The First Phone Call from Heaven is the kind of book that gives me a nice fuzzy warm feeling in my heart. That sentence may sound like I'm cheapening it, but I'm honestly not trying to. I've never read any of Mitch Albom's work. I know of The Five People You Meet in Heaven because it was made into a movie, but if you asked me what it was about my response would be something along the lines of, "...er, meeting people? In heaven? Maybe?" 
 I'll also take a moment to say that while I don't tie myself to any religion, I do believe that the basic points of each one are correct: to be a good person and to do right by others. I like to think that maybe there's something after this life. And let's be real, it's safer to believe than not to, right? Anyway, this book focuses almost entirely on whether or not you choose to believe in an afterlife. And when several people in one small town begin receiving calls from their dead loved ones, they are put to the test. 
 I won't ruin the ending, because I feel like the biggest draw for this is that you don't know how it ends. Maybe Albom's previous writings reveal more about how this book will end, but seeing as how I haven't read any of his other work I didn't have that background. Regardless, I really loved the ending. It managed to come full circle. It managed to be disappointing and uplifting and sad and touching all at the same time. It managed to make me cry, and I've gone through a pretty big streak without that happening for a while. 
 All I really want to say though is that this is a pretty great book, with beautiful lessons. I'm not too cynical to say that. And in all honesty, this is the kind of book I'll lend to others so hopefully it can bring a little to someone else, too. I know just the person to give it to....

This was a weirder book than I was anticipating. While it had had some cute and funny moments, it was pretty odd. 
 Harper is the stereotypical queen bee at her school, except she's not a mean girl. While we're meant to believe that she's an active over-achiever and good girl to make up for her older sister's fall from grace (an even that is alluded to a few times before we finally find out what happens and then is never really explored further), for the most part I found her pretty vapid and shallow. She was often commenting on how pretty she was and all of problems started because she didn't have lip gloss on. Really? 
 Then all of a sudden the school janitor dies and bestows upon her "superhero powers" and she's just fine with it. It takes like a chapter for her to come to terms with it. Later when she finds out she's to protect David and David finds out about her powers - and his own - he takes a couple minutes to process it and then he just accepts it. It's not like I want to read endless chapters of self-denial, but I felt like it should've taken them a little more time to get on board with things so crazy. 
 There wasn't really a whole lot that went on in the middle of the book. David's Aunt Saylor helps train Harper, which doesn't seem to be really necessary since Harper's abilities manifested instantly. There's a lot of Harper feeling bad about lying to her friends and having problems with her boyfriend and a lot of awkward sexual tension growing between her and David. However, the end got a little more action-y and the love triangle seemed to get resolved - for awhile at least. 
 While I didn't always like Harper, I liked the banter between her and David, which provided much of the humor in the book. And even though I know it's going to provide a lot of unnecessary melodrama in the next book, I liked the twist in the end. Overall, this book was a little odd, but was cute and an easy read. I would recommend to people looking for a light read, who enjoy YA fantasy/contemporary.

I really feel as if I was reading two different books. I knew they would merge eventually, but it still did not take away that feeling that we were walking on two parallel planes that would continue to exist close to one another but never touch. 
 In the first story, you have a lovely story of Adam and the many struggles that people suffer in day to day life. His world is falling apart (aren't all teenagers' worlds falling apart?), and as the day goes on, it keeps getting worse. 
 The second story is an ode to Mrs. Dalloway. A ghostly woman of a recently departed meth addict that blends with the queen of the spirit world.  This story seems a bit more far fetched, since it is within the realm of the unknown and inconceivable. 
 I cannot give an honest rating to the book as a whole, since I am still mulling everything over, but for Adam's story, I would say it is a solid 4.5-5 stars. For the ghost's story, it is more like 2.5-3 stars. I do not want to rate it too low because overall, I kept wanting to read this book because I enjoyed the premise and idea of it, but I feel guilty giving it 4 stars because I just did not understand what Ness was doing with the ghost story. Obviously, release is the theme of the book, but it seems like a very round-about way to get to the idea that there are many kinds of release.

 I thought I would like this book. It's basically Romeo & Juliet and paleontology. I really liked Romeo and Juliet, and I love dinosaurs. I also love the author's Airborn series. This book should have been an easy 4 stars. Instead, it's barely worth 2 stars. 
 The book started off okay. It wasn't amazing, but it was easy to get into. The characters were a bit flat, but I figured they would be fleshed out throughout the book. They weren't. Most of the characters were completely 1-dimensional. The book was narrated by the two main characters, Sam and Rachel, and I feel like I didn't learn anything about them even though they were narrating. Sam felt like a whiny kid, and Rachel felt like a robot. I love how they were both so passionate about science, but they had no other interests or personality traits. The rest of the characters weren't any better. They each had a single personality trait and weren't developed at all. 
 Romance is a big thing in this book. It is a Romeo & Juliet retelling after all. The romance sucked though. I know that in the play Romeo and Juliet's romance was completely underdeveloped and was based almost entirely on their raging hormones, but that was kind of the point. In this book, the romance was just as unbelievable, but it was dealt with in a different way. After Sam and Rachel got married, we're supposed to believe that they actually love each other? And that the best thing to do is for them to stay together? No! They are not in a good relationship. Neither of them are mature enough to be married! They probably won't even last a year.  To top it all off, this book had some of the most awkward and cringe-worthy sex scenes I have ever read. I don't read erotica, but I feel like there must be better ways to describe sex than how the author did. Kudos to the author for including sex in a YA novel, but the book would have been infinitely better there hadn't been any sex scenes in it. 
 This was a pretty awful book. I wouldn't recommend it.

 I really really loved this book! I thought the characters were so intriguing and I loved the idea of the psychic mind powers and how they were classified by color. That was really interesting to me. The only thing I didn't understand, and this just might be a personal conception, is why the government and authorities weren't afraid of those who were classified as "blue" when blues were telekinetic. THEY CAN MOVE THINGS WITH THEIR MINDS AND FLING PEOPLE AROUND. Why isn't the government more afraid of them?? 
 Other than that...I really loved all of the characters. Ruby is a great female protagonist. I loved that her biggest concern was helping other and keeping her friends safe. She wanted to learn how to master her powers in order to protect other people and not accidentally hurt anyone like she had in the past. I also really liked that she was so smart. For example,  the scene in which Clancy claims he's gravely injured and needs Ruby's help...everyone is like, it's a trap, don't go. And Ruby's like, I know it's a trap, does he think I'm stupid? And even though she still went to Clancy, I liked that it was because she was hoping to overpower him and control him rather than run in there like "OMG CLANCY I WILL SAVE YOU!" Except I will say I was a little frustrated that she didn't figure out earlier that he was playing her the whole time and that the voice in the back of her mind was him making her feel things that she didn't really feel, and not actually her own inner voice.  
 AND THEN THERE'S LIAM! Omg I finally get why everyone loves Liam, he is truly wonder and perfection rolled up in one. AND his southern accent and when he says "darlin'" SWOON. 
 This book gave me so much anxiety at the end however which is why I gave it a half star lower. It gave me anxiety because  the whole book Ruby was so worried about accidentally erasing herself from Liam's memory that I was terrified it would actually happen. THEN Clancy wanted to learn that particular aspect of her power and I started freaking out that he would try and erase Ruby from Liam's memory because he's a jealous little brat. But then when they got to the Children's League and Ruby wanted Liam to go because that place would break him, I knew she'd have to erase herself from his memory because there's no way they'd let her leave and there's no way he'd leave without her. AND THEN THAT'S EXACTLY WHAT HAPPENED. AND THEN I SOBBED (not actually this time but figuratively) BECAUSE LIAM DIDN'T DESERVE THAT! Even though I understand why it had to happen, it still made me very sad because I'm definitely a hopeless romantic and I just want the relationship to work out even though that's not the main plot of the book and there's still two more books for resolution to occur.  
 I also loved Zu and Chubs. Such great side characters!! 
 I need to read "Never Fade" soon! And I'm so freaking happy that "In The Afterlight" comes out in a few months because there's no way I could wait a whole year for that book. 
 I definitely recommend "The Darkest Minds" if you want a cool dystopian/paranormalish series that has a smart heroine and a swoony leading man!

I've read House of Suns and really enjoyed it, so picked up Pushing Ice to see if Reynolds can keep his streak of amazing books. 
 Bella Lind and her ship Rockhopper push ice, they mine comets. But when Jupiter's moon Janus suddenly takes flight as if it were a spaceship, the Rockhopper is the only feasible craft to follow. As they chase down Janus, there is mutiny in sight - and who knows what they'll find at the end of this journey. 
 Although I liked this book, in general, I had a few problems. 
 The pros: 
 - Plot was solid. This type of space opera appeals to me. It has enough space mystery, a few alien species, plenty of human questions, etc. 
 - Lots of interesting things in this scifi. Wang's tank that can create stuff, Crabtree and links to robots, alien descriptions, mysterious symbols, strange cubes that have messages. It's really everything I like in my scifi. 
 - I liked how we were able to see generations and the interaction of children who grew up not knowing Earth. The idea that flexies are like typewriters amuses me. 
 - There is huge potential in the tube world. 
 - I really liked Parry and Axford (the supporting characters). Great personalities that benefited the book. 
 The cons: 
 - I didn't like the entire power play between Svieta and Bella. It felt completely false. The idea that they would hold such a grudge over their beginning issues seems absolutely ridiculous.  So Svieta won't forgive Bella for not blindly believing her even though Svieta knows that's a logical decision; and Bella won't forgive Svieta for mentioning her dead husband even though she knows it's a sore spot? . I don't believe it. They are practical, intelligent women - and they can't see how utterly illogical their actions are? It reeks more of women being depicted as overly emotional than a true mortal enemies sort of situation. I really, really didn't like it. 
 - In fact, all of the power plays and political action felt contrived. That an entire regime could be overthrown by Jim? That cheapens Svieta's power. She didn't have any contingency plans at all for something like that? It's a little ridiculous. 
 - There is so much that is left unexplained!!! The tube world, Janus and its machine-like thinking for patterns, etc. I know some of it should be answered in Revelation Space, but it makes Pushing Ice not a very good standalone book - which is how it was marketed. 
 3 stars because although I did like it, I have some problems and it is not that rereadable. And I was not a fan of the main characters motivations. Would probably not recommend this book, to be honest. House of Suns is a better entry to Reynolds. I will read Revelation Space, but this book is a bit of a dud for me.

 This world is the next generation of Midnight Breed characters and it took me a minute to catch up but just like in the previous 11 books, I found the world building intense and all consuming. 
 This series is a sure thing if you love intense Alpha males, dark sexy vampires and an intriguing story line.

I read to my children every night. One is six, the other eight. We have been through a few of the Harry Potter books, the Swiftly Tilting Planet series and a number of other small books, but nothing has ever caught the imagination of myself and my two vastly different children like The Search for WondLa. 
 DiTerlizzi has again shown us that writing for children down not need to be simple or slow. His fantastical world and brilliant use of language is again a masterpiece. The Spiderwick Chronicles and Beyond The Spiderwick Chronicles are favorites around here, so it's no surprise that when DiTerlizzi took us out of Fantasy and into Sci-Fi he would do it with the same flare as before. 
 The Search for WondLa is an engaging book on the level of plot. A young girl who has been raised by a robot in an isolated underground Sanctuary must leave her home and try to find others like herself. Along the way we meet animals, plant-life and intelligent creatures unlike any seen on Earth. Each new discovery is described in detail so that the reader feels they are there, but still with the simplicity and speed a child responds to. 
 The book is long, coming in at 496 pages (in YA spacing and format) but one chapter a night rarely was enough for my girls. They were always asking for more. There were many nights when I had to stop myself from reading ahead, just to find out what happened. 
 I recommend The Search for WondLa for any reader. This is an interesting and delightful story to read as an adult. In such contrast with all the romance and blood in literature these days, a new kind of fairytale was a treat to lose myself in. And for my daughters, DiTerlizzi never spoke down to them - never made them think this was a "baby" book, but also took great care to involve them at their level. An great example is at one point the narrative uses the word "tome." 
 "Do you know what tome means?" I asked my girls. 
 "No," said the 6 YO. 
 "No," said the Ninja, "but I think it means book... I mean, they're in a library right?" 
 The Search for WondLa encourages critical thinking as well as a love for literature. I hope you enjoy it as much as I did.

This book was ridiculously too long. It could have been a couple hundred pages shorter and if it was I think it would've been much better. It was still a solid 3-star book, but I do have to admit I got bored for long stretches of it. 
 I liked pretty much all the characters. I liked that one of them is on the Spectrum and how he was written. I was a big fan of the romance, but found the ending regarding it completely annoying (though not as annoying as supposed incest like in some of other Clare's books...). Julian was my favorite. It was often repeated that he kept a lot of secrets, but I thought they were completely obvious. When he pulls Mark and Emma aside to tell them about one of the secrets, I was expecting something really shocking, but what he told them was something I thought we already knew? And did Emma really not figure it out before that? 
 While the book was almost completely predictable, I was surprised by who the Guardian was, so that was a good twist, even though it made me sad. I think the rabid Clare fans will really enjoy this book and the cameos from characters from the other series. For me, it was kind of average, but I'll still plan on reading the next book in the series.

I don't know why it took me so much time to read this book; it's certainly not that I didn't enjoy it. Covering events in the life of Queen Elizabeth I from her mother Anne Boleyn's execution in 1536 to her sister Mary's death and Elizabeth's ascension to the throne in 1558, much time and history is covered. We also get what seems to me like a fairly good insight into Mary Tudor. Most of the book keeps a fairly steady pace that made me think I was going to give this a solid three stars, but there were also times that I was shocked or on the edge of my seat. (I don't have the memory to be a good study of the history. Can you imagine going down a Wikipedia rabbit-hole looking at context and side details while trying to avoid spoilers for events 500 years ago? Haha.) Mostly it is the familiarity with and affection for Elizabeth developed through observing 22 years of her life and 3 weeks spent reading that sent me to the fourth star. I'm very impressed with her and honored to be a fellow redhead. :) 
 (P.S. I loved Katherine Parr dY~C/)

What do you get when you combine genetic mutants, large machines and an alternate timeline? 
 Well, apparently, you get Leviathan by Scott Westerfeld. In an alternate universe, the Great War (know currently as "World War II" to many of us) is fought, in a nutshell, by two side: the Clankers--the Clankers use, mainly, steam-powered engines and gears as weapons, and occasionally, just because--and the Darwinists--the Darwinists create fabricated animals (or "Fabs") out of original animals' DNA (they called it something else in the book, but I can't remember what). The Darwinist Fabs do not need all of the fuel, and are not bulky, but they can be easily damaged, are not very powerful, and some need entire ecosystems to stay alive.
One of my favorite classics!!

I'm glad I read this book, but I didn't love it as much as I'd hoped I would. The story about the "Rabbits" of Ravensbruck Concentration Camp was new to me, and definitely one worth telling. And -- as I learned in the author's notes at the end -- the story of Caroline Ferriday was also worth telling. However, I don't think the author did a good job of telling either story. Obviously, she did a ton of research for this book, but her skill at spinning these facts into a compelling work of fiction is limited. IMO, she made a huge mistake by telling the three main characters' stories from a first-person perspective. The alternating 1st-person narratives would have been okay if each of the characters had been fully realized and had a unique voice, but I don't think she was able to fully plumb their inner thoughts and feelings. This was especially true in the portrayal of Herta, the Nazi doctor, who came across more or less as a blank slate. Also, I think it was true with Caroline, the socialite who took on the cause of the Rabbits -- her portrayal was more the stuff of melodrama than one of the courage and dedication she exhibited in real life. Both Caroline and Herta were real people, and perhaps that's why it was difficult for the author to impart a real sense of them in this work of fiction. I felt like we got to "know" Kasia the best, but perhaps that's because she was an invention of the author. Another big mistake, in my view, was the emphasis on Caroline's love affair with the French actor. Not only was this kind of boring and trivial in light of the other things happening in the story, but it also disrespected the REAL Caroline, who had no such affair. Too late now, but I wish Kelly had stuck with the nonfiction format in telling this story. (BTW, I recommend the following website, which provides a lot of info about the Rabbits, including photos: http://www.elizabethwein.com/ravensbr....) With all that said, I'm still glad I read this book.

I see an actual possibility of the world going down the shitter one day and landing us in a reality like "Unwind" represents - I blame TWERKING if it does. I can even prove it. 
 Erm...In one way this was a very good read, but in another it lacked so much. My thoughts were divided between the meaning of the novel - which I liked, and the actual world building and character development- which I didn't like as much. 
 If I could choose a true main subject of this novel, I would name it "Current Popular Morality". 
 If we look at our world around us, the social acceptance is fueled by what society believes to be correct at the time. For example in this day and age, you are considered an enlightened, compassionate human being if you are a surrogate parent for a couple that can't have their own natural children for whatever reasons. A few decades ago you would be considered something akin to Frankenstein's monster if you chose to 'rent your womb out', mainly because it was considered extremely amoral, and people doing it cold and cruel, because what kind of mother is capable of giving birth and just giving her kid away. Our morality and the code of accepted behavior mutates with humanity, influenced mainly by the prolonged exposure of certain ideas and certain fashions. The longer you are exposed to 'shocking behavior' the more immune to it's shock value you become. Another example - a few years back, the dreaded 'duck face' was extremely popular on social media, now you're considered a loser if you do it. A few years back your passport photo would include your face, and now you are considered 'lame' unless that photo is actually an animated gif of you looking across your shoulder and exposing your quivering ass cheeks. What was considered extremely vulgar just a few years back became widely accepted behavior for women of all ages. 
 And we come to the conclusion- just because everyone does it, doesn't make it any less nasty. 
 If we apply the Current Popular Morality pattern to "Unwind", the culture in witch destroying a normal, healthy human being for the sake of it's 'spare parts' is completely plausible. But probable? Not so much. 
 Here is what made me not connect with the world described in the novel. Current Popular Morality is a human social construct. It is flawed beyond imagining, simply by being a human social construct. It can't hold a candle or even dream to compete with mother nature. And she is a ferocious beast when riled....because she is a mother. 
 So when Shusterman introduces us to a world of so much disregard, neglect and will to kill your own flesh and blood with so little emotional connection, I don't buy it. At all. You see parents that don't bat an eyelid but simply choose to have their child torn apart because they were being rowdy teenagers. It doesn't make any sense. 
 Then you have the fact that the entire Bill of Life defies the current direction of humanity which is overpopulation. The people in this novel are allowed to have as many kids as they make, and are allowed to dump them on people's doorstep, and are allowed to have them cut up for the progress and continuation of life of mainly already mature adults. Doesn't make any sense at all. If anything a global wide forceful implementation of contraception is more likely to be the outcome, not a decree that allows the populace to breed like rabbits. With no contraception are we to believe no more disease is spreadable sexually in the future? 
 So this is why I had a hard time completely liking "Unwind". As a YA, dystopian novel it focused more on the social aspect between the characters rather than interactions with the outside world. It was an original concept, but I wouldn't call it disturbing or creepy. Morbid maybe... Still it was a good read, but I won't be continuing the series.

What made me get interested in this book, you may ask? Well, it was by coming across a book trailer on YouTube, which Disney collaborated in and featured Bella Thorne as (surprisingly, when you compare her role in Shake it Up!) a bitter-looking narrator, dressed in black and wandering around at her own funeral. I was so intrigued by this, that, after also learning that it's a book trilogy, I checked out the other trailers they made. This is the first one for this book. 
 I never expected this to be such an intriguing read. I've never really read ghost stories before - well, I remember being read/reading bits of 
 Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark 
 and just snippets of 
 The Exorcist 
 - and I think this was the first time in actually reading a ghost story in a whole! 
 The suspense worked a lot more for me since I didn't read past the summary's 2nd of 3rd paragraphs, and instead, have the story unfold before me. I loved Alexis and how outspoken she was-- in fact, by the time I started to read this, I had two different friends who dyed their bangs pink, and Alexis's hair is described as pink a few times throughout! 
 I loved how much Alexis and her little sister, Kasey, really cared for each other! When I first read about Kasey's "creepy doll collection," all I pictured was the "Weird Girl" (the innocently-dressed girl with huge eyes and blank face, always carrying a white cat and predicting others' futures) from Tim Burton's 2012 animated Frankenweenie. As if that image didn't make Kasey as creepy as she was going to progress... 
 Yes, their parents are dysfuntional, but not at all to the point where they're extremely unlikable - In fact, you start to feel worried about one of them, too! (This was a relief to me, after I remembered reading about Val's God-awful parents in 
 Hate List 
 .) 
 And let's not forget about Megan: Yeah, the group of cheerleaders in this book are mean people, but one of them, Megan, becomes prominent to the story in such an unexpected and sympathetic way! 
 So, yes, the story is very well-constructed, as we follow Alexis's journey in the mysteries of her spooky-looking mansion, as well as her younger sister. I read this at a quick pace! Although not a jump-scare horror kind of thing you'd always expect from horror movies involving supernatural stuff, this has slowly-building suspense that involves questions wanting to be answered. The scenes that struck out to me the most were when Alexis was wondering about the closed basement door, the water boiling by itself (these two, because that's when I knew something paranormal was really happening, and could feel myself getting a bit tense), and Kasey coming into Alexis's room at night (that's the start when things really start going crazy! Unsurprisingly, that one's used as an excerpt on the back of the book's hardcover editon).  
 Now, I can't wait to put the next one, From Bad to Cursed, on hold at the library, followed by As Dead as it Gets! Thank you, Disney, for getting me interested in this book trilogy with your trailers! 
 My only complaint, though, is Carter. What was the point? What did he add to the story, other than he and Alexis being attracted to each other albeit being polar opposites? Was this just an excuse to have a romance subplot, just because it's a young adult novel? Well, hopefully, he'll become more important later on.

WARNING: Do NOT read this book, if the failure to use something as simple as spell check would bother and offend you. 
 We've all read those books; books you want to love, but can't for the life of you because the author didn't take the time to proof read their work. I swear I spent more time rewriting the sentences in my head then I did actually enjoying the story, which is a shame considering it had so much prospective. Still, I couldn't bring myself to write a good review with all the headache inducing run-on sentences and the overabundance of careless mistakes. 
 The concept had the potential to be a great good-girl-loves-bad-boy -tale. Potential, however, does 
 not 
 equate to rendering a proof reader unnecessary. Any redeeming qualities were lost on me after I came across the countless paragraph long run-on sentence that made about as much sense as an English Major taking Engineer physics--that is to say, none at all. 
 One word can sum up my biggest frustration: Comma's. The author either failed to use them all together or put them in places they had no business being. I can understand missing your own errors after spending hours writing, but that's why editors are such an important component to the writing process. The reader shouldn't be editing the "finished" copy. Please get one, or find another one, because this just isn't working. 
 I hate to write such a negative review, especially of one with such promise, but the mistakes were just too sloppy and overshadow the positives.

Without realizing this was a middle school book, we selected it for our book group's January discussion. The determining factors were that it was highly rated, had an important theme which would make for a good discussion and was short so it would be better to read during the busy Christmas holiday season. This book kept me, an adult in my late 30s, interested and even brought me to tears. It is heartbreaking while being uplifting and will be an exceptional weapon against bullying in school-age readers. Bullying and teasing are the main themes of the book since the main character is severely deformed and attending public school for the first time. The book begins with August Pullman's narration and we get a good feel for how his life has been, how he perceives himself and his family and his nervousness about attending public school. Once we have listened to Auggie's voice for a while, we are given different narrative perspectives from his family, friends, and even the bully. The book does a great job of allowing us to empathize with each of the characters from Auggie's sister Olivia Pullman to his best friends Summer Dawson and Jackalope Will. There is even a perspective from Auggie's main bully, Julian Albans. The book does a decent job of not turning anyone into a perfect altruistic good guy (except maybe Auggie) or evil bad guy (except Julian until the end when we hear his side.) If I had one complaint, it would be the bully's grandmother's story (it felt too contrived) and the way it immediately turned the bully around in the end. It felt like Julian did a 180 as soon as his grandmother finished the story and that didn't seem realistic.  I don't think that is too much of a spoiler for those who haven't read it.

 quite. 
 That... bothered me a lot. Like, I kept reading because I was engaged in the story and I NEEDED to know what happened, but at the same time it was like... okay. Please don't. It was a writing tic that bothered me a lot. 
 Cadence (who I kept thinking was called Candace for the longest time) as a character felt kind of blah. She doesn't remember anything that happened to her, she's in pain and she has meds, but I couldn't see her being as rebellious as she thought she was. I had a hard time pinning her down beyond "rich girl who has suffered amnesia, among other things" so that was a bit frustrating. 
 I liked the conflict between the adults. I though that was an interesting thing to include, mostly since you don't get a lot of adult-on-adult conflict in YA, unless it's a divorce. We had several adults here. Not strong enough for me to raise this up a star, but whatever. 
 As for that twist. No, I didn't see it coming. Yes, I should have. "We set a fire and ALL MY FRIENDS DIED IN IT AND I KILLED THEM" is what it boils down to, although I've gotta say this was one of the more successful uses of this trope that I've seen. I love The Basic Eight to death, but "Natasha never existed" doesn't hold up as well. I'd like to re-read the book and see if there were more hints planted beyond Mirren never reading the emails, Gat leaving, Johnny... Johnny what? Who exactly is Johnny, beyond bounce and snark? I always look forward to a new Julie Klassen novel. She's one of those authors that are on my "Automatically Read" list. However, The Dancing Master didn't quite live up to my expectations. 
 The story is a little Footloose meets Jane Austen. We know that there is an unofficial law that prohibits dancing, but don't find out why until about 2/3 of the way through - and it's wildly overdramatic and a little ridiculous. Then there's still so much more to get through. The book was long. The book clocks in at 419 pages, which isn't necessarily that long, but it seemed to be with such a slow pace and very little action. As in all Klassen novels, there are some secrets and scandals and twists. The initial twist I found surprising, but after that I thought everything was fairly obvious and it all was drawn out a little too long. 
 The story is told in 3rd person POV between Julia - the beautiful, impulsive "poor little rich girl"; Amelia Midwinter - Julia's strict, severe, No-dancing-allowed mother; and Alec Valcourt - the young Dancing Master who has just moved to the town without knowledge of the no dancing rule. I did not find Julia likable at all. She was selfish and reckless and manipulative. Towards the end of the book she learned the error of her ways and of God's forgiveness and grace, but I still found her insufferable for most of the book. 
 I mostly liked Alec. It's mentioned a couple of times throughout the book that he's a "dandy" and I found that a little unlikable in our hero character -he all but refuses the opportunity to work at the clay factory because of the manual labor and dirt, despite his bleak prospects for anything else at the time. However, he was kind and sweet and funny. I never quite bought in to why he was so in love with Julia, though - other than the fact that she's beautiful. 
 Amelia Valcourt was a character I wished we would've gotten more from. I enjoyed the few flashes of her back story and would have liked to have more of that. Like her daughter, she learned the error of her ways towards the ends of the book. There were some likable secondary characters, but they were pretty under-developed for me. 
 Perhaps my biggest problem with The Dancing Master was it's unoriginality. My favorite Klassen novel is The Apothecary's Daughter" and there were several moments that reminded me of that novel. One example is when Alec is teaching Julia some dance moves - similar to when Lilly is teaching Francis the moves to the same dance in The Apothecary's Daughter. 
 From The Dancing Master 
 "Partners must keep a proper distance apart," he primly intoned. "Bodies must not actually touch." 
 "Pity," she breathed, her face tipped toward his. 
 Oh yes, she wanted him to kiss her. His heart pounded at the thought. 
 From The Apothecary's Daughter 
 She looked away, focusing on her hand on his arms "Partners must keep a proper distance apart," she said, parroting the admonition of the Viennese dancing master. "Bodies must not actually touch." 
 "Pity," Francis breathed, his sweet breath warm on her temple, her ear...She knew she had but to look up and he would kiss her. Her heart pounded at the thought. 
 Overall, The Dancing Master was a little disappointing for me. It still had the mixture of faith, romance, and a bit of mystery that I look for in a Klassen novel, but it fell a little short on all counts. Despite that, I will still be giving Klassen another chance whenever she comes out with her next novel.

Cause how can you live your life within these factions, that are actually just personality traits - more or less? 
 Granted, maybe I just feel this way because I read Divergent in Dutch (my native language) and the faction names were horribly translated: Candor became 'Oprechtheid', which is actually a more apt translation of 'sincerity'. Not really the same if you ask me. Thus: confusion. 
 Needless to say, after page 1, 2, 3, I was a bit worried about the 'skeleton' of this novel. However, the 'flesh' of it cleared my concerns right up. It's actually quite a detailed, addicting and action-packed story, and - I can only imagine - probably pretty well written when you translate the crappy Dutch translation back to English in your mind. 
 So, final verdict: I really enjoyed Divergent and recommend it to anyone who enjoys books such as The Hunger Games, Matched and Starters. It has action, an interesting dystopian setting, a complex an subtle love story and even some memorable secondary characters. I think the story shows a lot of promise and look forward to the second book. But that one I will definitely read in English, in stead of Dutch :)

Julia Quinn shines when she's writing the dynamics of a big, close-knit family. She has a masterful grasp of the tensions, the hilarity, the instinctive protectiveness, and the petty annoyances of being part of such a clan. So The Sum of All Kisses is delightful when cousins call each other out, communicate with glares and raised eyebrows, and stick to each other loyally, and when the hero has to contend with the heroine's absolutely hilarious sisters, including unicorn-obsessed Frances. The story struggles, on the other hand, with the kind of high drama that is typical of the genre. Hugh's father is an over-the-top villain that is hard to take as a credible threat. The climax, with people repeated charging out into a storm on horseback, kidnappings, and life-and-death scenarios, likewise was difficult to swallow.  The part where Sarah "resolved" the whole Hugh/Daniel/Hugh's dad conflict made no sense. So she's going to refuse to sleep with Hugh if Hugh's dad went after Daniel? Would she really go through with that? It seems like the same kind of situation (though admittedly less dire) that Hugh's suicide pact was--pointless to actually go through with if the threat didn't work. Also, Hugh's dad has no respect for women, so if Sarah really did go through with it, what is to stop Hugh's dad from either raping her for heirs or from killing her so Hugh can marry someone else? Obviously, hopefully none of that would happen, but it seemed utterly ridiculous to act like Sarah brilliantly "solved" their problems because she made a DIFFERENT over-the-top threat than Hugh. . It seemed to belong to a different type of book entirely, one that Julia Quinn shouldn't attempt to write. Also, Hugh being a mathematical genius seemed oddly irrelevant by the end, despite how prominently it was highlighted in the beginning, and in the back blurb and cover. Overall, still an enjoyable visit with the Smythe-Smiths, who I actually love more than the Bridgertons.

I just reread this book 20 years after I first read it. How is that possible? How can so many years have flown by? At any rate, while I sit here feeling bad about how old I'm getting if 20 years can pass between readings... let me write a review. 
 I first read this book one summer (many years ago...) and was clearly a clueless reader. Innocent, perhaps. The story starts out with Sal missing her mom who took off a year ago and hasn't been seen since. Her paternal grandparents take her on a road trip to trace her mom's steps. Sal wants to bring her mom home. This where I went clueless all those years ago. I think I suspected that Sal's mom was in no position to return home, but I don't think I believed that she couldn't come home. Across all that time, I remembered that conclusion because it so surprised me. But there's much more to this story than just it's tragic ending.  
 On the road trip, Sal's grandparents ask for a story, so Sal tells them about her time since her mom disappeared and she and her father moved to suburbia. In that time, she makes a friend and discovers that her friend's family takes their mom for granted, resulting in her mom disappearing. As Sal tells the tale, she wonders how she had treated her mom, and how clueless she may have been to her mom's needs. Traveling with her grandparents, she realizes that decisions can be made that change your life, and you may kick yourself for them, but you can't let guilt eat you up for an innocent choice. I think this was the best part of the story for me as an adult; you can't live in a bubble. Small choices, like going for a swim, or climbing a tree, may irrevocably change your life, but not doing those things won't make your life better. It's just how life goes. I think that's a pretty impressive lesson for a YA novel. Even if I didn't get it 20 years ago, I got it now. Some things improve with age.

A few revelations I totally saw coming, others were just plain shocking to me (I was flabbergasted when the wine Fitz and Rurisk drank was poisoned and Rurisk died. I had to read it again to make sure I read it right. ). There really aren't a lot of lovable characters (hence the GoT comparisons) but most are sufficiently three-dimensional. What really stood out to me in this book was the (eventual) plot, the world building, and the political machinations. 
 Sometimes books start great and then lose steam. This is the opposite and it left me wanting to give it four stars, even though on balance I think it should be three. 
 My other criticism is that it seemed like the author was trying to create a world with some gender equality (e.g. the firstborn inherits whether male or female) but I think overall she failed. Molly, Patience, Jonqui, Kettricken, and various queens of the past have interesting parts to play in the story, but I think this fails the Bechdel Test. And I was annoyed that every duchy was ruled by a duke. Out of six, you'd think at least one would have a duchess worth a mention. 
 Oh and, Esperanza, if you're reading this review, take note: YOU DO NOT WANT TO READ THIS BOOK. DOGS ARE HARMED. REPEAT: DOGS ARE HARMED.

SPOILERS. 
 Such a wonderful book in so many ways. It has a very controversial point of contention for the protagonists. It has a fairly predictable plot that stays captivating the whole way through. It has characters that read real to me. And that, ladies and gents, is why I cried. 
 I think this book gives voice to all of those dashed hopes and dreams that come with a severe accident such as Will's. WIll went from literally being on top of the world (or at least, top of Africa), top at his career, and always on a new adventure to bottoming out. He hit rock bottom so hard he couldn't see the light from the bottom of the well he was lying in. I would imagine that having to restructure your life in such a dramatic fashion is hard enough living a regular lifestyle, let alone the jet-setting one Will employed. New countries, new physical activities, no shortage of women wanting attention. All that is gone in an instant. 
 Will, understandably in my opinion, gets very depressed about this. He tries very hard to kill himself, and fails only because someone found him in time. It is that kind of determination in Will that sets the tone for the whole book. He is determined to have his final nuggets of freedom, and he will not relinquish. 
 So he plans to do physician-assisted suicide. 
 This was a particularly interesting book for me because I have written several college papers on the subject. We were always told to write about something controversial, and I wanted to do something not really found in the limelight. And predictably, there is a fairly large chasm between the two opposing parties for this. 
 On the one hand: murder is murder, it should not be allowed. 
 On the other hand: if they are of sound mind, they can make their own decisions. 
 It is these two opinions that ultimately make up the book. Will wants to exercise the only freedom he has left, and everyone else is trying to convince him not to do it. Honestly? They all have really great points. Every single one of the characters have great reasons to back up their own personal opinions. I think that is why I appreciated this so much, because the constant ping-ponging from denial to acceptance for these characters seems so realistic. Knowingly sending someone to their death is not nearly so easy as it may seem. 
 Louisa and Will's attraction for one another felt organic, which equally made this an attractive read. I loved how they both adopted each other to be their pet projects. Louisa was hellbent on getting him to change his mind about killing himself, and Will was hellbent on forcing Louisa to actually spread her wings and explore beyond her little town. They influenced one another for the better, and I loved that it was an improvement on both of them. 
 The story is predictable. If a man with no mobility from his nipples down wants to commit suicide, and is wealthy enough to leave the girl protagonist well off, what do you think will happen? Right. He goes through with it (after lots of soul searching on Louisa's part) and leaves her a nice chunk of change to pursue her newly found interests in her career. There was no other way this could have ended, and I knew that going in. It was no big surprise, and yet I was desperate to keep reading. I wanted to feel what Will felt. I wanted to feel what Louisa felt. 
 It's a love story, sure. But I think more than anything it is just a story about growth, and I love that so much more. Louisa grew, and Will grew. Will's mother grew, Louisa's sister grew. I would not have had it any other way.

Consent by A.J. Rose is the third book in the Power Exchange Series. This is NOT a standalone, you need to read the other books in the series and read them in order. This story is told in First Person, Multiple POV, and the narration is impeccable. I am writing this review and going to try to avoid any spoilers from any of the books in this series, so if I appear to be really vague..I don't want to ruin any part of this series. 
 Before I go any further, this story is one that is going to test a lot of limits and is a story many won't like due to subject matter. There is kidnapping, rape, sex crimes, death of a supporting character, murder, and torture involved in this book, in multiple scenes, in graphic detail. I want to make sure you understand this going into the book, because the story doesn't deserve low ratings by those who are unable to read dark matter. As we saw in the first two books of the series Power Exchange and Safeword, A.J. Rose writes some dark, graphic, disturbing scenes - so take the worst scenes from books one and two and multiply by 10, you will have the level of darkness found in Consent. 
 Now, to the story - it is again the same characters from the first two books. The DeGrassi men and their significant others along with the supporting characters from police stations and the BDSM life. Ben and Gavin are finally getting over trauma of the past and loving life. When all of a sudden horror strikes the DeGrassi family again. The words It's Mya. She's missing! via a phone call at 2 a.m. have Gavin, Ben, and Cole on a mission as they fight to bring back Cole's wife and Gavin's best friend from whoever dared to take her. This journey the three take part in challenges a lot of different aspects of the men. Their very humanity is tested and their bonds with each other are strained as they go head to head with some of the world's biggest scum. There is a lot of angst in this book, as you find yourself flipping through the 350 pages as fast as you can to see...will they get to Mya in time. Worse, what will be left of her? 
 This is a rollercoaster ride and will keep your heart pounding as you try to figure out who, what, why...who will make it? In addition, we get to see some very emotional times between Gavin and Ben as they take their relationship to new levels "I want a collar around your throat, and a ring on your left hand. I have plans for us, and I'm going to do everything in my power to see those plans through." 
 I recommend this story to all readers who can read dark subject matter. Please read my warning ...take it seriously. This story will F*ck your mind in the biggest way!

 Oh my gosh! Geez louise. I do. I live here, and I LOVE it. How's abaht this book is in SET IN PITTSBURGH - and I didn't even know it until I started reading?! Tons of local references - complete with shout outs to Eat 'n Park and Edgar Snyder commercials. Plus, it was good. Actually, GREAT. I loved this book almost as much as I love Pittsburgh, and, that, my friends, is saying something. 
 At the root of this book is an ugly story about the cruelties of high-school hazing and the ineffectiveness of adults (parents and authority figures) in recognizing, addressing and preventing bullying. This book completely coincided with my own experiences with the inexplicable malice of children towards one another. My first real look at it was in the first week of junior high when boys in my music class turned upon another student for having dirty, old shoes. Now, clearly, this boy was not from the most economically prosperous families; but, the next day, he came to class in new, white tennis shoes. Did this spare him the indignity of being humiliated once again - no matter the cost or inconvenience to his family who bought him the shoes? Fuck no. They made fun of him for having cheap K-Mart shoes, the wrong type to escape their ridicule. It was then that I realized that kids are jerks. Real raging assholes with a pack mentality, willing to turn on each other, preying on the weak to avoid their own detection and criticism. This book is about how children are willing to hurt one another in the name of having a "good" time. It is about how adults are able to turn a blind eye to traumatic events in the name of tradition and toughening up their youth. It's about how growing up is hard enough without the pressure and anxiety of surviving in the social jungle that is high school. It's about the impact of hazing on the fragile juvenile psyche. And it's beautiful and real and ... did I mention it is set in Pittsburgh? 
 Thanks NetGalley for the opportunity to read this book in exchange for my honest opinion. I'm a Catholic school girl from way back when, and this read rang true to my heart. I'll be promptly recommending it to my local reading friends.

I've been wanting to read this for ages. I read a book a while back (years, though I don't remember how many) and Amazon did this really nice thing where they recommended other books similar to that. This was before I found goodreads, mind you. So when I finally took the plunge and renewed my 7 year old library card, this was one of the first books I reserved. 
 I'm so glad I did. There were so many elements to this story that I didn't know were going to be in here and I loved. Mental illness takes a pretty dominant stance in the storyline, never too far away from the main point. This has always been a fascination of mine, most likely the reason I took so many sociology and psychology classes. When it was revealed relatively early on I immediately got all giddy and rushed to find out more. 
 The characters were fantastic and well fleshed-out. Vida Winter was striking to me at first; her description was not how I had imagined her given the synopsis on the inside cover of the novel. However the physical transformation she underwent was decidedly effective. Her The "wolf" that stalked her was vivid imagery, when he attacked and when he waited patiently in the corner. 
 As for the story itself, I was captivated from the very beginning. The actions of Charlie, Isabelle, Emmeline and Adeline all were what kept me motivated to continue on. An unusual gene is passed down through the generations that made the family such an enigmatic and cruelly-fascinating presence. 
 Aurelius is probably my favorite character. The only one who seemed to naturally have a sunny disposition in the novel, I was drawn to him and his curiosity regarding his surroundings. Honestly, I kind of pictured him like Hagrid, especially given his description of seeming like a storybook giant. 
 My only complaint is that one question remained unanswered. I wanted to know who it really was that Vida had been taking care of all those years. Was it truly Emmeline? It is sort of hinted that it is. But it could just as easily be Adeline, I think. I so desperately want to know  
 The Thirteenth Tale is (of course) very autobiographical for Vida Winter. It is only logical to have the story hidden until the very end.

That was unexpected. You pick up this mammoth of a picture book expecting to hastily flip through 
 some decent grey-scaled pencilings that might mildly entertain. Instead, you get wrapped up into some dark themes for a kid's book; death, alcoholism and thievery topping the list. Fret not, fellow parents, as they are handled gingerly and don't give anybody any bad ideas that they didn't already have. 
 In addition to the 1930s Parisian steampunk-influenced clockwork theme, the illustrations merited the 2008 Caldecott Medal. What makes that a big deal is that the Caldecott is typically only given to picture books, not graphic novels or novellas. This book is a noteworthy and deserving exception. The pictures hook you in but the story keeps you flipping through. This format of alternating chunks of full page illustrations and text dumps is seamless and extremely very well executed. 
 The Invention of Hugo Cabret in hardcover is as big as a brick and packs an equally sized wallop. Don't let the size fool you, an adult can finish it easily in one or two sittings. I imagine the publisher originally had some reservations about pushing a black inked, hardbound hunk of pulp for kids. The end result is well worth picking up.

This is such an amazing story! I read this for my YA lit class that I'm taking in the fall. It does start off a bit slowly, but once it picks up, it is REALLY interesting. It's very clearly well-researched, and it tells the story of two British girls during World War II. One, Maddie, is a pilot from England, while the other is a spy from Scotland. Their friendship is amazing and I loved reading about it. I think this would be a really interesting book for a high school history teacher to assign during a World War II unit, but I could see it getting looked over in favor of books that discuss the Holocaust or non-fiction accounts of the war. Language can be a bit strong at times, but it's used to add personality and spunk to the main character, so I personally did not find it to be offensive. I recommend this to anyone interested in planes, spies, or history in general - this action-packed read will definitely keep your attention!
The entire trilogy is beautiful escapism with grippingly strong characters. A perfect modern fairy-tale.

I feel like I have unfinished business with this book. I look at all these 5-star reviews and I scratch my head. (Thank goodness there are a few other mixed ones out there pointing roughly to the same issues I had with the book, so I know it's not just me!) 
 I liked reading it, but it completely failed to grab me and pull me into the story. I really liked the start of the book, but more and more I felt like a witness, much like the falcon flying through the sky, wondering how Locke was going to get himself out of yet another situation. But I hardly ever felt any suspense. It never was a case of whether he was going to make it out of there, I knew he would, it was just a question of what other clever trick he had up his sleeves. I could close and pick up this book whenever I wanted, I could have left it closed for a week without an issue. 
 There is no doubt though that Scott Lynch is a really good author though: the whole construct of the book was smartly done. Not showing us all of Locke's history, but keeping that for interludes (although unfortunately the moment those interludes stopped being about Locke, I was bored to death with them). 
 Even within the chapters, he starts out by writing the meeting where the Gentlemen Bastards make their plans, but we never hear the plan, we only get to see the execution of it afterwards. Which is a smart way to make sure we understand when they are winging it and when it is planned, without having to repeat himself at all. 
 I thought he was especially good at writing dialogues. Every character had a different manner of speech which made the character into a real person, and the general dialogues were witty and clever. Some of my favourites: 
 Chains: "Oh. You have a magic boy. Magnificent. I'll plant him in the fucking ground and grow a vine to an enchanted land beyond the clouds" 
 Jean: "Throwing blondes at Locke Lamora was not unlike throwing lettuce at sharks"" 
 Locke to Bug: "What a stupid, reckless, idiotic, ridiculous damn thing to do. I haven't the words to express my admiration" 
 So we have good writing, witty dialogues, quotable lines and some really nice characters, why wasn't this book able to keep my attention? 
 I think the major issue is that I didn't really care. Especially after Bug and Chains were gone  I didn't care all that much about the main characters. This is an adventure story with a lot of "look how clever I am, even though no-one will ever realize it's me - which actually makes me even more clever". But there's no real connection with the characters, nothing about their motives, and what it all means to them. Why do they keep doing this after so many years? 
 This book combined with more emotional depth would have been an easy 5 star. But I find it a bit more of a struggle without that depth. I find it a shame that he left Sabetha  a ghost character , because perhaps she could have helped deliver that.

The Scar didn't blow me away with the same ferocity as his first New Crobuzon tale, Perdido Street Station, and I think that was partly because the world of Bas-Lag is much less-well developed in The Scar than the city of New Crobuzon was in the first book. In general, I think of Mieville as a urban fantasy writer who does his best work envisioning cities and their wild, magical, xenomorphic inhabitants. 
 However, The Scar does feature some interesting characters and a pretty exciting premise about a floating pirate city (!) whose leaders are questing to find "the Scar: a massive wound in reality" left by an ancient civilization. How and why they want to get there and how the main characters get involved are details I'll leave to readers to discover. My main beef with The Scar, compared to Perdido Street Station, was that the thrust of the plot lacks the epic urgency of "Perdido" (and people who have read that one know what I'm talking about), and it feels at times as though Mieville is making up the world of Bas-Lag as he goes along. 
 These are minor quibbles in an otherwise pretty intriguing read. Also, in my opinion Mieville makes up these deficiencies in the 3rd Bas-Lag story, "Iron Council", fleshing out the world and adding a high-stakes plot that also nicely ties into some elements of "Perdido". All the books are worthwhile, but people looking to get the best bang for their reading time should check out "Perdido Street Station" and "Iron Council" in that order; The Scar is tangential to the main story.

This is definitely not an easy book to read, though it was definitely interesting and worth the effort. 
 The difficulty stems, of course, from the subject matter, from the very experiences being recounted. Had this been fiction, I do believe I would have long since abandoned it, but it was not, it was someone's true and painful struggle, so I made myself read past the parts that made me cringe and made me want to look away because it was so painful to witness. 
 More than anything, I think this book changed my way of looking at mental illnesses in general, and at depression in particular. I do believe we as a whole do a lot of romanticising and fancy-fyng these kinds of ailments. Fiction books in particular tend to be accused a whole lot of this. 
 Me going off on a tangent regarding mental illness as portrayed in fiction books:A whole lot of the criticism regarding Made You Up was very much how it was wildly inaccurate as far as schizophrenia goes, romanticizing the bits that were more amenable to the story the author wanted to say instead of portraying the stark horribleness of it. I still don't think the author meant to romanticise things, but in the end I believe a book's own fiction cannot be held against it for not being non-fiction enough. 
 I am aware such is likely naive, since those kind of books can contribute to people's twisted outlook as much as anything else, but as usual there really is no perfect solution. Fiction has a right to be fiction, and to be judged for its own internal consistency and narrative and not because of its choice of being fiction. I do wonder if it'd help, though, if authors/publishers put in a cute little note somewhere near the beginning or end that read something like, Being a fiction book, X is not necessarily portrayed here as it manifests in real life. For those interested in understanding this crippling condition, read z or y or whatever..

A fun read, but not enough action and too little relationship development. I loved Kate in the beginning of this book. She was a tough young woman dealing with the responsibility of caring for her dying mother. She was so strong, but as the story went on I felt her character weakened some. I liked seeing her devotion to Henry (Hades) and they had a really interesting dynamic. He was very distant and protective and she was always trying to get him to open up. But, I don't think Aimee Carter did a good enough job of explaining why Kate was so into him. I admired Kate's dedication to the goddess test, but I didn't see enough of why she fell for Henry. 
 [Read more of my reviews at http://laurynapril.blogspot.com] 
 I wanted to know a little more about who Henry was. For a good chunk of the book the only thing the reader, or Kate, knew about him was that he was old, honest and attractive. And, while those were all great traits, I wanted more. As the story goes on Henry and Kate started spending more time together, but I wish we'd gotten to see more of it. I never really felt a strong spark between them. 
 Also, this book it set up with a twist. And, it was a good twist. I didn't see it coming, but the way the story is set up makes parts of the plot drag because you don't understand how important certain small moments are until the end. You don't find out who the gods are or what the tests were until the very end. It was a nice twist, but it made the plot drag. I spent a lot of time waiting for Kate to take a test just to find out she'd been taking them all along.  I also felt like the tension in the story could have been upped a bit. It's mentioned a number of times that it may be dangerous for Kate to stay with Henry as someone has been killing all the girls Henry bring to take the test. I would have liked to have seen a few more attempts on her life. 
 Overall it was an enjoyable read, and I'll give the sequel a shot.

Chaltas has done a great job of balancing the normal and the abominable, keeping Anke from being only a victim. I found the language to be especially well crafted, at once revealing and spare. 
 The finale comes a bit too quickly and too completely for my liking. Fans of Sonya Sones will feel at home with "Because I am Furniture," but readers of Ellen Hopkins may not be satisfied with Chaltas' lighter touch.

I want to smash something. 
 I guess it's a positive that Levithan made me so attached, so allegiant, to his character, Mark, that I want to throttle the fictional character who hurt him. I haven't felt this worked-up over a book since The Handmaid's Tale... 
 Okay. The suffering that Mark goes through in You Know Me Well is not comparable to the rape-y horror of Atwood's dystopian novel. Comparatively, it's mild. But goddamn if I don't feel utterly enraged, if I don't feel like injustice has been done. Why, oh why, Ryan ? Why, oh why? 
 How This Whole Thing Started 
 You Know Me Well starts at the beginning of Pride Week in San Francisco. Two teenagers, Mark and Katie, both gay, both attending the same high school, run into each other at a LBGTQ club. Mark is there with his best friend, Ryan, who is also gay. Mark happens to be in love with Ryan -- small fact. Mark and Ryan have messed around, but always in secret, because Ryan is closeted. Katie spots Mark after he wins a scantily-clad bar dancing competition, much to Mark's embarrassment. Katie, impulsively, asks Mark to be her friend. He agrees, bemused, and the two take off together when Ryan wants to stay behind to flirt heavily with another guy. Ugh. 
 Katie has her own problems. She's been in love with her best friend's cousin, Violet, from afar for a long time. That night, Katie and Violet are supposed to meet at a party through arrangement, but Katie takes off before the meeting due to nerves. After running away and ending up at the same bar as Mark, Katie wanders off with him to find adventure in the city, which sets off a chain of events that will leave them changed. 
 I'm Still Mad 
 Just to remind you, I'm furious. 
 LaCour and Levithan -- Who Was the Stronger Writer 
 As you might have seen, You Know Me Well was written by two (gay!) authors -- Nina LaCour and David Levithan. In my opinion, Levithan's writing blew LaCour's out of the water. I trudged through LaCour's chapters but ate up Levithan's greedily. I wish the entire book had been written by him. (Yes, even despite the fact that he emotionally demolished me with this book.) 
 In comparison to Mark, Katie's character was fairly watery. She wasn't as vivid or full of life as Levithan's character creations. Moreover, I didn't like Katie's strange combination of impulsive forthrightness and cringing hesitancy. Call me a critic, but those are some contradictory qualities right there. 
 Overall, Levithan was was electric. LaCour was only so-so. 
 So Do I Recommend This Book Or What? 
 I do! It's a short read and Levithan wrote a powerful half of a story. LaCour isn't bad enough to drag the story down to unreadable levels, either. 
 As for my rage... siiiigh. I'm still remarkably upset about Mark's lack of a fairytale ending . Maybe some reader's would be less upset than me, but the situation struck me hard. 
 Anyways, this book would have been a 4.5 read if not for LaCour's just-okay writing. I give the book 3.5 and recommend.

 This book is horrifying and great at the same time. I dont know what intrigued me to read it the most. I think it was the title at first then the book cover then the description then (when I researched about it) the movie's trailer. 
 I couldnt understand half of the vocabulary used in this book. I had to stop and search the words in a dictionary so that I would understand what Eva Khatchadourian was talking about. But this is a good thing, I learned a lot of difficult words and maybe I could use some of those words for The Untitled Book. 
 I also watched the movie after I read the book. Can I just say Ezra Miller is a really great actor. I loved him so much as Kevin. And I love him so much that he's playing Patrick in the Perks Of Being A Wallflower film with Emma Watson, Nina Dobrev, and Logan Wade Lerman. 
 Plot 
 When I read the description of the book I was super intrigued by it. It was so different. So unique that I just had to - HAD TO - read the book as soon as I can. But when I was reading it I had a lot of urge to put it down, lock it away, and never read it again. But I never did that because it was so good that I had to continue reading it, I had to finish it - it was that good. 
 Characters 
 Kevin. Kevin scared me but I also love Kevin, I understand Kevin. What he was going through. What he was feeling. Why he did what he did - I would never but I understood him. It was really confusing for me at first, knowing already - because of the description - that Kevin killed his classmates and destroyed his teacher's life but I understood why. Why he did it, why he had to.  The thing that I'm still confused about is why Kevin killed his dad. His dad who loved him so much and defended him through the very end of the story.  Maybe he did it because he really hated him or he wanted him to know that he was wrong about him and that he should've believed his mother. I really dont know. 
 Eva. I dont like Eva but I dont hate her either. I pity her. I'm sad for her. I feel bad for her. Its had when your own child doesnt want, like or love you. When your own child - who came from your womb - tortures you. But I admire her for her bravery, for her courage, for not giving up on Kevin. Yes, she hated her own son but she still tried to love him and tried to accept him and tried to make him happy. There was a moment in the book where Kevin wanted to spend time with her, where he wanted her to have a moment, he wanted her to be happy. And I think that's my favorite part in the whole book. 
 Franklin. I like him as a father for Kevin but why Kevin alone? 
 Celia. Celia is the sweetest little sister ever. She is the opposite of Kevin, need I say more? 
 Overall 
 This book is really interesting but I wouldnt recommend it to everyone. Read it if you can handle the nightmares you will have later on - after reading this book. It will test your beliefs, your morals, your values. You gotta have a really open mind if your going to read this. And you gotta be willing to read this and make sure to finish it. You will never understand if you will not finish it. 
 Happy reading!

First thing first. I rarely read thrillers or crime fiction. Its not quite my genre of choice. Despite this, however, the title and the premise of the book called to me, and I could not help but pick it up to see what it was like. 
 The story is told through the alternating points of view of Ted, who believes his wife is having an affair with his house contractor, and Lily, a woman he meets on an airport and to whom he confesses he feels the urge to kill his wife. The alternating viewpoint thing is a technique I see more often in the fantasy genre but which I thought worked incredibly well here too. At the same time, however, I found myself wishing that the story had been written solely from the point of view of its most interesting character: Lily. 
 I'd go as far as to say that it was she who carried the weight of the novel on her shoulders. Other characters, like Ted, felt as dull as a church on a rainy sunday, laying the groundwork for what would come but never in a particularly engaging faction. It was interesting enough that I slogged trough it, curious as I was about the premise, but I was also always happy to finish their chapters and go back to Lily. 
  I was also a little disappointed that Melisa was revealed to be such an obviously unlikeable character. Not because she planned to murder her husband but because she was written to be an incredibly shallow person with very little in her to redeem her. And don't even get me started on Brad. He felt like such a convenient tool, both in the universe of the story and from an outside point of view. The only good thing that can be said about him is that we did not get into his head.  
 Character gripes aside, I found the story to be rather well told and crafted. There were plot twists I did not see coming, though that might just be the aforementioned lack of familiarity with the genre. 
 I think the ending  ruined things a bit with its open, cliffhanger-ish nature too, but eh. I would have appreciated if the author had made it clear one way or the other whether Lily is going to get caught at last or not.

First, we'll address the 800-pound gorilla in the room. 
 "How you doin', Mr. Bananas?" 
 "Doing fine, E. How's the family?" 
 "They're well. Autumn's growing up too quick and Chris... well, Chris is a dude. You know how dudes are." 
 "I do, I do. So what is it that I can help you with, E.?" 
 "Oh, nothing. Just wanted to address you." 
 "Oh. Well you should know that this is a terrible joke and, if people laugh, they'll be laughing at you, not with you." 
 "I know." 
 "Good. Just wanted to make that clear. Say, do you have any bananas?" 
 "I'm sorry, I do not." 
 "Then what fucking good are you to me? Piss off." 
 Now that Mr. Bananas is gone, I should probably address the problems you might have with Lauren Beukes's The Shining Girls. If you do not read chapter titles, you will soon Amelia Earhart your way into history. I do not like chapter titles. All too often, authors ruin their own books by putting spoilers in their chapter headings. It's a huge pet peeve of mine, so when I come across a book with chapter titles, I skip them. I feel this way: the important information should be worked into the actual chapters and not lazily dropped into the chapter headings. Lauren Beukes not only uses chapter titles in lazy ways, but if you miss whose head and the time you're in, the book becomes a mess very quickly. More than twice I had to flip backward to make sure I knew who I was with and where in time we were. I shouldn't have to do that, Lauren. Shame on you. 
 Other than that, this book is great. The plot isn't the most original (serial killer bouncing through time ala Sherlock Holmes vs Jack the Ripper in that one old movie), but Beukes does manage to make what happens interesting. I think where Beukes shines (get it? DID YOU GET MY PUN????) is character development. She goes into deep detail concerning the smallest character. Most importantly, she made me care, or at the very least understand, the red shirts in this book. Every corpse had a pulse at one point in time, and I dig that she paid so much attention to their history. 
 Once I managed to get a feel for the flow of the story, I enjoyed myself. Are their problems? Sure. Several of them. But I didn't notice until after I finished reading. But the best part of this book is Beukes writing. It's smooth and seemingly effortless. I blew through 50-100 pages a sitting because, once I started reading, I couldn't put the book down. 
 In summation: Not everyone will like Beukes because she forces you to pay attention. If you skip chapter headings, you will be super fucking confused. If you don't like a huge cast of characters, you'll likely not like this, because every third chapter or so is from a brand new person's POV. She gets into the heads of every victim, so expect to learn some of everything about everybody. I didn't mind. In fact, the big cast was one of my favorite parts. 
 Final Judgment: Pay attention for full payoff.
