I received an eArc of this book from Netgalley in exchange for an honest review. 
 I imagined this book to be slightly more of a comedy in that our main character, Tom, comes from a Utopian 2016, travels back in time, messes up the timeline, and thus returns to our, as in the actual, 2016. (Note: I am going to refer to Utopia 2016 as U-2016 and the actual 2016 as A-2016 from now on.) I thought it would be funny in that it points out the flaws compared to the Utopia that it should've been and Tom would struggle with our technology and everyday life; that it would focus more on this aspect of the story and his adaption to A-2016 would be the general plot. That, however, is not really how it turns out. Yes, he does struggle with technology and life in A-2016, such as running into doors because he assumes all automatically open, but the plot is much more character development based. He has some bad stuff happen in his life in the U-2016 and those things don't happen in A-2016. At the same time, the people that he knew in U-2016, such as his family, are much different in A-2016. They have different personalities, different (though slightly related) interests and jobs, some even have different physical features. Other people he knew in U-2016 don't exist at all in A-2016. He has to thus adjust to these people and his relationship with them. He questions whether is is right to enjoy/prefer one version of that person over another. Mainly his father here. He also has to decide the overall morals of what he has done. Due to his time travel accident, the world is not the Utopia it should've been and several people don't exist due to this, but at the same time several others do exist because of what he did. 
 Tom also really has to question how he, as a person, fits into A-2016. He did exist as a person in A-2016 before the time travel incident and lived a normal life. He, however, was actually given the birth name John (not Tom) and lived a much different life and career path. Tom is able to recall John's memories of living and growing up in A-2016, but he still retains all his memories and knowledge of U-2016. This is really the point of the book here. He definitely struggles with finding out who he is and what it all means. 
 As for the science in the book, it explains time travel in an interesting way. That time travel is impossible for the longest time because you can't see it as just traveling through time, you must also go through space. This, to me, refers to the TARDIS from Doctor Who though. Thus,  I don't think it is completely original, but it gives a lot of considerations and how to get past barriers using some sort of science. Not quite hard scientific fact, like The Martian, but it gives more foundation to how time travel is possible in U-2016. There are other scientific inventions in the book which are explained for an everyday reader, but doesn't go into too hard of details/mathematics behind that either. It was nice, but I think the blurb from Andy Weir made me believe it would be based on more scientific fact, so don't expect it to be like that. 
 The overall flow of the book was pretty good. It dragged on in the middle a bit-- maybe some of those parts could've been trimmed. Thoughts about the ending:I did not see the ending coming at all. I was a bit angered at the twist of Lionel Goettreider being the "bad guy" of it all-- that he was angry over his love life with Ursula and even if he is dead in U-2016, at least he is famous for making the world a better place, so he forces Tom to go back to the incident in 1965 and fix the accident Tom caused in the first place. Oh, also that Lionel has all this fancy technology stashed up for his own personal use in a private warehouse/lab in Hong Kong. (WHAT????) Tom doesn't want to go since all his loved ones are nice and alive in A-2016. Lionel goes so far as to kidnap the ones Tom loves in A-2016 saying they will die anyway if he does not go. Tome gives in and agrees to travel back. Lionel's version of time travel however, is not instantaneous. Tom has to wait 50 years to travel back 50 years in the past. He has all this time to contemplate on how he will fix the event. This involves actually telling Lionel to stage a kidnapping of A-2016 Tom's family so he will go and time travel to fix his accident (since Tom ends up deciding this is the most moral thing to do for some reason). Despite 50 years of planning, Tom messes up again trying to fix it and creates a 3rd 2016 where his name is Victor and he has an even worse life, and its a post-apocalyptic 2016 where he is a trained soldier. He ends up being frozen in ice until time travel is invented in this 3rd 2016 so he can go back a 3rd time to fix it so the world doesn't end. When he does make it to the 1965 incident again, Victor doesn't want to die so Victor is fighting Tom/John to not fix the accident and it's just a mess. It's quite a climax but boy it all just rushes out at once. The fact that there are 3 people in one body, Tom, John, and Victor, is just a lot for a reader to adsorb. I understand that this was supposed to explain the part of the book where Tom/John essentially rapes Penelope and the intern, and that rape was actually done by Victor somehow, but to follow all this is madness. In the end Tom/John win over Victor, but U-2016 is sacrificed so A-2016 is the world that Tom travels back to and it stays as it. It then wraps up with Tom/John pairing up with Lionel to release the technology that Lionel invented to make the world a better place so it eventually is the Utopia that it could be.  There was a lot said in the spoiler section, but basically the ending is confusing at times, overwhelming at others, but exciting, too. Overall, I give it a 4 out of 5. I really enjoyed it, but it dragged at some parts and I think the ending was a bit too much/rushed.

The summary of this book calls it a mash up of The Wild West and Arabian Nights (though it is not a retelling). I think that's pretty accurate in terms of the setting and feel. I do want to acknowledge that there are many negative stereotypes about Middle Eastern culture and the historical US West that are used here, but I don't think the author has ever lived in either region as far as I can tell. Although I ended up loving this story, I don't disagree with people who have questioned if it was her story to tell and say the Middle Eastern influence was poorly researched. I have read a couple of own voices reviews that seem to be in conflict about the representation, and as I have no experience with the background it's hard for me to know what to think. 
 While reading, I was very engaged and found the story and world interesting and enjoyable. I kept being surprised at how much I liked it. I loved the world-building. It felt familiar AND fantastical. The magical creatures were interesting. I loved the creation mythology. I loved the magic system. 
 There isn't a ton about the main character, Amani, that stands out to me as something I loved, but there was nothing about her that I hated either. Jin on the other hand was a character I enjoyed from start to finish. I loved the dynamic between the two of them. 
 The middle portion of this book has kind of a survivalist tone and I'm always a sucker for that. Two characters with conflicting motives having to work together to survive? SIGN ME UP! 
 I loved the pacing. There was a part of the story right past halfway where the action lulls off and we start to learn more about new things. This is usually where my attention would take a nose dive. I was expecting to lose momentum here but then surprisingly, things were revealed in a way that kept my interest and propelled me on to the end! I particularly loved that some big things were revealed around 3/4 in because this gave us a little time to explore them and get excited for the next book without revealing too early, which can sometimes make me grow bored. 
 I love  Amani's power and everything about how it was revealed. I expected her to have some type of magic, but I wasn't expecting her to be a Demdji. When she was trying to figure out what her power was, I was really afraid it would be something like Noorsham's - control of fire. This is a power that has been done to death so when we find out that she can actually control sand, I was excited! It totally fits her character and the world and it's something fresh (to me at least). I love that her eyes were her only marker, and the iron of her guns kept her power at bay, which is why she never knew. It was SO bittersweet to watch her gain this new power, but at the expense of her sharpshooter skill, which she taught herself, since using a gun essentially "turns off" her Demdji ability.  
 I loved that there were many villains, and I especially loved how one of them (Noorsham ) is kind of a wildcard who you want to be won over to the good side but you can't tell how it will play out! I am so invested in seeing what happens with this one character! And the conflict they present to Amani! Ugh! My emotions were all over the place. 
 This book took the overdone rebellion-trying-to-overthrow-an-evil-overlord trope and made me interested in it! I will definitely continue the series.
There is a huge shift from The Thief to this book. The world is the same, the characters are the same -- but so much more -- and yet everything is darker, richer, more complex. It's beautiful.
3.5. Meh, it's a strange world we live in when the TV show captures the nature of the character better than the book. It's certainly not something I expected to be saying, but there it is.

A modern day retelling of Pride and Prejudice. I liked it but didn't love it. Was kind of angst ridden and a bit too much for me really but I'm glad I read it as it was a fun read in between the angst-y parts.

This book is amazing! 5 stars from me. 
 The plot is very simple but you'll actually end up rooting for the characters hope that they just get along. What a refreshing read. After all the books with leads that have dark pasts and heavy drama (not that I don't like them), this one is different. In fact, I was so deep into it that I never stopped reading until I finish it. 
 So they dislike each other but they have to work together and what a huge surprise it was when J.D. admitted that it was love at first sight for him. Oh how sweet!!! . I really love these kinds of stories since I'm still a young lady in the middle of strawberry fields. 
 And also the dialogues were pretty amazing that I feel a little bit smarter after reading it. The author really made the characters witty. 
 It's funny, witty, sweet, and it makes you feel-good after. It is somehow like you helped two people find each other. 
 Great job! I love it.

Yes, this is an angst-y teenage book about finding yourself and yes, the narrator does sound way too smart to actually be a teenager. What made this book worthwhile and a standout of the genre were the characters and the writing. Aristotle and Dante are interesting people who think about topics that grownups sometimes forget to have time consider. 
 And the writing! I was not surprised to find out, after looking up the author on completion of the book, that Saenz is in fact a poet as well as a novelist. If you think you won't be able to deal with all the drama of teenage-hood, the writing will get you through because it is beautiful.

I have to say, I am thoroughly surprised by what a fantastic find this book is. The last several books ive gotten for review from Netgalley have totally let me down. Haha 
 So... as the summary states, the basis of this story revolves around a girl who is branded as a sinner. In this future world, there is a Commander- the big bad- who enforces the rules of the new US. Basically if ANYONE just accuses you of sinning, you are literally branded a sinner and sent to the hole. 
 So... despite my belief that something like this would never happen and it is totally unbelievable, as our society as a whole likes to "sin" too much to ever try to actually outlaw it, the story was pretty cool. It was a good idea for a dystopian settings. 
 Our characters were all very believable and deep. I really like Lexi and her improvement as a person. She really grows a lot, from scared, sad, so-desperate-she-is-ready-to-kill-herself Lexi to a strong, independent, ready-to-make-her-own-choices Lexi. 
 I will say, sometimes she was kinda annoying, and her choices were kinda annoying... but overall, I really like her. 
 Cole... at the beginning, I thought he was dumb. Not actually stupid. But as a character, very lame... in that he was another-mostly abusive- male lead. Thankfully, all that changed and I grew to REALLY like him!!! Swoon. 
 Even minor characters were pretty great! 
 But what was really great about this book were some specific scenes/relationships. The build up of the Cole/Lexi romance. It really built well. It wasn't rushed- no insta love. NO triangle! YAY. They learned about each other. Helped eachother. Argued. Grew closer. It was FANTASTIC!! 
 The Alyssa/Lexi relationship. Gold, people! It was brilliantly written and executed! 
 Even the negative relationship of Lexi and her stepfather! The dynamic, perverse, gruesome, sadness of it all was SO well done. 
 There were about 3 or 4 wtf moments though... not in a good way. Some dialogue and scenes were pretty poorly done in this sense that it felt like it was written by an entirely different person (perhaps... one of the authors? Im not sure) I don't wanna get too spoiler... BUT I wanna give an example. SO... don't read this if you don't want the spoiler. 
  
 So... like when Keegan and Cole start arguing about whether Lexi can fight or not. The entire thing was... semi believable in that men think they know everything and can control everything. BUT when Keegan makes him leave. Im left wondering WHY?! Why was everyone ok with it? Why did keegan keep saying that he was not to be trusted, and just wait and see... hes bad? Why did Lexi just go along with it if she loves him so much?! 
  
 Anyways... overall a great read that sucks you in and entertains despite its misgivings! :D

It really bothers me that a lot of reviews of this book call Leonard a "school shooter," and compare him to real school shooters. Leonard is not a school shooter, he wasn't planning on shooting anyone at school, that's not what this story is about. 
 This book is about the day Leonard Peacock decided to die (and take someone awful with him). For me, the most meaningful aspect of Leonard's story is how obviously he does not want to do it. Every moment he is looking for a way out, making bargains with himself, and hoping to be seen. And as a reader, this is what I wanted for him as well - a way out, a bargain, to be seen. That suspense is what drives the story. And Leonard lives. I think this is a super interesting book in part because Leonard, while sad and weird and someone you root for to live, is also an unreliable narrator. The part where his horrible mother dismisses his suicidal impulse because his Nazi gun was so rusty it would never shoot! There's so much revealed in just that sentence.

This book doesn't really need another review; it's pretty popular, but I'll add to the pile anyway... 
 The protagonist, Lei, is a 20-something uniform police officer in Hilo, trying to make detective. She attends night classes; lives by herself in what must be a pretty nice little slice of paradise. She keeps orchids, and a companiable Rottweiler named Keiki. Between work and school, Lei seems to have her hands full. She is tapped to help investigate a double kidnap/rape/murder case. Meanwhile, it seem she's being stalked. As things move along, we also find that Lei has some creepy, unpleasant stuff in her own background. (The narrative doesn't dwell on any gruesome aspects, by the way, which is nice.) 
 I enjoyed Lei as a character: an island woman who also spent some years in California as a kid. Pretty savvy and independent on the outside, but she also has a bit of a golden gooey center. The small-town Hawaii environment is a nice place to read about, and she's a nice change from hard boiled eggs. I think the author knows her stuff and I slid comfortably into the whole thing, feeling I was in good hands. Oh, I also really liked the character of the police therapist. 
 And now for the nit you knew was coming... The preferred character for glottal stop (`okina) in Hawaiian orthography is U+02BB. But instead of that, or even just a curly quote or the old stand-by upright quote mark ('), the book uses the so-called "backquote", ASCII U+0060 (`), which is sometimes displayed as an opening single quotation mark in various fonts, but it can also look hideous in other fonts. That would have been my choice of last resort. I enthusiasticaly applaud the effort of indicating the glottal stops, but kind of wished another choice had been made. Since I got the book for free on an Amazon give-away day, I won't complain too much about this sub-optimal orthographic choice... But after I pay for the next book in the series, I may feel free to snipe at the author or the editor. ;-)  
 Oh, this is apparently an indie publication, and discerning readers might like to know that the editing was really good. Top notch, in fact. Dang, I found exactly one typographical error (a missing full-stop at the end of one paragraph) in what my e-reader claims is 255 juicy pages of prose. So Ms Neal deserves a silver rodent award for that heroic feat.
I don't have any words. This was so damn good.

No, I just.... can't. Definitely NOT a good book. SO REPETITIVE, gosh! I can't believe I read this. 
 Before: Wow this book was cool, kind of repetitive.

This is the first book in the series about Cat, the half Vampire. Born as the product of a rape, her mother encouraged her to go out and kill vampires from the time she was sixteen. She polishes off quite a few, before finding one that is a bigger bite than she can chew. 
 A fun read, this does bear a few similarities to Buffy, including Bone's resemblance to Spike.

Inspired by A Thousand and One Nights, The Wrath & the Dawn promises a compelling premise of romance and intrigue set against the enchanting backdrop of the Middle East. I always found the Persian-esque setting to possess a seductive quality, evocative of a rich culture and a dash of magical charm which often appears in fairy tales. 
 This is first and foremost a romance, which I tend to stay away from. I do however, appreciate a good story, and this certainly was one (a romance story). The story primarily aims to convey feeling, and it does so effectively; however, the lack of breadth and world-building ultimately detracts from the experience. The plot felt subdued, and never truly lived up to its full potential. It was a solid retelling, though not a particularly sophisticated one. The story relies on the rather angsty and provocative chemistry between Sharzhad and Khalid, though little else exciting happens. Their relationship is analogous to that of an intense, vexing encounter between two serpents, and it was enough to remain invested. I love a vengeance-driven protagonist as much as the next person-- not to mention, a dangerous and enigmatic Caliph too. 
 I do enjoy Renee Ahdieh's writing and will be looking forward to Flame in the Mist. (Inspired by Mulan and set in Feudal Japan? Count me in.)

Harry Potter is back for his second year at Hogwarts. Before being saved by Ron and his brother, Harry discovers Dobby, a magical creature who shows up in his bedroom and warns Harry not to go back. Once the term starts, things take a turn for the worse, students, teachers and ghosts alike are found petrified once the chamber or secrets has been opened. Mia, who was held hostage in an isolated cabin with her abductor for several months in the winter, has selective amnesia and claims her name is Chloe.

I hated any foundation to anything the author included, thinking that maybe Eve (Mia's mother)'s googling and research would be relevant to the story. (It's not!) Who cares if there is an umlaut over the e in Chloe? Not this girl. And Mia's therapist's pedantic descriptions of everything just talked down to everyone -- to Eve, to the detective, to us the reader. We are familiar with a lot of these terms, thx. 
 Second, I was not here for the obvious pro-life stance of the author, both by the language used in the story as well as the despicable description of the person who pushed the abortion. Fuck that shit.  
 Third, the author's implicit racism pissed me off. And I'm not one to immediately say "racism," 
 but seriously, Dalimar couldn't be a white criminal? He had to be blackest of the black, surrounded by black people in a bad neighborhood bar, described as the black of the "blubbery skin" of a killer whale? What? Yes, Colin was a product of some unfortunate circumstances, with no safety net given to society's poor/ill citizens, but he was given a redemption story. He died as an innocent in the eyes of the reader and his funeral was well-attended. Yet Dalimar's set up to be the bad guy, even though SPOILER at the end it's revealed that Mia set up her own kidnapping to out her father's corruption UMM.  
 I am not a stranger to a liking and defending stories with questionable and (let's say it) detestable characters and awful plots, but the writing was not compelling enough for me to give a shit about anyone. (Well, I cared about the cat.)

Still don't care about the characters - they're either underdeveloped or unlikeable. There was some clunky romantic angst that felt crowbarred into the narrative, and Thomas's view on women seems to be that they're either needy or duplicitous.

Izzie Goodnight is the penniless daughter of a serial writer of fairy tales. Her father foolishly did not amend his will to secure his daughter's future and left everything to a male cousin who hates her and took great delight in taking everything. [In HR the true antagonist is primogeniture.] Penniless and starving she receives a letter from a lawyer to say one of her father's biggest fans has bought her a castle and left it to her in his will. She arrives at the castle with one small bag and an ermine. 
 But the castle is still occupied and by a surly, giant of a man who seems to be the Duke of Rothbury. The castle is also a mouldering ruin inhabited by bats, rats and fleas - oh my. 
 Even if it is legally hers, she has no money to renovate it or go to court to confirm her ownership. 
 It takes her days to work out he's almost blind. He has been cut across the face in a swordfight and the handsome rake's face is a scarred ruin. 
 "Don't tell me you're one of those women with radical ideas." 
 "No," she returned. "I'm one of those women with nothing. There are a great many of us." (p. 45). 
 Indeed. 
 Even though she and Ransom are opposed, the only way to solve it is to go through the huge pile of correspondence and try to sort it out before a party arrives to judge his sanity. And as they do, they have to park the lust allowing their affection to grow. Plus, Izzie has a veritable legion of LARPers who show up to pay her homage wearing tea trays as armour. 
 She traced the scar with her fingertip, all the way from his brow to his cheekbone, then let her touch linger on his unshaven cheek. How ironic that the blow had just missed his right eye but taken the sight from both. 
 "Well?" he prompted. 
 "Well," she said, "it's plain to see that you were once a devastatingly handsome man." 
 "And now?" 
 "Now . . ." She sighed. "I really hate to say it. Don't make me say it." 
 His hand caught her wrist. "Just say it." 
 "Now you are a devastatingly handsome man with an impressive scar. That is the unhappy truth. I wish I could tell you otherwise. You will be impossible now." (pp. 199-200). 
 Izzie knows what she wants and she'll grab him with both hands. So his strategy of trying to seduce her to scare her off fails dramatically; but he keeps pressing his suit as it were...repeatedly. 
 And the scene in the library? Woo *fans self* [I had Atonement flashbacks.] 
 "I don't need to be a man who takes advantage." He sent one hand to burrow under her skirts. "Just one who takes an invitation." (p. 245). 
 *** 
 Duncan the valet. Bless. 
 "Give it here." The valet took it from her hand. He shook out the frail, tissue-thin fabric and examined it, clucking his tongue. "Dirt . . . grass . . . My word. Are these bloodstains? On silk embroidery?" 
 She bit her lip, praying that he wouldn't be angry with her for the duke's recent injury. Or worse, demand a full explanation of how it had occurred. 
 "Miss Goodnight, I don't know what to say. This . . ." He shook his head. "This is marvelous." 
 "Marvelous?" 
 "Yes." He gripped the fabric in both hands. "This is what a valet lives for. Removing stubborn stains from quality fabric. It's been months since I had a challenge like this one. I must away to the laundry, at once. If the stains have any longer to set, I'll never get them out."(pp. 203-204). 
 A man who loves his work. 
 I enjoyed this and read it quickly but as I go to write a review I'm seeing more issues. 
 It has a whole lot of tropes: yay! I love tropes. Who could love a beast? Ransom is scarred and blind. Izzie is so plain she's got to twenty-six without being kissed. Haters to lovers. Reformed rakes make the best husbands. Emily is frightened of the dark and that's where Ransom effectively lives these days. 
 Each has been starved of affection: Izzie is forever seen as the small pretty girl the fairy tales are told to, and Ransom has been blamed for his mother's death in childbirth. But they get to insta-lust pretty damn quickly. 
 There were very amusing scenes - Ransom hates the LARPers. 
 Gostley Castle? Really? It's almost like she tried to write a Gothic but didn't tick all the Gothic boxes. Izzie is not hopeless and waiting to be rescued. The odd noises at night are Ransom stomping around. There are literal bats in the belfry... you know. 
 But the ending was just too sudden. And it kind of doesn't work. It was romantic as he made his public declaration (which perhaps means it does work?) but in the storyline it wouldn't be the end of the matter. 
 And there are other plot holes: the male cousin comeuppance? The crooked solicitors? The wolf dog Magnus disappeared after a few chapters. 
 Who was the body in the priest hole? What happened with that? 
 If Izzie wrote the stories then it's gotta be her own damn fault that she didn't get her father to make a new will. She's supposed to be clever. She could have written under a male pseudonym - although I guess she was only thirteen and the sole breadwinner. *frowns* sign this or I'm not writing anymore, dad. 
 The Moranglians are a whole lot silly. Is she having a go at her own fans? 
 Where the hell are all the weird things the Duke supposedly bought to 'act' insane? The mustard plantation and the Arabian menagerie? 
 Signing over twenty thousand pounds to her at an insanity hearing is sweet, but well... insane. It'd just be torn up or offered as proof. 
 Ransom is a Duke. He doesn't have just one castle (or residence) or just one servant. He'd have literally thousands of people dependent upon him; bailiffs, estate managers, tenant farmers, housekeepers, butlers etc. And they're all just... non-existent. As is the hinted at person who wants his title and income who has conspired with his solicitors. We don't even know who they are by name let alone meet them and they are kind of the antagonist.  
 So... it was fun and sexy with good banter. But...

 I. LOVE. LUKA. KOTOVA. 
 She clutches my bicep around her collarbones like she doesn't want me to let go anytime soon. I'm not. I'm holding on forever. 
 For anyone who knows Krista & Becca Ritchie's writing, you will probably already be aware of the fact that this will have your emotions all over the board. Be prepared to fall, and fall hard, for all of these characters. A handful of times, I had to close my kindle and cry, just to soak in the emotions emanating from this story. If anyone knows how to sweep the reader into a world of characters that none will soon forget, it is KB Ritchie. 
 Awe-inspiring. Heart-warming. Off-the-charts. 
 The characters are timeless. The love is limitless. The passion is unforgettable. 
 "All I know is what I feel. And I'm in love with you, Bay. Right now. Not just five years ago - but here, today. Yesterday. Tomorrow. It's forever kind of love, and I'm not letting go. I can't let go." 
 While time changes us with age, Luka and Baylee come to see that hearts often stay the same. I don't think I've ever read a romance quite as tender and adorable as these two. Their childhood experiences, their struggles and heartbreaks, bleed through into present. Into who they have become. The question is if they can somehow manage to move forward together. 
 Our chests rise at the same time, and in a crowd full of people, with all eyes on me, I mouth, I love you. 
 Baylee and Luka aren't burning up the pages, they are warming our hearts. And it's simply precious. 
 Also, I'd just like to add that Luka is probably the kindest, sweetest, most empathetic character I've ever read. He puts his loved ones first. Always. Circus is family, and it's not just a motto, it's a way of life for him. 
 The family dynamic alone will have you wrapped up in this story. The love and support between these amazing characters is uplifting and inspiring. Nikolai. Thora. Dimitri. Timofei. Katya. Sergei. (Yes, even Sergei.) For the love of all things family. This group will dig into your heart and not let you go. 
 "I love you, brother. I need you whole." 
 Welcome to the circus.

This book surprised me in all the right ways. It's an unflinching and often brutal zombie story, and yet it's also hauntingly beautiful, moving, and told in the voice of such a unique and interesting character. In its themes and writing style, it really is very different from any zombie (or any paranormal creature) story that I've read before. 
 The main character is Temple, a wonderfully resourceful, thoughtful and independent teenage girl, who has been left alone in a post-apocalyptic world in which most of the Earth's population has been zombified. She has accepted her situation with surprising grace and maturity. Rather than long for a world that no longer is, or attempt to change it, she has adapted, and she finds beauty in all the little wonders of nature that still exist. This is not the kind of zombie novel where the characters are searching for a cure or a safe haven, or even battling against hoards of zombies just to survive. This is something very different. This is a story about survival, but perhaps more about survival of the soul than of the body. In that way, it is somewhat akin to Warm Bodies, another very unique zombie story that I've recently read and loved. Be warned, though; this has none of the romance of Warm Bodies. It is harsher, and in some ways an even stranger book, but just as clever and astonishing. 
 The zombies in the story are the slow moving, lurching kind. In fact, they rarely pose much of a threat to Temple, and only seem to be a problem if humans are caught unaware, or if people attempt to remain static and walled up in large communities. Temple understands that she is living in a new kind of world, the kind where it is better to keep moving, constantly, and she finds a quiet joy in this. She travels, discovering new places and new people, and she accepts that if the zombies get her, it will be because she has been careless. In this way, the zombies are more like predatory wild animals than monsters, and, in fact, the true dangers of this world come from other humans. I only really have one criticism of the zombie aspect, and that's the scenes with the mutants, which just felt a little too video-gamey and, for me anyway, didn't seem to fit with the rest of the book. 
 While staying in a community of survivors, Temple is attacked and forced to defend herself. She kills a man, and then must flee his brother, who wants revenge. Meanwhile, Temple has taken on a mentally handicapped man who cannot fend for himself, trying to take him to whatever remnants of family he has left. The story is therefore half quest, half chase, but the pace, while fast, is not frantic. Temple accepts everything that happens to her, even the basic unfairness of being blamed for killing a man in self-defence, a man who was clearly in the wrong. His brother knows this too, and even regrets having to kill Temple, but he is still set on this course, as if he has no other choice. Both he and Temple almost seem to be bound by deep, raw laws of the world, and both have a strong belief in fate, or at least in some kind of order and meaning that drives them. It is tragic that the deep bond between them is one based on revenge and death. 
 The feel, story and themes of the book give it a very Wild West feel, so much so that I would call it a Zombie Western. The new post-apocalyptic world seems to suit Temple's free spirit better than the old world would have; she is at home in a life without restrictions and the complicated rules of society. The revenge theme, particularly, based on a deep feeling of duty rather than justice, fits very well into the book's style. I found this fascinating, particularly when combined with the lyrical quality of the writing. It's not just a Zombie Western, it's a beautiful Zombie Western, which is even more surprising. 
 The Reapers are the Angels surprised and delighted me. I found it moving, tragic, and beautiful. It's a fairly short book, well paced, and I was captivated until the very end. (Proof of this: I read most of it on a train, with no seat, sitting uncomfortably on a suitcase with screaming children nearby, and as soon as I started reading I didn't even notice anymore. And let's just say, it's a good job that my stop happened to be the train's final station.) If you love zombies, or even if you're getting a little tired of them by now and would like something a bit different, you should definitely consider adding this to your 'to read' list.

 After nearly two weeks, I finally finished this absolute monster of a book (1396 pages!!) and although it wasn't what I expected, and there were times when I thought that I should just give up, I'm so glad I managed to finish it because I ended up really enjoying it. I expected to be terrified but once I got used to the idea that it wasn't going to be that way, that it would be more of a quietly creeping uneasy kind of read that would leave me thinking, probably for a long time, after finishing, I got along a lot quicker. I will not be watching the movie though - that I think would scare me half to death. 
 I really loved that at the centre of the book there is a strong friendship between the seven members of The Losers Club. They go through so much together and they all stick together through that summer of terror in 1958 and it makes me sad that for 27 years after they first defeat IT that they forget each other, apart from Mike who stayed to watch over Derry all those years. It makes me even sadder that when it is all finally over at the end, their sacrifice is the forgetting of each other all over again and all the happenings in Derry.  
 I did love most of the members of The Losers Club, they were very real and I enjoyed how even as adults they were still recognisable. I really did not like Richie though. He was one of the most annoying characters that I have ever read about. HIS BLOODY VOICES. I wanted to bash his head in, I wanted him to be taken by Pennywise, I wanted all sorts of bad things to happen to him. It's really bad because he's just a kid but THOSE VOICES. 
 There are so many fucked up things in this book. You've got the severe bullying (Henry Bowers was a truly evil little shit and I honestly thought he was more terrifying than Pennywise because he was an actual human child), racist abuse, homophobic abuse, parental and spousal abuse, animal abuse... and that's without the murdering of children by the evil in Derry. The book starts off with little Georgie Denborough meeting Pennywise by a drain and getting murdered by having his arm ripped off and that's probably the least fucked up part of the book! It was very uncomfortable reading at times but it was the part towards the end where poor little Beverley felt she had to have sex with the six boys one after the other in order to bring them back together to escape the sewers  that I really felt was unnecessary - they are eleven years old for crying out loud! 
 It may be really long but if you have the time, it's worth the read. Could it have done with being a bit shorter? Probably. However, thinking back there's not an awful lot that I would have cut. I'm definitely looking forward to picking up another Stephen King book at some point in the near future and I'm thinking of possibly rereading The Shining (which I really didn't like when I read last year) because I feel like I might have a new appreciation for it after reading It.

First impressions: Male POV! Yes! Not only is Cas a great male protagonist, he's funny. Swoon! 
 Lasting impressions: Great little horror book for the ghost hunting set. 
 Conflicting impressions: Can we have a new rule where nobody falls in love with ghosts? 
 Overall impressions: This book was so much fun, which feels weird to say about a sometimes gruesome, often scary tale about a demonic ghost. Kendare Blake sets the tone with our fearless narrator, Cas. He's witty, funny, quirky, and has an interesting occupation: ghost killer. 
 Cas has inherited a knife and an ability from his father that allows him to put murderous rampaging ghosts to rest. He grew up traipsing around the world after his dad, who followed leads on where to find the worst ghosts. His mother, a witch, sells candles and other Wiccan supplies online, thus supporting the ghost killer habit. When Cas's dad dies at the hand of a particularly brutal ghost, Cas takes over. 
 Now following tips of his own, he pursues a lead on a ghost in Canada known locally as Anna Dressed in Blood. Murdered in the 50s on her way to a school dance, she now haunts her old house, taking out anyone who dares enter. She proves this in epic fashion on Cas's first visit to the house, when a bully from school locks him in the house and Anna unleashes her wrath upon the bully. 
 There is plenty of violence and a smattering of foul language (f-bombs flying!), so this is one for the older set. I, for one, did not mind the language, but a few times it seemed to pop up so suddenly that it took me out of the world for a second. Maybe it's because I've been reading so clean lately? 
 Anna is as wonderful a character as is Cas. She's bold, confused, and full of hideous secrets she tries desperately to hide. I don't want to give too much away, because the joy of the novel is discovering Anna's story as well as Cas's. The two of them have to explore their histories and destinies in ways that make them uncomfortable, but it must be done in order to set things right. 
 This is a magical, dark, funny novel full of interesting characters. I loved the story, and its twists and turns kept me guessing. There were a few elements that could have been developed a little further, and I'm not a fan of the fact that this turned into a paranormal romance when it could have been a great standard horror book, so four stars from me. It's still a great read, however, and I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a great male protagonist. 
 Marry me, Cas!

I really enjoyed this book. I'm a huge fan of Jane Austen and Persuasion is one of my favorites. While I didn't enjoy this as much as Persuasion, I thought it was a really good read and a great way to use a classic to tell a new story.

 The partial epistolary style was excellent and a beautiful way to show the roots of Austen's work. The class conflict was more pronounced, this being a dystopia, but the story was much closer to the original than I would have expected. The names were mostly brought right out of Persuasion, with some slight tweaks. The story is just as heartbreakingly beautiful. Kai could be irksome, but I adored him nearly as much as the first Wentworth. 
 The writing was beautiful too. A very good read.

3.5 stars - This book was a visual feast. The whimsical descriptions and handful of scenes written in second person really let me experience the circus like I was part of the audience. 
 But aside from the beautiful writing, there weren't any other wow factors for me. The first half of this book really d r a g g e d. The pacing was painfully slow. So much time was spent describing every small detail of the circus and introducing several characters. The number of characters and time spent on the circus didn't allow me to connect with any of the characters, so there wasn't a lot keeping me invested in the story. 
 The only thing I knew about this book going into it was that it was about a competition between two magicians. The competition didn't appeal to me at all. It was a vague concept, and I didn't enjoy the way they played or the way it concluded. For this to be THE selling point of the book, it was pretty weak. 
 I also didn't enjoy the way the chapters skipped around in time, until the very end when it was evident what the two timelines had to do with each other. It was difficult to understand what was really going on at first due to these jumps. 
 I did really enjoy exploring the circus though, and the second half of the book began to be a bit more plot driven and characters began interacting with each other. The chapters that were dialogue heavy really sucked me in. 
 I saw many reviews saying the book starts off slow and lacking a connection to the characters but that it was worth it in the end. This is very true. So I encourage anyone feeling stuck to stick it out because I really enjoyed spending time at the circus.

 However, this book isn't so much about action and more about internal thoughts about the characters. It alternates points of view between the main female and male leads, Etta and Nicholas. Instead of focusing on the events that happen it is more about the internal thoughts of the characters and what they are feeling. Obviously this is a love story if you didn't get that from what I just said or the general summary of the book, but it is terrible insta-love. They even sleep together in this book despite the fact that Nicholas grew up in a completely different time period where people probably didn't sleep with each other until they were married, but he has no problem just going for it.  I can understand Nicholas's strong feelings a little bit better, as he is from a time where people got married very young, and he is very much a marrying age. I've watched the anime film of Vampire Hunter D, and was intrigued to see what the book's like. As January is vampire month for the Paranormal Challenge, I thought this seemed like a good time to give it a try. 
 I wasn't quite sure what to make of the book at first because it's written in a very odd style. I suppose this could be down to the translation, but to me it felt like a deliberate choice. It seemed to be going for a kind of 'pulp' style, which suits the weird setting and atmosphere, but it definitely slid over into the realms of cheesy at points. This includes a detached non-character narrator who occasionally appears to talk back to himself, sometimes talks directly to the reader, and who observes events without hindsight or omniscience, as if watching a film for the first time: there was a black shadow in the corner but D didn't notice it... D looked around the room... a cat rubbed up against D's leg - oh that must have been the black shadow! (Okay, so that wasn't an actual quote, but it gives an idea.) 
 However, though this was a little disrupting at first, I did get used to it, and I began to see why Hideyuki Kikuchi had chosen to write like this. Vampire Hunter D clearly owes a lot to old Hammer Horror films: there are constant references to them, the vampire count is called Lee, the book is dedicated to the cast and crew of Horror of Dracula ('58), and the author talks about the influence such films had on him. The sometimes cheesy dialogue and narration did actually capture a sense of this kind of over-dramatic, fun-yet-still-frightening horror. Combined with Japanese elements, the author's own unique style and vision, and a lot of manga/anime influence, this actually blossomed into what was quite a quirky, different, and fun style. 
 The story is a very simple white-knight and damsel-in-distress tale, made more interesting by the unique world Hideyuki Kikuchi has created. It's 12,090 AD, a far future in which mankind has almost ruined the Earth, blown itself up in nuclear world war, slid into another Dark Ages, been taken over by vampires, risen against the vampires, and now exists in a kind of uneasy state of freedom. There are futuristic gadgets and inventions, the horses are cyborgs, and the vampire castle has laser defence systems. Yet the world has also reverted into a kind of small-town, agricultural, past age, with a society to match. Pretty much everything technical the humans possess came from the vampires, and there is a sense that there is no innovation or invention anymore. On top of this, there are all kinds of bizarre supernatural creatures roaming the Earth, most of them bioengineered by the vampires for the lolz. 
 This is a fantastic setting, and the weird mix of fantasy, old-world, paranormal and futuristic works very well. I loved it. But, unfortunately, the story did not really live up to this amazing creation. Doris Lang is bitten by a vampire and hires D, a vampire hunter, to help her with her unwanted admirer. D runs off to the castle, and the rest of the story is a series of incidents designed to instigate as many fights as possible, while Doris is constantly whisked away, providing more chances for D to save her. This got old very quickly for me, as did the never-ending introduction of more elite bad guys. The story is full of people who are so quick and incredible at fighting that none of them actually appear to move. D is always the very definition of cool - calm and unafraid of anything, not because he's brave but because he knows he's the best - and this kind of character tends to irritate me. Where's the emotion, the tension, the character development? There were odd points where D did show a real person lurking beneath the surface, and these were the most interesting parts. It was a shame that this never lasted very long. 
 I also found Doris' character to be rather annoying. She starts out with an incredible strength; she is brave despite her fear, looks after her little brother and the farm with no help, deals with all manner of problems, is self-assured and determined, but also kind and well-meaning. She seeks help because she knows a vampire is a formidable foe that she cannot face alone. Then she meets D, and as D begins to do more for her, she gets steadily weaker. By the end of the story, a girl who took on everything and anything on her own can't even lift a bucket without D's help. She tells her little brother that she now doesn't think she can manage on her own. I understand that she would be tired and in shock after everything that happened, but I do prefer characters to grow with their experiences rather than become more helpless. 
 Vampire Hunter D is an interesting and quirky book, and certainly worth reading for its weird and wonderful world alone. The story is simple, and at points it lets the book down, as does some of the characterisation. A short and light-hearted read, often entertaining, sometimes frustrating, but very unique.

 The Beginning of Everything was a really great contemporary novel that is very character driven. It was filled with laugh out loud moments as well as those that made me want to burst into tears. 
 It follows a boy named Ezra who is involved in an accident that completely changes his life and sets him on a path of self discovery and the chance to figure out what he really wants for himself. 
 I really loved the writing and the humor in this book. It was definitely interesting to read from the male perspective. While I feel like it isn't as common of a voice in YA, I also feel like lately it has been making a huge surge in the genre. I really liked the character of Ezra because he wasn't mopey about how his whole life and future was going to change based on how the accident affected him. He kind of just rolled with the punches. I really liked how he reconnected with his childhood best friend Toby, as well as the relationship he developed with new girl Cassidy. 
 Cassidy transfers to Ezra's high school from a boarding school, and when she arrives she is immediately recognized by Ezra's friend Toby, who knew her from Debate Team tournaments. Cassidy is known to be very eccentric as well as a Debate champion. She has quite the effect on Ezra and helps him reshape his life without either of them really knowing it until towards the end of the novel when a bit of a bombshell is revealed. I really liked the twist at the end of the story even though it caused the ending to be bittersweet. 
 The bittersweet ending is the only reason I gave this book 4.5 stars instead of 5 stars. While I still enjoy a bittersweet ending and understand the necessity to not always have a truly happy ending, I am a bigger fan of the happy ending. I felt like in the case of this book, Ezra mostly got his happy ending, but there was still a bit of misfortune for him. 
 Overall, I loved this book and would definitely recommend it!

 I really enjoyed reading "Fifty Shades Darker" by E L James and I give it four (4) stars. I was excited to see what would happen between Ana and Christian in this second installment of James' "Fifty Shades of Grey" trilogy. Together, Ana Steele and Christian Grey experience some intense excitement, as well as some crazy highs and lows. This second story goes more into the secrets of the CEO and dominant, Christian Grey's, past. Ana was allowed some insight into his life and has to choose if she could still stay with this man that she loves even after learning what she did about him. Overall, I think "Fifty Shades Darker" is exciting and intense on many different levels. I would recommend this book to someone who is open minded and looking for a new branch of romance stories, like erotica. 
 Christian Grey, and innocent, college graduate Anastasia Steele have an interesting relationship. There is a deep emotional and sexual connection between them. 
 "He glances down at me, and it's there in the air between us, that electricity. It's palpable. I can almost taste it, pulsing between us, drawing us together. 
 'Oh my,' I gasp as I bask in the intensity of this visceral, primal attraction. 
 'I feel it, too' he says, his eyes clouded and intense. 
 Desire pools dark and deadly in my groin. He clasps my hand and grazes my knuckles with his thumb, and all my muscles clench tightly, deliciously, deep inside me." (Page 14). 
 Before meeting Christian, Ana was a virgin. Then after meeting Christian, Ana is all of a sudden swept up into his intimidating world of sex. And intimidating it is with all the whips and handcuffs and other unidentifiable objects. Ana wants to have "more" with Christian, not his usual Dominant and Submissive relationship. She tried the submissive thing for a bit, though she didn't sign the contract, but it just wasn't for her. Though when she left Christian she didn't realize how much she loved him until he was gone. The same happened for Christian-he realized he loved Ana. So, Christian and Ana came to an understanding that they will try a more normal relationship, as Christian would say "vanilla." Maybe, as time goes on, Ana will allow Christian to spice up the vanilla sex, especially if he could learn to trust her. 
 I think this book's title should be changed to "Fifty Shades of Wow." Wow=Great in this case. I really liked this novel. The only reason that I am not giving it five stars is because it gets a little repetitive at times. BUT! I am not a writer whatsoever and I am not bad talking James' style in the slightest. I really enjoy her work, I do. But for example, every single time Ana and Christian have an orgasm together it's the same line of Christian calling out Ana's name. No big deal really, but I just wanted to throw that out there because sometimes that is something readers want to know. Like I said though, I give this book 4 stars and I also give the first book 4 stars. I am about to start reading the third book, "Fifty Shades Freed" and hopefully I think that book is at least 4 stars as well. I will definitely let you know when I do though! 
 I found this book to be very exciting, unexpected, thrilling, and revealing. I also find it to be quite humorous at times. Ana and Christian both have a very dry sense of humor that I actually find refreshing. They enjoy each other's company so much, even if they are in the midst of an argument. This, yes, seems to happen a lot. But that is only because of how overprotective Christian is of Ana, and he has his own personal reasons of course. I also find it quite amusing when Ana refers to her inner goddess. She does this quite often throughout each book. She also refers to her self-conscious a lot too, but she is a lot more reserved and prudish than Ana's inner goddess who is sexy and needing. 
 "He is gloriously naked. My inner goddess is doing a triple axel dismount off the uneven bars, and abruptly my mouth is dry," (page 76). 
 I know I already said this, but I just love this book! It's a fun book to read. Of course, yes it is an erotica, but I really enjoy the romantic parts of the story. I like when Christian opens up to Ana, and how they find comfort in each other's company. They have grown a lot together in this book, and I can't wait to see where the next book brings them!!

 My faith in contemporary romance has been renewed. I took a huge break from all things contemporary romance. For a month or so I have solely read historicals because I was completely over the mind numbing brainless drivel I'd been reading. Seriously, I almost gave up reading all together because I'd become so frustrated that every book seemed to be the same and the characters all fell in love in ten seconds within three words of speaking to each other. I felt like I was loosing my mind. Like maybe there were chapters missing to every book I read where the characters actually spoke to each, got to know each other, and were justified in their 'feelings'. So for the sake of my sanity, I took a break. But then I got equally frustrated at how hard it was to find a good historical romance that was clean, that I hadn't already read. I kept reading solid three star books and well, I don't like settling for good when I could have great, so again I began to feel book-frustrated. 
 Anyway, unto this book. I've had this on my Goodreads to-read list for like 3 months. However, the reviews were mixed as to whether or not it was clean and so I hesitated in reading. For some reason yesterday I decided to try it out and thank God I did! This was so freaking awesome. I can't even deal with the relief and satisfaction that I feel after reading this. 
 Thoughts: 
 The attraction and tension in this was so freaking delicious. Like, it was palpable, tangible, thick enough to bite. It. Was. Delicious. But this book was the full package because although the tension was delicious, so was the actual story. Like I've read so many books and combined with the fact that some authours are sort of just churning out the same story, I'm hardly ever surprised anymore. But Penny Reid didn't go with the formulaic, cookie cutter, this has worked before so I'll just repeat it story lines. It was original. Like I could never have seen who Jon cheated with coming. I was legit surprised. I loved that there were actual conversations in this book, where they legit talked lol. I loved Janie's stream of consciousness, and will we ever learn about the Japanese kids and eye contact? 
 I'm gonna wrap this up because I have part two waiting for me. But all in all this was awesome, it was obvious that time was spent with this, the angst is minimal, so is the drama, the characters are all reasonable. It was quirky without trying too hard. And my faith in the genre is restored.

As for the plot itself started off really intriguing and basically became a magnet to me throughout the rest of the book. Boys, guns and dark family secrets- what more can you ask for??? 
 Kate (Nate) Thompson, the main protagonist of this story, could be a real contender to my favorite female kick ass character, next to Celeana Sardothien of the Throne of Glass series by Sarah J. Mass. Yes! That's how awesome she is and you all know how much I love Celeana! One of the main things that really stuck out to me about her was her attitude- her get - outta - my - way - or - die kind of gritty 'tude. In addition to that, I find her to be very admirable- crazy- but really admirable in finding out what exactly did her father die for. However, the supporting characters of this novel didn't really live up to the expectations that I had as I read about them. Of course, really interesting things happened between a couple of the characters, including Kate, but I felt like the supporting characters still kind of lacked something which then affected a certain event of the book. 
 Vengeance Road is certainly a 2015 release that everyone should definitely get their hands on! Of all the YA books that I've read my entire life, there was nothing that ever came close to this. As a matter of fact, this wouldn't really be the kind of book that I would normally reach out for because of it's genre (western, historical fiction), but I am so thankful to have read this. Otherwise, I would be missing out on a lot. I would like to thank HMH for providing an ARC in exchange for my own direct and honest opinion! Thank you so much HMH!!! 
 Vengeance Road comes out on September 01, 2015 :D Grab your copies!!!

One thing I have learned throughout my reading journey: once you convince yourself to try to love a book, you are fighting a losing battle. 
 So yeah, I tried to like this book and as expected, I failed at liking it. 
 My biggest problem is Sam's character. I don't have any issue with bad-ass heroines but the way the author created her character did not sit well with me. 
 My idea of a perfect story is one where the excitement builds, in Here Be Sexist Vampires, after the initial shock of knowing Sam's gift, all felt flat to me. She was portrayed as too perfect, better than the rest of the vampires and I bet if I continue to read on, she will even surpassed Antonio. 
 If you have that kind of heroine, will you ever be excited of knowing what will come next? I would appreciate it more if we get to see Sam grow stronger, it will become believable to me. And she's what? Only a three year old vampire? Know what I mean?

First of all, let me say: WHAT THE FUCK IS WITH THE NAME SERAPHINA IN YA RIGHT NOW? Seriously, this is the third book I've read this year that's intended for kids or teenagers and has a main character with that name. IS IT EVEN A NAME?! The world may never know. 
 Overall this was a decent book, although very clearly written for younger people by an adult who doesn't remember being a kid. It wasn't so much the content, which was at points as horror-filled and action-packed as you could want, but the structure, the simplified language, plot, and clear pointing out of important foreshadowing or explanations. (Seriously, the presentation of what a catamount is was a throwaway two-line conversation about an EXTREMELY convenient painting they see while doing something else. The fuck.)  I've read kids' books that don't explain themselves, ones that really make you feel like you're IN a kid's world rather than being shown a simplified world created FOR kids. This book was not that. 
 For all my griping on that point, though, Seraphina was a decent character. The exaggerated catlike thoughts and behaviors were obvious, but amusing. And the Man in the Black Cloak was a pretty terrifying enemy. A lot of the book read like it was intended to be adapted into a movie or show, and it does turn out there's a movie in the works. Unfortunately the movie's gonna be live-action; for some reason my brain depicted the events as an animated movie instead in the Rankin Bass tradition, but we can't have everything. 
 I don't feel like I wasted my time reading it, and if I know any kids who liked Coraline I now know something else to recommend them!

Alexis Baldizzi is upset that her younger sister has blown off her dental practice and started living at a hotel/casino with the owner. She thinks her sister has been kidnapped and brain washed so she storms into the casino, ignores the front desk attendants and bullies her way passed security and demands to see her sister. The hotel and casino owner, Ethan Carrick, is polite to Alexis but...despite being a prosecutor, Alexis starts pulling martial art's moves on him and trying to beat him up. It was pretty juvenile and I kept thinking she was over-reacting and Ethan should have called the police on her. I'm thinking her career would have been over but instead, Ethan got turned on by it. I, however, was turned off and decided not to like the leading lady. 
 Ethan Carrick is not only the hotel and casino owner of a successful casino on the strip of Las Vegas but he is also the president of the vampire nation and he is campaigning for a second term against a rather unsavory opponent. His campaign manager thought that Ethan's image would be improved if he settled down so when he met Alexis' sister, Brittany, an impure (someone born from a human mother and a vampire father) he thought it would be the perfect opportunity to impress his constituents by marrying her except for one thing, he wasn't attracted to her and had no feeling for her. 
 Brittany is a sweet girl but she has no idea she is half vampire. She's figured out that Ethan and his friends are vampires and thinks she needs to save their souls. When she tells Alexis this, Alexis thinks that Ethan and his friends are playing like they are vampires like people play Dungeons and Dragons. She agrees to take Brittany's place to play Ethan's girlfriend for a week so her sister will go home and back to her dental practice. She thinks Ethan and his friends are all crazy. 
 Alexis grew on me. After the disaster of the first meeting with Ethan, she stopped being so juvenile. She was still crass but that endeared her to me because I realized she reminded me of me the way she doesn't get all sappy and she just says what she is thinking. 
 I enjoyed the romance between Ethan and Alexis and I was intrigued by the secondary characters and the plot. The thing I liked the most was the humor. Humor goes a long way with me. 
 I'm not sure if I am hooked or not on this series but I have downloaded the second book and am going to start reading it tonight.

Overall I really liked this book, but I had mixed feelings about the characters. Grace was just such a hot mess. Her life was so tragic and heartbreaking. The adults around her were not helping her like they should have been. I realize they were grieving too, but the damage they were doing to Grace by allowing her to live the way she was made me angry. She was drowning and they were essentially pouring more water over her head. I often felt Grace didn't truly want to feel better either. I know she was plagued by extreme guilt, which kept her in a pit of self-punishment. I just really felt bad for Henry. He met Grace at the absolute worst time possible. For some unknown reason, he still completely fell for her. She continually tore his heart out, but he kept going back for more. All Grace did was hurt him and essentially use him, but he still daydreamed about marrying her. Masochist is all I can say. I really liked his character and wished that Grace could be better for him. He really helped her, even when she hated him for it. She just wanted to wallow and he would make her feel good again. Then she would punish herself for it, punishing Henry along the way. The poor sap. This was a messed up love story, if you could even really call it that. It definitely highlighted the ugly side of some relationships and dealt with the very real truth people are faced with when their planned out futures completely fall apart. This story is, at its heart, about heartbreak. We experience it at different levels with multiple characters. There are no happy endings, just the reality of life after love ends. Brutal and ugly and honest. Definitely not a feel-good book, but enjoyable in its own right.

This review will be short because I read through the entire Five Hundred Kingdoms series in quick succession, meaning I have to write about 5 reviews on similar topics. 
 One Good Knight is about a bookish Princess Andromeda who has to be sacrificed to a dragon. But somehow along the way ends up on a quest to save her kingdom from her own mother. 
 As per the last book, I very much like the premise of this series. I love the idea that Tradition moves a bit like fate and tries to make people's lives fall into a story-book trajectory. It's new and interesting, so watching Lackey manipulate the story and reference old fairy tales in a new way is just fantastic. 
 There were some great components. 
 I liked how Lackey lingered for a little while on Andie coming to terms with her mother's evilness. 
 I loved the fox. Every scene was just a mix of awww, hilarity, cuteness! Imagining it within dragon teeth like a cage, listening to it whine about not being free, etc. Absolutely delightful! 
 I do wonder, however, how evil she actually was. Was it tradition to moved her towards that path? We'll never know. 
 Also, we don't really see how the blood-sibling pact changed anything. I wish there were some addendum about that. 
 Three stars. It was a solid second book for this series. It didn't blow my mind or anything though.

In the beginning I wanted to strangle Alex with all her "my Seth" nonsense, but I knew it wouldn't last. The series is getting darker as the war grows nearer. I guessed correctly the god involved/responsible for Lucian and Seth and all the destruction/power play. I'm curious to see how both Alex and Seth respond to the encounter she has with the god. I'm also anxious for the encounter between Alex and Seth. Will she be successful in beating him and transferring his power to her? How hard will he fight and will she have to kill him? If she succeeds, what will Seth be like after the drain. What will Alex be like after the boost? Will she be able to control it, will Aiden be able to ground her? Will Apollo have to take her out too? Will she have success taking out the traitor god? Who else will be a casualty of war? Sentinel will be out in a couple months. Can't wait.

It took me a little while to decide what rating I wanted to give this story. I love the author's writing style and I found the story interesting and twisty. There were so many twists I just wasn't expecting. 
 But at the same time the modern day retelling of Peter Pan that wasn't really a retelling of Peter Pan and the YA love triangle really made me want to rate it low. 
 I ended up giving it three stars because if the author hadn't marketed it as a retelling of Peter Pan. It takes the character names of Peter Pan and places it on a beach in California, but that is as far as I would go in calling this a retelling of Peter Pan. 
 I am also not a fan of love triangles. I know they are popular in YA, but I really dislike them. I love the writing style though and I enjoyed the unexpected twists that come with the love triangle. 
 I would suggest this book to people looking for a YA romance that has a dream like quality to the way its written.

Perhaps the problem with this is that I listened to the audio book, which was read well by Gerard Doyle. If I'd read the pages, my complaints might seem less acute. When it comes to fantasy, I either need a briskly paced plot, or characters I can really root for. This book didn't offer either of these for me. Instead, the story plodded along with far too much history of Wonderland. That could have worked in a more adult novel, but not as YA. And there wasn't one interesting person in the story. Say what you will about J.K. Rowling, Hagrid and the Dursleys make the first chapters interesting. 
 Don't know who I'd offer this book to. It isn't bad or objectionable, just not charming or exciting.

Marchetta has spun a tale about a girl at a new HS struggling with new friendships, a boy, and a mother depressed and in bed. Garden-variety movie-of-the-week stuff, but with an Australian setting that has some charms. I can see why fans of Sarah Dessen would enjoy this. 
 I saw the one big reveal coming from a long way off, but teens probably won't have the experience to track it. They will probably enjoy Francesca as a relatable, flawed teen who could be someone they know. The many friends - male and female, from the new school and the old - may lose some readers, while others will appreciate the realistic rendering of shifting alliances and developing intimacies. 
 A bit of language and reasonable drinking might earn this a 'PG-13' rating. Its heart is in the the right, albeit earnest, place.

5 Sing Me Home Stars! 
 This is shifters TJ Klune Style - like nothing you've read before!! If you have not ever read anything by TJ Klune before then you will be blown away by this book. 
 Ox was twelve when his daddy taught him a very valuable lesson. He said that Ox wasn't worth anything and people would never understand him. Then he left. 
 Ox was sixteen when he met the boy on the road. The little boy who talked and talked and talked. Ox found out later the little boy hadn't spoken in almost two years before that day, and that the little boy belonged to a family who had moved into the house at the end of the lane. 
 Ox was seventeen when he found out the little boy's secret and it painted the world around him in colors of red and orange and violet, of Alpha and Beta and Omega. 
 Ox was twenty-three when murder came to town and tore a hole in his head and heart. The boy chased after the monster with revenge in his bloodred eyes, leaving Ox behind to pick up the pieces. 
 It's been three years since that fateful day--and the boy is back. Except now he's a man, and Ox can no longer ignore the song that howls between them. 
 So as everyone else has stated this is an amazing story - Our MC Ox Matheson and Joe Bennett are unique and unlike any other characters you have ever read. Ox, he has never felt like he fits in.. always waiting for the inevitable "sh*t" that his daddy said would be coming and wondering why he always felt out of sync. Then one day people move in to the house down the lane from his house and his life is never the same. On a random walk home he meets Joe Bennett who is a little blonde tornado talking a mile a minute and running around him eager to take him home and show him off. When Ox Meets Joe's family he immediately feels like a part of him has been found and he feels at home with Joe's family. After all, Joe said he is awesome and smells like "candy canes, pine cones, and epic and awesome who was Ox to argue with that - whatever Joe said, just was. Joe and Ox become inseparable. Joe gave Ox a miniature wolf on his birthday. Ox cherished that wolf. 
 Then one night, Ox is called to come out to the woods - and Ox's eyes are opened that night to the world of the supernatural of witches and werewolves, of Alpha's and of Mates. I have to say that Ox takes it very well and even when he is offered to be officially added to the Bennett pack he declines. 
 Of course this story can't all be happy though so when evil comes to town the pack and the witch band together and defend each other. However, when evil gets away - Joe Bennett goes on a journey to chase him down and for 3 Years. One Month. 26 Days. Joe and Ox do not see each other. Ox doesn't even know if Joe is coming back and Ox goes through an amazing transformation while Joe is away coming into his own rights as a leader of what is left of The Bennett pack and his friends who stayed behind. He is an Alpha of his own making. So when Joe returns - the two have to decide if they can salvage what they had before evil tore them apart. 
 Let me tell you this is a long book - but it goes by so quickly you will be wanting more when its done. It has amazing characters. The setting and the details - they are one of a kind and add so much to this story. What these two go through in the span of this story - T.J. Klune really puts them through the ringer! However, I think had he not made them work so hard for what they have the story would have been flat - these two needed to work for their HEA and to overcome what life through at them. And, they do! 
 So run to the store - and get this book. This is not your typical shifter story. It is an amazing story that will take you on a whirlwind of emotions by the time you are through all of it.. enjoy! 5 Stars!!

I read this during my freshman year in school, after watching the 2010 "Alice in Wonderland." It was the annotated version, because that was the only copy they had in the school library. But I read it, nevertheless, and enjoyed both stories very much. Not only did I learn that "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland" had a sequel, but also that there's pretty much more to explore, compared to the Disney animated version, which I watched only once, years ago. 
 Mid-way through reading this, I realized that the 2010 "Alice in Wonderland" didn't contain any of the witty language and nonsense from the original source, and I now realized why many disliked that movie. 
 You feel very bad for Alice, because just about everyone she meets is rude to her. At first, I wondered if the author hated kids, because of what he was putting little Alice through; but then got the idea that he, too, sympathized with her, like saying, "Poor Alice!" Carroll has a very visual style of writing, and I enjoyed picturing what was going on and what they looked like; also admired the Tenniel illustrations (I even copied some of them with pencil in Drawing/Photography class). 
 As for the last scene right before Alice wakes up, I remember having a grasp of shock when I read it, as if I were there. Just a bunch of cards flying right at you, ordered by the easily-tempered Queen, surrounding your now-grown body, and then, poof! You find yourself on your sibling's lap, who's brushing away the leaves on your face, which, a second ago, felt like cards.  It really felt as if I had just woken up from a nightmare. 
 "Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There" is very good as well. I again enjoyed the visual images that came to my mind, the literacy, felt sorry for Alice, and rememeber laughing at several scenes. 
 Of course, since I read it in "The Annotated Alice" first, I read quite a few facts that were noted throughout. Very interesting (like the scene where the dormouse tells a story of three girls stuck in a well -- their names are anograms of three young girls Carrol was friends with). 
 Then, a year later, I bought a copy of "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland & Through the Looking-Glass" at Barnes & Noble. 
 Literacy at its best. No wonder it's a classic. 
 They're definatley two stories I wouldn't mind reading again.
