 Divergent has been on my radar ever since last year but for some reason I did not pick it up because the feeling of reading any dystopian book depressed me. 
 So what changed my mind? For the past couple of weeks, my fb feed is full of Divergent-related news and I thought to myself, why not give it a try? It is very much hyped about. 
 After reading? Dystopian fiction isn't really my thing. I honest to goodness loved The Hunger Games (book 1), I struggled with Catching Fire and I gave up reading Mockingjay. 
 Why mention the THG trilogy? In almost every review of Divergent that I've read, the comparison between the two always comes up but here is what I am thinking, except for the dystopian thing, I do not find that many similarities between them. 
 Personally, I like THG trilogy more than Divergent but that does not mean that Divergent is not good. 
 It is good yes because for the first time in months, I found myself reading past midnight and after waking up I continued reading the book until I was finished. It was unputdownable in a way and I have to say that I was very curious about the book. 
 Perhaps what I like best about this book is how it kept me at my toes. I was dying to know what Veronica Roth has to offer and how the five factions come about. Still, after finishing the first book, I was left with more questions than answers. I would like to convince myself that it should be good thing (that I would have something to look forward to) but it wasn't. I was looking for something intense and that only came during the last part and even that isn't intense enough for me. 
 The thing is I did not feel any deep attachment with the world and its characters. I have tried but it did not come. Sure I was glued to the story but that was all. I found it hard to like Tris/Beatrice (there were traits of hers that I did not like). As for Four, I did like him. What I did not like is how "easy" it was for Four to show his like for Tris, it would've been better if it wasn't an insta-love kind of thing (but that is just my preference). And somehow the whole world isn't that clear to me yet or rather it is not that believable. Sure I get the gist of their world but what is the greater picture? Or will there be a greater picture? 
 Will I read the next two books? My honest answer? Probably not. But I will watch the movie :)

This book is very far from something that I typically read but I kept coming back to it because a later book in the series was on the bestseller lists and each edition was rated over four stars on average with lots of reviews. 
 I almost put it down because it was a lengthy book with a complicated magic system based on the main colors found on a spectrum and the fantasy sci-fi genre is not my preferred genre. The system of magic is complex and well-thought out but explained almost ad nauseum. I wanted to get past that and move on to the characters and the plot, however, the magic system is its own character and plot foremost. The magic is based on the color spectrum that results when white light is dispersed by a prism. ROYGBIV. The most powerful light-bending magician controls many, if not all, of the colors and is the leader known as The Prism. The pay-off for being the most talented of magicians, a 'superchromat' (like the Prism Gavin Guile himself,) is a limited lifespan that dwindles the more you 'draft'. Break your limit, the 'halo', and you are faced with suicide or the madness of becoming a 'wight' and being hunted down. 
 This first book is set a little over a decade after a war in which two brothers battled for supreme power over the land. The story focuses on five main characters. Gavin, Karris, Kip, Liv and The Prisoner. Gavin Guile is the Prism, the most powerful man in the world. He is high priest and emperor, a man whose power, wit, and charm are all that preserves a tenuous peace following the Prism war. The volatile relationship between The Prism Gavin Guile and Blackguard Karris Whiteoak draws constant sparks; the story gradually unfolds each painful fragment of their history and it seems that only further tragedy can come of it. When Gavin discovers he has a son, born in a far kingdom after the war that put him in power, he must decide how much he's willing to pay to protect a secret that could tear his world apart. The Prism must build a relationship with the illegitimate son he has suddenly inherited, sending Kip to learn about his magical abilities at the renowned school known as the Chromeria. But even that father/son relationship is underlain by dark secrets. Gavin's son, Kip, is awkward and smart-mouthed - and retains his character as 'brat' rather than 'chosen one' in an almost endearing way. From a lifetime spent with his tweaked out mother feeling inadequate and inconvenient, to discovering his father is not only the most powerful man in the land but also handsome, smart and charismatic, is just another injustice to add to the list. Along with Kip is childhood friend Liv, a less-talented drafter whose father was a renowned general that fought against Gavin, and whose sudden compliance to the Prism leads her to doubt everyone and everything that she knows. And just to spice up the mix, there is the mysterious prisoner that Gavin keeps locked away in a secret blue room. The prisoner is losing his humanity and his sanity while devising a long-term plan for escape. 
 The book twists and turns around the secrets and mysteries hidden in the past; hinting at and revealing the betrayals and lies in tantalizing ways while fast-marching through a current war between the Chromeria's and an emerging charismatic leader's crazed magicians. Frequent perspective shifts keep the reader guessing as to who is heretic and who is hero. Once I got past the fantasy parts (the world, abilities, religion and rules) and was able to follow who was who, I found that I did enjoy this tome and would like to read the next one. I put the audiobook version of book two on hold and once I picked it up I discovered that it was distractingly "A Movie in Your Mind." It was no longer a book and instead was highly produced with sound effects, a full cast, musical score and many other features. I'm not sure if I'll listen to it that way, get the book instead, or just put the whole series on the back burner as a result. Only time will tell.

I don't know, maybe it's just me, but I've just never gotten into the whole werewolf paranormal teen book craze. It just wasn't my thing. So I read Raised By Wolves partially because I had nothing else to read, partially it was recommended to me and I liked it. I didn't absolutely adore it, but I got through it. So I was sort of iffy about whether I should even continue the series. A few months later, I'm looking through the shelves in the library and I see Trial by Fire AND Taken by Storm sitting next to each other, side by side. So I just HAD to take them. 
 Once I opened Trial by Fire, and started to read, I just couldn't stop. It was a pretty quick read, and a lot easier to get through than it's previous book. Jennifer Lynn Barnes really stepped it up in this book. The writing was more smooth and the repetitive words in the Pack bond wasn't as annoying. To me, at least. 
 So in this book, Bryn has a dilemma. A major complicated-werewolf-politics-augh-I'm-the-alpha kind of dilemma. Lucas, a werewolf from a different pack is literally dumped on her doorstep. And he's beaten, broken, and bloody. Not to mention that lead of the pack he's from, Shay, really really really wants Bryn's head. Not literally. Well...maybe. He just wants her dead. And he wants his wolf back. But if Bryn sends Lucas back, Lucas is sure to be killed. And if she doesn't send him back, that's basically a declaration of war, so her pack will be killed. Either way, it all ends in blood. 
 Just when things can't seem to get any worse, Shay plays his trump card. He's not the biggest threat to Bryn and the well-being of her pack. A coven is. 
 Now I know what you're thinking. Coven? Vampires and werewolves? Again!? How many more books do I have to read about these two bloodthirsty creatures going head to head. But no, not this time. This time, the coven is made up of...well...let's just say, people who have knacks. Knacks that can kill. And these people (yep, they're human) really really want werewolves dead. 
 Tensions are high and stakes are too. Will Bryn find a way to protect her pack and save Lucas? Will she have to sacrifice him for the greater good? What about these freaky human killing people? And the biggest question of all, will Bryn prove herself worthy of being an Alpha? Dun dun dunnn 
 In this book, there's still the same things that we loved from Raised by Wolves. Bryn's rebellious attitude? Check. Lake and her tendencies to get overexcited when the word weapon is said? Check. And Devon? Check. And more characters are added and we also get to explore the fascinating past of an old character.... 
 So I recommend it to anyone who gave Raised by Wolves a chance, and isn't sure if they should try Trial by Fire. Also I recommend it to anyone who's into the whole paranormal supernatural thing but wants a fresh take on it!

3.5 
 Reader thoughts: Well, it wasn't quite what I was hoping, but it was still fun. I absolutely loved the first 40% of it. 
 Where to start? Curses. I loved the ideas of the two mirror curses. Laidra gets uglier every time she heals someone magically, but she can't help herself. So, she's crone/hag/wart-fully ugly. Her twin, Ellea, gets prettier every time she cruelly breaks someone's heart. Calen is a giant serpent any time anyone looks at him. His twin, Volen, is a giant serpent any time someone isn't looking at him. So fascinating. 
 The royal families hide Laidra and Calen, determining that no one should see them or meet them (except to kill them, eventually). Laidra is ugly enough that people run away screaming. Calen is dangerous in his serpent form and has probably killed people. Then Laidra and Calen meet eat other under the cover of darkness, and, of course, they're both very kind-hearted despite their childhood trials and abusive parents. 
 I loved this. Both are cursed so that no one should look at them, and they spend their days playing music together in the dark. They fall in love without seeing each other. It's great! But then they jump to getting married after knowing each other for only a couple weeks. Granted, they decide this because their lives are in danger, but still. 
 I must be a more callous person than Laidra. At the beginning, first page before I knew about her healing gift, I read about her rushing to help a little bird who had been crushed. I thought she should finish killing the thing to end its misery. No, she healed it. Well, that makes sense. 
 Later, I thought she shouldn't give up her healing ability to save Calen. She could have gone around the two kingdoms, saving people. Surely Calen would be willing to sacrifice his life to help the whole land. Laidra could have saved thousands of lives. She was already healing over a dozen a day! Was one snake's life worth it?  
 problems 
 I had some issues with the book. First, I wanted the book to be more PG-rated. It had sparkles on the cover, and it is a fairytale retelling. The characters are only 16. 
 How shall the curse be broken? True love's kiss? Nope. It's "consummation of a royal marriage." Yep. Get married, have sex once, and the curse will be broken! Then you can get a divorce (and this was contemplated and even discussed). What happened to true love's kiss? Why can't kisses still be magical? 
 Along with that, the bad prince and his bad father (yes, I think of characters as "good" and "bad") spent one scene fondling the same slave girl. Um, ew? Sex slaves are bad enough in the real world. I don't want to meet them in a book. 
 Then we have the way that I didn't feel like the MCs actually solved their own problems. The gods solved their problems. At about 75% of the way into the book, three gods manifest in a castle courtyard to argue over Calen and Laidra and their curses. Their solution? Go on a quest, and we'll help you. 
 It was handled well. I mean, the quest had a purpose (unlike in Ever), but it still felt like an odd shift for the plot. I wanted a book that had people helping each other and solving problems, not just a "well, this curse is impossible for mortals, and we deserve better" approach. I'm still not sure how that convinced the gods to cure them, but whatever. 
 I was disappointed in the end, partly because it was predictable. I knew she'd be asked to give up her healing powers. I also knew someone would make her beautiful, and I hated it when it happened. It's not that I wanted her ugly. I just didn't want her to feel like she couldn't have a happy ending when the character still had warts and scars. 
 What I wanted to happen was for Laidra to try to heal Calen out of his curse. Maybe she has to try so hard that she spends up her healing gift on him (without the help of the gods), and she gets so ugly that she's, like, covered in fur and warts (or scales?). Then I wanted him to have to sacrifice something for her in return (like, something with his snakeskin?) 
 Even better, she heals him to have a human mind in the body of a snake, and she ALSO gains the body of a snake (because she's now so ugly, I guess), and they can both live as snakes togehter. 
 Yeah. Because that sounds like Dragon's Bride, which I liked. And it is also by HLB.  
 After Laidra promises that her serpent won't hurt anyone, she turns around a threatens the captain with him. Could she not come up with a better way to talk to the king? 
 Then there's the idea that mortals deserve a nice life. In the argument between the humans and gods, the humans are upset at the curses. It's that "I don't deserve to die!" argument that is never logical. Everyone deserves to die. It's grace and mercy that lets us live. I just didn't like that scene. 
 Oh, and Calen breaks an entire tree, splintering it into kindling to use as firewood. Eh, what? Is that really better than making Laidra walk around for a few minutes to gather firewood? You just destroyed a tree for no reason! (No, I'm not saying that trees deserve to live more than humans. I'm just thinking Calen could have thought this through and come up with a better solution. Besides, live wood smokes a lot.) 
 Writer thoughts: Something left me unsettled about this book. Why? 
 Mostly, I think it's the literal deus ex machina happening all over the last third of the book. Having gods step in and solve conflicts for the human characters is unsatisfying. I wanted the humans to break the curse on their own. It's like the book changed the rules on me. Instead of being a boy or snake, Calen became a snake only. Then he became a snake with a boy's mind . . . all because the gods interfered.  It felt like cheating.

I finished this book entirely sure that I loved every emotionally manipulative minute of it. And I did, but I'm extremely aware of the parts which I loved, and what was just... okay. So here's what I loved, and why, and what I didn't mind, and why. 
 The main reason was An Imperial Affliction, and Peter Van Houten, and everything that meant for the story. (What follows is probably closer to an English Essay first draft than a review.) 
 I didn't mind that Hazel and Augustus talked in metaphors and ridiculously pompous language, and generally sounded like they'd swallowed a few too many French philosophers. Firstly, I had friends at 14 who talked exactly like that; it's not implausible (perhaps unlikely), and it's talking down to teens to say it is. 
 It's completely okay because of how very self aware the entire thing was. Hazel and Augustus were characters in the book which was written by Peter Van Houten. They were the perfect existential teens faced with mortality, and talking in cigarette metaphors. Hazel deliberately dressed as Anna to appear to Peter. She was his own damn creation *in her own mind*. Hazel over-identified with the character of Anna so much, that's why she needed to know what happened after the book ended. She need to know that her family would be okay. And that is why it was completely acceptable for her to be speaking like the existential ideal of a cancer kid who grew up and took on Peter Van Houten's emotional and philosophical stance. She wanted to be that kid. And so did Augustus. And they wanted to know what happened to their shrapnelled family. (And then we find out that Peter is The Tulip Man, who is a con, and Anna's mom is alone, and the hamster is the only one who survived the fall out of Anna's death because the hamster isn't human. There's an easy answer for the hamster. Because Peter isn't okay, and he is always the father who lost a kid who didn't get to become Anna.)  
 I loved three characters in this: Issac, Peter Van Houten, and the memory of Caroline. 
 Let's start with Caroline. She's nice. Then she's a bitch. She's made into a bitch by cancer. She dies. Everyone pretends to love her memory. Augustus is obligated to stay in a relationship with the dying girl, because she's dying, and because of that the relationship has an end date and so choices don't have to be made.  
 I like that shit happens to cancer kids, to the people around cancer kids, I like that that is not overlooked and romanticised. 
 Which is why I love Issac. 
 He knows the last thing he's going to see, and he loses his eyes, and he loses his girlfriend. And he cares more about losing his girlfriend because CANCER SHIT IS SHIT, and he already knows that, but another human being betraying you hurts more than the inevitable. 
 (Context: I'm in a long term relationship with someone who is registered blind. I still fuck up. I have made terrible blind jokes by accident, and on purpose. She still hates asking for concessions relating to her sight because she was shamed so much over it as a child. I can empathise with Melanie, okay, and I can very much empathise with Issac.) 
 The complications of being in a relationship with someone healthy makes the Hazel/Augustus romance insipid and inevitable and awesome all at once. By being with each other they minimise their grenade victims (yes, I loved that line, obviously). They get their 'happy' ending, even through all the grief and inevitability, and they don't have to think, in the back of their brains, that they're another Caroline, who has a relationship out of guilt and death, and their impact on the world will be tainted. 
 The complicated ones are in the background. Hazel/Augustus was more interesting when Gus was 'well', and Peter said their stars were crossed. The problems with Issac being NEC, but long term disability being harder for Melanie to deal with than illness is awesome to read. Augustus didn't have to dump Caroline, even though his relationship with her was rubbish, because she died. She checked out of life, and he was allowed to vent about what they didn't have. It's an emotionally abusive relationship which works on guilt, and Melanie did the absolute right thing to dump Issac, rather than choose him through guilt, and fuck him up more when she couldn't deal with it.  
 People aren't perfect, and they're allowed to not be able to cope. Yeap, I love that message. 
 I also loved that characters with disabilities and illnesses were allowed to be sexual beings. Disability and sex is a whole thing which isn't talked about, it is weird and strange and somehow not allowed. If you are disabled, that is all you are (Gus's Venn diagram is not an unusual idea in the disability activism world). I fucking loved that there was sex, and it wasn't really fade to black, it didn't fade at 'more than kissed', it went for the awkward and the real. Awesome. 
 Mostly, Peter. Oh, Peter, I love you. 
 Peter was what I was reading this book for. From the opening epigram (that's a cheat, John Green, now I want to read An Imperial Affliction), I wanted to be reading AIA rather than AFioS. 
 I wanted Hazel to be Anna. I wanted to end mid-thought. I wanted everything to be for nothing, with no resolution, no answers, no neatness. And that is Peter. 
 Peter is the aftermath. He is the depression and malaise and destruction that can come of humans who grieve. I love that he said he would change, but probably never would. I love that everyone thought he had potential to do more, and he didn't. He couldn't read the letters. He couldn't be what Hazel and Gus and Lediwij wanted him to be. Because he's the Dutch Tulip Man. He's a fraud, and he doesn't save everything, and he runs off to Amsterdam to hide.  
 And that is why the English Lit grad in me loves this book. Because of the layers of metaphoric talking about itself, and what it's trying to do, and what it would do in an ideal publishing world, and what it fails to do. 
 I still want to read An Imperial Affliction, though. Someone, get on that.

The premise is simple: Teens in a High School get a flu shot that gives them telepathy. Can you imagine? I mean, teens "normally" act as if they know everything, but the characters in this book can hear everyone's thoughts, they indeed know e v e r y t h i n g. 
 They of course find a way to take advantage of their new power. You read about dates, tests, and all the teen secrets, dramas and adventures that are made better because of the mind reading. You also read the fails this new power brings. Some are awkward: hearing parents' libidinous thoughts, finding out someone that works in your school was a stripper, etc. 
 The writing style is for teens. Simple dialogues and vocabulary. There is not one narrator. Actually you don't know who the narrator is, because it is written in the first person plural, as if all the telepathic teens wrote the story at the same time. How that would happen in real life beats me. I can't imagine 23 kids getting together and agreeing on how to tell their story. 
 The end didn't make sense (but then again, does YA make sense?). It makes grown-ups and even the government look dumb. The "problem" apparently had a simple solution. Nothing paranormal or futuristic. And as simple as it may be, it is not believable. Kids will get money and a new shot to fix the "problem". Just like that. And then some kids decide not to get the antidote shot and supposedly live happily ever after with the telepathy.  
 Anyway, this one is for the older teenagers. To some this might sound a bit exaggerated but I have to say it. I don't think it is for young teens as there is some sexual content. The parents are absent in the story and those who come up, are portrayed as distracted, horny parents. There is also a phrase that caught my attention: "They didn't have sex, but they did everything else." I know kids today are having sex and we can't prevent that, but really? I know there are still some innocent naive kids out there. It's hard enough for them to start finding out about their bodies and hormones, surrounded at the same time by sexual content in music and TV. Getting kids to read is a big deal, but please, let's fill their minds with edifying productive ideas. Any naive kid reading this would want to find out what everything else is, and of course try it ASAP. 
 Don't Even Think About it by Sarah Mlynowski is a fast read, for teen girls, I would say 16 years old and up. If you are an adult it is a very simple fast read to pass the time in between big adult-ish books.

This is one of the most riveting non-fiction books I've ever read. I actually carried it around with me everywhere and read it every spare moment. Besides the fascinating medical history, there's a lot of grappling with medical ethics, and the medical ethics of sixty years ago, and how they intersect with race, poverty, and education (or the lack of it). Through all these issues, Skloot maintains a sharp focus on the human side of the story in Henrietta and her family, especially her daughter. In Skloot's hands, all the big issues boil down to a family who is deeply bereft, and then kept in the dark about their loved one's legacy by the medical establishment. I really admire how Skloot opens herself so much to the Lacks family, how deeply she allows herself to empathize and how much she takes their story to heart, while still managing to portray the doctors in a balanced, even sympathetic way.

WTF did I just read? What is this steaming pile of cat shit? 
 This book is the WORST world building I've ever encountered. It's so bafflingly bad that I'm stunned and speechless. Did the author even attempt to consider the implications of ANYTHING? It took me thirty seconds to see the huge and OMG plot holes in this world building. 
 I'll give you the first example that came to my mind (because it's basically the whole book and that would take too long.) 
 We have here a 'pride' of cats. There are two ways that one is 'made' into a werecat. You're either born into it or are scratched and survived. Right out of the gate we encounter the first big-fucking-plot hole. Female werecats are *only* born, not made, and they are incredibly rare. The author states, for example, that there are only eight unmated werecats females in north America before all this started. They are then wed to unmated male cats destined to be the alpha's and their one goal in life is to have a girl. 
 Are you seeing the problem? No? How about this: prides consist almost entirely of born werecats. She has three or four brothers and their territory is spread over several states. How is this possible? If prides consist of born males, how is it possible to have a pride larger than ten or twenty at the most? How have they not devolved into incest and horrific genetic problems thereby? 
 The 'scratched' werecats are called strays and are (for the most part) considered to be terrible, terrible people (for some reason.) She never actually explains why this is so it's basically just a stupid plot devise. One of those 'just add water' things. Wam! Bam! Insta-supa' villains praying on innocent, virginal girls!

Imagine being handed a single book and being told this is the only book you can read. Now read it. Over and over and over again. 
 That is this book in the nutshell. The book starts with the birth of the main character. Then she dies. That's not so much a spoiler, it's pretty much the plot. She dies and the story zips back to her birth and re-tells itself again from that beginning till the next time she dies. Each time she is born she lives a bit longer and dies a bit differently. I got about half way through this before I just couldn't stand to go through the whole shebang again.

I think I'm the last person in the world who hasn't seen or read The Fault in Our Stars, mainly because, IMO, young adult so rarely gets the "adult" part right. It's as if many writers have forgotten how we really acted when we were teenagers. We certainly weren't the self-righteous and upstanding citizens of either The Hunger Games or Divergent. We were just...younger people, with all of our normal faults and foibles. 
 Luckily, John Green writes about real people. Teenagers who are looking to claim their own identity against the context of what really mattered to all of us - our peer group. School was just the background for what was really going on in our complex social interactions, as the kids in Looking for Alaska show us. 
 The pranks in this book were laugh out loud funny, the tragedy enough to make me cry, but it is the simple and honest prose that rings out through the pages of this book that will stay with you for a long time. 
 The back of the book compares this to Catcher in the Rye, but that comparison bothers me because Holden was always a little shit. Pudge is our everyman (or woman). We all remember that first intense crush, that longing to be part of the "in" group (unless you were in the "in" group, in which case you are probably not on Goodreads...) and the way friendship distorted out perceptions of events and even morality. 
 In the end, there are no easy answers to Pudge's questions, despite the neat summary that Pudge writes in the last pages. But it is here that we see the genius of this book shine through - showing us that beautiful hope that is present in all of humanity (but perhaps especially in the young): 
 "Those awful things are survivable, because we are as indestructible as we believe ourselves to be. When adults say "teenagers think they are invincible" with that sly, stupid smile on their faces, they don't know how right they are. We need never be hopeless, because we can never be irreparably broken. We think that we are invincible because we are."

What can one say about Brave New World that hasn't been said? This is one of those timeless pieces of literature that still has significant relevance and thus has earned its status as a must read. 
 This isn't the first time I've read Huxley's classic, but it is the first time I've read it in over a decade and once again I am in awe. 
 The premise of the book involves a futuristic, Utopian society where, through a combination of careful genetic engineering and rigorous social conditioning, social stability has finally been achieved and a perpetual state of hedonistic bliss is only one dose of soma away. Then in walks John, a savage from uncivilized society, who feels true happiness can't be real if it doesn't cost something or if it comes too easy. 
 Perhaps the most poignant scene occurs near the end of the book when John and Mustapha Mond, the Controller, discuss the merits of this brave new world. 
 Mond explains to the Savage why his view of what constitutes happiness is skewed. 
 Actual happiness always looks pretty squalid in comparison with the over-compensations for misery. And, of course, stability isn't nearly so spectacular as instability. And being contented has none of the glamour of a good fight against misfortune, none of the picturesqueness of struggle with temptation, or a fatal overthrow by passion or doubt. Happiness is never grand. 
 Mond discusses the merits of religion and why the God of the Savage's world is not necessary in their world. 
 You remind me of another of those old fellows called Bradley. He defined philosophy as the finding of bad reason for what one believes by instinct. As if one believed anything by instinct! One believes things because one has been conditioned to believe them. Finding bad reasons for what one believes for other bad reasons - that's philosophy. People believe in God because they've been conditioned to believe in God. 
 John's response. 
 "But I [John] don't want comfort. I want God, I want poetry, I want real danger, I want freedom, I want goodness, I want sin." 
 "In fact," said Mustapha Mond, "you're claiming the right to be unhappy." 
 If you haven't, read the book. If you have, read it again.

 If this were a non-fiction book, it probably would have a tag phrase like: love through the eyes of an asexual person. 
 What is asexuality? 
 That's the main issue the book tackles and I love it. We Awaken seamlessly manages to integrate the answers to that question without it being too awkward or dreary. Also, the main characters being asexual gives rise to a bunch of cute moments and there is so much fluff that I just can't help but smile. Now this is the kind of romance I enjoy reading about. No need for a two page kiss scene, give me a whole chapter of them hugging each other in their pillow fort and watching Singing In The Rain instead. 
 Truth be told, I was thinking of dropping the novel somewhere around 20%. Romance was never my favourite genre and Victoria and Ashlinn's rushed relationship kinda put me off. It felt much like an insta-love. But something made me keep reading, and that something was the writing (that and also I wanted to find out how a relationship like Victoria and Ashlinn's would pan out). The writing is beautiful, in the sense that it's neither too simplistic, nor too flowery. It made it really fun to read from Victoria's perspective. 
 However, I felt that the novel could be so much more in terms of the building of the dream world. Why are there only two people controlling dreams? How does Ashlinn create dreams for others while still being able to remain in Victoria's dreams? Does she like create multiple copie of herself? If other people are able to take over her job, then can't other people work alongside with her??  
 In the blurb, it says "or all of humanity will pay the price". Kinda sounds a bit apocalyptic doesn't it? But the way it was resolved was a bit anti-climactic and does not live up to this phrase at all. It was basically "hey let's meet up and let's just work out a compromise in a diplomatic manner".  
 Overall, I am impressed by We Awaken. I picked it up as I thought that I should try reading some books from the LGTBQ genre and it did not disappoint. I'm glad that the author decided to choose to feature asexuality, something that is not commonly seen of in fiction books.

This book sucked me in right from the beginning. The rhyme at the beginning of the first chapter sets up everything perfectly. 
 Don't trust the fire, for it will burn you. 
 Don't trust the ice, for it will freeze you. 
 Don't trust the water, for it will drown you. 
 Don't trust the air, for it will choke you. 
 Don't trust the earth, for it will bury you. 
 Don't trust the trees, for they will rip you, 
 rend you, tear you, kill you dead. 
 It's a child's chant. Children chant it while skipping rope. When you trip on the rope, that's the spirit that will one day kill you. And that is how the story starts. With a six year old Daleina sneaking out of her house (which is in a tree - all the houses are, whole villages are built on branches of trees - how cool is that?!) to take part in the tradition of the jumping rope to the chant. Against her parents' permission. 
 By the end of the first chapter, the spirits have attacked Daleina's village, killing nearly everyone apart from Daleina and her family after she manages to save them. Up until this point she has not shown an affinity for controlling spirits. This attack and the horrible realisation that if she'd known about her abilities earlier she could have saved the village and it's villagers leads to Daleina deciding to go to the academy to train so that she could one day be queen and to prevent anything like this happening ever again. To protect her people. 
 There are so many things I loved about this book. I really rooted for the characters. Daleina isn't a typical main character for a YA Fantasy. She isn't perfect. She isn't amazing. She isn't the strongest. She isn't naturally gifted. She hasn't got 549367398 guys running after her and a romance that takes all the attention away from the plot. She gets to where she is by lots of hard work, never giving up and some help from her friends. She gets to where she is by acknowledging her weaknesses and working around them, coming up with different ways to get stuff done. I love that she has lots of friends who are girls. They support each other. They're happy for each other when they are successful. There might be a little bit of jealousy and bad feelings but these feelings aren't something they dwell on and let poison their friendships. Okay, they might not always be 100% nice to each other but I don't think any decision is made spitefully. 
 There is a little bit of romance but it never takes over the plot. And it's not with the other main character, Ven the disgraced champion. Ven is more of a father figure to Daleina. I like their relationship. 
 I like that being the queen isn't something you can inherit. You have to train. You have to become a candidate. Then you have to pass trials to become an heir. There must always be a queen. The only thing stopping the spirits from going wild and killing and destroying everyone and everything. Only the queen has the power to control every spirit, this is a power that is given to her at her coronation by the spirits themselves. It's complicated. The spirits both hate and need humans and humans both hate and need the spirits. 
 I never quite knew what was going to happen and the ending... wow. Was not expecting it. I don't want to ruin it but wow. I actually think it was kind of perfect? I can't wait to see what happens in the next book.

I ended up disappointed. Jack started off really nice and didn't get scared off by Millie, Grace's younger sister who happens to have Downs Syndrome, like so many previous boyfriends had been. I never bought him as a nice guy, he always came off creepy to me although that could be because I knew he was going to be an arsehole and then BAM day of/day after their wedding he just becomes completely evil. If you're shocked by my rating, so am I. Let's chalk this up to the fact that I've been in the weirdest reading funk lately where I'm disappointed with everything. *cries*

 What I liked: 
 -Chapter 2. 
 -Chapters 7-9. 
 -The first paragraph of page 450. 
 What I didn't like: 
 -Endless war strategy. Look, obviously this series has always been about a war, but reading copious amounts of war strategy was tedious, boring, and slowly paced. 
 -Choppy battle scenes. Just about every other chapter is Arin riding (or sailing) off to some different battle. These would break up the pace of anything else going on. Toward the end of the book it got worse because... 
 -Too many paragraph breaks. The narrative is 3rd person, but it follows Arin and Kestrel separately. Even when they are in the same room, many scenes had ENDLESS paragraph breaks to switch between their POVs. As many as 5 breaks on a single page. The climax of the book suffered from this greatly when Kestrel and Arin were in different places. The narrative constantly switched back and forth between them, which held the reader at arm's length and prevented me from ever getting into what was happening. 
 -Anticlimactic. Didn't we always know these things would happen? Despite the cliffhanger endings the first 2 books threw at us, I've always felt that Rutkoski too quickly erases her plot twists. The stakes didn't feel very high to me.

 Margot being "dethroned" as mom in the Covey household was awkward as hell. I mean... I get it. I really do. Margot obviously felt like she got shafted with Mrs Rothschild stepping in, but come on GoGo, must you have acted like a spoiled two year old who didn't get the last fudgesicle??? 
 Lara Jean drunk at the bachelorette party was pure gold. I'm such a lightweight when it comes to alcohol, it was like reading about myself and how happy I am after one drink. 
 My annual ode to Kitty. She has really grown up, and I love that she doesn't let Lara Jean push her into a what she thinks Kitty should be. I adore her passion to be her own Song girl. She doesn't go for the fluffy bridesmaid's dress, yet she still kills at doing hair. I love that Jenny Han makes each Song girl so individual and a powerful woman/girl in their own right. 
 Okay, Peter. Good lord. I just want to wrap him up in a sleeping bag, and give him chocolate chip cookies to keep him safe from his douchey dad and his meddling mother. I raged so hard when his dad stood him up at graduation. I screamed harder when his mother gave Lara Jean the "talk". Woman needs to mind her own business. Peter is kind, important, smart, and loving. You can see that in how he treats not only Lara Jean, but her entire family. 
 I am so happy that Dan aka Dad found himself a partner in crime in Mrs Rothschild.

I've really come to love dark erotica and this is definitively worth a read. While I like comfort food slightly better, this was still amazing. Can't wait to read the second book and get on with the story (yay twice the length!!).

Too many crazy escapes. Too many crazy coincidences. Just too crazy to be as charming as the previous books. And I must say, when it comes to Jacky Faber, my crazy tolerance is pretty high. Higgins continues to be my second favorite character because he's the most reasonable character in Meyer's world of insanity. 
 What keeps me coming back to this series is the amazing audiobook narration. Katherine Kellgren sings and does a million voices and just makes it all so enjoyable. Bless you, Ms. Kellgren. 
 So now I'll complain a little via spoilers: I actually felt really angry at the author when Jaimy finally caught up to Jacky and she was naked in the arms of another man. That was just too terrible. I was so relieved that he took her back at the end of the book! I was also baffled when she got picked up by the tornado and carried off her boat. Do people really survive that kind of thing?

Wow - what an emotional rollercoaster ride! 
 The O'Briens are a happy and close-knit Irish-American family of six all living under one roof of an old triple-decker at the "Bottom of the Hill" in Charlestown. At 44, Joe O'Brien, patriarch and head of the family next to his devout Catholic wife Rosie, is enjoying the fruits of his labours after spending 25 years as a cop on the Boston Police Force and raising four healthy children into adulthood. He is thinking that after another ten years of working the job he loves he may be able to retire with a good pension and spend his autumn years watching his grandchildren grow up and having some quality time with his wife and family uninterrupted by the constant demands of his job. His plans are cruelly interrupted though when he starts developing some strange neurological symptoms - muscular twitches and temper outbursts he cannot control and can no longer ignore. 
 After Rosie forces him to seek medical help and have some tests done, the doctor delivers devastating news: Joe has Huntington's Disease, an neurodegenerative disease passed down from his mother who died when Joe was only a child. There is no cure, only temporary control of symptoms, and sufferers face a cruel fate as they progressively lose all muscle coordination. Instead of retirement, Joe may be facing a cruel death in ten years' time after having lost total control over all his bodily functions. But worst of all: there is a 50% chance for each of Joe's children to have inherited the disease. A simple blood test is all that is required to show whether Katie, Meghan, Patrick or JJ also carry the gene mutation causing Huntington's. But is it better to know and be prepared or live life in the moment not knowing what cruel fate awaits? 
 I have read all of Lisa Genova's novels, but Inside the O'Briens was definitely the one that touched me most - once I started reading I couldn't stop! Genova's neuroscientist background is obvious from the in-depth knowledge of the disease and its effect not only on sufferers but also on their immediate family, friends and neighbours. The reader watches in horror as the tight-knit O'Brien family slowly implodes and everyone faces their worst demons - their own mortality and that of the people closest to them. As Joe struggles to come to term with his own mortality and guilt about potentially having passed on a cruel deadly illness to his children, his wife Rosie is struggling with her faith, which in the past has given her strength and hope. Each of their children also face a horrible choice - would they prefer to know their fate or live life not knowing? There is anger, guilt, fear and despair, and each member of the O'Brien family deals with it in a different way. 
 Inside the O'Briens is written from the perspectives of Joe and his 21-year old daughter Katie, which gave a wonderful insight into family dynamics whilst not overdoing the psychological aspect of the story (as may have happened had Genova given each family member a voice). I really felt for Katie as she is struggling to make decisions regarding her future. How will not knowing if she is a carrier affect her? Will she be paranoid that each trip, each stumble or slip is a sign of Huntington's? But would going through genetic testing be any better? Would knowing she had the disease stop her from having a relationship, planning a family, embarking on a career? As a yoga teacher Katie tries very hard to live in the moment and look after her health. But she knows that if she is gene-positive for Huntington's, there is nothing she can do to make any difference - her fate is in her genes, it would just be a matter of time for the symptoms to manifest themselves. 
 There are so many impossible and heart-breaking choices in this book that it was difficult to fully comprehend the depths of despair a sufferer must face. And yet Genova manages to explore the topic with the family's sense of hope, humour and love and support for each other. All the characters feel real and genuine, and it is impossible not to feel for them. Genova offers explanations of different aspects of the disease, reflecting the way in which Joe and his family find out the details themselves - the preview copy contained some textbook-type explanations (which may or may not be in the final edition of the book) which provided some background information on this cruel disease. Despite the serious topic, the overall feeling after reading it was positive, engendering a deep and instant gratitude for the health we take for granted. As a mother, I did not even want to imagine some of the horrible choices and devastating emotions experienced by the parents and would-be parents in this novel. 
 Inside the O'Briens is a complex and layered story of the emotional effects of a cruel genetic disease on a family, which cannot be done justice in a review, so I will leave it at that. I think that Genova has done an outstanding job exploring this topic. Very highly recommended. Definitely a novel to go on my favourites list and one whose ethical dilemmas will stay on my mind for some time to come. 
 Thank you to Netgalley and the publisher for providing me with a free electronic copy of this novel in exchange for an honest review.

At first I flicked between thinking the author was on something while writing, and thinking this was one of the greatest things I have read of late. By the time I was about a third of the way through the book I was leaning heavily towards the latter. 
 I am not a Londoner, I enjoy my fields, trees and wildlife (other than rats and pigeons), but I was instantly transported to a London, but not as I would know it even if I did dwell. I thoroughly enjoyed the witty characters and funny scenes. At times though I did feel it suffered slightly from talking head syndrome, when who was speaking was not readily apparent, this caused me to read a few passages incorrectly

I have absolutely no doubt that I would have enjoyed this novel more if it was in fact a graphic novel. It wanted to be a comic so bad, I kept waiting to turn the pages and find an illustration. 
 Still though, I liked it. It was different. Instead of being your average superhero tale, it was focused on supervillains. Men and women that have inexplicable powers linked only to a light in the sky known as Calamity. What the world knows is this - Calamity appeared, the Epics followed. 
 Our hero is an eighteen year old boy named David. He was there at the beginning of the end ten years ago and witnessed the most powerful Epic of all - Steelheart kill his father in front of him and take his bellowed town. With his child's eyes he saw and remembered everything. He remembers his father shooting a gun and the bullet that grazed Steelheart's face. The only time anybody ever made him bleed. 
 Our hero is an unremarkable boy with remarkable skills. Teaming up with the only group of people ever to stand up to the Epics, he sets his plan in motion to discover what exactly is the one fault in the indestructible enemy that rules their world. Find it, and use it against him to finally avenge his father. 
 See what I mean? It's begging to be a graphic novel, or a movie even. (Not a TV series because they manage to fuck everything up royally when it comes to something good - Marvel's Agents of SHIELD??? I rest my case.) 
 Although the plot was entertaining enough, it had some drawbacks and problems on it's way. Like most of superhero films, outlandish shit just kept happening that continued to save them in the nick of time. The convo between the characters was flowing nicely, funny at times. Everything to keep you engaged.

Calling Invisible Women by Jeanne Ray is a unique novel that speaks for fulltime-taken-for-granted mothers who are all day doing household works and taking care of kids. It might sound really lame at first, but the twist is that, in the new millennium, majority of mothers are figuratively experiencing "invisibility" at home. For instance, (excerpt from the book) The boys can be looking at naked women on the internet and they don't so much as twitch when I walk into the room. I can ask Steve (her son) what time he wants dinner, and he keeps on texting like I wasn't even there. As you can see (read), some mothers are taken for granted, they do so many things for us, for the family, and they don't get something in return, including respect and mutuality. As for me, they deserve a lot of respect & a share of expressive love and care -- heck, they deserve a lot more. 
 The story started with Clover suddenly disappearing physically inside her home and then at some time she discovers that there are others like her, women of a certain age who seem to have disappeared as well. As she uses her invisibility to get to know her family and her town better, Clover leads the way in helping invisible women become recognized and appreciated no matter what their role is (goodreads summary). 
 This novel is hilariously written and emotionally stimulating! Perfect for a one-sit, one-time read!
The scariest book I ever read.

Fun Home does that, but it's also humorous, beautifully drawn and has a lot of charm, too. I know, I know; this sounds just like a book jacket blurb... Straight truth though.

Wow, I don't even know where to begin with this mess. I guess you could say that Kristin is going through a difficult and confusing time. She finds out that she is intersex which throws her for a loop considering how heteronormative her environment is. On one hand, I do sympathize with her but one the other hand it's challenging when the protagonist is selfish, a bigot, and immature. 
 There's the initial shock when she finds out about her diagnosis. Her doctors were nonjudgemental, informative, and encouraged her to talk about this before making rash decisions. Her father doesn't shun her and all in all was pretty freaking perfect in reacting to this. He researched to better understand about his daughter, yet Kristan can't even reach out to talk to others who are also intersex. It's all "woe is me, I'm the only one whose suffering (really?) from this). I get that not everyone handles adversity like a champ. But it was so offensive when she shit talked about the same women trying to help her. Saying that they weren't real women and neither was she. And you know what? I don't even know where this is coming from. Why is she the biggest fucking moron on the planet? 
 Anyways, there's this dumb conflict where she accuses her friend of letting everyone know about her secret. I get it, I really do. It's not people's business if it isn't. She should have had time to tell people on her own time. But you know what. This book is a joke on all fronts. The characters read as fucking 12 year olds in the way they speak and act. The way that the conflict was resolved was also a huge fucking joke. It's the worst when authors use the "misunderstanding trope" to move a plot along. It was unnecessary and pulled the more important part of the story down. 
 Finally, the issue with the love interest was once again pathetic. She gets herself into a sexual assault situation. Now what I mean by that is she follows a guy out and he recognizes that she's the intersex girl from rumors. He gets upset and demands to see her penis. Obviously she doesn't have one and he proceeds to rip her clothes. This is the time to yell for help but she doesn't. Darren comes out and sees her and offers her a chance to ask for help and guess what she says. "Oh, we're fine Darren. We just need to talk." WTF, you are about to be raped, killed, or both. This is how your bravery manifests?  She is a fucking moron and this scene was a sad excuse to bring Kristan together with Darren. 
 How can a book which preaches about supposed acceptance and understanding follow the very conventions that reenforces detrimental stereotypes.

This was a really interesting book. When it starts out, you really have no idea what's going on. You are kind of thrown into the middle of something horrible and have to discover the details. Em has been locked up in a cell for months. She is repeatedly tortured for information she refuses to give up. Her one consolation is the limited contact she has with the boy in the cell next to her. They cannot see or touch, but they can converse through the wall they share. When a chance arises for the two to escape, they take it. Armed only with a note stating, "You have to kill him," Em and Finn travel back in time to try to change the future. This is their 15th trip back. All 14 previous trips have failed. Each time they have tried something different, and it finally comes down to taking out the one person they have avoided harming in the past, their best friend. Can they do what needs to be done? I liked how the story used science/physics instead of magic as a time travel agent. I also liked that I didn't have a hard time understanding it.  The only confusing part to me was the timeline change, perhaps paradox, at the end. I don't understand how Finn and Nate are alive when James is dead and can't make Cassandra to send anyone back to save them one more time. As I understood it, the timeline where the young Marina was the only survivor should have been the last timeline. Are we meant to believe that somehow Cassandra still was built and it took one more trip back to make it right? Don't get me wrong, I love that the good guys all lived and all was wrapped up nice and clean. Finn was my favorite character and I love that he survived to win Marina again. .

 Spirit is a book which is totally satisfying, yet it leaves you feeling confused and wanting for the next book soon.

 You can't expect someone to face what he faces and not end up being how he is. I get it. 
 Hunter Garrity is not sure where his loyalties lie. He was bought up with the sayings like "Use them before they use you", after all! Calla Dean and cronies want an all-out war, by brings the Guides to town. As if all the fires which happened in Spark were not enough, Calla sets a Carnival on fire, and is planning for something more disastrous. 
 Meanwhile, a Guide- Silver and his accomplice Kate are really in town- their mission: to destroy all the Merricks and other Pure Elementals in town. Hunter also has a lot of problems at home, which results in him being thrown out oh the house. He ends up sleeping in his car, until the Merricks help him into their house. Hunter is sure they don't trust him. He doesn't know whether to trust them or not. He is not at all sure if all their actions are out of kindness or just to keep their enemy-him close. Added to this the problem of Kate. He doesn't trust her; He believes that Kate is using him. In the end, he also ends up in total disarray about his feelings for his father and mother-especially after some revelations. 
 Hunter seems to have a whirlwind relationship with Kate-first mistrust, then confusion, anger, followed by a little bit of trust and then to something he doesn't even know what.[ I'm really sorry for Hunter. Why is it that all the girls he likes somehow end up not lasting?]  
 This book contains some action, as usual, but also focuses on the emotion aspect. The confusion, loneliness and mistrust aspects are very well written- Bravo Ms. Kemmerer, for a well-written book! 
 I'm really looking forward to the next book.

Endure. Outlast. Outwait. Three little words that have gradually come to be emblematic of the Animorphs' struggle over the past 40-some books as their guerrilla war against the Yeerk invasion drags on. The Animorphs are increasingly fighting not to foil the Yeerks' plans but just to break even, to maintain, hold on by the skin of their teeth. And even then they're slipping. 
 Like Megamorphs 3, this is an alternate timeline book; but where the 3rd installment focused on altered versions of famous battles and other broad historical events, Back to Before alters the personal timeline of the Animorphs themselves. The story opens from Jake's point of view, in the aftermath of a horrific battle. He is already emotionally stretched to his breaking point when the Drode, Crayak's wonderfully slimy emissary, appears to offer him a deal: what if the Animorphs could get a do over? What if they never walked through the abandoned construction site that night? 
 Jake accepts the deal, and he, Marco, Rachel, Cassie, and Tobias go back to their ordinary, pre-Animorph lives. No morphing powers. No responsibility. There's just one small problem: the Yeerk invasion is still happening. 
 Back to Before is the ultimate "what-if" scenario of the series, an absolutely unflinching exercise in taking the Animorphs' hopeless situation, the power and responsibility they've grown to hate, and showing how ignorance to the danger is still a worse alternative. 
 Speaking of alternatives, I've had to restrain myself from spending most of this review on Tobias' alternate timeline, because his story just broke me. I've rarely wanted to rescue a fictional character from their situation as much as I did while reading his. Tobias' inculcation into The Sharing is chilling and plausible: he's exactly the kind of vulnerable kid this organization was DESIGNED to prey on, with zero support and love at home and a bully magnet at school. Even as I relived just how bad his life was before becoming an Animorph, I still hoped he would magically make a different choice than on my last reread. You can see his downfall on the horizon and it is heartbreaking : 
 Odret said to me. 
 To say that I hated myself would be an understatement. Odret had rifled through my memories, each one more embarrassing than the one before. I'd had to relive too many things I had tried to forget. 
 Most painful of all was the image of myself swallowing everything The Sharing told me. I had walked, willingly, to my own destruction. At the time I'd seen no alternative. Now I saw nothing but alternatives. 
 Was my home a dreary, awful place? Yes. Was I somehow marked as a bully magnet? Yes. Was I different, strange, not-quite-normal? Yes. 
 And to fight all of that I had destroyed myself. Brilliant, Tobias. Brilliant. All of life's pains combined could not have equaled what I now endured. 
 Even now no easy answers leaped to mind. I could not easily have stood the bullying. I could not easily have survived the loneliness. In my fantasies I could construct fantastic escapes, but in reality there was no easy way. My life was nonfiction, not some story where the endings are always happy. I couldn't simply become a different person. I couldn't just have some great insight that would save me from myself. 
 All I could have done, really, was wait. I could have endured. I saw that now. It wasn't a dramatic answer. Wasn't exactly inspiring. 
 Endure. Outlast. Outwait. 
 I might have been able to do that. I'm not a fool, I know that school was just a part of my life. You spend eighteen years as a kid, then maybe seventy years as an adult. And what you are as a kid isn't what you'll be as an adult, not always, anyway. 
 Endure. I could have done that. 
 Now, too late. My nose itched. I could not scratch it. 
 TOBIAS. :(((((( 
 We're not being infiltrated by aliens (as far as I know), but bullying and broken homes and feeling awkward and different are all real things. And feeling like your life is an unending circle of torment is still an all too common experience for teens. I just can't get over how important it is for teen readers to internalize the message that whatever's happening to them right now, things will get better, and to hold on to that. It's not dramatic, it's not profound, but it's so so important for kids who feel like the only solution to their suffering is to join a gang, or commit suicide, or bring a gun to school.  
 I want to take a moment to discuss the cover: it's haunting, a black and white portrait of the five human Animorphs (Ax is notably missing) standing on a black substrate riven with cracks suggesting the broken pavement of the war zone their suburban home becomes at the climax of the book. The grayscale tones suggest a photo negative, visually reflecting the dark alternate timeline of the narrative's events. Superimposed over the five teens is the ghostly image of a red-tailed hawk, in a symbolic inversion of Tobias' typical representation in which his human image is subordinated to the hawk body that is now his true form. 
 Quite simply, Back to Before is a masterpiece, one of the best installments of the series. Definitely not recommended for new readers, since so many of the details and developments are so much richer and more significant for readers acquainted with the 40+ books of material that precede it. But for fans who've hung in this long, it offers a darkly tantalizing vision of what could have been.  In the end, KA refuses to give us any hard answers about which timeline is actually worse: is it better to end the war quickly even though all the Animorphs and millions of humans die? Or is their drawn-out campaign in the true timeline preferable for minimizing loss of life, even as it slowly breaks the kids down?

I've watched the movie a couple of years back and was surprised by how much I liked it. The book is superior in many ways -though the movie is pretty good as well. There is something raw and wild about this novel. I'm not certain if I completely liked the writing style but it was certainly interesting. There are some powerful passages and Melinda is a character you can sympathize with. It deals with a huge, important, difficult issue -rape- and it does so thoughtfully and with great care and respect. The symbolisms worked and the writing felt like that of a teenage girl. Overall, a good book if you're in for some serious YA fiction.

Even though the book is a script, it reads like a novel. A very engaging and fun story even though Harry is kind of a sullen jerk. Lots of possibilities as to where the story might go and it did not disappoint.

I didn't like this book as much as I thought I would. I don't get what's so great about Bev. She's not even really cool, like Alaska or Margo Roth Spiegelman, or her friend Meg, from this same book. I did like that the band wasn't any good though. You never read novels about teen bands that, you know, kind of suck.

5 heart wrenching beautiful stars 
 I wanted to do a video review but I don't think I could talk about this book without bursting into tears. It Ends with Us hit me so hard on a personal emotional level. This is the hardest book I have ever had to read. I listened to the audiobook, which eased my pain in a way but it still hurt. Not only was this book beautifully written and heartbreaking it is one of the most important books I have ever read. I think everyone should read this. It deals with some really sensitive topics, it should come with a trigger warning but that would spoil the book too much. It ends with us quickly became one of my favorite books of all time. 
  Part of why this hit me so hard and was so difficult to read is because sadly I too have been in an abusive relationship. While he never hit me and I got out of it, the scars he left on my heart will never fade. This book brought back all the trauma, pain and emotions of that situation. I could relate to Lily so much it hurt how much. How thin the line is between love and hate, how no matter how much he hurt you, you were still madly in love with him. When you love someone more than anything who only hurts you, you hate them too. You hate them for hurting you when all you do is love them. But even when you hate them that hate is veiled in love. You never think of leaving them, your heart is filled with love for them. Oftentimes they convince you it's your fault they hurt you. If you had just tried a little harder to not anger him maybe he wouldn't have hurt you. The thoughts Lily had were similar to mine during that time, they were so hard to read. I never really liked Ryle I enjoyed the diary entries and her past with Atlas so much more. I shipped her and atlas together so hard right from the beginning. Despite her growing relationship with Ryle I wanted her to end up with Atlas. Part of me thinks I didn't like Ryle because subconsciously, due to personal experiences, I picked up on all the abusive red flags. Even in their first meeting he was overly violent towards a chair. That to me was already a red flag. Despite all of this when he first pushed her I was just as shocked as Lily. I was about to rewind the audiobook because I thought I had heard wrong. When Atlas came back I was so happy! I wanted them to be together. Allysa and Lily were so cute! I ABSOULTELTY LOVED THEIR RELATIONSHIP! It's sad that someone so sweet could come from the same family as Ryle. This book wasn't all heartache. The moments with Allysa, the diary entries, and a few moments with Ryle were happy. Another book that I read for my young adult literature class. I have to admit, I didn't have high expectations for this, because most of the other books that I've read for this class have fallen short of my expectations. But this book was WONDERFUL. It sucked me in from the very beginning and I couldn't put it down - so thankfully, I read it while I was at the beach and I actually had time to read non-stop, haha. 
 This book takes place in a fantasy world, with humans and dragons (who can take human form) at the forefront, but the world bears many similarities to medieval history, so it's very easy to adapt to as a reader. The world is easily understood and what isn't immediately understood is explained soon enough, and done so smoothly, without deviating from the story. 
 The characters are so wonderfully crafted, each with the perfect medley of character flaws and strengths. Sometimes, the narrator's decisions could be frustrating, but even when she made decisions that I disagreed with, her reasoning was so solid that I couldn't get mad at her. I liked each character so much that I couldn't get mad at them, even when I wanted to be. 
 The story had the perfect amount of mystery and adventure, tragedy and romance, magic and reality. It even had political undertones, but wasn't so overbearing with them as to distract from the story. This is truly the first young adult novel that I've read in a long time - especially from the fantasy genre - that I want to thrust upon every reader that I know. If you're thinking about reading this book, don't think about it any longer - just pick it up and read! I highly, highly recommend this book. It fully deserves all five stars.

I know I'm generous with my ratings, but this might genuinely be one of the most enjoyable books I've read. 
 1. If you want to get into Greek literature for the first time, I think this is a great place to start. Miller uses an easy, common language, yet, somehow she manages to capture the ancient and poetic feel of the era she is writing about. The story has a modern angle, focusing mainly on the romance between Achilles and Patroclus, including a lot of personal thoughts from Patroclus, unlike older books where the authors tend to not describe the emotions of their characters as much. I find it easier to form a bond with characters in the former type of book. Yet you do get a pretty good overview over the historic event that is the life of Achilles. 
 2. It is romantic, poetic and beautifully heart-wrenching. 
 3. If you are already familiar with The Iliad, I understand that this book might annoy you, as it is an adaption and doesn't include all the elements of the original work. Keep that in mind. 
 4. If you're not, and if you like beautiful stories and Ancient Greece, you cannot miss this book.

I bought this book because it was featured on Wonkomance and because of the blurb. I didn't even read Kent's interview. A heroine who pays the hero to take her virginity and a book that's recommended by Wonkomance for any reason is an automatic buy for me. 
 And it was really good book. I enjoyed the heroine's motivations and I LOVED the interaction between the hero and heroine at the beginning. I especially loved how the intimate scenes ARE the progression of their relationship. (In romance, the intimate scenes show progression. But in Escorted, they're THE progression. That's awesome.) 
 I also liked how the surrounding details weren't there--and if this book was traditionally published they more than likely would've been added in. We know the city, but the setting isn't overly described. Thank goodness cause I didn't care about what the city looked like. 
 Much of the first part of the book takes place in a hotel room. Thank goodness. Who cares about the rest? 
 The heroine's friend served very little purpose, except to keep uttering the phrase "Pretty Woman," and while a publisher might have rounded that out... That's all the friend needed to do. She transmitted some info we needed to know and then the attention was put back on the couple. 
 It's written in third person Heroine view only. Not bad. I would've liked to know more about the Hero and while the questions at the end helped give us details, I wish that had been rounded out a bit better. 
 I also wished Ander's arc would've been a bit more consistent. Things got a bit shaky after dinner at Hero's local/favorite restaurant. But they were fixed pretty quickly once the "grey" moment was over. 
 Another plus, this book has a grey, not black, moment. 
 In the end we have a self-published book that Kent admits to selling on Amazon in haste. She didn't spend much time editing because she thought no one would read it. So the little complaints--and they are teeny, tiny, tiny things--don't matter, because Escorted is Kent's draft for all intensive purposes. 
 Holy heck the world is blessed with an author who can create this story without help from editors and publishing houses. 
 It's a really good book and Kent has a GREAT idea. 
 Throw up some more of your outside-of-the-box manuscripts, Kent. I'd love to read them.

Just... wow. 
 This book was everything a sequel of City of Stairs could have possibly hoped to be. We met General Mulaghesh in book one as the cussing, brass to the bones leader. And here she becomes our main character after she is unwillingly pulled out of retirement and dumped into cold, godforsaken Voortyashtan to uncover a mystery about some potentially Divine dust. But... is it really that god forsaken? 
 I am always a little skeptical about book 2 in a series because the newness of the world has worn off, the characters have already been shown off, and now we're starting to inspect the nitty gritty. But just damn, Bennett kills all doubt with City of Blades. 
 There is a new country to explore, a new main character, new side characters, a new god, but still all the fantastic comfort and old characters as well. Voortyashtan is a brilliant new world, and I suspect that we could have delved a little more into its history, but what was shown was just enough to let me feel like we were in a new place. 
 There are some moments where I legitimately laughed out loud. Mulaghesh is pretty darn hilarious (especially plus Sigrud), and Bennett's comedic timing is immaculate. I don't think I've ever been more appreciative of cussing in a fantasy novel. Generally I am not a fan - but it makes so much sense with her character and this type of book that I loved every word of it. 
 I loved how we got to meet Signe, who is brilliant and beautiful and still not a Mary Sue. I love how Bennett writes female characters. I cannot emphasize this enough. He is not afraid to have a book full of main characters who are women. And they are all so different and still make so much impact. 
 I loved the peeks into Shara's life post book one. And how it really was not what we all expected. 
 The plot was tight and always interesting. There were no moments that did not connect. I found the mystery intriguing with a lot of speculation, and the reveal was quite satisfying at the end. 
 I absolutely admire the social commentary in his books. He discusses what it means to be a country that is war-torn and conquered, what it means to be the conqueror, the difference between those who fight in wars and those who build, what it means to be a soldier, what it means to serve. 
 I love that he discusses this aspect of the Divine  (i.e. the afterlife) . It makes so much sense that I would actually be surprised if he didn't already plan this book before starting book one. It's not a shoehorned plot to keep this book a series. 
 I literally have nothing bad to say about this book. 
 Five stars. Everyone should read this book. And seriously, I do not give five stars lightly. But this book and this series deserves it.
