I know it's weird that I'm typing a review for the second book before making one for the first book but I just finished it yesterday and I want to make sure I remember everything. That said, I can definitely say that I'm at loss as to which book was worse. 
 The first book, Fallen, is admittedly my little masochistic baby. I'll expound on that in another review or whatever. I'm aware that it's considerably poorly written and there isn't anything remotely likable about the book's heroine, Lucinda Price; however, the book - as explained by my bookshelf - strangely grew on me... for questionable reasons I'm not aware of. 
 Although I already lowered my expectations to the proverbial bottom of the ocean, Torment has succeeded in disappointing me. Ironically, it interested me as well. I blame the masochistic tendencies I developed after reading the Twilight saga. 
 Since first book Luce was impossibly annoying, I dared to hope for some character development in the second installment. I was met with a literary slap from Lauren Kate. Luce, if possible, has grown more spoiled and whiny and self-centered. Not to mention self-righteous. (I'm pointing at that "I have a boyfriend" comment Luce made towards that stranger during her flight. I hate to break it to you, Lucinda, but not every guy wants to sleep with a Mary Sue.) Furthermore, as the plot (Hah. What plot?) develops, she continuously insists that she deserves to be able to make decisions for herself. Usually, I'd applaud the heroine for her bravado because technically, it is her fictional life. In this case, however, Luce has just proven herself to be more conceited and bratty and stubborn than I initially believed. I understand that Lauren tried to make us picture the brain dead heroine as independent and spunky but to simply put, her attempt backfired... completely. 
 I was never truly a fan of Daniel. The boy has his moments (though I honestly can't remember them) but the amount of brooding he subjects himself to is almost nauseatingly. In other words: not attractive at all. A break from his hot-one-minute-then-cold-the-next personality is seriously way overdue... but alas! We didn't get that, did we? No. Even if Daniel isn't physically present most of the time in the book, 89% of it is basically about him. In this little installment, Daniel is depicted to be even more important than oxygen. What with the whole 'he will tip the scale between good and evil' crap situation and all.  Moreover, he continuously showcases his - really irritating - dominating douchebag-ish qualities. (I, for one, strongly believe that no matter how much of a pain in the ass Luce is, she, in no way, deserves to be with Mr. King-of-Heaven-to-Hell-and-back. As much as I hate to admit this: She deserves better than Daniel. But let's move on.) 
 Now, as for the relationship between Luce and Daniel, I think that it's now more nonexistent than ever - and I know that what I said is grammatically incorrect but whatever. The love that's supposedly been there for thousands and thousands of years of death and reincarnation is complete and utter imaginary crap. To this day, I can not see any chemistry between the two of them and the whole arguing-that-leads-to-heavy-make-out-sessions dilemma that appeared in 40% of the book is just revolting and sad. (That is not what a real relationship entails, okay? Get that in your head, Lauren.) To simply put: Luce and Daniel aren't right for each other, exclamation point. 
 The plot remains vague and at times, disorienting. Luce is clearly a part of something "important" and perhaps even "life-threatening". However, Miss Kate continues to keep Luce and all of her readers in the dark. It's insulting, to say the least, but at the same time, I admit that the lack of information keeps me interested as to what happens next. (How cunning of you, Miss Kate.) The introduction to the Outcasts has definitely earned a few brownie points from me but, they're considerably flawed. If they're blind and can only sense Luce through the so-called burning of her soul or something to that extent, why did they mistake her for Dawn? Any ideas? That's what I thought. There are still a number of plot holes along the way. Also, the angel mythology in this book has, unfortunately, not improved. 
 What I enjoyed in this book can be summarized in one word, or to be more accurate - name: 
 Miles 
 . As a supporting character, I'd give him five and a half stars. He is the complete opposite of Grigori which means that Miles is a total sweetheart who actually cares and shows it - Very essential, let me tell you. He is definitely the highlight of this book though I am somewhat irked that he ends up falling for Luce when she, in no way, deserves him. At all. . 
 I'll admit to skipping a few paragraphs every now and then just so I can read about Miles. In fact, if Lauren Kate manages to get her hands on legitimate writing skills and publishes a book about the charming, quirky, sweet, lovable, cheerful, open-minded, gorgeous Miles, I'd definitely buy it without a second thought and proceed to make love with it. (Just kidding about the last part... kind of.) 
 Honestly, I can type up more paragraphs of how much I adore the Nephilim descendant, but I must move on to the other sort of likable parts of this book... namely, Cam, Arriane and Shelby. 
 Cam is the only reason I survived the first book - well, aside from Arriane, that is - and it's saddening how he's barely in Torment. I mean, why can't we have less Daniel and more Cam and Miles here? Dear god. 
 Arriane is still the amusing spitfire and I continue to pray, to hope and to dream that Lauren Kate will rewrite this entire series in her point of view instead of Luce's. She is basically the kick ass, independent, quirky, lovable, headstrong heroine Lucinda is desperately trying to be. Never fear, Arriane, no one can do you better than you. 
 Shelby is an interesting character who is more likable than Molly (I kid you not.) and whom I applaud for verbally brawling with Daniel. At first, I felt a little bit of a 'hippie' vibe coming from her but her character definitely developed throughout the book which is more than what I can say for Luce and Daniel. Needless to say, I like her. 
 Looking back to what I've typed, I think that without Shelby, Miles, Cam and Arriane, Torment would be receiving a lot of negative stars... but since they are in the book (thank the Lord!), I'll be giving this 2 stars. What can I say? I completely adore Miles.

I received a copy of this title from NetGalley. It does not impact my review. 
 I had such a hard time putting this book down! It's a really character-driven story about friendship and relationships and learning from your mistakes. The chapters switch POV between four young women and the relationship and life troubles they face. 
 *While I don't consider any of the below descriptions a spoiler, some readers might find it mildly spoiler-ish, so proceed with caution* 
 Gabrielle 
 Gabrielle was probably my favorite of the bunch. However, her problem is one of my pet peeves in books, which is when one simple conversation could solve all the problems, but that conversation doesn't come until close to the end of the book. Gabby has had a hard life and when she meets a nice, cute guy in a bar she lies a little about her life. (I loved Tony, by the way. He was so sweet and pretty much just the perfect guy - I was just waiting for him to do something awful because no guy can be that great.) She doesn't expect to see him again, but she does and they fall in love and the lies spin out of control. The truth about Gabby, obviously, has to come out some time, though. I still didn't like how Gabby handled it, but I did like how it all resolved in the end. 
 Madison 
 Madison was probably the hardest of the girls for me to like. She was one of the youngest, recently graduated from high school, and had the most growing up to do. She's in a non-committed relationship with the cliched bad boy musician, has no real future goals, her dad has recently been diagnosed with cancer, and her family is approaching financial crisis. When her dad's former boss, George, comes to visit and shows a bit of an interest in her, she decides to milk it. While they both know what she's doing, it still came across as a little too manipulative to me. But on the other hand, George is in his early thirties so I can't feel too bad for what he puts himself through by pursuing a teenaged girl. 
 While Madison was probably the most selfish character of the group, she did grow up a little as the story went on. I did really like her close relationship with her father. I also liked how her relationship with George ended up. 
 Claire 
 I really wanted to like Claire and I did for the most part, but I just didn't respect her for so much of the story. She is the wife of a pastor, who is running a mega-church, even though he's in his very early twenties. Claire is also very involved in the church. When she finds out that Gavin is doing very un-pastor-like things, she doesn't confront him, but starts to question what she did wrong and then blames a third party, as well. When the confrontation finally comes with Gavin I still wasn't satisfied with it. There was very little emphasis about what this meant to his job as a pastor or to their church or the members of the congregation. In fact, we never even find out if there's any fall out, other than what it means to their marriage. I'm just disappointed that once again the Christian faith is so poorly misrepresented in mainstream fiction. 
 Laura 
 Laura dropped out of high school to marry and follow her football star boyfriend to college. She's planned her whole life around him becoming a professional player, but all that is put in jeopardy when he gets hurt and they have to move back home with his parents. Laura is another character who had so much growing up to do and I think she made the most progress. She decided to go back to high school and get her diploma. While there she befriends a new guy who challenges her academically and makes her really start to consider having her own goals and not just following Brian's. Though she wasn't my favorite of the girls, her story arc was. Not everything turns out perfectly, but it seemed the most realistic and I was really proud of all she learned. 
 Overall 
 Overall, I really enjoyed The Young Wives Club (and it's gorgeous cover!). It's a well-written, character-driven story that I could hardly put down. Though the characters weren't always very likable, I really appreciated how much growth all of them showed throughout the book. I also really liked that things didn't just magically work out for all of them, but they had to work at it and learn to be ok if things in their life turned out a little differently than they expected. I definitely recommend this to fans of character-driven novels. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 4 Stars

Fleabrain got somewhat trying as a love interest, so in my head her ultimate destiny is to become a certain shepherd's wife. Otherwise, I loved the setting on the wilds of semi-ancient Scotland almost as much as I loved the alternating chapters from Lady Macbeth's point of view, which strive to make her a sympathetic character whose treachery is born of grief and generally having been married too young. 
 Admittedly, I have only skimmed the original play, but I thought this book did an amazing job of unpacking, expanding, and re-examining it from the female perspective/putting women at the center, while envisioning a whole story of missing scenes with a wildly memorable and likable original character (her backstory was particularly brilliant). The elements of magic conflated with the power of mere suggestion drew me in. And I'm pretty sure that the magnificent black warhorse she borrows is among my top five favorite characters in the book. 
 Spoiler for ending: I also really liked that in the end of this one, Lady Macbeth's suicide is faked so she can go reunite with her long-lost daughter, who meanwhile has spurned all marriage offers in preference of freedom. To me this means since the nature of Collum and Caora's relationship got pretty murky by the end, there's no reason the destiny in my head can't come true several years down the line, when she's good and ready for it. A+ on the ability to provide closure to the story while leaving her future open-ended.

This is a very nicely done romance, set in my absolute favorite period: Regency England. The regency period lasted from about 1790 to 1820. The actual length of time the Prince was regent was from 1811 till he ascended the throne in1820. Why is it that whenever I pick up a Rick Riordan book, I find myself completely speechless. I've no idea what to say about the second book of Percy Jackson, but what I do know is that I immensely enjoyed reading it. 
 For the most part, things have been pretty quiet this school year and Percy even makes a new friend named Tyson, a giant of a kid who, it turns out, is actually a Cyclops and a son of Poseidon. Anyway, soon enough, monsters come in and attack the gym during a game of dodgeball and chaos ensues, and Percy learns that something terribly wrong has happened. The tree that signifies Thalia's sacrifice has been poisoned and Camp Half-Blood is no longer safe. This, of course, leads to Percy wanting to save the world his fellow demigods and everyone else. And he, together with Annabeth and Tyson, does exactly that. 
 ... Okay, that probably didn't sound as exciting as I wanted it to, but don't get me wrong, The Sea of Monsters is just as thrilling and amusing as The Lightning Thief. If anything, this book, for me, holds more depth... and has been infused with more Greek mythology. (Read: utter awesomeness.) 
 Now, the low points were the lack of Grover's presence, the introduction of a character named Tantalus, and everything about Dionysus. Despite these, I breezed through the entire book, smiling and laughing at times. The beginning was all right, the middle was well-written and well-planned, and the somewhat abrupt ending just killed me in the most spectacular way! 
 5 stars and I'm just itching to have my hands on the next book.

I didn't like this a bit. Throughout the novel I shouted, come on Liz! You got everything, don't you know how to be contented?! :| 
 How can a successful woman with a husband who loves and cares for her very much is not happy with her life because she has some sort of neurosis and feeling of being trapped?

 The story is as follows: Liz decided to abandon her husband and claims to find the 'real one' and herself. WRONGLY, LIZ feels betrayed. She uses few men and then throws them away. I really felt bad for her husband. I seriously cried because of Liz's stupidity...

 The Magician's Lie is theatrical as its protagonist, taking you through the vaudeville scene and cleverly making you forget that Arden is fighting for her freedom. The chapters where she narrates her childhood and her days on the circuit, are full of vivid detail. I only wished that there was more to it. It read how anyone would recount their past, but it felt at times that it was missing some human interaction. Yet, I kept telling myself that if one is fighting for one's life you'd leave out those details. The chapters set in the present between Arden and Virgil was a game of cat in mouse, with Arden being very much the cat.
This would've been 4 stars for the fantastic ending and cliff hanger if it weren't for the length. If you chop off about 300 pages of fluff it would've been golden.

I don't like beer. I'm not a big drinker anyways, so it's not a big deal, but I've always felt like I would be more of a Beer Girl than a Girly, Fruity Drink Girl. But no matter how many times I try it, I just don't like it. I want to. But I don't. And that's how I feel about Colleen Hoover books. 
 Hoover is a good writer, I don't deny that. Owen and Auburn are both pretty well-developed, sympathetic characters. I liked the idea of the confessions with the art work and wish that would have been a bigger role in the book, instead of just the springboard for the overall theme of confessions. There were also many cute moments between Owen and Auburn that made me smile. That's unfortunately all I can list for the positives in this book, though. 
 One of my biggest pet peeves in fiction is lying and miscommunication. While ok in small doses, it drives me crazy when it's the main plot. When one honest conversation could bring about the conclusion of the whole book within a couple pages, I can't get behind a couple hundred pages of angst to get there. 
 I also really wanted to like Owen and in many parts I really did. However, most of the time he gave off kind of a smarmy vibe to be. He lied to Auburn from the very beginning and he kept lying to her. Even when he finally told her the truth about most things, he still kept one very big secret from her and I really hated that. A lot of his time with Auburn seemed manipulative to me and he came off a little controlling even. But it's supposed to be hot and attractive because he's hot and attractive and he does care about her. It just rubbed me the wrong way. Yes, he had sweet, redeeming moments. But overall, he was just a little off for me as a romantic lead. 
 Auburn was a sympathetic character, but kind of drove me crazy most of the time. She put herself into bad situations and despite wanting to change it, was just kind of resigned to her fate. She was very passive in changing her life, despite being supposedly very determined, and made many bad decisions. When she did finally step up, she did so in an underhanded way that made me disappointed. 
 Overall, Confess was a fast, easy read, but pretty underwhelming. While it did have some cute moments, I felt like it was ruined by all the lying, miscommunication, and poor decisions of the characters. Hoover isn't a bad writer, but I really just do not understand the obsession with her stories. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 2 Stars

I'm sure that similar stories of opposite sides of war falling for each other is a common plotline, but I really enjoy the characters involved in this one. Kestrel is the daughter of a military general, a high-society lady who is either to marry at the age of 18 or join the military. This fact is true to all people of the Valorian society. Valerians are a militaristic people who have conquered the lands of the Herrani. Valerians have Herrani as slaves. The story starts with Kestrel buying a slave, Arin, and she is somewhat intrigued by him since he was sold to her as a singer. Kestrel loves music, and loves to play the piano. She isn't much of a fighter, but is an excellent strategic military tactician. Arin is a strong-willed slave who does not easily bend before others. He ends up working as a Blacksmith for Kestrel's family, but often acts as Kestrel's escort when she is out and about. (Taking slaves as an escort is a common and normal thing to do in Valorian society; a lady cannot be without an escort.) Naturally the two start to fall for each other, but Arin may have plans that conflict with the life of Kestrel. 
 I really like Kestrel. I love that she sucks at fighting but is a very strong thinker. It's nice to have a heroine with a brain. Her love of music is also a nice touch-- it partially allows her to be sympathetic to the slaves (herrani) since they were a people of art. It gives her more reason to fall for Arin. 
 I do get a little confused about Arin's side of the story. The end, which I will not spoil, gives me a lot of conflicting thoughts. I don't think Kestrel can possibly still have feelings after Arin's betrayal, but she does!!! But he wanted to destroy her entire life! I guess he ends up keeping Jess alive, but he still kills a lot of other people Kestrel knows..... I guess it is supposed to be a story of the heart wants what the heart wants, but it is incredibly hard to understand how Kestrel could ever forgive Arin. Then Arin thinks he can keep Kestrel as his pretty little dove.... its kinda weird.... At least the deal that Kestrel ends up working out in the end will be interesting for later books. I definitely want to know more about this arrange marriage with the Emperor's son.... but then I don't want a love triangle either. Just how will they handle this? AGH!  
 Okay, that spoiler tag shows how excited I am for the next book-- I hope to get it soon!

The Fire Sermon is one of the better dystopian novels out there just for the world building alone. The great disaster that causes this bleak future doesn't seem silly; a nuclear blast from one country attacking another causes irreparable damage. Millions of deaths, a dying ecosystem, an ashy winter that kills off most of what survived. Eventually, the surviving animals flourish (including people) with just a few minor modifications. 
 For the people and animals alike, this means deformities. Missing limbs, duplicated limbs, no eyes or ears or noses. The flip side (and the less believable side) is that there are twins to these deformed humans who are nearly perfect. No health issues like colds or flus. No problems with reproducing. No missing or extra limbs. 
 I got past that though when our story actually began to take shape. Cass was a girl with her head perpetually in the clouds--she had these very naive ideas about how to change the way things were done, and it didn't seem very realistic. She got on my nerves sometimes, but I enjoyed her journey all the same. The idea that conceivably every problem could be wiped out with suicide or the seemingly innocent murder of one person was a curious one to me too, an idea that kept me continually on my toes. I knew someone would commit suicide for the good of whatever cause they were championing, I just wasn't sure who it would be. 
 Our villains were perfectly done, too. They were ruthless and took no prisoners, but they weren't caricatures--they had real motives that made sense in the scheme of their world. They weren't bad just because. They were bad because it fit with their end goals and with their own personal fears and desires. 
 I had the idea that this would be a little bit like The Darkest Minds so I was pleasantly surprised to find I enjoyed this significantly more.

4.5 Not my favorite Sanderson, but still better than most books I read. 
 Reader thoughts: I can never fault any of Sanderson's pacing. There are just a few hints perfectly placed. The ones I figure out are satisfying as opposed to being giveaways. The ones I don't figure out make the reveals even better.  For instance, I guessed Bleeder was the governor about halfway into the book. I knew the special bullet was a spike, but that didn't give anything away. I had no idea about Lessie. I seem to be unable to connect anything Cosmere (except Hoid).  
 His characterization is also flawless. Wayne at the temple? Too awesome for words. The newspaper inserts? Very cool. Wax figuring out the buried pages riddle? Also neat. Marasi . . . actually she's not as cool. I like her, but more for her ideas than what she does. 
 Gum, electricity, and radios. This world is moving forward, and I wonder what the next book is going to be like. What era will the next trilogy take place in? 
 Trell? I guess we'll learn more about that later. 
 Writer thoughts: Having such old MCs is unconventional. It's done, but not popular. Usually MCs need to be young enough to have spark but old enough to be capable, and this tends to be ages 15 to 25. Wax is 40ish. This loses interest of some readers (myself included, except that this is a Sanderson novel). What does Sanderson gain by this choice? 
 Wax has more background. By making him older, Sanderson can pack in career choices and lost loves and old friends. If Wax were 20, this wouldn't work. 
 Wax has more experience. If he were 20, he wouldn't be able to realistically deal with the things he does. He also wouldn't be able to act so calmly to the responsibility and death he has to face. 
 Wax has more connections. The police and governor confide in Wax and trust him with important duties that would be unrealistic to give a 20-year-old. Sure, it's fun when we read about 20-year-olds doing the impossible, but it makes more sense when a 40-year-old does them. 
 Wax is slower. That's right, this can be an advantage. With everything else Wax has to deal with, he also has a body that is aging. Great, another conflict piled with the rest. Wax has to work harder to chase after bandits, and readers will appreciate that in him.

 The usual plot devices were abundant - oh no, look, it's another undefeatable monster! ok we totally slaughtered it, thanks deus ex machina - as well as short chapters that all end on cliffhangers. This book had some really awful transitions, as did the entire series. 
 It was difficult to keep the modern day Prometheus and the Danu Talis Prometheus straight, though the huge cast of characters narrowed down thanks to killing off a bunch of them. The only major character to die in this series was Hecate in book one, and then despite the Dark Elder's and Dee's attempts, the body count didn't change until the last book. I guess the writer thought he needed to make up for lost time. Anyway, the surviving characters teamed up and reduced the different settings I had to keep straight. 
 The big reveal about Josh and Sophie's "twins of legend" status was ridiculous. The more interesting reveal about Isis and Osiris took roughly 2 short paragraphs and was over within a few more. For the entire series, we've been reading about the twins of legend, which I figured would be Artemis and Apollo based on the silver/gold and sun/moon traits. Instead, we learn that they're not twins and they are not even related. They're just two kids picked out of different time periods and kept in storage. What a stupid, stupid, stupid resolution.  
 Three things saved this book: Machiavelli, Virginia Dare, and the event that "Everyone cried" at.

 "I wouldn't expect love from you. I can't love you back." 
 "I am incapable of love. I will not offer it to you." Beth wondered what was more heartbreaking, the words themselves or the flat tone of voice. 
 "What was it like?" His words were so low she barely caught them. "Explain to me what loving feels like, Beth. I want to understand." 
 "Is this what it feels like?" he whispered to her. "I don't like it, my Beth. It hurts too much." 
 I just want to hug him :(

Quite The Novel Idea ~ Novel Ink 
 I'm just utterly... flabbergasted. That's the perfect word for it. I have no idea what to rate this book or what to even say about it because... I don't even know. This book is a mess. If I can make any message clear at the outset of this review, I'd like that one to be the one. 
 This was one of those books that I think really benefited from amazing publishers and agents who really saw an opportunity in this story being one of the next teenage crazes ala The Hunger Games, Twilight and Harry Potter, so of course they're going to jump on that chance and promote the heck out of it up until its release date. To be fair, even the reviews that came out regarding the story before the book was actually released positively glowed. 
 Having finished the book tonight - I'm left wondering exactly what version of this book those reviewers read and where can I get that amazing copy? 
 Red Rising tells the story of Darrow, who lives as a HellDiver in a mining colony under the surface of the planet of Mars. To seventeen year old Darrow, blood, sweat and pain are all he knows; however with his wife Eo and their extended family he's as happy as a clam. That is of course, until tragedy strikes as it inevitably does and Darrow comes to learn that above the surface of Mars is an entire society full of colors in which the Golds rule. It is when Darrow is disguised to infiltrate the Golds' "Institute" to fight for vengeance that the story truly begins. 
 Let me start off by running through what is wrong with this book. First off, the Society. Who exactly in the future sat down and took the time to figure out what skill group each differently colored hair thrived in? The Obsidian-haired are the law enforcement, Golds are the rulers, Reds are the slaves, Browns are skilled at fashion and hairstyling, whilst Pinks are made for love-making. It literally makes no sense. I'm sure whoever was on that planning committee loved the fact that Pinks were forced to become prostitutes for all eternity. 
 Also, I really feel like Pierce Brown was trying to create the next Dune or Clockwork Orange with this novel. By that I mean, he has stuffed this book so full of his own made up terms that the first 15% of the book is nearly unreadable because you have no idea what he's talking about! headTalks, hellDiver, holoCan, frysuit, Tinpots, slingBlade, etc. etc. At times it feels like Brown really thought he was being genuinely clever with all these terms which just end up making you roll your eyes after the fourth or fifth randomly-capitalized word you come across. Then there are the terms the characters use: bloodydamn, gorydamn, Pixie, boyo, etc. and when one character uses one of these phrases, they tend to use it three or four lines in a row just to make sure we got the point. 
 Next, we have Darrow. I don't care what anybody says, Darrow IS a Mary-Sue. He is perfect in every way. As a HellDiver, he was the best of the Reds from the age of 13. When he was first exposed to Golden society, another character is shown playing with a very high tech puzzle cube infused with mathematics. While Darrow can't understand the math behind it, thankfully his quick hands make up for it and he solves it before that other character can. There are literally so many moments just like that throughout the story - where things are doomed by thankfully Darrow had an amazing moment of heroics, or an epiphany that literally saves the day. 
 When Darrow is "Carved" and that what makes him a Red is removed and replaced by Gold - he physically becomes a vision of perfection. There isn't even a moment told in the story where Darrow struggles to become accustomed to this new society he never knew existed before. Rather, he takes some magic intelligence potions, reads some Ancient Earth philosophy books, and suddenly is completely ready to act as a Gold and play their games. 
 Then on we get to the Institute. When Darrow arrived at the Institute and was put through the rigorous testing and eventual sorting ceremony, all I could think was how much this part of the story was designed to reflect and lean on the success of Harry Potter. When the students are sorted to their appropriate houses, they all head to a Great Hall with a holographic ceiling that reflects the true sky outside to have dinner! It was just completely amazing that Pierce Brown's editor or the publishing company even allowed that to make it to the final published version of the book. 
 Then we've got the houses themselves. Why are they all named after Greek Gods? And what luck does Darrow have that he is sorted into House Mars, while competing at (one of hundreds, on hundreds of planets,) the Institute being that he is also born on Mars. It was just way to corny to be likeable. Like, "look at how noble and good Darrow is - he can't escape his heritage even when he's disguised to look and act like a Gold from a distant planet!" And what is with the Society's love for Ancient Greek Gods? Why not design the story's own apostles and heroes? Also, this is when the story shifts fully from Harry Potter into the Hunger Games, and we discover that there is no book learning at the Institute, but rather these students will be fighting to the death. It was yet another moment that I couldn't really believe a publisher didn't stop and say: "Wait, didn't I just see Katniss do this in that other book? 
 Finally, because I can't write forever: the plotting of this book is just crazy to me. Most times, it feels like Pierce Brown was literally just sitting down and writing whatever came to mind. There didn't seem to be any planning or anything. When a twist occurs  like Titus being a Carved Red, or Mustang being the Jackal's sister,  there are no repercussions for them, or even any more exposition on the topic. Furthermore, Brown at times seems bored by the lengthy timelime of the story, and jumps hours, days, weeks, and months ahead multiple times, (especially during the last 30% of the story,) where the majority of the story becomes Darrow telling us things that have happened rather then the reader actually experiencing them. 
 It's all a shame really - because the story is interesting, and I would like to see where Brown takes it next, however I'm not entirely sure that Brown yet has the writing skill to fully bring to life the story of Darrow's future he has created for him in a way that will be satisfying for the reader.

 Sun Tzu emphasized the importance of positioning in military strategy. The decision to position an army must be based on both objective conditions in the physical environment and the subjective beliefs of other, competitive actors in that environment. He thought that strategy was not planning in the sense of working through an established list, but rather that it requires quick and appropriate responses to changing conditions. Planning works in a controlled environment; but in a changing environment, competing plans collide, creating unexpected situations.

This is a book that was quickly gaining a lot of hype and some incredibly good reviews, and so it moved right up my 'to read' list even before both online book clubs I'm a member of decided to choose it as their November pick. There was a lot to live up to - practically every review I read mentioned that this was bound to be nominated for all kinds of awards. Was it as good as everyone was saying? Yes! 
 Ancillary Justice just clicked with me. I loved the universe that the author created, the planets, the stations and ships, the characters, the plot - everything interested me. This is one of those books that I found impossible to read along with the book club; I couldn't help reading on and finishing it ahead of time. 
 Everyone has been talking about the gender politics in the book, so let's touch on that first. I thought this was handled really well, and not only provided a fascinating cultural backdrop for the story, but also challenged the reader, inviting us to examine our own relationship with gender. The people of the Radch just aren't interested in whether a person is male or female, and so the story, told from the POV of a person who has grown up in the culture of the Radch, refers to everyone as 'she'. How much does it really matter, how much does it affect the story, if we know a character's gender or not? In this case, it doesn't matter at all, and yet I would still find myself at certain points trying to assign gender to characters. It was also interesting to see how a culture like this might interact and think about the world. 
 This approach to gender added a fascinating and unique element to the book, without being as vital to the plot as the gender politics in something like The Left Hand of Darkness turn out to be. I liked this - sometimes it's nice to explore something like this without it also being integral to the plot. 
 Speaking of The Left Hand of Darkness, I think there were some clear nods to it in this book - the frozen world at the beginning, the two characters thrown together learning to understand and accept each other... and in some ways the relationship between the two main characters mirrors that of Ai and Estraven, but interestingly in terms of class and citizenship rather than gender. The style of writing also reminded me a lot of Ursula le Guin. It is strong, controlled, perhaps a little distant at points, with an almost mythical feel to it that I adore. Again, this kind of writing just clicks with me, and I'm so pleased to have found another author to add to my favourites shelf. 
 The Radch, then, don't discriminate based on gender, but they do find other ways to keep certain members of society down. The class politics are incredibly important in this story, as they are behind the split and changing ethos of the Radch empire. At the centre of this is Anaander Mianaai, the ruler of the Radch and the person that the main character, Breq, is determined to assassinate. I thought the class politics, like the approach to gender, were conveyed so well, and there was a definite Roman feeling going on with the client-patron structure of Radch society - anything to do with Romans is always a bonus for me! 
 However, my absolute favourite thing about the book was how the author managed to show Breq as both human and not-quite-human at the same time. It is so hard to write an A.I. that truly feels like an A.I. and yet is also sympathetic and relatable to. Ann Leckie pulls this off perfectly. Breq often feels cold, slightly alien, distant... and yet she is driven, opinionated, and perhaps almost a little romantic about certain things. She is a wonderful character who I really enjoyed reading about. And then there is the fact that Breq both is and is not One Esk, and they are but are not Justice of Toren, the ship and the hive mind in control of all its ancillaries. Again, this is hard to pull off, that sense of individuals within a group mind, but it comes across so well here. Finally, the point of view stretched across several bodies is a brilliant touch in the early chapters. It's a kind of first person voice of god, not like anything I've read before and intriguing without being confusing. 
 The plot itself is compelling and exciting, with just the right amount of world building, and flashback chapters that not only add so much to our understanding of the characters, but that turn out to be very important to what is happening later in the book. The pacing was very good, perhaps just drawing things together a little too quickly at the end, however. I liked the resolution of this particular story and look forward to seeing where the characters will go next. 
 A fantastic story with wonderfully written characters and several unique elements that make this a truly memorable read. I have to agree with other reviewers - this will surely turn up on award nomination lists next year!

Some Kind of Perfect by Krista & Becca Ritchie - 5 mindblowingly amazing stars 
 Ten years of laughter. Of heartache. And love. 
 6 friends. 
 3 sisters. 
 1 epic story. 
 And I can't handle life right now... 
 This is it. This is the ending we have all been hoping our Calloway-Hale-Cobalt-Meadows family would get. Not that we ever wanted their stories to end. This final book is so beautiful and heartfelt. So raw and real. It was definitely some kind of perfect happily-ever-after for the most realistic characters I have ever read. 
 Krista & Becca Ritchie are super heroes for writing these books. 
 I am distraught - yes, my emotions are that intense - that I have to say goodbye to all of these amazing characters. Their lives, their stories, their hearts are engrained in my very being. There will never be enough when it comes to this series. You'll fall in love every time. You might cry or get angry, but oh, you will fall in love. Every. Damn. Time.

And no matter whether they are going through something wonderful or something that rips you apart, the best parts of themselves or the worst, you stand by their sides because you know in your marrow that they would be standing right by you if the roles were reversed. This isn't goodbye. There's no way in hell. 
 And I know some people might be rolling their eyes at my love (that word doesn't even feel strong enough) for these fictional characters. Frankly, if you haven't connected so deeply to a story before, you're missing out. 
 You should read this book. Like, now. Right now. Shove all other books aside, and read this series straight through. That's right - all 10 books. Alive is a thrilling YA debut novel by Chandler Baker that will keep you on the edge of your seat, wanting more. 
 Alive is centered around Stella Cross who had been fortunate enough to received a heart transplant. However, weird things begin to occur after receiving a new heart. Things like nightmares and hallucinations begin to interrupt her daily activities. In addition, after a new kid transfers into her senior class, Levi Zin, she begins to have an undeniable attraction to him and finds that her heart would ache for him when they were apart- like literally. 
 The plot of this novel was definitely intriguing from the moment I had heard about it til after I had read it. I knew it would be a thriller but I didn't expect it to have affected me the way it did. The nightmares, the hallucinations had a very high creep factor that I almost could not read this book at night... alone in my office. The way the plot had unraveled itself and the timing of it all played a really big part on my enjoyment of this book. I knew that there was just something wrong when Stella began having nightmares and hallucinations and when her attraction for Levi began- the this all played out in the book, including the book's pacing was absolutely wonderful. 
 I'll admit, I'm not entirely a big fan of Stella's personality and some of the decisions that she made throughout the book. There were moments when she was selfish, self- centered, a bit of a brat sometimes. However, I feel like her personality and her character development was due to the plot itself. Does that make sense? For example, she stood up some of her friends because of this "thing" that she had for Levi or the reason why she did such careless things immediately post- op (without considering how it would make her mother feel) was because she's a teen with an unfulfilled need to explore and to just be a teenager and do teenager-y things with her friends. (Sorry, but that's the best way I could explain it at the moment). Anyways, though I did quite enjoy her as a character, I felt like her character development wasn't completely satisfying to me. I wanted to see a lot more of her as the book progressed. As for secondary characters, I really loved Brynn! I loved her spunk and her sarcasm- she's sooo awesome!!! If I had met her in real life, I think she and I would be BFFs <3 
 As for the writing... all I have to say is- this book would not feel complete if it weren't for Baker's wonderful writing. It was her choice of words, elements of the plot and the plot's pacing that really brought this story to full circle. 
 I am a big fan of thrillers, whether it's a movie or a book, and this novel had definitely satiated my craving for a summer thriller. Overall, this is one book that everyone has to check out especially if you're a fan of YA thrillers ^_^ I guarantee that you will not be disappointed! 
 I would like to thank Disney- Hyperion for sending me an advanced readers copy in exchange for an honest review! Thank you, Hyperion <3 #MuchLove

If I could, I would give this book 3.5 stars, since I did really enjoy it, but it wasn't quite the standard that I've put other 4/5 star books in. I'm a hard one to please! 
 City of Bones opens up a world mixing the modern with the supernatural world of demons, werewolves and vampires (and others!), set in New York. It uses the classic explanation of ordinary human's (called 'mundanes') inability to perceive the other world due to the 'glamor' - an invisible veil. However, the rest of the novel explores a rather original approach to a fantastical world. 
 The novel is about a young woman named Clary who seems to accidently come across some 'demonhunters', namely Jace, Isabelle and Alec and her world begins to unfold. Her mother Jocelyn is attacked by a demon and disappears, and it turns out that Clary is no ordinary mundane - but a descendant of the Clave, a cult of shadowhunters who are sworn to kill demons. It transpires that the person behind this attack is an exiled (presumed dead) shadowhunter named Valentine - and he is involved in Clary and Jace's lives more closely than you'd think. 
  While I thought the plot twist of Valentine being Clary's father rather unsurprising (it has happened in many fantasy/science fiction novels and adaptions. Namely, Star Wars, The Mortal Engines by Phillip Reeve, The Chronicles of Ancient Darkness by Michelle Paver, etc etc), I was wholly unprepared for the second twist being that Jace and Clary are brother and sister?? Personally I don't think this is true - Valentine's character is a master deceiver and 1) they look nothing alike, and 2) they're in love (kind of)so this makes absolutely no sense! But I do think we will find out the truth in the next book, in the I presume, waking of Jocelyn.  
 Cassandra Clare's writing is very rich and her poetic style is a joy to read, using some lovely original and interesting similes to describe action and appearances. The novel's pace is quite fast but easy to understand until the end, where I thought it dragged a little and became confusing. The characters are witty and relatable and I can't wait to read the next in the series.

First impressions: Can Harper be my new book BFF? In the first few scenes she is funny, irreverent, rebellious, and sympathetic. She is the most authentic teenager I've read, perhaps ever. 
 Lasting impressions: Beautiful. Heartbreaking. Magical. Hilarious. Although this one hit close to home for me, it was wonderfully cathartic. 
 Conflicting impressions: I can't think of anything that didn't work for me in this book. 
 Overall impressions: Harper has lived in the shadow of her sister her whole life, unable to understand why she doesn't have June's innate ability to exceed everyone's expectations. Feeling like the loser letdown of a daughter, Harper has carefully constructed a persona to match her perceived failings - black nail polish, a wall of truancy and detention slips, smoking cigarettes. June is the golden child and she is the black sheep, invisible to her warring parents. 
 When June commits suicide, there is no note, and everyone struggles to understand why she did it. Harper feels the weight of being the one that's left, and has a hard time shaking the feeling that everyone thinks the wrong sister died. While going through her sister's things, Harper finds a mix CD that June had been listening to right before she died, as well as a postcard of California - the one place June had always wanted to go. 
 Jake Tolan is a boy who seems to have no ties to June, but shows up at the wake. After Harper discovers June was tutoring him, and that he works in a record store, she realizes he made the mix CD. Soon Harper, Jake, and Harper's best friend Laney have concocted a plan to drive to California and put June's ashes to rest in the place where she wanted to belong. June wanted nothing so much as to escape the pressures of life and family, and to be free to do and be whatever she wanted, and Harper is determined to make that happen as a final gift to her sister. 
 As Harper experiences impromptu protests, concerts, and landmarks, and shares these exciting adventures with new people, she begins to find herself. The road trip experience is full of powerful moments that reveal things about her desires and strengths, as well as her feelings about her sister. We don't watch Harper change as a result of the trip, we watch her discover that the person she has been all along is nothing less than her sister. She has always been strong and capable, but her fears and insecurity colored her perception of herself. 
 Harper is without a doubt one of the best characters I read this year. I related to her and her struggles on so many levels, from her inability to cry at a funeral, to her need to just run away from it all and so something meaningful for the person she feels she failed the most. Hannah Harrington has written a girl so complete that I had a hard time believing she wasn't real. Harper lives far beyond these pages, showing us the way teenaged girls really think and feel. 
 This book is one that will definitely stick with me. With a love story that seemed genuine in its slow growth, and an exploration of music through the eyes of Jake Tolan that provides a perfect soundtrack to Harper's journey, this one is full of life and memories. For anyone who's lost someone close to them, especially from suicide, this is a cathartic story that allows us to process our feelings alongside Harper. This is a powerful treasure that should not be missed.

 I mean, the writing in this novel is just beautiful at times. I highlighted more than one passage ad will probably be thinking about the philosophical musings from the last chapter for the next couple of days.

 Historical fiction can be hit or miss, depending upon one's interest in the given subject and the author's abilities and execution. For those who are fascinated by witchcraft and/or the waning of Queen Elizabeth's influences on England (Gunpowder Plot, anyone?) this is a quick and enjoyable read. 
 Note that if you have any sensitivities or objections to depictions of incest or torture or rape, this is not the book for you. 
 William Shakespeare plays a minor role; many of the characters are based upon actual historical figures. Despite this footing, Winterson keeps her prose lively as her plot is quick which makes for fast page turning (short chapters also help in this regard). One of the historical figures who is alluded to--but does not appear in the story--is Edmund Campion, a Catholic priest persecuted by England in the early days of that country's reformation. This is of personal import to me as the first college which I ever attended was named for him.  
 Winterson has some great lines in this one; one of my favorites is the phrase witchery popery popery witchery which was recited by the McCarthy-esque government goon named Potts. The structure of the narrative employs some use of flashback although it is not nearly as intricate as Winterson's Gut Symmetries, which I also enjoyed (although I am hesitant to make any concrete comparisons between the two without rereading both after completing Winterson's published catalog). Suffice it to say that if you enjoy her writing (for either themes or style) than you will love this book, as it is certainly a tightly-honed little package that will leave you breathlessly contemplating the briefest glimmers at dusk.

3.5 stars. I enjoyed this and look forward to continuing the series. It was well paced and filled with characters I found rather enjoyable. There is just enough mystery to keep you turning the page. I just wanted to know more about the secret world Violet found herself suddenly a part of. On her 17th birthday, Violet learns that she is part angel, imbued with an angel's essence at birth. She spends the entire book trying to deal with this knowledge and the changes it brings to her life. She must decide if she will embrace her destiny and all the power that comes with it, or turn her back and take her chances at surviving the exiled angels that can now sense her presence. She feels betrayed by Lincoln, the man who she has been training with and falling in love with for the last two years. He has known all along what she was and never told her. Instead he did all he could to prepare her. Lincoln is her chosen partner, and Grigori partners can never be together. They both love each other, but being together will weaken them and put them in danger. Instead she turns to the dark and dangerous exiled angel, Phoenix. He is powerful and secretive. She never bothers to find out more about him, just decides to trust him.  Phoenix is the only surviving child of Adam and Lilith (father of man and mother of demons/evil). Of course he is an angel of the dark. I'm curious to see what becomes of him. I believe he truly loved Violet and wanted to be honest with her. He wanted her to love him and be with him. I'm curious to see what will become of him now that he's lost her. Will he embrace his dark nature and be a true enemy to the Grigori? Will he seek revenge for being scorned? I'm also curious to find out more about Violet's powers. I think she is Michael's daughter. Her power and rank are obviously greater than everyone else's. I think that her unique powers will allow her and Lincoln to be together without weakening them. We'll just have to see how long it takes them to figure that out. I think being together will actually strengthen their powers. I could be wrong. I'm sure it will be a while, filled with lots of angst and pain, but they'll figure out how to be together. . As the war between the exiled and the Grigori intensifies, Violet is forced to make her decision, embrace or walk away. Lincoln's very life depends on it.

This book surprised me a couple of times, I have to say. I went into it with a sketchy understanding of Crane's DisIllusionists world from one novella I had read (and enjoyed). At first I didn't enjoy this novel very much. I felt like I was being hit over the head with exposition, a stumbling sort of telling not showing style that I just don't like. Part of my dissatisfaction was also a lack of mystery. Everything was just so boringly straightforward. For a book that was billed as noir I just wasn't getting any shady intentions of depth of character. Justine was transparent, Packard was just too forthright, the whole set-up was a elementary. Although, I did love a few of Packard's insights... an example: 
 "I got it right, Justine. Feel into it. Your sense of being a misfit blinds you to what your heart really wants. When you get around solid, upstanding men, you're like a bird with tinfoil. It makes you incoherent on a romantic level." 
 So, as I have only complained this far, let me say - even in the first part of this book there were some smashing turns of phrase. And, of course, as you can see I have rated it 4 stars. As Justine became a functional Disillusionist, working targets, getting her "zing" on, and battling her attraction for Packard, I became much more engaged. It was like as she embraced the darkness and stopped fighting it so much, she became more relatable. Plus, it was hard to relate to her at the beginning when she was nothing but a raging hypochondriac. 
 I did feel like the plot was seriously telegraphed from the very beginning. I knew that  Otto was Henji . Obviously Justine and Packard are good together, but I didn't foresee that  Justine would fall for Otto (like, really fall for him) and actually choose him over Packard . This actually made me like her a little less. She just so obviously doesn't know what she wants, and it's kind of pathetic. This relates in no way of course to the fact that I myself would choose Packard a million times over the other guy. Smile. 
 So the reason I rate the book so highly is because of the strong psychological undertones. I mean, Justine goes through a supreme mindfuck in this one. And that was well-portrayed. Packard is a shiny, wonderful thing that I want more of. I definitely will read more of these to find out what happens to him. And I find I was fascinated by the concept of the Disillusionists themselves. Not so much the way they are paralyzed by some component of themselves that ultimately becomes mental illness, or even how they zing it off onto people. But the way they are portrayed, introduced, and interact with each other as if they are nothing but the embodiment of that one thing that inhabits them. When Justine meets Julio, he introduces himself as "Ennui". That's it. His whole existence, boiled down to one word. I find that a pretty profound concept actually; it communicates more to me about the disillusionists and what their lives feel like, than all the exposition (of which there is too much). 
 As for this being Crane's first novel, I find it highly promising. I think if she relies more on her excellent instincts about concepts and characters, and less on telling us the story I will love her work. I am definitely looking forward to more Packard.

It's not as easy to digest as the blockbuster thrillers and mysteries of past few summers (re: Gone Girl, Girl on the Train), but it has plenty of surprises and definitely pays off if you give it a little time. Emma's boyfriend Lucas is dying of cancer. When she enlists the help of a local witch, Emma performs a ritual that she believes will bring him back from the brink of death. When Lucas makes a miraculous recovery, Emma is the only person not surprised. However, her joy is slightly dampened by that fact that Lucas seems to be .... a little "off". He speaks robotically and lacks memories that he should have. Generally, he doesn't seem to be himself. 
 Scout came from another world as part of a scouting crew. When the ship his cruiser is attached to comes under attack, Scout is the only one to detach and flee. When his crew is obliterated and his ship is irreversibly damaged, Scout must find a way to survive on Earth...but how? 
 This was my first Karen McQuestion book. I can say "first" because after reading this one, I plan to read her entire collection! Besides a completely original storyline (how many of those are out there?!), this story is well executed. The author's voice changes depending on the character whose point of view the story is being told from. Even without a heading, I would have been able to tell who was narrating each chapter. 
 I simply can't say enough about how good the characterization in this book was. Emma and Scout were both loveable characters. Emma...her unfailing faith that her cure would work and everything would turn out all right, finding herself doing things she never dreamed to protect those she loved, and her keen observation skills all stood out. Scout's unusual way of looking at things and gradual understanding of the human race was beautiful. Every major and minor character was believable and well-rounded. I didn't have too much information or too little about anyone. It was refreshing to read a story and have everything so well connected. 
 The cover is beauitful and likely to grab a reader's attention as they browse the library. Fortunately, the story lives up to this cover!

 Seriously. With every book this woman writes, my heart suffers more! If she keeps this up, there'll be nothing left when I'm 5 books further. And each new book becomes my new favorite! This will be in my top 14 at the end of the year. For sure. 
 Maybe Someday is about Sydney Blake. She's in college, has a job, is in love with her wonderful boyfriend Hunter and rooming with her best friend Tori. And every day she goes out onto the balcony, listening to the musician playing guitar on his balcony. Everything changes when she discovers Hunter has been cheating on her with Tori for years. When she's left with nowhere to go, the musician takes her in. His name is Ridge Lawson, he's been in a serious writer's block for weeks. Now he's finally found his muse and they soon find themselves needing each other in more ways than one. This wonderful book is accompanied by a soundtrack that Colleen has made with musician Griffin Peterson. 
 This book took my breath away. it really did! It was so intense! But I guess I should've expected that. It is a Colleen Hoover book. Every new book of her instantly becomes my new favorite and ends up in my top 5 of that year. Last year Hopeless was number one and I'm sure this one will be too. It's funny, witty, breathtaking, heartbreaking, romantic, sweet, ... I read a big part of this on the bus and there are now a few more people in the world who think I'm absolutely crazy. I was laughing, giggling, sobbing, crying, laughing again and then crying some more. God, my heart can't take so many feels. 
 I was surprised how well the combination of the book with the songs worked! The songs were amazing and it was such a unique experience. I love them! I think this is one of those rare things that only Colleen can pull off. Colleen has a way of making everything seem so realistic and genuine! And only she can make a romance like this so perfect. I was on the edge of my seat the entire time. Like I said before, my heart can't keep this up anymore. It's not healthy! 
 One of the greatest things about Colleen's books are the characters. The feel so real. And most of the time they could be friends of mine. I would love Sydney as a friend. She's so sweet and talented and a little bit evil. Sure she has flaws, but I don't care. I didn't even bother remembering them because I love her so much. And Ridge! Oh my god Ridge! He's so amazing! I can't even begin to describe him. But I'll try. In spoiler brackets because something about him was quite a surprise to me and I want you guys to be surprised by it too! Yellow Crocus is an unputdownable book. I started it and had a hard time putting it down to get to my normal activities. I read it in two days. It's a great story that reminds you of the hard times families went through in Virginia back in the 1800s. And when I say families I refer to both, white or black families that had to face slavery and deal with all its consequences. 
 It is a story about the endearing unbreakable bond between two women: Mattie and Elizabeth. These two women shared a bond made of love and out of the fact that they both were victims of slavery. Mattie was born into slavery...she was a third generation slave. Lisbeth was a slave too, despite being born into a gold cradle. She was a slave to the ideals and duties that women of Virginia society were expected to follow: 
 Young ladies may speak to young men about the weather, meals, clothing, and their relatives. Avoid conversation concerning politics, finance, or religion. Though a gentleman may bring up such topics, and a lady must follow where a gentleman leads, a skilled lady will return the conversation to an appropriate topic. 
 When speaking with a lady who is older than you, you must follow her lead. Occasionally, though, you will be required to initiate conversation. Fashion, the weather and inquiries about relations are always appropriate topics among ladies. Do not allow a gentleman to overhear you speaking about courtship, literature or politics. 
 You cannot possible choose a husband based on the literature he cares for, nor can you reject a husband for how he treats the hands. You would be giving up everything. For what? It changes nothing. 
 Mattie and Lisbeth shared a bond that made them equals. These two undaunted women shared the courage that made them fight for their right to have a life of their own, a life they could freely chose. 
 I heard of this book, because it was recommended after I read The Help. This book is better than The Help IMHO. I recommend this book for those who enjoy historical novels, those who enjoy stories about strong bonds between women. It is a story about love, courage, suffering and hope. 
 Even though I enjoyed and liked this book, I couldn't give it 5 stars for two reasons: 
 1. The cover. One of the reasons I decided I wanted to read this book was the title. Yellow crocuses are special flowers to me, as my garden is covered in them. So I was drawn to the book immediately after reading the title. With that said, I have a question: Why does a book titled Yellow crocus have a purple crocus on its cover? Why? Ok, the purple crocus is reference to Mattie but still, why not put a yellow crocus? Why all the references in the story to the first crocus of spring and not put a yellow crocus on the cover? Why oh Why? This took half a star. 
 (The second reason might be some sort of spoiler so you can skip it if you want.) 
 2. The ending. I'm in a phase of my life where I like happy endings. As for me, this ending wasn't a happy one because despite of everything that Mattie and Lisbeth had to overcome to have the life they wanted to have, they weren't completely free. They didn't have the freedom to be the longtime friends they yearned-for. They even couldn't greet each other on the streets. Despite the almost 'mother-daughter' bond they shared, in the end they lived their 'free' lives apart from each other. This took another half a star.  
 And for those reasons this one gets a good solid 4 stars on my list. 
 Read Yellow Crocus. You'll enjoy it and will be happy and thankful that we've come a long way. :)

Lies of Locke Lamora is one of the best fantasy novels I have read in a very long time, truthfully the best one since being introduced to maybe Rick Riordan. The main difference is that Camorr, Locke's home, is entirely fictional. And boy howdy is it one hell of a place. The descriptions are fabulous--full of the typical comings and goings of any city, but also rife with gang life and a bit of whimsy. There's things like Elderlight, this amazing material that was left over by some unknown beings. There's Wraithstone, which is a gaseous material that turns anyone who comes into contact with it into a zombie-like, placid being with no thoughts. There is ridiculously awesome animals like all the bloodthirsty shark things in the water. The whole thing is just absolutely magnificent world building, and history building, and plot building... 
 I don't know if I can adequately describe why I enjoyed this book so much. I always have a harder time with glowing reviews than I do with "meh" or bad reviews. But essentially, the author created real, tangible characters that are full-bodied. We have Jean, the fattest assassin you'll ever read about. Locke, quite possibly the luckiest and sneakiest thief ever (known in legend as the Thorn of Camorr) and the Gray King--guess what color he wears? But the way all the different components of the story intertwine together is just absolutely great. Locke's scheme with one don ends up playing a bigger role than he ever anticipated. It turns out one very foreboding person knows exactly who Locke is, and who all of his friends are... 
 Basically, one diabolical scheme after another gets dumped on Locke. He's forced to play along with deception after deception in order to stay alive and to try and keep his friends alive. And the ingenuity in which it is done is the best part. It's clever without throwing in your face just how clever it really is, which in itself is a neat trick.

This book is definitely a page turner. It's fast-paced and unsettling, but is it worthy of all the hype? Is it really Hitchcockian? Mmm...that's a pretty high bar. Putting Hawkins on par with the Master of Suspense might be overkill. I know people are going bananas for it, and I can see why, but I'm not left with the urge to push it on my friends and say, "You gotta read this!" It's engaging, I'm glad I read it, and I'm sure it'll make a good movie (which you know is gonna happen). 
 Unsurprisingly, it's being compared to Gone Girl. A beautiful young woman disappears from her seemingly perfect life, the story is delivered through alternating viewpoints (which are ordered asynchronously), the characters are all wildly unreliable, and Hawkins doles out key information in a very piecemeal fashion. Great - a recipe for success. 
 Except...it's just not done quite as well. To varying degrees, the characters lack a certain depth and believability. I believed Rachel's character, she felt frustratingly real to me, but others - like the detectives - were pretty flat. It didn't quite reach the point of being a character study because, aside from maybe Rachel, we didn't really get into any of their heads. It lacks perspective entirely from a few key players. The creep factor was high at points, but I was never chilled to the bone as I was reading certain passages in Gone Girl. 
 I might have given it four stars, but there was one little detail at the end, a crucial one that I won't spoil here, that knocked it down a peg. Were this more pulpy throughout, I would've loved it. But it's not pulp, so it was just cheesy and totally took me out of the moment - one of those things her editor should have read and gone, "Yeah, I get it. I get what you're doing...but it's a little much." 
 All in all, would I recommend it? Sure. It's a good concept and it'll draw you in. You might guess the ending before you get there, but the process of getting there is still fun.

This is Book 2 in the Tanglewood series, but it can stand alone and it's definitely worth reading, as it's a very happy book. I love the Regency period and often wonder what it would really be like to live back then. Of course, it would probably be better if I had a title than if I had to be a servant. Cora is caught between the two worlds. Her parents almost force their way into society and in an effort to secure their position, they decide to marry her off to a most detestable man. So she runs away and becomes a servant--a housekeeper, to be exact. What would I do if I were in her shoes? I honestly don't know, but it would sure be miserable to be stuck with someone you can't stand. She knows what she wants and won't let anything stand in her way of obtaining it. 
 There's something about Cora, whether it's her teasing nature or sunny disposition, that draws those around her close. Her humor diffuses tense situations and breaks down barriers. Jonathan is considered to be somewhat of a tyrant, but Cora captivates him from first sight. I love the way they balance each other, especially when Cora is able to worm her way in and cause changes around the whole place. I love their relationship so much! I love the little misunderstandings and the slight groveling to resolve the situation. There are some shimmery sparks from the start and it's fun to see what happens, especially with the few little twists. 
 These are characters who are fun, interesting, and easy to adore in a beautiful country setting. I can't wait to get another story in the series!

I loved this book! I just loved it. Jojo Moyes has become one of my Must-Read authors and she did definitely not disappoint with One Plus One. 
 Jess is a young single mother, working multiple jobs to just barely pay the bills. Despite all the hardships in her life, she does the best to always look on the bright side of things and is determined that things will all work out. Ed is a rich software developer with poor relationship skills that has led to him being investigated for insider trading. When their paths cross while Jess is at her lowest point, Ed uncharacteristically offers himself as the solution. Thus starts a multi-day road trip with Jess's two very different children to get to a math Olympiad that could change their lives forever. 
 I'm a huge fan of character driven novels and Moyes really excels at that. All the characters in this book were well developed and grew leaps and bounds throughout. Though told in 3rd person POV, each chapter is dedicated to one of the characters' perspective - Ed, Jess, Nicky, or Tanzie. I honestly loved all of them. Though I got sometimes frustrated with Jess or Ed, I really found them all to be likable characters that you can't help rooting for. 
 I loved the way Jess and Ed's relationship developed and how the romance is subtle and almost takes a backseat to the rest of the story. I loved watching Nicky come out of his shell and start to accept himself for who he is. I really loved Tanzie, how wise beyond her years she is, but also still very much a ten year-old girl. And I also loved Norman, their big, lazy, loyal dog. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed this book. This little review does not do it justice. I would definitely recommend One Plus One to fans of Moyes and character-driven books. Though I got this at the library, I liked it so much that I think I'll end up buying a copy to keep.

The Shadow of the Torturer: Apprentice torturer Severian shows mercy for an imprisoned woman and helps her commit suicide rather than endure weeks of torture. For his crimes, Severian is sentenced to travel too the village of Thrax and take up the post of carnifex. Will Severian make it to Thrax alive? 
 The Shadow of the Torturer isn't your grandmother's fantasy. The tale of Severian isn't the hopeful quest story that's been written and re-written umpteen times in the past fifty years. The setting reminds me of Jack Vance's Dying Earth but much more developed and with the specter of space opera hanging in the background. Gene Wolfe takes the bare bones of the standard quest story and clothes it with literary merit, from the unreliable narrator, Severian, to references to classic works. The scene in the necropolis near the beginning is straight out of Great Expectations. Or straight out of Great Expectations if Pip was an apprentice torturer and helped Magwitch in a fight rather than fetch him a file... 
 Wolfe's writing is baroque and reminds me of the New Weird authors like China Mieville. The Book of the New Sun definitely isn't a beach read. Be prepared to divine the meaning of words from the context. 
 Apart from Severian, the cast isn't all that developed, but then, the unreliable narrator should probably be the center of attention. Dr. Talos and Baldanders steal the show with what little screen time they're given. 
 That's about all I can say without giving too much away. The world Wolfe has built is full of fresh ideas. How many other books do you know that feature two men fighting with flowers with razor sharp leaves? 
 The Claw of the Conciliator: Severian's journey to Thrax continues and his path brings him into contact with both friend and foe. Will he ever make it to Thrax? 
 Claw of the Conciliator continues Severian's rise from apprentice torturer to eventual Autarch. Wolfe's inventiveness grows as Severian encounters man-apes, a giantess, witches, an androgyne who might be The Autarch, a giantess, and many other interesting characters, including Dr. Talos and company. More is revealed about the Claw of the Conciliator, though much mystery remains. I get the feeling a lot of secrets are still lurking in the background. 
 One aspect of The Book of the New Sun I really enjoy is how Gene Wolfe has a lot of sci-fi elements lurking in the background, like aliens, wormholes and the true nature of Jonas, and the casual mention of what might in fact be laser guns. Wolfe's a sly one. 
 My favorite part, by far, is the bit with the alzabo and Severian injesting a piece of Thecla's flesh and experiencing her memories. I suspect this will continue to reverberate through the next two books.  
 I don't want to spoil too much but I enjoyed Claw more than Shadow, possibly because I was used to Wolfe's style. While I felt like I was still in the dark, Wolfe knows how to reveal just enough to keep you firmly ensnared. Like Severian says, it's a hard road. I can't wait to see where it finally leads.
