 OMG. Second time I've written this review because the site was down for maintence. So, this review will be short and sweet. 
 Gretchen Lowell = almost non-existant in this novel. She's mute and incommunicado throughout the majority of the novel - having not spoken a word since being recaptured. A courtroom scene is thrown in as almost an afterthought in the final few pages of the novel - but it's unsatisfying and not at all important to the main storyline - which is disappointing to say the least. 
 Portland is flooding and a serial killer is on the loose - attacking victims near the increasingly high waters with (LAME SPOILER ALERT) blue-ringed octopi. *shakes head and sighs at the ridiculousness of the plot* He's got a vendetta to pay for government-denied deaths relating to a flood that occured fifty-odd years before. (EVEN LAMER SPOILER ALERT) The death he is avenging is a suicide. *pounds head off of desk* Throw in a kidnapped child that the killer is manipulating to kill for him and you've got the novel in a nutshell. Lots of Archie and Susan. No Gretchen Lowell. 
 This novel took a departure from the most charming dynamic in the novel - the Archie-Gretchen relationship - and as such, wasn't near as good as the others in the series. It was a huge let-down in terms of the series and as such took me longer to read. 
 Will I read the next? Es possible - if I remember about the series when the next book is released. HOWEVER, if Gretchen's gone from the limelight in the next novel, I won't pick up another.

Hard to imagine a more satisfying middle-school/young high school read. This is action and adventure, reminiscent of "Pirates of the Caribbean", minus the supernatural elements. Jacky is as plucky a young heroine as you might wish for; her adventures are both extraordinary and plausible. The audio book is a brilliant working of accents and voices. 
 There is an attempted sexual assault and a violent beating, so know your readers. The 12 y/o in our house loved the story beginning to end, and we had some necessary conversations about some of the realistic dangers Jacky finds herself in. By the end, we were rushing out for the second book.

This is my twelfth Dessen novel. In the last two years I have read all of her published works and am now waiting for book thirteen. 
 But back to this one. I really enjoyed this overall. It was understandable why Mclean reacted the way she did to her parents' divorce. I had a hard time liking the mother at all, but she did grow on me a little. 
 All of the friends that Mclean and her dad make in Lakeview are great. Deb is my favorite. She does some odd things that really remind me of myself. I like Dave for the same reasons; I see myself in his character. Riley, Heather, and Ellis were each fun additions, though I wasn't sure about them at first. Opal was excellent. 
 And then there's Jason. He gets his own paragraph because I would like to see more of him. He was a jerk in The Truth About Forever and Along for the Ride, but he seems to have grown so much here. I would really like a novel where he's our main guy. Please Sarah? Can you give me that? I know you could make it great. 
 This isn't my favorite Dessen novel, but it was really good. It's quite well balanced and it, along with some of her other recent books, shows how much she has grown as a writer. 
 The basketball rivalry was fun to see from a distance. Very North Carolina in tone there. And the restaurant was a nice touch.

 This is a companion novel to The Lost Heiress. While we do see a few mentions of Brook and Justin and some of the other characters from the first one, and of course those blasted Fire Eyes. 
 Characters: 
 Lady Rowena Kinnaird - Heir to a Highlander Earldom. 
 Brice Myerston - The New Duke of Nottingham, 
 Lady Pratt - The widow of the late Lord Pratt. 
 As with the first one this isn't even half of the characters, but they are the main ones in my opinion. 
 This story follows Rowena Kinnaird the only Heir to a Highlander Earldom. Her father has been rough with her, her whole life always making sure she follows his every command, and makes herself be hidden inside the castle for the most part. He has also put her in an engagement that could very well cost her, her life later on once they are married. But then she meets Brice and he believes that God has put him there to protect her and take her far away from the Highlands with a marriage in order to keep her safe. She doesn't know what to do as a Duchess though, while she had gone to a boarding school and knows the basics. That was a long time ago, and she has lost a lot of her own confidence since that time period due to the abuse she has suffered at the hands of the two men in her life. 
 Once they are back to England, Brice starts introducing her to all of his friends, but he makes the grave mistake of keeping a big secret from her. While Brice is withholding information from her she becomes friendly with Lady Pratt who she feels is also an outsider to society. 
 As Rowena and Brice slowly start to trust each other, and become friends and later on a married couple. Brice is now one of my favorite male love interests (I can't believe I just said that.), not only was he patient with Rowena about being his wife, he never pushed her to tell him anything, and he was a good God fearing man. While he did flirt without knowing it, he never did it to hurt anyone and most of the time didn't even know he was doing it. 
 Once they start working together as team to try and protect their new family, and Rowena's father even comes to help. We see how strong they both can be together, and how unstoppable. Rowena becomes a strong woman again who will take nothing from no one anymore which I was so glad to see after everything she had been through. 
 Overall I liked this story.I didn't end up enjoying this book as much I did The Lost Heiress, but I still found it enjoyable. It was painfully slow the first 50% of the book, it did get better the last half that it made up for it. I can't wait to see what happens in the third book in the Ladies Of The Manor trilogy and who will make an appearance in it as well.

It is 1895, or so, and the night is the venue for a male dominated dinner. Interestingly, people are not named; they are labelled as the psychologist, the young man, the editor and so on. And, of course, the Time Traveller. Our narrator is, I suspect, not a young man. I suppose it is written in first person once removed- if there is such a thing? 
 After a short demonstration in which a tiny model of the time machine is set and disappears from the room, the guests discuss it amongst themselves and generally decide it is a trick. 
 The next week, they return, (two attended the previous week) but the time traveller is not at home. In an age of servants, they make themselves at home and await his arrival. When he does arrive he is injured, dishevelled, shoe-less, looks greyer and needs a few glasses of champagne to recover. He insists on dressing for dinner and eating before he tells them his tale. 
 Travelling eight hundred thousand years in the future he arrived in a very different world. The people (Eloi) are tiny, physically weak and unintelligent. They have lost language skills and most sentences have only two words. Their social group is flawed; they let one drown without helping or trying to save her. He does and she, Weena, follows him around afterwards. They live in ruinous buildings but huddle together in a kind of communal living. They eat only fruit, they do no work - merely play and make love - and they are terrified of the dark and sleeping alone. He also notices that there are no old or infirm Eloi. 
 But someone has taken the time machine and he suspects it is stored inside a giant sphinx statue that sits near where he left it, as it is too heavy to carry far and the Eloi did not touch it. It disappeared overnight and the Eloi are frightened of the dark. Why? And how can they live like this? Who makes their clothes and shoes? 
 Awakening early one morning, he went to see the sunrise and caught sight of an ape-like creature; a big-eyed nocturnal version of the Eloi. He decides that humanity has split along capitalist and labourer lines and that these two races are the final result. 
 So, in the end, above ground you must have the Haves, pursuing pleasure and comfort and beauty, and below ground the Have-nots, the Workers getting continually adapted to the conditions of their labour. Once they were there, they would no doubt have to pay rent, and not a little of it, for the ventilation of their caverns; and if they refused, they would starve or be suffocated for arrears. 
 He tries to ask Weena about these creatures and she tells him they are called Morlocks, but when pressed, she cries; the only time he saw an Eloi cry. They go exploring together and find a huge building that may have been a museum. He makes a kind of mace as a weapon (he did set out on this exploration woefully unprepared), finds more matches and a jar of camphor. On the walk back, they get caught out after dark and he suddenly understands that the Eloi are the meat the Morlocks eat. They are effectively cattle. The Morlocks attack and he lights a fire to scare them off but it takes hold in the dry forest. 
 He loses Weena in the turmoil and when he makes it back to the Eloi living area he finds the doors of the sphinx statue open and the time machine waiting for him. 
 It is a trap. 
 He escapes, and activates the machine but it is still set to move forward in time, he travels on to a world of complete darkness where the earth has stopped rotating and one side faces the sun. He immediately reverses until light is present in the world and then stops. But this awful, dying world is too much for him. The air is too thin and he returns to his starting time. 
 As he tells the story, he pulls two crushed flowers from his pocket. He has no other proof and although they enjoyed the story, his guests do not believe him. He has a moment of self-doubt where he fears it is all fading from his memory and he runs into his lab but the sight of the dirty machine reassures him. It has moved across the room; the distance from where it landed to where the Morlocks dragged it. 
 The next day, the narrator returns to check on him and catches him with a knapsack and a camera. The traveller asks him to wait half an hour and then he will speak with him and have proof of his ability to time travel. Eager to hear his story of another adventure, he waits, but when he enters the room, the machine is gone and the time traveller with it. 
 And in three years, he has not returned.  
 ~~~~~ 
 This story has been hugely influential in science fiction. Even the name 'time machine' is inextricably linked in our minds as something that travels through time when it could so easily be another word for clock. It has sparked half a dozen TV or film adaptations and maybe thousands of other stories. 
 The story surprises me for what it does mention: Kodak, his concerns about the separation of the haves and have-nots, evolution, psychology, climate change (the dying earth idea), and social degeneration. The same things we worry about today. So, even though it talks of fabulous unreal ideas like time travel, it also has a core of familiarity. 
 The one thing I do wonder about is who was Hettie Potter? The dinner guests amuse themselves with stories of her before the traveller returns. Was she a friend whose name he popped in? She is unGoogleable and was not an actress of the time. If so, like Ianthe he has written her name upon the sands of time*. It seems somehow, appropriate. 
 (*a reference to the poem by Walter Savage Landor) 
 Her Name 
 Well I remember how you smiled 
 To see me write your name upon 
 The soft sea-sand . . . 'O, what a child! 
 You think you're writing upon stone! ' 
 I have since written what no tide 
 Shall ever wash away; what men 
 Unborn shall read o'er ocean wide 
 And find Ianthe's name again.

A few years ago i saw the ITV-screen-adaptation of Persuasion with Sally Hawkins and Rupert Penry-Jones. I was sold immediately and watched it few times since then. I've now read the book for the first time and can happily report that i loved the book as well. It might actually have climbed to my favorite Jane Austen. 
 My favorite scene by far seems to be also the most memorable one, as i've seen it come back in a few reviews: Anne is talking to Captain Harville, Wentworth is sitting a few feet away, writing a letter and at the same time eavesdropping on their conversation. Based on what he hears, he decides to write another letter, that contains the famous words (famous amongst persuasion-lovers that is):  
 I can listen no longer in silence. (...) I am half agony, half hope. Tell me not that I am too late, that such precious feelings are gone for ever. I offer myself to you again with a heart even more your own than when you almost broke it, eight years and a half ago. 
  Aaawwwww.

What happened?! I really liked the first book; I've never encountered a sequel that fell flatter. In no particular order, some things that didn't work for me: 
 Fire, Archer, Big, Small, Horse, monsters--Someone buy Cashore a dictionary; she's in dire need of help in the naming department. On a somewhat related note, add Cashore to my growing list of fantasy authors who can't write horses. 
 I never particularly connected with Fire. It's a tricky thing when your character's special snowflake power is her overwhelming beauty. I don't think this premise succeeds in Fire. I understand Cashore's point: beauty can be a curse. But the vast majority of the narrative consists of men lusting, one way or another, after Fire. It's repetitive and dull, even if the attention is generally unwelcome. And after Archer dies , oh man, Fire becomes insufferable. I wanted to rip my hair out; I settled for rolling my eyes, repeatedly. 
 I swear, Fire spends half this book on her period. I suppose Cashore is trying to diminish taboos around menstruation, but it was a little ridiculous. Sometimes it's better for things to happen offstage. 
 To top it off, the writing wasn't even good. It was clunky and cheesy and filled with far too much exposition and info-dumping. Oh, and so much deus ex machina.
Ugh soooooo good! It's going to a long hard wait for number 3!

Read this in one marathon sitting. As YA problem novels go, this is a solid one, though not at the level of the best. Rainfield isn't a poetic writer. Or especially original. But, dang it, she keeps her plot moving along and her character's voice strong, and that's more than many of her contemporaries can manage. Fans of Ellen Hopkins will probably enjoy this. As molestation stories go, I prefer Such a Pretty Girl, but for cutting, this is way more engaging than Cut. The language is easy to read, even if the subject matter is difficult. 
 As other reviewers have mentioned, Kendra's Lesbianism is comfortably integrated without feeling preachy or sensational. And the focus really is on her abuse survival, revealing how cutting, while alarming and problematic, is a strategy that can soothe and make the intolerable tolerable. 
 On a side note: I've read that the image on the cover is of the author's arms and the author is thrilled with the image. I think this detail, not mentioned in the book, is another selling point. The author is a survivor.

 This is the best series I have read in a long time. It keeps me on edge and guessing at all times. 
 In the last book, the Flash happened...something akin to a solar flare that turned every living thing in its path to ash. Evie lost everyone she knew except Jackson Deveaux who is has turned out to be a very capable protector. 
 Before the Flash, Evie had nightmares, visions and even people talking to her in her head. She thought she was going crazy but now she knows they were all warnings about the Flash and to help her with the game. Yes, the game. She learned...through a boy named Matthew who talks to her in her head...that she is part of a sick and terrifying game that pits teenager against teenager against each other. Each teen or young adult is one of the 22 Major Arcana from a Tarot deck. Evie is The Empress. Each Arcana has powers and Evie finally came into hers at the end of the last book. This game has apparently been going on for thousands of years, the characters being reincarnated again and again. At the end, only one can live. 
 Evie doesn't want to play the game but has to since other players will be coming after her. At the end of the last book, she killed one of them and Jack saw it. She had been keeping it a secret from him but now he knows. 
 Already, two of the Arcana have allied with Evie. Apparently, in previous games, the Empress and Death have always been the last two players so everyone will either align with one of them or go after the two of them. Selena is the Archer and has aligned with Evie even though neither of them trust the other and Selena is hot for Jackson. Matthew is the Fool. He tells Evie that they've always been the best of friends. He sees the past, future and present. He's autistic and the information he gives is sometimes in riddles or doesn't seem helpful but what he says always comes true. He has also aligned with Evie. 
 In this book, Evie is on still on her way to see her grandmother, if she is still alive, so she can tell her how to end the game without having to kill everyone. She has to travel through dangerous territory where cannibals and bagmen live. Bagmen are zombie-like creatures who used to be human but the Flash morphed them into something else. They are super strong and attack people for their blood. They are constantly thirsty and will suck up any water source but prefer blood. Their bite is infectious so more and more humans are turning into bagmen. The cannibals are being led by some crazy person who could be one of the Arcana. 
  
 There are spoilers below. I'm going to try not to spoil the end of the book but there was a lot that happened in this book and this was a major part of it. 
 She gets abducted by Death who she believes is going to kill her. He takes her to his mansion where he is living in luxury while the rest of the world is struggling. She learns that she and Death have a long history. Death has won at least the last two games and is thousands of years old. The winner gets immortality. Death's touch is fatal to anyone except for Evie which he learned in one of the previous games. He went to kill her by touching her but she didn't die so he abducted her. I guess he was so desperate to be able to touch someone, he didn't care if she was his enemy. And apparently, Evie was not a nice person in previous lives. She pretended she liked Death and then tried to kill him and he fell for it twice. Death still seems to be holding on to some kind of feelings for her. He actually is a decent guy. Evie starts to have feelings for him. 
 Even though I felt bad for Death because Evie is the only one he can touch, my heart was breaking for Jackson. I like Jackson and Evie together even though both of them make things difficult on themselves because of their pride and insecurities. While I was reading, I was wondering if this is going to be the start of a long drawn-out love triangle. I certainly hope not. Either you love one or the other. I was just hoping Evie didn't choose Death because he can't have anyone else. 
  
 This book introduced many more characters and the game is getting more complicated. There's the army out there terrorizing everyone still. Evie learns that the Lovers who are a pair of sick and demented twins who like to torture people are part of that army. Their father leads it. 
 And then there are all of the other players out there that have yet to be revealed. 
 This series is so exciting!

I think the premise of this story was a great idea. Eliza's notebook of all her personal fears is stolen by the group of popular boys at her school and they won't give it back until she does some of the very tasks in the notebook that she's afraid of doing. I like! 
 However, I found the story to be overbearingly juvenile. 
 The main character Eliza didn't have a strong personality. It's hinted at that she's the smart girl, shy, curvy, unnoticeable. And yet the way she speaks and acts a few times doesn't fit into that stereotype very well. She seems like she could be the life of the party. It just came off as lazy characterization. 
 I really hated the false Southern stereotype of the friend Clarice. Such gems like 'Clarice is from the South so she's never heard of Cheetos.' FALSE. 'Clarice is from the South so she thinks it's normal to leave your doors unlocked.' FALSE. 'Clarice always dresses up, even at 4 in the morning. It must be a Southern thing.' Obviously the author has never been to the South. Sadly, we have a strong relationship with Cheetos, which causes us to be so fat we resort to wearing only sweatpants and are too fat to outrun all the robbers and murderers who break in even though our doors were locked. (I kid, I kid! but seriously, the South is not a different country. If Clarice doesn't eat Cheetos and is too trusting, that's a personal problem. Don't blame it on a region.) 
 More than once the main characters would have lightbulb moments where they come up with some brilliant plan and they all state in ALL CAPS that OMG it's SUCH A BRILLIANT PLAN, WHY DIDN'T WE THINK OF THAT BEFORE? But the thing was... these were such obvious things to me. 
 There was frequent, and strong profanity. There were frequent references to sex and drinking. It wasn't in there to be edgy or make a statement so it just made things feel a little shallow to me. 
 It was a fun and entertaining read, but honestly it failed to have any significance. It was straightforward with no twists. I came up with 2 theories while reading that honestly would have made things more exciting.  1- That Clarice and Marissa, the two BFFs were secretly the ones manipulating Eliza. These two ding-bats kept disappearing throughout the night and several items it was mentioned that they were texting right before Eliza would receive new instructions via a text. 2- That in the end Connor would have been behind it all to stage some big romantic gesture to win back Eliza.  Furthermore there was this giant lesson looming over the entire plot that was never actually pointed out-  that Eliza has been holding it against Connor that he dated her because of some list from his frat friends, when here she was doing the same thing and following their instructions to check off items on a list. She should have realized they were even and seen Connor's viewpoint of being bullied and then forgiven him . This plot set up these things so well, but without including any of them it just simply fell flat.

I never had the relationship with my siblings that Maya and Lochan have with theirs. In fact, it was the opposite of what they had. We rarely got along with each other. Even now. So for me, it was hard to imagine that you could in fact fall in love with a brother or sister. And I had my doubts about this book. Especially because of the theme of it. It's a heavy and serious subject and some people just can't handle it. But I gave it a shot, with my doubts and all. Thinking: 'how can this ever be a good book?' Boy, was I wrong. 
 "How can something so wrong, feel so right?" 
 That is the big question in this book. And through the course of the book I found myself asking why it is wrong? If I were Maya, I would've probably fallen in love with Lochan too. They're both so fragile, loving, vulnerable and protective that I could not NOT love them. I just couldn't hate them. I felt everything they felt and I cared for them. Really cared. It left me breathless at times. I sobbed and even cried because of them. Their brothers Kit and Tiff and sister Willa are such great characters! Willa and Tiff made me laugh and cry and sob along with all the kids of that family. That family is just so fucked up. Their father is a first class asshole that left them years ago and their mother... God, I hated that woman. At times I wished I could pull her out of the book just to give her a hard slap on her face. She is such a bad mother. What am I saying? Bad? She probably is a prime example of the worst mothers in the world. Yeah, I really hated her. 
 "The human body needs a constant flow of nourishment, air and love to survive. Without Maya I lose all three; apart we will slowly die. " 
 What else can I say about this story? It was written perfectly. I got to now the characters, the story didn't go to fast, it wasn't exaggerated. An ending I never saw coming. An ending I never wanted, though it is as perfect as the rest of the story in a way. I really am a mess because of this story, but I don't mind. I'm glad I've read it. Everybody should read it. In the end, you'll be glad you did. 
 This is a story about love. About two people who fall in love. They shouldn't, but you can't stop love. You can't choose love. Love chooses you. And sometimes, love is really hard. 
 I can hear you thinking. 'But their brother and sister, that's wrong!' blablabla. No. I had a fucked up childhood to, but that was partly because of my brothers, so I can't even think of falling in love with them. (Yuk) But the kids here in this story? Their home is falling apart. Their father already gone for years and now that stupid thing that calls herself a mother leaves them too for a stupid boyfriend. They are left alone and Lochan and Maya take responsibility in taking care of their brothers and sister. They have to grow up so fast in such a short time and it's not strange that they find comfort in each other after being pushed in parenting roles. Lochan is so shy and feels so alone in the world. I know that feeling. The feeling that you are alone in the whole goddamn world even when you are surrounded by so much people. The feeling that you want to scream very loud and nobody would hear you. I get that. I've been there. And then there comes Maya. Someone who knows how he feels, understands it. Someone who hears his inner screams. It's definitly not strange that they love each other as something more than brother and sister. In a way, it felt right. And that's why you should give this book a chance. 
 "At what point do you give up - decide enough is enough? There is only one answer really. Never." 
 To conclude this (for me) very long review I want to give you all my opinion on the subject. I think it's bullshit that these relationships are illegal. Seriously. Maya and Lochan are so much more than siblings. They are soulmates, best friends,... Their love shouldn't be forbidden. It should be celebrated. And the fact that I want to throw up when I even think of kissing my own brother doesn't matter. As I always say: love is love. The only thing that counts is the happiness of the ones that are in the relationship. As long as they get their happily ever after, it's good. Who do you think you are taking that away from to people just because it is 'wrong'? That, in my very honest opinion, is sick. Not the relationship they have, but the people that judge them because they are siblings. If you ask me, they are just jealous. Love is love and everyone deserves a happy ending. And it's sad that Maya and Lochan didn't get theirs.

Title: Will and Patrick Do the Holidays 
 Series: Wake Up Married, Episode 3 
 Author: Leta Blake and Patty Griffiths 
 Genre: Gay Romantic Comedy, Serial Style 
 Pages: 117 Pages 
 Release Date: November 23, 2015 
 Publisher: Leta Blake Books 
 Stars: 4 
 Heat: 4 
 Review: 
 This episode of the "Will and Patrick" saga was finally a book with some heat! For all of you who have been dying for a little sexy action between our two guys.. well this book delivers!! 
 In this episode we get to follow Will and Patrick as they spend time with Will's family during the holiday season. The way Will's family treats Patrick is so unfriendly and full of snide remarks about Will's ex-boyfriend Ryan. It really made me have some hateful feelings towards Will's Family and I hope they are able to redeem themselves in following installments. 
 The overall dynamic between Will and Patrick is changing in this saga. These two are going from strangers married to something more.. Will wants to spend time with Patrick. Patrick begins to enjoy spending time with Will and the chemistry between the two.. heats up. 
 For most of this saga the chemistry has been at a slow burn or non-existent stage, well the authors definitely bump it up a notch as these guys finally reconnect. To say their bedroom life will be boring.. would be very misleading. In addition to the chemistry heating up, episode three shows us a different side of Patrick as he lays claim to Will in more ways than one. Patrick is embracing his married life (well more than he was in previous episodes) and we get a sneak peak of Alpha Patrick, possessive and sexy Patrick, and doctor Patrick who is always worried about and caring for his husband. I think out of the characters, Patrick has done the most growth in this serial thus far and it will be exciting to see how far the authors take him. 
 In addition to the fun and sexy stuff in this Saga, I appreciate the author's ability to deal with a chronic disease and allow the reader to see some of what a diabetic and alcoholic has to deal with on a daily basis. The restrictions, treatments, and never ending pull towards alcohol are very real and the authors do a great job of showing this in the book. Creating Will with these chronic conditions and then having him meet a brilliant doctor and subsequently marry him allows Will to have someone who not only wants to help take care of him, but understands the disease process and issues that Will has to face daily. 
 At the end of this episode I think there are a couple sentences that sum up Will and Patrick's feelings. 
 "Despite everything, despite how stupid it might be, Will's happy, and Patrick is too. The Consequences can wait."

Wow, Jo. This is hella grown up. Sex, drugs, rape, abuse, neglect, and local politics. All very sad topics. In a way, this novel reminded me of a nonfiction book I read years ago called Random Family. They're both about the causes and consequences of poverty, and how and why efforts to help the poor fail so often. 
 Of course, Random Family was entirely about poor people, but The Casual Vacancy is also about the middle class. This book's main villain is Howard Mollison, a hugely obese man who owns a successful shop and is the heavyweight(!) in the local political scene. I thought J.K. made him a little too detestable, but it was all leading up to a point that really hit home well, the scene where the fat man is decrying the public funds spent on helping drug addicts and the doctor points out that (with socialized medicine) public funding has also been spent on his obesity-related illnesses . 
 I think this may be a book written by a bleeding heart liberal for bleeding heart liberals, so as a huge Harry Potter fan and a super bleeding heart liberal, how could I not like it? I also love what I think of as gossipy books: books about the nitty gritty dirty realistic details of everyday ordinary lives--stuff like John Updike or Anne Tyler. Who's cheating on whom? Who seems happy but secretly hates their life? Stuff like that. 
 Another thing I liked about this book is that the story was balanced between the adult and teen world. I think that may be why the book was overlong. There are like 12 main characters, maybe six adults and six teens (now that I think about it, maybe more--Wikipedia lists 19 characters). As we saw in HP, Rowling is especially gifted at capturing the worldview of young people. In HP it was angsty but in TCV it was downright depressing. Teenagers are crazy. But also compelling. We were all that young and stupid once. Well, maybe not as stupid as Krystal or as sociopathic as Fats or as depressed as Sukhvinder, but maybe more like Andrew, who I thought of as a zitty version of Harry if he'd never been a wizard. 
 I would NOT recommend this to fans of Harry Potter, unless you also happen to be an adult who doesn't mind reading super depressing stories about how our civilization fails people on so many levels. 
 Still, I liked it.

I can understand why this Jane Austen novel isn't as famous as most of her other ones. It just isn't as good as her other novels. 
 This book follows Lady Susan Vernon, her daugther Frederica and her sister-in-law Mrs Vernon; and it is the first time with a Jane Austen novel that i find myself cheering for the downfall of the lead character. 
 What bothered me the most about this book is not so much the story or the characters, but the method she used to write this book: via letters. We get to see letters from Lady Susan to her best friend, and from her sister in law to the latter's mother. That could be fine, if those letters where also really written as letters.  "Age of Miracles" is a modern coming-of-age story with an apocalyptic setting, exploring human reaction to catastrophe and the ability to adapt to altered circumstances - from the perspective of an 11-year-old girl. With her novel Walker challenges the reader to consider the impact of unexpected changes, threatening all the things we take for granted, including our own future. 
 Julia is on the cusp of womanhood, coming to terms with her own changing body, her friendships with her peers, the pressures of school and her confusion over her changing feelings about boys. One morning Julia and her parents learn frightening news - overnight the earth's rotation has inexplicably slowed, prolonging the interval between night and day and altering life as they have known it forever. As days and nights progressively lengthen and humans are confronted with the changes wrought by the phenomenon, Julia must not only come to terms with her own life's challenges, but also those of a changing world that poses a threat to everything she has ever known. 
 I am not normally a fan of apocalyptic settings (with a few exceptions), but since this was a bookclub read with a very promising and unique premise, I put my prejudices aside and spent a few lazy Sunday hours reading this novel - I don't mind to be proven wrong in my set ideas about certain genres. However, despite Julia's fresh voice and engaging narrative, I cannot say that I particularly liked the journey the book took me on. The rather depressing doomsday atmosphere aside, the story didn't work for me on several levels. Exploring a catastrophic event through the eyes of an eleven-year-old girl raised more questions than it attempted to answer, which made for a very unsatisfying conclusion. Furthermore, the fact that Julia is an only child, rather passive and a bit of a loner further narrows the perspective of the event, making it almost banal in parts of the novel, which I found extremely frustrating. Faced with a threat to humankind as a whole, I would expect more dramatic responses than, for example, the hoarding of food and arguments over which time to keep in the face of lengthening daylight and darkness hours. It's like worrying about missing your favourite soapie in the midst of a category 5 cyclone! I have experienced a major natural disaster in my lifetime, and expected to read about some of the intense emotions experienced when confronted with a threat to life from forces out of our control - the fear, the panic, the anger and only much later the resignation Walker describes. For me, this did not come across in the novel, which was somewhat disappointing and very unsatisfying. 
 That said, Walker's novel may appeal more to a YA audience, who are more in touch with the problems Julia is experiencing and may be satisfied with the lack of answers to all the questions the story instantly raised in my mind (Why is the earth's rotation slowing? How exactly does that affect the birds? Etc etc.). But compared to other classic apocalyptic novels, such as John Wyndham's The Day of the Triffids (which I loved, incidentally), the story falls totally flat, giving us none of the highs and lows and satisfying conclusion that would make reading it worthwhile. I do give points to Walker for coming up with an imaginative, original idea - and I did like her prose, which flowed very well. Not bad for a few hours of light reading on the beach, but don't look for too much depth or meaning or you will be disappointed.

This started out slow and then petered out toward the end, but the middle was really good.  That said, I think I understand some of the criticism I've read. For one, the three points of view were (at times) difficult to separate as POV changes were not always well delineated. Therefore, it requires some work on the part of the reader to keep track of who is speaking. 
 Not much seems to happen in the beginning of the book. I'm a pretty patient reader, though after about 60-70 pages I was still waiting for something to happen. 
 This book also doesn't really fit well into any particular genre, though has elements of several different genres making it feel as if Abbott couldn't figure out what she wanted this to be. 
 Still, it's well-written and though the themes are subtle, I think they are poignant. Honestly, I'm surprised by some of the negative reviews. 
 Personally, I can't wait to read more of her novels.

 As a kid, "Alice in Wonderland" was one of my favorites. The ides of diving down the rabbit hole and coming out the other side into a world of backwards rules and impossible imaginings was so great that I would dream of my own adventure. 
 So of course when I saw "Alice in Zombieland" I couldn't resist. 
 And I'm so happy that I didn't. 
 There was a rabbit hole, although it was more metaphorical than anything, and I dove down and into it. 
 For beginners, I'd like to start off with something spoiler-free: this book was one of the most hysterical horror-comedies I have ever read. I couldn't stop laughing, actually spit out water and tea from bursting into hysterics (I had to stop myself reading whenever I wanted to drink something because I was afraid to spit it onto myself... again), and in the end I was trying to piece everything together alongside Ali (a.k.a. Alice Bell). 
 Altogether I gave this book 4.5 stars. 
 That's right. 
 And THAT surprised me, too. 
 Now we're heading into the spoiler section... 
 ... which means you either have read it and are willingly following me down the rabbit hole (see what I did there?) or you haven't because you don't think it's worth it. And that's fine. 
 You're wrong, but it's fine. 
 The story flowed very easily through this novel. You have the protagonist go through something traumatizing and come out on the other side, you have her spiritual eye open - if you will - and have her life turned completely upside down as her whole family dies. And then attacked by zombies. 
 But they aren't normal zombies. 
 This is why I have to give Gena Showalter credit: she took a classic monster and CHANGED IT COMPLETELY. They are actually spirits infected by evil, feasting on a person's spirit (rather than flesh), and in order to fight them the slayer MUST be in the spirit realm as well. 
 So on top of the crazy spirit-eating zombies you have the slayers who are able to leave their bodies in order to fight them in the spiritual realm. Which was SO FREAKING COOL. 
 The characters were definitely unique, in that Kat was insane and amazing, Ali was hysterical and sarcastic as hell, Cole was broody with a reason and then lovable, her grandparents were ridiculous, and so on and so on... 
 I'm not running through the entire character list. 
 BUT! 
 Between the unique cast and this incredible hidden world on top of ours, just in spiritual form, made this book a gem in and of itself. I enjoyed the way that it was written, the way that the story flowed, and the originality was off the charts for me. This was definitely a zombie story I will never forget, nor is it an "Alice in Wonderland" retelling that will be forgotten. 
 I had one major issue, but in the grand scheme of things it pales in comparison to how I felt about the book. One characters - Reeve - dropped out of the book. No explanations, no mention except about her father, just... gone. 
 Which didn't change the story, but I felt like it was something that should have been addressed. 
 Whatever. 
 It was awesome. 
 And Ali's snark was perfect and necessary for keeping it feeling like the Walking Dead (I mean come on, lighten up guys). The humor kept me flipping the pages and never once did the story feel as if it were becoming stale. 
 It was fun, it was fresh, and I craved more. 
 And so I caved and bought the other three books. 
 I know. 
 I can't wait to read them. 
 This rabbit hole just keeps on going deeper. I just know it. 
 So overall, I had to take a half star away for the lack of explanation as to what happened to Reeve. I know it wasn't that big of a deal, but it was still an issue and therefore I cannot ignore it. 
 So... yeah. 
 That's about it. 
 The book deserves its 4.5 stars.

Elisa is the younger princess of a feudal fantasy kingdom. Her older sister is beautiful, poised, charismatic, and thin, while she always feels stupid, unprepared, and ungainly. She's quickly married to the king of a neighboring kingdom, in part simply to get her out of her own kingdom, where assassins already target her. For Elisa is not just a young fat princess who loves to read and worship God; she's also the bearer of a Godstone, and as such, fated to play some heroic part. When she arrives in her new kingdom, she finds that her husband hasn't even told anyone that they're married, and so she must endure the court's disrespect. But then she's kidnapped for her Godstone, befriends her kidnappers, realizes that she should (and almost more importantly, can) help them beat off their invaders, and then returns to her husband's court in triumph.  
 By the second half, Elisa was a little over-competent and confident for a sheltered teenager who until a few months before had only cared about food and religious texts. Though we're told from the start that she has a Godstone and as such will be called upon for a heroic deed, I thought her solution to the Invierne invasion was a little too convenient. I would've liked other characters to feel a little more fleshed out, and I want to know far more about the Invierne. My guess is that they're all a lost colony from a Spanish speaking country/countries on Earth, and have split off and evolved separately.  Overall, I liked this. I liked the world building, the descriptions of food (those coconut tarts sound so good!), and Elisa herself.

And even through they are constantly thrown together and he is still her greatest support they still just never seem to click (as a friend of mine would say- Gale has been friendzoned).

The rebel president Coin is actually just like president Snow even down to his hair colouring and eyes. She is definitely not above blowing up a few innocent children, including her own people and leading people to believe its the Capitol.  In the end Katniss isnt even the one who openly chooses between Gale and Peeta. It does become obvious that the new regime is a democracy, with representatives from each district. And there are never any hunger games and it seems that district 12 becomes completely self sufficient, yet you can only assume from these little tit-bit that its worked out better. Collins seems to feel that you need to decide that for yourself. In the end it would seem that Katniss looses everyone who she is close to and that the names of her children are never give, that she had to be convinced to have them and that she still wakes up screaming every night tells me that at the end of it all she is a very broken woman.

October 28, 2011 Reading "Room" by Emma Donoghue actually listening to the audiobook. It is about a woman who was kidnapped at age 19 and held prisoner in a tiny soundproof room for 7 years. She has a child while there. It is told from the 5 year-old boy's perspective which is precisely why I like it and why my husband Randy really doesn't. 
 To five-year-old Jack, Room is the entire world. It is where he was born and grew up; it's where he lives with his Ma as they learn and read and eat and sleep and play. At night, his Ma shuts him safely in the wardrobe, where he is meant to be asleep when Old Nick visits. -- Room is home to Jack and he is basically happy, but to Ma, it is the prison where Old Nick has held her captive for seven years. Totally plausible when you hear about people like Jaycee Dugard, Elizabeth Smart, etcetera on the news. Through determination, ingenuity, and fierce motherly love, Ma has created a life for Jack and educated him as best she could considering she was taken while still a child. But she knows it's not enough...not for her or for him. She devises a bold escape plan, one that relies on her young son's bravery and a lot of luck. What she does not realize is just how unprepared she is for the plan to actually work. 
 Told entirely in the limited language of the energetic, pragmatic five-year-old Jack, ROOM is a celebration of resilience and the limitless bond between parent and child, a brilliantly executed novel about what it means to journey from one world to another. The writing style wasn't easy to follow or read but that was much of the charm of the story. I got used to it eventually, just as I did in Push by Sapphire but that doesn't make it easier to read. The 5-year-old voice and perspective make this book bearable since it is a very emotionally haunting topic. I could not have read the same story had it been narrated with the mother's voice, thoughts, and reflections.

 Lady Elyne de Burgh or Ellie is the daughter of one of the most powerful men in Ireland who has aligned himself with Edward I. Her sister talks her into going with her to jump of the cliffs for the annual celebration of Maiden's plunge where all the virgins jump off the cliffs into the cold sea.  She swims back to shore via Mermaid's cave and stumbles onto a group of men who look like pirates having some kind of meeting. One man wants to kill her right then but Hawk, who she doesn't know, convinces the other man that he will take her out to sea and kill her and then proceeds to kidnap her and take her out to sea. Ellie thinks she is going to die and never see her family again but Hawk tells her that he is just going to keep her for a while and then return her after she is not a danger to his plans. She believes he is a pirate and might use her against her family so she lies and tells him she is a nursemaid for the Earl of Ulster instead of his daughter. 
 Hawk is meeting with some Irish mercenaries who will meet him on the 13th and with at least 150 men and who he will then take to another location to fight with Robert Bruce against the English. When Ellie stumbles upon their meeting, the Irish leader wants to kill her but he doesn't want to kill an innocent woman so he adducts her. He gets to open water and tries to sneak by a few English ships and would have succeeded but Ellie jumped out of his boat and starts screaming. The English spot them but Hawk manages to get Ellie back in the boat and escape. 
 At first, Ellie's family think she has drown but hear about the incident where the English sailors had witnessed Ellie with the pirates and now the English are out searching for her. 
 Now, he is laying low on Spoon Isle while he waits out the time until the mission with the bossy little nursemaid. He is used to getting his way with women but with Ellie, his charm isn't working. She is seemingly immune to his charisma and good looks. He can see the English ships and wonders why they are patrolling so heavily. He has no idea his captive is someone of importance. 
 I loved how the romance developed between Ellie and Hawk. I thought it was funny how Ellie just rolled her eyes and ignored Hawk's flirting which annoyed the heck out of him. And I was rolling with laughter when he told the people on the island that the reason she was with them was because she fancies herself in love with him and stowed away on his boat which everyone believed because most lasses fall all over him but Ellie was mortified by it. 
 This author has a way with making my emotions zigzag all over the place. One minute I'm laughing then I'm angry, wanting to slap Hawk for his misogynistic ways and then I'm sad because one doesn't feel the way the other does and I think they aren't going to end up together. It's crazy how Monica McCarty, the author, can manipulate my moods so well. That's some excellent writing!

Bitterblue by Kristin Cashore. 
 Quickie review: Confusing at first, and definitely a struggle to get through the first half. But it's worth the struggle (in my opinion, at least), because the second half is twisted and complicated and wonderfully convoluted. 
 Finally, it was just thought-provoking. This book was extremely thought-provoking. 
 Rambling review: This novel has left me feeling very conflicted. I don't quite know what to think of it. 
 See the problem is--and I'm willing to bet that many of you also dealt with this--that the first half was difficult to get through, to put it bluntly. Not because it was poorly written or anything, but because it was simply slow. So utterly slow. So slow that I've actually gotten this book from the library several times before, but could never get past the beginning because it was--as stated before--slow. It didn't immediately draw me into the story, and so I gave it up at the time. I tried to restart it several times after that, but each time, the same thing happened. Couldn't get into it, so I dropped it. 
 And then, six months later, I finally pick it up again and tell myself: "You are reading this. No matter what. Suck it up, and read man. Um, girl. Yeah." 
 Thus comes the first main point of this rambling review: Bitteblue requires a lot of patience. A lot of it. Buckets of that stuff. I also think it helps if you're a devoted follower of the series. And...if you hadn't done what I'd done and read Bitteblue an entire YEAR after Fire. Oops. 
 But! The silver lining in that is that if you do persevere through, then you will be greatly rewarded. Honestly. Because the second half of this book is phenomenal. 
 Why? You might ask. Oh I can give you the answer in less than five words. 
 Things. Start. Making. Sense. 
 Let's tack on a "Hallelujah" to that sentence too. 
 Another problem I had with the first, oh, a hundred fifty pages, besides the pacing was the way everything was sort of scattered. There's probably a fancier, literary term/phrase for this...but since eye dee kay what it is, we're sticking with scattered. 
 Scattered. There would be a bit about the Council and Katsa and Po here, then a little nugget about ciphers, then some random observation like, "Oh! That statue is of me!", some anecdote about Saf and his crew, the advisers being weird (and that is putting it very lightly), and more of Bitterblue's puzzlement. We are just as puzzled as she is, and also getting just as FED UP with everything as she is. 
 There were just so many random events and details that didn't make sense, and oh lord, the QUESTIONS. Heaps of questions. So many that at one point, I really didn't care enough about the story to actually wonder what their answers were. 
 Ouch. That sounds harsh. I may be making the first half sound worse than it actually is, but I'm just trying to give a fair warning to y'all. 
 But that's really my only complaint about this novel. Everything else was great! You might point out that my single con spans two hundred pages, and to which my reply would be...actually, I'll get back to you on that. 
 Anyway, the second half? Awesome. Just awesome. What started out as seemingly simple if a bit sporadic clue-hunt has evolved into this intricate, political and psychological crisis. 
 It just blew me away, how the pieces began fitting together and locking into place. 
 Oh, and just think about how much thought Kristin Cashore must've put into drafting and plotting this novel. Actually, I can't think about it. Thinking about it would make my brain hurt. 
 The plot is just so immense. And the damaged psychological effects from Leck's reign and how it affects the characters and events in Bitteblue and just the whole psychological aspect of it and how truly "messed-up" it is--ridiculously convoluted and absurdly complex. Cashore must've spent at least a year in planning and wondering if she could pull it off. 
 Oh, but she did. 
 Looking back, one just really sees how subtle Cashore was. Every single tiny fragment, no matter how miniscule it was, connects in the end. And then on top of that, there's the overarching theme or mood or feeling that keeps tugging at the reader: These people are traumatized. They need help. 
 I just cannot emphasize enough how convoluted and complicated this story turned out. In a good way. 
 The damaged advisers, their frail mental state--oh my word. 
 The whole plotline about about her advisers was raw to the bone. It tears at you; it's horrifying and shocking and gets so emotional for the reader. 
 I guess what I'm really trying to say is that the psychological hurting aspect of this novel is the strongest part of it--it rubs you raw. 
 Freakishly complicated to do, but Cashore has done it really well. 
 Final thought: The theme of this novel. Wow. How sometimes, in order to recover, one can't just try to move onward, and just forget the past because it hurts too much. How one sometimes has to remember, has to relive the pain, in order to learn from their mistakes and truly get redemption. But also how sometimes, some people are too fragile to do it. 
 See what I mean by immense and convoluted?! That theme is just one of incredible depth and philosophy. 
 Bitterblue is less of a 'plot' novel and more of a 'thought' novel. In blunt terms, it messes with your mind. Tampers with your emotions. 
 And you're left feeling very very conflicted.

If I am being totally honest this isn't a full 4 stars for me. It's more like a 3.8. 
 Cons: 
 -The writing is beautiful but it really made a grand entrance. The book opens with Lia describing the scene so poetically that I was a bit overwhelmed and it wasn't until later on that I started feeling any connection and ease of reading. 
 - Confusing characters. YES I KNOW THIS WAS INTENTIONAL. But I caught on very quickly that something was up and I kept going back and trying to deduce things from previous chapters and it just slowed me down. I don't think the final payoff was worth the confusion.  
 -I did not like the design of the randomly inserted songs and poems that came before some chapters. They was no organization to where they were placed, they did not occur before every chapter, or every chapter from a certain POV, they just seemed thrown in randomly and I guess a prefer a little order when elements like these are thrown in. Yes, I know this is a silly thing to mention in a review, but I could not get past it! 
 -That map. This map was the worst map that could be present in a fantasy novel and it did this book a HUGE disservice. While it was nice to see the general location of the main kingdoms, the map image did not line up at all with the directions mentioned in the story. Lia frequently comes across woods and rivers that do not exist on the map. She frequently heads east in the text, but on the map it's really north. She mentions some important town SEVERAL times that isn't on the map, and the location where it should be according to his is just an ocean. None of the cities are to scale, which obviously a fantasy map won't be 100% accurate on something like this, but when she enters one city she describes the landmarks to be remarkably larger than anything in her kingdom and yet they appear as a mere blip on the map next to her castle which takes up half the page. I would have preferred if the map had more prominently featured the main locations in the story more than trying to encompass the whole world. 
 Pros: 
 -Lia is a likeable main character. I was immediate impressed by her and rooting for her. 
 -I like Rafe, and the promise of what he will bring to the story in the future. 
 -It kept me reading. I read large chunks at a time and kept wanting to come back to this book. It sometimes wasn't the easiest read and didn't always have a lot of action but something just kept gripping me.

Many folks have fond memories of reading the Narnia books as children. I loved "The Lion, The Witch, and the Wardrobe" as a kid and enjoyed it as an adult. Now that I'm re-reading the series with children of my own, I'm struck by how un-charming, pedestrian and just plain 'blah' several of the other books are. "The Silver Chair" is my least favorite, and that's saying a lot, given my distaste for "The Horse and His Boy" and the even worse "Voyage of the Dawn Treader." Here, the characters are thin and wholly unremarkable. Lewis' narration is grating, smug, and superior. And his story telling is just a shambles. It is as if he decided climaxes were a bad idea and gave up on them altogether. But I'm an adult; perhaps my kids are a better audience? 
 The seven and nine year-old both give it a big, fat "Meh." The older one says that Eustace isn't "such an interesting guy." The younger one wants to know why it's called "The Silver Chair" when the titular furniture only appears briefly. The whole thing lacked any urgency and felt like a recycling of the first two books in the series. 
 I know successful authors can have lesser works ("The Butter Battle Book" isn't quite "Green Eggs and Ham," "King John" doesn't compare to "Hamlet"). But I really am astonished at the longevity of this series that begins well and then falls completely apart. Magyk, Half Magic, The Book of Three, Inkheart, Redwalland even The Field Guide are all better better fantasy series, as far as I'm concerned.

The first in a series of a modern take on the historical 'mail order bride'. 
  Ethan's friend Rob has taken a practical joke too far. He's set up a drunken speech on Youtube and used it as an ad to find a wife. Application after application comes in for Ethan, and Rob diligently goes through and finds a woman for his friend. But Ethan knows nothing about any of it. 
 Autumn applies to be a cowboy's wife in a desperate attempt to save her job. She is on the verge of losing her position at a magazine and figures that writing an expose about the desperate cowboy might be just the way to save it. 
 What neither of them counts on when Autumn shows up at the ranch is their quick attraction for one another. Autumn realizes she can't write the expose because she'd have to pretend that her feelings for Ethan didn't matter and that she was ready to walk away from him - which she most definitely isn't. 
 Ethan is mad at Rob for setting him up with this woman...the woman he just can't get out of his head. He comes around to the idea of having Autumn on the ranch and slowly, slowly comes to love her. 
 They did tell a lot of lies, or half-truths in the beginning which hindered their final relationship, but once those mis-steps came into the open, it was a quick path to love and romance for Ethan and Autumn.

This was nice. Strange and unexpected, but still nice. I particularly enjoyed the mythology of Anansi (the spider...or the rabbit depending on which stories you believe, but most likely a spider), which is effectively interwoven into a rather contemporary story of a man who after much turmoil and trouble finally comes to terms with who he really is, in this fun tale that is often quite funny. 
 The real appeal for me, though, was Gaiman's characters, 'cause I'm generally a sucker for interesting and original characters. Add to that my love of myth as a whole, and this was satisfying on many levels. 
 If you're a fan of Gaiman, you probably already know what to expect so expect to get him doing what he does well, and if not(a fan), well be prepared for something different, but in a good way.

The actual description of the story is awful, so here is one written by me: 
 Morgan Stockhour is a 15 year old girl who lives on Internment-- an island in the clouds that is ruled by a king. Since it is an island in the clouds there are several laws/controls put in place in order to maintain a steady living environment. One such law is when you are born you are assigned a betrothal. This is easily done because pregnancies are controlled by the government. When a couple wants a child they put their name on a waiting list and when someone dies the couple next on the list can create a child. The sex of the child is also controlled through science, so the betrothal will be to that of the opposite sex. Morgan's betrothal is to a boy named Basil. 
 Morgan has a family as well. A mother and father plus an older brother, Lex, and sister-in-law, Alice. Lex is a Jumper-- someone who has crossed the fence and peered over the edge of Internment and viewed the vast nothingness of the sky. Lex is disabled (blind) due to this and is part of a support group with other jumpers. Having a Jumper in the family is kind of scandalous, but none of the main characters we interact with in the story care too much. Morgan often catches herself daydreaming about the edge and wondering what would happen if she peered over. She tries her best to avoid these thoughts though as the edge drives people mad. 
 Our plot starts out when there is a murder on Internment-- something that has not happened in about a generation or so. This murder is different than the other one though, according to Morgan's parents. People are afraid and don't want to leave their homes. The patrolmen are all over the city after the murder, keeping watch. Someone is accused of the murder, and Morgan actually runs into this person where I will stop to avoid much more spoilers. 
 The side characters of the story are very well put together. I don't think there is one that is haphazardly thrown in there which is really nice. I like to care about characters. Morgan herself isn't that bad either. She is naive as a 15 year old but she does question the world she lives in which also helps the holes in the world-building (though not many holes, it just fits that we know what the character knows). Basil is my favorite character. This next comment I will put as a spoiler to avoid spoiler-ish opinions but it isn't that big --  I sincerely hope that there will be no love triangles later on in the series. I know that Basil is her betrothed and books like these like to have people break away from the dystopian rules, but can't we keep the fact that there was a boy born for Morgan? Can't we keep the idea of soul mates, even in a world where birthrates are that highly controlled? Please?  I love Basil and he is just the right amount of protective over Morgan. He is just a great match for her. 
 Basil may be my favorite, but Lex, Alice, Pen (Morgan's best friend), Amy (member of the Jumper group), others, and even up to Thomas (Pen's betrothed) are just so very well crafted. As a person who reads for characters I love it. 
 Small qualms about the book is that the last third or so are incredibly rushed and kinda random. I understand one event  Judas leads Morgan (who is supposed to be dead from poison from the government) off the flying machine underground they were hiding in to go "kill the king" for revenge of the death of her parents, but Morgan ends up kidnapped by the Prince and Princess of Internment. Her friend Pen is also kidnapped because Pen found Morgan as she was a concerned friend looking for her  is to bring another character or two into the scene, but it was just very rushed. 
 Overall I am looking forward to the next one and hope the story goes in a direction I like. I'm not sure what to expect. :)

I have to ask...What is the big deal with this series??? 
 I have read Foundation, and honestly, it left me flat. I have geared myself up for an epic SciFi novel, and found myself reading something resembling an instruction manual instead. The novel revolves around psychohistorians who successfully apply mathematics to social studies with an end result of detailed prediction of the future. The concept is very interesting I admit. However, Asimov's writing is not that ingenious and leaves much to be desired. 
 His characters are presented as dehumanized logic obsessed calculators, witch is a fact that doesn't help the story. I understand that these people are supposed to be extremely intelligent and can quickly apply a mathematical formula to any living situation, but if you don't allow a human factor into the equation you have successfully produced a novel in witch you describe how a computer computes. An incredibly boring read. The points that the psychohistorians made throughout the novel were not too groundbreaking, rather than common sense. What goes up, must come down. Everything has its birth, life and death. That includes an enormous Empire. Politicians lie. Religion can be used as a method of control of the masses. The more information you possess, the better chances you may have. Honestly, comparing to some other SciFi authors out there this isn't all that good. 
 Also lacking was the general plot. After twelve thousand years the Empire is predicted to fall apart and force humanity into something akin a dark age. The fall on it's own cannot be avoided, but its recovery can be sped up if the knowledge of the current Empire is preserved. So a bunch of scientists inhabit a planet on the outer edge of the galaxy and begin their work. Close to the publication of the first edition of the Encyclopedia the planet becomes strategically important to the fractions that arise from what is the beginning of the end of the Empire. 
 It could have been so much more, I expected so much more....but I was left disappointed.

Tough one to rate cos there were stretches of this I did actually quite enjoy, but... weighing up, there was decidedly far more that I didn't. 
 The bits I liked: 
 - The tough subjects addressed. They were dark and unsettling and thought provoking. 
 - The element of mystery running through. 
 - Drip feeding of info up until its grand conclusion. 
 - Much of Malachi and Harper's interactions with each other. 
 Now the bad: 
 - The humongous amount of word count spent on detailing them getting it on. Gratuitous. 
 - Malachi's hit-and-miss humour. At times, brilliant. At others, forced and pretty damn inappropriate. 
 - The ease with which Harper got over his trust issues with Malachi. Like, Oh, what if he's responsible for such and such! But, no, he wouldn't do that. I mean, yeah, I have major trust issues thanks to everyone I've ever known screwing me over. And, Yeah, I've known Malachi only a handful of days and despite me spilling my guts to him, I know almost nothing about him. But I absolutely trust him cos he's super funny and he says he believes me and he lets me f*** him. I've overreacted, I'll say sorry now and all will be well. 
 - The messed up account of how Harper spent his prison days. One minute he's saying he did try to make a friend only to be shunned, then he's all about how he rocked that solitude, and then he's on about how clued in he became to working the prison to work best for him. 
 - The sit-back-and-let-shit-happen-to-me attitude of both protags when it comes to their own personal demons. 
 - How 2D most of the secondary characters were. 
 - The wrap up. So neat and tidy. The *bad guys* spilling their guts in typical bad guy fashion and screwing themselves over, freeing our heroes up for their HEA. To nicely drip feed all the way through only to splurge in epic info dumps right at the end: Big-time disappointing! 
 - The sex in Conrad's games room. This did not sit well at all with me.  
 - The epilogue. Too sweet, made my teeth ache. 
 - Third person narrative. In my personal opinion, this would have worked far better in first person dual POV.

Obsidian (Lux #1) By Jennifer L. Armentrout is the first Jennifer L. Armentrout novel that I have ever picked up. I know, I know I know what you're thinking- seriously, this is the first book that you've ever read by her?! Yea, I get it... And to just be honest, I was a little hesitant to even pick this book up because the general idea of this book reminded me so much of the Twilight Saga by Stephanie Meyers. You know- girl is undeniably attracted to boy, boy turns out to be some paranormal being. And with the way that the Twilight Saga turned out, I honestly couldn't risk another heartbreak. To my relief, Obsidian did not break my heart- well, at least not entirely. 
 Despite it's similarities to the Twilight Saga, the plot had elements that stayed true to the unique concepts of the book. 
 Main male protagonist, Damon (or Daemon- as spelled in my kindle copy) was nothing like constantly brooding Edward. In fact, he was a "bit" of a douchebag to the main female protagonist, Katy, almost throughout the book. And I mean, he is the king of all douchebags throughout the entire book which made the "romance" between Daemon (Damon) and Katy a tad bit more entertaining than Edward and Bella's. Speaking of the main female protagonist- Katy was sure as hell a lot more useful than Bella Swan. At least, Katy had the balls to kick some alien ass when her bestie and boy toy needed some assistance in that department. Seriously, if I were being held captive by some supernatural monster and Bella and Katy were the only ones around to save me, at least with Katy my chances of living are better. I still may die, but at least I have a better chance. Oh yea if you haven't already noticed, this book was about aliens. None of that overrated vampy or wolfy high school mojo that seems to be the hype of every teen paranormal- romance novel. 
 The writing is- well, let's just say it's ok... moving on... 
 Obsidian was a great read and it definitely satisfied my unusual teeny bopper paranormal romance craving. The plotline was not all that bad- though some parts may be a tad bit cliche but definitely was not over played, the ongoing love- hate relationship between Damon and Katy may technically be insta- love (ok, well yea it is insta- love) but it was a way better build up than others (ehrm, Edward and Bella) and I'm curious to see how this whole alien concept play out. It was definitely a step up from the Twilight saga and could be a series worth investing my time in. 
 Overall, Obsidian is worth checking out if you have some extra reading time on your hands or if you're craving for some weird teeny bopper para- romance read. It is such an interesting story and it's fun and quick.

 I couldn't get into these stories. About the time I figured out who the people were and what was going on with them, their time had ended and I had to start over with another one. This isn't good because it represents human suffering during WWII, nor is it good because it provides martyrs like in The Nightingale. Don't get me wrong; I absolutely loved The Nightingale. It had me in tears at work while listening to the audiobook. 
 The Women in the Castle is different. It's different because it doesn't make you empathetic to the German citizen's plight during Hitler's reign. It doesn't make you think that maybe their actions were warranted, or that they didn't know what was going on. Maybe it's true they didn't know fully, but they were aware to an extent. 
 The reason this is a success is because it presents three women with radically different views of the war--one vehemently opposed, one affably indifferent, and one foolishly for. They represent the gamut of reactions, and it provides a way for us to envision life for each of them and how their experiences shaped their opinions. It's a surprisingly deep work if you think hard enough about it, and I appreciated the author's ability to create a framework where these women can speak out. Are any of them right? Maybe. Do we get a glimpse into conceivably real people without literary guilt making them all into heroes? Definitely yes.

I loved this book so very very very much until the epilogue. I thought it was a fantastic character exploration and was pleasantly surprised to not be able to find a true hero or villain in the piece. Every character is masterfully well-rounded and motivated by many opposing factors. The theme on the power of pride and how people let it shape them for good or evil resonated very deeply within me. After slogging through "A Song of Ice and Fire," this was refreshing fantasy. It has a fast pace and remains real without getting as graphic as ASoIaF. 
 Then I got to the very last sentence and about threw the book across the room. My book club specifically picked this because it was a stand alone novel without a sequel after the last two books caused frustrating time sinks for people without much reading time. That means that unless Mr. Kay has a change of heart (and he wrote this book over 20 years ago), we the audience are left with this awful pit in our stomachs.  My advice, read the book, stop at the epilogue.

Perhaps as a 23-year-old reader with a middle-grades novel, I found the mysteries rather easy to figure out. First, I always take the dust jacket off when I read a hardcover, and I noticed the cat silhouette on the back immediately. So, rather than be surprised by Serafina's mysterious origins, I spent the first few pages of the book wondering if the character was actually a cat rather than a human. Maybe without seeing the medallion on the back I wouldn't have noticed until it appeared in the second chapter. There were a lot of cat qualities through the book though, which I thoroughly enjoyed. But even as part cat, I have trouble believing that Serafina could climb the tapestries and curtains successfully... And the desire to knock the chess pieces off the table in the library went a bit far in my opinion. I did enjoy the inclusion of the catamount though (and greatly enjoyed the etymology lesson! I didn't know that) as a local term, and the execution of the mythology when Serafina finally met her mother. I'd never heard a legend of catamounts being human/shifters.Although the book did a good job of casting suspicion around as to who was the man in the Black Cloak--creepy Mr. Crankshod, Mr. Vanderbilt's shoes, etc--as soon as Thorne basically said he became a violinist overnight I was 90% sure it was him. That was chapter 3. Like I said though, there were still hints toward other people afterward.As for Serafina's mother, that was the one I second-guessed myself on the most. When she found the den and was playing with the cubs, I wondered if they were so easy with her because somehow they recognized that she was kin. When the lion attacked though I figured I must be wrong. Then when Sera was hiding in the den and the mother saw her eyes, I thought she would know and nuzzle Sera or something, but that didn't happen either. Well it turned out the lion was her mother, it just took a while to prove it!  I still had fun reading this though. I live a couple hours from Asheville and I've visited Biltmore several times over the years, so I was excited to read a novel set there, especially in the fantasy/paranormal genre. I enjoyed the way the story was told both in the atmosphere and the word choice. The bit that we got to explore the house was very fun, though in my opinion the feeling of being there could have been developed a bit more, instead of just using room names so much. I'm not sure how well the scene was set for anyone who's never been to the house. I hope the next time I go, to see this book in one of the giftshops! I do plan to continue reading the others as well. 
 I also loved the design for this book. The cover features gorgeous colors and a silhouette of Biltmore House, with an overlay that looks like antique paper with a tree branch as a sort of ribbon for the title and a silhouette of a girl. Taking the jacket off, the hardcover is the same color like antique paper with the two thorn silhouettes from the chapter ornaments, one on the front cover and one on the back. The deckle edges of the paper also add to the antique splendor aesthetic that fits with Biltmore.

I had mixed feelings about this book. For one, it just seemed a little long. For two, it is told as a letter to a boy that Cassie hurt, hoping to earn a second chance--but we never even learn the boy's name. That drove me nuts. Every other insignificant character had a name, but not the one who really mattered. Cassie was an interesting character. She was trying to deal with the aftermath of losing her mother and then finding a severed foot on the beach. After the foot incident, she starts to hear a voice that "makes" her hurt herself and do things she would never otherwise do. Her dad doesn't really know how to deal with her. She spends most of her time lying and sneaking around. Perhaps if her father knew that her sneaking mostly involved trying to deal with the voice through a support group, he would understand. She doesn't want to take her medication, she doesn't want to stop hearing the voice entirely. In the midst of all this, there is a serial killer on the loose, killing prostitutes. There is a lot going on in this story, perhaps too much. The bottom line is: the "boy" this entire story is directed at never really knew Cassie at all. She kept most of herself from him. He got to know parts of her, but this letter is an attempt to show herself entirely to him in the hopes he will understand, forgive and give her another chance. We'll never know though. It is up to the reader to decide how the story ends. Once the letter is sent, we don't get to see his response. I'm not sure how I feel about that. Overall, this book was quite different in many ways than your usual story. I would have liked it better if it had been shorter. I felt it just kept going on and on. There was only so much of Cassie's ramblings I could take. Too much inside anybodies head is too much for me.
