 THIS WAS BRILLIANT!! 
 WOW! WOW! WOW! 
 I'm overwhelmed with so many thoughts and feelings it's hard to express them properly without giving anything away. When I finished this book at 1 am I spent the whole night tossing and turning because the brilliance of OUT OF TIME kept playing through my mind. 
 "The world was rotten and so was everybody in it." 
 Gah, this was a true statement if I've ever one. 
 In 'Nine Minutes' we learned about Ginny's childhood and how neglectful her parents were in raising her but what we didn't see was WHY they were so neglectful of their daughter. I'm not excusing her parents behavior but in this book the reader sees what events caused her parents to become the people we read about in book one. 
 When it came to Grizz's childhood we travel back to when he was a young boy in the '50s and the events that lead to him in the motel where in 'Nine Minutes' we learn about him. 
 Last but not least, he's my favorite since book one, is Grunt / Tommy. We get a glimpse into his childhood also and see what kind of conditions he had to endure. Overall the insight we gain from going back to the past was beneficial in rounding out the characters. 
 "... heartless bastard." 
 Really, who wouldn't be under the conditions they were raised in. No one loved or cared for Grizz... let alone showed any compassion for him as a child. Being a heartless bastard was a result of the environment 
 "Everybody had their demons." 
 The revelations that are revealed left me speechless. We learned so much and our questions from book one are answered but this story isn't over which leads to new questions and speculations. Just when I think I had something figured out I'd learned that not everything was as it seems. 
 "It had to be on information overload." 
 All the information revealed about the characters, the situation, and the love stories had me grasping at straws because the minute I'd learn something I was jonesing for more. 
 "Both he and Grizz were guilty of letting her live her life based on secrets." 
 'Out of Time' is Ginny's discovery of the unknown. She spent her time living in a sheltered world. She knew bad stuff was happening but she stayed away from it. Staying oblivious to her surroundings was the key to her sanity during her time at the motel. Plus the two main guys in her life protected her from matters that were ugly and not necessary for her to experience. 
 I've been thinking about this book for days! When asked what's the appeal was I shared how it reminded me of the Twilight allure. I'm not saying this is a Twilight fan fiction or that it even has a similar story because it DOESN'T. What I am saying is - here is a girl who is the center of two guys' worlds. They'll do anything and everything to protect her while vying for her love. What girl wouldn't want to be the center of a man affection, let alone two of them? Both willing to sacrifice everything for her happiness and safety - HELL YEAH! Right there - that's the appeal. Another reason I love escaping into fiction - being able to live vicariously through characters. 
 Let's not forget the humor in this book. I laughed in several spots which I wasn't expecting. The banter helped lighten the tone of this INTENSE book. If you read Nine Minutes and you were left wanting MORE than this is your MORE. 
 Overall this quote summed the book up for me: PEOPLE IN LOVE ARE WILLING TO DO DESPERATE THINGS. It's the essences of the story!!! And yes, there's another book coming out in 2016 and I know to EXPECT THE UNEXPECTED while reading that one.

I grew up reading Sarah Dessen. I almost always love her books. This book was really no exception, even though it was not quite as great as I was expecting. I did enjoy it. I love how she gives her characters such complex histories and how she weaves family and friend relationships throughout. This book was fun and an easy, beachy read, though there were definitely some heavier moments. 
 Overall, I liked this book. Louna was a little grating at times (particularly toward the end), but her mother, William, Jilly, and especially Ambrose were wonderful characters who kept me very entertained. The banter between all of the characters was absolutely hilarious. Her history with Ethan had that magical summer romance feel that was lovely. I know it seems unrealistic to fall in love in one night, but it was very well written here. 
 I think my main complaints about this novel would be the under-tone (and sometimes blatant appearance of) negativity towards other girls. I also am not sure if I truly buy into the ending. I do like that it is pretty open ended, but it seemed a little haphazard to me.  I also think that Louna and Ambrose would have been marvelous friends, but I'm not convinced of their romance. I never felt that kind of chemistry between them. I honestly thought they should have stayed platonic... but that's just me!  
 3.5 stars for this one! Not my favorite Sarah Dessen, but it was very entertaining and I loved reading about weddings and wedding planning. The side characters really won me over as well.

This was definitely my favorite of the three. Even though I knew most things that were going to happen, I still was so engrossed in this book. 
 In order to find the antidote to help her mother, Clary must travel to the City of Glass, which is the home of the Shadowhunters. When she tells Jace, he doesn't respond the way she expects him too. 
 While Jace and Lightwoods prepare a portal to go to Alicante, Simon shows up. Jace asks for Simon to tell everyone that Clary changed her mind and didn't want to come with them. Simon refuses. While the boys talk, they are ambushed and rushed into the portal before it closes. 
 When Luke and Clary get there, Magnus tells them what happened. Not wanting to be left behind, Clary makes a portal, not kn0wing that unauthorized people get transported to the edge of the city and that Luke is no longer welcomed. 
 Hereafter comes the quote that sums up Clary to me. "Of course you didn't know, Clary. You don't know anything about Idris. You don't even care about Idris. You were just upset about being left behind, like a child. and had a tantrum." Luke's words to Clary describe her perfectly, 
 Everything gets resolved in this book. The battle with Valentine, the forbidden love of Jace and Clary and we are also introduced to a few new characters, most importantly Sebastian Verlac. 
 Clary's main concern is helping her mother, and once she does, she is not sure how she feels towards her mother or what to do next. 
 I loved the scene where Jocelyn tells Clary everything about Valentine and her first born. I especially loved climax scene where Clary is talking to Valentine. 
 Like the previous books, City of Glass has a few things I didn't like but scenes and dialogue I know will stay with me, I feel this would have been a perfect conclusion to the Mortal Instruments but Cassandra Clare added more. I look forward to see who the villain is, and how the relationships of Clary and Jace as well as the love triangle of Maia, Simon, and Izzy progressed. 
 I really hope that Clary matures more and becomes a better friend to Simon.

Good Heavens, I loved this book! Let's discuss why: 
 The Characters 
 As a group, I loved these characters! Not since The Raven Boys have I been so obsessed with a cast of characters. And while these characters as a whole don't quite match up to The Raven Boys for me, they are a very close second and have so much potential. They work together as a team so well, even if they don't always get along and there really wasn't a weak link. And The Banter. I love it so much! 
 Kaz Brekker. I love him. Like, I'm in love with him. It's a problem. He has become one of my favorite characters of all time. He's clever, strategic, sarcastic, vengeful, vulnerable, protective, selfish...there are just so many layers to him! I adore him. I just wanted More, More, More Kaz. 
 I also loved the comic relief that Jesper and Wylan provided and I loved how resourceful Inej was. It took a little while for Nina and Matthias to grow on me, but they eventually did and I heart them, as well. 
 The Story-Telling 
 I'm a big fan of Bardugo's Grisha series, but it's been awhile since I read it and I've forgotten how great of a writer she is. She's amazing. And as much as I love her first series, I think I love this series even more, even if it's just one book in so far. There was a lot of angst in the Grisha series and while there is some angst in this book, it's not a main plot point. I loved the overall story and I especially loved the subtle twists and turns throughout. There were times I was sure something terrible was happening, then realized it was all part of the plan. I love when a book can surprise me and Six of Crows surprised me over and over again. 
 The Romance 
 Ok, so the romance was not a major part of the book. In fact, it was a pretty small part in the grand scheme of things, but it was well done and we got a little bit of everything. There's the beginning of a cute flirtation. There are exes who will maybe reconcile (and were the main attraction for the angst in this book). And there are the friends who are trying to deny their feelings for each other. And yet another reason why I'm obsessed with Kaz - who doesn't love a guy who will tear someone's eye out of it's socket for you!? 
 Why I Couldn't Give it 5 Stars 
 I was thisclose to giving this book 5 stars, which if you know me, you know why that is such a big deal. But there were just a couple problems with it. For being a heist book, I thought it was just a little too slow paced. Now if all of the slower chapters were from Kaz's point of view, I probably would have had no problem with it. But, that brings up my second point, I thought there were too many chapters from Matthias and Nina's POVs. I could have used a little more Jesper and A LOT more Kaz. I was pretty happy with the amount of POVs we got from Inej, though I would've liked maybe one more small chapter from her at the end. 
 Overall, I just really loved Six of Crows. I loved the cast of characters, the twists and turns the story took, the romances, and KAZ BREKKER. Can I say that enough? I love Kaz! This is one book that definitely lives up to the hype and I strongly recommend it to basically everybody. Though it's a YA book, it read adult. And while I think it would be helpful to read the Grisha series first (there are a few mentions of characters featured from that series and some of the events that took place), I think you could read it on it's own and figure it out. So, go read this book! 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 4.5 Stars

I found the premise for this book to be cliche, which seems appropriate since the whole time I'm reading it, I'm thinking of another cliche...would you like some cheese with that whine. 
 Tony, the narrator, is not only unreliable, he's somewhat of an ass. I also thought the ending was too convenient, contrived, and predictable. Barnes' characters lack authenticity and thus become caricatures (annoying ones). I hated all the characters, not because they were evil or depraved, but because they were so silly and pathetic. 
 Oh...and the ending sucked or did I say that already. 
 Of course, I am in the minority here. Clearly, I am either too clever for this book, or it's too clever for me. Or maybe (and this is just a possibility), this is one of those works that has ridden the wave of critical acclaim and is good because some judges said it was not simply good but great and not because it really is. And now I'm just being (or trying to be) clever, so shame on me. 
 Final analysis...superb writing, good pacing, but unrelatable, unlikable, and annoying character(s) who lacked even a shred of self-awareness. And maybe that's the point. 
 In some ways this read like a monologue with a few passages of dialogue thrown in for good measure. 
 Seems only appropriate to finish with another cliche...to each his own. Read it and decide for yourself.

 Ginger Scott is now on my must buy list!!! <3 <3 <3

This book has been on the best sellers lists for a while but there are so many books on my to read stack that I hadn't gotten to it yet. When I noticed that it had been added to the book club kits list and was being made into a 2015 movie, I knew it was time to get it read. I borrowed it as an audiobook from the library and kept the discs in my car only getting to listen to it when I was driving somewhere until near the end when I couldn't stand to wait for the next installment and had to bring it into the house to listen to the last 2.5 hours. 
 The book deals with complex subject matter in post-World War I Australia. It is about Tom and his wife Isabel who live alone on an island where they tend to a lighthouse and are faced with a moral dilemma. They have lost three babies to miscarriage or stillbirth at the island. Isabel is deep into depression when Tom finds a boat washed up at the beach on the island. In the boat is a dead man and a very tiny dehydrated but living baby. Desperate to comfort and satiate the child, Isabel trusts her instincts and gives into her yearnings placing the child to her bare chest. Since Isabel only recently lost her last baby, her milk came back in once she put the baby to her breast. Tom and Isabel debate the issue and eventually Isabel convinces Tom that since no one knows their baby died and this child is parentless, they could pass her off as theirs. 
 Assuming both her parents are dead, Tom and Isabel keep the baby and name her Lucy. They love her with an intensity that no reader would want to see broken. Eventually, on a trip to the mainland for Lucy's christening, they discover a grieving mother who lost her little one, Grace, along with her husband. Guilt overwhelms Tom and Isabel but it is too late to turn back now, they love their toddler too much to give her up. 
 Will their guilt be too much? Will they slip up and get caught? Will the secret be discovered? Will the secret destroy the woman who clings to hope that her baby is alive? Will they be accused of a crime? Will they be forced to return Lucy to her biological mother? Will Lucy be too old to accept a change in family? I liked this book for the tension of where this little baby would end up. 
 Is the book realistic? Not really but it doesn't matter because it gets to the heart of family and love and heartache and that is what makes it great. Whose heartache is more worthy of the healing love? Sure, there's too much "it-just-so-happens-that" for it to be true to life: the couple struggling to start a family just so happens to be on an isolated island, and just so happens to find a boat washed up with a baby, who just so happens to be a newborn, who just so happens to be perfect for passing off as the couple's own, because it just so happens no one knows Isabel miscarried...yada, yada. You get the picture but you'll fall in love with both sides of the heartache and have a difficult time rooting for either one without feeling bad for the other. This book was emotionally a hard read. I developed sympathy and/or empathy for every character even though they were all in very different places and hurt each other in very different ways. I thought there were so many ideas and dilemmas that were thought-provoking. I definitely recommend reading this book.

 The Collector of Dying Breaths is a fantastic novel written by MJ Rose. I was attracted to this novel by its title and by its cover. They both seemed so mystic and somehow ethereally dark, if that makes sense. When I saw the cover and read the title I knew I had to read this. And if that wasn't enough, the author's name: MJ Rose. My name is also MJ. No brainer (bashful grin), I had to read it. 
 The Collector of Dying Breaths is a suspenseful journey that takes you back to Florence, Italy in the 1500s and to Paris, France in the present time. It is very well written in the sense that the going back and forth is very well achieved. Even though there are two different stories in a different time and place, they are cleverly intertwined. The transitions were done at the precise time in the story and I never got the feeling of being lost in time. 
 I absolutely enjoy novels with the alchemy/chemistry/perfumery theme. The research for this one felt well done in my humble opinion. The way MJ Rose describes everything is so vivid that you almost feel like you could smell the scents, visualize the procedures and places in the story. 
 The Collector of Dying Breaths is a novel of suspense, mystery, friendship, love, passion, betrayal, murder, ambition, seduction. It is definitely an adult read, as it deals with serious subjects like reincarnation, euthanasia, incest, bondage to name a few. 
 I gave The Collector of Dying Breaths 4.5 stars for the sole reason that the sexual encounters portrayed in the book were not quite my cup of Joe.  The incestuous encounter yuck. And that sex scene in the confessional at the church was unnecessary in my humble opinion. I'm no prude but somehow it made me feel uncomfortable reading that. The setting, where it takes place wasn't necessary. It would've been the same or even better and more time appropriate for the story if those two had escaped to some secret garden or hidden alcove to have sex. They would've been safe there too.  Other than that I would read this book again. 
 I recommend The Collector of Dying Breaths to others. I enjoyed reading this book. Producers out there, this would make a good movie. I'd watch it. :D It is a great book for book clubs too. I can see numerous discussions on the reincarnation theory, coming from reading this fascinating novel. As unbelievable as it sounds it is a subject from which many opinions can be shared and discussed. 
 The Collector of Dying Breaths is the best book I've read so far this year. I will definitely read the other books in this series by MJ Rose.

Good literature is transportive. And Louise Erdrich makes one feel that they are Joe, the narrator, viewing events on his Obijwe reservation through his eyes, experiencing what he does, taking us right through the shattering yet expected climax with him. 
 She is a novelist at the top of her game, weaving in alliterative phrases and unforgettable descriptions with such adroitness that we feel as if we had thought those things, even as if we already knew them. When she writes "There are Indian grandmas who get too much church and Indian grandmas where the church doesn't take, and who are let loose in their old age to shock the young," it is almost as if this was something I'd always known, but was hearing in new language. 
 She refuses to ever take the easy route in her characters; they are all true people, including Sonja, the protagonist's ex-stripper aunt. We see everyone as human, with all of their flaws. 
 This is not a feel-good, easy read kind of novel. But it is real and sobering and made me want to donate more money to the NALF. 
 I can't wait to go back and discover all of her other books.

Quite The Novel Idea ~ Words from the Clouds

 I have no idea how to start this review, honestly. This is the second sequel in a row that was very... meh to me. Great in some parts, but then not so much in others. Though, yes, this is more of a companion to The Shadow Queen (which I LOVED), it's still second in a series and it disappointed me a bit. And that gives me the sad. So now I'm confused because one half of me wants to flail about the great parts... and the other half of me wants to sulk because of the lesser parts. The life of a reviewer is not easy, I'm telling you. So for this review, I'll be using lists. Because lists are life. 
 WHAT I LIKED... 
 I loved the entire first half of this book. A LOT. It started out great with the prologue, then it kept my attention with great characters, great writing, great plot, great pacing,... Great everything basically. It was on its way to becoming a 5-star-read for sure. 
 The first chapter started with our MC, Ari, baking and hating corsets. So naturally we connected instantly. 
 There were glorious cameo's! First Lorelai & Kol from The Shadow Queen, then a bit later none other than Hansel & Gretel showed up! Not gonna spoil anything about either of these pairs so just read it and be happy with me when they show up! 
 I loved the writing. I love the dialogue and the narrative and the world-building and everything. There's just something about this author's writing that clicks with me and I love when that happens. 
 THE CHARACTERS! I loved Ari and Thad and Sebastian and Cleo. I even loved the villain, Alistair Teague. He was a great villain and I loved his backstory. All of the characters are so well-developed and real and I adore them. 
 ARI! She's such a great MC. She's resourceful, smart, witty, pro-active, stubborn, kind,... but also clumsy and she DOESN'T. HAVE. THE. PERFECT. FIGURE. And she LOVES FOOD. She's SO relatable and I loved her. 
 SEBASTIAN! (No not the crab from The Little Mermaid...) Sebastian is the new weapon's master at the palace and he's adorable and precious and fragile but also so badass and awesome and I just felt a very strong urge to protect him at all cost. And hug him. And wrap him in warm blankets. 
 Alistair Teague is SUCH a good villain. He's powerful and sneaky and evil and awful and dangerous. His backstory is ALL OF THE NOSTALGIA. Seriously. And I kept imagining the guy that plays Rumpelstiltskin in the TV-show Once Upon a Time as him and it fits perfectly honestly and I loved that. 
 I loved the romance... in the first half of the book. It was sweet and slow and adorable and gave me all of the swoons. 
 Sibling love! I loved the bond between Ari & Thad. Sibling bonds are life. Seriously. More great siblings in books, please? 
 WHAT I DISLIKED... 
 I don't know what happened, but the second half wasn't nearly as good to me. I just... the story took a turn around the halfway point and it lost me a bit there. So this might be just me. I just wasn't in it as much anymore for several reasons, which are spoilery so I'll mention those in a moment. 
 I also hated that there were quite a few side-characters hating on Ari because she was... not very skinny and had curves. That bothered me quite a bit and it wasn't necessary in my eyes. 
 The romance sped up a bit too much in the second half and it kind of lost me. But I still liked it?? Sort of?? 
 ... Around the halfway point Ari ends up at Teague's house and it just lost me. The romance went too fast, there wasn't much of the sibling love anymore, the ending was a bit too easy considering how bloody things got in that event in the halfway point and how cruel Cleo's death was... Also what happened with Maarit?? She kind of... disappeared?? I think?? The second half just really didn't work for me at all. Which is sad.  
 So overal it was good, but I wanted it to be great. The first half was a lot better than the second half, in my eyes. This is just my opinion though and you should absolutely read it and form your own. There's still lots to love in this book and I haven't read many retellings of Rumpelstiltskin before and this is definitely a good one. So read it. And I hope you love it.

 Mac and Barron's are back and I love them to death. They have a dynamic that I've never quite read before. The story continues and also adds the MacKelters from the Highlander Series, that's all I'm going to say. We find a little more about the Nine, about Mac, and of course, we see Dani.

My introduction to Outlander went something like this. 
 Comic Con 2014, there's a giant medieval castle in the middle of the exhibit hall floor, full of kilt-clad men and women dressed from the 1940s. I got to draw a ticket, and that ticket corresponded with a prize. I got a very nice Outlander shotglass, but since I didn't have any of the premium channels, I went along with the rest of my weekend and thought no more of it. 
 Comic Con 2015, the friend I go with (hi, Kelsey!) is obsessed with the TV show. Luckily, she knows someone whose dad is really high up the chain of command, so the first half of my Comic Con experience is spent discussing all kinds of things surrounding Outlander. She manages to get her book signed by the cast and the author, and got to go to the panel. I, meanwhile, am meandering around still trying to scoop up as many books as I can. 
 Lucky me, the guy working the booth was super cool and remembered me, so he saved me a (non-signed copy) of the book. Cool! But it's huge, and I had a massive pile I brought home, so I delayed it a bit. Until now. 
 This....it's a dreadfully long book, but captivating all the same. The back cover makes it seem as if Claire goes through a stressful time trying to decide between Frank and Jamie, but there really was never any contest. I suppose we needed Frank in the picture so that Claire had a reason to try and get back to her present, but it never really felt real. What felt genuine was the relationship between her and Jamie. It started off gently, as strangers who were forced together by chance (fate?). The forced to marry by a weird rule that Claire needed in order to avoid realistically getting raped and tortured, awkwardly trying to find a sense of normalcy. And slowly, it developed into something utterly realistic. 
 That is the ultimate charm of Outlander. They are rash, they are stupid, they are steadfast and strong. They were highly sensual, and animalistic at times. They were angry and hurtful. They were brave and in love. 
 It was so unbelievably entertaining. Their growth together through all the crap they had to endure was the best part of this book. Claire repeatedly gets kidnapped and almost raped. Jamie consistently has to save her. Clair consistently has to fix his wounds and injuries. It definitely was repetitive, but the written style that Gabaldon uses doesn't ever make it seem dull. Long yes, but not dull.

I can honestly wait a lifetime for every installment of this series but what I need to know this instant (or even in the next book) is what prompted Henry to marry that girl. Just that reprieve and I think I can be at peace.

I was on the edge with my star allocation but the dialogue was so good it pushed this book to 4 solid stars. 
 The writing was really good and I immediately felt for our MC Macy. She is 17, dealing with the normal teenage drama plus she is still feeling the raw emotions left a year and half after her dad died. She is coping with the only thing she knows how: control. She must stick to the routine, never deviating and always striving for perfection. 
 I'm not going to go into the story line. You can read the synopsis for that. 
 This was a pretty straight forward read but what really made this book was the characters. ALL OF THEM WERE WONDERFUL! And the dialogue. I was laughing, and cringing, and loving these characters all the more.

Holy cow I am officially hooked on this series! 
 The first book I kinda just pushed through, the second I began to really enjoy it and now... I'm addicted. This third book was so suspenseful, action-packed, and just overwhelming. Trying to process the many thoughts and emotions going through my head right now in the immediate aftermath of reading it (that ending!) 
 I hardly needed the recap at the beginning because I was plunged straight back into the Fever world as soon as we were taken back to the scene of Mac in the puddle near the Sinsar Dubh. I love how over the course of three books I've developed clear mental imagery of the setting and its many characters. Speaking of characters, Mac has finally grown on me. In the first book, I sort of hated her because she annoyed me with her vapidness and shallow interests. The second book saw her developing as a character, and now I am appreciating how far her character has come. She still loves fashion and other "girly" things, but now she's developed a tougher skin and is a better character for it. I loved how she became intent on working everyone around her to her own benefit and was determined to not be helpless. 
 As for the men in Mac's life, I am so crazy about V'lane. It's a good thing this isn't real because I'd be in serious danger for that. Ahhhhh. Tried to deny it because he's a possible baddie but oh my god this third book just solidified my affection (mostly because he was a lot more civilized and even considerate in this book). I realize that his actions and behavior are not the result of romantic or sappy interest in Mac (come on, that would be deluded), rather serving the interest of getting her to get the Book for him, but I love his character nonetheless. I loved the part when he accompanies Mac to the abbey and their little trips to the beach, as well as, of course, when he gave her his name. (I also loved implied jealousy on Barrons' part hehehe.) His antagonistic dynamic with Barrons was amazing. I must know more about the history between them and I'm sure it will be revealed in future installments. I never really got attached to Barrons as a character in book one but began to like him a bit more in book two. In book three I wished we could have seen more of him since I felt like he was missing for a lot of it. Either way, I'm at about the same level of affection for him as I developed during book two, which is an in-progress "growing on me" stage. I am quite anxious for things to come clean between him and Mac though. 
 It was almost a let down that the Lord Master was just Darroc, an outcast ex-fae.  I was expecting something a little more mind-blowing, but oh well. I still think he didn't really kill Alina, though Mac refuses to believe that. There is just too much hinting at him not, from him actually saying so to Barrons reminding Mac not to assume things right when they were talking about the LM being Alina's killer. Hmm... Also it would seem my guess at Barrons' true identity were wrong. I thought he was a Druid but now that the Druids have actually joined the storyline I see that I was mistaken.  So what on earth could he be??? It's driving me nuts not knowing. 
 Speaking of Druids, I found them an interesting addition to the scheme of things and I liked the character of Christian MacKeltar. He's the least dangerous and normal-seeming of Mac's various "suitors" (though I suppose this could change in some sort of future plot twist) and I hope Mac develops a further relationship with him. 
 Now onto the inevitable, that ENDING. I wasn't sure if the author was gonna completely follow through with it, but she did. I kept waiting (ok, hoping) that V'lane or Barrons or someone would step in to save the day at the last second but no I get this shocker and cliffhanger instead. Is Mac gonna be Pri-ya now?  I hate hiding reviews, but I cannot discuss what ruined this book for me without spoiling it. So, if you've read the book, clickety-click that spoiler tag. Go on. I dare ya... 
 Let's get this out of the way right off the bat. Maggots do not eat healthy tissue. They eat dead and rotting flesh. Any medical professional knows this. This has been common knowledge since the fucking dark ages, along with using leeches to reduce swelling. Just because you think they're icky doesn't mean you can break the rules to suit your fiction. So, no, the smiling child's brain was not being eaten. Good try, though, Mr. Banks. 
 After reading the nonsensical chapter "What Happened to Eric", I called my mother (a forty-year nurse), and then I called an old buddy from my hospital days. I asked them both to "Tell me your maggot story." Neither had to think very hard. Why? Because maggots are par for the course in the medical field. If you spend any amount of time within the walls of a care facility, you're going to come across them. 
 I won't share their maggot stories because I think mine's better. My point is, everyone who's ever worked in the medical profession has a maggot story. 
 Here's mine: 
 An old wheelchair-bound homeless man was brought into the ER. He'd been sitting out in front of a CVS in Montgomery, Alabama, "harassing" customers by screaming about how he couldn't feel his legs. Well, he was in a wheelchair, so no big shocker there. When 911 was called, EMTs showed up alongside the police. When he got to Jackson Hospital, where I worked at the time, they wheeled him in and laid him out. In his report, one of the EMTs said, "there's something funny with his legs. They feel weird." Good job, dude. You get a gold star for that comment. 
 Well, Mr. Homeless Man was wearing pressure stockings under his sweatpants, likely to help keep him warm on the streets. Lucky for me (the sarcasm drips...), I was tasked with cutting Mr. Man's compression stockings off. Wanna guess what happened? No? Don't wanna guess? Okay, I'll tell you. 
 I started at the top and got less than an inch down before a sea of maggots boiled out over the scissors and my gloved hand and onto my shoes and the floor. They came like pus from a lanced cyst. A tide of maggots dropping in writhing clots. Disgusting, but not the worst thing I've seen. 
 I guess that was my problem overall with this book. The shocks had no value because I've seen worse in real life. Not even the animal cruelty scenes affected me because I spent a month working for my local humane society one summer. I saw burned and tortured animals all the time. Mostly I helped take care of the aftermath of dog fights. It's more sad to me than horrifying. 
 That being said, the book is not without merit. It is extremely quotable. I highlighted whole paragraphs, but that doesn't mean I enjoyed myself. For the most part, this book was boring as hell. Like I said above, much of the shock lost its value due to scientific inaccuracies and my own life experiences. 
 That ending was fucking sillier than tits on a bull. Get it? Tits on a bull because it's the wrong gender??? HAHAHAHAHA! I'm so fucking funny! 
 I can't believe this ended up being a gender-swap of Sleepaway Camp. 
 In summation: My own history and medical knowledge ruined key scenes for me, and when I wasn't frustrated with the inaccuracies, I was bored to death. Some passages are terrifically written, but they are few and far between, making this book horribly inconsistent. 
 Final Judgment: NO PENIS FOR YOU!

Ok, so I have tried and tried to review this book and I don't know why, but I just can't write anything I like. I have decided to just go with listing the things I liked and didn't like. And it will be ***SPOILERS GALORE***. So if you haven't read it yet, don't read any further. This a great series that deserves to be read without spoilers. 
 *************SPOILERS FROM HERE ON OUT!**************** 
 -The character development in this book is superb! Like, for real. Mal is the least annoying he's ever been in this book. That's not to say he's still not a little annoying, though. He's decided to dedicate his life to protecting Alina and knows that he can't be with her. But he still loves her and though he tries to ignore it, he's still letting her know every time she turns around. A lot of the minor characters get a lot more developed, as well. Genya and David. Toyla and Tamar. Even Zoya. 
 -And then there's the Darkling. Layers and layers and layers of characterization. We learn his mother, Bhagra's, back story, that she is actually the daughter of Morozova. We learn that the Darkling's name is actually Aleksander and that deep down all he wants is to be Aleksander and have a friend. He wants Alina so much because he thinks she's like him and he doesn't want to be alone. But ultimately, he wants the power of the amplifiers. 
 -I still love Nikolai/Sturmhond. He's still one of my favorite characters and I almost wanted Alina to end up with him. I was a little disappointed that he's not actually in love with Alina, but I do enjoy their friendship. I was super upset when the Darkling turned him into some weird creature. But I liked that at the end he was ok, though scarred. I wish there would've been a little more of him in the story, but overall, his arc within the series was very well done. 
 -Mal's the amplifer! Why didn't I see that coming? He was obviously more than a normal person, but the amplifier? And why exactly did they have to find the firebird to figure that out? I'm still a little confused about that. 
 -There was a little too much wandering around the woods with Alina and Mal wallowing in their own thoughts. Things could have sped up a little here. 
 -I really liked the twist that after uniting all three amplifiers (RIP Mal! - but not really), Alina's power was distributed to the people. Her heroic journey ends with her sacrificing her power and she gets to be the normal girl she always wanted to be. Even though she has a hard time still wanting it. 
 -Alina kills the Darkling. Not with great power, but with Grisha steel. I agree with The Darkling when he's like "Like this?" That's how he ends. Just stabbed with Grisha steel. Which begs the question, WHY DIDN'T ALINA ALWAYS HAVE GRISHA STEEL WITH HER?!?! She could have just stabbed him while kissing him at the end of the second book instead of draining all her power. That seems a little bit of poor planning on Bardugo's part. 
 -I loved how Alina has mixed feelings on the Darkling's death. Yes, he was evil and needed to be put down. But also, he's sad, confused, lonely Alesander, who should be mourned. 
 -I got the ending I kind of always wanted, normal Alina and Mal together - at their old home of all places, but I'm a little disappointed with it. It seems a little anticlimactic after all the excitement they lived through. But, I liked that they're still friends with Nikolai and their other Grisha friends. 
 -Overall, I really did enjoy this book. I thought it was a good end to the series. Bardugo's writing and imagination is amazing and her characters are twisted and tormented and complex and lovable and wonderful. I'm sad to see this series end, but look forward to reading more from her in the future.

I wasn't sure what to expect with this book when it was handed to me at book club. It is an inspiring story of reaching out against odds to an unlikely person and trusting that a great friendship can be forged. It also teaches that living involves much more than just obtaining possessions or money. This is a heartwarming memoir about, as the subtitle says, "A Modern-Day Slave, an International Art Dealer, and the Unlikely Woman Who Bound Them Together". I liked the dual point of view method of telling the story but thought the speaker's name would have made it clearer whose parts we were reading. I also would have loved to have a third perspective from Debbie but I know that wasn't possible. Especially since over and over we are reminded that Denver couldn't read or write but he was supposedly capturing his broken English in the alternating paragraphs. It contains some eye-opening details about the reality of poverty which endures generations beyond the end of slavery and homelessness which continues as much by choice as necessity. The friendship, loss, love and trust aspects of the novel were "eyelash wetters" which endeared the narrators to me. The book tells an inspiring story of some folks who made a difference in each other's lives and touched many more on the way. 
 I'm not exactly the target audience since I am not a Christian and the last half of the book necessitates that the reader be a believer or treat it as completely fiction because the afterlife and words of God don't resonate to us. It is a wholesome story that is ripe to be made into a "Christian" made-for-TV movie which I would not watch. I would never have selected this book on my own, I don't read Christian books as blatant as this if I can avoid them and I hate when there is such a "direct line to God" in a supposed non-fiction book. Nevertheless, if you like books that affirm your faith, this one is a good choice for you.

 Gah! All the feels! I put off reading this book because I knew it would make me feel things & I wasn't exactly sure if I was ready to feel those things. I was also nervous to read this because I didn't want it to fall short after all the hype it had been receiving. 
 Unfortunately, one of my students spoiled the book for me by revealing the fate of one particular character, so that didn't help matters. I figured I kind of already knew what was going to happen & didn't know if I wanted to experience the book for myself. 
 I finally decided to read the book during April, along with Before I Die by Jenny Downham, as both books have characters with cancer, and April is Cancer Awareness Month. I also knew I needed to read the book before the movie arrives on the big screen. 
 Now to the actual review part... 
 OH MY GOODNESS! So many emotions! John Green has wonderfully crafted a teenage girl & has somehow made her leap off the page with such vibrancy and depth, all without being a teenage girl himself! Hazel Grace is a delightful girl with so many layers and feelings, you can't help falling in love with her, just as Augustus Waters does. 
 The writing style John Green uses elegantly & eloquently portrays the story of two star-crossed lovers, with an unfortunate side-effect - Cancer. The story takes you on twists & turns, ups & downs, leaves you hoping so much for the happy ending, but sadly, leaves you broken inside upon learning the fate of the characters. 
 I do really enjoy that John wrapped up the characters in such a wonderful way, leaving me feeling satisfied that the characters did live on beyond the pages of the book. The story continues in my mind, unlike the story Hazel loves in the book, which ends mid-sentence. 
 This book comes highly recommended with a broken, yet full & satisfied heart. Such a poignant, contemporary story of two teenagers who are faced with a fate they didn't plan, but battle with all they are.

Having seen the show (through season 2; any word yet one way or another on season 3?) prior to beginning the book, I have to say I was pretty bored. With all the shock value sucked out of it, I really have no comments on the plot, so I'll compare the book and show. 
 Now, I haven't rewatched any of the episodes since their original airing, so going off my spotty memory and wikipedia episode summaries, this is my list of similarities and differences between the first book and the show. 
  
 Houses 
 In the book, all the houses in Wayward Pines are Victorians. In the show, they are all cookie-cutter suburban houses. I give points to the book on this one. Although the house designs in the show fit in extremely well with the show's visual aesthetic, 1) I love Victorian houses and I'm super disappointed I didn't get to look at a ton of them for 2 seasons, 2) Victorians would make a lot more sense to keep people from getting suspicious/confused about what year it is. Victorians would have been before the time of anyone in WP, but still fashionable in their own way. They are immune to anachronism. 
 Age and appearance differences 
 I much prefer Terrence Howard as Pope rather than a blond white guy. Yes, for diversity's sake, but also because I just can't think of a time when I saw a menacing freckled blond guy? I read that description and pictured Owen Wilson in Night at the Museum and that just sort of killed book!Pope for me. 
 Rather than wacky, red-haired Arlene being the sheriff's secretary, we have Belinda, elderly and gray-haired. I don't know what the point was for this change, unless they just wanted that specific actress. Tbh there's not enough old people on tv so this was a disappointing change to me. 
 On the flip side of that, Nurse Pam is young and beautiful in the book, whereas in the show she is approaching old age and not markedly attractive. Probably this was done to make her scarier, without the audience being distracted by beauty/sex appeal. I give them points for that. 
 In the books, Theresa is blonde and green-eyed, a sharp contrast to Shannyn Sossamon's dark hair and eyes. I suppose her book appearance makes her and Ethan a more stereotypical perfect-looking couple, but Shannyn has such a command of the screen through her appearance alone, I could never side against her. Plus, is anyone not white in book!WP? 
 Ben is a little 7-year-old when Ethan disappears in the book, and when we see him again in WP he and Theresa have been there for 5 years already, making him 12. In the show, he's a teenager the whole time. Maybe this was just done to save on having an extra actor, but I like having a capable, more developed character for Ben in the show rather than a little kid just used for emotional manipulation of the audience and guiding motivation for Theresa. 
 There's also no mention of Wayward Pines Academy in the book, no indication that the children have inside information that the adults don't, no creepy/obnoxious Megan... That was the biggest difference between the two IMO and I'm not sure how I feel about it. I think maybe the show was stronger for having that added dimension. 
 Kate 
 Kate features heavily in the show but pretty much makes a passing appearance in the book. In both, Ethan is in WP looking for Kate and Agent Evans, and he's had an affair with her. However, her only real scenes in the book are when she and Harold find Ethan barely conscious, and when later Ethan goes to her house and finds her gray-haired and in her 60s, rather than just being about 10 years older in the show. In the book she does still have the conversation with Ethan where she hints at him that they're being monitored and things are not safe, but doesn't reappear after that. 
 Reckonings/Fetes 
 In the show, the elimination of a resident is called a Reckoning, and is a typical mob-mentality mass brawl/hunt leading up to a public execution by Sheriff Pope. In the book, they are called fetes, people wear elaborate costumes, and everyone joins in beating the target to death. Pope supervises, but doesn't take center stage. The costumes make it so much more outlandish and unsettling in the book, but tbh I'm glad the show went a little more civilian with it. To me it was so out there I really felt like that one aspect was in a world of its own and didn't fully mesh with everything else. 
 Plot 
 There are a couple other small differences between the book and the show, such as Beverly being from 1999 in the show and from 1985 in the book, and agent Evans being married as part of his new life in Wayward Pines in the show but not in the book. In the book, we get a lot of information about Ethan's past as a soldier and prisoner of war, whereas I don't recall it being mentioned much if at all in the show. 
 Episode 3 is actually where things go off the rails in terms of the show paralleling the book. 
 In the show, Theresa and Ben leave Seattle to find Ethan in WP and are abducted for suspension then. 
 In the book, Pilcher approaches Theresa at home a year after Ethan's disappearance and offers her the chance to see him again, if she and Ben drink the liquid-filled vials he's brought. She initially beings to accept, then changes her mind, and Pilcher gasses and takes them. 
 (I don't recall the book giving an explanation for Pilcher taking them. There's no collusion that I recall between Pilcher and Hassler in the book, but maybe he thought taking the family would somehow stop the secret service from looking into it further because no one would push the investigation? Idk, to me two more disappearances does more harm than good. And they couldn't have been brought in to settle Ethan, because of course at the time they were abducted the fall hadn't happened and no one had been brought out of suspension yet, so Ethan hadn't been found out as a troublemaker. Did they anticipate it to that extent? Idk. Plot hole, unless I'm missing something.) 
 In the show, Ethan finds Theresa's long-abandoned car while trying to escape WP and then is magically reunited with his family. 
 In the book, Theresa and Ben have been living in WP for 5 years, through 2 previous attempts to integrate Ethan, and he doesn't learn they're there and alive until the very end of the book. 
 In the show, Ethan takes Theresa and Ben and tries to get through the fence, killing Pope when he tries to stop them. An abbie drags Pope through the gate and the Burkes close it and stay. 
 In the book, Ethan hikes out of town after Beverly is killed and reaches a canyon, where he's beset by a group of abbies and kills them with some luck and rock climbing skills. Pope dies at the end of the book when Pilcher takes Ethan to see the Boise ruins and leaves Pope to the abbies, saying Pope couldn't be trusted to accept his place as second in command. 
 In the show, Ethan becomes sheriff, lives with his family, and starts reading residents' files at the beginning of episode 4. He does not know the whole truth about town and still thinks he can escape if he waits for the right opportunity. In episode 5, the audience is told the whole story through new student orientation for Ben and two other teens at Wayward Pines Academy. Meanwhile, Ethan is hiking out of town trying to get to Boise, discovers it in ruins, and is picked up and filled in by Pilcher. 
 In the book, Ethan is made sheriff at the end, after finding the warehouse, surveillance, and suspension tanks, seeing the abbies, and being taken to Boise by Pilcher, where Pope is left for dead. There is no mention of the school in the book and no indication that Ben or anyone else in town knows the truth. 
 As far as I can tell, everything from the first book is covered in episodes 1-6 of the show. 
 Conclusion 
 Now, I'm biased, because I saw the show first, but I think the show does a much better job of building the mystery and suspense and taking you through it. The book, especially at the beginning, was a big confusing blur to me as I tried to keep up with where Ethan was, how many times he had been unconscious and why, if he was waking up alone or in custody, etc. As I remember it, the questions and reveals were much better paced in the show, whereas the book is pretty much drawn-out chaos as Ethan never takes a break to assess the town and regroup but is physically running/hiding the whole time. 
 I wish I could temporarily block my memory of the show and read the book clean with no prior knowledge, but as it is, the book fell flat for me. I've read plenty of things before for which I'd already seen the screen adaptation and still really enjoyed them, but with WP being so mystery-focused, I feel it's really useless once spoiled. As an interesting exercise in comparing page-to-screen adaptations, this was fine; in terms of reading experience, I got nothing out of this. I give it 3 stars because I did really enjoy the show, so maybe the book would have been good if I'd read it first. I'm going to keep reading though just to see how the differences go, and hoping maybe things will diverge and the rest of the books and show will take different routes. 
  
 At this point I'm going to conclude my review and get into the second book.

I finally decided to read this after a couple things. First, a group that I'm pretty active in had it as a group read(which I failed to participate in--oops). Second, many of my GR friends have read it and loved it, opinions I tend to trust. Third: it just plain sounded cool. 
 What made me skeptical at first: Cassandra Clare said it was good. That scared me. 
 All that being said, I really loved it. It had all the elements of a story that I deem it awesome. There was a haunted house element, which had me jumping for joy--ghost movies are my favorite and are the only ones that manage to scare the crap out of me. This book didn't scare me, but I still loved the creepiness of it. I wish more of the ghosts had been described. Like the woman in the graveyard with the stones for eyes... 
 It had gore, my second favorite kind of horror movie. It wasn't overdone and it had a place, which was nice. It wasn't just for the gross factor. And I loved that the writing didn't shy away from the gore, either. Oftentimes YA literature likes to shield its readers from this kind of thing, which drives me crazy. I realize this may not be normal, but I watched The Exorcist and all manner of scary movie starting when I was 5. So I get super excited when books don't treat me like a child with blood and guts. 
 The romance is understated. Which is weird, since it's basically the main point, but it wasn't up in my face the whole time and there wasn't a whole lot of "she's just so gorgeous and I can't control myself and I have no other life outside of her" thing that YA likes to do. It was refreshing and I found I enjoyed the romance part because it wasn't so obnoxious. 
 Anna's story....Anna's story. I don't know what to say about that. I can't say that I enjoyed it, because it was horrible. But it was well-written and I found myself having extremely visceral reactions to what I was reading. The violence that Anna portrayed wasn't an issue for me; it was the violence that was done to her that had me sick and wanting to rip people apart, even if they weren't real. 
 I'm glad I chose to pick this up. I want to say a big thanks to those of you on here that read it first and (indirectly) recommended it!

I often tend to disagree with the hype surrounding popular books, which is why I was so pleasantly surprised by how much I liked The Wrath and the Dawn. It's not a perfect book by any means, but I really quite enjoyed it. 
 The Wrath and the Dawn is apparently an A Thousand and One Nights re-telling. I'm not really familiar with A Thousand and One Nights, so I can't tell you how it works as a re-telling. This story focuses on a young king, or caliph, Khalid who is in a routine of getting married one night and then having his new wife killed by the following dawn. Shahrzad is a young girl who volunteers as a new bride, her heart set on avenging the death of her best friend who was one of Khalid's wives. In doing so, she unwittingly becomes the catalyst to a new army uniting against the caliph, and to her father learning a dark, dangerous magic. 
 I have to point out here that one of the main plot points I found a little ridiculous. Shazi volunteers to become a bride so she can kill Khalid. You would think she has some sort of solid plan in place. But her whole fate rests on telling him a story and not finishing it by dawn, so he'll want to let her live another day to hear the rest of the story. Ummm, ok? But, it works and he lets her live. And because she's such a special snowflake, he keeps letting her live and they - surprise - start to fall in love. Even though it's obvious and predictable and fast, I was a fan of the romance between them and their growing relationship. 
 Shazi was not always a likable character. She was impulsive, immature, and arrogant. However, she was written in such a way that I still cared about her and was rooting for her. Khalid also had a lot of the same characteristics so they worked together. I did like Khalid a lot, though, because who doesn't love the whole tortured soul thing? 
 There are several side characters I liked, as well. Jalal is Khalid's cousin and captain of the guard. He's the stereotypical sidekick - charming, arrogant, comic relief, but actually very smart and loyal. Shazi's childhood sweetheart, Tariq, is on a mission to save Shazi from the fate he believes awaits her and his best friend, Rahim (who also serves as a bit of comic relief), joins him. One character I really didn't care for was Shazi's father. He's determined to make up for his prior weakness and he goes down a dark path of magic. I was actually kind of surprised by the magical elements of this book. While it was subtle, it's central to the major plot. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed The Wrath and the Dawn. I liked the relationship between Shazi and Khalid and that they both grew a little throughout the story. While there were several points I found the plot a little on the ridiculous side and the ending I found a bit unsatisfying, the well-developed characters and the overall story really makes up for it. I would definitely recommend this book to fans of YA and I'm eagerly anticipating the next installment

This is a gem. It's a book for booklovers about a bookstore for booklovers with lots more bookish elements thrown in, yet with plenty of modern technology that--for the first time ever?--is not presented as at odds with stacks of old books or as the new-and-improved replacement for old books, but a partner, a tool to get a bit else out of it. There's also a great big mystery which we discover right along with the narrator, fun details for artists, techies, and historians, and an intriguing cast of characters that (apart from Ashley IMO) never feel flat, despite brief interactions that, dare I say, actually mimic how we meet and get to know people in real life. 
 I feel compelled to put down that I didn't quite "get" the final message... but the rest of the book was so good I don't even care! I'll study up later. The epilogue wasn't quite what I wanted it to be, but it all wrapped up nicely and I think it fit with the overall themes and tone of the book. Perhaps these could be summed up in the now familiar phrase festina lente, which means "make haste slowly" and is symbolized by the dolphin and anchor, Manutius' printer's mark (and emblem of the Library and Information Science honor society)--everything comes together in its time, as long as you work diligently. 
 I think the only complaint that could be made about this book is that overall, all of the scenarios work out a little too easily, but it still has its ups and downs and it's still undoubtedly worth the read for all the nerdy goodness. And the glow-in-the-dark cover!

I loved this book so much. It's my favorite kind of romance, where the romance is really a vehicle for personal growth. Yes, Willem is dreamy, yes the immediate spark between Allyson and Willem made me alternately hold my breath and sigh, but that all takes place in the first half of the book and the book is about so much more than that. Willem's abrupt disappearance breaks Allyson's heart and sends her on something of a downward spiral, but she never would have figured herself out without that loss as a catalyst. Even when she goes back to Europe to search for him, it's not really about him. It's about herself. She wants to find that girl she was when she was with him that day, to see if that was really her "true self". I thought I'd be disappointed that easily half the book had no Willem, but I was so caught up in Allyson's journey that I really didn't mind. Allyson had to do that on her own. If they'd been together from that day, I don't think she would have taken any of the steps she took on her own.  I felt so proud of Allyson by the end. 
 Her steps forward into a new version of herself weren't easy or perfect. She made mistakes, she doubted herself and what she was doing, but she kept going, and by the end I really felt she'd made peace with what she had with Willem, no matter how it ended up working out. She was able to go back and appreciate the experience and what it did for her without being simply crushed by losing him.  
 Loved this book. I think I'm going to go back and immediately re-read, which I almost never do.

Overall this was enjoyable. This is not the first book I have read with the concept of the main character being able to see when everyone was going to die. In this story, Ivy is cursed with seeing everyone's numbers, including her own. Every time she looks at someone, she can see their countdown, to the second, displayed like an alarm clock over their heads. She knows when they will die, but not how. She has never been able to change anything. When her best friend is murdered, the entire town thinks she knows more than she is letting on. She has always been different enough as it is, but now she is a social pariah. The new girl, Amanda, seems to see too much. The two form an almost friendship. Ivy does all she can to keep people at a distance because her countdown ends in just a few months. She tries to live as much as she can, but it is hard to stay positive. She keeps looking into the death of Vanessa, especially when more victims turn up. The clues lead her to suspect a variety of people, like Vanessa's angry twin brother, Mitch, her ex-boyfriend, Myers, and even Vanessa's boyfriend, Brent. She knows the murderer is someone that was at her uncle's diner the night the second victim disappeared. As she continues to look into it, the killer starts stalking, threatening, even attacking her. She realizes that her death will come at his hands, but she is determined to take him down before her timer runs out. She will be his final victim. I enjoyed watching Ivy struggle with the knowledge she is cursed with. All she wanted to do was be with Myers, yet she was so adamant about keeping him at a distance, pushing him away, all to protect him from the grief of her death. Myers was an interesting character. I wish Ivy could have seen that he was going to hurt either way because he loved her, even if she kept him at a distance. It was interesting to watch her try to help her mom and sister so she wouldn't have to worry about them after she died. I'm not sure I liked how she kept the curse to herself. It would have helped her to confide in someone, even if they didn't believe her. Miranda would have been an ideal candidate, what with the Alzheimer's and all. Anyway, it was a daily struggle just to live when all she wanted was to be normal. She learned that she could take chances and be reckless, since she knew she wouldn't die. I don't know what I would have done in her place, but I probably wouldn't have gone to school on my last day, especially since she didn't have any friends anyway. Who knows. Overall, I enjoyed this mystery. I received a copy in exchange for an honest review.

This is a marvelously rendered fantasy world with complex economies and cultures. It had emphasis on social strata and how those influenced various markets, anthropological interpretations of the same texts or past occurrences, as well as the differences marring science and magic. It's a surprisingly in-depth piece of work, and I enjoyed seeing the different environments that Vic was thrust into. Seriously, I don't think we've hit a social level yet that she hasn't already experienced; maybe there will be more in the next book. 
 The reason I gave it three stars instead of four or more is because I couldn't understand Vic's head, and that's a big part of reading for me. I will root for our characters if I understand their mindset, even if I don't necessarily agree. Vic was broken down by a man. He broke her so thoroughly that she yearned for him and had no identity of her own at all. When she begins to build herself back up and remember who she is, she still loves him. Why? I'm not really sure. He didn't particularly treat her well. She turns into Bella Swan-- when she thinks she killed him, she collapses in on herself so thoroughly that no one recognizes who she became after. I was part of that grouping--I didn't get it. Where did the girl go who was bent on revenge and recovering her identity? Where was the strength we saw slowly building? She was weak in the beginning, to be sure, but after joining the military she seemed to find her stride. Her subsequent mental break just seemed like a convenient way to get her onto another path, and it didn't sit well with me. 
 I never completely got past that, and it made everything else that followed seem tarnished. I couldn't actually believe in her strength anymore because the author seemed to give it and take it away whenever she felt like it.

 Tessa has a secret: when she touches people, she gets visions. It has become such a problem that her parents have decided to uproot the family from Los Angeles and move to Texas, to be closer to her mother's family. Her father gets a job at a prestigious boarding school, whose pupils Tessa is instructed to stay away from for her own safety. She doesn't listen, as she's intrigued by Dastien, one of St. Ailbe's teachers. Dastien is just as fascinated by her. He tracks her down at a party and gives her a kiss...then a bite, then a scratch. Because he's a werewolf, and now so is she. 
 Someone needs to recommend me some good werewolf novels that aren't Twilight or True Blood (or Nightshade). I'm on a werewolf kick at the moment because I'm incredibly obsessed with Teen Wolf and until the obsession peters out (if it ever does), I need something to fuel the flames. 
 This book wasn't terrible. Glowing praise, I know, right? But it wasn't. It had a lot of potential, but it depended too much on cliches and the reader's own imagination. It wasn't that believable. Yes, I know this is a book where werewolves exist, but still. 
 My main problem was Tessa. Unfortunately, she's the main character, so if you have a problem with her, you're gonna have a bad time. She was not a very strong character. She was such a whiner, but it was approached in such a manner as to make you think that she's a tough girl who doesn't take crap from anybody. She gets visions by touching people skin-to-skin, yet she wears short sleeves and goes to parties where the chance of bumping into someone accidentally is astronomical. She explains her wardrobe choices by pointing out that it's really hot and humid in Texas and she didn't want to wear long sleeves. Then you don't get to complain about having visions. Suck it up. 
 She's surprisingly closed-minded, considering this is a girl who gets visions by touching people. She refuses to believe in werewolves, she thinks her mother's family is crazy because they claim to be witches, she doesn't really believe in vampires until she gets attacked by one. She's also a little too judgmental for my tastes, writing off the girls she meets at her new Texas school (whose names I can't remember) for being into clothes and country music. Apparently anyone who doesn't like the same "weird" music that she does isn't worth knowing. 
 On the subject of her parents, if they knew that werewolves existed, and that they were in close proximity to a school of them, why the ever-loving hell would they not warn their children about that? I know Tessa is a whiny brat who will do what she wants anyway, but maybe she would have taken their request to stay away from the St. Ailbe's people a little more seriously if she'd known they could kill her or turn her into a werewolf. 
 I know that Tessa and Dastien are super duper soul mates, but they didn't have much chemistry. Tessa spends a lot of time talking about how much she is drawn to him, but they know virtually nothing about each other. I understand that the whole mates aspect is rare even for the world of the novel, and that it's supernatural and they don't really get a choice in the matter, but I would liked to have seen at least some attempt for them to get to know each other as people before deciding to commit for the rest of their lives. I think they go on one date, and she knows he likes the kind of music she likes, but she gets really surprised that he knows the bands. That's because she's judgmental. No, she's quirky and weird and listens to obscure bands, I'M SO DIFFERENT NO ONE IS LIKE ME. 
 I gave this three stars because, for all that the world is sadly underdeveloped, like I said, I think it has a lot of potential. If Erin could just show us a little more about this secret supernatural world that only seems to be a secret from Tessa and her brother -- considering everyone in town knows that there's a werewolf school even though for some reason no one does? I got confused about that -- I think it would be a lot better. There's so much we don't understand, and I think learning more about the history and the politics would go a long way. How big is this pack? Are the council members part of the pack? How many packs are there? Is this not pertinent information we should know? After all, Tessa is told that she doesn't have to join the St. Ailbe's pack, but we're given nothing else about other packs. 
 The story itself, while predictable, was interesting enough to keep me reading. It's fairly obvious from the very beginning who Tessa is going to end up with, but I would have appreciated a little more character or relationship development before everyone just accepted that they're mates, tra-la-la. 
 I'm hoping that a lot of the issues that I have will be dealt with or addressed or built upon in the next books.

BETTER UNDERSTANDING OF LIFE. 
 When you get old or mature enough, you'd naturally learn and adopt the message that the story is trying to convey. Yes, that everything in this is world is not permanent and that life isn't fair. The novel teaches us to enjoy each day -- plus the "Amyotrophic Lateral Aclerosis (ALS)' and its devastating effects to human. 
 If something destructive is destined to come to your life, you must accept it, although accepting it is even harder, you must fight for the moment where you will be able to say: 'I accept' - but that doesn't mean you will just lie on your bed and wait for your death; you have to make the most out of it. The truth hurts, everyone knows that. Life is really just a game, a long fighting journey, so we must desperately try to reach our goals and fight for the acceptance of life and become a person with value. 
 People often say that life is unfair, which is true. Life being frequently unfair is a fact. That's why it can be similar with a game. There are some parts of our lives that in which sometimes we get upset and sometimes we have our sweetest and unforgettable victory. You make your own life, make you own decisions, live, laugh, complain and do anything you want on your own but it will never change the fact the life is unfair. That's the irony of life. Death is a part of living and it should not be feared. 
 Going back to the story, I cried how Professor Morrie's illness and imminent death can affect those closest to him (family as well as close friends) in both miserable and positive way. 
 'Tuesdays with Morrie' is a profoundly moving, deeply touching, life affirming novel. I cannot believe I just read this today. I've been familiar with this book ever since my elementary days. I missed this for almost 17 years now. I cannot recommend it highly enough!! 
 "Don't cling to things because everything is impermanent." 
 -- Mitch Albom, Tuesdays with Morrie

BEFORE 
 Of all the books that came out in 2016 (or that will), the one I'm most excited for is The Dark Talent. I mean, it might even beat out Calamity and Runaway Deception and No Good Dragon Goes Unpunished, but it might be a four-way tie. (It's definitely higher on the list than The King's Traitor and Defy and The Bronze Key, which are also exciting.) 
 I have no doubt Sanderson will deliver. I'm not ready for this amazing journey to end, but I crave more Alcatraz fun. 
 AFTER 
 Reader thoughts: Oh, Mr. Sanderson, you knew what you were getting into. 
 I was extremely upset at the end of the book. This wasn't just, "Main characters died, and how dare he!" but, more importantly, "Alcatraz isn't funny anymore, how dare he!" I was sad at the deaths, but it bothered me more that Alcatraz had to go through such trauma and stress that he lost his humor. 
 That's right, about the last 50 pages of this book are not funny. Alcatraz warns us in the forward, but I didn't heed him. My trust in Sanderson dropped a notch. (Not that it prevented me driving 9 hours to and from one of his book signings this week). 
 I felt a little betrayed, like when the two hilarious guys in Warbreaker turned around to murder the good guys. Funny doesn't pair with tragedy in my head. 
 The only time I remember reading a book where the author drastically changed the MC was in The Queen of Attolia. I hated that, too (when Gen went from joking and clever to brooding and spiteful). This happened a bit in Mockingjay, too (when Katniss went from badass hunter lady to a girl shaking from nightmares and PTSD). Yeah, I get that sometimes bad things change people for the worse, but it doesn't have to be in books. It doesn't have to be in these books. It doesn't have to happen in this children's book! 
 Alcatraz watched his father get tortured to death. The end note only slightly ameliorated the awfulness by 
 1, telling the reader that Grandpa Smedry is still alive. 
 and 
 2, having Bastille promise to write the final volume because Alcatraz won't. 
 Now, I am very excited to have another book (and hoping it fixes all the problems from this one), but I'm not sure how I feel about Bastille narrating it. It would be neat to see Alcatraz through her eyes, though. But, will it be as funny as the first four? 
  
 Everything else about the book was fantastic (except Dif, but whatever). I loved the Penguinator. I loved the wardrobe. I loved the elusive Dark Talent. I loved infiltrating the highbrary. I loved the cure. I loved the overpowered glass. I loved everything between Alcatraz and his mother. 
 And I especially loved the footnotes. Here's a piece of my favorite, Alcatraz's list of ways to die that don't sound very fun. 
 "eating rocks, being eaten by rocs, being punched by The Rock . . . accidental grenade ingestion, being sucked up a tornado, Avada Kedavra, being sued by J. K. Rowling . . . accidental teddy bear detonation, being eaten by a sentient romance novel . . . putting something metal in the microwave." 
 Writer thoughts: It really is a sign of true writing genius when a book can be this upsetting. When an audience can shrug off a supposed tragedy or roll their eyes at deep betrayal, that shows the author did a terrible job. In some ways, the fact that people are so upset only demonstrates how powerful Sanderson's writing is.

Catton's Booker-prize winning book is a real feat. It has the capaciousness of a Victorian novel, with the attention to detail and social awareness of Dickens, and the murder mystery story with supernatural elements like Wilkie Collins, but the formal framework is all her own. She's written the novel using astrology as the conceit to hang everything on. Every character represents an astrological sign, although the main movers and shakers are planets (which makes sense, as the signs are influenced by planets, just as men are influenced by men with more power or charisma), with the golden boy Emery Staines as the sun, and the prostitute Anna Wetherell as the moon. This is fitting since, even though it's not discernible for most of the book, all the actions and thoughts of all the characters revolve around these two. Even stranger, the main narrator, who quickly takes the story out of the hands of the man who begins the narration, is the sky itself! The celestial heavens tells you when a man is dissembling, when his knowledge is incomplete, when he is imperfectly understood by his interlocutor. And just when I thought she couldn't take it further, I found out that each chapter's word-count is half the previous one! Just as a formal achievement, it's astounding, but it's not done without a fumble here and there. The conceit becomes a little forced at the end, where the chapters become so short that the preamble describing each has to do most of the work of telling the story. There are many, many characters to keep track of, and the actual mystery at the center is pretty convoluted. Once I gave myself over to the story, and stopped trying to keep track of everything, I really enjoyed it. She gives you all the atmosphere of the New Zealand gold rush populated with villains, diggers, con men (and women!), opium addicts, Chinese indentured servants, (one) Maori, as well as double crosses, bastard brothers, forgery, fraud, and every other thing people get up to. Catton's book contains multitudes.

The Einstein Intersection: New Wave SF with style but story lacks discipline 
 Originally posted at Fantasy Literature 
 It doesn't get any more New Wave SF than this very slim 1968 Nebula-winning novel (157 pages), and it's hard to imagine anything like this being written today. It's a mythical retelling of the Orpheus and Eurydice story in a far-future Earth populated by the mutated remnants of humanity. 
 Being a Delany book, the writing is disjointed, jazzy, lyrical, playful, and tantalizing. The surface events are fairly obscure, but it's clear that the real narrative is buried beneath, and in case you didn't catch on, every chapter has several obscure (and fairly pretentious) quotes from intellectuals, not least of all the author himself, who inserts between chapters snippets of his journals from his artistic travels in the Mediterranean while writing this book, in classic meta-fiction style. Even in a longer book I'd view this literary device as fairly self-indulgent, but when the entire story is 157 pages, it's seems downright insulting to the reader. It's very clear that reader expectations and tastes have changed dramatically in the last half century. 
 The plot, to be charitable, involves Lo-Lobey, a humanoid mutant in the far future who sounds more like a Neanderthal with great brute strength but limited brain capacity. He is a musician who plays his sword like a flute, and when his love Friza disappears one day, he sets out on a quest to find her. His nemesis is a fearful super-being called Kid Death, a mutant with the power to kill seemingly at will who is intent on wiping out other mutants (which makes you wonder why he doesn't dispatch them all with a flick of the wrist). 
 One of the key themes of the book is the mythical overtones of the Lo-Lobey's Orpheus-like quest into the underworld, and by far the most amazing and intense part of the book is the extended sequence in which Lo-Lobey hunts down a massive minotaur underground and battles him. The writing is fantastic and if the book had been able to sustain more passages like this, I would have liked the novel much more. As it is, I felt that was the high point and the narrative collapsed afterward. 
 The other major theme is mutation as a metaphor for being "different", and when we consider that Delany himself was a gay black poet growing up in Harlem, that makes sense. He married high-school classmate poet Marilyn Hacker after high school, but they experimented with polygamy and had affairs with both men and women, and Marilyn later declared herself lesbian after their divorce. So it's fair to say Delany would consider himself different. The underlying theme of the story also strongly identifies with the mutants, and at the end of the story Lo-Lobey realizes that instead of imitating the traditions of the extinct human race, the aliens (for that is what they are) need to embrace their differences and live on their own terms. This may make sense thematically, but to shoehorn such a complex idea into the fragile vessel of this story is really over-reaching in my opinion. 
 Nonetheless, it's hard to believe this book won the Nebula and was nominated for the Hugo, since it wouldn't even get a consideration now and might only count as a novella. I wish I could have been in on the award committee deliberations. There must have been an old-guard group supporting Golden Age writers, and a much younger, hipper, coffee-house social activist group on the other side, locked in a deadly struggle for supremacy. Tracking the Hugo and Nebula winners through past decades is a fascinating barometer of the changing times and SF readership, something that an MA thesis could be devoted to.
