Okay, so I seem to be like the only one who was "meh" about Everneath. 
 Well then. 
 But I can say this. I'm in agreement with most of the Goodreads-world in this case. 
 Everbound was so much... better than Everneath, in my opinion. 
 This is one of those rare circumstances in which the second book actually surpasses it's first book! Whoa! Surprise! Brodi Ashton is keeping us on our toes. 
 I found Everneath to be a bland, sketchy retelling of a myth, that kind of stretched the boundaries of mythological retellings a little bit too much, with a weak heroine, and unappealing love interests. Oh, and all the characters were just...glum. There was just far too much brooding. 
 Everneath focused on the psychological happenings to Nicki Beckett, our protagonists. Her recovery from hell essentially, and her strive to redeem herself. How the other people reacted to it. It was definitely a more slow, deeper? book. 
 But I just found it oh so hard to get into. 
 But then comes Everbound. 
 And bam. 
 Everything changes. Right-side up is now upside down and vice versa. 
 Everbound is all about the quest, and dare I say it, a little adventure. For most of the book, Nicki, Cole, and Max are venturing deeper and deeper into the Everneath, farther than anyone has ever gone, to go to the Tunnels and save Jack Caputo. 
 It's...intense. Suspenseful. And Everbound just has the "more" I was looking for in Everneath. 
 I could actually relate to Nicki in this novel. I understood her frustration, at how everyone was trying to help her, and telling her that the only way they could help her is if she told the truth, but if she told the truth, no one would ever believe her. She appreciated their efforts, but in this case, she was really all alone. 
 Except for Cole. 
 I've always had my suspicions about that guy , but I never truly expected him to turn and become a full-on traitor to us.  
 But I still had a few qualms with this book. 
 1) The Ring of Water. Wasn't it supposed to mess with your emotions? But most of the obstacles that our trio came across in it were just...Wanderers. I was expecting an intense,complete emotional attack from something, but instead, we got Everliving zombies. Argh, it's a small detail, but one that kind of bugged me nonetheless. 
 2)  When Jack Caputo came back.  I mean, yeah, it was happy, reunion and everything, but I was just utterly perplexed at how it happened. There was some vague description about digging himself out, but for the longest time, I thought it was an illusion or something, or someone pretending to be him. Like, no one really saved him. And bam, he just pops up in Nicki's bedroom one day, with no explanation. And everyone accepts that? Bogus. 
 3) The pacing. I know these books are slower, but it took me like a third of the book to actually get into the world, into the story. The beginning...didn't grab me. Nicki being angsty about Jack's disappearance is not how I want to start a book. 
 But despite these issues, it truly was a good, and kind of spooky book. 
 The description of the Tunnels? With all the hands? Oh my word, that was so bonechilling and so freaky and so disturbing...*shudder* 
 Which is a good thing. In this case. Yeah. 
 But that's the point of it all. The Everneath is a seriously disturbing place. 
 I think that was my main problem with Everneath (the book). The idea of Feeding and everything was just so disturbing that I didn't really want to read 300 pages of stuff about that. 
 And the ending to Everbound. OH. MY. GOODNESS. 
 I hated it, but also loved it, for Ashton to spring something like that on us. It was really ingenious...but also ridiculously agonizing. My heart goes out to Nicki. 
 I loved her final words on the final page. 
 "You know the Everneath?" 
 "Uh ,yeah, I think I'm familiar with it." 
 "Good because I'm going to destroy it." 
 His smile faded. 
 "I'm taking the whole. Darn. Thing. Down. 
 Aaah, I need Evertrue now! 
 I recommend this series to anyone who's looking for a mythological retelling that's just really...chilling. 
 Wait, that's way to specific. 
 If you liked stuff like Starcrossed or dark fantasy teen novels, you'll probably like this series. 
 Everbound. Disturbing, but in a good way.

After finishing the Gabriel Inferno Trilogy, I discovered that Sylvain Reynard was writing a spinoff novel set in the same universe but supernatural and the main character was seeking revenge on the Emersons. I will be the first to admit they are not at all perfect, but I was not keen on the idea of something bad happening to them. So I read 'The Prince', and although I still had some uncertainty, I continued with reading this book. 
 I enjoyed the character of Raven Wood. She isn't thin, she has disability with her foot, but she works at the Uffizi Gallery restoring artwork. I could tell she had a past that no one knew about and was interested in learning more about her. 
 The story begins with The Prince two years after the novella of the 'The Prince' still seeking revenge on the Emersons for stealing his illustrations. Raven is leaving a party with some friends when she sees three guys beating a homeless guy, someone she knows. She tries to intervenes causing them to go after her. Close to death, she is rescued by figure. She wakes up the next day and notices that her appearance is different, she is thinner, her leg is no longer an issue for she can not run, and she no longer needs her glasses. Returning to work, she discovers that the paintings the Emersons lend to the Gallery were stolen and it hasn't been a day but a week since the robbery and her disappearance causing the police to be suspicious of her. Ease dropping on a conversation between Gabriel and Vittali, the name William York becomes a lead. So she goes to where she believes he is which is the turning the point in the novel, at least to me. Returning home, someone is waiting for her; telling her to leave, which of course she does. She wants to clear her name.  Mhhh... I am sitting here, having just finished this book, and really wondering about how I feel about it. 
 The first part of this novel is setting the scene for a pretty common captivity story - a young girl, off to Mexico despite her parents saying no, a charming young man who isn't so charming on the inside and well = the start of a living nightmare of forced sexual slavery. It reminded me of too many books I've read before. 
 The first 75% of the book 
 If I could say one thing about how I felt about this book up to 3/4 through, it would be that the story was going through the motions. Everything that should've been there, was there but I felt myself not fully being able to connect to the story and its characters. Speaking of the characters, I was left largely confused. I would not exactly count this Angela's story dark, again, it felt more like going through dark motions without ever really getting to the heart of things. 
 - Fernando (the initial captor) disappears from the scene quite early on. Now that was a character I would have loved to have around! 
 - Marco on the other hand I could not make sense of at all - he would be ruthless one minute and insecure the next. We never get to read this story from his perspective which I felt was a shame - somehow that led me to not feeling the psychological undertones of the story at all - I only ever heard from the 'good' side, never from the bad. I knew the undertones and emotions were there but they just didn't transfer. 
 - Angela was at one point just there - I could not fully appreciate how what she was going through emotionally. Although part of the books was written from her perspective, the writing was very descriptive. Whilst I can understand that this may have been in order to see her detachment to the situation, it really led me to sometimes just feel nothing at all either and it made it hard to keep being interested in the book. 
 - Colin again left me confused - strong and also bitter on one hand but so not in control of himself on the other - it just left me feeling irritated. 
 The last 25% of the book 
 Would have made it a four or even five star read for me. There were such intense moments between all of the characters that I enjoyed immensely. Part of me felt like finally reading the book I was hoping to read. Field really brought deep emotions out of the characters. Whilst up until the 75% mark I found everything that happened rather predictable, I could have never seen any of the rest coming. 
 It was raw 
 It was intense 
 It was heartwarming 
 It was everything I wanted 
 It was creative 
 Sadly, for me, it was not enough - knowing the first 75% are there, I would never pick this book up again. 
 On a final note, Field is a good writer and I am considering reading Josef's story when it comes out simply because I envision him being a deeply complex character. The reference to Fifty Shades of Grey caught me off guard for a moment but overall, the writing was pleasant, just not as intense as I would have liked.

When I first started reading "V is for Virgin" I expected Valerie to be this unassuming, shy young woman who is too bashful, religious, fill-in-the-blank to give up her v-card. Never assume! She was surprisingly strong especially in her convictions and reasons to remain a virgin until she married. You go girl! Don't get me wrong. I love a hot, panty melting story as much as the next girl. But, "V is for Virgin" was such a wonderful change of pace and attitude. It was not preachy, had loads of humor and delivered a great message in a non-judgmental, that's-okay-for-you-but-this-decision-is-best-for-me sort of way. Valerie stayed true to her convictions throughout and endeared herself to me by the way she handled the less-than-supportive attitudes of those around her. It was refreshing to see the author stay true to Kyle's character also rather than have him change just for the sake of a quick and easy (but smile-worthy) happy-ever-after or happy-right-now.  Kyle was not in a place in his life where he was willing to wait until marriage for sex with Valerie nor was he willing to marry her without a sexual relationship already established. He didn't want to take such a formal step as marriage if they were not sexually compatible. And, as an indulged, almost famous musician who has beautiful, willing young women throwing themselves at his feet everyday, he realizes he would stray and break Valerie's heart. Blunt and a bit harsh but realistic.  Good job Ms. Oram. I really wanted to like Valerie's best friend, Cara. While the banter between the two friends was a scream and a half, I found Cara to be very self absorbed, even in the beginning. Isaac on the other hand was adorable throughout the story. What a sweetheart. The only thing I did not thoroughly enjoy about "V is for Virgin" was the ending. It seemed there were too many events included in an attempt to tie everything up in a neat little bow in order for everyone to have their HEA or nearly so. Despite my feelings for the ending, I really enjoyed Kelly Oram's "V is for Virgin".

This was a lovely YA novel. I thought it was a storylover's dream because it amalgamates so many of the stories that are familiar to most people raised in a Western atmosphere and probably a lot of people who weren't. This novel integrates Celtic and Greek mythologies with Rumplestiltskin, Bluebeard, and Beauty and the Beast. I'm sure there are other stories that were woven into the intricate tapestry of Cruel Beauty that I was just not cool enough to pick up on. 
 I loved the characters in this story because they weren't entirely loveable. Everyone in the story is incredibly flawed, and everyone in the story has at least one endearing quality. 
 Nyx is intelligent, brave, strong, dutiful and... bitter! I like that she has a real darkness inside herself that she comes to grips with. All of the players in Cruel Beauty's plot are like that, they seem rather simple at first glance but through the events of the story the reader comes to see that, while their initial impressions weren't wrong, the characters are a lot more than what they originally seemed, kind of like people... 
 Nyx is upset that she is made to marry the ruthless magical tyrant that reigns over Arcadia because of the reckless bargain her father made before she was even born, but she is determined to make the most of her marriage by saving her land from their overlord's spell. She plans on seducing him, gaining his trust, and destroying his house with him inside, but when she is given to the Gentle Lord and slowly begins to unravel the truth of The Sundering she falls in love with him. 
 This book was pretty awesome but it was made even better (I think, I'm just guessing here because I have only done it one way) by the vocal talent of Elizabeth Knowelden. I liked listening to her voice, I felt that the fact that the book was from first person perspective worked well with her reading of the book's characters' idioms and attitudes without changing her voice very much. To me it seemed as if Nyx was telling the story and doing poor mimicry of the others in the story. 
 Some things I didn't like about it were that the world was not built up enough for me. We got glimpses of religion, politics, and magic, but it was all really focused directly on the plot and so I don't really know what is going on in the world. If this is a series, then I hope this is expanded upon in later volumes. The story is pretty self-contained though so I don't know that it will be a series, what suggests that to me is the fact that a novella exists by the same author that is dubbed "a Cruel Beauty novella" so if that's a thing, then a sequel might be also. I wanted to know more about hermetic workings especially. Nyx talked about nullifying, and balance, and referred to things as hermetic whatevers (replace whatevers with saying, device, study, experiment, etc.) so Hermeticism definitely occupies a significant place in society. Additionally, while I did enjoy this story I have to say I could have done with less of it. Parts felt drawn out that didn't need to be, like the ending, and many of Nyx's lamentations about her thoughts and feelings. 
 All in all a pretty good book. I enjoyed it a lot and appreciated all the allusion and homage to familiar stories incorporated.

The Alpha King is set in a dystopian reality in which shifters have risen up to rule the land and humans are subservient and owned by the different shifter regions. Set in what used to be the world as we know it, far in the future, the lands have been renamed and it is a different world. Each region has its own pack structure with leading families, the Alpha, betas, gammas, deltas, and omegas. What is missing and has been missing for sometime is an Alpha King and his Verum Omega. It has become the thought that such people never really existed, the scholars have since lost the records, and overtime the Alpha King and the Verum Omega have been thought as a myth meant to keep the packs in allegiance. So, imagine the upheaval when at the yearly mating rituals for all of age Alpha's, one Alpha-heir -Luca, starts presenting with traits beyond what is normal, he starts becoming the king. But how? He has no Omega. That is until he realizes that his powers strengthen and manifest when he is in the presense of a pitiful, scrawny, human slave - named Kit. He is drawn to Kit. Even though he knows as Alpha-heir he must mate with an Omega who can produce an heir, he can't control himself around Kit. 
 I loved reading this story. It had such amazing world-building and character definition. I loved watching Luca and Kit fall in love, and watch Kit transform from unwanted human slave to the Alpha King's mate and Verum Omega. Victoria Sue did a wonderful job not only doing a twist on the star-crossed lovers trope, but in creating a world that enamours the reader. I didn't want the story to end and my only problem with the story was it just felt to rushed in parts, not enough details to the little things that I like as a reader. This is a personal preference and may not even annoy other readers. I would have liked to see more love between the two, at times Kit wasn't even sure he was wanted, and that bothered me. In shifter stories, especially wolves, I like the mates to have a lot of passion and love. 
 Overall, 4.5 Stars and I am eager to see if there will be a book 2!

Not many books have moved me to actual crying with actual tears, but this one did. More than once. 
 It's going to take some time to gather all my thoughts about this emotional, powerful, gut-wrenching story, so I'm just going to say this review will be a work in progress for the next week. 
 This was another ebook I bought because it was a bestseller in Kindle's "Daily Deals," and I have to say, at first, I severely regretted my decision. At the beginning of the story, I hated--that's a strong word but "disliked" implies passivity--all the characters. I couldn't sympathize with the girl with murderous tendencies, the girl who's embarrassed by her religion, or the guy who thinks he owns the world because girls want to sleep with him. All their behavior was foreign to me, as a person whose high school was absolutely nothing like this one, and their language was disgusting. It felt like a bunch of annoying white teenagers with no morals or even brains, not to mention, a story. I thought I was going to have to DNF a quarter of the way through. 
 But like I said in one of my updates, this is the kind of book with "realistic" characters, who are annoying as heck on purpose at first, and then later you sympathize with them. 
 And boy, did I. 
 Lately, I've been in the habit of going into books not knowing anything of what they're about. So, with this one, I was not expecting the gravity of the sexual assault and rape culture themes. They're woven into every scene, every character, every conversation. This book will make you think about rape culture for real. Even as a person who couldn't relate to the characters' lifestyle, I felt for them. I was angry for them. I was devastated for them. And when Alex became a martyr for her cause, I was enraged. Motivated to do something different. To want an end to this.  
 Because even though the characters are kind of annoying at first and some of them seem unrealistic, this is a very serious and a very real issue, and this story handles it the way it needs to be handled: with a no-nonsense, angry punch to the gut. Or, if you're Alex, to Park's groin.  Or rather, a series of them. Repeatedly. 
 BUT with all that said, this isn't a totally dark rape-book. It's a story about teenagers and their everyday behavior and their friendships and their love lives and their worries and dreams and hardships and laughter. It's about senior year and puppies and prom and parents. 
 But it's also about danger. Because in this world, those things can't be separated. 
 "I live in a world where not being molested as a child is considered luck." 
 At this point in my review, I'm worried I'm scaring people away with all my talk of danger, so I'll touch on some of my favorite parts that are not dangerous at all: 
 There is romance. And it is unbelievably sweet. The kind where you read sentences that make your heart swell in your chest and you look like a weirdo smiling affectionately at your Kindle in public. 
 There are awesome girl friendships. Empowerment. Girls who call each other on their pettiness but don't judge each other and build each other up and comfort each other and it's beautiful. 
 There are good guys. In a book that deals a lot with rape culture, it's so important to have good guys in the mix, too, and this one has some really good ones. 
 There are puppies. And kittens, if that's your thing. Lots of 'em. 
 The only thing that really didn't work for me was the character of Branley Jacobs. She just isn't realistic. She's the only one who never broke out of her caricature of a typical annoying white teenage girl and fleshed out into a real person. I get that that's part of her character, that she feels all this pressure as a "female of the species" to be more pretty than real, but it was too much. 
 "You don't do that to me. I'm Branley Jacobs. Do you understand that? Branley Jacobs." 
 No girl talks like that, no matter how confident she's pretending to be. Branley just felt like the stereotypical mean girl to me, and I know there were reasons for that, and I think it COULD have worked well; it just wasn't executed as well as it should have been. 
 Alex's character was really important to me, though. I can't even go into detail about it because I don't want to give the story away, plus I can't exactly put it into words, but I will say that as a "mysterious" girl who definitely could've suffered from the Branley Effect, she did not. Her character was not only believable, but heart-wrenching and powerful. 
 I'm giving the book 4 stars because although it's powerful and I tore through it in just a few days, I feel like some things could have been executed better. HOWEVER, the only reason I even say that is because I feel like whoever reads this review should go into The Female of the Species knowing that even if some aspects fall flat, the novel as a whole is powerful (yeah I know I've said that 80 times but it's because that's the word. That's this book. It's powerful), and even though some parts could have maybe been a little more realistic, it deals with real life, and it works. It makes you think. It makes you want to do something.

First impressions: If there's one thing Maggie Stiefvater can do, it's write a good intro. I liked the tone of the prologue, setting us up for a not-so-happy ending. When the actual story begins, we pick up soon after the first book left off, and I thought things got going right away. 
 Lasting impressions: Even though I could see where the story was going, I really didn't want it to happen. This book suffered from "middle book syndrome," where there's enough of a story arc to get us through, but no real conclusion. Instead, we're left to decide whether we care enough to find out the end of the saga in the third book. 
 Negative impressions: Though I liked the introduction of the new character, Cole, I found the four narrators to be a bit much. I often found myself uncertain who was "speaking" and would read several paragraphs before realizing I was in Cole's head and not Sam's. Everything in these books reads exactly the same way, in exactly the same voice, which does not lend itself to two narrators, let alone four. 
 Overall impressions: In some ways, I actually liked this book better than Shiver. Grace was less annoying, but perhaps only because with four narrators I spent less time in her head. Sam became much less interesting in this book, but Cole was exciting and fresh, and his dark attitude brought something different. 
 The story changes a bit in this one, with the wolves less able to control their shifting, which leads to Sam, Grace, Cole and Isabel trying to figure out what's going on. When the book ends, they still haven't found a solution, and instead the ante is upped even farther, setting up the need to solve the problem in the last book, out this summer. I have to admit that curiosity is convincing me to give Forever a try, though the fact that I find these books only mildly interesting may change my mind. Stiefvater is great at thinking up interesting plots, there's just something missing in the execution.

"Left Neglected" is one of the most inspirational books I have read this year. It tells the story of 37-year-old Sarah, a busy, intelligent and hard working career woman, wife and mother of three young children, who sustains a traumatic brain injury in a car accident on her way to work. Waking up in hospital Sarah is told that she suffers from a neurological condition called "left neglect", also known as hemispatial neglect, in which her brain is unable to perceive anything on the left, even the left side of her own body. For Sarah it is as if "left" simply no longer exists, is no longer part of her reality. Unable to do the simplest things for herself, such as walking or dressing herself, let alone work or look after her children, Sarah's world is turned upside down as she realises that recovery is a long, hard road, and that she may never recover full function. With the help of her loving husband Bob and her estranged mother, who has moved in with the family to help Sarah look after her children, Sarah is trying to reclaim her life .... 
 I found this story fascinating from the very first page. Although my life only runs at about 30% of Sarah's pre-accident pace, I could relate to her struggle to juggle a busy career and a family, and her determination to function at 110% at all times. Both before and after the accident, Sarah is not one to give up easily, and never sinks into self-pity and despair, despite the daily frustrations of trying to reclaim her independence after her accident. In this daily battle to overcome her disabilities, and her never-give-up attitude, Sarah is a true inspiration to anyone who has ever had to struggle against adversity. 
 The author's knowledge of the neurological condition hemispatial neglect is evident throughout the story, and her thorough research has made Sarah a real flesh-and-blood character the reader can relate to. I had to remind myself that Sarah and her family were fictional characters, and this was not an autobiographical account of somebody's life story. With such vivid detail and personalisation of the condition, the book taught me more about the power of the brain than any textbook ever could - and how reality really is an abstract term, dependent on our brain's perception of "truth". Sarah's brain tells her that there is no left - and to her, the world is "real" and complete without a left. For Sarah, left simply does not exist, and is an abstract term much as "seeing" would be to someone born blind. Trying to understand Sarah's new reality was as fascinating as it was terrifying, maybe because it could happen to any of us, reality forever altered by a freak accident. 
 I was totally absorbed in this story and its characters and could not stop reading until I had turned the last page - and then felt poorer for no longer being part of Sarah's life. Genova writes with insight and compassion, and paints such a vivid picture that the reader is almost part of the story - a silent observer, smelling the coffee, hearing the baby cry, feeling the chill of the snow on bare skin. I absolutely loved this book, and must say that I enjoyed it much more than Genova's other novel, Still Alice. I recommend it to anyone who wants an inspirational, captivating read. 
 PS: If you enjoyed the theme of this story and are interested in novels featuring neurological conditions, you may also like The Echo Maker by Richard Powers. Though vastly different in style, it also pays homage to the power of our brain and "reality" being an abstract concept dependent on the function of neurons and synapses - and will challenge everything you have ever believed about what is "real".

I read Garden Spells a month ago after a friend noticed that I added this book (the second one about these characters) to my to-read list and she said that I had to read the first in the series before the next. I absolutely adored Garden Spells so I was excited to read another book about the Waverly family. This ended up being a good book too, not as magical for me as the first but a satisfying read. It had the tension of the threatening stranger and how he will wreak havoc on the family and the tentative love relationships. It also had more of the "ever after" for the two women who found love by the end of the last books. I would recommend reading Garden Spells first because it really helps to have all the background on all these characters. I don't think the book will have as much impact if you don't have that background. 
 This story focuses on three women in the Waverly family and is set many years after (I think it was 10 years after) the events in Garden Spells. Claire Waverly has started a new venture that uses the garden magic she is known for, she is running Waverly's Candies now. However things are starting to spin out of control and Waverly's Candies is so successful it is completely taking over her life. Sydney has settled into a happy marriage with Henry and has put her first abusive marriage behind her. Still Sydney is struggling with the fact that she wishes she could have another baby, a baby for her and Henry to call their own and it's just not happening. 
 The character we hear the most from though is Bay, Sydney's daughter. Bay's magical ability is to know where things belong. This ability backfires when she meets a boy at school, Josh Matteson, and knows that they belong together in some way. Unfortunately the Matteson and the Waverly families have history and it's not good history. In addition to all the above a strange man drifts in that is tied to Claire and Sydney's mother's past and he end up causing even more chaos. 
 This book (along with Garden Spells) is often classified as "women's fiction". I guess it kind of is, but is also a beautifully written story with lots of magical realism and some mystery. This story does feature the trials of women in their mid 30's as they struggle with balancing jobs, husbands, kids...and magic. However this book has a bit more of a young adult flavor to it as well because Bay features in the story so much. Bay is dealing with some very normal (and also some not so normal) growing pains, she is 15 years old and still learning who she is. 
 I really love the beautiful writing style throughout the novel. There is excellent imagery here and it really makes the scenes come alive; you can almost smell the candies and taste the autumn in the air. I also love the interactions between these families. There is a lot of conflict here but it is resolved by the characters being supportive and understanding of each other. I love the fact that each of these women has one very specific magical ability that influences her life in a crazy way. 
 While this book does have a more YA tone to it at times, I think a lot of the issues dealt with are ones that grown women will relate to a bit more. Sydney is struggling to raise a girl that is nothing like her and is upset that she isn't able to get pregnant. Claire is excited about the success of her business but concerned by how much time she has to take away from her family to run it. There are other characters that flit in and out of their lives. A character that is close to dying, a character that is trying to recover after betrayal from his partner of many years, a teenage dropout with a baby that is struggling to get her life together, and an old con artist that is sick of conning people but not sure how else to live. I really enjoy how all these life stories weave in and out of the Waverly's lives. 
 Overall this was another fantastic book by Allen. If you loved Garden Spells I think you will enjoy this book. I would recommend both books to people who enjoy a beautifully flowing story about women struggling to make it through day to day life...but with the added twist that there is magic in their lives that provides unexpected and crazy influences.

The Look of Love rating: 3 out of 5 stars 
 The Sullivans series rating: N/A (haven't read them all) 
 The Look of Love (published in 2011) is the first book of Bella Andre's The Sullivan series. 
 How are the sex scenes? 
 My iPad says this book is 279 pages. I'd say at least half that is filled with scorching hot, clever, bocce ball inspired, stranger sex. 
 How are the story lines? 
 Story line. You only get one for your money with this book, but it's a decent one. 
 Would you read it again? 
 Yes, especially if I finish the series. I might also print out specific pages and tape them to my bedroom mirror for reference... 
 Summary 
 Chase Sullivan is one of six ridiculously good looking, overachieving brothers who go through women like a flu victim does Kleenex. As a world traveled photographer currently shooting a high profile fashion spread, Chase is ready to spend some quality time on the job site that just so happens to be his brother's multi-acre winery. We all know at least one of these families. Real life's version of the Will Smith dynasty. 
 Chloe Peterson is on the run and suffering from obvious trust issues while delivering serious blows to Chase's heroic deeds by questioning his every attempt to help and remaining a tight lipped, obliviously seductive mystery. 
 The entire story takes place at the winery and over the course of one week, excluding the Epilogue. Chase and Chloe grow to "know" each other and ultimately decide whether their new found feelings are strong enough to develop a permanent bond of trust and love. The supporting characters are few, but very adequate and add just enough to the novel's singular purpose - to drive Chase and Chloe's relationship forward. Trust is a the recurring theme. So much so that the word is written 50 times during the story and I'd guess mainly in reference to Chase's feelings, thoughts and words towards Chloe. 
 Review 
 The writing is some of Bella Andre's finest. There are some repetitive words that appear within sentences of each other (i.e., take her to a motel, leave her in some dank motel, I told you to take me to a motel), but as a whole the story flowed. The plot line is not multi-dimensional, but Marcus Sullivan's appearances are entertaining and I'm curious to read the second book and hear his story. If the Epilogue was any indication, Marcus will be a wonderfully tortured and wounded soul in need of healing. 
 As whirlwind romances go, this one is pretty fantastic and we would all be lucky to find a Chase (or Chloe, for the male readers) of our own.

Admittedly, embarrassingly, before he took over for Jon Stewart at The Daily Show, I had never heard of Trevor Noah. I wasn't initially sure what to expect from Stewart's replacement, but to be fair I wasn't really a die-hard follower of the show in the first place. Sure, I enjoy Stewart and his humor, but I wouldn't be completely lost if I didn't watch every episode or even every day; I typically only even watched occasional clips online. Needless to say, when Noah took over I started watching more; more often and more regularly. His humor, his perspective, and his voice are precisely what we need today. Thus, when I learned that he was releasing a book, especially a memoir, I just knew that I needed to read it. I was not, by any means, disappointed. 
 Before Noah's voice even appears on the pages, there are three highly notable things worth mentioning about this book: 1. There is a picture of young Trevor with his mother right on the title page, 2. His dedication: "For my mother. My first fan. Thank you for making me a man," and 3. The Immorality Act of 1927. The weight of these three elements sets the tone for the book and, in retrospect, appropriately balances his attention to subject matter. His life with his mother, and even his mother alone, are by far incredibly prominent focal points for Noah's essays. The very nature of his existence, as technically a crime under the Immorality Act, is also a major factor as it dictated how he and his parents could interact in a society rife with such prejudices and, let's be honest, flat-out racism, as was the case in apartheid era South Africa. Each move he and his family made had to be precisely calculated. In many ways, there are incredible, and incredibly heartbreaking in every sense of the word and its meaning, parallels to the black experience here in America, especially in poor, underprivileged areas. Noah's reflections on his own poverty (at one time being so poor that he and his family slept in cars at his stepfather's workshop and ate worms) really provide a much needed perspective that everyone can and should appreciate. 
 Trevor Noah is also known for his comedy, so while there are definitely very serious and even scary (especially regarding his stepfather, Abel) stories between these pages, there are also some really hilarious aspects, too. Trevor generally seems like a guy who had a happy childhood (thank you, Patricia Noah) and was, quite frankly, a bit of a clown. I enjoyed the back and forth between him and his mother, especially when he tries to reason with her for getting out of going to church (a whole day ordeal, schlepping between three different churches: black church, white church, and mixed church; I can't say I blame the kid). I actually found that while I enjoyed this book in its entirety, I particularly and especially enjoyed any and every story involving his mother, Patricia. I became so invested in this strong, beautiful woman, that I almost skipped ahead to the last chapter (essentially an ode to her) to read over and over again. I remained patient, however I still have the urge to reread this chapter. Trevor's love and appreciation for, and dedication to, his mother is clear throughout this book, even in his reflections of tense, painful situations (e.g. cutting her out of his life when she becomes pregnant with Abel's second son).  'You're lucky to be alive,' I told her. 'I still can't believe you didn't have any health insurance.' 
 'Oh, but I do have insurance,' she said. 
 'You do?' 
 'Yes. Jesus.' 
 'Jesus is your health insurance?' 
 'If God is with me, who can be against me?' 
 'Okay, Mom.' 
 'Trevor, I prayed. I told you I prayed. I don't pray for nothing.' 
 'You know,' I said, 'for once I cannot argue with you. The gun, the bullets--I can't explain any of it. So I'll give you that much.' Then I couldn't resist teasing her with one last little jab. 'But where was your Jesus to pay your hospital bill, hmm? I know for a fact that He didn't pay that.' 
 She smiled and said, 'You're right. He didn't. But He blessed me with the son who did.' 
 Though we grew up in vastly different worlds and with vastly different experiences, I found so many common traits with Trevor: 
 I didn't have any friends. I didn't know any kids besides my cousins. I wasn't a lonely kid--I was good at being alone. I'd read books, play with the toy that I had, make up imaginary worlds. I lived inside my head. I still live inside my head. To this day you can leave me alone for hours and I'm perfectly happy entertaining myself. I have to remember to be with people. 
 Okay, so the above relates in large part to the fact that he often couldn't go out, especially in certain neighborhoods, because of the color of his skin: he was always considered either too white or not black, never just Trevor. I understand the lone nature, though; as an introvert, this has always been my general state of being. Being alone is not being lonely and it's perfectly cool to be content with entertaining yourself, especially when books are involved... 
 My books were my prized possessions. I had a bookshelf where I put them, and I was so proud of it. I loved my books and kept them in pristine condition. I read them over and over, but I did not bend the pages or the spines. I treasured every single one. As I grew older I started buying my own books. I loved fantasy, loved to get lost in worlds that didn't exist. I remember there was some book about white boys who solved mysteries or some shit. I had no time for that. Give me Roald Dahl. James and the Giant Peach, The BFG, Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, The Wonderful Story of Henry Sugar. That was my fix. 
 As a librarian and general bibliophile, I fell in love with the above quote. As an anthropology minor (undergrad) and ever hopeful (future) linguistic anthropologist, I found Noah's comments on the power of language to be really inspiring and meaningful. 
 Language brings with it an identity and a culture, or at least the perception of it. A shared language says 'We're the same.' A language barrier says 'We're different.' The architects of apartheid understood this. Part of the effort to divide black people was to make sure we were separated not just physically but by language as well...The great thing about language is that you can just as easily use it to do the opposite: convince people that they are the same. Racism teaches us that we are different because of the color of our skin. But because racism is stupid, it's easily tricked. 
 Nelson Mandela once said, 'If you talk to a man in a language he understands, that goes to his head. If you talk to him in his language, that goes to his heart.' He was so right. When you make the effort to speak someone else's language, even if it's just basic phrases here and there, you are saying to them, 'I understand that you have a culture and identity that exists beyond me. I see you as a human being.' 
 Trevor Noah is a polyglot, a necessary trait he developed while growing up in South Africa, where people were separated for so many stupid reasons (because, yes, racism is stupid) including language (aka tribe). By learning so many different languages, Noah was able to fluidly navigate difficult social situations as well as establish friendships, avoid being mugged (or worse), and understand others' cultural identity. We could all learn at least a little bit, if not more, from Noah's examples, especially here. 
 I highly recommend this book to everyone, regardless of your familiarity with Trevor Noah. I also recommend reading this book simultaneously with (or before/after reading) the YA book The Hate U Give for some beautiful/heartbreaking parallels (both with some much needed humor!) as well as important perspective into the black experience in America, especially today.

 There is just so much I love about this book. And then there's the main message of the story that I fundamentally disagree with. It's almost hard to reconcile the two, but it was a perfect example of a book that took me outside my comfort zone. 
 I usually read to be entertained, to maybe fall in love with a story. While I'm not opposed to big Thought Provoking books, I don't generally seek them out. But then came Me Before You, wrapped up in a romantic package, led by a character that initially reminded me of a Sophia Kinsella novel (that's not a bad thing, mind you, there's a time a place for chick lit fun) and I got so much more than I was asking for. 
 Will Traynor was a daredevil, world-traveling, successful, active man. Then an accident occurs that leaves him as a quadriplegic. Will cannot adjust to his new life, being paralyzed from the chest down, needing to rely on those around him. He has lost the will to live. Enter Lou. At first glance she's flighty and aimless, though cheerful. She begins a 6 month contract being Will's daytime caregiver and during their time together she begins to bring him out of his shell of depression and he challenges her to figure out what to do with her life, to travel, to make a plan. To love. 
 And then comes the twist. Will does not want to live as a quad anymore. He wants to die and he wants his family to take him to a facility in Switzerland that specializes in assisted suicide. His parents made a deal with him to wait and think about it for 6 months, hence Lou's 6 month contract where she endeavors to make Will change his mind. Does love really conquer all? 
 This is where the book became so much more than just an entertaining romance. It takes an issue that I completely disagree with - euthanasia / assisted suicide - and makes me really evaluate why I feel that way. It gives a real to life example of why it might be the right decision to make. Moyes made me fall in love with this character who is depressed and paralyzed, without any chance of getting physically better, who wants to end his pain. Is that his choice to make? Should it be? What would I want in such a situation? 
 Overall, I really loved Me Before You. While it didn't change my mind on the subject of assisted suicide (I still think Will is a selfish dick for even considering it - though a selfish dick I still love), it really challenged me to think and evaluate my own beliefs. I also thought the characters were wonderfully developed and the slow-burn of the romantic relationship felt natural and realistic. Despite the heavy content, it was also humorous and sweet. It was beautifully and evocatively written and left me a mess. I would definitely recommend this book.

There was a desert wind blowing that night. It was one of those hot dry Santa Anas that come down through the mountain passes and curl your hair and make your nerves jump and your skin itch. On nights like that every booze party ends in a fight. Meek little wives feel the edge of the carving knife and study their husbands' necks. Anything can happen. You can even get a full glass of beer at a cocktail lounge. 
 This is the opening to Chandler's short story "Red Wind" and the excerpt that brought his fine writing to my attention. After reading this I knew I had to not only read the "Red Wind" but also more of Chandler's work. 
 A little background 
 At the age of 44 after losing his job with an oil company during the depression, Raymond Chandler decided to become a detective fiction writer. He would go on to write 7 novels (a number adapted into popular films) and be elected as president of Mystery Writers of America, the year before he died. 
 He has been lauded for his sharp and lyrical prose that rival those of any literary great and criticized for his treatment of minorities, women, and homosexuals in his novels. Some have claimed his plots were chaotic messes. 
 Generally acknowledged today for his hefty contribution to the written word especially with respect to the crime genre, in his day Chandler was often received snippy criticisms of his work. 
 One response to his critics, "The thing that rather gets me down is that when I write something that is tough and fast and full of mayhem and murder, I get panned for being tough and fast and full of mayhem and murder, and then when I try to tone down a bit and develop the mental and emotional side of a situation, I get panned for leaving out what I was panned for putting in the first time." 
 You just can't please everybody. 
 My take 
 Personally, I think he's a genius. 
 His prose are probably some of the best I have read. 
 His characters or rather caricatures are skillfully rendered. 
 His main character, while wrapped in a macho veneer, is complicated and layered. 
 And the dialogue? WOW! A+++ 
 Politically correct? For the time, probably-yes, but if you're someone who is easily offended you may find some of the more misogynistic and homophobic references to be too much. Personally, I have a very easy time viewing books like this in the context they were written at the time they were written, but that's me. 
 Finally, as far as the plot--while "busy" it was not especially hard to follow, at least I didn't find it hard to follow. I actually like the layering, which ultimately comes full circle as it is exactly what I expect when reading a good mystery. 
 This was just fun to read and I want to read more. 
 Who would I recommend this to? 
 This will likely appeal to the fan of the crime novel, especially those who appreciate the "hardboiled" and/or "noir" subgenres. Honestly, I could easily see fans of The Godfather and The Sopranos eating this up. 
 A little taste 
  
 It was about eleven o'clock in the morning, mid October, with the sun not shining and a look of hard wet rain in the clearness of the foothills. I was wearing my powder-blue suit, with dark blue shirt, tie and display handkerchief, black brogues, black wool socks with dark blue clocks on them. I was neat, clean, shaved and sober, and I didn't care who knew it. I was everything the well-dressed private detective ought to be. I was calling on four million dollars. 
 She was twenty or so, small and delicately put together, but she looked durable. She wore pale blue slacks and they looked well on her. She walked as if she were floating. Her hair was a fine tawny wave cut much shorter than the current fashion of pageboy tresses curled in at the bottom. Her eyes were slate-gray, and had almost no expression when the looked at me. She came over near me and smiled with her mouth and she had little sharp predatory teeth, as white as fresh orange pith and as shiny as porcelain. They glistened between her thin too taut lips. 
 This room was too big, the ceiling was too high, the doors were too tall, and the white carpet that went from wall to wall looked like a fresh fall of snow at Lake Arrowhead. There were full-length mirrors and crystal doodads all over the place. The ivory furniture had chromium on it, and the enormous ivory drapes lay tumbled on the white carpet a yard from the windows. The white made the ivory look dirty and the ivory made the white look bled out. The windows stared towards the darkening foothills. It was going to rain soon. There was pressure in the air already. 
 I sat down on the edge of a deep soft chair and looked at Mrs. Regan. She was worth a stare. She was trouble. She was stretched out on a modernistic chaise-longue with her slippers off, so I stared at her legs in the sheerest silk stockings. They seemed to be arranged to stare at. They were visible to the knee and one of them well beyond. The knees were dimpled not bony and sharp. The calves were beautiful, the ankles long and slim and with enough melodic line for a tone poem. She was tall and rangy and strong-looking. 
 "Just who the hell are you, soldier?" 
 "Marlowe is the name. I'm a sleuth." 
 "Never heard of you. Who's the girl?" 
 "Client. Geiger was trying to throw a loop on her with some blackmail. We came to talk it over. He wasn't here. The door being open we walked in to wait. Or did I tell you that?" 
 "Convenient," he said. "The door being open. When you didn't have a key." 
 "Yes. How come you had a key?" 
 "Is that any of your business, soldier?" 
 "I could make it my business." He smiled tightly and pushed his hat back on his gray hair. "And I could make your business my business." 
 "You wouldn't like it. The pay's too small."

Short Review 
 A basically by-the-numbers Dresden book (brink of financial money, suckered by his "chivalry" toward women, unrelated seeming plotlines converging, etc.) that breaks away from the serious business type of storyline we got in the previous installment. It still manages to drop in a few major development points regarding Harry and other characters, but overall it was nothing special. If you like Dresden, you'll probably like it. If you're a bit sour on him, this is one to skip. 
 Long Review 
 This was not really one of the better Dresden books in my opinion. I'm committed to finish as many of them as I can, all of them if possible, but this one was rough. 
 I'll start with the things I liked though. First, I genuinely enjoy a lot of the side characters that Dresden's built up over the series thus far. Ebenezar, Thomas, Kincaid, Murphy, etc. are all people I enjoy spending fictional time with. The pacing was excellent, as always. There were lots of interesting action sequences and set pieces, and the 'mystery' that needed solving - while not quite up to par with previous installments - was well thought out if not kind of obvious. 
 That's... really all the good I can think to say about it. It was a fun book I guess, from an entertainment value standpoint. 
 Which brings me to the slightly longer list of things I didn't like. First and foremost, because I expect it to affect the rest of my time with the series, is I absolutely hate Harry Dresden as a character. 
 In essentially every book so far Harry has gone out of his way to make a point about how people may call him a neanderthal but he's just chivalrous and he can't help but overreact around women in distress and so on and so forth. I think if this were treated as more of a foible it would irk me less, but Harry is proud of it. Proud of it in an obnoxious, self-aggrandizing way. Sentences like, "Call me a Neanderthal if you like, but I get real irrational about bad things happening to women," are presented as something he's actually proud of. It reminds me of someone saying something like, "Call me a racist if you like, but I get real irrational about black people owning property." 
 It's presented in the book in a way that makes it seem like he's in the right for feeling that way. Like he is following some holier than thou moral code of chivalry that has been abandoned by loose modern society. It makes Harry come across like some reprehensible Red Pill men's rights activist trash. I'm just waiting for him to doff his fedora and call someone "M'lady". 
 This ties into him focusing exclusively on only the physical, sexual characteristics of every female character. I increasingly wonder if Butcher doesn't secretly want to write erotica. It also ties into his irrational behavior when Murphy wriggles out of her pants to disarm the anti-personnel mines. Harry is an ass. Not in the lovable way, like how you might root for an anti-hero, he's just an ass. 
 The final confrontation also totally deflates entirely because Harry, or maybe Butcher here, has to devote so much time on the theme of Murphy as a helpless little girl and how big tough Harry wants to protect her but he can't. 
 The family sub-plot with Murphy felt completely tacked on, and weirdly out of character for her. I seemed like something that got added for thematic contrast to Harry's new familial ties. Additionally, there were a lot of little things that felt like general laziness. 
 The statues that Harry refers to as 'Foo Dogs' are not dogs, they're lions. Thirty seconds on Google (this was written in 2004, no excuses) would have told Butcher that. A single conversation with anyone who knows even the most minuscule amount of information on East Asian history, or culture, could have told him that. Yes, I know the Japanese term for them translates into 'Korean Dogs' because they went from China to Japan through Korea, but their mistake doesn't mean they'e not still depicting lions. Besides, the person in the book who wants them recovered is Tibetan and he would absolutely not call them dogs. 
 Someone will jump in and say, "Yeah but in the Dresdenverse they're dogs." I don't care. Butcher clearly intends the books to suggest they are occurring in our universe and it shows sloppy research and disinterest in representing other cultures accurately. 
 Speaking of sloppy there are a handful of mistakes that jumped out at me. The Blue Beetle has been a manual car the whole series, but Harry puts in in drive when he starts it. Then he later shifts to second. If you know how to drive a manual car you see this discontinuity here. 
 Harry's staff is in one place, it's never said that it moves, and it's suddenly somewhere else like it had been there the entire time. 
 So overall, two stars.
It really started to get good around page 300 - unfortunately I stopped caring by then. I will finish the series because I'd like to know the ending, but won't get my hopes up.

 Guy In Real Life follows two characters, Svetlana and Lesh, who meet one night when one accidentally runs the other over while on a bike ride home. Svetlana is into tabletop games like Dungeons and Dragons, while Lesh is into heavy metal music. Throughout the book, the two grow closer and Lesh begins to become interested in gaming (both MMORPGs and tabletop games) 
 I thought the premise of this book was a really great idea, and I loved the beginning, but some parts in the middle were a little flat for me. The book was told in dual perspective as well as a few "video game character" chapters thrown in there, which were used to show Lesh's progression in the MMO computer game he became engrossed in. I thought these were really cool because I've never really seen anything like that in a book before (other than when fanfiction was incorporated in Rainbow Rowell's "Fangirl") and they were important to moving along the plot of the book. 
 I also really liked the cover of the book and the title. Once you get into the book, you find out what the title means, and if you look closely, you can see that the first letter of each word of the title spells "G.I.R.L." (Girl) 
 The only problem I had with this book is I didn't really connect with the characters much (not because they were into gaming. I enjoy different types of gaming as well) but because they just seemed really two dimensional to me and there were definitely times when I felt like Lesh was really immature and just couldn't make up his mind about his feelings or what he wanted. And I understand that he's 16, and 16 year old boys are indecisive. 16 year old girls are indecisive too. It just kind of bugged me a little. 
 The end of the book was a little bothersome as well. I felt like things were only semi wrapped up and everything was rushed. It definitely had an abrupt ending.

Ginny Blackstone lives a pretty normal, quiet, boring life. Except where her quirky Aunt Peg is involved. Peg brings adventure and fun and craziness into Ginny's life, and even after Peg's death, she continues to make her niece's life unpredictable. Ginny receives a package with thirteen little blue envelopes, each numbered and decorated and containing strict rules. 
 Her aunt tells her to pack a bag and use the money in the envelope to buy a plane ticket to London, where her adventures will begin. And sixteen year Ginny, nervous and naive and logical, decides to do just that. The decision takes her on a confusion, wandering, and ultimately rewarding adventure through love, loss, and several European countries. Throughout the adventure, Ginny learns a lot about life, her aunt, and surprisingly, herself. 
 I really enjoyed 13 Little Blue Envelopes. I loved the traveling, the uncertainty of a new place, the whimsical locations so vividly described in Peg's letter. Maureen Johnson had a real talent when it comes to descriptions; I felt like I was actually in all of the places that were described, and by the end of the book, I felt just a little bit more well-traveled. 
 Johnson actually is very good at writing conversations as well, and thoughts. Everything was sincere, believable. I understood what the characters were going through, and I related to them a lot. Actually, that was my favorite part about this story. Not only did I relate to Ginny on just about every other page (her fairly sheltered life, her craving to explore mingled with her nervousness and fear of the unknown, her awkwardness, her naivety, really everything), I related just as much to Aunt Peg. Even though we as readers only get to know her through Ginny's memories and recollections, some small snippets from Richard, her letters to Ginny, the way she influenced other people's lives along the way, and her art, that's more than enough. I love Peg, and I wish I had an aunt like her (though I think I will end up being the aunt like her.) Flighty, quirky, distracted, artistic...I think what I related to most was this line from one of Peg's letters: "The way I saw it, the great artists didn't want to be comfortable. They wanted to struggle--alone--them against the world. So I wanted to struggle." Even though I'm a writer, I still have this fantasy of writing as a starving artist, but I also have s strong connection to my home. Wanderluster and homebody... I just really looked up to Peg. 
 I really enjoyed this book, and while I was both frustrated with and resigned to the ending, I was very excited when I found out there was a sequel! All in all, I think this is a great coming of age novel with important, relevant themes, relatable characters, and important lessons to teach. I will definitely be looking into more of Maureen Johnson's work!

Short Review

 Long Review 
 I'm always a little wary jumping into series that have fan bases that bring to mind adjectives like 'rabid' or 'obsessive'. Half because things almost always wind up over-hyped and half because I realize I'm probably more critical than the average person and the prospect of drawing the ire of legions of fan boys and girls can be daunting. 
 Still, here I am, going through the entire Dresden Files series after tons and tons of recommendations. 
 I'm told they get better after book three, which I hope is the case because so far I'm enjoying them but I haven't found anything to rave over yet. I'll start with the stuff that falls a bit flat for me, then go over the stuff I do really like about this book. 
 The first thing that bothers me is that it's kind of cliche heavy. I won't consider the premise to be a cliche just because I feel like paranormal private investigator is basically a sub-genre now. Other things within it though kind of feel like Jim Butcher was just ticking off boxes. Murphy is your basic gruff, hardassed but lovable cop with a heart of gold. Her partner is the sarcastic skeptical cop with a chip on his shoulder about the protagonist. There's the grunting, cool headed bartender who's friends with the protagonist. 
 I know this was written originally for a creative writing course, and Butcher said he purposefully wrote it to be formulaic, but it shows and it can be a touch disruptive in my opinion to the reading experience. 
 The protagonist himself is what I imagine you would get if you printed out the TV Tropes listing on private investigators and then accidentally dropped it into a blender with an AD&D rule book. He is like what a geeky 13 year old might imagine themselves being in ten to fifteen years. 
 He lives in a basement, wears a black duster all the time, and falls into a ton of other geeky cliches. At the same time, he is made out to be 'bad with women' in a typical geeky person fashion but then gets hit on constantly and has several women trying to sleep with him. As someone who fell strongly into the category of 13 year old geeky kid, it felt super juvenile to me. Dresden seemed to have gotten stuck in his teenage phase, and as a result just came across as stunted and immature rather than relatable. 
 The book's also a bit misogynistic. I expect that from most books anymore - which is terribly sad for everyone now that I think about it. Harry self-identifies as a chauvinist, and seems pretty cool with it since he doesn't change. 
 His 'chivalry' is brought up repeatedly as a character flaw, but it still seems to paint the women as the bad aspect. So while he wails about how he's a sucker for feeling compelled to help the poor damsels in distress, the women themselves come out looking manipulative, sneaky, or deceptive in playing his weakness. 
 The female characters almost all use seduction in some way to try to get Harry to do what they want. Bianca, the vampire who (naturally) runs an escort service is defeated by Harry exposing all the ugliness hiding beneath her preternatural beauty. Murphy, who is played up as a badass, is subjected to constant thoughts by Harry along the lines of "Oh, look at her cute little hands. She'd kill me if she knew I was thinking that." His inner monologue about her totally undermines her role as a tough female character by making her sound like a puppy barking at a big, tough dog. 
 Harry also insists initially that only a woman could have been angry and emotional enough to commit the murders. Because you know how you ladies get. Never mind that it turns out the villain is a guy. 
 It all just grates a little. 
 All that being said, it was a generally enjoyable read. The story isn't complex, and you pretty much know who's really behind things well before the big 'reveal', but the pacing is good and the action is well crafted. 
 I know some people didn't like how it was handled, but I thought that magic was handled well enough. It has its limits, and Dresden didn't feel like some kind of walking invincible juggernaut of a wizard. It also felt like it was more the focal point of the story rather than the detective side of things which I thought fit well with what was going on. 
 I had enough fun with this that I'll read through the rest of the series, but I do sincerely hope they get better like people say they do. I always expect first books to have their issues, and my understanding is he had written most of the first three before the first was published, so I can see those following suit. I just don't yet understand why people lose their minds over these so much yet.

 I really enjoyed reading "Touching Smoke", the first book in Airicka Phoenix's "Touch" series. I was constantly surprised throughout the book. Just when I thought I knew what was going on, Ms. Phoenix pulled the rug from under my feet and surprised me again! This is a great YA Paranormal Romance - readers who enjoyed books like James Patterson's "Maximum Ride" series and Kelly Armstrong's "Darkest Powers" trilogy will really like "Touching Smoke" by Airicka Phoenix! I give this book 4 stars! 
 This book is about a sixteen year old girl named Fallon who lives life on the run with her mother. Problem is she never even knew she was running until recently. Fallon's first clue something was off was when her mother purposefully drove a motorcyclist off the road and left him there. Fallon had an instant connection with this man on the motorcycle, almost like they were soul mates, but she had no idea why. She had no idea who he even was, but she had such a driving need to make sure he was alive and well. Later, Fallon found out this man's name was Isaiah, and he was sent to protect her at all costs. She realizes that she would do anything to protect him as well. Fallon knows that what she and Isaiah feel for each other is not typical for teenagers in love, but they were made for each other - literally. Bit by bit, strange things have been happening to Fallon and she doesn't know what is going on because her mother never answered any of her questions. The things happening to Fallon is not normal. Fallon and Isaiah are NOT normal. Join Fallon in "Touching Smoke" by Airicka Phoenix, in her search for the answers to her many questions about her existence. See what happens with Fallon and Isaiah in their fight for their lives in this great YA Paranormal Romance. 
 I really enjoyed the characters in "Touching Smoke." I liked seeing Fallon progress from an awkward and frightened girl to a strong and brave young woman. The change was great to see. There were so many obstacles, drama, and pain in Fallon's young life. But, when the time came to stand tall, fight and protect, Fallon did just that. I loved how she stood up for what she felt was right, and tried to protect what and whom she loved. I also loved Isaiah's character. I loved his bad boy looks when he was first introduced in the story. I love motorcycles so his bike gave him added bonus points in my book. I like how fiercely Isaiah tried to protect Fallon, even before she knew who he was. SLIGHT SPOILEREven though Fallon and Isaiah's love was programmed, I believed in it.  
 I read "Touching Smoke" quickly even though it was not a short read. I read the kindle version and when I was finished and came online to write my review I noticed that there were 380 pages in the paperback version. I had no clue there was that many pages because it didn't feel like a long read at all. I like when I am reading and just so engrossed in the story that the length doesn't bother me. I hate it when a book is really long for no reason, when the story just seems to go on and on with no end in sight - "Touching Smoke (Touch, Book 1)" definitely wasn't one of those books though! I think that author Airicka Phoenix paced this story perfectly. There was the right amount of everything at the right time: suspense, romance, action, heartbreak, and more. The conclusion of this story left me satisfied yet yearning for more. I will definitely be looking out for the second installment of the "Touch" series. Airicka Phoenix is an author to look out for, and I would recommend her to Young Adult Paranormal Romance fans.

 As I usually do when I'm in a bit of a reading slump, I picked up a book from a series that I don't particularly enjoy (call me a gluton for reading slump punishment) to get me out of it. Don't ask me why that makes sense to me - it just does. 
 The chosen one this time around was Torment, the second book in the much hyped Fallen-series by Lauren Kate. I ha-ha-hated the first book. I hated the setting of Sword & Cross, I hated the characters and most of the storyline. So I was pretty sure the title of the second part of Luce and Daniel's story would be a self-fulfilling prophecy kind of thing. 
 Then I started reading and well, colour me surprised! I actually really enjoyed Torment (there's a sentence that could be interpreted way way wrong). 
 We are catapulted into a new environment that's a lot more hospitable and glamorous. Bye bye bleak grayness of Sword and Cross, hellooooo Californian sunshine! 
 Even though I thought it was kind of lazy of Lauren Kate to use the 'new girl at a new school'-routine twice in one series, I was very happy with the change of scenery. There were some great new secondary characters introduced to us, my favorite of which were Francesca and Steven, who I imagine as Rosamund Pike (Gone Girl) and Robert Carlyle (Rumpelstilskin from Once Upon a Time). I really liked Miles and would have probably found Shelby more entertaining had I read her quips in English instead of the translated Dutch. Regardless: a real improvement, setting-wise. 
 The character development in Luce was kind of amazing too. I remember being really annoyed with her in Fallen, but in Torment, she was rather relatable. Okay, she still did some pretty stupid shit here and there (DID WE NOT TELL YOU TO NOT LEAVE SCHOOL GROUNDS, LUCE???) but I liked how she questioned the whole "true love" affair. 
 Another thing I liked was how she didn't forget about Penn. A lot of times in YA's like this, the MC has so much going on that there's no time or room for grieving - or even just a passing thought about their lost friend, most of the time. Luce is obviously stills scarred from her friend's death and her rol in it, making her a more real and in-depth character. 
 The Outcasts (literal translation of the Dutch translation back into English, so I hope that's how they're called in the original book) were very interesting to me and I'm curious about their role in the greater whole of things. We get some new and much needed insight into Luce's past lives, which I enjoyed, and learn more about the Shadows (no idea what they're called in English - sorry, you know what I mean though). The idea of how Luce interacted with the Shadows was kind of strange to me and suggests that Lauren Kate played with Play-Doh a lot when she was a kid or something, but I got used to it I guess. 
 I also liked how the chapters counted down and of course, the cover is once again gorgeous. 
 Towards the end, when the old Sword and Cross-characters start to pop up again, I was kind of bummed. Did Arriane, Roland, Gaby and Molly rrrrreally have to come back? I liked the new crew a lot better. 
 But all in all, I enjoyed reading this second part of the Fallen-series and I'm giving Torment 3,5 stars - not 5 because I will never really love these characters and not 4 yet because I think there's still room for improvement and plenty of books still to read in the series for this improvement to happen in. Overall, a very pleasant surprise that helped me out of my reading slump - yay!

 Superhero by Eli Easton, is about two best friends Jordan and Owen. Jordan realizes his homosexuality in the sixth grade, and to his dismay his body and heart is set straight on Owen, who is in fact straight or is he? Owen is a wrestler set on going pro, he has a gay best friend, and he is totally cool with that fact, until things start to change within him and he no longer is seeing Jordan as just Jordan. However with facing this new brink comes a lot of issues that could change Owen's life forever, is he willing to give up his whole entire life that he constructed for himself on a deep attraction for his best friend? ... I know pretty darn deep for a short story right? 
 "Holy sexual paradise, Batman. I was so fucking glad I was gay! 
 The main character Jordan was the greatest thing next to cheesecake! He was dorky, talented, a dreamer, and just plain adorable. I instantly loved him on sight, add this to the fact that he had such a good heart; he stuck by his friend even though he loved him and knew it was never going to work out. I also love that the author was so very consistent with his character, it made him so very vividly real to me. 
 "Besides, if there was a secret way to my heart, it was Jordy." 
 If Jordan was the greatest thing next to cheesecake, Owen the second main character, was better than white cheddar macaroni and cheese! Owen truly was a superhero, he had the kindest and biggest heart, I too instantly loved him on sight! Owen was not judgmental and despite being the popular jock he never allowed other people to peer pressure him into anything he was not comfortable with. He stood by his friendship with Jordan, placing it on a pedestal above all things, and that made my heart melt. I loved the fact that the author created Owen's character as a very sensitive person, despite his very large and muscular physique. 
 "From that day on, Owen was my best friend- jelly to my peanut butter, fellow pea in my pod, Sam to my Frodo. And I was his." 
 Owen and Jordan's friendship was better than white cheddar mac and cheese, and cheesecake for dessert. They were both dorks, and complemented yet opposed one another. They honestly were a perfect match. I enjoyed how the author showed the readers when the two first became friends in the second grade (which was incredibly sweet) and then bridged into the difficulties of high school. 
 "Can you not say this was a terrible mistake?" I said, half joking. "Because it was fucking amazing for me. And if you hated it, I'd prefer to remain blissfully ignorant of that fact." 
 I always have a soft spot for homosexual characters that pine after their best friend (who is sadly straight), so to see that both these boys got their HEA was awesome. I liked how the author chose to show the issues the couple faced together, in high school and outside of it. 
 The writing was absolutely phenomenal and I am utterly amazed the author accomplished so much in hundred and something pages. The characters were very much real in my mind, and the story line was constructed beautifully. I am new to the whole genre of m/m but man lately the books that I have been reading are amazing!

Here's another example of a book that I didn't realize would ensnare me the way it did. I read Anna Dressed in Blood several months ago, so the urgency to finish the series was diminished. I'd forgotten the finer points of the story. But despite that it was extremely easy to jump right back into the fray. 
 Anna doesn't make an appearance in this until the very end of the novel. Girl of Nightmares starts pretty much exactly where Anna Dressed in Blood left off--Cas is unrelenting in his search for Anna, Anna's still stuck in hell with the Obeahman, whom she sacrificed herself to drag down with her. 
 Cas is left with Carmel and Thomas trying to find any sort of clue to bring him closer to finding her. And some of the stuff he encounters is downright fucking creepy. And I loved it. Particularly Thomas' family friend/grandma. A really awesome addition and so unbelievably entertaining. The way the Obeahman moved, with his several additional joints, was terrifying and gave me the chills. If I had to face that every single day and get shorn to pieces every day I don't think I'd stand it with the same stoicism Anna does. Because holy shit, that poor girl. 
 "He'll break my arms first," Anna says. 
 "What?" 
 "I'm just telling you," she replies like it's a matter of course. "I'm going to try to hold his arms, so he'll break mine. I can't beat him. Don't rely on me. I don't know if you can." 
 Total badass. And my god I'd never thought I'd be so emotional over a ghost--but Anna's ending was so damn emotional. It's one of those bittersweet endings where you know there wasn't any alternative, and you're happy that it ended that way, but still sad it couldn't be any other way. Anna finally gets to rest and have the life she wanted. And Cas rests easy knowing he set her and all the others free. But still, he didn't get to be with her. She got to be with him, though. So there's that.

4 1/2 stars. Station Eleven owes much to David Mitchell, Stephen King and really any writer that has ever taken a crack at an apocalypse novel. It does, however, stand extremely well on its own. 
 The storytelling device used here has been done before, but it's still effective and the characters are incredibly compelling. The only real quibble I had with SE is the fact that the characters in the foreground (or the new era) aren't as fleshed out or always as interesting as the ones in the background of the novel (or the past). 
 Other than that, this is an incredibly entertaining novel that, unlike what I feared at first, is not a stodgy literary novel but a tale that helps you appreciate the small things in life: a cappuccino, an orange, a cell phone call to someone on the other side of the country (or world).
