It seemed better the first time I read it: at that point I had read Desperation but had no knowledge of the connection between the two books, so it was an extra interesting layer. Last night I finished re-reading the book after many years, and it fell a bit flatter. 
 The ideas were good, but often felt like they could have gone further. For example, the Regulators/Motokops begin as ominous and mysterious, but since they never leave their vehicles to interact or invade the houses each scene with them ends up samey: drive, shoot shooty shoot shoot ("Shut up, Shooty!"), move on. I also found the novel confusing. There were various vans, regulators and Motokops: I tried to keep them clear in my head but it turned out to be pointless since none of them do anything different. Lots of suburban characters, many of them similar, to the point that I kept forgetting which ones were alive and dead. The leads seemed to be Steve and Johnny, who could easily have been merged into one character. Even the houses (despite the map at the start of the book) somehow merged together, so that I often forgot which house different people were in. I understand the desire to make this a full-street event, but the resultant name soup didn't help. 
 The ending was a bit of a Kop out, in that  Seth specifically asks Audrey to take Johnny with him. And it turns out that it is nothing to do with the plan - Johnny has no role whatsoever, planned or actual. No, the reason is so that the scene can continue on the page once the other characters are gone. Hardly something a character in the book would build into their plans. 
 I was left with the feeling that this was a good book, but could have been better. The writing is confident and smooth, and some of the details are striking, such as when one of the killers' bullets are examined and found to be a long spike like a pencil lead, or as a child would draw. A mixture of well-observed points (ouch) and believable nightmare reality come together. King excels at that kind of thing. 
 So I would certainly recommend the book, but maybe one read-through is enough. That's the thing with King: even when we complain, it's only because some of his books are so amazing that it is hard for them all to live up to that promise, and even a King "average book" is a good book, worth reading.

This book first caught my eye earlier this year, mostly because of the beautiful cover (I'd buy a physical copy just for that cover!), but I hadn't got round to reading it until now. I managed to get hold of the third book from NetGalley and that gave me the kick up the arse to actually start this series. It sounded like something I'd really be into as well but it ended up being quite disappointing. 
 I couldn't quite work out what the target audience was. The writing could be very simple at times. Lots of short, simple sentences. Lots of step by step sentences. Owen did this. Then he did this. Then he thought this. At times I thought it was an adult book written as if adults were children. Then I thought maybe it was a children's book that wanted to also be appealing to adults. I don't know. I don't know at all. I'm not someone who really knows anything about literacy terms - I tend to review on how much I enjoyed the story, the characters, and how pretty the writing looks on the page and how the words sound when I read in my head, I can never really work out what's showing and what's telling but in this case... I really did feel that it was far too much tell and not enough show. 
 The Queen's Poisoner is based on Richard III and the events of 1485 with a different outcome. I would have known this even if I hadn't read the Authors Note at the end. King Severn is King Richard who is believed to have had his nephews, the true heirs to the throne, killed. He had an Uncle Warrewik who conspired with one of his older brothers, Lord Dunsdworth, to take the throne... King Severn was made the Duke of Glosstyr at the age of nine, one of the murdered princes was the Duke of Yuork. At times it felt very lazy. If you are going to write a fantasy series based on historical events, at least don't make it so obvious and try to have a little bit more imagination. I shouldn't compare it to A Song of Ice and Fire but that is a series loosely based on history (The War of the Roses) that is done well. 
 I think one of the major problems with this book is the characters. I found the main character, Owen Kiskaddon, really difficult to like. He was so whiny and wimpy. I know he's an eight year old boy, but I wish he'd toughened up a bit. It seemed like he was forever crying or shaking with fear. It's believable that a boy of that age would be scared and prone to tears BUT it doesn't make a very interesting main character for me. I didn't need him to be oh so special never scared of anything, would kill anyone who crossed his path but I needed something more than what was there. And I feel bad for complaining about Owen because he was based on the authors son. 
 Evie was slightly better, although the constant 'My name is Elysebeth Victoria Mortimer' crap got very annoying. Ankarette... I'm pretty sure that she was only there to tell Owen stories so that he'd know everything that had happened before. Again, a lazy way to let the reader know the history. I honestly think it was a bit of waste of a character. King Severn... I was made to believe that he would be a terrifying monster of a man but that wasn't the case. Characters talked about his sharp tongue and his wit but I never really saw much of that. And he wasn't scary at all. Although I did appreciate that he wasn't evil. 
 The story was a little boring. Not a lot happened until the end and even that was a bit blah. There were one or two moments where I was a bit, uh oh, what's going to happen, but those moments were few and far between. I missed the sense of danger. Owen was taken to Kingfountain after his brother was executed for his father's failings, he was being used to ensure his parents loyalty, and there was supposed to be a worry that the king would kill Owen if his parents did anything wrong. I never got the impression that he was in any danger at all. Not even from those close to the king who supposedly hated him. Even the 'uh oh what's happening' moment, I didn't feel that anything serious was going to happen to him. 
 I was a little bit disappointed that there wasn't a better explanation of the magic but perhaps this will be explored more in later books. 
 Even though this hasn't been a great review, I will still continue with this series. The next book is set nine years later and by reading the blurb, I have a small amount of faith that Owen won't be as annoying or whiny, and he and Evie will be older. Perhaps the issues will resolve themselves now that they are no longer eight year old children. Plus, I've got the third book on my kindle so I kind of feel that I have to.

Fahrenheit 451 has been on my radar for years because my teens had to read this book in literature class. One of my daughters loved it and my other one didn't ... she thought it was boring. Can you tell which one is the book lover and the one who doesn't like to read? *lol* Even though I haven't read this book, until now, I've been discussing Fahrenheit 451 for years with my teens. 
 What is this book about? Basically, it's about a society set in the future where the citizens have decided that reading books is worthless. The firemen's job is to set any books they find on fire. They don't put out fires they set them. They are BOOK BURNERS. You get caught with books and everything you love and cherish goes up in flames house included. As with any society, there are those who RESIST the movement. There is a small group of citizens who are against destroying books and to keep from being found out they memorize the books and then burn the books themselves. The stories and information live on through word of mouth. 
 Above is an elementary description of the story. Don't let that fool you because there's a lot that happens between the pages. The whole concept of this book is very thought provoking. 
 Ironically this book used to be on the banned books list because "it contained an expletive they regarded as blasphemous." The words "hell" and "damn" sparked the ban. 
 It's been said that the author wrote this book out of his fear of tv's influence on our society. Television was invented in 1927 and Fahrenheit 451 was written in 1953. I wonder if Mr. Radbury could see how much technology has taken over what his commentary would be today? 
 After discussing this book with my girls a couple years back I've often wondered which books I'd memorize to keep their stories alive. No doubt I'd have many books that I would want to live on. 
 Fahrenheit 451 is a standalone dystopian set in future. If you're a book lover then this is a thought provoking story that will spark your passion for books.

In the last book, we got a closer glimpse into the relationship between Kayden and Jake. Kayden had always believed he was hiding something and we found out he used to be a detective, but left his old life after his wife was murdered. In Silenced we pick up with their burgeoning relationship. 
 While out on a rock climb, Kayden finds a dead climber. When the acting Sheriff, Landon (Kayden's soon-to-be brother-in-law), convinces Jake to join his short-handed police force and take lead on the investigation, Kayden agrees to help since she has climbing expertise and is in with the tight-knit climbing community. 
 While the mystery of the murder is interesting, the focus of the investigation seems mostly to advance the relationship between Kayden and Jake. They've never spent much time together one-on-one and they both enjoy it a little more than they should during a murder investigation. When the case comes to a startling close, something still isn't sitting quite right with Jake, especially when he continues to get threatening notes. 
 After a life-threatening accident on another climb, Jake figures out that the threats don't have anything to do with their initial case, but that his past is coming back to haunt him and he'll need the help of the rest of the McKenna's to save the woman he loves. 
 Overall, I enjoyed Silenced. I liked that we got to see Cole and Bailey finally get married and that we also got to see more of Reef (who the next book is likely to be about). I would've liked for the initial mystery to have tied into the central plot of the book in some way, though. While it was interesting, I felt a little bit like it was a waste of time. However, I still look forward to continuing the Alaskan Courage series.

This is, by far, the most difficult book review I've had to write primarily because I am still so utterly, hopelessly conflicted with how I feel about this book. Even as I write this, I am repeatedly debating on the accuracy of my star rating. I cannot adequately stress how difficult and confusing and befuddling this is. 
 In terms of content, numerous sensitive themes were explored in such a powerfully raw, explicitly personal manner that never failed to move me in some way. There were pieces that talked about rape, emotional abuse, grief and the death of loved ones. All these were taken from the author's firsthand experiences and she made no attempt to censor herself - which was a really, really admirably courageous thing to do. She did not hide behind vague allusions or colorful metaphors; she utilized a straightforwardly simplistic writing style with the sole intention to reveal rather than to convey a message while beating around the bush and dancing around figures of speech. 
 Another thing that I liked was how the collection was a carefully crafted web of stanzas and poems intertwined together, allowing all the pieces to be read together like a cohesive story unfolding on itself. Some of the poems in the latter part of the collection contained references to the previously presented poems in the earlier chapters, giving a sense of closure and continuity. I cannot count the times my heartstrings were tugged by the vulnerability within the stanzas. If I were to rate this book solely for the content and the emotion its poems evoked, I would definitely give five solid stars. 
 As someone who prefers form over substance in prose, I would have appreciated a lot more technical style and diversity. By the end of the day, my star rating is influenced by my personal preferences; however, this rating does not, in any way, diminish the quality of this collection. In spite of the number of my reservations, I do believe that The Princess Saves Herself in This One is a poetry book that's worth picking up.

 Welcome, welcome to my review of Caraval and all the hidden wonders you will find within. Imagine yourself invited to attend a world famous performance of the most magical show around. Before you walk through the doors, you decide if you wish to watch or participate. As a reader, you choose to participate because you wish to feel engrossed in the book, to be a part of the story. Caraval is a place of magic, but more so a place of mystery and wonder. While reading this, you want to be able to solve the mystery of the kidnapping of Scarlett's sister while the wonder of how it all comes together will leave you at the edge of your seat. The pacing of the novel is quick while providing wonderful descriptions of the show and events. While Caraval is a show, it is more about putting pieces together than it is an elaborate performance. It is a nice step away from traditional YA-fantasy troupes to give you something different but still magical. 
 Not to take any of the magic away, but it's not quite a perfect novel. Miss Garber's writing is very good for her first published novel, but at times the similes or metaphors feel off-putting or just plain silly. Upon Scarlett's entrance to Caraval, we get 
 "It tasted like light, bubbly on her tongue and sugary as it went down, making everything from the ends of her toes to the tips of her fingers tingle." 
 First of all, she isn't eating, she is entering a building. Second, you can't taste light-- it isn't something you eat, and thirdly, even if I could taste light, I don't think it tastes like pop. Now, that was a harsh dissection of the writing there, but I can see what other reviewers mean when they say they did not like or understand the metaphors. Not all of the metaphors are like this, however, some are quite lovely, but I did catch these odd ones every once and awhile. 
 The worldbuilding of Caraval is beautifully done, and I would refer to my first paragraph to see what I have to say about that, but the day-to-day worldbuilding is left a little unfinished. Perhaps we will explore it in detail in further books, but it has to do with the Isle that Scarlett and her family live on. Her father is governor of this Isle, but due to some history the Isle is not that important to the rest of the world. The history is mostly blown over and would hope that a better explanation comes along if there was any point to it at all. Otherwise why bother? Just make the father a Lord who would prefer to have better influence in the kingdom through a marriage alliance rather than set up this "Conquered Isles" aspect. This, however, is just me being nit-picky and a heavy high-fantasy reader. It isn't a glaring mistake nor the focus of the plot. I am just hopeful we get to learn more-- maybe even have a map of the entire world in the next book. 
 Overall, I rate this 4 out of 5 stars. We get a solid ending I wouldn't mind stopping at, but I definitely look forward to more in the next book.

Wow. This took a looooong time to read. It took me 3 months. It took half that time to get through the first 150 or so pages out of an 800 page book. Some parts were really interesting with characters that I liked, so very Uncle Stevie-like and parts were so mind-numbingly boring that I ended up resenting you. Remember: you are a book. I don't feel compelled to read the rest of the trilogy. Yay for movies? Pro: Pretty cover. Con: Too much minute detail, too many commas. Oh, and for a horror novel there were maybe 3 scenes that were genuinely scary and that adjective is a real stretch.

"Once upon a time, a girl had a father, a prince, and a society of friends. They they betrayed her and she destroyed them all". 
 It's hard to write in the view of a villain. You have to think about why they act the way that they do. You have to give them a reason and a personality to match. If you thought Adelina was a grey character. You'll need to reevaluate. Because she's definitely the bad guy in this book. Actually, there's not really a "good guy" in these books at all (which confuses me). Okay so now we've established that Adelina is evil. She has a voice that talks to her in the back of her head (Mistborn mirrors again!) and it tells her to make bad decisions. Thankfully, she doesn't always listen to said bad decisions. But somehow makes bad decisions anyways!? Adelina has become illogically bad. In a "why are you mad at me for killing your friend and getting your boss killed, YOU'RE BETRAYING ME YOU SHOULD DIE" kind of way. Like, what? So now Adelina hates everyone and wants everyone to die. That's the book. 
 New characters are introduced. Namely, a thief who inspired the word for Magic and then a mercenary who also used to be in the Daggers but was kicked out for his inability to use his powers. What a dream team. Magic is fun. But he falls in love with Adelina which is a horribly bad decision because it creates a highly unnecessary love triangle with the already DEAD Enzo. (Who Lu let slip in the last book might be able to be revived. Psst, guess what happens in this book). Poor guy, why would you fall in love with a crazy lady. The book does nothing in terms of helping me understand who the characters in the Daggers are. It does nothing to help me in terms of the world building. I have no idea what this country up north who apparently wants to take over are. I don't know who this Marie Jacqueline Kelly Corrigan person is or why her name is so long. I don't understand how her power is able to work. I don't have any idea as to who her brothers are. 
 Again, the politics in this book make NO sense. Somehow Adelina is bad and evil and angry at EVERYTHING and then gets the throne. Because all it takes is a little temper tantrum and affecting someone else's crazy to make them crazy and kill the one they love and obsess over because that makes sense. Somehow have more power than zombie Enzo who is supposedly TEN TIMES stronger than before. Get him to blow up an ENTIRE FLEET OF SHIPS. Then almost kill your little sister because you're crazy and then instead of repenting for your actions you decide- no fuck it. I DO WHAT I WANT. I DON'T NEED YOU. YOU BETRAY ME TOO. RaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaawrrghH! And what even happened to the powers of the queen? Do the people really all just turn to Adelina as the ruler just because she killed them? She has no political strength at all. I don't get itttttt.  
 But I've got to hand it to Lu. She has a diverse cast of characters: POC, disability, LGBT. Yaay.

Didn't like it as much as the first (though frankly, I had a hard time remembering details from Ember, lol), but found myself invested in the story towards the end. 
 This book felt more of a filler in the series for me, as I soon come to realize, this book is more about Helene - which I think is what made me not "like" it about halfway. I may not remember much about Ember, but what I do know is the reason why I didn't give it a full five starts, I just can't get over how Elias seem to love Laia and Helene at the same time (depends on who he's with), and in this book (especially in the beginning), we get to see more of that, not to mention Laia's feelings for Keenan (which I also disliked). 
 I am looking forward to reading book three because as much as this book offered some answers, I was left with more questions.

Recalling this book months after I read it, I remember mostly what a struggle it was to get through the endless minutiae remarked on by the narrator as he wandered first the streets of Manhattan, then Brussels. I was hoping that his wanderings would yield something a little more meaningful. I'm still not sure what to make of the revelation made at the end of the novel, although by then, the narrator's refusal to even address it was no surprise. The narrator seemed unable to acknowledge anything beyond the outward aspects of any interaction. He shunned almost every attempt to connect or to take responsibility. The fact that he's a psychiatrist emphasized to this reader at least, the opacity of his inner workings. Is this supposed to be a comment on the unfathomable mystery each of us carries around with us, even to ourselves? Maybe, but that point has been made in better books.

 I liked Truant's point of view but again, I am very confused about the ending of his section. My favorite points though were the house explorations (obviously) and how it affected the people inside of it.

Also, it was slow at points and found myself skimming. And lastly, I left this book very confused and kind of wish it ended more bluntly with everything laid out clear.

I would say this is actually a 3.75. I really liked it for the most part. I thought the images were powerful, which was in keeping with the subject of film throughout. I liked how dreamlike and disconnected it was because I thought it was using its epistolary style to make an interesting point. It was difficult to follow sometimes, but it was worth it. 
 What bothered me was that, after spending the whole novel carefully using all tools at her disposal to make that point, Catherynne M. Valente decides to state the point outright in the last few pages. It felt a bit like she was underestimating her readers' abilities to see what she was doing, and it was jarring after the round about way the rest of the book approached things. 
 When seeing is the focus of the novel the rule "show don't tell" becomes even more important, and for much of the novel she wrote that way, it felt like a lot of hard work was lost when it was just stated outright.

What can I say about this series.... Well its a Percy Jackson type story with some differences. For one there's demon-zombie-vampire type people. I loved this series because one it wasn't another story about a protagonist who has no idea what her roots are. She knows exactly where she comes from, just know the full extent of what she is. 
 Some parts of the series was predictable, like knowing who was really the mastermind behind all the destruction was a no brainer. And why it took so long for everyone to figure out is the one thing I JUST DID NOT GET! 
 How is it no one could think of the obvious answer!!! 
 Alex didn't complain about everything that she was forced to do, all she did was bite down and fight back, I like that in my female characters. But Aiden just annoyed the crap out of me, I'm sorry he was just too much, too overprotective, to much everything really. I found myself skipping over much of their romantic moments to get to the good bits. 
 Seth was a good character, but what there just wasn't enough time spent on developing him except for his volatile and self-possessed nature.

The book has a very nice introduction, quite well-written and intriguing. Then we move on to our own world and the twins and here's where things get complicated. I used to be a shy, quiet, bookish child myself who got teased a lot for liking books more than people, so I could initially identify with Alex. But then, instead of remaining someone relatable that you can sympathize with, she started coming off as a smart-ass, which ultimately led me to feel that Conner was far more likeable. I did enjoy the story up to a certain point, but round around the middle of the book, I started getting tired and, overall, I think the novel could have been several chapters shorter. It's very linear and very straight-forward, though I must admit there were some pieces of dialogue that I especially liked. I believe Chris Colfer has potential and I would definitely like to see more of him in his future work; several times I had the feeling that he was deliberately trying to hide how smart he is so that the book would be more accessible to children, particularly on one or two occasions he made jokes that a young child wouldn't get. In the end I'd say it's an alright first book for such a young writer, it shows potential and imagination, but I do think it was longer than it should have been and rather predictable (though I have to say I liked the explanation on the origin of fairy tales, that was really interesting and fresh).

I dub Jessica Sorensen, BREAKING NOVA, the new queen of New Adult Heartbreakers. -- . 
 I started reading BREAKING NOVA by Jessica Sorensen because the premise looked interesting and I was familiar with the author. I have read The Coincidence of Callie & Kayden by Jessica Sorensen and I really liked it so picking another one of her books was a no brainer. 
 There seems to be an onslaught of New Adult books that are all about showing us the dysfunctional, the broken and heartbreaking scenes of the human condition. BREAKING NOVA does this and more. I have never felt such bleakness in a character. The author painstakingly pushed me to not only relive these moments in time but I felt the heartbreak over and over again. I'm glad I read this outside that certain monthly window, otherwise I would have cried my way through, eating sleeves and sleeves of Oreo cookies. 
 The characters were well developed and felt very real. The storyline pushed the bounds of reality or maybe the author wrote so closely to the truth, I didn't want to believe that people could be so broken. 
 If you are looking for a raw, rip your heart out story that gives a twinkling of redemption then this book is for you.

The Duke of Denver--Lord Peter Wimsey's own brother--is suspected of murdering their sister's fiance, what? Don't worry, Lord Peter delivers his brother from the scaffold along with plenty of the ridiculous nonsense for which he's known.

Confession: this was my first-ever Agatha Christie novel. It was great! The character development was impressive, especially given the number of players. The plot felt classic and about halfway through reading it I realized that of course it felt that way because Christie defined the murder mystery genre! M. Poirot is a delightfully vivid character, it is very easy to see why she gave him so many stories, and why the legacy continues more than 100 years after his creation. 
 I will read more Agatha Christie novels. I also think these would be great for young, enthusiastic readers. Perhaps I'll give some to my niece for Christmas.

I felt the first part of this book was two princes being raised in abusive school systems and the occasional appearance of their sister. Seriously, there better be more of her in the third book. The boys devoured the page time. 
 Still. School ended and because of school they had the tools to survive the dangers that came their way. I especially liked the way the Rooted are treated and the issues that it touches on in the world today. Definitely reading the sequel.

4 stars -Friends to lovers Romance 
 On Point is book 3 in the Out of Uniform series by Annabeth Albert. This story focuses on Ben and Maddox and is a strong friends to lovers romance and full of angst. The romance in this book is a little slow, as you would expect with high angst, and the POV alternates between Ben and Maddox with time flashbacks as well. 
 Imagine the one person who has your back both while on a mission and when at home. He is your best friend and partner on your SEAL team. Now imagine you have found yourself to be falling in love with this man, you are afraid because you don't want to lose your friendship - yet it drives you nuts to see them dating other people. You want to be the person they are with, you want to openly love them and you want them to love you. Would you tell them? Would you go for it and risk losing it all? What if one night you had the opportunity to join in a little hot threeway action...would you do it? This is the situation we find our poor MC Maddox in throughout the book .. he is confused, lonly, angry, and he finds himself baking a lot! (Stress baking, it's real) 
 When on a mission, Maddox and Ben become separated from the team. It takes them relying heavily on each other to make it home alive, and at times Maddox wants to tell Ben how he feels as he fears he won't get another chance. However, they do come home. It's during the recovery that things start to heat up between these two. 
 The chemistry between these two is off the charts and Ms. Albert can write some smokin' hot scenes with dirty talk that makes you blush! Loved it! Watching these two each overcome their unique obstacles and learn to communicate their wants and needs to each other was great. Yes, I wanted to pull my hair out at times but other times - awesome! 
 I do have to be honest and say, I had some trouble with this book - it didn't hold my interest at first and I think it was due to the time jumping around. However, once we got past those flashbacks the story picked up for me well enough for me to still rate it highly. 
 Overall, this was a great story! I am hoping the rumor is true and we will get more hot, sexy, men un uniform from Ms. Albert - if not, she made sure each guy in the series got their HEA so all is good! I am eager to see what she will bring us next! 
 4 stars and I definitely recommend this book and series!

I got the first, but the second thankfully proved false. I fell in love with these characters, but I especially loved the love that we were able to witness.

I feel like the ending could have been better, maybe? All in all I kinda felt like the first half of Shattered was not last-book worthy (felt more like a first or second book) and the second part was kinda rushed and I didn't feel like all the puzzle pieces fitted together all that well, I mean you couldn't have figured it out on your own, could you? Love Teri Terry's writing style and the idea behind this felt very fitting with current day politics to me! (Brexit and Trump all, you never know).

This book had such a beautiful background and a heart-breaking romance that I loved it, despite the fact that I usually don't read these kinds of books. I thoroughly enjoyed the setting and the culture, having to sit next to my iPad in order to research something new and learn more about a culture that I am not familiar with. The story itself was well woven, showing us a glimpse into the Chinese afterlife and how they view it. I love this book.

First of I really liked how the story was narrated by both Cassia and Ky, up until the point where they reunite and then I just always get confused between the two and I'm always wondering who is talking. Anyways I really enjoyed this book. The story at times was boring because it was back and forth between finding Ky and then finding the Rising. I fell more in love with Ky and at this point I'm rooting for him. I did want to see more of Xander, but hopefully more of him in Reached. I do have a few questions about what is going on though. I mean, I really don't understand what Xander's big secret is, other than joining the Rising. Or wait was that his big secret? I don't know, I'm still very confused. And what about Ky, I don't understand his secret, did he put his name in the Matching thing? I DON'T KNOW, I'M CONFUSED. Also does the Society know that Cassia is missing? I don't understand that part. I mean won't they come looking for her or do they think she died? And what happened to her family? I have a few questions and hopefully they are answered in Reached. Other than Crossed being slow at some parts, it was a fantastic book and I can't wait to see what happens in Reached!

First Read: June 18-23, 2012 
 LOVED IT. As far as quick-reads goes, a pretty great book to delve into while nursing a stomach ache on the couch over the weekend. Archie Sheridan and Susan Ward are back, trying to nail (SPOILER ALERT) the disgraced Senator for pedophilic crimes from the past as well as trying to capture the NOW ESCAPED sociopathic serial killer Gretchen Lowe. If you've read the first and appreciated it for a good read, you have to read the second... and the third (which I'm now devouring - I was a bit late on updating the goodreads this time ;) ).

I liked this debut. Alexander introduces us to a twin brothers who may be in 8th grade, but who read a bit older, and their relationship is great. The play on the same team, except when they fight like only brothers can. Towards the beginning, I was a little confused as to who narrates the story; at first I thought that it alternated between the brothers, but I think only one actually talks. This title could easily work for Freshman and Sophomore readers who love basketball, family, and don't need R-rated activity. There's a honest, even earnest heart to the story that moved quickly and heartrendingly to the end. I might suggest following this with Boy21 for those who like the b-ball angle, Coaltown Jesus for those who like the message. 
 Props for having a mom who's the Vice-Principal. There's also a small but interesting female character who plays hoop, so there's plenty of cross-gender appeal, even as this works for guys who might be disinclined to the likes of Sonya Sones and Lisa Schroeder. 
 I hope Alexander has a few more of this sort in the fire. I know that he has a readership ready to embrace his stories if this is any indication of what's to come.

The bast way to describe Codex is complex. Think along the same vein as Da Vinci Code or Angels and Demons. Essentially this is a book about a book about another book that is a code for another book still. This is the literature version of Inception. 
 In this suspense novel, Edward, a money-hungry businessman, is hired by a Duchess to find a book that supposedly doesn't exist and has to run around New York to search for clues to its whereabouts. Along the way we get introduced to a variety of characters, including: 
 -video game geeks 
 -a female scholar working with Edward and whom is obsessed with the author of the supposed book 
 -several businessmen working against Edward and for the Duke 
 - and a business rival of Edwards who may or may not be trying to help him. 
 While Edward is trying to track down the mysterious book, he also gets obsessed with a virtual reality video game called MOMUS that takes up most of his time in the beginning and seems to reflect events that are happening in the real world. 
 It is obvious that the author did quite a bit of research for the book and really put his time and effort into it. The detail is very well done. The novel does seem to have a snowball effect that makes the pace go faster and faster as you get further into it. However, in my opinion,  the ending felt very anticlimactic and disappointing. Especially with all the build-up leading up to it. If there was a better ending, I would have given this another star.

This had some promise, being a regency-era romance that actually was about people who worked for a living, where the Napoleonic war wasn't just a thing going on somewhere, off in the distance. One gets tired of reading about the gentry. 
 But it turns out the french spy heroine is another fake strong female character. She starts out fierce and independent, fighting for survival, struggling with sexual tension in an uneasy the-enemy-of-my-enemy-is-my-friend alliance with english spymaster Grey. But eventually her autonomy is just slowly pared away until she ends up finding out in a twist that she's been an english double-agent her entire career, starting in childhood, without her knowledge!-it's a long story For one half of the book she's almost a Mary Sue. She has eidetic memory(she carries a plot maguffin in her head),speaks several languages, is a perfect mimic, is able to do battle triage while blind(!!). All good spy skills. Her blindness is a temporary malady that was bonked into her head a few months prior to the story, and gets bonked out of her about midway through the book, as in the manner of soap-opera logic. I allowed myself to suspend my disbelief for that much. But then this competent character must fall in love with her captor, as is the nature of the genre, and love apparently makes one stupid. The later part of the book I was just kind of bored. There wasn't as much give-and-take between the leads. The hero decided things for the heroine and she'd be incsenced and arroused- but conveniently, his decisions would usually end up being the best for her, and besides, you know she really wanted it...grrrrr 
 I expected more from this book, because it was a recommendation from NPR. It is better written than the abtacular cover would lead you to believe, but it's not mind-blowing. For many this would be good light entertainment.

Hellz to the Yeah!!! It's Will & Patrick Time!!! 
 These books just get better and better as we watch Will and Patrick navigate their feelings and admit to each other those three little words that hold so much meaning. 
 Both of these guys know they love each other, they are just really unable to say it to the other one. Directly, that is.. because it slipped out of both of their mouths - the other just either didn't take them seriously or didn't catch it. But it is coming.. I can feel it!! Then lets add it a Mafioso father coming to town and pulling what he thinks is a joke on poor Patrick, its a wonder these two survived this episode. But they did! And whether they recognize it yet or not, they are stronger for it. 
 There is some really hot scenes in this book, so make sure you bring a tall glass of something with ya while you read it, cause you will be on fire! As usual we have Patrick and all his quirky behaviors, which he doesn't want associated with being on the spectrum. I love this scene with his inner ramblings as he tries to figure out how to tell Will about his feelings: 
 Patrick shuts the door behind Will and leans against it, studying his whole body in the bathroom mirror. He's handsome enough; fit, and his cock is nice. He turns around and looks at his ass: round, high, and he'd eat it if he wasn't himself. Physically, he's happy with what he has to offer Will. 
 Love Patrick. Also, Watch out in this episode as Will has some true Italian Machismo shining through -- he isn't about to let anyone harm his husband. So good! 
 We get to meet and interact with more supporting characters in this episode, Will's Grandmother, Father, Mother - (its a Family Reunion) and we get to see Patrick show his softer, caring side. 
 All in all A WIN!! 5 Stars for this episode of Wake Up Married!! I cannot wait for the last episode!!

Junior in college. Star athlete. Constant attention from the opposite sex. 
 On this campus, I'm worshiped. While seven hundred miles away, back in my hometown, I'm still trailer park trash, child of the town tramp, and older sibling to three kids who are counting on me to keep my shit together so I can take them away from the same crappy life I grew up in. 
 These two opposing sides of myself never mix until one person gets a glimpse of the true me. I never expected to connect with anyone like this or want more beyond one night. This may be the real deal. 
 Problem is, Dr. Kavanagh's my literature professor. 
 If I start anything with a teacher and we're caught together, I might as well kiss my entire future goodbye, as well as my family's, and especially Dr. Kavanagh's. Except sometimes love is worth risking everything. Or at least, it damn well better be because I can only resist so much. 
 >>>>A new take on a student-teacher relationship. I've come accustomed to where the teacher is the boy. But this is a breath of fresh thingies. LOL! And I love that the author incorporates other author works, (hence the quotes at the beginning of each chapter) and based the chapters into that quotes.

I enjoyed the adventure. The mystery wasn't very mysterious, but I still enjoyed the story. It was obvious from the beginning who the bad guy was, but I enjoyed watching it unfold nonetheless. Cadie is an 18 year old girl who was forced to grow up too early. When her mother died, she was forced to take care of her family. All of her time goes to working, raising her four year old brother and holding the house together. Cooking, cleaning, and care giving is not what she had in mind. When she meets a cute boy at a party, she gives into to her desire for adventure and freedom and joins him and his cousin on a road trip. What starts out as fun, begins to turn serious. She doesn't know who to believe, who to trust, or what to do. One of the cousins is hiding a dark secret. He is not what he appears to be. Making it home alive is becoming less likely. I liked getting to know the characters in this story, seeing their backstories unfold bit by bit. I enjoyed watching Cadie learn to balance responsibility and freedom, learn more about who she is and what she is capable of. Overall enjoyable.

I liked it, but didn't love it. 
 Still very entertaining!

This book was so wonderful! Sweet, touching, and the perfect summer read! 
 Plus, it'll make you hardcore crave some gelato!
This book was a very fast, enjoyable read! Loved it.

Like Breathe, this was a fast read. There was a lot of action pulling me through the story. I still didn't care for the story being told in first person alternating point of view, I was having to look back to see whose words I was reading. It had been two weeks since I had read the first book and it took me a few chapters to figure out who everyone was and what was going on, I needed the author to give a few more reminders which weren't there, I can't imagine how much harder it would have been if more time had passed between the books. Nevertheless, we find out what happens to everyone (except the Jazz/Vanya connection) and are left with hope for our little Dystopian society.

Trying too hard. I wonder if I hadn't read this right after Jonathan Strange and Mr. Norrell if I would have liked it better. They were both trying to pay homage to the gothic/Romantic era writers, except that Strange and Norrell was brilliant, and this one was.. eh. I appreciated what the author was trying to do, but he didn't do it well enough to keep me reading. Yes, Romantic lit is full of cliche, but the thing is to do it in an intriguing way and with enough wit to keep your audience interested. This book did not have that balance. It had the formula, it just didn't execute things well enough, in my opinion. 
 To be fair, that could be because this book was originally in Spanish. It could have lost a lot in translation. I know it lost something, actually, because some of the sentences are rather awkwardly phrased. But Arturo Perez-Reverte's gothic-esque novels were also in Spanish, and they still had their magic in translation. So, I don't forgive this guy enough to finish the book. Which I didn't, by the way. Got about halfway through because I was hoping it would get better, but it was still not grabbing me, so. Onto the next!

 Maybe it was fate that I sat next to her that day, or serendipity, divine intervention, who knows? 
 Will & Mia meet on an airplane headed to New York. Their friendship was centered around their love of music and playing together. 
 Mia's lack of faith in Will is their undoing. Healing the hurts spoken out of lack of trust is the making of Mia. 
 "I love this." 
 "It's a lotus flower." 
 "I know." 
 "It symbolizes purity of the heart and mind." 
 I haven't taken it off since...

 Yes, I got it in my hands almost one week before the release date. How awesome is that?

We get to see more romance between Tris and Tobias than ever before.

Tobias is living in agony after two and a half years when the world is as perfect as it's ever going to be. But I can't stop crying like a maniac because of Tobias's grief.  
 What a finale!

Helen Grace is one fucked up lady. There are small scenes interspersed throughout with a dominant whipping the hell out of a woman, so much so that it draws blood. No names are given for this woman, but it is pretty easy to figure out that it is our main character, the incredibly competent Helen Grace. Why is she so f'ed up? Let me share with you... 
 But first, the rest of the plot. The first victims are Sam and Amy, a sweet couple completely devoted to each other. Eventually, out of desperation and starvation, one pulls the trigger.  Amy does.  Then Peter and Ben, coworkers at a law firm. One survives.  Peter stabs Ben in the eye, then can't live with it and jumps off his work building.  Then poor 14 year old Anna and her mother Marie, a differently-abled child and her devoted mother, are locked into their home with no sustenance and only a gun with a single bullet as company.  Marie suffocates Anna with a pillow, then dies of starvation herself.  There's more, but I think you get the idea. It is brutal, and slowly we learn a little more all the time. I had my ideas about who I thought the killer was, and I was delighted to see that I was totally wrong.  I thought it was the journalist who had acid thrown in her face, but turns out that Helen (whose name isn't actually Helen) has a long lost sister. Why is she long lost? Because when she was a young teenager she put Seran wrap over her mother and her father's heads and suffocated them. She did this because the father brutally raped her every night and her mother let it happen, and she didn't want the same fate to fall to her younger sister Helen. Helen's sense of right and wrong dictates her actions: she turns her sister in. Sister does not take kindly to this.  
 If you read the spoiler: see what I mean? It's just freaking gnarly. How can you not be totally captivated (and a bit sickened) by this plot? It seems incredibly similar to Saw, albeit a little more sadistic since none of the people that are kidnapped seem to deserve it. No junkies really, fairly normal and successful people. I am going to pass this around, I think there are a lot of people who would enjoy this demented little treasure trove.

With a tragic past behind her, Erika is still emotionally raw but determined to put her own feelings aside to solve the case and bring the murderer to justice, especially when she discovered that the same person may have been responsible for the brutal killings of other young women.  Brynza has done an excellent job with his debut suspense novel, and has delivered true-to-life characters I want to see a lot more of. As much as she can be cold and aloof, her humanity shines through in her interactions with the people around her - Brynza has achieved exactly the right mix of vulnerability and strength which make her a character to both admire and like. I also want to read a lot more about the supportive characters, especially as we were only allowed glimpses into their lives - Moss, Marsh, Peterson and Sparks. The storyline gripped me from the very start and I found it very difficult to tear myself away. And just when I thought I was on the right track to solving this mystery, the author brought it all to a breath-taking and totally unexpected finale. Brilliant! 
 I love a good murder/mystery and with so many good books out there, it takes a bit to impress me. And impressed I certainly was! This definitely belongs in my favourites list for this year so far, and I want to read a lot more from this author in future. I am very happy to hear that the sequel, "The Night Stalker", will be released later this year. 
 This is a must-read for fans of police procedural such as S.J, Bolton's Lacey Flint series, or Jane Casey's Maeve Kerrigan novels. Very highly recommended.

In Ruby Red, we get a crapload of awesomesauce mysteries and prophecies, and I was expecting some kind of explanation in this book. In fact, the only few answers we did get were actually so obvious it would have been weird if you hadn't worked it out for yourself yet. I am 100% convinced that Gideon can read minds. He could pull sentences right out of Gwyneth's thoughts, turn around to kiss her when she's doubting him, and considering he's a descendant of Count Evil, mind reading is not too far-fetched. If some catastrophic event caused hundreds of people to suddenly gain superpowers, what are the chances that the comic book dichotomy between good and evil would manifest? Or is it more believable that the strongest superhumans would create a new power structure where average people became little more than expendable labour? That latter scenario is what Sanderson imagines here in Steelheart, but not in the bleak dystopian style that seems to be so trendy these days. Yet despite the absence of altruistic superheroes, it's obvious from the get-go that beneath a cynical and hopeless facade, this is at heart an old-school superhero novel and a ripping good yarn. 
 As in many of his past novels, Sanderson again shows himself a creative genius in developing what amounts to a magic system. There is a highly-developed classification system to the superpowers of the Epics, which almost makes it feel like a novelized RPG. What I really appreciate about Sanderson's approach is that the explanations are always logical. That's not to say I buy them hook, line and sinker, but even if I'm laughing at the weak and tenuous link between action and result, I don't ever feel as though he cheated in the writing of it. Another thing I both laugh at and appreciate in Sanderson's writing is the PG writing. Curse words are substituted for make-believe words, and sexual innuendo is so mild that you'd miss it if you blinked. But the action and suspense are so incredibly well written that it still feels gritty and dark, and the lack of objectionable content really serves to almost subconsciously buttress the altruistic themes running throughout the book. 
 The audio narration by Macleod Andrews was fantastic, although with a mild caveat. The text was read so slowly that I was on the verge of gouging out my own eyes it was so drawn out. But bumping up the playback speed on my iPod to 1.5x, it was simply perfect. Andrews was exceptional in creating distinctive voices for all of the characters, and it often felt more like a radio play than a novel. In fact, his performance was so outstanding that this Canadian can even forgive him for using a Parisian accent for the French Canadian character (the difference between "zee accent" and "da haxENT"). This style of book makes for great audiobook narration in the first place, but Andrews really took it to the next level. Well, at 1.5X speed anyways, and that's enough for a strong recommendation in my book.

It did help me to understand autism more however, it's like Hadden took every symptom that he'd heard that perhaps an Asperger's child could have (most do not have ALL symptoms), cranked them to maximum, then tried to pretend that child that badly afflicted could write, at the moment it is happening, such knowing and insightful things about himself, but could only do it in the language and syntax of a 5 year old.  I received Behind Her Eyes from Book of the Month a few months ago, and after finishing Night Film, another psychological thriller, I was ready for this one. I love the entire book-the characters, the plot, the authors writing style. And then I read the last three chapters and my love for the book deflated. I have never been so let down by an ending in my entire life. It's funny how just a few pages can ruin an entire book for you. 
 Behind Her Eyes follows Louise, a single mother who is stuck in a rut, and Adele, the new girl in town who seems to have her shit together. And of course there is a man. David met Louise in a bar one night and they shared an amazing kiss. David is married to Adele. Oh, and when Louise goes to work on Monday, she finds out that David is her new boss. Nothing awkward about that. It gets worse when Adele bumps into Louise and invites her to coffee and they become friends. But Adele makes Louise promise that she won't tell David about their friendship because he doesn't like to mix his work and personal life. That seems innocent enough, but then Louise notices that David calls Adele a lot, and he prescribes her a lot of medication, and then one day Adele appears with a bruise on her face. To make matters more complicated, Louise has struck up an affair with David, and he is completely different with her. The more Louise digs into David and Adele's marriage, the more questions she has. Everything reaches its boiling point when David learns that Louise has cultivated a friendship with Adele and he tells her to stay away from them. But Louise cannot give up on Adele because she has finally has a glimpse of the David Adele lives with, and she fears for Adele. But maybe she should be fearing for herself instead. 
 The plot reminded me a lot of Gone Girl, with a third person involved. Pretty quickly I felt that Adele wasn't so much the victim of the plot, and I was right. But just like Louise, I found it hard not to like her. 
 A big part of the plot is that Louise has night terrors. Adele used to have them as well, but as a child, she taught herself lucid dreaming. Once Louise has mastered lucid dreaming, she finds herself in her own dream that she has formed when a second door appears. It takes a couple of dreams, but Louise is finally able to open the door, and she finds herself having an out of body experience watching her son sleep. Adele uses these out of body experiences to spy on David and Louise, which is how she found out about the affair. Because Louise is a newbie, she can't travel as far as Adele can though.  
 I feel like Sarah Pinborough is making fun of lucid dreaming and turning it into some re-write of Invasion of the Body Snatchers. It could have been done so much better. It ruined the entire novel for me. I don't think I'll ever read another novel by her. I understand that she was genre-bending, but she broke it. It went from something within the realm of reason to completely unbelievable and insulting. It made me feel like I wasted time and money. The characters that she spent so much time helping me love, I hate them. The plot with so much potential was ruined. If I had known that was going to be what happened before I started, I would have selected a different book to begin with and never ordered it. In summation, I'm disappointed.

 This was an interesting book with some original elements that I liked, but I still felt like I was reading the same thing as any other kind of dystopian novel. 
 I think it's really easy to come up with a new idea of how our future world can go wrong and easy to write about someone questioning this world to the point that a change happens. But I think it's hard to write that kind of novel differently than all of the other ones out there already. That's the main problem I had with this novel: it felt like a cookie-cutter YA dystopian. 
 But it was still pretty good. I really liked the idea of people coming back from the dead and being stronger, better, faster based on how long they'd been dead. I liked that the main character had the highest number they'd ever seen. I liked that the number one problem in this world was this virus killing people and bringing them back to life and how the world coped with this. 
 I didn't like that as soon as Wren was out of the HARC facility, her personality completely changed. I didn't like that after knowing Callum for roughly two weeks (I'm not entirely sure how much time really passed), Wren the Unemotional was willing to risk both of their lives to save him because he disobeyed orders that she'd been following unquestioningly for 5 years.  Mostly, I didn't like how bored I got three chapters before the ending. 
 But even though I got bored, it did end in a way I appreciated: without a major cliff-hanger. It leaves me wondering and wanting more, but I can end it here and not have to worry about the rest of the series unless I want to. And if I happen to pick up the next book in two years, it won't be frustrating for me to have to remember what exactly happened in the first book.

Don't let the slimness of this volume deceive you into thinking the story is light. This isn't a book through which one can skim quickly. The narrative is a kaleidoscope, and it truly takes all one's reading wits to focus the scattered pieces of the story into a coherent whole. 
 The strength of Woodrell's writing here lies in lacuna and elision; it's more in what remains untold and danced around. At points I would get a bit frustrated at his failure to flesh out the smaller details - to tell the story "properly", if you will. And then he would stun me by delivering a sentence or two so jam-packed with allusive detail that it stood place for chapters worth of writing. Take for example this description of a local penitentiary: 
 "Discipline inside the walls aped the medieval, with prisoners clubbed by guards or lashed at a whim--for making eye contact or not making eye contact, for slouching like a hoodlum or standing insolently straight, because they talked back or wouldn't answer at all--bats on the head regularly applied to encourage order or unconsciousness." 
 After finishing the book, I reflected back upon which elided details should have been more carefully spelled out. I couldn't think of any. To capture such a wide range of story elements - from both World Wars to the Bolshevik Revolution to the American mob scene - in such a small space, and without leaving the feeling of having missed out on a better story, truly makes this an epic writ small. In that respect, it's worth reading just to see how dense a story can be told with just the barest of details.

 I really wanted to like The Iron Trial. One of its co-writers, Holly Black, is a favorite author of mine. I'm eager to read any new material she produces. Moreover, there was a lot of excitement for this book amongst the online reading community. I'm not the only reader who loves Holly Black, and although I'm conflicted about the second co-author, Cassandra Clare, she has legions of fans. 
 There was some speculation and discussion about how the premise of the book was similar to Harry Potter: a small portion of the population can use magic, but magic's existence is kept secret from those who can't use it; children with magical abilities are sent to a boarding school where they learn to use their talents. Yes, the premise is very similar to that of Harry Potter, but I figured that the book would have its own originality and its own merit. I wanted to read it and decide for myself. 
 Well, I read the book and made a decision. It's a hard decision to put into words. It seems so harsh to write blatant and rip-off. But that is what I'm truly feeling about The Iron Trial. 
 I could never truly get into the story. The entire time -- the entire time -- I was comparing and contrasting the book with Harry Potter. And I argued with myself while I did this. Ellen, are you just making these comparisons because of prejudice? Are you truly being fair and impartial? But then, my mother saw me reading the book and asked, "Oh, are you reading Harry Potter?" 
 !!!!! 
 It turns out, she saw the little illustrations that appear at the beginning of each chapter -- so like the ones in Harry Potter -- saw a black-haired boy and a dragon, and made a connection. At this point, I committed firmly to my decision. Any originality that The Iron Trial has is overwhelmed by its similarities to J. K. Rowling's masterpiece. 
 To be fair, I'm going to take a minute to discuss the book without comparing and contrasting it to Harry Potter. If I'd read this book as a middle-grade-aged kid, I think I would have enjoyed it. The story follows Callum Hunt, a boy who has magical ability, but who has been taught by his father to fear and suppress his magic. Callum's mother was murdered in a war, and his father is embittered and has told Call that the Magisterium, the boarding school where young mages learn to manipulate the elements, confines and exploits magical children. When Callum turns twelve, he and other magical children are made to take the Iron Trial -- the entrance exam for the Magisterium. Callum tries to fail the test, but his plan backfires. 
 Callum is a bit of an anti-hero. He has slightly poisonous attitude, an inferiority complex, and a limp. I can't say that this is a genre break-through or anything, but it made for a bit of an unexpected twist. The narration was third-person, focusing solely on Callum's perspective. The tone was classically middle-grade with moments of levity and... HARRY POTTER HARRY POTTER HARRY POTTER!!! 
 I'm sorry, that's as much as I can discuss without bringing up the boy wizard. While I read, I started making a list of similarities. It contains spoilers, so I'm going to hide them all behind a spoiler tag. Read if you will. 
 1. Magic exists, with a small portion of the world population able to use it. 
 2. Those who can't use magic are prevented from discovering its existence. 
 3. Mostly magic is inherited genetically, but some children from non-magic families are magical. 
 4. There are boarding schools for magic that young magic users attend. 
 5. The main character, a boy, has ink-black hair. 
 6. There exists an evil mage, whose worst fear is death, who started a war. 
 7. The evil mage wants to defeat and elude death. 
 8. The evil mage disappeared a little over a decade ago and no one knows where he is. 
 9. The evil mage's soul is inside of the protagonist's body. 
 10. "All this time we have waited, Call, for you to be old enough. And here you are nearly ready." 
 11. Call woke up in the infirmary." 
 12. Call's friends at school are a boy and a girl. 
 13. The school is hard to navigate. 
 14. Call sneaks around at night. 
 15. The top mage at the school has a magical animal in a cage in his office and little magical doodads. 
 16. Published by Scholastic. Why, Scholastic? 
 17. I simply can't go on.  
 Really, this book is meant for kids, and I think kids will enjoy it. The only reason I read it is because Holly Black had a part in it. But -- and this makes me really uncomfortable to say -- I think her writing is worse for her collaboration with Clare. Worse, because the originality is not there.

The Last Colony is the third installment of the Old Man's War series by John Scalzi, and will probably be my last visit to Scalzi world. I really enjoyed Old Man's War, as it had the perfect blend of a sympathetic and wise-cracking main character, intriguing concept (recruiting 75 year olds with the promise of powerful new military bodies to fight aliens threatening humanity), basic training with the new bodies, first combat, and an exciting finale. 
 However, with each successive book I'm learning just how weak Scalzi's descriptive powers are, and while he certainly has a breezy narrative style and refreshing sense of humor, it is starting to wear thin on me since the stories lack the fresh ideas and precise pacing of the initial book. This problem was especially apparent in Redshirts, which had a great idea (what if you found yourself as one of those unfortunate redshirt-wearing ensigns destined for a horrible death in Star Trek) but got tiresome towards the end. 
 This time John Perry and Jane Sagan have retired to an ostensibly uneventful life on the colony Huckleberry as an ombudsman and head of security. Guess what, aparrently the Colonial Defense Forces are not done with them, or their adopted daughter Zoe Boutin. They get dragged into being in charge of a new colony made up of 10 planet's representatives, which is like being a kindergarten cop. Then the CDF plays a switcheroo on the colonists, and they become pawns in a chess match between the CDF and the alien Conclave on a world called Roanoke. 
 It's not worth detailing the remaining plot details, but suffice to say that Scalzi has to pull out increasingly unlikely scenarios from his hat to keep the action centered on this family. Is it really plausible that an entire Conclave of 412 hostile alien races cannot get their act together to beat into submission a single colony of 2,500 settlers who are basically unarmed civilians? And does it really make sense that the alien Obin would commit their race to protecting the daughter of the human traitor who granted them consciousness? Not to mention the dubious plot device of passing on military-grade combat strength and skills to someone by slipping something into their food? I wasn't buying that one. 
 To sum up, John Scalzi has a pretty reliable formula for churning out entertaining military SF, and he tries to vary it from book to book, but I don't think I can gain anything further by reading more of his output, with so many other books clamoring to be read. Not to worry though, I'm sure he'll do just fine without me.

An intriguing and exciting story begins to unfold, and there's a rumor floating around that there will be a book 2. I hope that means all the action is packed into book 2 because "The Bone Witch" was simply not for me. 
 I am a reader who craves action. While this book had plenty of character developing events, they lacked the bite that I was seeking. All of the elements are there; they just don't quite come together to make this a compelling read. For example: 
 Tea (pronounced Tay-uh for those like me who read it as 'tee' at first) has insane amounts of power and unbelievable things happen around her, but she is... egads!... boring. I feel like she's the Twilight movie version of Bella. "Yeah, I have tons of power, but I'm really not into it. I'm shy, and everything's like whatever." I hope that the events of this book make her into the badass I know she can be! 
 Early-on Fox (Tea's brother) is raised from the dead, and it doesn't seem to have as horrifying repercussions as I would have hoped. As a matter of fact, he's polite, well-reasoned, and just an all around nice guy. Usually magic has unintended consequences, but we don't see much of that here. 
 The creatures - when present they are breath-taking! My favorite portions of the book were about these guys. However, their appearances are few and far between. 
 The description. Whoever wrote it did a fantastic job! 
 Amazing concept! The details of this world are clearly thought out and often explained. I mean, heartglasses? Manufacturing hearts? How cool is that?!  The dual narration. Loved knowing that what I was reading was important later on.

 I have to say that between this and Monstrous Beauty I really am enjoying this new crop of folk & fairy tale retellings that are gorgeously atmospheric, poetic and largely character (rather than plot) driven. It feels more authentic in terms of evoking that dreamy, altered-reality feeling that I remember from reading my first set of Grimm's fairy tales where unfortunately, there are rarely any happy endings. 
 The first half to three-quarters of the book are slowly paced, as we are introduced to Mabel and Jack, a couple in their late forties who choose to move to cold and distant Alaska after Mabel delivers a stillborn baby. Each deals with the grief in their own way; Jack in the punishing physical labour needed to carve a farm from scratch in the wilderness, and Mabel in her need to escape from everything she once knew in search of solitude. Their first months are hard and both regret, but do not voice, their misgivings for their new lives. By the time winter arrives Jack is seriously considering working in the local mine for some money, even though it's practically a death wish, and Mabel is steadily growing more and more detached from everything around her. In a rare moment of lightheartedness they build a snow girl from winter's first snow. Jack draws the girl a face and Mabel dresses her in a scarf and mittens and paints her lips red. In the morning the snow girl is destroyed and they both start seeing a little girl running alone through the woods. In the months and years that follow, the girl - Faina - grows bolder and starts to interact with them in meaningful ways, enriching all of their lives and especially healing the rift between Mabel and Jack. 
 Mabel believes Faina is a snow fairy, created from their love, while Jack believes she is an orphaned human girl who has simply adapted to living alone in the woods. The truth is very gradually revealed and I actually found the ending to be very apt and fulfilling. The last quarter was a little jarring given the sudden six year jump, so I didn't feel as close to the characters as I did in the beginning. I also did not like the third character perspective that was added, even though it was an inevitable plot device. It felt a little cheap for it to be included before the final twist and reveal, but not after.  I.e. why did we see Garrett's views on falling in love with Faina but none of his grief after she's gone? IMO the epilogue would have been more fulfilling from his POV . 
 Other than that I thoroughly enjoyed the enchanting magic of The Snow Child, but it really is one of those books you need to be in a certain mood to really enjoy.

So this is basically 300 plus pages of "he says" "they say," a book that delves into the origin and evolution of Scientology, a pseudo-religion/cult with a special following within the celebrity community, touting dedicated members like Tom Cruise and John Travolta. 
 Sensational and shocking, Wright's book certainly characterizes Scientology as some wacky cult based on incredible claims that could only be spawned in the imagination of a science fiction writer. Yet far from silly-but-harmless, Wright accuses the Scientology leadership of violence, coercion, and brainwashing as it systematically exploits/subjugates/manipulates its followers. 
 The thing is every shocking charge made about Scientology could also be made against Christianity or Islam or Mormonism or you-fill-in-the-blank with a dogmatic ideology/belief system at some time in its past. And it occurred to me that the real difference between a "cult" and a "religion" is that the former, arguably in its infancy, is still a target for criticism because it is new and represents a minority, while the latter has been around so long that its deep cultural ties facilitate (even demand) a selective and collective amnesia and a big whopping heap of cognitive dissonance that allow it a free pass. 
 Seriously, talking serpents and bushes, walking on water, the parting of seas, virgin births, the dead resurrected, magical seer stones, magic underwear, ascensions into heaven in chariots...come on. And the Crusades alone certainly took religious coercion and violence to a whole new level. As far as brainwashing...well one could make a strong argument that just about every religion, especially in its infancy, depends on brainwashing to gain momentum. 
 So, yeah, this was entertaining, but in a National Enquirer sort of way. I don't personally subscribe to any particular religion, but it's easy to see how Scientology might offer its members what other more traditional religions offer theirs. The fact that it happens to have been born in our lifetime and updated its craziness doesn't make it any less meaningful to its followers. 
 I'm also not sure this is a book that is meant to enlighten as much as to sell and ultimately to prejudice or rather reinforce prejudice. Though Wright offered the church an opportunity to respond, much of the book and criticism was based on the testimony of members who eventually left the church for whatever reason. Again, one only needs to look at the history of other religions to see the similarities far outweigh/outnumber the differences. 
 Is Scientology crazy, full of hypocrisy and unsubstantiated claims that seem to defy logic and science?...hell yeah, but so is Christianity, Mormonism, Islam, etc...when taken at face value. Personal beliefs aside, it seems a little unfair to throw stones when most religions despite whatever longevity they assert still live in glass houses. 
 In the epilogue Wright makes an attempt to put the criticism of Scientology into perspective, pointing out some of the crazy claims made by other religions...still, I would have liked this to be more informative and less sensational. 
 Bottom line: it felt like he was picking on Scientology primarily because it's the new kid on the block and the easiest target. Overall, more entertaining than educational, but still a good read as a whole.

 I really wanted to like The Iron Trial. One of its co-writers, Holly Black, is a favorite author of mine. I'm eager to read any new material she produces. Moreover, there was a lot of excitement for this book amongst the online reading community. I'm not the only reader who loves Holly Black, and although I'm conflicted about the second co-author, Cassandra Clare, she has legions of fans. 
 There was some speculation and discussion about how the premise of the book was similar to Harry Potter: a small portion of the population can use magic, but magic's existence is kept secret from those who can't use it; children with magical abilities are sent to a boarding school where they learn to use their talents. Yes, the premise is very similar to that of Harry Potter, but I figured that the book would have its own originality and its own merit. I wanted to read it and decide for myself. 
 Well, I read the book and made a decision. It's a hard decision to put into words. It seems so harsh to write blatant and rip-off. But that is what I'm truly feeling about The Iron Trial. 
 I could never truly get into the story. The entire time -- the entire time -- I was comparing and contrasting the book with Harry Potter. And I argued with myself while I did this. Ellen, are you just making these comparisons because of prejudice? Are you truly being fair and impartial? But then, my mother saw me reading the book and asked, "Oh, are you reading Harry Potter?" 
 !!!!! 
 It turns out, she saw the little illustrations that appear at the beginning of each chapter -- so like the ones in Harry Potter -- saw a black-haired boy and a dragon, and made a connection. At this point, I committed firmly to my decision. Any originality that The Iron Trial has is overwhelmed by its similarities to J. K. Rowling's masterpiece. 
 To be fair, I'm going to take a minute to discuss the book without comparing and contrasting it to Harry Potter. If I'd read this book as a middle-grade-aged kid, I think I would have enjoyed it. The story follows Callum Hunt, a boy who has magical ability, but who has been taught by his father to fear and suppress his magic. Callum's mother was murdered in a war, and his father is embittered and has told Call that the Magisterium, the boarding school where young mages learn to manipulate the elements, confines and exploits magical children. When Callum turns twelve, he and other magical children are made to take the Iron Trial -- the entrance exam for the Magisterium. Callum tries to fail the test, but his plan backfires. 
 Callum is a bit of an anti-hero. He has slightly poisonous attitude, an inferiority complex, and a limp. I can't say that this is a genre break-through or anything, but it made for a bit of an unexpected twist. The narration was third-person, focusing solely on Callum's perspective. The tone was classically middle-grade with moments of levity and... HARRY POTTER HARRY POTTER HARRY POTTER!!! 
 I'm sorry, that's as much as I can discuss without bringing up the boy wizard. While I read, I started making a list of similarities. It contains spoilers, so I'm going to hide them all behind a spoiler tag. Read if you will. 
 1. Magic exists, with a small portion of the world population able to use it. 
 2. Those who can't use magic are prevented from discovering its existence. 
 3. Mostly magic is inherited genetically, but some children from non-magic families are magical. 
 4. There are boarding schools for magic that young magic users attend. 
 5. The main character, a boy, has ink-black hair. 
 6. There exists an evil mage, whose worst fear is death, who started a war. 
 7. The evil mage wants to defeat and elude death. 
 8. The evil mage disappeared a little over a decade ago and no one knows where he is. 
 9. The evil mage's soul is inside of the protagonist's body. 
 10. "All this time we have waited, Call, for you to be old enough. And here you are nearly ready." 
 11. Call woke up in the infirmary." 
 12. Call's friends at school are a boy and a girl. 
 13. The school is hard to navigate. 
 14. Call sneaks around at night. 
 15. The top mage at the school has a magical animal in a cage in his office and little magical doodads. 
 16. Published by Scholastic. Why, Scholastic? 
 17. I simply can't go on.  
 Really, this book is meant for kids, and I think kids will enjoy it. The only reason I read it is because Holly Black had a part in it. But -- and this makes me really uncomfortable to say -- I think her writing is worse for her collaboration with Clare. Worse, because the originality is not there.
