Thanatos, the most deadly Horseman of the Apocalypse, has endured thousands of years of celibacy to prevent the end of days. But just one night with the wickedly sexy Aegis Guardian, Regan Cooper, shatters centuries of resolve. Yet their passion comes with a price. And Thanatos must face a truth more terrifying than an apocalypse-he's about to become a father. 
 Demon-slayer Regan Cooper never imagined herself the maternal type, but with the fate of the world hanging in the balance she had no choice but to seduce Thanatos and bear his child. Now, as the final battle draws closer and his rage at being betrayed is overshadowed by an undeniable passion for the mother of his child, Thanatos has a life-shattering realization: To save the world, he must sacrifice the only thing he's ever wanted-a family. 
 Lethal Rider was a really brilliant read. I was hooked from the first chapter. Even though Thanatos is a total badass, I really enjoyed his and Regan's story. It's not steady and there are lots of up's and down's between Regan and Than but it makes for an interesting read because Than isn't the type that sticks to his characteristics. He knows who he is and what he is. He's a gentle giant at times with Regan yet he won't hesitate to kill his enemies. He may use some methods Regan doesn't agree with but in the end they work it out. With Regan, Than becomes a better character and understands how he can be a better person for Regan and his unborn child. He realises some things about himself that he's missed because he's been too consumed by his actions. 
 Which I think is also what I like about Regan. Once she's kidnapped by Than and as there relationship grows and changes and the storyline evolves you not only see more of Than but the growth of Regan and how she starts to believe in herself as a human being instead of just of her gifts and what use she can be. 
 Lethal Rider like the previous two books still includes the other characters and more of the overall storyline. You see how Limos and Arik are adjusting to being together and of their future plans. You see more of Ares, Cara and her beloved hell hounds. 
 The family support with each couple is just as vital and important as each couple and following their relationship. Which is what lies at the core of each book, even with Pestilence in the background reeking havoc they all stay connected, help each other in anyway they can and they root for each other. 
 Lethal Rider is a brilliant book, I have since also bought the paperback version of this series because I enjoy it so much. A definite must read but would recommend reading within the series to have a better understanding.

Give praise to Khaled Hosseini for weaving a tale of sorrow, brutality, horror, courage and shinning like a beckon of light hope, always hope. This novel is about two women; we watch them grow through their tragic life and where fate has placed them and watch on with fascination and horror as Hosseini finally connects the two women. 
 The novel starts off with Mariam at the age of 5 where she is deprived of the sense of family, community, and love "Mariam was an illegitmate person who would never have legitimate claim to the things pther people had, things such as love, family, home, acceptance." (Hosseini 4) however despite it all this does not corrupt her in any way she provides an eternity of love that only a child can give to her mother Nana despite the fact Nana's malicious and unhealthy behavior towards her daughter, her father Jalil is the love of her small life and the children that he has born with his other wives take a special place in her heart. It is a miracle under the circumstances that this child is not hateful and nasty but quite, kind, and loving. Mariam is a harami (a bastard) and must pay the price "nor was she old enough to appreciate the injustice, to see that it is the creators of the harami who are culpable, not the harami, whose only sin is being born." (Hosseini 4) For Jalil's unhonurable act he isolate's the two women from Herat and placed them on the outskirts of Gul Daman. As a reader Hosseini describes their home as a vast amount of open land with nature's finest work moutains, weeping willow trees, knee-high grass, and beautiful bright flowers and it freeze's in your mind like a wonderful painting that seems peaceful, remote, and a big cage with the obstacles to go with it in order to reach the nearest city which is Herat. Mariam's mother Nana is mentally ill placing the blame on everyone and is extremely miserable and her father Jalil is too full of his own pride in order to accept his daughter fully, because of these reasons she is left alone at age 15 in order to be bethrod to a man named Rasheed 30 years her senior and you watch on sadly as this little kind hearted girl takes what fate has placed in her path accepting it with her head held high. As the story goes on into Kabul where the newlyweds now live it is obvious that Rasheed is a man's man and believes in tradition and men stereotypes he takes full control of his wife; Mariam has moved from one prison into a far worse one however she is somewhat happy; "She felt prized by his protectiveness. Treasured and significant..." (Hosseini 81) Mariam is to wear a burqa (a head piece with a viel) when out in public as requested by her dear husband however she took comfort from the viel she no longer felt like everyone knew her shameful past- During one of their trips into Kabul Mariam is astonished and mesmerized by the modern women who wore make-up, high heels, showed legs, hem above the knee, and smoked whereas Rasheed was disgusted. As the book drags on it pulsesbuilding up awaiting the climax; Mariam becomes pregnant and she is desperate for the baby whereas Rasheed is desperate for a boy when Mariam loses the child we see a desperate tragic side of her and Rasheed grows hostile and abuse that was just piercing under his skin. In April 1978 Mir Akbar Khyber was murdered he was a prominent communist his supporters blamed President Daoud Khan's government. On April 27th military planes soared east and north, many people said Kabul was in the hands of the people when the rebels killed Daoud Khan and his family a new Afghanistan was born one with democracy and principles of Islam.

 Painting Sky is like a "everything is not what it seems" type of story. Jane is starting a new phase in her life; moving away from home, starting college and staying with a whole new set of roommates: her brother, her boyfriend, and her boyfriend's brother. One she loves. One she thought she loved. One she thought she hated. As she tries to adjust to a new lifestyle, everything changes and she doesn't know who or what to believe. She'll begin to doubt her own art skills and the people around her. When she truly discovers herself, it's the start of a new beautiful story. 
 Thoughts: 
 PLOT LINE - The story will get you hooked from the beginning and you'll get to the ending before you know it! When Keith comes into the picture, you'll want him to keep coming back. Although the story is from Jane's prospective. Keith brings a little something extra to the plot because he influences Jane in different ways. Throughout the story, Jane will unravel different sides of herself, ones she never thought she had. Then, she'll look at the world through a different set of lens. Once she starts to understand her past and present, she can think about her future. 
 CHEMISTRY - Everything about Keith is intense! So, everything between Keith and Jane is bound to be just as intense. Sometimes you will feel like you're getting whiplash from Keith. One day, he'll be all angsty and broody. Another day, he'll be kind and understanding. You'll never know what to expect, which can be kind of exciting. There is one thing you will get from Keith and Jane's relationship. You need someone in your life who can help you discover new things about yourself. Sometimes, changes in your life are for the better. 
 Overall, I liked the book! I hope the author will write another book because there is still some unanswered questions. Once you get to the ending...you will see!

First impressions: The immediacy of the present tense used in this narrative really drew me in. Victoria Schwab has an elegant way of writing that I found beautiful and hypnotic. 
 Lasting impressions: I couldn't connect with this one beyond the likable prose, however. I never fell in love with Cole, or even believed that Lexi truly had, and the story moved a bit slow for my tastes. 
 Conflicting impressions: I thought missing children would be enough to keep me interested, but the stakes never felt high enough for me to care about the outcome. 
 Overall impressions: This is one book where I am absolutely certain that the only reason I disliked it was because I just wasn't feeling it. I can tell it's a well-crafted, unique, and beautiful tale. I can see where some people would get really into this one and love it. For me, it fell a bit flat. 
 The setting, a secluded small town named Near located next to a spooky moor, is perfect. I loved the opening, when Lexi introduces us to local folklore about the old Near Witch who died long ago and is inextricably linked to the town's history. The first chapter is Lexi telling a bedtime story to her young sister, Wren, about the Near Witch. It's a quiet, intimate moment that made me want to curl up in front of a fire and keep reading. 
 The beginning was so good, in fact, that I think it set up my ultimate disappointment by the time I got to the end. Schwab's writing is dripping with detail, painting clear images in your mind, but without getting bogged down. It's the kind of writing you want to sip, and languish in, not hurry through to find out what happens next. Yet I still needed something to keep me turning the pages. Instead, I felt like I was fighting reading inertia, and that the more I read, the less I could actually continue to consume. Then I'd put it down and struggle to pick it back up. It was frustrating. 
 As the story continues, a stranger arrives in Near, and the children of the village start turning up missing from their beds late at night. The town quickly turns on this mysterious visitor, as strangers are not welcome in Near. Lexi, however, refuses to blindly join this lynch mob, and starts her own investigation into the strange events happening in Near. Lexi is headstrong and stubborn, refusing to listen to her somewhat controlling uncle, who just wants her to stay in the house where he feels she'll be safe. She disobeys him consistently, sneaking off to meet Cole (the stranger) or visit the homes where the children have gone missing. She wants to stop what's happening, not only because she knows these kids, but because she witnessed her own sister nearly escape through the window late at night. 
 Lexi's protective instinct didn't ring quite as true for me. I thought she was just nosy and curious. She seemed more determined to prove Cole's innocence than to protect her sister, and it bothered me that she got so swept up in the new boy in town. I felt they had no chemistry, and the romance that blossoms between them just didn't do it for me. He was an interesting character in his own right and I didn't get why he needed to also be a love interest. 
 The middle dragged on far too long for me. I had to struggle to get through this one, because neither the mystery itself, nor the beautiful prose, was enough to keep me hooked. The mystery is not much of a mystery as it turns out, and the story is much more effective as a lesson in how folklore and mass hysteria can influence human behavior, particularly in exclusive communities. Yet even this facet of the story seemed underdeveloped. While the overall tale is an interesting one, the details couldn't hold my attention long enough to get through more than a few pages at a time. 
 I recommend this one to fans of witch and folk tales, but this one just wasn't for me.

The setting and world development was cool (although we are still hungry to know what caused this magic wish stuff to occur - we assume it has something to do with Area 51, but...). 
 Two wishes: 
 1. That Eldon had grown as a character. Even my teen readers felt he was a jerk and whined constantly. I can't tell you how many times in the second half of the book my kiddos put the book down, looked at me, and sighed, "Why doesn't he just NOT make a wish? Does he HAVE to? What happens if he doesn't?" They weren't big fans of his internal and external dialogue. I also found him hard to like as a main character. However, if he had undergone a massive change throughout the novel, all of that would have been forgiven. 
 2. A more satisfying ending. Granted, #1 could have fixed this but my reading group felt like this was a cop out ending. Too easy! The story deserved better than that. 
 Here's the best thing about As You Wish: 
 It sparked a lot of conversations. A LOT. I would recommend it to read in a small group for that express purpose. 
 Thanks to Sourcebooks Fire for providing copies for my readers. <3

After being devastated by Rotters, I knew what I was getting into with Mr. Kraus. He is an unforgiving writer, who takes some familiar elements - a farm, a father, a wife, a sister, a boy - and distorts them into ghoulish relief. Fans of Stephen King will enjoy his work, or perhaps readers of Kraus will go onto become fans of the King and his ilk. 
 However, I didn't love this with the passion others describe. "Scowler" is so unremitting that is was genuinely hard to read. The violence is attenuated to extraordinary lengths, so that every sickening moment is available to the reader and it feels somehow longer than its 290 pages. Which might be a good thing, for some. I wasn't quite connected enough with the story and characters. And in the end, I wasn't really sure what I thought of the book, except that I was glad to be done with it.

I usually don't like retellings of legends or fairy tales. It's a lot to live up to, and the new versions never seem to be able to. But Gaughen did an excellent job. She changed the story just enough - with Maid Marian a runaway, dirty mouthed thief  - to make it fresh without giving up the essence of the legend. Scarlet is a kick ass character, bridging perfectly that gap between a rough and tough, knife wielding thief and a vulnerable and scarred young woman. And the angsty romance is done perfectly. Even the love triangle failed to annoy me. I just couldn't put this one down.

I was all set to give this four stars just for the cover and just because there's ghosts. Ghosts! Real, honest to goodness scary-ish ghosts! Not love ghosts, where you can make pottery together. 
 That was enough to make me pick up the book, and even enough for me to wait to read it--I wanted to leave a ghost book for myself after I read The Dead House. I wanted to pace myself and give myself time in between them. I did, though now that I've read this I won't say that I had to. 
 First: they weren't even mildly scary, which was a bit of a bummer. I like scary, I want scary. This just sort of seemed like a bunch of kids who aren't as trained as they act like they are doing wildly dangerous things. 
 The bad guy was realllllllly obvious, which made me sad. There was no twist for me because I already knew who the nameless person was from the beginning--there wasn't much done to throw me off the trail, so it felt a little silly when suddenly Lucy has a jaw-dropping moment of understanding. Come on sister, how come you didn't see it five days ago!? 
 Lockwood.... I'm confused by. I haven't read the first one, so I feel like maybe I'm missing something. Does Lucy have a crush on him? Is he a teenager, or is he a kid too? None of these kids have parents...? I'm a little lost with it. 
 But despite all those little negative bits, I did enjoy the story, if for nothing else that it is ghosts. Ghosts will forever be my weakness.

I cannot rate this book. Sorry but no. I will not deny that it keeps you reading, it makes your want more but...the way this book is written. 
 It is that BUT that just annoyed me. The first two books were all from Mare's perspective. All well and good now suddenly we're splitting between too many characters and that just chaffed me the wrong way. It would have made more sense to have this written from Mare and Cal's perspective, or Mare and even Maven's since he's the bad guy we are supposed to love/hate. I mean it't not supposed to be his fault his mother turned him into a lunatic, right? 
 And oh my fuck, everyone is so judgmental still, has no one grown up yet. Has fighting and bleeding next to someone no matter how different not made you realise that there is no difference. Aveyard makes some attempt at this when she points out that you can't tell the difference when everyone is in uniform and training together but then that's it. There is not one single character that truly grabs that realisation and runs with it. Is everyone that dense, that entrenched that not even a war even makes a dent in that prejudice? Of course this is bullcrap, cause if one where were ever to talk to any solider they would tell you it makes a difference. 
 Of course Mare stays an idiot, the only good piece of writing was her realisation about how much pain she caused others but that's as far as it goes. Because she is the one that truly refuses to see Cal for more than the Prince he was raised to be. She wants to force him to make changes the way she thinks they should be done not seeing that there might be more than one way to do things. That if she had Cal actually ruled a their little planet as equal rulers as he suggests then maybe that change would be better won, less people would die. But she is more guilty of the prejudice that she accuses Call from suffering since she cannot seem to see past her own anger against silver blood regardless of the good in Silvers that she has seen and the same ruthlessness in her fellow Reds she claims to hate in the Silvers. 
 Why the hell did this have to four books. Three would have been damn fine!!

A young woman who has faced terrible events in the past is now forced to find her path as a super-hero. 
 While there were some weaknesses, the writing was generally good and the characters were interesting. I will read more .

In the far future, humans cling to relevance through a combination of money and military. They are dependent on sentient AIs with impenetrable motives and on the Bose-Einstein condensates, which enable them to communicate and travel instantaneously through the universe. But the condensates are only found on Compson's World, and humanity's greatest scientist was just killed in a cave-in there. Catherine Li, a UN peacekeeper with secrets of her own, is sent to investigate Hannah Sharifi's death, and find what her latest discovery was. 
 The universe she lives in is fascinating, teeming with gene modded humans living in hive minded Syndicates, shunting one brain through another body, wiring fighters for greater reflexes and strength...And Moriarty mines modern quantum physics for sf ideas, coming up with teleportation that leads to imperceptible loss of people's mental states and memories every time they are reconstituted (because you can perfectly recreate their atoms, but not their constituents' spin). This is a fast paced thriller with excellent action scenes and...yet its also a beautifully sensitive portrait of Li's mind. I loved her vicious fighting style and pragmatic view of social interactions, but I also really felt like I got to know her, inside and out. Li has had to hide parts of herself to maintain her career, but when she starts opening up to Cohen she is forced to face the monstrous decisions she's made and lived with. I loved their romance; it's possibly the first time I've ever felt like the vastness and complexity of an AI came across. By the same token,  Moriarty also shows us what we might look like to other intelligence forms, ex: 
 She looked across the little distance between them and had a sudden shadowy glimpse of herself as he saw her. A fierce dark mystery, gloriously tangled in a too-fragile body, slipping away from him down a hall-of-mirrors perspective of increasingly pessimistic statistical wave functions. 
 I was so tempted to give this four stars, because the emotions and thought this book evoked were so intense and complex. But I felt like the mystery of Sharifi's death and final discovery were too convoluted, with too many players that I was expected to remember. Nevertheless, an excellent posthuman adventure.

First impressions: Rory is an incredibly friendly and authentic narrator. Her voice really drew me in, though I had a hard time picturing her with a Louisiana accent. 
 Lasting impressions: Jack the Ripper mystique aside, this is a good old fashioned paranormal murder mystery, and I loved every minute of it. 
 Conflicting impressions: As much as I liked Rory, she seemed a bit generic at times. I'm not sure I could tell you one unique quality about her, other than that she comes from an eccentric community in Louisiana. 
 Overall impressions: Oh good Lord did I gobble this one up! No, not just gobbled - devoured. This was no simple "Hmmm, wonder what's going to happen next?" It was "OHMIGOD I WILL KILL YOU IF YOU MAKE ME STOP READING THIS." I would count down the minutes on my commute and lunch hour, racing to flip pages as quickly as possible so I could find an appropriate stopping place. 
 There was no appropriate stopping place. It was too good to stop reading. Ever. 
 The summary pretty much says it all - girl moves to London for boarding school in the midst of a Jack the Ripper copycat spree and winds up entangled in the investigation while discovering an interesting paranormal element. So we have lots of things I love: 1) boarding school setting; 2)murder investigation; 3) Jack the Ripper history/trivia; and 4) paranormal activity. I fainted from swooning the moment I first read this book's jacket copy. 
 Believe me when I tell you it delivers in pretty much all of these categories. Rory's school is typical - grand buildings, quirky roommates, cute boys, skirted uniforms, and lots of studying. The murder mystery unfolds at a nice pace, with clues that stuck out upon reveal but weren't too intrusive when introduced (these are the best kind, in my humble opinion). There was lots of good Jack the Ripper information shared as the investigation went on, and when Rory discovers her new powers play a distinct role in catching the killer, I was fully on board. 
 Whatever unique qualities Rory may have been lacking were more than made up for with Maureen Johnson's breezy writing and distinct side characters. Everyone and everything seemed so natural and real that I bought in to the world completely without it ever seeming gimmicky. The tension and pacing worked seamlessly to pull me along through the plot, and around every corner there seemed to be something new and interesting to keep my full attention. Add in the Ripper timeframe counting down the days to the next kill and I was hooked. 
 This book requires a strong will to put it down, but enough entertainment to make you want to prolong the agony. Balancing fun, light characters with dark, terrifying events, this book is pure magic. You need to run out and get your hands on this one. 
 Now.

Regency romances are a guilty pleasure for me. I don't know why this quite short historical period resonates with me so much, but it does. That said, this story was one of the most enjoyable of the sort that I have read in a long while. It addressed the terrible difficulty of impoverished female gentry and of women in that period in general. It was quite wickedly humerous as well and I appreciated the heroine's dealing with the ton and icons of that time period. Oh, and if I had been the Duke, I should have banished the dowager duchess to a bleak and damp home in the Outer Hebrides for the remainder of her deplorable life.

Still notice that I gave it four star, so I'm still somewhat crazy about it. I loved the sylph and dragons in this one. The action was intense. I liked it. I didn't see the plot twist coming and the cliffhanger was so mean. I really did enjoy the book.

Wow. It's been an unfortunately long time since I've been this drawn into a book that I stayed up reading until I fell asleep and woke up early the next morning just to read it, simultaneously wanting to reach the end and dreading it all being over. 
 I also don't think I've ever read a better-executed love triangle. It wasn't easy to choose a "team," but instead you hurt and hoped along with all three characters because the love Tessa, Jem and Will all had for each other was so strong and beautiful that you wanted all of them to find happiness. I'm not quite sure what to think of the bittersweet ending just yet. 
 I'm a little put off by Clare's need to pair all the characters off romantically -- seriously, are there any single people in her series? -- but it's also kind of nice in a precious way. Cecily and Gabriel  are probably my favorite outside the main trio just because they're funny, along with dear old Henry. 
 Speaking of Henry, the scene where I thought he had died was terrible. We're talking Fred Weasley dying in Deathly Hallows, punch-to-the-gut, why-are-authors-all-heartless-people terrible. He's always reminded me a bit of one of my younger brothers, which may be why it hurt so bad.  
 I had had Jem's fate spoiled for me before reading as well, but even knowing he was going to be Brother Zachariah, Clare's writing was powerful enough I still believed he was dead. It wasn't as sudden and unexpected as Henry or Jessamine, but still hurt.  
 The Mortal Instruments series didn't give me much hope for Clare's stories. They were like fanfiction, good fanfiction, but still fanfiction, and didn't feel deep in the slightest. I didn't hurt for any of the characters, and while their stories were interesting, they weren't particularly involving. This series, though, was masterfully done. I'm a bit apprehensive about going on to read City of Heavenly Fire next (at least it's the last one?) but am looking forward to Clare's future series.

 Full Review: 
 When I saw that Megan Erickson was writing a Paranormal, Shifter - M/M story -- I was ecstatic! I expected a great book. I expected it to be cute, fun, loving. I should have known she would blow my expectations all to hell! This book was not fluffy. These shifters are not cute puppy dogs with fluffy tails. What Megan Erickson has created in her new series, Silver Tip Pack - is awe-inspiring with endless possibilities. She can literally take this series anywhere because not only did she decide to go beyond normal shifter lore - she created her own world and she kicked up the expectations for shifters for all authors to come! 
 In Daring Fate, you enter the world that is unlike the world we live in today. Humans, Gone. Luxury, Gone. Food sources, very limited. In this world, there are three species - Werewolves, Were's, and Nowere's. The difference? A werewolf is your typical shifter - two forms - human and four-legged wolf. A Were is a type of shifter that has three forms -- human, four-legged wolf, and upright wolf/human hybrid. Finally, a NoWere is an undead Were. They are stuck in were form and they roam around killing werewolves and turning were's into nowere's. So you have werewolves, hybrids, and undead were's all in one living in a dystopian world trying to survive; and of course, there is some love, some hate, some evil, some good, lots of hot sex and characters you are going to love! Before I even get started on how amazing the story was I have to applaud Ms. Erickson on her creativity that has blown me away - way, way above my expectations!! 
 The MC in this story are Dare and Reese. 
 Dare is Alpha of the Silver Tip pack. He is a were. He is not someone you ever want to mess with. In his human form he stands over 7 feet tall and is full of muscle - in his wolf form he is a large black wolf with a silver stripe down his spine and his ears are tipped in silver. His brilliant green eyes mesmerize Reese even before Dare has a chance to win him over with his personality - He is stunning according to Reese and who are we to argue? 
 Reese, a gray werewolf with a white throat - of the White Throat pack who has been living under Xan's rule in the Bluefoot pack. 
 When these two meet they couldn't be more different yet they know immediately they are true mates. The mating call and desires are high and it takes all of Dare's strength not to jump his mate straight away - but first he has to nurse his mate back to health. Because Dare and Reese didn't just meet on accident. No, they met after Reese and his brother Jude were exiled from their pack and Reese was left beaten half to death in an area that the Nowere's would find him and finish him off. If it hadn't been for Jude's quick thinking (which you will see he does a lot of) then Reese and Dare probably would not have ever met. However, Jude went to the Silver Tip pack for help and that was pretty much the start of an amazing relationship! 
 Were with a werewolf, how would it work? Werewolves were inferior to the Were's. Well, one thing for sure is these two don't lack in the chemistry department - once those pheromones start flying, it's on! 
 '"Mine," he growled against my lips. 
 Not gonna lie, I was fucking terrified. Dare was only half there, his Were pulsing inside his skin. I didn't know his Were, and I hoped to hell Dare had enough power to stay human. 
 I shifted my hands to grip his face, my fingers digging into his scalp as I rutted against him. The mating instinct overtook all my other thoughts. So, despite my terror, I was hard as hell. "Yours," I muttered back. 
 His chest rumbled, and he pressed our lips together -- hard, punishing, furious--before delving his tongue inside.

My head was spinning, my body on fire, ass clenching in anticipation for being taken. I wanted it. God help me, but I wanted him to pin me down and fuck me until I broke. I wanted to be owned. 
 I was going to be mated. To a Were. And there was no going back."' 
 Supporting characters include Jude, Reese's younger brother. G - who is one of Dare's guards and trusted confidant. Cati who is the mother of Dare's son, Mav. Then Bay Dare's brother. These characters were all brilliant in and of themselves and they all have stories to tell. I can't wait to read Jude's story and find out what makes him tick - I guarantee it's going to be another amazing story! 
 From the beginning of the book until the very end the story keeps you totally enthralled! I read this book in one sitting because I could. Not. Put. it. Down. There was just no way! I needed to see what happened next, then what happened after that - and my need to know just never stopped. This book has no low points. You won't be bored and you won't want to put it down. While I admit I am a huge Megan Erickson fan - my opinion of this book is not influenced by that at all - this book is JUST that awesome! If you don't like shifter books, I urge you to give this one a try - you will be surprised. It is perfectly balanced between paranormal, romance, hotness, Alphaness, sexiness, and mystery - add in a world that is intriguing and you have a winner! 
 I highly recommend this book - 5+ Stars!

Unteachable is basically a realistic and believable approach to a taboo love story that seems to be popular these days- I.e. Student/Teacher. 
 I loved how the author didn't sugar coat the attraction and tried to have the pair stay away and ignore said attraction. There was no justification given, or even needed. Just plan ole simple attraction. 
 Also loved the portrayal of Maise as a strong willed, go-getter who was no shrieking violet. Her almost Lolita feel was somewhat intriguing, as was her knowledge and use of it.

I wish I'd enjoyed this book, but I couldn't finish it. I don't want to criticize Paolini or his legions of fans, as he has created something that has a tremendous audience. And his youth while finishing such an opus is inspiring. However, I'm not a fantasy fan, so clumsy, derivative writing isn't something I have patience for, just because it is wrapped around heroism and magic. Perhaps the later books are better? I would suggest reading Terry Brooks, Piers Anthony, Anne McCaffreyor Mercedes Lackey to fans who believe Paolini to be the ultimate. Read a bit more; there are greater riches to be found.

 I read this following a book about mass murder, so I was not prepared to take on the sadness of child rape. The first several chapters of this were just heart breaking and I hated it, so much. 
 At eighteen, she was tired of living and resigned to the fact that nothing would ever change. 
 She wondered why she had even been born. For this, she supposed. 
 Take it or leave it. 
 God's truth. 
 And the only way to leave it was to kill herself. 
 Every time she faced that fact, every time she had the chance, her courage failed. 
 So Angel/Sarah starts out life pretty rough. 
 She is unwanted by her married father, her mother neglects her in favor of her lover, she eventually loses her home and her mother and is introduced to prostitution at the early age of 8. 
 Her only relationship with God is spoiled by her mother and a priest with apparently little mercy. 
 Enter Michael Hosea (whose name should have tipped me off to what bible story this was following but I did not recognize it. Who remembers Hosea, when Gomer is the name that really sticks with you.) 
 This one, beloved. 
 Michael felt a rush of adrenaline mingled with joy. Lord. Lord! 
 God speaks to Michael that Angel is to be his wife. This does not get off to a good start, Angel is of course deeply mistrusting of men, the idea that she can escape her life, and feelings in general. 
 Michael, fights with the Lord on this decision, and then it floods for a bit and Michael, feeling that Angel needs him, saves her from death and marries that woman (seriously, is it legal if she's unconscious?) 
 She preferred the numbness to this stirring of emotion. Hope was torment; Hope was an enemy. And this man was a thorn in her side. 
 Much like in the Biblical story, Michael loves Angel, she runs away back, he brings her back, she runs away.... etc. 
 At first, Angel wants to reclaim her gold, she wants to set up somewhere alone and be free. 
 Then Angel wants what she feels is best for Michael, a chance to be happy with someone who can give him children. 
 The third time, it's really for the same reasons but I'd like to think it's because she needs to deal with her demons. 
 I'm skipping Paul. 
 Ugh. This guy. 
 Good men were often destroyed by obsessions with fallen women, and he had worried about Michael. Joseph had never known a more mismatched pair. A saint and a sinner. 
 At first, I get what Paul is feeling. He's worried Michael doesn't know she was formerly a prostitute. 
 But afterward, it's his jealousy of having to share Michael with a woman, Angel wearing his dead wife's clothes (come on Michael, why didn't you realize that would be an issue??), and general lack of willing to overlook to prostitute thing. 
 Paul in a way represents the unchristian way. The lack of understanding, forgiveness, readiness to see redemption for someone. 
 Paul becomes really annoying and dickish, really. 
 The arrival of the Altmans is what sets Angel to open her mind/heart up. 
 Michael would not have been enough, I think, she needed female friends, a chance to see what a normal good functioning family looks like. 
 Michael is a great character. He is not perfect. He fights gods will at times, he gets angry and lashes out but he also has great patience and insight. It's a good balance and feels like a real person. 
 Over all, it was a good story. 
 Finding redemption, fighting your inner and real demons with Gods help. 
 A very real love story about unconditional love from God and the most awesome farmer ever. 
 I like that Angel trusted and believed in people and find our own set of skills. 
 I enjoyed Gods voice in this, that he called them beloved. It's a beautiful word. 
 And to end this, Wisdom from Michael: 
 "Feed the wolf in your belly, Mara. Then you can try fighting the one you think is at your door." 
 "I wish I could open your mind and climb inside with you." 
 "A woman is either a wall or a door, beloved." 
 "You're coming home with me." 
 "So you can kill me?" 
 "Jesus, are you listening to her? Why'd you give me this stupid, stubborn woman?" 
 "Your kind of love can't feel good." 
 "Does your kind feel any better?" 
 "You're a bird who's been in a cage all your life, and suddenly all the walls are gone, and you're in the wide open. You're so afraid you're looking for any way back into the cage again."

Where to begin? 
 The "best friends who have always been pining for each other" trope is a heavily used one, generally for a reason, but in the case of Kyler and Sydney in Frigid, I think it missed the mark. This book tells us things without showing us -- I didn't see any evidence of their deep and abiding friendship. We got a few anecdotes about Kyler climbing up to Sydney's window when she had mono, but not much else. I used to be a pretty big fan of this plotline, but the more I read, the less I like it. People will fall back on this and get away with not describing it well enough because all they need to do is say that they're best friends. They barely had an honest conversation during the whole book, and the multiple misunderstandings were completely ridiculous. 
 Not only did their friendship seem lacking, they were rather underdeveloped as characters. Sydney has some serious self-esteem issues (and I'm really tired of pretty girls who don't think they're pretty -- can we have some average-looking girls, or hey, how about not emphasizing appearance at all?), and there were not many redeeming qualities in Kyler. Considering they were both 21, they seemed immature for their ages. It was hard to like either of them, or really root for their relationship. A few days of sex does not equal forever. 
 And, really, someone was obviously out to get them. No one cuts power lines as a prank, especially not in a snowstorm. I can't believe they weren't more concerned with the fact that someone shot out the window and sabotaged their generator. No, it's more important that they have a sex marathon. Geez. 
 Also, Kyler's repeated use of the word "baby" was annoying. Seriously, he called Sydney "baby" pretty much every time he talked to her.

3 Stars

I felt like the ending where Brodie runs away was just an excuse to write another book.  It also felt like the ending was just drug out so that there could be a sequel, which I don't think is necessary. Also, I was really expecting some intense horror aspects in this book, and I got none of that. Nothing about it scared me or creeped me out, and I really wanted some American Horror Story Asylum creepiness. Overall, the "scary parts" seemed kind of childish to me. It was slow in parts, and quick in others. I did enjoy this book overall, and I will be picking up the sequel, but I'm going into it with lower expectations.

The creatures, called Darklings, are more animal than human. One of the main characters, Ash, is a twin blood. His father is human, his mother Darkling. I will read book two to see where the story goes, partially because I won a free copy of it.

 Meh....

This book was okay. I enjoyed it at some parts but I didn't become overly attached to any characters or anything. For the most part the plot was fairly predictable, and it wasn't funny or particularly witty. The world building of a futuristic United States was done all right. There were new technologies and the States themselves are no longer 50 (all the states have joined to one or two others to form a territory sort of thing, and the federal government itself is quite weak). Meh, It was OK.
This book is all kinds of adorable!

A fascinating story, but I'm just not a big fan of the journalistic reporting style that made this read like a 300-odd page personal interest story. 
 Skloot also rides a fine line between telling the story of the Lacks family, and telling her own tale of uncovering that story. There's a constant tension between justifying Skloot's efforts as an entirely altruistic effort, and having her express much-deserved pride in a journalistic endeavour fraught with more than its fair share of hardships and interesting personalities. 
 I think there is still too much of a societal gap for this story to be told to full effect. Skloot has done a great job of breaking the ice, though. My wish is that it would lead to a more substantial retelling from the family themselves as they benefit from the awareness raised by Skloot's effort.

This book started off slow -- the first say, 300 pages are all about getting to know 12 characters and their connection to the main plot. It was a bit tedious, and it was hard to remember all the details over such a long exposition. But once I had a grasp on all the characters, I really enjoyed this book! 
 The story takes place in Hokitika, New Zealand during the gold rush. It covers the strange, interconnected events leading up to the night of January 14, 1866 - a night where curious things take place. I enjoyed trying to piece everything together. 
 The writing is gorgeous and while the majority of the characters aren't very dynamic, they are characterized well. 
 I am not sure we needed the bits at the end where we found out "what really happened" -- I think the trial could have stood alone. It seemed a bit repetitive, and at 800 pages, repetition was not needed. I did enjoy learning the back story about Emery/Anna and Anna/Lydia, but perhaps that could have been incorporated in another way.

 Giving this 3 1/2 stars. Where to begin? This may be a convoluted review. I think this book should have been titled, "First It's One Thing, Then It's Another". This was a huge book and a big undertaking, and I am not sure I can recommend it. It was an interesting read, engaging and a lot happened, so it was definitely not boring. Good, but not great. I think any review on this novel is presented with the difficulty of how to fairly respond to a classic work of literature. These characters have become larger than life over the centuries, which should by any definition prove the worth or merit of Dumas' story. Yet I can't come close to thinking the novel as a whole was consistently enjoyable. There are also many elements which don't at all hold up to modern sensibilities. A new acquaintance, for example, gambles away his compatriot's sentimental and priceless treasure without the fellow's permission or even knowledge, yet the whole affair is accepted magnanimously and without question as a matter of honour. 
 As a side note, I began reading The Three Musketeers on account of the continual references appearing in Javier Marias's The Infatuations - particularly the mention of the woman whose branded shoulder escaped the notice of the marital bed. It seemed a ludicrous impossibility when Marias mentioned it, and it seemed equally ludicrous in the book. 
 Something else which hindered my enjoyment is that I'm not a big fan of the serialized novel (or its modern counterpart, the serialized television show). There is a tendency in that format to come up with some smashingly spectacular ideas, only to see them eventually spread too thin or stuffed with time-filling side plots in a effort to meet some marketing requirement for length. There are entire sections in this novel filled with vacuous moanings of passion where I can just imagine Dumas petulantly meeting his publisher's deadline by writing pages of whatever drivel came to mind. 
 Whatever might be said of the novel, though, there is no denying its timeless quality. There are several set pieces in the first few chapters that truly capture the imagination and almost single-handedly justify its inclusion into the canon of classic. Unfortunately, those moments were front-loaded, and getting to the end proved almost anti-climactic. It's like making the wine last longer by watering it down, cutting the cake into smaller pieces as more guests arrive, or trying to use a razor for six weeks when it should have been changed after one. But for those first pages, when things are firing on all cylinders, it's pure magic.

I want the character to stop and see what she is doing wrong because I want her to do the right thing. It isn't a, for example, New Moon (Twilight by Stephenie Meyer) where Bella gives up on life for the whole book because Edward left her and just mopes around stupidly and doesn't exhibit any character growth. Then overall it is just crazy that the prophecy of the Hero of Ages was changed by this higher power to make the world believe they will be saved when in fact they will be doomed. MIND BLOWN. Then just after all these thoughts I just have no idea what the crew will do now to stop this power!!! AGHH! I just did not see this coming at all!!!!!

 (did I a little bit love the fact that the journal of the missing girl, written ten whole years ago, made said missing girl my classmate? Of course. I also enjoyed how the romance was a very minor subplot, as Trevor's sole purpose seemed to be to sit on the sidelines, offering himself as a prize whenever Parker was ready to take him up on it. Bonus: mini road trip! 
 I didn't love everything about the ending*, but I loved every part of the journey. 
 *Ending spoilers in detail: I thought it was idiotic for Parker to decide on a whim she didn't want to go to Stanford, since from what I understood, she couldn't afford to go there without that scholarship money, and I feel like she probably could have found a way to defer acceptance and still gotten the money. This is a touching and sometimes haunting account of what it is to decline into Alzheimer's disease. I was moved by the struggles of the main character and her family. I read this book without any real prior information about Alzheimer's. I do not know anyone with this illness and I have never personally experienced any of the symptoms. I was so surprised to bawl through the entire last half of this book. The tale is harrowing, but full of love too. It was powerful and heartfelt and made for a great discussion at our book club this week. Due to a busy month, I read it all in one sitting the same day that we discussed it. I cried buckets then went to the group with puffy eyes. I haven't seen the movie yet but now I know that I must. 
 Alice Howland, age 52, a happily married partner in a power couple with three grown children and a house on the Cape, is a celebrated Harvard professor at the height of her career when she notices a forgetfulness creeping into her life. As confusion starts to cloud her thinking and her memory begins to fail her, she receives a devastating diagnosis: early onset Alzheimer's disease. 
 The potential to get the disease in the Early Onset version, can be predicted with genetic testing. Alice's three children have a fifty-fifty chance that they carry the genetic defect and have to decide if they want to know their future. Her husband, children, students, co-workers and others are affected by this disease but it isn't their story, it is hers and it is told from her oftentimes unreliable perspective. 
 "Still Alice" was an incredibly heart breaking story of not just a woman declining through Alzheimer's, but an entire family's journey. The story starts out showing how successful Alice Howland is. She is a Harvard professor, has a PhD, 3 grown children and a happy marriage. Slowly things start to change. Over the next two years, we see how this degenerative disease takes over the lives of Alice and her family. I found the different reactions of each of the family members interesting. Some members of the group perceived the husband as selfish and too scientific. They were angry with the husband and vilified him while myself and others felt that he did exactly what Alice would have wanted him to do. That he took the same advice that she gave to Lydia.  
 There were parts of the story that had me smiling because they are everyday things that could happen to anyone and then there were the parts that made me fearful for the future, and glad that I don't have this disease running through my family. This book gave me a look into the lives of the families that have this disease. They have my sympathy for what they have to go through, but more than that, they should be held in the highest of esteem and viewed with the utmost of respect. 
 One device Lisa Genova uses to chart the disease's progression is a series of questions that Alice devises to "test" herself before her dementia gets too bad. The idea is that if she can no longer answer the questions, she should open a specific file on her computer and follow the directions there for committing suicide. As the book progresses, the answers get shorter and more inaccurate--charting her deterioration. It was a brilliant device, and I was sobbing when Alice finds her letter to herself and struggles to carry out its instructions. 
 The only thing that bothered me was that Alice was given a tour of the Alzheimer's unit. When I had a loved one in a nursing home and was given a tour of the facility, the Alzheimer's section was off-limits to visitors. It was explained that this was due to the need to keep the doors secured so patients wouldn't wander off as well as the potential for confusion, agitation and disruption caused by a stranger in the area.

 YA books that deal with death and grief aren't exactly thin on the ground. As I write this, I'm looking over one of my bookshelves and picking out the Children's and YA titles. In almost every one, there is a dead parent, a dead sibling, a dead friend. This frequency of death and absence in literature has registered vaguely in my brain before, but looking over my collection now, I'm feeling some fresh realization. 
 In regards to Children's Lit, deaths become a sort of plot aide. Without parents underfoot, children can go on adventures, be resourceful, and express atypical cleverness. This is why Children's Literature is overflowing with orphans. The trope seems more than a little dark. But, for most children, death is not yet a real thing. I remember, as a child, how death was a comfortable part of my fiction. 
 In the YA genre, grief makes its appearance. Which makes sense. Unless you are fortunate, by adolescence, you will have experienced the death of a beloved person with the lucidity of a mostly-developed brain. It is your first grief, and this experience has its place in Young Adult literature, along with first loves and first heartbreaks. 
 Ava Dellaira's Love Letters to the Dead is quite blatantly a book about death. It explores the very peculiar and air-taking problem that follows the death of a person who in some way defined you. Who am I now without you? Who do I become without your presence? 
 Our protagonist, Laurel, comes to us just a few months after her sister May's death. From the start of the novel, we understand that May was a large part of Laurel's identity, and her absence leaves Laurel feeling like an utterly blank slate. Laurel decides to construct an identity for herself, and the plot unfolds from there. 
 On the surface, the narration is entirely epistolary, with Laurel writing notebooks of letters to famous dead people. However, I'd argue that the novel is really diary narration in disguise. To my understanding, Laurel does not know herself, so she addresses her diary to other people. This prominent device helps Love Letters to the Dead stand out from other YA issue-books, but did make for choppy reading at times. For each addressee -- Kurt Cobain, Judy Garland, River Phoenix, Amelia Earhart, and Allan Lane are the regulars -- Laurel writes a little summary of their life and accomplishments, which read, at times, like grade school reports. I met most of them with impatience, wanting to get back to the plot. The two exceptions were Laurel's breakdowns of Kurt Cobain's suicide note and River Phoenix's experiences as a child in a cult known for child sexual abuse. Both of these moments were gripping and enhanced the plot, rather than detracting from it. 
 Mostly, however, Laurel's remarks to the dead are entities detached from the storyline, which is populated with characters in supporting roles with supporting problems. Laurel's parents, aunt, and English teacher make up the only adult presence in the novel; mostly, the story is occupied by Laurel's band of high school friends. Each of these friends has a clear-cut issue, which often made them seem like case studies of at-risk teens, rather than three-dimensional characters. This is probably the main reason I can only give Love Letters to the Dead 3.5 stars. Excepting Laurel and May -- who is vividly present through Laurel's memories -- Dellaira's characters were flat as playing cards. Perhaps the diary/letter narration is partially to blame. The nature of that style of writing does not allow for the kind of rich description and close detail that can be accomplished when a writer does not have to accurately mimic a 9th grade voice. 
 This is not to say the book is without successes. Laurel's characterization was an accomplishment, consistent and complex. Aptly named, she has a strong poetic streak, which only occasionally veers into purple prose territory. She is an earnest, but unreliable narrator -- a liar of omission, with a warren of repressed memories. Laurel, the only person present at May's death, refuses to tell family and friends if her sister's fatal fall from a bridge was an accident or suicide. She keeps the secret from us as well, only tossing us small clues, until the end of the book, when the full scope of the tragedy is revealed in full. 
 May's character was another force in Love Letters to the Dead. She reminded me very strongly of Charlie Kahn from the incredible Please Ignore Vera Dietz. Both May and Charlie are only real to us through the memories of people maddened by grief. They are deified, preserved, distilled, and spiced with nostalgia. Sad and beautiful mysteries to unpack. 
 Ultimately, Love Letters to the Dead left me conflicted. I did not wholly enjoy this book, nor did I wholly dislike it. It had moments that left me very moved, and shortcomings that left me frustrated. However, I can say definitively that Dellaira was unafraid and admirable in exploring morally complex subject matter, and has given us a thought-provoking, if imperfect, read.

 Raisa traveled under an assumed name, Rebecca Morley, through horrible conditions with Amon and 8 of his cadets to Oden's Ford to attend military school. Here's where I became a little confused. Bear with me while I go on a side trip. Oden's Ford contains many schools; one for wizards on the other side of the river from the military school, and another school for temple dedicates where students learn music, art and philosophy. What I didn't quite understand was if Oden's Ford is the name of the entire campus which includes all of the schools or if it was a town or if it was a small country of its own. I tried following the directions on how each of the characters traveled to Oden's Ford but I got lost. I cheated and found a map from a spinoff series of the Seven Realms but I'm still confused. 
 Raisa is the princess heir of the country of Fells which is a mountainous region in the north of the continent. They traveled west through the mountains, past something called Westgate which seemed to guard the west border of the country of Fells yet they entered a swampland called The Fens where a people called Water Walkers live that the author described as part of the Queendom of Fells. They traveled southeast through the swamps to Tamron, the country connected to Fells. There was an abandoned guard house on the border. They then traveled south to Oden's Ford. Even with the map, I couldn't figure out if Oden's Ford is part of Tamron or a country all on its own. 
 Raisa enrolled as a cadet in Wien House at Oden's Ford. She may be out of Fells but danger is all around her. Students come from all over the Seven Realms to attend the schools at Oden's Ford. I've been a firm believer that this series should have ended after the third book (City of Glass). Books four and five were mostly awful and made me not as excited to read this last book. However, I was really pleasantly surprised with how well City of Heavenly Fire wrapped things up. I felt like relationships and friendships were solidified and the big threats were dealt with conclusively. 
 However, that's not to say that the book was perfect. I have about three major problems with it. 
 1. Too many POVs. There are a lot of characters in this series. A lot. While I don't have a problem necessarily with that or with using multiple POVs, there were just too many in this book. It seemed like almost every character got some time, instead of focusing on the big three: Clary, Jace, and Simon. I felt like there was not enough time spent with the characters that mattered to me and the transitions between POVs and scenes were not well done. 
 2. Using a "finale" as a "back-door pilot". I'm still bitter over Richelle Mead's treatment of Adrian in the final Vampire Academy book, just to set up his (much better) spin-off series, Bloodlines. While Clare doesn't mistreat any of our main characters in that fashion, she introduces - and gives a significant amount of time - to the characters of her new Dark Artifices series. While I've enjoyed the series, I'm not a huge Shadow-Hunter world fanatic and I don't really care about the spin-off. I might read it. I might now. What bothered me is the time dedicated to setting that up, detracting from the original story. 
 3. References to other series/books. I have not read The Infernal Devices series yet. I've always planned on it, but haven't gotten around to it yet. So when some of the characters from that series show up, I felt like I was missing important plot points in this book and I've also been spoiled for how the Infernal Devices series will end. There were also multiple references to Magnus' past that I assume were explained in his spin-off book. If I had read these other books, I probably would've loved the incorporation, but since I haven't yet, I found it really disappointing. 
 I don't know what else to say about this book without spoilers. I remembered why Simon was my favorite character in the whole series and have mixed emotions with how the story played out for him, but ultimately I think I'm happy with it. I think that fans of the series will enjoy this book, especially if they read the other series. If you haven't yet ventured into the Shadow Hunter world, I would recommend you start with The Infernal Devices series first, like I should've.

Steve, a normal "American" plumber who gets pulled into the Librarians' battle in The Library at Mount Char, often objects that Carolyn's explanations for how and why things are done don't make sense. To which Carolyn typically replies, "It doesn't matter." And it doesn't. But that's the mindset you need to really get into this story, you need to suspend your disbelief. Hawkins gives little teasers, but he doesn't reveal the secrets of the universe and he doesn't get wrapped up in the details. Instead he leaves much to the imagination. As Carolyn reminds us throughout, we're not reading a story about magic, we're reading a modern myth. The characters are complex, the mysteries run deep, and the plot is epic. It doesn't get much bigger than a battle for the power of the universe. Yet Hawkins delivers this story in such a modernized and unassuming way that it doesn't seem overdone. It's fast-paced, full of twists, and a total emotional roller coaster (in a good way). 
 While there is some gruesome violence in this book, I wouldn't say it's gratuitous. It's balanced with just enough humor that it's downright fun. David, for example, is equal parts terrifying and hilarious, slaughtering countless "Americans" all while sporting a lavender tutu. But more than that, the book's violence has a purpose. It circles back to the characters' humanity and the sacrifices they've each made, willingly and unwillingly, for the underlying message of hope. In the end, even Hawkins' cruelest and most horrible characters are redeemed, in a certain sense, and made into tragic figures. Even Father, who is perhaps the most complex of these monsters - the stuff of myths or an Old Testament god - embodies this process. He is fearsome, awesome, and terrible. Yet we are reminded that he is also the redeemer, the one who ended the darker ages (which, we're assured, were truly worse than anything we can imagine) and ushered in the light that made love, compassion, and life as we know it possible. 
 By the end I was left with a mix of intense emotions that I couldn't quite pin down. Reverence is the closest I can come to naming it, but I'm not sure it's the right word. (Maybe Carolyn could help me out on this one.) The various elements of this book - horror, tragedy, humor, myth, sorrow, loss, redemption, hope - all come together so nicely that by the end it's just...elevated. I truly enjoyed this book and look forward to Hawkins' next work. I'd recommend this to anyone looking for a wild and inventive read.

"President Obama came on the scene right as so many people in my community began to believe that the modern American meritocracy was not built for them." The feeling that the white working class has fallen behind, and can no longer identify with the present-day nation, is a central theme in this raw, eye-opening book that attempts to provide a view in to the white middle- and working-class Appalachian mindset. 
 "Barack Obama strikes at the heart of our deepest insecurities. He is a good father while many of us aren't. He wears suits to his job while we wear overalls, if we're lucky enough to have a job at all. His wife tells us that we shouldn't be feeding our children certain foods, and we hate her for it -- not because we think she's wrong but because we know she's right." 
 The two central questions this book talks about are: What is the nature of Appalachia, and what problems is it facing? And how did Vance escape the same fate as others around him? This book pulls no punches and offers a deep view of Vance's life, talking frankly about addiction, being forced to lie to authority figures, and violence. A few takeaways: 
 Vance escaped because he had uncommonly good support structures that gave him a sense of control. Mamaw (his grandmother) was always there for him, and implored him to focus on his studies. Papaw taught him math and made him excel in that area. He was able to gain control over his life, and escape the learned helplessness of the people around him and turned it into learned hopefulness. Gaining control and confidence, and having the right role models around him who sometimes implemented their rules with force--Mamaw threatened violence if she saw J.D. with his drug-smoking friends--led to him being able to succeed. 
 Economics leads to fragile communities. When factories close, like the factory that used to be in Vance's town, the community becomes fragile. People always relied on these jobs to be there, but after the Good Times where the steel mill always could offer a job, people no longer had the safety net that they thought they had. That's economics and larger society's effect. The steel mill always being available was an anomaly, I would personally say--but people took it for granted. 
 Vance thinks the problems facing Appalachia are mostly on the people, not the structure and society around them. Instead of government being able to enact policy to save these people, they have to save themselves, since, for the most part, he thinks these are problems that the people must solve. Being better parents, being better with money, all that--they have to be solved internally. That's hard because if it were a policy issue, it would be relatively easier than hoping people would solve the problems themselves. One example he gives is the cultural idea that it's "feminine" to be good at school. 
 I think it's a mix of both, and much more on the policy side--the failure to re-train people whose jobs went away before, during, and after the recession, due to automation and export of factory jobs, was a trigger or at least a catalyst for the state it is in today. Policy caused that, to some extent. It's harder for policy to undo that, but I still think there are structural things that make it hard for people, when they do have the motivation and effort to make their lives better, to do so easily. There are obstructions that can be removed, and I think this is more promising than he does. He does say, and I would agree, that there are certain things that are less receptive to a thumb on a scale than others. Yes, culture is harder to change. But I think there are structural things that can be more easily changed, and those things can lead to potential follow-on effects. 
 At the same time, he is also right to say that people shouldn't blame the government for all their problems. There are some things that they should be blamed for, but they also have to take responsibility for themselves. So this is a complex topic. 
 Honor was important--it was sometimes the only thing they had. People who didn't have much sometimes saw the only thing they had control over was their honor. So if someone did something that insulted their family, for example, that was one of the few situations where they could show their honor. In a sense, those were the times where they felt like independent, free-willed people, and sometimes that fueled the need for extremeness in their response, like violence. 
 Stress begets stress, distrust begets distrust. "Mamaw's life had been a constant struggle. From the poverty of the holler, to Papaw's abuse, from Aunt Wee's teenage marriage to mom's rap sheet, Mamaw had spent the better part of her seven decades managing crises. His community was very high-strung and stressed, and because they had a lot of life trauma, they found it difficult to trust people. 
 Being on guard means being less likely to associate with people, and more likely to distrust, and also leads to more stress. This also means that people are hardwired for conflict. This leads to many follow-on effects: children are raised in a less encouraging environment, which can lead to childhood trauma. Stress can increase the risk of miscarriages. Uncertainty exacerbated these kinds of issues. As a result, people just focus on self-preservation. 
 There's a culture of blaming your condition on society. People on welfare will criticize welfare. People who never went to work and got fired will criticize Obama for not protecting their jobs. There are people like this out there. Trump told these people they were right--Vance is telling them they're wrong. 
 Strong communities are truly more resilient, and religion is one of the few fallbacks for fragile communities. He brings up the example of Mormons in Utah, who were more resilient in the face of the recession and the difficult state for the white working class. He repeatedly talks about the importance of the church and religion as community--perhaps even more important as community becomes more fragile. 
 The feeling of persecution can make people ignore facts. When he started taking up Evangelical Christianity, partly as a refuge from his home life, he started believing in creationism and separating him from normal society. Other peoples became heretics. When he saw people waging war on Christmas, and hearing about Christian discrimination, made him feel stronger about his views and reject what science said, seeing those as "ideologies to confront, not theories to understand". 
 Patriotism--love of country--was so strong that it was part of people's identity, even though government was ignored or hated. People's identities were based strongly on one's love of country. The history of his town was based in WWII veteran pride, and that people and their families "did their part during WWII." But they felt like it was being lost. The modern American meritocracy, they feel like, is not made for him, whereas they did see it as being made for people like them. 
 Eternal hope. Even though life was tough, and continued to be, people still had eternal hope. Maybe this is a component of the idea that they see themselves as 'temporarily embarrassed millionaires.' 
 This is a complex, enlightening book, and an important read. It's hard to summarize it, and probably requires multiple reads to get everything out of it. Absolutely worth a read.

Wow, wow, wow. This was not an easy book to stomach, but it was one of the best I've read all year. Maybe even in the past few years. I was on the fence with Kang's last book, The Vegetarian, so I was a little skeptical as I cracked the spine on Human Acts. That skepticism was unfounded, it turns out, because this completely blew me away. Kang's exploration of the dark side of human nature is heartbreaking and deeply touching. Kang opens with the brutal quelling of the Gwangju Uprising in 1980, when government troops killed a staggering number of civilians, and traces its aftermath through the early 2000s. Each vignette offers a different perspective, following a different character's fate. 
 Kang takes an unflinching look at our seemingly limitless capacity for violence and uses it to examine how a communal tragedy is experienced and remembered. She uses Gwangju as a sort of meditation on perseverance and survival. As abundant as the violence in this book is, it doesn't come off as exploitative. There's nothing thrilling about the gore here, nothing exciting. It's horribly sad, even more so for the almost clinical, detached, and indiscriminate approach its perpetrators seem to take. She shines a spotlight on just how deeply depraved we can be when acting under the guise of authority and there's no such thing as accountability (a la the "banality of evil"). There's a lot to unpack here - questions of guilt, responsibility, grief, circumstance. Questions over how to memorialize the victims of such extreme violence and whose right it is to historicize these acts (and how). I definitely haven't processed it fully, yet, but it's one that will stay with me for a long, long time.

EDIT (October 28, 2015) 
 Gosh, looking back at this, I sound like a five year old. After reading both series all the way through, I feel now would be a better time to analyze the characters. 
 Clary- I still adore Clary; she's a great character: strong, independent, creative. She embodies what young adults want to see in a novel. She doesn't rely on Jace or Alec or Simon for protection, because she is perfectly capable of wielding her own weapons, thank you very much. She doesn't take any shit, and knows how to protect herself and fight for what (and who) she loves. Not to mention she was able to adjust to the Shadowhunter world, despite not growing up in it (and her adamant "I don't want anything to do with this" attitude.) She's a strong character, and even better yet because she shatters a lot of female stereotypes about women in fantasy novels. 
 Tessa- I do really like Tessa, and when I originally compared characters, I didn't really see her as a strong character. But now that I've read all of teh Infernal Devices I see she is indeed a strong character. For one, you can't really compare Clary's experiences to Tessa's. The time frames are too different and the standards (especially for women) are very distinct. Tessa proves she is a strong character by putting the harshness and unjust rules of the Shadowhunter world behind her to join her friends and fight. She doesn't hesitate to protect those she's closest too, and goes against every rule set for her gender at the time. She even fights in dresses, which is pretty kick ass. While she is close with Will and Jem, and both do go out of their way to protect her, she has shown in many ways that she is capable of holding her own. 
 Jace- I still really don't like Jace. He's a little bit of an asshole, and his character development did little to disprove that belief. He tries to distance himself from Clary because that's what he thinks is best; he tries to shield Clary, and while in some cases it's a sweet gesture, other times it's too much and belittles Clary as a character. Jace also crosses the line a lot from "acceptable sarcasm" to "Wow I'm such an ass" statements. For me, Jace and Will are extremely similar and thus many of the reasons I dislike Jace for, are also why I dislike Will. 
 Will- Many of the things I said for Jace still apply for Will (their characters are so similar that I have to wonder if Clare even went through the process of developing a new character or plucking parts from her originals that she liked.) The only real difference for me is that at least all of what Will does to Tessa and Jem and everyone else is justified, even if it's stretched justification. He though it would be best to push them away, but once he realized that was a shitty plan and his curse wasn't even real, he really does clean up his act and start treating everyone that cares about him ten times better. 
 Jem- I have nothing negative to say about Jem. Nothing at all. He's a precious cinnamon roll to good for this world, too pure. His character is amazing, and because of everything he has to go through, even more so. While he doesn't experience much character development, his character remains strong, loving, and hardworking. He lives life like he has something to prove, and overall I think that's what differentiates him from the other characters; he's been a Shadowhunter his whole life, but he's always seen himself as a weak one. Despite his strength, he's still dependent on the yen fin and that's what dictates how he acts until it's gone. That's why I think Jem is the best character Clare has written; he might not be a conventional protagonist, but he works harder than anyone in the series, and that deserves multitudes of recognition. 
 Simon- For the longest time, Simon was my favorite character, but as the series progressed (and I became more enlightened) the fact that he was spending so much time with Jace really started to show. He turned into a slight ass, especially regarding all the lies with Maia and Izzy. Out of all of the Shadowhunter characters, Simon has had to redeem himself so much more, from mundane, to vampire, to shadowhunter . He's had a lot to prove of himself, and with lost memories  to boot. Simon remains a strong, and dedicated character throughout the entirety of the series, and I'm excited to read The Shadowhunter Academy. 
 Whew. Hopefully those analysis' don't sound like they were written by a five year old.

 Carriger actually introduced a gypsy-like culture that I really loved.
