 Hello and welcome back to the third edition of Kelly Freaks Out Over Elena Ferrante Theater! 
 I hope that you didn't come in here with the expectation that this was going to be the time that I got disillusioned with Elena, did you? Because that seems unlikely to happen. Ever. At least not with these Neapolitan novels. These things are like crack brownie ice cream pot (insert more adjectives that indicate addiction and deliciousness here) sandwiches. I will never say no to another. 
 In this book our two darling girls are now in their mid-to-late twenties. Lila is dealing with the aftermath of her decision, in the second book,  to leave her husband and move in with a man who has loved her since she was a child (but never have sex with him). She is working long hours at a food processing plant, hired by someone else who once wanted to fuck her, and helping the man who took her in to study for a degree he is taking. Her family doesn't speak to her, her husband barely acknowledges the existence of her child.  Elena, meanwhile, has finished college and is married to her professor husband, from a good middle class family of lefty intellectuals and lives in a comfortable home in Florence. She has two children over the course of the novel and falls out of intellectual life and relevance after the publication of her first book, struggling with her motherly responsibilities and her growing understanding that her husband clearly wants a much more traditional marriage than he lets on. She is also cut off from her lower-class family now, in a way, since they do not want to deal with her, but she gets snippets of news from the old neighborhood and stays in touch with Lila. 
 So this is the part of your life, if you are following a life path similar to mine at least, where you start to lose touch with some of your nearest and dearest. Either that person is full enmeshed in transforming themselves, or you are completely absorbed by whatever project you're working on, and they disappear off your radar for months or years. It isn't that you don't want to see this person, it's probably more like you never divide your mental energy from whatever you're absorbed with for long enough to be able to have the energy to call anyone. That couch looks sooooo good right now. And even in late 1960s/early 1970s Italy, that formula pretty much hold true. You might get something here and there from mom, or you might arrange a call after four failed attempts and hear something. But damn, its tough, even for near lifelong besties. Even if you know that that person will come back into your life eventually. 
 What sucks about this though... well, I don't know if "sucks" is the proper word here. I think it needs something more- "maddening" perhaps, or probably "inevitable"... is it's not like your brain just stops working the way it always has just because you don't see the people you used to anymore. It's not like you aren't still measuring yourself against them with everything you do, wondering if they have time to write, if they are creating and growing and getting better while you drown, wondering if they'd still like you now, if you're falling behind and becoming the failure you always knew you would be, even if only by comparison. 
 Because comparison is all that matters. Let's be real. In considerations of success, which are usually tied up in class wars, in societal expectations, in your identity you built up for yourself, in family issues... it doesn't matter how successful you are, you'll only feel that way if your measuring stick isn't too far ahead of you. Honestly, that's what friends are for, sometimes- and sometimes it can be positive, it helps to push you and guide you and let you know when you've veered off course. And sometimes (more of the time) it's utterly misery making. But when you love someone that much, respect them that much, have shared so much of your life with them, that's how your brain works. You can't calculate your life and what it's worth without their presence. Wanting their approval and their love, even if only in your sick, sick imagination is part of how it goes. That's one of the shitty underbellies of getting into a relationship, romantic or otherwise, with someone you respect. That respect becomes like food and fuel and fire to you, unless you can root them out of you. And I guarantee you, if someone's got that many years and that much of a pattern in your psyche, they ain't likely to be going nowhere. 
 So that's the aspect of deep friendship we get this time- the kind that's a worm in your brain even when the person isn't even there. We already know that Elena and Lila are unhealthily entwined, and have only gotten more so over the years. Elena, of course, more than Lila, since she is the "inferior" friend in this partnership. Which I can't even... is just so true for someone who is insecure and who has met someone who has all the confidence and easy intelligence you never will. You can go to college, marry up, meet a great set of in laws, publish a book, have beautiful children and material comforts and still think that this person is better than you and always will be. I can name four people in my own life who fit this bill and just forced myself to stop before I went crazy. 
 Ferrante does such a great job of dealing with this part of our lives where we transition into full adulthood. The sort marked by the events that oblige you to take on a role and an authority that you never had before- becoming a wife (which comes with far more expectations in 1970 Naples), becoming a mother and being in charge of someone, becoming old enough for people to look to you as an authority figure, succeeding in your career and having people ask you questions they think you know the answers to. She shows Elena dealing with an "imposter complex" in such a true to life, agonizing way. This is the "why are you looking at me like I know something?" transition into adulthood before you're quite ready for the mantle- but there you are anyway. 
 I loved how she shows, even then, the pressure on mothers and wives to "have it all" and be it all, both to their husbands and lovers and to themselves. It's all just some history repeating- if you're not having kids, then you're heartless and unnatural in some way, of course. But beyond that- how you marry an intellectual who seems to want your opinion and your criticism, but really he just wants unconditional support that he can assure himself is educated and could disagree, because he's not an ape, god! How wives and mothers need to be obedient, but sexy and fiery enough to hold their man's interest at the same time. How you need to be daring in writing, but not daring enough that people call you a whore. (Again, a lot more of a death sentence at this time.) Ferrante showed me Elena scratching and screaming to get out, in all the passive aggressive ways that we do that- by yelling at her husband when he's had a bad day, by taking it out on the kids for a small mistake, by raging at the mirror when she looks like the mother of two she is. 
 I also, again, really liked the way that the surrounding world was woven into Elena's story. This time period was highly political and volatile (as Italy's politics have pretty much been, ever since WWII- pretty much a permanent hot mess with no solution). And if you pretend to be intellectual, or really in any way functioning and participating in society in an urban context, you're going to have to have opinions and take sides and be judged. It wove through the story here particularly with communism and how all the characters interacted with that- clearly that was the Cool Kid Thing To Be at the time, and how each character tries to contribute to it (or at least be seen to be contributing to it) is so telling then, of their rank, status and what I'm meant to think of them as a person. Lila, for instance, Elena's goddess she can never quite measure up to, even when she hates her, is the one who ends up doing the most concrete, visible thing that seems to make a difference, the thing that brings shame to all the ineffectual, pontificating intellectuals around her and shows them just how fake they are- while she is all the more authentic for being a worker herself. Another character reacts in a surly way to this, and then strikes a totally useless, bitter pose and becomes a layabout out of self-hatred. Elena is tongue-tied, writes some articles that she STILL gives full credit to her friend for, hating herself all the while for being less genuine than Lila. Her stiff, conventional husband doesn't want to get involved, and refuses not to fail a communist student leader who didn't do his work in class in order to help the class struggle- HOW UNCOOL CAN YOU BE, DAD! It was a great way to put us in the time and place without ever making some sort of preachy point of "and now here we are in this time" announcements. It's as organic and natural and seemingly necessary as ever. 
 And of course, for the intellectuals among us, Elena's journey towards trying to write a book after the success of her first and her years long break to have kids, rings super true. Her failed efforts, her feelings of self-loathing, her decision to give it up all together only to find herself writing again years later without any real intent to have done so, something entirely new and unexpected. That self-punishing creative process that we all think is special and unique the first time we go through it and then realize that that's just how some of us wrestle the beast out of us. How much energy she puts into the pose of being an intellectual, rather than just thinking the thoughts and asking the questions and reading the books that would make you one, apart from whatever image someone constructs of you. It's more important to be seen that way since someone did you the favor of giving you that label- you'll watch it like the world's most paranoid den mother to be sure it's never wrested away from you. 
 Because of course what's at stake, what's always at stake in these novels is identity. For so long, your identity is tied up in who you spend your time with- your family at first, the only ones you are allowed to be around. Then friends, then more carefully chosen friends. Then your choices start to be taken into account in a wider sense and it gets higher and higher stakes as the years go on. Elena's journey shows us how important forging an identity still is, even when you're past thirty, with a family and responsibilities and, presumably, a better understanding of the mundane things that really make the world go round. In some ways it becomes even more important to have a very strong core sense of self, because there are a million things to be doing every day and you'll never feel like you've done them all right, or enough of them. So you need to have a strong reason for doing everything that you do, otherwise you'll really lose it. Children, spouses provide that anchor of course, but they are only something you've built onto your Self. That Self still needs to be there to let you know why you put in all the work those relationships mean. 
 And of course, here... it's always going to be tied up in Lila. Elena will never be free of her, and that is what has made her who she is today. 
 I'm fascinated to see how we get from here to the sixty six year old woman we met in the flashback in the first book. I get where Lila comes from, what we've seen of her so far, but I really want to see her get over that hump with Lila. How does she detach, when do the fires go out? Does she really? Isn't this book proof that she hasn't? 
 See? Barely a single action sequence in these books and it's as suspenseful as anything I've read. I can't wait for the fourth book to be translated in September. 
 I can't wait until all of you who have told me you will read these books catch up with me. Please tell me when you do so that we can talk about it. I want to gossip about this and dissect it like this is English 101- but with more sex and cocktails. 
 It's incredible. I envy you if you haven't read it yet for still having it in front of you. Get to it, soldier!

Maybe I'm too cynical for this (and I'm definitely in the minority here) but I thought it was a dud. The Invoice is sweet and has an uplifting message, but it's ultimately forgettable. Although I liked the semi-absurdist premise, taking on cliches like "the best things in life are free" and "you can't buy happiness" is a dangerous move unless you can cut through the sappiness and provide something unexpected. Karlsson never quite got there. At some point I thought to myself, "Kafka for middle schoolers," and then I couldn't shake that comparison. 
 The thing is, I totally agree with the message! Life is all about perspective. Pain and adversity provide opportunities for growth and help us define our own happiness. You'll never be content in life if you only look for worth in material things. Did you feel anything reading those past 3 sentences? Probably not, because they're also cliches and as such are pretty flat when taken at face value. These sentiments don't become interesting unless we come at them from a new direction or introduce some sense of conflict. That's missing in these 200 pages. For me, each chapter read like a rewording of these basic concepts without any new spin. On top of that, there is no sense of urgency from our protagonist. He's unflappably affable. And yes, that's kind of the whole point, but what a bore when you can predict exactly how a character is going to react (or not react, as it were) to every new development. 
 To be fair, I read this right after reading Delicious Foods which is one of the most depressing books I've read in a long while, so I wasn't exactly primed for a feel-good, easy breezy, pick-me-up.

 Okay here is where it gets interesting. Y'know the last sentence I just wrote? Strangely enough it is only true for MalLory and not Kaleb. It's because Kaleb was given scenes that developed him as a character with the freaking annoying burden of instalove over his character self. He fought, he interacted with Zevi and tried to protect, he schemed and showed the reader his dilemma of being a cur, forfeiting and dying. He was skeptical of good intentions from Aya but had to deal with it. Even his decision to marry Mallory was an insight into this character. We were able to see something more from Kaleb than just dumb love. But from Mallory, all we get is a girl in love. Whoop de doo. What a waste of pages. 
 Aya was also by far the most interesting character from the get go because she had a greater, more desperate secret she had to kept quiet. Even from the readers. Every move she did was based on that secret motivation. But the readers did not know, but could only guess as she stabbed her ex fiance with a poisoned knife. That is what real characters should do. Have hidden motivations, change the world in some sort of way. Mallory made zero impact in the book. Aya, in chapter one, had already flipped the entire daimon world into recognizing upper caste women in battle. She concocts plans and executes them rather than just sitting around. Even her "romance" with Belias is interesting because it is a power play of some sorts. A question of true love or not. 
 However, when her secret was revealed, it seems like she is a little overpowered... Future books will tell. 
 I am not enthrall with the two world. Nothing is written to detail and everything seems to be compared to our world. I've noted many times where daimons were critical of their own world. But they know of basically no other world, so how would they know? It was jarring to see such sentiments because it felt like a human's perspective of the world rather than a daimon's. The lack of detail was frustrating. Caste system, a carnival of souls, red and black masks, curs, teeth and your true form. All of it was more like a necessity of plot rather than a revelation of the world. What do we know of the caste system besides Aya is the upper and curs are at the bottom? What do we know of red and black masks besides potential people who were them? The carnival of souls, what does it contain besides the battle for leadership? Does transforming hurt or feel good? Are there merchants in the caste level? Can a cur ever rise above the bottom caste system? 
 There is nothing in this book. It is a bare bones world that hints of blood and decadence but never delivers. 
 So. Subpar characters. A bare world. A mildly interesting plot.

I'm 1 for 2 with Melissa Landers. I borrowed Alienated from a friend, and I wasn't really impressed. For me it read like every other YA novel out there, and brought nothing new to the table. And while I may want to say the same for this, you'll notice my review is significantly more complimentary. Why? Because Landers pulled it off much better for me here. The suspension of disbelief wasn't as hard to do, the side characters were ones I legitimately enjoyed, and (as the author has mentioned) it has elements like the movie Overboard, which I love, so I'm a happy clam. 
 The story is that Solara, a girl with no money to her name, is trying to get to the outlying settlements to try and build a life for herself. Without the funds to finance her trip, she has to resort to indenturing herself as a servant/worker on someone else's ship. Of course, it just so happens that the one who picks her is the hot, arrogant boy from her class, and the two (over the course of the book) fall madly in love with each other. Is it surprising? Not really. I'm sure we all saw that coming as soon as Doran was described as the "rich, pretty-boy quarterback who made her life miserable in school" on the back cover. What was different this time around though was the background for the characters, and how they approach each other. 
 Doran loses his memory at one point and Solara decides to have him play her servant and enjoy it while she can. While Doran's head is all frazzled, he notices that the girl he's serving is pretty. Without the years of memory baggage, he's legitimately attracted to her. So when his memory comes back, it seems too far-fetched that he would just up and forget that attraction. And yes, he was absolutely horrid to her in school. He was the kind of boy who broke her self esteem down every chance he got, to the point that she didn't trust her own instincts anymore (which I also give the credit for. The heroine actually has poor self esteem and a reason for it! Not just a cocky attitude for no reason or a placid personality for no reason!) When his motives are revealed though, I could sort of understand why he treated her that way. Not condone it, never--but I can understand it. While he may partially have bullied her just to be a cad, he also had some underlying resentments that Solara didn't know about. It fleshed out his character beautifully, and I was much more willing to accept their romance as a result. 
 The side characters were gems. Obviously the author knew Kane and Cassia were going to be favorites, because she's already announced there will be a companion novel about the two. I particularly liked Renny, despite him not really having any screen time. An honest kleptomaniac. Brilliant, yes? The entire crew of the Banshee added a layer to the story that I appreciated all the more because they didn't seem like flimsy characters. 
 An aside: you gotta love that cover. It is so freaking pretty. Disney Hyperion has a really awesome team of cover designers, because their covers are always gorgeous and draw the eye. 
 Really though, if Landers sticks to somewhat more believable stories like this with less emphasis on instalove, I'll be so much happier. She's a good writer and I'd like to see more from her.

I'd bought this book at a clearance sale and it had been collecting dust in my bookcase for quite some time now, spine uncracked, when last week - whilst reading Shadow of Night by Deborah Harkness - I needed some lighter reading to alternate with. Once again, this was one of those books that went against my expectations and became a surprising favorite. 
 The Adoration of Jenna Fox raises some very interesting questions on the worth of a human being, the importance of a soul and the boundaries of scientific advance. The topic is tackled with a certain youthful clarity that will appeal to readers of all ages, making it a speedy read with long lingering aftereffects. 
 I hardly ever feel the urge to read a book in one sitting - even my very favorite ones (or maybe especially those) - but this one I could've finished in one day had I had the time. It's like a quite literal version of a "train of thought", which you can't get off of anymore after you've boarded because it just speeds on relentlessly. 
 However, when I tried to summarize this novel to my boyfriend to explain why I liked it, it turned out to be impossible to do so. When you recount the storyline, it sounds rather dull - which it truly isn't. I guess it's just one of those books you'll have to read to appreciate and understand. 
 In conclusion: the subject matter is current, the questions posed are well worth pondering and the writing is as fluent as the wispy thought of the teenage girl they accumulate to be. A special story that I will not soon forget and maybe even reread someday. 
 PS: I actually read this book in Dutch, and for once I have to say: kudos to the translator, Sabine Mutsaers! It was impossible to tell that this was a translated novel, which is so very rare.

 This is one of my favorite books ever. It's also one of the books that I read after losing someone in my life which created a great positive effect on me dealing with the loss of that loved one. I bought this right after the school year ended, literally on my last day of school. I think I read it immediately after and then watching the movie afterwards. 
 I found out about this story from the film of the same name. Judging from the mixed reviews, this book really works for some people. Unfortunately, I do not belong to that group of readers. 
 To be fair, let's start with some of the bits I liked: the intriguing and very promising premise, the very neat cover design, the description on the back cover (a master at work there, they know how to pique a reader's interest), the flow in terms of timeline (not too much, not too jumpy - since it spans a great chunk of time, I think the author made a good choice of points in the lives of the characters to describe). 
 As for the things that made it difficult for me to enjoy this book... 
 The language. Way too flowery for me. Is there such a thing as being overly descriptive? I understand that the author's writing style is actually one of the main attractions of this book for those who liked it; I thought it was too much. Every little detail - every sight, every sound, every sensation, every smell, every situation, every body part (!) is elaborated by a simile, a metaphor. Some of these analogies I found rather awkward. In the first couple of chapters, the babies' hands were likened to little stars (acceptable, but used more than once), starfish (ick), spiders (double ick), moth wings (uh...). Also, why must everyone be so 'delicate', 'frail' and 'vulnerable'? (Except for Bree, because she's supposedly the most kickass, edgiest woman alive). 
 The characters. No sympathy for the main ones. Especially Norah, at some points I wished that she just got sucked into that Electrolux vacuum cleaner of hers. The sudden appearance of random new characters did nothing for the story, so I didn't get their purpose. Phoebe, to whom the title of the novel alludes to, was rather underdeveloped as a character. The only impression I have of her by the end: short, stubby, chubby, dumpy, etc. with thinning hair (why had this to be repeated so many times! We know she's supposedly a classic case of DS), likes to sing, wants to marry Robert. So many POVs, but where is her story? 
 The multiple POVs. This, by itself shouldn't be a problem, except that everyone and their neighbour (except, as I mentioned, Phoebe herself) brought with them their own unnecessary subplot. I didn't need to know about Paul and Michelle, about Doro(thy) and T-something the swimmer, about Rosemary (named after her grannies, Rose and Mary) and Jack, Bree and Mark with half a foot. And the list goes on. 
 The repetitiveness. In each and every scene, we had to hear again and again how everyone was consumed by self-pity grief, regret, unhappiness. I don't mean to trivialize their lives' hardships, but they're caught in a loop. The same thoughts, the same feelings. It gets tiring. Some events were recalled way too often - for example, the discarded flamingo blouse fluttering in the sand . 
 The unresolved case of Dr. David Henry. He suddenly dies. How convenient. Perhaps meant to be a plot twist, but it felt like things were left hanging there. I think that many readers would expect a confrontation at some point (if only about Norah's affairs), and the author opted for skipping that and trying to add some other surprises. It didn't work for me.  
 The emphasis on so-and-so was (un)common in the year so-and-so. We know! Every section is labeled by their year. We know that things were different back then. I think the average reader would be able to conclude those things by themselves. 
 In the end, I'm sorry to say that I didn't enjoy reading this book. I wanted to. I've another by this author lying around, I guess I'll wait a bit before reading that one.

This wasn't a bad thing for me, I enjoyed the story and the mystery immensely. But I have seen some reviwers point out that this story wasn't original. I wouldn't say that's true. Yes, some of the themes present have been seen before, but I think this is different than what is currently popular. 
 Will I read the sequel? I didn't even realize this was a series and I felt that this book wrapped up the story and worked well as a standalone. But I loved the world and characters and can't wait for the sequel!!

 I wanted to enjoy this, I really did. I've been collecting the comics for years but at first I was very skeptical of them for a long time, and then it just never seemed like the right time to read them. But I felt like the stars were finally aligning--I'm finished with school forever, I found a stack of Buffy and Angel novels in a used bookstore a couple weeks ago, I was looking into some S1 stuff for a friend, and the anniversary of Chosen was a couple days ago. When better? 
 This just isn't doing it for me though. I even had to double-check that Joss wrote it because the dialogue seemed really off to me, plus the internal monologue bits. I would have never recognized Dawn by the illustrations, giant or not. Nor Andrew. And I just didn't do well with running headfirst into the middle of everything. I didn't get what they were doing at the beginning, I had to look online to figure out who was who in terms of new characters because I couldn't figure it out from the comics. I couldn't always tell when a scene was continuing or switching. The section with Buffy talking to Dawn honestly did not make any sense to me in terms of a coherent conversation. Are we somehow supposed to know what a thricewise is?? And so far I just don't like the story line, especially regarding the villains. I did like Willow's green outfit though. 
 I did like seeing Ethan Rayne, even if it ended up being for basically just two seconds... 
 Oooooh, I just got "cinnamon buns!" while reading plot summaries on wikipedia because I didn't feel clear after the comic. So, cinnamon lip gloss. Got it. I figured, because I knew about the big sex scene issue when it came out, but now I know.  
 I did like The Chain, even if I didn't totally get what was going on there either. There's good stuff that lives underground? There's fairies? What's it mean now that one of the decoy Buffys is dead? Are the demons coming to the surface now?  Who were the two women at the training center? Was the one supposed to be Rona or Olivia or someone else? I assume that guy was supposed to be Giles? 
 WHY CAN'T YOU DRAW SO I KNOW WHO PEOPLE ARE. 
 Amy's mom was perfect, go figure. I got Felicia Day from 1 panel of 6 on that commercial page, so I figured the other guy was Andrew (because who else?). 
 This is pretty much my first time reading comics, so maybe I just need to get used to the format, and with a bit more it will be better? I really hope so. I want to like these, I want more Buffyverse. And, well, I've already bought them all halfway through S10.

 The book was at its best when it gave characterization to corpses and inanimate objects, and at its worst when it tried to involve me with the plot. Like Strayed, I once set out woefully underprepared on a thru-hike, though my hike was markedly less intense than the PCT. I did a portion of the Camino de Santiago (about 200km) without a guidebook, hiking shoes, a hiking backpack, or a sleeping bag, to name a few things I probably should have brought. Needless to say, I could relate to a number of Strayed's mishaps and hiking pains. 
 But what's really impressive about this memoir is that Strayed can write. I honestly wasn't expecting that much from this book. But Strayed more than delivered. Her book is brutally honest and raw. Her descriptions and musings on the wild and on one's place in the world gave me pause over and over again. And now I want to do another thru-hike... with the right gear.

Once you start reading, you will not want to put this book down.

Fighting Dirty is the last book in Lori Foster's Ultimate series and finally gives us Armie and Merissa's story. If you've been reading the series from the beginning then you know Ms Foster has been teasing us with the relationship between Marissa and Armie. 
 Since we've been teased and tempted with the possibility of them since the beginning I didn't think I would really like Fighting Dirty. The previous books have shown Armie to be the ultimate player and implied that while he liked Marissa he wasn't going to go for her so I basically didn't have high expectations. Which of course was silly because Ms Foster always does a good job and Fighting Dirty is no different. 
 Fighting Dirty ends up being quite a sweet romance as Armie finally pulls himself together after Marissa gets hurt and can no longer resist her. There's nothing predictable about Fighting Dirty but it does flow in an order you can follow and fits with the rest of the series. 
 First line: 'Jesus Quick. You're a freak of nature. You know that, right?'Armie Jacobson, known as Quick to his fighter friends, ignored the complaint and threw a few more jabs, then a solid body shot, making Justice, a six-foot-five heavyweight, double over. 
 Fighting Dirty could be read as a stand-alone story but I would recommend reading the series in order because other characters are mentioned along with their story-lines and it would make more sense if you read the previous books. 
 Also if you've been a fan of Ms Foster for quite a while, like myself, you will recognise characters from Ms Fosters first MMA series SBC Fighters from 2007! 
 Although the Ultimate series might be over, Ms Forster is starting a new bodyguard series that will give us stories for Leese, Justice, Brand and Miles! 
 This review is based on the ARC of Fighting Dirty, provided by Harlequin

This book was okay. I would give it 3.5 stars, rather than just three. Well written with an interesting premise, but I felt like there were some holes, mostly dealing with the time-travel element. For instance, I don't understand how the loop was supposed to work. Meaning, inside the loop the peculiars were constantly doing things that would affect what happened on the island on the repeating day in 1940. So, thinking about the whole butterfly effect concept, was that essentially creating a separate alternate reality every day? I mean, which one of those days was the "real" day?  Does that make sense? In general, I found the time travel aspect to be fairly confusing, specifically how it related to the other loops that exist throughout history and how the peculiars could somehow travel to them, even though they're not in use. I don't think it makes sense that Peregrine has to restart the loop each day, but it still kind of exists whether she does it or not. On the last day, she wasn't able to restart the loop, but Jacob was still able to travel back to the present one last time. Just is a bit confusing. At the end, Jacob is left wondering if he'll be able to ever get back to his own time, but it seems like all he would need to do was go back to the island and pass through the cairn. Of course, Emma does say the loop will close when they leave, but it's not explained why.  Also, I thought what Jacob decided to do at the end was pretty crappy. Even with the "proof" he's essentially ruining his parents lives, and they seemed like generally decent people. I mean, they weren't abusive or anything. Maybe Riggs should've made them unlikable, so Jacob leaving would've been easier to accept for the reader (for me at least).  Anyway, it was a quick read and enjoyable and well written enough that I'll go on to the sequel to find out what happens.

This book was not an easy read for me, but it was compelling. Nor was it a lighthearted beach read. It touched on so many emotions and delved into the sacrifices of war (on and off the battlefield.) With the historical setting, intrigue and emotion, I was drawn in. However, because it did touch on darker issues, I had to put it down once in while. 
 The characters were all-too human - flawed and scarred. It wasn't overly graphic, but it was all too easy to imagine the suffering and feel the unfairness of the circumstances. The book had beautiful artistic moments and also showed damaged, human frailty. It talked about mental illness, social issues, and so much more. One of my favourite lines in the books was  "It was as if all the chaos of murder, adultery, suicide and illegitimacy had been reduced to mere social awkwardness.  I thought that pretty summed up a good description of the book, and yet it didn't feel vulgar or trashy... just honestly human. 
 As far as the mystery, I earlier told a friend that I had no idea where it was headed (but in a good way.) That was true right up to the last few chapters. Even then, I couldn't clearly say if there was ever a true nemesis or merely unfortunate souls dealing with unfortunate situations the best they could. If I could give 3.5 stars I would. For myself, I would rate this somewhere between really good and great. Recommended read for sure.

Judith is a girl who has lots of secrets. She can't say anything either because two years ago, she returned to her hometown with her tongue cut out. 
 Did I mention this is historical fiction? 
 The beginning of the story feels like some fantasy piece, until you start realizing that everyone lives like Puritans of New England because this is basically Puritans of New England. It was slightly bizarre reading this story because the realization that you're reading historical fiction doesn't get into your head until you make it through a few chapters. 
 Judith, with her tongue cut out, is as good as a leper, and because of this, the entire town shuns her and regards her as an outcast. Judith's own mother is the worst, barely treating Judith better than a slave in favor of her younger brother. Her only solace is Lucas, her childhood best friend, and who she has been in love with since whenever and the only one who brings any happiness into Judith's life. She wishes to talk to him so much she writes this book in 2nd person to Lucas as her "voice". However, Judith never confronts him person to person, preferring to admire from afar. Did I say admire? Judith is obsessed with Lucas. 
 This obsessive love makes Judith act ... really bizarre. Even for modern day standards. The only thing that prevents this from being creepo stalko behavior is the fact that she can't talk, so she can't actually confess her love to Lucas both because she is incapable and also because she feels she is unworthy of him. 
 Instead there is a lot of moping, staring, stalking and general creepy behavior expected of someone who can't tell their crush they like them. I accepted this as an excuse for her behavior. But then again  lying down next to their crush when they are sleeping in the woods  is a LITTLE beyond weird. 
 Then a bunch of bad things start happening to Roswell Station. And Judith is in the midst of it. When Lucas gets involved she realizes she must speak out even though she does not have a tongue. 
 Anyway, this story is a hodgepodge of mysteries and slightly nonsensical events. I can't really say much without giving it away, but Lucas's father is beyond strange, and his actions are behind the plot of the entire story. Unfortunately, nothing he does makes any sense. But if you can suspend belief and accept why he does what he does, the story will flow a lot better. 
 As for the writing, I enjoyed the 2nd person narrative minus when Judith was being stupid, cautious, ridiculously creepy, or just plain frustrating. Luckily this only happens when Lucas is involved. However, reading the book felt disconnected, both because of the medium of writing and the writing style. There are just so many mysteries you don't know where to start with first. The epistolary style doesn't help clear anything up either. 
 The ending was... unbelievable. The whole first 90% of the novel was dedicated to how the entire village is skeptical about Judith because they can't be sure if she came back as damaged goods or "whole". Yet when the trial begins and Judith is called as a witness, magically they believe everything she says without any doubt which undermines whole point of Judith's struggle with the other villagers in the first place. Too inconsistent to make me really accept the clean cut ending. 
 Other than that, one of the first epistolary books I've read that really worked this way. The set up of the story was also very original. If it wasn't for the several flaws of the plot and Judith's character, this had a good chance at being a 4 star.

What a cool book! Nalini Singh always manages to make the paranormal scene feel fresh. Here, vampires are Made by angels in exchange for 100 years of servitude. Elena hunts rogue vamps that try to skirt their contracts. When the archangel Raphael hires her for a special mission, things get tricky. 
 I loved Elena but I wish we'd gotten her full backstory. She has a very traumatizing past that's repeatedly hinted at but never fully explained. Hopefully that comes in later books. Raphael is frustrating but endearing, but Dmitri was more creepy than intriguing. I truly enjoyed the world building and plot, especially since the events of this book have set up an ongoing conflict. I'm excited to read on in this series!

This is a beautifully written, very creepy piece. It's an entrancing re-telling of the Snow White myth. Any fairy tale fan should read this, it may completely change your perspective on one of your favourite stories.

Maybe my expectations were too high after reading reviews of this book, but I found the story quite disjointed and hard to read, which prevented me from really "bonding with" or being able to emphasize with Susanna. Whilst the author offers some brilliant insights into the whole issue of mental health from a sufferer's perspective and the stigma encountered in the 1960's (which I guess hasn't changed all that much), the constant swapping and changing between snippets of different experiences and abrupt endings left me wanting for more depth and detail to truly understand what the author was going through. Because the other characters all appear so briefly, and with so little detail, they stayed shadowy and unreal, and I kept forever longing for more information. 
 All in all, unfortunately the book did not live up to my expectations, as there were too many loose ends and unsaid things. However, at times the author's astute observations and her wry sense of humour made up for the rest of the book, and I did keep reading to the end.

"There's no such thing as a normal highschool experience, Thorny. You assume everyone else is happy all he time and living an ideal life. You don't get that other people are pretending too." 
 MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS 
 Hawthorn is not a very likable character in my opinion. While yes she is very observant and admits that she wants to fit in like everyone else. She also does nothing to make herself more likable in almost any situation. Not only is she extremely self centered not just teenager self centered either, but truly so self centered that even her best friend gets tried of it after awhile. 
 I hoped to see things start to change once Lizzie Lovett went missing and Hawthorn started to become obsessed with the case. But instead Hawthorn ends up going down a dangerous path in my opinion. Not only does she start coming up with crazy theories about Lizzie, and how if she was able to find her that then Lizzie would help her fit in and be liked by people. So in order to do this Hawthorn decides to get close to those who knew Lizzie as how she was now, after high school. 
 "Lizzie could teach me how to ignore all the people who thought I was broken and strange. She'd teach me how to fit in, how to be likable. How to be like her." 
 Which leads her to Lizzie's boyfriend who I didn't like at all. Not because I thought he did anything to Lizzie, but because after awhile I could see most likely how things were going to end with him and Hawthorn and I didn't want her to do that. I wanted her to stop obsessing over Lizzie so much and hoping that Lizzie's boyfriend would care for her as much as she was starting to about him. 
 Now that I've talked about most of the things I didn't like lets get to the few I did. I liked how for once we had a real brother sister dynamic and mostly 'normal' family dynamic as well. Hawthorn didn't blame everything on her parents, and instead knew that they did what they were doing because they cared about her and just wanted the best for her. Plus the brother did truly care about what was happening to her, even if he didn't exactly understand her. 
 The add in of my hippies was also really enjoyable and was part of the reason I kept reading. They weren't a huge part of the story, but they were interesting and helped Hawthorn occasionally. 
 Overall this book fell kind of flat for me, but I know others will love it.

This is a great book, I'm very impressed once again. The world's history, lore and magic are getting increasingly intricate, and it is a fascinating look at a fictitious history when the mythological characters from several thousand years before are in the group telling the tales. 
 You should definitely start at the beginning with Pawn of Prophecy, you won't be disappointed.

This book felt like a YA version of November 9 to me. Where he only has a day to make her fall for him. In Colleen Hoover's November 9, the story is more widespread. I enjoyed that book more, but this I felt covered more important topics that should be touched on in the literature world. See below. 
 Still, I love the story line, the back and forth between the characters, the vast difference between them, but also the similarities. Natasha and Daniel are two completely different people from two different races. By a chance meeting, then another, the insta-love begins. They decide to put the idea of love to a scientific test to see if he can make her fall for him in the only day they have. Coincidences continue to line up, and Natasha refuses to believe in "fate" or a "higher power" or that "everything happens for a reason". But when push comes to shove, when is enough, enough? Daniel opens her eyes to thoughts she would normally shrug off, to considering beliefs she would typically scoff at. 
 NOTE: This book discusses topics like history & science, race, faith, loneliness, suicide... So while the insta-love factor is there, it wasn't making me run away from the story like they usually do. 
 The Sun is Also a Star is a beautiful tale of two people pushing the boundaries, not just of race, but of beliefs. That two people with open minds can still love each other completely because of those differences.

Amy Lane has totally blown me away with The Locker Room! 
 This is a book that I have had for quite some while, for some reason - I just never had the chance to read it. Then when the audiobook came out, and it was done by Sean Crisden - I quickly scooped that up and again.. it just never made it to my playlist. I can tell you I will NEVER put off an Amy Lane book, again. This book is a little darker than typical Amy - but it is every bit as perfect as all her books. If I had to compare it to another Amy Lane book, I would say its more of the tone of Beneath the Stain (Another amazing story) and The Johnnies series (a lot of everything and really emotional). 
 This is the story of two teenagers who find each other on the neighborhood basketball court and proceed to be bonded together by the game and their love of each other. Of course, they didn't always know they loved each other - but they knew they completed each other and they were what each other needed in order for everything to be okay. Xander Karcek, his story is going to rip your heart out. He is the character that will make you bawl your eyes out - the growth his character goes through in this story is amazing. How any author can capture such emotion, such heartache - put it into words and then make an secondary MC who perfectly completes him. It is pure perfection. Christian Edwards, he has the home, family, and life that every American boy wants - and when he meets a boy on the basketball court and feels a connection to him in his soul, he knows right then and there he will do anything for him. Its just the way it is. It's not even a choice between having Xander in his life or not - they are connected. That simple. I loved Watching these two learn to explore their feelings for each other, their first kiss, their first grope, their first time once they were eighteen and then their lives together as they go off to college and then are both drafted to the NBA. It was not always easy for these two - in fact there were times when Xander barely survived. But one thing for sure they knew - nothing was going to keep them apart. 
 Then as these two in the NBA have to start really worrying about appearances, it really broke my heart at the things they did just to protect each other and play a game they loved, while being able to love each other. With only the support of Christian's family - they make it for quite a while, before life catches up with them. 
 I have to give 5 stars to the story and then the narration done by Sean Crisden is worthy of 5 stars all on its own. I did a combo read/listen to this story and Sean totally nailed his narration. He added another layer or ten of emotion and depth to the story - pure perfection. 
 So, I highly recommend this story - the audiobook or eBook - or you can be like me and enjoy both! Don't put it off like I did - that was a huge mistake and I missed out on an amazing story all that time. If you haven't already read this - I suggest you go one-click it now and grab a huge box of Kleenex while you enjoy - The Locker Room! 
 5+ Stars

So I've finally finished this series! The Last Olympian By Rick Riordan is the fifth and final installment to the Percy Jackson series. This book follows Percy and his friends on their final adventure, leading to their battle against the Titan, Kronos and his army. This was an exciting ending but it didn't feel that epic, but exciting nonetheless. I enjoyed the general plot to this installment and like I said in my previous review on The Battle of the Labyrinth, with every preceding book, a new element specific to Percy Jackson's world is added and it continued to impress me.  This time around, the concept of Achilles was introduced which I really enjoyed reading about. I loved how the idea was intertwined with Kronos' ability to inhabit Luke's body. That was so brilliant. Oh, and the coming of the new Oracle... for some reason, I did not see that coming LOL! Also, it was awesome to see how automatons were put to use in this world. The concept was introduced in the previous book and it really got me excited to see the role they played in the war.  I also enjoyed the way the war was written. I think it really solidified the final book- like it really pulled me in. It had a lot of exciting twists and turns and I liked the sense drama that was included as well. However, the book didn't didn't reach that level of epicness that I was expecting and honestly, I wasn't all that moved when the final revelations to The Great Prophecy was revealed... Characters. I invested so many of my emotions (happy, sad, frustration at some point) on these characters, not only for this book but for the entire series in general. Rick Riordan did a splendid job in creating holistic, fictional characters, with a touch of realism. I was profoundly affected (in a good way) by the family aspects of this story. It made the characters seem real and relate-able, in a way. However, I felt unsure about Annabeth. I didn't really like how she was so hopeful (sometimes looking in love) with Luke but there would be times where she showed a bit of jealousy whenever Percy and Rachel were together. She was a total ass- kicker but her main downfall for me was when it came to sentimental issues about Luke and Percy. Rachel felt like a mediocre character for, even though she played a critical role at the end of the book. Overall, I really, really enjoyed this series even though it was a bit short on epicness. I would definitely recommend this book to anyone who enjoys adventure stories and even those interested in reading a fun, modern twist on Greek mythology. Also, Rick Riordan is such an awesome writer. He definitely has a spot on my favorites list :D I would definitely love to check out the spin off series. I heard that it is just as awesome :D

What did I just read?! All the Ugly and Wonderful Things isn't your typical love story. It's between a child and man. *Shocking, I know.* 
 While at lunch with my husband the other day I said to him, "So, I'm reading this really interesting story. It's about an 8-year-old girl and this 20-year-old guy." Let's just say my husband looked at me wearily as I went on to explain what I had read up to that point. When I made mention he should give the book a try he shook his head and said, "Nope! Not going to happen." . *LOL* 
 Okay, so this book isn't for everyone. And honestly, it's not my normal read either. But what it's not is some raunchy love story with pervy sex in it. It's about a young man who happens to care for a girl that no one else cares for and how their love (not sex) grows over the course of many years. 
 It's compelling because it's written in many different points of view. From the main characters to the teacher, to the family members, to the roommates... etc. Viewing the situation from their eyes was interesting to see how they interpreted the situation. 
 Two people in the story summed the book up for me: 
 "...., but the fact is, he loved that girl. He treated her good, took care of her, made sure she went to school. He looked out for her when nobody else did." ~Mr. Cutcheon (Kellen's employer) 
 "I wanted a fairy tale ending for Wavy, because if she could find happiness, there would be hope for me, too." ~Renee (Wavy's friend) 
 I was glued to the pages of this book because of the way the story was told. The author, Bryn Greenwood, brought a conversational story to life on the page of All the Ugly and Wonderful Things. This is a book that won't soon be forgotten. 
 Hey, mom, if you're reading this review ... this is NOT a book for you to read. Just sayin'.

"It was raining. 
 Isn't that the way all great love stories start? And also usually end?" Awe, it does seem like some of the great love scenes happen in the rain. Levee and Sam's story starts on a raining night on a bridge. Both of them are there for different reasons. Sam's there to ponder life when he see's Levee and wonders if she's there to jump. 
 'My career was soaring while, personally, I was plummeting.' 
 Levee has everything a little kids dream of -> being rich and famous. But behind the glamour lives a girl who feels a missing connection with the world. Her nightly visits to the bridge create concern for Sam who at the time is just a stranger on that bridge. He reaches out to her to let her know she's not alone if she's struggling. 
 'I was sick of fucking fine. I needed something - anything - to be great.' 
 Sam has his own demons that haunt him. Under the exterior of his tattoos and cigarettes is a man who searching for "something." 
 "Levee, I'd like to struggle with you." 
 By nature Sam is a caretaker. He holds other's needs in high regard. He carries their burden on his shoulders. Those nights on the bridge prove what a good guy Sam is because once he lays eyes on Levee, without knowing who she is, he reaches out to her to make sure she's cared for. 
 'It's just hard when your woman has Gibson [guitar] taste and a thrift store man.' 
 The relationship between the two of them started before either one knew who the other one was and once it got going it was with pure intentions these two fell for each other. It didn't matter that he wasn't rich and she was because they liked the stripped down versions of each other. Money wasn't going to be a factor in their relationship. 
 Ms. Martinez fans will love this story. The banter in the book will have you smiling and Sam will make you swoon. Plus there are other characters in the book to love such as her friend, Henry.

Collins has done a good job with the second in what is planned as a trilogy, and fans of the first book will enjoy this one, but it doesn't quite rise to the level of the first volume. It was a survival story; "Catching Fire" adds elements of political thriller while replaying some of the best notes of the first volume. Binti was a fantastic character, torn between a very traditional upbringing, and a desire to stay connected to her culture, and her innate curiosity and desire to explore the wider universe. 
 Unfortunately I think the novella tried to do too much in too little space. The "fish out of water" aspect is very abruptly cut off by a Meduse (space jellyfish) attack. That sharp left turn could have worked for me, but I found the second half of the novella too predictable. That ground -- enemy has been wronged, enemy becomes ally, protagonist becomes ambassador -- has been covered before. Plus, I felt like the ending was unrealistic: would the members of Oozma Uni really forgive the Meduse for the wholesale slaughter of a whole ship's worth of students and professors, to the point that they ask one of the jellyfish to stay as a student? Would Binti really forgive Okwu for murdering all of her friends? Was there really no other way to get that stinger back?? . (I'll also direct you to this review, which well articulates a lot of the issues I had with the story). 
 I didn't love it.

Nirvana's biggest strength for me is the world building. There isn't a great deal of detail, but what there was didn't seem too farfetched or unlikely. 
 In here, the world's population of bees has died, and with them almost all living plant life. When the plants died, the animals died. And when the world went to shit, people turned to virtual reality to escape it. 
 It's logical, it flows with what has been happening in real time, and it doesn't seem completely out of left field in reasonableness. Realllly strong there. 
 What I had a harder time believing: our main character is 17. Apparently she's a seasoned veteran at political activism, according to her. Like, years worth of it. So my automatic thinking is: I am mean to celebrate a 13, 14, 15 year old girl breaking into places and wreaking havoc in the name of justice. If anything, she sounds like a trouble-making teenager who thinks she's tough shit because she does stuff a lot of teenagers do. She's 17, lives with her boyfriend of two years, is apparently a rock star, and her parents are just nonexistent. I know it said her dad died, but I don't remember much about her mom. 
 It just seemed so ridiculous for a girl that age. Maybe if she was 22, or 26, I'd believe it. That's plenty of time to actually build up a following. But as far as this girl is concerned, she was a genius/prodigy with music, had time to tour, had time to break in everywhere and stage elaborate showdowns, and also to have a researcher boyfriend. Suddenly the world lets a teenager do a LOT of things they couldn't do before. 
 It was very fast paced, which was both a blessing and a curse. Sometimes it moved so fast I didn't feel like it was in real time, more like I'm being fast forwarded through the chain of events. But most of the time, it was perfect. There was a ton of action and Andrew's puzzle for Kenders was so enticing. Reminds me of when couples do those anniversary scavenger hunts--except, you know, more about life and death. 
 I liked how strong Kenders was, too. She didn't mope, she didn't shrivel at the first sign of hardship. When she had to hold her own against the conniving Paloma, she did so admirably. No whimpering, no outraged shouts, no losing control at all. I liked that. So many heroines are portrayed as brave and strong and then crack under the slightest pressure. Not here! 
 Good book, I think the characters should just be a little older. Especially with how seductive Lexie was being at 17 with middle aged men. *shudders*

Because of many favorable reviews, I read this with high expectations. In many ways, Reeve lived up to them by delivering a story of solid pacing and easy to follow dramatic action. He quickly constructs a world of mobile cities coursing a post-appocalyptic earth, feeding on each other, the weak falling prey to the strong. His action is brisk, combigining elements of Airborn and "The Terminator" and pirate yarns. If you read for plot, then this may be a book for you. 
 I hesitate to give it more stars because the characters didn't matter to me. The teen protagonists are flat, not even feeling like stereotypes but like place holders. Perhaps it is a result of the third-person narration that I don't know enough about Tom and Hester and Katherine. Or, perhaps I'm expecting more than the target audience of the book demands. Male readers may well love this more than heavily character-driven dystopian tales like Uglies and Unwind. There is some violence, but of the PG sort, making this appropriate for middle school as well as older readers.

So Many Reasons Why kept me compulsively reading. The subject matter was pretty heavy--the rape and attempted murder of a child being the stage for everything that happened. It was brutal to read at times, making me cringe especially when Emma describes what happened to her. Her being so scarred not just physically but mentally didn't surprise me at all; a trauma like that isn't something that a person just forgets about. The way that it manifested itself for her, through agoraphobia, was a unique twist to a love story. 
 Emma's interactions with Simon were great. While I am a bit skeptical about the time frame (everything happening in the span of like 3 weeks!?) I still enjoyed the relationship that developed between the two. The emails in the beginning were particularly my favorite part. The early stages of flirting and getting to know someone are always a little bit terrifying, let alone having the added baggage of not being able to step outside your home for a date. 
 For his part I thought Simon was a great guy. He certainly seems like a miscreant from the outside, given that he's an older man seducing his twenty-year-old student. Yet the way he talked and dealt with Emma showed tenderness and care. Even during the sex scenes there was still the constant presence of the feelings they had for one another, which was impressive. It wasn't like the author just inputted random sex scenes to juice it up. Instead, it was cohesive with the story; their personalities were maintained throughout. 
 I really liked the minor characters as well. Maddie of course was adorable. But the one I really loved the most was Cass. Cass and Tom were unequivocally the best friends. Having the strength to maintain a friendship with someone as broken and lost as Emma is a feat most people can't accomplish, and them sticking around through all of the shit was admirable, to say the least.

Dorky main character + manic pixie dream girl  (that turns out not to be everything that the main character hopes)  + a peculiar obsession established within the first few pages (e.g. Quentin's fascination with miracles in Paper Towns. Ezra's established, albeit rarely referenced, interest in tragedies was a little pathetically similar to this.) = predictable and somewhat basic plot line. 
 The story was chalk full of underdeveloped side characters and "endearing quirks" that tried to weave themselves in smoothly, but ultimately failed in doing so. Things like Cassidy's unexplained fixation with interesting words from other cultures came across as forced: I got the feeling that Robyn Schneider was just trying to show off her useless fact collection. 
 There were a few more inconsistencies of that nature that stood out to me as the story advanced. Ezra supposedly is not a reader. Which, well, okay fine. This is mentioned a considerable amount of times, Cassidy even going so far as to teasingly call him "Mr. Illiterate Jock". The irritating part is, for someone that doesn't read, Ezra was able to reference a pretty sizeable amount of literature, such as Animal Farm and Steinbeck. There was always an excuse for him knowing of these works. In the case of Steinbeck's tide pool poem, it was that he had read it for an extra credit assignment. Schneider having to explain that reasoning heavily interrupted the flow of the metaphor that was to follow. I mean, really, you could have just made him a reader. 
 Towards the end of the novel, the sentences tended to drag on and I found myself skimming a bit. The summary could have been half of the amount of pages that it was. Also, the only two characters that were fully developed by the time the resolution came a'rollin were Cassidy and Ezra. I would have definitely enjoyed more of Toby the other characters throughout the novel. 
  Another thing: Wow plot twist the main character's geezer of a dog dies how completely random and not at all expected. Even the death-via-coyote thing was predictable. It's not as if the reader is oblivious to the fact that the coyotes keep resurfacing in the story. We know it's not going to be for no reason! Seriously.  
 Overall, despite the book's flaws, I think Robyn Schneider has shown through a few cute moments (I loved the debate club party) that she has potential as writer. I am not opposed to picking up another book from her.
It wasn't too bad, but nothing exceptional. I think this might be the sort of series that gets better as the world fills out, so I'm definitely giving the next book a try.

I realized that I hated this book at the end of the first chapter. I'm not entirely sure why I continued to read it, but I did. I guess we all have to live with our choices. Fair warning: there will be many, many spoilers. 
 Turtle Alveston is a 14-year old girl living outside of Mendocino, California, with her abusive father, Martin. Martin physically and sexually abuses Turtle, and has for a very long time. Turtle's mother is dead, she went solo abalone diving one day when Turtle was very young and never returned. Or at least that's Martin's story. When we finally hear the story behind the death of Turtle's mother it is so loaded with heavy-handed uncertainty that I spent the rest of the novel waiting for her to either turn up alive after all, or for the revelation that Martin had murdered her after she'd caught him raping their daughter. But nothing ever came of it and ultimately Tallent wasted a lot of time imbuing the passage with ambiguity for no reason. 
 For all the mountains of praise being heaped upon this book, I am fantastically disappointed in the quality of Tallent's writing. He is the worst writer of dialogue I have encountered in years. Characters incessantly repeat themselves, there is far too much artless cursing, and no one - save Grandpa - sounds authentic. Jacob and Brett sound like caricatures of teenagers, and nothing from Turtle's inner monologue suggests that she'd be able to interact socially with them as easily as she seems to. 
 Tallent depends on the dialogue to help readers understand the characters and their motivations, which is largely why the character development is also poor. Martin attempts to blame his damaged psyche on his own father, accusing him of a level of hate and abuse that seems completely contrary to the way grandpa is depicted in the novel. Yes, Grandpa is clearly an alcoholic, but compared to Martin he comes off like an angel of mercy. Martin's accusations against his father fly in the face of the scenes where he and Turtle play cribbage, where he gives Turtle his beloved bowie knife, and encourages her to ask Martin to take her dress shopping and ask a boy to the dance. This is not the same man that Martin describes as hideously abusive. Is this meant to demonstrate how off-his-rocker Martin really is? Or is it a serious accusation of intense abuse, the legacy of which is now passed down to another generation? Perhaps it is neither of these? It is impossible to tell. 
 Tallent also goes way overboard on the description of the natural environment. We get it already, they're in the wilderness of the Pacific Northwest! It's verdant and wild and dangerous - JUST LIKE LIFE YOU GUYS. But by far the element of his style that I found the most grating was his tendency to turn nouns into verbs. At one point a man's arm is "sleeved with tattoos," at another point rain comes "sheeting off the roof." No. No no no no no. This is lazy writing. Not only are the lengthy descriptions of everything excessive and burdensome, but readers also have to suffer through the tortuous twisting of nouns into verbs because Tallent is too lazy to choose his words more carefully. BOO! 
 Speaking of choosing his words carefully, someone needs to ask Gabriel Tallent why he chose to write scenes of unimaginably horrible sexual abuse by a father against his teenage daughter with a tone of eroticism that is usually reserved for descriptions of consensual love. The first encounter they had I thought, "That was.... really weird," but thought that, perhaps, his intent was to demonstrate that while it's obvious to the reader that what Turtle is experiencing is extreme sexual abuse, she herself believes that when her father has sex with her it is him expressing his love for her. I found myself trying to remember Lolita, and how disquieting Humbert Humbert's feelings toward young Dolores Haze are; but then I recalled that in Lolita Humbert Humbert is the (very) unreliable narrator from whose point of view the story is told. This novel is not told from Martin's point of view, it's told from Turtle's, a 14-year old child who is being repeatedly raped by her own father. The tone Tallent chooses for these passages is, frankly, reprehensible. 
 This book is an orgy of weapons, especially guns. So. Many. Guns. Martin and Turtle bond over the weapons as he teaches her to use them, and then a rift forms over the very same weapons as her caution and knowledge surpasses his own. Notably, Turtle has a Sig Sauer pistol that she carries pretty much at all times, somehow - inexplicably - even to and from school without being caught, and she cleans it approximately 72 million times. It's clearly therapeutic for her, she has something important and powerful to take care of, but Tallent belabors the point until it ceases to carry any symbolic meaning before the novel is even half over. There is also a bowie knife which is given to Turtle and has great meaning and significance - a knife that sticks around and plays a very important role at the end of the novel - but somehow Turtle also carries that to school with her, along with her Sig Sauer, and remains - unbelievably - under the radar. 
 There are many, many other small details about this novel that are infuriatingly stupid. Her teacher, Anna, clumsily confronts Turtle about the abuse she suspects and while Turtle does her best to deny it NO TEACHER ALIVE that was alert enough to suspect an issue in the first place would be convinced by her insistence that everything is fine. Then a week after this conversation happens Turtle arrives at school, limping and black-eyed from her father beating her with a hot iron fire poker, and THERE IS NO POSSIBLE WAY that Anna wouldn't notice her injuries and contact social services - they JUST had a breakthrough conversation about it. Plus teachers are mandatory reporters! Also, when Turtle and Jacob are swept out to sea by the tide and she suffers compound fractures to three of her fingers, they just somehow magically heal in like, a week? With no residual problems with her dexterity or anything. Martin kidnaps another little girl later on in the plot and her whole entrance into the drama serves no real purpose that I can figure out. And the scene with the scorpions actually made me dry heave. And her name is Julia, but some people call her Julia, and her dad calls her Kibble, and she calls herself Turtle. Where did she get all of her names? Character names are usually kind of important.  
 In the end, I have nothing good to say about this book. I found it offensive, and the writing was terrible, and I'm angry that I wasted hours of my life reading it, and disappointed in all the authors that I admire who are heaping praise upon it. Do yourself a favor and skip it.

You have to read either just the first or all four books in order to make sense of this story. 
 These communities have constraints not unlike ours. The systems and fear of what's beyond the boundaries. Watching people obey, break away, adapt and establish makes me contemplate the construction of any social regulations and how justified they are. 
 Many words came to mind as I tried to summarise my inspired thoughts after reading the completed quartet: family, pain, rules, love, growth, society, knowledge, education... The most representative of all might be "once" -- it marks the starting place of people who move to Village, who withdraw from the old system, who open up themselves for possibilities that come from education and adventures.

The most accurate genre The Martian will fit into is "real science" science fiction. Andy Weir is a friggin' genius--in my very limited scope of knowledge of thermodynamics, physics, and chemistry, he did his homework and everything seemed plausible. 
 What makes this such a fantastic book is the voice. Mark Watney is funny. Hilarious, actually. Though I think there'd probably be a little more subdued tones and depression in real life, I couldn't help but root for Watney's unending brilliance. He was funny, he was damn smart, and he knew how to basically be a NASA handyman. A thousand osbtacles were thrown his way but he knows how to adapt and work with what he's got. 
 Namely, duct tape. 
 His jokes are insanely nerdy--ridiculously so. It had me cracking up laughing with how silly they were, because it was about pirate-ninjas and Aquaman and how he is technically a space pirate and he is the best botanist on the planet. (Really though--what kind of sense of humor would you expect from an intelligent botanist/engineer working for NASA? Smart jokes and nerd pop culture. That's what I expect.) Dumb, and exactly the kind of stupid humor I have sometimes. You can't really go wrong with those sorts of jokes. So ultimately, even though Watney's continued enthusiasm is probably on the far side of realistic, it made for a really awesome protagonist. I didn't want him to die. 
 Secondary characters were good supporting characters, but ultimately I would not have cared who played what had the roles been shuffled. They weren't the main event, and I treated them as such. To the sidelines with you, slaves! 
 Also, poor guy. Being stuck on an alien planet all alone for more than a year with nothing to listen to but disco and nothing to watch but 70s American television. Poor soul.

Ok so after finishing Paper Towns By John Green I found myself feeling a little... unsatisfied... Although it was a good read as what you can expect from a John Green novel. 
 Quentin Jacobson has had a crush on Margo Roth Spiegelman since ever since and when she suddenly climbs into his bedroom window one night and asks him to roam about time to complete particular tasks, what's a normal, red- blooded American boy do? He says yes of course. And when she suddenly disappears, he's left with a series of clues which he and his friends uses to find her. The more he works through these clues, the more he discovers a whole new side of MRS that no one ever knew about. 
 The characters. I like the characters in this book alot more, compared to the ones in The Fault in Our Stars because they spoke alot like "normal" teenagers, however, they weren't as interesting as Augustus and Hazel. Quentin, or Q as he's called, goes through a significant character development process which I really like and could relate to at some point. He starts off your average high school senior , who falls into the whole "geek/nerd" category of the social spectrum. Throughout his whole adventure, he does things that he wouldn't normally do; at one point you can actually feel him struggling between the things he would normally do and the new things he wants to do and eventually the new him would break free. Margo Roth Spiegelman, on the other, seemed like your interesting, popular girl character from the get go. However, as I continued on through the book, I find myself not really liking her because I felt like she was such a deceiving character. My thoughts on her were all based on the turn of events that occurred towards the end of the book soooo spoilers! 
 The plot. I really enjoyed the beginning of the book more than I did of the ending. The tasks were messed up- creative, but still messed up. LOL! There were parts of the plot that felt a bit slow to me. Although there were a few things that managed to pick it up. One of those few things were Q's friends who apparently loved to throw parties thereby completing the the stereotypical circle of high school nerds transitioning into the "cool" crowd post grduation. (Yay for reckless teenagers!!!) 
 Overall, I guess I had expected a bit more from this book. I think Quentin deserved a better ending that what he got, in addition to becoming a more wholistic character. The book was beautifully written as can be expected from John Green. Even though the plot was a bit... meh... I'd still recommend this book for a summer read :D Plus, with the movie coming out soon, I would recommend y'all to read it asap :D

This book hooked me on the first page when one of my favorite Ghostbusters quotes appeared, "Cats and dogs living together... mass hysteria!". I knew this was a book for me. I was immediately addicted and thought about canceling long-standing plans so I could read it. Thank you for that, Ernest Cline. 
 The synopsis of this book is difficult to gather in a few sentences, but I'll try: A Gates/Wozniack duo create alternative reality, OASIS, which the world can use for free to ignore all the problems around them (such as rampant poverty, disease, drug addiction, the energy crisis, etc.). The Gates-type, Holliday, dies. His will is a video game style quest for his easter egg held in OASIS where gunters (easter egg hunters) have to completely immerse themselves in Holliday's addiction with 1980s geek culture. The winner gets 240 billion, immortality in OASIS, and ownership of the company. Questing ensues. 
 It doesn't feel that complicated when I'm reading it. I love the diversity of the characters. There are some troupes, for sure, but that is one of the hallmarks of great YA literature. Yes, there is an evil corporation out for it all. But I don't think it impedes the plot. I also love that the book starts out with Wade identifying that the Media (capital A) has been getting his story wrong, so it's his turn to tell it. This immediately lets the reader know that he won, but the structure of the story and Wade's relationship with the other characters has us doubting at times. I think that's brilliant.  
 The 80s references were spot on. Cline surely did his research! He had lots of common references (Star Wars, Rush, Pac Man, Dungeons and Dragons) which most people, even those who didn't experience the 80s, know. He also had lots of obscure references. I knew a lot of them, but not all. And when I did my digging I found that they were impeccable. Eventually, the 80's-ness was so common I am sure I glossed over a few of the more subtle references. I liked that. It didn't feel like LOVE THE 80S I LOVE THE 80S YOU MUST LOVE THEM to the reader. It did to the characters, but the gunters we shared the story with also found they loved them. It was nice. 
 There were a few things that made this book 4.5 stars, instead of 5 for me. First was the endless techno-jabber. I love World Building. However, this novel had two worlds: The Real World and OASIS. OASIS world-building was fun to me, but Real World techno-jabber building was boring. I'm sure there is a group of people who loved it, but I don't fit in that category. The other...  was the ending. I was frustrated at how quickly it ended and everything got wrapped up in a neat little bow. As soon as Wade entered Halliday's office he immediately knew what to do and how to win. Plus, his arch-nemesis, Sorrento, was also somewhere trying to win, and we don't know how far he got. Did Sorrento make it to Halliday's office? Did he know what to do? How did Wade beat the clock there? Then, when Wade got out, he was just the winner. Lawyers were waiting for him, the media was at his heels, and he won the girl. It just... I wanted more. I didn't necessarily need more story, but I needed a stronger conclusion.  
 All in all, a well-written addicting read. I recommend this to anyone who loves the 80s, who loves geek culture, or who is interested in the future of video games and alternate reality.

I read this book thinking "no way this is going to be as good as the Percy Jackson series". I am so glad that I was proven wrong! Although I have read other books with Norse theme (Blackwell pages), I am not nearly as familiar with Norse mythology as I thought I was. I found that this book provided me with enough mythology to make sense of everything. In a way, the reader is put in the place of Magnus Chase who is also having the mythology revealed to him in bits and pieces.
