(This is not really a review, just some scattered thoughts.) 
 Good stuff: 
 -This novel does a scarily amazing job at realistically depicting an abusive relationship. Marcus is by turns kind and cruel, sympathetic and not, and it's easy to understand why the victim in this situation doesn't immediately fight back or cut Marcus out of his life. I think seeing abuse depicted like this is really important as far as being a precautionary tale and educational tool. 
 -I like that Hutchinson shows Henry finally getting help for his depression. Although... it's kind of worrying how often Henry told people about his suicidal thoughts and they didn't do anything. 
 -Jesse!! To me he was one of the strongest characters in this book even though he was just a memory. 
 -Audrey. A+ best friend. 
 -Charlie. A really complex character you'll both love and hate. 
 But I was meh on: 
 -Diego's character. He's a good guy and all. It's just... for some reason I just wasn't that invested in him. And I think you really need to be to care about his story arc, which is a pretty significant part of the novel. 
 -The melodrama and rather self-conscious poetics. In particular, the whole "save the world" metaphor went on way too long. I was so tired of it. 
 -The protagonist gets severely bullied at school, and I just have a hard time believing it could get that extreme. It felt exaggerated to me. But maybe other readers would disagree, idk. 
 -In general I just wasn't that crazy about this book. It didn't suck me in. I didn't really love most of the characters, and the writing style reminded me too much of John Green (not in a good way). 
 Content warnings (might count as mild spoilers, but I've tried to be vague): suicidal thoughts, bullying, abusive relationships, explicit physical assault, explicit attempted rape, alcohol abuse and drunk driving, miscarriages, um... I think that's about it? There's just a lot of dark stuff in this book.

Matthew Swift died. He tried to crawl to a phone booth and he breathed his last breath down that phone line. And the blue electric angels of the phone lines heard him. The angels of half whispered confessions, apologies, bad news, good news and everything else that people impart over the phone lines. The remnants of life like the white noise of the television. They always talked to him, much to the interest of his billionaire boss and master sorcerer Robert James Bakker. 
 So when he comes back to life and finds himself in his house - that isn't his anymore - he is understandably confused. He is more confused because the angels are now in him. 
 He tries to track down old friends to find too many dead ends; dead in the literal sense. And then the city and other magic beings notice his return. Matthew has to find his murderer, make magic blood treaties, start (and finish) an urban magic war, and sort out what he even is. And he has to do it in his human body; frail as it is. 
 *** 
 I love the idea that the older a city is, the more magic it builds up in itself. London is old and crammed with life and its own magic. The urban magic in this London comes from the streets themselves; from The Underground; from the Thames; from the animals of the city - rats, pigeons and foxes; from the ancient wording of laws carved into the stones and from the modern things - graffiti tags, phone lines, and computer cables. And from magic yellow pages volumes left on the roof of the bus shelters. 
 There are magical bike gangs that can fold distance as they travel, bag ladies that know what the pigeons see, a king of the beggars who is ancient and wise, and there is even a magical NHS (national health service) hospital for the magically injured. 
 I read something the other day about world building. It said that if you sell the reader well enough on the small things that when you get to the big things, they already trust and believe you. A dragon made out of old street signs? Sure... why not? 
 But jeez it was hard for me to read. I gave up and put it aside, but came back to it after a while. Even then, I really had to force myself to finish the book, and I shouldn't have felt like that. I get why the author needs to swap from singular to plural all the time, Matthew's body holds more than one person. It was an interesting story, great antagonist (the uber creepy Hunger), got some great ideas about urban fantasy and magic... but gah... reading it was like pulling teeth. Maybe it was the style of the writing? I ended up skipping some passages. There's a lot of the plot that remains a mystery for too long as the MC keeps things secret or tells us a big chunk of backstory in a memory. 
 especially things like Matthew's apprentice Dana, whom we don't even hear about until we are two thirds of the way through the book. Did he have an affair with Bakker's sister or not? The reader still doesn't know. I mean... I think so. But I should KNOW. This is his prime motivation - revenge for the hurt done to him and to the people he cared about. So when one gets hurt I didn't feel anything because I hadn't been told what that person meant to him.  
 I almost gave it 2 stars but pushed it up to 3 for the world building.

 I admit I read the Hunger Games only after I heard about the movie. I'd heard of the books before, but I'd never really got a chance to read them, and when I heard there was a movie I was determined to finish the first book so I could go watch it. And I'm so glad I did. 
  
 Hunger Games was amazing. The emotions were portrayed so perfectly that you could literally FEEL them. Catching Fire was brilliant as well and I was sitting on edge for Mockingjay. 
 Now a lot of people have said that Mockingjay was a total disappointment. But come on, I mean can't you see from the first book that this story isn't the 'happily ever after' kind? Fine, Gale fans might have been heartbroken by the end, but personally I was always, ALWAYS Team Peeta. Gale was way too much like her. And as Katniss herself has mentioned a million times, he's more like her brother. He even LOOKS like her brother. Peeta, on the other hand, complements every quality of Katniss by being her total opposite. Katniss and Peeta fit together like two puzzle pieces. It's inevitable that they should get married. 
 Of course I was awfully depressed about the number of deaths that happened in this last book, especially since a lot of them seemed so unnecessary. Finnick, Cinna and Prim did NOT have to die IMHO. But then again, the author isn't just writing to satisfy her audience. She's writing it like how it is, and how it should be, and she has every right to dictate the fate of her characters. She MADE them after all. 
 Overall, this series was amazing. I've read a lot of books and only a few of them ever make my 'best books' list. And Hunger Games is definitely one of them. Suzanne Collins has earned my respect. 
 Oh and need I add? #TeamPeetaForever

I read most of this book about eight years ago as a freshman in high school and didn't like it then. I thought maybe it was an age thing and I'd like it better when I was older. I was wrong. 
 The writing, especially the emphasis on describing everybody's eyes all the time, is simply horrendous. It feels like it's trying to be deep and artistic, but it succeeds about as well as a high school literary magazine. I realized I didn't actually care about any of the characters, and none of them had actions that made any sense. By the end, I was more relieved when I realized there were just pages left than I was interested in the non-compelling climax. 
 This book has an interesting concept -- a murdered girl watches her family from heaven as they try to solve the crime -- but it doesn't follow through.

I have very mixed feelings about this book and I'm not sure how to sort them out. It should be noted up front though that Revis drew on her brother's real experience with mental illness as inspiration for this story, so I am not doubting that this is a realistic portrayal. 
 You may want to avoid this review if you haven't read the book yet. I discuss things covered in the official summary, but I felt the summary gave away the whole story. 
 The premise of this story I've often heard is "Does the main character have superpowers, or does he have a mental illness?" It's in the book summary that he has a mental illness and that is how the book was recommended to me, and that's the only reason that I feel this premise is okay because I'm not very comfortable with relating mental illness to having a superpower (though I can't pinpoint all my feelings around this). However, I do feel as if it's realistic that their mental illness would come as a surprise to someone having delusions. Bo's experience felt genuine. 
 What really hindered my enjoyment is that the story relies so heavily on that question of superpower vs mental illness. It requires the reader to be unsure, but the summary told us the answer up front. This could have worked well as a character study if it hadn't had such an emphasis on the plot and that mystery. I don't enjoy stories that treat mental illness as a mystery to be solved. To be clear, I think it was responsible of the summary to tell us the answer up front, I just wish there had been more to the plot here because as it was, this story felt way too long, unnecessary, and repetitive. If you've read the summary, you know the whole story. The premise and the execution did not work for me personally. 
 It also did not help that the end totally leads you to believe that Bo had in fact seen the future with the earring scene, undoing all of the work toward establishing a story about mental illness.  
 I enjoyed Pheobe's few chapters and her perspective as the sibling of someone with mental illness, as well as the insight she gave us into their parents' lives and how they interacted with both her and Bo. The family aspect was the most interesting to me.

This book and my inept reading of it started a fascination with survival ism that eventually passed, but I clearly remember the thrill of reading about what would happen if it all fell apart.

But after reading some of his books, I've proved their worth as well-respected authors and strengthened my devotion to their work.

 I like the thought that went into this story and I like how intelligent Lemony was during his childhood or close-to-teenage years. Having really loved Swanson's novel Her Every Fear, it was a no-brainer that I simply had to read The Kind Worth Killing, especially after reading all the raving reviews about it. As I am always looking for captivating books for my daily commute in the car, I downloaded this novel from Audible, and I am so glad I did! The Kind Worth Killing was a fantastic read, the sort that made me sit in my car in the driveway on a cold, chilly night for "just a few more minutes" because I couldn't tear myself away. I can't remember much about my driving on those days, except that I got there safe and sound, but my mind was fully captivated by the book. Now there is a psychological thriller that lives up to its name! 
 Swanson offers us two female leads so chilling and malicious that listening to them sent shivers down my spine at times, and yet Lily intrigued me to a point where I silently feared for her safety and secretly hoped she would get away with murder (literally). She was both terrifying and sympathetic, which is a very hard thing to achieve in a protagonist, and I applaud the author for pulling this off so perfectly. It helped that Lily always had a perfectly reasonable explanation - at times challenging my own moral conventions. Is killing justified if the victim is a truly horrible individual with no chance of redemption, set to make a lot of lives miserable? Lily thinks so. In the airport bar, she says to Ted: 
 "Truthfully, I don't think murder is necessarily as bad as people make it out to be. Everyone dies. What difference does it make if a few bad apples get pushed along a little sooner than God intended? And your wife, for example, seems like the kind worth killing." 
 Sounds reasonable to you? No, no! *slaps face* - murder is BAD! I would love to delve deeper into the characters and discuss the storyline, but this is not the place and I would hate to give any spoilers. My advice is: plunge into this book blindly and let Swanson take you on his journey. The writing is excellent. The subject matter is chilling. It will mess with your mind - believe me! And the ending - I was worried at one point about how the author would pull this off, but it was perfect! 
 As for the narration: I loved that the publisher used four different narrators for the different characters, which made the story easy to follow and a pleasure to listen to. 
 The Kind Worth Killing was one of my favourite reads this year so far - one of those rare psychological thrillers that really mess with your mind and make you itch to find someone to discuss it with. I loved it, and am so glad I stumbled across it. If you love a good psychological thriller and are looking for something different, do yourself a favour and pick up this book today. You won't be disappointed.

While I am absolutely enthralled by the way Katsu weaves her words, the tone of the story has done little to hold my interest. After reading reviews both positive and negative on the nature of the book, I realize why: I'm afraid of the dark. 
 Shadows here and there add intrigue and danger, but the overwhelming black pit this book falls into has scared me away. I don't want to read about unrequited love to a man many feel unworthy of any admiration or redemption . I don't want to read about disturbing sexual acts, where the victim has no desire to leave her sadistic master . And I don't want to continue a book in which I have already read how blase the author mentions abuse. 
 For some, this book will thrill, entice, excite, and satisfy. I am not one of these people, so I will leave before I become too jaded.

Well, that sucked. 
 Okay I'm exaggerating,but it was disappointing. Blood Red Road was pretty awesome and I loved it, but Rebel Heart did not live up to it's standard. It also took me a ridiculously long time to read. 
 There's so many things that annoyed me about Rebel Heart. First, Jack. Why Jack, why? What're you doing man? I don't get you, plus you hardly showed up in the book. 
 Saba. OH MY GOSH SABA. I don't even know anymore. It's like you were a completely different person. Especially that Demalo thing. I am so disappointed in you. His whole crazy ass plan about only needing the 'young and the strong' and 'healing the earth', you totally agreed with it. WHAT IS WRONG WITH YOU. He's killing people and kicking them off of THEIR land to make the world a 'better place'. Uh-huh. For shame saba. I can't even mention what you did after that. 
 WHY IS THERE A LOVE TRIANGLE. WHYYYYYYYY?! -cries- I mean, if the guy was not a lunatic I'd be okay with it, but honestly! 
 And it's kinda strange how Saba had all these like inner demons due to her conscience after killing people, but then once they enter New Eden on their journey, it wasn't mentioned again, even though Auriel specifically said that the whole healing her thingy was not done and she was still 'open'. What happened to that? 
 Lugh was annoying, not worth writing about.

Culbertson has a wondrous way with words. At least once every other page, I would find myself impressed by a unique turn of phrase and trying to breathe in the smell of a beautiful simile. I also highly respected the main character for wanting to stay in her small town and work with her parents in their Cafe rather than ~escape~ to the bright lights of the big city, or anywhere else, for her narrative journey. ("People just assumed leaving what the best thing. What if I thought staying was the best thing?") I liked the detail about her job as well. 
 I did get tired of her parents failing to involve the cops in her thieving brother's ways, and found myself getting actively angry that she only took the job so she could use it to pay his debts. Dude sounded more in need of a beatdown from an enforcer by that point. I also cannot fathom a person who is like "meh" at spending time with a celebrity. Not screaming on the spot is a good approach, but this arrangement she fell into IS a fairy tale fantasy on the grandest scale. I'd do it for free (which I realize is precisely why they'd never ask me). The stylist's consultation of my wardrobe/makeup alone would be worth it. 
 The story gave me a good outline to imagine myself in the scenario, though, so that was enjoyable. And, by sticking with it, I gradually found Adam more tolerable as the story went on, though I still never swooned over him. The ending fell perfectly in line with my hopes, though. Thumbs up! For my future reference: [She accepts the breakup because she's leaving town, even though it hurts right now. Her brother gets his sorely needed beatdown, and then skips town rather than return to rehab and disappears from their lives, YAY! Last but not least, Adam returns in dazzlingly romantic style to finish off their tour of the town, and you get to decide what happens after that. A+ cinema quality ending!]

I need very little urging to tap into my Abandonment Issues side, so I was all on board for a story in which one's best friend and her family vanish with no explanation, and seeing how the character would cope with that. Added to that, the front and back covers are both magical, summer and best friendship perfectly encapsulated in two photos. I immediately wanted to be both of them at once so I could be friends with the other. 
 I love Emily because she's me, and I love Sloane because she's the kind of wonderful, creative, exciting, mostly-loyal girl that you only dream exists, and would never in a million years expect to just decide she wants to be your best friend and do everything with you. Aside from the dating fiasco, I loved pretty much all of their adventures. Sloane's love of scouring flea markets for vintage clothing and accessories just made her even more perfect. I rarely get to read books that are about two straight female besties with minimal boy distractions and no extraneous friends. Every time we flashed back, I'd sit up a little straighter in eager anticipation (even after the shine started to come off Sloane a bit). 
 I also loved all the descriptions of their small town, Emily's loving but completely scatterbrained playwright parents and the way their household turns completely upside down when said parents are like, "THIS PLAY IS GONNA BE SO AWESOME. *8 hours later* Wait, do we have kids?" Even the concept of the list itself held promise (and what a way to work your outline into the novel as a plot point). When she walked into the ice cream parlor and fell into a job offer, I was psyched that everything would turn out this cool. 
 But the farther into this book I got, the more annoyed I became, because the idea of pushing yourself out of your comfort zone is my #1 pet peeve. No one should ever do anything they find uncomfortable or that scares them if they don't have to. If something's worth doing, you'll already want to do it, and if for some reason you try something scary and end up happy you've done it, then I either judge you for not already having known yourself well enough to know you'd like it, or you've changed into a worse person, depending on whether or not I approve of the scary thing. (chances are if your parents/teachers/the police wouldn't, I won't either) Half the things on the list were great, but half were beyond stupid. 
 I'm also mildly offended by the suggestion that a person can go from being attached at the hip to one female friend, to suddenly having a 2-3 person mixed gender posse. In my experience, when you lose your best friend, you become as invisible as Emily was at that first party and you stay that way. At best, you might befriend a Dana, but definitely no boys if you didn't hang out with boys before. 
 The new friends do help round out the story, so for the most part that is a good writing choice, especially as they're clearly NOT replacing Sloane and are but pale imitations of placeholders. I even thought it was pretty organic how she met them...but her inevitable feelings for Frank and overly close friendship with him in particular felt so forced and uncomfortable. Instead of becoming instant running buddies, how about he visits his girlfriend every other weekend and you guys hang out, like, twice a week? I vote for more stories about what Emily does all by her lonesome. GO HOME, FRANK. 
 Ending spoilers: And stop trying to ply me with that weak "my perfect girlfriend and I have kind of fizzled out because we were too busy being complementary types of perfect to maintain any actual passion as soon as we were tested by distance" excuse for making Emily's crush valid. That is so overdone. How about a story where the perfect guy and the perfect girl actually are perfect together? 
 I wish the book had ended with her unwanted kiss turning her into a social pariah in that circle for good, but then it being OK because she and Sloane -- who is nearly 18 and juuuust about old enough to not have to be buffeted about by her parents' moving decisions, which no one seems to mention -- are busy making plans to move to the same area after graduation, thus putting Emily's world back on its axis. 
 I did love the fitting ending as it was, including the surprise reveal that Sloane's parents are trust fund babies-turned-bums who keep blowing through any money they do manage to get, and scrambling for places to rent/crash...I just wish Frank hadn't been part of it. The lesson should have been "Emily Learns That She Can Be Independently Awesome," not "Emily Learns To Rely On More Than One Person."

The first story was really good... it caught me right away especially with the mystery of the mirrors being draped over. This is one of those stories that are best told if rushed and that I love it even more that I didn't feel like it was. It just moved with the pace that I want the events to happen and when it was over I was completely shocked. I wanted more... 
 You see, I did not read the plot of this book. I just saw the incredibly beautiful cover and title and just read it right away. I didn't care about the plot, I didn't dare look at it. I just wanted to know what happens in the story. And being a BIG Cecelia Ahern fan, I just assumed it would be great. 
 Now, you might be thinking... if I loved it so much why did I give it three stars and not five or four? Well it's because the second story bored me. It was the complete opposite on how I felt about the first one. Again, I didn't know the plot of this book so I didn't know that it would only consist of two short stories and that the title was only meant for the first one. But this is not why I disliked it. Yes, it was boring but it also didn't have that "umph" factor unlike what the first story had. I felt like if I had just read The Memory Maker first I would have liked it but reading The Girl In The Mirror first made it seem so unoriginal and forced. 
 Also, I did not understand the message of The Memory Maker which is a HUGE deal for me since it's just a short story. I think if Ms. Ahern would completely remove The Memory maker from this book and make an individual book for it, it would be immensely better. So that I could read both stories at a longer length because I really want to know more on The Girl In The Mirror. It felt too short for me which I love and hate at the same time. And I guess maybe if The Memory Maker had a book of it's own I'd like it other than mix it up with The Girl In The Mirror.

When the movie came out a few years ago I promised myself I just had to read the book. But the movie (which I loved) on its own and the book on it's own.I finally had to force myself to put it down other wise I wouldn't have gotten any sleep. I simply love the book! Right from the beginning you begin to understand how both Sally and Gillian are each shaped into the woman they will become. 
 I found myself agreeing with the young Sally that love or more accurately passion can turn the most intelligent and independent woman into a desperate fool. And even from a young age these girls learn the kinds of lessons most adults never learn. 
 One of these things is that "sometimes the most dangerous thing of all in matters of love was to be granted your heart's desire." 
 The further I got into the book the less I wanted to put it down, you might not at all times be able to identify with everything that is felt and experienced by the sisters but you can understand and sympathize. The pace of the book was beautifully set out and makes you hunger for the next page. The lines flowing like poetry and sometimes like music in the mind. 
 At times you do feel sorry for Gillian and her feeling that she is not worthy of love and that the only love she deserves is from a man who only wants to control and hurt her. She has no idea of her own worth as a woman, as a human being. 
 And Sally who has become so disillusioned by the love she lost that she feels safer in making her children her world. Being a single mother I found myself identifying with her on this. But of course shutting out your feelings does not mean that they aren't there. 
 Even Sally's daughters separate journey's to woman wood and learning to accept one another is at times hair wrenching and painful, yet at the worst moment they are as one. Here again having a little sister I found myself identifying with the fights, arguments and dislikes of the sisters understanding completely that even through you don't always get along when it comes down to the nitty-gritty there is nothing you would not do for your sister. That includes keeping any secret, even burying a body or two. 
 The aunts, even through they did not play as significant role in the book as they did in the movie, they are still by far my favorite characters. Some feel that they where not as "substantial" but when you read how the aunt's feel about the sisters (Sally and Gillian) as individuals you know that is not true. They love totally without reproach or notes of disappointment. The sisters themselves are their own harshest judges not the aunts. They accept what they were and have become absolutely. It also expresses the sisters true feeling about the aunts that when all mighty hell hits the fan that they are the ones who are summoned. (I found myself wondering about the aunts and there ages, if they where in their nineties when they took the sisters in at ages 7 and 4. How much longer did they live?!) 
 As I said the book and the movie are two different entities but I love them both as they are. The only thing that links the book to the movie are the essence of the character (names included) the magic and the odd thing here and there. 
 And yet the sisters themselves and Sally's daughter are all touched by magic. Everything they do everything they are has magic in it.
Ty McCordle *sigh* :) ... He and Imogen seemed ill paired in reality, but the chemistry/attraction they had was something else.... My favourite pair in the series.

Wow, this book was a LOT better than the first two! I loved it! Even though the story line isn't super original or anything, I love the writing style (reminds me of Colleen Houck!) and there were some really dramatic issues between the main characters that really put the whole story in a different light. I'm really curious to see if Kaylee and Nash will get past this because oooh snap. Awesome read, just what I needed! I would recommend these books to fans of 'Starcrossed' as well.

Larry Niven is one of the first sci-fi writers I ever read. He is one of my dad's favorites, and my dad gave me all of the Man-Kzin Wars books when I was twelve or thirteen. My memory of them is very vague, but I remember really loving klingon tigers. Since that time, I haven't really gone back to Niven's works until now, and I've never read any of the Ringworld saga. 
 I started out enjoying the book a lot. Niven has a great sense of humor and the dialogue never ceased to entertain me. I love his aliens, especially klingon tigers. The cautiously coward puppeteers are also a unique species, and one I had fun envisioning. I got a little bit lost in the science, which is not unusual for me, but for the most part, I enjoyed the journey, which seems to me the main purpose of the book. 
 The idea of breeding for luck was an intriguing one although I found it similar to time-travel or clairvoyance as far as the confusion factor went. It's not something I believe would ever be possible, but it gives a kind of fantasy element to a science fiction book which I don't necessarily dislike. Niven seems to treat the 60s/70s attitude toward mind-altering psychic powers as a possible fact, which isn't all that believable, but it makes for a neat plot device. I had to think through events and their implications for Teela as often as Nessus or Louis did. It hurt my head in a good way. 
 That said, reading this as a modern adult left several things irking at me. Aside from the dated science ideas (tapes, anyone?) which are excusable, Niven falls right into the female character trap. There are only two women in this book, both of them are defined by their sexuality, and one of them needs a good slap upside the head. 
 Teela is thoroughly unlikable. She takes all the fun out of the hereditary luck hypothesis in that I spent most of the book wishing for her luck to run out. Niven seems to try and make her a human by excusing her behavior and attitude with the luck hypothesis and regularly stating how smart she is, but he never actually gives her an opportunity to demonstrate her intelligence besides finding a tourniquet. Louis Wu, age 200, falling for this 20 year old vacant trophy girl is also straining my disbelief. Luck may affect circumstance, but how could it affect another person's emotions? All the probability goes out of the theory at that point. Also, he more or less admits he only wants her to come along for sex. Did I mention he's 200 years old? I can't get past these things even in far future where age is really just a number. 
 Then Teela gets separated, which would be a great time for her to develop a character, but instead she finds a handsome barbarian (whom I kept envisioning as Kevin Sorbo... sorry) to take care of her and he's the love of her life because that's how lucky she is. Oh and it's fine if Louis Wu sells her to him. She has no problem with that at all if it makes life easier. It was such a let-down. I love the premise of Teela being a girl who can't be hurt, so she needs to learn what being hurt is like, but she never really does. She just watches other people get hurt, and it doesn't seem to affect her on an emotional level at all. 
 The other female character, Halrloprillalar, is a similar problem. Immediately, we find out she's a space-whore. And ... that's pretty much it. She has a flying castle, but we don't get much in the way of character development. But she'll join us in the end because earthlings need to learn to have better sex.  
 Let's not even get into the non-sentient sexes. The aliens presented are uniformly presented as "he's," so these non-sentient sexes are presumably female. I can't imagine an evolutionary advantage to this arrangement, and Niven never provides one, so it's just there to irritate me through the whole book. 
 I'm one who usually gives books some leeway based on their publication date, but things like this suck a little enjoyment out of the book for me. It doesn't overshadow any of the great fantastic-journey style adventures of the book, but it does diminish them a bit. I read somewhere that Niven is a "big idea" man and story/character are secondary to his writing. That's certainly true of Ringworld. The ideas are all there, but the lack of character made it harder to enjoy the ride. Might continue with the series someday, but not immediately.
I repeat--these are far from just mysteries! Nevertheless, the murderer is, for me, inevitable.

** spoiler alert ** 
 This book was not for me, to be honest. 
 I was convinced to read this book by the amazing ratings it received, and the dazzling reviews that declared a must read. I was excited - eager to discover who this handsome and charming Holder was. So I bought the book on my Kindle, and began reading. 
 Hopeless is the story of a young girl named Sky who meets this boy, Holder, and is immediately attracted to him. However, after confessing this attraction to her best friend Six, she is immediately informed that he is a "bad boy" and she should stay away from him. The story follows the relationship that unfolds between them, and a huge secret is divulged at the end that changes everything. 
 I know this book is a romance, so I expected the cheesy love quotes and love confessions (Colleen Hoover is actually a pretty decent writer), but I did not expect so much of it! Every single page detailed their love for each and how she felt when he touched her and all that romantic crap. At first, I was fine with it, but then after a while, I just kind of got tired of it. It was like, "okay, I get it! You guys really like each other! Now can we please move on to some actual form of a plot?!" I'm normally not that bothered by lovey-dovey situations like these, it was just the fact that the book made it seem like their whole lives revolved around one another's and that they had no life outside of their relationship which pissed me off. 
 Despite my ranting above, there was actually a plot and unlike many shallow romance novels, it actually contained very deep thoughts like child abuse, kidnapping, and alcoholism. The characters were actually very well developed with their own identifiable personality and it was extremely well-written. 
 All in all, the plot was very good and the characters were great, but it was the sappy, mushy romance infused into every single page that drove me a little crazy.

Book 2 in the rivers of London series. Peter Grant magic police wizard in-training is a little bit lost. Nightingale is still in recovery and he is left to his own devices a bit more. Lesley is in recovery too, but it will be a long trip. 
 The strange death of a journalist in a Soho jazz club is given to Peter; the man died after losing a part of his anatomy. Dr Walid says he met a woman with vagina dentata. Yep. Bitten off. 
 But other strange deaths are happening in Soho, too, and mostly to jazz musicians. There is a lingering magic sense that can be picked up from a place where magic has happened. One corpse (heart attack on stage) is playing so loudly that even Dr Walid can hear it. He asks Peter to check. Being the son of a jazz great, he recognises not only the song but also the artist and the version. He hears the song plus gets other subtle impressions; senses of sound or smell. 
 In this world, magic also leaves physical traces; it sucks life out of batteries leaving a sandy residue, it leaves bruises on the mind and eventually leads to death and a shrunken or damaged brain. A lot of jazz deaths written off as natural causes have these signs when Peter goes looking. And they go a long way back. 
 Peter has been conducting his own experiments on this. 
 This one didn't feel as well plotted as the first book. There were a few things that didn't make sense. And this cover annoyed me, too. grrr 
 The jazz journalist girlfriend of the first victim that Peter initially doesn't trust and then happily falls into bed with? What? And a clear setup of a bad magician; a black magic practitioner or bad guy for other books? It just felt like part of the story was missing. What was the bad guy's motivation? And I can't buy the argument that the jazz vampires didn't know what affect they were having; after 70 years? Nope.  
 And characters introduced in the last book, didn't have a big role here. To lose Molly, Lesley, Toby the dog and Nightingale? All at once? It left a big gap. Any one of which would have smacked Peter upside the head way earlier. Well, Toby would have yapped... a lot.

Her parents dead, her mother by poison and her father by being bound to his wife, Lourdes finds herself fighting to save her family and clan from the people who had formerly guarded them with their lives. As new maven, she makes a deal with another clan for their protection and gains herself a husband in the process. The question is, will she be able to protect all she holds dear and at the same time get justice for those she has lost? 
 I enjoyed reading this story. The characters were well developed and the world was unique. I wasn't thrilled with the canabalism aspect, but most of the aspects of the clans seemed to be based on different sorts of spiders. Interesting.

First of all, this book had way too much bad language for my taste. That being said, it was a well written story of a truly messed up marriage. Amy disappears on their fifth wedding anniversary and the evidence starts piling up against Nick. As the police zero in on him for her murder, Nick tries to convince them that simply took off and went to elaborate lengths to set him up for her murder. Is he telling the truth and if so can he lure Amy out of hiding before it is too late for him? These characters are so incredibly screwed up. WOW.

Elena Ferrante continues to astound with the second novel in a quartet detailing the life-long friendship between two girls from a working-class neighborhood in 50's Naples. The strength lies not in the plot of the novel (or in the first novel) but in how Ferrante uses the ever-changing passions and dramas of the neighborhood to draw the character of Lila (the brilliant friend of the first novel) and Lenu, the narrator. The two grow up so close, so in each others' thoughts and minds, that Lenu weighs every action, everything that happens to her against her friend's life. Their small circle is shocked again and again by Lila's audacity, intelligence, imagination, and ferocity. Lenu is also struck by Lila's qualities and feels herself, even while carving out a noteworthy academic career, a poor reflection of her friend's light. Lenu is relentless in examining her own thoughts and feelings: she loves Lila, she is jealous of Lila, she fears Lila, and is afraid for her, but everything she is herself is in relation somehow to Lila. Time spent away from her friend is tranquil, like a dream-peaceful, but unreal. Ferrante has written a fiercely honest, authentic story of a complicated friendship.

This part of the Baudelaires' journey moves rather slowly, but it functions well as a transition tying the past events to the last book. 
 The children continue to come up with ways to get out of trouble, though still unsuccessful, and many past characters reappear. Everyone chimes in when it comes to discussing the children and Olaf's innocence. And then the immediate threat is taken over by another sudden danger. 
 Oh, oh, oh... what's in the last book?

3.5 rounded down. There's some awkward writing and it's too short. The first quarter I didn't really understand what was going on, and that's a long time for a story so short. 
 The story--time travel and sexual identity with mama issues--packs alot in a story that takes only minutes to read. Haha, Heron--Her On, which isn't the case here. The new name should be Himon or Heon. Even the image of the heron swallowing a wiggly fish is female.
Love love loooooooove this book! Just my fix for a better mood and good vibes. Cute and romantic. I really fell in love with all, and I mean ALL, the characters. Must read!

A lot to like here. The author deserves credit for a establishing a bleak yet hopeful mood and sustaining it with well-calibrated prose. Certain parts of the book are really quite sublime. However, some of the descriptive passages went on the point of approaching tedium - "I get/Get to the point already" - and the fantastical elements were grafted onto the main narrative in something less than a seamless manner, in my opinion. And yet, more good than not-so-good here, this is a worthwhile book and a promising debut.

I read this on a suggestion form my mother who had watched the films many times and knew I find wartime exploits interesting. At first I was unsure if we were discussing the same storyline, but it soon got going and I was hooked. Every aspect we may be unfamiliar with is well explained without being condescending, but the story is where it really blossoms. A group of English women, most used to their comforts and in some cases maids, made to trek endlessly with no real destination. Then a smooth transition into a love story, very sweet and innocent. 
 I thoroughly enjoyed this novel. I would like to read both more on the subject and more from this author

Really weird format... I also didn't LOVE any of the characters. There were good parts and bad parts. It was definitely a very interesting read, but I also had some major issues with certain parts of it (for example, the main character is simultaneously endearing and incredibly frustrating). All in all, I'm not sure if I liked or disliked this book. I can definitely say that it was worth the read, because it gave me a lot to think about.

This zombie book didn't live up to the hype, but it was a fun read nonetheless. My biggest disappointment was that the zombies got less print than the blood testing devices. 
 The book begins post-zombie apocalypse with two young bloggers looking to move up to the top tier of the news world, which is now dominated by bloggers. We're never told, though, whether print and broadcast journalism are dead or just irrelevant. In fact, we're not told much of anything not directly related to these two main characters. Their ticket to fame and fortune comes in the form of exclusive rights to cover a presidential nominee's campaign, but we never find out how the government is structured post-apocalypse, or even whether Washington exists as a "safe" zone in this new world. In fact, we're really told nothing about the entire eastern seaboard. That creates a lot of gaps when the story essentially morphs into a political thriller. Moreover, this post-apocalyptic world somehow possesses a functional electric grid and factories that produce massive amounts of electronics and ammunition - despite the fact that the continuous zombie threat would make this pretty much impossible. 
 The book was an enjoyable enough read, despite some major personal issues with not giving enough details about how the post-apocalyptic world functions. Provided you don't ask too many questions when reading books, this would definitely rank as a worthy time-waster.

The Unbecoming of Mara Dyer (Mara Dyer #1) by Michelle Hodkin - 4 stars 
 Holy crap. Did that really just happen?! It did. And I am buzzing with anticipation to start the next book of this series! 
 I didn't know what was real, what was a nightmare, what was a memory. 
 The Unbecoming of Mara Dyer is the first book in a trilogy series and follows a girl -= yes, Mara Dyer - who has the unfortunate circumstance of waking up in a hospital only to hear that her best friend, her boyfriend, and her boyfriend's sister had died... And she was with them. The building had collapsed. She doesn't remember any of it. 
 Thrilling. Creepy. Witty. Enticing. 
 Mara suffers from PTSD, and convinces her family to move. She can't face the world she knows without the ones who stood by her every day. They move. Mara tries to start a new life in a new place while keeping her head on straight. But hallucinations and nightmares assault her mind more frequently. Or are they visions? Memories? Is anything real or is it all in her head? 
 Then Mara meets Noah Shaw, the most wonderful seventeen-year-old boy I've ever read. Ugh. He was instant swoon worthy. And the nose boops! I love the nose boops. He wants to get to know her, and she is attracted to him, but she fears getting close to this guy with a reputation that has Mara uncomfortable. But there is an undeniable pull, something else working to bring them closer. But is he real too? Can she believe him? 
 This is literally how I feel. Everything was good. Pieces were starting to fit together. But now?! Now, I just don't know what to think. I was left holding my breath at the very end. So get the second book right away. Don't be like me. Or you'll be left waiting with a buzzing mind and NO answers. 
 The suspense is intense and thrilling. The dialogue is witty. The story pulls you in and holds you in its grip. You will need to know the answers. You will be intrigued with the strange happenings. You will need more Noah Shaw. You will crave the next book.

All of her choices were lucky guesses and chances like we take every single day. There wasn't the surety of absolute badassery, and there wasn't avoidance of emotions either. 
 I LOVE, LOVE, LOVE, LOVE AUTHORS WHO ARE NOT AFRAID OF EMOTIONS 
 I don't know about you, but I am more than fed up of 'ice queen' bitches whose only 'attractive' characteristic is that they are rude and insult everything around them; and that somehow that is supposed to be more than enough for the hero to fall madly in love with her. 
 I am tired of cheating assholes who like to showcase their emotional inability to cope with the fact that someone stole their teddy when they were five, and now they use the repressed feelings of inadequacy to deal with the situation 'like a man', by inseminating everything that will stay still for seven point two seconds. 
 Whenever I pick up a book like that I see nothing but fake people who use the most basic of tactics to deflect from the fact that they are insecure as hell, and force everyone else to deal with their problems. That's why I don't like contemporary romance so much. 
 So when you get something like this, an insight in a young mind that is wholesome, that understands the concept of family, friends, love and devotion, and sees that there is absolutely nothing wrong with being normal, it flows like a fresh breeze. Honestly, normal somehow became abnormal with the current popular culture, and it seems that people aren't really doing much else, except competing to see who has more mental and emotional damage. So kudos to the author, she deserves praise at every chapter. 
 But I digress... 
 The novel itself is fast paced and absolutely filled with action, and there is plenty of it to be had. The world building was clever, not too much like some fantasy novels out there, not too little to seem unconnected, but just enough to keep you turning the pages. 
 I loved the Dragon. I loved the dynamic between him and Agnieszka. Yes sure, he treated her in a cold way, but not in a sexually charged cold way. He genuinely thought she was an idiot....and truth be told, she did very little to dissuade him. 
 Everything that developed between them, happened trough a long period of time, it grew slowly, but naturally and it was awesome to watch. 
 As the magical villains go, I think the Wood is in top ten faves of all times. There is something truly sinister I think, when you can't put a face on something that is hell bent on killing you. A true evil, that lies within every person, waiting to be let out, rather than a simple guy in spandex wearing a distractingly elaborate hairpiece. 
 This has been so far a good year for me, book wise. I haven't had many duds. It makes me happy to no end, to see that fantasy is picking up speed. I am aware that there are a handful of authors out there who made it big and inspired more and more people in the genre, and I am glad, as it turns out - there are many very talented authors out there, and in a world filled with magic, not even the sky is the limit.

 I've read some good book so far this year, but nothing that has really stood out. Unbecoming, while not what I was expecting, is easily my favorite book of the year so far. 
 I love a good character-driven novel and this definitely fits the bill. I didn't find this quite as suspenseful as the synopsis makes it sound, nor is it an exciting heist story. If you're looking for those elements, Unbecoming may be lacking for you, but for me the character study completely made up for it. Grace is a young woman hiding from her old life. She is the root of the reason that her secret husband and his best friend has been in jail for three years and lives in fear of them coming back for revenge. This is the overall plot, but the real story is just Grace herself. 
 It is not an easy thing for such an unlikable character to be compelling, even sympathetic, but Scherm really pulls it off. While there were a few times in the book where I completely loathed Grace, overall I really did like disliking her. She is not the psychopath you might find in a Gillian Flynn novel, but a quieter kind of pathological. She's selfish, a liar, and a thief, but you would never know it until you really get to know her. And she's smart enough to never let that happen. Told in alternate timelines, we meet Grace as Julie the amateur art-restorer in Paris. Interwoven with her present life in Paris, we travel back to Grace growing up in Tennessee, to her college semester in New York, and to her return to Tennessee as she tries to desperately live the life she's always wanted. 
 While the synopsis makes it sound that the robbery is the focal point of the novel, it's more of the midpoint. There is Grace Before it happened and Grace After it happened. The real psychological suspense aspect for me didn't come until the final part of the book when one of Grace's biggest fears come to fruition. There is no dramatic climax or fight scene or narrow get away. The story continues at it's methodical pace and I really had no idea what was going to happen next, how it was all going to turn out. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Unbecoming. One of my few complaints of the novel is the information overload of antiques/art and the restoration process. There were many times where less information would have gone a long way and one of those instances where it felt like the author had done a lot of research and wanted to make sure it was all useful. Other than that, I loved the style, the alternating timelines, the character development, and even how truly unlikable the characters were. I would definitely recommend this book to fans of character-driven novels and I look forward to reading whatever Scherm comes up with next.

 Judging this book by its cover: 
 Holy hotness, Batman. 
 Plot/Execution: 
 I absolutely loved the plot of this book! It was pretty much a 'scorned woman leaves everything she knows to start over from scratch' story. In this case, it's Tess, and she's left New York City and chosen a random little town in California to begin her new life. She ends up on a ranch, which she knows nothing about. Except that the owner's son, Ward, is hot as hell. 
 I thought the pacing of this story was perfect. The characters didn't meet and fall into bed two and a half pages later. I felt like there was a nice build to their relationship. They both were scarred from their pasts, but neither of them were bitter about it. I really liked that aspect of the story, as sometimes I feel as though main characters hold onto things for too long. Tess was a bit skittish, but I feel like she really grew as a character during the story. 
 It was a fun to see Tess learning about ranch life and the way Ward coaxed her into trying new things. 
 I loved that though Ward wasn't too keen on having a serious relationship again, as soon as he realized how special Tess was to him, he let it go and wanted to be with her. I don't typically like a 'jealous ex-' in a story, but I really think it worked here. I think it gave more depth to Ward's character and helped you see just how much he cared for Tess. 
 Also--I love, love, love when one of the characters is from away, and near the end of the story, they return home heartbroken. Mainly because I love it when the other party shows up and declares their love! The scene in this one was set up nicely, and I really love that Ward asked her parents permission before he proposed to Tess.  
 I also appreciated the accuracy with which the author portrayed a character with autism. I think a great deal of research went into that aspect of the story. 
 Characters: 
 As I said before, I really liked the characters in this story. It was easy to relate to Tess, as I think, at some point we've all beat ourselves up for our past mistakes, and I loved Ward's easygoing nature and how he was so patient with Tess. He never pushed her to reveal more about herself than she wanted to. 
 I loved this book and would definitely recommend it if you love cowboy stories or stories about someone starting over!

When we neared the end of the novel, which we'd been going through at a moderate pace of a couple chapters a night, I refused to go to bed until my husband had read straight through to the end -- all of about six chapters.  Walk on Earth a Stranger may just be the best YA Western I've read so far. It's all I ever asked for bundled into an exciting adventure that had flipping pages as fast as I could. Fair warning though, this book won't be everyone's cup of tea. 
 For as long as I can remember, reading books that feature journeys has been *my* thing. I mean lots of things are my thing, but I always find myself craving a good old adventure. Across a country, to the top of the mountains, WHEREVER. I love living vicariously through characters journeying to some place and reading about the hardships they have to overcome. But that is just me as a reader and not everyone wants to read an entire book reading about a character's journey. Some people will want more. 
 I don't have much to go on but I have noticed that all the YA Westerns I've read so far, parents seem to die and I am not sure how I feel about this trope. Wouldn't it be nice if parents actually got to live and if there were other catalysts to inspire these journeys across the wild west? There were a bunch of other tropes but I kind of just moved on from them once we got to the actual journey bits. That's when the book REALLY just grabbed my attention and I COULDN'T STOP. 
 Leah is a fantastic main character. I loved reading about her, I loved being inside of her head and I LOVED getting to be a part of her journey. When her parents are suddenly killed and it becomes obvious that her uncle, her new guardian was responsible, Leah decides to run. Leah is smart. A lot of female leads are smart, but I love that Leah is not someone who rushes things. When she decided to run away from her uncle, she actually decided to stay an extra couple days so she could plan and get things ready. She also knows how to take care of herself but realizes that when running away, groups are better than individuals. 
 This book also features a diverse set of characters which is awesome. We have the "confirmed bachelors", we have Hamptom who is a slave and Leah's best friend Jeff who is half Native American and thus has to deal with with a lot of prejudice and resist the urge to punch people (or was that just me?) 
 What I loved about this book is that it not only featured diverse characters, it also addressed a lot of important issues of the time. The book brought up the injustices being committed against various races by the Caucasians (trying to be PC here and not say white people) and it also showed us instances of where assholes did horrible things because of their assumed superiority. 
 The writing was also terrific although I did find myself sometimes slipping into the 'cowboy slang' from Vengeance Road. If you read my review for Vengeance Road, you'll know that the cowboy slang had actually bothered me in the beginning, but here I was finishing off certain sentences the way they would have been if this book were written in the same style as Vengeance Road. Having said that, I thought the writing style was perfectly suited to the situation and really did make me feel like I was right in the middle of it all, journeying across the continent with Leah and company. 
 The book also has a slight fantasy aspect, given Leah's gold-detecting powers but their origin wasn't really explored and to be honest, it really didn't bother me that it wasn't. I didn't need the answers to all the questions and I was okay letting her powers be (especially since there were so many other awesome things happening.) 
 There is also a subtle romance in the book. My shippy senses were already tingling as soon as I was introduced to the two characters so to finally see my ship sail towards the end of the book made me so happy! It's a friends-to-more kind of romance and it just made sense given how well they (yes, I am purposefully avoiding naming who the love interest is) worked together and how supportive they were of each other. 
 As I mentioned earlier, this book is all about the journey. In fact, after the first 20 percent or so, the entire book IS the journey Leah makes from her town in Georgia to Sacramento, California. The journey was so well written and SO DETAILED. I was FANGIRLING and was up until 5:00 in the morning reading the book! I literally couldn't take my eyes off the pages and all I wanted to know was what hardship they would have to face next and how they'd overcome it. I wanted to know how many people would make it to California (because people do die and it was heartbreaking.) 
 This book is perfect for readers who enjoy stories of survival and adventure. It is detailed, heartbreaking and at the same time manages to fill you with so much joy. I LOVE THIS BOOK and maybe you will too! 
 Note that I received an advanced copy of this book for review in exchange for an honest review

The plot for this novel was a bit...odd. Odd, but it really got me interested in the book and the main character, Jane Solis. 
 Jane is suicidal and is planning to kill herself on her plane trip home to New Jersey, but before she can, her plane crashes. And she survives. Jane Solis is probably the luckiest fictional person who ever lived. 
 Jane isn't alone at the crash site though, as fellow passenger Paul Hart has survived the crash, too. 
 OK, I knew from the moment that I read the Goodreads description that Paul was going to die. It said, "Only one will live..." for pete's sake. And I knew it wouldn't be Jane who died, because she's the main protagonist and the book is from her POV...so it would be strange if she died. 
 I'm just gonna cut straight to the part where she left Paul to save herself. I was having a full-scale crying attack by this time. When it got to the epilogue and she confirmed what I'd feared, that Paul had died, I through my e-reader on the floor and ran into the first person I could find. 
  
 The only things that were 'bad' about this book was that it was quite short for my liking, and there weren't very many characters.

I loved every little bit of this. The dialogue was so fun, and I very much enjoyed the friendship between Albus and Scorpius.

The copy of the book I read was a pre-publication version-- I only mention this in case I quote, though I usually don't.

She finds out several things about her family, so much that it might be a tad too much, but really it was all a good part of the story. It actually had a twist that I didn't see coming, though maybe I should've (That he human mother was actually not her human mother but was in fact a witch. Her step-sister that also attends Pennyroyal also turns out to be a witch but she had no idea-- that I don't think I would've caught even if I did pick up on the human mother being a witch).  Her male counterpart, Remington, is also really a great match for Evie. 
 I like the concept of the school overall as well were people can go to train to be princesses that do battle against witches, not just sit in a tower and be pretty. Knights are the boy counterpart to princesses (they battle dragons) and usually they are of royal blood. The twist in this storyline is that since there are so many witches to battle that the school is allowing admission of non-royals to train to become princesses and knights which is how Evie gets in. A brief mention of note is that there is one boy character who is training as a princess rather than a knight due to his mother's wishes of birthing one girl. It makes a small statement, but nothing that stands out. The school is immensely harsh, however, as a lot of characters (many unnamed) get cut from the program. This is due to the character needed in order to battle witches and dragons. 
 Overall it was a well-rounded storyline with strong characters. I would definitely recommend for girls of the age group (probably ages 8+ depending on reading level of child), but would recommend to any friend who likes a different tale on fantasy.

My mother and I had a deep discussion about that state of feminism a few weeks back (while walking my fat lovable dog Molly down a trail, it was definitely a ladies day out.) "I don't think I would consider myself a feminist," my mother replied when I asked her how she felt about the subject. 
 "Well too bad, mom, because you are one no matter what you say," I responded. I held up three fingers, " One: You went to college for criminal justice and not just to get married. Two: You have had a full time job your entire life while simultaneously raising three children. Three: Never once did you ever consider that you wouldn't work, and you have never felt like it was ONLY your responsibility to take care of us and the household. Dad is a feminist too. He has never tried to control you, my dear mother, and you have a equal partnership in your marriage. Women before feminism were considered to be what Molly is to us: a man's property." 
 My mother sighed, "I guess I am a feminist then." (I never understand that whenever I finally convince someone that she is indeed a feminist, she always seem to sigh, like it's a 'gotcha' moment. HA! I fooled you! You are actually interested in your rights as a person! You like voting and getting an education! I mean SERIOUSLY, it's not like you just discovered that you have aids.) 
 "How to be a Woman" by Caitlin Moran is a hilariously look at what it is to be a modern woman. So when you read this book expect lots of period/ Brazilian wax jokes (which, trust me is a good thing.) Moran does make quite a case of feminism, by asking A. Do you have vagina? B. Do you want to be in charge of it? Because that is what feminism is, women in control of their own lives. On the other side of the coin, if you are a woman who thinks that your husband should make all your life/ reproductive health decisions for you, then congrats, you are not a feminist. 
 This is not a hard decision ladies. 
 But then again, every woman seems to be rejecting the idea nowadays. It's like if African Americans started rejecting the civil rights movement. 
 So recommend this book for everyone..... 
 Yes, men especially.

As I'm sure you all know by now, I have a soft spot for a good zombie book. I will be damned if FEED was not one of the absolute best zombies novels -hell, novels in general- that I've ever had the pleasure of reading. DEADLINE has been a continued roller coaster of emotion regarding the beloved After the End Times news crew and I never wanted, for one second, to put this book down. 
 That, my friends, is the trademark of a good novel. When a person will, quite literally, debate on whether or not having dinner is as important as reading the next chapter...Well, you know you've written a damned good story. DEADLINE is a fantastic novel that I cannot praise highly enough. 
 DEADLINE picks up one year after the end of FEED. If you remember what happened at the end of FEED, you'll remember who our main character is and why. The whole After the End Times crew is still around, except for the few who were lost during FEED or who, during the last year, took off to do "important things" like become Vice President of the United States. As usual, we open on someone poking a dead thing with a stick. Okay, well, it's actually a crowbar, but you get the point. There are zombies, and we're poking them. 
 The action takes off from there, and never lets up for a second. Unearthing conspiracies that possibly span the globe? Check. Sexual encounters? Check. "Haunted houses"? Check. There's also escaping from locked down medical facilities, epileptic teacup bulldogs, and cross-country road trips. This book has just about everything one could want from a good sci-fi thriller. 
 Grant has really done some amazing things with the character development in this installation of the Newsflesh trilogy. We get to meet a few characters in person who, in FEED, were nothing but voices on the phone or faces in a video conference. It's refreshing to see their mannerisms, and learn about their pasts. Shaun, for one, has become one of my favorite characters. He learns so much in this book: about the world, about himself, and about Georgia. 
 The last hundred pages of DEADLINE left me feeling as though I'd been punched in the gut a few times, with the end of the story a giant "what the fuck?" cliffhanger. Grant has an amazing way of making the reader care for these characters, care that they live, and care about the fact that they or their families die. She's done a wonderful job turning characters who started out in the background in FEED to main players in DEADLINE, and making one care about them so much that it moves the reader to tears. 
 I don't think that Grant should have done anything differently with DEADLINE. This book was amazing, and an excellent continuation of the Newsflesh trilogy. I know that I will be reading this book, and FEED, again before BLACKOUT releases next year. Probably a few times, if I'm to be honest. I'm looking forward to the conclusion of the story, but at the same time I'm so sad for it to come to an end.

What I learned is that I like Star Wars books that do not focus on the characters from the movies. Because I read this, and Revan is a total badass. From reading other reviews I can see that apparently these characters are from a video game, but I know nothing about this, and it therefore cannot influence my opinion. 
 What I do know: Revan is apparently just ridiculously powerful. When he was on the good guys he was able to totally demolish everyone in his path, including the Mandalorians. When he was brainwashed into working for the dark side, he almost annihilated the Jedi. And now that he is good, he is pretty much almost single-handedly trying to bring down the remaining Sith. It is pretty freaking cool. 
 As for the bad guys--Scourge is just so evil. It's like he needs to prove to everyone how evil he is, so he does all evil things all the time and refuses to do anything non-evil because evil is EVIL and evil is important, damnit! With that being said though, he was deliciously evil and fun to watch being evil. I couldn't deny that I secretly relished his dark deeds. 
 But really, what did it for me was the ending. Because my biggest issue with Star Wars universe novels is that they don't seem completely accurate to the movies, and that doesn't make sense to me. It is the founding basis for all of this expanded universe, so shouldn't it be accurate? 
 So when I was reading about Revan, I kept wondering how this was going to work--if Revan kills the Emperor, then how can Luke do it later? Unless it's a different Emperor? But then it ended in such a perfectly suitable way, so much so that it actually makes sense and makes for accurate reading! Plus it is an awesome ending just because it is so far from what I was expecting, and I was just so excited about that.  Scourge and Revan team up to try and defeat the Emperor because he has this mad idea about defeating the Jedi without actually having the means to do so yet. But then Scourge has his first ever vision, and it is of him and Revan dying at the Emperor's feet, so he decides to do some last minute changes. He strikes out at Revan instead of the Emperor, and cementing himself inside the Emperor's inner circle. Which was perfect, because Revan can't be the one to defeat the Emperor! Luke does it! So Revan being all powerful and insanely awesome and still surviving in some horrible suspended state is just freaking ridiculous and cool.  
 K I'm done gushing now. But this was a pretty awesome book and I like it and Star Wars is cool.

4.25 stars! 
 Wow. Wow. Wow. 
 I just finished reading Between Everything and Us, and the writing in it is just incredible. 
 When I got to about 80%, work got busy and I wasn't able to read like I wanted. A couple of times I picked up the novel with the intent to finish it (finally) just to get another item checked off my to-do list. Time-wise I suppose it wouldn't have taken very long...but Between Everything and Us demands every ounce of a reader's attention. Because if you try to rush it, you risk missing that word or phrase or sentence that's so beautiful, so special, that you may never read anything quite like it again. (In the last 20% alone, I swear I highlighted every other sentence.) Thus, this review is heavy on quotes because Rebecca Paula's words are WAY better than mine. 
 Now that I've raved about the writing sufficiently, I have to be honest regarding the storyline: it's frustrating! So, if you take this one on--and I think you should--be prepared to ride out a series of ups and downs. The following quotes illustrate what I'm talking about: 
 "We always feel so unfinished." 
 "...there's this huge void separating us. A void that we put there for whatever reason--rules, plans, pride." 
 "If we could get out of our way, then maybe we'd stand a chance together." 
 I've never understood the "he/she deserves better than me" mentality (maybe because I'm just selfish), but it must exist in real life because written about so much, right? In any case, that line of thinking is Beau's angle...mostly. Although he does "decide upon" Mati first, he's also the one continually pushing her away. 
 "Mati is a someday-girl, the one you're supposed to meet later when you're less of a prick and have your shit together. Someday girls are lost to idiots like me now, and if I'm being honest, they don't exist in the future either. Because there's a guy who is ready, who does know how to be an adult and can love a girl like Mati as much as she deserves. And those guys turn someday girls into forever girls and leave us losers to keep chasing after a string of hookups while we're stuck remembering the one perfect girl who got away." 
 The constant back and forth, push and pull, between main characters drove me crazy, and there's very little of them actually being together at the end. I like more of that, generally, to feel really convinced of a couple's longevity.  But since this appears to be series with interconnected characters, perhaps we'll see more of Beau and Mati in the future? They deserve more "happy" to balance out the apprehension, tension, and disappointment that each earned at the hands of the other. 
 In spite of the novel's frustrating trajectory, there are definitely some cute moments--my favorites being the fort-building and the trying out of pet names. 
 Like I said before, the writing really stood out in this novel. Truly, the author is in a league of her own when it comes to crafting unique descriptions. Mati (one of the main characters) is an artist, and the writing seems to reflect that same level of creativity and talent. Take the following quotes, for example: 
 *	"He moves like oil paint dries--slow--as if he might change me and needs time to decide the final picture." 
 *	"He's that drop of water that runs and seeps into the paper, smearing the other watercolors until they've run wild as well." 
 *	"That wild drop of water that's so oblivious to the way it ruins the plans of the colors that came before in careful strokes." 
 *	"The painting is monochromatic, white on white. That moment when you find yourself lost in a birch forest in the winter. The longer you stand there, searching for a way out, you realize that even white has shades of color." 
 *	"...they sky is still tinged with pink above the horizon. The whitecaps swell, half-hidden by a rolling fog. The large rocks hold everything together, dark markers dotting the coastline. They're giants, and at their feet lies a gorgeous beach..." 
 *	"The rain patters against the tent, slowly hugging the sides before each drop gathers speed and cascades to the ground." 
 While there are a ton of things to brag about when it comes to Between Everything and Us, at least two elements are left unexplained or dangling: I needed to hear more (from Beau's perspective) about Reagan and about Layla (Beau says the latter "doesn't matter"; is there a story there?). Also, there's some skipping ahead--usually just a week or so at a time--but I know that time gaps and fast-forwarding can be an issue for some readers. The technique didn't necessarily bother me, although I did want the main characters' relationship to progress faster. But that's the nature of romance, isn't it? Each adopts and moves forward at its own unique pace. 
 Verdict: 
 Despite infringing on a few of my "reader sensitivities," this one is a GREAT read. I've already put #2 in the series, Anything More Than Now, on my to-read list, and I look forward to tracking author Rebecca Paula's success!

I know I watched the movie in the 1980s and had the "Illustrated Classic" which I gave away through paperbackswap recently but I wanted the more in depth version.

I love this book. This is the type of book I read over and over again. It is a futuristic book in a future where there are no lies because everyone can read minds and you can't stop people from reading your mind once your mind is open. 
 If your mind isn't readable no one trusts you because they can't tell if you are lying or not. 
 Kira is a "Zero" or a person with a closed mind. She has one friend who still talks to her and who clearly likes her. 
 But then Kira discovers that she is different from everyone, and that she is very powerful. My main complaint with this book is that Kira seems over powered at points, but it was still an enjoyable read delving into the reactions that people have to things that are different from what they expect. 
 This story also has multiple YA romances as well, but Its not your typical love triangle. Its more along the lines of how real people deal with romance and how love changes and people change. 
 I would recommend this story to any young adult and I love the way this story deals with the problems that arise.

Soundless did an amazing job with the question: What if no one you knew could hear? And what if you were suddenly the only one who could? I was interested in and captivated by both the way Fei originally described her soundless environment and then later how she coped with suddenly knowing sound and being unable to explain just what all these sounds... sounded like. 
 The relationship between Fei and Li Wei is also well done, coming across as real rather than forced for the plot. But they are also not so hopelessly in love that the story becomes all about their relationship. The story is clean, with only a couple of non-descriptive kisses, and there is no bad language. 
 What took the story down from five stars was the ending. Up until the final chapters, it seemed as though Fei was going to be able to convince their village of the danger in staying where they were and thus rescue them from death. Instead,  the village is saved by Pixiu; up-until-then mythical guardians which the people managed to wake by passionately screaming . While this had been hinted at, it still felt out of place because of the lack of supernatural events prior to that. It also made me question why Fei had been needed in the first place. 
 While I didn't like the ending, I would still say that Soundless it worth the read. If for nothing else, the way sound is dealt with makes it interesting.
