I received a copy of Ready to Run via NetGalley. It does not impact my review. 
 I really enjoyed Ready to Run! It was exactly the sweet, lighthearted book I needed right now. 
 Jordan and Luke were both really likable main characters. I enjoyed getting to know each of them and how their relationship progressed throughout the book. It was a little bit of hate-to-love, which I always think is fun. They had several funny and sweet moments between them and I shipped it. I also really liked Jordan's co-worker/BFF, Simon, and all the townspeople of Lucky Hollow. I'm originally from a small town myself, so I always enjoy reading about them. 
 I loved the concept of the Bachelor-esque reality show. I'm not really a fan of that type of show myself, but I do like other kinds of reality tv and I love behind-the-scenes type stories. I was slightly disappointed that this book didn't really have much in terms of behind-the-scenes, though. It was more early pre-production. It didn't take me long to get over the disappointment, though, once I got into the book and invested in Jordan and Luke. 
 Maybe it's because I've recently read a couple of mammoth-sized books, but I kind of felt like this one was too short. I thought that there was more that could have been explored - more quirky townsfolk, more funny/cute moments between Jordan and Luke before the romance progressed, more information about the show, more information on Luke's jilted brides, more time spent on the heavier emotional topics (but not too much! I appreciated the lighthearted feel). I just enjoyed the story so much I wanted to spend more time with it. The only other thing I didn't really like were the sex scenes. There's only so much graphic detail I can take and still be able to take a book seriously and Layne's writing usually comes close to that line. I thought it was funny that in the "About the Author" section it says that "she writes romantic comedies with just enough sexy-times to make your mother blush." Just think of me as your more conservative mother. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Ready to Run. I loved the concept and the characters and never wanted the story to end. I'm very anxiously looking forward to the next book in the series. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 4 Stars

The reason why I "love" FMA is also the reason why I "hate" it. 
 To date, I have read 13 volumes of the manga. I started reading the first volume last March and it was only yesterday when I decided to continue reading from where I left off (volume two). 
 I was almost ready to stop reading this but decided that non-romantic stories would probably end my book dry spell. 
 The world/story of FMA is just wow. I really, really admire mangakas who could come up with such types of story. The truth is, I don't understand half of the alchemy jargons used in this manga but I am drawn nonetheless. 
 The thing with loving what I hate? It is how the author created his heroes (the Elric brothers). How often do we encounter stories where the hero is basically the strongest man of the bunch? FMA's Elric brothers are quite the contrary. I "love" how they get beaten up quite frequently and how it is obvious that the enemies are far above the brothers' league, it brings much realism to the story. There are times (and they are like 90% of the time) when I wish that Ed and Al would just get stronger and beat their enemies senseless but I would prefer them just the way they are. In being "imperfect" heroes, they get to rely on their comrades and this brotherhood is a sight to behold. Though of course, having to witness our heroes losing is frustrating and nerve-wracking 
 The thing is, one can't trust anyone in their world but the beauty lies in the fact that though the good guys are a few in numbers, these guys are the ones who will readily give their lives to save you. Isn't that amazing? 
 Full review to come as soon as I am done with the whole manga :)

First off, I don't know anything about the military--the ranks, the lifestyles, jokes, etc. Considering I live just outside DC where it seems everyone has retired from the military and moved onto their second career, I should know more. But I don't. I was a young teen when Vietnam ended so I don't really know more about that either. 
 So O'Brien has done a great job discussing and telling about the military life and the Vietnam war to someone who doesn't know the abbreviations, politics or the training. He doesn't get technical. 
 And he doesn't get mushy. Plenty of sad stories, of course, but they're presented with objectivity. It helps that it's a short book. 
 It was very creepy at one point when he's describing a man he killed with great detail, and I'm thinking, how can he look at this horrible face and know he was the cause of it? About 50 pages later, he writes, "Here is the happening-truth. I was once a solider. There were many bodies, real bodies with real faces, but I was afraid to look. And now, 20 years later, I'm left with faceless responsibility and faceless grief. 
 Here is the story-truth. He was slim, dead, almost dainty young man of about 20. He lay in the center of a red trail near the village of My Khe. His jaw was in his throat. His one eye was shut, the other eye was a star-shaped hole. I killed him." 
 He talks about what war stories are and what they aren't. In the end, of course, a true war story isn't about war. I've always wonder about war stories that are too heroic, too wrapped up. 
 Really great writing--he captures the essences of life.

Tam is a teenage widow. After dropping out of school, marrying her musician boyfriend, moving into a cabin in his parents backyard, and planning an adventurous life with him she is suddenly confronted with her husband's untimely death. Now her whole life is off track and she must figure out who she is without him or if she was ever really herself with him. 
 If I can say anything about this book, other than that I really enjoyed it, it is that it has a real authenticity about it. It tackles some tough issues and I have to applaud it for not taking the most obvious or politically correct route when dealing with these issues. Tam is a young bride. Tam drops out of school. Tam gets into legal trouble. Tam has a relationship with a guy nearly 10 years her senior. There was a lot of opportunity for this book to be overly sad and mopey, but Tam's experiences (the good, the bad, and the ugly) make this a much more tangible read. This book also hosts a bevy of colorful and interesting characters that each, very uniquely, help Tam in the aftermath of her husband's death. The character development was very good. Even Noah, Tam's dead husband, who we only learn about through her memories, their big plans, and the people who knew and loved him felt like he was every bit part of the story as any living character. 
 I know there will inevitably be people who read this and turn up their nose at the fact that 17-year-old Tam gets involved with the 26-year-old Colin during her grieving period. There will be hands on hips and scornful glares. There will undoubtedly be cries for authors not to romanticize statutory rape to an impressionable audience. But I don't at all think that is the case here. I'm not saying this relationship between these two characters is right or wrong, I'm saying it's real. Each is a broken character dealing with a heartache unique to both of them and, to me, it seems natural that this sort of melancholy would drive them to find solace in one another. YA is littered with stories of perfectly packaged romances between starry-eyed boys and manic pixie dream girls. It's rife with love at first sight and love triangles that inevitably conclude in the most predictable way possible. Isn't it time for something genuine? Tam and Colin felt like it had integrity, to me at least, and the fact that they don't ride off into the sunset together at the end  makes it all the more genuine. And, for that matter, we really need to give actual young adult readers of YA more credit - they're not as impressionable as we like to pretend they are. 
 Oh yes, and this was an ARC via NetGalley provided to me for an honeset review. It was definitely a solid read that I heartily enjoyed so, thank you NetGalley!

"Please," she said, unable to keep the quiver from her voice. "I've done everything you said. I've been cooperative. Please tell me where my children are." Whiteside held her gaze. "What children," he asked. 
 Haylen Beck is the pseudonym of a well-known crime novelist and screenwriter, and his writing skills became instantly obvious as he quickly drew me in with the opening chapter to Here and Gone. It starts innocently enough. A young woman is driving along a lonely desert road with her two children in the back. She is trying to escape an abusive marriage, hoping to make a new start with a friend in California. But when she looks in the rearview mirror she sees a police car following her, flashing its lights, forcing her to move over. The sheriff tells her that her car is overloaded and asks her to step out of the vehicle, leaving her children in the back seat. She is scared. 
 He is an officer of the law. 
 He is armed. 
 He has all the power. 
 And her nightmare is only just beginning ... 
 I loved Beck's ability to paint the opening scene with the type of technicolour clarity of a bad dream, playing out in every small and terrible detail in my mind. The long, hot, lonely road. The sour taste of fear in Audra's mouth as she spots the police cruiser in her rearview mirror. The crunch of tires and spray of dust as she pulls over onto the side of the road. The slow walk of the sheriff, eyes hidden behind dark sunglasses, hands on his gun belt, as he makes his way over to her. "Please step out of the car." It sent a shiver down my spine imagining myself in the same situation! With such an imbalance in power, what options does Audra have other than to comply and follow the sheriff's orders? Her absolute horror and panic when she realises that her children are being taken away by a stranger is palpable in every written word. Beck's portrayal of a woman with her back against the wall as no one believes her is well drawn, as is the moment Audra summons her inner tiger-mother and begins to fight back. 
 With its claustrophobic atmosphere and constant sense of menace and danger to our hapless protagonist, Here and Gone was reminiscent of a Lee Child novel - I was waiting for Jack Reacher to come to Audra's rescue and kick some butt! Instead, we get Danny Lee, a fascinating character I absolutely loved! He would definitely make a worthy vigilante for many more future novels yet to come. Danny appeared at exactly the very moment in the book where I feared it would go down the conspiracy theory track, and immediately snapped my attention back into focus. 
 Perhaps my only gripe with the story was that it gave away too much too early, which took some of the thrill factor away. I am trying not to give any spoilers here, but basically we know very early on who is behind the children's abduction, and there are no surprises in store in that regard. A lot more suspense could have been created had the author kept back that bit of information until much later - there were certainly plenty of opportunities to create other suspects in the reader's mind. Instead, with the mystery solved, the story turns into a race against time to find the missing children, and I had plenty of faith in Danny Lee that this would be accomplished. That said, there was still plenty of action and a nail-biting finale that made it well worth reading on for! 
 Here and Gone is a fast -paced and atmospheric thriller which will appeal to fans of the Jack Reacher series and similar novels. Personally, I hope for a return of Danny Lee in future books, as he made for an intriguing protagonist worthy of a lot more missions. 
 Thank you to Netgalley and the publisher for the free electronic copy of this novel and for giving me the opportunity to provide an honest review.

The Baudelaire children being in the belly of the beast and the bad weather have given me a cold, which forces my brain to stop working quickly as I rest in bed, but does not stop me from reading this book on my hour-long ride home from work. 
 I like the setting at a carnival and the group of "freaks" who made me go "huh?", "wait..." and "really." about their freakiness. As usual, Lemony Snicket brings insight to word meanings, while putting the three young children through the least imaginable troubles. 
 The series has yet to end, meaning they all get away for now... but the children are getting closer to finding out about VFD, and a possible survivor of the fire.

These books were fun, even if the magic was all over the place.  Some Gods needed hosts, some didn't. Bast needed a (cat) host at first, but then didn't? Osiris needed a host although he was in the underworld?

Was up until 2:30am reading this bad boy. So much running around my head about this book! 
 Really great book, another fantastic addition to an interesting series that seems to draw me in that little bit more with each book. 
 Only thing to say is this book would have been a 4.5 stars if it wasn't that for that bit near the very end very disappointing for me although it didn't ruin it it did put a dampener on the book for me. 
 For a full review go read someone else's because their are a ton of reviews out on this book that could sum it up better than I ever could! 
 Behind with my reviews from September as I had a week's vacation and didn't review or blog a thing and struggled to get back into reviewing since.

Just finished my second read of Wolves, and i enjoyed it (like Wizard and Glass and Wind Through the Keyhole) much better the second time through. And listening to the audiobook really just submerges you into Mid-World. Such a clever, sometimes disjointed, series.

Normally I don't like to read plays because it disrupts my flow. I did run into that problem a little but there's not much that you can do about that. I enjoyed seeing a little bit more about the next generation. I really like Scorpius and the fact that  Harry finally told Dumbledore off for leaving him with is abusive Aunt and Uncle . I loved Ron and Herminone's relationship, it was rather sweet. I was floored at the villain. But all in all it was pretty good.

This novel was bought on a whim by my boyfriend in the second hand store; I love paranormal and romance combined and I could not put this novel down until I finished it however it was poorly written, poor concept, and weak characters.

I really liked it. It was very different and interesting. 
 I enjoyed the characters, they weren't boring and they all a little funny. 
 I'm excited to see where the 2nd book goes.

All the strong reviews backing this book up are true. I think what makes this book so good is just all the balance it has to it's story. Starr, our main character, balances life between a white prep school and her home in the ghetto. We get two sides to her story/life and it really helps an outsider see how one affects the other. Adding to this is the balance of Starr's family and friendships. She has a loving relationship with each of her family members, from her parents to her younger brother and older half-brother. She has friends from her neighborhood and friends from her school. She acts one way to her black friends and another way to white (and Asian) friends, all while still being herself, just one side or the other. She struggles a little bit with who she is because of it, but it also makes her a strong, smart character. Throughout the story she learns more about herself and exhibits a very believable growth along the way. 
 I think each person who reads this book can pull something a little different out of it, but for me it was to always consider perspectives of other people. It's easy to fall into traps of thinking only one way, but it's important to think past that and consider the side of everyone involved.

I feel like I need to give this bonus stars for featuring Jane Austen! I loved seeing the ton reading her books - especially the Duchess. I got a big kick out of it. The mystery was a good one, but it felt rushed toward the end. The confrontation with the killer was a little bit of a letdown to be honest. 
 I was excited to have Jamie Knox appear again. I am desperate to know his connection to Sebastian and am glad the next book will explore that relationship. I'm glad I picked it up from the library already!
Review to be posted when I get my $h!t together (sigh)

I enjoyed this book a bit. especially at the beginning but towards the middle (when she decided to take over Hell and overthrow all the overlords including the devil ) it became disgusting and tiring. 
 It's funny in some places but really annoying most of the time

Mercy is probably the most realistic BDSM story I have read so far. It was quite refreshing to read romantic book which was not so lovey-dovey. Moreover, the storyline was truly unexpected. Every coin has two sides and it is the same with this story. On the one side, I found their relationship disturbing and I had hard time to connect with characters. But on the other side, whole story was untraditional, interesting and it was hard to put down. 
 Lucy, main female character, has her dancing but otherwise she is unhappy woman who is confused with her life. She was confident about herself outside but very unsure inside. Mathew, main male character, was very rough and cruel with words at the beginning. As Dom, he was very strict and there were times I didn't know what to think about their relationship. 
 Mercy is a dark story. I was not OK with some stuff they were doing (especially sharing) , but the whole book was definitely very interesting. This story was also excellent example of how being untruthful may mess up with your life in various, usually terrible, ways. If you are not afraid to read some darker stuff, this book is perfect choice for you. But I was glad for ending, it balanced whole story in the best possible way. 
 My favourite quote: 
  
 "You know why they call it falling, Lucy? Why they call it falling in love? Because it is completely out of your control. And I hate being out of control."

I love this book as well as the other 3 in the Jessica Darling series by Megan McCafferty. I always enjoy books that are written diary or journal style and Jessica Darling's journal entries are funny and witty.

3 stars 
 I wanted to love this book - I really did. The concept is fantastic, and the story/plot itself wasn't bad. Unfortunately it just wasn't pulled off in the execution. 
 You can tell Mandanna is a first time writer just a little too painfully. Characters that are meant to be complex but come across contradictory, or are flat and obnoxious. Thoughts and emotions that need to be explained rather than revealed. A clear lack of connection between the echo and the other (and I don't just mean bc they don't like each other - shouldn't there be more of a thread?) And unfortunately, not enough backstory or any sense of like ability for the practice of weaving. Why does it exist? 
 I'm not saying she's a terrible writer, just too underdeveloped to give this story the proper telling. At least it's not sloppy, lazy or just plain awful like some other wannabes that are cashing in on the YA craze. I give her full props for trying to tell a fresh and original story, and hope that her writing will mature to give her ideas the voice they deserve.
I have a tip for those who wants to read this story or are already doing just that. - Alcohol helps!

What can I say about this book without given away spoilers for a new book. It is well written but that kind of goes without saying when you talk about Sanderson. The only complaint I have is I now have so many questions that I want answered and I have to wait, I honestly hope this is not going to be a trilogy and there will be more books expanding the world and pseudoscience involved in it because I don't know how one more book could do it.
A quick read on the nature of temptation, guilt, and influence.

This is a magical realism book with a bit of magic in the baking. Rose can taste emotions - and this affects her entire normal-but-not-really life. 
 Yes, it's a slice-of-life book. Yes, it's magical-realism. Yes, there really isn't that much of a plot. Yes, some of these characters are downright weird. 
 ... but I loved it anyway. 
 I come into this story entirely biased. I had my fingers pressed to my mouth for almost the entire book. It was too close of a mirror for me, it hit home a little too closely. Not in all ways, no of course not. But the younger sister who is a bit of a pest and trails behind because she doesn't want to disturb. The smarter older brother who fades away. A family that is not quite, but just slightly dysfunctional. I don't normally like slice-of-life books - but when it can evoke such emotion from me... Well. 
 And those real life things aside, like I've said before, I've always had a soft spot for food based books. And this one is no different. This is such a sad book, heart wrenching, tinged with sadness. Even the ending is so sad. Oh my gosh. Oh my gosh. 
 Yeah, of course there are a lot of flaws. There is a crazy wtf scene when  Joe turned into a chair . That was just like... are you serious? I was with you all the way until there. But I took it with a (huge) grain of salt and treated it as if  he really did disappear, like a suicide or something  and the book was just as strong. 
 It gets a little crazy (what the f is this author smoking?), but I love the silent tension. It's in the silences, in the things that the dad just can't say, in the mom's crazy talk, in the emotions. 
 It's about finding yourself despite the differences. 
 Also, note: I am super snobby about books - if it gets less than 4 stars on goodreads (which self-selects for higher ratings), I usually give it a hard pass. Heck, even if it's a high 4 stars and the one star reviews are unhappy enough, I pass. But here, I loved this book. 
 3.5 stars, rounded up. 
 -edit- 
 I reread this and still loved it; maybe it's a straight up 4 stars.

Wake has an interesting premise, okay plot line, poor writing, and no character development, and in those ways reminded me of a James Patterson novel. There are millions of people over the world who love books like this, and it's no harm I guess, really. From about the fifth page, when I realized the date, time, choppy third person narration wasn't going to go away, I thought, wow, this is going to be a really terrible book. And it was. Janie gets sucked into people's dreams when she is close to them, whether she is awake or asleep, and these dreams are mostly really simple, often to do with fantasy sex, and don't really have anything to do with the plot. Then she meets a boy, sees his dreams, and then won't talk to him. This "romance" back and forth-ing is what makes up most of the short novel. Things get resolved easily at the end but it's hard to care.
Yeah...this one was much better than volume 1. Onto volume 3! I really want to continue with the rest of the series!
Still a solid YA book, but nowhere near as good as its predecessor. While Rebel Belle felt fresh and new, Miss Mayhem dragged at points and seemed too reliant on unnecessary relationship drama.

I really enjoyed this book. He touches on some excellent writing ideas and really deals with his own approach. He's a cheerleader in some places, but I think it was all genuine. He wants to help. A good portion of the book is autobiographical, but this doesn't take away too much from the writing lessons found there too. 
 For those say, yeah but it's Stephen King. He also has a clear grip on who he is as a writer. He's not under any illusions of being a literary giant.
It wasn't bad but it wasn't amazing. I don't know. I guess I was just hoping for some background of the characters a little more and character development. But it wasn't that bad.

Just finished "The Voyage of the Dawn Treader," and it doesn't hold a candle to "The Lion the Witch and the Wardrobe." So many folks have such fond things to say about this chapter in the Narnia cycle that I feel like a cad offering less-than-glowing comments. But it just wasn't very good. The characters don't grow or change; the plot wanders aimlessly and at great length. More importantly, it doesn't really have much to say about the issues it strives to raise: faith, fellowship, doing what's right, redemption. Hours after finishing it, I struggle to recall much of anything, beyond Lucy's nauseating infatuation with Aslan. She really sounds like an obsessive fan-girl whenever he deus-ex-machinas into the story. 
 Lest you think my opinion isn't valid because I'm a jaded old fart and this is [trying to be] a story for children, my young kids weren't too thrilled with it, either. They much prefer Charlie Bone, Half Magic, Dragon Rider and a dozen other books. 
 I don't doubt that adults have fond memories of this story from childhood. Some of the books in this series are still favorites of mine. Looked at honestly, "Voyage of the Dawn Treader" is a lesser work that suffers in comparison to these others, but is none-to-good even on its own terms.

I feel so bad because I should've read Delirium first. I did not understand this story... I mean I got it but not completely. It was very confusing because I didn't know who the characters where or what was happening to them or why. 
 I have a feeling that if I read Delirium first I'd really like and/or appreciate this book. I will re-read this soon... after I read Delirium and maybe I'd change my mind on this. 
 Also... I read this first because I thought this was a prequel to the book but it isn't. It's like a pre-sequel. So shame on me. :(

For a moment there, I was like, wait! Are these characters actually going to date?! In the first volume?! Hahaha, no. Anyway, the male love interest isn't really developed, aside from "he's a jerk! but cute!" and also some kind of sad backstory. I didn't really like him.

Lovely. A wonderful premise, a slightly dark and creepy story, quick pacing, vibrant characters. The novella dealt with themes related to belonging and identity - all these children who have fallen back through their portals feel like they don't belong in our world anymore - which were handled beautifully. 
 And I do have to specifically mention the inclusion of diverse characters -- in particular, the protagonist, Nancy, is asexual. And that's rare-beyond-rare to see in a book, but so important. (If better visibility can save even one person from the kind of meltdown I had this year...it's more than worth it).

** spoiler alert ** 
 What a crazy ride and roller coaster of a book. Interesting concept, interesting situations with all hell breaking loose within a single book. I say this isn't a kind of book every person can enjoy. I happen to enjoy reading books that require me to put aside my morals and read mindlessly once in a while. If you're in for anything biblical while reading this book, I recommend you stay away from it. 
 I swear Kiera was a character that I was shouting at and cursing at most through the course of the entire book. I have to say these characters aren't particularly deep nor is their love. Still, it was an engrossing read. S.C. Stephens manages to write well and drew out a perfect love triangle with all kinds of immoral things. Thoughtless is the one with most angst that I have ever read till now. It was super duper crazy (can't think of any other word to describe it). 
 Kellan and Keira's story starts out very unlike how usual love stories do. It starts off with cheating, progresses through lying, hatred, contempt, jealousy, revenge and what-not. It didn't let me down except it was way TOO long. I felt like towards the end the author wrapped up the story neatly. She gave some time for her characters to breathe and for us too. 
 This was a very guilty pleasure kind of a read. I personally prefer these kinds of books to Fifty Shades-type books which never convince me of the love the characters have as opposed to obsessive lust. For me, when I am reading sex scenes I should feel excited and turned on rather than sick and turned off which happens with erotica. So I tend to avoid them as much as I can. 
 I think I only kept going for Kellan. He seriously sounds like a Greek God in this book. If only he was real *drools*. I was as addicted to him as much as Keira was. Lots of aspects about this book were also forced too fictional to seem true, but in its defense it was a lot more realistic than an average erotica. -_- 
 I loved another thing which was that it wasn't just the guy hurting the girl over and over. It's like, they hurt both each other equally by doing some wild and downright horrible things. Some moves like, when Keira slept instantly with Denny after 'making love' to Kellan made me cringe. So did Kellan's manwhoring. 
 I will read the next two books too because I want more of Kellan. I happened to read spoilers that Keira matures later on so yay for that. I recommend this to any female who doesn't mind dirty affairs and has a free weekend to indulge on something that gives you lots of guilty pleasure.

Five full stars for the quality of writing and the in depth feelings I ended up having with each of the very interesting characters. At first I wasn't sure I liked the writing... I'm not a fan of speaking parts in books without quotations. A silly peeve to have I'm sure, but after a few chapters, I became mesmerized with how the author really brought me into the story. Each character was brought to life, whether you liked one or not, and in a way that I could picture every detail. To me, it was a slow burn that was worth the wait. You decide if it's worth yours but I would highly recommend this read.

Don't Look Back By Jennifer L. Armentrout is a unique stand alone that will take your brain on a thrilling chase, full of mystery in every chapter. 
 After reading the first book to the Luxen series, I knew I just had to check this out. Although it was nothing like Armentrout's usual paranormal- romance genre, knowing Armentrout's talent for telling stories, I knew this was a story I couldn't miss. This story follows a girl, found wandering in the middle of the street with no recollection of where she had disappeared off to or what had happened to her. In addition to that, her bestfriend had also gone missing and everyone claimed that they were last seen together. 
 The general concept of the plot was rather intriguing although I couldn't help but notice a couple of similarities to the Mara Dyer trilogy. Girl-goes-missing, girl- is- found-with- no- idea- about- what- happened- to- her, guy- falls-for- her- and- is- supportive- of- her- unfortunate- situation... following me here. However, I do acknowledge and appreciate the elements unique to this story. This plot followed an entirely different social class compared to the Mara Dyer trilogy- the high class, the rich, the elites of ... high school- so one can only imagine the different personalities of numerous secondary/ supporting characters that would emotionally challenged the main protagonist, but I'll get to that later. 
 I did find the plot entertaining and it really did live up to the genre of the book. I was reading this book around 2am and it did give me quite a scare especially towards the end. I don't easily get so scared when it comes to thriller books but this book got to me so that was a big thumbs up! 
 The characters of this novel were interesting, but didn't quite stand out to me. The main protagonist, Samantha, became a bit of a Mary- Sue as the book progressed, but she did have a good backstory. On the other hand, the love interest, Carson Ortiz, (yes, this is a J.L. Armentrout novel so romance is expected) was a bit stereotypical and predictable. The way the relationship developed and the way the love triangle unfolded seems to happen quite a bit in books that follow this genre so I honestly was not impressed. 
 As I had mentioned before, the secondary/ supporting characters did emotionally challenge the main protagonist quite a bit and I found some parts quite amusing and mildly entertaining. Then, there were just some parts that were just so mean that I actually felt the struggle. It would've been nice to know what had happened to the supporting characters after the revelations of the plot had taken place. I think it would've been nice to see them get what they deserved. 
 Overall, Don't Look Back by Jennifer L. Armentrout would be a great pick around Halloween because it could give you quite a scare. This was one of the few books that live up to the hype. It was entertaining and it surely will keep you guessing. Although the characters wasn't quite relatable, they were surely entertaining. If Jennifer L. Armentrout wrote a book within the same genre as this (but hopefully not one with a similar concept), I would definitely check it out. I would recommend this novel to those seeking a mystery thriller in the YA world- you won't regret it!
My least favourite out of the 3 I've read from this author. A Thousand Splendid Suns is worth the read, The Kite Runner, perhaps. Wouldn't bother with this one, I'm afraid.

I know I'm late reading this but my god I haven't hated a book this much since probably 50 shades of grey. 
 If you've ever read British Empire-era studies of its colonies and the ways of the natives and barbarians, that's exactly what this book's descriptions of the 'Latino Blood' world read like, except obviously the Empire's prose was far more sophisticated. I truly believe I could have written this better, based on my knowledge of California rap and Coach Carter-esque films. 
 I also had a problem with the main Latino character's constant stream of Spanish, most of which by the way sounded suspiciously like the sentences I was writing after 4 years of high school Spanish. I'm not saying people don't interchange languages - I'm bilingual, I do it myself: with people who speak my language - NOT at school, to teachers and certainly not when I need to cuss someone who doesn't speak that language. 
 The book was supposed to be filled with all these heart-wrenching scenarios: memories of a father's murder, interactions with a disabled sister, confrontations with disconnected and self-absorbed parents, a murdered friend and most obviously some deep love. I felt none of it. The writing was so astoundingly bad - the type where feelings are just written in words rather than conveyed in the mood or actions - that not a single event in the book moved me to feel anything. I mean seriously, Stephenie Meyer's prose sparkles in comparison to this. 
 And if the male narrative voice was annoying, I don't even know what to call the female voice. I must have read a variation of the phrase "I have to look perfect to everyone" at least 15 times in the first few chapters. 
 I'm guessing one of the intended arcs of this book is for the characters to come-of-age by renouncing their commitment to keeping up appearances and being true to themselves. Supposedly, the thing that connects the two characters is this struggle to keep up their respective fronts and hide the depths of their inner souls. The problem was that the characters had no depth anyway, so when they 'became true to themselves', there wasn't much improvement. 
 I guess there was also supposed to be some message about strength in diversity or something, but that kind of got lost in the BLATANT RACISM AND STEREOTYPES. I mean, obviously brown hood-rat needs rich white-girl to improve and reform. Obviously, the Latino Blood ex-girlfriend was a cheating slut. (I don't like using that word, but this is so blatantly what the author wants to imply). Obviously there was no-one in the hood good enough to make Alex aspire to leave or change his life at first, no girl, not even his mother or brothers. 
 Also I can't be bothered to go into it in detail, but since I read 'The Outsiders' recently and that I guess is one of the original smart kid from wrong side of the tracks stories, I noticed a lot of parroting in the phrases describing the rich-poor divide. 
 Basically, this book was terrible and I find the fact that so many people like it, deeply disturbing.

Only took a star away because of Froi's attempted rape of Evanjalin and how I'm supposed to set that aside and continue to find him a sympathetic character . I felt like it was handled really poorly and shouldn't have been included at all. Otherwise, so fun unputdownable.

Interesting story. Olsen attempts to keep elements obscured to build suspense but instead only ends up creating a narrative that is not enjoyable to read because it is disjointed. Hayley and Taylor are rather flat characters so I don't care about them enough to want to read on. I finished the novel out of obligation to complete the task rather than a desire to know what would happen next.

I was surprised by how much I enjoyed this. Juneau was a very interesting character. I really enjoyed watching her grow and come to terms with the reality of the world. Growing up thinking the world was destroyed in a third world war, only to discover that your people lied to you and raised you in a remote backwater community. I really enjoyed trying to figure out what was really going on with her people and what she could really do. I enjoyed getting to know Miles as well and watching him grow up and decide what he was going to believe and what he was going to stand for. The story was well paced and well written. I am looking forward to seeing where this story will go next.

Evernight got so much hype that I caved and decided to read it. It was worth all the hype it received. A seriously good read. A bit of historical and paranormal thrown in with some elements of steampunk. 
 One of the best books I've read this year for sure!

What a weird, clever little book! Wishes and moonshine, murder and romance. The main character, Lennie, was a kind of unlikable most of the time, but I still rooted for her throughout the whole book. I liked her uncles and her friend Larry and the evolution of her relationship with Smith. I thought the end was really cleverly written. 
 I've read this author's previous books and really didn't like one and really liked the other, so this book was the tie-breaker that has made me decide I like this author's work.

Honestly? I didn't expect, in a million years, to enjoy this as much as I did. The concept is unlike anything I've read before and it could definitely be improved but this is a promising start. Also, the writing is incredibly pleasant. I'll be continuing this series!

LOVE ME SOME REAPER MEN! 
 Yay!! I've been waiting for Painter's story ever since we first got a glimpse of him. If you've read this series Painter is no stranger to you because we first learn about him when he sort of has a relationship with the club president's daughter, Em. I was losing hope that Painter was ever going to man up and claim a woman for himself. It was looking like bachelorhood was his future. 
 The Grudge 
 Throughout the other books we've learned little pieces about Painter. We know he's been to prison/jail 3 times. But we weren't ever sure why they weren't together after his stint in prison. This is the story about THE GRUDGE that caused a line to be drawn in the sand for this feuding couple. 
 One condition Painter gives Melanie - "No. Fucking. Bikers." 
 Since they weren't getting back together Painter gives Melanie one condition. To stay out of his world. She wasn't allowed to date any bikers EVER. Basically his world no longer exised for her. Sounds like easy proposition until it isn't. 
 "Sometimes it feels like you hate me out of habit." 
 The issues between these two had their friends frustrated. Basically their friends wanted them to fish or cut bait. Unfortunately for their friends, Mel and Painter weren't out to please others and were doing things their own way. If that meant that everyone was agitated at them then so be it. This was their life to live. 
 I love Ms. Wylde's MC romance books. Reaper's Fall is a second chance romance that takes us back to the beginning of Mel & Painter's story. The readers are shown what they never got from the other books about their story. I really love how this story was laid out.

One would think this wasn't written by the same author, or perhaps an author with a time restraint. Disappointing. Wasn't worth the time reading it. Won't bother reading the third instalment.

Beautiful Music for Ugly Children is really well done. There's not a ton of ya trans novels out there, and I liked how this one tackles a first-person, middle class, suburban experience. I appreciated how Gabe is able to find support and acceptance in his hometown, beyond what he ever imagined possible when he daydreamed about escaping to the big city to finally become who he was meant to be (common dream for suburban/small town youth of all genders). At the same time, Gabe's legitimate fears of coming out at home are addressed, and, realistically, a handful of people are cruel and violent towards him and his friends. 
 The radio aspect of the show was maybe less strong. I don't know. I understand the sentiment that music in our own time isn't good and musicians can be perceived as interchangeable, which is how the book described male singers in country music, but I don't think that people who are really into radio as a career are just into retrospective stuff all the time. The characters' dismissal of Britney Spears, Taylor Swift, and all of contemporary country music showed a kind of weird closed-mindedness for a book that is about "playing your B-side."

It's the final battle, the culmination of the series. It's when the weapons come out and the battle lines are drawn and redrawn and blood and death reign supreme as conniving minds scheme to gain the upper hand. It becomes a war of three factions, the Mayor, the Mistress, and the Spackle. And in the midst of it all, Todd and Viola are trying to do the right thing, to find peace in the world and to save each other. 
 I can't believe I'm giving this four stars. Well, it's more like 3.75, but it's basically four stars. I came into this book with low expectations because endings are so hard to do well. But this deserves more than three stars, more than 3.5 stars. In the beginning I thought Ness wasn't that skilled at writing war - and he isn't. His battle scenes are a little clumsy as he portrays characters talking dialogue in the middle of battle and other slightly unbelievable things. But he is great at writing subterfuge and the hidden tactics of war. And this book brings us further into war, brings it into the actual death and destruction of what war is (instead of the guerrilla fighting of book 2). 
 We also get 1017's point of view in first person as well. I love Ness for this: giving us a new perspective with each book. That broadens our understanding of the characters and gives new insights into the world. 
 His style is still fairly consistent, his strengths and weakness similar to the other two books again. It has the same quick pace with truces and plans and attacks happening every other page. It's an adventure book that shows these characters grown up, but still making those hard decisions all over again. 
 Again, there were some things that I don't buy again (spoilers: like the silencing of Todd's Noise just by thinking the phrase or how it's opened again by talking to Ben. Too quick.). 
 I loved how he makes the villains sympathetic and the protagonists guilty of crimes as well (who is to say Viola or Todd is correct for wanting to kill thousands for one person?). These characters aren't flat, and they make you hurt for them in all the right ways. 
 There are so many mini-climaxes towards the end (so many fake endings). While I really appreciated it, there were some parts where the heroes became villains unexpectedly - and there was just not enough transition moments to make that believable as well. But the resulting plot and action that came from those twists are freaking amazing. So I'll let it go. 
 The ending. At first I was like... ack that's a cop-out ending, but no... it was done well. He did it justice. It didn't exactly tie up all the loose ends, but it ended on the right note. And it's hard to find a book that ends on a perfect note, so I bumped it a little bit in the ratings. 
 4 stars because I really did like this book a lot and the way it ended. It was entertaining, thought-provoking, had well rounded characters and great villains. 
 Recommended for people who read the first two books. But I would really recommend this series to anyone who likes adventure books.

Lately, I've been on an Anne Frank kick, sort of speak. I've read her diary and the supplement book called Tales from the Secret Annex in the past few months. I just happened upon this book when I was looking on a bookseller's website and was instantly interested in reading a book from Peter's point of view. 
 I thought this was an interesting read in many ways. Although it doesn't flow as easily as Anne's diary does, it still hits most of the major events that occurred in Anne's diary. I really liked some of the conversations Peter had with his parents and seeing a new perspective of the van Pels that wasn't so tainted by Anne's annoyance with them. I felt that Dogar captured Peter's spirit quite well and his quiet thoughts he may have had. I also really appreciated Dogar trying her best to piece together what Peter must have gone through after they were discovered in the annex and sent to the death camps. That's something that is often not discussed or depicted because Anne's diary ends before we ever know what happened to them there. I felt it added a special touch to the book. 
 I had a couple issues with it which is why I gave it 3 stars. In the beginning of the book, the author notes that she tried her best to stay true to Anne's diary in what she recorded, the sequence of events, etc. However, this isn't true when it comes to Anne's and Peter's romance. While I understand that Dogar was trying to get a new perspective and trying to imagine what Peter was feeling while also keeping in mind how biased Anne could have been in her diary, I didn't feel as if their romance was accurately depicted. Dogar depicts Peter as being very uninterested in Anne for quite a while before he finds himself liking her. In Anne's diary, he teases her/flirts with her quite a bit before she ever becomes interested in him.  I think her approach was interesting but nonetheless inaccurate. I didn't mind some of the other inaccuracies, especially because this is a fiction book and the writer had an author's note all about it in the beginning, but something as vital to the story as their romance was something I felt should've been depicted more accurately. 
 I also didn't like how explicit the book was. A lot of people wouldn't find it explicit at all; however, I did and it bothered me. Peter spends all of his time thinking about sex. And that's pretty much all he cares about. Not even 1/3 of the way in, Peter is having multiple sexual dreams about a girl. He also is implied to only be interested in Anne because he wants to have sex with her.  While I understand that this would be realistic in some cases, it's not something I care to read about and feel that the book would have been better without this theme dripping all through the entire book. 
 Likes: Interesting take. Didn't lag in any way. Stayed true to Peter's character depicted in Anne's diary. Went all the way through to the death camps. 
 Dislikes: Inaccurate depiction of Anne and Peter's romance. Peter's obsession with sex. 
 Overall: 
 Recommend? Yes.

It's been ten years since the last time I read the Hobbit. It was one of my first Fantasy novels as a child, and as a teenager, I found it to be an accessible and gripping introduction to the expanded world of Middle Earth. Prior to this recent re-read, my rating was a solid, nostalgic five stars. Picking up the book again, I expected to be instantly drawn back into Bilbo's adventures. But probably due to my high expectations, I couldn't help but feel disappointed. 
 Tolkien is undoubtedly a genius at world-building, but instead of bringing me into the world and letting me explore it from within, it was like being lectured. His descriptions of the various races, their histories, and the geography of the land all felt as though they took precedence in his narration over Bilbo's actual journey and development. Secondary characters were incredibly one-dimensional. We learn nothing about Thorin beyond his lineage and desire to reclaim his inheritance throughout the entire book, and even that's more than we know about the 12 other dwarves. Gandalf is mysterious to a fault - coming and going without explanation and ending up more a tool of convenience than any sort of developed character. 
 While I find the actual journey with all its obstacles interesting and well-crafted, it comes across as more an extension of the world-building rather than the driving force of the plot. The company encounters both elves of the bitter and merry-making variety, dangerous and violent goblins and wolves, wise and powerful Beorn, industrious menfolk, and more; they trek across the haunting magical forest, traverse the dark mountain tunnels, cross a raging river - but instead of learning and growing from these diverse groups and experiences, they're just tourist stops on a visitor map. 
 The ending in particular is extremely rushed and undeveloped. After 90% of the book taken up by just getting to the dragon, Tolkien manages to completely take the thrill out of the climax. He kills Smaug at the hands of a completely new character within a couple pages, initiates a siege against the dwarves by a combined force of men and elves, then abruptly abandons that conflict for a sudden reappearance of goblins and wolves - ending in an epic battle the main character (and therefore the reader) misses when he's knocked out. He goes from Thorin angrily exiling Bilbo, to a deathbed scene of forgiveness and gratitude within ten pages. All of this culminates in the final few pages with Bilbo returning unhindered to his home, content with the simple life he left in the beginning of the story, largely unaffected by his adventure, and unwilling to put to use his experiences.  
 In the end, it's probably only my nostalgia that redeemed any value I still have for this book. But then again, it's probably also my nostalgia that makes me so critical this time around.

I read a review of this volume that talked about the various distancing techniques used in these novels- first, that they're being written in a present-day frame story, so everything recounted is already in memory. It's an interesting way to shroud Lila's arguably more dramatic storyline, and frame it through the eyes of someone who is always wanting more or feeling like she's missing out on something. It has a distancing, dissociative effect that I strongly identify with. I found the actual story dragged a little in the last third, but I was still so bowled over by the emotions conveyed and drawn in by the characters that it didn't matter. I love the continued examination of class and privilege, too. Ferrante doesn't shy away from complexity and it's really satisfying.

I'm happy to say that Karen Marie Moning has yet to disappoint me. This book was no exception, and I enjoyed every minute of it! Karen's books are one to grab you by the neck and drag you along for the ride, which is why I love her style of writing. 
 Many people were disappointed to discover that Dani (a 14 year old) was the female lead, but it in no way retracts from the story. This is not a YA, trust me! There is a madness to Moning's methods that only she truly knows, and I'm content to continue trusting in Moning's formula for EPIC paranormal romances. 
 The dialogue is genius, the pace is fast, and the characters are amazing and complicated! What more could you want in a good book? Don't blink while you're reading, because I promise you will miss something! Karen has a knack for throwing curve balls that you will never see coming. 
 Dani's mind is very interesting to see inside and much different than Mac's POV in the Fever series. I love her quick wit, and the black and white way she sees the world at the moment. There is no doubt that things will get more complicated and gray for her as the series progresses. 
 I've read other reviews where some think that Ryodan is just a knock-off of Barrons and that is just plain false! Karen explains it well in the book: 
 "Barrons breaks heads. Ryodan turns them inside out. Barrons f***s you up. Ryodan makes you f*** yourself up." 
 Ryodan is not only a deliciously powerful alpha male, but also complicated in a way that Barrons is simple. There is way more going on with this character than meets the eye! 
 I'm so looking forward to the next two installments! 
 ***SPOILERS*** 
 Christian is becoming a most interesting character who I think is going to be more central to the story in the next two books. His transition to an Unseelie prince is unnerving (in a good way!) and his disturbing obsession with Dani is almost comical if it weren't so creepy! 
 Dancer is fast becoming a wild card, and I have a feeling he is not what he appears to be!
If you think a story about a magical sourdough starter and underground experimental farmer's market might appeal to you, pick this bad boy up. Highly recommended. Incredibly charming and enjoyable.

 Clara Campbell has spent the past 10+ years running from her hometown, her family, and her secret. 
 Her brother is Schizophrenic, and a past drug user, her parents have spent her whole life focusing more on him and trying to help him, and leaving her to her own devices most of the time. But when she needs them most, they blame her and tell her they don't have the money to fight a legal battle against someone so powerful. Instead her brother West ends up taking matters into his own hands ending up getting the police involved and him getting sent to the psych ward of the hospital.

 "Note to self: Always remember how lucky you are to wake up next to someone who thinks you're the shit." 
 True words of wisdom spoken above. In a world where loneliness can be all encompassing it's nice to have someone on your side rooting for you. When you find your 'tribe' it's very freeing to allow you to be who you are meant to be. The problem is when someone else's idea of success is not your own and they alter your course with their actions. They think they're doing it for your own good but ultimately it's a failure all around. 
 When the main cause of drama is miscommunication it frustrates me as a reader. This was one of those instances where some communication could have cleared up the initial mess that was created. I know at one point the culprit went to explain themselves but was disheartened when they saw the result of what their actions had done. A lot of characters were hurt by nothing being done to shed light on the situation. 
 I really enjoyed the writing style but from the beginning, I never connected with the story or the characters. The one character I really enjoyed was a side character who got caught in the crossfires of the clusterfuck. I felt really bad for them as I knew they were ultimately going to lose the heart of the one they had fallen for. 
 I know this book was written in 2005 and the majority of my friends read it about 4 to 5 years ago and maybe if I had read it back then I might have felt differently about the book BUT the world has changed a lot in that time. There were some words and phrases that just aren't acceptable to use - 
 gay, lesbo and retard. 
 A few years ago in my son's Freshman English class, a student had said, "That's so gay." The teacher informed the student they couldn't say that because it would be like everyone saying, "That's so [insert student's name]." She reminded the students the use of those terms above have a negative connotation. When I read those terms in this book it took me a minute to remember this was written 12 years ago but I still found them to be distracting. The story felt like it could have taken place now and all that was missing to make it feel like current times were cell phones. 
 Overall, I'm glad I read it because I was able to see why this would be a classic Goodreads book. HOW TO KILL A ROCK STAR is on the majority of my friends' favorite list as a must read book. It's something that caused a lot of readers to flip pages to see what would happen next. It was also published when there wasn't a lot of contemporary romance to pick from. 
 It's a book where you have to experience it for yourself to see how it affects you.

I had a hard time with the believablity of this book. The "not so distant" future set up felt bizarre and it wasn't clear how much chroming and other laws were part of state governments versus the federal government. The author made it in a United States where the government had changed little enough that chroming was a constitutional issue but didn't give any sense how such a clearly unconstitional act would be ruled constitional. Because there was an economic depression? But the survellience and chroming etc. don't seem like a cheaper alternative. What's generally frightening about a dystopic novel is how you could see it happening, how something could sound like a good idea before you discover how much it impinges on your liberties. I couldn't see this here at all, not in the way it was set up. Also, the chroming and abortion issues became really separate around the middle, about where Simon says chroming is good, but not chroming of women. Wha? Other parts were explained too heavy-handledly. Hannah's growing recognition of gender inequality read like feminism 101, which would have been more believable if she were 15 rather than 25. We don't ever know Hannah as a sheltered and evangelical girl, we are just told over and over again that she was, so many of her insights sound strange, either too naive or too sudden. Finally, I hated Aidan. I hated the email or whatever he sent that she read at the library. At the time I thought, oh so this guy's a jerk and part of Hannah's journey will be realizing how he took advantage of her and her adolescent-like innocence, a kind of statutory rape, but - spoiler alert - she doesn't.

This short story needed to be longer. I say that as both a compliment and a critique. 
 The ideas of the book are great. Innovative angle on the superhero genre + funny & fluffy writing style + bisexual (and biracial? I think?) protagonist + queer romance = YES PLEASE. 
 But to me, this book should not have been a short story. The scope of the story would have been better fitting for a longer narrative. Superior just didn't go far beyond the idea of itself; there wasn't enough space for it to grow. The characters are beginning to show signs of life, but they're still far from fleshed out enough for me to care about them or their romance. There's even one central character, Captain Superior, who never says one word in this entire book as far as I can recall; everything he does is just relegated to background summary, so it's like he's not even a character, just a plot device. Since he plays a fairly significant role in the plot, I would have liked to see him as a person, not just a prop, but... no. 
 Speaking of plot, a lot of elements of the plot are not that surprising or innovative on their own, but it could be engaging enough if the characters involved in said plot were characters I cared about. So it's the bones of a fairly good story, at least, but I wouldn't say it's there yet. 
 I wish I could give this book a higher rating because I do admire the idea of it and think we definitely need more cute, happy queer fantasy stories. (Also because I paid $2 for it even though it was so short, which led to certain high expectations.) Maybe if Jessica Lack went back and expanded this story significantly, I'd give Superior another read, but in its current form, I found it disappointing. 
 A resounding 'Meh.' 
 P.S. Kudos to the artist who did the cover art, by the way! I've been a fan of their tumblr, ofsparrows.tumblr.com, for a long time now. If you like warm and innovative fantasy art, you should definitely check it out.

This young adult novel is the first book in the series "Age of Legends". The village of Edgewood, aptly named by its location, sees the rise of twin sisters Ashyn and Moria. Twins are, in general, a rarity and the children are immediately forced to go through a brutal ritual to see if they are to become Seeker and Keeper. Those two young girls passed the test. As the Seeker, Ashyn and her hound Toga must, once a year, enter the forest near her village to find the bodies of exiled men with a search party. Once she finds and groups together all the dead, she puts their soul to rest through chants, exiling the souls from the forest. Meanwhile, Keeper Moria and her wildcat Daigo stay behind with the villagers to protect them from the evil of the forest while the souls are cast away. This year marks their first Seeking without their mentors, but something goes wrong despite their extensive training. Ashyn meets Ronan, a young exile who did not pass away in the forest like he should have done. Then, dark creatures attack and kill most of their party while other creatures similarly slaughter the adults in the village. Soon after the macabre discovery, Ashyn, Toga and Ronan must race to a neighborhood city to find the kidnapped children. Meanwhile, Moria, Daigo and her bitter guard Gavril Kitsune follow behind to find the Seeker, hoping they are not too late. Add mysterious beasts, possessed individuals and menacing mercenaries, and Armstrong's "Sea of Shadows" is born. 
 I will admit that Ronan and Ashyn's quest bored me a bit at about 45% of the book, hence why I removed .5 of a star in my rating. I think that the older character's presence in the beginning of their walk could've been removed altogether. It felt like filler and it had no purpose whatsoever - a bit like the curse Moria reads in the beginning. There doesn't seem to be any meaning whatsoever in some parts. The confusion this brings is the only downside to the book, really.  Also, even though the description is beautiful in most parts, sometimes it gets a bit overwhelming and I did skip a few parts of description, especially towards the end of the novel. 
 For those of you who don't appreciate witchy rituals, this novel isn't too bad. I truly hoped that the rituals wouldn't be too bloody/demonic and I was pleasantly surprised. Armstrong keeps her audience in mind. The fantastic elements aren't unbelievable and Armstrong includes some well-written mythology (ugh, that worm!). There's swordplay and dagger-throwing involved alongside survival lessons, all wrapped in a nice adventure-driven young adult novel. 
 As for the characters, well, I love them. I dreamed with Ashyn, held my breath about Ronan, angst'ed with Gavril, and rooted for Moria. They each had their own sets of qualities and faults and were quite well-rounded. Even Gavril, who is despised by some reviewers for being cruel, has some mystery surrounding him that makes him appealing. In fact, everyone seems mysterious in some ways. The girls weren't annoying whatsoever, which is my biggest pet peeve with female heroines. I enjoyed the insinuations of romance through the book, and even though Ashyn is quite the romantic soul, it didn't overwhelm the novel. Yes, you've read right; this is a YA fiction without romance taking over the plot. Even where the plot might not be as tight as I'd like it to be, the beautiful way those characters were crafted made up for the few shortcomings I mentioned above. 
 Go treat yourself; pre-order that book! I recommend it to all young adult novel lovers out there. I'm pretty excited for the second book to come out, and I wouldn't be surprised if, in a couple of years, I'll be watching this story on film (can anyone anticipate the fandom going wild over those boys? Team Gavril vs team Ronan would potentially reach the status of Harry vs Draco, Edward vs Jacob, Peeta vs Gale, etc...) 
 I would like to thank Netgalley, as well as Doubleday Canada, for the free ARC of this novel in exchange for an honest review.

Legend is the first book in the trilogy by Marie Lu. It's a dystopian novel set on a post-apocalyptic state (Los Angeles). It is one of the most interesting dystopian novels I read so far. It got me thinking of the rise of the popularity of dystopian fiction amid both science-fiction and non-science-fiction readers. It appears that dystopian novels are a complete hit to all readers. Well, I can't blame them because dystopian fiction shares so much more than a fictional place where people live in fear. And when I say fear, it includes the abuse and misuse of the powers of the government, the government's break-down, not-to-mention WAR and Natural Disasters that will all lead the humanity into a complete mess. These fears are used as literary 'device' of the writers and put the protagonist to explore and conquer these ideas. Likewise, what made dystopian novels a real sensation is that it deals with real issues that we face every day, and turn them into a ominous prediction of what could happen to society if we don't change our way; if the government don't change their ways. 
 Here's a short plot of the story. This is taken from the goodreads, I didn't bother making up my own summary because I might end up giving more than I should have (or I'm just really worn-out to write some more. Haha. Forgive me!): From very different worlds, June and Day (our two protagonists) have no reason to cross paths - until the day June's brother, Metias, is murdered and Day becomes the prime suspect. Caught in the ultimate game of cat and mouse, Day is in a race for his family's survival, while June seeks to avenge Metias's death. But in a shocking turn of events, the two uncover the truth of what has really brought them together, and the sinister lengths their country will go to keep its secrets. 
 This almost had me into giving it a perfect score, but I was taken aback (negatively) by the following reasons: (1) the initial "cheesy" reaction of our protagonist during their first encounter. 
 E.G: "When I look to my side, I see a boy holding out his hand to me. He has bright blue eyes, dirt on his face, and a beat-up cap on, and at this moment, I think he might be the most beautiful boy I've ever seen" or Day's reaction be like: "I don't know if anyone's ever told you this, You're attractive".These are two of those scenes where I was quite scared that I might end up being utterly disappointed with this book. I feared that at the end of this trilogy (or this novel perhaps), I'll close the book and bring into conclusion that Marie Lu is yet another female writer that uses the very same tactic-- A CONTEMPORARY ROMANCE NOVEL DRESSED AS A DYSTOPIAN GENRE". On the contrary, there is nothing wrong with this tactic, it's just that, it will be a little too out of the genre; that instead of focusing on the seemingly interesting premise it was working with, it focused on romance. I'll never forgive the writer. (2) Second, (and by far, the last), I hate how young our protagonists are. In the novel, they're fifteen (15) years old and I can't help but complain how flirty they are; how (in such a young age) they knew how to drink; how mature they think (well, probably much mature than I am and I'm like five years older than them, haha) Anyway, this is just my opinion. 
 Overall, my feelings towards Legend consist of intense adoration; it contains nonstop action, suspense, and it is sure to entertain the readers as much as it gives. PLUS! It's a short, fast-paced novel that will surely burst you out of your seats!

 Augh. I wanted this book to be a little more perfect, because I picked it up Monday night and then read it in four one-hour spurts. It's that kind of book. 
 And you know what? There's so much that this book does right. We get a lesbian protagonist, but it's not a generic "am I gay? I think I'm gay" story that ends with her happily kissing another girl. Nah, there's more to it than that. Cameron is a complex character who has several different relationships, and doesn't necessarily question the fact that she's into women. She feels like she caused her parents' accident, but at the same time, there isn't a built-in shame whenever she kisses other girls in the book. I like that. I like that, at God's Promise, we get a girl with a prothetic leg (Jane) and a Native American guy who identifies as winkte , adding more diversity to an already well-written book. 
 Some of the stuff that happens at God's Promise was hard to read, and to be honest, I was expecting a bit more of the But I'm a Cheerleader! route, where the people at the camp are just overly ridiculous and objectively wrong. I still think they're wrong. But, again, they are painted in more than just black and white; the scene where Rick breaks down in Cameron's room because he doesn't have answers is kind of heartbreaking, because you are suddenly aware that this guy really thinks he's trying to do the right thing. Don't get me wrong, I still disagreed with him fundamentally and wanted to slap him upside the head, but I also felt sorry for him . 
 I am not crazy about the ending, though. Endings are hard, and I wanted something a little more resolved for Cameron and her friends. I wanted them to definitely have someplace to go, someplace to escape to, and someone she could call on the other end. Maybe Irene, maybe Coley, probably Lindsey. But the ending was just so darned ambiguous--have they escaped? Will people FIND THEM? What are they going to do?--that it bothered me a whole lot.  That's the reason I knocked half a star off this book. 
 In terms of writing, danforth is excellent with pacing and making this world breathe. There was so much to hear and smell and taste, as well as a lot of beautiful descriptions. At the same time, though, it never felt overwhelming. You know how it is when you read a book and literally everything is ornamented with unnecessary adjectives and the dialogue feels stilted and ugly, like nothing that would ever come out of someone's mouth? This book doesn't suffer from that, which is great. Props to danforth for accomplishing pretty prose without suffering from MFA syndrome (what I term a lot of "literary fiction" that crumbles under the weight of its own language). Cameron's voice was also believable, as both a person and a teenager (if that makes sense--there are some YA books that feel like they're being narrated by thirty-year-olds). And the, uh, I hesitate to call them historical details because it takes place in the 90s... but yeah, the historical details are good. It wasn't just "let's slam some 90s music references in here!" but instead it felt good. Real. 
 Read it. Please read it.

There's something very fun about a romance aboard a ship. The typical Regency romance takes place in England and it was refreshing to read about another place during this time period. 
 William is convinced that Amelia is a gold digger and isn't happy to have to retrieve her from her plantation in Jamaica to return her to England. He has an idea of what she's like and she proves him wrong at every turn. Amelia's marriage to William's brother is on paper and by proxy only. She has her plantation and doesn't want or need more. 
 Basically forced to leave her home, Amelia shows that she is willing to make the best of things. She is more than willing to help out aboard the ship--sewing sails, caring for the sick and injured, showing the cook new recipes, etc. She is completely unselfish and such a sweet character. I love the way Amelia is able to find common ground with those around her. She becomes dear friends with so many of the crew and is very personable. I love her strength and grit, especially in tough times. 
 I enjoyed watching William soften up. He's so used to ordering a crew around and being tough, yet kind and having a woman on board is a whole new experience. I loved watching the romance slowly blossom. 
 I experienced a lot of different emotions throughout the story and was engaged throughout. I thought it was a great story, especially for a debut novel! 
 Content: no language; some war-type violence/fighting with mild descriptions of death, blood, and injuries; mild kissing. I would consider it clean for an adult.

The plot and overall concept was enough to keep my attention and have the desire to somewhat finish the book, however, it was muddled by annoying repetitions and very poor character development. 
 My biggest complaint is the romance that tried way too hard. There was so much of it thrown in on seemingly every page that it stopped being romantic before it had even really started! A couple of times throughout the book I wanted to put it down simply because I was tired of hearing of how much Logan needed to protect Rachel. It looked to me that she was perfectly capable of protecting herself. 
 Except that she rarely did. There's not much that bothers me more in books than a female character described throughout the entirety of the book as tough and independant and then having her be saved countless times by her love interest. And that wasn't the worst part about Rachel, who I started to get the feeling she was more of a supporting character to Logan as the book progressed. The worst part was that she was never consistent. One minute she didn't want to talk, the next she decides that she does as soon as there's another character there to join in on her conversation. She's determined to withstand the Commander, but without any logical explanation, she changes her mind and does what he wants. She knows that she'll never be the girl the commander thought she was, but turns into exactly that at the threat of Logan's life.

So yeah, despite some faults, I really enjoyed this, enough to give it 5 stars. 
 Faye weaves a wonderful and multi-layered tale in a Gothic setting that is sure to appeal to those who appreciate a good mystery/piece of historical fiction. In addition to an engaging main plot, Faye manages a number of subplots that compliment rather than distract for the primary story line. And while a few of the secondary/supporting characters bordered on cliches, the key characters felt fresh and well-drawn (for the most part...obviously Faye is a Sherlock Holmes fan, too). I also felt that the mystery aspect was well done. 
 The faults? 
 Initially I had difficulty picturing the the protagonist, a man, as a man (Tim Wilde sounded like a woman--Faye--writing as a man), but by the end of the story I was sold. 
 Early on Faye went a little crazy with the period lingo/slang. There really is a fine line between adding a sense of authenticity to a period piece and simply annoying the reader. Yet as the story went on it seemed as if the author stopped trying so hard and as a result the story became more readable. 
 Bottom line: A thoroughly enjoyable read (faults and all) and I look forward to reading other books by the same author.

A good zombie book in the first half, which becomes a little slower in the second half. Too bad the pace didn't keep up, as the first pages were just what a zombie reader wants: death, puss, mindless and relentless killers. But as human villains appear, they just aren't as compelling as the mindless hoards. By the end, there isn't much momentum, and the climax isn't ghoulish, its political. At 440 pages, Higson could have picked up the pace and ended a hundred pages sooner and still offered up a satisfying read. 
 I wish I could offer this to reluctant readers, but I think the length, combined with the third-person narration that shifts between multiple characters will make this one a tough sell for weaker readers. Probably not the place to start if you're intimidated by Alexander Gordon Smith or Darren Shan. 
 In spite of the topic - and the carnage that comes with such things - "The Enemy" would probably be fine for young teens, as well as older kids seeking out a "Zombie Land" fix. There's barely a hint of romance and zero profanity or drug use: just good, ol'fashioned undead mayhem. There's room for a sequel, although I'm not certain I'll need it.

 Night Watch is widely reckoned to be one of the best Pratchetts, and rightfully so. I find it hard to say exactly why it works so well. Explaining the key plot device, that Vimes has to go back in time to become his own mentor makes it sound like Hackneyed sci-fi. But it really, really works. 
 I think there is an innate satisfaction to reading about something which happened in the past, even if it is fictional. It fills in the history of Ankh-Morpork a little, showing what life was like in the pre-Vetinari days. The pacing to me feels good -- earlier Pratchetts have had a problem where it feels like there is a lot of beginning, and then not much middle, whereas I think he gets the balance right here. Part of the joy of the book is watching Vimes at work. His love of the city, and his approach to policing, and the conscious effort he imposes to keep himself moral. A lot of it is the poignancy. It is easier for Pratchett to kill characters in the past, as the assumption is we are just there for a visit, and he makes good use of this, underlining the stupidity of the situation. 
 It is less funny than many of the others, but given how strong a book is, that's perfectly alright.

What a strange book. Having read some of Mr. Smith's other titles - In the Path of Falling Objects, Winger - I knew that anything might happen. Indeed, the first page tells that a bunch of stuff transpires within its pages. So yes, there's some skateboarding and mutant mantises and sex and packs of cigarettes and Polish boys and Lutherans and Catholics and....well, really the plot points are almost beside the point. Austin Szerba is a confused teen in a world becoming more confusing by the day. There are moments of sharp humor and other moments of sage thoughtfulness. Of course there's also a bunch of "what-the-hell-is-that-about." 
 All of it is delivered in the rich and ribald tones of Kurt Vonnegut. Perhaps that's why this topped so many "Best of the Year" book lists? It is obviously literary, layering on repeated images and phrases for an effect beyond the mechanics of narrative. I liked it, as something interesting always turned up, and frequently characters and events seemed to recur in delightful ways. 
 But I'm not as charmed by the book as many others. It certainly is worth reading. "Grasshopper Jungle" will stretch some readers who don't know that books can do completely unexpected things. But I didn't find the central character to be worth the amount of time I'd spent with him. Austin's friend, Bobby, was actually more interesting (sequel?) and Austin's other friend is also curious, if under-developed. But the ending just left me tired, not sated.
