Like many others, I first need to just stop and take a moment to remark upon the elaborately amazing cover design here. I mean, seriously; 
 wow 
 . Not only are the colors and pattern beautiful, but the tension in the strings that are being pulled in every which way seem reflective of the characters' own internal (and sometimes external) tensions and struggles. Just like the universe. So much meaning in such a seemingly simple cover design. I love it. 
 Okay, so now onto the content of the book itself. This story begins with Natasha Kingsley, an undocumented immigrant from Jamaica who has been living in the United States with her family since she was eight-years-old. She believes in science and facts; observable truths. Her father, an aspiring Broadway actor, makes a devastating mistake (DUI, which additionally leads to him unnecessarily reporting on their undocumented status)  one night, which sets in motion the deportation of her family. Determined not to let their "voluntary removal" come to fruition, Natasha takes it upon herself to change their destiny. One thing leads to another and Natasha is late for her appointment. This sparks a chain of events that leads to her romantic entanglement with Daniel Jae Ho Bae, a Korean-American teen who is also on a mission to change his future. 
 Natasha's dreamy-eyed romantic opposite, Daniel believes that it is fate that has led him to Natasha. If not for the security guard, Irene, who took too long with Natasha's personal items at the USCIS building, she wouldn't have been late for her appointment, or met Lester Barnes, or got the name of an attorney (Fitzgerald) who might actually be able to help, or be caught in a moment with her music on the same street that Daniel happens to be on after a strange mystical/spiritual (sort of) encounter on the subway. He sees all these signs where she sees mere coincidences, typical occurrences that have no real meaning other than they are things that have just happened. Through one action and encounter after another, Daniel convinces Natasha that he can make her fall in love with him; something that Natasha initially steadfastly denies is possible let alone even exists. 
 They spend an entire day together, butting heads, flirting, and trying to convince one another of the other's beliefs on love and science, which may just prove to be more intertwined than either could have imagined. At the end, Natasha and her family still end up going back to Jamaica, and another ten or so years pass by, but fate on an airplane has the final word.  
 Maybe part of falling in love with someone else is also falling in love with yourself. 
 I really enjoy how Yoon utilizes multiple POVs. In this book in particular, there are multiple voices, perspectives, and even factors that become narration and contribute to the view of the story as a whole. For instance, instead of just going back and forth between Natasha and Daniel, we also get glimpses into the lives of people with whom they interact, who end up contributing in some way or another to the creation of their universe. Some interactions are more positive than others, even potentially life-saving, such as with Irene the USCIS security guard (and later flight attendant). POV in The Sun is Also a Star also includes informational stories, such as about word origins or mythology (irie, the Fates). All of these touch and connect to Natasha and Daniel, just like the strings in the cover art. 
 I have been struggling with how I feel about The Sun is Also a Star, which is overwhelmingly positive with a healthy(ish?) dose of skepticism (realism?). In essence, my own internal struggles regarding love at first sight and relationships is as split as Natasha and Daniel at the beginning of their relationship. I want to believe like Daniel, but I'm also highly skeptical like Natasha. My skepticism steers me toward the views of other reviewers who comment on the somewhat annoying instalove between Daniel and Natasha. But then it's difficult not to get wrapped up in the beautiful prose that creates their story, especially if you leave out that annoying "this all happened in just the course of one day" detail. What if that's all it was meant to be? Stepping back and looking at the bigger picture, rather than focusing on "annoying" details, this is a beautiful story about two teenagers from vastly different cultural backgrounds and their "American Dream" experiences, first love, and, in essence, the truly mysterious nature of the universe.

I like myself a good sociopath. They make things interesting in a world of heroes and anti-heroes if well written. I found a new favorite in Jorg of Ancrath when I read Prince of Thorns and wrote this review. 
 In the second book of The Broken Empire series, Jorg is now King of the Renar Highlands and he's all grown up. Now eighteen, he's preparing to marry his young bride Princess Miana with an army knocking at his door. The Prince of Arrow wants to roll right over him with numbers Jorg can't hope to compete against, but if there is one thing Jorg is king of besides thorns, it's the long shot. 
 If you thought the first book was good, this one is better. Jorg has matured. He no longer gets all stabby-stabby if you look at him wrong, and the ghosts he created now haunt him. One ghost in particular is of a little boy that has grown over the years that Jorg has seen him. Jorg doesn't know who he is, but a little copper box holds the secret and he's tempted to open it despite the threat that he might loose his sanity. 
 But even with the fantastic character development Lawrence has put Jorg through, he still remains the same clever smart ass with questionable morals. Makin, Rike, and Gorgoth are still around. As are the Watch and Coddin. The new character that makes a splash is Miana. Even though she's only twelve, she has a quick mind and is capable of the same ruthless thought process as her husband. As it turns out, she was raised by a card player, and she's not afraid to make sacrifices for maximum damage... I mean gain. (That manages to sound worse.) 
 Like Prince, Lawrence uses the same structure. There is the present time the novel is set in - Jorg's battle against Arrow - and the past set four years ago after the events of the first book. The flashback story line deals with Jorg trying to help out Gog because the poor leucrota boy keeps exploding into pillars of flame. Jorg knows that he's mostly doing it to save himself, but you know he's attached to the kid. It's one way Lawrence shows the reader that Jorg is growing up. 
 The flashback also introduces us to his mother's family, who isn't trying to kill him. In fact, he rather likes them and is relieved when he doesn't need to off them for self preservation purposes. The alliance he builds with his grandfather by marrying Miana helps him out against Arrow, and gives the reader more time with his uncle who describes himself as simply "good with horses." 
 Lawrence does get a bit more complicated this time around by splicing in the memories from the little copper box. They flow nicely, and don't confuse, but I won't go any further for fear of ruining the story behind it. 
 The little descriptions of the Brothers are spliced in too, punctuated with pages from Katherine's journal. Yes, Katherine is still around, and she's learning the ways of dreams. 
 Then there is the Builders. In my last review of the first book, I brought up the computer that Jorg and his Brothers believed was a fairy trapped in a box. Now Jorg knows a ghost - a data echo - of a man named Fexler Brews that he met under his grandfather's castle. Fexler is made from the memories and personality ticks of a real person a thousand years gone. He wears a white lab coat and is a bit of a grouch. He bestows Jorg with a gift of Builder tech that relies on the satellites that still orbit Earth, giving Jorg an advantage over Arrow's forces. 
 Sure, it isn't all easy reading. The dog scene is a bit difficult to get through. I admit, it's hard reading scenes of animal cruelty as I learned when I read Chuck Wendig's Bait Dog, but it is a formative moment in Jorg's young life from before he hung in the thorns. And if you didn't think you could hate his father more, think again. 
 I could really go on and on about these books. They really were what medieval based fantasy needed. This genre bender is, in truth, its own thing. It can't be squeezed into the little boxes of science fiction, epic fantasy, or post-apocalyptic. If I had to define it, I'd say it's more like Game of Thrones had hot, satisfying one night stand with Fallout 3. But even then it doesn't seem right. 
 Just do Lawrence a favor and read his books because he is a good writer. A very good writer.

I adored this book and consider it an important addition to the African American Literary Cannon. It is written in an experimental style that has more in common with Slam poetry, Jazz or Orlando by Virginia Woolf than a contemporary novel. It can be hard to follow and demands a readers full attention and trust. Because of the style, it lends itself well to audio book or reading aloud. I did both as I alternated between audio book and ebook. I enjoyed the audio book a great deal as the narrator understood the content and matched tones to subtle historical references. In short, this is one of the best books I've read in the last couple years. 
 That said, this novel is satire, and race can be a difficult topic in the most careful of hands. By diving full bore into satire, Paul is able to approach ideas and questions that we are often too polite to speak about. He also gives voice to "inside voice" ideas that aren't to be spoken of publically where non-minorities can hear. Such as the idea that black people might just be better off building their own cities, economies ect because "whites are toxic" and giving up on the idea that racism can be cured. I have memories of hearing Farrakhan speeches as a child and listening to my father and his friends talk about isolationism or leaving the US altogether... the plot of this story is ridiculous but the core emotions will be very familiar and leave some surprised to see them dissected so bluntly. This is important and uncomfortable. He gets away with the difficult content by deft use of gallows humor. There is a LOT of cursing and racial slurs. They are in context and often used with multiple nuances and cultural references. In my reading, the racial slurs lend authenticity to the narrators cultural experience and allow the reader to get past those words until they are approaching highly uncomfortable ideas head on that can't be approached when trying to be polite. 
 The plot is absurd and not at all the point. A black man raised by an abusive sociologist grows up to find his town literally disappeared. This is an experience that features literally in African American history as towns that were bombed or destroyed in other ways by white neighbors. It is also an idea in the figurative sense... if we are post racial do we cease to exist? What exactly IS black. The narrator decides to bring back his town and in the process re-segregates the town and somehow ends up with a slave who doesn't really do any work that he has to pay Dominatrixes to whip. Eventually he is arrested and the case goes to the supreme court, and this is all intertwined with criticisms of black intellectuals, minstral shows, entertainment industry and black culture.  
 Personally, I didn't find anything about the book offensive but that is probably because I've grown up looking at and talking about race relations from all sides. This is a book that relishes in its inheritance from uncensored barber shop conversations and 70's comedians. So while the language can be crude, rough, racist, and sexist, the lessons are just the opposite and I am sure this book will still be read in 50 years as a classic right alongside beloved and invisible man.
On its own, the story was good, though a bit repetitive and heavy-handed with its themes. But the illustrations add so much (I love Jon Klassen's style) that I gave it an extra star.

 Gateway tells the story of Daiyu, a Chinese-American teenager living in St. Louis, who suddenly finds herself transported to an alternate world. In this world, Jia, as Daiyu quickly learns, it is the Han, a people very similar to the Chinese, who explored the new world, and Shengleng--the city Daiyu knew as St. Louis--is the most important city in the world. Because her Chinese heritage lets her pass as Han, Daiyu is recruited to infiltrate the upper tiers of Han society in order to eliminate the prime minister Chenglei. But as she proceeds in her mission, Daiyu has doubts. Is Chenglei really the evil man that her handlers, Ombri and Aurora claim? Can Ombri and Aurora be trusted at all? Complicating everything is Daiyu's budding romance with Kalen, a poor stonepicker boy. If Daiyu does decide to go through with her mission, can she bear to leave Kalen behind? 
 I have a kind of uneven history with Sharon Shinn's works, of which I haven't read as many as I probably should. I loved the world she created for The Safe-Keeper's Secret and its sequels, but General Winston's Daughter frustrated me on so many levels, not the least of which was the heavy-handed anti-imperialism message and the tacit approval for, essentially, a terrorist attack. When I picked up Gateway from my local library, I wondered which work it would resemble more. 
 As it turns out, Gateway is completely its own book, with a unique voice and style. While Shinn's richly detailed world-building is definitely present, as is her penchant for exploring the interactions of different cultures, Gateway didn't forcefully remind me of any of Shinn's previous books. Like General Winston's Daughter, it features a teenager girl entering another culture and becoming enthralled with it, but instead of trying to drive home a political message, Gateway simply seeks to be a romantic fantasy adventure. 
 Daiyu, the protagonist, almost represents what any savvy reader would hope to be like if they got swept into another world. She's open to the mysterious strangers, but she weighs her options before making decisions. She's eager to see this new world she's in, but she keeps an escape route handy. She uses people as she has to, but feels genuinely bad for any collateral damage, even just of the emotional variety, she leaves in her wake. She tries to avoid relationships that can only end painfully, but in the end her heart just can't help itself. Most importantly, she remains skeptical of everyone. I found this both interesting and frustrating. Intellectually, I approved of her reluctance to trust Aurora and Ombri. Emotionally, I longed for her to invest in one side or another. When she finally makes her decision and commits herself, the story rockets with intensity, but it's a little late in the story. 
 As a character, Daiyu is a little bland. She's a bit too much a placeholder, constantly responding to the actions of others, instead of shaping her own path. However, as placeholders go, at least she's an inoffensive one. Her voice is crisp and modern, in pleasant contrast to the ornate fantasy culture around her, but never jarring with slang or pop culture references. She quickly picks up on what's she's told, minimizing info dumps. Although she falls for Kalen pretty quickly, she doesn't spend pages drooling over him. Despite her initial irritating indecisiveness, when she does decide to act she handily proves herself no damsel in distress. Daiyu won't be joining the pantheon of most-beloved characters any time soon, but being inside her head for the space of a novel is a painless, mostly pleasant experience. 
 The plot, which mainly revolves around Daiyu insinuating herself into high society and trying to decide whether Prime Minister Chenglei is really a bad guy or not, meanders a little at times. Readers who are looking for fast-paced action will probably tire of Daiyu's detailed descriptions of the gorgeous outfits and intricate customs of the Han elite. Gateway chooses to focus on the world-building over the adventure aspects, probably to the book's benefit. It also places a lot of emphasis on the romantic subplot, which grows in importance until it's a little hard to tell whether this is a fantasy adventure with romantic elements or a romance with fantasy and adventure elements. Daiyu's relationship with Kalen, the poor cangbai (that 's Fantasy Chinese for "white") stonepicker, moves at a whirlwind speed. It could have benefited from a slightly slower pace and more development, however the interactions between the two always feel natural and the progression of the relationship, while rapid, doesn't come across as forced. Shinn keeps the romance as a thread entwining throughout the novel, never overwhelming the main plot, yet never wholly disconnected from it, either. There are some very sweet scenes between them that become very poignant by the end of the book. On my first reading, I "dinged" them some points for the cliched "I'd never met him before, but he seemed so familiar" routine, but the ending forced me to reevaluate as it brought some very teasing possibilities to my mind. 
 The real delight here, though, is the world that Shinn creates. Inspired by Chinese culture, yet not bound to it, Jia is a beautiful, exotic wonderland, yet with a palpable darkness to it as well. Shinn has an eye for "domestic" details, adding countless tiny customs, fashions, and other particulars that make her world feel real. Whether we're joining Daiyu for a formal tea with society's elite, or wading for precious qiji stones in the river with Kalen and the poorest of the poor, every layer and facet of the world resonates realistically. Because Shinn brings Jia to such vivid life, we are almost as enthralled with it as Daiyu is, which makes more powerful the poignancy of her inevitable departure. 
 Whatever gripes I had with the first three quarters of the novels, the last fourth is wonderful. The stakes ratchet up, Daiyu takes an active role, and the romance has fantastic emotional payoff. The very last chapter was both intensely enjoyable and frustrating. It made me completely re-evaluate the beginning of the book. I'm not sure if the possibilities it raises were intentional, but it would fit the rest of the book beautifully in a very poignant way.  The conclusion is somewhat satisfying, but I rushed to the computer hoping to discover that this was the first book in a series. Sadly, I could find no evidence of this. 
 If this was a first book in a series, I would give it 4 stars out of 5, but as a standalone novel, I can only give it 3 1/2. The premise is intriguing, and the world-building is excellent, but the characters and plot aren't always quite up to par, and the ending leaves a little too much hanging.

So. Hmm. Divided. I just don't know. I mostly enjoyed the first book in this series and have been looking forward to reading this one, but I found it a little underwhelming. 
 It's been awhile since I read Dualed, but I don't remember it ending on a cliffhanger. West Grayer (I love that name) is an accomplished striker (assassin) and has defeated her alt and should be able to live her life in peace with her best friend/boyfriend, Chord. However, West is still dealing with the emotional fallout of her past sins. When she's summoned to the Board, she's offered a way to not only make up for her past, but to protect her future. 
 This is where things start to fall apart for me. West feels guilty not so much for killing people, but not knowing whether she killed the right alt or not. If she killed the more worthy alt then she's put her city at risk by providing inferior soldiers to guard the barriers. The Board Operator wants to make a deal for her to work as a striker to kill the alts of Board children. He makes the case that they are the worthy alts and that it's just an extra precaution for them to not actually face the challenge. West buys this logic, along with what he's willing to offer her in exchange and sets out to relive her days as a striker. 
 There are some twists and turns while she's fulfilling her contracts and we get a lot more background information about the city origins. Some of this I found interesting, but mostly I was just trying to get through it. The pace was pretty slow and a lot of parts that should have been exciting seemed a little anticlimactic. I just couldn't get on board with West's rationale and thought process through most the book and that hindered my enjoyment. 
 I can't tell if this series is a duology or trilogy. I couldn't find anything about a third book. While Divided wraps up some things, it still leaves a lot of loose ends and if this is the last book, I found the ending a little unsatisfying. 
 Overall, Divided was an ok read. I enjoyed the extra world building and the background information and the twist with West's final contracted alt. I would've liked a little more character development of both West and Chord. If this is the final book, I would've liked more things wrapped up, but if there's more to the series, I'll read it to find out what happens.

Turns out it was...fine. Not great, but (thankfully) not terrible either. I'm not a fangirl for Four so SORRY I DIDN'T LOVE IT. I like whenever Tris talks about his sculpted shoulders and so on, but I'm too old for his brooding angst. Overall I think he's a bit of a bore and usually end up rolling my eyes and thinking "UGH" whenever he says anything. 
 The Transfer was the first time I felt like Four was actually a human person with human feelings. I wasn't sure what I felt about this book until the narrator's identity was revealed. The language is simple and direct that the story just flows on and you feel bits of it are so close to your own life. 
 This book is about family. About parents, precisely. Though, family or not, we need to realise there are people whom if we do not cherish now, we would regret for the rest of our lives. My heart is broken. I can't find words to explain the hole I feel in my stomach after finishing this book. 
 Having read this book only once before, not a lot of times like I read the others, I feel a little uneasy on giving a review. 
 This book changes everything. It grows darker, and darker, and it's painful to know that I'm reaching the end of the series, and I know what to expect from the ending. Pain. 
 Harry's sixth and last year at Hogwarts comes with the burden of the Prophecy heard in the previous book. That he will be the one who'd fight Voldemort in the end. And he will. Soon enough. 
 I think the rhythm of the book was slower than the other ones, and that's what makes me give it four stars, instead of five, like I usually did with the entire series. I think it's my least favorite book from the entire series. 
 It's a bit boring, the action doesn't flow as easy as in the previous books. 
 I hated that Harry dated Ginny, and I hate how book Ginny is better than movie Ginny, therefore it was harder to really hate her, as I do with book Ginny, but then, my all-time OTP is Harmony, and I'll stick to the opinion that Harry and Hermione are meant for each other. 
 I hated Ron for so many reasons during this book, especially for making Hermione cry, she didn't deserve that, just because he's a git.

 I hated that Draco Malfoy was going through so much, and he was alone, and misunderstood, and that was such an amazing character development created from the smug, bullying Draco Malfoy, to a scared, misunderstood, teenager who had found himself on the wrong side, and who had no choice. 
 And in the end,  I have cried so much when Dumbledore died, but I didn't cry for him, I have grown to dislike him when I found out the reason why he protected Harry so much was only to kill Voldemort, anyway, more of that in next book's review, but I cried for Snape. I cried because Snape felt uneasy with the task Dumbledore had given him, and he was the only one who knew what he was. I cried for him when he nearly lost it when Harry shouted at him that he was a coward. No. Like Harry says, at the end of the series, Severus Snape was the bravest man.  
 I fear to read the last one, because over the last month since I've started re-reading the series, I lost myself in the Harry Potter world yet again, and losing everything again it's just heartbreaking. 
 3rd read update: This has always been my least favorite book of them all, but this time, it resonated completely differently with me. Besides the Harry-Ginny pairing, which I still do not understand, it all came perfectly. 
 Still so pissed about how horrible the movie is, and how much is missing. How we have no insight into Voldemort's life, and how unfair it is for Snape. He is such an incredibly tortured character.

When I had the great opportunity to hear Linda Castillo speak earlier this week, she said that there's a new dimension to this book that greatly appealed to her: a ghost story. I wasn't quite sure how I felt about that, but I absolutely loved how she pulled it off. In what is one of my favorite Kate Burkholder books to date, The Dead Will Tell is a fast-paced, twisty mystery that grabbed my interest right away and kept it until the very end. 
 As always, Castillo dives straight into the crime that sets the stage for the rest of the book. (As an aside, while we were waiting for Castillo to arrive at the event, my mom started reading the book - which is not her usual genre of choice - and when she had to put it down, she told me she had to read it when I was done.) In this case there are two crimes. The first happened in 1979, when a family of 7 brutally turns into a family of 1. Flash forward to present day and those responsible begin to turn up dead, one by one. 
 I felt like the mystery unfolded at a great pace and even though I started to guess who the killer actually was, there was a great twist that I didn't see coming at all. 
 In addition to the case, the story delves a little into Kate and Tomasetti's home life, as they finally seem to be happy and together. However, Tomasetti - who has come oh so far since the first book, is thrown when he finds out that a man responsible for his family's murder has been released from prison. While he doesn't turn back into the addict that he once was, there's still definitely a darkness and need for revenge/justice inside him. Kate struggles with his dishonesty and the ghosts of his past. 
 While we get to see some of Tomasetti's POV and how he handles this news, I wish there would've been more. I also miss him and Kate working together. However, I'm happy with their relationship up to this point and how they have real conversations in this book that they've avoided in the past. I'm definitely holding out hope for this couple! 
 Overall, I really enjoyed The Dead Will Tell. It was a great mystery with an end I didn't see coming and had just enough romance written in to continue to develop Kate and Tomasetti. One thing that I was surprised about, but necessarily upset about, was that there was no reference at all to the Daniel Lapp storyline that's been present throughout the series and especially the new developments in the last book. I would definitely recommend this book to those that have read the series and definitely recommend the series to those that enjoy mystery/crime/suspense and Amish!

Ignite Me has been one of my most anticipated books of this year. And overall I think it was a wonderful end to the series. 
 I want to talk about Juliette's character growth. It's amazing to see a character grow as much as she does throughout the series. I can definitely see her growth, and I love the new stronger Juliette. Where she's at at the end of the series is incredible, and I love her. In Shatter Me she narrated with numbers, crossed out lines, repetitive thoughts. They decreased in Unravel Me, and are nearly gone in Ignite Me. While I believe she has grown beyond that fragile state of mind, and therefore this style of thought wouldn't have fit with her development in Ignite Me, it was still something that I missed. It's what hooked me to the series. So, when choosing my rating, I had to consider that I enjoyed the narrative in this one slightly less than the first two books. Not that it wasn't appropriate, this is just a personal preference. 
 Ignite Me was a super fast read, it was still easy to slip into the words. And Tahereh has not lost one inch of her poetic genius, even though the narrative is a more mature style. There were so many beautiful metaphors, and that is the way in which Juliette maintains her old self. 
 A large part of why I gave it only 4 stars is because I felt like too much of the content of the book was unneeded or repetitive. I'll go into the specifics more below (*1), in the spoiler section. But there was a lot of what I felt were lengthy dialogues that were trying to sway the reader to feel a certain way, but I didn't need a lot of persuasion, I was already there. 
 Also, as the end of the book got closer, I started noticing how few pages I had left and that we hadn't encountered any conflict yet. The ultimate climax of the book was INCREDIBLE, but it was so short. That end in and of itself is 5 stars, but I would have liked it to have been more stretched out, perhaps not as easy as it was. I felt like these books have focused so much on only the romance aspect of the plot, which is sad considering that the action that we do see is incredibly written and feels like it's right out of a movie. I would have loved if this finale had spent more time on the action. 
 As an overall ending to this series I think it was perfect. I have some doubts about one thing (will mention below -*2) but it ended up in a way I thought was fitting. It's almost a little bit of an open ending because you know that they are going to face more challenges. It reminds me of Requiem actually, only done better. You know there is more to happen that we won't be around to see, but it's wrapped up in a way that I was satisfied and felt I knew the outcome, or at least the general direction things were headed. 
 I would say that this series is one of my all time favorites, because of the writing. If I had to rank the books, I'm not sure I could pick a favorite, I feel like maybe Shatter Me was the most appealing to me because it pulled me into this world, had that unique narrative that I loved, and I feel like more things actually happened in it. 
 Spoilery section: 
  
 *1 - The repetition I mentioned was that I felt a lot of time in the beginning of the novel was spent on trying to sell the reader on Warner, trying to redeem him. And in the middle, there is a lot of arguing between Warner, Adam, and Juliette, making Adam look bad. Juliette has at least two long tangents where she is weighing Warner and Adam against each other and she goes on and on for pages about growth and how she's different, how Adam sees her as weak, where Warner makes her feel strong. I didn't need to be convinced. I was already on the same page as her, and I felt like these long dialogues trying to turn the readers to Warner weren't needed (especially if you have read the companion novellas) and took time away from advancing the plot. In fact, more time is spent on swaying the reader to ship Warnette than on actual plot. Every conversation the characters have up to the last 50 pages are all about Warner/Adam. 
 *2 - I do think Juliette is strong now, I saw that in book 2. However, I couldn't quite take it seriously that she was going to be the new leader of the entire country. At the beginning of Ignite Me, Juliette literally falls on the floor because she can't deal with her emotions. So it's difficult for me to reconcile that image of her with the image of her as a leader. She has little to no world experience. True, Warner will be at her side and he has the political and military experience, but I didn't understand why he wasn't the one in charge, or why she couldn't have said "We" are your new leaders. 
 3 - Who else was rooting for Adam to die? I have never turned against a main character so quickly. Get out of my book man, you are ruining it. 
 4 - I am SO happy that Juliette ended up with Warner! I for one did not end up with the first boy I ever dated. You are young and inexperienced and don't know what's best for you right off the bat. Too many YA books stick a boy and girl together and call it "fate." But that's so unrealistic. Although I said before that Juliette's musings about the two guys were a little long, I have never had a book grasp so perfectly the rose colored glasses of first love, and speak about SELF instead of just fawning over a boy and why he's so great. It was refreshing to have an author GET IT. I'm so tired of having first loves shoved down my throat, that isn't the real world. 
 5 - Anderson's death was SO easy. Juliette tells us in detail about 20 different doors she knocks down as she searches for him. Why?? Why this pointless detail? It took away from the time able to be spent on the conflict, which I felt was lacking. I was hoping Anderson would be more of a threat, and that we'd get to see if he had a power or not, since he has 3 sons with powers. This felt a little bit anticlimactic to me. 
 Ah, I suppose I'm done. ;) Discuss with me! Did you feel the same about any of these things?

 Let me start by saying that I was intrigued by this novel the moment I read the blurb for the dust jacket a few months ago. Truth be told, I thought the book was about something completely different before going into it-- I honestly thought it concerned a mother and her young son trapped in a zoo after hours with a lion on the loose (or something along those lines). Obviously, that's way off. What the plot actually turned out to be wasn't necessarily a letdown, but I was disappointed that my theory was wrong (admittedly, I don't know how I got that original idea in my head from reading just the synopsis). 
 *I'll keep the spoilers appropriately tagged to preserve any kind of surprise for future readers, although it will be hard to do while I tear this book apart.* 
 I was expecting a Cujo-style thriller, but ended up with a different beast... and one that wound up being exceptionally boring. 
 As soon as I realized this was to be a book about gunmen/mass shooters  I was a bit turned off, but gave it a shot (no pun intended) anyways. We follow Joan and her four-year-old son, Lincoln, as they hide themselves away, and make irrational, unrealistic decisions for the remainder of the novel. I'd like to say here that Ms. Phillips made some inflammatory comments at the start; Joan's first line of thought once she understands what's going on is "Aren't all mass shooters white?" and further on she says something along the lines of, "they're white. Just as she expected". Okay. Gin Phillips needs to get her facts straight and check her prejudice: people of all races and ethnicities are capable of and responsible for many mass shootings since 9/11/01. Not just white folk. . I was rooting for Joan even after these comments. I wanted to like her, but then there came the whole deal with tossing her phone away to get rid of the light, countless times calling/texting her husband instead of the police, leaving the safety of her sanctuary after only like, an hour and a half to find a vending machine, because her son can't go three hours without a snack. 
 It was really too much for me to suspend my belief that any rational person would act this way. Then there is the instance of the baby in he trash can. Joan makes some harsh comments about the mother, even though Joan herself leaves the baby where she found it. Granted, she checks her attitude regarding this towards the end, but we never do find out the fate of that trash baby or it's mother . So many loose ends. So many plot holes. 
 One of the major issues with this book is that it focuses too closely on Joan and Lincoln. Their dynamics are about as interesting as a wet cardboard box, and most of it had no bearing on the actual situation at hand. By the time Kailynn and Margaret came into the picture, my annoyance was eased a tad, but focus only shifts to their perspectives briefly, and then we're back to Joan's. And from there, Joan slowly starts acting like a bitch! She is judgmental of Kailynn talking, of Margaret's religion, she eventually seals their fates, too, by being a total moron. 
 Lastly, I just have to publicly decry the countless instances of animal abuse, and downright senseless animal murder, in this novel. It serves no purpose setting this shit in a zoo. Really. Ms. Phillips saw a gimmick-y setting and ran with it. And you know what, from my perspective, failed miserably. If more attention was paid to characterization (and not just unnecessary and pointless backstories), plotting (taking time to fill in details and avoid all the holes in the plot itself), and tying up multiple loose ends, then maybe I'd have given this a higher score. In the end, Fierce Kingdom ends quite abruptly, and quite unremarkably.

I've been wanting to read this book for a long time (since middle school maybe?) and when I saw it at a used book store I decided to finally get it. I'm glad because I really enjoyed this book. Maybe I shouldn't have, as it does have some of the more common tropes within the YA genera. Still, I feel like the author handled them pretty well and I had a lot of fun reading it, which is the most important thing! I finished The Summoning in less than a day, and I've been in a reading slump too! 
 The book opens up in a perfectly creepy setting that I loved then jumped to when 15 year old Chloe is a freshmen. Like all paranormal YA she finds out she has powers yada-yada-yada. Except that isn't exactly how it goes. Instead of hiding them and trying to go on figuring out high school, she freaks out (like any normal person) gets sent off to a "group home" aka a sort of mental recovery institute called the Lyle House. They tell her she has schizophrenia which is why she was having hallucinations. Though she has a mild form as she doesn't have all of the symptoms that schizophrenia presents but hey, not seeing ghosts! Yay! However, as Chloe settles in and gets to know the other kids, they encourage her to be wary of the Lyle house and what they say. Soon, she begins to wonder if she really does see ghosts or not. Before duh, she is a necromancer (can see and yes, raise the dead) and finds out some of the other kids have different powers too (sorcerer and a werewolf) and that they are all part of the 'supernatural' crowd. I'm not that interested in finding out about their society, doesn't seem as interesting as some I've read about I'm sure it will be fine when I do actually get to that part. Armstrong isn't very descriptive about that in The Summoning.  
 I like a book that focuses on characters and doesn't get sucked into a bunch of romance and this book checks those boxes. Well, focuses on some of the characters. I wish that I could have seen the friendship between Rae and Chloe grow but it was subverted by the brothers Derek and Simon who introduce her to the world of the paranormal. And so yes, there are some love interests but, at least in this book, there is no real romance. I really liked that Chloe felt she had better things to do. And the 'plot twist' at the end was fun! It definitely made me want to pick of the second book ASAP!

Same feelings basically as the other books in the trilogy, but I started to get tired of Gemma's angst. It felt like so many of the chapters ended with her expressing again how alone she feels, and I get it at this point. I had less patience for the stuff in the realms again, and wanted more of the social negotiations of the Victorian world. I think I wanted everything to be more...supernatural, rather than fantasy. The fantasy elements took away from the gothic-ness of it. In fact, I didn't really feel the gothic at all, which is quite different from how I felt about the first book. Oh well. I still liked reading it. I don't think I was really in the best mood for this book right now (her constantly questioning her decisions, hesitating at making them, etc.), but overall it was fun. I think I just needed different timing and had incorrect expectations.

After a promising first book and a disappointing second, this series is finally starting to hit its groove. I'm just not sure from this perspective whether it's a groove or a rut. 
 The book begins with an odd murder in the underground, and Constable Peter Grant is called in to work his magic (literally). Although the story really pulled me in, it ended far too abruptly and without addressing some larger issues. My impression was that it felt more like an episode of a TV series than a novel--not surprising, considering the author's history. It's not necessarily a bad thing, either, but one that I'll be keeping in mind before reading any more of these books. Two issues that have loomed since the first book are the faceless wizard and Peter's need to be better trained in the magical arts. Both of these are mentioned in the book, but then left unaddressed. Again, it's like a TV series where one issue becomes the reason for the show, and the viewer is strung along episode by episode without ever solving the biggest issue at hand. That's what I'm seeing for this series, although it really is fun enough that most people won't mind. 
 One of the best recommendations for this book comes from the subtle racial commentary. Peter Grant is of African descent, and there are plenty of jokes and pointed comments about how his heritage influences reactions. My favourite line was the "trio of disreputable-looking white guys," simply because I've heard the reverse from so many ignorant white folk. There are even more magical characters introduced in this book, and that same racial discussion happens at an all new level, hinting at the same issues from a different angle. 
 All in all, this was a fairly solid read, but I was really hoping for something more developed.

 Deathless is the kind of book I want to read because I saw some of its quotes and promptly fell in love. To be honest that's not a good method to choose book because the actual whole thing will be a colossal disappointment and I got my heart broken a few times already. 
 Deathless, however, does really live up to the potential of its fragments floating around on tumblr. I love mythology and folklore to the last bone of my body, the gritty kind, the ones where the world comes to be in the most tangible way, the fabrics bloody and magical. Add to that a setting that incorporates the modern world and characters that are both beautiful and ugly, and you have me hooked. Valente's Deathless is a complete retelling of the Russian folklore Koschei the Deathless, set in Soviet Union. Marya Morevna, the main character, lives her life between the two world, the street of Leningrad and Koschei the Deathless kingdom - Buyan. There is no gentleness in this book, and if there is, it exists in flashes and dies down like the last spark of burning coals. Valente's writing has a great poetic quality about it ( I think I overuse the word now, poetic), making the story to become even more wrenching, as the characters grow and change in the face of war and revolution and love. 
 Marya is child that has been carved into adulthood by another person, by another force once was much greater than her. Therefore, there is no positive message coming from the her relationship with Koschei at first. Love in Deathless is terrible and brutal,that's for sure. But in the end, Marya is still her own person. She is not a being made up of metaphors, she is as real as she is magical. I'm as happy as I can with that.  
 If you don't like confusion (because that's how folklore goes, things happen because they happen), if you don't like a bloody world meeting another bloody world, this is not the book for you. But if all I have describe are what you're looking for, then Deathless is a great option for you.

 Review originally from over on my blog. 
 This is not going to be overly coherent I suspect. 
 I have been obsessed with Harry Potter since I was eleven years old. That's a long time, I'm old (almost thirty, gasp!). So of course I picked this up on Sunday, having spent the previous week re-devouring the seven Harry Potter novels for the umpteenth time, my expectations cautious but optimistic, not expecting this to really be the next Harry Potter book but a fun little addition to the Wizarding World. 
 And I'm really glad I was thinking that because this really is not the next Harry Potter book, it is not in the same league, it can't even see the league it's so far off, it feels very different, you can tell these aren't JK Rowling's words, and it lacks that little magical something that sets the novels apart. Don't get me wrong though, I liked it. I did. I still really want to go and see this performed in London if I get the chance, I'm sure that this would look absolutely fantastic on the stage, and I'm dying to know how they pull off some of the magical elements, but I think something gets a little lost in translation. 
 First of all, this is a script, obviously, so this is a very different experience from reading a novel, I have no problem reading the play format but I much prefer to watch plays if I can, and this is a prime example of why. Reading rather than watching this means we have all the limitations of the stage without the benefit of its advantages, the pacing is by necessity much faster which leaves little space for things like character development or the quieter moments of the novels, while we are missing out on the spectacle of the surely phenomenal production values and performances that would help make up for that. 
 The story was alright, a little predictable and nothing enormously new, a rather generic time-travel story with a Harry Potter twist, a little nonsensical at times but generally quite fun at the same time, it kept me turning the pages and the Part One cliffhanger was pretty exciting. It's a shame that the story relies so heavily on what came before, it would have been more interesting to get an entirely new story, just about the world of nineteen years later but I won't begrudge them the decision to throw in some Harry Potter highlights, the name is the reason everyone's here. There was one element that I really, really did not like but we'll get to that in a minute. 
 It was truly wonderful to see some of these characters again, even if a few were not really in keeping with their novel counterparts, every time a new beloved character showed up I grinned like an idiot. And after something Rowling said a while back I was very happy that we had some confirmation that Ron and Hermione are still happily married. The new characters were a mixed bag, I was a little disappointed that Rose wasn't in here more, and that she was kind of mean, but I loved Scorpius, what a delightful little nerd he was, I want a book series about him! In fact the Malfoys were my favourite part of the whole thing, it was fascinating to see how Draco has changed since his troubled teens, his redemption solidified and now with an almost grudging friendliness between him and the Trio, and I think Scorpius is likely to be the highlight for most people, he was a shiny beacon of loveliness, though can we stop with the queer-baiting already? 
 Also on a random side-note, the revelation about the trolley-witch was an amazingly insane idea and I love it. Ten points to the Hogwarts Express. 
 Ok, now, let's talk spoilers. Because, ho boy, there is one thing that I was really not a fan of. 
 WARNING. HERE THERE BE DRAGONS. AND SPOILERS. 
 The villain. The second Delphi showed up I went, "yep, that's the villain" it was so blatantly obvious. And just... holy bad fanfiction Batman! The idea that Voldy and Bellatrix had a baby is just... what even. I really wish that they had just had a new baddie who was unconnected, or just... basically anything but Voldemort's kid because what the heck even is that about? I rolled my eyes so hard I'm surprised they didn't fall out of my head. It goes against everything we know about him as a character, he would neither accidentally conceive a child (I doubt he'd even be human enough to be capable) nor want one. He spent a great deal of time and effort attempting to become immortal, he has no need or desire for an heir, he'd only see one as a threat to his own position. So yeah, not a fan of that idea at all. 
 Her plan was a really interesting idea though and it was really quite fun to see the AUs the meddling created, and the prophecy was a clever idea, the spare being spared was a lovely little nugget, just a shame they couldn't come up with a less... well, idiotic villain motivation. 
 Also I was a little bit heartbroken when Sirius didn't show up at the aftermath of Voldemort's attack on Godric's Hollow, I had a moment of utter excitement, he's my joint favourite character, and then had my hope crushed. Way to stomp on my dreams Jack Thorne. Not that I'm bitter.  
 HERE ENDETH THE SPOILERS. 
 So yeah. I am just a big ball of conflicting thoughts about this book. I think there is some great potential here for the stage, I'm sure seeing it performed would up its star rating a bit, but it just doesn't quite have the magic. I think that I am going to keep this in a little box in my head, separate from the Harry Potter canon, its own entity, like a piece of very weird fan-fiction that just happens to live on my shelf. If you need me, I'll be over here having an existential crisis about this... I can't believe I just gave something Harry Potter related less than five stars.

Back in my teenage years, I was very much into the murder mystery genre. Add a little bit of a puzzle, then some horror elements, and you can basically sum up everything I read between the ages of 12 to 16. But after a while, I became a seasoned sleuth, and the 'mystery' was no longer a mystery. Like an episode of Law and Order,the first suspect is never the killer, and its always the quiet bookeeper who is some sort of stalker, and his slip up was leaving his unusual olive green glove at the scene. So I stopped reading the murder mystery genre because I was just bored with the tired plot. 
 This book was recommended to me via Goodreads, and the summary read to me as a sort of novelization of 'Death Note,' a Japanese series I always found intriguing. Much to my surprise, the book was more like A Tale of Two Cities than Death Note. Suspect X, or Ishigami is so devoted to Yasuko Hanaoka and protecting her from the murder of her ex-husband, that he hatches a brilliant plan, one that she or even me as the reader does not understand until the very end. 
 The ending is quite good, and plot is very different from those that I read in my teen years (I am looking at you Lois Duncan). Even I, the seasoned sleuth, was pretty shocked by the twist at the end (well not too shocked.) However, I found the middle to be a little slower than I would have liked (which meant I was actually able to put down the book and live a normal life) and the "cat and mouse" game that was promised in the summary was much to be desired. 
 So I recommend this book to those who like a little challenge when reading a mystery. And to my fellow seasoned sleuths out there, see if are capable of solving a unsolvable question.

I received this from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. 
 Ruby, Nick, and Alexis are three teens who are part of the Portland Search and Rescue volunteer squad. On their first SAR callout, instead of finding the missing man for which they are searching, they instead stumble across the body of a murdered teenager. As the story goes on, crime buff Ruby begins to suspect that there is more to the girl's death than the police believe, and she convinces Nick and Alexis to help her investigate. 
 YA seems to be populated by dystopian and paranormal books, so it's refreshing to see a believable teen crime story. The Body in the Woods has a great mystery and interesting, realistic protagonists. Ruby, Nick, and Alexis all had relatively normal issues and insecurities. 
 My main issue was with the abundance of side plots. While helpful in fleshing out the personalities of the three main characters, I felt that Ruby and Alexis's parental plotlines detracted from the main story. Alexis's in particular introduced several characters who served little to no purpose in the grander scheme of things and seemed to be tacked on for whatever reason. 
 Overall, I enjoyed it, and I hope it starts a trend of more YA crime novels.

I loved this book!! I loved it so much I had every intention of continuing the series....until I realized there's 5 total. Is anyone else tired of not having a single standalone book anymore?

 Arlen, after seeing his father's cowardice prevent him from protecting his mother from demons, vows never to let that same cowardice rule him. His whole life is aimed toward the goal of conquering the thing that everything fears--the demons that stalk the night. Demons that are immune to everything, with the exception of wards (runes) that no one remembers the origins of. But they work! 
 Leesha is a whiny girl who I liked in the beginning then got annoyed with later on. She's the type that I'd expect to be all weenie about killing zombies. She doesn't mind combating demons, but how about three men that rape someone over and over again? Nope, we should be nice to them and let them keep all the stuff they stole and let them go and rape more people. Yup. 
 Rojer is someone who let everyone else do the fighting until he couldn't (not by choice, really. Just ineptitude.) Then discovers he has a gift for something that staves off the demons (music, everybody!) 
 Really the whole thing is just a build up to those three meeting each other in the end, but I loved the stories independently. Each one brought something different to the story, each character had a different path to grow up on. 
 Plus, demons are cool. Even though we find out in the end that they're all just drones for the big bad demons that are still below the surface, but whatever. Still terrifying and gory and deliciously evil. Definitely the wind and rock demons are the most terrifying. Having nothing but some scribbles on your door frames to keep you from being gored is a good way to succumb to fear. And though Arlen slowly (as the Warded Man) gets people to break away from that, it's easy to see how they all fell into their hidey-holes.

I think I've been too harsh on this series because I'd already watched the drama. Now that I've passed the point of HBO, I find the story a hundred times more compelling and two hundred times more frustrating. 
 The most frustrating aspect about this installment was just how *close* the characters are at every turn, at every bend. They just need to take one step further to be reunited with their loved ones, to find a true ally, to achieve some goal. Sometimes they physically are that close, but they are stopped by pride or foolishness or blatant misunderstanding. Bran is so *close* to Jon at the wall, Brienne is so *close* to Arya on the road, Sansa is so *close* to Tyrion who could be a real, true ally.  I just wanted to smack characters together and say, "She's RIGHT THERE!" a thousand times. 
 This frustration is only compounded by Martin's love of killing people which I'm going to say is worse than Joss Whedon's. He sends me into a frantic state of mind whenever the novel turns hopeful or peaceful. Any time things seem to be going well, I know someone is going to die, probably horrifically. I was a bit sad about Robb though more because it felt like dropping the plot than any actual caring for him. He lost that right when he got married for no reason. I see why HBO changed that plotline up. Catelyn I was almost happy about because I found her chapters the hardest to read. Interested to see what that sequel is going to mean. I'm sure I was singing "Ding Dong Joffrey's dead with the rest of the crowd, but that was compounded by knowing my happiness at one thing spelled someone else's doom. Sure enough, Tyrion. Oh my Tyrion. I hope there is more in these books for you. They don't actually "say" that he died yet, but I flipped through the chapter listing of "Feast for Crows" and he's no longer narrating. That is sad enough for me. Likewise I know Lysa dying, sweet as that was, probably spells Sansa's doom.  
 The compelling part though is that I don't think an author has ever made me wish so hard for the wrong thing. Most of the times when reading a story, you see the protagonist's choice clearly outlined with an easy choice and a right choice. They are crystalline and the hero is obviously going to make the write choice. Martin regularly presents his characters with a wrong choice and a worse choice. Melisandre is a good example. Martin spends half her descriptions convincing me she's is soulless, pretender harpy. Then he spends the rest of the time making me wish she wasn't. I end up as confused as Davos and Stannis, and I think that's brilliant. 
 I'm not sure how people made it half-decades between books. I'm very pleased with the next move for Arya, Brienne, Bran, and Jon, whose chapters are finally becoming interesting. I'm deeply saddened that Sansa cannot catch a break, but I look forward to seeing what happens next. As for the Lannisters... what can I say about the Lannisters? Debts! Debts to be repaid all around, I think. Also zombies. I look forward to lots more zombies. 
 I realize I've about forgotten about Dany, just like the rest of Westeros. I think that's also part of Martin's intention, saving her for book five. Then again, Martin never does what I think he's going to do, so why do I try?

 The Handmaid's Tale is a very terrifying, very possible dystopia. We follow the story of Offred through her experiences as a Handmaid. In a world of declining fertility and increasing sexual activity, there is a coup in America. The world changes, seemingly overnight. The Sons of Jacob rule and the age of Gilead begins. Offred remembers "the before times", but those memories are fragmented. Partially she is choosing to forget as a coping mechanism. Partially she is unable to remember since there is nothing but her mind to hold these memories. 
 The most fascinating part of this is book is how the story is told. Time and place are often unclear. Offred frequently slips between "the before times" and now. She jumps from describing what she's doing to living in her mind. It can be a challenge to keep up with sometimes, but it was also a fascinating way to experience Offred's mental positions. 
 Throughout the entire book, I was looking for an explanation of what happened and how this happened. How did the world turn against women in this way? Very logically, Offred did not provide this insight. I think if my world turned around like this, I wouldn't be able to place my finger on it either. The fall of America and rise of Gilead was not Offred's story to tell. Instead, at the end of the book, there is a transcript from a keynote speaker at a convention. This keynote speaker talks about the validity of The Handmaid's Tale, as well as loosely addresses the events leading up to and following this moment. It offered a view of Gilead I had been longing for while still keeping Offred's story true to herself. A stroke of genius in my opinion.  
 All in all, a surprising novel. I greatly enjoyed it, even thought I felt horrified most of the time. 
 I recommend this book for lovers of dystopia, feminists, and those fascinated by the embroiling of religion and politics.

Sophie Talbot is one of the Talbot sisters. New to the ton, their father made his money in coal and is now an Earl. Rumour is that he bought the title or won it in a card game with Prinnie. Either way, his wife and daughters are on the search for marriageable husbands. The eldest snags a duke, but when her sister Sophie catches him in flagrante in the greenhouse... she pushes him into a fishpond. And shatters her own reputation in the process. 
 Running away, she saw a man climb out of a window, and she stole his Hessian boot. 
 He is a rogue so rascally he's named 'king'; Kingscote, the Marquess of Eversley, and heir to a duke. He refuses to help her and calls her 'unfun', so she pays his footman to swap clothes, and hangs onto the back of his carriage. That's before she realises that he isn't even IN the carriage and it isn't headed to London. It's going North. 
 NOW what does she do? She has no cash left, she's hanging onto a carriage, disguised as a boy, and if discovered she'll be ruined. 
 He notices her immediately... such is her luck. It might have been the yellow silk shoes she's wearing. But she lets him know what she thinks of him. 
 "Let me be very clear. I am headed north to escape everything you are, and everything you represent. You are all I loathe about the aristocracy - arrogant, vapid, without purpose, and altogether too reliant on your title and your fortune, which you have come by without any effort of your own. You haven't a thought in your head worth thinking - as all of your intelligence is used up in planning seductions and winning silly carriage races. In case you have not noticed, I was perfectly fine in the stables until you came along and revealed me to be a woman. And when I left, with every intention of finding my own way north, it was you who followed me! And somehow I am looking to trap you into marriage?" She paused. "I do not know how I can put it more plainly. Go away." 
 When she accuses him of destroying engagements, he argues: 
 "Isn't it possible that I ruined her for the marquess?" 
 Who was several times the lady's age. [Oh ho... so that's it. Clever boy, king. It takes her FAR too long to work out what he's doing.] 
 So she sells his carriage full of spare wheels (for curricle racing) and catches the post carriage. 
 When it gets held up by highwaymen, she leaps out to defend the small boy she just befriended. 
 At this point, King catches up to them but for once in his life, he's too slow, and Sophie is shot. 
 King's pretending she's his wife to the only surgeon he can find. *Snorts* as if that lie isn't going to bite them both in the ass. The moniker Mrs Matthew has stuck from the footman's name she used on the coach. 
 *rubs hands* Bring it on. 
 The surgeon he finds has been thrown out of the medical society for washing his hands. [yessss] And he uses honey as wound antiseptic. 
 King knows she is a cyclone of scandal for him. But he can't help himself. 
 "I like you fine," he tells her. 
 And then they both discuss how the labyrinth on his estate is their favourite place. And then he gets a little carried away rubbing the honey on after her bath. *fans self* 
 And then he messes it up. Sighs... BOY does he mess it up. He basically seduces her, won't leave her alone, tells her he will never marry anyone let alone her, and tells her he can't/won't love her, but takes her to bed anyway. Then he takes her to see his father - in an attempt to pretend he's marrying her and upset his father. Rubbing salt in her wounds that she's unsuitable, unlovable and worthless. *FROWNS* 
 His 'wound' is a bad one but the entire thing is skewed by his eighteen year old understanding of the situation. Grow up, King. 
 By this point, I was very conflicted. I had liked him, but he just kept making an ass of himself.  
 Ch 21 miserable marquess makes massive mistake. 
 Certainly does... 
 Then Sophie's whole family show up, insist that she fix it all - the pond Duke has destroyed her father's business - duh. And she can fix it by marrying King. At this point, I dislike ALL of her spoiled brat sisters, and their useless lovers. 
 But I am concerned about her sister - the one who married the Duke that fucked the woman in the glasshouse and brought this entire situation down on all of them. She tells Sophie that it was her fault 'because she didn't tell him she loved him before she trapped him'. *blinks* and after they are married and she's pregnant... and... WHAT??? 
 And this is why she tells Sophie that if she loves King, she should tell him, and still coincidentally trap him... that her cheating husband would not have cheated if she'd just told him she loved him. She's pregnant with his child and heir. AND he's cheating on her. Why is she blaming herself for this? I know men could cheat with impunity. But it's the blame that freaks me out. 
 Sophie KNOWS King's nightmare is to be caught but she beds him anyway. He has decided by this time that he really does want to marry her, but doesn't tell her... and then I just want to shake everybody including Sophie's father. 
 Cute that Mary and her light fingered children get their HEA too. And squee... he bought her a bookshop. 
  
 I mean... it started off so well and then the last third just... made me annoyed.

7 years ago, when I was 12 years old, I watched a movie called 'Twilight' then discovered it was a book series. I immediately went to a book store and purchased the books then marathoned them all. Thus beginning my obsession with Twilight and also the beginning of my reader life. My review may be a little biased but you can be the judge of it. 
 As I've said it's been 7 years since I read Twilight so I feel like I can't properly review this because I didn't reread Twilight before reading Life and Death so I don't know exactly what is the same and what is new material. However reading it with fresh eyes, I can say I really enjoyed this. 
 When it was first announced about the gender-swap I was super excited but I was also really unsure if I would enjoy it. I was scared it would change my perception on the series I loved dearly. But I was wrong. This book totally worked for me. I actually really loved it, it gave a new spin on the story and kinda made it into it's own without being a completely new story. Same story just more fresh. 
 At first, it was a little hard to imagine that Bella was now a boy; Beau, and Edward was now a girl; Edythe, but as the story went on it, it wasn't that weird anymore. And because it's been so long since I read Twilight it was actually difficult for me to imagine how it was written in the original book. It was also fun trying to figure out who was who, it definitely gave me a few laughs. Obviously some things had to be changed because it wouldn't have made sense and that was perfectly fine with me.This book reminded me in so many ways why I love Twilight to begin with. It was really interesting to see how this story was the same and how different it became just based on the gender-swap. 
 I love Bella and Edward but I also love Beau and Edythe and I feel like I love them all equally even though they are pretty much the same characters. Although Bella and Edward both had their faults (I mean what character doesn't have their fault though) I personally never saw Bella as a 'weak' character, I've always loved her. And I never saw Edward as 'controlling'. Now gender-swapped, I didn't think of Beau as 'lame' or 'weak' because he's not the typical stereotyped male character. I found it refreshing to not have the typical male character that we always see in YA novels. I also didn't find Edythe to be controlling, I actually found her hilarious and kick-ass. Also I really loved the ending, and how it closed the story. 
 I also forgot how much I loved Stephenie's writing. I really do hope she comes out with something new eventually. Also for those who think this was a 'money grab' I personally think you're wrong. Stephenie clearly loves these characters and wanted to play around with her own world that she build. And the fact that 10 years later and things still bothered her about the original material and the criticism that came with it, does not scream 'money grab' to me. She explains all the changes and why she did what she did and I'm happy she included that because it help me make sense of what she did. 
 Regardless of what you think, I think this gender-swap was a good thing for the YA community to open their eyes a little at all the stereotypes that go on in literature. 
 Anyways I loved this new version, it was interesting and fun! This book definitely made me feel nostalgic so maybe that's part in reason why I loved it so much.

Delany's off-kilter semi-poetic examination of myth and its uses, using Orpheus as the main pattern, set in a post-apocalyptic actually, as it turns out, post-human too  Earth. Delany's fascination with the subject is clear, the atmosphere is unique, and some passages are beautiful, but sometimes it wavers between too slipperly allusive and too on-the-nose here's-what-this-symbolizes. For instance, I liked the mutant 'minotaur' in the underground cavern 'maze', but the coy computer whose acronym spelled PHAEDRA seemed too cutsey. Likewise, Spider's sudden transformation, once Lobey finds him in the city, into the info-dumping gatekeeper of the underworld seemed awkward. I mean, it was very useful for clarifying what Delany was playing at, but in terms of story and character, clunky.  
 So that sounds like a three-star book, right? Well, it's obviously flawed, but with enough powerful scenes, images and tantalizing ideas to merit four-stars.

Anna and the French Kiss is a debut novel by Stephanie Perkins. The genre of this book is Young-Adult contemporary romance and/or Chick-literature which means the majority of readers are girls, most likely teenagers (and/or high-schoolers). I find it pretty hard to rate this novel because I don't dig chick-lit but this book received favorable reviews from my Goodreads friendlist. So I thought, I might like this book; but then I was just being too optimistic. 
 Another reason why I read this novel is because I thought this book maybe fun; that this may not be another romantic-shiz; that maybe the girl protagonist will not be just a stubborn and whiny hypocrite who seems to be always on menstrual period; And that MAYBE the guy-protagonist will not be just an Edward-Cullen-like man who is so attractive, shiny, charming and has brilliant accent. SO MUCH FOR MY EXPECTATIONS. SO MUCH FOR MY UNANTICIPATED BUOYANCY. 
 This book tells the story of Anna Oliphant, a girl who has parents who are separated and a senior (in school) that is forced to attend a boarding school in Paris. She was "FORCED" to leave behind things that she loves such as her best friend, younger brother and her crush. "Sad" and "Forced" as the novel says it does, the story goes on indulging into the life of our whiny, stubborn and flirty girl whose moods always swings from the moon and back. Anna met a charming boy with a perfect accent Etienne St. Clair and who is perfectly taken by his steady girlfriend. As the story progresses, Anna discovers that she may actually have a chance with Etienne yet. Amazing.... Naaat -___- 
 Conversely, there are some points I appreciated in the novel. First, Perkins did a great job of making Paris come alive as a place to live in through the descriptions of Anna's adventures and exploration; and second, there were scenes in the novel between Anna and her little brother Seany that made me quite happy because it was sweet and touching and it reminds me of my funny relationship with my baby brother. But a lot of my feelings towards Anna and the French Kiss consist of intense dislike, and now I keep on telling myself "this is the reason why I don't read chick-lit!". On the contrary, this book may be a fun, cute book for anyone who's looking for a light romantic story with a picture perfect setting.

 Windfall is my first novel from Jennifer E. Smith, a very popular contemporary author who first caught my attention years ago with her other novel, The Statistical Probability of Love at First Sight. I set a pretty high set of expectations prior to reading this, but ultimately, in the end, Windfall swept me away and left a hurricane of mixed feelings brewing inside of me. 
 For one thing, with a title defined by the dictionary as "a piece of unexpected good fortune", Windfall's plot was fairly and generally predictable. The book had very few surprising revelations and even sparser twists scattered around its narrative. 
 Unfortunately, as much as I liked the other characters, I cannot say the same about Teddy, the actual love interest. In fact, I'd even go as far as to proclaim that I hated Teddy. It's not only because of his annoying personality but also because, fortune or no fortune, he just isn't an interesting character at all. He's shallow, short-sighted and poorly developed. While I completely understand that Teddy's turning point for the worse (e.g. becoming unreasonably extravagant and increasingly selfish) was inevitable, when he finally decided to change for the better, nothing he did was enough to win my favor. Probably because he never had any favors from me to begin with (since I disliked him even before he won the lottery). 
 Teddy aside, the bulk of Windfall had me emotionally reeling, and that's primarily because of the dynamic family relationships in the story. I can't really articulate my thoughts on this aspect, but it's a story element I thoroughly enjoyed reading about. 
 Overall, I might not have completely loved the book, but I would still recommend Windfall. This contemporary novel explores grief in a way that's deliberately thorough and painfully realistic. Many scenes in Windfall definitely hit close to home. Smith writes so beautifully that when she tackles delicate topics like family and healing, she is effortlessly able to induce emotions that just bleed through the pages. 
 Actual rating: 4 stars

This is another book club selection and with good reason. There is so much to talk about after reading this book. The Glass Castle is a captivating story of abject poverty, adventure, and survival. Jeannette Walls beautifully and simplistically shares the story of her childhood. 
 Jeannette Walls had an unusual childhood. Her memoir is a stunning look at a family experiencing extreme poverty. Her dad was an alcoholic with big plans and her mother was an artist uninterested in playing the role of mother and always on the lookout for an adventure. But maybe it's not the story you expect. Are they irresponsible or eccentric? Do they live outside of the norms because they are too intelligent to conform and perhaps know something we don't or because they can't maintain in traditional society? Together these two had four children, including the author. The family moved around a bit and money was always tight. The children were often forced to fend for themselves when it came to basic needs. Necessity breeds creativity and until the children become teenagers, their life is hard, but poverty is not their focus. They are fun, loving, warm, and a bit madcap. 
 Amidst the addiction, unemployment, starvation, and often the hopelessness of this family there is a beauty in the journey. I was immediately drawn into this family's life. There were times during my reading when I wanted to reach into the book and strangle the author's parents, Mary and Rex for being so selfish and stubborn. I'm all for raising kids to be self-sufficient, but it is a parent's responsibility to care for their children. I did admire the parents in ways and despite their seriously flawed parenting style, or perhaps because of it, their three oldest children turned out just fine. There is a scene in the book where as adults the children get together for Thanksgiving and they muse about all of the food and how it wasn't that hard to provide it. 
 In some ways I could identify but in others my life was strikingly different. I would not have wanted to grow up like they did, but the Walls family did have some good times and I did agree with Mary and Rex on some points regarding parenting. Poor Maureen, the fouth child, seemed out of the loop with her older siblings. She had missed out on happier times with her parents, who no longer had any 'skedaddle' left in them by the time they reached the town of Welch, and she suffered because of it. She did not receive much attention from her parents and was not as self-sufficient as her siblings were. I felt bad for her and I hope she turned out alright. The story is bittersweet; it ends well for some members of the Walls family, and sadly for some others. I really enjoyed this book.

 The Royals series is such a guilty pleasure for me. They are not the type of books I usually read, but I picked up Paper Princess because of all the hype and found it totally addicting. I felt like that addictive quality was lost a little bit in the following books, but it was back in full force for me with Fallen Heir. 
 Fallen Heir shifts the focus from Ella and Reed to Easton. I really enjoyed getting his 1st person POV. I was expecting the story to be told in dual POV between Easton and the love interest, newcomer Hartley, but I'm actually really glad that it wasn't. I can't really think of many Romance books that are told solely from the male's POV and so that set it apart a little bit. And while there was a lot of brooding, I did like the insight into his behavior and I enjoyed it a lot more than I had enjoyed Reed's POV. 
 As expected, there was all sorts of behavior I don't approve of when reading about young adults (or regular adults for that matter), but I felt like it was toned down a lot from the previous books. I really appreciated that the story didn't rely so heavily on shocking or graphic content. This book focused more on Easton's destructive behavior and that there were actual consequences to it for both him and the people around him. I am really hoping that Easton gets into a rehab program before this series is over. 
 I enjoyed the slow burn relationship between Easton and Hartley. While at times Easton did come across a little too stalkery, being in his head we know there was no ill intent, so it didn't really bother me that much. I liked that we got to see Ella and Val and I liked Easton's friends Pash and Bran a lot, too. There was some more high school mean girl drama that kind of annoyed me, but I didn't find it as over-the-top as it was in previous books either. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Fallen Heir. I loved getting Easton's POV. Sometimes he's a hard character to like, but I was 100% rooting for him the entire time. I felt like this book recaptured the addictive writing that the first book in the series had and I can't wait to read more - especially with those major cliffhangers this one ends with.
