 Shadow & Soul opens with a poignant dedication that sets the tone of this story. 
 "This story is also dedicated to the children no one looks out for, and to the adults they become." 
 I knew right away my heart was going to be in my throat for this book. 
 Shadow & Soul is a forbidden romance that progresses into a second chance romance with the heartiness of Michael ("Demon") and Faith's tumultuous love story. Demon's story begins in book one; Strength & Courage, and becomes the main focus of this book. When we first meet this broken man I knew I was going to love his story because it wouldn't be an easy, peasy, cheesy love story. Ms. Fanetti's muse, Lola, loves to play with her beloved characters and Demon was no exception. Lola's been quoted as saying, "Sure, I love a good torture. Blood and guts is my meat and potatoes. But angst--tears--that's my Dom Perignon. When Susan cries while she's writing, I am intoxicated." *shivers* 
 Faith was born and raised in the MC where she grew up feeling connected to the lifestyle. While Demon was raised in foster care where he had to learn to fend for himself. Even though, their childhoods were shaped differently these two were immediately attracted to each other. 
 The shadow of their past love affair still haunts them ten years later when they meet again. At this meeting it's as if all those years had vanished and their souls were intertwined together. Despite the fact their relationship was no longer forbidden the fear they felt from the earlier years still lingers in the shadows of their re-acquaintance. Along with their past fears both of them have personal stuff they are dealing with that test the strength of their newly formed bond. 
 I loved how emotional this love story is with both characters battling their own "demons." Ms. Fanetti is a favorite author of mine because she isn't afraid to write a story that has realistic aspects even if it breaks the readers hearts. Lola's ability to make a story come alive with the facet of realness adds to each story. The characters never travel the easy road but instead they battle uphill for their happiness. 
 Thank you for another well told tale from the mc world, Ms. Fanetti.

For the first time in my life, I can say I felt embarrassed while reading a book. 
 In my time I've read some nonsense, but the sheer ignorance the author displayed in "The Queen of All That Dies" was cringe-worthy to say the least. It came to that point where I couldn't even laugh at it anymore. What made the entire experience bad was all the opportunities the author had but missed to research some points that she chose to incorporate as vital elements of her story. What made it worse is the fact that majority of those were common sense. 
 If you ever wondered how to write a cheesy fluffy romance novel, then try to unconvincingly disguise it as politics and intrigue, thus proving you are absolutely clueless about either subject, then by all means, read this book, it will give you some excellent pointers. 
 The world has been divided to eastern and western hemispheres by a horrifying nuclear war. Serenity Freeman is living in the burned, barren landscape of the Americas. She lives underground in a kind of military base, with a handful of other survivors. Food is scarce, there is no sunlight. A true post-apocalyptic world. You get the gist of it, now listen to this.... 
 She is an ambassador's daughter, and in the new world order where every move could mean the difference between life and death , the author chose to apply ancient distribution of power; inheritance, rather than merit as Serenity is called to attend with her father a meeting with the dreaded King Lazuli to negotiate the surrender and survival of an entire hemisphere. I thought OK, maybe she's a badass, highly educated diplomat with mad fighting abilities. The author simply chose to say this, "Next to my father I've learned useful skills." - what those were, we never discovered. Another thing that stunk to high heaven was the described condition of Canada and Central America. As the author said herself, the things are so unsettled and dangerous there and a ruling government was non existent. Yet, here is this irrelevant girl, 
 surrendering 
 a territory nobody has any control over. It goes so far to say to the reader to disregard her father who happens to have experience as a diplomat, and simply focus on her, because she's speshul and beautiful, and stuff, that on it's own would be enough to dazzle a conquering force...... 
 Seems legit. 
 In the midst of all of this 
 incredibly clever stuff 
 , the author launches herself in thinly veiled backhanded praises of just how beautiful Serenity is. She is so malnourished from hunger everybody is suffering from, yet her friend feels sad for her and the look of her hipbones and her collarbones sends them into a grief fest. Never mind that her friend is starving just like she is. Just so we know our MC is super thin guys. The supporting cast keeps subtly hinting how pretty she is, while she selflessly laments her life by having to wear a dress in front of the King, because she is above and beyond superficiality. Oh, and she has a scar, so I guess we were expected to believe she is above vanity as well. To all of those still not getting it, this is the part where the author pretends that by pretending not to like all the frilly, trivial nonsense our MC is actually displaying a sign of incredible depth of character. And, if you wish to continue reading this novel, this is the part where you pretend to believe her. 
 But fuck it, even that isn't bad on it's own. It's the science.... 
 Most of the developed countries on this planet possess nuclear weapons. Most of the undeveloped countries possess them also. There are a shitload of nukes around, and no matter how turbulent our world becomes, or how violent, nobody ever seems to use them. Why do you think that is? Majority of third-graders out there have an idea. The times of 'Little Boy' are far behind us and most of today's weapons measure in yield up to fifty times more. One single blast from those things and the fallout would encircle the entire Earth in a matter of days. If more then one bombs would detonate we would face a nuclear winter, engulfing the planet in a cloud of smoke that wouldn't lift for decades. Nuclear blasts and radiation are apparently magical in this book. A bomb strong enough to 
 level 
 DC goes off, our heroine survives it in a basement, not a bomb shelter....but a basement. She steps outside after a couple of hours with no ill effects whatsoever, she simply strolls away. 
 Many more bombs detonate, across TWO continents covering one half of the globe, 
 razing the soil, making the atmosphere toxic, and our heroine simply prances around in a dress and heels, waiting for a flight over to Europe. No hazmat suits, no precautions, no Geiger counters, no decon, nothing. 
 On top of being magical, the radiation is extremely polite too, as it stayed where it was originally dropped, as Europe continues on with life unscathed, and lush as always. As our Serenity says, the sky is even bluer there... 
 Just think about it... This colossal stupidity is the backstory of the ENTIRE novel. I mean, ignorance on a subject is easily rectified by a little research. If you don't feel confident enough, perhaps don't feature the elements of that subject as carriers for your story. Some time spent with Google at least could save you a shitload of embarrassment. 
 Example: Dunning-Kruger effect 
 The Dunning-Kruger effect is a cognitive bias wherein unskilled individuals suffer from illusory superiority, mistakenly assessing their ability to be much higher than is accurate. This bias is attributed to a metacognitive inability of the unskilled to recognize their ineptitude. 
 As David Dunning and Justin Kruger of Cornell University conclude: "The miscalibration of the incompetent stems from an error about the self, whereas the miscalibration of the highly competent stems from an error about others." 
 Did Wikipedia just send you to the BURN UNIT? Oh Yes, I think it did. 
 It seemed to me that she was simply too lazy to look anything up, she just tossed all that in there as fluff until she had the chance to focus on the romance. If that is the true case, don't try to sell this novel as something it's not. I simply couldn't go trough this story with a straight face, because the author tried to portray serious characters going trough an incredibly hard life, by saying things that make no goddamn sense at all. Cringe....just cringe.. 
 PS: 
 Aw hell, i just couldn't keep it in....King Lazuli??? As in Lapis Lazuli??? I kept imagining a smurf. It made those scenes hilarious where she was silently pissed at him. I mean what was she going to do? Choke a smurf? smh...

This is a book that I always saw on the shelves throughout high school, but never picked it up until I was in college, and I am upset that I waited all this time to read this book!

Oh, how I so desperately wanted to like this book! Yet, I step away from it feeling an overwhelming sense of meh. It's not even a matter of making comparisons to Thirteen Reasons Why, as that never even crossed my mind while reading What Light, however I think it may have been a case of overdoing it with the expectations. The writing was so well done, the characters so carefully, thoughtfully crafted (Thirteen Reasons Why) that I suppose I expected something similar for What Light. Instead, though, I found the characters to be flat, the plot was underwhelming, and the conflicts were...lacking to nonexistent. The writing was okayish, but I constantly caught myself involuntarily rolling my eyes at some of the descriptions, especially with the "peppermint mocha" (teehee! -subtext) descriptions and...I don't know, maybe I sound all bah humbug, but I just really wasn't feeling this one. 
 So, as a general overview, Sierra's family owns and operates a Christmas tree farm in Oregon. Each year, just before Thanksgiving, they migrate south to California for one month where they set up their trees to sell for the season. Though they are only in California for one month out of the year, they have been doing this so frequently that Sierra has been able to establish a deep friendship with a girl named Heather (in addition to her two best friends back home, Rachel and Elizabeth). This seems a bit odd to me, especially the whole approach to the foursome's friend dynamic; I personally find it a bit difficult to believe that friendships of this magnitude would be approached both so maturely and without jealousies among sixteen-year-olds, but the Pacific Northwest has always been so progressive, so...I don't know. Anyway, Sierra's parents always hire "ball players" to help with their tree sales. This one kid, Andrew, is always hitting on Sierra, who has refrained from getting involved with anyone due mainly to the timestamp on their time in California. Heather pressures Sierra to date while she's there this year so that she won't be alone with her seemingly clueless boyfriend, Devon. Sierra initially insists that she's not interested in partaking in the dating scene...until she meets Caleb. 
 Caleb has an adorable dimple on only one side of his face and Sierra is pretty much immediately taken with him. Of course, this is the one boy Heather tries to dissuade Sierra from dating as he "has a reputation" for supposedly "attacking his sister with a knife." Oooh. Okay, sure; this sounds like a clue that this dude might potentially have anger issues (I picture Andy from The Office, punching his fist through that wall. Twice.), but to be fair it's all just rumors until she hears it from the source. Okay, so it happened, but there's (parental divorce, bratty sister) backstory. The general gist is that Sierra spends time with Caleb and intuits that he "isn't that guy" and forgives him for his past behavior. But can Caleb forgive himself?  
 By the end of this book, Sierra has blown off her friends in Oregon, missing Rachel's first "big break" in A Christmas Carol (to be fair, that's a long train ride for a two hour performance, but I also get why Rachel's mad; Sierra blew her off to spend more time with Caleb), fights with her parents, gets really close to Caleb...then they call it quits? Because of the distance. Then it's all "I don't want to lose what we have," but without any real turnaround or depth. Essentially, this relationship escalates quickly (though they only kiss; not a complaint, just an observation) and by the end of the book they're going to make it work since they "love" each other.  
 Besides the relationship between Sierra and Caleb, there's the strained friendship between Caleb and Jeremiah, who was there the day that Caleb went after his sister. By the end, they are friends again, which is perhaps a parallel to Caleb forgiving himself? Or maybe I'm reaching for a deeper meaning. Heather ends up not breaking up with Devon after Christmas, as he's not as clueless as she thought he was. Caleb gets others involved in his mission of spreading Christmas joy, where they buy and bring Christmas trees to families who otherwise would not have had a tree.  
 It's a sappy (pun semi-intended) story without too much depth, which wasn't really doing anything for me. Others have mentioned that reading this book is like watching a Hallmark Channel Christmas movie, which is definitely the cheese factor level I was feeling here as well. If you like these movies, there's totally nothing wrong with that. They're just not for me and neither was this book.

Making Faces is... rough. There's a lot of really tough issues within these pages. Spousal abuse. PTSD and scarring. Self-esteem. Deteriorating diseases. 
 The thing is, this author makes it work. The whole story is one big melodramatic meltdown, but Fern's philosophical views and Bailey's (almost) constant optimism make it seem less so. They're all very real characters fighting their own individual battles. Fern, the plain girl who finally learns what it's like to feel beautiful. Bailey, the boy whose body doesn't match his insides and who probably won't live to 25. Ambrose, the boy who ran away from responsibility, convinced all of his friends to go with him, then had to suffer the mortal consequences of losing his closest friends, as well as his physical beauty. 
 Ultimately, it's a story of acceptance: acceptance of oneself, of others, of emotions. It's a gorgeous one, and one I wish had a different ending for some. 
 I don't know. This was a heavy one so I'm not really in a good place emotionally to write competently about it. It's a damn good book though.

Short Review 
 One of the weakest offerings in the series so far. A majority of the plot elements resolve themselves in a way that leaves less explained than when we began, others are covered over by what amounts to thematic hand-waving. Upon finishing the book it left me with the feeling that entire novel was just there to set up later events. All of that gets topped off with the creepy sexualization of underage Molly to make this a solid two-star for me. 
 Long Review 
 This was easily the worst Dresden book for me in a while, primarily because of the plot construction and the way the novel ended feeling like it's sole purpose was to set up future storylines. 
 First though, I'll go over the things I did like. 
 With the exception of Harry, whom we learn nothing new about in this book for once, there's a lot of good characterization. We learn more about Thomas, get a little more into Murphy's feelings toward Harry / opinion on how a potential relationship would go, and get to see a side of Charity that finally makes her feel like a well-rounded, human character rather than a caricature of a strident, overprotective wife. We also get the set-up material for larger plot lines that will become important later, which is something of a strength and a weakness for this book. 
 It's nice to see bigger things happening, but at the same time the desire to pull things together and make everything look connected robbed this book of a lot of its individual plot. 
 Which brings me to my biggest complaint about this installment - the plot. 
 By the end of it we're left with a whole lot more questions than we are answers about anything that transpired. Madrigal Raith, our resident red herring for this book, presumably got manipulated into being there by someone through his half-djinn. That's never explained, and we forget about it to rush after the phages Harry pinged back to Molly. 
 The phages themselves and their presence are never really explained. Molly only gave Nelson and her other friend nightmares and a fear of drugs, she didn't call the phages. They were presumably sent from the Nevernever, but we don't find out who sent them. 
 It could have been the biggest Fetch, but why? The Fetches are Mab's servants, did she start all of this? If the Fetch sent the phages through then why did they get redirected to Molly when Harry used his spell to send them back to who called them since she didn't call them? 
 The presence of Hellfire suggests whoever attacked Arctis Tor was in league with the Denarians - and by extension maybe the Black Council - but why were the Fetches still there? Did the attackers lose the fight at Arctis Tor? Where were the bodies of the attackers if they lost? What were they trying to accomplish if they succeeded? Why did it take Summer Fire at the wellspring to bring the whole Winter army back home if the place had already been basically crushed by the attackers using Hellfire? 
 The whole book feels like the author arranging pieces for a later story while ignoring this one. Madrigal Raith's involvement is pointless, other than to set things up a bit for Thomas and more White Court stuff. Nothing really was accomplished - the phages were stopped but it feels empty because there doesn't seem to be a clear reason for their presence to begin with. We just end with Molly as an apprentice and a bunch of plot elements set in place for the next book. 
 Harry, to no big surprise, is still a creepy, sexist pig of a man. I'm certain I've filled my lifetime quota for reading about shirts 'straining against chests'. Everything with Molly (her being underage and all) is extremely creepy. All the talk of piercings in private places that Harry insinuates he's enjoying imagining, all the little off-hand remarks about how he has to keep reminding himself she's underage and off-limits, they clearly show Harry considering it. 
 I know people will fuss that he turned her down at the end when she showed up naked, and didn't do anything, etc., etc., but that doesn't really make a difference. The way it was written makes it clear Harry wanted to, whether he indulged his creepy side or not, and the way it played out seemed like really disturbing fan-service. It felt like the author made Molly behave in such a bizarre way just so he would have an excuse to put her in the book naked. 
 All in all, this book came across as more of an interlude than a real novel - just something to set things up for further installments without much thought put into making this installment into an enjoyable story in its own right.

 As a volunteer at a shelter for lone shifters--the same one that rescued her--Makenna Wray has dedicated her life to finding homes for its residents. And when she discovers that a teen in her care is related to Ryan Conner, the broody, handsome-as-sin enforcer of the Phoenix Pack, she's eager to help connect the two. She just wasn't prepared to feel a connection of her own. 
 Lone wolves are loners for a reason--and most of them bad. Or so Ryan assumes until he meets the mysterious Makenna. Quirky and sensual, she seems to enjoy riling him, especially when she refuses to discuss her past. Although there is no mating bond, he's sure she's the one. All he has to do is be patient and wait. But when another pack's sinister Alpha comes sniffing around, threatening Makenna and her shelter, this enforcer is ready to let his wolf off the leash... 
 I've been reading Suzanne Wright books for several years and I'm really surprised I've never actually reviewed one of her books before. Savage Urges is the fifth book in The Phoenix Pack series and is my second favourite book in the series so far. My favourite being Dark Instincts! 
 The Phoenix Pack series consists of great alpha male characters and strong, vibrant and funny females characters who won't take crap from anyone and a bit of crazy thrown in just to keep things from being too smooth and Savage Urges continues this with this great series with Ryan and Makenna. 
 I love the way Ms Wright, writes her male characters and Ryan is no different. While he may be an alpha male and not the alpha of the pack that's where the similarities end with the other male characters. Ryan holds his emotions close to his chest and is often described by others as being closed off, cold and unfeeling which isn't true and while his back story is sad it really worked well for him. I loved how determined he was of what was between him and Makenna and how he never wavered with his feelings for her or the decisions he makes to protect her. 
 Now Makenna, she's an awesome character. To be honest all the female characters in this series are awesome and it's hard to say who a favourite is as they are all wacky and brilliantly written but Makenna is definitely one of my top choices. Makenna has a complicated past that doesn't feel over done or overwhelm you and doesn't get dragged out. Makenna brings a lot of light and humour to Savage Urges and to Ryan. Makenna brings crazy to Savage Urges by being extremely superstitious and it was so funny to see Ryan's reactions to the superstitions she said and how others react too. 
 "Finding an unconscious shifter on your doorstep was a definite buzzkill. 
 Frowning in surprise, Makenna Wray double-blinked, half expecting him to disappear. Nope, he was still there, which just went to prove that Friday the thirteenth really was an unlucky day." 
 The amount of crazy in Savage Urges, is much less than compared to others in the series but it works really well as I mentioned the crazy is a lot less because it's more contained with Makenna's superstitions, which honestly cracked me up. I loved the way Makenna could get past Ryan's shields and get to him like no one else could. 
 It was great to see everyone from the pack and to meet some great new characters in Zac, Dawn, Madisyn, Riley, Savannah and Dexter. 
 All in all it was a really good read and not only do I recommend Savage Urges but this series too!

I'm on a really great streak. The last few books I've read have all been great ones, ones that I would easily recommend to others. On the Island is no different. I received it from a friend as a Christmas present; obviously it took me a bit before I got to it, but I'm glad I did. It's a beautiful story. 
 The essential plot is this: a young teacher takes up a position to tutor a newly cancer-free teenager while he's on vacation in the Maldives. Circumstances force them to ride together and separately from the rest of the boy's family, and while flying to the island their pilot has a heart attack and they crash into the water. 
 Anna and T.J. survive the crash thanks to their life vests, and T.J. brings them both to shore on a deserted island. And they live there in total isolation for three years, forced to make due with supplies washed ashore from the wreckage and whatever else they could find on the island. 
 I loved the plot. They are forced to face virtually everything while stranded on the island: sharks, starvation, disease, wild animals, tsunamis. I think the only thing they didn't have to face--which in my opinion would knock anyone to their knees--was loneliness. I loved the developing bond between T.J. and Anna because it seemed natural to me. Anna fought it for so long because she knew what the implications would be. T.J., however, was gung-ho about it from the start. I was only surprised to see that his ambitions to be with Anna weren't just sexual in nature. In fact, I was amazed at how much he wasn't bothered by what he had missed. Perhaps his time missing school because of the cancer had already forced him to adapt to not having a typical experience. That seems most likely to me. Yet his determination to be what Anna needed--no, that's not right. John was the one that tried to force himself into being what Anna wanted. T.J. embodied what Anna wanted and needed, because he truly wanted the same things, and I love that. He bought Bo! 
 It's a fascinating story. I cared about the story, and I cared about all the characters. And I admit, I really loved that Anna got the happy ending she wanted.

Bully was a book that I did enjoy, there is enough "what the hell is going on" to keep you reading, cause lets face it you do want to know why the male protagonist Jared is being such an assHOLE to Tate. 
 Okay lets start with what I liked: 
 What I liked 
 This wasn't a girl sees guy around school, likes him, pines for him, he doesn't know she exists, then something happens and he begins to see or she changes herself, new cloths, hair, make-up etc to impress him type love story. 
 Tate at least had a strong personality and didn't just flow with the crowed and at least she doesn't pretend not to care what others think of her, she makes it quite clear that she does. 
 What was even better about this book was that the language in the book didn't pretend that teens sensor themselves verbally or mentally either in private or in a group. Yes teens swear and some swear a lot, they also think about sex quite a lot and its not just the guys, girls too. The book also didn't make high school out to be a fairly tale, it pointed out that there where different groups of people and different types and just about everyone no matter who they were gossiped and spread rumors about one another. Majority of high-schoolers are not innocent from that at all, and that often people help a bully, encourage, or incite bullying in high school. Even just be pretending not to see whats happening aids bullying. 
 Tate tried to handle situations as best she could, she didn't always make the right choices and often she was fully aware of the fact, later, that she could probably have handled things differently. At least she decides to stand-up for herself and wont allow herself to keep letting the situation be something that would hurt her. 
 What I DID NOT like 
 Bully was not really the best title for this book, because although in the beginning we are introduced to Jared's horrible treatment of Tate and others encouragement and also no one doing anything to stop him, that's about the only real bullying you see. Yes you feel sorry for her in the beginning and it establishes that Jared is an asshole who deserves to get a taste of his on medicine and when she gets back after her year away and she makes the decision to not allow it any

 And it became very clear that both Jared and Tate where, for want of a better word, "Hot for one another". Tate's reaction was clearly because of past hurst and trying to mask her true feeling for Jared so as not to be humiliated by being in love with a guy who treated her like crap for three years.

The entire book is fulled with negative criticism against other girls who are not like her. Just because a girl wears short shirts and tight tops, which she also did at one point, and has big boobs does not make her vapid or stupid. I also didn't agree with the fact that she was always referring to other girls as slutty or coming down on them for having sex. That goes against ever feminist bone in my body. 
 for example: 
 "Being a bitch could be a survival technique. They get respect. There was no honor in people thinking you were a slut." 
 There is so much wrong with that statement I cannot decide on where to start, so I'll just leave it at that. 
 At no point in this book besides the fact that Tate usually ends up trying to beat up someone or is thinking about it does she really have a conversation with any of the girls in her school except her best friend, KC, and Jess the girl on her cross country team.

Because here are two people who went through their pre-teen years working on cars together, playing together and they're ending up in love. He encourages her to race and not to hold back, and Tate has no problem staking her claim over Jared and has even less of a problem with telling him that. 
 and of course quotes like this :

Not that I was in a love triangle, but I never understood how a girl can't know whether or not she wants a guy. We can be confused about what is good for us but not about what we truly want."

I won't go into detail as I realize I may be spoiling some big things for people, but GUYS. SO MUCH STUFF HAPPENS. The real meat of the revelations comes within the last, like, fifth of the book. BIG THINGS. BIG BIG THINGS. A thing that stunned me, and a thing I clapped and laughed delightedly over, and a thing that made me cry a little.

 Look at this pretty flower! 
 Hey. I want to know if you like me, but I can't say that, so here's an awkward flirtation instead. 
 Where are you? 
 I'm here. 
 Where? 
 Here. 
 There? 
 No, here. 
 Oh. 
 Look at my kid. 
 Look at my dog. 
 Look at me. 
 Look at me holding my kid and dog. 
 Hey, everyone. I took a huge koala this morning.

I think I was pleasantly surprised by this fantasy book. To be honest, it holds a lot of the old tropes without that much innovation. But it was still a fun read. 
 The king is dead and the peace and equality he and Falcio Val Mond have been working for has been for nothing. Now the Duchies are clawing for power, bandits and thieves are running rampant, and Greatcoats -once heroes- are now spat on as villainous. But Falcio and his two friends are Greatcoats and they have a geas from king to find his greatest jewels. 
 I loved the opening - great hook, great start. 
 However, ultimately this is an unpolished fantasy book. There are multiple times that were very jarring - to the point where I reread it and went "what?". None of it grammar or syntax, but flow of the story. Another editing eye would have definitely benefited this book. (When Aline meets Brasti for the first time - she scolds him familiarly. What? The random insertion about paying a scribe to write this novel. What?) 
 I am not that enamored with the characters, as fun as they might be. I never really get to understand Falcio fundamentally. He is more of a stock hero than anything else. He doesn't feel real to me. But oh! He has so many unique traits: like being a berserker, a righteous guy, revenge for his loved ones, etc. I think it's mostly that his voice doesn't feel unique despite this whole thing is written in first-person. 
 And Kest and Brasti feel more like minor characters than part of a grand traveling trio. What can I say? I don't particularly feel attached to anyone. 
 The romantic angle was just really freaking weird. So he is given near-absolution in the span of a night with a prostitute? And she comes on the command of a god? 
 That's the other thing. There's just so many things crammed in that aren't developed. It's a world that is barely shaded in. The gods and Saints are important, but we know next to nothing about it. The magic is hinted at and only used in a minor plot point. The political maneuvering is only barely touched upon, but it should be super important due to the revelation of who the Lady is. And the worst thing: we don't even really get to know the main villain! How can we go through the entire book and only meet the main villain in the slimmest of moments? 
 On the positive side, the climax of this book, for me, was the scene in the dungeons. The scene with the Fey horse and the torturer. Well done. 
 But moving on to the ending... I was just not a fan of the ending because it highlighted how unpolished the book was. It felt like de Castell wasn't sure how to end the novel, but had to end it somehow. Too many new elements were thrown in at the very end. This, to me, is a sign of a weak ending. Too much deus ex machina with the Tailor, the random appearance of the Saint, the explanation behind the hidden gems, the reappearance of the Greatcoats... no. 
 You can't cram that many plot appearance/resolutions in the span on 50 pages or so and expect me to nod my head willingly. 
 Three stars. I think this is a good start to de Castell's first fantasy series. But honestly, I wish I would rather read his second series after he has figured out a couple of kinks. I'm not dying to pick up the second book - but when it does come out, I'll probably check it out.

Mare, Kilorn, Maven, Cal... what is this called, this relationship? Is it a love square? A rhombus? Whatever it is, I never really felt a strong bond between any of the characters, friendship or otherwise. With that weirdness aside, Red Queen offers up Mare Barrow, a girl who in the eyes of her family is a screw up. She thieves. She lacks any real skill to help support her impoverished family. Fate steps in and she becomes a servant to the palace. 
 This isn't a rags to riches story, it's about an inferior race serving the tyrannical elite. You can draw parallels between the Silvers and the Reds to the Civil Rights Movement of the 1950's and 1960's, and even to what is happening today. We get glimpses into the mistreatment of the Reds by the Silvers, and each race's disdain and mistrust for each other, yet it wasn't as fleshed out as I hoped it would be. It felt too generalized, by Mare. Several pages in, you gather that Mare hates the Silvers. I don't recall her being personally victimized by a Silver, unless you count the conscription. I wanted the injustice to feel personal. Perhaps her father's war injuries should have been played upon more, or her seeing how the Silvers treat Gisa as she works as a seamstress. 
 What I wanted more of was these gladiator tourneys. Mare hates them. Kilron loves them. I was fascinated by them. I kept waiting for an appearance of a tiger. 
 With every appearance made by Farley, I laughed. When I hear Farley, I think Chris Farley. 
 All joking aside, Red Queen is a decent read. It leaves you with a few unanswered questions, most notably how did a select few Reds get Silver abilities? When do these abilities manifest in Reds? Is it stressed induced? Red Queen also does a fairly decent job at showing how a rebellion led by young adults, isn't a smooth operation. I appreciated this. No rebellion is flawless, it is even less so in the hands of the inexperienced.

There's no book hangover quite like a Zadie book hangover. I woke up today, having finished Swing Time last night, already mourning the fact that I didn't have any new Zadie left to delve into. I might as well shut the blinds, pull the covers over my head, and go back to bed. Her latest work follows an unnamed narrator over 20 achronological years, interspersing episodes from her childhood in North West London with those she has as an adult, working for an Australian pop star. Many of the themes Smith works with here will be familiar to devoted readers - complicated family relationships; deeply internal identity crises; fame and notoriety. 
 There is, at the beginning, a hint of some salacious betrayal that takes roughly 400 pages to come back to, though by that time you know it's coming and the reveal isn't the point. In fact, it's not even the most interesting betrayal in the book, which is probably the actual point. As always, Smith's writing is melodic and flat out beautiful. She is, of course, an expert at character studies, though they didn't seem to breathe as much as those in The Autograph Man or On Beauty (perhaps with the exception of the narrator's mother who practically stepped off the page). I get the sense that Swing Time is one that will stick in my brain and gradually prove itself to be much more intricate than it seems at first glance.

 I was really hoping to like this book more, but I was left a little unsatisfied and disappointed. 
 The book told a story of a country doctor, Dr Faraday, who became involved in affairs of an old English family, the Ayres. Faraday had known the family since he was a boy through his mother who used to work for the family. The house, Hundreds Hall, had made a strong impression with Faraday even as a young boy. His feelings were rekindled when he was given the opportunity to visit the Hall as a doctor answering a house call. After a while, series of strange incidents started happening in the house with its members--the mother, Mrs Ayres, the son, Roderick, and the daughter, Caroline. Roderick was the first to have strange events happening to. He was later committed to a mental institution after unexplainable fires broke out in his bedroom. A while later Mrs Ayres began to show strange behaviors. She said that she could feel the presence of her dead daughter, Susan, and that she had been hurt physically by her. She ended up hanging herself, though it was unclear how it could had happened considering she was heavily sedated. Caroline was the last of the family members. She was found dead on the floor of the house and was presumed to have committed suicide by leaping from the second floor, even though she had never exhibited any troubled signs. 
 At the center of it all stood Dr Faraday. He was the narrator of the story, but was a biased observer. He insisted that all the strange events could not be supernatural, but were explainable with scientific reasonings. Faraday concluded that everyone was suffering from some degree of mental illnesses, even though there were times when he was conflicted and thought that supernatural phenomenon was possible. He went seeking advice from another colleague, Dr Seeley, on what was happening at the Hall. Seeley planted ideas in Faraday's head that strange force might be possible: 
 'Is that so surprising, with things for that family so bleak? The subliminal mind has many dark, unhappy corners, after all. Imagine something loosening itself from one of those corners. Let's call it a--a germ. And lets say conditions prove right for that germ to develop--to grow, like a child in the womb. What would this little stranger grow into? A sort of shadow-self, perhaps: a Caliban, a Mr Hyde. A creature motivated by all the nasty impulses and hangers the conscious mind had hoped to keep hidden away: things like envy, and malice, and frustration... 
 This statement turned out to be very significant to the story. At the end, when things were falling apart at the seam for Faraday and Caroline, she called him out that he was the one who wanted to save Hundreds and that was his only goal. She said that he didn't really love her, but actually the house was what he loved. I think this is when the story really unfolded. Faraday was exposed as somewhat a fraud. After Caroline's death, I was left to wonder if Faraday was actually the "little stranger." The family members all experienced different things, but as Mrs Ayres put it: "the house knows all our weaknesses and is testing them." Different family members had different weakness. I think that was why Caroline was the least affected until the very end. At the inquest of Caroline's death, it was revealed by Betty that Caroline yelled out "You!" before she leapt to her death. That implied she saw someone she knew... Could that someone be Faraday? Nothing was happening to the family until Faraday's arrival. The author certainly left that for the reader to wonder. 
 The story was entertaining, and some of the passages were definitely spooky, but it also dragged on in some parts. The story also left a lot to the imagination. Unfortunately, something was lacking in the book for me.

This was a book that bubbled over with authenticity, imagination and passion. The prose manages to be lyrical and formulaic at the same time, capturing the essence of the best fairy tales. Yet despite all these wonderful ingredients, I found my interest to be continually sidelined. This frustrated me, because the concept of the novel--a fairy tale fantasy superimposed over the tragedy of real war--is more or less the same as Pan's Labyrinth, a movie which absolutely transported my imagination. 
 I thought my struggle might have been grounded in my unfamiliarity with the Russian folklore, which serves as both the scaffolding and flourishes of the story--and that may have indeed played a part. What I think was a bigger issue, and probably what held me back from my expected enjoyment, was the rigid application of what I assume to be the conventions of storytelling used in Russian fairy tales. Numbers were used incessantly, and the exact same facet of the story would be told three or four successive times with minor variations. I can honestly appreciate how this could be mesmerizing or romantic, but it felt like I was reading the scriptural book of Leviticus. 
 The quality of the writing is such that I can't give two stars, despite the fact that it barely moved me. I can see glimpses of a tapestry of literary magic here, but it simply remains beyond my grasp.

I had this book on my to-read list for a while but finally read this book for my book club and loved it. It will provide a great discussion. This book was intriguing; I couldn't wait to find out how the Victorian language of flowers played into the plot. There are many flashbacks detailing how the main character came to be so wary of attachments. I had a little trouble following the dual timeline, but the complexity of the main character pulled me in and kept me going. Despite her problems it is not a depressing book but one filled with hope. 
 Victoria Jones, the main character was emotionally damaged as a foster child. She has spent her entire childhood in foster care. Her only constant has been her social worker. The book opens on her 18th birthday which is her emancipation from the foster care system. She has been a difficult child with failed placements and her caseworker is tired of it all but never gave up since Victoria's failure would be the caseworker's failure too. She does not last in the halfway house intended to help her adapt to society. Instead she ends up sleeping in a park and eating food left uneaten by people. 
 The story is told in alternating chapters of the present and eight years ago when Victoria was a 10 year old. At that time she was placed with a single childless woman who cared for her and wanted her to thrive - Elizabeth. Elizabeth teaches Victoria the Victorian language of flowers but something happened and Elizabeth didn't raise Victoria after all. Victoria absorbs all the information about flowers and later uses it to create a customer base in the floral shop. 
 The only thing that Victoria seems to care about is flowers. She knows their proper names and more importantly the meaning of each one. A chance meeting with a florist opens the door for her to shine. 
 This book was so incredibly good that I read it within one day. The agony of Victoria's life sucked me in and wouldn't let me go. She has been independent so long that she can't let go and trust others. Her relationship with Elizabeth is so complex. Then we meet Grant, someone who understands her flower language. What a tortured couple! 
 Victoria has had such a tough childhood that she doesn't know how to deal with emotion. She makes wrong decisions, hurts those around her, and has trouble loving anyone - even herself.

 Maybe Someday is the first book I have read by Colleen Hoover and it has opened my eyes to her beautiful writing and amazing stories, and I can't wait to read more. 
 Maybe not right now. Maybe not tomorrow. But maybe someday. 
 Sydney and Ridge don't really know each other. They live across the courtyard from each other and when he plays guitar on his balcony, she can't help but sing along, making up her own words. Though these stolen moments are the only times they see each other, they can't seem to tear their gaze from searching the other's balcony. There is a pull between them that can't be explained but there is no intention to understand why they are drawn to each other. 
 When Sydney finds out that her boyfriend is cheating, her world is flipped upside down. Nowhere to go, she finds herself accepting a room in Ridge's apartment, making her his fourth roommate, thus putting in motion a relationship that will forever change her life. Ridge writes music for his brother's band, Sounds of Cedar, but has been in a writing slump. Sydney ends up being just want he needs. With her ability to write lyrics, she becomes his muse and a gorgeous connection is formed. They are a great team and soon the music flows. 
 There's a complication to this duo though. Their attraction is crazy strong and they do everything to fight it. 
 I'm convinced that people come across others in life whose souls are completely compatible with their own. Some refer to them as soul mates. Some refer to it as true love. Some people believe their souls are compatible with more than one person, and I'm beginning to understand how true that might be. 
 What follows is a rollercoaster of emotion that will rip your heart apart and then slowly piece it back together. Well worth all the pain you go through to feel the love that's waiting at the end, this story delivers all the feels - I cried, I smiled, I laughed, and I loved. 
 The characters were amazing and unique! Sydney was wonderful, down to earth, and completely relatable. I loved her personality and her big heart. She had a way with lyrics that just meshed with Ridge's music. They were perfect together even when they could not be "together together." She fought her feelings and I felt her pain as she did so. 
 And Ridge, sweet Ridge had so much love and commitment in his heart and I felt that too. He was amazing, sweet, sexy, and honest. He has his vulnerabilities but he was a brave and wonderful. He was so loyal that even when he wanted something else, he wouldn't veer from the decision he made years earlier. I knew he would stick with it and it hurt my heart, frustrated me, but ultimately I understood him. 
 There isn't a doubt in my mind that we could be perfect for each other's life, Sydney. It's our lives that aren't perfect for us. 
 This story was full of feels. There were butterflies in my stomach and my pulse was racing. I was nervous and had a sinking feeling deep inside. The tension that surrounded Sydney and Ridge became more intense the closer they became. They couldn't be more than friends with road blocks placed long ago, and watching everything they went through while trying to fight their attraction was painful. No matter how they denied it, there is this pull between them and I felt it all. I had happy and sad tears running down my face. I felt the turmoil in both their hearts along with the love. 
 I failed miserably at trying not to fall in love with you. 
 ... 
 I failed first. 
 This story isn't all about the angst though. At times it was light-hearted, funny, and sweet. I also loved the music and enjoyed the role it played in Sydney and Ridge's life. I loved watching them connect over the music and I believed in the beautiful friendship that developed. They were honest with each other and put everything out in the open. I loved this aspect of the relationship because it strengthened their bond even more. 
 I have to touch on the love triangle. 
 Usually I do not love stories with a triangle but this one is unique and unlike any I've read before. Ridge is dating Maggie when he meets Sydney. I wanted to hate Maggie but I couldn't. I tried. Trust me, I tried. She was sweet, friendly, and I liked her immediately. And because I liked her so much it made the story that much more angsty and real. How could I love Sydney, Ridge, and Maggie and still get a happy ending when obviously they can't all have a HEA? Well Colleen has done a fantastic job with this story and how it all played out.  
 This story is emotional, angsty, and unforgettable, and I devoured it. The ending was beautiful and my heart was full of love. 
 Overall, I loved this book. I know I will continue reading everything Colleen Hoover writes. I can't wait to read 
 Maybe Not 
 , the novella featuring Bridgette and Warren, Ridge's other two roommates. 
 *Make sure you check out the EPILOGUE to Maybe Someday on Colleen Hoover's website. It's the perfect conclusion to the story and I loved it.

I've read Jane Eyre quite a few times. I even taught it the one semester that I actually got to teach Brit Lit. Obviously, I like Jane Eyre and I enjoy retellings, so Jane Eyre set in 1950s/60s Scotland sounded pretty darn awesome. 
 For the most part, I was not disappointed. I think Livesey did a great job of capturing the essence of Jane, through the character of Gemma who is lucky enough to live in a time when girls are beginning to have more options in life. The overall plot of the book is very similar to the original: after the death of our heroine's beloved uncle, she is treated terribly by his widow and their children, eventually sent away to school, until as a young woman, she find employment caring for the ward of a mysterious man. After nearly marrying her employer, she discovers a secret from his past, runs away and is taken in by caring strangers, almost marrying a passionless man, before returning to forgive the former employer with whom she will now find happiness. Livesey changes enough of the details to keep it fresh and interesting. I did find some of the plot changes a little underwhelming, but I appreciated her efforts. 
 Some complaints from my fellow book group members (which I understand, even if I don't completely agree): 
 The setting didn't feel consistent -- some parts felt like the 50s, but others more like the 70s or later -- particularly some of the overtly sexual behavior of female characters. A lot of what they referred to would have taken place in the mid to late 60s, so perhaps it was a bit ahead of it's time, but I don't think it was too far out of line. 
 Some plot elements seemed thrown in the follow the original, but didn't really go anywhere -- i.e. the mysterious man who tries to pick up Jane in his car at the beginning. 
 The ending was anticlamactic. I have to agree with this a bit. I was hoping she'd find something more dramatic in Iceland. Also, the fact that Sinclair chased after her, rather than her returning to him, changed the tone of the ending. But Gemma is more independent than Jane, partially (as I said before) because she has that luxury in the 1960s. I was really, really glad that Sinclair didn't go blind or become otherwise helpless. I always really hated that part of Jane Eyre.

 I was a bit hesitant before starting with Will Grayson, Will Grayson because I didn't know what to think of John Green's books: as much as I loved The fault in our stars, I found nothing amazing in Looking for Alaska. So I couldn't know if this one, co-written with David Levithan (whose books are still unknown to me), would suit my liking. In the end, it did, and I'm very glad I gave it a chance. 
 For some reasons, at first I was certain it was a paranormal book, that the two Will Graysons were either clones, or lived in parallel universes. And apparently I'm not the only one who got tricked because at the library they had put it on the fantasy shelf. But let me warn you: it is everything but a fantasy book. It takes place in Chicago somewhere in the 2010's, and our protagonists are humans beings just like you and I, they just happen to have the same name. And the same age, too. 
 So, who are these two Will Graysons? The first one, written by John Green, is a pretty reserved boy who doesn't want to feel emotions. He has a rule: "shut up and don't care". He sounds quite distant and cold at first (and that's the desired effect, I guess), but I liked him a lot nevertheless, because he really looked like a male version of me back when I was 16. 
 The second Will Grayson, which I'll call low-case will (because he always uses lower case) is a goth who seems to hate the entire world, except one guy he has online chats with, yet in fact he just craves to be loved. I also liked him a lot; he has a great sense of humor. will was written by David Levithan and it makes me think I should definitely try one of his books. 
 And there comes Tiny Cooper, Will's best friend, whose name should be in the title, too, because he is one of the most important characters of this book, if not THE most important character. Without him, nothing would have happened; he is what connects Will and will. Tiny really doesn't have the right name because in fact, he is enormous. The largest gay person, or the gayest large person. Seriously, this guy is hilarious. You cannot not like him, even if he has a handful of flaws, like being unbelievably self-centered (he is even setting a musical about no less than his own love life, which is more twisted than a Sex and the city episode), and mentioning that he's gay a hundred times a day, like if his sexuality was the only thing that defined him. 
 This book wasn't quite what I was expecting, as I said before I first thought it was a paranormal book, but even when I realized it was contemporary and changed my expectations; it still wasn't what I was expecting. I thought that when Will and will met, it'd be a complete turning point in their lives. But let's face it, their meeting doesn't change much. And they really have few interactions with one another. Really, the central character here, the one who plays the most significant role, is Tiny. However, I still found it interesting. It's a nice tale of friendship and love (love in general, not just romantic love). There were some hilarious parts, and some very emotional ones. 
 The main flaw, in my opinion, lays in the ending. It's too much, and definitely not realistic. Okay, several things in this book weren't really realistic (I strongly doubt you could find a Tiny in real life), but the ending was beyond unrealistic (I mean, who on Earth is going to attend a gay musical and tell a stranger that they appreciate him, just because they share the same name?)  Yet it was very musical-like, so since Tiny's musical is a very important part of the book, I guess it makes sense. But still, I think this book deserved a better ending. 
 To conclude, I'd say that this book isn't flawless, but it makes you feel good. We need more books like this! 
 I recommend this book to you if: you like teenagers who think out of the box, and you want a story that will put a smile on your face. You also have to be okay with gay characters, because it deals a lot with homosexuality.

 Defiant is a 1760 historical romance located near Albany, New York during The French and Indian War. 
 Lord William Wentworth sends his greatest enemy - and best Ranger - Major Connor MacKinnon to rescue his niece Lady Sarah Woodville from the Shawnee Indians. When Sarah is found, Connor must watch Sarah endure torture before he can negotiate her release.

 Defiant. Wow. 
 I get that "wow" isn't much of a review, but that is my first reaction as I sit here to write. 
 The first time I read Defiant I was shocked by the Shawnee tribe's brutality. They burned people. They scalped people. They stole women and kept or discarded them at will. It's tragic. It's accurate...and they weren't the only ones who did it. 
 As Pamela Clare has pointed out, historical romance fans don't read novels about the French and Indian War. They read Georgian Era stories, London-based and full of ballgowns. 
 Defiant isn't your carriage ride in the park, sleep until early afternoon novel.

 In the midst of scandal, Lady Sarah Woodville is sent from London to New York where she writes a pleading letter to her uncle. Her uncle responds, asking she travel to meet him at Fort Edward. During that journey she is abducted by the Shawnee tribe. This is where Chapter One begins.

It took me a few pages to actually get invested in the story of Cecile de Troyes and Tristan de Montigny, but I eventually found myself enjoying it. 
 Cecile de Troyes is the daughter of a famous soprano and, fortunately for her, is just as talented a singer. On the evening before Cecile is supposed to leave the farm and head to Trianon to become a singer just like her mother, she is kidnapped and sold to the Trolls. 
 Cursed by a witch 500 years ago, the Trolls live under the Forsaken Mountain, unable to leave the city of Trollus. Desperate to break the curse, the king orders Cecile and his son, Tristan, to be bonded in hopes of breaking the curse. 
 Cecile pissed me off at first. I'm not entirely sure why; she wasn't particularly petulant or Mary Sue-esque, but something about her rubbed me the wrong way. Tristan was largely unlikeable as well, only in this case, my dislike of him lasted throughout most of the book. Their romance- while expected, given that it's a young adult fantasy novel- felt forced to me. While the two shared some kind moments before the big declaration of love, it didn't feel very developed to me. 
 I really enjoyed the idea of trolls being the ~otherworldly~ romantic interest.  When I found out that wasn't what they really are, I quite literally turned to my cat and said, "of course they're fucking faeries. Of fucking course." Because truth be told, I'm becoming oh so very tired of faeries.  It definitely was a new take on the idea and I really want to applaud Jensen for going in that direction. She definitely combated the image of trolls being short, dumpy, and all around ugly, while maintaining some of the characteristics that the word "troll" brings to mind. 
 I found Stolen Songbird to have a very good balance of dark and light, although there wasn't much humor or many outright hilarious moments. 
 I wouldn't mind continuing on in the series, but if it takes as long for me to be invested in the second book as it did in the first, I'll probably end up placing it low on my currently reading list.

So I was turned off by the first chapter, because I wasn't fond of Szeth's scene. The prose was stilted, and there was a LOT of telling and not showing. The next few chapters were equally taxing, with cheesy elements (I found the sprens to be an unneeded bulk), terrible dialogue, and a steep learning curve. 
 This is my first foray into Sanderson's work, but I've read The Wheel of Time before, and all I could think to myself was, "THIS was the guy they chose to complete the series?" 
 I put the book away for a week while I worked on the rest of my books in my reading pile. After that, I found myself without money to buy new books, so I sighed and picked up The Way of Kings again to pass the time. I'm glad I did. 
 I'm not sure how, but Sanderson's voice seemed to evolve as the book went on. I found myself not being annoyed by the prose anymore, and I was beginning to root for Kaladin. 
 Of course, readers are thrown into the deep end of Sanderson's world, but things start to make sense halfway through the book. Fabrials, soulcasting, parshmen, broams, all these words slowly become a part of you, and by the end of the book, you'll feel more equipped to tackle Sanderson's other works. 
 I like how he tied up the loose ends, despite the book being a part of a series. Finishing the book leaves you with a sense of completion, with a healthy desire to find out what happens next without the needless cliffhangers. His resolutions also evoked some emotions within me, and I found myself moved by some scenes in the book. 
 The dialogue is a little out of place however, as I feel like the characters speak like modern city-dwellers instead of how I imagine people should speak like in that world. 
 I can understand how this book isn't for everyone, but in my case, I really enjoyed it, and would love to check out his Mistborn series as well. Now if I can only save up enough chips for his other books...

Oyeyemi's book isn't a retelling, and if you're expecting Snow White, you'll be disappointed. Rather, it takes up the themes of fairy tales: beauty and appearances being not quiet what the seem, the relationship between stepmothers and stepdaughters, as well as mother and daughter. Oyeyemi allows herself the same liberties as the spinners of those tales. She's not tied to realism and instead makes free with symbolism, but takes on real-world issues like race in a way that feels new. The book is split between Boy's point of view and that of Bird, her daughter. Boy's voice is a 40's Barbara Stanwyck, which is chronologically appropriate and fun to read, but feels a little lacking in emotional depth. Bird's is equally unbelievable, but warmer. Still, emotional depth is often missing in a fairy tale, isn't it? The elements are always told in such a straight-forward way: the children are lead by their father into the forest and abandoned. The girl is despised by her stepmother and sent away. There's not much dwelling on it, it's just the back story to set up the next part. In any case, Oyeyemi's tale struck me as a more exciting way to explore race than, say, The Help, and more fecund in terms of creating meaning. The Help can really only tell what it says, while one can delve deeper into Boy, Snow, Bird and come up with different interpretations.

Where do I begin...

 HOLY HELL WHAT AN EMOTIONAL ROLLER-COASTER.

 Ok so the stakes have gone up by several notches to say the least. Every step of the way you can sympathize with just about every single person you meet. Yes I said person. Hunter isn't overly descriptive about each character. As the story line moves along information about each character is thrown in. Like when Kylie, Della and Miranda talk about boys and their breasts or the way Della will look good in Miranda's new miniskirt because of her legs. 
 Also the most important things are given to you so you know what you're working with but mostly it's left up to your entire imagination.By now we've gotten to know the basic natures of each person around Kylie, the story is no longer completely just about her. It's become about everyone she care's about and the life they're all helping her to build. 
 Derek left because he couldn't deal with the emotional ride that Kylie was every time he was near her (oh well see yah, I like Lucas more anyway), now Lucas and Kylie have a chance to develop more even though she still misses Derek, it's just the reverse of when Lucas was away. Sure she's still confused but hell what woman wouldn't be. Both Lucas and Derek are both great just in different ways. 
 Kylie's powers are more developed and I didn't know if I was reading faster to try and find out what she was or so see where everything was leading. 
 She can heal people, she manages to heal Sara, her childhood friend, from cancer. 
 The plot is more complicated and the lines that where so carefully drawn in the beginning of this book start to blur. 
 And once again Hunter starts to tackle issues that other YA authors seem to shy away from. She has begun to explain that in the supernatural world there is a heaven and a hell which are not just abstract concepts but places that do exist. There are demons and angels and each has their roll. Not all vampires and werewolves are good, or any other supernatural being for that matter, but neither are they all bad. But those who are bad can be very bad... 
 So grandpa rogue vampire, who is definitely not just a normal vamp, and his crazy vamp grandson, nicknamed Red, have gone out of their way to abduct Kylie because Red had fallen for Kylie and good ol' grandad has decided that Kylie will marry his grandson or die...(nice old man isn't he, oh so cuddly). 
 So no way out, no problem, since Kylie can now dreamscape, she just lets Lucas know. So Kylie finds out, when someone she cares about is in danger, she can break though solid metal chains and break own walls. Now thats cool! 
 Red and his Grandfather are evil and they want Kylie, and hell just when we thought both Lucas and Derek would do anything to have her, Red takes it to a new level. 
 Every time something bad is about to happen an animal saves her but the animal is no normal animal it feels evil to Kylie. So then why keep saving her? 
 On top of that Derek is back and I'm back on the fence because Lucas does so many things that makes you wonder where his loyalties lie. Is it with his pack?, Fredericka? or his family name that he wants to clear? 
 Then he fills Kylie's room with roses and tells her, he'd not only kill for her he'd die for her... 
 Damn! and I'm back on Lucas's side...(sigh) (so what if I'm being all girly about it!). 
 Kylie has a vision that a vampire is going to die, but who will it be... 
 Meanwhile Red keeps trying to talk to Kylie in her dreams, but vampires aren't supposed to be able to dreamscape so what the hell. 
 Red goes so far as to freeze time, in Kylie's cabin, with Della and Miranda there, during the re-vamp of the camp into a boarding school. He wants her to know that he wants her to make the choice, to choose to be with him because he's falling for her. And that's because she's good and through watching her he wants to protect her, that's his reason for freezing time cause he knew that his grandfather would try to kill her. And although Bernett and Lucas would make it in time to save her Miranda would die and he knew that would hurt her and he didn't want her to be hurt. 
 This is where the lines between good and evil begin to blur. 
 She has the impression that it might be Ellie, Derek's old girlfriend that he brought back to the camp and who she decides to be friends with. 
 And as it turns out she's right, Ellie is killed by the grandaddy rogue and Derek is badly injured. They then go after Kylie and because Red chooses her over his family, his grandfather has no problem killing him either. 
 The emotional ride in this book isn't just about finding love, it's about family, they don't necessarily have to be blood relatives, people who care about you and will stand by you. No matter how much Miranda and Della argue there is nothing they wouldn't do for one another or for Kylie. Every person in your life is there for different reasons and everyone provides you with different things that you need in life. But no one is less important. 
 And most of all, nothing is either or, black or white. Things and people can surprise you deeply.

Lauren Halstead is trying to open a school. It needs to be cheap but functional and well designed. She's tried a lot of architects and none have any ideas until she meets Matthew Walsh. His family firm specialises in renovation architecture and he is full of ideas. 
 Of course, most of them concern Lauren's body, not her school. 
 *** 
 This started off really well, but now the heroine is giving me whiplash. 
 She's naive but she's sexy. She wants privacy but she wants to fuck against his warehouse windows. She's trained by her SEAL father and does krav maga but she falls over all the time. She's never had cunnilingus but she wears a necklace with a clitoris on it. She sexts him then deliberately doesn't return messages for hours. 
 It makes no sense. 
 There were a few editing errors but they weren't enough to throw me out of the story but now I'm irritated with the heroine, I'm noticing the errors. 
 "Why not just hire a couple architects?"(p. 153). 
 Of... missing an 'of' there. 
 I have to say that the hero, Matthew, is just as confused as I am by Lauren's behaviour. 
 Lauren is... awful. She doesn't return messages, she keeps trying to find ways to leave him (she's been doing it since their first night together), she tells him she's 'busy', except when she wants sex from him, or architect work. She makes herself friends with all his siblings and then tries to dump him all the time. And then she shows up and they're together almost every night. 
 He suggests she move in with him and she tries to avoid the conversation by reaching for his cock. Then says this when he slaps her hand away. 
 "It's ludicrous that we're having this conversation. I've known you for three months," I said. 
 "And you feel exactly the same way, and it's bullshit that you're pretending you don't." 
 I sensed my beautifully crafted existence, with all my rules and rebellions, and treats and cheats, was crashing down around me, dissolving into something I didn't understand. (p. 310). 
 How does she not understand a normal healthy relationship? She's the one with the awesome parents who are still together. He's the one with the abusive, horrible father. How does she think that Matthew is a 'treat' like a goddam cupcake. The woman has issues. 
  
 And then she decides that she has to sleep at her place because she has a period. She's obviously had one before in three months so it's a dumb lie. Be an adult, woman. 
 And then she tells him this: 
 "No. You said what you needed to say. We can't force it anymore. I have my priorities, and I can't let you be one of them." (p. 321). 
 And dumps him. And then his siblings blame Matthew. Dicks. 
 What is wrong with this woman? 
 Why would Nick the paediatric surgeon be handling their father's stroke case? I mean Angus behaves like a five year old... 
 But when Lauren goes to the hospital and tells Matthew that she loves him... there's nothing. The scene doesn't work for me. She hasn't earned it; it FAILS as the theatre cheer scene (that's what they call it in romance movies - you know when they dash to the airport, or stop the other wedding or whatever). And why would Angus die holding Lauren's hand? She's not his kid. Realistically none of his kids will hold his hand; they'll be fighting over who gets to pull the plug.  
 There are a lot of 'dead' scenes; setup for the obvious stories to follow. Matthew has five siblings and a good friend, and they all obviously rate a volume. 
 Matthew can do better.

First, as always the cover. The cover doesn't really do it for me. The moon is creepy looking, but the title being all lower case blends into the background, along with the series name. I did really enjoy the fact that the bloody crescent was on the beginning of each chapter of the e-book. Onto the novel, there was a certain Twilight-ism to it. This made it very predictable to me. The second Taye was gone and the wolf showed up, I knew it was him. I knew instantly Lucard was a vampire. The reason this book was so much like Twilight was because the characters, and components of the vampires and werewolves. Now, if the elements had been traditional vampire/werewolf characteristics this wouldn't have stood out, but Meyer's vampires and werewolves broke all the rules, so the features that were so similar made it impossible for me to separate the two. For example Kade's and Meyer's vampires both: 
 1)Are cold and pale 
 2)Eyes that turn red when they feed on human blood 
 3)Have special talents that make them even more super 
 4)Have intoxicating features that are hard to ignore 
 5)Are complete possessive freaks 
 Onto the werewolves: 
 1)There is the Indian tribal connection 
 2)Are shape shifters not really werewolves 
 3)Are hot in temperature (which didn't make sense to me when Meyer made it happen, so I don't understand this inherent hotness in this book either) 
 4)Bad tempers make them "phase" (which is the exact word that Meyer uses to describe her wolves) 
 5)It's a big deal that a girl is a werewolf 
 6)Are complete possessive freaks 
 These are only a few of the examples of the vampy/wolfy similarities, but it didn't stop there.  The characters are eerily similar, with the edition of a secondary creep/physco named Lucard. I found it almost impossible to like any of the characters. There was Amberlynn, naive, whiny, complainer, and SO weak. There was Tayelon, instantly possessive, overbearing, darkly hot and immature even though he's a Senior in college, he acts like a Freshmen in high school. There was this Tristian character, who I don't even know why he was there, other than for Amber to say was immature, even when she was acting like a complete toolbox herself. Then there was Lucard, the biggest toolbox of them all. This guy was 
 creepy 
 , crazy, possessive, always showing up at the oddest moments and saying odd things. I still don't get why his butt was there, but he reminded me of Larant from Twilight. Then there was dream vampire, who Amber has never met, only in her dreams, and when he's real she acts like a complete mush pile. He's just as creepy with his quiet, supposedly caring, but totally possessive and phsyco-ness. There was one character I did like--Luna. She was funny, cute and a good friend. She seemed to have a brain, which made me even happier. There were a lot of things that just didn't make sense to me--like the fact that the wolves phase but don't know who they are. They just change into killing beasts, but somehow Amber has the talent of making them not kill her...because she's special.  The ending was also kind of what the, but it saved the whole thing for me because now I have to know what happens in the next one. So I'll pick it up because it ended so strangely. 
 As for the writing--I found it overly descriptive,describing things that I didn't care about (like what she chooses to eat each time she eats). Then again, I am known to really live by and read by the "show don't tell" tenant. The sentences were also at times choppy, and it caused the pacing to go from slow to fast, back to slow. Then there was the huge lecture that Taye gives about the wolves, which Amber just listens to without questioning for four pages. I understand that some things can't be drawn out and shown through the length of the book, but I would have rather skipped the descriptions about food, looks and needless things and learned about the wolves slowly instead of all at once. Overall, this book held my attention and the ending makes it so I must read the next one. I highly suggest this book for those that loved Twilight and were on Team Jacob--this book is Twilight in reverse.

 I've read nothing but great things about this series, so I was excited to finally read it. Unfortunately, it did not at all live up to my expectations.

I could the similarities to the Dr. Who and BBC Sherlock franchises but this book has more to offer than just that. In addition, I thought that the pacing of this book went better than I had expected especially since that book was surprisingly short (Really, Mr. Ritter, must it really be this short?!) This ties in with the overall plot development as well- I think the story would've turned out a bit awkward if the pacing was off. Thank goodness it all turned out well :D 
 Now, the characters! OMG the characters!!! I do not know where to begin in explaining my gi-normous crush on R.F. Jackaby... seriously... gi-normous crush.  I love Airicka Phoenix's work! This book is a prime example why. IT ROCKED! 5 STARS, hands down - I really loved it. From the moment I read the first page, I didn't want to put "Games of Fire" down. I swear if it weren't for that thing in life called responsibilities, I wouldn't have put it down. But you know...someone has to take care of the kids right?! How can Sophie convince him not all girls are the same? While Sophie and Spencer figure out exactly what they mean to each other, there is an ever-present shadow watching their every move. At first Sophie is oblivious to the stalker's presence, but as her relationship and understanding with Spencer increases, so does the stalker's boldness. Find out who the stalker is, what they want, and why they are after Sophie and Spencer. Is it random? Is it jealousy? Or is it revenge? You will have to buy and read "Games of Fire" by Airicka Phoenix to find out! I know you'll want to see what the verdict is on Sophie and Spencer's relationship too! 
 Ahh! I LOVE this book! I know I already said this but...this book rocks. Airicka Phoenix rocks too Seriously. You need to buy this book right away and read it. I absolutely love the characters of this novel. I feel like there wasn't a single character that was unimportant or should have been left out. Ms. Phoenix is very talented and has a way of writing that everything you read in her stories is significant. I was instantly in love with Sopie. She is the kind of girl that I would love to hang out with. Sophie is just a real girl in her vintage tees and jeans. I'd love to swap clothes with her sometime! I related with her on many levels, her situation with Spencer one of them. As for Spencer...he is just an all-around rock star. From the first scene he was introduced, I was in love - even though he wasn't the most polite man in the world. But what can I say? I fall for the bad boys...but the ones who are secretly good guys on the inside are the best. I understood why Spencer was so guarded towards females. I would have thought it were crazy if he didn't have any type of wall up to protect himself. I just loved how Sophie and Spencer clicked though, even when they were arguing. They had such strong chemistry between each other and their attraction was palpable. I am a sucker for happy endings and I just wanted them to have theirs; I was routing for them from the very beginning. You'll have to read "Games of Fire" to see if they got their fairy tale though. 
 This novel is for Young Adults. However, some of the language and sexual content is not suitable for readers under the age of sixteen. I would recommend this 5 STAR novel to readers interested in YA, Romance, Thrillers, and Mystery. Also, if you enjoy the New Adult genre then I think you will like this book as well. I definitely think that you should add "Games of Fire" by Airicka Phoenix to your To Be Read list, along with the rest of Ms. Phoenix's work...it will be worth it!

That part isn't as prominently featured as one might hope, though, so if you don't take a near instant shine to Very like I did, you won't like the book. I admit, I'm still having trouble explaining why Very draws me in. She just does, makes me want to hang out with her wild-child adventures. And that's a really wonderful thing to find in a book. 
 I do have just one issue with the end, though: Very's roommate, who was my hero for being a virgin (and not of the waiting-for-marriage type, but simply because she was determined to be in love with someone prior to sleeping with them), and who spent the entire book patiently informing Very that she was not gay...turned out pretty gay.
