I finally finished this book after a freaking month and a half. I can't believe it, it's the longest I've ever spent reading a leisure book. But! I am glad I read it. 
 This book reads a little like a 18th century soap, filled with drama about affairs and love interests and stealing people's boyfriends and whatnot. It's not my most favorite type of genre (I don't like stupid love books where people have nothing better to do than just whine about their love lives and create drama for themselves), but Tolstoy is a master of characters. 
 I swear, no matter how much I didn't like most of the characters, I still kept reading because Tolstoy managed to make them so very real and different. A lot of authors have a problem where they aren't really able to make characters too much different from each other, except for the obvious story tropes they fall into. But here, Tolstoy manages to show us how humans react emotionally to different situations - all of them so very different in mindset and background and situation, but all showing this nature of humanity in interaction. 
 Okay, I'll stop with the flowery words. I sound like an English paper, really. (But I can see why an English class would want to read this!) 
 But anyways, he does this by skipping through each person's thoughts when writing a scene. Sometimes it's a little disconcerting because we start one paragraph in Levin's head, and then end up in Anna's, or something like that. But I really think it works, I really love this style of writing. We see how perceptions are so different depending on the perspective. What one character does and says for a specific motivation can be interpreted so differently by the others listening. (Example, Anna thinking that Kitty hates her for who she is, when Kitty just feels pity.) 
 My absolute favorite parts are when we tag along with the characters to different parties where three or more of these character we have slowly gotten to know interact. These moments are where you see the hidden motivations behind such simple words and sentences, and why characters react as they do. We have the third person omniscient view and we know everything - and it is absolutely delightful to see Tolstoy capitalize on this. 
 But Tolstoy ends up adding so much more to this book than just the romance. I might even dare to say that this book isn't a romance, despite that it would seem to revolve around Anna Karenina's affair. But that's not the case. Tolstoy adds major issues to this work, ranging from politics, to spiritual enlightenment, to dealing with death and in-laws, the education of women and civilians, of course divorce, and so much more. I think these additions are what elevates this book from just a mere romance to a classic. 
 But... at the same time, sometimes he would go on and on about a certain topic just to get it across, and I always struggled to get through those times. So good and bad. 
 One interesting thing is that Tolstoy manages to present both sides of the argument for whatever issues he's talking about - so the reader doesn't actually know exactly what the author believes. Some books are so heavy handed in their support for a touchy issue, but Tolstoy manages to weave it into his conversations naturally. It's quite lovely to read. 
 Let me also just say that I hated the characters. They were so stupid, so silly. But... then, you could empathize, almost feel for them. When Levin is pulls his heart out and offers it to Kitty, when Dolly struggles to stay afloat after making the hard decisions of staying for her children, or when Kitty goes on a soul-searching journey to find herself after a love gone bad. Or maybe even feel deep sorrow and pity for Anna and Vronsky's love gone so bitter. All of them made such stupid decisions, such stupid choices. But they were real, with their thoughtless passions and raging emotions. And for that, I love them. 
 The ending was a disaster, in my opinion.  I don't mind that Anna died, there is really no other way that I could see the book ending. But to make the last part, the quasi-epilogue, all about Levin and his spiritual change... that is a cop out, in my opinion. It makes the book about him. About him and also about the author's own spiritual change, trying to show the reader what he is about. I am not a fan of that.  
 I could write a lot more, to be honest. About the characters, about nit-picky details, about my own thoughts of the issues he brought up, but it might take a book report that I'm really not willing to write. 
 I'm just glad I read this on my own time instead of in a high school class - I'm sure I would've just skimmed it and disregarded most of the book in those years. 
 Two and a half stars because it was okay. I didn't "like" the book in commonly used term where you liked the story and the characters and the setting and whatnot. Instead, I found myself appreciating the author for his writing ability and prowess with words. Although long, I do think this book is worth reading (at least some of it) just to get a grasp of how he manages to weave different characters into a conversation without losing anyone's personality. 
 Recommended only for those with time and those who want to read a classic. I don't think there are many books that are terribly similar that I've read. 
 For me, it was worth reading. Once.

The Devil DeVere series rating: 4 out of 5 stars 
 "The Devil's Match" is novella #4 in this novella series and 
 can be read as a stand-alone novel. 
 How are the sex scenes? 
 A twist for Georgian romance. 
 The East's Harem has an influence in this novella as the heroine learns there are many benefits to a...erm, massage. 
 How are the story lines? 
 Wonderful, if a bit rushed. There's a strict word count 
 and sometimes the scenes would read better with more transition. 
 Setting 
 "The Devil's Match" is a Georgian historical romance based mostly in Woodcote Park, Epson, Surrey, England. It prologues in 1778 with a scene from The Devil You Know, then jumps to 1783, just days after The Virgin Huntress ends. 
 (Remember, novella #3 is a prequel to the entire series.) 
 The Epilogue starts in 1794, and to tell you the location would be a spoiler. 
 Review 
 The Virgin Huntress's couple, Captain Hugh and Lady Vesta, are being wedded and everyone's attending Woodcote Park for the big celebration. Diana is making plans to leave Hugh's estate since her place as Vesta's caretaker is no longer needed. The Devil is determined to have Diana back in his bed after five (or four?) years. 
 A wager forces our love birds to confront their still-burning attraction and the novella takes a turn for the exotic, erotic and unpredictable. (Sorry - more detail would spoil the story.) 
 Our Devil has a juicy, juicy secret and it's revealed quickly - hidden during a conversation between him and Diana. It tempts me to reread the series and confirm if he's telling truth. Given his preference for receiving oral sex, I think he might be. 
 Vane's strength lies in creating lifelike, complex characters who are not always heroes or villians. Vesta is irritatingly spoiled, yet finds understanding for Phoebe. DeVere shows random acts of kindness, but is still The Devil at heart. Like real people. 
 Remember to stay tuned for the Epilogue, because it's not the blissful cherry on top of the story you'd imagine.

I rated it 1 star out of 5, not because I think it was THAT BAD but because 1 star literally says "Did not like it" and I felt just that.

Enough to almost have me return it (I wrote a short "Please stop using the word 'materialized'" review, when I was a bit into the book and was getting insanely frustrated) Come on, use a thesaurus or something! 
 I'd say the only reason why I bothered/managed to finish this book was because I was curious of the ending, though I hated it. I just can't start something, and not finish it... The whole idea of "it gets better" really needs to be drilled into lesbian and gay novels, since I'm sure lots of teens are reading this book not just for the sappy love story, but for the possibility of achieving love and peace. 
 Maybe I'm a pervert, but there really wasn't enough romance for me to classify this book as romantic. 
 I was hoping that there would be more meat in the book, both romance-wise and content. Not just, "Tears welled up" and such but real descriptions of emotions and thought-processes. Can Holland express anything other than passiveness? The beginning of the book dragged on a little, and the end felt very rushed. Days were skipped, and although I get that Holland was in some sort of trance, still felt weird.  I didn't fall in love with Cece at all, I felt sympathy for Holland, but otherwise I didn't believe they were as powerful a couple. Sure, Cece was there for her, and so was her family, but were they really in love? Does a ninth-grader know what love is? I don't know. Sometimes I think it's easier to just go with "Yeah Mom, I'm straight" in order to get the funding for education and whatnot. I'm not saying that you have to use your parents, but in the end, Holland did realize that she had let a lot of things go, including her future. I can't believe she decided to go with an undecided major, it felt like she had literally given everything up. I honestly expected a different ending. A lot of the book is dedicated to how smart and determined Holland is, and how much she gets into the things she loves.  
 Somehow, I don't believe that this could all happen... For one, I don't believe Holland is as smart as everyone said so in the book. It felt as though I was constantly reading about someone praising her smartness and grades,  yet she only seemed to read novels and by the end, had dropped with all her marks. If she was truly smart, wouldn't she know enough to keep herself together? Especially when her mother referenced her history, and how she made it... I think Holland's mother was even more dedicated to success, though Holland says she hardly had any in her teens.  I do realize that some form of homophobic bullying still occurs but everything felt very unrealistic, and extreme. Maybe it's just because I haven't experienced it, but the book felt very very very over-exaggerated all the time. 
 Maybe I'm not in the right mood to read this book. I did finish it quite fast because I was hoping that it would become better, which it didn't really so that was a disappointed. Maybe I need to graduate out of the YA section already?? 
 I guess the main things I didn't like about the book were as follows: 
 -Lack of real character development besides just lust and electric pangs in stomachs 
 -Lack of actual romance 
 -Scenarios were sort-of unrealistic 
 Read it if you have time, are willing to be uninvested in the characters, are gracious in giving books slack, and are currently not going through any sort of traumatizing lgbt-related issues. Some parts can become pretty emotional if you are going through the same thing, I guess...

Received a copy of the ARC from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. 
 The Mime Order picks up right when The Bone Season left off. Like literally right after. When The Mime Order opens, the escapees from Sheol I are still on the train they boarded at the end of The Bone Season. From then on, it follows what happens to Paige and some of the other refugees after they return to their lives in Scion London. Paige must go back to the Seven Seals and work for Jaxon, as she is now the most wanted person in London, but she grows increasingly frustrated at his lack of caring about what is really happening to the voyants in the city, about the reveal that Scion is simply a puppet government for the Rephaim. 
 I loved the world that Samantha Shannon created in The Bone Season, so I was anxious to return to it, and I was not disappointed. I will say that The Mime Order does seem to drag at times, because you may forget (as I did) that this isn't a trilogy -- this series is going to have seven books in it. It's nice to have a story that isn't rushed so that it can happen in three books, but there are points where I was wondering when something was actually going to happen. Unlike the Harry Potter series, these books don't encompass an entire year. The Bone Season I believe took place over about six months, and The Mime Order is less than that. 
 As much as The Bone Season was about introducing the Rephaim, The Mime Order is about introducing the syndicate that rules the voyant underground in London. Paige is forced to return to work for Jaxon, despite having left his services at the end of the last book, for protection, as her face is now plastered all over London as public enemy number one. After the Underlord and most of his employees are murdered (with Paige being the prime suspect, having discovered the bodies), Paige learns more about the syndicate and discovers with horror that it is just as corrupt, if not more so, than the actual government. 
 In this second book, we are introduced to ever more voyants -- some of the refugees from Sheol I, other members of the syndicate -- and we get to explore the relationships that Paige has with her fellow Seven Seals, whereas in the first book the emphasis was mainly on her relationship with Nick. Now that Paige's eyes have been opened to what's really going on, she is anxious for the syndicate to do something and frustrated when not even members of her own gang are willing to help. 
 The rebel Rephaim return, led by Warden, and pledge to help her expose the truth and take down Nashira, but even though they have a common enemy, it is clear that these rebels have little regard for human life. Warden has been branded the worst kind of traitor, accused of consorting with a human, which even his fellow rebels find abhorrent. Thus Paige and Warden must continue their...whatever they have...in secret. Their relationship is both compelling and confusing, and they are both aware of that fact, but the attraction between them is too big to be denied. 
 The Mime Order is more of a mystery than The Bone Season was, focusing primarily on Paige's investigations into the murder of the Underlord and the mysterious Rag and Bone Man, who seems to secretly control more than anyone realizes. I like trying to solve mysteries, which is one reason why I enjoyed The Mime Order so much, even when it was moving a bit too slowly for my tastes. The more Paige learns about the syndicate, the more I want to know. So it's a good thing that there will be five more books to satisfy my curiosity. 
 That doesn't mean there isn't any action, though. The last quarter of the book has plenty of thrills, including more murder and a giant, twenty-five person cage-death-match to determine the new leader of the syndicate. Paige and Warden's connection is explored a bit more -- the mysterious golden thread that no one seems to know much about -- and we visit Jacob's Island, the slum within a slum where you learn that there are certain types of voyants who are detested even among their own kind. 
 There are plenty of lingering questions left at the end of The Mime Order. What happened to Michael, who vanished near the beginning of the book and hasn't been seen since? What is going on with Paige's father, who is clearly distressed about his daughter's disappearance and subsequent "outing" as a voyant? Is Paige's cousin Finn really dead? (Okay, that one might just be a question I have, but hey, no one ever found his body.) No matter how much time is left until the publication of the third book, it's too long to wait. 
 If you enjoyed The Bone Season, then chances are you'll like The Mime Order as well.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I did a little bit of research after I finished the novel to see what others had to say about the subject, and what I found was that there was very little information online from other readers. The most I was able to find was essentially that Waters, being a vocal lesbian, liked to write about lesbian affairs. 
 The Little Stranger, based on what I've read of Waters' other works, is nothing like them in terms of the relationships of the characters. It is a gothic thriller; set after World War II in England. The Ayres family consists of Mrs. Ayres and her two adult children: Caroline, 27, and Roderick, 24. Generations of their family has lived in their estate, Hundreds Hall. After the war and the loss of most of the family members save those three, the estate fell into a perpetual state of disrepair. It quite literally began to crumble around the family, along with their finances. 
 When Dr. Faraday, the narrator, is called to the house to treat the sickness of the family's maid, he inevitably enters the family's lives just as a chain reaction of events occurs. The novel starts out somewhat slowly, spending much time on the descriptions of the estate how Dr. Faraday remembered it as a child and how he sees it in his present day. What I learned later in the book was that there was actually a purpose to divulging so much minute details about the once-stately mansion. We learn that Dr. Faraday has always had a fascination with the estate and despite its dilapidated state still admires it strongly after all that time. 
 Dr. Faraday immediately strikes up a friendship with Mrs. Ayres and Caroline, while Roderick is hesitant to allow him into their family business. Mrs. Ayres is a woman who still believes that she must keep up the grandeur of her generation, despite the war bringing about more change than she would have liked. She still follows her upbringing, which taught her to always be aware of the public eye. Caroline is a rather ugly looking girl--as stated many times within the novel--who would prefer to be trumping around outside with her dog than being the dainty woman her mother was raised to be. Roderick seems always to be on edge, a badly scarred man with a permanently messed up knee from flying in the Air Force during the war and being hit. 
 What I love about this novel is its dark setting. Even the happier moments--and there are very few--seem to be tinged in gray, as if something is always casting a shadow. Bad luck strikes the family again and again as, one by one, they begin to succumb to something. They believe it to be a ghost of some kind; an apparition bent on keeping the house for itself and yet unwilling to let the inhabitants flee. Numerous occurrences happen that seem to substantiate their theory; mysterious knockings within the walls, fires bursting to life with no apparent reason, Caroline's dog being unsettled. 
 Eventually we find that despite Dr. Faraday's repeated attempts to get the family to forget the phantasm nonsense, they still believe it. Roderick essentially loses his mind and ends up in a mental hospital for the remainder of the book after his room is almost burned down. Mrs. Ayres believes her firstborn daughter Susan, who died when she was 8 and before Caroline and Roderick were born, is the spirit and she wishes her mother to come into the afterlife with her. Mrs. Ayres is later found hanging from the back of her bedroom door dead, an apparent suicide. Finally, it is only Caroline left. She and Dr. Faraday began a courtship that was heading toward a wedding, but within the last few weeks she calls it off and tells him she will be selling the estate and moving out of England, stating she loves him dearly as a friend but nothing more. 
 Heartbroken that the life he has seen laid out before him was now not going to happen, Dr. Faraday goes back to Caroline multiple times, in the delusion that she was only deluded herself. Eventually he gives up on winning her back and resigns himself to his work, just as he had before he had met the family. 
 We find that Caroline had an accident a few days before she was scheduled to move. The maid heard creaking as if someone was walking around in the middle of the night and gets up to investigate. What she finds is Caroline on the second floor landing, stumbling backward as she says "You!" before tipping over the banister and falling to the floor and cracking her head open. We never actually know who it is that Caroline sees before she died. 
 As a result, the estate has a kind of rumored curse around it. No one moves in because it is so decrepit and it falls steadily into worse condition. Dr. Faraday and the maid who found Caroline are the only two left who knew the events that happened firsthand. Dr. Faraday, knowing that no one is taking care of the house, takes it upon himself to try and mend it one small issue at a time on his own. 
 I'll try to explain this as best as I can: Dr. Faraday was inadvertently the apparition that was haunting Hundreds Hall. During the novel we find that Caroline has been doing some research into the supernatural. Basically, if someone was in a deep enough state of some emotion (usually negative ones such as agony or anger or depression), their subconscious self--the one who houses all these hidden-away emotions--can physically separate from the conscious self and do what it pleases. Caroline believed this, but failed to recognize who was actually breaking free. She believed it was her brother, Roderick, once he was admitted to the hospital. The mother believed it was Susan, her firstborn daughter who'd died previously. 
 Instead, Dr. Faraday is to blame. His fascination and desire for the house was so strong that he effectively drove everyone else out using their weaknesses. Roderick's constant stress about finances and keeping the estate running proved to be his undoing, unraveling his mind. For Mrs. Ayres it was the idea that maybe the ghost of Susan was beckoning her to the afterlife. And for Caroline, we can only assume that after her and Dr. Faraday's falling out she was surprised to see him creeping along her hallways in the middle of the night. It was his apparition that she saw and shouted, "You!" to. 
 This is all speculation of course. Given the information we are provided by the author, it seems the reaction she was going for. Another option is that the family was mentally unstable from the beginning, though there was never any indication of this with previous generations. 
 I love how this dark story is reminiscent of Edgar Allen Poe. It has a distinct gothic style and has a supernatural quality to it that is not overdone. It is a haunted house story, but it's so well done you don't quite realize it until much later on. And it's enough to get your skin crawling sometimes. 
 The fact that the cause of all the problems is the narrator is something I personally have never seen before. Even once the book ends Dr. Faraday has no inkling that he may have been the cause of all the misfortune. He still believes the business of phantoms is ridiculous. 
 It makes me wonder, though, if he would truly feel regretful if he did know. Would he be sorrowful because of his deepest desires? Or would he accept it easily and without a second thought? 
 I like to think it would have bothered him some. Yet even his engagement to Caroline seemed entirely focused on moving in with her into the house. It was once he found that this was no longer an option that something seemingly inexplicable happened to her. 
 If this book weren't so long, I would sit down and read it again given the opportunity. I feel it would be an entirely different experience reading it with the information I am now armed with; to see if I would still come up with the same conclusion, or maybe see clues hidden that I had not noticed before in the text. 
 So basically what I'm saying is if you like dark novels set in the past, check this out. If you can stomach the long descriptions, that is.

I'm having a really difficult time with this one. It is very provocative. While reading it, I could only think of Lolita but set in a much more modern context What that means exactly, I'm not sure. For those deeply horrified by the Santa Barbara shootings or the Stanford rape case, it could be deeply triggering. 
 I don't want to go into any details because the narrator is unreliable as hell and if you're familiar with those cases of entitled, cisgender, heterosexual white males and how they are so nice and deserve everything, you can put two and two together pretty easily of how this novel plays out. While that may not be so remarkable, this is definitely a well-crafted novel that really puts you into that very entitled, sociopath mind-set. It's, at the very least, a safe way to enter that space. 
 "Teddy Wayne's captivating and increasingly disturbing Loner features a character that you'd like to hug if you could be assured that he wouldn't try to stab you. It's a wonderfully unnerving and unreliable first-person account of a dangerous stalker who is also a shy teenager just trying to get a date with the popular girl in school. This impossible-to-reconcile character, mixed with Wayne's wry charm, makes Loner as thrilling as it is cautionary." --Jesse Eisenberg 
 "Teddy Wayne perfectly conjures the mind of a keenly observant, socially ambitious, and utterly heartless college student. Yet no matter what outlandish things David does, I couldn't help but root for him--until the book's gut-punch ending." --Adelle Waldman 
 I am bothered by some of the reviews for this book, these two in particular. David isn't just a shy teenager and he was stalking Veronica from very early on in the book. There is nothing to root for. I don't feel that there is really any room for interpretation, but I guess if Vanity Fair can call Lolita "the only convincing love story of our century," there are going to be multiple ways to view this novel. 
 David is a stalker. He is creepy and entitled as fuck and very dangerous. He  date-rapes his girlfriend,  Sara, whom he is only dating because she is Veronica's roommate. He follows her around to get into her same classes, makes very stupid homophobic jokes, and basically views everyone in relation to whether they can improve his social status. He is so VILE. This book is so much more than a shy, nice guy just trying to get a date with a 'popular' girl. 
 It's a fascinating, enthralling entry into the mind of a man so entitled he excuses his own criminal behavior and still believes in his feelings. But those reviews make me feel sicker than the actual novel. That's how those cases of murder and rape happen. It's not a shy guy who wants a date or needs to get laid. It's an entitled creep who thinks he deserves this woman who only needs to be convinced of his merits, and if not, well...consent be damned. She's his by right. 
 This is a really good book. It's very, VERY well-written, the pacing is perfect, and the characterization is great. There are one or two surprise twists. The ending was talked up a lot, so I expected more, but it's not surprising. I only worry that, just like with Lolita, David and this story will be misinterpreted for something that they both are not.

Boyne focuses on the action rather than observing the main character's surroundings: but he does so in a way that is far more telling than showing. Most of the things that take place in the novel is crammed in a few small sentences, rushing us through all of the parts that could have added some layer and complexity to the overall story. He doesn't spend enough time describing the house and he also skims over the 'mysterious' happenings that make Eliza realize that there is something afoot. The characters too felt rather thinly depicted; they make such little impact on the story that it renders them completely forgettable.

Light and just the right amount of cheekiness for a Spring Afternoon picnic read.

A very good end-of-the-world novel, that manages to be realistic about what things are like without completely abandoning the idealism of humanity. 
 Being written in 1977, it's not perfect about a lot of things (e.g. race and sex politics), but it does address those pretty well for its time. One scene really struck me - it's a small thing, but early on, a group of white farmers are talking about how they don't want n*'s in their territory, and then they look briefly at the one black family in the room and say "But not you guys, you're okay," and the black family is described as "trying to look as small as possible." I'm probably not explaining it well, but - that really stuck with me. 
 I also appreciated that the women were, overall, more competent than the women in "Alas! Babylon!" - even with some reversion to old sexism (and with some characters being *happy* about that reversion), it wasn't all "ohhh let's all become hysterical about stuff." 
 The main characters had some pretty clever strategies for survival (dehydrating meat, stockpiling black pepper). Also appreciated how crucial amateur radio was. And FEUDALISM. Yes. A lot of people (like the guy in the Army who ended up having them all go cannibal ) think that come the end days, they'll be king of the world, but....nope. King of the world is whoever can build the best feudal system the fastest. And for that, you need land, peasants, and LOYALTY. 
 The book's take on Communism was surprising - most of the characters hated it, but in the end, some vestiges of it still remained in the world. 
 I don't have a full casting in my mind, but I think I would have Matthew McConaughey play Johnny Baker. At least, that's how I pictured him in my mind. 
 Pretty sure Neal Stephenson read this book during his research for Seveneves. And I'm okay with that. 
 Overall, 4 stars, because I expect I will read this book again before I die, but it's not a "definitely reread every year if I can" kind of book.

Having read Siobhan Davis' book True Calling, I knew I was in for a good read when I started Saven: Deception. I was wrong. It wasn't just good. It was fantastic. 
 5/5 stars for me. Siobhan Davis is a fantastic pulse-pounding, frantic page turning action writer. Her romance portions are even better - get out your fan! (We've already ordered this book and are anxiously awaiting the paperback of Book 2). 
 Some of my favorite things about this book: 
 -Oh, Nelly, can this woman build a world! You can completely visualize Thalassic City and put yourself in Sadie's shoes. Never is there a moment where you have to completely suspend reality for something that just isn't plausible. 
 -The title makes sense. You'd be surprised how often I read a book and think the title should have been something else. When you read the key line in the story that connects to the title, it's an a-ha moment. 
 -Characterization is outstanding. You want characters you can sink your teeth into? Here. Feel like you've known them forever? Here. Love or hate? HERE! 
 -Dystopian fans (think Hunger Games, Divergent, These Broken Stars, 5th Wave, Article 5, Atlantia) will pick up on the many cues provided by Davis that something is not right from the beginning, although it does not turn out how you think it will. Taking that familiar story line and twisting it in a new direction, I was completely captivated. 
 -It combines the familiar beats with unexpected elements: espionage, evil government, romance, lower class, aliens. There's something in this book for everybody and I think that sums up why I like it so much! I know there will be many readers for this book. It's going to be a sound investment for our high school library. 
 -The sequel comes out in April. I love a book with a quick sequel. I hate waiting and I forget so much of the story! Siobhan gets that. 
 -Does it make my heart happy that she's a self-published author? YES! Boys and girls, you don't have to get an agent and go through the big publishing companies to get your voice heard. Self-publishing is easier than ever and, obviously, good writers do it too!

 "Come, sit," he says, his fingers curling gently around the tips of mine. 
 I plop down on the beanbag beside him and yelp. 
 "You are hurt." He frowns. "Let me take a look." 
 He scrunches the edge of my shirt, but I clamp down on his hand. There's no way I'm admitting that it's my butt that's sore, and no way am I ready to let him inspect that part of my anatomy. Yet. 
 Get you, my inner devil teases. 
 "I'm fine." I pin him with a "drop it" look. 
 "You are so stubborn." Shaking his head, he unscrews the cap from his bottle. 
 "I'm stubborn?" I level an incredulous look his way. "Have you not looked in the mirror recently, dude?" 
 He laughs and the sound sends warmth flooding through me. 
 "You've a lovely laugh," I blurt out. Ohmigod! I can't believe I said something so cheesy. 
 "I do?" He looks amused. 
 "Yep." I'm resorting to one-word replies now for fear of what else might inadvertently tumble out of my mouth. 
 He stares intently at me, his fiery eyes penetrating my soul. The cord buzzes with anticipation. I might've forgotten how to breathe again. "You are beautiful, through and through." 
 With each passing second, my heart pounds faster and faster. He inclines toward me and I move closer. Butterflies are throwing a mad party in the pit of my stomach. Like magnets, we inch closer and closer still. As my pulse throbs, he zeroes in on my lips and his eyes linger there. 
 I've imagined this moment so many times without ever really believing I'd get to experience it. Now that I'm here, seconds away from my first real kiss, I'm terrified of the strength of my emotion. I never knew it could be like this. That I could feel such a strong connection to a boy; that my body could tremble with such intense desire. And our lips haven't even met yet. 
 We are a hairsbreadth from one another. I bridge the final distance and close my eyes. His fingers brush my lips and I'm tingly all over. Reopening my eyes, I see the adoration glistening in his gaze. For me. 
 "Ala beatra." The words roll seductively and respectfully off his tongue. 
 I've no idea what it means, or what language he's speaking, but it sounds beautiful. 
 And like a form of worship. 
 Though it's possible I'm deluding myself. 
 He closes his eyes and presses his mouth to mine. His touch is feather soft and it unravels me. I kiss him back equally gently and he moans softly. His lips exert more pressure as he draws me in flush with his solid chest. I've never felt this much emotion before. It's almost too much, but at the same time, not enough. 
 Gaining in confidence, I encircle my arms around his neck and melt into him, savoring the feel of his body as it presses against mine. Angling his head, he extends the kiss, and it grows in intensity and fire. I'm matching him, kiss for kiss, and my need for him is reaching an all-time high. I can't get enough of him. He is everywhere, and yet I need more. 
 ___________ 
 I recommend this book to fans of The 5th Wave trilogy, Insignia trilogy, Across the Universe trilogy, and Unwind series. Atlantia would be a loose comparison, but if you enjoyed the underwater aspect, Saven: Deception will NOT disappoint.

I take this book with a grain of salt, because I know it was a different time, and a different style of science-fiction. However, the subpar characterizations and overtly Freudian framework really killed it for me. 
 The ideas were great. I loved the structure of a murder thriller where the detective already knew who the killer was, but the chase was all about the burden of proof. It added an interesting twist to your typical mystery. I could even get behind the incredibly obvious Freudian twist that Reich had actually killed his father, and succumbed to his own internalized guilt , but the characters were just so weak. None of them had depth, and any hints at depth (Dishonest Abe, Reich's mother/family life) were glossed over for the sake of a flashy chase scene or tense confrontation. 
 Still, I was on board with a lot of that until the very end. Everything was so rushed and forced. Barbara and Lincoln can be together because she's secretly an Esper too (putting aside how unpalatable that relationship is to begin with); the computer was right all along; Reich doesn't die because he's too valuable, he's just brainwashed (ugh, also hard to digest); and life will be just grand when everyone is an Esper, because there's certainly no obvious concerns about the Esper community and hierarchy already...  
 I'm glad I read it for the sake of it being a classic, and I did enjoy much of what it was trying to do. But it definitely had its flaws, and I'm not a particularly big fan.

 Sometimes I have this gut instinct about a book that tells me I have to read it because something inside me is screaming at me that it'll be amazing. Symptoms of Being Human is one of those books and when I finally listened to that voice inside my head, it ended up being my first 5-star read in more than a month. 
 Symptoms of Being Human is about Riley Cavanaugh. Riley is many things. Punk Rock, snarky, funny, rebellious, and gender-fluid. Some days Riley identifies as a girl, other days as a boy. But Riley isn't exactly out yet. Not in Riley's new school, not to Riley's mother and congressman father who's running for reelection. On the advice of a therapist, Riley starts an anonymous blog to vent those pent-up feelings and tell the truth about what it's like to be a gender-fluid teenager. But then unexpectedly the blog goes viral and someone in Riley's new school finds out about everything and threatens with exposure so Riley has to decide what to do. Run away from it or come out and risk everything. 
 Gender identity is something completely separate from sexual orientation and it's not something I'm completely familiar with yet because I don't hear much about it. So I read these books partly because I love learning more about these different things. Gender-fluid was new to me. I had heard the term but I didn't know anything about it really. So in my opinion, these types of books can serve as a means to educate people about these topics, which is a really good thing! I celebrate all types of diversity in books and I'm a very open-minded person, being a part of the LGBT+ community myself. And on that part, Symptoms of Being Human certainly did its job very well. I'm very happy to have learned more about what gender fluid means and what it's like to be a gender fluid teenager. So props to that, Mr. Garvin, sir. 
 Of course there's more to this book than just that and what makes me so happy is that the other stuff is also so very very good! The story is touching and has a lot of moments that hit me right in the feels. Riley's journey throughout this book and the things Riley experiences touched my heart and I felt for Riley all the way through. Riley is an amazing character, so inspirational and strong while also being a bad ass, punk rock, snarky and so very funny. But next to Riley, there's also Riley's parents who were such a great part of the story, a rare thing in YA these days. Riley has amazingly supportive parents, which is something I LOVE to see. And then there's Solo and Bec, Riley's friends, whom she meets in the new school. I loved both of them so very much and they were great friends. All of these characters get so much love from me. Is there romance? Well... I'm not telling. I went into it not knowing and I want you to do the same. So... Be surprised! Whether there is a romance or not shouldn't be a deciding factor for you to read this book or not. You should read it. Period. 
 Symptoms of Being Human is a very touching and important story to read. Not only because YAY DIVERSITY!!, but also because it's just an amazing book period. While I do have to mention that this review was challenging because I tried to avoid calling Riley he or she as I do not know which to choose this day and by the time this review goes up, who really knows how Riley will feel that day? So go get this book on Edelweiss or pre-order it or both, just make sure you read it.

 The Shades of Magic trilogy follows Kell and Delilah Bard through the worlds of Red London, White London, and Grey London as they fight unknown evils that are seeking to return power to Black London, a London that has been locked off from the rest of the worlds because it craved magic more than life itself. 
 By the time I made it to A Conjuring of Light, I was extremely glad that I had the book in my hands and was in a position to read it right away because the cliffhanger from Shadows left me with whiplash. This one was the hardest for me to read though, because the amount of death left me extremely melancholy. 
 The whole series was unlike anything I'd read before, and was what I was needing at the time. It takes all three books to get to know the characters, and I love that. It made them more like actual people. You don't learn everything about them at one time, it takes days, weeks, months, and years to learn the dark and twisty parts of a person, and that is exactly how Schwab wrote the characters.

Miss Lydia Charingford misses her best friend Wilhelmina Pursling who is now a Duchess but she keeps herself happy. Lydia is always positive about everything. She even finds a bright side to her recent loss of a fiance after he was charged and sent to gaol. The one dark spot on her life is the young doctor in town, Doctor Jonas Grantham. He is routinely sarcastic, always blindingly truthful, thinks of himself as a little dark raincloud and told her that she ranked only 11th prettiest girl in town. 
 That was before he recognised her. 
 Five years earlier, he had been on rounds with the local doctor before he was left his practice, and he heard the man tell a couple to put away their fifteen year old pregnant daughter. That she was already dead, they should let her really die. 
 "Once a girl is ruined, her life is over. Even if you can conceal the truth of her unfortunate state from those around her, the girl is worth nothing. Her life will follow one of two paths. If she acquires no moral sense, she will continue on in her sluttish ways, a burden of humiliation on all who know her. One of the moral diseases will shortly find her, and she will perish in ignominy." 
 Then he prescribes a tonic for her that contains Prussic acid; a poison that these days we call Hydrogen cyanide. 
 She miscarries, of course. 
 The young doctor knew that everything the old man did was wrong, but he didn't speak up and he has hated himself for it ever since. He thinks of this girl every day and the memory of her drives him to be a better medic. He washes his hands and doesn't wear gloves in case they transfer disease. Groundbreaking stuff for the time. But he is shocked to see that rather than being dead or banished she is healthy, happy and a charming socialite with an intact reputation. Still loved by her parents and as yet, unwed. 
 He's ready to be married himself. 
 Also, he had decided it would be best not to mention his main reason for wanting to marry--that he thought it expedient to procure a regular source of sexual intercourse without risking syphilis. 
 Oh... Jonas... 
 He falls in love with her, but he can't convince her of this, and he has spent sixteen months flirting outrageously badly. Cringingly badly; to the point of rudeness. And that makes me like him less to start. 
 But she did hear part of the old man's message. She is utterly terrified that she will be a slut. Her baby wasn't a product of rape or young experimentation. She was seduced by an older married man who told her sweet nothings. And she liked it. She enjoyed the sex but her experience has led her to tamp all that down so hard and plaster over it with this thin veneer of happiness. She focuses utterly on the good to the exclusion of all else. Lydia knows she is shockingly good at lying to herself but she can't get out of it. 
 And Jonas unnerves her. He makes her remember things she would rather not; he reminds her of her shame. And the miscarriage happened at Christmas time and even the smell of pine trees throws her back into that memory. He makes her think about things she has convinced herself are wrong. He makes her want... 
 He loves sex, too and has no shame about discussing it in clinical detail. She hears him advise a woman pregnant with her ninth child how to use contraception. They discuss her lack of a hymen. 
 He raised his eyebrow at her. "I'm a doctor, Miss Charingford, and even I can't always tell on close examination whether a woman is a virgin. Besides, the hymen is just a membrano-carneous structure situated at the entrance of the vagina. It is of substantially less physiological relevance to a man in the throes of passion than the vagina itself." 
 He tells her about French letters and that he hasn't used one for sixteen months. 
 He takes her to visit his father. A scrap metal collector who has been ill and is in the early stages of dementia. He's hoarding metal inside his house and Jonas doesn't know how to help him but his rubbish is injuring others and it has to go.  
 So he makes a bet with her: 
 "I wager," he said, "that I could show you a situation before Christmas that would be beyond even your capacity for good cheer." 
 She frowned. "What do you mean?" 
 "I see the worst of Leicester. In five minutes, I'll leave for my next appointment. You smile and you wish and you see an entire world set forth in the most optimistic terms. I wager that I can find you a situation that lacks a bright side." 
 If she wins, she demands that he not talk to her again. If he wins, he asks for a kiss. Worst case scenario, he thinks, is that he gets to spend time with her. 
 He loses the bet, but she has met her match. 
 This one didn't work for me as well as the others in the series, so I'm marking it down compared to them.

I didn't realize this was a bible fiction when I picked it up from the library and even though I'm not into church stuff, this book doesn't read like that. It really is a novel. I did appreciate the historical details in this book. The red tent is the place where women gathered during their cycles of birthing, menses, and even illness. Like the conversations and mysteries held within this feminine tent, this sweeping piece of fiction offers an insider's look at the daily life of a biblical sorority of mothers and wives and their one and only daughter, Dinah. 
 Told in the voice of Jacob's daughter Dinah (who only received a glimpse of recognition in the Book of Genesis), we are privy to the fascinating feminine characters who bled within the red tent. In a confiding and poetic voice, Dinah whispers stories of her four mothers, Rachel, Leah, Zilpah, and Bilhah--all wives to Jacob, and each one embodying unique feminine traits. As she reveals these sensual and emotionally charged stories we learn of birthing miracles, slaves, artisans, household gods, and sisterhood secrets. Eventually Dinah delves into her own saga of betrayals, grief, and a call to midwifery. 
 I found this an interesting read. It takes the biblical characters and, with literary license, weaves an interesting view of life during the beginning of the formation of the Jews culture. The previous gods (religions) are not abandoned as would be logical in a developing society. The separation/differences of men and women create the drama in this story. I was pleased with how it was wrapped up.

Cahalan's memoir is a recounting of her harrowing experience with a rare brain disease that took her from living an independent, normal life in New York, working as a journalist at the New York Post to acting erratically, to having seizures, to psychosis, to near catatonia in the space of a few months. I don't see how that can be anything but riveting and horrifying. Cahalan suffered not only a loss of reasoning, but underwent personality changes, and memory loss that to this day spans the months of her ordeal. The most frightening thing about her disease is that the doctors had no clue what was wrong with her until it was almost too late to save her. Using her skills as a journalist, Cahalan has painstakingly assembled the story of those months through interviews, hospital paperwork, her parents' journals, and footage of herself from the hospital. Cahalan does a good job conveying her family's increasing desperation and determination while a parade of doctors cycle in and out of her treatment as her case becomes more mysterious. Less impressive is her skill as a writer, which I found workaday and repetitive. 
 Cahalan was extraordinarily lucky to find the doctor who could solve the puzzle of her illness, and she's devastated for the people who have not been as lucky. While this book had failings, I admire Cahalan's mission to raise awareness about this disease so that more people can make the kind of recovery she did.

I have to say I'm disappointed. This was a really great idea, and for me it kind of just fell flat. I had really high hopes for Enchantment. And while I think the idea is there, I wouldn't say the execution is. 
 First: I didn't get immersed into the story. So much information was thrown at me in the beginning that while I'm still trying to figure out how the whole magic things works the whole family just up and moves and throws me into a whole new situation. The emotions Channie had bounced back and forth so much it was unlikely, especially with her parents. She's angry, she's guilty. She's angry, she's guilty. She has no problem cursing the heck out of them, then tries to hug them. Then wants to ask for chamomile tea. 
 Which brings me to the next main thing: the characters were too "out-there". Her parents are just plain horrible people. They're vindictive and impulsive and abusive and don't bother to think through any of their actions. There are no redeeming qualities whatsoever and I had a hard time figuring out why Channie would care in the slightest about them. Josh was the opposite. He's just so darn perfect in every way, isn't he? At first he was described as being extremely skinny. Later he's described as having amazing abs and a nice body, and is then suddenly drop dead gorgeous because of Channie constantly meddling in everything. Which brings me to... 
 Third: Her lack of thought about throwing magic left and right was annoying. She's supposed to be hiding and keeping it a secret yet she zaps basically everyone she comes into contact with. Her parents do that too, but at least they don't pretend to be all martyr-like. 
 I don't know. I just was let down by it. I'm in the minority on this but I wanted to be honest. I wouldn't feel right if I said something I didn't believe.

 I feel like P.S. I Still Love You suffered from trying to be too much, without every really defining itself. It acted like a "cause" book for awhile, calling attention to slut shaming and the double standard between males and females when it comes to sex. It had a bit of a love triangle/love square (but not with the person you would expect) and it didn't take up the majority of the book like I thought it would (not that that's really a bad thing, though). There were a lot of scenes and dialogue where it almost seemed more like a middle grade or very young end of the YA spectrum book, but then there were other scenes and language that seemed more appropriate for the more mature YA crowd. It made so many parts of the book just seem so awkward. It was kind of the book equivalent of a little girl playing dress up and instead of playing house, plays Sex in the City. They tried very hard to sound grown up, but instead just come across cringe-worthy. 
 The flow was kind of choppy, as well. There would be really random scenes of Lara Jean and her sisters or Lara Jean and her friends at the nursing home that just didn't really seem to add anything at all to the story. 
 The book wasn't all bad, though. There were still some cute scenes between Lara Jean and Peter, though not as many I would have liked. Her relationship with her sisters is solid again, which is nice to see. The lack of Josh is kind of surprising, but I liked the addition of John. 
 Overall, I found P.S. I Still Love You to be very underwhelming. It was not at all the book I was expecting it to be. I feel like it could have been much more focused. Perhaps the story was trying to combat the critics of the first book who thought Lara Jean was way too naive, but unfortunately her "growth" in this book just made for an awkward read. However, fans of Han will probably still enjoy it and if you've read the first one, you might enjoy this one, too.

First off, I should say that when reading a novel by Mrs. Clare, one should expect happy endings where pretty much all the characters survive and are paired off with someone else. Why should you expect this? Because, Mrs. Clare is a fangirl in the end, and fangirls always want happy endings and their favorite character marrying or kissing their one true love. I am a fangirl myself, and while it may be a little dare I say boring to know you are getting that happy ending, I don't care because I love the characters. I read books because I enjoy good characters and I want my favorite characters to be happy. So does Mrs. Clare. 
 I don't have too many problems with the overall plot, but one glaring one from a global perspective is that it is okay to give up. From this, I mean  that they just gave up that there was no way to cure the poisoned shadowhunters. Maybe having to kill them all was Clare's way of making a semi-sad ending, but I feel like in most YA stories there would be an attempt at getting a cure that works. Instead it was, oh, the silent brothers didn't find anything. The warlocks didn't find anything. I guess that is it. True, they consulted good sources of information in the shadowhunter world, but there were not even attempts at like, trying to reach the inner person (like Clary trying to save Jace from Sebastian by trying to call out to "her Jace").  
 Here I am going to talk about relationships, but it will all be spoilers.  I am happy that Maia broke up with Jordan but there was no good way to refute the original forgiveness Maia maybe thought she had for the boy. I don't think it is forgivable in any form, and I don't see how she could ever date him again. This was obviously thrown in for the backlash Mrs. Clare got for having a white male violently attack a colored female. I never saw it as an issue of race in all honestly. I just saw a problem that a girl who was in an abusive relationship decided to forgive the boy and date him again..... Even if the person changes there is no going back on it. Anyway, at least she tried to break up with him before Jordan dies. Though this is probably a reason Mrs. Clare saw that it was okay to kill Jordan. I don't think he would've died if Maia and Jordan stayed together. I don't think it was necessary for Maia to find a new relationship afterword though. Mrs. Clare didn't heavily focus on it, but she did throw it in. As I said, she is a fangirl and likes to pair everyone off, but come on.... 
 The interactions between Isabelle and Simon are adorable and geeky. They made me laugh the most. I know a lot of people think they shouldn't be together because Simon should still be getting over Clary, but nonetheless Isabelle and Simon are an adorable funny couple. 
 I've never been a big fan of Alec and Magnus. I still am not. I like them separately. Just not together. At least towards the end Magus finally admits he will try to reveal his past to Alec. Relationships should be open like that.... 
 I am excited for the potential relationship between Emma and Jules. They become parabatai at the end of this one, and of course they will fall for each other in the new series. But parabatai cannot marry/love each other, so what are they to do?  
 Mrs. Clare tries to repair the mess she made with Alec and Jace's parabatai bond. I'm sorry Mrs. Clare. I know you are trying, but you did it right with Will and Jem. You will never fix the mess you made with Jace and Alec. Never. 
 The ending of the book had of course the bad guy losing and the good guys winning.  I think in the end I am happy with Simon's ending. Was it selfish of Isabelle and Magnus to try and get him to volunteer to come back to the world of shadowhunters? Maybe. But I think he will fit well into it as he did before (though awkwardly as a vampire). He also agreed to it even as a human. He knew deep down he was missing a part of his life. I hope he lives through the process of converting to a Shadowhunter. He is my favorite character and I would be sad if he did not (fangirl). I am sad he lost all his memories of Clary and the shadowhunter world, but at least they get to be recovered. Plus, it is great he isn't a vampire anymore-- he was a bad one anyway.  I think it was a pretty good ending to the series overall, but I still think that maybe the series should have stopped after three. The 4th and 5th were not so great. But this one isn't so whiny about Jace and Clary at least.  Though this ending is nice that Simon is human again!!!

You must give praise to Laini Taylor for creating a world like Eretz right smack in the middle of the start of a Revolution. In the first novel Daughter of Smoke and Bone you are plagued with the mystery of 'Who is this girl, this narrator?' as we travel along with her in the discovery of herself and new found love. I enjoyed the first novel I bought it on a whim and the creativity and the imagination that erupted was nothing like I imagined it would be however that paled is comparison to Days of Blood and Starlight. 
 In the second novel Laini Taylor weaves a tale of war, vengeance, and hope, always hope. Again I was astonished by the imminence imagination Taylor wrote with- Creating different perspectives one from those suffering, those in battle, and those who dreamed of a different world, those who hoped. I will not lie during the novel there were some drier moments in the novel which I felt could do without however it picked up paced once again. 
 Throughout the novel all character's experience moments of achievement only to be countered with misery which outshines the victory, throughout the novel I kept hoping those deceased would someone emerge and it would all be okay again however this novel is a story about war therefore it took on a sense of Realism which I enjoyed however my heart did not. Unlike this first novel the main focus is not Karou and the bright shinning love she finds - unfortunate for me because I have a romantic heart but Taylor makes up for this with the climactic sequences of events overlapping one another. 
 Like I said before; The novel started out great in the beginning- not where it left off in the first novel so that as a reader your left to pick up the pieces, in the middle is where I experienced confusion (with the Serphiam) and boredom however this passes and when it does it's like a runaway train excruciating, fast, exciting, and has you seating at the age of your seat turning pages until you are left with; 'to be continued' and left in complete shock. During the middle of the novel I found myself believing the first was so much more better but as I reached that one chapter that started the snowball rolling I realized as I closed the book that I cannot wait for the third.

So if these books keep getting hotter and hotter as we go on, I'm not sure my heart or kindle will be able to handle the next one as it might just go up in flames!!! 
 The second book in this series is just as good as the first one, and I thoroughly enjoyed it....

I was quite pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed The Wrath and the Dawn. Unfortunately, The Rose and the Dagger surprised me by how underwhelming I found it. 
 For a long time it felt like NOTHING was happening. There was really nothing going on that was advancing the plot in any way. This wouldn't be so bad if we were diving into deep character development, but there wasn't much of that either. We kept jumping perspectives between Shahrzad, Khalid, Irsa, Tariq, Jahander, and Omar and we never spent a lot of time with any of them at any given time. 
 Things finally began to pick up when Shahrzad figured out how to use her magic carpet and met a new character, Artan, who knows about magic and curses. I did like Artan, but we did not get enough of him for me to really grow to love him. There was much hinted at in regards to his family and his aunt's abilities, but barely anything is really done with it. We don't find out any more of Artan's history or why his aunt want's Jahander's book destroyed so badly. It feels like a big loose end that was never tied up and thus a little pointless? 
 Where the book shines is when Khalid and Shahrzad are together. They are a great example of a romantic pairing being a real team. I enjoy their banter and I enjoy their romance and I can't say there was really a scene that I didn't like when it involved both of them. While there is more to this book than a romance story, I felt like it floundered just a bit when the romance wasn't involved. 
 While I felt like nothing was happening for much of the beginning of the book, the plot did really pick up towards the end. The talk of war becomes a little more than talk and there's kidnapping and double-crossing, and a few deaths - one of which was pretty emotionally impactful (**VERY MINOR POTENTIAL SPOILER** and I think it was a real missed opportunity that none of the children mentioned in the epilogue was named after this person). 
 Overall, The Rose and the Dagger was just ok. After how much I enjoyed the first book in the series, I was disappointed that the follow up did not live up to my expectations. However, I really enjoy the relationship between Khalid and Shahrzad and that enough is reason for me recommend this series. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 3 Stars

I first read this book when I was 16 and, for whatever reason, could only get one book from the library (I assume I'd racked up some massive fines, as I'm notoriously bad at giving books back, and my parents let me check out one novel on one of their cards. Naturally, I went for the fattest one.) It was the first Stephen King book, with the exception of On Writing and The Eyes of the Dragon, that I was allowed to read, and I definitely had nightmares while reading it. 
 We meet seven children -- Bill, Ben, Beverly, Eddie, Richie, Mike and Stan -- who grew up in an odd little Maine town named Derry. As children, they come close to defeating the monster, It, which has plagued the town for generations. Twenty-seven years later, six of them return to fight It when It again awakes from hibernation. 
 The story is told well, managing to combine wonderfully developed characters with bone-chilling terror. I really enjoyed the way the narrative skips back and forth between the children of 1958 and the adults of 1985. By the end of the novel, these scenes segue in an eerily parallel way, with a chapter cutting off in the middle of a sentence in one year, only to see the sentence finish in the other year in the next chapter. 
 Another part of the book I really enjoyed were the Derry interludes. Several times, we take a break from the main story to hear librarian Mike Hanlon's tales of other years when It was at It's worst, and these serve to fully establish It's corrupting power.

 Girl On a Wire is a taut, gripping read. (Ha. Taut. As in wire tension. Guys, I made a pun.) There was so much that I loved about this book, even though it's a bit of an obvious retelling of Romeo and Juliet. (The protagonists' names are Romeo and Julieta; not exactly subtle, but I'm willing to look past it.) 
 I read this book while flying from New Orleans back to my home in Louisville, which was perhaps not the wisest idea. Not because this book isn't engrossing--because it absolutely is--but because the experience of high-wire exploits combined with those dips you get in the air when flying was flat-out frightening. Bond builds tension so well in this book, most notably with the high-wire scenes; my palms were sweating as I read of Jules' feats on the wire. Making your reader scared for your characters' safety is a pretty good talent to have, especially when you keep remembering, "These people are fictional. This world is fictional. It's okay if they fall--there are no real-world consequences." With a novel like this, that logic is bull--this feels believable. 
 The central romance was also well-built and teased at in an agonizing way. Since this is a retelling of Romeo and Juliet, you get a good idea from the start who's gonna fall in love. And it takes them two hundred pages to officially get together. Definitely what I'd call a slow burn. The romance is not the be-all end-all to the story, but it was definitely worth reading. 
 Speaking of the plot... there's a lot going on here. Circus mysteries! Romance! Plot twists galore! For the most part, I found Bond's plotting excellent. There were several twists that I didn't quite expect like Sam's death which actually kind of wrecked me , and everything went well until the ending, which felt a little flat compared to the rest of the book. Still, this wasn't the kind of ending where I felt like throwing the book out the window, so it didn't ruin the book for me--it was just a little frustrating. The ending reveal of Whodunnit felt anti-climactic, and I'll agree with the "Scooby Doo" assessment that others have made; it really felt just like, "Oh no, someone needs to confess! So they'll just confess to everything suddenly at the end it's okay though."  
 Odds & ends: I have a lot of Dita feelings, as we get a character who is figuring out her (bi)sexuality--not quite a coming out story by any means, but she's very obviously questioning, which I thought was great! (I wanted a LOT more of Dita, to be honest. I cared so much for her and wanted to hug her all the time--but she's hardly ever there. Oh well. She can live on in my mind's fanfic?) Also, holy wow, there are some beautiful sentences in here. "Butterfly wings splashed with a sparkle of colours, twisting vines that gleamed green, fox ears that curved above golden cheeks" (16). How can I learn to write this beautifully?

I want to give this book-no, the series-ALL THE STARS! 5 stars is not enough! I can't believe I waited this long to read this series because I know this will be a series that will be read again and again by me! This series brought up feelings I haven't felt when reading a book since reading Harry Potter. Yes, I am putting it on that level! 
 This book is the last of The Lunar Chronicles and it does not fail to bring in all the stress and excitement and love that it's previous books did. 
 Again, all of our beloved characters are constantly torn apart from each other and we have no clue if they'll all survive, if they'll see their lover and comrades again, or if the Levana is going to use her Lunar gift to torture them and their loved ones (not so much of a spoiler, she does). 
 What I loved about this book: 
 -Cress finally gets some gumption! Praise the Stars! She finally tells Thorne that she loves him, and that she is sick of him flirting with all the other girls, and that she realizes he was trying to not hurt her and she let herself fall anyways, but she is done with it.  I needed Cress to do this. As a girl who has fallen one too many times for the wrong guy, I needed Cress to stand up for herself for all the times I haven't. 
 -Thorne tells Cress that he loves her! I'll admit, I needed this too. The romantic in me wouldn't have been satiated if he hadn't, because we all knew he was falling for this woman. And the more dependent she became, the more he fell for her. I really needed this. 
 -There wasn't just one big battle and it was all over. I feel like that is what happens in so many books and movies. Wars don't happen like that, life doesn't happen like that. If there was an evil dictator ruling part of the world right now and we all rebelled, it would not be fixed after one big fight, it would take multiple fights and rebellions to be rectified. Although this just makes the book more and more stressful because with every battle, more people die, our beloved characters become more distraught and damaged themselves, and Levana almost wins more times than one. But it makes it so much more real. 
 -It almost had a completely opposite ending. Levana almost successfully killed Cinder and had Cinder's instinct not kicked in, Levana could have won. We were so close to having the opposite ending that reading the chapter where this last battle is going on was so stressful for me, I switched sitting positions at least 6 times because I could not handle it.  
 -It does not end in a wedding between any of our couples! As much of a romantic as I am, these people are all 16-20 years old.
