This was better than I expected. The story follows a 20-something girl named Camryn as she leaves her humdrum life in North Carolina behind with a spontaneous trip across the country via Greyhound bus. While traveling, she meets Andrew, an extremely attractive bad boy who is going on his own personal journey. Without giving away any of the twists of the plot, I can say a few positive things. For the less prominent negative things, I will hide it with a spoiler. 
 The story is really sold by the reality of the characters. Cam and Andrew are both completely believable, real people. The level of detail not only to their thoughts and observations, but to the casual descriptions of places they visit on their trip, made me stop at points and wonder if the author based this on something that really happened to her. (She didn't; I read an author interview she did after finishing the book.) As this is a romance, liking and feeling for and believing in the characters is an absolute must. There are no good romances without good characters. You can get away with it in almost every other genre, but romance is definitely a genre where character matters more than plot. 
 I have some gripes with the events of maybe the last 10% (it felt a little rushed), but in general I couldn't put this down. I was on vacation for the week with constant entertainment, and I was looking forward to getting back to the hotel for some reading every night. If I had had nothing but free time, I probably would have read this in one sitting. It's just really addicting. 
 So it's very good, and totally recommended. Why four instead of five stars? Well, now to some of the negatives, which will give away big things in the plot. If you are still on the fence about this book, just give it a chance and start reading it rather than reading the rest of this review. Then come back here and see what you think. 
 Anyway, some things that held this back from being perfect. Four things really bothered me about this book. 
 1. The first is what I thought from the description would be a really big, exciting scene: when Cam decides to get on the bus for the first time. Maybe my expectations were too high, because imagining this scene was what made me excited to read this book. I pictured it as this big movie moment sort of thing, where she would at least have a moment where she looks around at her life and decides to leave. And I mean, literally look around her and look at her life. In a scene. And then have this rush of excitement as she packs up everything, and gets on the bus, which is very much the craziest, wildest thing she's done all her life. But instead, getting on the bus is kind of tame and extremely detached. For one, it's not even a scene. The book is told in first person present tense, and we're in Cam's head for the first few chapters in the present. But then suddenly, after a bad night at a club, she's already on the bus, remembering and telling us how she spent the last few days moping around, and then telling us she got on the bus and is already there. ... Seriously? This was a huge let down. It didn't help that she also talked about how she didn't care much about what she was doing, because she was depressed. I get that, I do. I get that she might have been in a daze while packing or whatever. But at least let us feel what she's feeling in the moment, rather than tell us when she's already on the bus. It was such a big moment and such a lackluster presentation, I felt kind of cheated. Luckily, the story picks up right away once she's on the bus, but I wanted that transitional scene and the emotion of that scene. 
 2. Emotional transitions in general. There was one big transition that did not work for me at all, and took me completely out of the story. It's pretty far along into the book, after Cam and Andrew have been together on the road for a while. It's when Andrew suddenly decides to disappear, leaving Cam alone all day, and then sneaks back in at night to leave her the note that he'll never see her again. She catches him, reads the note and is rightfully devastated. And what does she do? She shouts out "I want you to own me!" And then, not even wiping away her tears, has a really wild and rough fuck with Andrew. Like a paragraph later. And she's totally into it. Not feeling sad at all, everything's suddenly better. I guess my problem isn't that they have wild sex right after this big dramatic leaving scene, but that it happens so fast, they are practically having sex during the leaving scene. She just gets over it so fast, faster than even I as a reader could get over it, and I'm only reading about it. 
 3. The "big reveal" about Andrew. Okay, so I saw this coming. I kind of predicted this about midway through the book, and I get the feeling, as the author is layering in the hints, you're kind of supposed to catch on about a hundred pages before you get the full story. But... it didn't work for me. First, it kind of felt like cheating. The book alternates between the first person narration of Cam and Andrew, and it's pretty stream-of-consciousness at times. How could he not think about the fact that he has brain cancer AT ALL until the climatic chapters? I mean, he'd obviously be dwelling on it the entire time. He thinks about everything else, including giving all these backstories about his father and even himself, telling the story of his life and leaving out that bit. I thought that was kind of M. Night Shyamalan of the author, to have that kind of twist so late in the story, when by her own rules of narration, it should have been revealed really the first time we hear Andrew's thoughts. So I don't like that it's cheating, but I also really don't like what I'm being told either. Or rather, how it's handled. I'm willing to go along with plots in some pretty crazy directions, but this climax/ending was sooo Deus ex Machina. Very conveniently, after they finish their road trip and after the reveal is finally made, Andrew suddenly has the first sign of symptoms through the entire story. In front of Cam. In a really violent, melodramatic seizure. Nice timing for the story, right? And then, rather than deal with the illness with the same realism and time that the story's other events are given, Cam sees him once in bed and that's it. More time is given to their damn fucking singing performance than to the fact that has has a FUCKING BRAIN TUMOR! I mean, with the singing, we got all these scenes of rehearsal, and of course the earlier scenes at the bar with Andrew singing alone, all these new bar characters, and then all this talk about how suddenly Cam is a great singer out of nowhere and blah blah blah. And to make matters worse, these damn singing scenes (which were some of the most unnecessary of the book), were only a few chapters before all this damn brain tumor plot with Andrew, so they were very fresh in my mind. Anyway, back to why the climax didn't work for me--oh right, he lived. He's been ignoring a FUCKING BRAIN TUMOR for what? a year? that is already big enough for really melodramatic seizures, after watching his father die because he had the same thing, and then what happens? He gives Camryn a letter telling her good-bye (again), we skip ahead two months later, and get an epilogue where EVERYTHING'S FINE. False alarm. Turns out that brain tumors are no big deal; it's a condition that is only fatal if you're a minor character. 
 Only, everything's not fine... 
 4. The epilogue. It's very very rare that an epilogue is done well, and doesn't hurt the book. So many terrible epilogues, and this one is right up there. Not only do we have everything being fine with Andrew, suddenly we have a few other major plot developments that either conflict with reality or totally make it a Very Unhappy Ending After All. First, the tattoo. The other half of it, I mean. Have you ever gotten a tattoo? Do you know anyone else with a tattoo? For a really intricate, big tattoo, it takes a while. You have to go to multiple sessions. And not only is this a really intricate, big tattoo that Camryn suddenly has, but it also perfectly aligns with Andrew's matching tattoo. Which implies that he was there by her side as she went through these sessions. Which, even if she rushed through them, with healing and appointments and such, it would probably take the whole two months to get it all done. Given that Andrew was recovering from FUCKING BRAIN SURGERY, and A COMA, is it likely he was able to be by her side during these sessions? Maybe one that she had a week ago, but it's unlikely that the doctors allowed his unconscious body to be wheeled to the local tattoo parlor for some commemorative body art. So... maybe it's one year later, not two months? Okay. I'll pretend it's a year later. BUT there's also one big huge other thing: Cam is fucking pregnant. That's right: unprotected sex can do that, even if you are being owned. Given what the novel is about, and what they were attempting to do (and avoid), is this pregnancy actually a happy ending? 
 I say no. Here's why: well, let's look ahead at what will happen. During the next seven months, Camryn will continue to get more and more pregnant, and naturally refuse to go back to her job at the department store. Meanwhile, Andrew will be going through chemo, and probably barely able to get out of bed. They'll already be broke when the baby is born, and in massive massive medical debt from Andrew's treatment. I don't care if they have insurance; cancer treatment is expensive in this country. And while Andrew's family is represented as well off, the father who made the money is dead, and the mother, as loving as she is, appeared to be a stay at home mom. And also way beyond the point where she can start a new career. So we got a broke, possibly still happy family. 
 Let's flash forward a few years. The kid is growing up. That means enrolling him/her in school, and staying in one place for the next eighteen years. Kids are also expensive, so Camryn will probably have to beg her way back into that department store job she loathed. Andrew might end up fixing cars, but not much else, as he was banking on dying by 25 and didn't finish college. I also imagine that while "being owned" is hot when you're on the road, after a long day at the mall on your feet and then a long night taking care of a kid, Camryn won't really feel so "in the mood." Meanwhile, Andrew will just drink and get in bar fights. His violent streak will no doubt intensify with age and disappointment, and it's not impossible to imagine that his rough sex play with Camryn could turn to just rough treatment and black eyes. 
 And what'll happen to Camryn? How will her life end up? I just have this picture of her as a defeated forty-something woman, not traveling the world but standing behind a counter at a department store, begging people to try perfume samples. And then when she goes to the bathroom on her break to cry and wonder where her life went, she's just sitting in a stall alone and wishing, wishing, that Andrew had just fucking died before he got on that bus. 
 That's what I pictured when i finished that epilogue. Maybe it'll be in the sequel? 
  These things made me deduct a star, but overall, it was an engrossing reading experience, and what works outweighed what didn't. I still recommend it, even with its flaws.

I think it's safe to say that the vast majority of the Goodreads population knows about the Holocaust, and Hitler. I think it's probably safe to take it one step further and say that most people in the Goodreads community have read at least one book about the Holocaust and its victims. I put myself in that same grouping; I've read my fair share of Holocaust books both for school and for leisure. My heart has been seriously heavy at times and my eyes have gotten extremely puffy from crying while reading these books. 
 The Book Thief doesn't follow the Jewish community. It follows the Germans. In particular, it follows kids who are in the Hitler Youth program, whose fathers sign up to join the Nazi Party. It is largely about childhood in general, with WWII building in the background. What I really like about this book is that humanizes the bad guys. 
 Generally, WWII is viewed like this: poor hapless Jews being slaughtered by mean Germans, rescued by the Allies. Which I suppose is ultimately true. But what I think is really fascinating is that while in theory I'm supposed to hate these people--as much for their lack of action as the Nazis for DOING the action--I found I really cared. They are the people who do not have a lot of money, and are just trying to get by without ruffling any feathers. And I think Zusak's ability to humanize them was phenomenal. Because a lot of us who weren't there say the same thing: How come no one ever stood up for them? Never fought? How could they just sit back and watch all the atrocities? 
 Here we have our answer, the first being that maybe not everyone was aware of just how bad it was. Liesel certainly had no idea early on, and it wasn't until she got older that she began to realize. Hans Hubermann did what he could to help one soul, and worried the rest of the time about protecting his family and not treading on any toes. I think as much as everyone wants to say they can't relate, they really can. Most will not risk the lives of their loved ones for a cause that is not on their doorstep, especially since Liesel and her loved ones rarely saw the physical ramifications of Hitler's reign. At least at first. 
 It is obvious that toward the end of the book, they all feel the ramifications. And that, despite being the bad guys, had me tearing up and wishing for a different outcome for the many characters.

Content warnings: (since there are so many, I'm hiding this so you can choose to see them or not, but be warned it's a heavy book that explores awful things.) 
  Abusive romance, abusive parents, suicide attempts and suicide ideation described in enough detail to be very triggering, rape, some fat shaming and slut shaming that is challenged on page immediately, flippant teenage attitudes and language toward mental illness which is only sometimes challenged.  
 I'm going with 5 stars on this based on the personal meaning this book had for me and how much I appreciate it. Though I don't think it's perfect, this story and these characters will stick with me for a very long time and I have not been so impacted by a book maybe ever. Most of the reason for this is because I had my own bad romances and this book eerily reflected many aspects of one of them. It felt like reading about myself at times. If you've had a different type of experience, it may strike all the wrong chords for you. This is certainly only ONE depiction of an abusive relationship and should not be taken as a guidebook for what to expect in every abusive relationship. 
 My favorite thing about the book was the format. Grace is essentially writing this book as a letter to her abuser after the relationship was over (she does occasionally speak to him as "you" but I did not find this distracting). Because she already knows the relationship was abusive, this allows her to portray their romance as it unfolded and show us how she fell for him, but then take a step back and point out exactly what actions were abusive. I just loved that lens, that we could watch her fall without the book romanticizing anything. 
 Because of that format, I do think this book would good for readers who have not experienced an abusive relationship. It may help them see which actions are not okay. Things like possessiveness, jealousy, manipulation, which are often romanticized in books and can be very overlooked when you are in love and swooning are always called out here. 
 And for those who have been in this type of situation, I think there is still room for you to unpack the story yourself. There were times when I was allowed to draw my own conclusions and I could see where a situation might lead without the words actually being on page. So I do think this book is written for both the people who have and have not experienced a bad romance. 
 Some more things I appreciated: 
 -Demetrios tells us in her author's note that she wrote at least partially from her own experience. I could really tell she knew the mindset of a young abused girl and I am so thankful she wrote this story. It's easy to see that Grace is making the wrong choices, but equally easy to see exactly WHY she makes them. 
 -There was no hitting (in the romance). I'm SO glad to see a more nuanced portrayal of abuse that shows it's not all about a partner who beats you. Other physical aggressions like grabbing are shown as just as harmful. 
 -Sexual assault and manipulation between romantic partners is something explored, which I appreciated shining a light on the fact that many cases of sexual abuse are committed by a partner. 
 -There was relateable examination of both partners' roles in the relationship. Grace sometimes blames herself, and sometimes blames only Gavin. I did not agree with all of her conclusions about this, but it showed the mindset of a victim well. 
 -There was a wonderful support group in Grace's friends who helped her realize her relationship was not healthy. 
 -Pretty decent examination, at least from what I inferred, of how Grace had internalized toxic ideas about romance from the examples her parents set. I usually hate when victims of abuse are portrayed as all having daddy issues, but in this book the use of her parents' relationship as a mirror and foil to hers worked very well. 
 -Somewhat decent discussion of mental health and the importance of medication and therapy. 
 Things I thought could use improvement: 
 -Words like "crazy," "insane," and "psychopath" are thrown around a lot by teenage characters to describe the abusive characters. While these things are said by teenagers who don't know any better, and while MI does certainly play a role in these situations and many real life situations, some readers may or may not see this as villainizing MI. I didn't feel that way, but I can't tell if that's due to my own reasoning outside of what was on page. To me, the characters were developed well enough to avoid stereotypes. 
 -I would have liked more exploration of Gavin's home life, or involvement from his parents. 
 Diverse elements: 
 -Side character Lys is lesbian. 
 -Side character Nat is Cuban. 
 -Portrayal of poverty in MC's family. 
 -Barely seen side character had an unspecified eating disorder. 
 -Barely seen side character had PTSD and addiction problems. 
 -Mother is speculated to have had OCD. 
 -Abuser is speculated to have depression and codependency.
This is, perhaps, my favourite short story, ever. The irony Chopin uses to her advantage allows for the story to remain with readers long after they've completed reading it.

When I cracked open Bad Feminist, I was ready to embrace it as the feminist bible for a new generation. When I finished it, I was left with mixed emotions. I wanted to love it, every single word of it. I'm so tired of this anti-feminist bullshit that I was already fully on board with a book that goes after it aggressively, intelligently, and in a way that's accessible and engaging for young readers. I just wish she went harder and I really hope her next one (please write a next one) is more aggressive. That said...everyone should read this book. No matter where you stand on feminist issues, Roxane Gay will challenge you to broaden your perspective. 
 Many of these essays were originally written for the web and have that feel about them. That's not a bad thing - it's the tone her readers are familiar with and if it makes it more inviting, then I'm all for it. However, at points it also sacrificed a level of complexity that I was hoping for. There were several essays, for example, that could have been reworked and combined to create one longer, harder-hitting, more in-depth essay. Overall it was a very mixed bag. At times it was scattered, redundant, confusing, contradictory, and surface level. Yet at other times it was hilarious, biting, urgent, powerful, nuanced, and moving. 
 That said, I'm probably not her primary audience and I was bringing expectations to this book that Gay never promised. This wasn't billed as a collection of peer-reviewed, scholarly research articles. It's a collection of personal essays. She's not having this conversation in the academic realm, but with a broader, pop culture based audience. Which is absolutely a good thing. The feminist movement has stalled out and needs new voices and perspectives to bring it up to speed. It needs to shift in order to stay relevant, and Gay is helping that shift take place. 
 I'm already 100% on board with Gay's definition of feminism and have been for as long as I can remember. I don't need convincing and I don't need it to be friendly. BUT, to a young girl or a young woman who has never heard these opinions articulated before, I can only imagine how mind blowing it would be. To readers who had a misconception of feminism or could never discuss their feminist beliefs openly, I'm sure this book was a godsend. To girls and women who are vastly and embarrassingly underrepresented or ignored in broader conversations on feminism, it must be incredibly validating to read these essays and see your own frustrations and struggles given a voice. For that alone, Bad Feminist is an important book and worthy of your attention. 
 Plus I thought the Scrabble tournament essay was hilarious.

Eric Drake is a pure blood dark wolf that has thrown his lot in with the half breeds - the Runners - who act as pack policemen. 
 Chelsea Smart is looking for her missing sister. When last heard of she followed a guy into this mountain area. Intent on finding her sister she doesn't see the private property signs and doesn't know she's now on pack land. 
 *** 
 I subscribed to a Harlequin romance website and got a pile of free books. This was one of them. 
 It is book #4 in a series but it wasn't hard to pick up what had happened earlier. The recaps proved useful. 
 Eric is dealing with a lot of fallout from his father's behaviour and tensions between the various packs. 
 Chelsea gives me whiplash. Everyone says she's beautiful, but she doesn't think she is. She freaks about not being in control or being held down, but there's no explanation for this. She did say her mother was a doormat... but that's not the same thing. She thinks her sister is in trouble with NO evidence that she is. The sister hasn't called her to ask for her help. They aren't close, so it's not like she phones her every second day or whatever. 
 She says she's been called frigid in the past, but then is confident in bed and says she gives amazing blow jobs. (there wasn't a demonstration to confirm this) 
 She has the most appalling double standards. She literally goes from apologising for her awful behaviour to doing it again in the next paragraph. And she works in women's shelters and then resorts to violence against her lover. AND she has sex under the influence of a drug but says it's okay because she wanted him to. *frowns* NO. 
 I have no clue why Eric bothered with her. 
  'I thought you were my friend and on my side,' she snarks at someone she has know for a DAY when she is cutting and running away... again. 
 When you've had sex with an alpha wolf, he tells you that you are his mate, that he and the wolf only get ONE mate... do NOT tell him in the next sentence that you're leaving and that 'he'll get over it.' 
 Everything he told her, she either didn't believe or she acted as if she didn't believe him. Your sister said she's staying... my sister would never do that. Etcetera. 
 She shot someone dead... which given her character seems like it should have been a big deal for her... nope. Not even mentioned again. Other than the wolf loving the fact that she did it for 'them'. 
 I would argue that if the drug the guys gave Chelsea was supposed to work on making a mating bond, then it worked on Eric. And that means that everything they are both feeling is driven by that drug. That feels like it ought to be a bigger issue for both of them, but it was blithely mentioned to explain why Chelsea didn't forget her experience when the raped women did forget theirs. First off ewww... but it does raise an issue. 
 And just who was going to be the drug-mate otherwise? 
 And how do they make these drugs that: remove their scent, make them incredibly strong, resistant to pain, make women bond with them, and make other women insatiable so that they can be gang raped for three days, but then able to forget the experience later? And more realistically WHY would a wolf pack need these drugs? 
 I am fairly certain it is not possible to make a drug that removes your scent enough for a WOLF to not smell you. 
 Please, can we lose rape as a story point? Pleeeease...

There are some things I like about this book and others I don't. You get to see what this whole messed up situation does to her. She is in love with A, but can't deal with him/her changing bodies everyday. She tries to focus on just the driver, A, but can't help but be hung up on the car on some days. It did bother me selfish A was being at times. He only cared about what he wanted, namely Rhiannon, and not what he was doing to the life of his host. Rhiannon drove me crazy too. Her whole inability to leave Justin infuriated me. He was obviously not a good boyfriend and not a good attachment for her, yet she refused to let go. At times it felt like she wanted him as her fallback. If it couldn't work out with A, then she wanted Justin as her consolation prize. No matter how much I disliked Justin, it wasn't fair to him and made me lose all respect for Rhiannon. I realize her character is stuck in a horrible situation, but she doesn't handle it very well either. A deserves a lot better than her. I appreciate what he does with Alexander at the end. If only Rhiannon could accept it and go with it. Perhaps in book three A will find a body he can and is willing to permanently inhabit and the two can make a real go of it. I guess there will have to be coma victim or accident victim who has checked out but not died yet. Perhaps that is how A will find a body. I keep expecting it to be Justin he inhabits again. I know it is against the rules, but perhaps Justin will get in a drunken car accident and when his spirit leaves his body, A can jump in and take over. That way Rhiannon will get what she wanted all along. Justin's body with A inside. Who knows. This whole series isn't exactly one I love. I don't really know what I even read book 2. I didn't really like book 1 all that much. I guess I was just curious to see what was going to happen next. I do sympathize with the characters, but I just don't like them enough to care on a deeper level. Plus, the whole tolerance, gender, sexuality agenda just bugs me. I'm not surprised, based on the author's other titles, so I guess I should know what I'm getting into. Not really for me.

Quintessential King. Like most of his other memorable books, this is rife with Americana and side trips that would have been irrelevant rambling in the hands of anyone else. 
 Like his Dark Tower series, there is a lot of narrative roaming. Although the novel is ostensibly about JFK's assassination, the bulk of the story involves people and places that have absolutely no relation to that event. And like that other series, I can't help but feel some element of cheating when it comes to climactic plot points. The narrative hinge just doesn't seem substantial enough to carry the weight of my expectations. 
 Oddly enough, the wandering narrative serves to minimize the effect. With King's writing I usually become more invested in the personal story than the plot (or at least whatever the marketers would use to describe the book on the jacket). I can shake my head at some of his climactic set-ups and resolutions, but it's closer to a reading speedbump than a roadblock. I'm still more interested to find out how the personal story resolves. 
 Although King is usually sycophantic about the '50s--and this book is no different--it was nice to venture into some caveats this time around. Yes, the '50s would have been a great place to live...assuming you weren't a person of colour, or a "subversive", or even an independent woman. 
 This ended up being a fun read that I would recommend to just about anyone, but prepare to be disappointed if you were looking for some hard questions to asked of anything. This isn't a book about difficult concepts or philosophical what-ifs. It's American-style entertainment written by a master of the form, and it's all too easy to find yourself settling in and asking to pass the popcorn.

Mockingjay. The anomaly that, in the world of Panem, never should have existed. Quite like our heroine, Katniss Everdeen. Mockingjay is a story about hope, overcoming adversity in times of terrible strife, and war. 
 But mostly... It's a story about hope and never giving up what you've earned. 
 As with The Hunger Games and Catching Fire, Mockingjay centers around Katniss Everdeen and the country known as Panem. Most of the novel takes place in District 13, with the climax happening in the Capitol. 
 District 13 is a sterile place, everything kept in strict order. The people who live there are assigned tasks, and and every bit of their day is scheduled for them. Katniss ignores her duties, instead choosing to sleep most of her days away. Until one night, she sees Peeta giving an interview from the Capitol. 
 In this novel, Katniss really comes into herself, learning to choose between what she wants to do and what is best for the people. In the end, they are one and the same, but making the initial decision is the tough part, especially when the lives of others are at stake. 
 This final portion of The Hunger Games trilogy really stresses the importance of working together, and perseverance. Without the others, Katniss never would have accomplished her goals, and without perseverance she never would have saved the person who meant so much to her. 
 This book is about sacrifice, and hardship. It is everywhere, even in the Capitol; people are leaving their homes, going without food, without the comforts that make their lives bearable. Katniss is forced far out of her comfort zone to become the Mockingjay, the symbol of hope of hope for the rebellion. She watches as those she cares for are killed before her eyes, and she struggles with the repercussions of harming those who would oppress the freedoms those of Panem deserve. 
 Overall, I enjoyed this book, and I enjoyed this series. As many have stated, I was a little let down by the ending of Mockingjay; I feel that the author tried very hard to give her characters the happy ending that they all deserved (this is what I like to call "The Twilight Syndrome"), and in the end fell a little bit flat. However, I thought that this book was enjoyable, and I would definitely recommend it, and the rest of the series, to readers who enjoy dystopian fiction.

He made me super swoon-y, almost embarrassingly so. The whole bit with the Fire Night and such... Yeah. 
 At first Feyre annoyed me a bit by being too stubborn, but I think that was mostly because I just wanted her to get together with Tamlin already. Other than that, she was an enjoyable narrator and certainly wasn't spineless. But you have no idea how frustrated I was when she didn't say "I love you" back to Tamlin after he said it TWICE, and even more so when we found out that if she had all their problems would've been solved.  Oh well, without conflict there can be no plot, right? 
 As for the other characters, I liked Lucien. He was entertaining and snarky. I felt Alis was kind of a flat character, but whatever. She served her purpose of ominous warnings and such. Now, for Rhysand/Rhys. Why did we only get to learn more about him towards the end? I need more! Although I loved Tamlin, I also love those dark characters (and he is a dark fae). I wonder what will happen with his deal with Feyre. I'm caught between wanting something (but only a small something) to happen between them and wanting them to remain entirely platonic. Either way, I hope the cliche love triangle will be avoided (it was successfully avoided in this book so I have hopes). 
 This doesn't have to do with the story itself, but I found it a bit irksome that the author overused ellipses in the dialogue. Almost every other line the characters said was broken up by ellipses, it felt like. Thankfully this faded away as the book went on, because while it was happening I started noticing every single time it was used, a feeling akin to noticing the sound of a clock ticking. 
 You have no idea how much I freaked out when the book ended, because I had been dreading reaching the end. Imagine my relief when I checked GR and found out it was just the first in the series. Then imagine my aggravation upon finding out the sequel would not be coming out until May 2016. Ahhhhhhh. 
 Overall, I thought this was a great book with a strong plot and characters. I could definitely see the connection between this story and Beauty and the Beast (both the original fairytale and the Disney version, the latter of which is one of my all-time favorite movies). The villain was evil but with logical (okay, not really logical, but understandable) motivations and the thing about the stone heart  all came together in the end. I didn't even come close to guessing it despite the hints dropped, and I love when a book can blindside me with a plot twist like that, as long as it's not really just out of nowhere. There were so many times where I just had to pause and gasp when dramatic events began to happen. I even laughed out loud at some bits. Highly recommended!

What a fun little read! It has the same kind of vibe as Sideways Stories from Wayside School, which I absolutely loved as a kid. Clueless parents who are blind to all the action. It's been quite a while since I read book 1, it was sometime in 2012 I think. I wasn't writing reviews then so I can't honestly remember why I only read book 1 and didn't keep going. If I hadn't committed myself to a couple of read to review books this week I can really see myself devouring this series. It's completely addictive! 
 What's not to love?! Alpha males, tough leather wearing vampires to be precise. A lot of action and politics, romance and tension, family dynamics, and a horrible deity type figure that has the power to weild ultimate control. Oh yeah I hate her. It feels too easy a get out clause for whatever unresolvable difficulty develops in the plot. It's there in the back of your mind, 'oh the Scribe Virgin will sort it out in some twisted way'. Nevermind though, the world would have lost something if there was no tradition or culture underpinning it. 
 It was the one thing I didn't like about this book though. It ended so abruptly. I was all ready to experience the heart shattering pain of the illness. I had faith all along there'd be a HEA but I really expected things to get a lot worse before they got better. 
 Minor point really though. Otherwise I loved this book and the world that's been created. I was concerned that the big gap I'd left since book 1 would mean I wouldn't remember all the details about the world. It came back to me very quickly though. The world is built in a natural and sublte way that makes it feel normal, like the world really is that way. It gels, it doesn't seem at all absurd, it just is what it is unapologetically so I as a reader just accept it and let the characters, relationships and action develop without pesky scepticism getting in the way. No information dumping. 
 I love the brothers characters, I love that I'm getting to know them each slowly. There are little peices pulling together all the time. Little peices that build the relationships, that tease out their histories, that give hints as to what may be in store for them. In this case I was already getting excited about what was obviously going to be the focus of book 3. The characters flaws are what make them unique and interesting. There's depth and tensions and growth. 
 This was Rhage and Mary's story and it was a beautiful one. Mary was such a sweet unassuming character but with a strong will and desire to care for others. It was clear how it would play out with his alter ego, to me at least, but I never the less enjoyed watching it play out. Watching the coming together of the two sides of Rhage's character, his acceptance of the beast and being at peace with himself. 
 Mary's growth was also emotional to watch. The pain of her loss was so fresh but she clearly needed to love, it was so obviously fundamental to who she was, to see her allow that to happen and allow it to be reciprocated was both beautiful and heart breaking. 
 I have to admire the author here in how she weaves in the meta plot of the battle with the lessors and the evolution of the vampire culture alongside what's fundamentally a romance novel. I'm literally itching to keep reading the series. The story of John and his transistion is going to be fascinating. The story of Zsadist and Bella is going to be intense. I'm nervy about what horrors O is going to inflict (although I'm afraid to admit I skim read the lesser parts). I wanted so much more out of this book but really I think it's that I want to be completely emersed in the world. It's great that it was focused on one couple but I did miss Beth and Wrath and I am desparate to learn more about each of them. 
 Fantastic series, lots of depth and interweaving threads, multifaceted flawed characters, intense romance and a network of relationships creating a world I'm coming to love and feel part of.

It isn't up to par with "Burned" or "Impulse" and on its own, "Glass" is a pain. I slogged through it because it will be so popular with students at the high school where I teach that I needed to be familiar with it. Anansi Boys is the tale of a man named Charlie whose father is Anansi. Yes, that Anansi, the spider trickster god of west Africa. Of course, being the son of a trickster god isn't all it's cracked up to be. Charlie, who is ignorant of the powers of his father, spent a lot of his childhood being tricked by his father without understanding why and lived a very embarrassing first few years of life. He was even nicknamed "Fat Charlie" by Anansi and it stuck with him ever since. Now that he's an adult, with a lackluster job and beautiful fiancee, he just avoids his father. 
 Unfortunately, dear old dad dies one day, and Charlie must attend the funeral. Charlie finds out that he has a brother named Spider. Spider barges into Charlie's life and starts ruining much of it, including stealing his fiancee, and Charlie is desperate to get him away. So he manages to initiate a ceremony where he trades his brother away for the Anansi birthright with Birdwoman. 
 Okay, getting into the ending of the story is going to take too long, but Charlie's evil boss at work, Graham Coats who has been cheating his clients tries to destroy Charlie's life. Along with Graham, Anansi's long lost enemy, Tiger, also seeks revenge of the bloodline of Anansi for taking away his stories. There is a lot of mythology in this book, as well as Mr. Gaiman's own masterful storytelling. 
 I admit I had a little bit of a qualm with the fact that Mr. Gaiman chose to write about Anansi. It is just weird that a mythology so associated with the African culture be somehow written by an English author and center around an English protagonist. Is this racism? I don't even know. Culturism? It just doesn't feel right, like Arthur Golden and Memoirs of a Geisha. Honestly though, Anansi Boys is really not about the mythos of Anansi and more about Mr. Gaiman's own legends which are a continuation of his American Gods. Which is alright. But I think he could have written about any trickster god and this book would have been okay. 
 Second. Your damn red herrings Mr. Gaiman! It's not that I hate red herrings, but your red herrings are more like rivers I expect to lead to the ocean that just dry up. The entire feather bit, I was expecting something to happen with that but NO. NOTHING. NOTHING AT ALL HAPPENS WITH THE FEATHER. I felt a huge letdown after reading the end of that plot point. 
 Also did Graham Coats deserve to  spend eternity with Tiger after some white collar crime?  I mean, we are aware that he is the bad guy of the story, but his crime wasn't any more devious than what thousands of people have done throughout history. His only falling point was that he went against a son of a god, which immediately means his punishment is way overdone. 
 Well, Anansi Boys at least ends with just desserts which is all I really ever wanted. 
 The best thing is Mr. Gaiman's actual writing. He is quirky and funny in interactions, even if his plot fails from trying-to-do-too-much syndrome. 
 "I'm Charlie Nancy," said Charlie Nancy. "Who are you?" 
 "I am Dragon," said the dragon. "And I shall devour you in one slow mouthful, little man in a hat." 
 Charlie blinked. What would my father do? he wondered. What would Spider have done? He had absolutely no idea. 
 Come on. 
 After all, Spider's sort of a part of me. I can do whatever he can do. 
 "Er. You're bored with talking to me now, and you're going to let me pass unhindered," he told the dragon, with as much conviction as he was able to muster. 
 "Gosh. Good try. But I'm afraid I'm not," said the dragon, enthusiastically. "Actually, I'm going to eat you." 
 "You aren't scared of limes, are you?" asked Charlie, before remembering that he'd given the lime to Daisy. 
 The creature laughed, scornfully. "I," it said, "am frightened of nothing." "Nothing?" "Nothing," it said. 
 Charlie said, "Are you extremely frightened of nothing?" 
 "Absolutely terrified of it," admitted the Dragon. "You know," said Charlie, "I have nothing in my pockets. Would you like to see it?" 
 "No," said the Dragon, uncomfortably, "I most definitely would not." 
 There was a flapping of wings like sails, and Charlie was alone on the beach. 
 "That," he said, "was much too easy." 
 Brilliant.

I recently lent a book to a co-worker -an adult mystery from a series that I really like. It's a good mystery with well-developed characters and includes some (though I didn't think a lot) graphic details of a serial killer. She gave it back to me saying that I'm more dark and twisted than she ever thought. I wonder what she would think of me if I handed her a copy of Dangerous Boys. 
 I've become a fan of Abigail Haas in the same way I am a fan of Gillian Flynn. In awe of her writing and a little bit terrified of her. Both are masters of writing psychological thrills and ca-razy psychopaths. 
 I expected this book to be similar to Dangerous Girls, but with male protagonists. I was a little disappointed at first that it wasn't, but that disappointment didn't last long. Dangerous Boys gives us the story of Chloe, a teenage girl looking forward to heading off to college. Those plans derail when her father leaves and her mother begins a downward spiral of depression. Chloe finds herself putting off college so she can pay the bills and take care of her mother until she's better enough to go back to work. 
 Ethan Reznick is new to town and falls hard for Chloe. While she's not interested in any more attachments to this small town that she hates, she is interested in a distraction. Ethan proves to be a good distraction and she falls into an easy life with him and his parents. When his older brother, Oliver, sweeps into town unannounced, everything changes. 
 Oliver is smart and charming and worldly. He accepts no responsibility and offers no apologies. He seems free in a way that Chloe never has been. Though she knows it's wrong, she finds herself increasingly drawn to Oliver, who leads her down a dark path she never thought she was capable of, but embraces it along the way. 
 This is a pretty dark book, guys. Way darker than Dangerous Girls was, for sure. There isn't any one big shocking twist, but there are small, subtle continual shocking moments that lead us to the end of the story, which is really just the beginning for Chloe. 
 My biggest complaint is that Chloe is the only really well developed character. I would've liked much more of the Resnicks. Not just crazy Oliver and seemingly perfect Ethan, but of their parents, as well. 
 Overall, Dangerous Boys is another compulsive read from Abigail Haas that will creep you out and keep you turning the pages. I enjoyed the use of multiple timelines that helped build the suspense throughout the story. I would definitely recommend this book to fans of Haas, Gillian Flynn, and other psychological thrillers.

 This story has a lot of potential. Unfortunately, it fell short of the mark for me. I expected more connection to the modern world than there was, so that was surprising. Not necessarily a bad thing, but I felt that it was all mythological gods and things when I was expecting more connections to reality. 
 The author, Ana Franco, from what I understand, is not a native English speaker or writer and still wrote this novel in English! The language usage was confusing through a lot of the novel and the switch from perspective to perspective could be a bit abrupt, but I think with some more polish the story would flow much more smoothly. 
 The story itself deals with Celtic and Norse gods. The mythological aspect was quite interesting, but I don't think things tied together very well. There would be strange bouts of conflict that would suddenly end or be ignored for a while before popping back up again. I found this both confusing and rather off putting. 
 The characters were likable in most cases, but I didn't feel that they were very developed. And relationships were rushed. Along those lines, the passage of time didn't seem to make any sense at times. Sometimes it seemed like only a few minutes were supposed to have passed and then it would be a week or two. It left me rather confused. 
 I think the story has a lot of potential and could be a fun mythological tale with romance and humor, but it needs more polish and some development to be really enjoyable.

Julia Quinn, Eloisa James and Connie Brockaway joined together to write an entertaining regency romance. 
 Three lovely young women and a raving ninny are kidnapped from a winter ball and taken to a draughty castle in Scotland, because Laird Taran Ferguson has decided it is time for his nephews to wed. 
 The four young girls find that there is also a Duke in the carriage, asleep, who wakes as they are leaving, racing toward the castle through a growing blizzard. 
 The passes are closed and the women are trapped until they reopen. 
 I very much enjoyed this story, as it was lighthearted and sweet. It did not have a lot of steamy scenes, but the romance sufficed. Despite having been written by three, it was seamless. 
 If I had to pick one thing to criticize, things seemed to fall into the happily ever after line to easily, but this is a romance and that comes with the territory.

There's something so deliciously perfect about an opposites attracting story. John is a slightly tortured Navy SEAL, who is set on discovering secrets of his past. Nora is a very old-fashioned, vintage librarian who thrives on genealogy. This story completely captured my heart, hard subject matters and all. 
 I absolutely adored Nora and her sisters. I have two sisters and there's such a special bond and relationship they all share and it makes me miss my sisters. I can't wait to read their stories and dig into more of this family's lives. The importance of family is prevalent in these pages. 
 John's quest is a tug on the heart, but I thoroughly enjoyed the way this story came together, especially the gradual way the friendship and romance develops. I love the way John and Nora incorporate their strengths and faith into the story and come to fully rely on God to do so. As I mentioned before, I can't wait for more in this series! 
 Content: moderate+ religious elements; mild romance; talk of abuse/rape, nothing to graphic.

** spoiler alert ** 
 The relationship drama was overpowering. 
 Juliette: I don't have much to say about her. She spent 1/3 of the book complaining about how Adam didn't understand her, 1/3 saying how much Warner understood all of her, and 1/3 of the book telling everyone how great Warner is and how they misunderstood him and training for the ''epic'' battle that lasted 5 minutes.  Warner: Oh poor poor Wanrer. It turns out that he was misunderstood al along and he's just a lonely boy who wanted to be loved.The inexcusable things he did were all misconceptions. Warner was a prince undercover all along. And now that his secret identity has been revealed to Juliette, Warner is finally free to be the perfect gentleman he was along. He's always saying/thinking/doing the right thing and doesn't have any flaw anymore. He's now the perfect love interest. No wait, not the perfect love interest but the perfect human being! 
 Adam: Gone is his gentle nature. The new Adam is a jerk full time and what used to be one of the main character is now barely a side character. Even his relationship with James has become non nonexistent and even Kenji and Warner have more significant moments with James than him. 
 My problem is that while reading Ignite me, I almost felt like I was being manipulated to love Warner and hate Adam. And I could have been okay with the new Adam if some part of the book would have gave him the attention he deserved and gave him some kind of redemption but instead he just faded in the background. 
 To summarize my feelings about this book: 
 -Addictive as ever. I have to give it to T.M., that woman's writing is one of the most addictive writing I've ever came across. 
 --The war was not given much part in the book . No epic battle. No epic confrontation. 10 pages and it's over. It didn't feel like an ending. If I didn't know better, I would say that there was at least one another book in the series. 
 -Insulted. I feel insulted by the person Adam became. I wanted him to be flawed, not a usuless jerk. 
 -Annoyed and angry with the person Warner became. I liked Warner when he was complex and interesting. If I wanted to read about the perfect love interest I would reread The Hunger Games (Peeta). Thank you. When I read Shatter me, I didn't have a ''team''. I liked both guys but I wasn't ''in love'' with them. Same thing for Unravel me. Then I read the novellas and reread Shatter me and Unravel me before the release of Ignite me and became a fan of Wanner. I chose my team and I was so sure that I would love the romance in Ignite me because of that....I din't. I still like Warner and Juliette. I'm glad they ended up together but I'm not a fan of how they become ''together'' and how unfair and convenient it felt at times. And sometimes, they were bordeline ''corny'' and the Warner and Juliette or Unravel me were a lot of things (sexy, intense....) but corny wasn't one of them. 
 -No plot. There was a plot but it was outshined by the romance. I'm all for romance. And it's true that it was a big part of what I liked about this series. But that doesn't mean it's all I wanted for the last book. 
 I'm sorry if I sound harsh. It's only been a few days and my emotions are still ''intenses''. I still have a lot of respect for the author and what she did with the first two books and I'll definively read anything she write in the future but to me, Ignite me was a disappointing conclusion.

Lethal nightmares feature heavily in Lair of Dreams, the second book in the Diviners series. A deadly sleeping sickness is sweeping through Chinatown, eventually affecting all of New York City. Only the Diviners can follow the clues to discover and eliminate the supernatural source of the illness. 
 One of this installment's most interesting features is also one of its stumbling blocks: it introduces a number of new Diviners and incorporates their stories into those of the characters we came to know and love in 2013's The Diviners. The new characters are an exciting addition, but their inclusion pulls focus. It's problematic too that most of the known Diviners have gone their separate ways at the start of this story, and their multiple storylines don't always seem to gel. The Diviners eventually assemble together for the grand finale which contained the camaraderie and supernatural action I loved in the first book. 
 Despite these issues with the book, I really, really loved it. I believe that Lair of Dreams introduces characters and sets up events that will drive the main action in the last two books in the series. It feels like it has a few too many threads as a result, but I know that the framework established here will mean a hell of a ride for books to come.

About the time this book came out in 2011, I discovered the first book, Daughter of the Blood and subsequently read the first three books in quick order. Over the course of the year I read books 4-8...but my enthusiasm for the story had waned and I never got around to reading book 9. In an effort to complete the series I picked it up from the Library this week. 
 Those first three books were so memorable. Anne Bishop created an interesting, witchy world that felt fully realized with a complex, yet coherent mythology. It was a matriarchal world, corrupted, sexual, and emotional. She filled this world with good to great characters, everything I wanted with a summer read. 
 This book is a collection of four short stories, as was the case with four other books in the series. The thing is...all stories come to a natural conclusion, and by book 9, there wasn't much more story to tell. The biggest fail is that there is no real conflict or stakes, no threat is really concerning, there is nothing epic or even centralized to the conflict. The ferocity and power of the characters at this point is all lip-service, (and rarely a paragraph goes by where this service is not lipped). Tragically, the heroine of our story, Witch herself, has become a secondary character. The men become the more compelling characters, taking over as central leads ...really sad in a world that is supposedly matriarchal. The stories end up being about an opportunity to spend time with the characters, and nothing more. In all honesty, it feels a bit like fan fiction...granted, better written than fan fiction generally is. 
 It starts off with quite the clunker of a first story. Essentially a Christmas tale (aka Winsol). I have zero desire to see Warlord Princes named Deamon, Lucivar, and Saetan, playing clueless family men guarding presents under a Christmas tree from kids and puppies. It's an insufferable window in a chaotic and ultimately catatonic family holiday. 
 The best of the four stories is the 2nd one, which actually contained a plot, even if the antagonist is never perceived as a real threat. I found myself wishing the time had been taken into drawing it out into a larger story, polishing the themes of caste distinction, and really culture conflict. Also, really liked that we saw the guys show their teeth, and didn't just hear about it. 
 The third story started off good and just...petered out. It did contain some quite excellent grotesquerey if you're into that sort of thing. 
 The forth and final story is probably a bit of a risk, and for that I appreciated it, even if it ultimately left me cold.  Taking place nearly 90 years after the first story is written and then spanning about 16 years, we see what Daemon Sadi is like once Jannelle and Saetan are gone.  It's ultimately a romance, which has never been my strongest attraction to this world. 
 At the end of the day, I wish we'd gotten more of a glimpse into the culture and caste complexities and conflicts. I really wish we had explored the other realms (especially Hell) a bit more. Less forced romance and family drama, and more political drama would have rounded the stories out.

I read White Teeth ages ago, in the midst of all the hype of a first novel from a phenomenal new talent. I remember almost nothing about the book, only my reaction of colossal indifference. So I wasn't eager to read another Zadie Smith, even as her reputation grew. But then she made an appearance at a tiny independent bookstore in Brooklyn in conversation with Hari Kunzru, and she was so thoughtful, so articulate and interesting that I knew I had to give her another chance. I'm so glad I did, because this book was fantastic! What's it about? What isn't it about? It's about academia, about marriage, about children and their parents, about art, but most of all about love. It reminded me a lot of the play Phaedra, in which the titular Queen is brought low by Aphrodite who makes her fall helplessly, fanatically in love with her own stepson. Phaedra's driven mad by her passion for Hippolytus, much like the characters in this book are seduced, betrayed and betray each other, how they are made at least temporarily mad by beauty and love. Smith shows how we can be venerable academics, ambitious young things, or anyone in between, Aphrodite can still tie us up in knots when it suits her. My one quibble is how she never really got beneath the skin of the beauty herself, Victoria, only once or twice letting us glimpse what's beneath the surface of all that extraordinary lusciousness. Smith seemed bent on portraying her as someone who most of all is at the mercy of her own beauty, trying her best to inflame the desires of others, and to make them answer to her own purposes, to figure out who she is, to feel something, to be someone. I'm left a little unsatisfied by that, but it's a small failing in such a wonderful book. Smith's treatment of Carl is more interesting, as someone who, until the denouement, has perhaps been unaware of his effect on people. All in all, a real winner.

I think my eyes are chapped from reading this book because it was so dry. When I initially heard of the first book in the series, The Passage, I was excited to read it. However, it took forever to slog through it. It wasn't a disappointment, it just didn't live up to the hype that surrounded it prior to its release. 
 Fast forward to the second novel in the series, The Twelve. I thought that maybe I was just in a different state of mind when I read the first book so I dove into the second book with one goal: to read it without getting distracted by other books. It seemed to work because I finished it much faster than the first book, and generally, I enjoyed most of it. 
 Finally, the third, and final, book of the series is released this past spring. I was ready to read it, but not to the point where I wanted to drop everything and become absorbed in the ending. I wanted to read it, but wasn't necessarily excited about it. 
 My apprehensions were justified. 
 While not a bad book, it certainly lacks something. I tried to figure it out as I read through it and by the end of the first chapter, I had finally put my finger on what was wrong. It is the characters. They are all so flat and one-dimensional. No one has an arc of self-discovery. They remain fixated on their own problems and complications of day-to-day living. I had difficulty differentiating from one person to the next because they all had the same issues with no individualizing characteristics. In other words, they were boring. Until we are formally introduced to Fanning, a.k.a. Zero. He has an entire chapter devoted to his backstory, and for the first time in the series, I felt like I finally knew someone and his motivations in this book. Not all was right yet though. Just as his story is getting interesting and he is about to reveal how he became Zero, it simply says he was infected and that was that. WHAT?! I wanted to know more. Maybe it was hinted at or explored in the previous books, but by this point, I didn't want to revisit them for this trivial matter. Even though I was less than 1/3 of the way through this book, I just wanted the story to move forward and end. 
 The end was long in coming and an arduous journey at that. Along the way, I had difficulty understanding how one character could be in town one day and the next he's gone and no one knew where he went. Sure, there were eventually some who knew where he was, but no one seemed interested to tell his family where he'd gone. Yes, his plan was risky and secretive for a reason, but if he was about saving people, then he would have let his family know where he was and what he was doing. That's what would have made sense to me. When Dunk is murdered, no one knows for years (or was it less time?). He's a major figure in running an outlet of vices for the people of the area, but no one questions that he is missing. If he was such a threatening and important figure, why didn't anyone question his whereabouts? That didn't make any sense to me. His death seemed like a side note of little importance. 
 Back to Michael. When he finds the Bergensfjord, it is understandable that he doesn't want to tell anyone prematurely. But no one ever wanders out there and discovers what he's doing? Yet they are able to divert tons of fuel without much speculation? It's all murky. 
 It is evident that Justin Cronin, like Gregory Maguire of the Wickedseries, loves language and putting together prose. Unfortunately, many times it seems like the writing gets in the way of the story. I found it difficult to envision geography, settings, and locations because nothing ever seemed very concrete. It seemed like a rush to get from one section of prose to another without stopping to really show what was happening. I just couldn't become absorbed in the story because the parts that should have been important were vague and foggy. 
 Another annoyance was the Prologue. In the second paragraph, it says that three were lost: Theo, Mausami, and Sara. I remember Theo and Mausami dying along the way, but I don't remember Sara being lost. And then she plays throughout the book. What's going on here? It was confusing and made me wonder if I should have read the first two books again before plunging into the third. Maybe someday I'll revisit them, but for now, they'll stay on the shelf. 
 Remember the end of the film "The Return of the King" back in 2003? When I saw it in the theater, everyone, myself included, kept thinking that it was over, but then another ending happened. It went on and on and pretty soon no one knew if it was going to continue to just keep going. That's how I felt about the end of this book. It just kept going on and on and on. Things could have been resolved much quicker, but I guess someone had to reach a word quota. It ended up being tedious and mind-numbing. My mind periodically drifted and I found myself wondering what else I could be doing. By the time I reached the final page, I was just glad that it was over. It was exhausting. 
 The same is true when it came to characters and their respective deaths. Many times a character died only to have another scene ten or twenty pages later. "Oh, they weren't quite dead." It was difficult to become invested in anyone or anything when rules of life and death didn't apply to anyone. 
 In regards to Zero's end, I am very disappointed. We were granted an exclusive look at his life and afterlife; his dreams and aspirations; hopes and disappointments. But he never expressed remorse for what he had done and what chaos and misery he had caused. To him, it was all justifiable because he lost the woman he once loved, Liz. So for him to be reunited with her in eternity, I imagine, seemed cheap and unfair. He never repented or felt sorry for betraying humanity and driving them to their demise. He wanted what he wanted and consequences be damned, but in the end, he still got the dream eternity that he always wanted. It was a ridiculous, annoying, infuriating copout.  
 Like I said, I wanted to like this book, this series, but it fell flat and read unemotional. Maybe someday I'll read the books again back to back. Perhaps the book and/or the series simply wasn't for me. Or I'm too picky. Like any piece of subjective work, it isn't meant for everyone, and it doesn't matter. For now, I have many other things to read and, I hope, enjoy.

I was fortunate enough to get to read an ARC of this book back in May, after attending one of Amie and Jay's signings with a friend of mine who WON THE ARC! 
 I then convinced/bribed my friend to let me read it first, because I was the one to introduce her to Illuminae in the first place... Mwahahahaa.... 
 I will begin by saying, this is my favorite book of 2016 (as I expected it to be, as Illuminae was my favorite of 2015) and I am 100 percent sure nothing else will top it. 
 So let's begin with the basics of why I loved this book... 
 One of my favorite things to find in a work of fiction is an already established relationship, platonic or otherwise. Amie and Jay went this route in Illuminae with Kady and Ezra, and they've done it again with Nik and Hanna, to an extent. While the journey of a new relationship in a novel is always enjoyable to see play out, I LOVE an already established relationship. The fact that these characters already have a history and know a little about each other makes their snarky interactions that much more believable. (And BTWs, the snark in this book is ON POINT, guys!) 
 The characters themselves are so fun to read about. Every single one of them is different from the others and with such a wide cast, that's quite impressive. Hanna it tough and badass and girly and everything I'd want in a best friend. And then there's Nik...oh Niklas Malikov. I swear this boy is my spirt animal, solely for the fact that his CAPS lock key is almost permanently engaged. (The jokes about the CAPS lock had me dying with laughter.) 
 The villains were formidable, the Lanima were one of the scariest alien species I've ever read about, and the PLOT TWISTS! HOLY CRAP THIS BOOK IS PLOT TWIST CITY. As mentioned earlier, Illuminae was my favorite read of 2015, and upon 2 rereads/listens of the audiobook, it has cemented itself as one of my favorite books in general. I honestly did not think anything could top it but I'm pretty sure Gemina just did. The plot twists are more extensive and gut wrenching and brilliant. Every time I thought I had something figured out, I got slapped in the face with an even better explanation of what was really happening. Amie and Jay's writing is as clever and beautiful as ever, and it just gave me ALLLL the feels. 
 The diversity in this book is incredible, as well as all the little details threaded throughout within both the artwork and the words. I want to point out specific examples so badly, but I'll save those to add to an "under the cut" spoiler section after the book is released. Just be aware that you're reading a book written by a pair of evil geniuses. 
 This was a book my soul needed to read, which of course makes me just a little nervous for what that says about my soul, needing to read a book about a covert terrorist squad overtaking a space station while a privileged "princess," anti-hero drug dealer, and his hacker cousin try and take them down all while avoiding being killed not only by said squad, but a whole lot of scary-ass serpent aliens that wanna feed on them all. 
 This book is everything I love about science fiction, relationships of every kind, snarky language, and plot and character development. The mixed media format will ALWAYS be a favorite of mine and I wanted to savor every word of every page of every document. The artwork in the ARC is already fantastic, so I can only imagine how mind-blowingly amazing it's going to be in the final published edition. I cannot wait to reread this beauty when the final edition is published, as well as listen to the full cast audiobook, because the audiobook for Illuminae was stunning and I have all the faith in the world the one for Gemina will be just as good, if not better. 
 THE BIGGEST BOOK HANGOVER OF MY LIFE RESULTED FROM THIS BOOK AND I WOULDN'T HAVE IT ANY OTHER WAY. 
 Oh, and If I ever saw either of the authors crossing the street, I'd absolutely without a doubt slam on the brakes, roll down the window, and offer to take them to coffee.

I've heard Grave Mercy mostly described as "Nun Assassins", but that doesn't feel entirely correct. Apparently the old pagan god of death (now referred to by the church as a Saint), can sire children and give them special talents or powers to serve him - known as Handmaidens of Death. I was a little confused by this in the beginning. I thought that Ismae's father was actually her father and her mother was just a bit cray-cray. But, later it's said that Mortion actually impregnated her, though there are no details of their relationship. Anyways, Ismae eventually is taken to the St. Mortian convent. Here the "nuns" serve Mortian as a god and teach their young pupils numerous ways to kill a man, as well as "womanly arts" to manipulate them. After a couple of years, Isame is sent out on assignment. 
 You can guess what happens when she's instructed to team up with the Duchess's advisor, Duval. While the initially can't stand each other, they slowly begin to trust and respect each other, until - surprise!! - they fall in love. While this was typical YA and predictable, I did actually like their relationship. I liked both Ismae and Duval as individual characters, as well. The rest of the characters could've been a little more developed for me, though. 
 The pacing of the story was a little inconsistent. It was slow in the beginning, then really picked up. Then slowed down again. I also wished that with so much emphasis put on Isame being an assassin, that we would get to see her in action more than we did. I enjoyed all the political intrigue, but at times had difficulty keeping all the supporting characters straight. 
 One unique aspect to this book is Ismae's devotion to Mortian. I've read several books that involve Greek gods, but the characters don't really serve them. Only in Christian books have I seen the characters really love God and want to have a relationship with Him. While Ismae's devotion disconcerted me a little since Mortian is a pagan god, it made me realize that there may be a bigger audience for Christian Fiction, if the rest of the story is solid. 
 Overall, I enjoyed Grave Mercy. While at times it was confusing and fell prey to a lot of the typical YA conventions, the story was unique enough to make up for it. While I'm in no great hurry to do so, I'll probably continue on with the series.

This is not going to be a hit for everyone. Hell, even when I first started reading this I thought the hype was detrimental to the enjoyment of the novel, but the truth is, Watchmen is laced and intertwined with layers of subtext and symbolism. You simply can't comprehend the sheer complexity of the alternate universe painted by Moore in one sitting. It takes multiple readings and viewings, for the two are quite mutually exclusive in this scenario. 
 None of the superheroes have superpowers, with the exception of Dr. Manhattan, who in himself is a product of human scientific development. In this world of fear and ignorance, decadence and despair, each superhero dons their mask and/or costume for their own reasons, their own sense of right and wrong, of what it means to be human or perhaps to not be, and ultimately the inner struggles and moral dilemmas that pervade the Watchmen has huge repercussions for humanity as a whole. 
 I ended the book wondering, "is that it?" But as I read it again and again I discover some seemingly small point that suddenly seems significant. Such is Moore's thoughtful, potent language coupled with Gibbons' raw, unrepenting artwork. Watchmen definitely blurs the line between the graphic novel artform and literature.

I wasn't a huge fan of Open Road Summer so I wasn't expecting much from The Start of Me and You. I am quite pleased to say that it definitely surpassed my expectations and I really enjoyed it! 
 Paige was dating Aaron for about two months when he tragically drowned on a camping trip. While she mourns his loss and has suffered from some PTSD related nightmares, what she really has trouble coping with is The Look. The way people give her pitying looks and identify her only as the girlfriend of the boy who drowned. She's ready to really start moving on and being happy again. She makes up a list of things she thinks will help her do this and embarks on the new school year determined to make it happen. 
 My problem with Open Road Summer is that I felt it tried too hard to be deep and meaningful, while still being a cute contemporary. I think that The Start of Me and You does much better at balancing the cute with the Message. The characters were relatable and likable. The problems were never too melodramatic. The romance, as well as the growing friendships, were a slow burn. 
 One thing this book does really well is the friendships. Paige has a core group of friends - Tessa, Morgan, and Kayleigh - who are all pretty different, but are always there for each other. That doesn't mean they don't ever fight, but they always make up. While there was opportunity for great girl drama (my crush has a crush on my best friend, you're spending more time with your boyfriend than you are with me, etc.), it never went there and I was really grateful it. There were no frenemies here! While the friendship between Ryan and Max isn't as explored, we know that they are really close, as well. I also liked how Paige's and Max's group of friends converged throughout the book. 
 I also liked that there was an "adult presence" in the book. So many YA books have completely absent or oblivious parents and that always gets on my nerves. Paige has present parents and she has a realistic relationship with them. I also really liked their English teacher, Ms. Pepper. She provided several humorous moments throughout the book. 
 The relationship between Paige and Max was very cute, as well. They start out a bit uncomfortable, but slowly become friends. It's several months before Paige even begins to realize that she may like him as more than a friend. I loved their banter and inside jokes. His nickname for her reminded me of Gansey and Blue from The Raven Boys so while they have nothing to do with each other, I think it endeared them to me more. 
 The underlining message of it all was about overcoming tragedy to live your life and the journey it takes to get there. I think Lord does a good job of weaving this into the other storylines about Paige's friends and Max and her grandmother. While there were a few times it almost got a little "preachy" about it, I didn't feel as brow beaten with it as with Lord's former book. It seemed much more organic and less forced. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed The Start of Me and You. The characters were likable and the romance was sweet. The writing was often humorous and I found myself smiling a lot while I was reading. I would definitely recommend this to fans of YA Contemporary.

Oh, Red Queen, I so wanted to like you. I could forgive you for the dystopian cliches (because, let's be real, all dystopians are pretty cliche) and how predictable everything was. I could forgive you for the unlikable characters. Unfortunately, the most interesting part of the whole book is the cover. 
 Before I go to spoiler city, I will just say that I had to pretty much force myself to finish this book, which I only did because of some great reviews I read. It did get better towards the end, especially the well-described action sequence in the second-to-last chapter (I think it was second-to-last, might have been the last two chapters?), but it just did not make up for how bland the rest of the book the was. The pacing was slow, the characters were not well-developed, and I was just bored. I didn't connect to the characters so I didn't really care what happened to them either. I will say a lot of people seem to love it, so it might be worth a try, but if you try it and are struggling, I would suggest just forgetting about it. 
 ***SPOILERS FROM HERE ON OUT*** 
 I think I'm just going to list some of the more specific things that didn't work for me. 
 -Mare's best friend, Kilorn, came crying to her when he found out he would be sent to the war. She does everything she can (which isn't much) to keep him from it, and eventually saves him after the royal family finds out what a special snowflake she is. But the first thing he does with his freedom is join the rebel army. He not only joins, he is immediately part of the inner-circle. If he was a stronger person I could overlook that, but he was too weak and scared about the idea of going to the war front, so I can't buy him as a great rebel. 
 -There's a very half-assed love square. A romance between Mare and Kilorn is vaguely hinted at, it's more of a "what if" scenario if the world was different. I think their relationship would have benefited from being just a stronger friendship. Cal is the obvious love interest in the beginning - the one that realizes how special she is before anyone knows there's anything special about her, but there's not really any development with their relationship besides a couple of dances and longing looks. The story seems more caught up in trying to pull one over on the reader by focusing on Maven as the surprise hero and love interest. I could almost get on board this ship, but Mare swings back and forth so much about which brother she likes more that I couldn't really root for either of them. Eventually she tells Maven she's choosing no one, so that was a nice change of pace. However, her circumstances has thrown her together with Cal, and all of her following actions make it seem like Cal is the answer. 
 -When I was trying to decide to keep reading or not, I read some reviews. I came across one that was not marked as being spoilery and it mentioned something about how surprising the big betrayal was. I wasn't far into the book at this point, but I was far enough to realize that the only betrayal that could hold any sort of emotional impact would be from Maven. I didn't really trust Maven in the first place, but I might not have been expecting his turn around if I hadn't read that first. So, unfortunately, I spent the whole book waiting to see Maven turn against Mare. 
 -Obviously Shade wasn't killed. No one should be surprised when he shows up in the Epilogue. 
 -Overall the pacing of the story was just slow. I was really bored most of the time. The character development for everyone besides Mare was pretty poor, and while she was more developed her character didn't really grow at all. I found myself not really caring about what happened to any of them. As I mentioned earlier, there was a really well-written action sequence towards the end and that was the only time I really got into the story. If the whole book would've been written that well, I would be able to recommend this. I might read the next book, just because the ending was more interesting, but I'm not sure. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 2 Stars
