First impressions: I'm generally a fan of the alternating time perspective, and it worked really well here. Letters from a woman who came to America on the Mayflower are interspersed throughout the book, giving us clues about the mystery as the story progresses. Loved it! It felt spooky and different and gave the book a touch of old world classiness that mirrored the high society lives of the present time. 
 Lasting impressions: I thought the book was a giant success and am really glad I decided to try out this series. It was a great cross of paranormal with a contemporary feel. I must say, this whole boarding school theme is growing on me. 
 Conflicting impressions: I figured out the mystery just a little too easily, and this coming from a girl who NEVER figures out the mystery. 
 Overall impressions: I breezed through this book in just a day or two, and thoroughly enjoyed it. Prissy, preppy New York girls are not usually my go-to characters, but here I felt they were all fleshed out well, with real personalities that didn't seem ultra thin. I especially liked Schuyler Van Alen (and what a name!), who both fit in, yet didn't. She marches to her own beat, yet can hang at a fashion shoot no problem. Sure, I'll model these designer jeans for you. Sure, I can get us into this club. Yet just when you thought she'd veer off into Mary Sue territory, she'd bring it right back to reality. 
 The world and setup here is quite interesting. Vampires are some of the most powerful members of New York society, called Blue Bloods because, well, they have blue blood. As teenagers, when they start to turn (because it's hereditary...kind of...but really reincarnative...sort of?) they are at their most vulnerable, and this knowledge is being exploited by something out there killing off the vamp kids, one by one. The narrative follows a handful of these young kids, some are vampires, some aren't, as they sort through these events. 
 The story builds nicely, and as the kids stumble through discovery after discovery, they eventually start to piece together what's happening. The book does at times feel like one big, long prelude to a larger story arc that will build in subsequent novels, but as a stand alone it is also completely satisfying. I loved de la Cruz's incorporation of the Mayflower history into the story, and I hope that we get to learn more about the vampire culture and how it is exactly that they regenerate. This is a quick, fun read, especially for fans of the vampire genre.

Each character's choice of genre actually highlighted the characters' personality. Such a clever techinique Gale Forman, very clever. 
 I also loved the reactions I gave while reading the book. Especially the start -again, I'm not spoiling I want you to buy this book and read it yourself - I got so surprised and it just made me kept going, kept reading. It made me focus my attention to the story, the plot, the characters. I also loved how Gale Forman wrote each chapter, how she goes from present to past then present again. It's brilliant! 
 I am truly inspired with her (Gale Forman) style of writing. I'm truly a fan. 
 I also love how I saw myself through Mia's eyes. How would I deal with such situations? How would I feel through all that she has witnessed? What would I choose? How could I make a decision? How? While reading the story I thought of how I could I feel or do in a situation like that. It makes you re-think your life, your experiences, your strengths, your weaknesses, your achievements and failures, yourself - in general. 
 And the message of the story - Oh My Gosh! Oh my, my, my - just so heartwarming, I swear. At one point in the story I actually and literally shed a tear. It was so pure, so believable that my heart just felt the emotions the character, Mia, felt and I just teared up. The emotions I felt at the time was just so powerful I had to let it out. Yes people, that's just how amazing this book is.

I didnt want to finish it because if I finished it the story would be over. Its like when you're watching a show and it ends with an open ending or a really good ending and you're just like, "That was it? NOOOO! I WANT MORE!!!" That's exactly how I felt about this book. I didnt want it to be over. I wanted to keep turning pages and keep reading. Its just that good. Soooooooo good that I didnt want it to end.

I swayed between three and four stars on this one and finally kicked it up to four. Why? 
 elevator description: Robinson Crusoe on Mars without pal Friday to keep him company. Has to figure out how to survive until the next Mars mission arrives. 
 Annoying things: 
 1. Although much of the novel is written in 'diary style' and colloquialisms such as 'yay' and 'lol' are meant to emphasize that, they were just sometimes annoying. I know the explanatory line from Mark Watney's (the main protagonist in the story) psychologist (interviewed at some time in the book) told us that he cracks a lot of jokes, and that seems to be a central part of his personality, but I didn't really warm up to his 'voice'. There were a few parts that were truly funny, but I had the feeling those parts worked best because the author wasn't trying overly hard to convince us that Watney was a funny guy. 
 2. The point-of-views in the book alternated between the first person log entries (Watney), a sort of omniscient narrator looking down on Watney, third person limited POVs from some of the earthbound people and the Hermes crew. I found the omniscient viewpoint distracting and some of the third person as well. 
 3. Stereotypes and stupid decisions. Scientists on earth. These characters seemed designed just for the plot and did not seem to have any real reason to exist on their own as characters. Least favorite line in the novel: '"Sheesh," he said nervously. "We're scientists, for Christ's sake. What the hell!?"' This was made in response to the crew commander for the Hermes getting emotionally involved about the decision NOT to let the Hermes crew rescue Watney. How stupid is that?  Not the decision itself, but the crack about scientists. As if scientists do not ever get emotional. Nooooo. We're all robots, right? 
 4. Watney. He always seems to know what to do *right away*. Sometimes he figures it out after a good night's sleep. I find it hard to believe that he could sleep at all with some kind of death-inducing event threatening on the horizon. But that's just me. He had a sort of shallowness/immaturity about him that reminded me of the main character in Ready Player One who could be excused for his behavior because, well, he is an adolescent. Watney should be beyond that. But this is also a good thing (see below) because we are spared a lot of whininess. 
 5. Predictability.  With the whole planet watching, we know there is going to be a good ending. I also guessed the Hermes maneuver early on.  
 Good things: 
 1. Pacing. Excellent. I read the book in two days. I had already read the sample beforehand - which almost made me jettison the book completely, but I'm glad I got through that part. It gets better after that. Much better. 
 2. Suspense. Very good if a bit overdone. Everything Watney does brings up a new crisis. It was believable, if in a strained way, but it certainly made for good reading. 
 3. Lack of Emotion. Watney doesn't wallow in any sort of depression about his situation or any of the crises he is faced with for very long. I found this a good thing if not very believable. But he is an engineer, so I could be wrong about that. It makes for good reading because there isn't a whole lot of introspection. Instead, there is a lot of discussion about 70s television and disco music. Okaaaaay. 
 4. The Writing. Doesn't get in the way of the story. Very good. Despite that, there is a lot of visual imagery so we know what the setting is, the weather, etc. and can get a good picture of what all the vehicles look like (sort of). 
 5. The Physics. I didn't even skim it, found it fascinating and interesting and didn't even go through and check everything. I believed the author had and that was enough.

Decent second installment in the Oak Knoll series.

 As a whole, I really like Hoag's writing, which is competent and smooth. The characters in this series aren't as strong as some other series I've read, but they're good enough. What I really find compelling about her books is her efforts to explore through fiction the anatomy of a killer. Mysteries and who-done-its are fun, but they are more fun when they seriously address the why in a way that only fiction can. Hoag has obviously read her share of books by experts, which I think imparts her books with a level of authenticity that is often lagging in other similar reads. 
 Of course, as is often the case with this type of book, the coincidences abound, at times to the point of absurdity, but that's more a function of this genre than it is a deficiency in the writing.

The proper title for this would have been "The Exposition at Styles"; that's pretty much the only method of storytelling Agatha Christie seems to have known how to employ. We don't really see any of the action here, it's basically verbalized to us in long endless descriptions. I can understand that this was the beginning of the modern murder mystery, but I'm really glad that fiction has come a long way because I didn't find this suspenseful at all. The denouement is a lot like the end of Psycho, where you're told (and not shown) about everything that makes Norman Bates the way he is.

I feel that this book is in large part unnecessary. Firstly, the entire main thrust of the novel was given away fairly obviously very early on (two of the team members returned when we know for a fact that they are dead, the odd smell permeating the facility which only the person who hasn't been contaminated either in thought or person can smell) . The majority of the time is spent with Control as he attempts to wade through office hostility and crazy while getting a grip on his predecessor and Area X. The previous book made use of flashbacks during the course of the narrative and I see no reason why this couldn't be condensed as well. I think the subtlety which would have to be employed would better serve the mystery anyhow. 
 Secondly, I don't like the emphasis of Area X as being the sole main protagonist of the series. It makes sense, sure, that area and its mystery is the background and impetus for the whole series.  Original Review: 
 This book is a little inspired by Beauty and the Beast but is definitely different enough to be worth the read. 
 Feyre is a 19 year old girl who hunts for her very impoverished family and is the one who keeps them alive. He father is crippled and her elder sisters don't do anything to help survive. While out hunting for a deer, she encounters a large wolf who she kills more to protect herself from the Wolf (after all, he could be faerie who are dangerous creatures who hate humans). As it turns out, he is indeed a faerie, and a vengeful faerie friend comes to claim Feyre as a captive for violating a treaty between humans and faeries. This faerie friend takes her back to his home (otherwise Feyre would die in exchange for the wolf's life) in the faerie part of the continent across the Wall. There she must spend the rest of her days unless she can figure out how to get out of the treaty. 
 All right, so its pretty obvious Feyre falls in love with her captor faerie. It is a great romance. I loved it as a romance because there really wasn't a love triangle for once. All right, a little bit of one but only a little teensy bit, but it was so refreshing to not have any of that TEAM ***** crap. You know? I am just getting so sick of the prevalence of love triangles in YA fiction, especially in fantasy which is what I mostly enjoy. Thank goodness this exists. 
 It's also most jam packed with lots of interesting/action/things that happen versus you know, oh I love him but I can't (and then insert long chapters of nothing happening but the character complaining or something else dumb). I enjoy a book that gets to the point. 
 The worldbuilding is nice, nothing too unique. The faerie lore is interesting and I would like to learn more about it. I'm not sure if this is a series but I can see Mrs. Maas expanding upon it. There is definitely content that she could continue on with. I would definitely pick up the sequel. :)

For the most part, Stroked is a fun, light-hearted affair. Blazing chemistry, an in-depth look at Olympic swimming, and several sources of conflict made this an enjoyable, rollercoaster ride of a read for me. 
 Although the premise is a bit far-fetched (not a deal-breaker), the author does a superb job of establishing chemistry between the two main characters. The narrative's focus on the publicity angle of Olympic swimming added another layer of depth to the sport that I enjoyed learning about. The sources of conflict are well-managed, meaning that angst didn't overshadow the story's positive, more heartwarming moments. 
 I've seen in other reviews that readers are divided when it comes to Bellini's chapters. Personally, I thought they were hilarious and that they really stood out as a different "voice." 
 As for constructive criticism, I have to admit that the narrators sometimes went off on tangents that took me out of the story. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Stroked and would definitely read Meghan Quinn again.

I guess the only redeeming quality of this novel to me is the superlative artwork by Jim Lee and co. Everyone, be they villain or good guy, has never looked better. 
 The plot grows ever the more bizarre, but the tighter it becomes the more coherent it feels, though I'm still too busy ogling at the sumptuous detail of the visuals. 
 And the sequence where Catwoman practically straddles/wraps herself around an in-dire-need-of-a-shave-and-bath Batman at the lion's cage = very sexy indeed.

Of course, the story is not what it seems, and the romance between Sharzhad and Khalid is swoony and sweet. The setting and the writing are lush and absorbing - I can't wait for the next book.

This book was amazing. 
 I absolutely love Curtis' books, but this one might be my favorite. The family dynamic was so great, I just loved how all of the Malone's talked to each other and really stuck by one another. It was both funny and touching, especially when things started to get tough for them. 
 Like his other books, racism is handled very deftly and powerfully. Poverty is as well, since this takes place during the Great Depression. The story is both heartbreaking and heartwarming. 
 Deza is a fantastic character. She's a perfectionist who loves to read and write. She's very concise and matter-of-fact about everything. While she tries her best at everything she does, she learns to cope with falling short of her own high expectations and her family's struggles during the depression.

Unfortunately, I didn't like this start to the Mortal Instruments series as much as I thought I would. I kind of felt like the main character Clary was missing...something - maybe I just didn't connect with her for whatever reason - and I wished that she was more active, more able to kick-butt. I get why she can't fight since she was raised as a mundane and wasn't taught to fight demons, but I still wish that she had found some dormant butt-kicking skill or something. Also, I felt that there was just a bit too much happening in the book, a bit too many twists and turns of the plot. It got a little distracting by the end. And maybe it was that I read Clockwork Angel first, not knowing it was technically a prequel to this series. The plots are so so similar: the orphaned girl who gets pulled into the Niphilim's world and ends up being cared for in the hospital wing of the Institute, the teen Niphilim left at the Institute alone, the two blood-brother warriors and the one lone female Niphilim, the love triangle between a nicer, gentler boy and a bratty but oh-so-cute and secretly-fragile boy, even where the first kiss takes place is the same. As a result, City of Bones felt too familiar to me. And the final twist, the sort of Star Wars ending, drove me nuts!!! Ugh, I'm so mad at this book for that.  
 But, the book was certainly entertaining. I may go on to read the next one, if only to find out what happens to a few of the characters.

And then, there's her accomplishments. I remember not so long ago, the popular consensus opinion was that women weren't funny. Fey and Amy Poehler may be the second or third wave, but those attitudes persist. Fey's advice about working around that kind of sexism is invaluable for women in any profession. What a terrific novel by a great new(ish) author!! 
 Kate comes from a family who is often the subjects of gossip and scandal. Her father sits back in oblivion, while her mother flirts with any man she can get her claws into. Her sisters seem to be following their mother's footsteps. Kate is determined to become an old maid and travel to India with her spinster aunt, but her mother won't allow it unless she receives...and rejects...three marriage proposals. Kate asks her longtime friend, Henry, to help her out so that she can live her heart's desire. But some bargains are hard to drive... 
 My heart went out to Kate. She was known as Kitty as a child and no one, save Henry, will let her break that mold and grow up. She is forever correcting everyone on her name. Her family is so selfish and Henry's mother is just plain mean toward her, yet Kate is the most unselfish and kind person ever, always thinking of the feelings of others. I really liked her and felt a connection to her, which for me, draws me into the story even more. 
 Henry was such a gentleman and true friend. He goes against his (mean) mother to help a friend have a dream come true. Those stormy gray eyes... Any girl would be lucky to have someone like Henry on her side. 
 I loved the friendship and chemistry these two have together. I loved the flashbacks to the past that Kate had--they were the strings that tied the story together to help the reader understand what makes Kate tick. This author has a way of drawing the reader in--I really felt like I was a part of their lives. 
 Put this one on your "to-read" list because you don't want to miss out on this one!!

I absolutely adored this book. I have a son with Asperger's, so I have a special place in my heart for people on the autism spectrum and their families.

Oh, yes, I felt that, too. But that's a spoiler, so I'll separate that. I could not put this book down. Wonderful, wonderful story.

 And his mother? Let's put aside the whole leaving without telling her son first. I know it was hard raising Christopher. Believe me, I get it. However, she writes weekly letters to him for 2 years and never once thinks, "gee, maybe I should go visit him in person"?? Really?? I was so furious with her! How do you do that??? I was glad that she finally did choose to put her son's needs first. 
 I really liked that Christopher's dad was willing to give him the time and space he needed to trust him again, and did not force the situation.

Sigh. It took me an hour and a bit to read this book. There is a heat wave in Australia and I couldn't move off the sofa. 
 I am kind of disappointed. I'm not sure if that is because I have seen so many rave reviews for this story that I expected it to be better and it just didn't meet my expectations or what? 
 First off, it's written in first person pov. It started in third and I was hopeful and then the next chapter, it switched. Dammit. 
 Second, Leigh has dealt with the issues of the Russian errors elsewhere. In essence, her response was 'I did my research and left it and so did my editors/publisher etc'. I think that's kind of poor. You can't stick Saint Basil's cathedral on the cover, mention samovars, tsars, and troikas and call your elite grisha and then say it isn't based in Russia. Read Anna Karenina and you will comprehend the different names for males/females. So the main characters name is just... wrong. She is a female and should be Alina Starkova not Starkov. That isn't hard and we are not talking a minor thing; this is the main character's correct name. It's the equivalent of a boy named Sue. 
 Alina is the standard YA (young adult) heroine; she has brown hair, is skinny, clumsy and plain looking (I fear she said mousy). The guy she loves, Mal, doesn't notice her as they grow up orphaned together and join the army and he sleeps with all the pretty girls and still doesn't notice her. Mal is, of course, beautiful. 
 And then, voila... she discovers her gift in an attack by scary monsters and goes to mean girls school... I mean the Grisha training academy where she transforms into a beautiful woman, is now top of the defence class (trained by Yoda), all the girls hate her and the boys like her. Which is amazing because everyone there is so beautiful. Gah. 
 I kind of went with it as I read the book but now as I sit here to write my review it all seems too easy and too damn familiar. Alina isn't just talented, she's unique. The magic world is divided into different strengths or abilities; healers, heartrenders etc. and she is a sun-summoner and they haven't had one of those for hundreds of years; if at all. I couldn't work out how they knew they existed if they'd never had one. She is taken to the palace in a mad rush to be protected but then doesn't have bodyguards or anyone with her half the time. 
 The other unique magic person is the Darkling. I love a good bad guy and he redeems the book for me. The magic abilities are grouped by colour; he wears black like Alina should. But she doesn't want to be different. Right. 
 And does he have a name? He's all ready to swoop her into bed but forgot to tell her his name? I get why the Darkling wants her, but I just couldn't buy Mal's about face where she was concerned. He discovers he loves Alina after she's not around. 
 And the plot? Besides being all action to start, then a fill in of the boarding school bit, where Alina got frankly whiny, it switches back to scary monsters again. But leaves it with no resolution. 
 The priest seems to be just added in to be creepy. 
 Alina believes everything she is told until one person tells her the exact opposite and then she believes them, gives it all up and runs away - immediately. The darkling is not the greatx5 grandson of the guy who made the scary monster valley, he IS that guy. What? Really? And nobody noticed? And she believes it? A better plot twist would be if grandad showed up to break them up. 
 And the last part? Whoever kills the magic stag will use the horns as a magic enhancer/amplifier. She doesn't kill it; but she still gets the power. Logic train derailed. Yeah, she spared it, so she gets the power. Wait... what? So should every other person who didn't kill it. The stag can't choose who gets the power; it's dead. Sigh.  
 Please give me book sets where each book has an actual ENDING. I am soooo tired of series with cliff-hangers and no resolution. I take that back; my copy has some early chapters from the next book and after reading those (in my head) that was the end. The first book does have an ending and switches back to third pov... why? 
 It was an easy read and I might read the sequel to check up on the Darkling, whatever his damn name is.

Overall I really enjoyed this. The story takes place in an interesting world with likable characters and a cool magic system. I just had a few problems with it that kept me from really loving it.

The world building was quite weak and the various types of magic users (Knacked, Marked, and Privileged) were not ever explained very well. What an utterly delightful read! I am very grateful for having stumbled across Shelleyrae's review of this book on her blog "Book'd Out", which initially made me put it on my to-read-list. My only regret is not having picked it up a lot sooner! A Man Called Ove is easiest one of the best books I have read all year, and one that will definitely make it on my all-time-favourites list. Told with both humour and wisdom, it follows the story of a 59-year-old Swedish man called Ove, who has recently lost his wife and his job and decided that life is no longer worth living. Always considered a somewhat taciturn and grumpy old man by his neighbours, Ove is sure he won't be missed by anyone, and makes his plans for a clean exit from this life. But one by one all his plans are foiled by the arrival of new neighbours next door - a pregnant "foreign woman", her tall lanky husband and their two little girls, who will not accept that Ove wants to be left alone. 
 Written with laugh-out-loud humour as well as tender insights into his characters' lives, Backman instantly drew me into the storyline and made my daily commute richer as I laughed, cried and pondered the meaning of life, love and death with Ove. Very highly recommended. I absolutely adored it!

 This story is about a girl, Kaitlyn, who only exists at night. She and her sister, Carly, inhabit the same body--Carly surfaces during the daylight hours, Kaitlyn during the night. She has never known the sun, or a classroom full of people. She has never held a real conversation with her sister--only messages left on Post-Its, or birthday cards, or in notebooks. 
 The first thing that already made me love it was that they truly WERE sisters inhabiting the same body. Two souls. I have literally just finished two books (almost in a row) where it was the opposite. The main character thought she was possessed, turns out she was both people, and she had Dissociative identity disorder. In another one, she thought she had a twin sister and it turns out SHE has Dissociative identity disorder as well.  It's apparently a fad, because I've seen a lot of media go this direction. Movies. Other books. So when I first read about it, I was blown away. Now, on my fifth version of it, it's not a cool twist ending. 
 And that's a big portion of why I liked this book. It makes you think it's going to go one route, and then (fairly early on) it goes the other way--and I was so freaking excited about it. 
 And after that, it was a pretty great traditional ghost story for a while. Kaitlyn starts to deteriorate after Carly disappears and Kaitlyn wakes up during the day, instead of at night  She starts to see things, see people, who aren't really there, hear voices whispering--all the sort of stuff that gives you the chills while you're reading. I was outside taking a walk while I was reading and I jumped so bad when a heard something rustling through the bushes near me. It was 10 o'clock in the morning, there was sunshine, plenty of cars driving by, and I was so immersed in what was happening I didn't notice any of it until the loud noise that had me jumping out of my skin. 
 Good job, author. I was absorbed. 
 It does get a bit convoluted, and at one point I had to stop and rehash a little bit of what had happened so I could make sure I had it all straight. The reason for the title DEAD HOUSE doesn't actually show up until pretty far into the novel, but by then I was hooked. I was reading it so quickly that I was jumping through the major plot points practically instantaneously. 
 Plus, I loved loved loved loved LOVED the ending.  Because it ends precisely the way a creepy ghost story sort of thing should end. We don't know ultimately what happened to her. We don't know if she won, if she found Carly, or if she simply perished. Rumors abound that she still haunts the place, looking for her lost sister. People, years later, visit the spot to try and detect paranormal activity. Though I can definitely lean toward one ending after what happened with Kaitlyn's psychiatrist.  
 Plus, I freaking love the cover.

 Throughout this book, Em constantly apologizes for not letting Gavin beat the crap out of her ex. Here she is, trying to keep Gavin out of jail, and from escalating the cycle of violence. But no, Gavin has to be A MAN. Yes, that's right. The word that they used throughout the book is "being a man". 
 And of course, poor Em, she's so sorry - like crying hysterically sorry - that she doesn't want him to do this. Because she's keeping him from being a "real man". 
 .....Sorry, I had to walk away for a moment so that I could vomit in my mouth. 
 You know, if this was a historical romance set in 1206 before we had fully formed foreheads, maybe this would make sense. But, really? I can understand feeling violent if somebody hurt someone you love. What I can't understand is how it apparently makes him have less testosterone if he doesn't act upon it, and she's clearly not a supportive girlfriend for stopping him from going to jail for assault. 
 Oh, and OF COURSE there's a baby. What NA book now doesn't end up with an unplanned pregnancy that makes everyone ecstatic even though they're 21 years old? At least he didn't find out bc she kept the peed on stick test in her drawer or her purse. I've read at least 4 books where that happened, and all I can say is - EW.  
 Finally - WHY DOES SHE KEEP GIGGLING? Doesn't anyone know how annoying if a sound that is? It makes me feel like Em is a teenage airhead. 
 I suppose I'm being a hypocrite, because by the time I threw down the book in disgust, I wanted to bitch slap her silly. Maybe I'll have a cell between Dillon and Gavin.

Wendy Walker's stories are all a little bit "out there". They are extreme circumstances and people doing things that are extremely out of the norm, and it gives me an eye roll as well as a bit of excitement. 
 It starts just the way it sounds--two sisters vanish on the same night. Then three years later, one of them returns, and won't rest until her tale is told. It alternates between her point of view and the doctor studying her. You would think this would provide unique insights--one person who knows what's going on completely, and another trying to figure out the situation. Only Cass doesn't reveal very much at all until the very end of the novel where we get the explosion of drama. 
 The mother was the most fascinating part, which may seem obvious. She was demented and provided a very obvious case of narcissism in its true form. For me, she was the most fascinating piece of the story. Yes of course I wanted to find out what happened to Emma, but for me it was more important to see why her mother acted so outrageously, and to see what specifically she did. 
 Still a severely dramatic story but I greatly enjoyed it.

An amazing book. I bought The Lovely Bones several years ago, thinking I would read it before the movie came out. I never got around to reading it, but I saw the movie anyway. Pulled it off the shelf yesterday and thought "why not." The fact that I'd seen the movie made no difference. You already know who Susie Salmon's killer is by page two, so that wasn't spoiled for me. In fact, I'd forgotten almost everything that happened in the movie, except that Saoirse Ronan and Stanley Tucci were in it. 
 This book is so well-written. It actually reminded me a lot of King, though King is somewhat more compelling to me. Unlike King, The Lovely Bones is what I would call "literature" but it does have a supernatural element. Still, this was a gripping read. It's not a murder mystery (which I originally thought it was when I first bought the book). It's really a family drama, centered around an extremely tragic event. It examines the question, how do you live after something like the brutal murder of a child, how do you continue to be a family after that? 
 TLB is told from the perspective of the murdered girl, Susie Salmon. And because she is a spirit, she can look in on each of the characters, jumping between them at will, even jumping from one character's thoughts (including glimpses of their pasts) to another's. This is a bold perspective choice. A lot of books I read are in first person (supposedly the easiest perspective to write from). Some (like King's works) are third person. I don't know if I've ever read something from an omniscient perspective, definitely not first person omniscient. I would think it would be near impossible, but, somehow, Alice Sebold pulls it off. 
 I think this is one of those books that will be part of college lit courses someday. I definitely recommend it. Be warned, though, the subject matter is very, very dark. People make choices that you might not like, but that's just like life. 
 I think I'll rematch the movie sometime and see if I thought it did the book justice. I can see why it didn't do so well, I think. Heavy, heavy source material.

I was amused, I laughed out load several times, it was nothing I'll probably find all that memorable or re-read, but I did enjoy it.

 The main theme continues to be identity, and what makes you who you are. Is it your genes? Your family? Who are your family? And how do you overcome a clouded past for the future you hope to have? How much do your choices matter? Does it matter why you make them? 
 In a lot of (good) ways, this book reminds me of The Blue Sword. A young woman struggles to grow into adulthood, and tries to turn her handicaps into assets. She discovers unanticipated skills, and finds love in unexpected places. She has (wonderfully-written, well-developed) important friendships with horses and dogs. 
 I highly recommend this book. And maybe someday I'll get through a whole review of a Cashore book without referencing The Blue Sword.

Armstrong traces the history of the television show and the culture that grew around it, from the original concept that emerged out of a conversation in Lee's Market between Jerry Seinfeld and Larry David, through the production of the show over nine seasons, to the finale, and beyond--the Curb Your Enthusiasm "reunion," for instance, as well as the emergence of Internet fan sites, such as the Twitter sites Modern Seinfeld and Seinfeld Current Day. 
 The book is not a work of criticism, so although various episodes are mentioned, they are not discussed in detail. Nor is the book a reference work or a collection of trivia: it mentions, for instance, a few of the catchphrases associated with the show, and names some of the celebrity guest stars, but does not attempt comprehensiveness with these or other comparable subjects. And although Armstrong interviewed numerous subjects in researching the book, it is not a collection of reminiscences by the main actors. 
 In fact, it appears that Armstrong did not interview Seinfeld, David, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Jason Alexander or Michael Richards for her book. Instead, many of her interviewees include both writers who worked on the show and people on whom different characters were based. In this way, Armstrong explores something she terms "Seinfeldia," a space between the show and reality where the lines between the two become blurred, such as in those moments in the show that, while seemingly surreal, were in fact based on real events, or in those instances in which fans continue to interact with the show, even almost twenty years after the last episode aired. For example, although I was not surprised to read that "Festivus" has become an actual celebration among some fans of the show, I did not expect to learn that the "holiday" had been in existence since 1966, some thirty years before the episode of Seinfeld that brought it to the attention of the show's audience.  
 I laughed a few times while reading the book. At one point, I interrupted reading to re-watch one of the episodes. 
 Extra points for the inclusion in the text of George's marine biologist monologue.

From the very first sentence, this book grips you by the throat and doesn't let go. I devoured this book in two sittings, staying up late into the night, furiously wiping away tears so I could finish. I was so thoroughly invested in Lina's story that I had a hard time letting go. 
 Lina, along with her mother and brother, is ripped from her Lithuanian home by Soviet secret police late on a June evening in 1941. They are given 20 minutes to pack a bag before they are whisked away on trucks and herded onto train cars bound for Russia. From there, we follow Lina's harrowing journey of survival by train to Russian and Siberian forced labor camps. 
 The book moves quickly thanks to short chapters, often punctuated by Lina's memories of moments from a better time. These snippets give us a glimpse into the girl she was before she was taken. They serve as a jarring juxtaposition against her situation in the camps - starving, worked near to death, fighting disease and failing health. Her memories are those of any girl, and remind us of her humanity and innocence. 
 Lina meets a number of people on the train and in the camps, and they all captivated me in different ways. Ruta Sepetys, who researched this book by visiting Lithuania and hearing survivors' experiences, created such vivid characters despite their dire circumstances. I felt for each of them in different ways, much like the way they each process their situation. No one person reacted the same way to what was happening - we saw denial, fear, shock, outrage, defiance, and defeat. Nothing can prepare you for the gamut of emotions that Sepetys paints onto each page. 
 This is a gorgeous, haunting, and incredibly moving book. I highly recommend it, but be sure to keep some tissues handy.

An acceptable sequel to a Anatomy of a Boyfriend. Dom is a driven, pre-med student, home from her freshman year of college and still smarting from the end of her first serious relationship. For a book that doesn't flinch from explicit details of casual sex, it is as earnest as an after-school special. Dom may test the casual-sex waters, but not before checking every medically-recommended box. Would it be out of line to describe the rendering of Dom's pelvic exam as 'clinical'? Snadowsky leavens the all-too-correct pre-connubial STD testing with plenty of humor; I laughed out-loud at Dom's reveling in post-coital joy on p. 159. "So...how many other people know about this?" Indeed. Fans will want to spread the word about this trifle. 
 While the frank, uncommitted sex Dom has will turn off many readers, but I had a different bone to pick with the story. At one point, there is fight between Dom and Amy during which they trade cruel words, unless "pathetic nymphomaniac" was yelled in the good way. They then don't speak to each other for a few days (this is what friends as close as sisters do, after all?). When they reconnect, these two brush their visciousness aside as incidental. Mutual apologies all around; hugs and kisses. While I understand that people say things they regret, I wish Snadowsky had allowed these women to fight fair, instead of like reality-TV B-listers. There are boundaries in relationships - with guys, with girls - that can't be crossed if we are to remain healthy. Dom is great at setting boudaries for maintaining her sexual heath, but isn't so great at maintaining equally firm ones for her friendships.

This is fucking great. 
 It's like a slow burning version of The Twilight Zone mixed with The Ring mixed with anything having to do with the Salem witch trials. Plus, I met the author when he signed my book and he was a super nice guy, so brownie points for that. 
 Story: Present day Black Spring is haunted by a 300 year old witch. Seeing as how they're in the year 2012 (there's mention about the presidential race between Barack Obama and Mitt Romney) though, they're quite modern about their haunting. They have cameras all over the town, and they have an app on their cellphones. It's all part of their infrastructure for keeping an eye on the witch. She pops up in random places and they never know how long she will stay. Once she stood my someone's bedside for three straight days without moving. 
 She's just as creepy as you would expect too. Her eyes and lips are sewn shut, but all the townspeople can swear they feel her eyes on them, like she's biding her time. Doctors back in the 60s tried to unthread her mouth once... the results were disastrous enough that no one ever tried again. 
 Just don't get too close to her, because her whisperings can lead you down a very dark path. 
 Where Hex starts up is focused on one family, and how their decisions drastically alter the trajectory of the townspeople's lives forever. It starts out slowly, but holy crap that ending is worth it. If you've ever watched The Twilight Zone, this is just like an episode called The Monsters Are Due on Maple Street. It's magical and dark and freaking psychotic and I loved every single minute of this book. Easily my favorite so far this year.

Uh, wow. Where to start with this? 
 I haven't read Fangirl, which was apparently the book that spawned this one, and maybe if I had I'd be feeling better about Carry On. Idk. As it stands, it took me a long time to get a good feel for this world and what was happening in it. The whole first half (at least) is very in medias res. 
 So, because of that, I kind of wish this had been a series instead of a standalone, since so much of the story is in the past. But at the same time, I doubt I would have the motivation to slog through a whole series. 
 I say that because yeah, I found this pretty enjoyable and it kept me reading, BUT I wasn't in love with this world or these characters. I didn't really like this book at all until Baz came along. He's definitely my favorite character and one of the things that made me give this book 3 stars instead of 2. I definitely shipped the ship and all, but all the tension/anticipation kind of went out of it for me before they even kissed. I can't pinpoint why their first kiss and everything after fell kind of flat to me; it just did. Maybe because I didn't understand why it happened when it did. Sure, it was dramatic, but I didn't feel like the characters were at that point yet, emotionally. More so Simon than Baz. 
 As for the villain, and I won't say who that is because spoilers, I didn't find him very scary or interesting. More time needed to be spent interacting with him, and not just in flashbacks to stuff that happened before the start of this book. Reading about the defeat of the villain was just kinda meh for me because I didn't want it enough yet by the time it happened. In retrospect, that might be the same problem I'm having with Simon and Baz getting together. 
 There's a lot of positive stuff I could say about Carry On. Rowell does a lot of clever things in building this world and making it distinct from Harry Potter. The writing is often funny and great at keeping me hooked. I very much enjoyed Rowell's choices for the epilogue. I adored the way she developed Baz's character. And Agatha's--she turned an unlikable, flat character into someone I was surprised to find myself rooting for and really liking. 
 That said, I have no strong feelings about this book and am not sure it lives up to the hype.

I know I said I wouldn't give Siobhan Davis a 5 star rating yet because I know she will get better and I'll have to invent a new rating system... That being said, this book gets a 5 star rating. And I may have to reinvent my rating system. 
 Immersing you immediately in a new world along with Sadie, intrigue abounds as the mystery about Sadie's past and purpose unravels. Every single point is so well developed, you are completely comfortable as a reader in a new land, and it is very exciting to experience things alongside Sadie. Although Siobhan asks you to suspend your disbelief, it is utterly unnecessary to do so because the plot is so finely crafted that you are already willing to buy into it hook, line, and sinker. I appreciated the innovative perspective she brought on time-travel. Without spoiling anything, here are a few of my favorite things about Saven: Denial: 
 1. Sadie finally grows! I know she's grown throughout the first two novels (I was there). However, I always disliked her a little bit. She was whiny, weak, and completely blinded by her love for Logan. It was almost like she wasn't her own person. (Funny, because she really kind of wasn't and that is explained in this book.) Sadie comes into her own towards the end of the book, making hard choices and sacrifices. Her choices aren't always the best, but they are fully her own. Look out, Saven and Tor! Sadie is taking charge! 
 2. Axton. Can we just .... for a second? I could not be more thrilled with this development!  And I'm totally #TeamAxton right now. He really knows her deep down and he had to suffer through watching her with Logan all that time. Bleeding hearts of the world, unite. I hope he wins out for her affection in the end. We shall see!  
 3. World building done right. The next time an aspiring writer asks me for a book that is a good example of world building, this is it. This is my recommendation. Of course, it piggy backs off the first two books. It stands strong on its own as well. Building a complete new world, plot, and characters successfully in so few pages. 
 4. I've had such pleasure in watching Siobhan Davis grow as an author from True Calling to now (and will continue beyond!). Her skills are really showing in this innovative, breathtakingly suspenseful, beautifully crafted series. I am anxiously awaiting book 3 and I am invested in the outcome of this series. I am wondering if she will take advantage of the many spin-off novellas that she can do to flesh out characters and backgrounds even further. 
 Disclaimer: Yeah, I received an advance copy of this book in exchange for an unbiased review. Everything I said is really my own opinion, even though I got to read the book before its release date.

Slayers: Friends and Traitors: "I Blame it on Christopher Paolini."-Bess 
 What Bess said is true though. Maybe it's because we've grown up reading stories about majestic dragons, benevolent dragons, wise dragons, magical dragons, etc. that we harbor a slight fondness for the creatures. Or maybe it's something else. But the initial prospect of groups banding together to slay dragons--malicious or not--tugged at our hearts and saddened us a bit. 
 Anyway. 
 I'd forgotten how much I loved Bess and her razor-sharp wit. Actually, I'd forgotten how much I'd just loved Slayers in general. I read it two summers back, and now I remember being blown away by it. The exciting action sequences, the awesome concept, Tori's quips (although not as good as Bess's), Dirk's sass, the betrayal, the summer camp "feel", Tori's character development, I just loved it all. 
 Although I must admit, Tori can be a handful at times. Hence the star deduction. She and her infatuation with a certain Slayer boy can be slightly irritating, especially when she's in moments of peril and peoples' lives are at stake. But then she'll come back with a hilarious one-liner and then suddenly pull an epic move out of thin air  like killing a dragon with parachutes and mind control , leaving you dumbfounded and thinking to yourself, "Tori, why can't you be like that all the time?" 
 The rest of the crew was great. There's just this sense of camaraderie about them that's so fun to read. They all complement each other and balance one another perfectly--Jesse reining in Kody's recklessness, Rosa soothing Alyssa and Lilly's fury, and Tori taking a ton of jokes at her expense.  And I know I'm not the only one who's really interested in how Ryker and Willow will integrate themselves in. It's such a spunky group.  
 Also, Friends and Traitors dived so much deeper than Slayers did. One of my favorite scenes was the interaction between Dirk and Tori, where they squabbled over whether anything in life was just good or evil, black or white. And we see that thread of thinking reappear several times in the story as Tori questions the morality of slaying dragons and more broadly, war and battles. Maybe Dirk's influencing her, maybe it's the dragon lord part of her emerging, or maybe she is right to question it. We don't know, and that's what's great about it. 
 And Dirk. Oh Dirk. Such a conflicted, interesting character. He hasn't severed all ties with the Slayers yet, and it's obvious that he still has some lingering loyalties to his friends, but then on the other hand, he has the natural familial instinct to trust his father. And then he's insistent on protecting the Slayers, but he also wants to turn Tori to the other side. Ah, inner turmoil. Wonderful. 
 Friends and Traitors was just such a wonderful sequel to Slayers. Without a doubt, this novel did its predecessor justice. It was every bit as fast-paced and thrilling, while also being every bit as entertaining to read. 
 Favorite quote: "How can people be protectors and hunters at the same time?"

A detective straight from noir fiction and an idealist down on his luck are brought together when their separate quests for the truth collide. A behind-the-scenes political thriller, this fast-paced novel takes themes and plot ideas that could be just as much at home in a modern-day story. 
 The science-fiction element in this book is of a "lite" variety. Ship drives, weapons, comm devices and the like are all just assumed as a reality, so we aren't even sure how electricity is generated or what fuel source powers space travel. While undoubtedly depressing to lovers of hard sci-fi, mainstream readers will appreciate the fact that the story takes off without being bogged down by analytical details. This is definitely more thriller than sci-fi, which can be a pro or con depending on your taste (or even your reading mood). 
 Many reviewers also seem to take issue with a self-described Space Opera novel being confined to this solar system. Personally, I think it's a brilliant move. Humanity will never be able to agree on one way forward to the stars, and division and strife will undoubtedly make the road bumpy. The continuation of internecine strife beyond the reaches of Earth rang true to me, and the setting made me consider many aspects of how we would theoretically need to progress in our quest to become an intergalactic species.

 (copied review) Sweeping and lyrical, spellbinding and unforgettable, David Ebershoff's The 19th Wife combines epic historical fiction with a modern murder mystery to create a brilliant novel of literary suspense. It is 1875, and Ann Eliza Young has recently separated from her powerful husband, Brigham Young, prophet and leader of the Mormon Church. Expelled and an outcast, Ann Eliza embarks on a crusade to end polygamy in the United States. A rich account of a family's polygamous history is revealed, including how a young woman became a plural wife.Soon after Ann Eliza's story begins, a second exquisite narrative unfolds-a tale of murder involving a polygamist family in present-day Utah. Jordan Scott, a young man who was thrown out of his fundamentalist sect years earlier, must reenter the world that cast him aside in order to discover the truth behind his father's death.And as Ann Eliza's narrative intertwines with that of Jordan's search, readers are pulled deeper into the mysteries of love and faith.

 Writing this review is going to be hard for me, because I want to be sure to convey what a big punch this book packed without giving too much away. I'm afraid the word 'covet' is going to turn people off to reading this book, but it is so much more than the title suggests. 
 First of all, I have to say the cover of this book is absolutely stunning. I could be in the grocery store during rush hour in a hurry to get home, and I still think this cover would bring me to a screeching halt. It's breathtaking. 
 It's not often that a book makes me rethink things I think I know. The person who does the cheating is always the one in the wrong...right? I'm not going to go into what I think, because cheating is a very controversial topic and everyone has their own view. I'm just going to say that I think by writing this book from the perspectives of all three characters involved in this scenario, Tracey Garvis-Graves gave the reader a lot to ponder. 
 I thought the pacing of this book was absolutely perfect. It felt like everything was moving in 'real time.' Nothing was rushed or forced; everything seemed to occur naturally. 
 Though you get everyone's point of view, it's Claire's that dominates the story. You get a glimpse into her day-to-day life as she navigates multiple roles, including wife, mother, friend, and neighbor. Her relationships inside and outside of her home allow you to see how caring and compassionate she is. 
 Claire's friends made enough of an appearance that you come to care for them, but not so much that they overtake the story. They were so much fun to read about-it was almost like Desperate Housewives with a bit of Xanax tossed in. 
 But despite the people surrounding her, Claire is lonely. Her husband, Chris, has closed himself off emotionally from her, and she feels like there is no way to get through to him. 
 It would have been easy to be angry with Chris-except that you're privy to his point of view and realize he's not trying to keep himself closed off from his family. The amount of weight he feels from losing his job is all-consuming, wreaking havoc in his head and questioning his masculinity because he was unable to provide for his family. In an effort to try and keep that from happening again, Chris throws himself into his new job until he's so spent there is nothing left. He always means to go up and crawl into bed with his wife; he means to be there for her and tell her he loves her, but time slips away and it just doesn't happen. 
 Chris is also suffering from side-effects of his anti-depressant, and is unable to perform sexually, thus driving a bigger wedge between the two and making Chris feel even more inadequate.  
 Daniel was an 'OK' character for me. I didn't think there was anything especially fascinating about him, but I think that was a major point in the story. It doesn't take someone extraordinary to make you feel special or loved; it just takes a bit of effort. 
 I thought the author did a fantastic job with the male points of view in this book. 
 Covet was an emotional roller coaster ride for me. Reading all three points of view makes you realize that there is more to every situation than you know; nothing is cut and dried. 
 At it's core, this book was about how you can have all the good intentions in the world-you can love someone with your entire heart and soul-but if you don't back that up with actions and show them, it means nothing. 
 This was my first Tracey Gravis-Graves book, but you can bet it won't be my last! 
 If you are looking for a story that packs an emotional punch and will stay with you for a long time, I highly recommend this book.

Although this book was super long, I don't think anything too exciting happened in the first half of the book except for when Roger was hanged. This booked droned on and on about every day ordinary life on Fraser's Ridge. If you ask me, most of the book needs to be edited and shortened. Half of the book was just meaningless dribble and could have been left out of the book. 
 Because this book was so long, I'm having a hard time remembering what happened in it but I'll try to summarize it the best I can. 
 In the last book, Claire, Jamie and Ian went off in search of Roger since Jamie had given him to the Iroquois. They travel through the wilderness and discover that Roger had been given to the Mohawk so they travel even further to the Mohawk village. Roger had been living amongst them as a slave for quite a while by the time Claire, Jamie and Ian reached the village. 
 Jamie had been making whiskey which was more profitable than any of the other things they did on the ridge like farming. In order to get Roger back, they had brought their share of the whiskey along with them to trade for him. The whiskey was worth a lot and would have supported them for at least a year with its profits but it was the only thing they had that the Mohawk would accept as trade for Roger. They hid it before they reached the village. 
 Somehow, the men in the village got ahold of the whiskey and got drunk. A fight broke out in the village during the execution of a Jesuit priest and one of the Mohawk was killed by Roger. The Mohawk demanded a life for a life so they took Ian and tattooed his face, scrubbed him with sand in the river and adopted him into their tribe. Claire, Jamie and Roger left without Ian who said he would be happy with the Mohawk. 
 Roger ended up not going back to the ridge right away with Claire and Jamie because they had told him about Brianna being raped and being pregnant. He had to decide whether he wanted to stay or go back to his own time in the 20th century. He had found a place like the standing stones in Scotland where he could travel back to his time out in the wilderness. In the end, he decided to be with Brianna and accept the child as his own. 
 The beginning of this book was all about the Regulators and an impending battle. The Regulators were a group of about a thousand or more men who had grown weary of the corruption of government officials in North Carolina so they would go into certain towns, drag out the corrupted officials and beat them and sometimes kill them, and start riots in the town. Governor Tryon who gave Jamie his land called on Jamie and others to get together an army of men to fight the Regulators. 
 Claire went along to the battle to help the wounded afterwards. On the morning of the battle, Jamie sent Roger over the creek to speak with Herman Husbands, a Quaker who was basically the leader of the Regulators. Roger was to try to reason with Herman and to convince him to stop the battle. I felt like this series had a lot of potential. Ideas that were squandered by the mediocre execution. The first book in the series, Divergent, is the most fully realised of the series. It's clear that the necessary time and care was taken with that book to improve it before it went to print. It feels like after the success of Divergent, the other books in the trilogy were rushed onto the market and their quality really suffers for the haste. 
 The biggest problem is the completely one-dimensional and forgettable characters. Looking back I don't think there is a single fully-realised character in the series. The lack of development was ok in Divergent, because the first book in a series should obviously set up questions to be answered in later volumes. Satisfying answers never came. The lack of development was most obvious in Allegiant, as the perspective switches back and forth between Tris and Tobias, but their narration is indistinguishable. Sometimes my mind would wander, bored, and when I dragged my attention back and reread the page I'd have to flip back to the start of the chapter to remind me who was supposed to be talking. They both sound totally the same, and they both sound like characters in the first draft of a dystopian young adult novel: mere simulations. They seemed to be robotically reciting whatever messages the author wanted to get across. Sometimes they spoke in soundbites of fortune cookie wisdom. 
 My indifference to one of the major storylines, the romance between Tris and Tobias, was the inevitable result of my general indifference to the characters. While the first book did a good job of setting up their romance, the follow through was completely lacking. The later books somehow simultaneously overplayed the romance and undersold it: Tris and Tobias are constantly making out and having melodramatic arguments / making up, but apart from that they never really seem to spend any time with each other unless they're facing some kind of oncoming doom. They never hang out just for fun. The narrative tries to make out that it's just because they're ~so busy~ but they both seem to have time to spend with other people, and there are plenty of opportunities to spend time together that they don't bother seizing. Without that kind of evidence of their genuine attachment to each other, all their romantic melodrama is completely meaningless. 
 The underlying message of the trilogy is seriously underwhelming, in part because of the lacklustre worldbuilding. An effective dystopia should tell us truths about the world we already live in, or the world we might inhabit if we don't change our ways. Otherwise, what is the point? If the Divergent trilogy was supposed to be critiquing some aspect of our civilisation, I'm still not entirely sure what it was. It felt like even the book didn't understand its own metaphor. Halfway through the trilogy it got bored of its first allegory and set up and entirely new one. 
 It probably doesn't help that I read this trilogy immediately after rereading the Harry Potter series from start to finish, as all of the severe deficiencies of Divergent are strengths of HP: characterisation, worldbuilding, and those little details that turn an abstract and distant reality into something that grabs your heart in its mighty fist and squeezes.
I just kept reading onto the end to find something I could hold on to and say " Wow". But this book failed to amaze me, let alone give a second thought. Bad-read.

I was approved an ARC of this book by the publishers via NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. This review in its entirety was originally posted at eclectictales.com: http://www.eclectictales.com/blog/201... 
 I admit, the first few chapters of the book was a bit hard to get through; it almost felt as though the reader was thrown into the fray and it took some adjusting to the world, the magic system, what is going on. The setting was really interesting though-late twentieth century but rather post-apocalyptic after events of a Great War between the Great Houses. Post-war Paris feels familiar with all the famous landmarks and buildings but otherwise feels eerie and different with the Great Houses and the darkness and roughness of its streets. 
 As I mentioned it did take a while for me to warm up to the book. All of the characters felt rather remote to me; granted, perhaps that was what I was supposed to feel about the characters as the Fallen were pretty outerworldly and disconnected from everything else, even though they did fall. Nonetheless I was interested in them enough to keep reading, especially as the mystery of the curse and shadows haunting House Silverspires finally makes an appearance in the story. The mystery not only expanded on the history of the Great Houses, the characters involved, and the overall worldbuilding and magic systems that operated in this world, but it also added to the atmosphere of the story and the danger in which these characters were facing. 
 The conflict between the Houses was also very interesting and weaved into the mystery quite nicely. I wished there were more scenes about the politics going on between the Houses, as I was interested to read more about House Lazarus' own goals and the chippy arrogance of House Hawthorne as well as what led to the demise of the lesser Houses. I liked that the consequences of the Great War is still being felt in this story, and you get hints as to why things are the way they are and what caused the war to begin with. 
 Overall I really enjoyed reading The House of Shattered Wings. It was slow at first, but once the mystery is revealed and the conflict established, it was hard to put the book down; I ended up reading most of it in a day. The worldbuilding and magics involved are definitely a highlight, but the mystery was intriguing and the all-around ominous nature of the shadows lurking around House Silverspires really creepy. Readers of fantasy will definitely want to check this title out!

I really am not sure what I think about this book. There were parts that I absolutely loved, parts that itched under my skin, and parts that flat-out confused me. In the end, it's a book I'm glad I read even if I don't fully understand it. 
 One of the things I love best is that this is the most diary-like piece of fiction I've ever read. A lot of authors (especially in children's books) will use phrases like, "Let me go back to the beginning..." or "Maybe I should explain." Well, no you shouldn't because this is not meant to be read by anyone. Diaries are personal and free the author from needing to include exposition. Mor writes like she doesn't intend this to be read by anyone but herself, and as such she never explains anything she isn't working out for herself. This makes for an amazing amount of suspense as reveals happen so very slowly. The reader's mind is always buzzing with questions, and I found myself urgently rushing to the next entry, hoping it would explain the one before. This structure also means fantastic events are dealt with in a very commonplace way because they're common to Mor. It cements the story firmly in reality and is by far my favorite part of the book. 
 A close second is Walton's use of magic. What a fresh and fantastic take on an old theme. Walton's magic is grounded in connection and seems to only work when that makes sense in the user's mind. Mor's magic is grounded in her sense of the earth and how the earth works and in her connection to the people around her. There are no spellbooks, no classes, and no rules other than the universally imposed ones. It's also infinitely deniable and ends up looking like coincidence. This makes the entire novel entirely deniable, and indeed if you take out the magic, you have a perfectly acceptable coming of age story. If you believe Mor is an unreliable narrator (and she is clearly trying to paint a picture of her own character through her diary), then you could deny all of the magical events in the story. Each one serves to emphasize a change in Mor's life, whether it is a normal adolescent transition or a far more traumatic upheaval specific to her. Whether or not the magic is real, it still serves a purpose in showing Mor's growth and change. 
 Walton's treatment of fairies is also quite original and yet sensible. She never fully explains what they are or how they are, just gives the readers hints that we can make our own conjectures. Their variety and communication is fascinating, and I wish I understood it better. They are not Mor's focus though, and Walton never lets them steal the show away from her protagonist. 
 All that said, I still don't find Mor particularly likable. It's odd because I should clearly identify with her. She's an awkward teen without many friends obsessed with books and longing to be older than she is. Everything about that describes my adolescence, but I didn't like myself much then and I don't really like Mor now. It's something in the way she denies feeling and criticizes her classmates and even adults in her life as stupid and dramatic. I think it's appropriate to her history for her to think like this, but she comes off as too harsh for me and really never makes any effort to get to know people beneath their veneer (until Wim), despite expecting them to look beneath hers. I think I'm supposed to admire how contrary she is, and certainly this aspect saves her life, but most of the time I just wish she'd cut other characters a little slack. The references also make it sound like she's desperately trying to be an adult too, but that could be the fact that I'm used to people referencing Heinlein and Zelazny to sound smart. It's different to talk about contemporary authors who were out of the mainstream. Actually, Mor's something of a late 70s hipster. 
 There's a lot I still don't understand about Mor  (I'm still not entirely sure which Mor she is, why she chose to sign Morganna but makes everyone call her Morwenna, which name is on the death certificate of her sister)  and I did find watching her cope and change interesting, but part of me reacts to her in the same way I react to all teenagers. 
 On similar confusing notes, the ending. I think I am so used to Hollywood endings that this one seemed painfully rushed. If this were a movie, the showdown with the fairies and with her mother would be lit up in blockbuster lights and 3D CG. As is, the ending is just another entry in a diary, and an understated one at that. It sort of encourages me in my theory that Mor is using a lot of metaphor to deal with losing her sister and coping with her insane mother (what a risk to have a shadow antagonist like this and only show her for a page at the end). She defeats the fairies by emphasizing her will to live. She defeats her mother by literally rooting herself in the earth. Mor's a clever girl, and it's entirely possible she's crafting a novel out of her life, and I love that, but I wanted a lot more closure than I got. I didn't dislike it, but it left me a little dissatisfied.  
 Among Others isn't like any book I've ever read, and I'm very happy S&L tossed it my way. It's definitely a story that will stay with me and make me keep asking questions.

I'm really left wondering why this book has so many stars on Goodreads. I thought it was a pretty light, easy read but it didn't capture my interest and it took me FOREVER (literally months) to read this. I'll just sum it up quickly why it took me so long: I don't like Armentrout's writing style and I never liked Daemon. 
 Armentrout's writing style is VERY similar to A.G. Howard's (author of "Splintered"). Lots of people like their style, but for me, it's boring, hard to follow and lackluster. Same thing as in "Splintered," the characters jump from conclusion to conclusion, conversations between characters are awkward, there's a strange attempt at sexual tension. I just can't. My brain just couldn't read it and enjoy it, I was too busy thinking "This is such a weird conversation. How did you jump to that? Nobody actually talks like that" the entire time. 
 It definitely does have some unique parts to it such as the whole aliens  thing but it did definitely feel like "Twilight" as many other people have pointed out. There are so many similarities between the two and I won't bother listing them because I'm sure at least one reviewer has listed them before here on Goodreads. But the plot runs pretty similar to "Twilight," especially at the end, and although there is some unique qualities to Armentrout's characters because of them not being vampires, it didn't feel unique by the end of the book because of the plot. 
 Katy was an interesting character for me because of the same thing as is relatable to most people here on Goodreads: she's a book blogger. She loves reading. She actually posts book reviews on her blog and nerds out over new books being sent to her. She makes videos reviewing them. She's a pretty fun, relatable character. I like that she stood up for herself and kept her head on her shoulders for most of the book. Daemon was pretty insufferable for me. Although I can see where most people point out that he's just a complex character, he just reeked of jerk to me and I just couldn't get on with him regardless of some of his sweeter actions. Dee was a fun character and probably the only one that didn't get on my nerves the whole book. I flew through the first part of this book because Dee dominated much of it but when she started to peter out a bit towards the middle it because increasingly difficult to read for me. 
 Regardless of my feelings about this book, I think I will still try to continue the series and see if it becomes any better for me. A retelling of "Twilight" with a twist or not, I don't regret reading this even though it became very boring for me. 
 Likes: Katy for the most part. Dee. A new paranormal character type for YA. 
 Dislikes: I just couldn't get on with Daemon. "Twilight" retelling pretty much. The dialogue between characters felt awkward to me. I just don't care for Armentrout's writing style. 
 Overall: 
 Recommend? Yes.

 "She's a child that that thinks she can play with adults, and she needs to understand that this isn't a game."

There's all kinds of computer and hacker lingo that comes across very well and makes it clear that now only is our heroine Wick fluent in binary but Romily knows a thing or two as well. Everything Wick has to do, no matter how much she may love it or hate it, she does for her family and for Griff, the boy she loves. 
 The only thing that bothered me in this book was the introduction of Milo. He was pretty cool, but I am seriously not a fan of love triangles when I already adore the first love interest. Beatrice has reached the age of 16 and as thus takes part of the choosing ceremony where she will choose which faction she will become a permanent part of. There is the candor, who value honesty; the dauntless, who value bravery; the erudite, who value intelligence; the amity, who value peacefulness; and the abnegation, where she was raised by her parents and they value selflessness. Different factions are assigned different jobs, such as the abnegation being in charge of the government because they put other's needs before their own and the erudite being the researchers and scientists since they are so smart. Before this ceremony, she takes a test to see which faction she fits best in, but finds out she is divergent. No one gives her a definite answer of what this exactly means, but the results of the test were nonconclusive, so she does not exactly know which faction she would be the best part of. Which faction will she end up choosing? 
 I don't know how to put this in that nice little summary without any spoilers, and though it may be obvious which faction she chooses, after she chooses the faction, she is put through a series of test to learn the factions ways. One of her instructors, Four, is quite the mysterious guy, and of course she falls for him. It isn't like whiny ohmygodilovehim sort of writing, which is really nice. As she was raised in a selfless society, she is a little confused as to what her feelings are towards him, but he makes her feel uneasy at times and causes her heart to beat fast... etc. It is a settle way of expressing a teenage girl's feelings who is suddenly out on her own away from her parents upbringing. It works well because again, she was raised in a selfless society, so a sudden switch of character like that is ridiculous. 
 I'm not sure if I liked this book as much as I expected but it was still really good. I liked that this dystopia actually sets place in a real place setting. It was a little confusing, the setting, at times. I believe it to be some sort of Chicago where buildings are abandoned and run down, but then I am a little lost as to where the citizens actually live. I also wonder about different parts of the world/country of US. The five factions all live in the Chicago area, what happened to the rest? 
 I also really like the family dynamics that are in the story. Beatrice has a brother who also chooses his faction the same time she does. That causes an interesting development, and Beatrice's mother is also pretty great. You probably will be surprised by her. The father character doesn't get much development though. I would like to have a little more background on him. 
 In case you are wondering, this ends up being a trilogy because of the growing tension between factions and the possible war that may result, not a whole series of books about Beatrice's transition into a full faction member. I don't think the book summary really says anything about that, and I think it is important to mention. I would like to know how long society has been living under these factions though. Why did it take this long to get to this point? 
 Anyway, I will definitely be finishing the series, and maybe I will find time to go see the movie in theaters.

Sometimes I hate being so interested in history because it makes it abundantly clear that most urban fantasy authors did little to no research. Unfortunately, it seems like most love to take their inspiration from the past. 
 It's just the little things. Mead isn't clear if Georgie is from Greece or Roman but some rather simple details are all wrong. If Georgie was from Greece, for example, she would've kept her dowry in the event of a divorce. The whole point of a dowry was to provide for a widow or a woman who gets divorced. If she's Roman, well, she would've been married long before she was and her name would've been after her father. You see, women were so insignificant in Rome that there was no female names. It was just their fathers name with a major or minor, depending on birth order. We still have those names floating around today. For example, Julius Ceasar had a daughter. Her name was Julia. 
 In both cases, these girls would never have left their homes, a short distance or not... 
 /sigh

 I spent just about all of high school reading Stephen King, and I've read my fair share as an adult. I'm a fan. Not always of his writing, some of which I find a bit self-indulgent, but of his ability to really spin a yarn and to keep your interest through a seven hundred page door stopper. Good news: he still has that ability. I read past my bedtime every night I was reading this book. He draws characters that feel realistic, but still call on archetypes that make them feel bigger than regular people. The Upstanding Capable Man. The Gifted or Precocious Child. The Eeeeeevil. So it's interesting to follow the Gifted *and* Precocious Child from The Shining on his windy path to becoming the Upstanding Capable Man. But the lows never get that low, which make the highs a bit anti-climactic. The truth is, he doesn't want us to dislike Danny. Fine, I like Danny. I'll go as far as to say I like him a lot. But it's symptomatic of everything wrong with this book. Abra's too powerful, Rose the Hat and her cronies aren't powerful and menacing enough. The denoument is never really in doubt, and so when it's all done, it's not that exciting. There's no big sacrifice. Everybody's happy and there are hugs all around. Dare I say it, Stephen King has gone soft. In the old days, if there were deeds to be done, some Capable Man or Gifted Child would step up to do them, but they usually wouldn't come back from it all hunky dory, if they came back at all. Maybe it tore my heart out, but it made a better book.
