The original Abhorsen series meant a lot to me. I read Sabriel the summer I was eleven, when we'd come back to America after living in England and evacuating Saudi Arabia; it (and the following books) became comfort reads. I got all my friends to read them, and in adulthood, I've been pleased to discover that the original trilogy has held up well. (I will be honest and say I have yet to read Across the Wall: A Tale of the Abhorsen and Other Stories, so if you know me and are looking for a future Christmas present... well, there you have it. 
 So when Garth Nix announced he was writing a prequel I was over the moon. Although it took me a little while to get into it, Clariel did not disappoint. 
 Let me first say that I was THRILLED to have an actual asexual protagonist in a YA novel. I am twenty-three years old. I have read other books with (hinted-at) asexual characters, but this was the first time that it was a major part of the protagonist. I cried twelve pages in because Clariel is immediately established as not wanting anything to do with romance or sex. As someone who is on the asexual spectrum, it felt pretty great. I was so glad that this wasn't, "Clariel doesn't like people! But that's just because she hasn't found the ~right one~ yet." Often, asexual stories focus on feeling "broken" or "unnatural" compared with everyone else; I enjoyed how Clariel faces some of this (mostly in the form of her parents being like, 'Why don't you want to get married?') but is also secure in her own identity. Basically: GREAT. 
 I also found watching her choose what she chose to do difficult. It's not necessarily that I didn't relate; I absolutely understood all of her motivations. When someone is caged for so long, it's understandable that they long to find freedom, especially someone like Clariel who has dealt with people not giving her the freedom she wants. Towards the end of the book, she's in a bind,  and she makes the stupid mistake oftrusting Free Magic (which is like OH GOD NO, WHY , but she makes that decision herself. She's reached a point where she realizes nobody will fight for her but her. I liked how this prequel gave added backstories to characters we've seen in the original series (Chlorr of the Mask  and Mogget)--will be interesting to re-read the originals now knowing how Mogget acted in this book. 
 You don't have to be an original fan to read it, although it does help to already know some of the stuff about the Old Kingdom (what the Abhorsen does, for example, or what the Clayr do--there are things to help guide those unfamiliar, but it's one of those books where prior knowledge enriches your reading experience). Please, though, read it--it's really, really, flipping good.

 3) Scenario: You killed your classmate. Spend approximately 2 paragraphs feeling bad about it and forget that peripheral character! She's literally of no consequence and was introduced only to be killed off in this scene!

 4) SO PRETENTIOUS. It oozes off the page. Quentin says of Fogg: "He spoke...as if he wished he had an English accent but wasn't quite pretentious enough to affect one." I don't think there's a better description of Grossman's own writing style, or even of the whole plot of this book. It'd be acceptable if it were just a nod or if he did something clever with it...but he doesn't. And it added a layer of distraction, having to constantly remind myself that these kids were supposed to be American. Had I not known, I never in a thousand years would have guessed Quentin was from Brooklyn. 
 5) The only character who shows any kind of development or maturity is killed. I didn't feel anything for any of the other characters in this book, Quentin included. I don't need my characters to be likable, but I appreciate it when they make me feel anything other than annoyed. For 400 pages. 
 6) Back to it being pretentious. Good fantasy is fun and exciting - Grossman is like the kid at the party who thinks it's cool to be too cool for it. If you think fantasy is dumb why didn't you write a different book? Maybe that's not fair, maybe it's Quentin who thinks he's too cool for it, but I couldn't tell where it was coming from. 
 7) The world building was sub par. 90% of it was pilfered from Harry Potter and Narnia and 0% of it felt real. Can I picture Brakebills? Not really. Can I picture Fillory? Negative. What about this New York place? Never heard of it. The characters were mostly flat and entitled, the relationships all felt superficial, aside from Quentin nobody had their own voice, and their adventure lacked gravity because they only took it seriously for like 5 pages. 
 8) Quentin's got obvious problems with women but I can't tell if that's his character flaw or Grossman's. 
 9) This is the first book about magic that's ever made me feel like I'm not missing out on anything. 
 to be continued.

I'm still pondering this one, the day after finishing. Did I like this book? Can I appreciate it without enjoying it? I think, finally, the answer I've come up with is "yes." 
 If only for the sheer determination it takes to plan, organize, and deliver a plot that caters to highly intelligent, three-steps-ahead characters, I must reward Gillian Flynn with 4 stars. Not to mention the guts to write an ending that literally no character can be completely happy with (or reader, if the reviews have anything to say about it). 
 Like life, this one has no good answers, no full resolution. Nothing is tidy or easy, for anyone. Is it a pleasure to read a book that insists on heaping great mounds of shit onto already shitty characters? Not always, but I think Flynn took care to not make every moment miserable. The brilliance is in the way she builds up hope, only to dash it to pieces. 
 Flynn manages to manipulate her readers just as the characters manipulate each other, and it's through that process that we come to understand them. While I found the ending personally unsatisfying, I applaud Flynn for giving the characters what they probably deserved. There is not always a clear winner or loser, and sometimes, even our ability to be cruel is a sign that we ultimately care. 
 Genuinely thought-provoking, this one. I have no doubt the movie is in capable hands with David Fincher behind the lens, but knowing that the ending has been completely rewritten has me curious to see if they can pull it off. Total sidenote: I absolutely cannot picture Ben Affleck as Nick.

In many respects, I'm not sure what to say here. I quite liked this novel in some respects while reading, and I decided on keeping the book, but in other respects I would be critical of the novel. 
 This book does have some fun ideas. The idea of a probability storm that gives and takes things away from people at random is an intriguing idea for a set-up and creates a world where everyone must be on edge, no matter how high up their position in society. The Protectorate is the authoritarian regime in this society that essentially exists to produce order out of this chaotic mess. This makes sense that people would desire someone that could try and create order out of such a society. There are things that attack humans called revenants that the Protectorate kills and portrays itself killing. So the set up is generally enjoyable. 
 Where I would probably be critical is perhaps the characters, more so Moa, because I think she's a bit too much of a damsel in distress, and when she does make a strong choice it feels out of character rather than character growth. I'm thinking in particular the scene where she decided to drag Vago along with them even though Rail is against it. It's even pretty much lampshaded that this is out of character. The book says she's in a 'stubborn mood' (p. 97), but it more felt like ' we have to get Vago to go with them for the sake of the plot, so I'll warp the character in order for this to happen'. It didn't feel organic.  
 As regards the plot, I found the story a bit up and down regarding my interest levels. The first bit of set up didn't drag me in, but once we got into the adventure I started getting more interested. However, it then went a bit flat through part III and then got going again near the end. 
 In conclusion, good ideas, good in parts despite problems. I would cautiously recommend this if you see something you like in the ideas.

After reading Legion, I don't think I'll ever be able to pass up a Sanderson novella. Sure he pulls off doorstopper-thick tomes of epic fantasy without even breaking a sweat, but the novella format whittles his thoughts down to lean essentials. The Emperor's Soul in a sleek machine in terms of both concept and execution. The whole plot revolves around just one event - creating a new soul for a comatose emperor - that must be completed within 100 days. Chapter names are simply day markers, which serves both to let you know how much time has elapsed since the last scene and how much remains. It instantly establishes the setting while at the same time ratcheting up the tension as the deadline approaches. Brilliant. 
 What impressed me more than anything, though, was how deftly these characters were developed. 175 pages isn't an awful lot of room for this when the genre demands a thick plot and a well-explained system of magic. Yet the characters Sanderson sketches in this short space are more real and interesting than many I've encountered in much longer books. Short though it is, The Emperor's Soul made for a most satisfying diversion.

This will be a review of Book 2 and 3 since all the books run into one another and are not really separate. 
 So Alison's body has been found under the would-be-tennis-court, right? And an investigation has been opened into her murder. All the girls are being re-questioned about what happened the night she went missing and the days leading up to it. 
 So if Ali is dead, who is "A", is this someone else? But how could they know secrets only Ali would know and why is this person blackmailing them? 
 In this book more is revealed about Alison, and looking back they each begin to realise things about her they never wanted to admit to themselves or about their individual relationships with her. 
 The girls are still hovering between friends and not friends, each still choosing to keep away from the other's, mostly it seems out of fear that the secret that they all hold might be revealed, and that they remind one another to much about the past. But there is another part to the secret that the other girls know nothing about and it's about to come out no matter how badly Spencer is trying to keep it quiet. Neither is A letting her off the hook so easily, she doesn't want Spencer to tell either, but why? Is it because it's Toby? Is Toby actually A? 
 Toby is Jenna's older stepbrother, everyone things that Toby is extremely creepy, in fact he has never been anything but creepy. But if he is A, how does he know all the same things as Ali did? Was he spying on them all the time? But still some of those secrets he couldn't know, he wasn't in Rosewood all the time after Jenna's accident, his parents sent him away. 
 By now Aria's secret that she and Ali caught her father kissing one of his students (Meredith) in his car is about to come out what makes it worse is that her father has resumed his affair and A is giving Aria an ultimatum or maybe it's a choice. Make it go away or tell her mother, what will Aria do? 
 No matter how hard all the girls, Aria, Hanna, Emily or Spencer try to keep their lives together nothing seems to work. A's cryptic messages are making them a fall apart and they don't seem to have anywhere to turn, not even too one another. 
 Hanna 
 Hanna is trying to keep it together but no matter what she does it doesn't work. She loves Sean, and she plans to tell him. He has taken a virginity pledge but she's convinced that she can seduce him out of it. Mona, her so called best friend, doesn't think he's worth it. What guy would take a virginity pledge, he must be gay. He can dress after all and he is just so super perfect. 
 Hanna tries to seduce him at a party, practically stripping down and throwing herself at him, literally. But as far as I see it. Sean is a jerk. Telling Hanna that she has no respect for herself and even when she admits to loving him he brushes her off. 
 Hanna is so infuriated by his indifference she proceeds to get herself even drunker at Noel Khans party, thrown by his parents for all the school kids in the area - kegs and alcohol included, and when Sean strips off his cloths to go swimming with all the boys she plans to steal his cloths but ends up stealing his parents car instead and totalling it along with Mona in the car. They ditch the wreck thinking they've gotten away with it but instead as it turns out the next morning the only one to be so lucky is Mona. 
 Hanna's mother...what a trooper she is. Once again she "takes care of the problem" getting Hanna out of trouble (by seducing the cop in charge) and all Hanna has to do is do community service for Sean's father at his plastic surgery/burn clinic. (Hell my mother would have handed me over to the cops gladly) She even goes so far as to call Hanna's father to get him involved. For the life of me I can't figure out why she'd do something like that. The man hadn't spoken to, or seen his daughter in three years. Not only that but Hanna had to find out her father was getting married through media sources. As far as I see it, she shouldn't have bothered. 
 Hanna, although she feigns indifference is hopeful that this is the start of something new and special between her and her father. Everything seems to be going just fine, she even ditches a party that she's been looking forward to, to go to supper with her father (after he claims he really want to spend a weekend with her) only to find out he's invited his fiance and her daughter along. Hanna goes along with it. 
 After Ali's memorial service, A became quiet, on the night of the supper (and of course the Foxy ball) she get a message that Sean is with a new girl. Kate (her would be stepsister) offers to cover for her and even takes pill that Hanna stole from the clinic, saying it will be fun, of course this isn't true. After a disastrous...well everything at the foxy ball, Hanna returns to her father only to find out that she's been betrayed by Kate. And surprise surprise daddy dearest wants nothing to do with her. 
 This actually in a way validates not only is her father an asshole who doesn't deserve to have children but that he expects her to be perfect. 
 Aria 
 Aria's father is back to cheating and the secret Ali promised to keep is about to come to light. And will not only hurt her mother but most probably destroy her family. Aria is also sneaking around with her English teacher, who she could possibly be in love with, but A is not only threatening to tell Aria's mother about her father's infidelity but also threatening to out Aria's relationship with Ezra the hot English teacher. But of course as fate would have it Ezra misunderstands texts he finds on her phone and they are over. Of course, somewhere along the line Aria had to find a connection with Hanna's ex-boyfriend Sean. 
 To make matters worse Aria's brother Mike as also found out about their cheating father and is falling apart. 
 Although Sean and Aria seem to have things in common, can it work when she's still not over Ezra. I completely get that Ezra is only a few years older than Aria but she is only 16 after all. That should scream stay away even if the girl is falling over herself that is just wrong in more ways than one. In the first book Aria seemed more collected than her other three friends but now she is coming across as just as self-centred. Not as much about cloths and social status, although she wants to be accepted, but there are some things about herself that makes her feel as if she is better than her three other old friends and better than the other students. She classes most boys and most of the girls that go to Rosewood day as "Typical Rosewood..", yet she doesn't really know any of the people she goes to school with. She doesn't realise that she's treating them exactly as they treat her, by assumption. 
 She follows a tip "A" sends her and ends up meeting her father's mistress, and even admits to herself that in an alternate universe they could have been friends. 
 Spencer 
 She continues being completely obsessed with outdoing her sister, the things that stress her out like receiving a B minus on a paper just makes me want to slap her. I mean here someone is threatening your life and you're worried about a paper? Priorities! 
 So after he's caught with her sister's boyfriend and completely shunned for weeks, and her credit card is taken away, you'd think she'd learn her lesson right and keep her hands to herself...wrong. Since her sister is back with her high school ex Ian, Spencer is back to drooling over him. Just giving A more things to blackmail her with. 
 Since Spencer is falling apart because her family pretends that she doesn't exist and her sister's ex boy friend (not Ian) has broken things off, not to mention A's constant taunts she's becoming paranoid. She sees someone following her everywhere she goes. 
 Emily 
 As I said Emily seems to be the saddest case of all her friends. It turns out that she didn't just love Ali as her best girlfriend but she was actually in love with her. As in her first crush. So she's gay...ok, that's a twist. And it just so happens that after she realises that she actually as those same feeling for her new friend Maya who as luck would have it is bi and very much wants her to just admit that she's into girls she gets her old lover letter, that she wrote to Ali, from A... 
 What the hell?! Does A just have all these things lying around somewhere? 
 Of course A uses this to further blackmail her into keeping quiet about the messages and to get her to do what exactly? Nothing. A just likes torturing Emily about her sexuality. 
 Yet she still manages to sneak off for quiet moments with Maya, knowing that A is watching. How dumb is that? I mean why would you give someone more physical proof? 
 Enter Emily's asshole boyfriend Ben, who starts sexually harassing her because she's not interested in boys. 
 Alison 
 Ali was definitely not a friend and how her friends never realised that is something that I just cannot understand. She was manipulative and it is very clear that the only reason that she was always willing to be there as a support was so that she could have something to hold over their heads for her own enjoyment. 
 A 
 What I would very much like to know is why exactly it is that A hates them so much, if you consider the fact that they were always making fun of others, sure I get why they could have had enemies. Yet for the most part the fun making seems to have stayed within the group. And how is that A, just seems to be in the perfect place at just the right time to spy on them...that's a lot of leg work for one person. 
 Pet Peeves 
 Why is it that every item of clothing and accessory as well as designer name has to be noted? Yes, I'm a girl and I like fashion but, really it isn't like I'll die if I don't know WHAT and WHO the characters are wearing every second of the day, really I won't. 
 And how is it that all these kids are drinking so much and no one seems to notice, or care? There were points that I kept forgetting how old they were because they were drinking so much. Only to be rudely reminded by their manner of speaking that they're only 15! 
 And is it just me or do all these girls parents seem just way to wrapped up in themselves to really care about their children? 
 Aria will do anything she has to just to keep her mother from finding out about her father's affair, do anu of her parents see what effect it has on her? No. Hanna's is making herself sick with trying to be perfect and popular, it's so bad that not only has she gone back to binging and throwing up but she's having panic attacks. Does her mother notice? Is her father even around to? No. Spencer, well with Spencer I'm not sure who's more obsessed with her being perfect at everything, her parents or herself, Do her parents realise what they are doing to her? No. And Emily is to afraid of being anything her parents don't approve of that she is so miserable that it's a wonder that she's not clinically depressed or has tried to kill herself. Actually I think the only reason she hasn't attempted suicide is because her parent's disapproving attitude might bring her back to life just so she can feel the guilt. Do they think that they are being unfair to their daughter? No.  
 Everything about Rosewood is based on everyone trying to be perfect and on fitting in. But underneath it all everyone has some kind of secret. At first Spencer is convinced that her sister Mellissa has something to do with Ali's disappearance, then they all start to believe that maybe it's one of the old group of friends. Maybe Ali shared everyone's secrets with someone in the group. 
 Even though Shepard tends to repeat herself a lot about past events and, when Ali went missing, or information from the previous books, I suppose it is important to keep it fresh in the readers mind and also she give bits of extra information about events from the four characters points of view. It can be tiring but I also see why it's essential. 
 Also the fact that she provides hints that has you thinking ok ladies don't be dumb it's not who you think it is. Then it turns out that after all that it wasn't who you or the characters thought it was it what keeps you reading. It's like Desperate Housewives teen edition.

Assassin's Apprentice had me captivated for the entirety of the book, then let me down. It seemed that we were building up to several different big endings, all of which were kind of brushed off to the side to make room for an ending that is just as good, but wasn't portrayed dramatically. 
 FitzChivalry, the bastard son of Chivalry, is dropped off at the doorstep of Buckkeep, where his family resides. Taken in by Burrich, he learns how to be a stableboy and that he has an ability called the Wit--an ability to commune with animals. He can experience an animal's senses through this connection, but is taught early on by Burrich that it is a bad thing and to hide it. 
 And so Fitz goes through life just kind of bouncing along, until King Shrewd decides the boy will be educated in the ways of the assassin. He learns swordplay, he learns to maintain the health of the animals, he learns how to mix herbs to kill a man. None of this really comes into play at any point until very brief moments more than two-thirds of the way through the book. But I kept on truckin' along, because I figured something would happen eventually. 
 As he gets older the king decides he needs to learn the Skill, apparently a kind of mind control. If able to do it, he can communicate telepathically with others trained in the Skill, and can garble the minds of others with intense concentration. His training in this skill is essentially abuse at the hands of a man who hated him, and he suffered physically and mentally has a result of it because the man used his own Skill power to make Fitz think he was failing and that his life was worthless. 
 Later in his teen years he comes face to face with Patience, Chivalry's wife (and the one he cheated on with Fitz's mother, resulting in Fitz being born). She just barges into his life, makes him all flustered, and demands he be taught in the ways of his proper birth. Apparently her only contribution to the story is to give him a new dog to use the Wit on and then just kind of drift out of the storyline. 
 Meanwhile, we learn about the Red Ship Forgers who are these pirates who go in and just want to screw with everybody, so they take what they want. They kidnap half a village, then tell the other half that if the villagers pay the ransom for the prisoners, the pirates will kill the prisoners. If they do nothing, the pirates will return the prisoners back to their homes. Which sounds backwards, right? Except when they return the villagers, they're different--totally devoid of anything that makes them human. They retain all their memories, but they live in the moment. If they're suddenly not hungry anymore, they will drop their food where they stand and trample over it in their comings and goings; they won't plan for the next meal. They attack and pillage simply because they want to. The villagers must then make the horrible decision of whether to let their loved ones continue in this animalistic way, or pay for the pirates to kill them. 
 But this is only a precursor, which is weird to me. Because despite how cool that whole thing is, the real focus is on one Prince Verity needing a wife, and his brother Prince Regal prancing around and finding him a suitor. When he finds the suitor, Fitz is sent along for the ride so he can assassinate the wife-to-be's brother. Which apparently is all a clever plot by Regal to get Fitz in trouble (aka dead) and to also kill his own brother Verity for his place on the throne. Which is awesome! Except it's all handled so deftly that it kind of feels like a narration of a garden or something instead of a narration of multiple assassinations and assassination attempts. 
 Plus I was a little disappointed with how it was just wrapped up in like five pages. What happened with Chade, Fitz's mentor in being an assassin? What about the Fool, who is apparently prophetic and a little omniscient, but never really mentioned again? In the end we are under the assumption that Fitz is speaking to his son or grandson, but how did that happen? Is he still in good graces? Did he find Molly? Does he still use the Skill, or the Wit? It all felt very unfinished, especially since there was so much build up for all of these things. I want the ending to match the rest of the book.

This book certainly gives you a lot to think about. When I finished, I wasn't sure that I liked it. But yesterday I had the opportunity to hear Levithan speak, and I think he changed my mind. Sometimes I accuse other people of sloppy reading (usually when they don't like a book I love), but I think this time I was the sloppy reader. 
 Before I began this book, I'd heard two opinions about it. The first was that it was seriously amazing, one of the best books of the year. The second was that it suffered terribly from one chapter - one day - in particular, when A inhabits the body of a fat kid and is rather cruel about it - crueler, probably than he'd (this gender is made-up; A doesn't have a body and therefore doesn't have a gender) been about the drug addict, the girl who killed her brother by drunk driving, and the mean girl. This is a notable chapter, and I think it's kind of the turning point of the book, as you're reading a long and wondering whatever is going to happen in the end. 
 In his talk, my pal David said that he went into this book in explore two questions he had about the scenario he made up in his head (waking up every day in a different body). What is our identity - our inner self - when we have no body, no family, no culture, no community? What would it be like to be that person? And, Can another person really love a person like that, whose body is changing every day? He said that if you read his book, you'd learn his answer to that question. 
 Well, he's not exactly cut and dry in the novel, but I think I get it. So A is moving along in different bodies day to day, and when he meets his Manic Pixie Dream Girl, of course he wants to stay with her. But when he discovers that there is some possible (possibly evil) way to continue inhabiting a body, he  decides not to. Why? I was thinking about an identity I might have outside of family and community and body and all those little things that make us unique, like talent and interests and style, and I don't know what that would be. So what it comes down to, and I think this is maybe the point, is that being a different person every day, THAT is A's identity, and really nothing else. If he stayed in one person, who would he be? How much of the inhabited person's identity would remain? All he has are his rules for his day to day life, and he decides to keep it that way.  
 The question of loving someone like A is more of an obvious theme when you read the book. And I think Levithan's answer comes down pretty clear:  no. Whatshername isn't interested in A so much when he's in a woman's body, and when he's fat she's basically like, "call me when you're in a hot body," which is why it's the turning point for the novel. The scene when they're getting hot and heavy, he even notes that what she wants is the body.  
 This book can come off a bit didactic, but maybe we, as readers, should fight reading it that way. I think that's what got me hung up. A inhabits girls and boys, popular, unpopular, happy, depressed, athletic, gays, and straights, and transgenders, and the way he talks about them (in a really hot girl, he notes how girls shouldn't have to put so much work into their bodies and appearance, etc) can come off as after-school specially. This is what makes the chapter with the fat kid so noteworthy. Levithan stops being didactic. Is this on purpose? What's his point? Is it a failure of his personal beliefs OR is he trying to make a point in the novel? My other criticism is that the episodic nature of the book can get... well, a bit dull. I was kind of bored there for a while. 
 It took a few days for this book to catch up to me, and I think that had I not seen Levithan yesterday, it may not have. The heart of this book is the questions it explores, and I wasn't exactly taking the time for them. Now, though, I think it'd be a great book for a book club. Can we really separate our identity from our body? Can we separate other people's identities from their bodies? 
 David also said that there might be a sequel. Maybe. Don't hold him to it. But possibly.

Yeah, I'm jumping on this bandwagon. 
 This would have gotten 5 stars from me save for one last twist that happened at the very end of the book...like, the last twenty pages. There was already one previous twist during the (long) climax, and with that one I was stunned and absolutely in love with this novel. Color me impressed. 
 What works so well for me isn't necessarily the love story, but that's to be expected for my reading style nowadays. I rarely enjoy googly eyes and starcrossed lovers beyond the occasional one or two stories a year. So it is not surprising at all that this particular part of my reading experience, while not the stupidity I was expecting, was not the deciding factor in my rating. 
 Here's the story: Kady and Ezra broke up. The same day, their tiny icy planet way out in left field (with an illegal mining operation) is brutally attacked by a rival corporation. 
 Once that happens, Kady's world blows up. An amateur hacker, she and Ezra are suddenly thrust into the middle of this corporate galactic battle, where millions of lives are sacrificed for some bucks. Throw in an AI making life or death decisions it has no right to make, an arrogant commander who decides to court-marshal everyone, and a virus that turns people into psychopaths, and you've got Illuminae. 
 Honestly, as much as I hate to admit it, the gimmick-y stuff worked for me. The way the pages are laid out where fun and I felt like a little kid when I had to turn the page different ways to read the lines. I loved the pages that showed a picture using numbers or words. Especially the ones in the end......so freaking gorgeous and confusing because it's binary but still pretty. I didn't mind most of the plot being told through IMs between different characters, or of video analysis. I loved that we got to see inside the AI's artificial head space. I am pretty surprised that something so silly would work on me, but damn was it great. 
 The characters are more like caricatures, but for the first time that I can remember in my reading lifetime, I actually enjoyed this. Ezra and Kady were pretty one-dimensional. So was the captain, so was the best friend, so was the whiz kid genius hacker that takes Kady under his wing. All of them had a role to play, and all of them did it brilliantly within their confines. There is a very heavy message of girl power here which, while heavy-handed, was still ultimately appreciated. I liked that the women here were all along the spectrum of success. Biologist. Captain. Lieutenant. Hacker. It was pretty refreshing, and I will wholeheartedly accept your shove of feminism down my throat and run away with it. 
 But ughhhhhhh--what really did it for me was that twist. That incredibly rude reveal that totally shook up what I was expecting out of a YA sci-fi romance novel. Kudos to these authors for throwing that monkey wrench into the design. 
 And then damn them for going back on it.

wow. this story really makes you think. about humanity, and war and nationality and morals..and right and wrong. 
 the setting is post World War 2 Hamburg...where British soldiers are requisitioning German homes while they attempt to tear down and rebuild the city. a British Colonel sets his family and home up alongside the previous German occupants (and rightful owners of the property) instead of sending them to the camps. 
 this sets off a series of relationships and events that don't really surprise the reader, but definitely made me think about situations and experiences...wondering how i'd behave in each of the subsequent character's places. 
 i think the characters were a bit one dimensional...but i honestly liked the story enough that it didn't matter all that much. i think this would make a great film...with all the intrigue and deception and secrets going on inside the house...and all the devastation and disagreement going on outside the house. 
 the real clincher that makes this story one that i didn't want to put down, of course, was the moral ambiguity going on in both places...in the ranks of the military, in the marriages and familial relationships of the characters, on almost every page of this novel. it was an interesting way to view this time period...not coming from war or peace or good and evil..but from a moral perspective. it's a quick and solid read.

 Actual rating: 3.5 stars = Liked more than I disliked. 
 Hmmm. This was a bit unfulfilling to me, but I did enjoy it more than I expected. 
 I think you'd enjoy it if you like stories about processing the loss of a loved one. That isn't a theme I tend to gravitate toward because I lost my mom at a young age and I don't enjoy reliving that feeling, and books about grief can be VERY hit or miss for me. I did enjoy the portrayal of grief in this book though. I think that's where the book shines. 
 I also really enjoyed the friendships, all their ups and downs included. 
 What I was less than enthusiastic about was the romance. I just did not ship it. It was a trope I do not enjoy (bad boy with tragic backstory). And the mystery left a lot to be desired from me. That mystery element did give an added layer of investment and I think this story would have been pretty bland without it, but it just didn't work for me in the end. 
  There was so much build up of finding out who YOU was, and it was just dropped and we never learned who it was. I appreciate how Juniper was able to let go of it in the end, and I think that's an important lesson, but the book was constantly spoon feeding us specific clues and we came SO close. As a story, it was a big let down.  
 Debut wise, the writing was pretty solid. I think some things could have used more development, and some tropes could have been toned down, but I would read more by this author. 
 I listened to the audiobook, which is narrated by Abigail Revasch, and she did a PHENOMENAL job with the narration. Her acting and emotion was some of the BEST I've heard all year. She really gave the story a ton of personality and I want to hear more narrated by her!

 Ok, lets give this a try. I promise to be as coherent as possible but CANNOT guarantee anything. 
 The synapses for the second book as as follows: 
 When Sofia Claremont was kidnapped to a sunless island, uncharted by any map and ruled by the most powerful vampire coven on the planet, she believed she'd forever be a captive of its dark ruler, Derek Novak. 
 Now, after months of surviving an endless night, the morning sun may soon rise again for Sofia. Something has possessed Derek's heart and he offers her a gift no human slave has ever been given in the history of his cursed island: escape. 
 High school, prom and a chance to move on with her life now await her. 
 But will she be able to forget the horrors that steal her sleep away at night? ... Or the feelings that haunt her for that tormented prince of darkness? 
 That description, is so far off about what the book is actually about, its about everyone whinnying and feeling sorry for themselves. 
 I think it's wiser just to hide the reset of my ranting...sigh 
 first off... 
 Sophia didn't really suffer any horrors when compared to Ben, she was never tortured or used as a sex slave. Derrick (yes I know his name is spelled with one R but in my head I tend to draw it out because he is so annoying), was nothing if not respectful, if very bossy at times. The only one who threatened her life was Lucas but Derick did very thing in his power to protect her. So I repeat SHE DID NOT SUFFER ANY HORRORS. 
 The first book had very great potential because some of the ideas where quite unique, other idea's that we've seen before could have been interestingly re-worked and to some extent was, but Forrest or even her editors could have expanded on these ideas a lot more. 
 The flow in the edition to the series is much better, a bit slow in some places but not to bad. 
 The problem is that here we have a 500year old vampire still acting like the teenager he was when he was turned! Everything for this really Vampire-all powerful-prince is a woe-is-me pain in the butt read. And Sophia is even more annoying. In the first installment she had spunk and now she's just whinny. 
 Derick asks her to stay, but after taking all of 5 seconds (tells him she needs to think about it) to think about it she decides to go back with Ben. The guy who knew, by his own admission, that she was in love with him but thought she'd always wait for him so because he wasn't ready to commit (said the 17year old) he flaunted his flings with other girls, basically rubbing it in her face, but choose me because I love you and now I will make my past stupidity disappear like magic. 
 Forrest basically gives Sophia a choice between Bad Stupid and Stupid Bad. 
 So she picks Stupid Bad and keeps agonizing over Bad Stupid So she picks Ben but keeps agonizing about Derick, day dreaming about him and his kisses and touch (said in high pitched fluttery sarcastically laden voice) driving her self and Ben even more crazy (if that were possible). While simultaneously, questioning why oh why does the Shade have such a hold on her, NO she'll never go back there it was her worst nightmare come true. 
 REALLY! I MEAN ARE YOU SERIOUS!? 
 Ben is an unlikable character, angry, unstable and completely insecure to the point that I was unable to feel any form of sympathy for what he had endured. I suppose the fact that Forrest also skims the description and focuses more on his desire for revenge and his blindness of his treatment of Sophia also aids in my complete dislike of his character. What bothers me is also the fact that Ben's flippant attitude is what Sofia loved about him. How can you even consider being with someone who admits to willingly pushing you aside infavour of other girls when he knew you had feeling for him and he had feeling for you which he was fully aware of? 
 I'm sorry this just didn't fly with me. 
 As for Derick...so he just lapses into Mr. Evil-I-can't-control-myself-because-she-left-me guy, stomping on everyone and even retorting to torture as well? Then he suddenly just becomes Dr. Jekyll again? For me the Derick Character is week because he needs Sophia to be good, it's not that she makes him better which is what a healthy relationship does, but if she isn't around then he's Hitler incarnate, he's character is not stable enough to maintain the positive changes Sofia brings unless she's physically around. So to me he's not all that good a character. 
 I do like the changes that have been reveled about Vivienne. This is an interesting insight into her personality. And you actually come to realise that Vivienne might have tried to change things but a number of things where forced by her Father and Brother Lucas. 
 Everything about book two is about blaming someone else, so I was extremely frustrated by all the characters. And found myself skimming through paragraphs. 
 Also the Authors choice of words just didn't seem right. In one instance one of Derick's Harem, Ashley, tries to help Sofie under stand why Derick slept with other women and she the sentence ending read.... 
 "Ashley droned on..." 
 If your friend is trying to give you reasoning behind why your boyfriend slept with other women when-he-said-loved-you-but-you-left-him-anyway-and-were-then-in-a-relationship-with-another-guy, would you describe her as droning on. 
 When droning on means to talk in a boring way? 
 and ALL the characters where always scoping something out. I now hate this word. It grates in my nerves every time I read it.  
 I did like the two twists near and at the end. I anticipated that it would be something like that but it was still something nice and it will interesting to see what Forrest has planned (fingers crossed that its good). 
 So as you can see this was not a good read for me. Not at all.

I actually really enjoyed this book in spite of the negative feedback it has received on Goodreads. The first chapter piqued my interest, and the remainder of the novel kept it. I read the novel in a day, and it has stuck with me since, which serves as a testament (I think) to its compelling story. 
 While I wouldn't say that I actually "liked" Riley, I would say that she kept me entertained. I can't count the number of times I laughed out loud while reading...and not only at her, but at characters like Audrey and Evan (who are fantastic, by the way). Even though Riley would undoubtedly get on my nerves in real life, I continued reading because I wanted to see the characters' story play out. Frankly, not all main characters need to be likable for narratives to be successful, and I think to some degree we see that phenomenon play out here. 
 Plus, Max is really great. 
 Additional thoughts: 
 In many places, the inner monologue technique was either overdone or completely unnecessary. However, I think it worked well in some spots--like when the sex scenes emphasize that Max wants to make Riley feel good (as opposed to reaching his own orgasm without any regard for her pleasure), or how both of them overthink even their most basic interactions after they transition from a friendship to a romance.  
 Max refers to Riley more than once as smart, but I did not get that vibe. Am I missing something? She doesn't seem to excel academically, she frequently makes poor choices where Noah is concerned, and she has little common sense when it comes to the job market and life after college. Instead of telling me she's smart, I would prefer to be shown that she is. 
 Finally, I would have liked a clearer picture of what Max looked like. While several characters referred to him as "cute," it was frustrating that I couldn't actually picture him. 
 So based on this review, I would recommend Besse's work to some people but not to others, depending on their interests, preferences, and patience when it comes to the experience of reading. As far as my own reading is concerned, I wouldn't hesitate to pick up another book from this author: Although Since Forever Ago has its flaws, it's a satisfying read.

 This is the first novel that I am reading for Mental Health Awareness Month that was suggested by the Penguin Teen. I have never read a John Green novel before, but I have seen The Fault in Our Stars movie and I know how much I cried during that one and the emotional turmoil that occurred in the movie, multiplied it by 10 and decided that that was probably what I would feel during Looking for Alaska. 
  
 This book perfectly paints what depression is like. Although the characters didn't register that Alaska was in anyway severely unhappy, the feelings that Alaska carried around with her after her mothers death affected the way she lived her life. She has carried this guilt around since she was a child, and her behavior was a very obvious sign when you're reading about it secondhand. To her friends, she was just occasionally moody and didn't want to answer who, what, where, when and why questions. She and the Colonel had known each other since they were freshman, but he had only just learned that her mother was dead. She drank like it was going out of style. 
 To someone right there on the front line, it's not clear, that was just the Alaska they knew and loved. But being someone who has been there and watched loved ones be there, I could see what was happening as it happened. 
 Dealing with the death of a loved one, especially one that was unexpected and may have been suicide, that's not ever going to be easy. There aren't classes that you can take to make it easier. Everyone grieves differently and at a different pace. I knew that my Grandma Peterson was going to die, we went to the hospital to visit her; I was 10 years old. When I was 18 years old and graduating, it hit me that she wasn't around to see it. I don't remember what even made me think of it, but it hit me like a ton of bricks, and I had to mourn her loss all over again, this time as an adult with a better understanding of death. Death, when expected, is hard enough. This book beautifully illustrates what unexpected death feels like. 
 I don't think Alaska meant to kill herself. Should she have been driving? Hell no. But do I understand why she was driving, regardless of the fact that she was inebriated and hysterical? Yes. And although I wouldn't wish what happened to Alaska on my worst enemy, I know that she found peace. I wish she could have opened up more to Pudge or the Colonel or her boyfriend, anyone. I wish that Takumi or Pudge or the Colonel didn't let her get in the car and drive away. I'd like to hope that in that situation, I wouldn't have let me friend get behind the wheel.
I can understand why these books are so popular, but they are just not my cup of tea. I like the main characters, but the struggle they have to be together is just not something I want to read about.

Fair warning, reading this book to is akin to reading a pinterest board full of inspirational quotes in swoopy hand-lettering on nature backgrounds. Live boldy. Live your life to the fullest. Every moment counts. Every effing moment. It's not like I disagree with the sentiments, but it would be difficult to find a book that takes every cliche and delivers it with so little effort at massaging it into something original. Also problematic is the reliance on cliches about class, where the woman from the lower class is irrepressible and vivacious, so full of life! While the upper class characters are trapped in their stiff manners and unable to reach each other. I'm not saying it never happens that way, but it doesn't make a terribly interesting setup. What I give Moyes credit for is an actual understanding of a middle class that is just holding on to "middle class" by their fingernails. A good blue-collar job for the father is about to be eliminated. The mother has a full-time job at home, caring for her elderly father and keeping up with the endless cooking and cleaning that a family of six necessitates. These pressures are so common and so little explored in literary fiction. I read so much about the upper middle class because that's where most literary fiction takes place. These days, I know the story of the struggling middle class from the newspapers, but there's not much fiction where it takes center stage. And then, it got an extra star for Moyes' cojones. She's taken what should be a light, chick-lit romance and made it into the anti-romance. Turns out love can't conquer all. And she's delivered this message wrapped up in all the confectionary twaddle we've come to expect from chick-lit (n.b. I speak as someone who sometimes enjoys confectionary twaddle). Just a spoonful of sugar, right?

 Blackhearts tells the story of a young Edward "Teach" Drummond, son of one of Bristol's richest merchants. He's just returned from a year at sea and dreams of going back to chase adventures in faraway lands. Instead he finds himself engaged to a girl he doesn't love and sick of the high society he was born into. The only one standing between him and his dream is his father, who will never allow him to leave again. But on his first day home he meets the new maid Anne, who was left broke and with nowhere to go after both her parents passed away. She dreams of leaving Bristol and sailing away to find her mother's family. Together they must decide whether they should follow their heart and dreams and go, or do what's expected of them and stay. 
 I went into this novel expecting a lot more piracy. Who wouldn't, though? You see the name Blackbeard, you think pirates, right? I thought so. But this is more or a historical fiction. A retelling of Teach's pre-pirate years. The author herself has called it a pre-pirate novel before even though I didn't know that until after I started it. I know the name Blackbeard but I wasn't awfully familiar with his story to be honest. Then again, not much is known about his life before he was a famous pirate. I did like this reimagining of him a lot, though I wanted more piracy and swashbuckling. 
 I'm not the biggest historical fiction fan, so I really am surprised at how much I loved this book. Most of that is probably the writing, which had me hooked from the start, and the characters. I loved both Anne and Teach and I shipped them furiously all throughout the book. Their romance was done very, very well in my opinion. I also liked the other characters. Though maybe not Teach's father and Patience, Teach's fiance. Yeah I really didn't like Patience. I do however love the fact that this gave us an explanation as to where Blackbeard got the name for his ship, the Queen Anne's Revenge. At least, I get the Queen Anne part. I'm really hoping for a sequel that'll dive more into him as a pirate and maybe also tell us where the Revenge part came from. 
 Blackhearts is a fascinating and romantic reimagining of a famous pirate's life before he became said famous pirate. I'd recommend it to fans of historical fiction and retellings, or those who are interested in Blackbeard himself. All in all, it was a good first book to read in 2016.

ALL OF THE STARS BECAUSE IT GAVE ME ALL OF THE FEELS! 
 Victoria continues to be one of the best storytellers and world builders around. The plot was so intriguing and unique, I loved every second of reading it. August and Kate are fantastically developed characters that go on quite the journey. One of my favorite things about them is the juxtaposition of their character. 
 August, a literal monster, wants so badly to be human, while Kate, who is human, wants to badly to prove herself to her father, in ways that may make her out to be the more monstrous of the duo. These traits made them a very interesting set of characters to follow, and I cannot WAIT to see where their story goes in Our Dark Duet. 
 Victoria is one of my all time favorite authors, and I can honestly say the only bad part about her work is the inevitable book hangover that comes after finishing a novel. 
 So, so wonderful! Pick this one up now!

I'm going totally the opposite direction than everyone on my friend's list with this. I absolutely loved it. Why? 
 Here's the thing: I love scary. Halloween is my favorite time of year because of all the haunted houses and activities. I get all excited whenever there is a new horror movie coming out, and if I don't see it the night it opens you can bet I will be there before the weekend is over. Slasher movies are okay too, but by and large I love me some ghost stories. 
 They're the only thing that legitimately can creep me out, because the one thing that scares me is something I can't fight against. How do you fight a ghost? If there is a shadow standing in the corner of your room at night, making the hairs on your arms stand on end, how do you drive it away? You can't call the police. You can't fight back with a gun or a knife. If it wants to get close to you, there's not a damn thing you can do about it. 
 And because I'm a little bit of an adrenaline junkie (only a little bit, I swear), I like the little surge of adrenaline I get when I'm freaked out, that fight or flight response. (Did you know watching a scary movie burns as many calories as walking for thirty minutes?) 
 So when I saw this book cover on NetGalley, I jumped on it. Because for all of my love for ghost stories, the one place I never seem to find anything satisfactory is in books. They usually get distracted with some kind of love story, or they'll have one creepy moment and then diverge into a regular plot with no more scaries. And it's disappointing. It was with some hesitation (but way more excitement) that I requested this, and I was absolutely stoked when I was approved for it. 
 This was precisely the kind of book I was dying for. I'm in my slump of the year, when it's too far away to start planning my September and October Halloween activities. And here I trip over this beauty. 
 The Girl from the Well gives me a bit of background about the original Japanese myth that spawned The Grudge, The Ring, Shutter, etc. All of which are American remakes, but that's beside the point. 
 Already with that information I am sucked in, because I love mythology and if I can learn a little more than I already knew than I am golden. 
 So already I am happy, because I learn an old myth. Then the opening scene is Okiku (the ghost) doing her creepy Grudge thing and being all crickety neck and black eyes and dirty hair hanging in her face. 
 I loved the way it started, and I loved that this wasn't the only time we got to see her do this. She does it a few more times throughout the novel, and each time I got excited that I got to see it. 
 As for the plot: Okiku is the avenger. She goes around murdering people who have horrifically murdered children, and then sends those children to the afterlife after releasing them from the chains that keep them tied to their murderers. As she's going about her business, avenging people and just sort of meandering through purgatory, she comes across a 15-year-old boy with tattoos and a weird sort of presence. She's drawn to him for two reasons--one, because there's a pedophile nearby who wants to take the boy, and two, because the boy's tattoos do weird things. She follows him around to use him as bait to get at the pedophile and make him pay for killing children, and then sticks around with the boy (Tark) because she sees another ghost. 
 Anndddd that's when it gets weird. Because apparently a sinister ghost was trapped inside the Tark with those tattoos, a last defense to prevent it from hurting others. The whole novel is about Okiku deciding to help Tark and his cousin Callie stop this evil entity because it's harming Tark, and Tark falls under Okiku's domain because he's a child (or angsty teenager, whatever). 
 I just love it so much. There's an actual plot, there is no stupid romance to get in the way. Okiku still gets to be creepy as hell with her disjointed movements, hanging from the ceiling, and standing right next to the characters just in the corner of their vision. I could plop myself right into the story and feel like I was about to see a jerky ghost in the corner of the room. 
 And it was ultimately that atmosphere that did it for me. It was just like watching a scary movie, only I got to reread the parts that were creeping me out. There was even a night a couple of nights ago where I was reading it before bed. I got so unnerved by the descriptions and my own imagination that I started to get paranoid and expect to see a girl on my ceiling. So I had to put the book down and turn on the television (and the small light) so I could calm myself down. 
 I love it. I love it I love it.

To be honest I wasn't looking forward to Bare It all because it is yet again another human trafficker storyline and Ms Foster seems to be doing a lot of these nowadays, and after a while they don't stay very original and fresh. 
 That's not to say Bare It All is a bad book, the character's are great and the chemistry and relationship between Alice and Reese is really well done and Bare It All is the best so far out of the Love Undercover series but I just wish the storyline had been a bit better. 
 Alice is a previous character from Trace of Fever although it's been so long since I read Trace of Fever I don't remember her but it's mentioned in the book and there's a brief scene with Trace although he seems very much like a different character from what I remember originally. 
 I really liked Alice as a character while she's suffered and it has changed her, she keeps to herself she doesn't trust other easily she's still a good character. She has a backbone and a sense of humour and she still feels able to reach out to people. I liked Reece too he's a good protective hero without being all alpha and smothering Alice because he knows she's keeping secrets. He lets her get to know and trust him and only pushes her when it comes to her safety. 
 While Bare It All was Alice and Reece's book, there will be at least another two books. There's the set up for the next book which is Rowdy's. Rowdy really shined through in Bare It All his possible next steps and his good guy/bad guy blending the lines approach and how how he's so protective over women even if it's not romantically make him a good and interesting character. 
 Overall I liked Bare It All but so far I haven't found this to be an amazing series and am pinning my hopes on the next book. We shall see.

I was really excited for this book because it got great reviews and it sounded extremely interesting. But from the very beginning it was hard for me to get into the story and I found myself putting it down multiple times out of boredom. And as the book went on it got worse for me because it's actually the exact kind of book that I don't like. I have to put it in spoilers because it'll ruin the whole book if I tell you what exactly I didn't like about it. 
 Aliens. Extra Terrestrial life. People living on another world. I just can't handle it. I find it very difficult to read or watch shows with this kind of element and I'm not entirely sure why. All I know is that I get very bored very quickly, and for some reason they give me a stomach ache. I know, weird. The weirdest thing is that this was actually more of an alternate dimension kind of thing (which I love) rather than a UFO kind of thing (which I can't stand), but it didn't read like one for me. But that's really why I rated this book two stars.  
 The writing wasn't bad and the overall story wasn't bad. I really can't find much fault with it - besides how I really feel like the main character didn't do a whole lot, which greatly added to my boredom - and I feel bad that I didn't like it. But this is just a genre that I really don't like, and I couldn't have known that without being spoiled and you can't know what genre it is without being spoiled. 
 This is the kind of book where you just have to take a chance (if you didn't read my spoiler above) to read it. This is really a hit or miss, love it or hate it kind of book. And a lot of people are loving it. There are definitely worse books out there.

I think that this is one of those novels that suffered from a too detailed synopsis. I didn't feel like anything was really a surprise because so many major plot points are already given away. 
 That said, it was still a mostly enjoyable read. I really liked the cast the characters. The kindrily (like a clan of Elements - souls that can choose to retain their memories when they reincarnate and have special abilities) is large and it took awhile to get them all straight, but I think that Hooper does a good job of giving them all distinct personalities. I enjoyed reading all of their interactions. 
 I'm still a little confused with the explanation of the whole Kindrily process and all the rules. I feel like information was given a little too sporadically and I would've appreciated a more detailed explanation given at one time. I also thought that the subplot with Dedrick, the big villain of the story, was not well developed. 
 Overall, I enjoyed Grasping at Eternity. It was an interesting premise with some well developed characters. While much of the plot was predictable and the explanations a little confusing, I'm still looking forward to reading the next books in the series.

Going into the fourth book I had already gotten the vibe that I would not like it, (which is such a huge disappointment considering how much the third one had me). I did not understand why Maya Banks chose to make this one about Nathan. I felt the furthest connection from him because in all the previous book's the twins (Nathan and Joe) have been stationed in Afghanistan, not really being a strong presence in either brothers books. I felt more connected with Rio, Steele, or any of his teammates rather than Nathan. Which is why I guess I was so hard on his character. Nathan was extremely mushy and repetitive, it was really getting on my last nerve to be honest. He constantly spoke about how his love interest was his miracle etcetra, which is probably true but I did not need to here it in every chapter. What I also could not understand, is the fact that when he got back from being held captive a part of himself was holding back from actually coming home, because his "miracle" had disappeared. A part of what got him through his captivity was the fact that he wanted to get back home to his family desperately, and when he is finally home he pushes everyone away. That made negative sense to me. Another thing that I was excited for was that huge connection between Nathan and his twin. However they had hardly any interaction whatsoever, which was really upsetting. 
 The other reason as to why I was so unsure about this one, is the fact that it had a supernatural twist. I cannot comprehend why she would do that it was really random, and the whole time it felt like a predictable Hollywood/ sci-fi/ military movie. 
 So already I do not like the main character, as well as the concept. What is left to save the day? The heroine and the romance... which sucked on both ends. 
 Shea Peterson is Nathan's "miracle," and I hated her. Maya Banks creates great female character's which I have had the pleasure of reading. Like I stated before usually they are involved in a tragedy, and are often battling their inner demons while trying to remain strong. Shea was no exception to this, but for her I felt it didn't quite work. She was more weak then strong, and a constant contradiction to herself. What I am assuming Maya Banks was aiming for Shea, is that she spent majority of her adult life being strong and on the run. So when Nathan and her brothers came into the picture, she gave up the reins and was able to be a scared girl and allow others to worry/ protect her. I did not like it, at all. Shea would always do the most annoying thing in the world, she would state how she would be fearless, then in the next paragraph she is scared shitless and crying for Nathan. Shea like Nathan, was extremely repetitive and mushy. Their love scenes were really disgusting and they had far too many moments of confessing their love for one another. All in all they were really gross, I felt like screaming the whole time, "PDA PEOPLE!!!!!!!!!!!!!!" 
 This book wasn't a total disappointment because going in I already knew I wouldn't like it that's why I put it off for so long. I liked the fact that Maya Banks did not make Joe fall in love with Shea's sister Grace, because that right there would be totally predictable and one hot mess. So good job there Ms. Banks on that one. That being said, I am super excited for the next one which is Rio's book who I have been dying to read about. It will still have that supernatural twist (because it involves Shea's sister), but I'm hoping Rio will make it worth my while.

This book was not on my radar until the librarian handed it to me for our next book club discussion. It sounded fascinating and it was. I couldn't stop reading until I had finished the book! It is a captivatingly written story of a young woman surviving through a year when the plague decimated nearly all of her neighbors, friends and family. I felt transported back to 1665 and the entire world was painted in vivid detail for me by the author. This is a very engrossing story told in amazing detail some of the imagery is still with me. I highly recommend the book but be warned - it is one horrific tragedy after another, and the author spares none of the gory details. 
 It is historical fiction inspired by a true story - the author read of a small village in England where the people decided to quarantine themselves to avoid spreading the disease to neighboring towns and villages. She built the character and other details around this framework. 
 The ending seemed contrived (the author's other books center around the locale where we ended up and I think that is why she writes such an unlikely journey and character transition into it.) Because I was so engrossed in the rest of the book I'm willing to forgive the fantasy ending and appreciate the rest of it.

3.5 stars - rounded up. 
 Great concept, well executed. 
 Like many others, I preferred the first half. The survivalist tension was great and Amy really established herself as a strong, resilient heroine. I really loved this version of the post-apocalyptic world, and feel the sudden urge to invest in solar panels and electric fencing, haha. 
 The relationship between Amy and Baby was built up beautifully which was carried on well to the second half. I found the past and present passages here really disorientating at first, but of course this was what the author intended. I did end up liking this narrative choice though, as it broke up and reduced the tedious "Ward" time that so many other YA novels have featured prominently. However it also made the ending twists a bit too obvious for me, so I never experienced a big "oh my god" moment as intended. 
 Whilst I didn't love it, I would definitely pick up the sequel to see where this is going. I'm really intrigued to find out what happens between Amy and her mother, and even Rice, although he was disappointingly underdeveloped in this one.

I would actually give this book a 4.5. Best book of the series in my opinion. The story was good--very good--and I was unable to put the book down. I enjoyed this book more than the others because things were actually happening, and for a reason. It wasn't Thomas and his friends saying "Well, we have literally no idea what's going on, but some weird people told us to do something, so let's go do it and see what happens," and then something bad happens, and they get angry and sad, and then the cycle continues. This story was about survival, it was about doing whatever had to be done to make it through another day. Even though the characters didn't always know what was going on, there seemed to be more purpose in their actions, more direction in the story. Learning what actually happened with the sun flares, the PFC, and the Flare disease from a first person narrator who is actively going through all of the hell that those things entail was so very insightful. Mark is a great character, and seeing the story through his eyes was the best way to experience it. I just feel like this book had so much more depth. For example, Thomas never even bothered to learn most of the Gladers' names, whereas The Kill Order is all about personalities, details, and relationships. I also liked that the dangers were more real. This book wasn't about creepy monsters with chainsaws for arms or silver balls that eat your head or mutants covered in blades and light bulbs; that aspect of the series always seemed so contrived to me. This book's dangers are natural disasters, a disease that makes people either die or get progressively more crazy until they die, and ultimately, the very real danger of losing your own mind, and losing youself in the process. 
 This was just such a well-written, interesting, thrilling book that kept my attention the entire time and gave me chills as I was reading the last page. The epilogue in there also sheds some light on the beginning of the next book, and the files from Theresa at the end were really something. I could justify reading this book before The Maze Runner if it weren't for that bit at the end. I read it very last, and I'm satisfied now with how the series ended, though I would still say that this was the best installment.

WINGER isn't one of those cliche, sappy, manipulative, stereotypical coming-of-age book that takes you on a 'life-lesson journey'. It doesn't force you into understanding the moral of the story and it doesn't force the protagonist to sound like a perfectly wise 'zen-master-type' of guy that says things typically a 14-year old wouldn't. Its simply beautiful in the sense that you get to be inside a "so-called-ordinary" teen guy. And believe me, he is far from perfect. No matter how wild, wierd, twisted or perverted his mind is, it was an absolute pleasure being inside his head. I've never related to a character as much as I did with Ryan Dean West. I swear, he is my male alter ego. 
 The little drawings and quick-comic along the way were a fabulous addition to the story. I didn't expect to enjoy Winger this much, in fact, if I were to be completely honest, I didn't expect to like it at all . Winger made me effortlessly smile and laugh out loud plenty of times, even when I try unsuccessfully to resist the laughter and tears while reading in public. 
 I'm not a huge fan of Rugby. Never seen a game, nor heard of any of the rules- not going to bother to look them up either. Surprisingly, Winger managed to avoid making the rugby part of the story feel like one of those fillers; it didn't feel like it existed in the story just to give the character some personality. It felt like a genuine part of the story, and I had a delightful time reading about it. This is pretty much a light-comical read most of the way - nevertheless, a powerful one too- but towards the end, it takes a darker turn. 
 In fewer words, WINGER is one of the most original, emotionally raw, honest, somewhat kinky and beautifully executed contemporary I've read in a long time. All credits to Andrew Smith.

Welcome to the Dark House - an atmospheric, suspenseful YA horror that will have older readers reminiscing about the guilty pleasures of the past. For me, this book was immediately reminiscent of my pre-teen favorites penned by R.L. Stine and Christopher Pike. Like those books of yore, this one immediately grabbed my attention and wouldn't let go until I had finished it- all in the dark, all in the course of several very late-night hours in bed. It was scary. It was fun. It was frustrating. (Why, oh why, must authors torture me with cliffhanger endings and promises of sequels? I NEED RESOLUTION, DAMNIT, and I really can't be bothered by waiting several years for answers. Okay, I probably can...but... I don't WANT TO! And, my apologies. Apparently, reading an abundance of YA lately has put me in the adolescent frame of mind - what with all the angst and whining. I'll survive, and, yes, I'll read the sequel. I'm just astounded by the number of YA series that they are churning out nowadays. Regardless of the books' individual merits or worth, I occasionally just want a standalone - one with all the answers. But alas, this is not to be had - at least with this book. And maybe that's not a bad thing). 
 This book centers around 7 teens, contest winners, who have earned the opportunity to preview a new movie put out by one of the most popular horror franchise directors, Justin Blake. Each have submitted their greatest nightmare (in a thousand words or less) - but will their "great" reward outweigh the personal risk in exposing their inner vulnerabilities? Me thinketh not. I mean, this is a horror novel, right? 
 Invited to spend a weekend in a hotel designed to resemble a locale out of Blake's movies, the horror-loving adolescents are living out their greatest (see also: scariest) fantasies. Characters from Blake's movies populate the hotel, adding to the authenticity of the experience. BUT when one of the winners is discovered to be missing AND a strange message...in blood... is found in her absence, the teens aren't sure what is real and what is smoke-and-mirror movie magic designed by the director to be part of the weekend's thrill. 
 I can't go into too much detail - as I don't want to spoil any of the fun - and trust me, this book is fun - if not somewhat predictable, as is the plight of most horror. Yes, some of the characters were somewhat crumbly at the edges, falling prey to the cookie-cutter that helped shape them. It's YA. It's horror. I make allowances for these things. Standout characters were dear, hair-plucking twinsie Natalie (because she was the most dynamic, CRAZY original character of the bunch) and badass goth Garth Vader (because... his name, really). My only real complaint (besides the *cough* lack of an ending) was the undefined shift in narrative perspectives. The book frequently shifts between the seven teenagers; however, my galley didn't allow for distinction between their voices, and as such, I spent the first several pages after every "shift" trying to determine just who I was reading. Regular readers, have no fear. I've read that this has been rectified in the book's published form. NetGalley, I forgive you the confusion that you inadvertently caused, and I, once again, thank you for the opportunity to read this...even though you have apparently suckered me into yet another series where I am forced to wait for resolution. *sigh* It's a love-hate thing, NetGalley. Okay. It's more of a love-love thing, but - remember - I'm feeling angsty after all this YA ;) And now, if you'll excuse me, I'm going to go cry in my poster-covered room while writing in my secret diary about how horrible my parents are. (God, they just don't understand).
Uuuuum...it was the most interesting textbook I've ever read. I guess.

While I was reading this, one small detail bugged me. Why did Doug Swieteck get invited to the gym to meet the Yankees with Holling and Danny? What did Doug do to deserve that? Was it just so he wouldn't try #166 on Mrs. Baker? I feel like I must've missed something. 
 Anywho, I both really liked and kind of hated this book. Excepting Holling's family, most of the characters were kind of unbelievably earnest and emotional and pure. It made the story seem fake and dippy. But what it lacked in sarcasm, it almost made up for in good writing and a decent look at the life of a 7th grader in 1967 (air raid drills, Vietnam, hippies, etc.). 
 In the end, I think I'd only recommend this to 5th-8th graders who have to read historical fiction. It's definitely one of those kids' books that adults love, but actual kids...not so much.

Map of Fates is backstabbingly fun. It's a YA Jason Bourne thriller. Bullets fly. Assassinations are happening left and right. Every corner Jack and Avery turn, the list of people who they can trust is cut dramatically.

Actually 3.5 stars. 
 Overall, I enjoyed this book. I think the dystopian setting lent itself well to Persuasion and helped to make some interesting points about life in Jane Austen's time that we often forget as modern readers. However, I ultimately had too many concerns about Elliott and Wentforth's relationship to call this a completely satisfying retelling. (If such a thing exists...) 
 Successes: 
 - The dystopian setting helped put new perspective on the class divide that Wentworth and Anne were dealing with when they first got engaged in Persuasion. 
 - The science fiction elements demonstrated middle class vs. landed gentry priorities and pursuits. Honestly, I've never sympathized or understood the gentry position better than when I saw it through Elliot's eyes in this book (she was responsible for the health and safety of all her tenants and was essentially shackled to her land). It's cool when a dystopian SF book can do that! 
 - The changes to and/or deletions of a few side characters worked well for me. 
 Disappointments: 
  
 - Wentforth never went into the barn room or even saw that Elliot had kept all their letters. I AM SO UPSET. He was standing outside that locked door at least three times over the course of the book. The buildup for that emotional payoff was HUGE. I wanted a realization of how Elliot has been feeling and how big of a dick he has been. Sorry not sorry. 
 - After Elliot HEARS Wentforth say that he loves her, she just kind of stares at him across a room, shares a look, and then decides not to pursue it?! I MEAN, WHAT?! Again, emotional buildup, people. I need that revelation to prompt action in Elliot. I personally feel that's a huge part of the Persuasion story. She may have been persuaded once, but there's no way in hell she'd be persuaded a second time, as long as she knew Wentworth loved her. Love gives her agency at the end. But Elliot... gives up without even trying?! 
  
 When all was said and done, I needed more emotional payoff and at least one chapter more to the story for Wentforth and Elliot. However, I was pretty happy with Elliot as a character and her storyline about being a landowner. Sigh. Retellings... they never have it all.

I haven't been reading much literary fiction lately so it took me a while to get back into the groove, to be patient with the plot, and open up to Adichie's deep-dive into her characters. Around the 150-page mark, though, I was all in and read the rest in a matter of days. Americanah is a big, sprawling novel that follows the divergent paths of two Nigerian teens, Ifemelu and Obinze, after Ifemelu immigrates to the US. While the thread of their young-then-lost-then-rekindled love trails throughout, Adichie uses their relationship as a touchstone rather than the story's central focus. 
 It's hard to summarize Americanah or to distill it into a few central themes. It explores race and class across several continents; offers several takes on the immigrant experience; provides political and social commentary; and something I can't quite put my finger on but can sort of describe as several iterations on the coming-of-age theme (Ifemelu and Obinze both "come of age" in in the traditional "childhood to adulthood" sense, but Adichie leads them through this process of self-discovery several times as they mature). 
 I'm not sure why I'm even trying to describe it. All I know is that it was a pleasure to read and I desperately hope Lupita Nyong'o really does make this into a movie because I can't wait to experience these characters all over again.
