 I'm happy as always to see the children mature though in dire situations, and waiting to see what wicked ways Olaf has up his sleeves. Also, I'm picking up on Snicket's clues about his "whereabouts" when he wrote the books... He sure has me ready to read his autobiography, the companion to this series!

After reading a string of so-so books, Whitney's book reminds me of why I read YA. Here's a book that introduces a strong character, Alex. She plays piano, loves Beethoven, has room mates and friends and a sister who isn't always easy to relate with. Alex also has a problem: on page one, she wakes up in the bed of a boy, unable to remember how she got there. While the 'problem' of rape has a lengthy pedigree in YA (Speak, Putting Heather Together Again, Target, anything by Ellen Hopkins) "Mockingbirds" is realistic without being relentlessly grim. 
 There are several strengths to the story: gobs of references to Harper Lee's book, geeks and jocks receive fair and friendly treatment, scholarship generally gets an enthusiastic green light. The students at Whitney's fictional Themis Academy are reasonable and mature, although not quite perfect. And while the story never strays far from the central conflict, there are several other side-lines that lighten the tone of the story and add interesting nuggets to Alex's world. 
 The weaknesses of the book are small-to-middling: the students are a little too reasonable, the adults a little too clueless, the system of justice is a little too smooth, everything works out a little too-well in the end. As a parent, I'm concerned that kids in this book so universally understand that talking to adults is futile. As a human being, I wonder if the "justice" meted out by the Mockingbirds is actually just, but teens may not see either of these as issues. While "Mockingbirds" isn't especially complex, the many characters will make it a challenging book for reluctant readers. Still, girls will respond well to Alex, her predicament, and the hopeful tone of the work. Don't think it will have much guy appeal, which is unfortunate because there are several characters who present guys as effective allies working against the 'problem' vised upon Alex.

Part One: A Hot Spell. Holly. Summer, 1984 
 I was hooked on this book from the start, always thinking about it when I had to be doing other things. I totally fell for Holly, in a reader/main character way. 
 And then part 1 ended on a total cliffhanger. And we jumped years into the future. And to a new narrator. And boy, was I mad. 
 Part Two: Myrrh is Mine, Its Bitter Perfume. Hugo. Dec 1991-Jan 1992 
 I wasn't nearly as invested in the next narrator. I was reading slower, not itching to come back. And then a good bit of part 2 ended up being in French. Thankfully, my phone came with a handy app that recognizes text and then translates it. Never got to use that before. 
 Vinny cropping up out of nowhere was exciting, a thread to hold on to. But I nearly cried when Holly showed back up, although she's so different. 
 It was nice to have a glimpse at Holly in this part, and Hugo's story wasn't so bad. The end of course was very interesting, although I felt that it stopped a bit short. And then, poof everyone and everything disappears for years, just like at the end of Part 1. 
 Part Three: The Wedding Bash. Ed. April, 2004 
 I'm sorry to say I found Ed's part rather boring and irrelevant. I'd been wanting to see how he was doing and what happened with him and Holly, but again it was such a big time jump and he and Holly had changed so much. 
 The deaths of Nasser and Aziz were sad, but aside from introducing us to Ed's job (which could have been much shorter and simpler) it all seemed drawn out and irrelevant to me. 
 The important bits from this part were really just that Ed and Holly had Aoife, Ed's conversation with Aunt Eilish, and Holly's moment about the room number. 
 And it all seemed like a lot of build-up just to have him totally disappear from the story after this. Just a small mention of his death, years prior to the mention. 
 Part Four: Crispin Hershey's Lonely Planet. Crispin. May 2015-December 2020 
 Now imagine my confusion when I realize the star of Part 4 is Crispin Hershey. Rando author guy mentioned in Hugo's part. 
 At least Holly has more of a starring role, all things considered. I was very interested to find out she'd written a book, but for the first bit I was very sad that she was such a side note and that Crispin had so written her off. Of course, they eventually become good friends and I really enjoyed seeing her at this stage of her life, comfortable with herself again and just living life with Aoife. The fact that I was very interested in Ed during and after Part 1, but had no emotional response at all to news of his death goes to show how flat Part 3 was for me. 
 I also liked having more insight into Holly's abilities and knowing that she didn't totally lose them when she was younger. 
 And then Hugo finally reappears! After all the name-dropping of people he knew and no discussion of what we must assume was his mysterious and total disappearance! But it's just ever so briefly for a violent confrontation, echoing Holly's encounter with the scary murderer in Part 1. Which so far we've had no more mention of, nor any indication of why it was so important to talk to her in the first place. I mean, she's famous now. Do they not care since her eye's being tamed by whichever one is hiding in her head? I've even forgotten who it was. Even when Hugo interrogates Crispin, it's been years since her book came out and there's no indication that they're going after her then. 
 Unless they made her sick. 
 And oh, how I really really don't want Holly to die. Especially of cancer. 
 But the time skipping in this part just goes and goes and goes. That bugged me every time. 
 Part Five: An Horologist's Labyrinth. Marinus. April 2025 
 Here, things finally start to come together. We learn a lot more about how Horology works, about Atemporals, Returnees and Sojourners, and the Horologists that are living. We learn Marinus' history, Esther's history. We learn about the war between Horology and the Anchorites. We get the details on Jacko. All the characters are finally in play together (aside from Ed and Crispin, rest their souls. And Aoife, off safe in Europe). We go on a rescue mission and a suicide mission. 
 And Holly finally finds herself in Jacko's labyrinth. 
 And it ends on a bloody cliffhanger again, and a time-jump again. One part left. 
 Part Six: Sheep's Head. Holly. 2043 
 We're back to dear Holly. It's only right. 
 Well..... I've reached the end. 
 So suddenly the world's a dystopia. Holly's living in Eilish's place on the coast at Sheep's Head, Ireland. Aoife and Orvar have died in a plane crash caused by a geomagnetic climate storm or some such, and Holly is raising her granddaughter Lorelei (Lol for short). She's also taken in Rafiq, a refugee from the Middle East (I've forgotten which country and I can't find it again) who got separated from his brothers when their boatman tried to pass off Ireland as Norway to save fuel. 
 China and Russia seem to have taken over the world (there's basically no mention of America), the net is spotty at best, electricity is mostly run from solar panels, all oil and fuel is scarce, and ration boxes are getting smaller and smaller, supplemented by home farms and gardens, seaweed, and the like. The three surviving radio stations (one Irish gov broadcasting survivalist tips, one Irish independent, and one Chinese) finally go out. 
 And that's really all there is to it. 
 Marinus appears (this time as a 20-something man) to take Lorelei to Iceland since she has citizenship through her father, and suasions Rafiq's way too since he has diabetes and insulin is running out everywhere else. Iceland is very well off since they're an island and all. He leaves powdered meals (fully nutritional, but unfortunately all Hawaiian pizza-flavored) for Holly and her neighbor Mo to live on for a few years. Holly's cancer is back, though there's no medical equipment to confirm and certainly no medicine to treat. She has a suicide capsule the militia gave them when they stole the neighbor's solar panels. Oh, he also gives her a tablet that somehow connects to 3 others without internet, so she can see the kids and Marinus. 
 And that's it, that's the show. 
 Apart from Marinus acting as deus ex machina, there's nothing at all psychosoteric about his part. We know Marinus and Hugo got out of the labyrinth, though no information at all about specifically how it went down or what happened to Hugo. L'Ohkna and Roho are the only named Horologists that seem to be alive. Holly's abilities have not come back at all. (We do get the briefest description of Holly leaving the labyrinth.) 
 We don't know what happens to the world, if it ever gets better, details about how exactly it descended into total chaos to start with (I mean, obvi climate change and nonrenewable resources, but, be more specific), how long Holly lives, if she kills herself or the cancer gets her, if things ever improve and she ever sees Lol and Rafiq again, or Brendan in England near a nuclear reactor meltdown, or Sharon in Australia that no one's been able to contact. ... I dunno 
  
 I have so many mixed feelings about this book. 
 Soooo many time-jumps. 
 A new narrator in every part. Dear Holly's our thread, she connects them all, and I ended up feeling attachment to all of them, but still, it's jarring. 
 Cliffhangers or unanswered questions at the end of every part, with minimal, scattered resolution at best. 
 Scattered explanations of Horology, this big, mystical concept that comes together bit by bit and only coalesces just before the big action. 
 And the last part. I'm glad we got to follow Holly through her life, but it just really turned out underwhelming for me, compared to everything else. Although I don't think the dystopian feel was farfetched by any means, it was such a departure from the rest of the book, and the events just didn't hold the same interest for me. It all seemed like a sidestory rather than the main action. 
 But I loved Holly. And I loved the concept. 
 And I spent a month reading this, between all the switches and not wanting to let it go. 
 So 4 stars from me.

 Recently I decided that there are some books that I want to re-read. Books from high school that I had to read for school and didn't appreciate, books that I might have been too young to appreciate the first time I read them, books that mean more now that I'm older, and some just because they are good books and deserve to be read again. Speak is one of those books. I definitely understood it when I first read it sometime in my high school years, probably around 07-ish. But it had a bigger impact on me this time. I have known people who have been raped; I've been in situations where I was uncomfortable with a guy but didn't know what to say or do. Rape is a topic that is talked about in hushed tones and sparks a lot of controversy. It always seems to come back to if the girl (or guy) was "asking for it" because of what they were wearing or where they were. I am of the belief that it is always, 100% wrong. No one asks for it. This book does a brilliant job of saying just that, and I love Laurie Halse Anderson for writing it out so beautifully so that people who haven't been through it can understand the pain the victim feels a little better and so that people who have experienced it can know that they are not alone in what has happened to them or what they felt.

Alley Carter departs from her normal style of writing and gives us Grace, a teenage girl who saw her mother murdered and is dealing with PTSD. Can Grace be trusted in what she sees? Is what is happening even real? It's a Hitchcokian premise, that hooked me from the beginning. Yet, the less than stellar plot and ending left me with that feeling of that was it? It wasn't a terrible read. Some scenes felt rushed and problems were too easily solved with characters who miraculously had the skills needed to fix it. I'll give the second book in the series a read, but I'll wait for the library to pick it up. 
 The players: 
 Grace: She feels broken. She's been to doctors. Taken medicine. Felt the effects of the medication turn her into a zombie. Now, she's living with her grandpa as her dad fights a war, and her brother is in school. We get inside her head, and see what it's like to survive a tragedy and question everything you see and hear. 
 Noah:"I'm Noah. I'm here to be your best friend." Ummm... let's back dial it back down to a one dude. Having someone introduce themselves like that is like tattooing boundary issues on their forehead. Luckily, Noah turns out to be fine... but it started off on shaky ground. 
 Megan: Filled the roll of computer/tech geek as the plot called for it. I wish she stood out more, but in short she was a generic character. 
 Alexei: Mysterious Hot Russian. Need I say more? 
 Rosie: Is the youngest of the Embassy Row kids and former gymnast. Like Megan she was a plot device to help get them in and out of situations. 
 Lila: Is the Regina George of the book. She's the sister of Noah, and really has no other role. 
 Jamie: Grace's older brother whom is only mentioned. My problem with this is he tells Alexei to look after Grace, but being such a doting older brother he never contacts Grace himself. It seems odd he'd go to such great lengths to keep Grace safe, yet not call or even email her just to say hello. 
 Grandpa:He's risen from a low ranking employee to the position of ambassador. He's lost his wife and his daughter, yet he survives. He comes off as cold and aloof, which keeps you reading, wanting to dissect his character. Is it grief that makes him this way, or is there a darker thought process behind his behavior. 
 Ms. Chancellor: She is Mary Poppins. She is Donna from Suits. She is there to ensure that the ambassador's life runs smoothly. Grace is a small interruption in their lives, and Chancellor does try her best to help Grace. 
 Anyone else think there is something romantic going on between Grandpa and Chancellor?

An unforgettable childhood classic, and hopefully everyone's first introduction to the joy of books with pull-out letters. The short rhymes are nothing special, it's the contents of the envelopes addressed to fairy tale characters that make the magic happen, which I'll hide in case you want to discover them for yourself: 
  
 a handwritten/illustrated apology letter from Goldilocks, a fold-out poster advertising all the best witch products for sale (from Little Boy Pie mix to boots in 5 fetching shades of black), a publishing company's letter to Princess Cinderella complete with a mini-book detailing her classic story, a postcard to the giant at the top of the beanstalk, a cease-and-desist notice to the Big Bad Wolf occupying Grandmother's cottage, and back full circle with a birthday card for Goldilocks.

Waste Not... 
 Three intertwined stories are beautifully imagined and written in this book. Each of the storylines deals with "waste" in a different way. From the literal (a "freegan" couple who lives "pure" and "off-the-grid" by squatting in NYC and eating food from dumpsters), to the more abstract (a man who studies dead language and who is dealing with all of the material remains of a marriage, a man who makes a fortune collecting on old debts), the theme is ever-present in this book without feeling overly preachy (as books with characters like Micah tend to be). 
 Additionally, there are world-binding tidbits that show up in each characters stories - like the "Half Way to Healthy" diet, in which you throw out half of your food. Another theme is the idea of knowing who a person is from their waste - what does "what we leave behind" say about us? What secrets would a loved one find when sorting out the "stuff" of your life if you suddenly died? 
 One of my favorite storylines was (only a mild spoiler)  the idea of deep-time communication. It's an interesting problem which I have never thought about before. If you are burying radioactive waste that will be dangerous for 10,000 years, how do you warn future generations about it? All of the languages that we know today have been around for less than 1000 years. Who can even imagine what life and communication and civilization and even humanity will be like in 10,000 years? Could the citizens of civilizations in 8000 B.C. have communicated with us in present day, even if they wanted to? This is a really interesting take on the "waste" theme that I found to be truly intriguing.  
 While this story does have an interesting plot (especially towards the end -- it takes a little while for the action to start), at its heart it is a character study. In Want Not, the characters are deliciously complex - I have complicated feelings about each character. I sympathized with each of the main characters, but also see and understand their flaws. Each character has a strong back-story which I feel helped me understand their widely varying points of view. 
 The prose in this book is beautiful. I highlighted many sections to be remembered in the future. I would definitely read another Jonathan Miles book. 
 My only complaint is that I wish the ending had some more intersection between the 3 storylines. I know that Alexis and Micah's stories obviously intertwined, and Matty interacted with the Drs. Cross. The stories definitely aligned thematically, but I was hoping for a more bombastic, all-encompassing ending . However, I found the rest of the book so strong that I still rate it 5 stars. 
 As Dave Eggers says, "there's no one I would not urge to read it...".

 Here is my full review: 
 I generally enjoy sports romance and this one does stand out among them since it's about the sport journalists and not the players, but the game and the fan love for it is so very strong and noticeably present in the story. It's was such a sweet, funny romance I greatly enjoyed. 
 This is a spinoff series but I haven't read the previous set of books and this didn't affect my enjoyment of the story in the slightest. 
 Irresistibly Yours is my first book by Lauren Layne and I liked her easy, comfortable writing and the smooth flow of the story as whole. There was the right balance between drama, humour, sex and tender emotions. 
 Penelope (Tiny) is not your typical romance heroine - she is a tomboy, a real sports fan, who tries to act as one of the guys because she ultimately doesn't believe she is attractive/sexy. This self-depreciation could easily come off as annoying and too contrived but that was not the case. I found it fitting her character and when it came to being with Cole she didn't act shy despite her inexperience and insecurities. 
 Cole was an interesting character as Penelope, though certainly more typical than her. A sports writer, a lady's man but also someone who starts feeling the pressure of being all alone, of being his brother's only support system. His gradual realisation of his attraction to Tiny was sweet and it did take him by surprise. 
 Taken on its own some elements in the story should not work for me - a tomboy heroine who doesn't realise how attractive she is, a womaniser hero who falls for a woman who is not his usual type at all and he is all baffled by it. Surprisingly put together these elements the way Ms Layne did, I found them true-to-life and strangely attractive. 
 I loved the sports aspect of the story as well, the sense of loving a game, caring about it and respecting the players. I liked the easy camaraderie between all the characters, the sense of community and friendship which I always appreciate in a romance novel. 
 Cole's secret side, his relationship with Bobby was also wonderfully done, without going overboard in sentimentality, just real, emotional but also messy and at time tiring and confusing. 
 Overall, this turned out to be a very enjoyable, sweet and light romance and I'm very much looking forward to reading more in this series!

It took some time to get used to the style of this narrative. The story is told in the present tense, and the voice of the narrator seems to drift constantly between Cromwell's first person (almost stream of conscience) to a third-person omniscient who confusingly calls everyone "he." Most of the time, "he" is Cromwell, but it's a distraction, or perhaps Mantel means for you to read some passages twice. The present tense is an interesting way to remind the reader that while these events are now dusty old history that everyone knows, at the time it must have been like trying to ride out an earthquake. Luckily, Cromwell is just the man for that. Shrewd and calculating, brilliant, unafraid of change, you could have guessed all that from the facts. But Mantel softens the portrait of Cromwell with such tenderness towards his family, loyalty to Wolsey, and overall sympathy for almost anyone in a pitiable position. It's hard not to like this Cromwell and be on his team. In a reversal, Sir Thomas More comes off like a self-righteous prig. Of course, as with every time I read any historical fiction, I couldn't go a few pages without thinking, but is that *really* how it would have happened? I'm always wondering how it measures up to the real deal. I'm still not sure, but this helped, and there are plenty of straight histories to read after all. I'll definitely read the sequel. I know what happened to the real Cromwell, but I want to see how it happens to Mantel's Cromwell.

well, well, well. What have we here? 
 A most anticipated book of a popular YA series? 
 Bound to be awesome to some, a huge disappointment to others. As with most hugely anticipated conclusions, I say: don't expect anything, and you won't be disappointed. 
 Don't say: "It should end this certain way in which I will be completely satisfied...all the nonsense should be explained this way, or there should be lots and lots of X character in it, because I love reading about X. Oh, X is barely in there?? That means this book will suck." 
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 
 After taking a few days to digest this, I stand by my original 4 stars, but maybe it's a 3. I like this story enough, I like the characters enough, and darn it, the ending may not be perfect, but it'll do. 
 My biggest complaint about the previous two books was the 1/2 page conclusions. In Graceling, we meet Leck and poof! he's gone and all is well. 
 In Fire, it's the same thing...one paragraph to explain all the mysterious mysteries. Although I did listen to Fire on cd and didn't read it...it just wrapped up really fast considering all the build up. 
 Of course, I do have the habit of over-liking books because I can't stand the thought of being disappointed over something I've looked forward to for so long. 
 The Bad: 
 It's pretty long...and the same sorts of things keep happening. Lots of paperwork, headaches, frustration, etc. So much so that I felt the plot wasn't moved along fast enough for it. 
 There are quite a few little side plots. While all of them added a little something to the overall story, they just added to the length as well. 
 As for figuring out why everyone was acting crazy, it's figured out pretty early on that Leck was a crazy SOB and obviously created a Kingdom to satisfy his fancy. This involved experiments on animals, weird sculptures and the kidnapping, raping and torturing of his subjects, mostly young girls. We at least finally learn WHY he was doing this and not because he was just some sick bastard.  
 The Good: 
 I liked the maps, the pictures, the ciphers and the overall design of the book. It's shiny and pretty. I usually don't give a rip, but it's this kind of thing that you miss on an e-reader. 
 I liked Bitterblue. I found myself wanting her to succeed and live happily every after. I liked her interactions with Saf and Teddy, although there were long intervals between those scenes in the middle and end. 
 I liked the scenes where BB, Po, Katsa, Bann, Raffin and Giddon. Po especially. He's just such a likable character. 
 I loved Death (rhymes with teeth) the Librarian ... He had a Grace we ALL would have loved to have. 
 Despite all the deaths that occur for the sake of finally getting out from underneath Leck's reign of terror, I think the story ends on a high note and that BB can get down to the real business of building her kingdom to greatness.

Science fiction writers often shy away from dealing with religion in their works. I don't know if it's because they aren't religious and don't feel comfortable writing from a perspective of faith, or were raised religious and are now aggressively secular/atheist as a form of revenge. If religion is mentioned at all, it's usually as a backdrop, antagonist or straw man the writer sets up only to knock down in favor of science-minded rationalism. Rigorous in-depth examinations of religion and faith are rare in sci-fi. And that's a shame. Because otherwise we might get more books like The Sparrow. 
 Author Mary Doria Russell was raised Catholic and trained as an anthropologist, and strands of both scientific inquiry and questions of faith inform the story, which weaves together two timelines: in the year 2060, Jesuit priest and linguist Emilio Sandoz has just returned from a disastrous first contact mission to the planet Rakhat, crippled and dealing with a trauma that for him is quite literally unspeakable. 
 In the past thread (which starts in 2015), we see just how the expedition played out and what went wrong. One of the things I most love about Russell's writing is how she withholds information from the reader, waiting to reveal details of plot and character at the moment they have greatest impact. The double-stranded narrative is an excellent device for laying on this kind of suspense: we are put in the position of the Jesuit tribunal investigating the ill-fated expedition, sympathetic to Emilio's obvious struggles yet apprehensive of what exactly we're going to learn. All we know at the outset is that the mission altered the native culture on Rakhat, and anyone with a passing familiarity with the history of first contacts knows this change is rarely for the better. 
 Yet Russell eschews any easy narrative about the evils of imposing beliefs on others. The expedition to Rakhat is made up of conscientious, well-meaning modern people of different beliefs and educational backgrounds. I truly believed in the good intentions of each and every one of them: 
 "The Jesuit scientists went to learn, not to proselytize. They went so that they might come to know and love God's other children. They went for the reason Jesuits have always gone to the furthest frontiers of human exploration. They went ad majorem Dei gloriam : for the greater glory of God. 
 They meant no harm." 
 Yet harm is caused, not through bigotry on the expedition's part but through a lack of data and understanding of a culture profoundly different from their own. There are no good guys or bad guys here; the expedition members mean well but still make mistakes, and the antagonists behave in ways that, even at their most shocking--and there are some shocking acts in The Sparrow--make sense within the context of their culture. 
 Another thing that really sets this book apart is the writing. As much as I love science fiction, as a genre it tends toward spare prose crafted for the clear communication of ideas. On the other hand, a lot of literary fiction reads to me like pretty sentences with little story behind them. Russell's prose achieves the task of both, creating sentences of great power and beauty that develop the ideas, arc, and characters wonderfully. I'll leave you with a selection of favorite quotes: 
 "He slept, after that. Sometime just before dawn the next morning, he had a dream. He was sitting in the dark, in a small place. He was alone and it was very quiet and he could hear himself breathing, the blood singing in his ears. Then a door he had not suspected was there began to open: and he could see a flare of light beyond it. 
 This dream first sustained and then haunted him for many years afterward. " 
 ~~~ ~~~~ ~~~ 
 "Most exciting, in some ways, was that individual Singers came to be recognized, after a time. Of these, the most compelling had a voice of breathtaking power and sweetness, operatic in dimension but so plainly used in hypnotic, graceful chant that the listener hardly noticed its gorgeousness except to think of beauty and of truth. 
 This was the voice of Hlavin Kitheri, the Reshtar of Galatna, who would one day destroy Emilio Sandoz." 
 ~~~~ ~~~~ ~~~~ 
 "There were no more walls to be scaled, no more fortresses to defend by the fifth of Stan'ja, a month that marks the start of summer on Rakhat, when the nights are very short and full of stars and racing clouds and moons. But that first night was long enough for him to lead her in a private wedding dance, seeking the rhythm of her heart. And the moonlight...was very good for finding the way together to moments worthy of a Rakhati poet's song. 
 Later that summer, as rain fell, such a moment shimmered and paused on the brink, and then began the ancient dance of numbers: two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two, and a new life took root and began to grow. And thus the generations past were joined to the unknowable future." 
 ~~~~ ~~~~~ ~~~~~ 
 " 'There's an old Jewish story that says in the beginning God was everywhere and everything, a totality. But to make creation, God had to remove Himself from some part of the universe, so something besides Himself could exist. So He breathed in, and the places where God withdrew, there creation exists.' 
 'So God just leaves?' John asked, angry where Emilio had been desolate. 'Abandons creation? You're on your own, apes. Good luck!' 
 'No. He watches. He rejoices. He weeps. He observes the moral drama of human life and gives meaning to it by caring passionately about us, and remembering.' 
 'Matthew ten, verse twenty-nine,' Vincenzo Giuliani said quietly. ' Not one sparrow can fall to the ground without your Father knowing it.' 
 'But the sparrow still falls.'

It's a testament to her ability to create an amazing leading man and craft a swoony, epic love affair that you find yourself lost in the love story even though you know it will end badly. The whole time I read the last quarter of the book, I kept whispering in my head "please let it not happen... please let it not happen..." 
 However, if there had been some eleventh-hour deus ex machina that saved Jacob, it would have entirely undercut everything that came before. It has you by the throat because you know it won't last. 
 In the end, I don't have a problem with Jacob's story line. If I have an issue, it's with the resolution after that. I guess the point of the whole story is that Trixie finally opened herself up to fully love and trust. She was willing, in the end, to throw it all away and run off to chase this dream of Memphis with him, and her journey to having that sort of faith in him was really the arc of the story. 
 So what happens when he's gone? I felt like the Trixie resolution post-Jacob was incomplete, or not nearly as fleshed out as what had come before. She raised some big issues. The loss of a love like that really does leave a hole that time can't heal. So what does Trixie do in the face of that irreparable loss? We don't get to see. She literally rides off alone into the sunset. We know he was her soul mate and that she overcame her issues to fully throw herself into him (and let him fill her own God-shaped hole), but we don't know what happens after. What does she fill her God-shaped hole with when she doesn't have him? Idk idk... maybe that's the point. If so, that part didn't really work for me. 
 In the end, I have to say I liked the book, even if certain aspects left me personally unfulfilled.

Reader thoughts: This book was aiming for fun, I think, but the plot and characters made too many mistakes for me to enjoy it. 
 There were several things that were too easy. Like, the bad guys never found them despite their carelessnesses (leaving the radio in the truck, getting separated from Jaime, etc.). Sure, a mob saw them, but that was only once. 
 The things that did cause trouble seemed avoidable. Michael and Tessa decided to roll boulders into the road in a jungle. They waited to do this until the bad guy cars were passing on the road below. Surprise! The jungle is too thick, and the boulders did not make it. Well, he could have rolled the boulders yesterday when he first decided on the ambush! 
 Rebooting guards. This was WAY too easy. Then, a random couple guards had helmets on. This would have been way more interesting if ALL the guards had copper helmets to block Taylor. Oh, and why bother to reboot the guards anyway if you're going to just zap them? Here's how the scenes went.  
 Guards: "Who are you?" 
 "We're, ah, surprise inspectors!" 
 "I wasn't told." 
 "Hence the surprise!" 
 (And other mundane dialogue that's supposed to sound witty.) 
 Then Taylor reboots the guards, they look around in confusion, and Michael pulses at them to knock them out. 
 Why waste time talking with the guards if you're going to reboot them? Why reboot them if you're going to zap them? 
  
 The jungle ambush was poorly handled. Jaime should have explained his "safety" precaution, not tackled Michael. And then he should have turned his alarms back on while he and Michael and Tessa were in the tent, not let bad guys catch them. If Michael can click buttons and remove Jaime's dart, he could have helped Tessa. But, no, I guess it's more interesting to torture her for half an hour? 
 The characters kept complaining about the food. Hello, you're in the jungle! You can live if your sandwich doesn't have mayonnaise and the like. And they wanted the sandwiches to be pizza. Oh, how sad. They sat and complained about not having milkshakes at one point, and that the soda was cold. Gar. Still, maybe this was supposed to be a theme. The children were, perhaps, supposed to learn how to live without American food? Except the author kept giving them American food, even in the jungle! 
 Tessa's "I can't walk anymore" would be more believable if she didn't have breath to argue. Maybe it's to show she's a spoiled teenager, except she's been living in the jungle for six months. Surely she knows the limits of her endurance, yes? 
 There was also quite a bit of telling rather than showing. The book would say, "The darts hit me, and I fell to the ground." Where did the darts hit him? Why did he fall? Was he in pain, drugged, shocked, suddenly out of energy? Did his legs feel like noodles? 
 Writer thoughts: So, what went well here? Why 2 stars instead of 1? Why did I even finish the book? 
 1st, I finished it because it was an audiobook. 
 2nd, at least no one got new powers (although Michael still has a combination of about half the others' powers). 
 3rd, the book was well-balanced. 
 What do I mean by that? 
 The book had a good mix of combat/action/fighting and personal/relationships issues. The book has guilt and death of friends and trust and distrust. Some of it seemed simplistic (especially Hatch's takeover of the Ampere), but it still made a nice blend to even out the fighting and ambushes and interrogation and sneaking.

 The first book you read in a year is an important decision for this bookworm. I feel it sets the mood for my entire reading year. The Readers of Broken Wheel Recommend by Swedish author Katarina Bivald is the first book I've read on 2016. I couldn't have chosen a more perfect title to start my reading year. It was all that I expected it to be. It didn't disappoint me and it left me with a smile on my face. It left me feeling like it's going to be a good reading year. 
 The Readers of Broken Wheel Recommend is a book I chose to read because of its cover, title and description. More about this on the full review on my blog 
 The Readers of Broken Wheel Recommend is the story about Broken Wheel, an almost abandoned town in Iowa and how the power of books can transform a society. 
 The Readers of Broken Wheel Recommend is also the story of Amy and Sara. Amy, an elderly resident of the town of Broken Wheel, Iowa, and Sarah, a young woman from Sweden, are pen pals that form a lovely friendship through handwritten letters and exchanging books. After two years of correspondence, Amy invites Sara to visit her so they can finally meet in person. However, when Sara arrives, she finds out her beloved friend is dead but is quickly adopted by the people and the town of Broken Wheel. Sara's arrival to Broken Wheel is not inconsequential; as it brings the little almost dead town and its people back to life. 
 The Readers of Broken Wheel Recommend is a book for bookish people. Whether you call yourself a bookworm, book lover, avid reader, etc., this book is full of references, quotes and bookish facts and humor that you will highlight and keep in your bookish heart forever. SPOILER ALERT, I must say the book has a lot of references to other books, which will be spoiled for you if you haven't read them! 
 It also poses a lot of bookish questions and interesting answers for them. Questions like: are people better than books? If you were a book character would you be a main one or a minor one? Do you judge books or people without knowing them? Have you ever smelled a book? (Tell me you pictured Rory smelling a book after reading that question!) And a lot more interesting questions of the sort that will leave your bookish mind thinking of your answers to them. 
 If you're looking for a book about how books can transform lives, this is the book for you. If you're looking for a book about friendship, family, and love, this is the book for you. If you're looking for a book with romantic love stories and adorable heartwarming stories about small-town people, this is the book for you. If you're looking for a story about a little town and how everyone in town comes together for common good, this is the book for you. If you are a bookworm, this is the book for you. 
 The following is one of my favorite quotes from this book: 
 There's always a person for every book. And a book for every person. 
 The Readers of Broken Wheel Recommend has it all and like the quote above says, it is a book for every person. I'm glad I read it.

There is no way Go Set a Watchman cannot be compared to To Kill A Mockingbird. It's the same characters in the same town by the same author. I had read that Harper Lee had written a novel before To Kill a Mockingbird, but that her editor encouraged her to go back and try again. Watchman supposedly is that first draft of Mockingbird. But it's not a version of Mockingbird; not at all. We read Mockingbird through the eyes of Scout, ages 6 -8. In Watchman we find her, now Jean Louise, age 26, visiting Maycomb, Alabama, home from New York. 
 So, of course, I was expecting, hoping for, To Kill a Mockingbird, Part II. It's not. My initial reaction to the writing is that it seems chocky, disjointed from time to time, unpolished. There are lots of flashbacks, little vignettes, remembering a childhood that sets the scene. But of course, the scene was set by To Kill a Mockingbird. In these flashbacks, Scout and Jem are a bit older than they were in Mockingbird. There is one in particular that I became annoyed with. In chapter 5, Scout and Jem and Dill are playing make believe. It seems to go on forever, pointlessly, until finally culminating in the goldfish pond baptism, which is really the whole point of the chapter and an especially good point - but the preamble seemed interminable and boring. Another time is in chapter 7; way too much time is spent worrying about how the church musical director played the Doxology. It just isn't something that I, as the reader, care about and it seemed to contribute little to the story. Aunt Alexandra hosts a coffee of young Maycomb women, but they aren't Jean Louise's friends and she has little interest in them. The whole chapter about Alexandra's coffee seems a complete waste. These little bits and pieces give credence to the notion that this was a failed novel, that her editor encouraged her to do a complete rewrite. I will say that a flashback I thoroughly enjoyed was Scout's misconceptions about pregnancy - most amusing. When Jean Louise goes to watch the Citizens' Council meeting, that's the turning point in the book, both in the plot and in grabbing our attention. 
 The novel takes place in the 1950s, in the deep south, against the background of a US Supreme Court decision regarding racial segregation. I don't think it was ever named in the book, but it had to have been Brown v The Topeka Board of Education of 1954, overturning the separate-but-equal doctrine. In To Kill a Mockingbird, we get to know Atticus Finch as a strong fair minded champion of justice. In Go Set a Watchman, Jean Louise is appalled to see him as a white supremacist. In the arguments between Jean Louse and her Uncle Jack and between her and her father, Atticus, much of what they say to one another goes over my head - I don't follow the heat of argument - but their tone is clear. Jean Louise lambasts her father and is devastated by his support of the segregationist Citizens' Council. 
 It struck me as incongruous that Jean Louise was comfortable with class discrimination - unlike the Finches, Henry came from trash. It was an everyday cultural bias - but she seemed to be completely unaware of racial bigotry, at least among her kith and kin. Uncle Jack said she was color blind - boy, was she ever. When she discovered the racial bigotry of Henry and Atticus, it was so reprehensible to her that she rejected them absolutely. It was as if she had no idea at all that such attitudes existed. How could she not. This, to me, is a flaw in the novel. She simply could not have been that naive. And I found it equally difficult to swallow, as Jean Louise is packing to leave in haste, that with a wave of his hand, or a smack, actually, Uncle Jack was able to make her see the error of her ways, to accept things the way they were, an almost instant reversal of her previous furious condemnation. The End.  
 Unlike To Kill A Mockingbird, Go Set a Watchman is not a great novel. Really, it's only partially good. It can't escape being compared with To Kill a Mockingbird. I think that's the way it should be. It was written before To Kill a Mockingbird, a discarded first attempt, and it needs to be evaluated in that light. So, it's not the literary sensation that was To Kill a Mockingbird, but, if not standing on its own, it is perhaps edifying to our understanding of that novel. 
 We have to keep in mind that Atticus Finch in Go Set a Watchman is not an older version of himself in to Kill A Mockingbird. It's not as if the true Atticus Finch is finally revealed. The great literary hero of To Kill a Mockingbird is the true Atticus. In Go Set a Watchman he is merely a discarded fictional prototype. Everyone should read To Kill a Mockingbird. One should read Go Set a Watchman only after having read To Kill a Mockingbird. One need not read Go Set a Watchman at all. 
 This book was written as a contemporary novel. Now, at the time of its publication, it is an historical novel. If it had been published back when it was written, it probably would have gone unnoticed, an unknown writer's first novel, at least until after To Kill a Mockingbird garnered its acclaim. I wonder what impact it might have had, back when the civil rights movement was beginning to change our culture. And even now, in light of recent events and the controversy about the flying of the Confederate battle flag, it seems a timely comment.

I've been trying graphic novels on for size more and more this year and I still can't decide if they're for me. It isn't the stories that are making it difficult for me - they're some of the most creative and enjoyable stories I've read this year - it's the comics. Maybe I just need more practice so it feels more fluid and natural to me. Or maybe you really can't teach an old dog new tricks and I'm just too old now to start picking up comic-style reading. Who knows? All I can tell you is I'm looking for dialogue and action bubbles, my eyes are darting all over the page, I'm trying to follow the panes, fuck, it seems like an awful lot of work to read a story and it's goddamn distracting. It probably doesn't help that the story jumps back in time every so often with no warning. I just want to read a story, man. That is the only reason that this is a 4-star review instead of a 5-star review. 
 Reading preferences aside, this was hilarious and highly enjoyable. It's one of the strangest plots in the history of, like, ever. So strange that writing it out just makes this sound like a ridiculously laughable joke that no person in their right mind would want to read but, I assure you, it's surprisingly well executed. Here goes: it's about this woman, Suzie, and this guy, Jon. Through the power of orgasm, they can stop time. You know, like Hiro from Heroes ... but with more genitalia involved. Suzie is a librarian and her library is about to be foreclosed on (which I'm not even sure is a thing... is that a thing? Can public libraries go to the bank?). She and Jon hatch a plan to use their orgasms to stop time and rob a bank. But they're apparently not the only ones with this talent and they soon find themselves confronted by sex police. The characters could probably use a little more attention than they got, not much development beyond backstory here, but I don't think the story suffers much for it and it is a developing story that I can see expanding on this in future issues. I had some head scratching moments - like why Rachelle, Suzi's openly promiscuous friend and roommate, suddenly has an attack of moral conscience and feels compelled to rat out her friend - but I'm giving it the benefit of the doubt and assuming eventually there will be a confrontation where all is revealed. 
 I was audibly laughing through most of this read. It's clever, dripping with sarcasm, and raucously funny in the most unexpected ways. The artwork is very colorful and pretty (as you can see above); if you're a fan of comic art, no doubt you'll enjoy that aspect. It doesn't take itself too seriously (no, really, someone totally gets slapped across the face with a dildo) which I think makes it that much more entertaining. It's definitely worth a read.

I didn't read this because I thought it would be good or exceed my low expectations. I read a lot of different reviews and came to the conclusion that is book was definitely not for me. 
 I read it, and wanted to review it, because a lot of the negative reviews I wanted to like also talked about wanting to punch Nora in the face. Or die. And all the other usual violent ways to express hatred for a main character. 
 So, I wanted to read and review this without all of that. Because the author should be getting the flack. Not violent threats of course, but why give Nora the short end of this deal when she is clearly at the mercy of a lack of thoughtful revision and editing? 
 There are plenty of reviewers who talk about how creepy Patch is, Nora's not-so-logical decision making, and the similarity to Twilight. So I knew all that going in. As well as the completely nonsensical Biology class. That was initially what sparked my interest in picking up this book (with a glass of wine). 
 Outside of all of the above, I think the writing is what makes this book the worst. 
 It's nowhere near amazing, but then it can get real awkward real fast. Here's a description of the stereotypical mean-girl, Marcie Miller (in first person, mind): 
 "Her strawberry blond hair was combed into low pigtails, and like always, her skin was concealed under half a bottle of foundation. I was fairly certain I'd guessed the right amount, since there wasn't a trace of her freckles in sight. I hadn't seen any of Marcie's freckles since seventh grade, the same year she discovered Mary Kay. There was three-quarters of an inch between the hem of her skirt and the start of her underwear...if she was even wearing any." 
 I'm curious, as this is all through Nora's perspective in first-person, how she would know exactly how much distance would exist between Marcie's underwear and skirt? I'm really genuinely confused. Nothing before that was much better, but when I read this, I was like "WHAT?" 
 Not only that, but the typical girl-on-girl hate...it's so old and tired. Bullying is a huge problem, but this isn't even that. It's senseless and shallow drama. I had TERRIBLE acne starting in fifth grade and I fell under the sway of Mary Kay to try to hide it. Does that mean I was terrible and shallow in middle and high school? I don't have freckles, but again, my acne was TERRIBLE. And it did not take half a bottle of foundation to cover up. 
 I don't choose to wear make-up anymore because I'd much rather sleep in than mess with making it look really nice. That's my personal choice and it's just as valid for someone to make the choice to wear make-up. Patch compliments and tells Nora not to wear make-up and that really pisses me off. I really hate the trend of guys complaining about girls wearing make-up, whether it's 'too much' or just at all. It's still controlling if a guy is telling a girl NOT to wear it. 
 (Make-up rant over). 
 Beyond all that, there are very weird descriptions and metaphors. When Nora has a run-in with a homeless person, this is her description: 
 "Her eyes were raisins, beady and dark, and they twitched their way over me in almost predatory evaluation." 
 That is just such a strange metaphor. Not only that, but this woman is continuously dehumanized by Nora, Patch, and Jules. She's only referred to as 'bag lady'. She's also killed because she's wearing Nora's coat and no one gives any fucks whatsoever except, 'Oh man, that was meant for Nora!'  This book is full of strange things like that, which wouldn't be a super huge deal if it wasn't constantly pulling me out of the story in confusion. When Nora finds what is obviously a conspiracy website about Fallen Angels and Nephilim, she 'mouse-clicks' to get the link. Why not just click? This was published in 2009, so it's not like Googling something is a super new concept. 
 Also, this could be because of the classes I'm taking this semester, but there is so much excessive descriptors that were very redundant. Or, would immediately be contradicted with the next sentence. It was like reading a rough draft before any kind of revision. 
 Anyway. This wasn't fun to read, with or without any alcohol, because I had more homework to do over Spring Break than I anticipated. Reading this all in one sitting with alcohol and no interruptions is sure to be the best way to read this book.

I always read Leadership/Self-Help/Improvement type books with a skeptical eye. I constantly feel like the writing in these books is pandering and condescending. That was... only marginally true in this book, and I felt like I could forgive it due to the fact that this is a Fable. I feel like the message from this book is a good one, though. 
 The 5 Dysfunctions of Team:  
 5. Inattention to results 
 4. Avoidance of accountability 
 3. Lack of commitment 
 2. Avoidance of accountability 
 1. Absence of trust  
 And the reason they are listed in that order is because you should envision them like a pyramid: You need the foundation solid before you can build towards the top. 
 Now, I can buy into these. However, the Fable itself was very poorly written. The story was focused on Kathryn, the CEO, but was written from third person omniscient. This means we'd encounter a single sentence occasionally (about once every two chapters or so) which explained the thoughts or feelings of another character. Since that rarely happened, I found it disjointed. I would have preferred a fully omniscient narrator, or perhaps even a first person perspective more. I just don't think the point of view helped the story at all. 
 The last chapter describes the method. I definitely think that there is something to the method. There are a few examples on how to work on improving each of the dysfunctions in there, but I would have liked to see more. I feel like I can now see the problem, but I don't really know how I can get in there to reverse these dysfunctions. 
 All in all, a decent read. I'd recommend this to anyone who sees dysfunction in their team or other teams around them. Perhaps you can take more action on improving these issues than me.

While reading this I couldn't shake the feeling that I'd read something very similar before, something similar but much, much better. Mansion, dead wife who died under suspicious circumstances and who still has an effect over the house, young girl/woman marrying an older man... at times it felt like a poor, modern time copy of Rebecca. 
 I found certain things really hard to believe. Rachel, a young woman from a council estate in London, met and married an older man, David, after two months and moving to his mansion in Cornwall to live with him (on weekends) and his son. I really struggled with how quickly that relationship progressed, it might have worked in different times but in a modern day setting? It just feels weird. It also felt weird that Rachel was constantly described as so young. She's 30! While I don't class 30 as old, the way she was described made it sound like she was 18 with no life experience. Definitely not the case with Rachel, especially when you find out her backstory - some of which is utterly ridiculous. 
 The chapters hop around a lot, there can be weeks or months between chapters and I don't think it worked. While I liked the countdowns as the chapter titles - 120 days until Christmas etc. - it jumped around too much for my liking, it disrupted some of the tension and it made whatever character development there was come out of nowhere. For example, the breakdown of the relationship between Rachel and David seemed to escalate really quickly, it was really unbelievable. One minute he's all nice, the next he wants a divorce because she's mentioned something about his son, and the next... well, what an arsehole. The escalation of Rachel's mental health issues suffered too because of the time jumps. 
 I did like the photos included in the book, that added to the creepy atmosphere of the abandoned mines and the loneliness of rural Cornwall. 
 There were quite a few twists, none of them too exciting or unexpected, and I thought the ending was completely ridiculous.

Even though I enjoyed Dragonfly in Amber slightly more than its predecessor, Outlander, they were both immensely enjoying reads that kept me hooked from beginning to end, and so I've given them both 4 stars. 
 Dragonfly in Amber is not a mere book so much as a tome, and its plot matches the size of the book. It takes place in the 18th century and the 20th, in France and Scotland, covering wars, political intrigues, medicine, time travel, witches and magic, and, of course, love. There's something here for everyone: humor, romance, adventure, friendship, a little sci-fi, and some really excellently developed characters. 
 In the midst of all of this, what I enjoyed most was the realness of it. Gabaldon doesn't hesitate to share with her readers the gory details. The love story she tells does seem somewhat idealized (as with Outlander, some of Claire and Jamie's dialogue seemed sort of cheesy to me), but there are still plenty of all-too-believable bumps in the road, such as Claire's painful miscarriage and the three-month period in which she never wants to see her husband again . Gabaldon doesn't shy away from the follies and vices of men and the gross and grubby aspects of life, esp. wounds and the treatment of wounds, in the 18th century. 
 As for the book's ending... It left me with two frustrations. First, I wonder why the time travel between the two centuries was always parallel (when several years passed in the 1740s, the same span of years passed in the 1940s, so that when Claire returned, she really had been missing in the 20th century for the entirety of her time in the past) until Geillis Duncan traveled back more than two hundred years, arriving in the 18th century ten years before Claire would. My dad, who's read all the books, says this is never explained. Grr. My other frustration had to do with Claire. Upon returning to her own time, she refused to look to history to find out what had happened to Jamie during the Battle of Culloden. Not only did she remain willfully ignorant, she remained willfully ignorant for roughly two decades, while her daughter Bree grew from fetus to young adult. If she had faced up to the facts and looked through the evidence, she would have seen much sooner that Jamie survived the battle, and then perhaps she wouldn't have had to spend so many years "making do" with Frank, her second choice husband. Oh, well. I can't wait for Jamie and Claire's reunion in Voyager! (It WILL happen. It has to happen. I'm going to throw the book at the wall if they don't get back together.)

 I recently watched the first 8 episodes of the Outlander television series and fell head-over-heels for it. Wanting to stay with the characters and reluctant to wait for the rest of the TV series, I decided to pick up the first book from the library. And realized that the show is much more to my liking. The few irksome things about the show were sooooo much woooorseeee in the book - first and foremost Claire not really being in too much of a hurry to return to Craigh Na Dun and her husband. This is simply a matter of personal preference - but I am usually not the biggest fan of historical romance. 
 I eventually came to the conclusion that, in this situation, I am more interested in experiencing this series through the show than the novels - and my final verdict is that this is not a bad series, but the novels are just not for me.

In this sequel to The Shining, Dan Torrance is all grown up and trying to not end up an alcoholic like his father. Unfortunately, that isn't the case. And through his nightmares and alcohol fueled years, he eventually finds a small town to reside in permanently. 
 While Dan is becoming a part of this new town, there is a storm of evil approaching in the form of a caravan of Winnebagos. A group of "people" are traveling the country killing children that possess the "shining". But they aren't after Dan, nope. They are after another girl, a girl more powerful than Dan Torrence. And her, Dan, and a few other characters have to team up to stop them before it is too late. 
 In the first few chapters of reading this book, I wanted to throw it on the ground or throw it away. But I kept reading. I wanted to see Danny Torrence suffer. He does some very horrendous and despicable things early in the novel that made me hate him with a passion. But I kept reading. 
 And as I read, Danny began to grow on me. He redeemed himself in my eyes. His character changed and grew, he made mistakes and atoned for his sins. And he redeemed himself long before the ending. I stopped wanting him to suffer and I cheered when he did something just and right. 
 This is a book that you will want to put down, but won't be able to. You will read it long into the night watching the main characters be human, take chances, make mistakes, learn, and grow.

This is a powerful story of a suicidal narrator who's days away from another attempt, one she expects to be more successful than her prior attempts. I read it in a couple of evenings. The opening takes a while to find its way, but Daelyn's voice was irresistible. Yes, there are some large plot holes involving computers and those old parents who can't-figure-how-to-make-em-work. Still, the tension built well and by the end, I felt a kinship to a sort of character I don't know well outside of fiction. 
 A big complaint about the cover: the girl in the tub gracing my copy is eye catching. The narrator plainly states that she isn't thin and is treated badly because she is unattractive (p. 111). She's uncomfortable taking off her shoes, let alone posing nude in a tub. The cover isn't really true to the character, and seems to feed the very beast Daelyn abhors. 
 Back to the story. Peters doesn't offer simple answers to the hard issues at work in this book. The destructiveness of bullying is made painfully clear, but the antidote is only hinted at, to name my biggest frustration. Still, I think many teens will read this for its emotional grip and realistic grit.
Thought it a complete waste of time. Shelved unfinished.

The most basic law amongst vampires good or bad is not to let humans find out about them but Corky broke that law. 
 Now, it is up to Gregori Holstein to convince the President of the United States that Vamps are trustworthy and are willing to work with them and the video has to be shut down and declared a hoax. Gregori was transformed into a vampire 18 years ago when Casimir attacked him outside Romatech where he was picking up his mother from work. She knew that her boss, Roman Draganesti, was a vampire and begged him to save Gregori by turning him into a vampire. Gregori has never had to survive by biting humans because he was transformed after Roman Draganesti invented synthetic blood so he is the perfect vampire to convince the president that he is trustworthy and that vampires mean no harm to humans. The president has his own agenda. His wife has lupus and his eldest daughter, Abigail, is a scientist working on a cure. She's heard of some rare plants only found in some remote areas of China that could help with the cure. The president wants Gregori to teleport Abigail into China to find and retrieve these three plants without anyone ever knowing they were there. 
 Of course, Gregori and Abigail are instantly attracted to each other on sight but even if the president accepts an alliance with the Vamps, he would probably never accept a vampire dating his daughter. That could blow the whole deal. 
 I had to roll my eyes at some of the ridiculous stuff that was in this book. The president allows his two daughters to go out to a vampire club with just two agents from the Secret Security guarding them. I can't even imagine that first daughters are allowed into regular nightclubs unless the entire place has been gone through with a fine tooth comb beforehand and then there would be agents scattered all over the place watching every little detail but not in this book. Okay, I know you're probably thinking that vampires are far-fetched also but let's just pretend I believe in the vampires since I have read 11 books in the series now. The reason I buy into them is because Kerrelyn Sparks is such a good writer that she has made fall in love and hate with the characters so I'm willing to overlook certain things but as an American, I would hope the president would provide better security for his own daughters. 
 Besides the few things that I thought were ridiculous the rest of the book was full of adventure and conspiracies. In this book, we learn that his slaves are humans with super abilities derived from a plant called the Demon Herb which is one of the plants that Abigail is searching for to cure her mother. We find out that it is called the Demon Herb because a demon named Darafer invented it, the same demon who was in book #10, Vampire Mine, and he is working with Master Han. It will be interesting to see where all this leads. I love this stuff! 
 The books have taken on more of a serious tone but the author still includes some humor. I am really missing the humor that made me fall in love with this series in the first place. I hope to see more of it in the following books.

This book dragged a little for me, but it's Franzen so I knew it would going into it. (Sometimes it's like his whole goal is just to make you suffer.) It's preachy, snooty, and melodramatic. It paints a pretty dismal portrait of the modern American experience (for the privileged class, at least) and it's full of "big picture" questions like: "What is freedom?" "What is the price we pay for freedom?" and, "Am I an asshole?" I can answer the last one with an emphatic "yes." Freedom is the story of an asshole couple, their asshole friend, their asshole kids, and their asshole neighbors. It will remind you of at least a dozen assholes you know IRL. 
 But...that's the point, so whatever. I hated it, but not because it's bad; I hated it because you're supposed to. That's what we do, right? We're a society of disingenuous, self-absorbed assholes, pseudo intellectuals, and haters. Sigh. I'll give him that, it's hard to talk about why you don't like this book without it looking like you're proving his point. *shakes fist, mutters "Franzen!"* 
 Jonathan Franzen excels at writing characters who are just the worst, and the characters in Freedom are a prime example. Though thoroughly unlikeable, he's an expert at character development, so I felt as though I knew each of them well. They're flawed, layered, and almost unbearably real, reminding us that while we might not like what we see in them, we certainly recognize traces of them in ourselves. 
 Aside from the jerk factor, this book's one major shortcoming is the total lack of Jessica's perspective. Leaving her out was an enormous mistake and one that I'm just kind of confused about. Franzen included Joey's weirdo story line, Jessica's would have provided a nice counterbalance. Or maybe not, maybe she would have been even more infuriating. In any case, it's total absence was strange and disappointing. But...whatever. I'm over it.

 Wow, where do I start with this much anticipated release? There really is so much in this book it's hard for me to really know where to start and with what. I'm going to do this chronically I think and start at the beginning. 
 Edge of Dawn is the 11th book in the much loved (by others not jut myself!) Midnight Breeds series. I have read every book in the series and have to say that Edge of Dawn would be the perfect book to jump into the series if you have not read any of the other previous books. However, I would highly recommend reading this series in order right from the very first book because it is a great series with lots of action and each book contains a brilliantly written romance between the hero and heroine. 
 Now that's out of the way lets get too the heart of Edge of Dawn. I have such mixed feelings about this book because there's a massive jump of twenty years from the last book Darker After Midnight and as a loyal follower and avid fan of this series I feel a little cheated, we missed so much in that time and it irks me! Lots of the main characters have had children, who are now all grown and everybody is in such a different position that I was annoyed that I'd missed so much of their storylines. 
 Yet as a reader I know that it will make the series so much more, because we have lots of new characters to explore and get to know. We get to see how they all interact with their families and how they meet their breedmates and grow with them. 
 However, I not sure I'll be able to overcome my 'I feel cheated' rant until the next book. The primary reasons for this are that Mira and Kellan were both in the previous books so you saw them, loved them, rooted for them, then they grew up out of the books and we missed it all including the something dramatic that happens and we're slowly, oh so painfully slowly, given the details of what happened in Edge of Dawn. 
 Kellan isn't the boy you once cared for in the previous books, in Edge of Dawn he is a man a man that is a total asshole, primarily to Mira. Even though he doesn't want to be, even though he regrets it. He is an asshole. It's way too angst for me or from what I've come to expect from the Midnight Breed series. 
 At some points I was able to distance my opinions that I had from the first ten books and look at this as a new series and when I was able to do that, I was able to enjoy the storyline a lot more than I had first been able to. Although it was still a little too angst ridden for me. 
 Despite all of this, it was lovely to revisit older characters that we 'met twenty years ago' and see how the events from Darker After Midnight has changed them and made them follow a different path than the one they were first on when we were originally introduced to them. 
 Overall, I did enjoy Edge of Dawn and I will be sticking with this series for at least the next two books to see how this newer part of the series turns out.

 This is my first John Grisham novel, purchased for a dollar at a local consignment shop. It's the story of a young attorney who decides he wants to represent a grandfather he only recently learned he had and who is on death row for his part in a KKK killing decades earlier. Although the grandfather was only an accomplice in the crime he was convicted of, it turns out that he had participated in several other murders, adding a layer of complexity to the story.  
 In many ways, this reads like southern Gothic fiction, which I generally enjoy so it's no surprise that I liked this as much as I did. 
 In addition to exploring racism in the south, Grisham tackles the morality of the death penalty and also seems to be delving into the topic of "free will." For those reasons alone, I thought this was a compelling read. 
 The argument made against the death penalty is a familiar one, that state condoned killing is cruel and immoral and doesn't really solve anything. Interestingly, I'm reading one of his earlier books called A Time to Kill where he makes a moral argument in favor of a father charged with killing two men who brutally raped and beat (almost to death) his ten-year old daughter. 
 Both arguments, while seemingly at odds with each other, are strong and thought provoking. 
 The two criticisms that seemed to appear in many of the less enthusiastic reviews I read are 1. This is much different than his other books and 2. It was way, way too long. This being my only Grisham book, I can't speak to the first complaint. I do feel as if the book was long, maybe longer than it had to be. Yet on the flip side, I think the pacing of the book and its length mirror the death row process. So in that sense, it almost seems appropriate. 
 GR friends that have read this seem underwhelmed. Most awarding only 3 stars. But I liked it. Really liked it. Grisham is a phenomenal writer.

I recall the Orphan Train making an appearance on an episode of "Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman", so I was a bit surprised to see that this book takes place in 1929, the last year of the train. Apparently the real orphan trains ran for over 50 years. Basically, a train arrived in town with free orphans. You could pick one, or two, or however many you wanted on the spot (very different from my friends' experience who waited 3 years to adopt their daughter after having every aspect of their lives investigated). 
 This book is not really about the orphan train, but rather a dual story about a very elderly woman and an angsty teenager who have more in common than one might think at first glance. Both are quasi-orphans. The story alternates between Vivian's first-person account of her early childhood in Ireland, immigration to America, the tragedy that turned her into an orphan, and her placement on the Orphan Train in hopes of finding her a new family. 
 In sharp contrast, we have the third-person narrative of Molly, a modern teenager tossed from various foster homes like a hot potato. Molly's story is far less interesting than Vivian's, and comprises only a small percentage of the novel. I don't think it was necessary for the story, other than to perhaps show that orphaned children still have a hard time - well, duh. 
 Vivian is an odd character. She yearns for her family, yet eventually admits that her father loved alcohol more than his family, and that even her own grandmother cast them out. She suffers greatly at some abusive homes, and yet pushes away a couple who lovingly adopt her. Same with Dutchy . We see evidence of the preference of couples for babies, contrasting Carmine's honest adoption with Maisie's illegal one . I'm not sure what the book's message was - is adoption bad? Is a horrible biological home better than a loving adoptive one? 
 The book gets some things right. Dutchy's demeanor when he recounts having his shoeshine kit taken away broke my heart. Vivian's affection for little cross-eyed Carmine is so sweet. And the author absolutely nailed Vivian's emotions when she is curled up in the arms of the man she loves. 
 I think a better way to write about the orphan train would have been to tell the stories of several orphans in the same way to show the range of the program's successes and failures. This would have made a nice illustration of how today's adoption programs have that same range. Ultimately, something needed to be done for parentless children instead of leaving them on the streets. There were no social benefit programs for them other than private charities. The orphan train was a radical idea for the time with the optimistic goal of making families. The key part missing was the children's consent.
The love triangle(s) was interesting. I honestly don't see how that can work out peacefully. It didn't quite live up to the first one but it still counts as a good book.

For a rough book dominated by men, Cornwell draws some well-rounded and interesting female characters too.

I also think that we weren't left with much of the titular mystery of the disappearance of Bernadette. It was hard to relate to rich people who care so little about money that they seem bankrupt. This book was fun though. 
 Quick recap of key characters: 
 Bernadette - Award winning architect turned recluse who hides out the days in an airstream camper she had installed by her house so she can avoid the house which lies in ruins and other people. She also has a virtual assistant in India who she hires to basically handle all the day to day duties she has including ordering food, shopping, and planning all the details of their upcoming vacation at only 75 cents an hour. She seems like a nut job who is out of touch with reality but she is a woman who loves and fiercely defends her child. 
 Elgin "Elgie" - Her Microsoft genius husband who really has no clue of the life that exists around him, including his own family. Such an enigma that he thinks it's totally appropriate to walk around at the office with only socks on his feet.  Balakrishna "Bee" - their daughter. An only child who is an extremely intelligent person. She narrates the book and is probably the most normal adult in the book except that this makes her an odd outsider child. 
 The Gnats - What Bernadette calls the other private school moms who are a bunch of self-absorbed and narcissistic women. Their antics constantly had me laughing, while another part of me wanted to poke them in their eyeballs. I actually respected Bernadette a lot for her reserved way of dealing with them instead of giving a karate chop to the neck. 
 The majority was written in various forms of correspondence format as if Bee collected it to support a case file. I was really pulling for Bernadette despite all her flaws (because are we not all flawed? Just in different ways?) to turn back up for Bee.
