Violet is an honorary member of the Brothers Sinister; she is even invited to Oliver's bachelor party, such as it is. She grew up on the property half a mile away and Sebastian Malheur has been in love with her since he was six years old. And now she is the widowed Countess of Cambury, they are still close friends; best friends. But much closer than any of their other friends realise. 
 Sebastian is the clown of the group; he charms everyone and he has a winning way with the ladies (he's known as a scandalous rake) but recently it is his science work on breeding that has caused a major outcry. How dare he speak of genetics and sex differences in mixed company? Gasps! His work is so scandalous, coming on the heels of Darwinism, that he is now a household name and protesters show up to his lectures to throw vegetables at him. 
 There's just one giant problem: it isn't his work - it's Violet's. But who would ever believe that the Countess of Cambury had brains and wrote scientific papers? She may be titled but she is just a woman. 
 *** 
 History is chock full of women whose scientific efforts or inventions were stolen from them. Hundreds of them. 
 The dedication for this book is this: 
 For Rosalind Franklin, whose name we know. For Anna Clausen, whom I discovered while writing this book. For every woman whose name has disappeared without recognition. This book is for you. 
 In the author's note, she explains that Fru Clausen did all the work for her husband's experiments on violets but is not credited in any other way than a quick note to thank her. Clearly the author did her research as well. Violets, naturally, are important to this book. 
 *** 
 Sebastian and Violet are clever, clever people and they upset some people around them. They buy adjacent houses, they have secret codes, hidden meeting places, and an entire false life that they get away with for such a long time. He is no fool. As she tells him, he's an expert in this area simply to understand enough to give the lectures, answer questions and to help her. It is Sebastian who cracks first; and for the right reason - he doesn't want to take the credit from her any more. 
 But his brother Benedict, sees him as a pointless, frippery who - even though he may be dying - will not let him have guardianship of his son. When he tries to prove his worth in his brother's profession of shipping trade, he causes more problems by being too good at it too fast. 
 Her sister Lily, compares Violet's childless existence with her own eleven children and finds Violet wanting. She never hesitates to ask her for advice and to speak to her eldest daughter, but is never supportive of her sister. She knows nothing of her life at all. 
 And... gah... what a life! Violet hurts my heart. She is so incredibly damaged. Part of the story conflict is Violet with herself. She doesn't believe she deserves anything; she tells herself she is selfish to even want it. To want credit for her work. To want Sebastian. 
 She has been trying so hard, and for so long to not make any scandals or ruckus, that standing up for her own work at this stage will cause a riot. This is a world where women can't go to university. Her family has avoided scandals (just...) in the past: the unfortunate accident (read - suicide) of her father and the accidental death of her husband when he fell down a flight of stairs. 
 She thinks of herself as a stone, steady unemotional and unyielding.  That phrase hurt on a personal level - that's exactly how I used to think when I was in a bad marriage. The litany against fear; it'll pass over me and I will remain.  
 But Violet always shows up to help out her friends, and now they show up for her. And luckily, Jane brings her fake blue dye to use on microscope slides. 
 And Sebastian is so wonderful. Endlessly patient. He asks permission before he even touches her. Always charming and always uses his words to his best advantage. 
 "How many lovers?" (she asked.) He could have given her a straight answer. Dozens. Or, more specifically: Thirty-seven. Thirty-seven, if you counted mutual versions of the conduct he'd just engaged in, and Sebastian did. But what he finally said was, "Too many. And not enough." Her face was in shadow. He couldn't tell if she was disgusted by him, or if this was just a matter of idle curiosity for her. 
 She exhaled. "How many would be enough?" 
 He smiled sadly. "One more, Violet." He looked over at her--at her arms folded around herself, at her head, turned from his, as if that would be enough to distract him from the ferocity of his want. "I've only ever wanted one more." 
 Damn... 
 He gives an entire lecture on the breeding of violets to tell her he loves her, and she is the only one in the audience who understands. *sighs* 
 She's like the mad scientist; when she's reading or working, she forgets to eat, she doesn't notice when it gets dark, she doesn't hear him come into a room. He has learned from experience the foods that are the best at sitting on a tray for however long it takes Violet to notice them but she still drinks a lot of tepid tea. He sits next to her for an hour as she is writing him an angry letter, and she doesn't notice he is there, and he doesn't peer over her shoulder at what she is writing. 
  
 Nineteen miscarriages... of course she nearly died. 
 Violet contemplated the mirror. When her husband called her selfish for refusing to go to bed with him, what had he meant? 
 I deserve my chance to have an heir more than you deserve to live. 
 Ugh... 
 Dr Jonas complained about this some books back. He said a farmer would not put his prize mare up to breed two years in a row but thought nothing of doing the same to his own wife, but people didn't like it when he compared them to brood mares. Indeed. 
 And Violet's mother... dear God, could we all have a mother as formidable if we ever needed one? 
 I've noticed that Courtney Milan changes the language of sex scenes to suit each character. Dr Jonas was clinical with the proper medical terms for body parts used; Robert and Minnie were tentative virgins, and Sebastian and Violet are wordy and scientific. It's very clever and very subtle. 
 But dammit, Sebastian... you took her on a train and missed the chance to act out your train fantasy scene. 
  
 And every female character in the series is a very different kind of woman who is expressly supported in their differences by their men. 
 5 philology of rake stars

3.5 stars rounded down 
 Louise Rick has just been appointed technical manager of the Special Search Agency, a division of Denmark's Search Department that is responsible for investigating unsolved missing-person cases. 
 When Louise and her partner Eik Nordstrom identify a Jane Doe as a mental patient that supposedly died decades earlier along with her mentally-ill twin, the new partners embark on an investigation that leads them down a path of rape, murder, and family secrets--a twisted path which intersects with Louise's own troubled past. 
 The good: 
 Blaedel's prose are a pleasure to read, and she weaves several subplots seamlessly into the main plot. The mystery is strong and develops slowly, allowing the reader to employ their own deductive reasoning. The premise is engaging and the main characters are well-drawn. I also enjoyed that this was set in Denmark. 
 The bad: 
 About two-thirds way into the book, the story becomes less credible.  I didn't buy the relationship that seems to develop out of nowhere between Louise and Eik. In fact, IMO the story would have been more interesting if the author had continued to develop a love-hate relationship between them or maybe even a love/but hands-off approach.  
 The ending feels contrived and way more complicated than it needs to be, which coincidentally makes it lack credibility. I might have bought the ending if the author had taken time to explore the psychological implications of both Bodil and her brother...another missed opportunity especially since so much time was spent developing Camille's character (who ends up only being a distraction in the story)  
 Finally, a few of the characters were just way too one dimensional to be effective. The best bad guys are the ones that aren't all bad. And if they are bad, you've got to convince the reader. 
 Final thoughts: 
 All in all, an entertaining read, albeit with some flaws. This will most likely appeal to die-hard mystery fans who enjoy strong female protagonists. Though, this book didn't wow me, I would read another book by the same author as I did feel the writing flowed well and the first two-thirds of the book had me thinking four stars all the way.

Okay. I've now read all of Gillian Flynn's books up to this point. I started with Dark Places, back before I'd heard of her and before she'd blown up as super popular. Then I read Sharp Objects after she blew up. And now I finally made it to the front of the waiting list at the library to read this. 
 Here is my rating of how much I liked her books: 
 1. Dark Places 
 2. Gone Girl 
 3. Sharp Objects 
 When I first finished and put the book down, I was already thinking I liked this the least out of her novels. The ending felt anti-climactic, like she wasn't sure where to end it and therefore just kind of piddled it away until she just picked a random stopping point. Which, after deep thought hours later, I still kind of think. It was anti-climactic. 
 But the more I think about it, the more I realize, holy shit, Gillian Flynn is a genius. 
 She knew exactly what she was doing. Yes, the ending is anti-climactic, like she drew out the ending. But she did it on purpose. Because really, there ISN'T an ending point in this story, at least not yet. There's more to it. The "main" story has concluded, but the epilogue isn't really an epilogue, is it? Nooo. No no. Not by a long shot. 
 The thing with this book is I can't really go into detail about what made it so great without revealing things. Parts of it were a bit weird (late reveals of information that should have been available up front) but the overall story was on of Flynn's typical commonalities in her books: really, really fucked up people. Beyond the grounds of anything normal. Maybe I like Dark Places the most because it was my first book from her, so everything was such a surprise. I wasn't expecting any of it. With Gone Girl and Sharp Objects, I now know Flynn's gimmick. No one is normal in her story; the main character, in particular, is always really really fucked up. Really screwy, really unnerving. It is what makes her books work. Because we love reading how fucked everyone else is, right? It's why Stephen King got popular. 
 And also why I read them. I've never encountered people like this in my life, and it is a guilty pleasure of mine to read about people beyond the boundaries of my own personal experiences. And that's precisely what is at work here. I get grim pleasure out of reading books like this, because then my life seems insanely easy. Do I have to deal with psychopaths or sociopaths? Nope. And after reading Flynn's novels, I very much like it that way. 
 Not that I wanted it before. 
 BIG BIG BIG BIG SPOILER 
 Amy is a psycho who decides she's going to frame her husband for her death because he cheated on her. Makes perfect sense, right? Right. And then forces him to live with her because he understands her and don't you see we're perfect for each other? I'll make you into the best husband and father you can be.  
 In-fucking-sane.

It was a great idea in theory, however this book has now ended up in my DNF graveyard because every time I pick it up lately, I find myself cringing rather than looking forward to what comes next. As an avid fan of the YA sci-fi/fantasy genre, I don't make unrealistic expectations of books geared at teens, but this one was a disappointment for me. 
 So basically, the premise of the book sounded AMAZING from the summary. Had to have it. Time travel, parallel universes, space travel, this kind of stuff has always been interesting to me so of course I picked this up. 
 The first few chapters were great and the beginning of the book sucked me in right away, so I will give it credit for starting on a high point. The introduction to Liam, Maddy and Sal and how they were brought from their respective time periods was written flawlessly, and I found myself wanting more because Scarrow came out swinging from chapter 1. 
 The book eventually slows down however. While I found it interesting that Liam was from 1912, and I loved his introduction chapter, as well as the fact that Maddy and Sal were from the future...Loved the character building in which Liam always seems to be at a disadvantage because he's missed out on 100+ essential years of history (essential to the plot since he's the front runner for correcting havoc wreaked by time travelers, etc) and so on and so forth..... I even LOVED that Scarrow used one of my favorite techniques in writing - switching POVs right at a pivotal moment, which makes you want to read more because each character whether protagonist or antagonist left you on a cliffhanger. 
 So how did this story end up on my DNF shelf? 
 Easy. 
 The pacing died down. Like I said, Scarrow came out swinging from the very beginning, however by page 161 which is about where I stopped reading, I was cringing. The plot progression slowed more and more and it was taking longer than necessary to find out where the timeline skewed off into a new timeline in which Germany had won WW II. I understand the three teens in the story were new to time travel and correcting it, but the antagonist's POV just dropped off completely (understandable if you want me to figure it out along with the protagonists) and chapter after chapter just became a snail's pace of trying to figure out where the true timeline had been altered. 
 When a book takes too long to get to the point, I find it personally harder for me to continue reading it. I don't think 20 - 30 pages of "oh no what happened!" is bad per sei. I just think that it could have been better. If you're going to drag it out, at least make each moment become something that's essential to pushing forward that plot progression.  
 Anyway. I hate to say it, but I won't be picking up other books in the series, this was just way too disappointing. I am also not going to force myself to finish reading it. This is why DNF graveyards exist.

Warning: spoiler tags are in this review for a reason. I spoil everything and then I spoil some more. 
 Why only three stars? This is why: the biggest spoiler about the final twist in this book is that it doesn't have any. No, really. It starts with Mallory having killed Brian. It ends with Mallory finding out through a twisty, supposedly mindscrewish trial... that she killed Brian. There is also the boarding school mystery, but it is quite unremarkable and no one really seems to care, including Mallory herself. 
 I shall repeat it once more. There. Is. No. Twist. 
 Yes, we find out her ex was with her moments before. But it doesn't change anything. He didn't do anything. He doesn't do anything interesting later, either, just appears in order to deliver the explanation and then exits stage left. 
 There is no ghost. 
 There is no other mysterious person having snuck in to kill Brian. 
 No one "followed her", like the back cover says. 
 Basically there is not even an actual reason for Mallory's big hysteria-filled trip down the thrill lane. Yes, she doesn't really remember the murder scene (which, by the way, we only figure out halfway through the book through little flashbacks), but as it turns out, she didn't really forget anything important. 
 So I'm left wondering what was the point. 
 Three stars for having a cool premise and being entertaining up until the revelation. 
 Also, one of the cover versions lies. Love might hurt, love might kill, but here, love had nothing to do with any of the murders.

I'm pretty sure this is the Jacky Faber book I left off with once the Marcos de Niza library stopped being my second home, which means everything from this point on should be new. Unfortunately, there are still seven books left in this series, and based on the last two, they're all probably going to be longer than they should have been. 
 The story picks up right where In the Belly of the Bloodhound left off (literally -- lines are copied verbatim from that book's last chapter), with Jacky under arrest after being rescued. She, of course, escapes, and on-again off-again childhood sweetheart Jaimy follows, beginning a rollicking journey down the Mississippi. 
 Parts of the book had me questioning my own knowledge of American history, as I could have sworn religious revivals were not taking place as early as 1805, nor were Bunyan-like characters as rampant at that point. However, I may just need to study up on my history. 
 Meyer began writing these books after being inspired by hearing sailor songs on a public radio station, so I understand his desire to put in many song-and-dance routines. However, for me, they took away from the plot. He'd easily lose 10 percent of the book if he trimmed the songs. 
 Character development suffered majorly in this book. Five books in, I still haven't quite got a handle on Jaimy and whether we're supposed to like him, and his contradictory actions in the book didn't clear anything up. None of the characters introduced in this book really appeared to be anything other than the frontier versions of earlier characters, and the returners (Higgins, Katy Deere) didn't really change over the course of the novel. 
 This series is beginning to struggle more and more with simply having two many characters with indistinct personalities. It's enough that I didn't really remember the two big baddies of this book, both of whom were introduced briefly in Curse of the Blue Tattoo and Under the Jolly Roger. And it's a problem I imagine will only get worse as the series continues.

It's been several months since I have read a John Grisham novel. He has yet again done a great helluva a job in this novel, The Racketeer. John Grisham's works oftentimes include virtuous or upright lawyers as protagonist, but this time, he walks into the Dark Side. I don't know if this was his first novel where he clings into the bad side of a person, a lawyer to be exact. Well, judging from almost sixteen (16) J.Grisham novels that I've read, this was probably his first. 
 A Racketeer is a person who engages in dishonest and fraudulent business dealings. But who is really the Racketeer? This novel will get you thinking who the Racketeer is to the extent that you wouldn't mind skipping meals just to discover who it is. The story started with the man named Malcolm Bannister. He is an ex-lawyer charged with a federal crime --money laundering, a crime he only technically and innocently committed. When he is about halfway through a ten year prison sentence, a federal judge is murdered. As an intelligent man, Mr Bannister sensed a loophole -- a chance to obtain liberty; he challenged the FBI, negotiated his release by telling them he knows who the murderer was and his motives. What appears to be the MOST INTERESTING TWIST in the story is that we begin to find out that Malcolm Bannister has an entirely different and new agenda of his own. 
 This novel has a very interesting story. It is so entertaining that I could actually die! Haha. There is an ultimate high level of suspense throughout, enough to maintain our utmost interest in the story as we follow Malcolm's everyday activities and his mysterious plan to stay out of prison. 
 "I guess under the right circumstances, a man will do just about anything." 
 --John Grisham, The Racketeer

A fun, straight-forward fantasy romp through a steampunk-lite city with HOLY SHIT SOOO MANY MALE CHARACTERS. Like where my ladies at? There's maybe three lady characters in this whole book. Our main character, and then two antagonists who both try to kill our main character I was hoping that the gang leader would've joined the heist team right up until the end, though . 
 This ebook is available for free through Amazon and you can also read the story on the Wattpad site, but I'm not sure if there was enough here to get me to pay for the subsequent books in this series. I had a good time reading this and had a couple of laughs, but as far as debuts go, this one was a bit clumsy. 
 Amaranthe is an Enforcer (city guardsperson) who finds herself on the wrong side of the law through no fault of her own. She quickly uncovers an insidious plot that endangers the Emperor, and her strong moral code leads her to concoct a scheme to make him aware of the machinations of those around him. Oh yeah, there's also this weird creature killing people all over the city but whatevs. 
 So unfortunately this book had a few pet peeves of mine: 
 - The perpetrators of the mystery aspects of this book were not known to the reader until the MC was like "omg these people!!!!!!". I feel like that's not worded as well as I could, so let me rephrase a little. The antagonists were not characters we (the readers) were already introduced to - we didn't even know that they exist until the MC puts it all together. This irks me because I want to figure the mystery out with the characters and not just be told the punchline. 
 - Most of the characters have names that I can't figure out how to pronounce in a way that makes them sound like names real people would have. Okay, okay, okay. I get it. It's fantasyyyy they don't have to have "real people" names. But like, at least give me a pronunciation guide somewhere. I even Googled it! Maldynado. How the fuck that sound like a name at all. "MAHL-din-ah-doh"? "Mahl-DIN-ah-doh"? "Maldy-nah-doh"? I can deal with it if it's just a few names for uppity flavor, but like almost everyone had names like that. Sicarius. Akstyr. Basilard. And then we've got Books. ?????? 
 - Amaranthe's a total Mary Sue character at her core. Being a Mary Sue isn't automatically a bad thing! And I still enjoyed Amaranthe, but any time she was in trouble you knew without a shadow of a doubt that she was going to get out of it and that she was going to be okay. 
 - The plot in general was a little weak for me. It was a lot of tell and not show, and you knew our team was going to be okay at all times. I need higher stakes to really feel invested. 
 - And because it needs to be said again, VERY FEW FEMALE CHARACTERS. This is inexcusable. There is no reason why at least one of our main team members (other than our MC) couldn't have been a female. Instead it's like: Main Character, local playboy who thinks the MC is hot, lethal assassin guy who the MC thinks is hot, troubled teen boy who is touched emotionally by the MC, and older man father-figure who also thinks the MC is hot. Where is my lady-friendship?? 
 All of that being said, though. This book did several things that I appreciated: 
 - Amaranthe was not dumb - there were a few times where a character would be explaining a plot thing and I'd be sitting there going 'okay but why can't they do this other thing that is totally do-able and not dumb?' and every time Amaranthe would open her mouth and go "Okay, but why can't we do this other thing that is totally do-able and not dumb?". And I would just praise the heavens. 
 - The interactions between our rag-tag band of misfits were fun and I laughed at a lot of their antics. They were funny without being stupid (most of the time). 
 - Sicarius's personality. Give me all of the stoic, sly, sarcastic loners who try to appear emotionless. I really loved that he was written in a way where he didn't stand out from the others unnaturally, but his dialogue still sounded unique to him. and his dialogue totally reminded me of my boo Fenris 
 - The action scenes were well-written and I could fully visualize just about every one of them. 
 I would recommend that most readers give this book a try. It is a fun, quick read with a good group of characters - but give me more ladies next time, please!

My all time favorite author is Dean Koontz, and I used to think nobody could write a mystery/thriller/paranormal story like him. Well, Santino has done it and he did it well!! 
 Full Review: 
 Insight is book one in Santino Hassell's new series, The Community. This is a paranormal romance/psychic thriller that is full of suspense, twists, turns, and of course hot as hell chemistry. To say I was blown away by this story is putting it too light, this story left me breathless and kept me on the edge of my seat the entire book. I really shouldn't have been surprised by Santino's ability to write in the paranormal realm, after all reading his earlier work,In the Company of Shadows, one can see his ability to jump into the paranormal world with ease. That is exactly what he has done here as he takes us into the world of pyschics and cult-like living with the landscape of NYC as a backdrop. 
 The MC in this story are Nate Black & Trent Castille. Nate is an empath with no training, from a family that is well-known in the psychic world and also full of secrets. These twisted secrets are eventually revealed throughout the story and there is lots of creative foreshadowing to clue the reader in. Nate really doesn't like his family, in-fact he detests them and everything they are about. Nate just tries to stay in his lane while his messed up family does their thing. 
 When Nate suddenly starts getting visions of his estranged twin, Theo, drowning, he knows he won't be able to rest until he figures out what happened and how he is getting these visions. So, after the funeral for Theo he plans to get to New York, the only way a person can with no money or car. He plans to hitchhike. 
 Nate lucks out when a black Chevy Nova pulls over for him and he finally gets to meet, Trent. These two spend the next 3 or 4 days traveling and getting to know each other as they make their way from Texas to NY. The thing you quickly realize about empaths is that they are largely influenced by their environment and people around them. Nate was around negativity in Texas and he felt dark all the time. Now Nate is around Trent in the confines of a car and he can't help but absorb the emotion that Trent exudes, happiness, peacefulness, calmness; not to mention eventually lust. During an impromtu stop in New Orleans, Nate learns how combining his feelings with Trents makes for an explosively hot time! 
 Once these two arrive in NYC neither of them want to part. They have bonded and developed this attraction to each other that makes them yearn for each other after they part. Nate starts trying to retrace his brothers footsteps, find who he was associated with, who he lived with, where he worked and what he uncovers is a multifaceted cult like organization known as, The Community. 
 The layers of The Community are slowly uncovered as Nate digs deeper and deeper, all while continuing to get random visions. The Community, quickly tries to bring him into their fold, at which point I was screaming for him to run away! The more people he meets at a club called Evolution, the thicker the web of craziness gets. Nate quickly finds out that there are so many more layers of psychics out there, empaths, precog, postcog, mediums, telepathics, and more, and The Community is gathering them all together. It isn't until he meets the members of Theo's band,The Dreadnoughts, that pieces are connected for him. 
 Once Trent and Nate reconnect, Nate is able to start seeing things more clearly. Trent is his center. His calm. He quickly becomes his heart, but he fears that Trent may not really feel the same and is instead acting out Nates emotions as he projects them. Eventually, after some pulse-pounding occurences these two get on the same wave length and Nate realizes that Trent wants him, all on his own...no influence needed from Nate. 
 This story ends with a strong HFN and we get a glimpse into book 2 at the end. I have always loved paranormal psy/thrillers, my favorites being from author Dean Koontz. I will now add Santino Hassell to that list of authors who know how to write a gripping thriller. I can't wait for book 2!!

First impressions: Opening a debut novel in 2nd person narrative is ballsy. But, oh man, did it work in this case. By introducing the reader to the wonder that is this night circus through gorgeous prose and the immediacy of the perspective, we are hooked from the first sentence.  Lasting impressions: I relished this book in a way that rarely happens for me - slowly. For the week I spent reading it, I rarely thought of anything else, yet I prolonged the reading experience in order to get the most out of it. This is a book that inspires reflection in all of the best ways, and rewards you for taking the time to read every word carefully. The story builds slowly, but purposefully, until the exciting climax threatens to turn the entire world of these characters upside down. It's a beautiful journey to witness. 
 Conflicting impressions: I confess that I read all of the negative reviews of this book first. Surely no book could live up to the kind of magical hype this book has had heaped upon it, right? So I read the most blistering, scathing reviews, preparing myself for a slow, boring, overly dense novel with wooden characters and little action. And you know what I got? Subtle characters deftly written by a master puppeteer. Erin Morgenstern fills the pages with lush details, yes, but they all serve to inform us about the characters and the setting. I understood this world so well that I wanted to live in it for as long as possible, which is why I took so damn long to finish it. And why I bought a copy for my shelf the day before I returned my library book. I didn't want a single day to go by without having this book in my possession. 
 Overall impressions: This book is magical, but not because it contains magic. This is not Harry Potter. Our young protagonists learn magic through natural ability and frustrating lessons by their parental figures - no straightforward schoolteachers to be found. They learn through trial and error, cruelty, and their own perseverance and curiosity. 
 Celia and Marco do not spend a lot of time in each other's company, and as readers we are often much more knowledgeable than our characters. For me, this made the plot that much more enjoyable, as I had an inkling of where the story was going, but no idea how it was going to get there. As the story unfolded, I was more than willing to go along for the ride. This is a novel you either succumb to completely, or resign yourself to frustration. I think by the end of the first few chapters any reader will be able to tell if this is the book for him/her. 
 The Night Circus has rich period details, lots of colorful characters, and more than a handful of intrigue. This was not only one of my favorite books of the year, but one of my favorite books, period. If you're looking to be entertained by something truly fresh and surprising, you must get your hands on this one.

 The Retribution of Mara Dyer is the third and final installment to the Mara Dyer trilogy, written by Michelle Hodkin. Considering the amount of times that the release of this novel was pushed back, I honestly expected a lot more than what iHad just read. Not to be mean or anything but a lot of elements of this book fell short of 1. my expectations and 2. the elements of the first two novels. The Mara Dyer trilogy started out really strong. I was intensely hooked when I picked up the first book and after reading the second novel, I just needed to have the third. When this was finally released, I heard a lot of good things about it and, unfortunately, a lot of bad ones as well. I picked up this book with an open mind and I wouldn't allow other opinions to affect mine so this is what I came out with. 
 The plot. I think this played a really big part in how I ended up feeling with this book. The first two installments were headed down one road and with this one, the plot suddenly took a sharp turn and I felt like I found myself on a completely different road, reading a whole new plot except with the same characters (kind of, I'll explain more on this in a bit). I personally feel that the first two books really didn't build up to the way this book ended because I felt almost lost as I went through the novel. There was just so many new aspects to this book that weren't even hinted on, while the older aspects of the first two books were suddenly disregarded in this installment. It irked me out alot because I felt like Hodkin was taking this story down one direction but suddenly changed the premise of everything just as the trilogy was about to end. It left me with so many unanswered questions. Was that the cause of why the release date kept being pushed back? 
 The Characters. When it comes to this subject, the main person that comes to mind is Mara. Like the plot, her character also took a sharp tun for the worst, literally. Due to her major character development, this trilogy took on a lot more violence towards the end compared to the amount it started off with. I'm not against nor for it, I was just so surprised. Til this day, I'm not quite sure where I stand with Mara, whether I like her or not. She wasn't the same Mara this trilogy started off with but her character development did fit well with the sudden change in the plot. When it came to Noah, I felt he got weaker as a character; he wasn't badly written, he just kind of sucked as the dude because as his falls more poetically in love, his girlfriend is becoming more of a psychotic killer.  Oh, but the end of the story tried to soften her around the edges by explaining that Mara has the ability to give life in exchange of torturing someone else.... uh yea, that's still horrible.  
 The Writing. This wasn't so much of a problem to me. However, I did noticed that there was an increase of foul language being used in this installment. Again, I didn't find it offensive, I was just taken by surprise. I just hope this won't be something that will trend in the YA genre otherwise, I'd have a full hypothetical swear jar. LOL!

On the one hand, Tretch is one of my favorite male characters in all of YA. He's charming and polite to everyone, he loves to read (even if I roll my eyes at most of his taste in Pretentious Male literature) and frequents a used bookstore, he likes all the same music I like, he doesn't swear and is only gross in one scene, and he is definitely a hopeless romantic. His emotions run close to the surface and he cries quite a bit, mostly without shame. The choice in cover models is perfect, too. 
 He's also the master of that in-love-with-my-straight-friend trope, which is helped considerably by the fact that his best friend is equally nice, very tactile in his affection, and has no sense of boundaries or personal space. ("I'm gonna hop in the shower, but why get undressed in private when I could just strip while we're talking? Also, since you're staying over, let me loan you a pair of PJs before we get in bed. The same bed.") 
 On the other, the story kind of ran out of steam around Christmas. I kept expecting it to build to a big, major event, but instead it was like a previously-opened and shaken bottle of pop that's been left so long, the carbonation has vanished without even being opened a second time. I was already mildly let down when he got over his crush, unsustainable though it may have been, but I really felt all the wind go out of my sails when Matt announced he was moving away. Suddenly it felt like the message was "nothing will bother you as long as you accept and are comfortable with yourself." Nah dude, I vote codependency 4 lyfe. And more to the point, that was such a great friendship, I just don't know why any author would want him to have to finish high school without a buddy like that at his side.  
 I was also disappointed that I didn't connect with Tretch's family quite as much as I should have, but I got quite a kick out of Matt's dads, so there was that.

As I was reading, I kept thinking "this reveal about Elizabeth better be fantastic, otherwise I'm done." 
 I'm done. 
 Why was our hero behaving irrationally, ignoring the sound advice of her friends, and hurtling toward a prison sentence. I figured she was protecting someone, but when it was revealed that Channing, the teenager Elizabeth rescued from a horrifying sexually abusive captivity was really the one who shot the suspects 18 times, but that Elizabeth was taking the blame because she just knew the system would treat Channing terribly and that she would never get justice, I was done. 
 Really? A seventeen year old white girl is kidnapped and sexually abused by two men who are then going to kill her and when the girl manages to kill them first I'm supposed to believe a prosecutor is going to charge her with murder? Yeah, I don't think so. That Elizabeth is willing to go to prison to "protect" Channing over this only makes Elizabeth seem stupid.  
 It also didn't help that I figured out who the killer was in the first hundred pages. I'm giving the book two stars because it is clear Hart knows how to write great sentences, but I confess I'm baffled by all of the love Redemption Road is gettting.

 I like the idea of this, but these linked short stories are not created equally, and the ones I disliked far outweighed the good. And not just disliked: there were parts that really bothered me. 
 Specifically: 
 - the main character never really becomes more than a MPDG. She's supposed to be a mystery for much of the book, so this device could have worked, but she never gets beyond it. I think that her ending section was meant to elevate her into a real girl, but I didn't think it was successful. Women don't need to be written this way. 
 - She knows people better than they know themselves after less than 24 hours, and drops truth bombs on them. When is it okay to encourage someone to miss his college interview because you KNOW that he would be happier as a small-town mechanic??? 
 - the main character often "tells it like it is" (sometimes obnoxiously using song lyrics). I hate when authors portray someone being "put in their place". In this case, a hotel manager is berated because she won't give out someone's room number (in a not-life-and-death, everything-would-have-been-solved-in-a-few-hours kind of situation). UGH! So someone should give out personal information and get fired? Then the manager turns "cool" and secretly gives it out. UGH. 
 - a young man is rejected romantically by his best friend, but instead of respecting her decision, he is encouraged by the main character to not take "no" for an answer and to prove his love in an extravagant public display. And then of course she decides she was wrong. Why is this still portrayed as romantic? I'm tired of seeing the culture of "no doesn't actually mean no" perpetuated in a book written in 2014. This was insulting and disrespectful. Despite what men like to think, women are not into this crap. 
 On the other hand, I legitimately enjoyed the section about a woman trying to move on after her boyfriend's death. Adi Alsaid isn't a bad writer, and there were parts of each story that I thought were smart and profound; unfortunately, he usually chooses the cliche as the ultimate message.

The pacing of this book is, in a way, faultless because Butler kept me reading even when I didn't really want to. But that said, there were many parts of the book where I wondered why I had kept reading because nothing much was happening. 
 The writing was strong and very character-central and that helped the story progress despite the lack of any Big Events happening regularly. 
 The story is billed as 'sf' but at the most I would call it 'science fantasy' as there are clearly fantasy elements (i.e., the main character Anyanwu is a shaman-healer with shape-shifting abilities) involved in addition to the not-very-technical bioengineering (breeding experiments) as well. 
 The story starts out in Africa during the blossoming (this is probably not the best word to use, sorry) of the slave trade and follows the main character Anyanwu, a very long-lived if not immortal shaman, after she is captured by another spirit of a less than benevolent nature, Doro. 
 Doro takes Anyanwu with him to America  and forces him to marry his son in order to further his plans to breed supernatural children. His goal seems to be to, through his breeding program, create other creatures like himself.  
 In Africa, Anyanwu is a powerful shaman and clan matriarch, is used to leading her life the way she sees fit and shepherding her children through their lives. She practices healing but also occasionally has the need to frighten villagers into respecting her. 
 Her demeanor changes drastically when she falls under Doro's control. It's as if her already very long life has all been for naught as she becomes meek in so many ways. 
 People/relatives/children die. Anyanwu and Doro don't. They have a mostly antagonistic relationship. That's pretty much most of the story. Near the end, things change, but not necessarily for the better. Perhaps the story becomes more interesting in the later sequels. I may never find that out. 
 The very short time that the main characters spend in Africa was perhaps the most interesting part of the book. I really wish it had stayed there. 
 Late 17th and early 18th century America would also seem like an interesting and challenging setting for two (probably) immortal Africans to play out their relationship drama. But for all that, the setting did not play as great a role as it probably should have. 
 The character motivations, although clearly stated, were not shown with any great conviction. This reader thinks the book deserves a rating of around 3.5 stars but is rounding up to 4 stars based on the strength of the writing.

Where to start? 
 Overlong, with an ending that's a bust, this is very flawed, but still incredibly compelling at the same time. Hallberg also has never met a $10 word that he didn't make into a $20 one instead. As someone said of Justified's Boyd Crowder, "I love the way you talk... using 40 words when four will do." You get used to his style though and when you do, things move a lot faster than you might think for a 900+ page work. 
 Things do break down at certain points throughout, though, especially when we are treated to much of the same plot by various viewpoints. Thankfully, the 70s NYC atmosphere helps pull things along and keep one entertained. Some critics have felt that this is a Gumpian theme park type of look at America's post 60s hangover. I can't really speak to that since I was -2 when the novel is set, but the research seems meticulous to the point of the novel feeling authentic and lived in. 
 The aspect of the novel that I found the most divisive were the characters. They remain compelling throughout for the most part, except they do try one's patience and wear a bit thin at times. This is particularly true of Keith and Charlie, who I felt less and less sympathy towards as the novel went on. Strangely, one of the main characters, Mercer, is completely dropped for 200 pages in the middle section of the novel. I don't expect every character to be given equal "page time", but since Mercer is kind of the moral compass here, it's especially weird that he's offstage for so long. 
 In this now post-Bowie, post-Reed, post-Ramones world, it's nice to have evocative reminders like this of what counterculture once was. It's also interesting to see what the Mad Men era gave birth to, as this novel and the most recent season of Fargo can attest to. That's why, even at its most strained, frustrating and overlong, this was still a ride worth taking.

The Unbecoming of Mara Dyer is one of those books I instantly put on my to read-list, just because of the original title and pretty, mysterious cover. It took me a while to get around to reading it though. Anyways, I feel the totally random urge to do this review in a plus-and-minus kind of way, so I'm just gonna roll with it if ya don't mind. 
 On the plus side: 
 *	I really enjoyed the voice in which The Unbecoming of Mara Dyer is written. It's realistically teenage-y without being annoying towards readers that are a bit older (as opposed to the House of Night-books for example, which are most definitely annoying). 
 *	Pop culture references usually bug me because they keep the book from being timeless, but they were perfectly placed and and picked in this novel. Loved the references to Harry Potter, LOTR etc! 
 *	Learned some new vocabulary as a non-native English speaker. I really appreciate it when YA is not 'dumbed down'. Yeah, you go ahead and use those big words, Mara! Meanwhile I'll just ... Look them up in the dictionary. 
 *	The chapters had a nice length. Is it weird to actively like that about a book? Because I do. I love me some perfect-length chapters. 
 *	Though I don't have any brothers of my own, I found the relationship between Mara and her brothers to be very realistic. Everyone should have a big brother like Daniel. The same can be said for the relationship with her parents, who are - as rarely seen in YA - really involved in Mara's life. 
 *	The way the romance develops is very realistic. They have that hate-love thing going on. I would've loved that if Noah wasn't such a skinny hipster bad boy. I'm too old for bad boys. And hipsters. 
 On the minus side: 
 *	3/4 of the book is building up the romance and Mara hallucinating every now and then. It's only in the last quarter of the book that things get (somewhat) interesting. Some author on the cover advised readers to 'read with the light on'. Whatever for? There was nothing even remotely thriller-y about it. The story is kind of dull, but the solid writing makes up for it. 
 *	Noah smokes. Why does Noah smoke? Cute boys should not smoke. Never ever. Bad guys in books are allowed to smoke and then die of cancer, but the main love interest? No. Unresponsible. When a character lights up they have to pretty amazing (and obviously stop smoking) to get back in favor with me. Adrian Ivashkov (Vampire Academy, Bloodlines) is slowly getting there, but Noah Shaw still has some way to go. 
 *	Information dump much in the last part of the book? It would've been better to spread the info out a bit more or at least give the reader some inkling of what's actually going on instead of putting waaaay to much revelations in one conversation/chapter. That crap came out of the blue. And not in a 'wow, plot twist' kind of way. More in a 'the author did not think this through' kind of way. 
 *	Ouija boards, kids going into a haunted asylum ... Sigh. Then she goes to a fancy school and has a blonde nemesis! Sigh. Then her sorta-boyfriend turns out to be super duper rich! Sigh. Minus points for originality! 
 *	I have a feeling this trilogy will turn out like The Adoration of Jenna Fox (which I loved by the way). Just putting that out there in case I turn out to be right so I can come back and gloat.

Cracking open The Night Circus, I was expecting to uncover an epic odyssey of magic, love and intrigue - yeah okay so maybe I was hoping it was going to be Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire-meets-The Hunger Games - but...no such luck. 
 The best part about The Night Circus is Morgenstern's atmospheric prose, which for the most part matches the mood one would expect from a book about a magical traveling circus at the turn of the 20th century. It's sultry, it's enigmatic, it's - dare I say - enchanting. 
 (Unfortunately, it also has a tendency to imitate a special consortium of writers* who believe that anything that takes place in a mysterious or dark setting in the past needs to be described in forced, hyper-stylized language. Fortunately, this is only a tendency, and Morgenstern seems to control it for most of the book.) 
 The worst part about The Night Circus is that Morgenstern appears to have forgotten to include a plot. (Oops!) There's some vague nonsense about a duel between two magicians that doesn't really happen . There are straggling storylines that the author (unsuccessfully) tries to tie together at the end through a contrived "revealing conversation" between two characters. There are loads of unexplained actions and rules and circumstances that are overly complicated and don't really make sense when you try to put them together, and finally, there's a total lack of urgency throughout the whole book. Someone might die? Don't care. The circus is in peril? Sucks. 
 This does not bode well for the gentle reader. 
 And yet. I'm a sucker for language, so even though a whole lot of nothing happens, I can get behind that, to a degree. Case in point: I think I'm one of the three people in the world who enjoyed the 10-page description of what a pear is in Beatrice and Virgil. 
 It's worthwhile remembering that this is only Morgenstern's first novel. It was perhaps a touch too ambitious for her now, but I would keep reading her work in the future. She'll grow into that imagination of hers and all will be well.

Well, right off the bat, I am going to tell you NOT to read this review if you haven't read First Touch because Last Kiss is book two in the First & Last series. 
 Consider yourself warned. I'll try to use "spoiler" tags. 
 Picking up where we left off, Emily and Reeve are spending time on his ranch in Wyoming. Faced with the opportunity to search Reeve's office for surveillance that may provide answers to what happened to Amber, Emily chooses not to proceed. Whatever is building between her and Reeve, Emily decides she's all in. She wants him and is ready to give him her absolute trust. 
 Then Joe shoes up... and it turns out that Amber is in fact alive. 
 For months, she's been holed up with Michelis Vilanakis, Reeve's uncle and head of the Greek mob. Joe decided to continue his investigation into Amber's disappearance and death. Completely by chance, he finds the broken and battered Amber as she's attempting to escape Vilanakis and brings her to the only safe place they know - Reeve's ranch. 
 Immediately, Emily is racked with her own insecurities. She's thrilled her best friend is alive and that they can be reunited. But Amber is different. She confesses she was wrong to leave Reeve months ago and is desperate for a second chance. Emily, remembering the incident that drove them apart, vows not to stand between Amber and the man she wants. 
 But Reeve will not give up so easily. 
 And with Vilanakis seemingly on the hunt to retrieve what's his and to ultimately force Reeve back into the fold of the family business, Emily has to decide to either bow out or fight for what she wants. 
 There is still her own lingering doubts? Is Reeve too controlling? Is he truly capable of bad things? And does he want Amber or Emily?  
 Immediately, Last Kiss was a bit different in the overall feel and motivation of the story. Paige is much more focused on the dynamic between Emily and Amber, how they got to their current lots and life and what that means for them and the people they hold dear. We're still left with Emily's lingering doubts for Reeve. But instead of wondering if he's responsible for Amber's death, we spend much of the book mulling over his general trustworthiness in Emily's head. She questions her loyalty to Amber, the ability of Reeve to not only protect them but to put an end to the threats presented by Vilanakis, as well as her own self-esteem. 
 So the focus changes from suspenseful, psychological romance of doubt versus desire to a cat fight between girls over a man who may or may not be worth it. The funny thing is, throughout Last Kiss, I never once questioned Reeve's honor or intentions, not the way I was perplexed in First Touch. I actually enjoyed the mind games he played. But once he comes clean - and doesn't really put up much of a fight about it in the second book - he became just another guy who likes to be a bit dominant in the bedroom. He was no longer a mystery, but actually a likable hero. Reeve has his flaws, but he's the kind of guy you actually like because he's not so immature or douchey that he can't learn and grow from his past mistakes. I honestly felt bad for him because he's the one who keeps getting hurt but has enough courage to continue to love. 
 Where does that leave me? Well, reading 300 pages of drama between two woman who have outgrown each other - one who is much stronger than she believes, and the other weak and miserable unless she's engaged in manipulation - wasn't exactly what i was expecting. And that's really what this is all about - the girl who finally realizes her best friend is a spiteful bitch. 
 I wasn't totally disappointed in the direction Paige took the second book. Surprised a bit because I thought we'd get some good mob boss feuding. But I was pleased with the final outcome.

It's okay that Aileen and Blake fell in love (one cannot help that) but it's definitely wrong to sleep with the man who is going to be the husband of your sister. Even if your sister doesn't want (but thinks she needs to) and Blake thinks the engagement was a big mistake. They are STILL engaged. They should have waited till the moment the engagement was dissolved BUT here comes the funny thing: Till the end neither Tara nor Blake BROKE it. Aileen was sleeping with Blake the night before this wedding, she walked up the aisle with Tara and was accepting the fact that Blake would marry Tara and he did the same. In the end Tara took the happiness in her hands and ended the engagement at the altar (a pretty selfless action for a girl that was selfish and naive before). If Tara hadn't done it Blake would have married her with Aileen in attendance!!! 
 Sorry, this is neither romantic nor acceptable in my eyes. At least they told Tara midway through the story who was angry and felt betrayed (understandable). But she didn't break the engagement because she felt as though it would be her only chance to marry. I'm sorry but the whole concept of the story was a deal breaker for me, I just didn't work for me. It would have been okay for me if they started dating while he was engaged and they would have told Tara soon after it happened and dissolved the engagement. Tara would felt betrayed but it would have been a better love story for me. I feel so bad not finishing the story but I just couldn't.  
 Fourth: Although Tara wasn't the heroine she was important to the story and I didn't like her. (I cannot say a thing about Aileen and Blake because I didn't see enough of them to judge their character. But I think I could have liked them if not for point three. Tara was a different story she seemed too selfish but naive at the same time. She is expecting the man who loved her and she left because she thought she might someone better to still love her after three years and is angry because she realized she loved him and he moved forward? She wasn't loving him in the first place because she left him for selfish reasons! And then she comes back into his life and thinks they can go on as if nothing happened? 
 Well this where the main reasons why I didn't finish "The Bride Says No".

Review 
 Title: Ruin & Rule 
 Series: Pure Corruption (book 1) 
 Author: Pepper Winters 
 Genre: Romance, Suspense, Contemporary 
 "We met in a nightmare. The in-between world where time had no power over reason. We fell in love. We fell hard. But then we woke up. And it was over . . ." 
 RUIN & RULE 
 She is a woman divided. Her past, present, and future are as twisted as the lies she's lived for the past eight years. Desperate to get the truth, she must turn to the one man who may also be her greatest enemy . . . 
 He is the president of Pure Corruption MC. A heartless biker and retribution-deliverer. He accepts no rules, obeys no one, and lives only to reap revenge on those who wronged him. And now he has stolen her, body and soul. 
 Can a woman plagued by mystery fall in love with the man who refuses to face the truth? And can a man drenched in darkness forgo his quest for vengeance-and finally find redemption? 
 My review 
 Received an advanced copy by NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. Reviewed by Sarah for Alpha Book Club. 
 Five stars for this fast paced tale 
 When I saw that I could review Ruin & Rule, I immediately jumped on that chance. Ever since we met Killian at Diamond Alley in Third Debt, I've been intrigued by him. You know he had been hurt badly and I was most curious to know his story. Who left scars on his heart? Why was he seeking vengeance? We get some of those answers in Ruin & Rule, but we're left with so many more. 
 There were times that I hated Killian - he was so cruel to Cleo and I hoped that he would see the error of his ways. But then he would do something so sweet that my heart would melt and I knew this was who he is deep inside. And Cleo, I admired her for being so strong when she had no recollection of anything. But she believed that she had a connection with Killian and I loved that she pushed his buttons. 
 Pepper Winters takes us on a fast and furious ride through the past and present of the Pure Corruption MC and this book is filled with so many twists and turns that I was biting my nails as I anxiously read to see what happened next. Yes, the book ends on a cliffhanger and to say that I'm excited for the next book is an understatement. I'm dying to know who is good, who is bad and what the hell is going to happen.

Fair warning: I am biased. As a kid, I read Madeleine L'Engle's Time Quartet (the first three especially) until my copies were falling apart. This book will reach in and squeeze the heart of any L'Engle fan. Not only is Miranda a dedicated L'Englite (made that up), but the story feels just as urgent as Meg Wallace's story ever did. Next to that feat, time travel is practically a bonus. But Stead has done more than paid homage to a classic. She's created a book that remembers all the slights and frustrations of being twelve, from the petty social squabbling that feels momentous to the confusion of dealing with the grown up world of class and race when you're not quite sure what's going on. In that way, Stead reminded me of another classic author from my childhood, Judy Blume. For weaving these two together, Stead has my undying devotion. (Why not five stars, then? I have to say that I was a bit disappointed that the denouement seemed familiar from certain movies that shall here remain nameless out of spoiler considerations. I actually like these movies a lot, but was looking for something a bit more from Stead.)

 There's so much I want to talk about and I can't, because I really don't want to spoil you. There was major crying, I can tell you that. And so many smiles, laughing out loud moments, a lot of swooning and flailing going on at this side of the screen. 
 During my journey of blogging, which has taken years to reach this point where we're at today, I have gone with the hype and left things unsaid or raised ratings a star at times when I've stood in front of a choice of "how to rate" a particular book and didn't know whether it was "x" or "y" stars. I have learned from it, because if I don't have my honesty, what else is there? Nothing. So here I am being honest. I am never ready to part with these books, I don't ever want them to end. Same with this book! I love the twin's prose that's complex and poetic yet simple and relatable; the kind that really makes you think, but brings out a thousand different emotions in you. It's gorgeous! I will never stop craving to hear their words speak to me in such a hauntingly beautiful, passionate way. 
 However, it's my honest opinion that while everything was necessary either for characters, world/scene building or plot, some of the thoughts could have been cut a few paragraphs shorter. It's not to say that Ryke and Daisy's thoughts don't matter, they DO! Each and every one of them. And I absolutely LOVED reading them! But I simply found some things the tiniest bit redundant, I guess? I see how these thoughts all complete one another in a specific scene and the importance of the message they convey, and merde! They're beautifully, soulfully written! But I thought some things could have been cut a little shorter, because those things had been said before, just in a different setting. It doesn't affect my rating though because this book spoke to me and I loved it more than words can describe. I'm easily moved by a lot of things, but it's rare when a book touches me this much and Ryke and Daisy's encore most definitely touched me in many, many ways. 
 With all this being said, I loved Long Way Down so much and I'm forever thankful for what these books have given me. I've loved every single moment spent reading and re-reading them; making friends all across the world and finding people who love these books, characters and authors just as passionately as I do; the time spent time on making graphics and playlists; simply gushing with friends over the silliest things; (day)dreaming about these characters and their stories and so, so much more. It's been such a wonderful ride and I can't wait to see what the future holds for the next generation who will surely continue this wonderful, emotional legacy that is the Addicted series. Thank you for everything, Krista and Becca! These books have truly changed my life.

Confession time: I hated Nanette. She was a pretentious snob who looked down on everyone and anyone, and had no real criteria to go on. I can see from all the 4 and 5 star reviews that I'm very much in the minority with this, but I just couldn't do it. I tried to be profound and insightful like Nanette, but then I kept snorting with laughter at that and couldn't do it properly. 
 Here's why: Nanette's an idiot because she asks ridiculously stupid questions all the time. She's a snob because she thinks she's so original and speshul compared to all the kids at her school. She's a bitch because even though she recognizes she's being a hypocrite, she treats the people in her life like crap and uses them up until she doesn't need them. Then she'll drop off the face of the earth again and it's like those people never existed. She even says that, at one point. That they're all characters in a book and she's done with that book. 
 I am always on board to embrace the weird. I don't think there's anything wrong with letting your freak flag fly or announcing to the world that yes, you are a furry! You are fluent in Klingon! You like going to shitty dive bars to see bands no one's heard of! You like being a hipster and only listening to songs that aren't mainstream! There's nothing wrong with any of those. Go do your thing, girl. I just got offended by how much Nanette backhands all other forms of thought. Like only hers is the correct one, and if you aren't on her wavelength then you're just stupid. 
 I'm going to do some introspective reflection, here. I know why Nanette bothered me so much. Why? Because I was extremely active in high school. I had a lot of people I was really, truly friends with (not just acquaintances), I did multiple sports, I was in clubs, and I was excited for college. By Nanette's standards, I am a nobody because I follow the flow and am therefore not worth looking twice at. Now to be fair I didn't hand out blowjobs in exchange for liquor, but other than those issues I didn't hate Shannon like I was supposed to, I felt more drawn to her than Nanette. She parties, she drinks, she wants to play soccer on a scholarship at college. Her biggest flaw is probably that she's self-centered. But here's the catch: NANETTE IS INSANELY FUCKING SELF-CENTERED. Why is it okay for Nanette to be an asshole but not Shannon? Because Nanette's assholey-ness has been pent up for years, whereas Shannon is more adept at dealing with stress and just calls it like she sees it? 
 Now I am making Shannon out to be the hero and Nanette the villain, which isn't what I wanted to do. I just wanted to portray the fact that Nanette is just as much of a jerk as Shannon. But Shannon is still lesser than Nanette because Shannon wants conventional things. So I'll just circle back around to my opening line: I hate Nanette, and she is a pretentious snobby bitch.

First, the cover: it's slightly typical of New Adult novels, but this novel borders on the age of Young Adult anyways. I do like it, but I'm not in love with it. 
 The first thing that stuck out to me was the fact the book was written in present tense. I didn't like that aspect at all, so I found myself naturally changing the tense in my mind. Eventually I didn't notice it as much. In it's entirety the book was a bit of a roller coaster for me, but in a repetitive way. The MC was up and down, all over the place, but the same places over and over. It perfectly embodies teenage angst, over and over. It was Colt, no Jordan, happy, sad, angst, angst and horny, horny, horny, horny. Colt, no Jordan, happy, sad--you get my point. Thus, I skimmed major portions of the book just to get to the core of the story. 
 As for the characters, I didn't really love any of them. I also didn't really feel like I knew anything more about them by the end of the book besides the basics. 
 Charlotte seemed like a pointless character, who if removed, wouldn't have changed the story much in my opinion. 
 Colt was just a giant jerk. He was supposed to be, but I don't understand why at the end he's suddenly somewhat nice. If someone treats you like that, kick their butt to the curb--don't be friends with them! 
 Jordan was sweet and said to be a geek, but for the life of me I don't know why. Does he participate in chess club, mathletes or something? He underwent the typical geek to chic transformation, and has been in love with the MC even though he's never talked to her. 
 Onto the MC, she's suffered the loss of her father and hates the world for it. I understand where she's coming from, but her relationships develop so quickly and are so all over the place that I really believed what she needed was a straight jacket. Her relationships all also seemed superficial, but this may be because I didn't feel I saw any relationship building. There was a lot of physical, but very little of anything else--then she's suddenly in love with Jordan. She also confused me with her constant pestering about her v-card, and her vileness at Jordan being a pastor. She's waited 18 years, she can't wait a few more? She acts like Jordan being a pastor is the end of the world, but pastors can still marry and do it, so I'm not sure why she was freaking out. I know she no longer believed in God, but she constantly harped on the sex part and not too much of the God part. 
 Overall, I felt the novel had a strong message about God and faith, but it felt clouded by the lack of relationships of the characters.

Childhood's End, as seen from a 2016 reader's perspective, is seriously lacking in many things we regard as standard for novels nowadays - first and foremost, though, would be immersion, in a rough sense. 
 The protagonists, if you want to call them that, are bland. Instead of offering a character with a definable agency and an interesting point of view, they're mostly just tourists gawking at the author's worldbuilding. Often enough literally. 
 That is a common problem of certain older science fiction novels. Yet especially when hearing this book instead of reading it, one notices this fault way more distinctly; instead of being able to gloss over some part of the "look at this strange and marvellous idea I had!" infodump, you have to listen to it. And it drudges on and on, to a point where you want to give Clarke a stern "WE GET IT, MOVE ON FROM THE POINT" - and that's from someone who thinks that Tolkien's landscape tourism is quite bearable. 
 In general, the book expresses some interesting ideas - a few topics are timeless and not made obsolete by the computer age, as one could call it, which is often enough a breaking point for older scifi. The sad thing is that Clarke uses a very broad "this is how I envision it to be" amateur sociologist approach that is rather unrefined in how simple it expects human reaction to be, and intentionally leaves out big swathes of time where logic dictates something should have happened. Essentially, he Mary Sued the antagonists, except they're not antagonists, except they are. 
 And that's the main issue with it. The books reads like a "I think humans are heading for the end and even super-powerful space aliens will just come over to say "chill" and then euthanize the human race ". At no point is the possibility explored of showing more than slices of pseudo-posthuman  existence in reaction to the major plot point, there is no story arc instead of over-generalized societal snapshots, and the one subplot where someone actually does something is, essentially, pointless. 
 I really thought this classic would detail more than a simplistic broad-stroke "society tourism" with no meat to it.

 His father, who may not really be his father, treats him coldly and is angry that he is a part of the magical world.

A very fast read. The characters aren't particularly likeable, and the main character succeeds in being the most likeable precisely because the others are so awful (with the possible exception of Nina who is awful but funny). That said, there's something wonderful about their awfulness, kind of a literary equivalent of one of those great Come Dine with Me episodes where the contestants outdo one another in their varieties of awfulness, while Dave Lamb slates them in the background. 
 The basic premise of the book is this - Nora is invited to a hen do for an old school friend she hasn't seen for years. Other invitees include her closest friend, Nina (sarcastic, bitchy, sweary, funny) Tom (pretentious middle-class middle-twenties middle-of-the-road theatre guy who thinks he's a rebel), and Mel (overworked mother of a 6 month old who frets frequently her first time away from home since the baby was born). The instigator of the invites and party is Flo (unstable, intense, Single-White-Female-territory) and the hen is Clare (perfect. Too perfect?). 
 The hen do is to take place in an isolated woodland house in Northumberland. For our friends Nora, born in Reading and living in London, going to the Dreaded North is obviously not going to end well. Because obviously the North is where BAD THINGS HAPPEN TO GOOD SOUTHERNERS. Anyway, pretty soon bad things do start to happen. The mix of old and new people, all connected to Clare, stirs bitchiness aplenty, and this is the most fun part of the book. It's like one of those Come Dine with Me episodes I mentioned earlier - there's sniping, bossiness, drunkenness, terrible entertainment ideas, hysterics, bitching and general tension. It's fantastic. But then things take a turn for the worse, and someone ends up dead. And no, they were not killed by a bunch of Northern peasants with torches (as some of our poor ickle Southern characters feared) but by (dun, dun DUN!!!!) one of them. 
 The story flips between Nora, injured and in hospital trying to remember what happened, and flashbacks to those two nights which ended in murder. 
 I have to admit, the final reveal was my second guess for the killer, I had someone else as my No 1 suspect. While the memory-loss/hidden secrets theme is a little overdone, that's not the author's fault, and I think she handles the plot very well - it is certainly gripping and kept me wondering just what happened. However, the ultimate reveal seemed like a little bit of a disappointment after so much build up. 
 I also didn't get why  no one is at all worried when they hear the first 'break in' that Flo of all people is not only the one to take the gun, but then *keeps* it. She is a notably unstable character who is obsessed with Claire to the point that she loses all rationality when Clare's happiness is 'threatened'. As in, she threatens to kill Nora for wanting to go to bed early, and flips out when Mel leaves. I know *why* Flo has to have the gun, it's part of the plot, but seriously, not one character questioned it? If I was there I would have been like 'um, let's not give the weapon (deadly or not) to the most unstable person in the group, maybe? Also, I got the impression we were ultimately supposed to feel sorry for Flo. I didn't. Whatever issues she had, she was shrill, hysterical and annoying.  
 Great read to curl up with on a dark evening or read on the beach or a long journey.

Though The Golem and the Jinni isn't really that long of a book, it reads as though it is. I'm usually a pretty quick reader, but I found that when I was reading TG&TJ, when I felt as though I'd read 10 pages, in reality I'd only have made it through something like 3. On top of (or perhaps because of?) that, I found that the plot could really drag for long periods of time, with very little actually happening, despite a lingering hope that something is about to shake the world up. I think the narrative could have been edited down a bit more and maybe paced a bit better. 
 That being said, the premise of this book was brilliant. I really liked the characters, the history, the cultures, the fantasy, the fairy-tale elements and the overarching plot line. I liked the way Helene Wecker wove her characters into a web of connections that felt real. And I loved the way the ending tied everything up. The conclusion was interesting, unpredictable and most importantly, satisfying. (Whilst, of course, leaving room for a sequel... when you're playing with immortal characters the possibilities are endless). 
 I also liked the very slow and natural way that the romance between Chava and Ahmad developed. I really didn't know whether or not they would end up that way (and honestly didn't care, they had a great dynamic just as friends), but when they got there it didn't feel rushed. It was a real love that had been built on a long and interesting friendship. That's not something you read every day.  
 And can we just talk about how great this would be as a movie? The filler would have to be cut down, but the story and characters are very translatable to film. I can imagine a dark and fantastical old New York. I can see creepy old Schaalman, eyes aglow. I can see them giving Sophia a bigger part, making her a little more sassy. And some real life Aladdin would play Ahmad. I would watch that. I would like it. 
 Overall? I would recommend TG&TJ to people who have an attention span when it comes to reading, but not to someone who struggles with long books or slow-burning plots. I think it's a great transitioning book for people who are interested in fantasy but don't want to dive all the way into some monstrous series.

 His son, the heir and new leader, Lord Nagrad, demands a huge amount in compensation. And one other thing... her, as his wife. 
 They call in the Duke; a retired diplomat who has never failed yet. 
 *** 
 This is a short story from the couple who brought you the Kate Daniels series. 
 Here, negotiations stall over details... ahem... how shall we say it? Sex. Just what is she willing to do for the marriage? 
 "Our traditions are rather binding. There are certain things a man could ask of foreign woman that would be considered unclean by the women of the Reigh." 
 "What kind of things?" 
 "Things of sexual nature. Do you consider yourself open-minded in those matters, Lady Deirdre? Would you do all those things at my request?" 
  The prospective groom asks in vivid detail... so they one-up him by responding in even more detail. She wants details of what (exactly) she is expected to participate in. 
 Nagrad slid the card into his reader. It took him a good minute to scroll to the end of the list. His eyes blazed. "How many entries are here?" 
 "Five hundred and forty five." The Duke's voice couldn't have been sweeter. 
 "I request all of them," Nagrad said. 
 "In accordance to entry two hundred and three, will you then submit to having a cast of your anal canal so the dildo employed to penetrate your anus can be made to perfect proportions?" 
 Bwahaha... 
 Of course, there is mostly the money to deal with; enough for a decade of costs... but there is something more between the two of them. Deirdre has studied his people and society for a long time. She, more than anyone knows just what they are and why they can't ask for payment for mercenary services rendered. But clearly, Lord Nagrad has more than a passing interest in her. 
 Deirdre says: 
 "The Reigh don't submit. Not even in battle--when they surrender, they raise their hands to the sides, daring a thrust to the stomach. The kneeling... It's more a gesture of ultimate respect. A Reigh kneels only before his Lord and only once, at the acceptance into service. A Reigh Lord kneels before no one." 
 And at the end, he kneels in front of HER. 
  
 Very amusing sci-fi short.
