I received a copy of this title from the publisher via a Good Reads giveaway. It does not impact my review. 
 This book has been on my radar for such a long time, but for some reason I just never really felt like picking it up. A part of me just thought, "eh, it's just another dystopian." BUT I WAS WRONG! It's so good (bloodydamn good, you might say). This story, while it can in a way be considered a more intense Hunger Games, is so much more than your average dystopian. While some themes are obviously familiar, Brown's writing breathes fresh life into a story of the oppressed and the start of their revolution. 
 Darrow lives in a primitive, strictly regulated society on Mars. Though there is little to no luxury or freedom, he is more or less content with his life. He's the best at what he does and he loves his wife and his family. He believes what he's been told, that he's helping prepare Mars for the weaker race of humans to be able to inhabit it. His wife, Eo, though, is not content with their lot. She believes they are slaves and that they should have more, be more. It is through her sacrifice for the dream of freedom that Darrow is able to find out just how right his wife was. Mars is already inhabited and he and his people are slaves, considered the lowest of the low in the hierarchy. Darrow joins the revolution to honor and avenge his wife and begins the process to become a Gold member of Society and join the Institute, where the leaders of the Gold are made. 
 Red Rising moves at a pretty steady pace, but it took me well over a hundred pages to really get into the story. There was a lot of information given early on about how the society works and I was a bit confused at times. However, once Darrow gets to the Institute the story really begins to pick up. This is where comparisons to the Hunger Games come in, but it is much more brutal and intense and it also provides a lot more opportunity for strategy and intrigue. The betrayals and the deaths are more shocking because in this game, they shouldn't be necessary to win. 
 Brown's writing is really quite brilliant. He doesn't rely on big, shocking twists, which I have come to expect from these type of stories, but there are so many subtle shifts and surprises throughout the story. There isn't a lot of what I would consider banter, but the sarcasm is clever and biting. He also made many seemingly unlikable characters, people I could root for and care about. 
 I'm afraid this little review does not do justice to how great this book is and how much I enjoyed reading it. Though it took a bit to get into the story, once I did I was heavily invested and couldn't put it down. The characters are empathetic, the plot was forever evolving and surprising, and the writing was beautiful. I highly recommend Red Rising and am very excited to start the next book in the series. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 4 Stars

The close to this trilogy is every bit as good as the two that preceded it. If you're not familiar with The Knife of Never Letting Go and The Ask and the Answer, don't even bother with this final volume of the trilogy. Go back and start at the beginning; it will be worth it. 
 Although there are many impressive things about this series, I'm humbled that Ness has taken each book in different directions, constantly expanding and shading the story. Rather than simply continuing adventures of a couple of characters, the books of Chaos Walking seem to expand over grander and wider themes. 
 I now want to sit down with all three and re-read them in one sitting.

I'm not really sure why it took me so long to read this because it's an easy one and by all rights, should be a quick read. I think that the first half is a little bit of a slow build, but it really picks up in the second. Eleanor is a really well-drawn character and even though I was able to see the twist at the end coming, I still enjoyed this. It's a very sweet, yet not cloying, novel that is further enhanced (MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD!) by the fact that it depicts an actual true friendship, instead of lazily devolving into a pat, simplistic love story.

I really enjoyed seeing the outcome of this series. This book definitely built upon things that had happened in The Infinite Sea, so in hindsight I can see the purpose that the second book had, although I felt it was a little weak on its own. I had faith it would pay off and I felt it did! 
 There were a few things I was left confused about, but overall I enjoyed the way that Yancey played with different narratives. He approached the story from several different angles and some events and stylistic choices in the end lent a really unique reading experience. 
 The change in format was a big improvement. In the first 2 books, each section was narrated by only one character, meaning that we sometimes had to rehash the same events to backtrack to where the new narrative hadn't covered yet. In The Last Star, the sections of the book are now by day instead of character, with many narrative changes happening throughout each section. This created a smooth flow and was a great improvement in my opinion! 
 I did notice 2 cases near the beginning of the book where the narrative changed from past tense to present tense for no reason. I'm sure these were typos. Yancey does use past tense for some characters, present for others, and sometimes a character will narrate using both at different times. Some characters also narrate in first person, while others have a third person narrative. I'm not sure why he chose such variety, but I assume it was to create distinct character voices. I can see how this might be confusing, but I ended up thinking it was an interesting stylistic choice. 
 So, there's a big thing that happens at the end and I'm going to hide it as a spoiler, but want to talk about it! Cassie's death was one of the better treatments of a main character death in YA that I've read. I admit that I didn't find it heart wrenching, but I felt it was handled very well. She made a true sacrifice and showed a real understanding of what she would be facing that was not undermined by surprise villains, immunities, or magic solutions popping up to negate her sacrifice. The plan she carried out had been worked toward and brought about a solution that was truly deserved.

I have come to the opinion that an ending to a story is more important than anything else. The conclusion is the last thing a writer leaves her reader. She may choose to leave behind a sweet aftertaste, or a bitter one, and it lingers on the readers tongue as they close its pages forever (well, I mean you can reread it, but it's never the same.) I recently had to say goodbye to one of my favorite shows, How I Met Your Mother. The ending left me bitter and reeling, angry and unsatisfied; but more importantly, it unmasked a truth: this show may not be as clever as I once thought. My favorite show felt polluted, and I would never be able to watch my favorite gang without the shadow of the finale weighing on my mind (YES I HATED IT THAT MUCH. GOD DAMN IT TED MOSBY!) 
 I also felt the same about the Divergent series, because in my opinion, the conclusion revealed just how much of a amateur writer Veronica Roth is, and she spoiled her first two books, which were good/ passable to me. 
 So OBVIOUSLY I feared reading the end of this series, which I was more invested in than Divergent. 
 AND 
 To my surprise and relief, 
 I LOVED IT. 
 SPOILERS BEYOND THIS POINT. 
 As last we left of heroes, Karou and Akiva, they have come to some sort of understanding. No more pointless bruiting, there are more pressing matters at hand. Jael has flown to the human world in order to gain weapons to wipe off the remaining Chimera off the face of Eretz, and to start a war with the Stelians, another race of Seraphim. (I think he just doesn't like their faces, but whatever.) The Misbegotten and Chimera join forces, but not without a little drama, killing, and a resurrection. The group hatches a plan to save humanity and Eretz from this brother slaying emperor. 
 But that's not the part of the story I was particularly drawn to, and I would give this a three star at best. No, the storyline that I found engaging was anything dealing with the fallen angels. It disturbed me the fuck out, it was slightly "trippy" and had a resemblance to Neil Gaiman. So, of course, I LOVED IT.  I liked the idea of the Seraphim as explorers through dimensions, that they carried it too far and unleashed a darkness that threaten to eat everything that was light, also how time is not linear but circular, and that a myth we have heard before may not yet have come to pass.  But I have always been one for slightly ambiguous endings, since it gives me something to think about time to time on my long commutes. As much as I hated the novel A Sense of an Ending, I still wonder what the narrator discovered about his lineage that he decided not to share with his audience, two years later. There is something to the unsaid, the space between novels, that ambiguity, that while immediately may cause distress, in the long run prompts a reread. 
 So IN CONCLUSION, unlike the creators of How I Met Your Mother, I will read any future endeavors by Ms. Taylor. And let's face it, an author who can write a good ending is a rare find.

First in a new paranormal romance series The Sentinel Wars. 
 They are Sentinels. Three races descended from ancient guardians of mankind, each possessing unique abilities in battle to protect humanity against their eternal foes: the Synestryn. 
 Helen Day is haunted by visions of herself surrounded by flames, as a dark haired man watches her burn. So when she sees the man of her nightmares staring at her from across a diner, she attempts to run but instead ends up in the man's arms. Drake, is a Theronai warrior, whose own pain is driven away by Helen's touch. After years of bearing this pain Drake is determined to keep Helen. 
 This is the first book of the series and it's also the first book I've read by Ms Butcher. Even now two days later after I've read Burning Alive I still don't know how I feel about it! It's a really interesting story overall about the Sentinels and how they're protecting mankind from the Synestryn, who are monsters/demons that are wolflike, with a wide jaw of a shark, rows of serrated teeth, black holes where eyes should have been surrounded by singed flesh with rust coloured fur all over its body. They want to eat the Sentinels and any human who find out about them, they're drawn by the smell of blood and are night time creatures. 
 I really enjoyed seeing how Helen evolved through Burning Alive and how she tried not to let her fear of fire stop her from doing what she needed to do and that in the end she wasn't 'damaged' as Gilda and Logan thought but she was being protected. The chemistry between Helen and Drake was pretty great and I'm looking forward to reading more about their progress in the next two books. 
 I really didn't like Gilda, the Gray Lady and I don't see myself warming to her anytime in the future. 
 I'm looking forward to reading Lexi and Zach's story Running Scared which is the third book in the series! 
 Burning Alive is a really great paranormal romance and I'm really looking forward to reading the rest of the series and seeing how everything turns out.

Nemesis is very much like Virals, the series Brendan Reichs co-wrote with his mom, Kathy Reichs. Min is Tory. Tack is most assuredly the boisterous Hiram, and Noah is Shelton. In a way, Nemesis is an alternate version of Virals, which felt a bit like cheating. The basic premise is the same. Min and Noah have mysterious things that keep happening to them, that stands them apart from the rest of the kids in their class. Tack is sarcastic as can be while pushing buttons of his tormentors and authority figures (at times) to a point where I wanted to throw the book. Don't get me wrong, I am just as sarcastic, but there's a time and a place. Pushing someone that is intent on killing you then and there, isn't such a good time to keep pushing them towards pulling that trigger. 
 The premise of Min repeatedly dying, is what kept me going. However, it got old really quickly through her interactions with her psychiatrist. I started to question why he just dispensed Min's medication to her through the office. That sent a big red flag up, which is later explained, but still it irked me. 
 I did like the juxtaposition between Noah and Min's reactions to what was happening to them. Noah was more cautious, scared, and prone to panic attacks, while Min was angry, determined, and questioned everything. It made the book more believable, especially when the man behind the curtain was revealed. 
 I feel like there was too much time leading up to the big hurrah. I found myself having to go back and reread things, because my eyes would cloud over. I'm still trying to figure out how Nemesis worked. My brain is not working with the science very well. I was left with so many questions. The major one being How were Min and Noah repeatedly brought back to life? Where they long dead before the mass gassing? How did Project Nemesis remain a secret for so long? I can't imagine the United States being the only people with an apocalyptic back up plan.  
 I know this is a series, but I just don't think I'll be to continue on with it... at least not at my own expense.
I tried, I really did. But the overemphasis on the romance (i.e. "He's sex on a stick" "she's so hot") overshadowed what was an interesting plot and world building. Too bad.

Nose Graze -- Young Adult book reviews 
 Fluffy, quirky, a bit unrealistic, and totally unexpected--all words that describe 
 The Boyfriend App 
 . None of those are necessarily bad things, but I think they pretty accurately fit this book. 
 There are some very specific things I liked about this book, and some things I didn't like. So I'm going to break it down list-style: 
 Likes 
 * For the most part I liked Audrey. She was nerdy and imperfect. She wasn't always the smartest person (which I'll get to in the dislikes), but I mostly enjoyed her voice and attitude. 
 * I really liked the coding parts! When Audrey was building the app, I was geeking out over the programming and the language. I LOVED it! 
 * I like how The Boyfriend App version 1.0 was realistic. At first I thought it was actually going to work properly and legitimately match you with your perfect boyfriend, but then it kind of backfired, which I thought was a realistic approach, and more along the lines of what I was expecting. 
 * There were some really funny moments in the book; mostly just small sentences here and there that made me chuckle, but I really enjoyed them! Just random things like this: 
 I rolled over and stared at the current love of my life: Hector, my custom-rig desktop I built myself. Hector was like the best kind of boyfriend: smart, trustworthy, and always there when I needed him. I watched his green light blink and listened to the purr of his fans as though he were trying to signal he felt the same way about me. 
 --The Boyfriend App by Kasie Sise 
 Dislikes 
 * I really didn't like the technology substitutes. Instead of this book talking about Facebook, iPhones, iPods, iTunes, and Apple/Samsung rivalry, it made up alternatives. We got: 
 Public Party (a social networking site), buyJams (music-for-purchase website), the buyPlayer (handheld device to play said music), and then, of course, the buyPhone, the Beast (a handheld computer), and the Fiend (a laptop). 
 --The Boyfriend App by Katie Sise 
 Is it just me or are those the most lame names ever. buyPhone? No thanks. At first I was annoyed that the author used alternatives at all... especially when "real" things like Twitter are mentioned. So why have a substitute for Facebook? And instead of talking about the real Apple/Samsung rivalry, we had whole new companies called Public and Infinitum. When something is being marketed as a contemporary book, I just don't like it to have all kinds of fake, made up companies and technologies. But once it got to the end, I think I understood why the author chose to make up companies instead of using real ones. Portraying Apple as some kind of company that illegally brainwashes teenagers into buying its products might be a bit awkward.  
 * I was REALLY confused by the romance. At the beginning of the book, Audrey tells us she's obsessed with Xander, the unobtainable, super hot boyfriend of the queen bee bitch. But then whenever she looks at Aidan she gets all girly and blushy. It took me so long to figure out what the heck was going on. Does she like Xander or Aidan? Or both? Who the heck knows. 
 * Audrey was always going on about how she needed to start waitressing so she could help pay for college. WHAT? Waitressing is crap money. Audrey is supposedly an AMAZING programmer. Why would she not seek out programming freelance jobs, which actually pay a decent amount of money (unlike the laughable minimum wage that is waitressing)? You can easily find freelance jobs online. 
 * When Audrey decided to make The Boyfriend App 2.0 and utilize Public's big brainwashing software thing, I assumed she knew exactly what would happen. Since she's submitting the app to Public, they would obviously look at the code and immediately know that she knows their big secret. And since she already knew they were capable of blackmail, they were obviously going to try to blackmail her too. But when we actually got to that part, it almost seemed like she was SURPRISED that they found out, and then so unsure of what they would do to her. I thought it was super obvious.  
 Summing It Up 
 At about the 50% mark, this book took a very different turn. It went from being cute, funny, and fluffy, to having darker undertones and a lot less realism. The story became extremely unbelievable. It was still fun and enjoyable, but just be warned: it does start to border on kind of ridiculous. 
 I'm pretty confident that The Boyfriend App won't be a good book for everyone. Some people will hate the programming technical stuff, others probably won't like Audrey, some will be caught up with the absolute bitch that is Blake (Audrey's ex-best friend), and I'm sure a lot of people will snicker and roll their eyes as the plot progresses. That being said, I enjoyed this book. It was a bit quirky and it certainly wasn't perfect, but it called to my nerdy side. I actually wish that there was more programming in the book. The actual creation of the app--the bulk of the programming--was over in a heartbeat. 
 I think the book definitely did fizzle out at the end. It never felt fully resolved. Audrey gets some closure with her father, but we never actually get closer with Public, which is the big central conflict.  But overall, this book was entertaining and it made me laugh. I'm glad I read it!

This was my fifth Dessen novel and probably my second favorite out of the five (behind Lock and Key). What I enjoy most about Dessen's novels is how much time you just spend in the main characters head, hearing her thoughts. Sometimes those thoughts can be frustrating, but as a person who likes to think a lot, this appeals to me. There are things I liked and disliked about this novel, so lets get into them. 
 Auden was a likable character, but I didn't find her brilliant. She made some stupid decisions occasionally that didn't really seem to fit her character all that well. She did grow throughout the novel and I enjoyed watching that growth, even if it was slow going at times. 
 The novel doesn't really pick up pace until over half way through. Even then there isn't a whole lot happening, but what was happening kept me interested. It was nice to see Auden having to question her opinions of Heidi and Maggie. She thinks they are superficial at first, but learns over time that nobody can be categorized so simply. 
 The thing I disliked most about this novel was Auden's parents. I just found nothing about them appealing. I know they were supposed to be self absorbed and annoying, but I was hoping for a little more growth than we got. Her mom was working on it and her dad was too, in some ways, but I was constantly frustrated by these two. 
 What I loved most was Eli. Out of the five Dessen novels I've read I haven't liked a guy character as much as I liked Eli. He was complicated, but caring. He wanted to help Auden experience the things she missed out on growing up and their adventures together were so much fun. Honestly, I think this novel would have been better with more of Eli. 
 Overall this was an enjoyable read. It wasn't as emotionally charged as some Dessen novels I've read, but in some ways that was a good thing.

This is one huge ad for Google, which I found rather disturbing in a novel that is ostensibly about a love affair with printed books. Google simply dominates the pages. Even T-minus countdowns flash in the colours of the Google logo. I have to admit that I was a little depressed when my novel about books became a Google love-fest. 
 The publisher marketed this novel as literary fiction, and I think that was an even bigger disappointment than the Google obsession. I expected a lot more substance. Beneath the mystery that propels the story, though, there isn't really much of anything. The characters are all pretty flat, every chapter seems to employ a deus ex machina of one sort or another, and the incessant pulse of the plot leaves no room for thematic exploration. Just because it's a book about books doesn't make it "literary" by default. 
 Most of my negative reactions stem from feeling deceived or wilfully misguided as to the content. This is a solid book with a driving plot that zips along, but just don't expect the thematic exploration or character development that would normally appear in a book marketed as literary fiction.

Wonderful book, quick read. Gaiman is a master at taking reality and fantasy and blending them into something that's not quite real and not completely fantasy. This book is so small and sparsely written that there's tons left to the imagination. Normally I don't like stories that leave lots to the imagination, but in this case, it helped make it scarier and more lush. 
 At the outset, the story seems to point you to a young girl, her mother, and her grandmother who have extrasensory skills. They can read minds, see items not in front of them, conjure a toothbrush from nothing, and even create a moonlit night when it shouldn't be. By the end of the story, I was convinced I was reading a religious allegory. The bulk of the story is about Lettie and the narrator trying to send demons? creatures? back "home". They wind up invoking more dangerous demons to do battle and it backfires.  Lettie winds up sacrificing herself to save the narrator against the demon birds. Yet she's not really gone. Her mother places her in the titular ocean with the hope that she will come back some day. In some form, she does, though the narrator nor the reader doesn't ever see her as a girl again. She may have returned as a kitten. Apparently, our narrator has returned repeatedly to the ocean at the end of the lane, but he doesn't remember it.  The story invokes Lettie as a Christ-like figure, with her mother as God and her grandmother as the Holy Ghost. The bad guys that are constantly being fought are creatures of Hell. Or maybe it's just a rip roaring fantasy. With Gaiman, you never know.

Like a lot of others, at first I was very sceptical about this book. I thought it will be all about battles, powered suits and futuristic weapons. But then I changed my mind, also like a lot of other readers. Now it's about futility and absurdity of war. And the best way to show that is to describe the war itself in all it's colours. By choosing the genre of science fiction Joe Haldeman may be losing a large part of his audience, but he is doing a great job by putting this mind blower into a heap of war-glorifying books. There's nothing to glorify, he says, and it's hard to argue with him after reading this book. 
 What he doesn't say is that there's only one kind of heroic war which still needs glorifying. It's war for freedom, a guerilla liberation war against invaders and tyrants. (Not much of a spoiler but reveals the ending, in a way) --> But even the revolution that led to the end of Forever War in the book seemed to be peaceful, but then it also led to some kind of a Brave New World, a society that doubtfully can be enjoyed by a modern man. Not a best counterweight to a war. If it's the only way to live without war, I probably still choose war. But after all, there's a lot of planets left for the old-timers like our Mandella.  
 What seems very unlikely to me is the Army sex regulations described in the novel. Haldeman was probably inspired by hippie 'free love' concept, but it's hard to believe that they can encourage sexual promiscuity in the Army and it won't cause any troubles. Heinlein's Starship Troopers is more credible with it's gender segregation. 
 Update 
 After some thinking about the ending and thanks to one great discussion I had, I decided that Haldeman really messed up his anti-war message which he tried to deliver throughout the book. What happens in the end is complete ideological defeat of humanity, because humans took model of society of the enemy. What the author offers as an alternative to war is some hive-mind communism with no place for personality. I'd rather choose war. 
 Thus I changed my mind about the book. If you read it to escape from reality (which is very likely in case of war science fiction novel with strong main character) and put yourself in place of William Mandella while reading, then all is fine for you. You have your happy end and put the book aside being satisfied. But if you try to think about politics behind the war and it's ending and try to analyze what the author tried to convey, you realise that he is weak at politics and this deus ex machina ending was written because nothing better came to his mind. He just gave up the plot line for war and future of humanity and concentrated on the love story of main characters. For me, it is bad.

This is the kind of book that requires a lot of attention and careful reading. Not because there are hidden clues or details that can missed that are terribly important later on. It's more because it's very easy to get lost in the constant changing environment and motives when you're not paying close enough attention. 
 And really, that's the biggest problem I had with this book. It was just as fun as the previous two, it had just as much thieving and conning going on, and the characters were just as wonderful as they'd been from the very beginning. 
 However, I found myself reading the same paragraph over and over, trying to make sense of what exactly was going on and what it had to do with the next paragraph. Honestly, I did get distracted very easily throughout the book, but I found it annoying that I couldn't just pick up where I left off with no confusion like I usually do.

If they were reading Demons of the Ocean or The Way of the Warrior, this could be the next rung on the reading ladder. Fans may also want to look at Croak.

If there is such a thing as a literary thriller, this is it. This is Terry Hayes's first novel and all I can say is...I want the sequel NOW. 
 The basic building blocks (global cat and mouse chase, ultra secret agent, Middle Eastern terrorist) are standard, but the novel itself is certainly not. Hayes's characterizations, ingenious plotting (it's scary real in terms of plausibility) and flat out gripping writing are all superb. The character of Pilgrim is well-drawn, as are the supporting characters. 
 Hayes's descriptions of exotic locales are great, too. He creates fictional places so believable that I had to Wikipedia them to see whether they really did exist or not. 
 I simply could not put this down and I would go so far as to say that it might be the best thriller I've ever read. I also loved the way that he set things up for a sequel, but didn't necessarily create a cliffhanger that has to be resolved. Even at 600+ pages, I was really sad to see this end.

Megan Hart is so accomplished at switching the traditional romance male/female characteristics. In traditional romance novels it's the hero who is tortured, damaged, love-averse. And the heroine who sweeps in and opens up the hero to love and life. In Stranger, Grace, a funeral director who experiences death on a daily basis, avoids suffering, loss and emptiness by forsaking romantic relationships. Instead she experiences a different type of emptiness by hiring "rentboys" like Jack. Sure the sex is hot, hot, hot with Jack but it's not enough with Sam in the picture. Sam is sweet, sexy, irresistible, and most-importantly, persistent. 
 Sam does win his way into her Grace's heart. But not without breaking it...In the end being apart from Sam was just as important life lesson for Grace as letting love into her life in the first place. Grace learned that she was strong enough to move on and be without him. 
 "I learned that I didn't want to live without you, but that I could....Because before you, I was so afraid of being unable to live without someone, I could never live with someone."  
 This book, like Hart's other books that I've read, Broken and Dirty, is more than your average fluffy romance. It's intense, gut-wrenching but still very hot. I can't wait to meet more of Hart's angsty-flawed-but-relatable heroines and the heros who fall for them.

I Capture the Castle is a coming-of-age novel of 17 year old Cassandra Mortmain. She lives with her family in an old English castle which they lease. Her family is poor but she has a pretty positive outlook on her life. She has a famous father who wrote a critically-acclaimed novel but has gone on the decline after an incident that throws him in jail for three months. He has not published nor written anything since. She has a 29 year old stepmother who is Bohemian and very nice. She previously modeled in London for artists but would not be able to support the family on such an income as most of her earnings would be spent on her time in London. Cassandra also has two siblings, an older sister, 21 year old Rose, and a younger brother, 15 year old Thomas. Rose is very selfish and cannot stand being poor. They also have a servant boy who lives with them but is not paid, 18 year old Stephen. The story starts with Cassandra receiving a journal so she decides to write down her life's adventures, aiming to be somewhat of an author to create a good narrative to read. There is quite a buzz in her life as the landlord of their castle passes away and his heirs come from America to England to claim his property. 
 This novel started out all right-- Cassandra is a pretty good narrator, at least at first. After a time however, I am so frustrated over all the details she decides to include. I realize this is supposed to be a journal on her personal life, and it isn't so much about a plot, but after reading so many small details and events I grew very bored. Then, after a point, Cassandra grows to be a whiny teenager given the events. She finds out that she loves Simon, now engaged to her sister, and just cannot bear this fact.  She now is an incredibly annoying personality while also being annoying on everything she includes in her journal. I was disgusted and barely wanted to continue. Really, I was rooting for Stephen to "capture" Cassandra's heart, but after a kiss with Simon she is convinced she loves him and no other. Sure, she does kiss Stephen but somehow that kiss is just not love but surely Simon's was. She has a very fickle heart. This will be a review of the entire series, as I'm a lazy asshole. 
 First, it should be said that I'm not in the target audience, and that might be the main issue I have with this series. I read this at the urging of a friend who has loved this since childhood and it appears well loved here; I assume it reads better for kids. 
 Anyway, pros of this series: 
 -Strong female knight!! But this is known. 
 -Main characters have flaws, and their flaws are acknowledged by themselves and others 
 -Alanna knows what she wants and how she deserves to be treated. She demands respect and is a good role model. She grows up slowly over the course of the series and her character development is believable. 
 -The morals shoved forcibly down the reader's throat are worthwhile morals for kids, if heavy-handed. 
 -Alanna gets three romances that are all handled (fairly) believably and respectably 
 Cons: 
 -The writing is weak with many exposition dumps - classic mistake of telling instead of showing - but it is the author's first foray into writing. 
 -Good guys are good, bad guys are bad - the gray area in books like Harry Potter is entirely absent. 
 -Good guys are ALWAYS right, and nobody has to learn from their mistakes. 
 -Very weak world building that is largely built on established fantasy tropes. 
 -Plot makes absolutely NO sense at times:  ex. Thom's bizarre decision to raise the evil that was after his sister and king over... a bet??? what the FUCK dude  
 -As much as I love George , he flirts with teen Alanna while he's seven years older..? uhhh 
 -Most characters aside from Alanna, Jon, and George entirely dodge development and stay with one note. 
 -Probably more, but it's 4AM so it's time to stop ranting. 
 End Verdict: I didn't find it worthwhile to read. As great a character as Alanna was, her world and plot were weak. Today there is a lot of fantasy with strong, female characters so that virtue alone doesn't forgive the multitude of other faults. 
 However, the author gets markedly better later on! I wouldn't give up on Pierce books, but this quartet is eh overall.

Oh, the horror of dead-end, retail, big-box employment! Just such employment is necessary for Amy to keep her life going, which mainly seems to be about living in an apartment instead of at home. Fair enough, I don't want to live at home either. Amy is cowed enough by this situation that she accepts her daily attendance as an adequate cog in the giant ORSK machine, but the mind-numbing corporate doublespeak of the management, and the insistence that she perform her duties, not just with diligence, but with mandated enthusiasm makes her defiant. ORSK is a IKEA knockoff store, and the chapters are interspersed by descriptions of various pieces of furniture with fake-Euro/Swedish names like Liripip as one might find in a store catalog. As this was an audio version, I'm not familiar with any features of the physical book other reviews mentioned. Amy doesn't have a plan, beyond staying employed long enough to transfer to a different store and away from her present manager, Basil, who--horror of horrors--thinks she has potential! Then comes the assignment to stay at the store overnight to catch a vagrant making his home in the ORSK showroom. But is Carl the Homeless Guy the only thing going bump in the night? Amy, Basil, and model employee Ruth Anne are going to find out! Horrorstor is half comedy/half horror, and it's kind of an awkward combination. If Hendrix's earlier book "My Best Friend's Exorcism" was coming-of-age horror, this is workplace-comedy horror. Still, Hendrix executes the premise pretty well. In this workplace, he has a lot of grist for the mill, between the nonsense names of the furniture, the corporate-speak language, and the marketing and staging tricks ORSK uses to confuse and seduce its shoppers. You'll recognize the tricks--who hasn't gotten lost in an IKEA? Hendrix also has a way with graphic, over-the-top images that would fit right in on American Horror Story, images you won't soon forget. I won't spoil the ending, only say that it will solve the mystery, although Hendrix has his eye on a higher prize: how do you find meaning in a job you detest?

This book held such promise from the initial synopsis. As soon as I read it on Amazon, I knew I had to have it; "...perfect for fans of the high tension and expert pacing of The Secret History..." Using my second favorite novel of all time in the premise of a book, and likening the two, how could I not want to read this? As you can probably tell, my expectations were sky high with the hopes of reading something on par with Ms. Donna Tartt. 
 And let me say this: Everything about this book fell flat. 
 The characters, the plot, the game itself... there was nothing that gripped me. 
 For one, the shifting POV of first person present to third person was an odd choice. It threw me off aburptly, and continued to do so throughout until both POVs finally came to the same place in time. The characters themselves were utterly forgettable. Four extremely bland, and two slightly less, people converge to play a game. Of course, I had high hopes the game would make everything more interesting. Instead, it was an annoyance. First off, it wasn't explicitly explained. If this is to take up a majority of the book I'm reading, I want to know the ins-and-outs back and front. We don't get that here, only a vague idea of how the game is played. Now, where's the fun in that? The game continued being lame, and the players managed to become even more boring as the plot "progressed," focusing more on their day-to-days and school life, than the mental mind games of a supposedly psychologically deranged game. 
 Everything was so utterly predicatble, too. The final players (mentioned within the first 50 pages) being revealed early on, the tricks and deceits all completely obvious. I truly expected the final face off to be a roaring extravaganza of the most brutal kind, but it was the exact antithesis of everything fun. Talk about anti-climactic. So disappointed in the way the climax was handled. 
 Lastly, the two "main" characters (if you want to look at it that way), I loathed; Absolutely HATED! Really, I could not find anything redeeming about either. As much as the author tried to portray them with good qualities, their attitudes and their actions outweighed any kind of connection with me. The fact that there was one particular character Chad , who was portrayed as almost 'villainous' was absurd. Let it be known that Joylon is one of the most annoying characters I've ever read in literature. I hated him. Scratch that, I STILL hate him. How does he get portrayed as the victim in the end? Sure, he was a complete mess, but rightfully so! Mark, anyone? I just don't get it... I would've loved to see him continue playing that game til his demise. . 
 I thought I was going to read something on par with my beloved The Secret History, but instead, I crawled through the sludge of another weak imitation of far superior works. 
 In the end, I can't say anything good about this book. I had to force myself to finish it, when I should never have even bothered in the first place.

Thank you, Tahereh Mafi, for not crushing my soul with this book! I was so nervous to start reading Ignite Me because I love the series and all the other series enders I've been reading lately have not been good. While Ignite Me may not have been perfect, it kept true to the story Mafi started in Shatter Me and didn't end with me throwing my Nook against the wall. 
 Ok, Spoilers Galore from here on out! 
 Plot 
 We pick up soon after we left off in Unravel Me. Juliette is alive and she's pissed. She's ready to go after Anderson and take down the Reestablishment - with her bare hands. Warner is hiding her in his private rooms at his base and informs her that The Resistance and Omega Point have been wiped out. When he takes her to see for herself Kenji shows up and lets her know that Adam, James, Castle, and a few others are still alive and are staked out at Adam's old apartment and they head there. 
 Juliette is looking for them to join her in her plan to fight Anderson, but they've all lost their will and their spirit and Adam has basically lost his freaking mind. When he finds out she's been with Warner, wants to work with Warner, and defends Warner, he goes ballistic. Ugly, very un-Adam like things are said. We found out in Fracture Me that Adam isn't quite the saintly, loving guy we've always known, but I felt it was a little extreme here when he reacts to Juliette. Like almost every interaction Adam has in this book is him being an obnoxious, hateful, jerk. 
 Long story short, the remaining Omega Point clan comes to stay on base in Warner's private gym and they all begin training. Juliette and Warner's relationship changes and languishes and then blossoms. Yes, Juliette chooses Warner! And I love it. 
 Juliette and her friends perform a demonstration to Warner's soldiers to let them know about their plan and to ask for help. It works and soon Anderson and his troops are coming to shut them down. Juliette goes after him, kills him, and takes on the role as Commander. It ends with the first small victory in the battle to take back their world. It ends with hope. 
 I'm sure there will be some people that will be upset that everyone in Juliette's group survives - that it might be unrealistic. But I think it's great. And it makes sense. They're basically super heroes. Of course they'll survive. And Juliette has become basically unstoppable and with Warner by her side, they can do just about anything. Like he's been saying since the first book. 
 "So the two of you" - Ian tries to find his voice- "I mean, together-you two could basically-" 
 "Take over the world?" 
 Characters 
 Ok, can we talk about the character development in Juliette!? She's grown so much throughout the series. In this book she finally starts to stand up for herself. She lets go of her fear about almost everything. She's ready to not only fight back, but to lead the fight. She also stops feeling guilty about her feelings for Warner. Though we all fell in love with Adam at first, it was a little too "insta-love" to ever really make sense. Juliette realizes that it was more the fact that he was the first person to ever be nice to her and to ever be able to touch her that drove her to him. And he was in love with the idea of the girl he once knew. Her relationship with Warner, especially now that we know more about Warner, makes much more sense. And with him, she becomes the strong, determined character we always wanted her to be. 
 Though Juliette is developed and then some, the rest of the characters don't get quite the same treatment. There are a couple of minor characters from Omega Point that I don't really remember or care about and nothing about them in this book made me really care for them either. 
 There is a lot more Kenji and I really like him in this book. But when did he and Juliette become best friends? He was one of her only friends, but I don't remember him being so attached to her. I feel like I want a Kenji novella now. And am I the only one who was surprised that he isn't gay and in love with Castle? I thought that was hinted at in the previous book, but I guess not. 
 And then there's Adam. Oh, Adam. He's the ex-boyfriend from hell in this book. He's just horrible. There's too many scenes of him yelling the same hateful things to Juliette. He finally realizes that Juliette really is a different person than he thought and he stops being a jerk. When he finally tells Warner that they're brothers, I thought things got resolved just a little too easily. Warner is "not unhappy" to have brothers and no longer hates Adam. Adam agrees. 
 Readability 
 Mafi has a distinct style that I've always enjoyed. What impresses me most is the way it's evolved since the first book. As Juliette becomes more stable and more sane throughout the series, the writing becomes less frenetic. There are less crossed out sentences and words and in this book there were none at all. Because Juliette is no longer afraid of her thoughts. Brilliant. 
 Enjoyability 
 I loved this book! It was a great end to the series. Though I feel like there could be more story to tell, I like how it left off. I appreciate that it was the continuation of Juliette's story and didn't go off track like other series have. My only issues were really how uncharacteristically horrible Adam became and that the minor characters were kind of just filler. 
 Rating (out of 5) 
 Plot: 4 
 Characters: 4 
 Readability: 4.5 
 Enjoyability: 4.5 
 Overall Average: 4.25 stars

You know I'm going to say it because... ugh, how can I not? That cover! That wonderful, beautiful, spectacular cover! If covers could dream, they'd dream of being this cover. Yes, Ten Thousand Skies Above You, I'm coming for you in 2016! 
 A Thousand Pieces of You is the story of Marguerite (not a name I would have picked, I'm gonna just throw that out there now, but whatever) and an invention crafted by her brilliant parents. This invention, the Firebird, gives it's bearer the ability to traverse to alternate realities. The Firebird is so bad ass that it is worth killing for. Marguerite's father is murdered and Marguerite commandeers a Firebird to chase his killer through these alternate dimensions. Is the science sound? I have no fucking clue and I rarely read books like this with a burning desire to prove or disprove the scientific integrity. If you say it allows you to jump to parallel universes, hey, I'm on board. Sounds good to me. 
 What I love about this book is the promise of what awaits you in those infinite realities that mirror our own. Literally anything could happen and it really makes for a fantastic amount of material for storytelling. For me, Claudia Gray mostly nails it. Sure, some of the destinations were not quite as exciting for me as others, but that wasn't a real deal breaker for me. The characters felt a little more mature than most of the characters I read in YA, which I enjoyed, and I actually, quite surprisingly, caught myself getting a little swept up in the romance of it all. Romance in YA is not generally my thing. It tends to be my least favorite part of any non-romance specific book because I feel like nine times out of ten it is predictable and/or unbelievable. I actually bought the romance here and, if you can believe it, got a little swoony. 
 One major flaw for me, though, was... when you're dead, you're fucking dead. Stop pretend killing characters, authors, it almost never makes sense. Take a page from J.K. Rowling or George R.R. Martin - there is something so emotionally impactful about killing characters that people love. It's real. Do it and regret nothing.

The Regency period is fascinating to me. All of the balls and etiquette really attract my interest. In this story, Sir Horace visits his sister and tells her that he is sending his daughter to stay with her for a time. No one expects Sophy. She is bright, witty, daring, and completely goes against the grain. She brings the younger children in the family a pet monkey. Really...who does that? She buys herself a phaeton and races it like no other. She doesn't act prim, proper, and shy, like most of the other girls her age. There's no one she irritates more than her cousin, the one in control of the finances and properties--Charles. And annoy him she does! 
 Sophy is an extremely fun character! She really could care less what people think of her. How would it be to really not care and to be yourself? Especially in a day when everyone tried to fit in the mold. She does what she has to do to help those around her, even if she finds herself in unusual and seemingly dangerous situations. One of those situations was my favorite--I loved it when she went to visit the money lender. The way she handled him had me laughing out loud--especially when $$$ finds out. She's a busybody, trying to manage and arrange the lives of all those around her, yet she does it in an almost endearing way. She's a master of reverse psychology and really knows how people work. 
 Charles is so stuffy and uptight, yet we get a glimpse of why he is the way he is and it all makes sense. Still, I felt that sometimes Sophy acted the way she did just to get a reaction out of him. She seemed to love to catch him with his own words and turn them against him. 
 All in all, a perfectly delightful book that really shows the Regency period at its finest.

So a review of a book reviewer I like to follow said that this book has a shocking plot twist you don't see coming at all. Well, I must say, I have no idea what that book reviewer was referring to. I suppose I have about 2 guesses, but neither of the events did I see as a HUGE shock. Maybe this caused me to dream up a HUGE shocker that I thought would be out of this world, and I was trying to guess what that shocker/plot twist might be throughout my reading, so maybe that's part of it. Nonetheless, I must say I was not shocked at much. 
 Part of the reason for me to dream up a huge plot twist throughout my reading is due to the fact that nothing really happens in this book. It is about a girl who decides to quit being a Princess because she doesn't want to have an arranged marriage. She wants to marry for love. She runs away on her wedding day with her charge (who is a really good friend to completely throw away her ENTIRE life to go with this Princess, I must say. A bit unrealistic in fact, as she has a love of her life and everything to stay for in the capital. She really shouldn't have run away....) to a town about 10 days south of the captial, because the Princess is great at tracking so she pretends to head North and then hide her tracks and somehow manages to not be found when she is staying in a pretty decent size town only 10 days away.... Crazy, but I just keep going along with it. Now, even though no King's man/soldier can find her, the Prince she was betrothed to and an Assassin from a country across the continent manage to find her not long after she has been in town. The two even run into each other and pose as friends, each for their own individual cover up. Crazy. Nonetheless I keep reading. 
 Nothing happens. The Princess has attractions to both men, and the author just plays at the reader's head at which one she will choose. So a love triangle, yes. Why am I giving this 3 stars? Despite nothing happening, it managed to keep my attention, and I enjoy a decent love story, so playing with my head sometimes entertains me. One thing that I really liked is that once the Prince and the Assassin meet the Princess, the reader, though knowing that one is an Assassin and the other a Prince, does not know which one is which, and the author leaves it as you to figure it out. I enjoy a good puzzle, and this is a love story puzzle! It was the first I encountered that was written in such a manner, and I must say I enjoyed this. 
 As for the fantasy element, not really there. It is kinda there and probably will be relevant in later books. This one is just more of a romance. Not really a curl your toes romance, mind you, again, just play with your head love triangle. 
 It leaves off at a cliff hanger. It's a decent cliff hanger. I can't say I care that much, but I do plan on continuing the series. The Princess isn't that bad of a character so I care a little bit. Through bratty, she does want to prove her worth as a human being, and she is pretty loyal to her good friend (WHO THREW AWAY EVERYTHING TO COME WITH). The writing itself wasn't bad either. Not beautiful or breath-taking like some others, but not terrible.

The twist at the end threw me off completely, I thought I had figured out most of the plot line, but I most definitely had not. 
 As much as I enjoy the graphic novels of the main series, I LOVE the fact that these books are actual novels.
I could've done without the love triangle, and I probably shouldn't have read Destroy Me before this one because it really makes you wonder about the better couple.

Born of Fire was much more enjoyable than I had anticipated and now I'm annoyed at myself for putting off reading it for so long. Why did I put it off, well Shahara Dagan is a bounty hunter, she's a kick-ass heroine and I was put off by that. After reading plenty of other reviews on Born of Fire I was sure that I wasn't going to like it, as Syn is the ultimate tortured hero and I couldn't see how a kick-ass heroine was going to be a great match for him. But I should have know better. Ms Kenyon has never let me down with any of her books and I should have know I would love it. Ms Kenyon was the first author I read for paranormal romance two years ago and I will still happily read one of her books today! 
 As a child Syn was raised as a tech-thief until his livelihood uncovered a truth that could end his life. Now trained as an assassin, he allows no one to threaten him. He is the darkness that swallows his enemies whole. Shahara Dagan is the best bounty hunter in the universe. She needs the money from capturing Syn to help save her sister. There's only one problem, Syn is a close family friend of her brother, he's helped out the Dagans countless times. But if she saves him, both of their lives will be on the line. Shahara knows Syn is innocent of the crimes he's been accused of but she believes in the justice system and the only hope Shahara has of saving Syn is to find the evidence he buried long ago. 
 This is a brilliant series! I truly loved the first book Born of Night and was swept away with the pace of Born of Fire. It never slowed once and I found it hard to drag myself away, even for a cup of tea! Syn is an amazing tortured hero, you get all of his background through the story and it is such a heart breaking story you can't help but sympathise for him. In a way you can respect what Shahara does, she does what she thinks is right not out of fear but in the end out of love for Syn. She's a brilliant blood thirsty kick-ass heroine that you can't help but admire after everything she's been through.I really enjoyed the opening of the book with Syn in all his kick-ass glory putting down the assassin's sent to kill him. 
 I really can't explain how much I enjoyed this book and was shocked when I read the preface that publishers weren't willing to buy this book from Ms Kenyon when she first tried selling it. There loss and now it's are gain! 
 This is a brilliant series I can't wait to read the next book Born of Ice and I can hope that the series may continue. If not it's just a great small series. 
 I would happily recommend any Sherrilyn Kenyon book to new readers and would say if you pick up a book from any of her series always go for the first one.

An interesting story on its own, and a fine companion to Boxers. Especially interesting for how it renders faith and religious devotion with nuance and humanity. The parallels between the two books are fascinating, even as the individual stories hold the reader's attention. Well worth reading.

I read this book in one day. There's always a hidden twist at the end, and this one does not disappoint. Even though it's an easy read, I enjoy her character dynamics: what people say and what they choose to keep unsaid. The alcoholism was oversimplified: both alcoholic parents drank to the point of passing out in the living room, and while that may be, many alcoholics are not that extreme, and have other ways of damaging their children.

Around Britian, there have been attacks against Britains by Indians. They are stripped and hung with a note on them. It is up to Earl Phantomhive and Sebastian to figure out who is doing them and stop them before it happens again. 
 While walking around London, Ciel and Sebastian get threatened by a group of Indians, who have been forced to live in the slums. Two suspect that this group are the ones responsible. Before they are able to do any harm, the two male strangers we saw at the end of the previous volume shows up and "saves" them. They are Prince Soma and his servant Agni who has his right hand and forearm bandaged which is said to be called the Right Hand of Kali. The pair are looking for a young woman who was taken by the name of Mina. Because he saved them, Some and Agni, makes themselves in the Phantomhive manor, despite being told numerous times to get out. 
 On first impression, Soma seems to be a brat and immature, viewing his world in Indian as the way it works all over. Not realizing that different places have different customs. And not everyone is going to bow down to him. Soma is very devoted to Soma, and sees him as a God, because he took him away from his old life and gave him a new one. 
 While searching for Mina and the person responsible, Ciel tells Soma that had he not been kidnapped and tortured, he would be just like him. Immature and believing the world revolves around him. They discover that Agni knew where Mina was along and was working for the person that took her into order to protect Soma. He was the one responsible for the attacks. With Agni on his side, the man knows he will win the Royal Warrant and the Curry Contest. It is discovered that Agni's Right Hand of God, is not called that because of its strength but because of its god like ability. Sebastian is going to enter the contest too to hopefully win the Warrant for the company. 
 I can already tell next volume is going to be really interesting.

I had a hard time figuring out a bunch of different portions of the plot. First: the space between stars seems pretty minimal, considering how easy space travel is. There wasn't any focus on any of the technology or the time period, so I'm not entirely sure when it is. They don't seem to have cellphones or anything, but all of our power by then is pretty much renewable. We've almost figured out DNA and genetic coding but still haven't figured out cancer. 
 Also, I'd like to do ask a question. Let me set the stage: you are on a ship that has a total of 7 people on board. You get an incoming transmission from someone on a planet that offers to let you refuel and to trade some goods. He also mentions that his planet is almost entirely men. Do you: 
 A) Dock, have everyone keep a safe distance from the locals just in case, get your shit and get out 
 B) Be friendly to those who are close by, but still get your shit and get out 
 C) Send your two women that are of child-bearing age into a world of men that were just told that humanity almost died out? 
 I mean COME ON. As soon as the guy in the transmission said that I knew what was going to happen. Why was it that every single person on board ignored that little tidbit? Of course they're going to go after the two women! They think they're all going to die out! Imbeciles. 
 That was my problem throughout the whole book. Rena was a nonstop nutcase the entire time, and no one thought to actually listen to what she was saying. It's like ignoring the kid at school who says he hates everyone and wants to kill everyone and then brings a gun to school. You can't really say you didn't see it coming, can you? 
 It wasn't just with that one stop though. It was also when they docked on Alegria and figured out everyone was on shut down. Again: WHAT DID YOU EXPECT? I saw that crap coming a mile away! And never mind that Jamie was never in any kind of mindset to actually be reacquainted with her ex. That was just moronic from the start. 
 The longer I think about this the less I like it. Initially I was going to give it three stars, but after writing this I'm going to stick with two.
A clever, creative, humorous, semi-poignant first novel that rewrites history and comments on the similarities between the U.S. now and 100 years ago.

I WAS SO EXCITED! And, for the most part, I enjoyed the ride. I'll even go so far as to say this was a good book. I'd've rated this a 4 or 5 star book but the two things really got to me -- so this may very well be a 5 star book to you. 
 So, moving along, there were two things that really kicked me out of the story: 
 The Lesser Evil (One star off): The relationship between Peter and Mel. I like Mel. I think I'd even like that relationship in another setting. The problem I had was that it seemed to be the authors attempt at Peter 'getting over' what happened last book and I think that's shitty. He's in love with Leslie so we just chuck another girl he can screw and he'll be so over her? Maybe I could buy that as character growth from a lesser author but not Aaronovitch. He can do much better. 
 The Greater Evil (Two stars off): There is absolutely no explanation or reason why everything in the book happens. Absolutely none. We don't know why the girls were taken. We don't know the relationship between the village people and the others. It's just like he comes, runs around, screws Mel, gets the kids back: The. End. 
 Here we have a character that love to ask why questions and I love him for it. Yet he doesn't do that at all. What do cutting trees have to do with things? We never know! What about that river? Who knows! Why, if their purpose was to switch children, did they take Peter? Who knows! 
 It's maddening! All this new shit happens and it's like suddenly no explanation needs to be given. And then we get all these mysterious calls/texts from Leslie and they have no explanation or need to be there either. 
 In the end, this book left me deeply, deeply dissatisfied.

I like the main character most of the time, and the world building and pace of the the story was good. The mystery was ruined for me by how much I hated the character Knight. Having read other reviews, I seem to be in the minority. Usually I can ignore romances I don't care for, but I couldn't just skip the parts with him in it because he was in too much, and everything he said and did just made me want somebody to smack him. I hope it's not too spoilery to say I think the abuse of authority and sexual harassment is not OK because perpetrator is good looking, and that a true "alpha" type would respect others enough not be so condescending, rude and high handed. I also was disappointed that she seemed to keep putting up with it (with a minor show of verbal sparing) instead of doing something to put him in check.  The part where she lets him get away with sleeping in her bed was particularly annoying. Her boss's boss used his position and power to push an unwanted sexual situation, and`then told her to lighten up. She treated it like a minor annoyance. It really pissed me off.  I think that if she grew up and made him act like a professional and found another love interests who treats her like an equal, then I could like this series. For some people this is a safe fantasy where the overbearing man is sexy and therefore the situation is hot and a tease. If that floats you boat, this is a fun read. I do like the author, so I am hoping she will write something that won't hit my "She should file a law suit." buttons. If so, I'll probably give it a better review.

What a great sweet story from Sue Brown. Forty year old Peter takes his dog Harry to the vet since the dog is not doing well. It is the end of the road for Harry but the beginning for Peter and Evan the vet. 
 Peter has two kids and has been divorced for some time after his wife cheated on him. Evan is in a relationship with another guy. But can it be called a relationship when he barely ever sees the guy? They are both lonely guys who fall into an easy friendship. But Evan is attracted to Peter and so is Peter. 
 This book brings you a slow build up in their relationship. Peter is quite open-minded and while he is OK admitting he likes Evan he still needs time to assimilate what it means to be in a relationship with a guy. Plus Evan also has to deal with ending his relationship with his "boyfriend" before taking in on one with Peter. 
 This was my first Sue Brown book and not the last. Pick this one up if you are in search of a nice comfort read. But beware that there is a bit of sadness at the beginning due to the loss of Harry.

Rothfuss has impressed me with this book. While I would love nothing more to tell you that the book was packed with new and original ideas, I cannot. It is however like a welcome breeze on a hot day, familiar but thoroughly enjoyed anyway. Most books it takes me a few chapters to get into the world and enjoy the characters, not this one. By the middle of the second chapter I was hooked. I was hesitant to pick up a story telling book as I usually don't enjoy them very much. Kvothe story is different though, you can feel the emotion behind it and at times you just wanted to scream because of what is happening to him. When his family was killed  I saw it coming and was still almost in tears for him. The ending ties enough of the loose ends up to leave you feeling satisfied while leaving enough open that you can't wait for more, i will be starting "The Wise Man's Fear" immediately

Beautiful language. Hauntingly realistic and gave me the shivers a couple of times. 
 The build-up of suspense was skillfully done and Stiefvater brings the pieces of the puzzle together in a way that doesn't leave you thinking she came up with it on the spot. 
 I don't want to give you the feeling that it's horror, though. (i'm just a scaredy cat.) The dialogue between the characters left me collapsing in a hopeless heap of catching my breath and not quite succeeding giggles. 
 My one complaint is: 
 The sequel HASN'T COME OUT YET! >:( Hmph. >.<

 What is it about books with warnings? 
 I love them!!! They push us and make us squirm in our seats. Warnings give us a sense of unforeseen danger ahead. And, at the very least, we know something is about to happen. 
 Early on in the story the reader gets an inclination on the direction this story is headed. But the majority of the book is told from the heroine's pov and that creates a mistrust in the reader's thought process. The heroine becomes crazy with suspension to the point of making some foolish choices. Her suspensions make the reader doubt themselves... 
 Maybe I'm wrong and this isn't going in the direction I originally thought? 
 Maybe the heroine is right to think and feel this way. 
 Even though, I was right with my initial thought process, I loved how the heroine's opinions and actions made me skeptical of the situation unfolding across the pages.

Spoilers ahead: 
 This book had the most unappealing, irritating, annoying, female lead EVER. 
 Hush hush is a story about a self-centred girl named Nora Grey who was apparently an average teenage girl until the oh so mysterious Patch came along. 
 So here goes, the only thing I liked about this book was the concept. I liked the concept of Fallen Angels. The concept of them falling and being brought back and all that technicalities was kind of cool, but as usual, what's the use of a concept if you cannot execute it in an awesome way. 
 Nora 
 This is what I feel every time Nora opens her mouth. 
 Nora is a bipolar, selfish, self-centered, assuming,stupid, lying, spineless girl. Maybe to some she wouldn't appear as spineless after that sacrifice at the end but after reading the VA and Bloodlines series, Nora is the most spineless female lead I have encountered. Though my reading list is not that broad, I don't care and that doesn't change the fact that she's a horrible female lead 
 I really hate her. I mean she almost spent half of the book making up her mind about Patch. She's like a girl that's always on her period. The song Hot & Cold perfectly describes her. I literally wanted to pull my hair out every time she does that. Oh wait... she's like that for the entire duration of the book. I probably would've gone bald by now if i did pull my hair out. haha. 
 I can't blame anyone who's trying to kill her. If I was a character in this book I would've been one of the people vying to kill her. She'll also be at the top of my priority list. 
 Patch 
 Now Patch, i don't really get what's the fuss about Patch is. Aside from having badass tastse for his mode of transportation and his badboy aura, I don't really get what's all the hullabaloo about. He's got no personality, maybe there were some instance that i saw some spark that would have potential to be in the list of my hot-fictional-guys, but he was always "barely-there". He was kinda useless. Aside from almost killing Nora (which if he didn't change his mind about, would've put him on my hot-fictional-guys list. Not like anyone cares if he's on my list.), he was as I've said was barely there. 
 Patch is like a cop from the action movies, they seem to look like badass but in reality they arrive when the commotion's almost finish. Patch is a pretentious badass. The author made the readers feel like Patch is your typical badass male lead but he seems to always be missing in action. 
 the writing also didn't help in warming up to the story. There were times that i went from "okay" to "What the fuck did I just read?" There were also times that the transition from one scene to another felt like there was something missing. That Nora was kind of having memory gaps. haha. It sometimes gave me a hard time in imagining things. The only redeeming quality of this book were the times that Nora's being humiliated because of the consequences of her stupid choices. 
 I'll probably finish the series just to see how everything will end and because I sort of don't like not finishing things that I've started but I will not read the second book after this one. I need a break from Nora the annoying female lead (yes I have officially gave Nora the title of annoying female lead and that's after reading Fifty Shades of Grey...) 
 Actual rating 1.5. The .5 is for Patch's motorcycle, jeep, concept and the cover. I love the cover despite the awfully terrible experience of reading this book, I can't deny that the cover is good. :D

I didn't really have any expectations for this book when I started. The premise sounded promising, it's set in Louisiana, and is classified as a mystery/suspense. Now that I'm finished, I have very mixed feelings about the book overall. 
 I didn't really find any of the characters that likable or well developed. Meg (I'll refer to her using the name she used for most of the novel) was hard to relate to. The difficulty of the situation made sense and her feelings about it were understandable, but some of her reactions were not. She was impulsive, but not in an intelligent way. And she was very hot and cold when it came to other people. I didn't like that. Her family was equally frustrating. I didn't feel like there was really anything done with them. Ethan seemed like he could be an alright character, but he was too friendly too fast and their insta love relationship was a bit much. 
 The story itself was fairly interesting, but the interactions and actions of the characters detracted from the overall story for me. The novel ends without every really wrapping anything up and that was kind of frustrating. I haven't decided yet if I like it enough to read the second book or not.

This book just had too many misses and not enough hits for me. The characters weren't really that great, except for the dead twin sister. And no, I didn't like her only because her name was Courtney. Some, if not all, the truly believable emotional scenes involved her. I won't be surprised if she is in the rest of the series more and we find out she was a time traveler too. It's probably what caused her cancer. This book just tried too hard to be a successful Sci-Fi/Romance/CIA smorgasbord. The different elements just didn't mix well for me. Plus all of Jackson's actions are driven by the guilt over a girl he doesn't even decide/realize he loves until the end of the book. If the plot surrounded an epic love story, maybe it would have been more likeable. If everything was about saving the love of his life, maybe. Instead it jumps back and forth from testing his powers, to popping in on his dead sister (in the past), to digging into his father and the CIA. Half the time Holly seems like an afterthought, but she is supposed to be his whole reason for doing everything he does. Maybe I'm wrong about that, maybe she isn't supposed to be the drive/reason. I don't know, it just didn't resonate with me on any level. I gave it a two because there were some scenes throughout that I really enjoyed. Mostly to do with Courtney, sometimes Adam.
It keeps getting better and better, but I think some scenes are kinda repetitive with the previous ones.

I dislike stories told in first person present tense and I am not a big fan of angels in UF either. And this sounded like young adult, when I picked it up. So the book had a huge uphill struggle to make itself likeable to me. 
 It took more than a third into the book for me to become really interested in the story. Forget the post-apocalyptic part, this is UF, the post-apocalyptic setting is just a vehicle for the story, without any real consequence.. 
 I would have liked my heroine a little older, but I did not really get a YA vibe off this book, so it was not that important. Good fight scenes and some good characterizations, Obi and Dee-Dum were instantly likeable. The mother though was like a cardboard cut-out in those first few chapters. 
 The set-up of the book could have been better. The world building at the beginning did not win me over. The info dump is minimal, I would have preferred more of a backstory. Also, how convenient that our heroine had martial arts training throughout her teens. Somehow that didn't gel with me either. I did not really buy the tough-chick routine, not sure why. 
 The ending is very over the top, but also very entertaining. A bit of Istalove and a slightly too sweet HEA left me a little frustrated. Despite my bitching and complaining, I liked most of the book, while trying to ignore the bits that annoyed me. I am seriously considering to get the next book of the series.

 The Fault in Our Stars is focuses on Hazel Grace, a sixteen year old with cancer, and a boy she meets at a support group, Augustus Waters. The two become close and inevitably fall in love whilst both sharing the ups and downs of cancer. 
 This book would be categorized as a cancer book but it's not. In my opinion, it's a book about life. Or you can cliche it as a romance because it is pretty much just a normal book except the fact that the characters do have cancer. 
 So basically I fell in love. I fell in love with each and every character in the book. I fell for Grace's intelligence, Gus's wit and charm, Isaac's life. Honestly, I loved Isaac too much. But anyway, I frequently cry over books but this, this destroyed me. It broke my heart in a way that a guy could never. The beauty in this book was relentless. I'd never read a book like it. The words John used were incredible. I always look for good, interesting words in books because they just draw me in uncontrollably and John Green mastered the art of words. They way his mind works is honestly insane. The things I would do to have the power to string sentences together the way his does is never ending. 
 The book didn't only make me cry, it also made me laugh and smile at myself in a crazy manner. No other book has ever had the power to do that. 
 Overall, I gave this book 5/5 because there is no book better than this and I thought the day would never come when I'd say this. I can read it multiple times and my emotions for the book and still there. I recommend this book to everyone, no matter who you are, read it. It'll change your life.

I'm wavering between three and four stars with this one. I liked it, but I'm not sure it's going to match all the hype because it's not mind-blowing in any way. It doesn't really stand out in the still-growing market of post-apocalyptic YA fiction. It's, dare I say, a bit predictable. 
 The apocalypse has come by way of alien invasion. But not the alien invasion we have all envisioned (except we HAVE envisioned it in many sci-fi novels and movies, just not the ones alluded to in the book. It has, for example, obvious elements of The Host and The Body Snatchers and Ender's Game ). First comes the first wave - a electromagnetic pulse and all electricity is out. Second is an enormous pole dropped from our upper atmosphere into a fault line, causing massive destruction on the coasts. Third is a plague spread by birds that is so terrible and gross I will describe it as Yancey-esque. Fourth is the drones, the alien snipers that search and take out the last survivors. 
 What is the 5th Wave? And where are the aliens? 
 Cassie, short for Cassiopeia, is the star of the 5th Wave, although it does have some notable secondary characters who carry scenes in either first or third person. The book unfolds as you read it, and can be described as twisty, though I don't think many of the twists are surprising. IN FACT, I was waiting for one big twist that never came (I was kind of hoping that the twist of the book would be an "it was Earth all along"/"the carousel is a lie" kind of scenario where there were no aliens and that it was some kind of human baddies carrying out the apocalypse, but looks like the aliens are real or I'm being duped by Evan's character ) Anyway, the twists that come, the character reveals, the romance, and etc. are easily spotted by fans of the genre, and despite marketing efforts to convince me otherwise, the storyline is just not all that original. 
 But the layout and writing were well done. I like how the story is told and that we are kept at the same pace as the characters. There is a lot of action, but also time for relationship-building and a romance. (I've read other reviews say the romance isn't a big part of the book, but they're wrong. It's a big, major, honking part of the book; there's not much swooning, but it's there, like well, like most post-apocalyptic YA novels.)I like how the book ends. I believe there are sequels to come, but it would be interesting to end it just there, with kind of a play on what Cassie wants pre-apocalypse and what she gets post-apocalypse. Of course, I do want to know what happens next.
