 This book was all right, but long-winded. The first half moved at a snail's pace and the writing was terrible. Dialogue works for Mr. Hill, but when it comes to descriptions, there is a lot of room for improvement. However, with the second half of the book, the action picked up and the writing improved. It makes me wonder if more than one person worked on this book. Hmmm... I found the characters to be very unlikable. A few had some redeeming qualities, but most of them, I didn't care about their fates. This book has a lot of violence. That didn't particularly bother me, but what did bother me was how the author seemed to use violence not to move the story forward, but to shock the reader. This pattern was repeated over and over and over throughout this lengthy work. In moments of crisis, the characters had a lot of exposition. That didn't make much sense and ended up really slowing down the book's pace. The dialogue also had shock value in it. I'm not opposed to swearing, if the situation calls for it, but in 98% of this book (my estimate, not actual), the characters would spew random obscenities. Was it to establish character? Perhaps, but I don't think it was necessary every time. This book also had a lot of weird and odd sentence structures. There were a lot of random fragments in the middle of the paragraphs that made sense, but they would have been more powerful had they been actual sentences. The ending in Christmasland lacked polish. After all of the buildup, I had difficulty visualizing what was happening. It pages of descriptions were missing. It never really explained how ANFO worked. I guess it is simply assumed that we can figure that out. The last 40 pages (before the final section) were a lot of telling rather than showing. 
 Also, I believe that Joe Hill says he publishes his work under a different last name than his famous father. That's fine because his work should be judged on its own merit, not the expectations of what his dad has accomplished. That being said, Mr. Hill needs to move beyond his father's shadow and start making and incorporating his own mythology. With references to Shawshank Prison and Mid-World, it doesn't give me the opportunity to get lost in this work, but I find myself wondering why he's making comparisons outside of his own body of work. Overall, I enjoyed most of this book. It just could have been edited down for a more concise story.

This book is overflowing with messages of teamwork, not giving up on your dreams, being there for your friends even when things aren't going well, adapting to different roles and trusting other people even when they do something considered out of the ordinary or impossible, and having faith in yourself and your friends. 
 I only had two concerns with this book: even as an adult, I was very uncomfortable with Flora not realizing for so long that she was brought along as food, and it was so awkward when she thought she was going to be head of the sled team but her friends took her out to hide and would not tell her what was going on for so long.  I was also sad at the end that Flora never (as far as we know) got to go back to her family and Luna to let them know she hadn't been eaten and tell them about all her adventures. I think in part this was done to leave an opening for future books, but it also brings up the uncomfortable spectre that she might not actually have a family to go back to. I am not a vegetarian and I know the anthropomorphism is fictional, but this story brings up a lot of ethical/moral questions for the reader, I think.

It's a long time since I have read a real capital R romance novel. This was offered as a free download with the warning that it is the first story of the Braden family but features others from her earlier books. I had no trouble picking it up. 
 The hero is Treat Braden (try saying that fast three times). He's a super maxed out romance hero; he's super successful in his resort business, super rich, super tall, super hunky, super nice and super angsty. The last one caught me off-guard a little. Even his family are all super successful. I get it; it's fiction. 
 The heroine is Max Armstrong. She has a great job and lots of nice friends but she's a bit of a disaster inside. By the end of the story, the reader understands why she's like that, but there were a couple of times when I wanted to shake her. 
 First off, Treat gives her a judgy look when he thinks she had a one night stand with one of his staff - that's at their first meeting and he had no right. But each can't get the other out of their head and then Treat sees her again when he comes home to see his sister Savannah and Max is working a film festival. He is determined to try again but Max is doubtful about the whole thing. 
 There is the true to formula misunderstanding that tears them apart, but it happened three times. Max reacts, not to what was said, but to what she thinks is happening, and she's already plummeted off the deep end before she talks or checks with anyone. She doesn't even hear half of what Treat says to her. 
 When she goes to his holiday house and tracks him down, that felt like the ending and then she spun off again. 
 I was fine with it whilst I was reading, but later I went for a walk and I was thinking about writing a review and I felt that she was almost too neurotic. 
  
 Being the first of an obvious series, there was a lot of time spent introducing the rest of the Bradens. I just checked and there are 18 books in the series as I write. Phew. 
 I quite enjoyed it and teared up at the right places. But, then again, I cry at Hallmark commercials.

Honestly this book frustrated me like no other but damn it was addicting. 
 I couldn't help but enjoy it so sue me.

Picked this book up because it was touted as an anti-hero book with a dark/gritty tone. 
 In a world where the EO (ExtraOrdinary) are becoming more prevalent, Victor Vale has to go up against an old friend who has taken it upon himself to destroy all EOs. 
 Overall it was a good read. Good writing that shows actions and is fairly window-pane invisible throughout the book (nothing flowery, just solid prose), good pacing where we jump between present and past with development of the final showdown between the two characters, pretty good characters that feel real, a mildly unique story in a time where superpower media is way oversaturated. 
 I do like these kinds of books where it's two friends-turned-enemies that are perpetually against each other. (If interested in other similar books, try Pushing Ice by Alastair Reynolds or The First Fifteen Lives of Harry August by Claire North.) 
 However, my main quibble is with Eli. I really, really dislike the author using religion as the character's justification for serial murder. Not for any religious purposes, but because I think it is lazy writing. I can't empathize with the villain because he is freaking crazy and his logic doesn't even make sense. So it makes me completely on the side of Victor, which is hardly an "anti-hero" anymore because Eli is such obviously a criminal. I would much rather have a villain who I can believe his justification. 
 The climax was worth the slow build and I thought the ending was pretty darn perfect. 
 In the end, three stars because I thought it was a good book, but not much more than that. However, I doubt that I will reread this book. I would recommend it casually if you're looking for a decent to good read.

I loved this book when I first read it as a ten or eleven year old. I wanted to fight with a sword and have purple eyes and save the day with my awesome gift. 
 I'm glad I read this book at that age. If I didn't have such fantastic memories of it and my reactions at the time, I probably wouldn't be giving it as high as four stars today, but I enjoyed re-reading it. Everything was just as I remembered - just slightly less exciting. I'm looking forward to re-reading the rest of the series.

Just in time for the scariest of all months, a quick-and-easy Gothic YA novel that provides an inventive back story to Edgar Allen Poe's "Annabel Lee." I'll preface my review with the disclaimer that I received this galley for review from one of my favorite websites, NetGalley. (Psst... NetGalley -thanks for all the exciting new reads lately. You sure know how to keep a bookseller/avid reader flush with plenty of possibilities for my next read. If only I could review as fast as I read, we'd be in good standing. But alas, I need to read LESS and review MORE. I'm working on it. Chipping away at the reviews sitting in my notebook, just ready to be hashed out on the computer screen. ANYWAYS, I digress). 
 If you've read some of the reviews this book has recently garnered from fellow GoodReaders, you'll find that not everyone has the pleasure of enjoying this work BUTi I didn't take objection to it. I thought it was a fairly suspenseful, quasi-frightening read that would appeal to the young audience for which it is intended. Despite some of its potential downfalls, this book could serve as a fabulous introduction to those young readers not familiar with the writings of Edgar Allen Poe. Granted, the author certainly took liberties with poor Mr. Poe's life, but I don't hold that against her because its all in the name of good fun...and reading!Like I said, if one teen/pre-teen picks up "The Tell-Tale Heart" or "The Cask of Amontillado," then this book has served a mighty purpose indeed. 
 At the heart of it, there's recently orphaned Annabel Lee, who has been sent to live with her estranged (and downright strange father in Philadelphia. Annabel comes from a simpler life in Siam, a life where she hasn't been privileged with wealth or a lady's manners. She has a difficult time settling into her new home where her solemn and difficult father spends most of his time in his basement laboratory. To pass the unpleasant time she is having, Annabel makes the acquaintance of his two assistants, Edgar and Allen, and befriends the housemaid, Molly. But strange visitors lurk outside her window and there is a murderer on the loose, terrorizing Philadelphia. Will Annabel survive her new surroundings? 
 I enjoyed the book, for the most part, until the cliffhanger ending - seemingly a popular trend in today's YA. Of course there will be a sequel (and most likely, it will be stretched into a trilogy). Its not that I'm not going to read it...its just that I'm tired of adding new series to my reading list - especially when I have to wait for the subsequent books to be written and published! #readerproblems

I did not like this as much as the first volume of the trilogy. For one thing, we're not in Area X anymore, with its mask of a seemingly peaceful natural world overlaying a deeply weird, fleetingly glimpsed reality. We're in an office. Blech. At least it's the office that's in charge of figuring out Area X. For another thing, I found the narrator frustrating in a different way than the redoubtable Biologist of the first book, whom I could admire for her strength and doggedness. Still, I never got the feeling that VanderMeer didn't know exactly what he was doing with Control, Grace, Whitby, and the rest, while I was disliking them all. A few of the questions raised in the first book are addressed, but often with confounding answers, or answers that lead to more questions. A second book in a trilogy is always the weakest, I think, but it did its job in that I can't wait to read the third.

I... did not like this book... at all. 
 I was interested in the premise of the story; a kid is on the run, trying to just make it through in his life without being killed, and he takes a chance to finally do something that he really, really wants to do and that's to play Exy. And by "takes a chance" I really mean "he's pretty much forced to do it, and not even in a polite kind of way".  
 I always jump into things feet first. Go big or go home, right? What I did was see all the great reviews and immediately buy the complete trilogy. What a deal, right? 
 What I should have done was download the first book of the series cause it was free and see if I would like it. But I didn't do that. Shame. 
 This book was absolutely BORING. I got to the point where I was just skimming large chunks of text only to focus on dialog to see if anything important was happening. Unfortunately, since I bought the complete trilogy, I feel compelled to read the other two books in the series because, yanno, I spent money on them. But I think I'll just take my $2.00 loss and call it a day.

I found myself enjoying this a lot more than I expected to but I felt like the end was... very sudden? I almost felt like someone had ripped off the last few pages of the books. It felt more like the middle of a chapter than a proper conclusion. 
 *Read in french*

Can't review this. Just. Can't. 
 Feeling like I've lost an ARL friend here. And it is brutal. So, yeah, I'm just gonna go off now and fall apart some. 
 Wallow like a motherfucker. 
 Damn you, you awful, cruel, beautiful book, you. Damn you straight to hell.  
 That is all.

Vin is a pretty standard fantasy hero - she is a girl, though. Yay! But the only one... sighs. She discovers she has exceptional skills, has a teacher adept in those skills, finds a new bunch of people to hang with, and goes on a quest of a sort. Initially that quest is a little different though; it's a heist job. Kelsier wants to rob the Lord Ruler and steal his supplies of the most valuable metal. It's only later that the real quest emerges. Kelsier really wants to start a revolution, lift up the downtrodden Skaa and defeat the Lord Ruler... problem is, he seems to be immortal. He has already ruled for a thousand years and the Skaa are so downtrodden they can't even imagine fighting him, let alone have the strength or the weapons to do so. The Lord Ruler can't rule alone so it makes sense that he has The Steel Ministry and the Canton of Inquisition, to administer and punish. Steel inquisitors sound terrifying. 
 The world building is huge; a Sanderson trait but I think this is a very early one of his books. There are some issues. How do you grow food in a world without flowers and sunlight? 
 Maladroitly is clearly his favourite word. 
 I got confused in some places. I don't understand why the skaa are considered lesser if you put a skaa girl in a pretty dress and nobody can tell she's skaa. Perhaps Sanderson wanted to avoid any racism parallels with making them a different colour? But I don't see how the nobles could consider themselves so different and superior if they look just the same. A little taller on average from a better diet. I guess it's like an old English peasantry? Or is it the allomancy? Is it really just limited to the upper classes? And not every noble person can do it but they aren't considered lesser. (like squibs in the HP world). Vin didn't know what she was and there is probably a whole legion of Skaa who are the same; it's not a blood thing, it's an education and knowledge thing. The nobility know what to look for. Vin just thought she was lucky. 
 Snoop has a local dialect that they all laugh at in one scene. Vin can't understand him and that seems odd if she's lived on the streets for years, surely she'd know it? 
 I got screamingly frustrated with how slow the group was to put together some information. I was walking and shouting at my audiobook. 
 It clicked for me the second I heard that the Lord Ruler always castrates Terrisman like Sazed. Why would he do that? The only reason would be to stop even the possibility of a child. He doesn't want the new/real prophet to arise. It's like Edmund Hillary being killed by Tenzing Norgay. I know he hasn't been seen very often but surely Kelsier should have recognised his preferred young visage as a Terrisman? And, by the way, if a man is castrated he just has his testes cut off, and he still should have a penis. So Vin can't have seen just a scar between Sazed's legs... and now I am trying to imagine what Terrisman genitals look like if they aren't human. *frowns* This is not where this was supposed to go. 
 The Feruchemy fitted with what had been described in the journal and I could not get why nobody put it together earlier. It was a story point that Kelsier made everyone read it. 
 And why is he lugging around a journal big enough for a girl to hide behind as his dear diary? And why would his replacement keep it? 
 [70% Wait up... Kelsier is talking up religions that go on after their leader is killed *eyes narrow* if this is foreshadowing, I don't like it. sighs... and I was right. Sniffs.] 
 Vin is asked to deliver a pretty important message by the lady Tris and she never does. She kept forgetting to impart information she had learned when at other times people repeated whole conversations. 
 I don't understand why the gold and the eleventh metal show Vin an image of the actual journal writer (and the man who should have been king, as it were). Surely it shows two versions of the same person? (even leaving out the fact that there must be infinite versions of yourself branching off from everyday decisions). 
 How exactly did Marsh survive? I was also shouting 'just pull the damn metal spikes out' as I was walking, too. 
 Why on earth would they make Elend Venture king? I get why Vin likes him, but I didn't. 
 Did the Deepness win? Did the lord ruler make a deal with it a thousand years ago? Is that why the country is colourless and covered with ash? So do they have to defeat it, now? And they've killed the only guy who knew anything about it. Oopsies. And he's unlikely to have kept a journal like the whiny guy. That did make me laugh when Vin described the Lord Ruler as a whiny boy. I suspect that the huge stores of Ateum being missing means they are fed to the Deepness, not stolen by someone else as the crew suspected. I could be wrong *shrugs* if I'm right then Kelsier destroyed the mines and that action will have major consequences.  
 Guess I'll find out in book 2. 
 The audio book was well read. The chapters are soooooo long, though. The book is reduced to 21 audio chapters, some of which are nearly two hours long and they are cut in odd places. But initially having listened to Words of Radiance recently - it's the same narrator. So instead of thinking 'that voice is Breeze' I was thinking 'wait that voice is Lord Saddeus.' Took me a little while to get over that. 
 4 stars

I listened to this on audiobook, and I kind of wanted to throw it out my car window until the point that we were officially out of college and these pretentious, entitled, obnoxious kids graduated (if this is in any way an accurate representation of 20 year olds in the 80's, I'd like to call for the official end of the "millennial" entitlement stereotype because these people were THE WORST). If I had been reading it, I never would have made it past this section. WAY too much exposition, too pretentious on the part of both the characters and the author, too much gratuitous literary name dropping, and while I can only assume it was satirical, it bothered me as much as if the story took it seriously, so I don't think the satire was handled very well. Strangely, this kind of worked out for the audiobook, because the voices for the dialogue were unbearable, so the exposition was better to listen to. 
 I enjoyed Mitchell's journey to India (and weirdly made me want to visit India, despite how unappealing it sounded like it was), and Leonard's first person section had me on the edge of my seat. I thought the foreshadowing/backstory type of narrative was a lot more effective toward the middle and end sections, and I was satisfied with the resolution for the most part. I really wasn't expecting the mental illness theme, which was well explored, but got a little heavy handed. Do people with manic depression really say the words "manic depression" in every other sentence? I doubt it.
Moore delivers again. This is funny, compelling, and very readable. My only problem with it is it's about 100 pages too long. Some editing would have benefited this.

Given my total lack of anything resembling interest in baseball, I was surprisingly moved by the story. Was it the part where the love interest had cancer and the romance was subtle and understated and involved two instances of literally sleeping together and nothing more? MAYBE. But it also prodded my empathetic grief bone throughout at the idea of missing your father no less five years later.

No, seriously this organ in my chest, I don't need it. That's not a spoiler, that's a warning. This book is such a riveting installment, but be warned that it will not pull at your heart strings, rather it will pluck them until they break. 
 Okay, I love June. She's a fantastic heroine. A little too young, but I get Lu's reasons for making her 15. 
 The reason I gave this four instead of five stars, well there's a couple. The first is I didn't love Day as much in this book, and I really needed to. He was seriously irritating at times, but real people are. There's a storyline with Tess and it made me so freaking mad. Here's the thing Love triangles are great as long as they involve two boys and a girl. NOT two girls and boy. Come on.  
 I also didn't love all the dreams June and Day kept having. I think they are cheap devices in literature and yes that's coming from someone who coined the term "Dream Travel." It's just dream travel is real and what happens in dreams isn't and so it feels like they don't really move the plot along. They just dump info. And one final nitpick, at one point Day is put under for surgery. In most cases people cannot have dreams when they are under anesthesia. That one is a small one, but I had to note it. 
 The second book is really great! Gripping and fun. The ending to me was a little wrong. I get why it happened that way. And yes, I immediately went out and got third book, but it was definitely a crafty device for ending the book. Honestly, I'm torn on what I want to happen to the characters. Very good book, which delivers a lot of exhilarating emotions. 
 Oh and one final note, bathroom scene. Nice one! :)

This book should be taken at face value, written for humor and entertainment purposes of the best kind. I read this for two straight forward reasons; I wanted to see the movie (but wanted to read the book first and I'm so happy I did) and because it's Abraham Lincoln. 
 My first thought was that it was just going to be written as a humorous joke like a sort of parody that just pokes fun at random things. Ha ha, bad-ass president made more so by hunting vampires. I was so sure that this was going to be the case that it's probably what drove me to loving this book when I was proven so wrong. 
 I loved everything about this book; 
 -The vampires weren't sexualized or transformed into non-human like beasts so they still held that scary 'human but not really' feeling. 
 -The parts of the story that were woven in with what we know in history.(The ending! Of course we all know the ending, how could we not? Its history! But it still pulled through to be heartbreaking.) 
 -The surprise characters that I hardly ever expected to see. 
 -The feelings. Ohgosh, the feelings of Abraham's struggles and losses. 
 But, there were some bits that weren't so great; 
 -The writing style. It's confusing at the beginning, like you don't understand where the perspective is coming from until you realize that you're actually reading what the shop owner guy is writing . It's sort of blotchy in some parts and in others its like reading a history assignment back in middle school. 
 -Another thing, and this might me a spoiler for some but I view it as something people need to know because it is a trigger (so I'm not going to put it under a spoiler tag, I'm sorry) is that there is mentions of children's death or dying.

Based on all the reviews my friends have written for this, I'm the odd man out. This is becoming more and more frequent now. It isn't really something I worry about too much; it just means I'll end up trying out more books for myself instead of deferring completely to their opinions. Which isn't such a bad thing, right? 
 I loved this. It was like a more science-y and less wacky version of Pacific Rim. Have you ever seen that movie? It's basically giant Transformers fighting Godzillas. It is absolutely fucking amazing: 
 And that's what this book builds up to. Sorry if you don't like spoilers, but whatever. We already knew it was going to be science fiction; them opening a door/mouth/portal to a different location tells us that pretty quickly. What we don't know is just how much shit is going to hit the fan when it happens. 
 The premise is a bit weak, but overall I enjoyed it. I liked that our main character was like a modern day Mycroft Holmes. I liked that the big bad secret the scientists were hiding wasn't something I predicted. I even liked how Mike followed the little quirks to clue him in to what was actually happening. I thought it was all pretty solidly done, to be honest. I was invested the moment I started reading. 
 But the ending? The ending that everyone hates? I fucking loved it. It was demented. The patchwork man was absolutely mind-boggling and I kept flipping back to reread his description over and over again. That thing will give you nightmares, man. 
 I'm a sucker for well written monster stories. Give me Frankenstein, give me Godzilla, give me The Fold. I will gladly read this author's books again.

NOTE: Review contains multiple quotes which may contain spoilers. 
 One word. PHENOMENAL 
 Tyler Hamilton was a successful professional biker and one-time friend and teammate of Lance Armstrong, who like Lance eventually got "popped" for his doping. His captivating story, told with the help of Daniel Coyle, not only sheds light on the doping problem in cycling (with a spotlight on Lance) but also fosters empathy for the athletes (even Lance) who ultimately had to decide whether to lose/quit or give themselves a shot (literally) and join the "brotherhood". 
 After the race, I felt a new level of frustration as I watched the white bags get handed out. Now I could measure the injustice. Marty used to be a few groups behind me; now he was a few groups ahead. I could count the number of seconds those white bags contained. I could see the gap between who I was and who I could be. Who I was supposed to be. 
 This was bullshit. 
 This was not fair. 
 In that moment, the future became clear. Unless something changed, I was done. I was going to have to find a different career. I began to get more stressed and angry. Not at Marty--after all, he was only doing what a lot of others were doing. He;d been given an opportunity, and he'd taken it. No, I felt angry at myself, at the world. I was being cheated.  
 Here's an interesting number: one thousand days. It's roughly the number of days between the day I became professional and the day I doped for the first time. Talking to the other riders of this era and reading their stories, it seems to be a patter: those of us who doped mostly started during our third year. First year, neo-pro, excited to be there, young pup, hopeful. Second year, realizations. Third year, clarity--fork in the road. Yes or no. In or out. Everybody has their thousand days; everybody has their choices.  
 So what exactly does doping involve? A lot of things, including the uses of testosterone and cortisone, synthetic blood, blood transfusions and the use of EPO, often referred to by its code name Edgar, as well as other things. 
 What does being on EPO feel like? It feels great, mostly because it doesn't feel like anything at all. You're not wiped out. You feel healthy, normal, strong. ?You have more color in your cheeks; you're less grumpy, more fun to be around. These little clear drops work like radio signals--they instruct your kidneys to create more red blood cells (RBCs), and soon millions more are filling up your veins, carrying oxygen to your muscles. Everything else about your body is the same, except now you have better fuel. You can go harder, longer. That holy place at the edge of your limits gets nudged out--and not just a little.  
 The two most effective ways to enhance biking performance are blood transfusions and EPO. Both increase the number of RBCs in the blood and thereby increase the bodies oxygen delivering capability. For years there was no test to detect EPO, and so as long as you maintained a hematocrit below 50, you were safe. 
 Blood transfusions are especially hard to detect since you are essentially injecting your own blood back into your body. 
 The difficulty in proving a biker was doping had to have made it that much more of a temptation. 
 During my career, journalists often used the term "arms race" to describe the relationship between the drug testers and the athletes, but that wasn't quite right, because it implied that the testers had a chance of winning. For us, it wasn't like a face at all. It was more like a big game of hide-and-seek played in a fest that has lots of good places to hide, and lots of rules that favor the hiders.  
 I got to where I could estimate my hematocrit level by the color of my blood. I'd stare at the little drops when Ferrari stuck my finger with a lancet when he gave a lactate test. If it was light and watery, my hematocrit was low. If it was dark, it was higher. I liked seeing that dark, rich color, all those cells crowding in there like a thick soup, ready to go to work; it made me eager to train even harder. 
 Training felt like a game. How hard can you work? How smart can you be? How skinny can you get? Can you pit yourself against those numbers, and can you reach them? And the behind all that, was always the anxiety that drove you, that kept you working: Whatever you do, those fuckers are doing more.  
 I have to admit, even knowing these guys cheated, even knowing that when they got caught they lied, even knowing they often became indignant and attacked their accusers unjustly, I still couldn't help but feel some level of compassion for the lot. It almost seems as if they didn't have a choice. It was either take the drugs like all the other contenders or forfeit their dreams. 
 To win the Tour, you needed only three qualities. 
 1. You have to be very, very fit. 
 2. You have to be very, very skinny. 
 3. You have to keep your hematocrit up. 
 Rule number 3 was regrettable in Cecco's eyes, but ultimately unavoidable, a simply fact of life.  
 Was it possible to win a professional bike race clean during this era? Could a clean rider compete with riders on Edgar? 
 The answer is, it depends. 
 According to Hamilton, drugs like EPO and blood transfusions delay fatigue and decline more than they spark performance. Thus, a clean rider could still be competitive during short races, but once the race exceeded a week, those not doping were at a huge disadvantage. 
 This was the moment, the fork in the road. Everyone who gets popped experiences it: That eerie calm before the storm, those few hours when they can decide to tell the truth or not. I'd like to tell you that I thought about confessing, but the truth is I never considered it, not for one second. Confession felt impossible, unthinkable, an act of insanity. Not just because I'd spent years playing the game telling myself that I wasn't a cheater, that everybody did it. Not just because it would mean the shame of being exposed, or the loss of my team and contract and good name, or having to tell my parents. Not just because confession would implicate my friends, possible end the careers of my teammates and staffers--after all, it wasn't like I'd done all this solo. But mostly because the charge didn't make any sense to me. The UCI was claiming I had someone else's blood in my body--and I was 100 percent sure that I didn't. Should I ruin my life and others' lives by pleading guilty to something I hadn't done? To me, the answer was clear: NO.  
 Ironically, when Tyler was finally "caught", he was accused of doing something he hadn't done, and he spent upwards of a million dollars to clear his name, but lost. 
 At the time this book was completed, his ex-teammate Lance Armstrong, who is discussed at length in Tyler's story, was in the midst of a civil trial and was still adamantly denying the doping charges, while spending a fortune to prove his innocence. Of course, we all know how that turned out. 
 One has to wonder what the future of professional biking will look like in the aftermath of the scandal. Tyler for one is hopeful, encouraged by signs that the sport is finally getting clean as evidenced by recent winning times, which are substantially lower than they were at the height of the doping era. 
 The winning time up Alpe d'Huez in the 2011 Tour was 41:21; back in 2001, a rider would have finished 40th. 
 Would recommend this book to anyone with an interest in the Tour, and or the pressures facing elite athletes. This is a well written, face-paced book, with lots of substance.

The author was kind enough to provide me with a copy of this book in exchange for an honest and unbiased review 
 Ok when I first started this book have to admit it felt a little too young adult for my tastes but it really won me over. Actually, it was Nat that won me over. She is such a great female main character. She is tough enough to be herself and not be too bothered by expected behaviour but vulnerable and 'real' enough to be believable. Oh and I laughed out loud frequently at the things she thought/said. I was so amused by the sarcasm and wit in the dialogue that I soon forgot that it was in a high school and is really the cheesiest idea ever. I mean really, a bored innocent high school girl gets 2 gorgeous rockstars falling for her?! 
 You have to believe me though, you completely forget about how cringeworthy that is because of how beautifully written Nat, Alec and Demetri are. Nat cracks me up, but she's also sweet and clumsy and open and caring and I don't hate her for the love triangle thing, which for me is amazing given how much I hate love triangles. This one is ok though because the Author actually made both lovable, although there's no question which 'team' I was on! Demetri is full of fun and life and Alec is all caring and protective. I just ignored all the cheesy rockstar parts, which are kind of completely unnecessary, unless of course you're a teenage girl and still like to dream about that kind of thing. (please remember it's not real!) 
 This book quickly became an intense passion-full new adult book that I was completely swept away with. I literally read from cover to cover stopping once for a 3 minute comfort break. For any lovers of New Adult contemporary romance this is a must read. You will love this story and love the boys. It has it's fair share of drama and intensity too. I cried my eyes out at an unexpected part The bit where she hugs her Dad at the hospital, oh god I'm tearing up again just thinking about it now! . The last part of the book was so intense my heart was in my mouth, I was so worried about what would happen and if the right choices would be made. The ending was beautifully satisfying without being cheesy. I'm not great at gushing (feel a bit foolish being over the top given I'm in my 30's, married with children) but this really deserves gushes, I feel like a teenager again. This book would have been my teen fantasy, tears 'n all. Sad I know, but the author really sold the love well for me. 
 To summarise, (and stop gushing) I loved this book!!! Nat is a wonderful character who wears her heart on her sleeve. I could easily tell why a boy would fall for her which made it easy to believe, and I could feel her emotions. Being such a loving open character it was obvious how she got herself into this and how she managed to have so much love and forgiveness to give. I don't usually do the whole 'favourite quote' thing but several of the things she said amused me so much but I'm going to share this one with you to demonstrate how great Nat was (and not at all a soppy pushover like many heroines!); 
 "I rolled my eyes and pushed away enough to look up at his face. "You're so romantic. Really, you take my breath away. I almost swooned just now. Good thing I'm lying down."" 
 To me it says a lot that I want to talk about the characters as if they are people rather than about the authors prowess or shortcomings. All I want to do is have more of that. Next book please!

I love this book. 
 Do you hear me? I LOVE this book. 
 I love it so much that I just spent the past 3 hours reading the last 80% of it rather than sleeping like I typically would. 
 I love that Jennifer and Beth's emails remind me of my best friend and I's emails. I love the snark and the fondness and the honesty; the shift between irritations like food odors at work and serious life-changing events. I love all the pop culture references, especially all the nerdy ones. I love that I loved Lincoln's character without feeling like *I* was in love with him. I love the balance of the book - the shifts between Lincoln's active pov and when he's reading the emails. I love that things are explained just enough, not overly detailed or drawn out, but still with full and satisfying explanations. I love that the ending was just how I wanted it, despite not knowing what exactly I really wanted to happen.  I love that it was all 'just enough,' and yet, so much more. 
 "Perfect" is not a word I use often, but in this case, it's suiting. Even past the afterglow of having just come off reading it in its entirety, I doubt I'll have anything to nitpick apart. (As with most Kindle novels I've read, there was a handful of typos. I can only assume they don't exist in the print edition. Even if so, it didn't detract from the story past a glancing notice.) I was drawn in the entire time reading. I didn't once feel the urge to skim and skip ahead to the next good part - they were all 'good parts.' And the ending... what a perfect line to leave off on.  I felt satisfied once I reached the end. Though I would love to know "What happens next?" I don't feel like I'll die if I don't know what happens from that point on. 
 I already want to read it a second time. 
 Maybe I loved it so much because I could relate to Lincoln. Maybe I found it cathartic in a way, to see him work past so many things I feel I've experienced in the past handful of years. Maybe it held that special kind of magic that so few books have - hope. 
 All I can really say is that it's easily become a favorite, possibly "the" favorite. I can't recommend it enough. I'll very quickly be purchasing Eleanor & Park next, and keeping my fingers crossed that it's just as delicious as this one was.

This is probably one of the most difficult books I've ever had to review on here, mainly because I'm of two minds about the book in general. 
 The Red Knight is the first of the Traitor Son Cycle series, and tells the story of a mysterious captain of a company of hired sell-swords who suddenly finds himself in the midst of a war against all manner of hideous and powerful creatures when he accepts a contract to protect the fortress convent of Lissen Carak. The Captain is used to accepting minor contracts for small amounts of money, and moving on quickly once the job is done. However, Lissen Carak is sat upon a font of power that the Wild outside its walls will do anything to reclaim, and the Captain finds himself having to make decisions he'd really rather not, and utilize his own mysterious abilities in order to ensure survival. 
 This book is clearly a herculean effort on Cameron's part to write and establish a new high fantasy world akin to Tolkien's Middle Earth with the numerous characters and settings, epic battle scenes, and dozens of plot threads. However, it all just falls a bit short for me due to a somewhat lacking execution. 
 I don't know if my copy was missing pages or what, (I live in America, and I have the edition with the dark cover focused on a knight's hands holding his sword,) but my book didn't come with a map of the world. One thing I really need when I'm reading a fantasy book full of made up places is a map to orient me to the locations or I have an incredibly difficult time getting immersed into the story until my mind can create the map for me. Of course, that requires details which unfold over the course of the story about where these cities or fortresses are in correlation with one another. 
 Also, there are a number of editing errors in this book that in some instances completely destroyed the function of entire sentences. While I don't have any examples handy while writing this, I find it odd that this book clearly wasn't edited by a professional editor (if at all) who was focusing on things like spelling errors, or ensuring that the characters names were spelled correctly (there was a few instances of Ranald's name appearing as "Ranulf," as an example.) There were also a few instances of the directional relationship of Albinkirk and Lissen Carak being mixed up, which makes it even harder to orient yourself as a reader in this new world. 
 POV was another area that I think suffered in this book. There were way too many. I'm all for books that switch it up a bit and give you a few different perspectives on events, however, this book did it every three or four pages! We'd see the events unfold from the Captains perspective, and then we'd see them again from Thorn's, and again from another character, before Cameron suddenly decided to switch it up and tell us about what was happening in the city of Harndon or Albinkirk and make us forget all about what was just expanded on before. It made it hard to fall in love with the characters because just as I started to feel a connection to them, it was severed again. 
 Cameron is clearly a very intelligent man, and as someone who is involved in medieval roleplay in his time when he's not writing, he has a unique perspective on medieval style that lends itself to his writing. I feel like I learned a lot from this book, but at the same time, it was exhausting to constantly have to set my book aside and look up some tiny piece of armor that was referenced by its medieval name that I had no understanding of. Along this line, I can understand why Cameron felt the need to include religion, and God in the book because it plays a large part in chivalry of the characters, however, I can't help but feel like it's all a bit pandering, constantly reminding the reader about the power of Christ, even in a fantasy land where they could have had their own God(s) that they found faith in. 
 A few other areas I found lacking: 
 The love story between the Captain and Amicia. Their relationship was meant to read as exciting and passionate, but just felt boring to me. There were a number of times when they would either be kissing or fighting, (or kissing and then fighting,) when a battle was starting just outside the walls and it just felt unbelievable. 
 Also, what was up with the ending? Thorn survives the final battle, only to run off into the woods and the Captain and co. just take that as the end of the threat and leave?  It just doesn't make sense! The threat wasn't destroyed, and there was no satisfying conclusion. I understand that this plot thread will likely come up again in Book 3, but I think that books in a series should also be able to stand alone on their own, in which this book doesn't do that in a satisfying way. 
 All in all, it wasn't terrible, but it wasn't great either. I plan on checking out the second book at some point, but I'm not rushing out to buy it today either.

Sara Farizan got her MFA in Writing for Children & Young Adults from the university I work for, and I'd already read her first book, so I figured I'd give this one a go. I thought it was a lot stronger than If You Could Be Mine, in part because this one does not have the same kind of instalove (i.e. from the literal first paragraph--if you didn't buy Sahar/Nasrin in that book, a lot of the ensuing feels were not ideal). While If You Could Be Mine was perhaps a little more thematically adventurous, this was a lot more slice-of-life flavoured. I loved listening to Leila and I appreciated that from page one she knows she's gay, but she isn't sure how to come out yet. It was a variant on the coming-out story where the character doesn't know they're gay until they kiss someone, etc--made it interesting. 
 There were some bits that moved a little too quickly for my liking, and some character details that didn't quite make sense (several people have pointed out the classmate who is wasted all the time yet gets high grades). There were also a couple of parts that felt either a little exposition-y or over-explained, whereas I think they would've done a little better to be shown. I suppose my biggest qualm was with Saskia. I really wanted there to be more backstory, more of a reason as to why she toys with Leila and then proceeds to out her. I wasn't sure if she was closeted--which might have been the easy move--or if she was a sociopath or what. There's mention of her being expelled from other schools and that she had other "victims," but I wasn't sure if she just went from school to school outing people, or if it was just general bullying. I also wanted a little more clarification as to why she was in town, living in a hotel, sans parents--I believe it was mentioned briefly, but if it was, it was *very* briefly.  She was a fine creation, to be sure, but I felt like her character had a lot of untapped potential that I wanted to see more on the page. 
 Overall, though, I had a lot of fun reading this one, and I am excited to see what Sara writes next. God knows we need more diverse queer YA books, and this was a welcome addition.

 This was such a fun book! And just what I needed too! It's the perfect book to read on a hot summer day on the beach. Or a cold day in the winter snuggled up under a warm blankett. You don't have to do much thinking and just enjoy the book! I love those books from time to time. 
 When Claire's dying mother asks Claire to break up with Jared, the only boy she's ever loved, she's left with a broken family and a broken heart. But that soon changes into anger when she finds out that her biggest regret became Jared's big break. Jared suddenly is a rock-star and every time his song plays on the radio, Claire's heart breaks. 
 The summer after her senior year, months after the break-up, Claire is trying to keep her head down and make it through a trip to the beach with her family. And then Jared shows up and old feelings resurface. 
 This was a very quick and light read. You don't need tissues for this one. If you've read a lot of heavy and emotional books lately, this is just the thing you need. This is a story about family, mistakes, love and making the right choices. If it would be turned into a movie, it would be a great family movie. And I loved how music was such a big part of this book! I just... Yeah I liked it a lot! 
 I don't know if you can really call it a book about romance, I'd say it's more about second chances. Sure, Claire and Jared have great chemistry together and in the memories she has, there are a lot of sweet romantic scenes but in the present, not that much. Even so, I liked it. 
 I liked Claire okay. I loved her sarcasm and her taste in music, but I don't really love her as a character. The thing that I didn't like that much is probably that she broke up with Jared because her mom asked. Sure okay, she was dying, but still it's unfair to ask that! If she's happy with the guy and he's good to her, why break up? I'm just saying... I wouldn't have done it I think. I liked Jared, but not at first. But after a while he's really a pretty good guy and he's sweet! I'm on his side for sure. There were also a lot of other characters, a bit too many in my opinion. I didn't really care for most of them. 
 So like I said, this is a sweet book about family, second chances, ... And I recommend it to fans of contemporary who just want a light fun book instead of all the heavy emotional ones for a change.

This is an anthology featuring 3 novellas. My least favorite of the 3 was the Jill Myles story. I didn't hate it, but it didn't resonate much for me. Just another on the pile of promiscuous shapeshifter stories I guess. The whole idea of a woman's sexuality being driven by what type of animal she turns into isn't terribly unbelievable. But in this story it just seemed like a device to me, to allow her to shack up with 2 guys. And neither of them had any depth at all, they were pretty much cardboard cutouts who just fell into bed with her. Maybe I'm being too hard on this story, but given the company of the other two really great stories, this was the odd man out for me. 
 The Blushing Bounder by Meljean Brook is why I bought the anthology, this is a story set in her Iron Seas world, and frankly I just cannot get enough of that world! This is the story of Mina's assistant Constable Newberry, and tells us why he moved to London from America - to save his wife. It's a sweet little love story, perfectly set in the London of the Iron Seas. We get more fascinating glimpses of the steampunk setting and the aftereffects of Horde occupation. It was not as great for me as The Iron Duke or Here There Be Monsters... but I loved it. 
 The third and longest story included in this anthology is by an author I have never read before - Carolyn Crane. This is apparently book 2.5 from her "Disillusionists" series. I was really impressed with this story! In this imagined alternative America, there are regular humans and others who have telekinetic or telepathic powers. The two characters in the story are Sophia, whose power is memory revision - she can go into people's short term memories and revise them, wiping events out, adding new events in - and Robert. He is a force field guy, he can control geographic features and buildings with his mind via force fields, if he touches them. It sounds pretty Fantastic 4-y or something, I know, but the story of these two people is really a beautiful thing. The way Crane gradually reveals it is well done, especially in a novella of this length. There is a strong psychological component as well, within their relationship, in the way they use and are impacted by their powers. It is definitely on the darker side. I felt that the ending was not quite as strong as the buildup deserved but all in all I was very impressed and definitely plan to read this series! 
 Update: I just re-read Kitten-Tiger and the Monk after having read the first two books in the Disillusionists trilogy, and it's like a whole new story. The best part is at the end where Sophia has decided to tell Shelby something big - I am thinking the truth about who killed Avery in book 2! Which means it will get back to Justine... I mean, after a surely twisted path of course! :) having read the other books certainly makes you appreciate what a shitty person Sophia has been, that's for sure!

Countless discussions can go on about symbolism in this book. The sheep itself could represent anything we chase after in life. But on top of all thinking, this is a journey in words with a process good enough to not dwell on finding a purpose. 
 The narrator both stands out and blends in with the everyday crowd. He's not hugely successful or attractive, nor does he go through the most fatal fights. Rather, he is divorced, has casual sex, and barely knows what to expect during the wild chase. In many ways, he is like any other person, except for the strange encounters and his (the writer's) profoundly poetic perspective in seeing everything. I believe the narrator's urge to find the sheep is inspired by the Sherlock Holmes he often reads. 
 Although the adventure is wild and quite out of nowhere, it probably doesn't seem so to those who are in the centre of it. As Murakami writes, "On a telephone pole, three plump pigeons burbled mindlessly away. Something had to be on their mind to be going on like that, maybe the pain from corns on their feet, who knows? From the pigeons' point of view, probably it was I who looked mindless."

High off of Cloud Atlas, I went out and bought Mitchell's latest, and started it nearly immediately. But after a few pages in, I found I couldn't get into it as much immediately the way I had been with Cloud Atlas. It was only much later that I began to push through it, and after I got past the initial couple of chapters, I began to get really into it. I think what is really impressive about Mitchell though, is that he's so versatile. To go from something as inventive as Cloud Atlas to this, which is essentially a historical novel, is part of what makes me admire him as a writer. But about this particular novel: once I got into the story, I was really drawn in. The intrigue and mystery becomes heightened as you realize that what you thought this novel might initially be about is actually something else, and the perceived heroes of the book might actually just be witnesses, at least initially. Craft-wise, I found some passages confusing, in the way they were written or how we jumped from scene to scene, but for the most part, I found I could overcome these issues. Overall, I think this was well-written and well-wrought, and I enjoyed it a lot, but unlike Cloud Atlas, this book didn't stay with me once I was done with it. Still, a great read.

A wonderful start to a new series from a debut author!I love the world-building and the thought that the author has put into creating this series!It's a completely new take on demons and I've loved it so far! 
 Molly has just turned 19 years, and though she wishes to lead the life of a normal human, she has abilities and powers that set her apart from others.This causes her to keep people at a distance, with the exception of her best friend September.After a incident at the party, she realizes that her parents' warnings were true.She is indeed betrothed to a demon, due to an unfulfilled promise. 
 And the demon who is supposed to marry her is Tensley Knight, the one who saves her. 
 Tensley isn't interested in marrying her, but he is duty bound.As a demon, he can't feel emotions, and doing so would result in disastrous consequences. Now that Molly is in danger, he has to find a way to keep her safe and fulfill his obligations. 
 Molly is totally confused by the demon who keeps being rude to her, but shows up to save her the next moment.She doesn't want to be tied to him, but she also doesn't know who to trust. 
 Will these two make it out safe and together? 
 I loved the slow development of the relationship between Molly and Tensley from mutual dislike to love.Molly was a little naive in the beginning, but unlike other heroines she underwent tremendous character development, and her true strength came out.I could understand Tensley's attitude, but his hot and cold behavior grew old too fast.But I still loved the push and pull between them.The chemistry was too good! 
 The action and the events had me waiting to know what would happen next.The cast of secondary characters were also amazing!And I believe the writing was the most beautiful part! 
 Thing aren't resolved fully by the end, I am really eager to see where the author takes Molly and Tensley in the next book.Now that I have Body of the Crime in my hands, I am going to jump into it immediately! :D 
 P.S. Don't you just love the covers?They're absolutely dreamy and beautiful!

I really enjoyed Uninvited. The topic feels cutting edge and thought provoking. I felt that a possible future in which scientists have discovered a gene that causes violent tendencies was very realistic. A large focus of the novel is how these people who are marked as carriers are discriminated against by the rest of society and it felt to me like that discrimination in and of itself seems to be what actually causes them to act on their tempers. It's a great study of self-fulfilling prophecy. Ironically, reading this book made me feel very angry at the situation and I was usually hoping the main characters would just haul off and start punching people in the face! And then I'd get to thinking, omg if this were real, would I have the HTS gene? It's sort of terrifying, thinking about if you were in Davy's situation. It leaves you thinking about the world and about yourself. 
 I also really enjoyed that in this novel we are seeing sort of the beginnings of a dystopian government emerge. There is an agency in charge of handling the gene testing and dealing with the carriers. Throughout the book we see this agency gain more and more power within the existing US government, which other than this agency seems much the same as it currently is in 2014. (This book is set in 2021.) I know this is marked as dystopia, but I don't see it as that. In most dyspotians a corrupt government is already in place and being rebelled against. I'm sure there will be some rebelling in the sequel, but I have to say it was refreshing to see more of a pre-dystopia setting. I have actually been looking for this, to see how things started. I loved it! 
 These things above, I would rate a 5 star experience. 
 The reason I gave it 4 stars were personal quirks (4 stars is still very good to me though), and they are probably spoilery, so I'm going to hide the next part.  Davy gets bullied or beat up quite a few times throughout the novel, and WITHOUT FAIL Sean always come out of no where to step in and defend her. He would be no where around and then all of a sudden Davy's attacker would be pulled away from her and she'd realize he'd swooped in. Did he have a radar? Not only did I think this was a little too easy, but I wanted to see Davy win her own fights, and also it gave me a mental image of Sean being not much more than a gorilla, pounding someone's face in and beating his chest in triumph. For personal reasons, this made Sean unattractive to me as a love interest. I understand that coming to her defense and being protective was endearing, and yes the topic of this book was violence and anger, and being put in situations that would make you act out. But having dated some men who probably would be carriers of the HTS gene in this universe, it's just a personal turn off to see a love interest act in that way. So it failed to have the romantic swoon for me. Again, that's just personal.  
 Basically though, I do recommend this book!

This was a good book. I really liked it. I did. However, I am a little disappointed in it. I thought for sure this would be a 5 star book. That this would immediately be shelved as "favorites". That I could see myself reading this book again and again. Why? Because there are so many people that label this book as "perfection" and its one of their favorites. Because it is a Brandon Sanderson novel and he is considered one of the fantasy greats of today. Because I've read 2.5 other Brandon Sanderson novels and I loved 1.5 of them. 
 So with that, what was my problem with this book and why doesn't it get that 5th star? I just couldn't get adsorbed into the story. I think this was mostly due to the two main characters, Vin and Kelsier. They didn't stand out to me as characters. They felt very generic, which is the problem I had with that 1 Brandon Sanderson book I did not like so much, which was the Rithmatist. My opinion on Vin is going to contradict itself, but what I liked most about her was that she was very suspicious and untrusting of people. It made sense given her upbringing. However, due to her heavy suspicion, she was so boring and unemotional. She grew up hiding her emotions and it makes sense and I agree, but she was stubborn to do anything because she has a hard time trusting people. She does however get opportunity to grow from this, and she does grow, as a character, but she never really grew on me. I will continue on with this series and I hope to see her grow more and then in time, grow on me as a reader. Kelsier, on the other hand, like I said, very generic. He is the legendary guy who gets this movement to defeat the Lord Ruler started. He has secret powers and is going to use them to change the world. He is a leader of thieves and acts as one should as a leader of thieves. He is inspirational and people unquestionably follow him. True, a guy like this had a strong place in this sort of storyline, but I wanted a reason to single him out. To make him different. I don't want to make any comparison here, but the .5 Sanderson book I read is "The Way of Kings". Yes, I only read half of it as of Feb. 2016, but I needed a break from it for whatever reason that I don't have. I really enjoyed the first half. I even bought the 2nd book. In any case, I really like the .5 Way of Kings better than this first Mistborn book. The characters were much more developed for me and I found myself caring a lot more for them. (I know, it sounds bad when I couldn't finish it right away, but its a big book and I think halfway through I just wanted a break from fantasy and then I just never got back to it. One day this year though, I promise.) 
 Now, all those complaints and it still gets 4 stars? Well, for one, like most Sanderson books, the worldbuilding is glorious. He spends a lot of time developing the magic systems for his fantasy settings as well as the setting overall. It is very interesting to read and see how it ties into the plot, which of course is also done very well. I love the ending of this book, too. It gives a good stopping point, both as a trilogy and as a sort of standalone. There is more to explore but if you didn't like this one and don't wish to continue, you still get a full storyline and can at least get satisfaction from that. The side characters are also pretty fantastic. I really like Sazed, Elend, and Marsh. Even a lot of the Allomancer crew of Kelsier's are pretty great guys. It's a great fantasy plot and world, and I want to read more about it. I just wish I didn't hype this book/series up so much, I think that also affected my expectations way too much. That's not to say after reading all 3 that this won't end up on my favorites list, it definitely could if the main characters continue to grow, but as of right now, it is just going to be as a "really liked it" on my fantasy shelf.

I recently traveled to Maine and had the chance to visit The Mystery Cove Book Shop. It's a great little shop and if you're ever in Bar Harbor just the kind of place I love to browse, full of wonderfully hand selected books and wonderful little gems. I was able to pick up the paperback ARC of The Peculiars and sat down to read it as soon as I got home. 
 The Peculiars is YA, which I don't read, Steampunk, which I have never read, and fantasy, which I usually shy away from. Based on the math I shouldn't have liked this book, but I adored it. Despite a few little niggling issues, this book was just about perfect. I can't wait for this book to catch on so I have someone o talk to about it. 
 Based in the late 1800s The Peculiars is set on the East Coast of America near the outlands of Scree. The main character, Lena, is more than likely half Peculiar, a breed of humanoids who are outcast from mainstream society. Her smart and inquisitive nature drives her to set out alone to find her deadbeat father. The thing I loved the most about this book is the way McQuerry weaves in historical philosophies and inventions. From Darwin to Lister, she intersperses the excitement of the late 1800s around progress and invention. 
 At the beginning of the book there is a strange device used where we switch from first person memory (in italics) to third person narrative. It's odd because it only appears again once during the course of the novel. I hope that in the process of taking this from the ARC I received to the final product these sections are removed or reworked. It was distracting and unnecessary. 
 Overall, this is a top notch book with all the qualities of a great story. It's definitely intended for the YA audience, however, the annoying new YA-Supernatural-Romance-Stupid-Girl tendency is completed avoided. The characters are smart, relateable and completely fascinating.

I'm liking this trend of intense bird-knowledge in children's books. 
 This book has some similarities to Okay for Now since it's about a displaced kid who is dealing with family issues with their own brand of escape/rebellion, but I think this one is little heavier in that there's no feel-good quest towards the end. The main character, Chirp, has to deal with a whole slew of issues: being the only Jewish family in town, older sister's teen rebellion and bad choices, her mother's diagnosis with MS  and subsequent depression, long stay at a psychiatric hospital, and finally, suicide. Yeah, this gets super dark , her psychiatrist father's helplessness, and her neighbor's abusive parents and unnerving OCD tendencies. 
 It sounds super depressing, but it's not written in a way that got me down. Chirp loves bird-watching, and her interest manifests itself all over the narrative. Every nod and gesture follows with a specific bird simile and is quite cute. Netgalley has a scary passage about quoting (to not to) so I won't, but trust me! You want to know all about the way loons nods across species show off different feelings, I swear! 
 There is something unstrained and organic about the story, and while there are many shocking moments, they are dealt with so honestly that there was no need to be flinchy about them. Esther Ehrlich just looks at you firmly and wordlessly tells you to follow and you do because you don't want to show her that you are a wimp. And that pretense makes you better at dealing with the blows. 
 This is a lovely story about a girl who has too much piled on her, and who manages to stand up strong and look back at the world. No fighting, just letting the world know that she's there and she'll keep standing and looking back equally firmly. And then she'll notice a red-throated loon and get out her binocs and ignore everything until she's again alone in her special place. 
 P.S. I felt that Joey, Chirp's neighbor, was a little too much of a wreck with the OCD. The hinted violence was realistic and painful, but the OCD on top of that was overkill. Esther, by all means, talk about all the scary things kids have to deal with, but maybe stretch it across several novels so that it's not crammed into one book, edging out the main issue. Love you though <3

I started listening to this audiobook fully expecting to think Rainbow Rowell was overrated and that I would spend my days at work rolling my eyes at some sappy dialogue the whole time. I did laugh a couple times before I was able to get over the male narrator mimicking a female voice, but that was it. 
 Eleanor and Park takes place in the 80s. When Walkmans were the only way to listen to music on the go, short of carrying around a big boombox, and you actually had to call someone on their home phone to get a hold of them. 
 I don't really care about all that. What I care about, and what doomed me to sitting quietly at my desk fighting small tears of happy, was the realism. I haven't forgotten what it was like to fall in love for the first time. But I haven't thought of it in a while, and I forgot just how many emotions go through you when experiencing every part of a person for the first time--both physically and emotionally. Rowell's writing really shined in that way. I was instantly brought back to those moments when I was 15 (jesus, almost 10 years ago already?) when there were constant butterflies--butterflies over what to say, over what to wear to school, over something as simple as touching a hand. It's a rough but beautiful time, and I loved how vividly I could throw myself into Eleanor and Park's tentative love story. 
 Park was the one I was really drawn to. Eleanor came from a broken home so her way of dealing with it was to lash out, most often at Park. Park, being the boy with loving parents and grandparents, does not have this issue. Maybe partially because of this, he is a beautiful human being. He's endlessly kind, endlessly thoughtful. I feel like he is the sort of boy whose quiet presence immediately makes one feel more at ease. It was an added bonus that he wasn't a traditional "boy"--he wasn't masculine. He liked wearing black eyeliner, wore black clothes and a long trench coat (or at least, it's long in my head). He isn't run-of-the-mill. 
 Eleanor I was less enthused about. While I understand her plight is the reason for her lashing out so much, I had a hard time seeing what Park would like about her. I would have liked her to be a little more deserving of Park's affection, but all the same I couldn't help but root for their love. Park's sexual desire for Eleanor was handled extremely well; it never felt too sudden, or over the top. It was surprising for me to find that I actually very much identified with that part too. The initial lust of a new relationship is sometimes a hard thing to describe. I always find that romance novels tend to overdo it, like the only thing anyone ever thinks about is sex. Everyone is sex on legs, everyone is obsessed with looking at chiseled muscles or high cheekbones or dramatic eye colors. The dramatic hair/eye colors are still present here, but Rowell did a magnificent job of making everything poignant. I think this one will stay relevant for a long time.

Okay there are two extreme emotions. And its not an either or feeling. It is both a love and hate or frustrated emotion. 
 So Katness and Peeta find themselves back in the Games, just when you think okay they just might be forced to be married and she'll never have the boy you think she wants, Gale. Yes I like the unpredictability of the story line. One minute you think you're headed in one direction then it reverses so sharply you're left thinking...okay now where the hell did that come from. 
 But most of the time I found myself frustrated with Katness and how dense she is about everything including her feelings for Peeta, that's when I have to remind myself; she is after all only sixteen. Everything she might have been thrust into has matured her in some things but that doesn't mean that she knows anything about love really. What sixteen year old really comprehends that feeling. Most adults don't. Although the second books focus is still on the love triangle (although its not so much a triangle anymore but Katness not being sure how she feels about Peeta). For me Gale has become a non-entity. Okay okay, I am totally team Peeta. I can't help myself, he is so sweet and understanding and selfless and of course so completely inlove. Who wouldn't be team Peeta. 
 I love that Collins has given Peeta the "gift of gab", his extraordinary ability to weave a spell of words around people to draw them to his way of thinking, and to be able to evoke the emotions he wants them to feel is perfect for the type of character image she has built. 
 The story also makes your think about a number of things, the evil and indifference humanity is capable of. As well as some terrifying ideas of government.

So the back of the book describes the story as a "bleak allegory about surviving the human experience". I do not understand the story at all. I get that the bright cheery artwork is done on purpose for this horrifying story, but I was incredibly confused by the end of it. Nothing was really resolved and a lot of things lead to nowhere. I get that I am also supposed to interpret a lot of things just from the artwork, but there is just too much that is skipped around and I just didn't understand the story at all. There is no reason that I can come up with as to how the little girl that all these characters appeared to emerge from has died. There is a part in the story with the maggot eating character that shows a flashback, so I thought the maggot eating character was representing the girl's death or a lost spirit or something, but after an incomplete flashback, nothing is explained. I also don't get the random man in the woods, was he the guy who killed her?? I guess I'll never know.

I like Amanda Hocking. When I first read her Trylle series (when they were free on Amazon) I thought that she was a pretty decent author compared to a lot of others that seem to do self-publishing. The writing was smooth and the characters were awesome. But in this series... 
 I just don't know. I liked the first book, I read it a long time ago and thought, "that was pretty good." But the second book just felt so repetitive, like everything was happening all over again. She had to find Max, she lost people, she had to kick ass even though she was supposedly weak as hell. I don't like how she just basically forgets all about Lazlo. He's barely even mentioned in this book. 
 The one thing that just really irked me was Remy's hypocrisy. When she found Nolita and Daniels making love (I'm going to call it that because I think they really did love each other as much as two people could during the end of the world) she was disgusted! She thought that they shouldn't even be thinking about stuff like that during an apocalypse. Yet at the end, she just goes right ahead and screws Boden even though it doesn't seem very likely that she's in love with him. I know she saved Nolita and Daniels' life by interrupting, but she didn't had to be a hypocritical bitch about what they were doing.  
 Sorry if you don't like my review, I usually try not to leave 'bad' ones, but this book just irked me. I like Hocking and her works, but I feel like this one could have been thought out better.

So I will be completely honest... I don't do many of these reviews but I feel something should be said about Cursor's Fury. I am a *huge* fan of the Codex Alera series. This was my intro into Jim Butcher's world, and once I got past the first chapter of Furies of Calderon this series really took off for me. 
 I love that these books have been page turners for me. I have always liked multi-character POVs if they are well done. Jim Butcher does a great job here, because there's always a cliffhanger just before he changes characters, making you want more.

I bought Half Bad in London early this year, before there was any considerable hype to speak of over here. So if I'd had read it right then, I could've beaten everyone to the punch and have been all hipster about it. It took me until now to finally crack the spine though, so I guess I'm lagging behind in the hype-department once more. 
 Half Bad is not an easy one to review. I guess you could say it wasn't "half bad" (puns! <3) but in my opinion it wasn't very good either - certainly not worth all the fuss. 
 The first 50 pages were extremely off-putting to me. I wasn't sure if the entire book was going to be written in that same unbearably clipped, deranged style so I didn't really want to read on. I hated - absolutely hated - the chapters that were written in second person perspective and hope I never ever come across it in any book ever again. The whole first 50 pages seemed to me a desperate attempt at being original. 
 I asked the Goodreads-community for advice: continue reading or give up? They unanimously urged me to read on, and I'm glad I did. Because after those first 50 pages, the writer sort of gave up on being strange and off-putting and "original", which makes the whole thing even stranger - I mean, what was the point? I ... really don't get it. This entire style experiment was lost on me. 
 Anyways, in general, I did not like the style in which the rest of the book is written any better. If you'd ask Mike Skinner of The Streets to write a book, it would probably be something like this. I actually do like The Streets though! But using 'cos' in an actual book instead of ''cause' is just plain wrong to me ... 
 The story ... I don't know, it's quite boring isn't it? There's a lot of build-up, a lot of feeling sorry for Nathan, a lot of 'eww'-moments. A very boyish book as well. I didn't appeal to me in any way. 
 Whilst reading, I had this idea that Half Bad was actually just a Harry Potter re-write: 
 What if Harry Potter were the son of Sirius Black, raised by witches who looked upon him as if he'd be just as 'evil' as his serial-killer father. However, in this world, the good witches aren't very good and the magic isn't always all that magical. Poor Harry/Nathan grows up in a cage instead of a cupboard under the stairs. Even worse! That poor boy. And the not-so-good good witches want to use him as bait to catch Sirius Black! Whom he has never met! Oh the tragedy. The end. 
 I did however like the last 100 pages, after Gabriel (like!) and Rose (like!) showed up and stuff started moving along. Even so I am not very inclined to read the next book. I simply don't care for Nathan very much, the setting depressed me and the writing style is not one I'm partial to. 
 Overall, this was just a very 'meh' book to me, with a terrible beginning that is not referential to the rest of the book. It gets better as you read along, sure, but this one's just going to be labeled: "Not for me, thanks". 
 Thanks to the last 100 pages, I'm rating it ***, otherwise it would've probably been **.
