This book had a slow start for me, but that was due to the way the author built/introduced the world. She throws you right in and you have to figure things out yourself and gradually you learn/understand more about it. After I got past that point, and I'm not quite sure where that point was, past 100 pages though, but I totally got into it and I could not put it down. The world is just so unique, I can't quite compare it to any other popular series. It is definitely high fantasy though. I think I would have a hard time describing certain types of witchery to people though, especially Threadwitchery. That one took me forever to wrap my head around, but I stuck to it to trudge right through. It actually is amazing since it allows me to be really excited for Iseult's (the Threadwitch) point of view chapters because I want to see how other characters are feeling and what their threads are doing. It created so many teases for romance between Iseult's Threadsister, Safi, and the ship Captain they run into (Merik). 
 Going off that, the characters are great as well. I love the relationships between the Threadfamily-- Safi and Iseult; and Merik and Kullen. It's great to have a novel that focuses on strong friendships. I kinda wish that we got to see some more "magic" or effects that thread-family can create, but right now it just seems that they are best friends who always have each others' backs and will risk their lives to protect each other. I am so sad about Kullen's death-- I loved that the main love interest had a Threadbrother to match the fact that Safi has a Threadsister. It just allows the couple to be able to relate to each other more since they understand the feeling of having a friend so close. Kullen was just so strong too, and it was awesome to see his witchery come alive.  
 I also love how romance was approached in this-- it is what I want for a romance. It teases the reader and mostly the book focuses on developing the world and setting the stage for the plot for future books in the series, but just that little bit keeps me on the edge of my seat. And since I know it is not the focus of the book it always leaves me wondering of what is going to happen between the characters. 
 By the way, there is an antihero in the plot as well-- he is a bloodwitch. I think he may become my favorite character down the line-- I am a sucker for those types. Right now though, Merik is probably my favorite (though Kullen is a close 2nd). 
 It will be a long wait for the next novel, but I am sure it will be worth it!

There are odd psychological aspects of Hartman's story - Seraphina's 'mind garden' - that take a moment to get used to but which I ending up enjoying.  A quick, engaging read with a sleek, alternating triptych narrative structure that deals in graphic themes that are not for the faint of heart. 
 ***TRIGGER WARNING*** for those sensitive to descriptions of extreme violence. 
 Based upon a tragic incident in the history of the region of Uganda and its bordering countries in which an entire school of young girls was kidnapped by marauding thugs known as the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA). A courageous nun tracked the LRA contingent responsible for this abduction and negotiated for the release of all but thirty of her students. Those girls entered a program for reintegration into society where they were treated for Stockholm Syndrome and Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. Unfortunately abduction of young people by the LRA is ongoing within this part of Africa. The country has been unable to fully eradicate the rebel army as they have used guerrilla tactics and brutality to elude authorities. An organization of concerned parents of girls in this situation sought international aid for this ongoing crisis. 
 Susan Minot first became aware of this issue while on a journalism assignment and chose to collect interviews from those affected. These interviews became the basis of this novel, solidified within the voice of a single narrator-victim who was one of thirty girls who was not allowed freedom: Esther. Esther's voice is both cautious and scared, befitting the tragedies which she witnessed and endured. 
 The author's journey to Africa forms another section in the exploits of her alter ego Jane. While working on a film, Jane encounters a wealthy young woman who invites her to her villa in Sudan. When Jane learns of the LRA's kidnappings, she flees the emotional trauma of the death of her ex-husband and falls for a young African man from a well-to-do family who is somewhat younger than her. The descriptions in this section are more sparse than the others; despite detailing excessive drinking and feasting and wild sex while Jane processes her personal grief and that of those affected by the LRA's kidnappings. 
 Parts of the sections detailing the girls' subsequent healing process is made visceral by its use of second person narration. Other parts of this rehabilitative process are told by Esther. This duality shows how rehabilitation is a collective endeavor as well as an individual journey. 
 All three of these narrative voices depict starkly different viewpoints of female emotional trauma. While the book would have been arguably more strong without the sections on Jane, the author's choice to represent herself in this way provides a stark contrast to the extreme poverty common in Africa.  
 Reads as if Cormac McCarthy took to the The Green Hills of Africa. stands on its own to merit attention, both for its focus on an overlooked tragedy in recent history.

I'm really surprised this has such a high rating! I read this for book club, and its the first William Kent Krueger I have read. If it's typical of his work, I'll know to avoid his books in the future (unfortunately). I found the whole thing very poorly crafted. 
 There were some things, to be fair, that worked. Ordinary Grace gets two stars for being a Minnesota mystery, my very favorite subgenre. I live in a rural MN town between the train tracks and the river, and Krueger's descriptions were dead-on. Not just dead-on, he has a gift for scene setting and descriptive language. I found that part delightful. 
 Things that did not work: 
 * ALERT ALERT, someone has gone through this poor man's book and stolen all the commas! I don't know if the book was just poorly edited or if the author (or publisher) insisted on all these run-on sentences to maintain some kind of voice, but it's distractingly awful. Examples, quoted verbatim punctuation and all: 
 The hole was already dug and Gus was waiting and Sheriff Gregor was there though I didn't know why and moments after we arrived Mr. van der Waal drove up in the hearse and my father and Gus and the sheriff and the mortician slid the coffin from the back. (page 70.) 
 (Take a deep breath!) 
 We said our good-byes and Jake called shotgun and got in the front seat and I slid in the back and Gus and Ginger French spent a moment talking quietly several paces away from the car and then he kissed her on the lips and she held his arm as if she wouldn't let him go and then the connection broke and she lifted her emptied hand and waved to us as Gus drove up the dirt lane and headed back to New Bremen. (page 239.) 
 If it was once or twice, I would shrug it off, but the whole book is written this way. Beyond that there are a handful of spelling errors that surprised me in a published novel. The overall impression is one of low quality and it makes for a difficult read. 
 * There were several story lines that Krueger developed and then just discarded without taking them anywhere. Examples:  The original murder of Bobby Cole, the second murder of the itinerant (super spoiler: there is no serial killer, despite the setup), the domestic violence in the Klement family, the feud between Ruth / mother and Julia / Kal's mother, even Engdahl's story is half-heartedly ended.  These plot lines don't do anything for the story. They aren't resolved, and they don't further the main conflict. They muddy up and weaken the book. 
 * I found the murderer easy to identify, by about a third of the way through the book. The red herrings Kruerger tries to include  such as Warren Redstone's supposed guilt  are unconvincing at best. The writing even clearly shows that character's innocence. No one is falling for it, and it makes the book tedious. The reveal was done in a series of increasingly obvious clues over a chapter or two, and came way too early in the book. Once we know who did it, we still have a chunk of run-on sentences left to get through, and without a story left they're nothing but boring. 
 * As I say I have not read other books by Krueger, so I don't know if this is true of all his writing or just part of this book because one of the characters was a minister: This is awfully, awfully preachy on the religion front. Some of the monologues about the love of God and His forgiveness went on for several pages, added zero to the story, and irritated the heck out of me. Why reproduce a Sunday morning sermon in its entirety? Why devote so much story time to the discussions characters have about God? This felt much more like Christian fiction masquerading as genre fic to me, and that made my eyes roll so far I could see my own brain. Not necessary. 
 Overall I can say this read felt to me like nothing but a waste of a few hours. It's poorly done. There's a lot of great character and scene descriptions, but without a decent structure or resolution they can't go anywhere. 2/5.

My Big Fat Disclaimer 
 In the interest of fairness, (and maybe only a teensy bit of pride [but totally the Mama Bear pride and not the gross look-at-me pride]) I should disclose that I know the author, M. Molly Backes. Over the past few years she has been my teacher, critique partner, and friend. While this does not prevent me from stating my honest opinions on the quality of her book, I am probably in a position to like it as a person familiar with her personality and writing style. With that all out in the open, let's move on. 
 Shit just got real... 
 Go back up and read the first bolded line of the summary above. I'll wait. 
 Back now? Good. I point it out (for the lazy set: "What does it mean to do wrong, when no one punishes you?") because I think understanding this theme from the outset greatly impacts your enjoyment of the book. This is not a story about fluffy bunnies and sparkly unicorns and beautiful rainbows (even though, in my mind, that cover is just asking for a rainbow). This is a story about real things that can, and do, happen to teenagers. 
 The situations in this book punched me in the gut. I dare you to read the prologue and not connect deeply with at least some portion of it. Molly Backes is a master of Getting It. She wrote a character, Paige Sheridan, who is struggling to understand consequences, or the completely unjust and unfair LACK of them, that accompanies the life of a high school student, in a way that was believable and thought-provoking. Backes peeled back the superficial layers and forced Paige, and us as readers, to acknowledge the ugly sides of human behavior and the ease with which cruelty and convenience can influence even the best of intentions. 
 Life is not fair. Things don't always end up the way we want them to. And I love that Backes portrayed this so truthfully in her narrative. Not everyone agrees with me. 
 "Issue" is such a loaded word... 
 Is this an issue book? It deals with the impact of a drunk driving accident on a group of girls. It illustrates common teen situations of homophobia, bullying, partying, and sex. But I didn't see it as an issue book. It wasn't pointing out the perils of drunk driving and why teens should avoid it. Were there severe consequences from the accident? Yes. One girl was seriously injured. But that wasn't the point of the story. Nor was the point of the story to show us how destructive homophobia can be on a community, or how teen girls should handle their drunk boyfriends trying to rape them. The drinking and the sex and the gay slurs just happened to be a part of Paige's life, and all of these things impact her growth from a narcissistic princess into a contemplative writer. This is Paige's story and journey, not an issue book passing judgment on the behavior of its teen characters. 
 I appreciated that Backes didn't gloss over any aspect of Paige's life. She has a manipulative best friend, a weak-willed boyfriend, and a self-absorbed mother. Her friends drink too much, Paige cares too much about what people think, and everyone in this book is capable of bad decisions. The beauty of this book is the subtlety with which each character's growth is illustrated. There is not one cathartic event that pulls everyone together. Instead, there are a series of events that impact different characters in unique ways, setting all of them on a different trajectory. 
 Sisters, man... 
 One of the best devices I noticed to show a subtle change was the name Paige used for her sister. In the first half of the book, Paige's younger sister Miranda repeatedly has to remind everyone that she prefers to be called Mirror. As with many flights of fancy with young people, she is ignored. Paige refers to her always as Miranda, since that's her name, and she thinks calling her Mirror is dumb. 
 I don't know when exactly the shift occurred, but toward the end of the book I noticed that Paige was consistently calling her sister Mirror. While finding acceptance of herself, Paige began to understand that something as simple as a name change was also an important way for her sister to find her own identity. Though Paige may not have given herself a unique nickname, I think she subconsciously realized that Mirror did so because she wanted to be taken seriously, much like how Paige now wanted to be viewed as more than just a vapid princess. And she finds common ground, as well as a fresh starting point in their relationship, by using her sister's preferred name and therefore validating Mirror's perspective and identity. As someone with a younger sister, I really connected with this concept. 
 What I'm saying is... 
 I'm no expert in contemporary YA fiction, but this one spoke to me on so many levels. It's a book that will make you think, which is always a good thing. It sheds some light on the power of cliques and group thinking that can take over a teen's life without them even realizing it. Backes finds a way to validate experiences without passing judgment, and without needing to find a lesson in every difficult event that her characters encounter. Life doesn't always hand us teachable moments, nor do we find answers in the immediate aftermath of major events. It's how we process our experiences into making the choices that feel right to us that truly matters.

Gretchen, Grace, and Greer are finally united and determined to fight the monsters heading their way while they attempt to face their destiny. This requires finding out what their destiny is, as all they know is that they are the Key Generation. The people who do know, Eurydale and Sthenno, have been kidnapped and taken to either the Abyss or the dungeons of Olympus, two equally dangerous places. The girls need to rescue their mentors while dealing with their own increasingly messy lives. Greer is trying to keep up with her rich, high-society peers and plan some elaborate tea while keeping her monster-killing hobby a secret. Grace is excited because her crush, Milo, likes her back, but how can she start a relationship when she's got a secret life she's keeping from her family? Grace is also getting increasingly worried about her (adopted) brother Thane who ran away from home without explanation. Meanwhile, Gretchen, the only sister who isn't leading a double life, has her own troubles in the form of Nick, the cute guy who called her in the last moments of Sweet Venom and saved the sisters' life by warning them about the house blowing up. Gretchen knows Nick is hiding something, but can she let her guard down a little and let him in? 
 This was a fantastic sequel. I said in my review of Sweet Venom that it felt more like an prologue to a novel than an actual novel, and Sweet Shadows was good enough that it made the first book worth the time, if only to get to book 2. Again, I was not a fan of the Greek stuff and I think the novel would have worked just fine without being based on mythology, but it was so far off from the Greek mythology usually incorporated into teen novels that it was easy to forget the connection at times. The story moved pretty fast, which was good because if it hadn't then I would have given up pretty fast. My patience was worn through after completing Sweet Venom, and if Sweet Shadows had continued at the same slow pace then that would have been it for me. 
 I don't remember if I wrote this in Sweet Venom's review, but the characters, especially the triplets, all seemed flat and one-sided. Each of the girls had a stereotype, and each stuck to her stereotype throughout. Although one could argue that Gretchen softened a bit, which went against who she was supposed to be, I think the whole point of having a character so tough and closed-off is to later open her up. She let everyone in too quickly, much quicker than a real person with that personality would, which made her seem even more one-sided in my opinion. My favorite character was Greer, because she even when she does feel gooey and emotional, she puts on a stoic face and says sarcastic things. Greer is the most real, despite her cliche rich girl attitude. 
  
 My favorite scene in the novel was the one in the Abyss where Gretchen discovers that not only monsters live there, and that not all monsters are evil. It was especially cool because it messed with Gretchen's head and made her rethink everything she's done for the past four years. It also complicated the girls' non-plan, because it made them realize that there is no way to save the good guys without saving the bad guys, and no way to kill the bad guys without killing the good guys. 
 Is it just me, or was there something between Greer and Thane at the end? Not quite love at first sight, but definitely something at first sight. Which is really nauseating when you realize that Greer looks exactly like Grace, who is Thane's little sister. Thane was definitely shocked to see Greer because of her resemblance to Grace, but Greer definitely has a bit of a crush on her sister's brother. The incestuousness here is a tad uncomfortable, but since they technically aren't related, I guess it's okay? I think the only element of this that makes it disturbing is how Greer and Grace look alike, so if Greer and Thane were to get together, he'd be dating a girl who is the spitting image of his sister. Another reason for not wanting Thane and Greer to hook up is that as of now, Greer is the only single sister. The point of a novel such as this is that the author wants you to believe that this is happening in your universe, or in an alternate one, but in no universe does every person end up with a great boyfriend at the end. For Greer and Thane to end up together, one of the other couples would have to break up/die, which strangely doesn't bother me and I find myself inclined to wish Milo or Nick dead. What's happening to me? Where's the sweet girl who wants happy endings??????

Time travel novels tend to be fun, but discussion on theories of visiting the past usually leave me cold. That, in a nutshell, is why I give this book a three rather than the (at least) four it otherwise deserves. 
 Ned Henry is an historian of the early 21st century, which by this point means a first-hand witness of historical events by means of time travel. 
 Funding for time travel ran dry once investors realized they could not pillage the wealth of the past, but Lady Schrapnell has agreed to underwrite costs. The catch is that the department must allow her to use historians to help research the now-destroyed cathedral at Coventry to ensure a completely authentic restoration. In a typical deal with the devil, Lady Schrapnell's zeal is all-consuming, and she exploits all resources at her disposal without regard to human limitations - let alone the possible destruction of the space-time continuum. 
 When Ned suffers "time lag" from Schrapnell's tyrannical jump schedule, he is secreted away to Victorian England for a spot of rest. This quiet location inevitably becomes the suspected locus of a possible rift in the space-time continuum, and Ned and his fellow historians attempt to solve the mystery using the appropriately literary-historical examples of Agathie Christie and P. G. Wodehouse. 
 The dialog and humour are masterful, and the constant allusions to Three Men in a Boat (To Say Nothing of the Dog) serve brilliantly to knit the story together. 
 Although I found the time travel theories to be almost risible at points, the comments of others seem to prove me as the exception. Keeping that caveat in mind, this is a book that I would recommend to any reader.

There was something about him that drew you to him, that made you want to see more of him, that might even (if you were James' age) make it very hard not to smile and wave. Maya could see that was the case. She could feel that call of his in her very bones. 
 Have you ever read a book where a feeling begins to grow in your chest, coming up your throat, until you find yourself smiling? That is what I did after I finished reading this book. This book is a short, pleasant, read. The style the author has, and her descriptions, are utterly amazing. 
 The author is able to transport you into this world and create a feeling of 'ennui' (the actual word for a book-hangover) in the rest of the world after you are finished. It's not as strong as some of the other books I've read, but I just had that feeling even while reading the book. While I wasn't thinking about it consciously, I didn't want it to end. Even so, the languorous ending felt like the right conclusion when put in perspective with how the rest of the book was written. 
 What is this feeling? So sudden and new? 
 I got the moment, I laid eyes on you? 
 Oh Cabinet of Earths 
 Because even though I really enjoyed this book, there were some minor problems (though that may be because this is an ARC copy). First off, there isn't much action. Yes, her descriptions are great, but there isn't much actually happening. Mostly, it is Maya having certain feelings about people and acting accordingly. All in all, the book feels a bit vague sometimes, although I like that since  there are people who ARE vague. They have been stripped of what makes a person special, and noticeable, and are left invisible and horrifyingly ordinary.

There were aspects of this that I really enjoyed but it was too long, too repetitive, and too ridiculous for me. I've admittedly never been to the opera, so maybe for opera fans this book is right on target. It's certainly very theatrical, very high drama. Plenty of jewels and lavish gowns. Lots of plotting, schemes within schemes within schemes, back stabbing, love, and betrayal. My main problem was the repetition, each go 'round getting increasingly absurd but not really progressing the plot or bringing us any place new. If this were 200 pages shorter I would've liked it quite a bit.

This story is told in an Alternating POV or Third Person Multiple. This POV allows us to get inside our characters heads, and follow them each as they all work on saving the world from the Crazy General Madigan while working against someone on the inside who wants Madigan to succeed.

I really do not want to go into details about the story because I would hate to ruin anything for any reader out there.. this is a story you MUST experience as it is intended. I will warn you that if you are going into this story looking for a lot of hot man on man action, you will probably be disappointed. While there are plenty of scenes that are appropriate to the storyline, after all, you can't really stop and get it on with your lover while you are trying to save the world from madman - I think what was there was perfect. 
 Throughout this story, we get to see all the characters as mentioned and our couples are all there in one way or another - there is President Jack Spiers and his First Gentleman, former Secret Service agent Ethan Reichenback; Russian President Sergey Puchkov and Sasha Andreyev; and Lieutenant Adam Cooper and Prince Faisal al-Saud. There is a lot of emotional times between these three couples as they are uncertain each time they see each other if it will be the last - will they all make it out of the arctic alive? One thing is for sure, these six and their teams are Outnumbered, outmaneuvered, and outgunned yet they don't ever give up. 
 While Ethan, Jack, and crew are all out trying to actively save the world, there are people among them who are working for Mad-Man Madigan - people they trust, people they know, people who are reporting to Madigan their every move. Who? Why? When? Those are all thing you are going to have to find out as you read the story. 
 Make sure when you start this book you literally have all day and night to read, because once you pick it up - you're not going to want to put it down and it is a long book coming it at over 450 pages. Cover to cover it is packed with action, mystery, breath-holding moments to pulse-pounding excitement-- I laughed at some of the crazy things that happened or certain moments and cried during certain moments. I totally could keep reading about these characters, there is soo much more that could be written, not that there was anything left gaping open, no cliffhangers, It is just one of those storylines that could easily go on...Overall, totally loved it!!

 I gave this 4 stars immediately upon finishing. Maybe the most important thing you need to know about this book is that I found it absolutely gripping and it messed up my sleep schedule 2 nights in a row. I haven't had a book kidnap me so wholly in a while. 
 However, upon further thought and space, I am changing my rating to 3 stars. Although it was quite an enjoyable reading experience, a few things just BUGGED me. 
 Spoilers below, please only open if you've read this book. 
  
 First of all, I hated the fact that Meg's suicide was treated as a mystery to be solved. It is very much human nature to want to assign blame to something (or someone) tangible, so I understand Cody's motivation for setting out on her mission. But I was very uncomfortable with the fact that the book very much gives us a villian. Bradford was portrayed as responsible for making Meg pull the trigger (So to speak), he was painted as a "murderer." I have a problem with this. 
 Now, I have no experience with losing someone to suicide, and I'm not trying to make a generalization that this scenario could never happen. But I DO have experience with depression and I felt like turning this story into a mystery with a bad guy INVALIDATES MENTAL ILLNESS. 
 There was never a mystery. Bradford was just some guy on the other side of a computer screen. He could have been ANYONE. He could have been NOONE. Meg was DEPRESSED. She knew it, her parents knew it, and some of her college acquaintances knew it. The only person who didn't know it was Cody, who Meg has hid this secret from, but I felt like just one simple conversation would have given Cody the understanding and closure she needed. Turning it into a thriller felt like a bastardization of suicide and mental illness to me. 
 Secondly, this was basically a story about GLORIFIED STALKING. Cody does some shady and somewhat illegal things to track down Bradford. She finds out his name, place of work, and home address and then proceeds to show up at his door unannounced. HOW IS THIS OK? With recent events that have happened in the book community I was shocked to read about this behavior from our "good guy" and it never be addressed that maybe she has gone too far. 
 I am pretty much appalled at seeing the very same people in the reading community who were some of the loudest voices of outrage during the Hale/Harris debacle turn around and now praise I Was Here as a touching and accurate portrayal of loss and grief just because this is a favorite/well known author. No. Just no. 
 /drops mic 
  
 And for the record, I know I've taken a critical approach in my review but it is in no way a hateful review. Gayle is one of my favorite authors, and I enjoy that this book gave me lots of food for thought.

Station Eleven is a post-apocalyptic science fiction novel with a realism and relatability that I have never experienced from a novel such as this. 
 Our scene opens in Toronto, Ontario where a formerly-famous film star just collapsed on stage as he plays King Lear. Arthur Leander dies as a newly minted paramedic, Jeevan Chaudhary, attempts to resuscitate him. Meanwhile, a child actor named Kirsten Raymonde is on stage and is marked for life by witnessing Leander die. As the event dies down, Jeevan's friend, a doctor at Toronto General Hospital calls to make good on a promise he made years ago to Jeevan: Yes, there is a real epidemic going on. Clark Thompson, Leander's best friend, is meanwhile tasked with alerting all Leander's ex-wives that he has passed away. This includes successful executive Miranda Carroll who is currently in Malaysia. Then in Toronto Jeevan's phone rings again, his doctor friend advises him to evacuate the city. 
 The Georgian Flu kills 99% of the Earth's population in only a few days. Now the world must learn how to continue on without internet, phones, electricity, etc. We suddenly wake up in a world devastated and barely able to survive. But, unlike most dystopian novels we have no zombies. No Mad Max-esque road warriors. No action scenes. No crazed government plots. Just humanity struggling to survive. 
 The main players, as addressed above, are all loosely connected to each other. As the story moves forward we are constantly flashed to the past and experience these tenuous ties being drawn tighter only to be pulled apart again. For example, Kirsten survived and as a once-child-actor now travels and performs with an acting troupe: The Traveling Symphony. Here they put on concerts and performs Shakespeare. Shakespeare and his world, also ravaged by plague- but not as roughly, serve as constant metaphors. 
 Station Eleven is haunting, terrifying, beautiful, and captivating. It taught me to appreciate the little things and helped me recognize what I take for granted might not always be here.  There is no incredible revelation at the end of this book. However, the ending was perfect in my mind. After all this death, misery, and sadness, the reader is able to walk away from this novel with the briefest glimpse of hope. This hope was very real, and in turn, made this whole novel so much more possible. Unlike most post-apocalyptic novels, we are left knowing that life moves on and the world will once again be whole. Just a different kind of whole.  
 I encourage you to read this. It's a wonderful ride.

Noggin is surprisingly heartfelt and had me tearing up a couple of times. It's a rough emotional ride, in that it deals with a situation that people will never have to go through. 
 We've all seen the futuristic TV shows or movies where someone wakes up years into the future, with all of their loved ones dead and gone. Noggin follows a similar story, only Travis wakes up just five years after his "death". On the surface this is an amazing thing--his family is still there when he wakes up, many things are still very recognizable. When he goes back to school he still has to deal with the terrible teacher he dealt with the first time around. 
 But five years can be a very long time. In that time, Travis' girlfriend Cate has grown up and moved on. She's engaged to another man, and though it has been five years since she last saw Travis, for him it only feels like a few weeks. His best friend Kyle has moved on to university, and everyone he grew up with has moved on to other things. And Travis, still 16, must start down at the bottom and try to catch up in the world. 
 And really, that's where the heart of this novel is. Travis made this ultimate decision because he wanted to maybe come back for Cate--only to find that Cate is engaged and 21. It's hard because you can't really blame anyone. Cate would have been drowning for five years had she never found a way to move on. And Travis isn't suddenly going to mature to an early twenties level overnight simply because his best friend and old girlfriend are. And it was heartbreaking to see the difference between the two. And Travis reliving his past moments with Kyle and Cate and comparing them to his present moments were really why this novel shines. 
 I couldn't help but be desperate for Travis' case. I just kept thinking, "wait four more years, Cate! Then he'll be 21, you'll be 25!" The age difference isn't so drastic that they couldn't somehow make it work. It's just that Travis is a teenager NOW. And I was really really hoping the end would have an epilogue that maybe showed them reconnecting with a little chemistry. Alas, my wish did not come true. 
 Really, though, I was highly impressed. When Travis relives his last day with his friends and family, I finally just gave up trying to keep a straight face and started crying. No shame.

Short Review 
 A lot like The Final Empire if you slowed things way down. The little bit of development that was present in the first book in regards to character is absent as well. Given its length, it's difficult to justify actually reading this over just reading the Wikipedia summary and jumping to The Hero of Ages. 
 Long Review 
 Despite its faults I didn't think the first Mistborn book was all that bad. I enjoyed it. I assumed most of the problems would get cleaned up by the next book since Sanderson was a relatively new author. Sadly, the problems seem to have just compounded. 
 First, because I try hard to be an upbeat positive sort of fellow, the things I enjoyed. The way the plot is structured there are some interesting things hinted at and revealed that make events in the first book more understandable and hint to thing I hope are explained in the third. 
 The Lord Ruler is humanized a great deal, Preservation and Ruin are foreshadowed well, and there are things like the spike in Zane and Marsh's descent into insanity that I expect to tie into things in the third book. 
 Additionally, I liked a lot of the little exchanges and small bits of development given to the 'side' characters like Ham, Breeze, Clubs, Sazed, etc. I also enjoyed the action sequences a lot, much as I had in the first book. 
 Now, onto the problems. Sorry. 
 The first thing I'll note is what I'll call Walking Dead Syndrome. If a character has a sudden burst of touching, heartfelt moments - they are going to die. Clubs has his little heart to heart with Sazed and gets the religious token from him, he gets killed. Tindwyl has her touching 'I love you' moment with Sazed, she gets killed. Dox has his heartfelt moment coming to terms with Elend and the nobility, he gets killed. 
 I have nothing wrong with an author trying to make us like a character, I have nothing wrong with an author killing characters off, but when it's structured like this it makes me feel like Brandon Sanderson's editors called him up and said, "Hey, we don't really care about Clubs dying. Can you get us a little better emotional response?" and so he just threw in a single heartfelt moment rather than building him as a character throughout the book. 
 To me Vin regressed as a character in this book. I know the idea is that the 'betrayal' of Kelsier leaving them all and dying as part of his plan is supposed to be the thing that reawakens this mistrustful side of hers but it feels so damn forced. It seemed like she was swinging between the extremes of badass murdering assassination machine and angsty insecure teenage girl - placing her more in the middle or acknowledging some kind of gray area would have been substantially better. Not the mention the half-assed love triangle with Zane. 
 The twist with the Deepness and the Well was expected. This is half of why I say this book is skippable - its primary purpose seems to be to establish that the Deepness is the next big bad guy and to set Elend up as being equal to Vin in power by making him a mistborn. 
 The dialogue is still painful, and the repetitiveness is dialed way up. Either that or I just noticed it more. When not rehashing the events of the first book, there are lots of sequences like this: 
 "Oh no!" Elend cried, "X happened! What will we do? That means Y and Z are definitely going to happen." 
 Breeze nodded. Sazed smiled. Ham nodded too. 
 Y and Z are definitely going to happen then, Vin thought hesitantly. She nodded. She smiled at Elend, and wondered how long it would be before he left her, and Zane left her, and her brother came back to life with Kelsier just so they could leave her again. 
 "Y and Z won't be easy," Clubs grunted grumpily. "Do remember when this, that, and that other thing happened in the last book? That means that A, B, and C will happen too." 
 Vin angstily angsted some angst about angsting. 
 Am I being too hard on the book? Possibly. The hype surrounding this book though makes it difficult to give it too much of a pass. I expect better by this point. 
 Also, there are still lots of 'but commas' as mentioned in my review of the first book. Sentences where a comma always follows a but, even when it is in no way appropriate for the sentence. After a while it just gets to be a game of find the but commas.

Part of me just wants to write, I LOVE RAINBOW ROWELL, and let it be the end of the review. I don't really think it's even possible for her to write something I don't like. Even the idea of a magic time-warping phone being a major plot point. 
 Landline has all the things I've come to expect from Rowell - witty dialogue, great characterization, and lots of emotion. What's different in Landline as compared to her other novels, is that instead of watching the main characters fall in love, our main character, Georgie, has already fallen in love - and gotten married, and had kids. It could be the post script to any of her other love stories. When the happily-ever-after may be a little light on the happy. 
 When the idea for a sitcom that Georgie and her long time writing partner, Seth, have been working on forever is given a possible green light, she has to skip her vacation to Neal's mother's house in Omaha for Christmas. She expects Neal to reschedule the trip (because he's always been the one in the relationship to sacrifice things), but instead he decides to take the girls and go without her. Her mother is convinced that Neal has left Georgie for good and invites her over. While Georgie insists her marriage isn't over, she begins to worry that it's heading in that direction - that it's been actively heading in that direction for awhile. With Georgie's cell phone always dead and Neal never answering his, Georgie uses the old landline phone from her childhood bedroom to call Omaha. Except the Neal she reaches is Neal from the past, specifically Neal the week before he proposed. Georgie begins to wonder if she is messing with fate, if she should save Neal from herself, if she could save her marriage before it starts, or if she's going insane. 
 I wasn't really sure what to think of the magic phone when I first read the synopsis. I'm still not even sure how I really feel about the magic phone. But, the magic phone is really not the story. The story is Georgie coming to terms with her faults and knowing that while there are some things she's never going to change, there are some things she can work on. For Neal. Which is really all he's ever asked of her. 
 I really loved the characters in this book. They all have the witty banter ability that I love. Her kooky mother and her teenage sister are both supportive and funny. Her kids are cute - and weird - and full of personality. And Neal. Neal is sweet and loving and wonderful in a way that only Rainbow Rowell can write. (I'm pretty sure I would marry ANY of Rowell's leading men. Maybe the next book can be about a magic pen that writes them into existence.) The only character I didn't completely love was Seth. Seth reminded me a little of Nick in Fangirl - using Georgie because his writing was better with her. However, unlike Nick and Cather, Seth actually cares about Georgie. They're still best friends, even after all these years, even though he's always been a point of contention between Georgie and Neal. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Landline. I love Rowell's writing and the way she seamlessly flows between past and present to tell Neal and Georgie's story. I love that it's a different take on "love being enough" for making a relationship work or last. And I just love Rainbow Rowell. She has such a distinct style and it just makes me feel happy reading it - even when it sometimes is making me sad. I would recommend Landline to fans of Rowell, marriage, contemporary lit, and a little bit of magic.

In the world, there are places like Bone. Places that are forgotten by people with privilege where survival is a struggle. 
 In Bone, there is a girl who spends most of her existence being ignored and neglected by her mother. Then one day, another girl goes missing and Margo decides it's time for things to change. 
 I read back in the winter and immediately became enthralled with Tarryn Fisher's writing style. She is very raw, emotional, and at times bare. She chooses her words so very carefully that if you aren't paying attention, you'll miss the subtle nuances in the characters and plot. And if you manage to become lost in the story, then you'll actually miss the bigger picture. You'll miss the twist. 
 Mud Vein and Marrow are both written from incredibly dark places. The central characters struggle with depression and psychosis, with the unreliability of the people in their lives so central to their foundation as humans with incredibly loose anchors to sanity. 
 I'll freely admit that when I finished the book, I was actually disappointed because I had absolutely no idea if what I was reading through the character's point-of-view was real or imagined. I was so frustrated in fact, I had to think about it a bit, reread a few paragraphs. And finally, it clicked for me. 
 Like I said, Fisher is subtle. So very subtle, I am questioning my own sanity. 
 Without giving much away, my recommendation is to read Mud Vein first. While both are standalone novels, Marrow contains a very subtle spoiler in the form of one Chekhov-style prop and one minor character. It took me until her appearance to really put everything together. And because of that one minute element, I was left scratching my head for the remainder of the book. 
 So, the ultimate question: Is Judah real?  Based on what I realized after finishing the book, my answer is a resounding yes. 
 While her minute Easter eggs are very clever, it doesn't really change my overall reaction to the book. It's flawed. The characters are very hard to like or feel any sort of empathy for. And rather than cheer for the vigilante justice that Margo delivers to her albeit deserving victims, I never feel like she carries out her acts with any sort of rationality. Of course, that's the draw of an unreliable narrator. We're relying on Margo to tell us what it feels like, what's on her mind. Essentially, she carries out her actions with almost the same level of sociopathic detachment. It's difficult for me to feel like she's done the right thing, that she's returned the world to some sort of moral balance. 
 And that is possibly Fisher's intent, to make it so that Margo is constantly teetering on the edge of hero and criminal, sane and insane. The end result is a train wreck I can't exactly turn away from. But I'm not enjoying it either.

First Impressions of this book were pretty muddled. When I found out that Santino was writing another book featuring #Rayvid I was ecstatic - over the top happy. I loved my guys the first time around, why would I not want to read more about their happily ever after? Well, therein is the issue - Santino put these poor guys through the ringer in this book. There were moments, Not gonna lie - that I wanted to reach out "virtually" and smack Mr. Hassell, because how dare he do this to Raymond and David?!? 
 Then, after I finished the book and really thought about it - which it has taken me a LONG time to write this review I can appreciate all that happens in this book and all that our couple is put through - because that is life after all. It's not pretty. It often doesn't come with happily-ever-afters and everything is rosy. No. In life, you have to work for happiness - every.single.day. That is what we see in this book and in the end, I think we get a stronger couple for all that they put into their relationship. 
 ..."As much as I love being in love, I know that the existence of it isn't a magic ticket to a happy ending. And I know that as much as two people love each other, relationship don't always work, and then people split up and find other people to give it a go again. It's a horrible cycle, and I'm afraid that we're becoming part of it" 
 If that fear of David's isn't something we can all connect to - then one has never been in love. 
 So, about the book. This is a book that will leave you feeling raw. emotional. exposed. pissed off at times. happy. confused. breathless. Interborough is full of moments that you can probably apply to an aspect of your own life, whether that is relationship growth or troubles, awesome friends, love, self-doubt, life struggles, and more. I think that is something that is great about Mr. Hassell's work - it's real. There are not fluffly flowers and puppies thrown in the storyline just to make it appease the crowd - no, his stories tell the story in a way a real person would experience it. So while we still get to escape from our reality while reading the stories - we are reading something that very much fits into our normal. Allowing for a deeper connection with the characters and the storyline. I think this is why - as a reader, we are able to develop that "connection" and talk about these characters as if they are real. They become real to us. That is the sign of an amazing story. 
 The passion between these two has not grown cold with time - it's more of a trying to find time to be together issue. Again, real life - anyone? When they do find the time - these two still know how to burn up the sheets! Have no fear - the sex scenes are hot enough to make your kindle melt! 
 Some of my highlights from the book: First, it exists: yes, even though it pissed me off at first - I loved it. Second, I loved the relationship aspect - the nitty-gritty that was shown and how this story didn't gloss over issues that occur in relationships as people grow together. Third, the sex. Yeah I guess I am a perv. But who doesn't love to read about these hot as hell guys going at it and when David Refers to Raymond as a "Sex Marksman" I lol'd. Fourth, the epilogue - Michael and Nunzio. Fifth, Characters from other books were plentiful - loved it! Sixth, although not a highlight of this book per say - but knowing there will be a 5th and 6th book! Until then - I will have to read this one and books one-three again! Thank you Santino for an amazing series and a 5 Star Story!

My son was given this book as required reading for his schooling. After reading it myself, I released him from that requirement. This book may have won an award in the 1970s, but it has no place among my children's generation. I grew up near Oakland, California at the time this book was winning awards and I cannot say that this book helped to fix any of the racial problems I experienced as a child. Perhaps this kind of racial hatred still exists in parts of our country, but where I live we do not identify friend or foe by the color of their skin--and if I can help it we never will again. 
 As I read this story, I kept hoping to find redeeming value at its end. Instead, the author's toxic rage only increased. Consistently throughout, the author very explicitly identifies the antagonists and protagonists by their race. At one point in the story, one of the characters blames the evil white man's motives on the way his grandmother brought him up to remember the "old ways" (by which she means slavery). Oddly enough, the entire book succeeds in encouraging its readers to remember the "old way" of segregation and racial hatred that many of us had hoped would die off by now. Keep in mind that this is a story written in the 1970s about the 1930s. It is one thing for the author to document the segregation, the persecution, and the politics of that time. It is another to pass that same hatred on to the next generation of her readers. 
 The sub-plot that I had most hoped to redeem the story at the end succeeded in disappointing me the greatest. One of the young characters in this tale is clearly depicted as a fool, and his foolishness gets him into dire trouble by the end. However, in the last few pages, the narration clearly blames this young man's misfortune on the ethnic antagonists. Not a lick of real responsibility is laid on the young fool's own actions.  
 When my family gathers to fellowship with friends and kinfolk, the house or yard is full of children of all race and colors. This last summer, seeing my children playing with no awareness of ethnic differences, I could distinctly hear Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s words: "Free at last, free at last. Thank God almighty, we are free at last." Once upon a time, that freedom was threatened by the way people lived as described in this book. However, that dream of freedom is now threatened by the proliferation of this kind of literature beyond the generation to which it was relevant.

Teia was the only active character, that had a climactic role in the whole novel, but still we read chapters of nothing before and after that scene. By the end of this book, I don't even know if there was an actual antagonist, nor who it was. Everything pretty much happened as I expected it, with the exception of a few revelations (which happened in an anticlimactic scene). 
 I'm not asking for an epic battle, the building of another wall, or any more maiming/disfigurement. But what I am asking for is the characters that we've grown to love, doing what we love them for, in a way that is entertaining and believable. Is that too much to ask?

Hanover House is EXACTLY what I was in the mood to read, and the cover played a big part in piquing my interest. I love the black and white photo and striking red text. The structure itself, presumably Hanover House, is just creepy enough to intimidate without being too obvious. While the building resembles the manner in which haunted houses are portrayed, the reality of what--or who--will be housed there is much scarier than anything supernatural might be. 
 Dr. Evelyn Talbot has worked tirelessly to create a facility in which to not only incarcerate, but also study, psychopaths who have committed especially heinous crimes. Thus, this 40,000-word prequel sets the stage for future installments by contextualizing the doctor's interest in psychopaths, establishing her relationship with a few of Hilltop's townspeople, and giving readers a glimpse into what dangers might accompany her endeavor. In doing so, author Brenda Novak lays sufficient groundwork for suspense in addition to a potential romance: the perfect blend for satiating my reader's sensibility. 
 I, for one, can't wait for the release of Her Darkest Nightmare in 2016, as the prequel has me interested, invested, and impatient for more. Hanover House has successfully hooked another reader.

I'm missing the point here apparently, because I found Anna to be insufferable and annoying and a two-dimensional character. To me, it was painfully obvious that Anna's thoughts were written by a man. She deteriorates into insanity through paranoia and jealousy, when just ten months before she was poised and the belle of the ball. Every woman wanted to be her, every man wanted her. Who hasn't come across that yet? But I just couldn't follow how she went from a strong and independent woman to a sloppy mess of a woman. 
 Plus, I couldn't really be sympathetic for her because she brought all of her issues on herself. Look, I get it. Part of the emphasis is showing us that women are the ones who have to deal with the social fallout of an affair, whereas the men aren't hurt by it at all. I get that. But for me personally, cheating is cheating. Anna chose to pursue an affair, she chose to ignore her husband's request to stop, and was consequently pregnant with a bastard child and leaving her husband for another man. Even now, that wouldn't go over well. But I'm supposed to feel sorry for her..... 
 Tolstoy also had a tendency to get extremely distracted. There was way way WAY too much time spent on that damn horse race. I don't care about the stupid horse race. I don't care one lick. Stop going on and on about it. Go away.

This was one of those books that I opened to read a chapter before bed and ended up staying up until three:thirty to finish it in one sitting. I had read a comment online about the book, before it came out, saying that it was going to be the book of the summer and then... that was it. I somehow missed all the hype around it, I missed the people saying to go into it blind, I missed the spoilers that were probably everywhere. And I think that let me enjoy the book a lot more. Really. Go into it completely blind. 
 The only thing I will say about it outside of my hidden spoilers section is that the way it was written - poetic, filled with purple prose and lots of line breaks - annoyed me at first. It just seemed unnecessary. But there were some parts that the writing was so perfect, that you needed those line breaks, that it had to be read as a poem to properly convey the emotions. And by the end, it didn't annoy me at all anymore. 
 Apparently a lot of people go into this book knowing that there's a THING that happens, a huge twist that will blow their mind. I didn't. I mean, I realized pretty early on that Cadence was an unreliable narrator. She would get lost in these long metaphors and she was very obviously Sick. I also figured out the twist really early in the book, but at the same time I kept doubting myself. Almost immediately, I thought that the Liars were dead, but then the Sinclair family was just so weird that, you know, maybe they weren't. There were clues that were popping out all over the place, but they could also be read differently. They didn't seem to exist to most people on the island, but that could be because most people were angry with them for starting the fire.  Expecting it, though, made the experience of reading it no less enjoyable. I did think that with all of the foreshadowing of the BIG TWIST, the fire was handled a little poorly. It never occurred to me to question the way that Cady got injured. It seemed like the one thing she was sure of. And there were so many little references to it later (the flat rock with Gat, jumping off the ledge with the Liars, the repeated lines of going down and seeing the bottom of the island). It seemed like sort of out of nowhere she was just like, "Oh yeah, it was actually the fire." I was waiting for her to jump into the water after the fire, for it to be at least partly true, but it wasn't. Oh well. 
 This was the kind of story that you get swept up in the plot and the writing. You get lost in the narrator's head. You hate the Sinclairs even while feeling sorry for them because Cady paints them so negatively while still loving them for being her family. You like the Liars and some other characters (although actually I see that most people didn't), but you don't get too into them. It is not a book driven by its characters. It is a book driven by Cady, her relationship with others as they exist in her head, her healing and grieving and coming to terms with reality.  
 Overall, I thought it was a good read, and I'm immensely grateful that I somehow managed to avoid everyone else that thought so before reading it.

This book covers a lot of ground and it is no wonder that it has survived the test of time. It acts as an allegory for mirroring aspects of society much like Frankenstein's Monster did. It is written in the form of a journal of a shipwrecked man named Edward Prendick who ends up on the isle of strange creatures. Throughout the novel, Wells (through Prendick's observations) examines the qualities that separate humans from animals, and eventually comes to the conclusion that we may not be as different as we think. Wells suggests that human and bestial qualities rest under the surface of all life, and only the chains of society keep us human. Moreau shows Prendick that it is quite easy to turn beasts into men, and we come to learn that it is even easier for men to act like vicious beasts. The entire premise makes the book feel more like a long metaphor than an actual science fiction novel and I liked that.

An Ember In the Ashes By Sabaa Tahir had exceeded my expectations considering that this is a debut novel. And I also heard that there is a movie in the works! How crazy is that?! 
 AEITA is centered around two main protagonist, Laia and Elias. In the beginning of the novel, Laia is a character scorned as her family is murdered and brother was captured the the soldiers (called masks) of the ruling empire. Elias, is the Empire's greatest soldier, looking to escape the life within the empire, away from the life of a mask. Their lives intertwine when Laia is hired by the Resistance as a spy within the walls of Blackcliffe Academy, for them to rescue her brother, while Elias plays the course of hat is expected of him in exchange for his promised "freedom". 
 Personally, the plot and the execution was the plot was hands downs the most interesting I've ever read so far this year. There wa just so many things happening, politically, that there was just no time to be bored. After hearing that this is a "stand- alone" (I'll explin later why I put quotation marks on that word), I was a bit skeptic on the world building of this novel, but I was so wrong. Apart from the two maps in the front part and back part of the book, the descriptions of this world was extremely captivating. At least for me it was. I say that confidently because it was really easy for me to imagine and engage within the world as we follow the characters through their plight. 
 Yes, there was bit of romance to this story but! BUT! It did not overpower the dominant elements to the story. It was more like that drizzle of chocolate on a sundae, or that cherry on top of a vanilla ice cream scoop. I found the romance to be really intriguing and it left me wanting to know more which bring me back to what I had mentioned earlier. 
 This is why is had placed a quotation mark on the word stand- alone. The way this book ended did not close off on all the main plot points and if you read the book, you'd know what I'm talking about. [spoilers] This book pretty much ended when Laia saved Elias from being executed. However, the fate of Laia's brother was never revealed. Did the Resistance try to rescue him? What's going to happen to that other dude that liked Laia What's going to happen to Laia and Elias now that they've escaped Blackcliffe Military Academy? Will the Commandant go after them?! [/spoilers] So many questions that only another book or possible a series can answer. 
 Aside from the plot, the characters made a huge impact of how the story turned out. I found them to be so complex and torn y what their world has done to them. In addition, I absolutely love the character development of both characters. You want to see a complete 180 in terms of character development, then read this book because of Laia. Do want to see the endurance and perseverance of a truly dedicated character in a passionate search for freedom, then read this book because of Elias. Furthermore, the main protagonists would not be anything if it weren't for the secondary characters and the bad guys. All I can say about the bad guys, kiss my a**, Commandant!!! 
 Overall, if you are looking for an exciting, adventurous read for the season, this is it! It's got great characters, a gripping plot and a movie in the works... and that says a lot about a novel since it is a newly released novel for the month of April. And the news of the movie came out waaaaaaaaaay before the book even hit the market. So read this! Let me know if you do and we shall discuss!!!

Room deals with a dark theme and there are trigger warning with sexual and emotional abuse. Not recommended for under 18, despite the fact it's narrated by a five year old boy. 
 I'll start off with the fact that I didn't want to read this book. I have been watching this pop up on my Goodreads home page on multiple occasions, more so after the movie release last year, but I restrained myself because judging from the content and the blurb, I knew this is a book that will emotionally burden me. 
 But then the Oscar nominations came out. Room the movie got several nominations. If nomination for the best actress wasn't enough to lure me to give this book a second thought, it certainly was for the Adapted Screenplay category. And I had to read it now. 
 Minor spoilers ahead, but none you already don't know if you've even watched the movie trailer. 
 First of all, the blurb lies. I thought the main plot will be whether or not they manage get out of the Room, but it's not. Quoted from the blurb ...What she does not realize is just how unprepared she is for the plan to actually work.. However, the actual escape plan is not all that huffed upon in the book. Halfway through the book, they are successful in their endeavor to get out of the Room and the grasp of their captor Big Nick, which if you ask me, was a little too simple, considering Big Nick is someone who went ahead and put metal fence all over the room, including the floor. The catch that he never even considered to check whether or not Jack was actually dead was kind of baffling.  
 But anyway, they get out, at about halfway point of the book. Then the actual story starts. Jack has spend the first five years of his life in the Room. While it was a prison for Ma, it was a sanctuary for Jack. Jack doesn't know how to function with other people, or with Ma who suddenly has other people who wants her attention. Ma believes Jack is her savior, but other people (i.e. Grandpa) can't even look at Jack. When people from the outside world accuse Ma for not taking the initiative to put Jack in the outside world rather than keeping him all to herself like a selfish, Ma just about loses it. 
 People here are complaining about how emotionless and irresponsible it was to portray this story from the eyes of a five year old child whose speech patterns aren't developed enough to be soothing to the reader, and how the author tried to sell this book by using a different approach or whatever, but I think that's the whole point. A story that is based on abuse and such a dark theme is supposed to be emotional as it is. The fact that we are being able to see it from Jack is the entire point of this book. If I had wanted to know about how the woman, captured at the age of 19 went through this turmoil, I would've preferred reading the case stories of actual scenarios of which this book was inspired from. 
 Anyway, I can watch the movie now, so that's a relief.

FOUR POINT FIVE STARS 
 LITTLE BIG LIES centers around a group of kindergarten moms and an incident that reveals both big and little lies told by everyone. 
 Kindergarten is the foundation of learning. It's where we learn the golden rules that will carry us through life. 
 Share everything. 
 Play fair. 
 Don't hit people. 
 Put things back where you found them. 
 Clean up your own mess. 
 Don't take things that aren't yours. 
 Say you're sorry when you hurt somebody. 
 Wash your hands before you eat. 
 Take a nap every afternoon. 
 But those rules are lost when you get a bunch of overly eager moms together. Each mother thinking their child is an angel and would never do anything wrong turns into a nightmare to deal with. The conflict and strife created between these moms have them doing some nutty tactics. 
 "All conflict can be traced back to someone's feelings getting hurt, don't you think?" 
 The incident that takes place at a school function happens right away in the book. The story takes us back prior to the event so we can grasp a deeper understanding what lead to this tragedy. 
 There are 3 main kindergarten moms who the story centers around: 
 A remarried mom, Madeline, whose daughter from her first marriage is a teen and wanting to live with her dad. Madeline's ex is remarried and his daughter from his new marriage is in class with Madeline's youngest child. 
 A well to do mom, Celeste, with twin boys. Celeste appears to have the ideal life; twins, rich husband, a luxurious lifestyle. But behind closed doors, she lives a life of abuse. 
 A young single mom, Jane, who has one child, Ziggy. He's the new to the area kid and his story is what ties all these moms together. 
 Since I listened to the audio it took me my awhile to figure out all the characters. I'd hear a name here or there and wonder if I should be paying attention to that person or not. Once I figured out who to focus on the story became easier for me to follow. I really enjoyed listening to the narrator's accent. The way she said certain words sounded much better than the way I say them. *lol*

I received this book for free from a Goodreads giveaway for an honest review and I am so glad that I did. I loved this story, with just a few things that bothered me. But first, the good! I loved the world she built. I loved the incorporation of the Greek gods and I thought all of the magic and powers were fantastic. I absolutely adored getting lost in this world. I loved the circus and the people there and I only wished we got to see a lot more of them. They were great, had wonderful powers and personalities, and I really hope that we get to see a great deal more of them in the rest of the trilogy (which I am DEFINITELY going to read!) I realize I'm using the word loved a lot but I can't think of another word. Cat was amazing and I thought she was really well written. Now to pepper in some of the things I wish were a little different. First off, I don't normally read abduction that turns into romance. While I love Beauty and Beast and Belle's my favorite princess, there is that part of me that can't help screaming Stockholm Syndrome. And this was a worry here. But I think this was handled as well as it could be, and the author had Cat fight for her freedom and hold out for quite some time, which I appreciated. And even though I knew from the beginning who she was going to fall for (and I wanted it to happen), I was rooting for her to escape and didn't mind her complaining through the first half of the book because I thought it was completely justified. The author did make the abductors sympathetic so I was on board as she started to fall for her captor but it is a fine line to walk.  I also really appreciated that he released her from her vow eventually and that Poseidon showed up in a vision and confirmed that they were meant for each other, that he was created for her. I will say making them predestined mates made it easier for me to accept the romance.  The other problem I had is difficult to explain without spoilers, in a broad sense I wish she had wrapped up a little more of the plot in this book. Very specifically  I think she should have had Cat tell Griffin that she is the lost princess in this book. I was shocked that he didn't put it together himself and I really was waiting for him to tell Cat that he knew and so I think it is a weird thing to draw out and reveal to him in what I assume will be the next book. Hopefully, it isn't so drawn out that it takes until the third book for him to find out.  I know that it's going to be a trilogy. As I said, I can't wait for the next book. But there are plenty of places for the story to go, I think this one point should have been resolved by the end of this book. But overall, I love "A Promise of Fire", I loved the magical world, and I can't wait for the next book

This is another book club selection which unfolded slowly and reverently into subtle writing revealing a beautiful message of love and hope. It is slow, some might say boring, but if you stick with it, you'll appreciate its subtleness. It is written as a memoir from a dying elderly (at least third generational Protestant minister) to his seven year old son. Right away I was struck with the unique perspective from which it is narrated. The protagonist's voice is gentle, the entire book is addressed to his beloved son, and the diction is elevated, with a lot of biblical references. I'm not religious at all and could still appreciate the messages since it wasn't preachy and was more about family, friendship and the mature reflections back upon a life well-lived from the the perspective of pending death. This book doesn't follow an obvious plot-line and there are no chapter divisions. It is written in a rambling, stream-of-consciousness style as the writer records his memories and thoughts when they come to mind. It's not one story, but a collection of them. 
 Old Reverend John Ames had his son late in life, in fact, he's in his 70s and his boy is only 6 years old. Ames lived alone as a widower for many years before his second wife, more than 30 years his junior, walked into his church and his life in the 1950s the period when this jounal is written. The Iowan minister is keenly aware that he won't be around to provide his son the love, encouragement and counsel that a dad usually has the opportunity to contribute to his children's lives, so he is keeping a journal -- writing down the stories, observations, reflections, and advice that he wants to leave his son after he is gone. Although Gilead is a work of fiction, I felt as if I had discovered an old diary and was reading the private thoughts of a man sharing his heart with his beloved son. 
 If the book could be improved, I would suggest an introduction of the son as an adult in the beginning and/or the end. Perhaps he found it and is reading it for the first time or perhaps hecherished it his whole life and is passing it on to his son. I just wanted a tiny bit of his perspective since he was such a powerful impetus for his father's writing.

The man in black fled across the desert and the Gunslinger followed. 
 Roland Deschain, the last of the Gunslingers, is on a quest for the Dark Tower, a mysterious edifice that is the axle of worlds and holds all existence together. In this, the first volume, Roland pursues his nemesis across the Mohaine Desert. He follows the man in black's trail to a little town called Tull, then through more desert, encountering a boy named Jake from our world, and then into the mountains. Will Roland finally catch his arch-nemesis after years of pursuing him? And what means will he go to to achieve his goal? 
 When I first picked up this book, I had no idea it would shoot to the top of my favorites list. I wolfed down the first four books in three weeks, then entered an agonizing period of waiting for the last three to be published. I think I've read the first four books five or six times each. The whole Dark Tower series, while on the surface a fantasy-western, is really the story of one man's obsession. In this volume, we get a hint of what Roland will do to get to the Dark Tower. 
 The writing is great and it warmed me up to Stephen King. Roland's world is unique. Part fantasy, part western, part post-apocalypse. While it's the first book in a series, it's quite satisfying to read on its own. 
 If your looking with fantasy with a different flavor, look no further. 
 Additional Thoughts from the April 2011 re-read: 
 Some of the additions in the revised edition of this book were much-needed and brought the first book into synch with the later ones. Others seemed a little ham-fisted and took away a bit of Roland's mystique. 
 I like the idea a certain curmudgeonly Kansan reviewer proposed that the first edition of The Gunslinger and this one are from different cycles in Roland's quest. 
 I think it's a testament to Stephen King's skill as a writer that even on my sixth or seventh go round, I was still hoping Roland wouldn't let Jake fall. 
  
 Additional Thoughts from the 2014 reread: 
 In the forward, King mentioned he pushed everything else aside to finish the last three books because he felt like he had a sense of responsibility to his readers. If only George R.R. Martin felt that way... 
 It is mentioned that Roland is the kind of man who straightens pictures in strange hotel rooms. Is this a hint of his obsessiveness? 
 I notice something new every time I read this book. If I had to pick one book that made me want to write, it would be this one. 
  
 The following concerns my speculation regarding the end of the series. BE REALLY FUCKING SURE YOU WANT TO READ IT BEFORE YOU CLICK ON IT. 
 The Man in Black tells Roland he must slay the Ageless Stranger in order to reach the top of the Tower. Since Roland learns that HE is the Ageless Stranger in The Dark Tower, I think it means that he's going to have to put his obsession with the Dark Tower to rest if he's ever going to reach the top. 
 Also, I caught myself hoping Jake wouldn't fall AGAIN.

This is Pike (Josiah's friend) & Zack's (Ryan's Friend) story and we get to watch these two navigate their way to HEA. We met them both in the #Gaymers Series and now we get to watch these two learn to adult and fall in love. 
 This story is set more in the military world and deals with a lot of Homophobia. If homophobia, slurs, the thought that being gay is a choice, and mention of ways to help the gay person get over being gay are trigger subjects for you - this story may not be a happy read. In addition, Zack's family are Ultra conservative and religious (his dad carries a Bible in his pocket) - needless to say they are a huge issue in the story. Know these things going into the story - because Annabeth Albert has written a story that is pretty emotional and in your face with homophobia. 
 Zack - he is so far in the closet, even Narnia is closer to the door than he is -- and Zack has no idea how to even begin to find his way out. When he meets an energetic, sexy, ginger man - with sexy freckles and gorgeous eyes. Zack starts looking for ways he can be the man, the SEAL, the son he was raised and trained to be -- all while being a man that Pike would want as well. 
 "You. Are. Not. A. Distraction." Zack toppled Pike backward, loomed over him. "You're my everything. And I won't let them have you. Won't them ruin this." 
 Pike -"Pike was the type of guy who would flirt with wallpaper, but he seemed to have singled Zack out for special attention ever since their first meeting at a LAN party." Having never been in the closet unless it was while changing clothes - and he refuses to go in the closet for anyone. Even a sexy, muscled man - a man that makes his heart go pitter-patter and makes him think of happily ever afters, homes, family..going from me to an us. 
 When these two find themselves spending a lot of time together - feelings and sexual attractions grow. Then Pike finds out Zack isn't just in the closet but he is also a Virgin... 
 "A virgin SEAL--""Shut up." He shoved Pike's shoulder. Pike neatly sidestepped his grip. "I'm just saying, you must be rarer than a fucking unicorn. I thought you guys got all the ass-- of any gender-- you wanted." 
 Let's just say...Pike and Zack have a lot of fun during Zack's sexual education! Zack earns A+ in all subjects! 
 The chemistry and passion in this book is perfect! When these two fall... they fall hard, even if they don't acknowledge it right away.. 
 "Kissing Pike always felt like breathing-- necessary, important and vital to his well-being-- but right then it felt more like a sacrament . Or like super glue instantly sealing their bond together. And that's what this was-- a bond . His mouth might not be able offer many promises to Pike, but his body could pledge an oath, swear to Pike with each thrust that this meant something, meant everything." 
 Overall 4 stars -- great book. I would have liked to see more of the happiness, the fallout with the family just sort of stalled out, and a couple other areas were not fully resolved - but it's a great story and an awesome start to a new series!

DISAPPOINTING. It came nowhere near the hype the surrounded the novel and subsequent movie. If I had spent more than a dollar on it at a garage sale, I would have been even more disgusted. The book starts off with a bang and continues with a long, drawn out whimper that tested my patience. Susie Salmon is a young girl who is brutally raped and murdered by a neighbor, who is an unapprehended serial offender. She narrates the dissolution of her family unit in the wake of the tragedy from her afterlife, occasionally making efforts to communicate her presence to her father, mother, siblings and friends. The novel drew out the static tension surrounding this murder, again, focusing on the emotional impact of Susie's disaapearance on her loved ones rather than the resolution of her death. SPOILER ALERT: Her murderer is never apprehended for his crimes though the family and police suspect his invovement through the entirity of the novel. What took the slow, tedious novel from bad to worse was Sebold's attempt to resolve Susie's unconsumated junior high love affair through the bodily posession of one of her peers. With that, I was offically disgusted by the book. What made me even angier was when I read in the adknowledgements that the author is a close friend of Amy Hemple - Amy-Mother-Effing-Hemple was a first reader of this monumental borefest. *shock and horror but mostly jealousy* I respect the emotional honesty and the author's attempt to capture the heartbreak that surrounds a tragedy of this magnitude - but the tragedy seemed to fizzle when the author lost sight of the action and movement of the plot by wallowing in the family's loss without much reslotion. It may accurately communicate the stagnent hopelessness that surrounds childrens' unsolved disappearances, but it doesn't make for a compelling read. 
 So, the two stars were a gift. I was expecting something more and received something less. Maybe if I had read it without the expectations (largely based around the hype surrounding the movie), I wouldn't have been so disappointed. Plus, knowing that the author had Amy Hemple at her disposal during the creation of the novel, makes my disappointment even greater. Because if anyone can move me, Amy Hemple can. Alice Sebold clearly cannot. Side note: Even Marky-Mark cast as Susie's father could not entice me to now watch this movie. And that, my friends, says alot.
