So, dark and hardcore BDSM erotica is so not my usual cup of tea. If not for the recommendation of a very trusted friend, I would not have touched this book with a ten foot pole.

I mean, in some ways it is - there are ridiculous amounts of equally ridiculous sex, to the point where I skimmed a lot of it because you can only write about the same thing so many ways before it starts to get old - but there is also an astonishing amount of philosophy, introspection, and religion, of all things. Take a look at some of the quotes that I liked to see what I mean...this shit is deep, complex, and dark...and yet unexpectedly witty and humerous at times. The book left me feeling vaguely depressed, even though the ending was mostly "happy", but I loved it anyway. 
 Ms. Reisz's characters are so strong and vivid that it's almost overwhelming. They scream from the page, grabbing you by the throat and forcing you to hear their story...even when you don't necessarily want to. It takes a hell of a lot of talent to make me fall in love with a sadistic priest that gets off on caning his lovers, but somehow Reisz managed it. I'm still trying to figure that one out. @_@ 
 Anyway, this was one hell of a read. It's dark and disturbing in so many ways, but it also makes you think and drags you right into the characters' lives and world. I don't think I could read several of these in a row, but I will definitely check out Kingsley's story soon. Ms. Reisz is a fantastic writer!

Firstly, I would like to thank Eric Smith from Quirk Books for sending me a physical review copy of Hollow City or this post wouldn't have even existed :) 
 This book was a lot better than I had expected *whew* and it proved that I was accurate about the first installment being more like an intro to Peculiardom. In the second installment of Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children, Hollow City, we follow Jacob and the rest of the Peculiar Children as they race against time to save their beloved Miss Peregrine. Along the way, we meet a lot peculiar and non-peculiar characters and we learn more about the Peculiar world. 
 Although the plot line of this book was a continuation of the first installment, it was nothing like it- the plot line to Hollow City was BETTER!!! I felt the excitement as Jacob and the rest of Peculiar Children ventured through war time London. The world building was absolutely ah-mazing and very descriptive. I could see their world as I read through this book- it was terrifyingly gripping because I didn't want to stop reading so I wouldn't leave their world behind!!! The vintage photographs within the many pages of the book were great reinforcers for readers to grasp Jacob's reality. Each photo more stunning and peculiar than the previous. Now the twists and turns of this book was really cray. It had me glued on the edge of my seat and at some point, made me gasp out a little too loudly because the revelations were just so- unexpected... IT WAS TOO DAMN BRILLIANT!!! Of course, what's a good story without its ah-mazing characters?! 
 I saw a lot of growth and character development within Jacob and the other Peculiar children and this time, I felt more connected to them than when I first read about them in the first book. In this book, Jacob discovers more about himself and as he makes these discoveries and abilities, he begins to learn to trust himself as well until the end- when he finally gives into his abilities and finally, trusts himself to put his abilities into good use and save lives. Now, that was quite the development. When it comes to Emma, my opinions have not changed since the first book. I felt that her emotions and what she feels isn't really directed towards Jacob, but to his grandfather. Like she sees something in Jacob that reminds her of him... which is kind of sad and I don't like that about her at all. Millard is still freaking awesome!!! He's like Mr. Know- It- All >.< And I really enjoyed the new characters. They were interesting and some of them were sarcastically funny, which I loved!!! 
 Overall, Hollow City was definitely a step up from the first. I really recommend for people to jump onto this book after they're read the first and for those who have not picked up this series, to do so because it just gets better. I can't wait for the third installment to come along because there are a lot of questions that have been left unanswered, and with the way this book had ended, it looks like there was a lot more to Jacob than what he had expected...

Wow, I came to Wolf Hollow with a fair amount of indifference, but it was stunning in so many ways! It affected me so much that I couldn't sleep because my heart was racing too fast. I haven't been so worked up about a novel since Yaqui Delgado Wants to Kick Your Ass, and just like in that book, the stakes are really high. Betty isn't a low-grade threat: the things she does are truly terrible, and the consequences are shocking. The author perfectly captures a child's reactions to such threats, even though I, as an adult, kept thinking "You have to tell someone! No, don't do that, you'll make everything worse!" Kid logic is not adult logic, and the choices that Annabelle totally make sense in that context. I ADORED that she had solid, reasonable parents who supported her, since the trope of the doofus parent is something I can't stand. Most importantly, this book has an amazing moral of what it means to care for the outcasts of society, and to have true compassion for those who are different from us. There are so many great things going on in this book, and I hope it gets some attention during awards season.

The Graveyard Book had been in my wish list for months. I became thoroughly interested to this book because of its uncanny and (seems-to-be) creepy, gothic-like plot (yes, I'm interested to those kind of stuff) but sadly, upon reading this book, my expectations were not met. I was expecting something akin to Coraline's gloomy theme and atmosphere. Regrettably, I hated some of the book's trying-hard-to-be-unique-mysterious-eerie catchphrases and names for characters, especially for the main character, "Nobody Owens". Ugh. When Nobody/ ('Bod' for short) name was revealed, I wanted to stop reading this, the only thing that stopped me from putting this book back on the shelf was that I hate having unfinished books. It gets me the "O.C. Feeling". 
 Anyway, The Graveyard Book tells the story of a boy (Nobody 'Bod' Owens) whose parents were murdered when he was still an infant. He was then raised by souls and a cemetery guardian in a known Graveyard in their town.

The Emperor is dead. Treachery is afoot. But for the heirs, there are still more dangers to overcome. Kaden, the heir to the empire and the blazing eyes of the royalty, is a monastery where the lessons are trying to teach him something more important than empire politics. Valyn, the second born, is just trying to survive the Hull trial. And Adare is left holding the Unhewn Throne even though she will never inherit; the only one of the three left to avenge their father and play the political game. 
 My only problem with this book is that it is technically two and a half different books. Since we mostly follow Kaden and Valyn, we can consider them our two main protagonist. Adare is more of a placeholder character to show us what is going on in the kingdom - her story is hardly fleshed out. Her story is bare bones minimalism. 
 As for Kaden and Valyn, their stories are completely disparate except that they are both children of the emperor. They are isolated in their own realms until the end of the book. In that sense, each of them could a protagonist of their own book. It isn't like GRRM where each scene has impacts on another character's life. 
 But really, that is my only quibble. And it barely bothered me because I was so engrossed in their stories. I am notorious for hating these multiple perspective books because I inevitably like one character more than the rest and hate another one - and then reading the hated character's POV is tortuous. But I really liked all three - which is rare, exceedingly rare. Stavely does a fantastic job writing characters. This is his strength. None of them are perfect, but not of the mare stupid. They have flaws (Kaden is stubborn, Valyn is a little too hot tempered, and Adrose is impulsive). But they are stronger for it all. They feel three dimensional. 
 I have to say, I am a fan of these types of "training" story lines where the character is beaten up somehow and ends up becoming a leader or achieving a certain skill. It's great because if it's done right, the change is so gradual that you are always taken by surprise at what a dumbass moron the character was at the beginning by the time you're reading the end of the book. 
 The scope of the world is intriguing. There is something more than just court politics in this book, and I like that. I want to know more. 
 Staveley is not afraid to stick his characters in crap situations and watch them crawl out, bleeding and desperate, but pushed to the last tethers of their mind and strength. What happened with Lin... damn. I did not expect it at all. That whole relationships was written perfectly. 
 This book could easily be three times as long. (And I almost wish it were so I could have more pages). As such, sometimes there are details lacking (how is Adrose actually holding onto the kingdom?), etc. 
 Even though there are flaws, I quite liked this book. I was thoroughly engrossed, felt very connected to the characters, and was intrigued by the plot. 3.5 stars rounded up. I rounded up (which is actually really rare for me to do with these books that hover one the 3.5 mark) because at the end of the book I found myself desperately wanting to read the sequel instead of merely like "eh if there's a sequel I might read it". I'm looking forward to January 2015. 
 But really... WHERE IS THE SEQUEL!! argh you can't leave us on that incomplete ending, Mr. Staveley. 
 I would highly recommend it for anyone who reads empire books. It reminds me of Inda by Sherwood Smith in a very good way.

 This was a great read. Well-written, compelling, and fun. It first came to my attention when a number of my favorite reviewers gave it five stars and glowing reviews, and then when I saw that Orbit was its publisher. Orbit, a science fiction and fantasy division of Hachette, has been publishing great stuff recently. 
 It took me a few tries over a month to get past the first few pages and start genuinely reading the book. I think the reason for that start-and-stop was the mysterious wording of the blurb and how gradually stuff is revealed early on in the narrative. But, having completed the book now, I see this as a plus. The slow revelation of certain details made for some really fun moments, especially when unexpected pieces start coming together to form a picture. 
 Another strength of the book is its balance between being a character-driven and plot-driven narrative. Many books are either-or, but M.R. Carey managed to combine a cast of solid characters who develop realistically and quickly paced action. 
 In regards to the characters, the narration is split between five of them: Melanie, Sergeant Parks, Ms. Justineau, Dr. Caldwell, and Private Gallagher. Carey does a fantastic job of giving each narrator their own, distinct voice, while making each character slightly archetypal. Melanie manages to be both child-like and clever. Sergeant Parks is pragmatic, dry, and determined. Ms. Justineau is questioning, ethical, and feeling. Dr. Caldwell is clinical, logical, scientific. Private Gallagher's narration is the least frequent and the weakest of the five. His voice is that of a self-aware red-shirt. Usually, a book with so many narrators will frustrate me with its chopiness, but as these characters are usually in the same geographical location and participating in the same plot, the narrations managed to not be disjointed. Instead, they gave the plot a certain richness in being related by disparate, realized points of view. The book would have been weaker if Melanie was our only narrator. 
 My favorite narrator turned out to be Sergeant Parks, which surprised me, as his character is perceived as villainous by our early narrators. But, pretty much all of my kindle highlights wound up to be Sergeant Parks' lines or lines about Sergeant Parks. He is the comic relief of the book, and his dry humor is one of the best aspects of the book. 
 In regards to plot, the book has three distinct parts, with the pace building in each part. The first takes place over a series of months, the second over a series of days, and the third over a series of hours. It's neatly done, and this organization, along with the tied strings of the ending, gave me no small amount of satisfaction as a reader. 
 Despite this pat-ness, the themes of the book still manage to engage complex questions regarding humanity and disaster. This thematic nature is what gives the book five stars instead of four. There is no doubt that the book is a fun read, but it also raises subtle questions and suggests different perspectives of philosophical dilemmas. Because of this, I can see The Girl With All the Gifts being a great book for a group discussion. 
 All in all, I recommend this book for all genders, for both young and old adults, and for fans and skeptics of the recent zombie craze.

Illegal Contact is book one in Santino Hassell's newest series, The Barons, and this story may well be one of his most romantic yet! When I started this story, I had no idea where Mr. Hassell would go with the storyline, rest assured his first venture into sports romance is a huge success - Super Bowl worthy! 
 The MC in our story are football superstar, The Barons tight end, Gavin Brawley and Noah Monroe, a recent college grad looking for a job when he interviews to be Gavin's personal assistant. You see, Gavin has found himself on house arrest in his Hamptons mansion and will be unable to leave the property for several months - he is also on a suspension from The Barons while he serves his sentence out. This is what leads the secretive man to bring an assistant into his life and home. I don't think he planned on meeting his match; someone who wouldn't bow-down, didn't think he was a god, and couldn't careless about football. It's quite hilarious as we watch these two scrimmage for top dog. 
 The immediate desire and attraction between these two is evident to the reader, even if the characters take a little bit to catch up. This lapse just makes the UST practically jump from the pages of the book as you can imagine our guys vibrating with need...yet, trying to fight it. As with most forbidden things, all it takes is just one taste and these two are on fire!! 
 "He was so addictive. Like candy. Or drugs. One taste of him had me fiending and my heart beating out of my chest." 
 These two make their own little bubble and the time of Gavin's punishment moves quickly. When the real world starts to encroach in their happiness, hard choices have to be made and secrets have to decide to stay secret or come into the light. Mr. Hassell appropriately dedicated this book "For the scared, the closeted, and the hopeful" and all of these realities play out for Gavin and Noah. Gavin has to make a choice and risk losing football, the only thing that has held him together in his life...or he can choose to stay closeted and lose Noah, the man he has fallen in love with. 
 "I do love football, but I love you more. And your ass is less likely to decide I'm too old once I hit thirty-three." 
 Could he hope that maybe he will get to keep the man and the sport? Would that be too much to ask...you are going to have to read this amazing book to find out! 
 I thoroughly enjoyed this book from beginning to end. The romance between our MC was not smothering; yet, it was clearly evident to all who were around them. Noah was the reason that #ThatBrawleySmile existed and Gavin wanted nothing more than to keep Noah in his life and his bed. A bed that got a LOT of action as our guys tore up the sheets and shook the walls down during their hot as hell sex scenes! Just a warning some parts of this book may make you blush profusely if you read in public! 
 5+ Stars for this amazing story, I adore Gavin & Noah and am sure you will as well! I can't wait for the next book in this exciting series!

I don't know how large the market for 600-page space-opera-teen-romance is, but this should go a long way to filling it. Kady - a scrappy computer hacker - and Ezra - an untrained but remarkably gifted pilot - have been blasted off of their home planet, only to limp away from the perusing attackers as part of a rag-tag fleet, who's super-computer has gone haywire and may be trying to kill them as zombie-plague virus runs amok. Yes, there a bit formula at work here. 
 Initially, I found the book's formatting to be distracting: an email chat, an incident report, a memo, a diary entry, more email exchanges, notes attached to many of the documents. This may make it slow going for fans coming off I Am Number Four. But then the lower word-density allowed me to fly through pages, making it feel far shorter than a fore-mentioned 600 pages. While the story is action-heavy, the Ezra/Kady back-n-forth is also central to the plot, which is either entrancing or aggravating, depending on which parts of the narrative fires your crackers. 
 The Illuminae is set up as a dossier (French for "long report") recounting the events following a corporation's destruction of the competition's mining colony on Kerenza. The opening was a bit herky-jerky, but by page 80, enough momentum had built up that I didn't want to put it down. The plot twists and turns along, with several genuine surprises. The conclusion sets up subsequent books in the trilogy without leaving this one unfinished. All and all, worth reading entertainment.

First impressions: BANG! Did you hear that? That was me racing through the front half of this book. Cannot. Put. Down. Even. To. Eat. Feeding myself was far less of a concern than finding out what was going to happen next. 
 Lasting impressions: I am in love with Justin. He is my official book boyfriend until further notice. The love story here is so sweet and real and satisfying. Even if I did sometimes want to punch Justin in the face. 
 Conflicting impressions: Seriously Justin? You put work over personal happiness? Your seemingly well-meaning chivalrous attempts to protect Maddie don't make any sense. You either want her on your side or you don't. 
 Overall impressions: Okay, so maybe Justin and I are in a time-out. He can be so irritating! 
 See, Maddie is not the innocent I first assumed her to be. This is part of what I loved about this book. She's a bit of a rebel, and is on probation for hacking into her uber-powerful dad's computer and helping the resistance movement try to take down Digital School. After a rash of violent incidents years ago, Maddie's dad developed an online educational system that has quickly spread to almost all facets of life. It's like the internet on steroids, where people rarely leave their homes because everything can be done online. 
 Kind of cool. Kind of scary. 
 Justin is one of the folks that thinks this is more scary than cool. He wants to bring people out of their homes, offline, and back into open society. He reaches out to Maddie, and she soon realizes that he's trying to recruit her. She's not sure whether or not to tread back into Bad Girl territory, but Justin is quite the temptation. Her unraveling relationship with her super strict dad only pushes her harder into Justin's arms. 
 This is mostly a love story, after all, despite the dystopian (ish) setting. Digital School had its drawbacks, but it wasn't all terrible. In fact, it was kind of mostly awesome, especially for people like me who prefer to avoid awkward social interactions. Sure it's also a cautionary tale about the internet taking over our lives/world, but at heart this is really about Maddie coming to terms with her own views on society's direction, and how her feelings for Justin influence that viewpoint. 
 So why is Justin so irritating? Well, he has this hang-up about his little underground rebellion. He works to recruit people to his cause, and this takes him on the road for long periods of time with little to no reliable means of communication. Despite Maddie's strengths and abilities, he continually insists that she's too valuable to be out in the field, so OBVIOUSLY they can't be together. 
 Please. 
 I'm so sick of the "we must protect the fragile female" perspective! For once I'd like to see the dude go "SICK! You're beautiful and smart and capable of man-handling the organization we're fighting with one hand tied behind your back - and you WANT to help? Let's go take them down and be super happy love partners in crime together!" 
 But no. That never happens. Instead they just whine about how much they want to be with the girl, but do The Right Thing and protect them by quarantining them somewhere away from the action until the manly men types save the world for them. BARF. 
 I forgave Justin, though, because he's so darn cute. And even though Maddie didn't step up as much or as often as I would have liked, she reminded me so much of myself that I forgave her too. They're just too awesome! Maddie is brilliant, funny, shy, and a bit of an adventure-seeker. I so related to her willingness to go with the flow and get caught up in the wild capers that start to come her way, not wanting to turn down the opportunity to just live a little and maybe meet some cool people. You never know when you'll meet that person who changes your life, in either a good or bad way, and sometimes you just have to walk on the edge of good and bad until your choice reaches its consequence. 
 Bottom line? Loved, loved, loved this book, but the end and the Justin-isms were enough to knock it down a star. If you're in the mood for a great love story in a futuristic setting, definitely pick this one up. Immediately.

 There is a small piece of my heart that is gone knowing that this series is over. I had a lot of reservations going into the Hush, Hush saga. I was just discovering the book blogging community, I hadn't read a lot of young adult and certainly hadn't read any books about fallen angels before. When I looked it up on Goodreads so many people were saying negative things and giving it poor reviews I thought for sure I wouldn't like it. Once I read A Need so Beautiful by Suzanne Young I realized I really did in fact like angel books so I swallowed my reservations and just decided to pick it up. And I didn't stop until I finished Silence. Holy Smokes... I fell in love with this series, I fell in love with Patch and I fell in love with Becca Fitzpatrick's writing. I didn't do a review on Crescendo and Silence as they more or less blended together as the same book for me... I literally dropped one and picked up the other. And I'm sad to say... now I have to review Finale. The last one. A closed-door :( 
 When I say I was highly anticipating this book, that is no stretch of the imagination. As soon as the book was in my hands I started reading it. This was the one for 2012 for me... and then about 2 chapters in I had a small debate with myself -did I really want to finish this? Maybe I'll just wait awhile... to keep the story alive. Needless to say, I didn't stop(obviously... I can't resist the urge to read about Patch when it's right in front of me) and I sucked up the whole book. 
 Becca Fitzpatrick is back at it with her incredibly easy to read writing style. I absolutely adore her writing... it doesn't even feel like you are reading and then suddenly 3 chapters are gone. 
 Finale leaves where Silence finished... with no break in between, It's literally the very next day. Nora is now Nephilim and has sworn an oath to lead the Black Hand army. Nora of course doesn't want to go to battle as her boyfriend, Patch is a fallen angel and she is not turning her back on him. Finale goes on to tell of Nora's training, and discovering more of the Black Hand's mysteries. 
 I liked Nora the best in Finale. She is much stronger and definitely not as whiny. She is not my favorite character but she doesn't display that annoying weakness that she does throughout the first three books. Patch of course, is absolutely perfect. Scott is amazing in this book... I absolutely adore him. He is so sweet to Nora, and him and Vee have a little something-something. And Vee... oh my Vee. She was my favorite from the get go, she is so spunky and has such a wicked attitude. Well... Vee is back and better than ever for the final book, with secrets of her own 
 There was certainly a few flaws in Finale. Two that I can name specifically and they are only the real ones that stand out. But... I can't tell you either of them because they are major spoilers and would defeat the purpose of reading the book as they take place at the very end. One of them made me happy that it was done but completely pointless and felt like it was thrown in nonetheless, the other I cried and cried and cried because it was not necessary and hurt my heart. That's all I will say. Despite those flaws, this book is still 5 out of 5 for me. I thought the ending, or at least what I was wondering the most about the ending was completely satisfying and it was a perfectly acceptable ending for one of my favorite series of all time. 
 Becca Fitzpatrick made me fall in love with Patch, made me fall in love with Nephilim and most of all... she made me fall in love with Fallen Angels. Now as soon as I see a fallen angel book, it's a must read. I'm so crushed that this series is over, but so happy I read it. 
 Sidenote: It sounded like I just gave a Eulogy. Bahahaha.

Kiersten White is funny. Not 'hmm that looks kinda funny?'-funny, but good old 'haha'-funny. 
 SPOILERS FROM HERE ON OUT 
 I was a bit disappointed about Lend being (mostly) absent from the story. 
 Evie and Lend basically went through the typical 'second book in the YA-series' relationship issues: perfect boyfriend suddenly off doing other stuff, doesn't understand what main character is going through - enter new character who understands perfectly! (This being Jack) 
 Examples: New Moon (Twilight saga), Angel Fire (Angel trilogy) and Spells (Wings saga). 
 For me the best part was the bit in the Faerie Realms. White's style is perfection to my standards, so no complaints there.

Space romp set far from now in the enrapturing post-Singularity 'verse that is just one body short of an orgy. 
 Features a strong exploration of political theory of the Marxist and Feudalist flavors as well as the long-term ramifications of more current issues affecting any individual who happens to read this review. 
 Very strong techno-theological overtones that will make you think and stuff. 
 Two excerpts which highlight those overtones: I am the Eschaton. I am not your god. 
 I am descended from you, and I exist in your future. 
 Thou shalt not violate causality within my historic light cone. Or else.& 
  "Consider the hypothetical case of a power that intends to create a localized causality violation that does not produce a light cone encompassing its origin point. (We are implicitly assuming a perfectly spherical zone of sinfulness expanding at velocity c with origin at time TO.) If the spherical volume of sinfulness does not intersect with the four-space trajectory of the power's initial location, we are not dealing with an original sin. Consequently we do not expect the Eschaton to condemn the entire sinful civilization to damnation, or a Type II supernova; redemption is possible. However, damnation of the sinful agency that causes the causality violation is required. 
 2. Does the Eschaton always intervene destructively? The answer is probably "no". We see the consequences of intervention in issues of original sin, but for every such intervention there are probably thousands of invisible nudges delivered to our world line with subtlety and precision. The agency by which such nudges are delivered must remain unknown for them to be effective. They probably flee the scene after the intervention, hiding themselves in the teeming masses. The agency may even work in concert with our own efforts, as Eschaton-fearing human beings, to ensure no violations exist. It is possible that some Eschatologically aware government agencies amy assist the Eschaton's secret friends, if they are aware of their presence. Others, secret agents of sinful powers, may attempt to identify them by evidence and arrest them. 
 3. Of course, few people would contemplate breaking the law of causality without at least a very major apparent threat. One wonders what the invisible helpers of the Eschaton might do when confronted with the need to prevent a causality violation in the face of such a threat? At that point, they may find themselves with split loyalties: on the one hand, to defend the prime law of the anthropic cosmos, while at the same time, not wanting to surrender their misguided but nevertheless human peers into the claws of a great evil. Under these circumstances, I feel sure that the Eschaton would tell its agents to look at their fellow humans' interests immediately after preventing the rupture of space-time itself. The Eschaton may not be a compassionate God, but it is pragmatic and does not expect its tools to break in its service. However, the key issue is determining which side is least wrong. This leads us deep into the forest of ethics, wherein there is a festival of ambiguity. All we can do is hope the secret helpers make the right choices--otherwise, the consequences of criticism will be harsh."  
 The detail on space ship travel gets a little boggy but the themes therein are strong enough to make this a quick read. 
 Plus there's a totally sweet metafictional hook at the end!  
 As Bruce Sterling has noted, "A Singularity has no business model, no major power group in our society is interested in provoking one, nobody who matters sees any reason to create one, there's no there there."

I love this book. First off I regret waiting so long to start reading it (and possibly the series). Secondly I have no idea why it took me so long as I love assassins and princes and castles, and this has all of those things! Thirdly, I want to write a quick review so I can go read the next. Here goes... 
 Celaena Sardothien is a renowned assassin who was caught (possibly by betrayal but unknown) and her imprisonment is slavery in the harsh mines of Endovier. A year into her lifelong sentence she is summoned out to meet with none other than the crown prince of Adarlan, Dorian. He tells the assassin he has chosen to represent her in a contest to become the King's Champion, a skilled warrior to perform the crown's dirty work. If she wins the contest and becomes the King's Champion, she can serve him for four years and then be free. She decides to accept his offer to get out of the awful mines and finally have the chance to live as a free person. She travels back with the Prince to the kingdom's capital and its castle of glass. There she begins her training to compete in the contest with her trainer, the Captain of the Guard, Chaol. She must defeat 23 other warriors, assassins, mercenaries, and the like in the contest. 
 Celaena is a great female character. She is someone who has a slight temperament problem which is different from many other young adult heroines of today's literature. It makes sense though, she is an assassin. She also has a tragic past that we don't get to learn too much about in this book, though I have a guess or two. I also love her interactions with the prince. The comedic affect those too bring together made me squeal in delight as I read. I hope I am not disappointed in the inevitable love triangle, but I feel I might be.... maybe? I don't know!! xD Anyway, Prince Dorian and Chaol as also great and the pair are good friends. I would have liked to see them interact more together on their own as their personalities also compliment each other very well. 
 One slight complaint is that the book for a brief period of time seemed like it was going with an unpredictable plot point but then turned back to the one that was predictable. Would I have hated the outcome of the one that was unpredictable, yes, I would have very much so. But would it have been different and, what's that, unpredictable? Yes, it would have. Oh well. I get to be happy with it being predictable, and at least the author made the thought actually cross my mind even though I was having a hard time believing it, especially when it didn't quite follow-up right away. By this unpredictable plot point I mean when Celaena thinks the attacks and killings of the competitors were from the Princess Nehemia. I loved the Princess as a good friend for Celaena and was heartbroken at the possibility. However, it was obvious once it didn't follow through quickly that it was not her. Or at least to me.  
 Anyway, I'm off to read the next book. :)

This is one of those books that once you read it it'll change your life forever... or at least it has for me. 
 I read this book four times now; (1) when I was a 4th grader - it was for a book report, (2) when I was in first year high school - another book report, (3) when my family went to New York for my summer break and saw a pop-up copy in my aunt's house, and (4) when I was a junior in college - for my class' GLR project. 
 I've always loved this book! It's one of those books that just touch your heart, even if at the first time I read it I didn't fully understand what it was about. As I gradually read this through the course of my life I found that every time I read it at a different age my understanding and perception of the book changes. It's like when my older sister told me that some people prefer to read The Chronicles of Narnia at different stages of their life because it gives them different meanings of it each time they read. Like when you get older and you read it you see the presence of God more in Aslan or how you should let go from things in your life because you have to grow up. 
 This is similar to The Little Prince because when I was in grade 4 I didn't understand the meaning of the story at all. I just appreciated the friendships The Little Prince had with the Pilot, Fox, Snake, and the Elder people. For the second time I read this I understood the friendships more - that you'll find friends that may be different in their physical appearances or personalities but they'll be there for you in the end, in short; diversity. When I read it during the summer time, when I saw the pop-up version, I understood the relationship of The Little Prince and the flower more - true love/care. And just last year I discovered the meaning behind The Little Prince's death or disappearance - (*hint hint*) acceptance & reality. 
 I also love how I found a connection with The Little Prince and the pilot when he was a child - I never understood how elders can't see/understand the artworks that I've done. Most of the time they misinterpret it to something else like the boa constrictor that ate the elephant for the pilot. And also I felt for The Little Prince on his search for knowledge - at times I feel stupid and naive because I don't understand a lot of things besides the fact that I'm twenty years old. 
 [image error] 
 I learned so much from this 100 and less paged book than any other 400 or more paged book. And it is because of this that I love this book unconditionally.

I really don't have words, as someone in the LGBTQ community, to express how disgusted and betrayed this book made me feel. Is the writing beautiful? Sure. Is Einar's story one that should be told? Absolutely. But this is not that book. 
 The Danish Girl, instead of talking about what it might have been like to undergo the first sex reassignment surgery ever performed, takes a highly fictionalized story about an intersex person who almost certainly has multiple personalities, possibly schizophrenia, and presents it/names it as a story about the transgender experience. I mean, everyone's experience is different, but nothing in this story even comes close to capturing what it's like to be trans*. This does unbelievable damage to the trans* community, a group already severely marginalized, by both confusing transgender and intersex as well as associating transpeople with mental illness. It plays into every harmful stereotype out there. 
 I don't understand what could possibly have motivated Mr. Ebershoff to do such a thing, especially as a gay man himself. I really don't understand what would have compelled Penguin to publish something so inappropriate. And how on earth did this win awards? 
 I hate that I wasted hours of my life supporting this nonsense.

Adventure, adventure and more adventure. This is what you can expect from Riordan. You're just recovering from a really action packed scene then suddenly there's another one coming. This book is like the definition of adventure filled book. haha! Riordan clearly patterns Percy's first three adventures from popular Greek Mythology. The first one was from Perseus, the second one I think is a mix of Odysseus and Jason and the Argonauts then the last one was from Hercules. It's kinda fascinating to read a modern take or retelling of these adventures. I like how Riordan made the Greek mythology adapt with the modern times. As a lover of Greek Mythology I have enjoyed the first three books and I really find Percy's narration very funny. So yea giving this book 4.0 stars. Though I liked the second book better, because I found Tyson and Percy's relationship really amusing :)

This is the first of the Wolves of Mercy Falls trilogy, and is about a girl called Grace who was attacked by wolves when she was young and grows up fascinated by the wolves in her town. Sam is a werewolf, and is the wolf who spared her life. Together, they try to solve the mystery of the wolves and in particular a boy called Jack Culpepper who is attacked by them. Grace and Sam fall in love, and set out to cure the werewolves, since they change into wolves every winter, until they simply stay wolves, and its Sam's last chance as a human. 
 I quite enjoyed this book, although in parts it stuck to the genre's cliches which I've noted before - however it managed to deviate a little to create a surprisingly maturer take on a very done-before story. Personally I'm a sucker for werewolves so I may be a little biased on that front, but most of the stories ideas and characters make sense and mercifully, the protagonists Sam and Grace are not mind-numbingly whiney and stupid. They act fairly reasonably for most of the book. 
 The side characters are not simply hashed out (with the exception of perhaps Rachel) but have dimensions and are fairly relatable. Grace's parents however, are generally copies of Bella Swan's - detached, good-natured, and useless at supervising or cooking for their daughter. At least Charlie Swan got angry when Bella went missing for two days. Grace's parents don't even notice, and while Grace is saddened but used to this behaviour, in real-world terms it is quite close to neglect, and one instance in the book (mentioned below in the spoilers) is an actual case of neglect and should have resulted in her father's arrest. 
 This book was quite sad in parts, especially since it deals with suicide and the struggles of being rejected by your family. The romance in the novel is not over-indulging or too unrealistic and quite refreshing in its casualness and awkwardness. I was afraid the plot would simply be a case of forbidden love but it wasn't like that at all (and I really hope it does not turn into that in the later books). The ending is fairly questionable and deals fairly casually with a serious implication, so I'll let you decide how you take that. I'd definitely recommend this book for people who liked Twilight or fantasy romance and wanted something new. 
 Spoilers review/talk below (only read after reading the book!): 
 Okay so you're wondering about how casually Grace mentions her father leaving her in a heated car to die too, right? "The doctor said I should have died, but I didn't" Grace recalls. I am sorry but shouldn't your dad be arrested for neglect and potentially committed homicide??? I don't care if it "cured" her werewolf-ness, something should have been addressed there. Okay... I just had to let that out, it was annoying me so much. That and curing it with meningitis. What a horrible thing. 
 I would also like to discuss how much I loved there being no "forbidden love" or love triangles or any abusive or manipulative crap being in their relationship. Thank you Maggie. Don't make me regret this. They were able to fall in love and have sex without becoming unhealthy about it. They wanted to do it, Sam decided it was too soon, they waited a little longer. When they did sleep together they had a good time and continued their next day as normal (if a little giddy). THIS IS SO NORMAL I LOVE IT. I WANT MORE OF THIS IN TEEN LITERATURE. They also used protection, more like this please. I shouldn't be so pleased about this, but after reading so much teen literature about it being wrong and uncontrollable etc etc I was ready to vomit. They seem a cute couple. I like.

I've read this ages ago. I never really processed the book, and the only reason I remembered it is because I've donated my old paperbacks to charity recently. 
 This type of books were a dime a dozen riding into popularity on a trail of stars like Vampire Academy and the like. Touch of Frost was uninspired, filled with cliche's and tropes. It based it's school for superfreaks on Greek Mythology. 
 The romance was your classic bad boy meets the unpopular girl, while the mean cheerleader and her cronies conspire against her. 
 The rest of the plot was so random and unconnected, truth be told - I found the story not worth the paper it was printed on. But hey ho, the kiddies loved it.

Rafe Sullivan is burnt out. He works as a PI and he's the best at catching cheaters but it has left him with the idea that 100% of relationships end in the bitter acrimony that he sees several times a day. His sister Mia, a real estate agent, tells him their childhood lake house is for sale and she has already negotiated a good price for him. 
 He buys it; if only to get Mia off his back. But when he goes out to inspect his purchase and have the kind of childhood holiday he dreamed of, he finds the house almost destroyed by the last owner. The only good thing is that his neighbor inherited her house from her grandparents. And he's real pleased to see her. 
 Fifteen years ago, Brooke Jansen had spent the whole summer as a part of the Sullivan family before they had lost their lake house. She is the only child of over protective parents and has finally fought free enough to run her truffle making business from the lake house. They disapprove, but they seem to with everything she does. 
 She's every bit as pleased to see Rafe; he's been her own personal benchmark of 'wild' for as long as she can remember. And he's right there. And looking at her like that. 
 Brooke is ready to be wild. 
 *** 
 This is one of those stories that I fell for (didn't see any typos - yay!) and then I think about it as I go to write the review and say... wait a second... it's a formulaic romance. Insta love based on a long ago meeting, insta lust, too and the standard misunderstanding in the third act thing before it is all made right. 
 But... I have to frown at an eight year old girl who has a crush on a fourteen year old... really? That's freaking decades apart at that age. She's what? In grade two? Three tops. He'd be in middle school... *frowns* nope. 
 I expected Brooke to have done something truly heinous at sixteen (she mentioned it like a dozen times) and it turned out to be got in a car with a boy driver and he was drunk... that's serious but I honestly imagined her having unprotected sex and hiding her baby off somewhere... (yes, I know I have a vivid imagination.) I really don't understand why her parents spent all their time reminding her of this awful deed as if it was so bad as to release all the evils of the world out of a box/urn or something. She's like the most safe teen ever! She made one mistake. 
 And the dominance thing with Rafe? What was that??? 
 Rafe was like dom-lite. He said some stuff and he tied her wrists for a minute and a half before undoing them. What the? I mean I didn't expect whippings and handcuffs... but jeez... make a girl expect some kinky sex and it had damn well better be kinky! (this is your fault Tiffany Reisz.) A bright silk scarf tied around a wrist for a minute and a half is not kinky. They didn't even do it doggie style! Vanilla all the way. 
 But yeah... I'd tear strips off him for doing a background search on me... and I get why he did it. But they got over it super fast.  
 But I will allow that Bella Andre can write an entertaining romance. This is book 9 in the Sullivan series and in the only-in-GR-category book 15 has a 4.2 star rating and she hasn't even written it yet. 
 3 stars

I really tried with this one. I checked it out about three times and finally gave up about 3/4 the way through. It got great reviews so I kept thinking, any time now the book with get good but it never did. 
 I thought the world the author created was cool but the book was SO SLOW moving and I didn't like any of the characters. 
 Maybe I will try again some day (not a quitter) but until then I wouldn't recommend to anyone I liked that this is worth the read. 
 "Friends don't like friends read 1 star books."

A book about a super-competitive performing arts high school, you say? Well, I don't know about you, but that has "GLEE AU" written all over it. Sadly, my initial plans to visualize a Rachel/Marley/Blaine/Ryder-or-Sam core four largely fell apart for lack of physical similarity, so I GUESS I will have to describe them on their own merit: 
 (not really spoilers, just long and a bit superfluous) 
  
 Sophie: brash, bossy singer/actress, not as talented as most classmates, and desperate for fame at the expense of everything else. Honestly not redeemable, but since I was reading her through a Rachel lens, I still had some sympathy for her. 
 Emme: obvious darling of the book. Sweet, desperately shy redhead with a true gift for composing and a near-inability to see the bad in people. Lone girl in a four-person band that formed the first day of high school and has been together ever since, she appears to have close friendships with all three members. Don't forget about Jack and Ben! They're good guys; they don't get first-person POV chapters, but they're central to the story. Even though I'm cramming them into Emme's paragraph, oops. 
 Carter: All-American golden boy type, immediately down-to-earth and very likable (my second favorite), not least because of the way he's drawn to Emme's refreshingly real and honest conversations. SHIPPIN' IT! Even though their relationship is purely platonic. 
 Ethan: dark horse jerk. He's hinted at having low self esteem, but instead of making him sympathetic, his only character traits seem to be turning to liquid courage to overcome shyness, and cheating on his girlfriend over and over because deep down, he was just so gosh-darn in love with Emme this whole time that Nothing Compares 2 U. Yeah, not buying it. They lacked romantic chemistry, and this is possibly the first time I've honestly seen a heterosexual male/female friendship as sibling-like instead of potentially romantic.  
 ---- 
 All in all, despite my dislike of Ethan, there were a lot of good stories about friendship, following (or sometimes finding) your passion, and every aspect of young musicianship from practice to the stage.

I found it very difficult to get into Red Queen at first. I couldn't help feeling as if I'd read this all before and it didn't help that I just couldn't connect with Mare. I was being told what she was feeling but I was left feeling almost empty. It was just words on a page and no feelings coming from them. At some points I was getting a Katniss/Gale vibe from Mere/Filorn, the only difference being that I actually liked Katniss and Gale. 
 Things did pick up though and somewhere along the way I actually began to care about at least some of the characters and there were twists that I was not expecting, although I probably should have guessed most of them. 
 I'm glad that I haven't read a lot of young adult fiction in recent years. I'm not sure I would have ended up liking this if I had read a lot.
Very cute book with great imagination and story.

Sincere compliment to Kathleen Kent that I did not realize this was a sequel to her book The Wolves of Andover! It stood on its own and I would never have realized it is a follow up to "Wolves" if I had not been looking for more of her books at my local library. Original review was 3 stars, boosting it up to 4 for that point alone.

I received an ARC from the publishers in exchange for an honest review. This review in its entirety was originally posted at caffeinatedlife.net: http://www.caffeinatedlife.net/blog/2... 
 I don't know anything about Panfilo de Narvaez' expedition, so I was intrigued by this novel. The choice of telling the story from Mustafa's perspective was what intrigued me about the book, and provides the author with creative room to approach the expedition and the experiences of these characters from another angle. 
 The storytelling itself was very interesting, initially going back and forth between the exploration in the New World and flashbacks to Mustafa's story prior to his inclusion in the expedition. I honestly found his backstory more interesting than present events in the New World, which in the process revealed the realities of slavery and the times in which he lived in. But his story in the "present day" of the exploration was also revealing and just as gritty: the hunger they experienced, disease, the in-fighting amongst the survivors, the uncertain terrain they faced...It was all quite realistic and brutal. 
 Overall,The Moor's Account was a fascinating look at 14th century Spain and the experiences of being on a New World expedition from a different perspective.

The blurb describes this book as "one of the strangest, funniest, and flat-out scariest books you will read this--or any other--year." This is entirely correct. It's also a very difficult-to-classify book. I would go with urban fantasy with thriller elements. 
 It won my heart immediately by being about a museum curator. There are not enough novels about museums and curators. In addition to that, the curator in question (Billy) is well-drawn and believable. There are people just like him working at the National Museum of Natural History just down the street. (Where, sidenote, we have an Architeuthis in a tank.) He was engaging, and I was interested in him immediately, even when he was just walking around giving the tour. Then the museum's squid goes missing, and all heck breaks loose. 
 This is a wild romp of a book, with plots, and subplots, and tiny details mentioned once that suddenly become very important later on. It's a book that keeps the reader on her toes, and one that (occasionally) disturbs her sleep. While never anything (very) overtly gory, there's some very well-done creepy squickiness. 
 This book kept me guessing right up until the end. Mieville does a very good job of introducing and tracking characters organically. In some books, you meet someone and immediately know they are a Character. Maybe this happens in other people's real lives, but it certainly doesn't happen in mine, so I appreciate writers like Mieville who introduce people slowly, without a bunch of physical description and back story to drive home the fact that You Should Be Paying Attention to This Person. It was really refreshing. The relationships and loyalties were also nicely organic and believable. 
 The story was incredibly imaginative and engrossing. The characters, even the most absurd, were well-drawn, and the concepts were just outstanding. I loved the angels of memory, Wati's union, the embassy, Perky the helpful pig, and all the other characters Mieville created and brought together for this extraordinary story. At root, this is a story about the nature, and importance, of belief. Mieville handles it dexterously and with rare humor, so it never bogs down. 
 My biggest (and only gripe) (and maybe isn't a gripe so much as it is a question) has to do with the last few pages of the book.  I understand what Vardo was trying to do and why. But what about Alfred Wallace? Wallace was stumbling toward the idea of natural selection at the same time as Darwin was, just in a different part of the world. Don't get me wrong, I know Darwin was important. But he didn't invent natural selection. He merely discovered it. It's there, and true, even if the Beagle went down, with all hands, in the Pacific. Wouldn't someone else have just discovered it? Or is the way the time fire works so precise that burning out Darwin's records mean that natural selection never gained dominance as a theory? I'm a bit curious about this. Though I was very touched at the squid's behavior, and the loyalty Billy feels toward Darwin, biology, and the museum.

Wow better than I expected! I rather enjoy the world of Chimeras vs Seraphim. Reminds me of Saga a little because of the Chimeras (Madrigal) with horns..falling in love with a winged species! I was kinda slammed by the last third of the book... wishbone part! It came out of nowhere it felt!
This book is pretty hilarious. I wish all my problems could go away by giving them a bus ticket and a suitcase ;)

Yes Cruel Beauty is an adaptation of Beauty and The Beast but like you've never seen it before. I was/am and am not in two minds about this book. 
 That doesn't make sense does it? But this is how this story makes you feel most of the time. 
 This entire story is a mixture of different fairly tales as well as Greek and Celtic mythology also the practice of Hermeticism, because of that it can become very confusing if you don't have some idea of what this is about as the author makes no effort to explain anything at any point. So often you have no idea why she mentions some things or keeps repeating others and she uses a lot of hermetic phrases which would mean zilch if you don't have the inclination to look things up (and not everyone wants to do that). 
 So for this review I'm gonna break it down just a bit. 
 Hermeticism 
 is an actual religious and philosophical tradition/practice. In a sense it is both science and magic. Isaac Newton was an a faithful follower and practitioner of it and said it helped him to better understand the why the natural world around him worked and aided in his research findings. 
 Basically hermetic's believe that everything is in everything and part of everything. And we see this in the story where it is talked about the hearts of the elements and that one element cannot exist with out the other. There are 3 parts wisdom of the universe according to these beliefs and the author makes use of two. That is Alchemy and Theurgy/Goetia (mostly the latter), Alchemy as we know is the ability of changing things but it is more than that, it is also about birth, death and resurrection. How people or energy (elements) move from one phase to the next.And Goetia was the ability to summon the dead or demons to gain knowledge or perform deeds for you. 
 So with that basic knowledge we can continue (a lot to swallow isn't it). 
 This story is not for the faint of heart or someone looking for a beautiful well wrapped love story, as yes it is beautiful but it is also very messy and in some ways heartbreaking. 
 Nyx lives in a world that has been separated from reality, Arcadia. It is a world somewhere in a void, where there are no stars at night and the sky is made of actual parchment, like the image of sky drawn on paper. This world has been ruled by the Gentle Lord for 900 years, he has no name, and he is a demon who makes pacts with people giving them their wishes at a price. You might gain the love of the man you want but you could loose your eyesight in return, or your lovers husband might die and you could have her but you or her might not live long enough to enjoy is. Before Nix and her twin sister where born, her mother was unable to have children and it made her sick with want, so their father made a deal with the Gentle Lord to give his wife healthy children (like Snow White's mother who wished for a daughter and the wish was granted by a frog - well in the story I read). He agrees stating that she will give birth to twin girls and he must then choose the daughter that will come to him as his wife when she turns 17 ( like Rapunzel's mother who craved a certain veg so much it made her sick and the witch allowed the man to take it if he would give her their first child). But there is a twist, although Nyx's mother has two beautiful daughters she dies some time afterward when the girls are older and they are taken care of by their mothers sister. 
 Nyx is told when she is 7 that she will be given to the Gentle Lord as his bride, as according to the bargain with the demon lord, who caused her mothers death but she will also be used as a tool to kill him and free Arcadia as she will be able to get close enough to destroy him. 
 Nyx then spends the rest of her life knowing that she will grow up to die, while her sister will live. She is trained in hermetic knowledge of how the elements work as the magic that holds the city captive is made up of the 4 elements and if she can break them she can set them free. But as a result it will either kill her or trap her for eternity with the demon while everyone else is free. To add insult to further injury, she is shown no affection by her father, who is only concerned with not only his revenge but the freedom of his people. An aunt who, is also the "evil" stepmother in a sense as she is sleeping with Nyx's father and constantly criticizes her and is only there to train her to be a good wife to gain the Gentle Lord's trust. And her sister is kept in ignorance, as although she knows Nyx must kill the Gentle Lord she is told that all her sister must do is get close enough as a virgin to slit his throat. Therefore her sister lives a happy life and Nyx resents her family for this. She feels hate and resentment everyday of her life and although she is prepared to do her duty this grows and festers in her heart. 
 What makes this story different from other Beauty and the Beast adaptations is that both Nyx and the Gentle Lord, also known as Ignifex, are both beautiful on the outside but inside they know how to hate others, they know what fear and resentment and loneliness feels like. Ignifex is evil, not because he is a demon but because he makes bargains with people knowing that they will never actually get what it is they want and as a result they will suffer for their choices. He isn't looking for someone who will love him or see the goodness within as he has accepted what he is. 
 And Nyx is a beast all in her own right because of the hate she feels, she wants to hurt others because of the pain she has had to live with. Wereas the traditional stories have been about a man who has been punished for his cruelty until someone can love him for the goodness that they can find within his soul and the character of Beauty was always someone of total kindness and love and because of this was able to bring out the goodness in the Beast. 
 The relationship between Nyx and Ignifex is volatile and fun, they never really have moments of sweet innocent kisses or pretty rainbow revelations. There is at no point that Nyx pretends that she wouldn't kill him if she could and yet for a demon, he never lies to her nor does he make her do anything against her will. She has been raised to hate Ignifex and she is fully prepared to do that, while she falls in love with his shadow, Shade, who she realizes is just as much a prisoner as what she is. He is both part of Ignifex and separate from him, he is what is left of the last prince of Arcadia. He is bound to do his duty to Ingifex, to follow his orders, keep his secrets and do him no harm. 
 I think the author must have watched the made for TV movie of Beauty and the Beast growing up (with Rebecca Demorne) where the Beast's castle is alive. There are no physical servants but the house in some ways bends to Nyx's will. Allowing her to watch her family through a magic mirror and giving her what she wants, to some extent. But the house is also dangerous as it holds the same spirits that destroyed the world when Pandora opened the box. 
 Against her will, as well as the advise of Shade, Nyx begins to fall in love with Ingifex. She realises that he is not all powerful, and he has his fears and gentle side. And his gentle nature only surfaces to protect her, to make her happy. She also realizes that it is not only herself and Shade that are captives but Ingifex himself as well. He is not master as she thought but also a servant created to serve demon lords. And when Arcadia was separated Ingifex was created and his name taken away, and if they can find his name, he will be free from his servitude so she begins to help him and falls deeper in love with him. In the process she tries to forget her duty to her family, her vows of vengeance because for the first time someone realizes that there is darkness in her heart. Someone knows who she truly is through all the pretense and he still loves her and she doesn't want to loose that. 
 Shade, who she trust betrays her, and she comes close to dying in the process and while Ingifex nurses her back to health she finds that she can no longer hate him in anyway. Even knowing what he is and what he has done and still does she can no longer hate him, because he loves her. 
 The reason I think this is a beautiful story, although confusing at times, is that neither character is perfect, and neither do they pretend to be anything but flawed. For me it was not Ingifex that was the beast, but Nyx herself. 
 She did not know how to love, as she had never known it. She had become a vessel filled with hate and bitterness. What made this worse was that for 10 years she had to pretend to be happy to simply do her duty, while hoping for love that never came from her family. The being in a demons house, someone who was supposed to be evil and happy to inflict pain, she finds acceptance. 
 It is as she tell her sister, when Ingifex allows her to go home to see her, that it was through the love and kindness that Ingifex showed her that she was finally happy to forgive and love not just her family but her sister. If it had not been for him she would never have been able to truly love her sister without hating her. 
 This story of Nyx and Ingifex shows us that when someone truly loves us, they accept both the good and the bad, they never expect us to be wholey good. They also don't expect us to change our true nature but their love of us brings out the goodness in us. It also shows that it is often those that we don't expect to hurt or betry us that often do and the person who we expect nothing from might just be the one who give us what we never had. 
 Nyx sister forces her, for her love to betry Ingifex. And Nyx for that acceptance agrees. And through love of Nyx, Ingifex is finlly able to face his fears. He faces his past and what he is truly lacking in himself. Thereby undoing the curse of imprisonment for everyone but himself. For love he was finally able to make the one sacrifice he was never able to. The sacrifice was only doing what was good for himself. 
 Everything is undone and is as if it never happened, but Nyx can feel something is missing in her life. She isn't sure what until she sees Ingifex's ring and everything come back to her. Remembering that Ingifex once told her the Demon lords leave clues for breaking their deals everywhere. The castle over Arcadia is in ruins and she remember a myth about a dead god who was allowed to walk the earth one night a year. 
 In the end she bargains with the Demon Lords, but she doesn't want anything in return. She simply asks for them to allow her to share his punishment so that he will never be alone and she wants nothing in return. She is warned that eventually she will hate him, and they will hurt one another. Nyx realizes this is true but it still means that he will never be alone in the darkness and they will still have one another. And the Demon Lords grant her wish. And it is the memory of love, and the loving of someone enough to give without receiving anything in return that saves them both. 
 Definitely a beautiful read. 
 Oh and Side note (if anyone is interested): Nyx means night, she was a goddess of night, daughter of Khaos (god of Chaos) and wife to, Erebos which means deep darkness/shadow (basically a god of shadows. So if you look at the story if Nyx and Ignefix she was a goddess of night and he was the god of the shadows)

The 2011 re-read:

Can Roland and Eddie convince Calvin Tower to sell them the lot where the Rose grows? Can Jake and Callahan find Susannah before she has her baby? 
 Song of Susannah was my least favorite book in the Dark Tower series the first time through. Susannah has never been my favorite character in the Dark Tower saga and this book is really Susannah-heavy. On the second read, I had to raise it another star. The Susannah/Mia conflict had its moments and did a lot of setting up for the big shebang coming in the seventh and final book. A lot more background information was revealed. 
 I'd be lying if I said Susannah was the reason I upped this one a star upon re-reading. The other reason is that Jake and Eddie seem like bonafide Gunslingers in this book, even more than they did in Wolves of the Calla. I have a feeling their fates in The Dark Tower are going to be almost as painful the second time through.  The relationship between Eddie and Roland has developed quite a bit since The Drawing of the Three, as has Roland's character. I still love Long, Tall, and Ugly, even though he'd probably leave me along the Path of the Beam the first morning I bitched about not having coffee. 
 There is something else that I liked a lot more the second time but it's pretty spoilerific. Now that I've had a few years to digest Stephen King writing himself into the story, it doesn't really irk me like it did the first time.  
 While it's not my favorite of the Dark Tower books, it's still good and it lays a lot of the cards down on the table for the final volume, The Dark Tower. See you all along the Path of the Beam.

Note: This is told entirely in dialogue form, mostly in the form of interviews. If you're averse to this kind of storytelling, stay very far away. 
 With that being said, I loved this!! At first I was supremely skeptical of the quote on my arc about this being a mashup of World War Z and The Martian, but once I started reading it I could see where the comparisons were. The World War Z comparison is immediately obvious--both of these novels are told predominantly through a single person researching and interviewing others who were directly involved. Purely an observer, never someone in the thick of the action. 
 The comparison to The Martian was less obvious. Really, the only thing that was similar was that it was science fiction, but with a positive realistic science-y spin to it. Sleeping Giants did a darn good job of providing realistic scenarios to an outrageous event. What if we found alien technology? What would we do: as a nation, as a race, as the entire population of the Earth? It always seemed grounded in more realism, and I appreciated that. Nothing seemed overly grandiose and obnoxious. 
 The choices the characters had to make were probably the most interesting part for me. When a cataclysmic event happens to Vincent, he has to undergo a change that drastically alters his involvement in the project. The way it was handled was harsh and I loved it. 
 The only criticism I have was my annoyance at there still being a love triangle even in a book like this. WHY? Why does there ALWAYS have to be a love triangle? It's just annoying. Stop it.

An awesome, fast paced, hard to put down book. :) 
 First reactions? 
 Upon first reading the book, my first reaction was that the writing style was..well...different. I wasn't sure what it was but I knew I didn't like it. After reading further, I realized that its a bit chunky, with a line of dialogue followed by so much internal monologue or description that we totally lost the jist of the conversation by the time the response comes along..so we're like "What?" "Oh yeah...*goes back to last line of dialogue to refresh*..THATS what she was talking about. 
 The story world is very unique, and a refreshing change to most YA books out there. It's not exactly dystopian, but it appeals to the lovers of that genre. Some previous reviews didn't like the fact that the author didn't explain where on Earth this was taking place, or if it was another planet, or what. But in my opinion, I really liked that the location was kept vague, focusing only on inner details. I found it helped me to just imagine this amazing magical world. It could of been anywhere, which I loved. 
 BACKROUND 
 There are barrons and healers who represent the "skilled" society. They go to an academy and train (without a concrete end, I might add), until they are deemed ready to go and fight or help in the unending war. There are also the unskilled people who are not allowed to know anything about the skilled. We never find out why though. Healers and Barrons are soulbound at birth, an idea I was totally drooling over. The thought of having a definite partner decided for you at birth that you will find one day inevitably is just..wow. I was so in love with this idea and  was so so so annoyed when Kaya found out that hers was dead. I was just like "Come on you just gave us the best concept and now we can't even take part in it? What unfairness!" But I have no idea now..was Darius Kaya's soulbound person all along? And I couldn't stand that they killed off Avery so quickly, without us really getting to know her at all so I was just like.."Oh, okay" I sort of wish we could have know her more for a stronger reaction at her death. Also, Kaya tended to forget about her often throughout the novel, later even referring to Maddox as the best friends she'd ever had.  
 Although most reviews didn't mention her, I really REALLY liked Maddox, Kaya's new best friend at the academy, and all she added to the book. She was snarky but strong, and had a strong characterization with a solid background. The scenes with her were funny and interesting and she was a fabulous addition to the book. Go Maddox!! 
 The world building could have been a little bit more strong, as I was left with bounty's of unanswered questions, like for example, Why, WHY I ASK YOU was Melanie so obsessed with Trayton?, or What was this war even about.....and...lots more I can't think of now. 
 The story plot was one you just fall in love with though, for who doesn't love a strong female heroine who can totally kick butt? Especially when people tell her she's not allowed to but she does anyway. Its a pretty common story line but I fall for it everytime. Going against the social norm and all that. 
 The romance with Trayton is actually the most confusing thing though, it moved much too quickly and didn't seem to have any real chemistry. Although that kind of sucked, the romance(ish) with Darius was enough to make up for it, for you just eat up when he shows some kindness in stark contrast to his usual gruffness. While Trayton is always SO sweet, realistically I think a girl might like that, but in a novel this can sadly get a bit drab and pretty annoying. 
 Overall, the book was a wonderful read that I was totally sucked into until I finally finished it. (And you can tell I'm still thinking about it now, so it hasn't quite left my mind yet). Though it might have some flaws, (Doesn't everything though), it has some great moments, and it was a super fun, and different read. Give it a try!

This is one of those times where I wish I could give half stars, because this book is more of a 3.5 for me. 
 Things I liked: 
 - Different POVs, giving us insight into many of the major parties involved in the Pell situation. Giving each facet of the conflict a voice helped bring a depth to the politics of the universe, and for much of the book I wasn't entirely sure who was "right" and who was "wrong." 
 - Josh and Mallory, for very different reasons. Josh is the character I'm most sympathetic to, from his troubled origins and Adjustment, to his loyalty to Damon and Elene. I was most interested in his story, and I wish I could have gotten more of it. Mallory, on the other hand, is a straight up jerk. She does some super questionable things, and I'm not sympathetic to her at all. But she's very REAL, and one of the most complex POVs we get in this book. Her actions, her thought processes, and her loyalties are very much analytical and calculating. Emotions do not factor in much here, and when they do it's pride and selfishness. Even when she decides to help Josh and Damon, it's less about her being humane and more about what's best for her crew, believing that Mazian has gone too far. She respects them both for being strong and determined even under duress, more than any affection she has toward them as people.  
 - The complicated politics and multifaceted conflict. This isn't a straight up good guys vs. bad guys situation. There are many factors that throw a wrench in any attempts at a two-sided showdown between Earth Company and Union, and each one is intriguing. 
 Things I didn't like: 
 - The writing. The first couple sections were particularly dense and hard to get into, thanks to the necessary info dump. The first chapter was just 300 years of history to set the stage, and while that's important, I feel there might have been a better approach. Her writing style is odd, dense but also fragmented. It reads almost like stream-of-consciousness, and important events are revealed too subtly. I don't like authors taking me by the hand, but I also don't like puzzling out meanings in the text itself. 
 - The Hisa. At first I hoped the Hisa would bring more to the story than just being loveable and sweet. I'm entirely sympathetic to them, and I love their society, but they're pretty pointless in this story. 
 - The Konstantins. Not that I didn't like them as people, but they were a little too straightforward. The rest of the characters have nuance and depth. The Konstantins are just the Good Guys, and this is evident because they're actually ~nice~ to the Hisa. This is literally the only role the Hisa have, to show how good the Konstantins are. In fact, the Hisa refer to good men as Konstantin-men, versus all bad guys as Lukas-men. This is pretty silly. In 300 years of humans being on Pell and interacting with Hisa, only the Konstantins have ever been nice to them and only Lukas has ever been mean? No one is in between? Humans are pretty much an invading species on their planet and recruiting Hisa labor for their own supply bases, you'd think there would be more to Hisa/human relations. Another thing which doesn't really make sense, since the bases are pretty rudimentary and still in the process of being built, even though Pell has been supplying stations with food and water for centuries. 
 I'm definitely interested in Cherryh's universe, though. I will likely read more of her books in the future, if I can get a better grip on her writing style.

I'm glad I reread 13LBE before picking up this one, as it had been a few years. 
 The Last Little Blue Envelope does a fairly good job of picking up where 13LBE left off, with Ginny back in the States and struggling with college essays. It's clear in the first few pages that she is having trouble moving on from her whirlwind summer, and it's also clear that her "kind of something" with Keith is kind of nothing now. 
 It was great fun seeing Richard again, though Keith seemed far different than he did in the first book. I greatly enjoyed the two new main characters, Ellis and Oliver, Ellis because she is the type of girl anyone would love to be friends with and Oliver because I really wanted to figure him out. I thought some of the romance in the book was a bit heavy-handed and too obvious -- there was the occasional moment when it seemed that Ginny might surprise us, but it was pretty clear who she would end up with -- and I disliked how hard Johnson seemed to be trying to make Keith into a bad guy. It seemed really out-of-character for him, especially just after reading 13 Little Blue Envelopes. 
 This next paragraph contains a pretty big spoiler, so, you know, don't read it if you haven't read the book and want it to stay fresh. 
 The only other thing that really bugged me about the book was Ginny's apparent lack of any connection to her life in the States. At least in 13 Little Blue Envelopes, we see her writing to that friend occasionally. In the sequel, even though she has full access to phones and email, she doesn't seem to call anyone but Richard. She's even prepared to move entirely across the world for college because of people she's been with in person for just a few weeks, which also seems unrealistic and makes me wonder just how sad Ginny's American life is.

I recommend The Spellman Files books all the time. To fans of Janet Evanovich, to fans of funny books, to people who just want something good to read. Somewhere in my pitch I usually say something like, "They're mysteries, but not really traditional mystery-genre mysteries." In this the sixth (and final?!) Spellman book that last part is more true than ever. Sure, there are mysteries in this book. And, of course, they get solved. But more and more these books are all about the characters and the relationships between the characters. I think that's why I love them so much. I actually teared up at the end of this one, and not just because it may be the last. Though the epilogue made me hope there will be a spin-off featuring Rae!  
 To people who ask, "Can I read this book without having read the others?" I say, "What's wrong with you? If you want to read this one, just read the others first!" (Now available in paperback!) 
 To people who ask, "Is this the best Spellman book?" I say, "I'd have to re-read them all to decide. Excuse me, I'm going to go do that now." 
 Incidentally, How to Negotiate Everything showed up in my library recently cataloged as easy non-fiction. Non-fiction! Way to go, Lisa. You are shaping young minds.
