This is definitely a werewolf book for grown ups. Duncan references everyone from Shakespeare to Charlotte Bronte to T.S. Eliot to Matthew Arnold. It makes sense that someone with an extended life and a literary bent would find their own writing full of allusions. It's fun to try to spot as many as you can, if that's the sort of thing that rings your bell. I can admit, it totally rings mine. The writing otherwise is...gory! It's filled with the viscera of the change, with popping and crunching and snapping, as well as a lot of blood. As much as Jake abhors himself for murdering one person a month to feed the wolf inside him, as the wolf, he glories in the kill and that's all conveyed in the writing. He employs the same approach when it comes to sex. The effect isn't erotic for the average reader, used to the soft sighs and gentle strokings of other novels, but I can see if you're bloody-minded Jake, it would be. In all, Duncan has done an admirable job. I'm a little mystified I didn't enjoy it more. Jake is gloomy company, either self-loathing or murderous and that wears. It might prove to be a book better enjoyed in hindsight, when I can appreciate the novelty of a literary horror book and all the grisly details have faded.

It's not a bad book, but maybe overrated. 
  In the first part of the book, Green does a good job of developing the characters and establishing a plot. Hazel and Augustus, two teenagers with cancer, meet at a support group and start falling in love. They share a fascination with An Imperial Affliction by Peter Van Houten, a novel about a teenage girl dying of cancer. They contact the author to resolve some loose ends and he invites them to visit him Amsterdam to discover the fate of those characters who survived his novel. A cancer kids wish fulfillment organization arranges their trip to meet the author. Van Houten turns out to be a rude, boorish drunkard who throws them out. Their trip is not a total loss however as they see the sights and physically consummate their love. After returning home, Augustus' suffers a relapse, and the story telling seems to suffer. The chapters get shorter and more fragmented and the story deteriorates. There is a poignant moment in a pre-funeral in which Augustus arranges for Hazel and Isaac, their blind-from-cancer friend, to eulogize him in the basement of the church where their support group meets. Augustus dies a few days later. Van Houten's appearance at Augustus' funeral is unexpected, and ultimately for the story, rather pointless. He is still a drunkard and Hazel rejects him. Later Van Houten's assistant sends Hazel by email a copy of a deathbed letter Augustus had sent to Van Houten. End of story. 
 I felt that Green dropped the ball with Van Houten. Van Houten was a jerk when they met him, he was a jerk at the funeral, and he was a jerk at the finding of Augustus' letter. The only role his character really played in the novel was to deflate the feeling that Hazel and Augustus shared for Van Houten's novel, which was an important element in the first part of the book. The final bit, Augustus' letter to Van Houten, which ultimately seems intended for Hazel, was an okay wrap-up, I suppose, but it could have been so much better.  
 Despite the predictions of other reviewers, I moistened no tissues during the reading of this novel.

All in all, a great book which leaves you wanting to find out more because there is so much left to explore about the Norse gods.

I don't even know where to start with this review. I guess I'll start with the fact that Goodreads STILL won't let us provide half-star reviews. So, I'll start with: 4.5/5 stars 
 Cath is an incredibly relatable character to me. When I was in high school I definitely wrote some fanfiction. I wrote more of my own characters in existing worlds, however, and I quickly realized I should just make my own. But, I wrote a lot. Also, Cath struggled with starting college. Anyone who knows me knows I don't struggle to make friends. But knowing where the cafeteria is? Deciding how to walk in late to class? Finally realizing that there is a severe physical difference between an 18 year-old boy and a 21 year-old man? Those I can relate to. The awkward roommate situations. The lack of a car. The self doubt. 
 And if anyone who went to college tells you they can't relate to that, well, they're lying. 
 This is my second Rainbow Rowell book. The first was Eleanor & Park. What I learned I love about Rowell is that she is a master of relationships. She knows what matters, what needs to be illustrated, and the complexities of relationships comes through. I love all the characters because of this. Even stupid Nick I enjoy. He and Cath have a special relationship. Watching it form, and repeatedly bend (sometimes drastically) were fascinating. 
 The best relationship in this novel is the relationship Cath has with herself. There is the person she is on the inside, and then there is the person she presents to the world. I'm not saying Cath is hiding, or not authentic, but everyone is a bit different on the inside compared to the outside.  I absolutely loved the moment Cath was super down and threw herself an Emergency Kanye party. That was the biggest moment in the first half of the book where inner Cath and outer Cath met up. Once Levi was pulled in she couldn't back down-- she just let herself roll with it. And it was perfect.  She grew in this novel. She didn't grow in any cliche or stereotypical ways Coming-of-Age books tend to have characters grow, either. No, instead she grew exactly as we expect her to. 
 This book only gets 4.5 stars from me because I struggle a bit with the ending. As my friend Kara said, "Felt a little long and then just kinda ended." I don't agree that it felt long. But I do agree that it just ended. There was resolution, but this book didn't end with the same sense of contentedness I felt at the end of Eleanor & Park. (I think I just ruined myself by reading that book first.) I was looking for more... resolution. 
 All in all, it's still incredible and you need to read it. Now.

 I think I went into this book with my hopes too high. I love Greek mythology and stories of starcrossed lovers, so I thought that Starcrossed would be perfect for me! I did enjoy the book, I just didn't love it as much as I thought I would. 
 Helen lives her life trying to get by under the radar. She lives with her single dad on the small island of Nantucket. From the beginning of the story, we get hints that Heleny isn't quite.. normal. She seems to have super human strength and speed, but tries her best to hide it so that she still appears normal. She also has major issues with attention, which is where my first gripe comes from. 
 Helen hates the spotlight. She avoids any kind of attention at all costs. When the spotlight is cast on her, she feels physically sick. Helen is also very self-degrading, always going on about how she's not pretty, she's a huge nerd, she has a horrible reputation in school, complaining about people hate her, etc. This really, really bothered me. Towards the end of the book we do learn that the whole "feeling sick when she gets attention" thing isn't really her fault, but it still bugged me a lot. During most of the story, Helen felt like such a weak character. I couldn't like her when she was constantly complaining, feeling sorry for herself, and generally acting childish. One of the other characters, Hector, actually told Helen that she needed to grow up. I definitely agree with that statement! 
 So, moving a head a bit, Helen meets a new boy at school named Lucas. For some reason, she has an uncontrollable desire to kill him. She's filled with so much rage and hatred towards him but has no idea why. We later learn that this is because of The Furies. The Furies basically turn the different 'Houses' (based on lineage) against each other. But Helen and Lucas fight against this, believing that they're actually destined to be together. And so, they fall in love. Cue issue #2. 
 I kind of feel like there was no "falling in love" phase for Helen and Lucas. One minute they hate each other's guts, then Lucas saves Helen's life and suddenly they're holding hands and stuff. But then here's the even more annoying part: Lucas is always holding Helen's hand and making remarks that suggest he likes her, but then he tells Helen that they can't be together. But even after he says that, he continues to hold her hand every chance he gets. Talk about leading a woman on! I thought that was just so annoying... I would be so pissed if a guy did that to me in real life. If he thinks they can't be together, he shouldn't be treating her like he wants to date her! 
 The last character I'll talk about is Claire. Claire is Helen's best friend. As Helen is figuring out that she's actually a demigod, etc., she doesn't tell Claire about any of it. Eventually Helen tells her and Claire is basically like "I knew that already." How did she know? She found out she could fly by pushing her off a roof when they were kids (just to find out if she could fly). She also tried stabbing her once just to see if it would hurt her. At first I liked Claire's character but after that, I just thought it was a bit weird. I thought it was too convenient that Claire did all those things (which is psycho in itself) and then actually put the pieces together. I mean if I pushed my friend off a roof and saw her "float gracefully to the ground," I'd think I was going crazy. I wouldn't automatically think, "Okay, she can fly." The whole thing just seemed too 'easy' to me. 
 Also WTF at the whole "Helen and Lucas are actually cousins" thing? First of all, I'm really sick of characters falling in love and then being related. I didn't like it in City of Bones and I didn't like it in Starcrossed. I was seriously like "WTF?" It came out of nowhere. Then a few pages later we find out that Helen's mom was actually lying and Helen and Lucas aren't cousins... Okay... another "WTF" moment. I just felt like I was being jerked around and it wasn't done in a tasteful way. It was just a bit annoying, and even confusing.  
 Overall, I did enjoy the Greek mythology aspects of this story and the whole blood feud, but I think I overhyped it for myself. I went into it desperately wanting to love the story, but there were too many let downs for it to be a 4 or 5 star book. I probably will read Dreamless eventually, but I'm not in a huge hurry.

"Maybe they didn't want you to realize that every civilization has its weakness. There's always one thing we depend on. And if someone takes it away all that's left is some story in a history class." 
 I loved Tally in this book. She was a trickster and a person who just wanted what she had always been told was the thing to be. But when she learns that there are others out in the world "smokies" and see starts learning that all she had been taught wasn't what she thought it was. She started changing and she was growing and learning, and when she realized that she couldn't do the thing she was pretty much forced into doing, she tried to end it. Sadly this didn't go as she thought it would and she ended up causing an awful thing to happen to the community she was now calling home. But she does her best to fix this and try to make it right and protect the people that she had by accident ended up hurting. 
 "History would indicate that the majority of people have always been sheep." 
 It's true even if you go back centuries from the time were in now, it shows that people have always been followers. Most to good people, but some to awful people. It's sad to think of but it does make you realize that sometimes we don't learn and we just go with the crowd even when the crowd is doing something that's wrong. 
 This book is very similar in ways to how we are as a society today. Which makes it scary and was what made me love this story so much I think. Because maybe we still have a chance to change how we see things and how we live. 
 The only real problem I had with this story was the insta-love between two characters. I know it's because there young and all but I still feel like more important things were happening/needed to be dealt with. 
 That ending was really good, I can't believe she told what she had done even though she knew it would change everything. It did make me love Tally even more though because she didn't just keep hiding it until she couldn't keep it a secret anymore or someone else told it for her. 
 Overall I loved this story and I am so glad that I have the second book so that I can just continue on and find out what happens next.

10 GOLDEN STARS!

 "Audaces Fortuna Iuvat" 
 Fortune favors the bold... 
 When the old legends of heroes are told, time erodes away the piss and shit of those trampled by the hero's march until nothing is left but the gleaming purity of sacrifice and devotion. Funny how life is never as simple as that. 
 Pierce Brown has a spectacular mind. He gets that one thing perfectly, that one thing that escapes the grasp of so many aspiring and veteran authors. Train of thought. Not any single thought that goes trough our minds is simple or singular. It always develops, forms, mutates, jumps from one point to another and it's never alone. It is always accompanied by emotion. Sometimes it can even seem like shards with jagged edges that stab one another and bleed trough, carting you off in a different direction in a of a blink of an eye. Our thoughts live and breathe with us. To have an ability to capture those transitional moments is true talent, one that Brown has in abundance. 
 I've felt Darrow. I felt his triumph over his enemies, I've felt his confusion and loss of identity. I was lonely with him, I hurt at his side. I found joy in the moments when he thought about his lost love and the innocence that marked another life he lived. 
 Brown has built the Empire in it's true form. An organism, a massive beasts that digests everything in it's path. Created for a nobler purpose, but wherever we find the human element, sickness follows. Greed, power, survival of the fittest. It's amazing how humanity most often creates the very weapon that kills them. They have created gods that enslaved the world and in turn created slaves, but they forgot that all true gold is found in the dirt. The Society is a mother that nurses her children with cruelty and now has nothing else left than to embrace her Golden Son... 
 I am the type of person who never judges a person on their tastes, but if you don't like this particular series....something seriously wrong witcu....

 It's been so very long since a book kept me drawn in like this. Yes, I was still a bit slower reading it than I used to be, but I was always thinking about it even when I wasn't reading, itching to go back, even when the story was still building up. 
 First off, I have to say that I identified with the narrator right away. We're not even all that similar--I'm certainly no runner, I'd have to have a cat, I do get lonely even more than I used to, and I don't write. (I do like raspberry.) But something about her had me clicked in like a puzzle piece from the very first pages. After that, all the suspense, all the mystery and twists kept me anchored to this story. 
 I borrowed this from the library, and I'm loathe to give it back, and sad that I couldn't make notes in the few places I wanted to. Things I noticed, knowing they'd be important later. I know there was one somewhat early on that I can't remember now--the shoulder bruise , I think? (Though that was actually a red herring, all in all.) And the name. And the gloves (I was only just a bit ahead on that one). I suspected an abortion almost the whole time, but couldn't confirm it until the end, and I certainly didn't expect it to be Clare. Even when I noticed it said "Lee," I thought it might be his parents. Only later did I realize they must have known her as Leo, too.  
 Oh, I don't know what to say. I think most of the time when I rate a book 5 stars, it's got some great sweeping moral theme to change the world or change a life, and I think that's what we all idealize literature to be. "Entertaining" is too lowly a word for this book, but that's just it--it was so good because it was so suspenseful, keeping me on edge the entire way through, keeping me interested even during the bits that would've turned me off a more regular book. 
 Soooo. I was a bit nervous when I first added this book as currently-reading because all the reviews seemed to be bad. But I loved it--so if you're reading this, do give the book a chance!

I read this book because I was doing a project about how it was banned at the public high school in Republic, MO because, the school board said, it sends a message (primarily about sex) that they don't want to be sending to their teenage students. I wanted to see what all the fuss was about. 
 This is a story about Anna who falls in love with the twin brother of her best friend, Frankie, weeks before he dies and before they're able to tell Frankie about their relationship. The majority of this book takes place one year after his death as Frankie and Anna both deal with having lost someone important. Anna has gone into a kind of tail spin and acts increasingly bold and brash - smoking, dressing sexy, etc. - in order to get her parents' attention, while Anna tries her best to just take care of Frankie and ignore her own pain. When Frankie's family takes Anna on a summer vacation to the beach, Frankie decides that Anna needs to start having fun and that they will flirt with 20 boys over their three week vacation. (Note that the goal is not to sleep with 20 boys, but just to flirt with them. And they don't even get anywhere close to 20.) She also pushes Anna to lose her virtinity as a kind of rite of passage. 
 So, yes, there are 16 year old girls talking about and having sex. Also, Anna and Frankie do a lot of lying to Frankie's parents, who are basically oblivious, sneaking out of the house every night to hang out with these two boys that they befriend and even going to a big party on their last night where they both drink and play beer pong. 
 But I think what is so often ignored in this rush to ban books is the context in which these details occur, and that makes all the difference. While Frankie claims to have lost her virginity earlier in the year and then to have had sex with a boy on the vacation, it turns out that she actually lied (due to her emotional turmoil) and is still a virgin. And while Anna does lose her virginity to a boy she meets on vacation, she does so in just about the safest way - both emotionally and physically - that she could have. In fact, just about the best thing in this book is that Anna has sex and it doesn't signal the end of her life (via pregnancy or shunning, etc.), as so often happens in teen books when a girl has sex. It's something that she choses to do freely and because she feels ready. The whole boy/sex thing is part and parecel of what Frankie and Anna are going through in coping with the loss of Frankie's brother. It's not thrown in there just for kicks, but rather is used as part of their psychological and emotional growth and healing throughout the novel. And, let's face it, teens are going to parties with drinking and they are having sex. Literature for them should reflect these realities if it's going to take the audience seriously. Ockler does that responsibly and without sensationalism.

"With murder, the victim is gone, and not forced to deal with what happened to her. The family must deal with it, but not the victim. But rape is much worse. The victim has a lifetime of coping, trying to understand, of asking questions, and the worst part, of knowing the rapist is still alive and may someday escape or be released. Every hour of every day, the victim thinks of the rape and asks herself a thousand questions. She relives it, step by step, minute by minute, and it hurts just as bad. 
 Perhaps the most horrible crime of all is the violent rape of a child. A woman who is raped has a pretty good idea why it happened. Some animal was filled with hatred, anger and violence. But a child? A ten-year-old child? Suppose you're a parent. Imagine yourself trying to explain to your child why she was raped. Imagine yourself trying to explain why she cannot bear children."

Austin feels the pressure of time, as he wants to finally settle down and do the whole family thing. Fast forward and Sierra and Austin are exploring their relationship with each other, and suddenly a curveball is thrown their way in the form of a son Austin didn't know he had. 10-year-old Leif comes into their lives after his mother passes away. I was very apprehensive to start reading this book, as I had heard it was a 'love it/hate it' book. I was also not sure what to think because I bought it on a whim after hearing some people talk about it, but then I read a different Jenny Han book and didn't really like it. 
 So I am pleased to say that I actually did enjoy this book! 
 I started out reading slowly, likely due to my apprehension with the contemporary YA romance genre, but as I got more into the story, the reading picked up. 
 I did like the characters, although I have to say there was little character growth and development, when there was so much potential for these things. I do feel that Lara Jean did grow somewhat, but there was a lot of potential for further growth - I'm not sure how much growth we'll see in the sequel to this book, but I do believe I will read it to see where the story goes from here. 
 I wasn't a fan of Peter at the beginning because he didn't seem like a very nice guy, but as the story progressed, I realized that he really was a nice guy and I started to like him more and more. By the end of the story, I was rooting for Lara Jean & Peter to end up together. 
 The one part that probably annoyed me the most about this book, was the fact that Lara Jean was actually nearly 17 years old - the writing and her thought/speech patterns made her seem like she was somewhere between 12 & 14, going back and forth depending on parts of the story. 
 I did, however, quite enjoy the overall plot. The romance between Lara Jean and her 5 boys was subtle and classy, and there was no time in which I felt the romantic elements overshadowed the main points of the story. 
 Overall, I rated this book 4 stars, because, although there were a few things that didn't work out just right for me, there were a lot of things that worked out just right!

I picked up Darkfever as a free ebook promotion and had no idea what I was getting into. Before I knew it, I'd purchased and devoured the first four books of the series and was kicking myself for not checking to see if it was complete because I was going to have to wait for the last book to come out. And then re-read them all. (Don't worry, the series is finished now.) 
 This is not the kind of series that you can just chill out between books. It's intense, it grabs you, and you can't let it go. But you have to have a little faith that the blond, pink-obsessed main character is going to change along the way. It doesn't happen in the first book, but trust me, her world gets turned upside-down and she becomes far less air-headed and annoying. 
 What really grabs me in the beginning is the old-world feel of Ireland where this takes place. It's the kind of place where you can imagine a fine line between Earth and Faerie. And the kind of place where you find musty old book shops to get lost in. Then we have a mysterious, hostile male, resigned to helping the naive female for unknown personal reasons. Yeah, he definitely makes the series. 
 There is one big negative for me, and that's the sexually explicit content. The overall story was good enough for me to gloss over it, but I still don't see the necessity. Especially the part where just being in the presence of a Faerie causes mindless stripping and orgasmic experiences . I've just had to block that out, but the cataclysmic action is that good (again, talking the entire series here). It's saying a lot that this series remains a favorite that I'd re-read - although it could have been worth 5 stars if I didn't have to partition my brain to enjoy it.

This book had a lot of things going for it, which is why I pulled it off the shelf at the library. First and foremost, a pretty cover - I cannot stress enough how much a good cover will do for a book! The description promised me fantasy, a female protagonist, and the reclaiming of a throne. Check, check, check, all things I like. 
 Let's take them in order, then. The world was, at fist blush, a standard medieval-analogue with some interesting backstory hinted at. Feudal system, queen/king, regent, with you so far. And then the narration started dropping hints about something called the Crossing. The words British and American were used. So in fact the book is something more like fantastic future history. But I wasn't clear on when, in our timeline, the Crossing took place. So then there were more hints - Kelsea talks about recessive genes. The Red Queen is a former geneticist. (mild). Ebooks are mentioned (as being the death of the publishing industry, which made me laugh). Heroin. So clearly this is more of a post-apocalypse (or at least post-present) regression to a feudal state. Though there's also magic, so. 
 This freaked a lot of reviewers out, based on my quick skim of some of the other reviews on here. Personally, it didn't bother me. If you're going to harp on how exactly they lost all their technology and why it happened so fast (though, honestly, it's not totally clear how fast it did happen) then skip this one, because those feelings seem to cause a lot of rage. Personally, I didn't mind. I just accepted it as it came and went back to enjoying what I was reading. Actually, I thought it was an interesting path to take and I wonder how it will affect the future books. 
 Next up, our protagonist Kelsea. First of all, I had to tamp down my own weird response to her name. It's very similar to the name of the protagonist in my current WIP (Kelisin), enough so that I did a few double takes at the beginning of the book :) 
 Kelsea is a good character - a bit black-and-white, morality-wise, but she's a young woman, and idealistic. I was rooting for her, and I think she does a decent job of maturing and coming into her own over the course of the book. 
 The plot was somehow fast-paced and slow-paced at the same time. By which I mean, everything got a lot of words devoted to it (hence why some people complained about pacing). On the other hand, I read the whole book (and it's long) in a day. I didn't want to put it down. 
 In the end, I'm really not sure why this is getting so much hate, except maybe that it's a case of strong reaction to serious over-hype. I'm not the kind of person who gets asked to review in advance, so I actually missed all the hype, but I've gleaned that it involved comparisons to the Hunger Games and Game of Thrones and a whole lot of praise. I don't think either of those are particularly apt comparisons, but that's marketing for you. 
 It's certainly not the best new book since sliced bread, but it *is* a really good, promising new fantasy. 
 Is it really worth a seven-figure advance and a movie deal (more gleanings)? ...Eh, maybe not. Though if the movie does get made I would totally watch it - Emma Watson is rumored to be interested in the lead. There aren't enough good fantasy movies made. 
 But it is worth a read, if it sounds like the sort of thing you like. Read the cover copy, ignore the hype, and decide for yourself.

When I picked this up, I certainly didn't expect it to be such a enjoyable read. A school where young ladies are trained in espionage and assassination in addition to etiquette does sound interesting indeed. I did find some similarities between Finishing School and the Harry Potter series, but isn't that the same for all books in a boarding school settings? 
 First I'd like to express how much I like the covers for this series. Just WOW~ They are so simple, yet beautiful. Also, the title is as intriguing. I like how both words start with the same letter but at the same time depict the two sides of the school - the public and the private one. Yet it seems the public profile of the institution is as important, if not more, for the application of the other classes. Etiquette is actually the means to acquire certain information and if you want to be a good spy, you'd better be a proper lady first. 
 The story follows Sophronia Temminnick, who enters the school as a recruit due to a recommendation from a certain someone. She is quite boyish in her adventures and interests, yet she refuses to wear anything but a skirt which baffled me. But I guess that was the way girls behaved in the 1800s. Of whom Sophronia reminded me? The answer is easy - Flavia de Luce. They are both smart with razor-sharp brains, observant and make the best out of any situation. Simply put, little girls with much potential. 
 The supporting cast was as interesting and fun to read as Sophronia herself, but among them are some who made a bigger impression than others. Such were Vieve (the girl-inventor who discarded her skirt for the comfort of loose pants), Soap (who apparently is the only person who is not a Caucasian), professor Braithwope (a charming gentleman vampire) and Captain Niall (a top-hat wearing werewolf who walks around naked under his overcoat). Pretty cute bunch, aren't they? Especially the werewolf. Har-har-har! 
 The idea of leaving the Headmistress in the dark is very unique in my opinion. She is the only one who has no idea her own academy trains spies and assassins under the disguise of being a finishing school. The teachers, however, are awesome - besides the vampire and captain Niall, Lady Linette is often giving Sophronia advice how to act when confronted with accusations, true or false, how to put the blame onto someone else without being suspected yourself and how to make others do whatever you want them to using only your charm. There are also classes on self-defense and assassination taught by the only male teachers, which is kind of strange; like, real ladies shouldn't brandish a weapon in the open, but only when needed and where you wouldn't usually be seen. That's just like women shouldn't learn boxing because it isn't a lady's sport... 
 And last of all, how did Sophronia realize it was Mrs. Barnaclegoose who recommened her for the school when the only scene with her was at the very beginning when there was truffle in her hair all thanks to Sophronia playing in the dumbwaiter? I'd prefer it to have some more clues and hints to lead the reader to consider anything of the sort - you can't just drop this on me and expect me to be all like, what a great twist! Because it can't be a twist if there is nothing leading to it. 
 Another thing I found lacking was the prototype - the center of the whole story. I couldn't imagine how this small part looks like. Also, the device superior to the telegraph (which by the way wasn't received well enough for mass production) was poorly described. May I say it wasn't described at all - I only understood that it was "big and complicated", that really helps... 
 P.S. Forgot to mention that the dialogues are so cute, so English, so Victorian, so lovely...

First impressions: I was so excited to get back into this world, and it picks up almost immediately after we left off in Matched. I admit I had to take a minute to think back - now where were we? I think this is one of those series that is better read close together. 
 Lasting impressions: While I won't go so far as to say this was a disappointment, it did suffer a bit from middle book syndrome. We didn't learn a whole lot of new information about the Society, and a majority of the book revolves around Cassia trying to reunite with Ky. 
 Conflicting impressions: I was so invested in Cassia and Ky's relationship in the first book that having to spend so much time with them apart made the story lose a little magic. The chemistry that connected me to these characters was missing, so the book dragged for me. 
 Overall impressions: This was probably my most anticipated book of the year, so it's too bad that it turned out to be just okay for me. Good, not great. I loved Matched so much that it's not likely the sequel would have measured up, but this felt like an entirely different story. 
 Cassia spends most of the book trying to sneak her way to the Outer Provinces by pretending she's not a Citizen and joining work camps. Ky, meanwhile, is faced with the grim reality of being used as bait in an ongoing war with the people outside the Society. He makes a few friends and bolts with them into the surrounding canyons. 
 There is a bit of tension surrounding the blue pills and whether or not Cassia will survive and/or be reunited with Ky. She also tries to find out more about the Resistance and what kind of role she wants to play in it. Similarly, Ky must also determine whether being with Cassia is worth accepting a prominent position in the Resistance. 
 With just enough nuggets of new information to merit this sequel, there's still a lot left to discover in book three, out next year. I think it's worth a read for fans of the series, but would wait to read it until closer to the release of the conclusion book, so you can move straight into what will hopefully be the more exciting end of the story.

We pick up right after the ending of The Emperor's Blades and quickly dive into the looming troubles of the Empire. 
 The biggest problem with this book is that other people's plots in this book seems to lead the direction, not the characters. 
 Also there is this strange phenomenon that characters are too similar in a strange way. They are obviously different, but both main characters (Valyn and Kaden) seem to suffer from being too kind to innocents despite their backgrounds. (Think of Triste like Saliena for both of them) It's annoying. and also... they're very stupid. 50% into the book, I don't know if they've made one smart decision yet. All the decisions they make on their own inclination ends up being a really, really bad decision. 
  Letting the Ungar go (and then getting captured), trusting the Csestriim (basically trading his mentor for two enemies), the whole stupid pilgrim thing, holding a spear up in the middle of a lightning storm. Yeah. . 
 I feel like this world is a little too big for the characters, at this point. Unwieldy is how I might put it. Like Staveley is struggling to move all of the characters around the map, get them to certain places, and make things happen. Because we lose a lot of the character interest that I loved from the first book. I don't think Adare was that believable. Valyn (as a character) suffers a lot from this sequel, along with his flight - which honestly was one of main reasons why I liked book 1. 
 Another point of annoyance from me: I feel like Staveley deliberately adds in extra characters from the beginning just to kill them off. As if he needs extra bodies to kill, so gotta make sure you add them from the start. It makes for a weird feeling of a too-big cast in the beginning and a too-small cast at the end. Not to mention I seriously question if those deaths are meant for faux-realism-of-war purposes and are necessary, or if it's more for the shock factor that this character died. 
 But there are moments of brilliance. A lot of reveals that I really enjoyed. Also, every time Stavelely introduces new characters, there is some sort of "easy to like" quality about them - no matter the type of character (villain, old fart, Csestriim, etc). And the bit about the gods. Just wow. 
 2.5 rounded down. I'm sorry, it hovers between "it was okay" and "I liked it". And there were more problems than pluses - so rounded down. Regardless, I am still very much looking forward to the sequels. And Brian Staveley is on my authors-to-watch list for sure.

Teardrop had more that I disliked than more that I liked. By a pretty considerable margin. I'll start with the stuff I liked, because I think it's nicer to start with positives. Plus the list is shorter. 
 Good: 
 -The cover. I went crazy over that cover! Such gorgeous blues and pinks and I just love staring at it. Her dress is made out of water. How cool is that? And in the background you can just see some structures, like pillars....hint hint 
 -I liked the setting. Given that we're dealing with a girl that can start hurricanes with her tears, it only makes sense to put the setting in Louisiana where they happen so often. The descriptions of the places Eureka went were beautiful. I went to New Orleans earlier this year to visit a friend and I loved the atmosphere of the place: the humidity, the greenery, the fog that made everything seem so mysterious. It makes sense to me that a legend says the first vampires to get to America congregated in Louisiana. But that's getting off topic. 
 -I found it incredibly funny that it was in fact a woman's fault that the hurricanes happen. People bemoan how the hurricanes are always named after women, that it's sexist or something. I don't really know. But I cracked up when I realized that this book was essentially saying that yes, it was a woman who caused this disaster. 
 -Cat was a pretty good character. I liked her the best out of everyone in the book, and gave her serious brownie points for putting up with Eureka's moodiness and total disregard for anyone else's feelings. And for sticking by her when all that crazy stuff went down in the end. 
 -...I'll come back to this section. Maybe I'll think of some more later. 
 Bad: 
 -That name. Eureka. It's so....transparent. Clearly we're meant to know that Eureka is special and different than everyone else. She has a fancy name, so that must be the case. 
 -So much buildup and hardly any payoff. This book is something like 400 pages and the entire thing is Eureka doing mundane things while moping. She bails out on classes. She runs. She goes to therapy. She eats dinner. She thinks about her dead mom. She runs. She listens to Cat's babble. She pines after Ander. She pines after Brooks. Then some cool glowing stuff shows up! Yay! And then it's gone again for another 100 pages. And then a shield bubble! And then she doesn't investigate it because apparently it's more exciting to pine after boys than investigate awesome powers. Oh and feel guilty for stuff. 
 -The caricatures. I can't call them characters because they're not. They're cardboard cutouts. Eureka needed a wicked stepmother to make sure she was thoroughly miserable at home as well as school, so she got one. Who apparently does not say anything besides what a wicked stepmother would say. She's condescending and rude and just plain bitchy. She has no redeeming qualities; even her love for her children is bastardized into selfishness and single-mindedness. 
 Cat is the same. I liked her the best, but she was still a caricature. We're purposely told that she's a genius, and that she is in all these advanced classes and does smart things because she's smart. And then the entire book, LITERALLY THE ENTIRE BOOK, she talks about boys. About hunting them. About going on a diet because she's afraid one will think she's fat. About reading the newspapers so she can impress college boys. Wearing a lycra dress and heels to a track practice on the fucking football field. She's so one-dimensional I couldn't understand how Eureka had supposedly been best friends with her, because Poor Eureka is so moody and different and not into normal things anymore and Boy Crazy Cat is so flamboyantly boy-crazy. It was inane. 
 Eureka's dad. Do we need a weak, pliable man to follow wicked stepmother's bidding? Yes we do! And we got one! All he does is bow his head and make fancy popcorn and pretend he follows what Wicked Stepmother says and we have a winner. No personality. No traits of any kind. Just a puppy to follow Wicked Stepmother around and provide a double assault on Poor Eureka. Poor thing. Because really, what other kind of person would force her to go to therapy and then force her to pay for it? Makes perfect sense. 
 Maya. Literally, so stupid. She had no point to the book except to provide the Bitchy Bully. And she plays her part so well. She does nothing except drape herself all over Sexy Brooks and sneer at Poor Eureka and make comments. Do we need a Bitchy Bully to make sure Eureka is miserable at school as well as at home? We got one! Eureka is not safe anywhere, and this is made very obvious through miss Maya's garish attempts at putting herself between Poor Eureka and Sexy Brooks. Because, you know, everyone's first reaction to someone back from trauma is to harass that person even more. 
 Now let me stop here for a moment. 
 I realize that my experiences in high school are way different than what others went through. I realize that bullying happens. I was lucky enough to go to a school where this wasn't too much of an issue. There was some trash-talking, but nothing as cruel and as hurtful as what Brooks and Maya say.  They all play a game of "Never Ever". Where you have to say thing you've never done ("never have I ever...") and then if others have done what you haven't they're supposed to drink. In the book it's a bit different, but the basic idea is the same. Maya chooses to say "never have I ever been in a car accident" when she knows that's how Eureka's mother died. And Brooks follows that with "never have I ever attempted suicide".  This pissed me off so badly I had to put the book down and walk away from it for a while. I know people can be cruel. But I can't wrap my head around the fact that the author needed a Bitchy Bully so badly to warrant something so incredibly cruel. To be so humiliating, and mean and horrible. And it pissed me off even more that no one did anything about it. I was a bully TO the bullies. If you were mean to someone and I saw, I was mean to you. There was a kid who tried to molest my friend in front of a crowd of his friends and I punched him. Gave him a nice swollen face for a while. And I couldn't believe that everyone just sat there and watched Eureka have to deal with that kind of hurtful bullying. That's bullshit. NO ONE should have to put up with that kind of shit and I was infuriated that it was used to further the plot. Incredible. 
 Okay, done with that. Point is, all caricatures, no characters. 
 -Ander. And Eureka's fascination with him. Let me ask you this: If a guy rear-ended you, then got out of the car and put your tear into his own eyeball, would you find that sexy? How about when you go to the police station to report him, he's standing outside watching you? How about showing up on your doorstep (even though you never told him where you lived) and making vague threats about staying away from someone? How about following you miles and miles out in a rural area where there's no other people and making more vague threats? Is this really considered romantic? Why yes, it is, actually. I'm so sick of YA books teaching girls that as long as a guy is Drop Dead Gorgeous he can be as creepy and possessive and stalkerish as he wants. Because he's sexy, so it's okay. 
 It's not okay. 
 The entire book is spent with Ander doing the creepyish shit and Eureka going "I want to shove him because he said something mean, but if I try to do that I know I'll embrace him instead". I think it was like 4 or 5 times that she wanted to run away from him--but no, she didn't, she wanted to run to him. Because you know, he's Drop Dead Gorgeous with his halo of blond hair so it's okay for him to follow you around and lie to you about everything. Because as long as he's gorgeous all you'll want to do is run into his arms. Oh, and then when creepy stalker who's made vague threats decides to announce his undying love and devotion to you, you just kiss him. Because that's what you do with stalkers, didn't you know? 
 -I dislike that the thing that makes Eureka special is crying. Now I'm going to stop here for a minute and bring up Harry Potter. Which I love. Wanna know why? It has its faults, but what it doesn't have is weak female characters who do nothing but mope (emo Harry had all of book 5, but we'll overlook that for now). Every single strong character in that series was strong because of their own talent and hardwork. Not for something so inane as crying. But Eureka can save the world! Or destroy it! By crying! Because that makes for an awesome heroine, doesn't it? One that springs into action and can actually fight her foes? Not a passive one who just stands there and cries? Wait... 
 All that being said. Beautiful cover. I like Atlantis stories. I like Cat. and I like the setting. Oh, I also forgot to mention that as someone who ran cross country in high school, I love that my sport was represented in a book. Even if I didn't much care for the character.

The Ocean At the End of the Lane was the first Neil Gaiman book that I've ever picked up. Yea, I know, I know... 
 Anyways, I heard so many ah-mazing things about this book especially about it being an awesome fantasy and when my local bookstore finally had it in, that's when I saw an opportunity to finally pick up a copy :D And here we are... 
 The Ocean at the End of the Lane begins with the unnamed protagonist returning to his hometown for a funeral, only to find himself drawn back to a place where he used to hang out at as a child. Soon, all of his memories from a significant part of his childhood came flooding back. I found the plot and the overall world development really fascinating, although there were certain parts that had somewhat confused me and had to read it over twice. Nevertheless, it certainly was a world that I've never seen before and it was quite impressive. 
 I found it intriguing how the main protagonist was ... well, nameless. It was ah-mazing how the book flew by without the mention of a name! Haha! I found Lettie and her family to be quite the interesting bunch. They certainly are different than your average human family- if human is what they are. Focusing more on Lettie, I enjoyed reading about her. I thought that she was such a fun character. In terms of character development, no character had gone through that much change than the main character himself. He goes through quite the adventure with so many complex fantasy aspects at such a young age. And though he may not have fully understood them all, he certainly handled it pretty well. I would've been freaking out the whole time if I had went through what he did haha! 
 Oh and his writing! Neil Gaiman is such an ah-mazing writer! His words pulls you into his world and keeps you there! I say this because I was pretty busy with some Life stuff so there were some days when I couldn't pick this book up to read. It's a pretty short book too! The copy I had only had about 170+ pages. I could've finished this in one sitting if I wasn't so busy at the time. But anyway, when I did have the chance to finally sit down to read, I felt like I had never left. His words totally pulled me in just like that!!! 
 Overall, I could now see why people have been raving about this book. It's a really, really good book!!! Though the world building was a bit confusing for me at times, The Ocean at the End of the Lane is an overall fantastic read and would be enjoyed by everyone, especially by fantasy lovers!!! I definitely recommend this book for the summer when you do have a sudden craving for something fantasy :D

 Wow. Some Boys really caught me by surprise. I picked it up on Netgalley because it sounded good, but I never had very high expectations. I didn't know the author and I didn't know if it would click with me and all that jazz. You get it, right? But then I read it and it just blew me away! 
 Some Boys is about Grace. About a month ago, she accused the town's golden boy, Zac, of raping her and nobody believed her. Since then they all bully her, calling her names. Everyone hates her and even her parents don't seem to believe her. When her supposed best friend gets her in trouble, Grace is stuck cleaning lockers during spring break with Ian, Zac's best friend. But Ian doesn't call her a slut or a liar. Ian is nice to her. Spending the days together cleaning lockers, they start to bond, but it's not that easy when everything and everyone seems to be against them. Against her. 
 Some Boys is very emotional and tough to read at times. It deals with a hard topic and the fact that this story is so realistic, is probably what makes it so sad in the first place. But I loved it and I was so invested in it, I couldn't put it down. I read it in one sitting, engrossed in Grace's story. I felt so bad for her and I just wanted to hug her and tell her everything'll be alright. Grace is so brave and so strong. If I were her, I'd be a sobby mess in the corner of my room. But she keeps her head up high, putting on her brave face. She doesn't want anyone to see how broken she is inside. I'm glad she didn't run, I'm glad she fought back. 
 On the other side you have Ian. We get to know him through the alternating POV's between him and Grace. I thought I'd hate him, but I didn't. I understood his side of things too. Someone called his best friend a rapist and honestly, it would be hard to believe for me too if I were him. But he likes Grace, a lot and eventually he saw what was really going on and he did the right thing in the end and that's all that matters for me. I hated Zac, Miranda and Lindsay. And a lot of the other characters too. They were mean and pathetic. I loved Grace's family and Ian's too. 
 The romance was perfect for this story. It built up nice and slow and I liked that. They both had stuff to get through and if the romance had been rushed it would've ruined the story, but it wasn't. It was perfectly paced and in the end I do think they saved each other. I rooted for them all the way. Still, I was always on Grace's side. When Ian was acting stupid, I was angry. But he always redeemed himself after being an ass, so I still loved him. 
 Some boys was surprisingly emotional and gave me tears in my eyes a lot. It's a heartfelt, deep and powerful story with a romance that made my heart melt in the end. I do recommend this book to everyone who loves contemporary books a la Katie McGarry or Colleen Hoover. I will be watching this author closely from now on.

Sanderson always delivers. Rithmatist is another gem, filled with quirky yet realistic characters, a healthy dose of humor, a nice helping of myster, and some truly awesome action. Not the same as his epic fantasy, but that in no way works against him with this YA book. 
 In a lot of ways it feels like Sanderson took the idea behind Harry Potter, who was always a reactionary character, which was always my biggest qualm with the series and the character, and turned him into a truly active character and competent character who drives the story along rather than the other way around. (Please don't take the Harry Potter reference to mean that this is in some way a Harry Potter clone.) The magic system alone, the fact that it has rules yet can be understood, puts the book ahead of most other YA out there right now, where the magic just seems tagged on to sell more books. 
 Melody Muns is my new favorite person. 
 I really want to give this book 5 stars because I enjoyed every page and I am very much looking forward to the sequel, but there is one thing Sanderson did that made me feel... cheated. Don't worry, no spoilers. Granted, this one thing has set up something for the sequel to have potential to be amazing, but I'll hold back that final star until I have turned the last page of Rithmatist 2.
The characters, although enticing, the slurs left me uncomfortable and the ending seemed unexpected but not entirely bad. Just didn't grab me as much as the others.

Agnieszka is a challenging daughter to her villager parents. Her father is the woodcutter. She is constantly tearing her clothes, and messing them up and she also strays too far into the woods that surround the village. The woods are not safe, and they seem to infect animals and people with a kind of madness that sometimes literally transforms them, and not in a good way. It has been this way for so long that the villagers are used to it. They live in a war zone and it seems the wood is winning lately. 
 The wood took over an entire village recently; just up the road. 
 Twenty years ago, the queen ran into it - allegedly holding the hand of her lover, a prince from the rival kingdom - and she never came back. Both countries are still at war but currently have an uneasy truce. Her sons are now adults and heroes to the common people, and the king still rules alone. 
 But when the wood attacks the village, it is the Dragon that they call. 
 He always comes, and he always helps, but he is only one man. 
 And the wood is winning. 
 *** 
 I saw a promo for this book a long time ago and the first paragraph just grabbed me. Recently it was half price on book depository and I lashed out and got the hardback. (being thrifty, I usually wait for the paperback edition.) 
 "Our Dragon doesn't eat the girls he takes, no matter what stories they tell outside our valley. We hear them sometimes, from travelers passing through. They talk as though we were doing human sacrifice, and he were a real dragon. Of course that's not true: he may be a wizard and immortal, but he's still a man, and our fathers would band together and kill him if he wanted to eat one of us every ten years. He protects us against the Wood, and we're grateful, but not that grateful." 
 The person that everyone thinks the Dragon will take is Agnieszka's best friend, Kasia. She is so pretty and accomplished that her parents have raised her sure in the assumption that it will be her that is the chosen one. But he chooses Agnieszka when she shows an unexpected magic ability. 
 Kasia tells her that she has seen a tree reach for her that's why she is so clumsy, but she didn't say anything at the time. Agnieszka always found food in the wood, as if the forest gave it to her, or conjured it for her. 
 The dragon looks like a young man but has to be at least 150 years old. He lives in a massive castle, all alone and he has forgotten how to train a person, or how to comfort a homesick girl. Especially one who was ill prepared to be chosen. He's traditional, rigid, happy with order and things in their proper place, and Agnieszka is chaos incarnate in his well-ordered world. 
 She messes up constantly and he always shouts at her. 
 For Agnieszka certain books in the library clamour to be read and they are often the works of witch women rather than the formal schooling of the men. She finds a tiny notebook that belonged to baba yaga. The Dragon tells her the books are useless. She tries to explain to the Dragon that he does it wrong. It's as if you walk in the forest and you need to change your path if there is a fallen tree; but the Dragon finds it hard to use her green, living, and changing magic. 
 I thought this idea of women's magic was fantastic. 
 Within months of her arrival at the castle, there is an incident and the Dragon has to leave. That night, she sees the warning lights go up in her village. She raids his potion cupboard and goes to help, rationalizing that she is better than nothing. 
 Somehow she gets through the attack. He grouses at her that she has wasted expensive potions. 
 But days later her friend Kasia is taken by some walkers (a kind of praying mantis like wood creature). She and the Dragon rescue Kasia and drag her out of the heart tree that holds her, but she is forever changed by it, and the two magic wielders working together have thrown an almighty stone into the magic pond and the ripples reach everywhere. 
 Next, princes and political emissaries are knocking at their door. 
  
 The Dragon is wonderful. He seals letters with his name and it smokes a little and looks somehow burnt. He is incredibly powerful and really dangerous. I think it would be a huge issue to live an extended or immortal life; to constantly outlive your children and grandchildren, and to keep losing the ones you love. He is frightened of this. He doesn't want to put down roots, as Agnieszka tells him at one stage. 
 There are a dozen ways that the title fits the contents - (I am so jealous of this, as I am crap at titles) our girl is uprooted, the wood moves, the Dragon won't put down roots, and so on... 
 Agnieszka follows her gut, even when she is in the center of the city and in a maelstrom of politics and crafty allegiances she doesn't understand. 
 There is a prince charming character, but he really isn't - he brags about killing a day old hydra, he uses people, his ego is worth more than the lives of his men, and he tries to rape Agnieszka in her servant room at the castle. She magically changed her clothes to heavy brocade corsets to deny him access, and then brained him with a tray. The Dragon just growls, "If you don't want a man dead, don't bludgeon him over the head repeatedly." But he helps her patch him up and wipes part of the prince's memory to protect her. 
 This is why I love the main character - she thinks outside of the box. 
 And the Dragon grizzles and grumps, and then helps her do it. 
 When they do magic together the whole is more than the sum of the parts, and they both know it. 
  
 All the women in the book are well written. Kasia is a true friend and deals with her new life remarkably well until she finds a place of her own. There is an ancient magic female blacksmith of color, who makes extraordinary weapons. The queen is terrifying and the wood? It'll give you nightmares.

This was an interesting "love" story. Not your typical romance at all. This was filled with very interesting characters. Reggie is a girl with a tragic past that sent her spiraling into Depression. She survives with hate and meanness to keep people away. Unfortunately for her, Snake thrives on her hate-filled words. He too suffers from Depression, and perhaps the two unlikely friends can learn to feel happiness again together. Bring in Carla, Snake's pregnant ex-girlfriend and Reggie's longtime "enemy" and this story makes for some interesting interactions. The three develop a rapport of sorts that leaves all of them a little bit better. Overall, I really enjoyed watching these characters grow and find themselves with each other, albeit reluctantly at times. Reggie starts out so messed up and by the end there appears to be hope for her after all. This was an interesting look at the way depression affects not only people themselves, but those around them. These characters were a bit refreshing. They were dealing with huge issues that turned their lives upside down with no end in sight. Even through Reggie's negativity and hate, there was a light at the end of the tunnel. Friendship may not be what she wanted or expected, but she couldn't avoid it and it was exactly what she really needed. This book was different, but I enjoyed it.

Wow! This book has everything in it! Romance, suspence, action and adventure and MYTHOLOGY! 
 The story is told by Nikki, who you learn right away made a devastatingly bad choice. She choose the easy way out, and went to the Everneath so she didn't have to feel pain any longer. Now she has Returned to the Surface for only 6 months before the Tunnells come to take her away forever to feed off her energy. 
 This story was unlike anything I had ever read before. I love mythology, but this is a very unique twist on the story of Hades and Persephone. 
 Characters: at first it was hard for me to like Nikki. She seemed young and naive and chose to give up her entire life and those who loved her all because her boyfriend hurt her feelings... ButI really grew to love Nikki as she learned from her mistakes and realized that her love for Jack was worth more than anything else. 
 Jack was AMAZING! He waited for her everyday of the entire 6 months (on the surface it was 6 months, in the Everneath she was gone for 100 years!!) while she was gone, hoping she would return to him. 
 And Cole... well I don't know how I feel about him. He is power hungry and has no problem feeding off humans so that he can stay immortal. AND wants Nikki to be his Queen so they can rule the Everneath. But for a while I kinda believed he loved Nikki, I just don't know. 
 Plot: Like I said earlier, this story had it all! At first it was kinda confusing, as the author switches back and forth between the time leading up to when she left, and the present time, leading up to when the Tunnels return. But after a while, I really enjoyed that she did it that way. 
 Romance: WAS PERFECT! I already said how amazing Jack and Nikki both are, so it was obvious that their romance was good as well. They had been friends for years before they decided to be together. It wasn't too fast, nothing was unbelievable, everything was perfect. 
 Overall, this book was EVERYTHING I expected and I cannot wait to read Everbound, the second book!

I was really pleasantly surprised by how much I liked Uprooted. Fans of Robin McKinley's core works like Sunshine and The Blue Sword will likely enjoy this as well. Novik reigns in the traditional romance and puts all the spark and interest into her plot and platonic character relationships; her female friendships and interactions remain my favourites in the fantasy genre. Even in male-dominated series like Temeraire, Novik has more depth and complexity between her female characters than many writers are able to manage with main male characters, and this knack is very evident in Uprooted. 
 I feel like some sections may have been over- or hastily edited (there are a scattering of callbacks to things that were evidently once in the text but later cut out) but the resulting plot is still tight so I'm happy to give it five stars.

Hmm. I think the gushing reviews I've read of this are mostly a result of people being enamored with the Gillian Flynn brand. Entertaining? Sure. Dark? Sure. Interesting characters? One at least. Complex? Debatable.

What I was expecting, based on the title and cover art: A nice retelling of a Russian folk tale, maybe with a bear and a nightingale. Like Golidilocks. 
 What I was not expecting: zombie vampires. 
 Also Death, a cruel Russian Jack Frost, and the Devil all messed up with crazy feminist witch-women and a power-hungry village priest who also just really likes to paint. 
 This book is intense. 
 Katherine Arden creates the most wonderful, complex, and moving Death character since Pratchett, and I would love to see more of him. Her other characters are also vivid and three-dimensional, with flaws and powerful hidden motivations, and they move the story. But Death, Morozko, is so ... enchantingly human, but better. 
 Now my one complaint about the read is that things don't really get moving until halfway or more through the book. The first half, while well-written and full of great characters, focuses more on rural life in 16th c (?) Russia and palace intrigue. It didn't always keep my attention and it took me several days to read that part. If that's you, too, keep reading - I hit the right section and finished the whole thing in one night, with every light in the house turned on because I was home alone and damn, this book gets creepy. 
 Slow start aside, this is one of the better books I've read all year, and there's very strong competition. Unique, beautiful, strong. There are characters like Vasha who are never going to leave my mind. The descriptions and setting were chilling even to this Minnesotan. It made me want to sleep on an oven and talk to little brownies that live in the corners. Fantastic.

I would like to start off the review with how I read the first three books of the series (though I should say trilogy, because that is what is originally was) awhile ago, and my mind is quite fuzzy on all the details. I do not really have an intention to re-read them anytime soon, as they were mostly okay for me. I know I liked the second novel out of the three best, and the third one just sorted dragged on for me. However, I own all three books, and as she one came out to continue the series, I thought I should keep going. 
 I LOVED THIS BOOK. The male lead is just so dreamy. Jonah is a survivor of the Thorn Hill Massacre, and as all survivors are, he has an after effect. Each survivor has a unique one, and Jonah's is that his touch can kill people. It is a little fuzzy, but it appears that touch by hands or lips are a definite kill, but sometimes I am pretty sure that other bare skin contact was made, such as someone touching the back of his neck in a hug, and there was no death from that. Originally it seemed that all types of direct-skin contact are deadly, but maybe that isn't quite right. I wish this part was a little clearer. Anyway, like most survivors of the Thorn Hill massacre, he goes to school (most of the survivors are children) at The Anchorage, a sanctuary for survivors of the massacre created by an adult survivor, Gabriel. Jonah also works as a nightshade for Gabriel which means killing the shades-- the dead spirits of the massacre can take over a dead body and inhabit it. The body still rots though, so the shade must kill a new target and live in that one until the cycle starts again. Jonah is very skilled as a nightshade, even if his deadly touch doesn't work against already dead creatures. 
 Emma comes into the story after her grandfather dies and she must move to live with her father whom she just found out existed. From her father Emma finds out she is a sorcerer like her parents were. He also explains how the mother died in the Thorn Hill massacre, but how she survived since she was home with dad for Christmas. It seems as though Emma's father may have more information on Thorn Hill which leads to Emma and Jonah crossing paths. 
 Both Emma and Jonah are great. Emma is a very strong female lead. She likes the truth and just goes straight for everything, no hesitation. Jonah is just very dreamy, and you get to see from both characters points of view, so from Emma's view Jonah may seem aloof but Jonah can't share his deadly secret. The side characters of Jonah's friends from The Anchorage aren't as dynamic, but they aren't terrible either. 
 One slight other problem I have with this book is the amount of music loving people. The anchorage is sorta disguised as a music school due to Gabriel's work in the music industry. Gabriel is actually so famous in the music industry he is on a Rolling Stones cover, for example. Then all of Jonah's friends play in the band. Jonah joins this said band, as does Emma.  Jonah writes songs for this band with his brother, Kenzie, also a Thorn Hill survivor. Emma's grandfather made guitars for a living, and Emma learned from him, so she loves to make guitars and she can also play them well. Emma and Jonah can also sing and they will sing for the band  Emma's dad plays as a bassist in a band and that is his actual profession. I don't know, for me, as someone who doesn't know many people who play musical instruments or sing or play in a band, it just seems like a lot of music people. It is a part of the plot it many ways, but just.... so much music..... 
 Aside from my confusion about Jonah's ability and the overabundance of musically inclined people, I am really glad I picked up this book, even if I wasn't looking that forward to it. Maybe the author really improved herself over her last set of books, I don't know, but 5 stars.

 I really really (really) loved this book! I wanted so much to give it 5 stars and I hope very much to be able to give book 2 that honour. I'll go into the missing star later, first, why I loved it. 
 This book has such an interesting atmosphere. It is not your typical ya/na book with relatively 'normal' characters with conventional tastes, lifestyle etc. Sunshine is about a group of pretty alternative people and it makes it so much fun to read about them. I think maybe because they sound like people I knew at 16/17/18 so I relate to them. It's great to be reading about characters with Magenta hair and tattoos and band t-shirts, who have lots of fun and create music together. I think also I particularly found the suffering that Sophie went through very realistically portrayed. The author went into a great amount of detail and took a long time to explore Sophies mental state. It was a fantastic example of demonstration, of show rather than tell. The way the book was written meant I felt her physical pain, I felt when she was anxious, when she felt sick, her nerves when people touched her, her love/anguish with her mother. I felt it all. 
 Sophie is such a unique, delicate, beautiful, troubled individual. Her voice was authentic, which made it even more heart breaking. 
 I was also pretty impressed with the general cast of characters. They weren't at all 2 dimensional, each had individual characteristics and we learned about them in the right way through witnessing interactions rather than that boring thing that authors sometimes do of just having the main character 'tell us' what they think of their friends/relatives. 
 As for the plot and pacing in the book I can see where a few people have criticised the twilight similarities. I get what they're saying. However, any similarity is merely on the surface. If you get down to the essentials of what happens in this book it is mostly about a very broken girl who has had a lot happen to her and a lot to deal with. It's about her finding a healthy way to cope and about her learning to trust and to love. That's not what's twilight is about. So there are vampires in it. Well that is actually kind of weird I have to admit. It almost doesn't seem necessary as the story is so powerful without it. On the other hand, I love pnr so I'm game for a good vampire tale. I do wish however that the plot isn't spelled out so much in the blurb. Having the truthes reveal themselves naturally would have had real impact I think. The pace was kind of slow but anything else would have undermined the seriousness of the mental health issues involved. 
 Because this is a pnr I feel I must talk about the world building. I didn't miss it much because I was so involved and invested in Sophie's growth and the romance, but when we got stuck into the action it did start to play on my mind that I didn't really understand who/what the vampires in this world were. I'll forgive it because it sits right with the fact that Sophie isn't quite part of the world yet. I am pretty intrigued about where the story is going, I feel that Sophie isn't all she seems to be. There are some threads in this story that have my brain churning, I'll be reading book 2 no doubt. 
 Now, the romance. It was so brave and entirely appropriate that the author took her time with this. I have read a lot of books where the main character has experienced similar things to Sophie but never have I read a more authentic account of the effects on mental health. Sophie could barely allow herself to think about moving on, she had very unhealthy coping mechanisms, and she had intense physical reactions to invasion of personal space. So the romance was suitably slow and painful and careful. It was kind of beautiful to see it evolve. Myles was a complete sweetheart. I need to know him lot better to love him as there is too much hidden and at arms length at the moment, but he treats her so delicately and with such love it is just beautiful. Oh god did I cry! When she said she loved him, oh that really got me, I'm getting emotional just thinking about it  
 The writing style and quality is rather exceptional I have to say. This is because what it did was create Sophie, create the atmosphere. It was her voice so every word told us something about who she is. I loved the wit, the honesty, the blase and sarcastic attitude she spoke/thought with. The streams of consciousness were insightful but not over lengthy, letting action and interactions drive the story. There a few little things that together brought me to come down to 4 stars though and partly it was the quality of the product. I had a review copy so I don't mean grammar etc as you I appreciate that I didn't read the final edit. But there were a few times where I felt there were abrupt endings or changes in scenes that completely threw me. I would stop and have to reread to process the change. I just had the sense that the author needs to work on flow of prose a little more, that an editor would be beneficial in sharpening up a few scenes/sections and really making this shine as much as it deserves to. 
 I do believe this author and this series has a future! It was this, some world building gaps and not being yet in love with Myles that brought me down a star. But you know, it's a strange thing, but there are some 4* books that I actually like more than 5* books. I wanted this to be 5 stars, I did love it, the atmosphere particularly.

This is a teen novel with timely and relevant content. The novel focuses on issues such as corporate power, consumerism, information technology, data mining, and environmental decay, with a sometimes sardonic, sometimes somber tone. I listened to this as an audio book and I think that really added to the experience. The "feed" that was in the kids' heads also blared in ours. We heard little snippets of news and commercials and other stuff that the kids were bombarded with. I thought this story was a neat concept, the NextGen version of being plugged in. Instead of Google Goggles or watches, these kids have the feeds installed in their heads before they even become school-age. 
 It didn't have an amazing story to go with the concept but by having an understated plot, readers have time to consider the implications of giving corporations too much control/access and the impact that technology can have on our lives. The plot is typical teenager's fighting boredom by taking a trip to the moon (which equates to our going out for pizza on the easy scale) and then having their feeds hacked which "destroys" their lives for a while. Their school is owned by corporations and they are not educated to think for themselves. Personally, they also have a difficult time with describing their world or feelings and dealing with them. 
 Titus is the main character and he meets Violet, a girl who had the feed installed much later in life (school-age instead of infant,) and she has major issues with the device after their feeds are hacked and they end up in the hospital unplugged and confused while they wait for the repair. Their feeds are fixed and they are sent on their way. Violet tells Titus that her feed isn't completely fixed and has been severely malfunctioning, and she may even die, having had the feed installed later in life (and so with greater accompanying risk). Due to her deteriorating feed, various parts of Violet's body are shutting down.

 I kind of take offense with the people who hated this book because it was too convincingly like it was written by a fifteen-year-old boy...I mean, sure he said "like" too much and kind of rambled, but it created a pretty distinctive style and I for one was impressed with how different it was from McKinley's fairy-tale-centric stories...I honestly had to check the cover a couple of times to make sure it wasn't secretly a DWJ book. It's obvious that this "immature" writing was a conscious decision, given McKinley's other books, and not just an attempt to disguise horrible writing (*cough* Hatchet *cough*), so I say it was well done. 
 Still, not her best. Kind of disappointing, actually.
Not bad at all. Not as funny as many Julia Quinn books. And I do like the humor. But not bad.

Elena is perfectly fine living her utterly normal life with her caring and loving boyfriend Phillip. If you'll excuse her enormous appetite, strangely powerful strength, and her night running times in which she turns into a werewolf. Yeah, Elena is the only living female werewolf in the world. But when a murder goes down back in her old werewolf pack home, she's called back to figure out what's going on. Her old life is calling to keep her home and she's not willing to stay. 
 A really quick read because I was craving PNR and werewolves. Yep. 
 I think it's a stereotypical PNR. It's about a "strong" and special girl trying to choose between two guys. A murder mystery and plot against her life. I think it's a little bit eye rolling sometimes (e.g. when she fucks her old flame even as she wants to go back to her human life. Like, are you serious?) But overall, it was a fast paced read. Sometimes i think the murder plot was more of a side plot for the romance rather than the other way though. Which is... kinda dumb. 
 But really, they didn't really flesh out the villains or motives. It was really just a romance story of Elena getting back together with Clay with a backdrop of a murder mystery. The ending of how they solved the entire premise/problem was so anti-climactic I literally face-palmed. You had this much trouble for two hundred some pages and all it takes is that? Just wow. No. Regardless, felt super sorry for Phillip. 
 It's a two star sort of book. I don't really like Elena as a character. She isn't really anything. Sure, she's "special" and the only female werewolf in the world and ultra desirable, and the only girl in the midst of a mouthwatering harem of buff werewolves. And oh yeah, trying to be a strong, independent woman who don't need no pack. Ha. But what else is she? Not much. She doesn't really change throughout the book, she doesn't really learn anything (except that she's in love with Clay). 
 Meh. Two stars. Maybe even 1.5 to be honest.
