3.5. I probably would give it 4 stars if I hadn't read The Lost Prince first. I really enjoyed it, but since I knew ultimately what is going to happen by the end of the series, I had a hard time getting wrapped up in the suspense. I really wish I didn't know what was going to become of all the characters. Not knowing who would live or die, who would fall in love, what would happen and what would or wouldn't work out would make this series so enjoyable. I read the Lost Prince because it is the start of a new series, but all the back story--which is referenced repeatedly throughout that book--takes place in this (Iron Fey) series. I was curious about the details of that back story. It is a lot more difficult to enjoy the story and character progression knowing how it ends. I am definitely not one of those people who likes/prefers to know how a book ends before I start it. That said, I enjoyed getting to know Meghan and meeting Puck and Ash for the first time. Even though I knew what was going to happen to Ethan, I still enjoyed the story of it happening. I absolutely plan on reading the rest of the Iron Fey series and will do it before I read the Iron Traitor.  I really wish I could have met Ash and Puck without knowing that Meghan and Ash end up married. I liked Ash's character, but I'm curious what I would have thought of him had I not known the two would fall in love and end up together. I just kept waiting for their first romantic moment. Would I not have seen it coming? Would I be anxious about what would happen next? I know from the description of the next book that Ash disappears on her, but obviously he will come back. I wish I didn't know the fate of their relationship because I would be able to enjoy the development of it a lot more. It's my fault for reading book 5 first. I shouldn't have listened when told I didn't need to read the first 4. .

I wanted to like this book more than I actually did and I'm a little bit torn about it. Sweetbitter follows the story of 22-year-old Tess, who moves to New York City without a plan. She finds herself training and learning about food, wine and drugs at an upscale restaurant in Union Square. 
 The writing about food and wine is fantastically sensual, as if once can taste the food and feel the wine. It made me want to cook, or to go out for a fancy mean I can't afford. I just found the characters to be rather superficial. While we watch Tess blossom from know-nothing new girl to seasoned (and maybe a bit crazy) waitress, I found that I still didn't truly understand her motivations, or those of the people she worked with.

Lots of folks love this dystopian tale of a future totalitarian state. I love it for the ideas it presents, of the 'shadow children' who stand in for all those in society who are relegated to the margins, unable to fully participate in society. 
 I do think it takes too long to get going, and in the first third not enough happens. So while it isn't a complicated book, I've noticed some reluctant readers struggling to stay with it. I also notice that I'm not particularly excited to read the rest, even though some readers adore the series.

I have read the first book (Crank #1) and solely stated that it didn't catch my heart a bit but I was forced by my best friend to read it. Just as I expected, it still didn't catch my heart and mind. lol :)

Spooky read for October. Cool concept - end of the world occurs when people see...something...they go violently insane. Those that are left learn not to go outside without blindfolds. You can tell it's first time author,since character sketches are bit thin and the writing is a bit tortured in places. However, there are some pretty vivid, harrowing set pieces, making this a worthwhile read for post-apocalypse buffs. IAs one of my October spooky reads I found it enjoyable.

This was the best-touching book ever yet. I was moved and it bought me realization that how life can be a struggle. 
 It carries all sorts of emotions. This is the first book that has made me truly reflect.

Probably 2.5 stars. A stranger, Amelia Anne, turns up dead on the side of the road the morning after graduation. The small town residents turn to the gossip mill whenever any theory about who she is, how she died, or who killed her comes to light. I liked how the small town gossip chain is depicted. It shows exactly how lynch mobs begin. It also shows how a story, whether true or false, can sway public opinion. I liked the character of James, a local boy with basically no future, trying to hold on to the last summer with his girlfriend before she leaves town forever to move onto bigger and better things. Other than that I didn't particularly like it. What probably bothered me most was the constant shifting of perspective. At least when it was told from Amelia's point of view, it was obvious. At other times it was told in first person from Becca's POV. Then in the middle of the chapter it would jump to third person and/or jump time periods. All of a sudden we were experiencing a memory or event from a few years in the past without any obvious lead in. I could follow it, but at times it would take me a minute to realize it was the past and then it would jump back to the present in the same paragraph. Then, change POV again. As far as murder mysteries go, it was pretty thin. I realize the story was supposed to be about Becca trying to come to grips with the reality of the outside world and truly being ready to move one, with the murder as the catalyst to her uncertainty. Amelia's murder was almost a side story as we saw how the town was affected by the event. Either way, the two main suspects were pretty clear from the beginning in my mind,  and then the author went and made them both involved/responsible in some way. At times I thought it had to be Luke and at other times I was sure it was James. Then it ended up being both of them. Lame.

An average read. There were some really fun possibilities, espcially in the moments it touched on The Handmaid's Tale territory and some serious tensions over religion. Morality is on stage here, and pleasantly there aren't any easy answers. It is a fairly simple idea: a boy and girl seem to be heading towards matrimony on their long deep-space voyage when something dramatic separates them. Loads of possibilities. But none of it worked to build an effective whole. The first act comes of implausibly. I didn't feel Waverly's story intensely - and it should be affecting - as Ryan has a preference for telling and not showing. When Kerian's narrative returns after a long hiatus, it feels incomplete and too short compared to the many pages devoted to Waverly's saga. The main characters are thin, their motivations too simple, while there minor characters sprout up without much explanation. 
 Many sci-fi authors have worked over similar subjects. Ryan may be a good place for readers ready to make the leap from twee-YA to something speculative, and those curious about faith may like the comfortable, non-specific-Christian story element. But there isn't enough here to recommend it to a wide audience. The ending is unsatisfying on its own, but I'm not curious about the sequel.

 A wonderful reimaging of Kiplings "The Jungle Book," relocating the setting to an ancient English cemetery. After Bod's parents are killed, he is taken in by the denizens of the graveyard and given the "freedom of the graveyard" -- which means that he can go anywhere, while he is inside the cemetery, even to the extent of passing through the walls of the crypts or fading into the shadows when humans are nearby. 
 As he grows older, Bod learns about the others in the graveyard, has close encounters with ghouls and eventually comes into contact with humans. One girl, in particular, befriends him. But he also learns that the man who killed his parents is still hunting for Bod and Bod ultimately has to rely upon the skills he learned in the cemetery to save himself and his friend. 
 The book was highly entertaining, with wonderful characters and Neil Gaiman infuses the story with an eerie sense of the macabre -- but nothing that young people would find disturbing. I read ghost stories like this when I was seven or eight years old and I loved them. 
 If I have one complaint, it's that Bod is eventually turned out of the cemetery to go live with his "kind." This is the way "The Jungle Book" ends, so this book rightly ends the same way, but it bugged me in Kipling and it bugs me in this. It's not like children never go back to visit their parents, after all, even when grown. I think it would be delightful to picture Bod returning to the cemetery for the holidays!

This is an excellent book! I loved every word! To set the scene imagine, if you will, that you are with your boyfriend and modeling crew flying to location for a photo shoot. It's something you have done millions of times. 
 You're not worried about the travel, the shoot, or where you are staying...it's all been arranged by your people. Instead, you are flying high above the Alaskan wilderness and heartbroken because you just asked your boyfriend to marry you...he said No. Before you guys can even talk however there is a loud noise, screaming, terrible pain -- then nothing as you float away to blackness. When you wake it's freezing cold, your leg is in agony, and you see something moving next to you. You try to move but the something, a man dressed in animal skins, tells you "Don't move!" That's when you realize you are not alone with this man-beast, no - there is a really big, scary looking, bear with huge teeth and claws, rummaging through scattered belongings and eating...your dead friends. 
 This is the way author Adrienne Wilder introduces us to our MC in Wild. August Vallory had it all. A modeling career, a man he loved, and the extended family heaEUR(tm)d acquired in the business. He is a bit wrapped up in himself in the start of the book, but he quickly gets over it. Keegan Brooks has secrets darker than night, more dangerous than wolves, more brutal than an Alaskan winter. Keegan as we find is living in the wild in order to survive. He has some very bad enemies -- and if they knew he was still alive, living in the wild, they would do everything in their power to fix that. Then, I would be remiss to not introduce "She-Bitch" as Keegan has coined the grizzly bear which makes frequent appearances throughout the story. 
 Keegan isn't really sure why he is rescuing and saving this stranger, it will be another mouth to feed, another person to keep safe, and on top of that -this man, August, is injured from the plane crash. It will be a miracle if he survives the injury without a hospital, rescue team, or any means of immediate communication. Keegan knows the only chance August has is if he can get him safely to the old vets cabin where he can keep him warm, fed, and wait for Doc to show up in the spring. He also knows that putting himself in anyone one place too long is risky and he isn't sure Doc would appreciate them essentially moving in to his cabin. It's August's only chance though, so the choice is made. Keegan treks across miles of wilderness while pulling August on a quickly made sled, all so he can save this strangers life. 
 Once they get to the cabin, which turns out to be very minimalistic even if it does have the luxury of an indoor toilet and water. August is so out of it, delirious with pain and infection, it isn't until he wakes up that his primadonna attitude starts to show. He wants to go home. He wants to go now. He is used to getting what he wants. He doesn't understand that the only means of communication are an old two way radio with a missing antennae. He wonders if he is doomed to forever in this small cabin, with a man who smells like dog, and wears dead animals for clothes. He wonders why he was even saved if he is doomed to this life. 
 During this part of the story I tried fo remain epathetic towards August, but his attitude and lack of gratitude got a little old. He does however pull his head out of his arse rather quickly. 
 Keegan on the other hand comes to enjoy having someone else around. He finds himself admiring Augusts amazing body and wouldn't mind exploring it a bit, A with his tongue. A The sexual tension builds between these two rather nicely. I mean what else is there to do when you are stuck in a cabin all alone? I think these two put great use to their idle hands and other body parts! Let me tell you Keegan is all top - he may have been living alone for the past few years but he still knows how to turn a man inside out! 
 The things these two do to each other by the light of the fireplace is pure, animalistic, pleasure - Wilder knows how to write smut worthy sex scenes! 
 I loved the relationship that grows between these two. They literally have nothing else to do but to survive, take care of each other, and get to know one another. If it wasn't for being stranded and in danger I would say it is the perfect way to fix a relationship. There are little things that Keegan does which annoy the hell out of August, but they move forward and work it out. Even if they are not in an official relationship -- its always in the back of their minds that if they can't get word out via the radio, when Doc Anderson arrives -- August will go home. Theirs is a temporary love. It has an expiration looming in the background, which is maybe why they both fall so deep, so fast. 
 Then one day while out hunting Keegan finds Daisy. He brings her home against all his better judgement. He knows when the wolf-pup grows up she will leave. He knows that even though she fits in the palm of his hand, she is still a wild animal -- still will answer to the call of the wild. But he brings her home anyways. August melts. 
 Daisey & August become inseparable and even if she puts holes in Keegan's long johns -- he loves her too, in his own way! 
 August, Keegan, and Daisy settle in to life as best they can and Keegan is content. Trouble comes to the wild though and life changes quickly as Keegan, August, and Daisy fight to survive. While Keegan fights to both hold on to August and let him go so he can be happy. 
 I loved this book! The world building was excellent and I felt like I was right there in the small cabin with Keegan and August or hiking through miles of treacherous terrains to help August get back to civilization. I experienced every emotion while reading this story and seriously didn't want it to end! There is so much that happens in this book, but I felt like I could read about this couple for another 300 pages and still not get enough! I don't know how realistic Wilder was with the depictions of Alaskan Wild terrains-- but I don't even care, because the world building in my eyes was spot on. I loved it. 
 I was able to empathize with both MC which is not always possible. I felt Augusts pain and adjustment problems as he was shuved into this new world. I felt his anger and self-pitty as he adapted to his new reality. I also felt Keegan's longing, desire, his need for companionship, his drive to do what was right warring with his want to keep August forever. I loved it all even if it left mean emotional wreck! 
 I highly recommend this story ~ bring a warm jacket and welcome to Wild!

This is a book that I didn't really like, but recognize that it is interesting and has a lot of potential for book club discussions. The only thing for sure that we know about Micah is that she is a compulsive liar. She likely also lives in New York, has a white French mother and black American father, and is a teenager. 
 The unreliable narrator thing is interesting, but I think Larbalestier took it too far; so far, in fact that there is basically nothing in the novel you can pick out as "true." I know the story is supposed to be about lying, and possibly about psychosis, and about not knowing what is true and what is false, but by the end I couldn't help wondering if Micah is just a teenager who thinks she's clever writing a story for school that doesn't make any sense. Novels aren't supposed to point so obviously at the writer, are they? 
 The one thing I thought could be really meaningful was the issue of gender identity that ran through the novel - from Micah telling everyone at school at first that she's a boy, to the details of transformation that are very female-specific, to her reiteration that she is "half girl, half boy," to her teacher at the end telling her, "it's okay to be a girl." Could this book be a gender narrative a la Charlotte Perkins Gilman's "The Yellow Wallpaper?" 
 But then I read on Larbalestier's website that she has been "shocked by that reductive reading of Liar." Oh well, I still think it's the most interesting way to read the novel.

"There is no dishonor in losing the race. There is only dishonor in not racing because you are afraid to lose." -- Garth Stein, The Art of Racing in the Rain 
 There are books that are made for foolish-"laugh-box" burning laughters, unimaginable madness, wicked mysteries, heart-thrilling suspense, mind-boggling twists and some books are made for ugly crying. And this is one of those books. The Art of Racing in the Rain is not your ordinary type of book which talks about life and how to live it; most of the books tackle life in a cut-and-dry manner: dying man trying to save time for it is truly the very important thing in the world --with romance and tragedy as unexpected (or totally expected) sidelines, this novel, on the other hand, talks about life as a race, life in a race and a race for life. Literally and Figuratively. 
 The story is uniquely told from a wise dog's point of view. His name is Enzo, unlike any other dogs who are under the influence of the usual dog habits like barking and biting, Enzo is different, he is more like a human disguised wholly in the form of a dog; he feels and understands a person's life beyond the limits known to man and his kind. In other words, he thinks more than a human.

You know those authors that just have a way with words? They can paint a picture in your mind so vividly you can almost touch it? Yeah well, Nicholas Sparks is one of them. 
 First, if you've seen the movie and loved it, and now want to read the book, you do need to know that there was a fairly big change between the two. While the movie is set somewhat recently, the book is set in a 1950's small town. I personally liked that. It made me feel like I was there with them. It just had a really homey feel. 
 And having the book written in the first person also made me feel closer to the person. I don't know if anyone else has noticed that, but it just makes me feel like I can identify with them more, because it seems like I can understand them better. As if I am inside their head or something.

First Reading: June 14-16, 2012 
 I've had this on my "to-read" list for quite some time, but I kept passing it over in favor of more exciting (see also: literary prospects). This weekend, my fiance and I went camping, and I had an abundance of down-time to read; I worked my way through the novel in one day. A lawn chair, a stream, direct sunlight, and no outside human connect is quite possibly the best way to read a novel that is otherwise so unsettling. One of the reasons I had been putting-of the reading of this novel is because I've pegged most serial killer fiction as passe or juvinile - at the best, vacation/airport novels like James Patterson - something I will read but would rather not. I have appreciated thrillers in the past. I loved Thomas Harris' Silence of the Lambs - but I associate books and books of this nature with my junior high school years - guilty pleasures for small minds - sticky candy for toddlers. 
 I must admit. I was plesantly surprised with Heartsick. It seemed more mature and faster paced than most. The novel opens with a scene of torture and carries that suspense throughout all of the pages. I think what I most appreciated was Archie Sheridan's weaknesses, his deranged and deeply disturbed connection with Gretchen Lowell, the woman who had kept him hostage for ten days of physical torture and mental mind-games. It seemed Cain was worried of treading the same trail as Harris did with Silence of the Lambs; she actually references the novel, having Lowell call the pink-haired (admittedly too stereotypically "punk") reporter, Susan Ward, who is covering The After School Killer story, Clarice. I feel foolish for wanting more, but I know I'll shortly be reading the others in this series.

This is my weird, rambling, multi-media re-read of TEotW... Slightly spoilerish and loooong, as I wrote it whilst reading and it just kept growing. It's not really a review either, more a ramble of my non-reading progress. 
 Read first time in 2002 or 2003, followed by The Great Hunt in 2003 and The Dragon Reborn in 2007. I never continued the series. I want to give it another try, as a buddy read with some goodreads friends. 
 The first 10 chapters I re-read as a comic in Kindle format. For reasons unknown to me, the comic split that up into seven chapters only. The comic grew on me, I liked it. 
 Some of the earlier chapters have a pretty strong LOTR flavour to them. Sometimes I wonder if he took the plot outline of The Fellowship of the Ring and some of his favourite scenes, and then just worked his story around them. It really pissed me off, when I read the book for the first time. I'm more relaxed about it now. 
 *~*~* 
 Parallel to the comic I read the Wheel of Time Re-read: The Eye of the World by Tor: 
 Chapters 1-9 
 Chapters 10-18 
 Chapters 19-26 
 Chapters 27-35 
 Chapters 36-41 
 Chapters 42-47 
 Chapter 48 to the end of the book. 
 Another good website to read summaries and reflect: 
 http://library.tarvalon.net/index.php... 
 All of these can be a bit spoilery, read at your own peril! 
 *~*~* 
 The plan was to just read chapter summaries of the first three books. But I got hooked. I skimmed to where the comic took me and then started to read TEOTW properly. 
 Chapter 15, Min's prophecies, as an easy to find reminder for myself: 
 - Sparks swirling around you, thousands of them, and a big shadow, darker than midnight. The sparks are trying to fill the shadow, and the shadow is trying to swallow the sparks. You are all tied together in something dangerous. 
 - A wolf, and a broken crown, and trees flowering all around him (Perrin). 
 - A red eagle, an eye on a balance scale, a dagger with a ruby, a horn, and a laughing face (Mat). 
 - A sword that isn't a sword, a golden grown of laurel leaves, a beggar's staff, you pouring water on sand, a bloody hand and white-hot iron, three women standing over a funeral bier with you on it, black rock wet with blood, lightning around you, some striking at you, some coming out of you (Rand).  
 Chapter 19, liked all the boys up to this point. They all are still very similar in their characterizations, but are starting to develop and become more distinct. Although they do behave very juvenile, considering that they are supposed to be about 20 years old. Especially Mat seems to be TSTL. I know it's a plot device, but he is painfully stupid at times. The female charactes are still pretty flat. 
 Chapter 21, the first POVs other than from Rand's perspective. Nice. But I still don't like Nynaeve, I want to slap her upside her silly head! Many reviewers like her a lot and dislike Egwene. During my first read I pretty much couldn't stand Nynaeve and really liked Egwene. That still holds true the second time around. 
 By the end of chapter 26 I don't mind Nynaeve that much anymore, but now I really want to slap Mat upside the head instead. Can't tell you why, sorry, you have to read it yourself. 
 I can see why I gave this four stars way back when, this is really good storytelling. I like the underhanded humour. It is not the most suspenseful story, but Jordan spins a compelling yarn nonetheless. It also gets a lot more interesting, once the fellowship traveling party splits up. 
 Chapters 27 to 34 I read as a comic again, Volume Four of the graphic novel version of the book. Strangely enough, it really dragged and I needed four days to slog through it. Not sure, if it was the comic or the story. A lot of traveling about on horseback and in carts. I liked the whole dancing thing and there was more channeling... I honestly can't say if I picked up on this, when reading the book for the first time. 
 I went back to the book for another five chapters or so, from the arrival of Rand and Mat in Caemlyn... I know I wrote about the good storytelling a little further up, but I started to loose interest and began skimming at this point in the story. Around chapter 40 or so I switched back to just reading the Tor Re-read chapter summaries, because I did want the reminder of what happens, but didn't actually want to read the book. Sorry! Not sorry... 
 I did some cross-reading with the book and have to say that the Tor Re-read of the book is very well done and captures the gist of the various chapters well. 
 "The Prophecies will be fulfilled," the Aes Sedai whispered. "The Dragon is Reborn."

I have to say that this was an EPIC love story. It was dark, it was gritty, it had a man i hated in the start that turned to be a character i loved. 
 These type of stories are hard to deliver, and Phal did it well. The emotional nuances were delivered with such an impact, i was reeling from them after i finished the novel. True emotional abuse, that was described just right, not over the top and not to little to make you feel that the heroine was overreacting. She was described as an interesting woman with really humane thoughts and emotions. I was drawn to her, to him and to the story. This was a damned good read. 
 The only problem i had with this book was the way it was written. It is clear that the author is eloquent, but the sentences in this novel would make a Shakespearean actor cry. Throughout the book, in certain places it seemed forced to that extent it sounded pretentious. The constant bejeweling of normal, non important sentences took away from the shine of those moments when such lyrical prose would make a deep emotional impact. description of how the MC wore his coat was followed with the same fanfare as describing the key points of his love affair. Think of it as glitter, in some places a sparkle or two will leave you with a glamorous effect, while if you freely shower yourself with it, you wind up looking tacky. Unfortunately for me the overwriting dimmed the sheer awesomeness of this story. 
 Still i will be reading more of her work.

Mr. Gladwell does write pleasantly, a raconteur of high order. Here, he tries to connect the Biblical David with the Troubles in Ireland and the American Civil Rights Movement and Huguenot Resisters in Vichy France and Impressionism and teen basketball coaches and so on. It would seem his main points are: 
 1. Sometimes, things aren't what they seem. 
 2. Sometimes, being a royal a-hole is necessary 
 3. Sometimes, a traumatic childhood makes for accomplished adulthood. 
 4. Inverted U shaped curves are everywhere. 
 Don't get me wrong: this book is enjoyable to read. It suffers from a lack of sharp conclusions, but is otherwise pleasant pop-science. It may provoke some interesting conversations, especially among the anxious bourgeois who desperately want their progeny to get into the Ivy League, but who suspect that even that won't be enough. And if that conversation dies out, fear not! Gadwell will have another book out soon enough.

4.5 STARS TO A FRUSTRATING AND HEARTWARMING HISTORICAL ROMANCE READ! 
 Love is composed of a single soul, inhabiting two bodies. 
 A Lady by Midnight is the 3rd book in the 'Spindle Cove' series. I have read the previous 2, and i absolutely LOVE, LOVE, LOVE them. They are amazing! Even though this book wasn't as good, it was pretty damn close! 
 I was a tiny bit hesitant to read this because i didn't really like the characters when i first met them in book 1, but now? I'm happy to say my opinion changed. 
 Meet the main characters! 
 His embrace is all she's ever wanted. 
 Kate Taylor finds friendship and acceptance in Spindle Cove after years of fending for herself. She finds everything, accept love, that is. 
 The very last place she'd look for it is in Carporal Thorn's unwelcoming arms. The militia commander is cold to the bones but brutally handsome at the same time. But when mysterious strangers come searching for Kate, Thorn steps in as her fiance. He claims to only have her safety in mind, so why is there smoldering passion in his kiss? 
 Long ago, Samuel Thorn devoted his life to guarding Kate's happiness. He wants what's best for her, and that's definitely not him. To outlast their temporary engagement, he must keep his hands off her and block out her warm smiles out of his empty heart. It's the toughest battle of this warriors life... one he's destined to loose. 
 " You're like a gift," he said, his voice rough. "All wrapped up for someone else. A man can't look at you, but think of loosing those bows, one by one." 
 I think i would enjoy this book so much more if it wasn't for the main characters. They were seriously getting on my nerves most of the time. 
 Thorne was a very....cold character in the beginning. I really didn't like how he treated Kate, he kept on ignoring her and being rude. But he had his reasons, and i understood why he was the way he was. And even if he was sometimes a cold hearted asshole, you could still see the good in him. He is probably one of the most strongest characters i have read about. It's hard not to love him. I really liked how crude he was - 
 I'm not a smoothly spoken man. If i put my wants into words, i'd have you blushing so hard your frock would turn a deeper shade of pink." 
 What i didn't like was how he constantly kept thinking he wasn't good enough for Kate. Throughout the ENTIRE book he thought of himself as unworthy and as a result did things that just made me want to put my fist through a wall. 
 "Am i causing you pain?" she asked. 
 "Always. Every time you're near." 
 She turned her face away to hide her wounded reaction. "I'm sorry." 
 "Not what i meant." He souded drunk. With his healthy hand, he nudged her jaw until she faced him. "You're too beautiful. It hurts." 
 Kate was a great character that i kinda loved. She had such a good heart! She was kind to everyone, even those who tried to bring her down. She was smart and funny. 
 What i didn't like about her, and what was most annoying, was how hard she tried to make Thorne like her. She literally begged him for complements. Even when the man pushed her around like shit, she was still clinging to him like freaking glue. Ever heard of something called dignity, girl? 
 "Katie, i want you. I can't make it poetry. I can't make it sound anything other than crude, because it is. I want you in my bed. I want you under me, holding me. I want to bury my cock so deep inside of you." 
 Wow. If that doesn't make you swoon, then i don't know what will! The sex scenes between Kate and Thorne were so passionate and hot, but also sweet and tender. Loved them! Especially naked Thorne *wink* 
 Overall,A Lady by Midnight was definitely not a disappointing read! It was funny, passionate and entertaining. A beautifully written Historical Romance that i recommend to anyone! I'm really looking forwards to reading book 4! :)

I have to say this, even though I will come back to it later in the review: I knew nothing about this trilogy, no spoilers and I am still good, but the one thing I kept hearing about was Kestral, whom I love, but no one speaks about Arin. I will get back to it. And you will see why I am surprise. 
 This entire book took me by suprise. The world. The characters. The plot. The romance. The plot twist not so much, because I realise I knew it, but in my mind this was happening in book two. I will leave the characters in the end, because I really want to talk about them in spoilers and details. 
 The world and the world building are so beautifully crafted. Given the fact that this is fantasy, with no magic, at least form what I know and read, the way the world works is still pretty intricate. I love how we see things from Kestrel's perspective, which after a while made me think why was she seeing all this like normality. Because to her it was. That was the society and she couldn't change that. Nor, from what I saw in the beginning thought of such a thing. Like I said, the world building is amazing (and *screams with joy* I've seen a map in book two), because Kestral is a strategist and sees things from a political point of view, thus showing how and why this came to be. 
 The plot is not that straight forward. It suprised me where I was where I ended this book. Even though there are hints, because we see from third person's perspective, the plot is shaped into the actual plot (I am confusing everyone, I know) I think somewhere towards the half point. As for the action, I can say the first half is pretty slow, but that helps build the momentum, not to mention helps you know the characters and the world. So I say it is well deserved. 
 The characters. I loved both main characters, and even though I really really liked Kestrel's way of doing things I was taken by surprise by Arin, because I never heard things about him. The focus with this trilogy always seems to be on Kestral, and is well deserved, because I love political plots and she helps with it, and I love intelligent characters that are not necessarily assasins. Plus I saw character development in her, which was big, by the way. 
 But Arin, I never heard about his intelligence and funny remarks. About his strength and motivation. And I can't talk about him without spoilers, so sorry, but just letting you know he is an awesome character. Based on how the society works in this book: having Valorians and Herrani, one being the conquerer, the other being the conquered, thus slaves. The thing is that at some point is was hard to choose sides, because there was killing on both of them, but thinking about it, the Herrani had all the right to strike back. Let's remember the time Kestral was put by Cheat to wash his feet, yes he did exagerate with everything, but that does not mean on the Valorian side people like him did not existed. Arin, who was not strong enough to resist Kestrel, who let her go, even though it meant he might kill his people. This Arin was a surprise to me. Seeing him hurt when he let her go, made me stop for a second. He had tried everything to make her not see him as a threat. In the end giving up and letting her go. He is that one character who has been through a lot and shit keeps coming at him. I like that even though Kestral did a mistake she took it back, by agreeing to the emperor, which is one straight forward dude :'I have a son' - no way? Really?  
 I conclusion, I really, highly recommend The Winner's Curse, for its characters, in the first place, for the world and plot and the romance, which I have not talk about, but it's beautiful and forbidden. And I think book two is going to torture me. Can't wait. And for the beautiful writing style. If I could give more than 5 stars I would, this was just amazing.

 First impression of the book was I liked his voice. Casual storytelling always appeals to me, and I've been known to like Neil Strauss and Douglas Adams so this wasn't any different. The combination of funny and scary was nice because I haven't actually read a book of this genre before (I haven't read much yet). 
 The gory scenes got kinda repetitive because I somehow get a feeling that Wong likes exploding/melting eyes, which brings me to the downsides of this book. It was a tad silly. I know, it might've been the exact thing he was going for, but I don't really fancy scenes that seem like it was pulled out of Wong's ass. Frozen turkey with deer tongue to speak with and ribs as legs? Casually strolling into another world and shooting hoops then coming back like nothing ever happened? Monsters from another dimension with high-school dirty sense of humor? Adams and Pratchett do a better job in that regard. 
 Overall, this is a funny book. With Wong's style, I find it hard to take the scary parts seriously. There's just a jovial no fucks given attitude to it all that any scary situations the protagonist finds himself in, he'll get out of it just fine. It reminds me of Jack Sparrow and his uncanny ability to stumble out of any predicament he has. 
 An entertaining book, but not the best. I'd still read the next book, just not so soon.

There's something about the way Rainbow Rowell writes that feels like you're having a really good conversation with one of your closest friends. Like her previous novels, the characters in this book were interesting and realistic, like they might actually exist in Nebraska somewhere. Characterization is definitely one of her strongest writing traits. The concept and plot were unique. She balanced reality and flashbacks with the ever-so-slightly supernatural really well. It wasn't a fast-moving plot by any means (which is fine!) but it definitely made me keep reading, wondering what was going to happen. 
 There were a lot of things I loved about the book. It really turned over traditional gender roles with Georgie as the working, TV writer/producer mom with Neal being the stay-at-home dad who is also an excellent cook. I would have loved more diverse main characters (the main three are white and straight) but the supporting characters were fairly diverse in race, age, gender, and sexual orientation which was so great. I really liked Heather in particular and her reveal. Despite the age difference between them, I enjoyed the sibling relationship between Georgie and Heather had and how they sort of learned to cultivate it. 
 My only complaint is that the ending is a little anti-climatic. I wanted a little more explanation or at least some kind of reason for present-time Neal not talking to Georgie at all when he was away. I felt it was pretty dick-ish and I wanted more of a resolution on that. Was he really pissed at Georgie or was she overreacting? (But you could also say that it was realistic in that the imagination blows things up when in reality it's not a big thing?). 
 I would definitely recommend this book and just this author in general. Rainbow Rowell can write about anything and I would want to read it.

Scarlet is the second book in the Lunar Chronicles series. The Lunar Chronicles are loosely based on fairytales, but set in the future with androids and cyborgs and aliens called Lunars. It doesn't sound like it would be good, but it is. 
 I usually don't like sequels that change the main point of view, but I didn't mind this one since Cinder was still a large presence in the book. The story was told through alternating points of view between Scarlet, Cinder, Kai, Thorne, and Wolf, though predominately between Scarlet and Cinder. 
 I enjoyed all the new characters. We still get to see my favorites from the first book - Cinder, Kai, and Iko - as well as introduced to Scarlet, Wolf, and Thorne. While Scarlet has some of the teenage girl qualities that annoy me in most YA books (impulsive, blames everyone else for her problems, thinks she can go against people much stronger and more powerful than her, falls in love after a day), I generally liked her. And she and Wolf provided the requisite romance that I was afraid was going to come up between Cinder and Thorne. 
 I liked Thorne. He's arrogant, but in an amusing way and his bantering with Cinder provides almost all the humor in the book. I was concerned that it would turn into romance that would eventually lead into a love triangle with Kai in a future book (I'm so not a fan of the love triangles), but I felt like it became more a friendship and partnership than anything else. 
 The book seemed a little longer than necessary, but I felt it was paced well, rarely dragging. The change in POV was well placed, not leaving cliffhangers at the end of every chapter only to return to three or four chapters later. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Scarlet. I think I liked it better than the first book and look forward to the next in the series, which will be loosely based on Rapunzel.

I remember when I found out that Aaron Sorkin would be stepping down as screen-writer for the West Wing series; I said, no more watching the show for me. But I went back on my word and tried a few episodes. Luckily, I saw what changing writers did to the characters and I stopped myself. No more. I collected DVDs of the first four seasons, and watched each episode over and over again, happy in the fact that the characters were safe from destruction, not growing into semblances of their past selves. 
 Sadly, Ms.Roth did not warn me against her changing voice--I plunged into Book #3 with the expectation that she would guard her main characters with care and strength. Unfortunately, she is no guardian angel of Tris and Four. Turns out, Allegiant deflects the potential of this series, and makes it just another trendy YA trilogy. Not one to re-read on rainy nights. Not one to savor. Yes, to live is to be brave, no matter the outcome. But I wish someone would have told me that the writer had checked out, and would leave my heart in tatters at the door. 
 ***A few days later*** 
 I've come to terms with this loss. Writing these books were how Roth came to terms with her anxiety. I have to learn to let go of characters I've fallen in love with. Perhaps that way, I learn to really love those who I'm really with.

Alright, so walking into this I was very unsure of what to expect and ultimately how I'd feel about it when it was all said and done. I'm still not totally sure; this is the first real time I've ever felt a book deserved a half star rating. I tend to adapt my rating style based on where I'm rating, so it was fairly easy for me to switch to full stars for GR. With The Casual Vacancy, though, I'm stuck. I want to rate it 3.5. 
 I'll go into the plot later if anyone is curious, but for now there's a couple of things I want to address. The first: 
 It took a really long time for the book to hit its stride. For me, this book had the same problem that the Harry Potter series had (I know, I know, I shouldn't bring it up), that Rowling introduces way too many characters all at once. I had this problem with HP in elementary school and actually skipped the first book and read the second one instead; with more emphasis on story and less introduction I found the flow much easier to handle. Now that I'm older, I faced the same issue with this. The only difference is I now have better reading comprehension and was able to follow the story despite finding myself taking notes about who was who. 
 I find myself wanting to compare this book to several others. For me, this had a touch of Needful Things (by the perennial king of fucked up Stephen King) to it; a town of people who bring about their own downfall. It reminded me a bit of Gillian Flynn's writing, in that many of the characters didn't really have me believing they were basically good. In fact I disliked almost all the characters. 
 But I LOVE this. I don't have to like all the characters in a story to still be invested. This is like a guilty pleasure read; it was deliciously cruel and slanderous. I felt like I was spying on these people's lives and watching them gossip and be malicious to one another. And I had some grim satisfaction out of reading this book; like peeking out my window to watch the neighbors have a fight on the front lawn. That's what this book was like. 
 Each character was three-dimensional and felt very real. They all had different motivations and different ideas about what was going on around them. Shirley believed she could do no wrong, that she was above everyone else. Gavin foolishly ran from any conflict he was confronted with. Fats believed himself to be the only really "authentic" person, aside from Simon. There's so many characters I could write a whole review just on them, but I'll refrain. 
 PLOT: Guy dies who wanted to keep a trashy part of town still within town boundaries and keep a clinic open for rehab. After his death everything blows up with people trying to sway politics the way they want but only succeeding in screwing up their own lives.  I just realized we never even find out whether or not the political agenda is pushed through! I'm a horrible reader if I only just realized this..s  
 Their actions were just crazy. There was hardly any real regard for consequences in any of the characters, and that's what sped the plot along. Again, it felt like I was seeing everyone's dirty laundry--like the neighbors talking loudly about an incident with their windows open and their voices broadcasting across the street. 
 It was merely the great lag in the beginning that brought down the rating so much for me. I found that once it hit its stride I was feverishly reading to see what hell the residents of Pagford would put themselves through next.

It's a powerful experience, shitting. There's something magical about it, profound even. I think God made humans shit in the way we do because it brings us back down to earth and gives us humility. I don't care who you are, we all shit the same. Beyonce shits. The pope shits. The Queen of England shits. When we shit we forget how famous or rich we are. All of that goes away. 
 Trevor Noah has the perfect blend of politics, insight, and funny. That quote up there is a perfect view of that. It's funny--he's discussing the act of pooping. By default, it is toilet humor. But then he brings you around to this magical idea about how poop is the ultimate level playing field. You make six figures a year? You still shit, and you still have to wipe your ass. 
 He brought this kind of funny thinking process to every essay in this book. His mother pushing him out of a car. Being a criminal (insofar as creating pirated discs). Being adrift in a sea of black and white, and not quite belonging to each. Plus, it's totally worth reading just so you have Trevor Noah's voice in your head. His voice is so smooth, and when you tack on the South African accent it's just magical.

There the story is slightly different: we have the young in love couple, not rich, but not poor either, living content day after day. Then a great inheritance arrives and they are suddenly in front of the possibility of becoming very rich. He remains indifferent to everything at first, but because of his wife he decides to fight for that inheritance, but then the war starts and he needs to leave for the front. What happens in all this time? The wife spends his money to emancipate herself and cheats on him. So, yeah, money don't bring happiness, and in this case, they only destroyed the happiness and peace he had at first with his wife. 
 In The great Gatsby we see this sad man tortured between his memories of a girl he once loved and the same girl that is now in front of him, being more distant than ever. He creates this aura of perfection around her and fails to see the true Daisy. He spends all his time and energy to find new ways to make her happy and she shatters his dreams one by one. He is a dreamer, that's for sure. In the end he dies for her (murdered for a crime that he didn't do).  Overall, The Great Gatsby has a strong moral and the way the world of that time is described, it makes this book very charming from some perspectives. Yet, I can't say I enjoyed this book. It left a bitter taste in my mouth just like Ultima noapte de dragoste, intiia noapte de razboi did.

This is going to be a weird review for me. 
 Why exactly? 
 Because I actually think this book is more of a three star book, but I gave it a five anyway. 
 Now this, my dear reader, may not make much sense to you, but it does to me. So let me explain my crazy to you so therefore you see that I am not a crazy mess who likes starting her reviews with off the wall introductions just to grab readers attention though they may be disappointed with the outcome and be all like, "Well damn! What a waste of time. She likes to ramble on and make comparisons that don't really work and doesn't say much about the actual prose. It's off to Reddit for me where people stay on point." 
 So anyway... 
 This book does deserve a five star, but not the way that most reviews are done on Goodreads, and my biggest qualm. WoR might be the best epic fantasy I've ever read, but it far from the best book I've ever read. Something I hate about Goodreads is this comparison that stars imply, 'BEST BOOK EVERZZZ!!!' But how could I possibly compare Sanderson's epic to something like the The Yellow Birds by Kevin Powers (which changed they way I thought about soldiers returning from war, how I viewed the Iraqi Conflict and made my cry multiple times?) One is literary fiction, another is epic fantasy. It would be like comparing a sculpture to a painting. Both have their own rules to follow, both engage it's viewer in different way, but they are both considered 'visual art.' 
 This book is far from perfect, yet executed perfectly well. Yes, I know I'm full of contradictions. 
 I have three big gripes that keep this book from being in my favorite books of all time list: the dialog, the length, and some of the characters. 
 I could not stand how cheesy the dialog was. NOBODY TALKS LIKE THIS. Shallan, sadly, was the biggest offender, but Kaladin, Adolin and Dalinar could be just as bad. Shallan was never funny, and when her and Kaladin were arguing I felt like I was in a rom-com. I know where this is going! They don't like each each but then they do! Same with her dialog with Adolin (ummm HOW DO YOU POOP?). I mean, who talks like her? (Wait, I do know someone who talk like her... my brother. And we all find it hilariously annoying.) Shallan, my dear, just stay away from men. They seem to make you talk like a fool. 
 My second point, the length. I have never been a fan of long books. To me, it seems like a the editor took a vacation or something. There was just so much unnecessary stuff in this book that just kept me from the good parts. For example: the horse riding chapters. I have no idea why this was included. It's not like Kaladin is gonna ride a horse now anyway since  he can fly or "fall" . If it doesn't serve the plot or build towards the conclusion then BE GONE WITH YOU. 
 And last, (and probably where I will get the most flack) the characters. Now it may surprise you that it was actually Shallan who was my favorite character in this book (like I said, contradictions.) Not because she was terribly likable, but DAMN was she interesting. And I'm sorry everyone, Dalinar was not interesting in this book. He is to me a lucky Ned Stark. Maybe this will change in the next book, which is about him, but when someone is just so RIGHT about everything and just awesome at everything he does I tend to mentally check out. No need to invest! Everything will turnout alright! Now Shallan, by comparison is DARK. We have never seen the real Shallan, she lives in some sort of fairy world in her brain, blocking out terrible memories. Not to mention  She not only poisoned then strangled her father to death as she sang him a lullaby, she killed her mother too (out of self defense) . She is one messed up character, and I LOVED IT. Stay classy Shallan, I'll follow you on your dark path (I just wish you would stop this nonsense with the male characters! You are way better on your own. You don't need a love interest.) 
 And (I'm sorry everyone) Kaladin could be somewhat of a bore too. Oh you hate lighteyes! You won't change you racist ways! He was the most interesting when he was powerless with Shallan, who basically saved his ass multiple times. I think it was a good humbling for him. 
 And Adolin.... eh. Just as boring as his father. Far more interesting in the last book. 
 Now you a probably wondering, "What then, Barb, made you give a five star if you basically hate all the characters (especially my precious Kaladin who I totally fangirl over?!?!)" 
 Never fear everyone! I liked Kaladin quite a bit actually. And Dalinar too. And Adolin. In fact, I loved everyone. It doesn't change the fact that they could be quite boring at times. 
 It deserves a five star for multiple reasons in which would take me forever to list, so I'm just gonna talk about the main one I enjoyed: The world building. 
 BUT BARB YOU SAID YOU HATED THE LENGTH WHICH WAS ALL NECESSARY FOR WORLD BUILDING YOU MAKE NO SENSE. 
 And you're absolutely right... but not really. 
 Sanderson's world is so... creative. I haven't read anything like this before, and I read a lot. His magic systems make sense to me. They have limits; they can be used up. There is really danger in this. 
 And really, right there is why it deserves a five star. 
 If only it was 200 pages shorter. It is still possible to write a interesting world in 800 pages. 
 Anyway, this review is way too long so I'm just gonna stop and I hope you understand my reasoning for why I gave it a five star but really it was a three star review! (I was never good with conclusions anyway.)

What he doesn't do is protect her heart and self confidence when other girls are chasing him in high school. 
 Although partly her fault due to her low self esteem and feeling that she isn't good enough for Noah, their friendship is rocky all through high school. Noah eventually mans up and tells Amanda how much he loves her and always has. He tells her its always been her and not the whores he has dated. Amanda tells him no, they can only be friends. 
  
 Whats a boy-turning-a-man supposed to do? He tried several times and she is set on him finding someone better. She even admits to herself that she loves him but can't have him. The problem is, she won't let anyone else have him either. So high school becomes a war of "you hurt me so I'll hurt you back" by the two going out with different people. 
 This book was hard to believe when they were going through all the problems in high school, but not enough that I had to stop reading. The plot kept me interested to where I could look past Amanda's insecurities. I understand low self esteem. I have totally been there. It was especially bad in high school, like Amanda, however I still never turned down a hot guy because I thought he could do better. Maybe I was just selfish, but that's the guys problem, right? Who am I to deny him the pleasure of my company. ;) Ok, side note....I had low self esteem in high school but am also extremely narcissistic. Really weird combo, I know. 
 Moving on, so fifty percent into this book and after a bad night of bad decisions on both Noah and Amanda's part, they have it out. What really irks me is that Noah just accepts Amanda's choice and doesn't fight for her. They move on to college and other people. 
  
 This is where I can't tell you anymore. It gets very emotional from this point on and things start happening that you never saw coming. Suddenly friendships mean more than they ever have. Life has become more important. Time is more important. If you read my reviews you know that I listen to my books while I am at work through Kindle Fire's text to speak. Today I literally was sucking up snot and gulping knots in my throat trying to hold back the tears. I wanted to be home so bad so I could have a good cry. 
 I think there is a great lesson in this book if you look behind the words. That lesson is you can't duplicate love and as the old saying goes, the heart wants what the heart wants. Amanda and Noah wasted sooo much time not being together. If they would have just given into each other ...however, then we wouldn't have this book.

Egan's 1995 novel imagines a near-future (2050) intertwining of software simulations of humans ('Copies' of ambiguous legal, ethical, and metaphysical status) with virtual reality in a still quite fresh, and often mind-blowing way. It leans heavy on the exposition to get its fascinating concepts and intersecting reality set-ups communicated to the reader, but its characters are not as thin as in some idea-heavy science fiction: Maria is pretty well-developed, Durham's calm monomania is well-portrayed (as is Maria's complex reactions to it), Riemann's guilt gave him a little depth, etc. But clearly characters and narrative flow take a backseat to Egan's obsessive and thorough working through his ideas. 
 Those ideas, as well as sometimes being the best dizzying mind-candy I've encountered in a while, also occasionally strike rich, disturbing chords. Egan is concerned with the human implications of everything he explores, even if he only sometimes smoothly portrays that through his characters. Basically, if you have any sf interest in the themes of virtual reality and simulated selves, or just want your mind compactly blown, I'd say this is essential reading, just be prepared for an idea-driven ride. 
 (The A-life aspects of the story(there's the top-down simulation of humans in the Copies, but there's also complex (and eventually sentient) artificial life that evolves in a separate virtual world whose physics are determined by the rules of cellular automata)  also made we want to re-play Creatures:Exodus and Maxis's SimLife.)

Not that the frequent comparison to Draco Malfoy went unappreciated, but adding some depth to his character would have gone a long way toward making this a more memorable read. 
 My secondary issue is that there's almost no conflict. (If Ada was supposed to be it, I just couldn't take her seriously. And neither could Blair.) Not that reads have to be angst-filled or riddled with plot twists to appeal to me, but something should keep a novel's plot diagram from being an uneventful flat line. While it's true that dramatic things do happen (the library fire, the grandmother's unexpected death) , as a reader I didn't feel the impact of them like I should have. 
 The final word: UnWritten isn't terrible...but it's not special either.

*Read at work for review for ROYAL* 
 Romancing the Throne tells the story of Charlotte and Libby, two sisters from the upper crust of London society, who attend boarding school and live a charmed life. The best of friends and sisters forever, Charlotte and Libby depend on each other for almost everything, but when Prince Edward comes into the picture, things take quite the turn, ultimately testing the bond they share. 
 The main plot point for the first half of the book is a love triangle, which is already my least favorite trope to read about. But then, throw in the added bonus of two points of the triangle being sisters, and the trope becomes even worse. Often times we see young girls and their relationships with each other portrayed negatively in YA. They're pitted against each other, most frequently when it comes to boys. This book is no exception and it's even more saddening to see it reflected upon two sisters, who up until the introduction of Prince Edward were each other's best friend and closest confidant. 
 Another problem I had with the book was the point of view. Charlotte is the only narrator, and in a story where both sisters are main characters and play a big role, it would have been nice to get Libby's point of view as well. We as the reader are frequently told by other characters how Libby is feeling, but it would have really added to the book if we could have been inside Libby's head for a while and experienced her thoughts and feelings directly and more in depth. 
 I did really enjoy most of the supporting characters. Charlotte's best friend India was fantastic, very rational, and very supportive in every situation toward both sisters. She never picked sides and she offered insight to Charlotte when she was being unreasonable. I also really loved Robert, who played a bigger role in the second half of the book. He was sweet and quirky and really helped Charlotte with her business ideas. I wish there could have been more of him. 
 The second half of the story is where the book's redemption arc takes place, and I don't mean for a character, I mean for the book itself. Charlotte gets over her issues and is a much better person for it. The business venture she undergoes with Robert and his brother entailing a beauty app was interesting to read about, and I wish the whole book had focused more on this plot point rather than the love triangle. I think the author really shined in this portion of the story because she was using her own knowledge of the beauty industry, which is clear when looking at her back catalogue. 
 One aspect of Charlotte's character I did really appreciate was her ability to stand up for herself. She dates Prince Edward but when her sister Libby shows up, he starts getting distant with Charlotte, and pays more attention to her sister. Charlotte is the one to stand her ground and basically tell him "hey, I'm not going to be treated like this, whether you're royalty or not" and that was a great moment for her character. 
 Romancing the Throne is fast paced and mostly fun, albeit a few problematic areas, but overall not a bad read.

Like the title character, Cujo, this book reads like a rabid animal: fast and frenzied. While not perfect, it is an entertaining novel. However, if I hadn't read it before, as soon as I learned that the main character drives a Ford Pinto (by choice!), I would have known that they were screwed. 
 I still like this book even if some of the roles (domestic housewife with no ambition outside of raising their son) the characters take are dated. The only flaw that bothers me about this story is Frank Dodd. Yes, the idea of this boogeyman "haunting" the town is disconcerting, but it never really takes off. It makes some peripheral movement throughout the story, but never takes the narrative front and center. If there is a boogeyman hiding in the shadows, I eventually want to see it and have the protagonists confront it and either defeat it or die trying. The fact that this character's name pops up here and there in the story isn't enough. The story isn't a supernatural story, so Dodd doesn't belong here. Maybe if his previous crimes had been mentioned and the family heard about them and planted the idea of Dodd into Tad's subconscious, then it would have made more sense. As it stands, introducing Dodd seems like a missed opportunity. Regardless, I have to hand it to Sai King when he actually kills off the kid. The first time I read this book, I was shocked and had to read that section a few times because I couldn't believe that Tad was dead. Pretty shocking.  
 It is the little details and how this story grabs hold and doesn't let go of the reader that it has endured, remained relevant over the years, and earned its right to be called a classic. 
 One thing is for certain: I am more wary of dogs.

I just finished this book, and I'm anxious to capture my post-reading glow of good feelings before they begin to fade. It took me less than a day to read it, and I took to perusing others' reviews soon after finishing to see what any of my friends had thought of it. While only one friend has read it so far, I read some other pretty critical reviews and negative feedback in the other reviews posted on a fairly regular basis. I was, honestly, a bit surprised - as I think it was delightful. That's honestly the first word that came to mind - which is weird for a book that is part science fiction time-travel, part teen star-crossed romance, part dystopian, apocalyptic future fiction - and pure delight. 
 To address some of the more common complaints about the book: Do I think it was scientifically plausible in the time-frame provided in the book? No, Do I think it was a realistic road trip romance - especially when set against the science fiction of having teen lovers from different, incompatible time periods (lovers, as in, the emotional sense of the word - not the physical sense, though lord knows Ethan tried to consummate the (primarily) chaste relationship the whole book)? No. Did I still love every second of it? Yes. It was romantic and sweet and fuzzy - especially a midst the impending doom of the situation for planet Earth in the future. Was it silly? Yes, a bit. But silly in the way that most YA is - endearingly dorky, you might say. I expect a bit of that with every YA romance I read. 
 That said, the scientific inconsistency and implausible relationship didn't bother me. I bought into the story, got wrapped up in the characters, and fell in love alongside Ethan and Prenna. I liked the road trip. I liked the card games and lessons. I wasn't bored in the least. It was charming. Call me weird and simple, but I would recommend this to others without much reservation. I wouldn't send it to Stephen Hawking for review, but I wouldn't balk setting it in the hands of a teen girl or those in search of another now ever-popular dystopian YA. In my humble opinion, it was well-done YA. 
 Here's to you, NetGalley. You're the best. Thanks for ANOTHER solid recommendation.

The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao is one of the seemingly thrilling novel about a life of a Dominican boy named Oscar and his family. I was extremely slow in pace since I need my ipod nearby the entire time, with Spanish to English translator open. This was also annoying because it meant that I couldn't really read on the car or elsewhere without an internet connection, unless I wanted to miss half of the story. 
 I will skip my rage and proceed to what makes this novel beautiful. 
 One of the interesting things about this novel is that it covertly tells the effect of recent democratic changes, independence and slavery, arrival of the Spanish and the Americans in 1492 in the modern Dominican Republic. [FYI, the Dominican Republic was twice been a colony of Spain (1821 and 1865) not to mention the Three (3) Gs: "God, gold, and glory".] 
 I'm sure most of us who have read this had been contemplating what the Dominican History has to do with Ghetto Geeks and Oscar but at the same time it's hard to wonder why Oscar has to go through so much trouble. People exist in geek circles, but does Oscar's atomosphere of geekiness produces dirty air in public and among Dominican people? And what does any of this have to do with the sad history of the Dominican Republic? These are the crazy questions I asked myself upon finishing The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao....and then, it hit me. I realized that the answers were all the same. Diaz illustrates through Oscar the sad truth of people who have suffered in pain and are rarely made better in Dominican History. Diaz's history of the Dominican Republic describes a nation that went through colonial rule and dictatorship to a military state in which neighbors betray one another for personal and material gain and sadly, to avenge petty fights and misunderstandings. I will not forget how the story depicts a corrupt modern era in which cruelty is the order of the day. -_-

2.5 rounded up. The good--great true-to-life characters, a beautiful cover and a relatively unknown bit of history. This was an extremely easy to read book and very little adult content, so it could have easily been classified as YA. (I put this in the good because it really boosted my yearly pages read stat.) 
 In historical fiction, the writer knows point A and point B, and the idea is to fill in the gap with what could have happened. Pataki (the daughter of NY governor George) writes a plot that has too many suspensions of disbelief and (I wish) lack of other historical facts...and that's too bad because there is a great story there. Pataki's afterword was more interesting than the novel. 
 The story is told through Clara, a new maid to Peggy Shippen and with her being a "ladies' maid" it's bogged down with way too many details of clothes and capital-C Champagne on every other page. Areas that just didn't make sense to me were  1) that BA didn't recognize a coded letter when he saw one, yet he was a general, 2) that he needed help from a maid, vs. his wife, or needed help at all and 3)that Clara didn't just walk out at the end, she had to threaten blackmail--it wasn't as if she had to pay indentured fees or anything like that.  
 I would have liked much more military info, but I wonder if all the details on clothes and food were to bring in more female readers? I also would have liked more chapters of the life after, when they were in England, and information about BA's first marriage and children (which were never mentioned in the novel). Online I saw where BA may have had an illegitimate child later, in Canada. He may not have been the push-over we think he was! 
 I didn't realize her character was in Turn, Washington's Spies, so I may look for that series on demand.

This is an entirely decent book. Especially for someone up all night desperately needing some distraction. It's perfect entertaining reading. And let's all note that it was published in 2008, a good two years before Downton Abbey premiered. It's good to note that to be fair to Morton, because I'm sure she's tired of hearing the comparison. 
 However. It is an apt description. Very upstairs/downstairs, and told from the point of view of the maid, who is now a very old woman looking back on her life. There are mysteries and intrigues, though nothing earth-shaking. The major plot twists are all clearly telegraphed. 
  
 The "twist" about Grace being Frederick Hartford's daughter surprised no one but Grace. Anyone familiar with the genre guessed it 50 pages into the book. Grace never expresses any curiosity about her father (nor does she mention him at all until someone else brings him up. And when she figures out her mother was a maid, fell in love with the younger son of the house, got pregnant, and left in disgrace she spends almost not time mulling it over and realigning her worldview. She just accepts it and moves on. 
  
 The lack of introspection is what dropped the book from a four to a three star for me. The book was an interesting look into how societal expectations can make people dishonest and miserable. If Grace could have been frank with Hannah about the shorthand the first time it came up; If Hannah could have lived the life she wanted without a husband as a cover; If once the marriage failed Hannah could have left Teddy; if, if if.  
 It's also an interesting look at relationships without a balance of power. Grace sacrifices much for Hannah's sake. And, in the end, it turned out Hannah barely knew her at all. 
 Also, I'd like to just go on the record and say I hate plots where the two sisters are fighting over one man.

Mind-blowing! 
 I don't think I ever read anything quite like it. This book was just so brutal, violent and on more than one occasion made me feel very uncomfortable. It was horrible, it was ugly, disturbing, upsetting and I loved every fucking page of it! 
 I started reading it in the car during one of our frequent road trips and from first page onward I was hooked. It was kind of funny actually, while everyone enjoyed nice views and tourist attractions, I chose to remain in the car and read this book. I'm sure I did not miss much... I hope! 
 As for the story, there was no warm up, no lengthy descriptions of characters or world, no slow plot development. From very first prologue page - bam! - shit was happening. Like a breath of fresh air in the world of high fantasy! 
 The plot kept me on my toes the whole time, no such thing as "oh this part is boring" or "nothing really happening, so I can put the book down". It took me, I think, around 6 hours to finish this volume with occasional sight-seeing and some time behind the wheel. 
 And I was so impressed with the characters! It is indeed a rare occasion when I like both protagonists, it is usually the one or another. Damen's character development was beautiful, he was strong and smart and could keep up with Laurent's wits. Everything he did made sense in one way or another. There was no stupidity in his actions, even when his pride was concerned. Yes, he made some errors but for a royal who woke up one day as a slave I must admit - he adjusted well. 
 Oh and Laurent. He is everything I admire in a good MC villain: intelligent, gorgeous, vicious, witty, and cruel, without mercy and still has depth in him. Half of my brain was thinking: 'I want to be your slave!' and the other (smarter) part was like: 'you are joking right?! This ass-hole will torture you to death in 2 minutes'. I just hope Laurent will not turn into soft little marshmallow within next 2 books. I love his brutality! Just love love love it! 
 Chemistry between Lauren and Damen was scalding hot to say the least. Jeez... 
 World building was very well handled, no information overload, just perfect amount so I was able to keep up without resting my brain. Realm itself was simple enough, you have the map in the beginning of the book which was basic enough for everyone to understand. I was fascinated with cultural differences between countries, how it was considered OK to rape in Vere but totally not cool to do so in Akielos. And why in Vere masters only kept same sex slaves etc. 
 Very well written book! It can take the place of honour in my all-time favourites shelf.

First impressions: One of the first things I loved about this book was Alexia's voice. She's a stickler for etiquette, and her commentary on the manners of others, even in the most ridiculous of circumstances, is hilarious. 
 Lasting impressions: What a refreshing take on the paranormal and steampunk genres! I loved the mash-up of steam and clockwork technology with werewolves and vampires in Victorian society. 
 Conflicting impressions: The first third of the book moved pretty slowly. It wasn't until the last third that I got truly hooked on the story. 
 Overall impressions: I've been meaning to read this book for a long time, and I'm happy that I finally did. Although this is a steampunk novel, it's really more along the lines of "steampunk light." I think if I had read this a few years ago, when it first popped up on my radar, I would have had a much different idea of what constituted steampunk. There are some elements of steampunk to the story, but it's not nearly as integral to the story as, say, Leviathan. I definitely recommend this one for folks looking to ease in to the steampunk genre. 
 The paranormal elements are what make this book really shine. In Alexia's world, vampires and werewolves are a part of society, even if they still inspire some trepidation and fear. They pose no threat to Alexia, however, as she has no soul. As a preternatural, her touch returns supernatural beings to their human state - vampires lose their fangs, werewolves shift back. Alexia's abilities are known to select members of society, but she works to keep it away from friends and family. 
 Alexia is strong, stubborn, willful, and of course, proper. Yet her Italian heritage, abrasive (for the time) personality, and advancing age (I think she's 27) have resigned her to life as a spinster. If I have one complaint about the book, it's the incessant beating to the head we take on these three facets of Alexia's life. On almost every page, and certainly in every scene, we are reminded that Alexia is old, Italian, and not suitable as a mate. She constantly refers to herself as a spinster. Later in the book there are hints that this has been drilled into her by her family, but through most of the story it is simply presented as fact so I never felt bad for her. Since these descriptors didn't serve to elicit empathy, they just became annoying. 
 Lord Maccon is the best sort of love interest. He's a dashing alpha male who still respects and appreciates Alexia. He can be condescending and brusque, but all in good fun as he matches wits with the equally snappish Alexia. The verbal sparring between these two is lots of fun to witness, and were some of my favorite parts of the book. 
 The mystery and plot were not nearly as exciting as the characters and world, so the story seemed to drag at points. Still, the ending sets up a new chapter in Alexia's life that holds lots of promise and I'm eager to start the next book.

The problem with books that have been turned into movies is that you start reading them with certain preconceptions influenced not only by the movie, but also the media hype surrounding it. I admit I was initially reluctant to pick up this book but was in the mood for something different to my normal fare of murder mysteries, so decided to give it a go - and I'm glad I did! I really enjoyed Cheryl's account of her journey to self-discovery. She has been criticized by many for her unpreparedness for hiking the trail, but to me it seemed gutsy and determined. Having lost my mother young I related to the journey through grief Cheryl experiences, the emotional roller coaster of sadness, anger, fear and risk-taking. It did not surprise me that she sabotaged her marriage and her own health in the aftermath of her mother's suffering and protracted illness. Everyone deals with such a profound loss in their own way. I enjoyed reading how, in the wilderness, her perspective of life slowly changes and she starts to discover herself underneath the layers of guilt, grief and loneliness. Some parts of the journey are funny, some are sad, and some inspired me to question how I would react to being on my own for such a long period of time, just trying to survive. All in all, I really enjoyed the journey - listening to the audiobook was perhaps a good choice, as it carried my away at its own pace whilst travelling along in my car. Thumbs up from me!
