It wouldn't have done this to me--there is no preview chapter in it, and if there was it'd probably have shading on the edges). 
 The other thing, there was just something about the storytelling style or whatever you wanna call it. The best thing I know to call it is explanatory, but it wasn't boring like a textbook or anything. It was just fairly matter-of-fact. Kind of like if your friend told you about his weekend or something. The main character narrates, and since this is a dystopian future (sort of anyway--not inside the OASIS where we spend a lot of time, but very much so outside) and we're dealing with more or less a big trivia competition, there's a lot of history and context to explain if you want people to really know where they are and what's going on. 
 I've never been very into '80s stuff or video games, but I still enjoyed reading this. I appreciated the geek culture and obsessiveness, information compiling, all that good stuff. I bookmarked the part talking about libraries in the OASIS, and Parzival's Firefly-class ship. I appreciated the mention of a Whedonverse planet, though was hoping for at least an explanatory sentence there mentioning Buffy. I really liked the quest / clues / riddles aspect. 
 I had a big crazy theory toward the beginning that I kept waiting and waiting for, which turned out to be totally wrong, so that was sort of disappointing. I thought that Aech was Halliday and he hadn't really died, but was being a control freak and wanted to know who exactly was gaining control of the OASIS before he retired, and had gone undercover to find a nice geek kid and sort of chosen/coached Wade. Alas. Real Aech was a good twist though.  Toward the middle though I got really excited, when Wade escapes from IOI and everyone meets in the Basement and freaking Ogden Morrow shows up like "Surprise! Btw I'm gonna fly you all to Oregon!" . Like, wtf. And at that point I had to go back to work, so it was killer. 
 But yeah, the very end was sort of underwhelming to me, what with thinking I still had several pages left, and my big theory never coming to pass, and everything wrapping up in a nice happy bow. It was just a little too neat and sunshine-y and at that point there wasn't enough info dumping about the consequences and future. Like, this was not a love story to me, but that's how it ended. . 
 So yeah. I don't have anything big to say. I feel like this is a very lackluster review, but I wanted to say something.

 Have you been searching for an amazing book to read? A book with substance? Humor? A book that has won awards but is still immanently readable? Have you been looking for a book that will change the way you think about life, in a way that's not sweetly-inspirational? What are you waiting for? Read Please Ignore Vera Dietz. 
 This book is many things. It is a contemporary YA novel, a love story, a ghost story. It's a book about destiny, about grief, about perspective. It's about Vera Dietz and Charlie Kahn, two best friends who are separated by the grave. 
 I read this book around a year ago, and when I look back, it's not the particulars of the plot I remember. What stays with the reader is the palpable emotions of the characters, the dark humor inlaid in the language, its quirky narrative design, and the overall quality of King's book. It is a character and language driven novel. 
 There are many narrators, but our primary is Vera. She's an intelligent teenager and has the potential to go places, but she's weighed down by what feels like her unescapable destiny. 
 Well, if it's as easy as catching my future from a blood relative, then I guess I'm due to be a drunk, pregnant, dropout stripper any day now. 
 I happen to love the narrative voice of intelligent teenagers. Vera's favorite classes in school are Vocabulary and Modern Social Thought, which describes pretty well her style of narration. When we meet Vera, she's coping with the death of her estranged, ex-best friend, Charlie, who she loved. She happens to know a secret regarding an unfortunate event that occurred prior to his accidental death, and she is visited by his spectres (yes, plural) who urge her to clear his name. 
 Note: This is not a paranormal genre book. Some might argue that the ghosts in this book give it a supernatural element, but unless missing someone severely is supernatural, then this book just portrays the way bereavement makes you feel insane. However, it also gives the dead a chance to speak and narrative voice to a pagoda. 
 The first night it happened, I followed them into the strip mall parking lot. They were all stuffed into a silver-gray Honda--all thousand of them... When I followed them to the mall, they stopped outside Zimmerman's Pet Store and all thousand of them got out, holding hands and two-dimensional, like cutout accordion dolls. They climbed into the front window with the black Labrador puppies and beckoned with flat, paperlike fingers. 
 As for Charlie, it's usually a drag to read a book that deals heavily with death, but Charlie's character is so vivid and present, it's like he is merely separated from the living by a thin curtain. He rivals Vera in regards to reader connection and identification. Charlie, an eccentric, charismatic, and troubled young man, sells himself entirely too short and engages in extreme self-sabotage, which ultimately results in his early death. His character starts out as an enigma, but is eventually fully unfolded. He remains one of my favorite fictional characters. 
 The thing you don't see while you're still there on Earth is how easy it is to change your mind. When you're in it and you're mixed up with feelings, assumptions, influences, and misconceptions, things seem completely impossible to change. From here, you see that change is as easy as flicking a light switch in your brain. 
 Vera's father, Ken Dietz, is also a standout narrator. In so many YA novels, parents are generalized presences, but King manages to make Ken a character in his own right. In a novel about how the past affects the present and future, Ken's reminisces to his own teenage days and his struggles to overcome genetic alcoholism were crucial to the thematic makeup of the story. 
 When Vera turned sixteen, four years after Cindy Sindy left, I brought her up to the pagoda and flew paper airplanes with her. I asked her if she wanted to know the story of how the pagoda was built, and she said yes. So I told her, and it was like everything was right in my life again. I watched the planes soar down toward the city, and I felt redeemed and whole. I remember thinking,Kenny Dietz, you have finally grown up, son. 
 I estimate that I spent over $2,300 on self-help books, workshops, and videos to make myself into the man Cindy Sindy wanted me to be. But all it really took was seeing Vera all grown up--nearly the same age as her mother when we sat in the very same spot, doing the very same thing. 
 There are many opportunities to identify with characters in this novel, many instances to feel that nose-burn that preludes crying. There are also many times where you'll smile and even laugh. The entire time, you'll feel connected to what you're reading. You'll grow in comprehension of King's message, as the story unfolds, and when you close the book, you'll feel as if you understand more about life and death than you did before. 
 Then, they are here. All thousand of them. Maybe a million. The field is wall-to-wall Charlies. They are glowing blue-white and I can hear them breathing. They exhale a word. Rest.

 This was massively disappointing for me since I loved Delirium immensely and was looking forward to this being an epic conclusion for the series.

 Requiem starts a few days after Pandemonium's epic cliff-hanger - Alex is alive but deeply resents Lena for moving on with Julian. Subsequently, Lena is plagued with doubt and guilt and turns into an incredibly unlikeable (and Mary Sue-esque) protagonist. Requiem also sees the return of Hana as a secondary POV character, which started off great but really fizzled out by the end. I was annoyed by their anticlimactic reunion which had the potential to be a really intense and emotionally satisfying moment given the build up from the alternating POV structure of the book. Instead it was rushed, flat and overshadowed by the other actions happening at the time. It also made Lena seem like an (even bigger) bitch by forgetting all about Hana as soon as she leaves the house.  This is one of unfortunately many wasted opportunities in Requiem. 
 And speaking of emotionally satisfying...that ending...wow. And I thought Mockingjay was a cop out for craptastic love triangle resolutions. Now I just think - at least it had an epilogue. I honestly considered buying another copy because I was sure that that couldn't be it. But...it was. Ok, yes, Lena has her moment with Alex but how can the book fade to black without a last scene with Julian? Does she even go through with it or is the reader just supposed to imagine their preferred ending based on who they ship? That is so not good enough considering the romantic relationships are actually the major theme in this series.  
 Plot wise I was disappointed that Oliver didn't go for something more epic, given that the series is about LOVE of all things. The resistance had a relatively micro focus in terms of focusing on 'liberating' individual towns rather than say, organizing a massive network to topple the autocratic government as a whole, or driving an ideological campaign of love and freedom that would start to change everything. Instead I can easily imagine the final battle backfiring on the resistance about 1 week after the book ends. Thus again, the need for a cohesive epilogue. I would also have been interested to know if the cure and Book of Shh ideology extended outside of America, but though the question is raised it is never answered. 
 One thing I did like was the use of the 'King Solomon' story. That was quite sweet. Also, Oliver's prose was a joy to read, as always. And as previously mentioned, Hana's story is great - especially in the first half. She has some very touching moments dealing with Lena's loss. 
 In the end, I don't know if my expectations were just too high, or if this really did fall so far from the mark as to be borderline unenjoyable.

This book was so close to being 5 stars. It had so many things going for it: excellent writing, fast-paced plotting, well-crafted world-building, unexpected twists, intriguing characters (one of the few books where I enjoyed each character's chapters almost equally), and witty banter that actually had me chuckling. 
 But there were a few things that kept bothering me. I really think this should have been an adult book. There was no reason to keep all of the characters 18 or under, except to cater to a YA market. Maybe a few of them could be teens, but the text explicitly states all of them are 18 or under. And that aspect felt so forced and unrealistic. I couldn't buy that the scheming mastermind Kaz is a teen. Or the burly soldier Matthias. Have you seen high school seniors? The characters' appearances, emotions, and schemes spoke to years more of experience; I don't care how rough their upbringing was. I would have gladly ignored this issue, but for whatever reason, the ages of the characters kept coming up again and again. 
 I also really could have done without the budding Kaz/Inej romance. Both those characters are stronger independently, and their relationship is so much more meaningful as a friendship. Unfortunately, it's also looking like all six of the Crows are going to end paired up. Sigh. Does every YA protagonist need to find love before 18?  
 My last quibble--and this is very minor--is that the first chapter really should have been a prologue and the last, an epilogue. How much stronger of a last line is "Dirtyhands had come to see the rough work done."  than "Right now there was money to be made." ? 
 Overall, this is a fantastic book. It's so great, in fact, that its few flaws stand out all the more.

 Hills like White Elephants by Ernest Hemingway is a short story about abortion, feminism and relationship. The story is set on a bar section of a train set to Madrid. Simple as they can appear, an American man (who is not named) and a girl named Jig are sitting and having an intense and enduring discussion over whether or not Jig will get an abortion. The American man, however, tries to convince Jig that undergoing abortion is just easy as pie which is completely insulting. At the end of the story, the train is about to arrive to its destination and the outcome of their discussion is still unclear because the last words she said were: "I feel fine". We are now left wondering if she went through with the operation or not. 
 Significance of the Title: 
 Hills like White Elephants 
 Hills: Hills are curved land formation. If we draw a hill vertically (position it on a portrait vision) it will look like a pregnant woman (the hill acting as the womb of a woman). Take for example the letter 'b'. :) 
 White Elephants: White elephants signifies a precious item. In the story it describes the hill (The baby inside the womb). A white elephant is very rare and a beautiful gift to some culture but its cost perhaps surpasses its usefulness. Suppose, you give someone a gift like White Elephant, it will become totally useless to the recipient. And that is exactly the reality of what Jig is going through. She has received a gift (the baby on her womb) which is, at that time in her life, useless to her because it was unexpected. It is also a gift that could be priceless to another.

 She actually felt like a person and not some sort of wish fulfillment. Not the "look how awesome my life is" "you'll never achieve this because I'm special" sort of book.

 I plan out my paintings with excruciating detail, and every paint stroke feels like a misstep. There is crying, long drawn out nights. At one point, I spent over 100 hours on one painting. I love/hated every minute of it. (If you want to check out my paintings from this era follow the link: http://www.barbarawilliamsonline.com And also, I can totally relate to having someone steal the URL address you want...  Also my obsession in college with getting good grades, my social life be damned!

I worked my ass off to get an A but, since art is a very subjective field, he was still able to give be a B. I remember after that class fantasizing about ripping off his stupid hat that he wore all the time and yelling, "WE ALL KNOW YOU'RE BALD UNDER HERE." I continued to get A's in other classes after that.

 So mostly what I'm trying to say is that Felicia Day and I would be best friends if we ever met in the RL.

High schooler Becca Williamson makes money in an unconventional way: she breaks up couples. She's seen more than a few classmates turn into completely different people once they start dating, dropping their former interests and their former friends in favor of "love." As the Break-Up Artist, Becca plants misinformation to force relationships toward the breaking point. But when she is paid to break up Steve and Huxley, the star football player and her former best friend, Becca finds the task more challenging than she'd anticipated. And shockingly, she's falling into a relationship of her own... 
 I loved Becca at first. She reminded me a little of Veronica Mars - sly, snarky, and smarter than her peers. This was a girl who had it all figured out: so many teenage girls base their entire self-worth and identity on their boyfriends, and Becca was opting out of that charade. Sadly, my high opinion of Becca was shattered about halfway through the book when  she falls for her best friend Val's new boyfriend Ezra, with whom Becca seems to share no palpable connection. The Break-Up Artist lost a lot of credibility for me here. It's difficult to believe that a girl who is vehemently anti-love would so randomly and willingly succumb to the advances of anyone at all, much less the person her best friend is dating, much much less someone with the personality of a shoebox.  
 As annoying as I found this subplot, there's a lot to like about The Break-Up Artist. Teens could learn a lot from Becca's tirade against coupling up too early, and as long as they do as she says and not as she does, Becca gives some sound advice. Her comeuppance too is swift and largely well-deserved. This is a likeable book with which nearly every teen would be able to relate.

Silver Bastard's is a spin-off series to Joanna Wylde's famous Reaper's MC series. The Silver Bastard's and Reaper's are allies in the MC world and are even featured in a few Reaper books. Silver Bastard's is Puck's story who majority of readers met in Reaper's Stand , ending with him and Painter taking the fall for their club and being sent to jail. This book picks up a year or so after that incident during their coming-home party and when Puck gets his colors, and is finally inducted in the club. This party is also where he meets Becca, the main heroine for out story. 
 I can really understand why some people did not like this book it took me a bit out of my own comfort zone, but once I got over it I was able to appreciate it for what it was: a good messy romantic story. There are tone's of reviews out there so I'm just going to keep mine pretty general and just cover a few things. 
 Joanna Wylde never ever fails to please me, she is slowly becoming one of my favourite authors out there. Everything she writes is golden, even some of my least favourite books from her get rated at least a three star, for the writing only. It felt really good to read another one of her books again, and I had the same experience as I did when I first read Reaper's Property : 
 - I laughed 
 - I squealed 
 - I sweated 
 - I died of mortification 
 - I gasped in horror/ shock 
 - And I screamed/ shouted/ yelled out my frustration on my poor Kindle 
 ... Any book that makes me do that HAS to be a good one. 
 There is just something about her writing style and her characters that I just completely love. I know that it is a fictional book and that in reality we would never live in her MC world, but there is just something so genuine and realistic of the decisions, thought process, or actions of her characters that make it very relatable. I find myself understanding some of things they do because I could imagine what I would do in that situation. I also like her story lines, they aren't perfect neat and tidy stories, they are messy, wild, and crazy and that's what makes it more fun and relatable because let's be honest life ain't all that neat or tide. 
 Puck and Becca which are the main couple in this story are not my favourite couple in the world, but there was something about those two that I really liked separately and together. 
 - ".. the guy was mysterious. Kind of like Batman. On a motorcycle." 
 - "Puck watched us silently, his face grim. Just. Like. Batman." 
 Becca was just this girl who had a rough life and was trying to find her normal, and get her shit together like every twenty-one year old out there. Yes, it was twisted that sometimes with Puck the fear and the lust would get mixed up but I also understood it. Puck was the one who had unintentionally took advantage of her but he also saved her life... so yes that is very confusing but it also made sense. 
 "I'd actually sat alone in the darkness lusting after a girl like some fucking Robert Pattinson wannabe. At least I smoked instead of sparkled." 
 Puck was a simple man he wanted what he wanted and he accepted his life for what it was: the MC world. Despite the past between him and Becca he had always remained the only constant in her life, and when he realized his feelings for her: "That's when it hit me. Someday I wanted to have kids and in my head they looked like Becca." *silence* ... I know right? 
 On some level their relationship started out twisted but in the end in turned into something so beautiful, that epilogue? Man no words. 
 Puck and Painter are also really good friends, so Joanna Wylde sets up a bit of Painter's book in this story, and surprisingly I am actually anticipating his book after reading Silver Bastards. In the end I really liked this book and am happy I read it when I was ready for it.

 I requested this book because the premise is intriguing. Sadly, that was where my interest ended. There are very few characters in this book worth rooting for, and the ones who are only make cameo appearances. (I really liked Fred. Why wasn't Fred in this more?) 
 The main character, Becca, is bitter and cynical about love and relationships because her revered older sister was dumped on the day of her wedding and has since been lost in a pit of wallowing, sweatpants, and reality television. That isn't the reason why Becca starts breaking up couples for money, it just reinforces her biased belief that she's only speeding up the inevitable, because despite the fact that her parents are still married, she thinks that all couples eventually break up. 
 Becca breaks up couples for money because there is a stigma against single girls at her school. (And possibly because she's still a little pissed that former best friend Huxley abandoned her for her boyfriend - and popularity - about three years ago.) Because there are far more girls than guys at her school, and your worth as a human being is apparently tied into whether or not you can land a man. She does it because she doesn't believe that love exists, especially not in high school. 
 Becca continues to cling to her beliefs even as she develops feelings for Ezra, the boyfriend of her best friend Val. Holier-than-thou Becca, who is convinced that she alone sees the truth among the love-hungry populace of her high school, pursues Ezra behind Val's back. What she and Ezra have is different than all of the other relationships she ruins because it's real. Even though Becca was quick to dismiss his romantic overtures when they were directed at Val. As soon as they're meant for her, though, she completely changes her tune. 
 A note on Becca's role as "The Break-Up Artist": we don't know the details of most of her jobs, but some of them do seem to be for the better. After Becca is outed and shunned accordingly, a girl approaches her and thanks her for helping her break up her friend's relationship, because the guy was telling her lies. With the exception of Huxley and boyfriend Steve, who seem to genuinely be in love, the couples break up for silly reasons, or for a good cause. This, of course, only convinces Becca that she is doing a good deed. 
 I am truly horrified by the portrayal of women in this book. Never mind that Becca is really not a great person, someone who ruins relationships and causes who knows what kind of psychological damage for the low, low fee of $100. Not everyone in literature has to be likeable, and unreliable narrators exist. Pretty much every girl in this story is shown to be vapid, shallow, and driven by one desire only: to get a boyfriend. Most of the conversations between the various female characters revolve around men, even tangientially. Becca's sister Diane believes that all of her friends, who are happily married, are laughing at her because she was left at the altar. Because women, especially women who have been friends for ages, are so callous and cold-hearted that they will just trash a friend who has been heartbroken. 
 It's also interesting to note that - aside from the man who solicits her help in breaking up Huxley and Steve - everyone who approaches Becca for her services is a girl. Because it's only the girls who ruin their friendships due to a relationship. Apparently guys at this school have no problem maintaining their own friendships while dating someone. Also, many of the girls compromise their beliefs and opinions in order to snare a guy - like Val, who stops being a vegetarian because Ezra likes burgers. It's implied that none of the guys have to do this because they can afford to be choosy about their girlfriends - there is a 65/35 ratio of girls to guys. 
 Something else that really bothers me is that no one solves their problems on their own. No one arrives at their own realizations. No one comes to their senses without intervention. All of the women in this book arrive at their conclusions because of someone else forcing them to see the light. 
 It ends the right way, which is that Becca and Val are friends again, cheating Ezra is out of the picture, and Diane reconciles with her own friends. Becca isn't quite so cynical about love anymore, and everyone lives happily ever after. But by that time, it's too little, too late.

Helena lives in a content world with her husband and two daughters. Happy to keep the past buried, she tries desperately to live a normal life. Then she hears that the infamous Marsh King has escaped from prison and her world turns upside down. He's known for kidnapping a teenage girl and keeping her imprisoned in the marsh for years and starting a family with her... he's Helena's father. Now she has to take everything she's learned from him to hunt him before he harms her family, seeking revenge. 
 Purely from Helena's point of view, the author takes us into her past, the way she viewed the world, living without any other human contact but her parents for more than a decade of her life - to her present, where she struggles with emotions she kept hidden for so long. So long that her own family has no idea of this torturous past. This is not a happy story. This is somber, real, emotional, raw and atmospheric. The author pulls you right into Helena's psyche and holds nothing back. In my fascination with the human mind, one subject that has always been extremely interested has been the concept of learned helplessness. "There is a psychological component to controlling a person that can be just as powerful as the physical pain you inflict on them...." Just how much can a human take, physically and emotionally, before they completely break? And how much stronger do they become when someone else's life becomes more important to protect than their own? A compelling novel that has you reeling, Karen Dionne knows what she's doing. This is not your typical psychological thriller. There are no full on twists but if you like to dig into the mind of a person's journey from child prisoner to primal mother, you'll love this book as much as I do. 
 Huge thank you to Putnam Books for this ARC in return for my honest opinion.

 Misadventures in Wonderland 
 Take fae, mages, demons, and mythical creatures then throw in a healthy dose of an awkward outsider discovering she is royalty and a smidge of Robin Hood and you have The Last of the Firedrakes. While the premise sounds intriguing, and definitely like something I would adore, the actual novel is far from that. 
 I feel like I am the only person to have truly disliked this novel. At one point, I believed it was going to be a DNF. That is how bad it was. The writing initially was abysmal, frequently telling the reader what was happening instead of allowing us to see and discover. Couple that was the most idiotic and self-pitying "heroine" and you have a book that is difficult to swallow. I am going to assume it was written with younger readers in mind, as it read more like a middle school novel that a true YA. I believe my 12-year old self may have loved it. It was juvenile and filled with tons of cliches and tropes, particularly from the Young Adult genre. 
 *	Dark "mysterious" love interest - check 
 *	Comical villains - check 
 *	Plain Jane protagonist - check 
 *	Evil popular girls - Check 
 *	Insta-love - check 
 *	Dead parents - check 
 Basically everything wrong with the young adult genre was present in this novel. I became so frustrated at points that I had to put the novel down for a minute and breathe. I rolled my eyes so many times I lost count. It became a bit ridiculous at some point for me to even try to read on, although I am glad I did. The last quarter of the novel was a significant improvement from the beginning. The protagonist grew, as well as the writing. While I still believe it is targeted towards the younger side of YA, at least I was able to tolerate the ending. 
 Characters 
 Aurora Firedrake 
 Her name is badass. Other than that, no part of her is awesome. She is whiney, hard headed (and not in a good way), self-pitying, and frequently dependent on others. She is incredibly moldable to anyone's ideas and is exceptionally naive. As in, trusts people based off of looks and a "feeling" level naive. And it happened over and over again. She literally decided if she liked or disliked a person depending on how they appeared. "I instinctively liked Kalen. He talked strangely and extremely fast, but I could tell immediately he was a sincere person," (p. 43). Lord forbid if a person is unattractive, or overly attractive (unless they are male), they will most definitely be a villain. Every. Single. Time. "First I met Lord Larney, the thing one who looked like a crow. He had oily, black hair, which was thinning at the temples.... The second man, who had not looked up from his food, was Sir Gothero, and I thought that he looked like a far, angry toad...I disliked them both at first sight," (p. 126). I will give her a little bit of praise in that she grew as the novel progressed. She stopped the self-pitying (thank goodness!) and started accepting responsibilities. However, she continuously made poor decisions. Quite a few times she should have died, except her special snowflake status prevented that. I believe I could have enjoyed this novel infinitely more if the protagonist was not such a twat. 
 Rafe 
 Oh how I wanted to love you. I did enjoy the fact that for once the love interest had a happy, somewhat pleasant personality. He was not overly controlling or broody all of the time. He smiled and laughed frequently, a rarity in any novel. However, that was where the enjoyment ended. His character was not well developed at all. While I understand that the author wanted to maintain some mystery, it is possible to do that while giving the reader a complex character. In this case, he felt flat and cookie cutter. He was a hot piece of ass for the MC. Which was unfortunate, because he had the potential to be infinitely more interesting than Aurora. Even the big twist involving him being the prince  was easily guessed. I honestly hope for the next novel to be alternating POV with him being one. 
 Damien 
 I am pretty sure you could change his name to Draco Malfloy and they would basically be the same character. I kept waiting for him to sneer, "Scared Potter?" but alas it never happened. There were quite a few characters that seemed based off of Harry Potter characters (Professor Dekela comes to mind). He was yet again another underdeveloped character (actually majority were). He was the typical bratty rich boy who casually travels down the path of darkness. 
 Morgana 
 Our antagonist of the novel, yet we primarily just hear of her vs witnessing interactions with her. While this has worked in other novels, it fell flat in this one. What happened instead was just basic factual information about her, then brief page time, then gone again. Her fight with Aurora was underwhelming. An incredibly powerful adult mage thwarted by a teen that can barely use her powers. A lot of attacks hitting a shield, then Morgana panicking and running away, then Aurora casually murdering people in anger over her horse dying.  
 Love Story (light spoilers) 
 Insta-love abounds! Aurora and Rafe barely spent enough time to become friends, much less develop a relationship. Yet low and behold, they loved each other from the moment they laid eyes on each other! Gag! It was not a plausible relationship development wise. They knew nothing about each other besides official titles and that the other person was attractive. Hell, Rafe is engaged to another woman. But alas, that barely matters. Their souls are connected *rolls eyes. At the end, they are holding out on being together, but I do not see that lasting long. 
 In general, I had issues with this novel. A main character who feels no guilt after casually killing people bothers me immensely, even if they are the bad guys. She is 16; she should not handle that well.  While I may give the sequel a chance (especially to see how the new villain develops) this book was astoundingly underwhelming as a whole, and did not live up to my hopes for it.

 Paul has spent the last eight months in England recovering from a fall from Gullfoss Falls (is that even possible?). After this long recovery he is left with a limp and short term loss memory. He can't remember anything that happened during his one year living in Iceland. But it is now time to go back to Iceland and Paul's return brings him a lot of frustration and confusion. He can't remember anyone of his friends, colleagues or anything that happened. 
 I think JL Merrow did a great job at portraying Paul's frustration, confusion and loss of confidence from his short term memory loss. I found myself wanting to reach out and shake him and tell him to "just ask what happened already!" Anyway, I could really feel the frustration. 
 I also found myself at times a bit broken hearted for Viggo. Paul feels Viggo is familiar to him and can't deny their attraction, and well he doesn't. These two jump in bed fairly quickly after Paul gets back even though Paul doesn't actually "know" him (well, remember him really). But it broke my heart a bit to see that things to Viggo mean more than to Paul initially and he restraints his feelings for Paul to give each other a new start. 
 All I want to say is that I loved this book because I loved Viggo even though we don't learn very much about him. But we do learn that he is a lonely, caring and sweet guy. And this leads me to my only real complain about this book No "I Love You's" are exchanged, although you know the feelings are there from both MCs . 
 This book also gets the thumbs up from me for poking fun to Icelandic, British and American cultures. The jabs are subtle but they are there and I enjoyed them.

Edward is the architect who built the house and has a distinct personality - on the OCD side - in which he lives by certain rules and want his women to do the same. If they don't, it's no longer perfect and he moves on. He pretty much caters to no one but himself and yet women are drawn to his "nonchalant" yet take charge attitude. 
 One Folger Street is affordable because whoever decides to live there are automatically test subjects. They live by certain rules and must answer various surveys... certain features such as the shower, may be disabled until the surveys are complete. They will be monitored and lifestyle changes will be strongly suggested to help them live a more perfect life. But to what cost? How far will Edward go to create the perfect life? (Side note though - a shower that automatically knows my temperature setting is a win for me!) 
 I was engaged throughout this entire book. I needed to know what happened from chapter to chapter. I did feel there was some repetitiveness but that certainly was to show the similarities in Emma and Jane's parallel world. I was kept on my toes all the way til the end of the book and loved the little twists thrown in at the end. There isn't really much I can add to the (undoubtedly) thousands of reviews of the LotR trilogy. But this is my fifth reading in something like thirty years, and I can only say that the series is that much better this time than the last time. 
 I paid more attention to the descriptions, to the pacing, to the inferences sprinkled through the book about what was to come, and I can only say that this continues to be my favorite epic/heroic fantasy of all time. The rich tapestry of myth and folklore in addition to the use of language, both native English and derived, makes this an unforgettable read. My personal opinion is that it is 'The Odyssey' of our time. 
 The books surpass the movies by at least an order of magnitude. And RofK is incomparable. Tolkien even manages to make the denouement interesting and action-packed (The Scouring of the Shire).

Everything about this book is so convincing, it's hard to believe this is Susannah Clarke's first novel. I don't mean the footnotes and what must have been the Herculean task of keeping track of an alternative history of about a thousand years (I think it took her ten years to write); I mean about her writing itself. She has a confidence about her voice that make you want to invest your time and energy and a certain amount of love in these characters and her world. And what a world! It's as if the characters from Pride and Prejudice or Persuasion were relocated into a book of British fairytales. I enjoyed this book more than anything I've read for a long time, but since Victorian lit and fairytales are two of my favorite things, I might be a bit biased.

I felt disgusted and hopeless and tortured by the experiences of the protagonist as well as her accounts of the actions taking place around her . . . but it was a good pain. The kind that makes you feel more capable of being a compassionate human being and the kind that makes you want to fight so fucking hard against that sort of unfathomable human cruelty and ignorance.

If you don't take it seriously in a story how seriously are you taking it in real life??? yanno. 
 One more thing. I appreciate when groups of characters (especially characters in jobs that are usually male-dominated, like fighters) are explicitly stated to have both women and men.  When Becca can't get into college, she drives across the country to give herself a year to make it into the acting world in Hollywood. This type of coming-of-age story is so interesting to me because it seems that so many 18-24 year olds struggle to launch into the real world successfully (without parental help). This story took me back to my late teens/early twenties years, although Becca's experiences differ vastly from my own. 
 As I mentioned previously, my main problems are with the content. I have a daughter only a year younger than Becca and there's no way I would be happy with her doing the things that Becca does. I do love at how hard she tries to be self-reliant and how she makes a check list of things to accomplish, but she seems fairly naive and finds herself thrust into the grown up world without someone to help her navigate the channels of adulthood. Her story does give me hope for my kids--that they can find a way to support themselves in this big, crazy world.

Only the last hundred pages earned this one the third star. This book fell into the trap that many sequels to even good series (which the first Nightrunner books were) do, especially ones that take place after the main characters have fallen in love. For some reason the author doesn't feel the need to give either of the parties much of a personality characteristic, other than being in love with each other. Its like since they don't have to woo each other, or unwittingly fall in love, therefore they don't have to be enticing to each other.. which has the unfortunate downside that they are not interesting to me either. Instead, the book substituted with rehashing events from books past and melodramatic thoughts and dialogue that made the two protagonists entirely different characters from the ones I remember. 
 I just have a real problem with the idea that people suddenly cease to be themselves when they fall in love, and may have no other opinions or thoughts other than 'I love you.' That is not what happens after happily ever after. At least I hope it isn't, and if it is, stop trying to sell it to us, writers, moviemakers and song-singers of the world, because that should not be something that we should want. 
 However. I will admit that both main characters suddenly got interesting again in the last hundred pages of the book, when they suddenly became people again, with conflicting opinions and shades of grey in their thoughts. Only then do any interesting questions or ideas come up, or does the reader feel any interest in the outcome. Before that, the most interesting character was Khenir/Ilar, the former enemy/lover of one of the protagonists, and he's kind of despicable, if pitiable, in a lot of ways.  
 I also felt the book suffered from pacing problems. The first three hundred pages were repetitive descriptions of our protagonists' life as slaves, thoughts of escaping.. and doing nothing about it, pretty much over and over, and just "playing the role to the hilt," until they get a real chance to escape. Also, she dropped anvils like she was Coyote looking for Road Runner, man. Unbelievable. Her writing tone was very uneven. She often used a more archaic tone with older word choice and descriptions, and then would drop into a more modern feel very abruptly. It threw me out of the story a bit. 
 There's clearly an open ending, and there's clearly another book coming. I'm hoping that that last hundred pages indicated that the quality of the first trilogy will be back in the next book. We'll see!

There didn't seem to be much depth to the characters themselves, and that combined with a lot of the dialogue made it seem like they weren't real people. 
 I understand that Macallan and Levi's friendship started because they both liked a cult, British television show, but once they were older and had been friends for a while, it seemed like that was still all they had in common. Oh, the narrative hammered it home a number of times that they were best friends and each other's better halves, basically, but I don't think it came across very well other than that. There were times when it just wasn't realistic -- I'm still puzzled about the scene where Macallan takes Levi to her mother's grave. That strikes me as weird and a little creepy. 
 I was intrigued by the premise of the book, because I was hoping that it would deliver on what the title says -- that these two were better off friends. But nope. It fell to the same tired stereotype and had the two of them fall in love with each other and end up dating. I think I would much rather have read a story where the two leads either attempt to date and realize they don't work as a couple or never bother in the first place because they truly have no desire to take their relationship to the next level. Because men and women can be friends, yet they almost never are, unless they are different sexual orientations. 
 All in all, the story was cute, but it was kind of meh and not all that memorable.

While I thought the storyline was maybe a bit too extreme, I do believe this is a very important book. It is the completely uncensored story of a girl who is raped and later isolated and ridiculed by her community. Anyone who have experienced any form of sexual abuse, will relate to both the thoughts of the main character and the way she's treated by friends, family and the people in her community. 
 I really enjoyed O'Neill's interesting perspective on social media. Having online support and twitter trends can feel like a massive support, but it can also be overwhelming and isolating. Does it really help to have the support of thousands of people if your friends and family treat you like you're partly to blame for what happens? O'Neill also, of course, explores the dangers of social media and how quickly something can spread. The spreading of sensitive pictures or messages can be extremely damaging on people and their lives and I think this book really showed both the positive and negative sides of it. 
 Even though 'Asking For It' is a work of fiction, it is also very much a reality. Rape culture is a real issue in today's society, whether we like to admit to it or not. Victims of sexual abuse are way too often made to feel guilty for what happened to them because they wore "revealing clothing", drank too much alcohol etc.. We need to emphasize again and again that nothing can ever excuse rape and that the victim should never be blamed. We need to live in a world where we instead of teaching girls how to avoid being raped, we teach everyone that it is only acceptable to have sex with someone if you have their willingly given consent. 
 'Asking For It' is not necessarily the best written book I've ever read, but it is a very important book. I hope it gets read by many people and that these issues keeps getting discussed. We need to talk about it, we need to understand it and we need to change.

 I felt like things were wrapped up a little too neatly. Of course, I love a happily ever after ending, but with so much conflict with Caymen's mom and her family, it was just a little to quickly resolved for me. I guess I wanted more story!! :)

I wish I had enough words to articulate how much I enjoyed this book, but I don't, so I'll give you a wordy review anyway. 
 I wanted to read this book for ages and held off on it for so long. I don't quite know why I waited, but I will say that the wait was worth it and I was SO GLAD to discover this book was as good as I hoped it would be (and then some). The writing is beautiful, the characters amazing, and LA breathes so much life into the book. 
 First, I'd like to address the movie-making aspect of the book. I got a minor in film studies (which doesn't qualify me to make movies by any stretch of the imagination), but I loved how it was worked into the book. Emi's job as a set-designer was fascinating to read about, and made me consider some of the stuff I'd already known about from my film studies classes in the past in another light. Everything's chosen so carefully to dress a set, even if it's only in the background for a few shots. It says miles about the characters. You need the plates, the sofa, the prints that they would have, not that you (as a director) like yourself, and you can tell a million different stories with those choices. I also liked how Emi realizes her initial choice of sofa was "wrong" and it wouldn't fit the film; it felt like she learnt more about her job rather than just thinking "I know everything all the time." It was such a lovely detail and I wanted her to get that sofa, but when she didn't and saw how well it worked out, I was just as pleased.  Even though Emi's a wunderkind and is already talented, it was nice to see her grow within her own profession. The descriptions were, frankly, magical and spell-binding; I wanted to spend more time in that world. 
 But one of the other things I loved about this book is the dichotomy between fantasy and reality. Emi realizes that real life isn't always as neat as it is in the movies, much as she wants it to be. I worried for a while that this would just be "rich girls in LA," and I was pleased that it didn't turn that way. Ava and Jamal have had radically different lives than Emi and Charlotte, and there were a few conversations that addressed this aspect rather than glossing it over entirely. It felt more realistic than the Gossip Girl style of "everyone's rich all the time, what poor people?" and I was pleased that LaCour included this. (Also, can I just say that the moment I decided I loved this book was when Emi describes her parents' academic interests, namely pop culture and black studies? AMAZING.) 
 The characters themselves were fantastic. I loved Emi and Charlotte's relationship--it was a great, supportive friendship, where they seemed concerned with helping one another. Ava was wonderful, and I loved watching Emi fall in love with her (and vice versa). By the end of the book, I felt like they were real people. The danger with writing a book with so much Hollywood in there is that the characters run the danger of becoming caricatures or over-the-top, but they all felt believable. 
 And the romance! God, it was adorable. I like Incidentally Queer Characters and Emi hits that right on the head. At the beginning, we know she's broken up with Morgan, and she's upset about it. That's it. Not "oh god, I like girls, what does this make me?" Coming out stories have their place but it's also nice to read something where Emi's sexuality isn't the focus of the story, but more of her career and her falling in love. The romance itself was a slow build and, again, felt real and satisfying. Emi and Ava belong together. Maybe a little fluffy? Maybe. But it was enchanting all the same. 
 Anyway, if you're looking for cute lesbian YA, this will satisfy your cravings.

Lizzie and Diesel are after another magic stone - the one for lust. They go on a magical scavenger hunt across Boston trying to stay one step ahead of Wulf and his assistant Hatchet, and the truly evil Dierdre or does she go by Anarchy now? 
 Carl the monkey says 'eep'. 
 *** 
 I think I read book 1 as a library borrow. Honestly I can't remember. And that's the issue with these books. They are an easy read. But I read 103 pages the first night and could not say what it was about the next morning. It just slides past. And not because it's easy reading. What was that old saying about easy reading was hard writing? Not here; it's just fluff. That's fine, if that is all you want. But do not expect anything to strain the little grey cells here. 
 It is supposed to be a magical realism world. Lizzie is an 'unmentionable'. They each have different skills and there are some unexplainable things that they do. She met Diesel in book 1. Here, he's still around because he needs her to help him. She can tell which object is magic; that's her special skill. 
 Diesel can find things. His cousin Wulf is the dark Diesel. Wulf's helper Hatchet is just... singularly annoying with his constant medieval speech. 
 The agency that Diesel works for provides him with everything he needs. His car blows up, a new one is delivered. He has endless credit for shopping sprees. His assistants walk out the door carrying a large framed Van Gogh painting, a movable model and something else (I've forgotten) and they disappear within seconds. And no, they didn't get in a car because they just drove two there for Lizzie and Diesel. There's magic realism and there's handwavium. 
 And Glo? I have no words for Glo. 
 Even if it is magic, it has to follow the rules. 
 The magic stones they are searching for engender each sin. I remember now that gluttony was in book 1 and it made Lizzie overeat. Here, she holds the stone of lust (transformed into the stone of true love) and it doesn't affect her. Or her friends. 
 Evanovich has a formula and this series is the same. There's even a Grandma Masur character - an old man, Sandman, who can bend spoons. 
 It's a 2 1/2 but sliding towards 2 stars. 
 Wulf constantly disappears in clouds of smoke like an amateur magician. A person's magic shop gets burnt down and she just says it's okay because she was over-insured and wanted to rebuild. wtf? Hatchet slices Glo up with a knife and she still thinks he's okay. He's creepy and messed up. Even Wulf can see that.

This is fanfic. Straight up. Sometimes, it's clever, enjoyable fanfic, the kind that makes you look at canon in a different way, subtly fixes problems, and enriches the original. Sometimes, it's fluffy, indulgent kind that exists to satisfy fans' cravings for things that a professional author (and editing team) cool judgement ruthlessly excludes. Sometimes, it's the headbangingly stupid, OOC, cliche-storm kind. 
 Also, it's a script-fic, so Fanfiction.Net wouldn't accept it. 
 Even if you go in knowing that it's a play, and not a novel, it's hard to adjust your expectations of Harry Potter's typical prose to what's on the page. I kept flip-flopping between trying to visualize the story itself, and trying to imagine what the stage play would be like--and I got quite curious, sometimes, of how all the various effects (like characters subtly aging while onstage) would be managed, how the audience would ever be able to see the exact expression in a Patronus's eyes, and, if all these other wonders could be managed, why the Sorting Hat evidently had to be an actor walking around on stage). Sometimes the stage directions are quite detailed, almost lapsing into prose, while other times they are so sparse that I was confused by the actual action and what characters were "on stage" at the time. 
 The characterization of Harry, Ron, Hermione, Ginny, and the others from the books is uneven. Sometimes, they feel like logical progressions of their young book-selves, while some aspects are awkward, forced, or come out of nowhere. The whole conflict between Harry and Albus is central to the whole story, yet we are never given any kind of satisfactory answer of where it comes from. Yes, sometimes parents' and kids' personalities just don't click, but aside from one messy scene in the middle of the play, we never get any hint that Harry actually did anything to make Albus feel undervalued or unloved. It's as if the story wants to play with the idea of Harry as a less-than-ideal father, but refuses to actually commit fully to the concept because of fear of irritating fans. The result is that Albus comes across as mostly whiny and irritating, and incredibly self-absorbed, something he gets called out on a total of one times (but it was great. Thanks Scorpius.) All the angry teenagers and bumbling parent drama is a big part of why The Casual Vacancy was a DNF for me, and I did NOT appreciate it scumming up Harry Potter. 
 And then there is a big honking pile of fanfic tropes that makes up the plot. It would be funny, how much this story seems to think it's being original, if this wasn't, by some monstrous quirk of reality, the official eighth story. Harry Potter may have more fanfic than any other fandom (I said MAY), and it has tons of its own conventions and typical plots, as well as those common to the medium. This story seems to want to dip its toes in all of them. There's Time-Turner shenanigans, of course.  The ending of Act Three was incredibly reminiscent of "How It Should Have Ended"'s take on the franchise  Alternate universes, set-right-what-once-went-wrong, shipping... Gratuitous emotional scenes  The whole conversation between Severus Snape and Scorpius, ending with him saying that he was proud that Harry named his kid after him, was so cheesy it was impossible to enjoy, even though I wanted to ... and a ridiculous freaking Villain Sue who turns out to be  Voldemort's secret daughter  of all things. Even My Immortal is better than that, Rowling. 
 Scorpius was delightful. I would so much rather read about a lonely, goodhearted Slytherin nerd than the suave, less-bigoted Draco-Xerox that had been previously making the fanfic rounds under his name. I was pleasantly surprised that the story chose to re-affirm certain canon couples, despite some of JK's recent comments about them. Albus was sometimes okay. 
 Overall, an entertaining story that I probably would have enjoyed a lot if I had read it on a fansite. As an official sequel...well, there's a reason Fanon Discontinuity is a thing (omitting the TV Tropes link out of mercy for those who had things they wanted to do this week).

I felt like I was travelling with him, seeing what he saw, hearing what he heard, feeling what he felt. The fact that this book is non-fiction made it feel even more real.
