At times this felt a little repetitive or as if Diamond were hammering home some pretty obvious points. But! I think the scientific approach to history is important, and I also believe that deliberately misunderstanding history and science is the number one tool of racists and bigots, so a clear, straightforward rebuttal of those ideas is really valuable. Diamond's writing is to-the-point and easy to read, and I would have read another four hundred pages about the things he goes into in the Afterword- about how environmental factors play into modern economies. If you wanted to teach the most depressing history class ever, this would be a good companion with Zinn's A People's History and Brown's Bury My Heart at Wounded Knee. This book is actually surprisingly apolitical considering its subject matter, which would maybe make it even more appealing to the kind of people who need its message most.
I couldn't keep the book down. I would wake up in the morning wanting to read more!

At first I was kinda hesitant to read this, that I'm thinking it would be another story just like Twilight. But I'm wrong, I loved every page of Patch and Nora. Patch is swoony, and Nora is one little bugger that can't be tamed. It's my first time to read stories of fallen angels and I really like it.

First read 4-10-2012. Picked it up again April 2015. Second time reading this and I've also watched the movie. Love what this book says about love and family in an imperfect situation. A definite chick flick with smiles, tears and romance. Favorite scene is the wedding and all the versions of Henry who came together to make it happen.

The Ice Twins is by turns a thriller, a mystery and a ghost story. It was an awesome read which was recommended to me as part of a reading challenge on our group's Goodreads page. Thanks Lisa Palmer! 
 Lydia and Kirstie, identical twins, were born on a frigid day in winter. For that, and for their "ice-blue eyes and snowy-blonde hair," their grandfather dubbed them "the Ice Twins." 
 Sarah and Angus, the twins' parents are reeling after one of the 6-year-old twins dies in an accident. A year later, they have moved and tried to start over with their remaining daughter. But then, this daughter starts saying she is the one who was thought to be dead. This book twists and turns around the identity of the girl, whether the accident was actually an accident, and how much culpability the parents have in these situations. 
 I loved that it seemed like a straight-forward incident and then it was altered as we heard more information from each of the characters. The ending was amazing even though you are left reeling and wondering exactly what happened. An amazing read.

*****You can read my full review at Darling & Co.***** 
 A lot happens in the 3rd House of Night book, and it all only takes course over a few days. I found myself becoming annoyed with Zoey more in this book; she is making a lot of basic mistakes that people in books/movies/TV shows always make. And just like every other character, her mistakes pile up, they're found out, and she falls hard. 
 During this series, I have spent a lot of time thinking about the phrase "the path to hell is paved with good intentions." Zoey has a lot of good intentions with trying to handle everything on her own, but she could have handled everything a lot better. She could have filled her friends in on it once Neferet left for her vacation and they could have taken care of Stevie Rae then, and they probably would have understood better why she hadn't told them when Neferet was around. 
 My hopes for the next book are that we learn more about Stevie Rae; that we figure out what the hell happened with Aphrodite; and that Zoey's friends give her a hard time about all the shit she's pulled, but they find a way to work through it and can take down Neferet.

I have really enjoyed this series. I find that while I'm not really much of a steampunk fan, I absolutely loved the characters. I was very happy with how the series ended. I've heard some of the characters show up in The Custard Protocol, so I'll be reading that soon. 
 I have to mention that I laughed out loud many times while reading this book. However, that scene where we thought Conall was dying/dead? I cried buckets. Really. I hoped he was not actually dead, but there was enough uncertainty that it really affected me.

A sequel that's better than the original? Given that the most interesting character - Jeffery - from the first book is offstage, Birdsall has managed quite a feat. My second grader was enchanted by the Penderwicks in this incarnation, and that's probably an even better indication of its quality than my own calmer reception.

First, the cover of this novel is totally awesome. It really depicts the main character as I see her. As for the book, I also thought the main characters of Fenn and Aurora were totally awesome. YA novels seem to currently be plagued by female protagonists who are, well, for lack of a better word, soppy. They whine a lot, and it gets horribly annoying. I never once felt this about Aurora. She was a strong person, who even when confused about what was going on, was determined to rise above it. She was stubborn at times, and you might find yourself telling her to just stop and think. This was actually amusing for me. She was so realistic. This says a lot for a fantasy novel. Onto the wonderful Fenn. He was realistic, perfect in Aurora's eyes, but you were able to see that he wasn't perfect. He made some bad decisions, but he admitted when he was wrong. That made him a strong character, plus his blue eyes reminded me of someone special!So, without putting spoilers in, the story line was excellent. It flowed nicely, for it wasn't rushed, and it wasn't too slow. At times it was confusing, but in a good way. I enjoyed this confusion because it allowed you to feel as Aurora did. I try to be honest with my reviews, so here is the reason it wasn't five stars for me: I did spot a few times where the novel went from present tense to past tense in the narrative, and there were some descriptions that I wasn't fond of. It wasn't that they weren't well written. I am just not one for lots of descriptions, but this is completely a personal preference and should not hinder your choice to read this novel. I recommend you do. This is a series that I fully intend to complete reading, and believe me, that says a lot, for I am not a fan of many serialized books!

"Those who don't build must burn... There's some of it in all of us" 
 The premise was relevant, chilling and scary in fact -- because I am reading an actual book that focused on a setting that destroys them and treat them as a taboo. The book "predicted" the takeover of television and mass media in written literature and this gave it a timeless grade to it. 
 However, the story felt short and the last several pages were a bit underwhelming. I felt that the storyline didn't progress in the same rate as the first two parts. I also thought that the characters and scenes can be fleshed out more (like for Clarisse, Mildred and even Faber's part), but instead we got more of Montag's inner thought. Apparently though, Bradbury thought that letting Clarisse live is a great idea (he got it from the movie adaptation that didn't follow most of the book's element) and he eventually employed it on the stage adaptation of the book. Last complaint will be that setting didn't feel futuristic enough (especially for his writing time), but I guess it's good too because we had more focus on the story and (a bit of) the characters. 
 This is still definitely a classic and I have to give Bradbury a break with all these as the book was written 50 years ago! Recommended for that and for being a quick read.

The Bone Clocks is the first David Mitchell I picked up and I wasn't quite sure what to expect. I've caught bits and pieces of Cloud Atlas on HBO and each time I flipped to something else a few minutes later feeling intrigued, but absolutely baffled. I try not to read a whole lot about books before jumping into them so I don't spoil anything for myself, but from what I gleaned from Cloud Atlas and the blurbs I'd read about The Bone Clocks on GoodReads, I gathered that this was scifi-ish and a little weird. Perfect, two areas I enjoy thoroughly. 
 What I was not anticipating was something quite so sprawling. It spans 7 decades (plus a few centuries if you factor in the Marinus/Esther backstory) and features five distinct narrators. The characters are all wonderfully flawed and expertly voiced. It's self referential and self indulgent. There's a subtle humor threaded throughout which makes it especially fun, human, and grounded. Perhaps what it does best is mix the elements of hard knocks real life (which can mean anything from first heartbreak to catastrophic global meltdown) and fantastic, escapist occultism. If scifi/fantasy isn't your cuppa, you'll probably disagree. If nothing else, I was totally engrossed in this book and couldn't put it down once I'd picked it up. 
 As much as I enjoyed it, however, there were a few things I got stuck on. From what I gather, Mitchell uses some of the same characters in his other books, so maybe had I read those I wouldn't have felt like a few of the story lines were just a matter of convenience rather than significance. What I'm mostly talking about here is the Crispin Hershey story line. I loved how utterly terrible he was, but looking back oh him now, I'm not sure what point he served. First off - this guy is absolutely terrible. He's a pompous, elitist, misogynistic prick who's coming to grips with the fact that he's washed up as a writer, his marriage is over, and he's reaching middle age. But he's so perfectly rendered that it's hard not to enjoy reading his section. It seems that Mitchell mostly uses Hershey to anticipate some of the criticism The Bone Clocks would receive. Which...fine, but unnecessary, and could have been done just as well with Hugo Lamb and his friends. The whole Hershey/Cheeseman subplot didn't end up going anywhere either. It just reintroduced a peripheral character who turns out, in the end, to remain a peripheral character. I thoroughly enjoyed the Hershey character, but when all's said and done, he doesn't seem all that significant. 
 And then there's the final section of the book - we return to Holly in Sheep's Head in the year 2043. Through our over consumption, exorbitant waste, and general recklessness, humanity pushed the world past its tipping point. Electrical grids are failing, the internet is a thing of the past, food and medicine are in short supply, and most major governments have essentially disbanded. This final section serves as a pretty stark contrast to the preceding 500 pages or so that revolved primarily around a fantasy/scifi battle replete with reincarnation, clairvoyance, multiple dimensions, and body snatching. Mitchell slams the brakes on this action and pulls you out of the dream world before you know what's happened, and I'm not sure I liked it. Jury's still out on that. It felt a bit like an addendum that he tacked on to the end so he could wax on about our path to disaster. Or maybe the whole jarring juxtaposition is the point. Like I said, jury's still out. 
 Overall I definitely enjoyed this and am a little less intimidated by Cloud Atlas now.
All I can say is, Elise effing deserved it.

I enjoyed it. I like the idea of a virus that kills all the girls at age 20 and the boys at age 25. In an attempt to wipe out disease, genetic tampering left one generous healthy and long-lived, yet the following generation with a ticking clock. It makes you not want to waste a single minute. I wanted to smack Linden for being so absolutely ignorant about the world around him and the bubble his father has him living in. How can he be so blind? Also, how come nobody (including Rhine) has dared to clue him in. He seems to be a gentle, caring young man. I kept wanting Rhine to tell him about Rose and their baby, about what's going on in his own basement, about her brother, about how his prospective wives were really gathered up, about Jenna and her sisters, etc. I just didn't understand why Rhine didn't even consider telling him. I guess she was too scared of what his father, Vaughn, would do. That he was just too powerful and telling Lindon the truth would bring her more danger and foil any chance of ever escaping. Cecily drove me nuts from the beginning. I wonder if what makes Rhine so special is that she was somehow born naturally, without any messed up genetics from the previous generation. If her unique eyes are a marker of her unique genes. I wonder if she won't get the virus and somehow Vaughn knows/suspects that. If that is the case, he will never let her go. There is nowhere she can run to escape him.

I admit, I feel a little guilty giving Written on the Body only 3 stars. You should see my copy of this book--I've highlighted favorite lines liberally. She's consistently poetic--like, "I barged my way through a herd of cattle, hooves braceleted with mud. My own feet were clod-fettered" (p. 177). Lovely. 
 There are whole passages that are simply masterful. For example, the narrator (never explicitly gendered) sleeps with a woman named Gail Right; sleeps with her in the most literal sense of the term. The scene when they wake up and she's still there is a brilliant movement from general depression to intenser and intenser disgust and even panic. This may sound odd if you haven't read the book, but one of the most powerful instances in the book was when the narrator sees that some of Gail Right's chipped red nail polish is getting on her greasy sandwich--it's something so particular, yet it's a turning point and really made me feel what the narrator was feeling. Winterson really knows how to use detail for emotional resonance. That said, I did indeed give this book 3 stars. I enjoyed it, it's just not one of my favorites. I wanted to know more about the main characters, the unnamed narrator and Louise. Most of what I know about Louise is physical; from the book's beginning to its end, I felt very distanced from her, as though I weren't really meeting Louise through the narrator's eyes but merely hearing someone talk about her, someone I'd never met myself. That made a lot of the flowery language about love read as too abstract and therefore not emotionally resonant. I also didn't care whether the narrator found Louise in the end or whether she died of cancer or not, because I simply didn't know these people well enough . 
 So, as a novel, I was kinda 'meh.' That said, as a work of poetry, I can't recommend it highly enough. So exquisite and interesting. 
 I'll end with the quote that pretty much summarizes the whole book: 
 "Don't you think it's strange that life, described as so rich and full, a camel-trail of adventure, should shrink to this coin-sized world? A head on one side, a story on the other. Someone you loved and what happened. That's all there is when you dig in your pockets. The most significant thing is someone else's face. What else is embossed on your hands but her?" (p. 181)

This one was just as good as the first book and it wasn't AS boring in the beginning. It didn't take 100 pages to get into, but it was still a little slow moving. But let me tell you, once the book begins to pick up speed it became impossible to put down. 
 I won't go into plot details because frankly, everyone I know has already read this book, or heard about this book and I also just don't feel like it. The main appeal for me is the character of Lisbeth Salander. She is a kick ass heroine who you don't really want to piss off. 
 My one complaint, which is the same as the first book, it's hard for me to keep track of the people because of their names. They are confusing to me, what can I say? Other than that, the book is awesome.

Finally, the children have come near the headquarters of the V.F.D., but for the first time the journey begins with Sunny separated from her siblings. 
 Almost nothing definite about the V.F.D. has been revealed, but having the events happen on its grounds helps bring the pieces together. With so little clues discovered, the children recall names and incidents from the past, eventually grasping a general idea about V.F.D. -- and feel like being a part of the organisation. 
 Reaching the end of the series... I'm starting to fear Snicket would really make the orphans be unfortunate forever.

If you've never known anyone who has told a giant whopper of a lie, then you might read this book and think, "This is silly, no one would EVER make up a peanut allergy." But I've known two people, one a college freshman, the other a 30-year old professional adult, to tell a Big Fat Lie in situations where they were about to meet a whole bunch of new people that they would inevitably know for a very long time. Both of them told their lies for the same reasons that Sadie does, but being older, the stakes were higher, and things didn't work out so well once they 'fessed up. One lost a lot of friends, the other lost a job. 
 I think this would be a great book for middle-school aged children to read, to help them see the long-term consequences of lying and (hopefully) choose to avoid it at all costs!
Interesting series idea. Full of action and kick ass females and rather alpha males.
Glory O'Brien reads kind of like a commencement speech in novel form, which is both good and bad.

Dark demons, mad gods, angels driven insane... this book has all that and makes a fine, but disturbing tale. 
 A man and his partner from Elise and James' past arrive in the city and begin a series of attacks, including wiping out all of Elise's funds. For protection for her collegues and friends and for a source of income, Elise makes a deal to aid the Night Hag, the area's Overlord. Still, it seems she may not have been quite specific enough and perhaps did not think things through enough.
I've come to realise that I'm never to old to read such a book, one I would have thoroughly enjoyed 35 years ago. Magic.

After We Fall, my first read from Marquita Valentine, unfortunately fell into "mediocre" territory for me. And I hate to say that because I've heard excellent things about the author. 
 I liked Hunter and Evangeline overall. However, taking their respective backgrounds into account, aspects of their personalities didn't seem to ring true. 
 Hunter's character, for example, seemed contradictory at times: like his comment in Chapter 9, "The last thing I would ever do is lay a hand on another person," and his hobby of underground fighting (chapter 3). For me, this discrepancy was never resolved.  His job, on the other hand, made far more sense to me; I would have loved seeing more of him in that role. 
 Given Evangeline's reservations about men, especially an ex-husband who'd deceived her so thoroughly, her trust in Hunter seemed rushed and a bit unbelievable. While I wanted for her to trust and love and heal, I wasn't convinced on her behalf that she wasn't getting duped again. Yes, Hunter was sweet and patient with her, but so was her ex when putting on a show. So, while readers are privy to Hunter's inner monologue and know him to be a good guy, I wanted "proof" for her beyond gestures and a mutual friend. 
 Little seemed to actually happen in the novel, other than the MCs bumping into one another a lot and subsequently dating. In a few spots, the narrative seemed to be building up to some big moments, which then flickered out instead of combusting like they should have. The villain is an interesting character, and the novel's opening and climax are well-executed. Overall, though, I wanted to see more depth, more build-up, more time spent on developing the characters and their relationship. 
 Based on other reviews I've seen, this perspective on After We Fall puts me in the minority! For many of those who'd been following the series, Hunter and Evangeline's story was an anticipated read.
4.5 stars. review coming soon.

This is an enjoyable story with some suitably dark elements. It has a dash of teen angst (which is to be expected in YA)and sometimes I thought the main character should have been more fae savvy considering the stories she was told as a child and her stated interest in books and libraries, but she did learn from her mistakes eventually. The story was magical and well written. It makes a good vacation book.

This one so made up for the last one! Why did I wait so long to read this one? (I mean I know why, I didn't like 5 so I wasn't in a hurry and then I moved so it got stuck in a box for forever.) But this book was wonderful! It brought back all the wonderfulness from the first 3 books. 
 Simon's story in this one is the saddest, closely followed by Magnus. I love Simon because I can very much relate to him. I'm usually the odd person out, I'm usually the nerdy one and no one understands my references, and I have loved the person who is way out of my league (only he never loved me back). Simon proves that he's a hero multiple times throughout the series, but in this book, he gives the ultimate sacrifice, worse than his life, his memories. He does it so that way all the people he loves can live, so that Alec and Magnus can have a life together, so that everything will go back to being okay and that the woman he loves will have a life full of joy, even if he isn't a part of it. I'd like to think that I would do this too. Of course, Magnus is able to make everything right by making Simon into a Shadowhunter and slowly returning his memories to him. He is eventually reunited with Izzy, and although he doesn't yet remember loving her, I can tell that they will have a long, loving life together (watch me be totally wrong). 
 Magnus's story is almost just as heartbreaking. He has spent all this time hiding his history, his story, because he is ashamed of it and wants nothing to do with it. But now he has to call up (literally) the part that he is ashamed of the most, his father, one of the Nine Princes of Hell. I mean, I think anyone to be ashamed of having him for a father. But he calls him up so that way his friends and loved ones, and Alec, can continue living life, even it means he is mortal and cannot live out his time with Alec. This is of course when Simon steps in. But then after everyone (minus Simon) is back safely, Magnus tells Alec in the sweetest way possible that he loves Alec completely and fully buy giving Alec a journal of his life's history. 
 Of course Jace and Clary end up together very happy-shocker. 
 Jocelyn and Luke finally get to get married! Now that all the wars are over, everyone is back together, and everything is fine, they can finally get married. I mean, the rehearsal dinner was only 3 books ago. I would have just found a Justice of the Peace and got hitched.

3.5 Stars rounded up 
 I found this book a gentle and romantic MMM story that was not all about the sex. So if you like your MMM less about three bodies working together and three people coming together in a relationship you may like this story. 
 I liked this story just fine BUT I had a couple of issues with it that ultimately made me give it a lower rating than I would have. Just a quick recap of the story. The story is told from all three MCs POV at different points in time, although Charlie (Chase) serves as the narrator. The story starts with Charlie being 15-16 yo. and meeting Scott who moves in next door and becomes his first love. Charlie and Scott are together for what's probably about 4 years until Scott moves to Las Vegas and leaves Charlie behind. Then about 5 years pass until Charlie (then going by Chase) meets Adan. Adan's and Charlie's bit is told by both Adan and Charlie. These two date for what's almost a year. Then 10 years or so pass until all three meet again. The last third of the story is told by Charlie and Scott. 
 OK. so what I didn't like about this story happened on that last second third or when the MMM begins: 
 First, I found utter crap one of the reasons why Adan and Scott decide to go for Charlie and that is because they are both tops and they "need" a bottom. Sure, Adan and Scott love each other and have been together for five years but their "problem" is that they are not 100% compatible in the bedroom because they are both tops. So what does that mean? are they both settling? Call me crazy but dissatisfaction in the bedroom is a sure way to head to splitsville. Whatever, the guys have hung in there for five years and now Charlie can fill that void, neat huh? Well, not really in my book. There is honestly so much more about Charlie that just his hole, so the fact that needing a bottom features so predominantly as a reason for them to pursue Charlie rubs me the wrong way! 
 Also, I was not brimming with joy about the way they come together again. It is by total chance! Yet Adan and Scott are both SO happy to see Charlie again and immediately want him back YET in ten years they never thought to seek him out? I am mostly more appalled that Scott never made a move to do this. After all he was friends with his sister for all those years so he had the connection to get in touch with him. At least when Adan and Charlie split Charlie disappeared from Adan's life not leaving Adan a way to find him. In the end Adan who treated him the worst is the one who seems more worthy of him. I get that for 5 of those years Scott had Adan but if he had loved Charlie for all of those years he should have been more proactive in seeking him out and at least knowing he was OK. Instead at the end of 15 years we have Scott and Adan leading a "happy" life whereas Charlie (who was always sweet and worthy of happiness) has become a bitter man. That's just not right. 
 Finally, and I understand that this was to create a dramatic effect, if Scott and his sister were friends he would have been at the funeral which means he would have seen Scott before he actually does.  
 BUT, in the end this book may be a great way for those who normally hate MMM stories to read a romantic one that ends in a HEA.

LOOOOOVED! 
 The dark heroine/origin of an anti-heroine is so intriguing! I loved it, and can't wait to continue with the series.

Great first book to a new trilogy! 
 Also props for a few mentions on a lady's time of the month.

4.5 
 Loved it!! Such a cool world filled with great characters and scientifically explained magic which was a nice change of pace. I know everyone is totally in love with The Darkling, but UNPOPULAR OPINION TIME: I AM NOT A FAN. 
 Can't wait to start book two!

This is such a hard book for me to rate. I can't decide if I want to give it 2 or 3 stars. My first reaction was that it was decent, if nothing I'd remember even two weeks from now. But the more I think about it, the more my opinion goes down. And I only just finished it last night. 
 Thing is, I think my expectations were already pretty low. I have gotten to the point now where I expect absolutely despicable writing and stupid plots and cheesy romances with any YA paranormal romance, so when I find one that's even mildly above that I get excited and automatically want to tack on an extra star. It has gotten to the point now that I just sort of sigh to myself and accept whatever they throw at me. 
 Everyone just seems too fake to me. Aleyx is such a ridiculous name to me (I'm not even sure I spelled it right) and seemed like a convenient way to have a weird spelling of a name. Same with Syrine and Eron (Serena and Aaron? No?) Tori was a complete Hispanic stereotype, and apparently all she's good for is cussing in Spanish and being a backstabbing bitch friend. 
 Aleyx is cold hearted, and he will be melted by the fiery Cara Sweeney. She has red hair of course, and he is tanned of course with sparkling clear eyes of some kind. 
 Not to mention that apparently two entire worlds depending on TEENAGERS WITH HORMONES GETTING PLACED TOGETHER. Who are the most irrational people on the planet? Right. Now let's put them together and make them mankind's only hope of survival. 
 Yeah, the more I think about it the less I like it.

Dear Miss Lee, 
 It has been far too long since we've been graced with your sweet voice. 
 Love, 
 The Scout in all of us.
Such an emotional ride.

Thanks to the publisher for an advance reader's copy. 
 When I was a kid, I was very very very obsessed with the Titanic, but in a sort of unhealthy way. It TERRIFIED me. If I thought about it too much around water, I'd get lightheaded and have to sit down. I wanted to learn everything possible about it, but was so deathly afraid that I couldn't touch the pages of my books about it. By the time the movie came out, I was much more reasonable about everything, but looking at pictures of the wreck still makes my heart race. 
 I was a little skeptical to request The Midnight Watch because YIKES TITANIC BOOK! and because I'm so often disappointed with historical fiction (I think it often works too hard to establish the world without giving enough substance), but the idea to tell the Californian's story was too good to resist. I haven't been able to stop thinking about the book since I finished. It starts a bit slow, to establish personalities and relationships between the characters, but I got to a point midway through where I couldn't put it down. I loved David Dyer's speculated reason why the Californian didn't respond to the Titanic's distress rockets, and  that it didn't resort to a big shocking secret. His proposed answer is far more subtle and revealing of human nature, and I loved it.  Reading this reawakened my (hopefully more grounded) interest in the Titanic while adding new insight into the disaster. I'm so pleased to have found this book!

(Full review to come later, hopefully) 
 Some parts of this book are more interesting and useful than others, but all of the chapters were well written and engaging and contributed to his overarching arguments about predicting violence. De Becker is clearly an expert and an engaging narrator, successfully blending humor and instruction and gravity. 
 If you have to read just one chapter of this book, definitely read the chapter titled "Survival Signals." It's about how you can be aware when someone is manipulating you and/or is considering or preparing to do you harm, and it's such important information for everyone, especially for women. On second thought, also read "In the Presence of Danger," because that first chapter contains a crime story that he then uses as his example to deconstruct in "Survival Signals."

FAMILY. DAD. MOM. GRANDMA. OSCAR. 
 EMOTION. LOVE. LIFE. MEMORIES. GRIEF. 
 EXTREMELY LOUD AND INCREDIBLY CLOSE 
 (You'll get my caption once you have read this book :3) 
 "I like to see people reunited, I like to see people run to each other, I like the kissing and the crying, I like the impatience, the stories that the mouth can't tell fast enough, the ears that aren't big enough, the eyes that can't take in all of the change, I like the hugging, the bringing together, the end of missing someone." 
 -- Jonathan Safran Foer, Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close 
 This is a sorrowful yet heart-warming novel of a boy's journey of keeping his father alive in his memory. I typically get highly emotional when a story talks about his/her father that is why this novel truly moved me. Now, I perfectly understand and feel deep compassion and empathy for people who have suffered tragic events.. 
 (I quote) "I regret that it takes a life to learn how to live." 
 -Ironically, this is how life moves...constantly. 
 I really felt bad for Oskar and his troubles. The story made me want to help him myself. I cried for Oskar's love towards his Father. I think it's really a curse to lose a parent that way :( 
 Oskar Schell will stay with me for a very long time. :') 
 Overall, I was inspired and impressed by Foer's writing style. I consider him now as one of my favorite authors. 
 THIS BOOK IS ABSOLUTELY ONE OF THE BEST EVER.

Lily is a child. She is a five year old who hates bad words, who cries when she doesn't get her way, and thinks all things related to boys are icky. 
 Never mind that she's supposed to be in high school, or that that she has a boyfriend whom she supposedly loves. Her course of action when she doesn't like something is to shut everyone out, run away, and mope and whine about how much her life sucks. 
 Would you like to know how her life sucks? Her grandpa (who is OLD) is slowly dying, and his quality of life is waning as a result. Her brother wants to move out with his long-term boyfriend. And her own boyfriend is not reading her mind. 
 HOW DARE DASH NOT READ LILY'S MIND. 
 Ok look, I get being upset about her grandfather. Her family is very close, and part of that is wanting the best for one another. I totally hope for her sake that he doesn't suffer more pain. 
 The rest of it, though? Bugger off, Lily. You aren't a child who gets to throw temper tantrums when your family doesn't do what you want. Your adult brother wants to move out--so what? GROW UP. You want your boyfriend to understand you and your needs? Then grow some mother fudging (because your delicate baby ears can't handle bad words) balls (are balls too icky for you too?) and TELL HIM WHAT YOU WANT. 
 Christ, she annoyed the hell out of me. All cuteness with this book is totally and completely undermined by how idiotic Lily is. I hope Dash breaks up with her.

I kind of knew going in that I would not really enjoy this book because well me and her don't like the same books and this one just wasn't up my ally. Yes, it sets up the pace for the book, and I do love when a novel grabs me right in, but I am a big fan of a slow brewing novel. I like to put the puzzle pieces together and collect the data as I go, the prologue seriously gave me a headache my mind was trying to process everything so fast. Reading is an enjoyment it should not feel like I am in one of my lectures listening to my professor. 
 Once I moved past that things got a bit interesting, the two main characters: Wynter and Khamsin were, I don't know let's just say they weren't my favourite characters. There was just so much shit going on, so thankfully Goodreads provides a synopsis for readers who are interested. The writing was not bad, it had good vocabulary that matched the time period, and good grammar but it was so wordy! The author used so much WORDS like holy crap it took paragraphs and paragraphs to describe what the characters wore or the setting of a new environment. It took pages and pages to explain the politics.mythology and what the main characters were thinking. I don't want to sound illiterate or dumb but seriously waaaaaay too many unnecessary words to the point that I skimmed a lot of shit and still knew what was happening. I think why I also did not like it is because my mind kept comparing it to one of my favourite series The Fantasyland series by Kristen Ashley. Obviously this does not bode well with his court and his people back in their lands, which leaves a very miserable and lonely Queen. Does Wynter do anything about this?... NO! The Queen is tormented, lonely, depressed, shunned in her own bloody home and Wynter does nothing until 60%. This also means that he does not get to known her and spend time with her until 60%, which means the time before that what were they doing you ask? Having mindless crazy wild ass sex (which wasn't even hot if you ask me).

 1."Truth be told, she was probably healthy enough within a week of the poisoning, but stupid me, I thought you might use the time to get to know your wife, not avoid her like the plague." ... see Wynter even other people notice that you should probably get to know your wife.

"How could she give him such passion in their marriage bed, then plot against him?" ... all he has to go off of her is the passion she shares when they have sex, hmmm maybe if you got to know her you would I don't know be more trusting of her possibly because then you would know her personality and know that she has nothing but good intentions? Just a guess Wynter.

Like what an ass, I swear I would have left him from way back when. AND in the end he claims he loves you? ... really like how from the three dates you spent with her? 
 From the start of their relationship to 60% they had nothing but desire and lust between the two of them, and that's okay you need that in a relationship, but it must be a starting point to build something off of otherwise it's just lust. I hated how when they were finally getting somewhere they ended up having sex instead of hashing out their problems, because like sex, fighting is very fundamental in a relationship. I liked Wynter when they were traveling to his kingdom, he was caring, blunt, and had ultimately good intentions but once he made it home he transformed into a major ass... and Wynter my man it's supposed to go the other way around.

This book not only kept me on the edge of my seat, it kept me guessing right until the end, which is not something that usually happens (although the slow middle is what kept it from getting five stars). 
 There are many reasons why I loved this book. One is the structure. In this book the story is told more or less linearly but using a variety of formats (parts of a novel, newspaper articles and private recollections). Another is the blending of genres. I enjoy reading literary fiction as well as SF and fantasy and I think this book is probably one of the best melding of the two I've come across. 
 Yet another reason I loved this book was the characters. Women in fiction often tend to be flat, one- or two-dimensional characters. This book doesn't do that to the two main characters, sisters Iris and Laura. There are the usual cookie-cutter villains in the story but both Iris and Laura are not from any standard mould. They are at times incomprehensible, irritating, ignorant, a whole host of traits. Sometimes you want to slap them upside the head for their obliviousness. All of this just serves to make them more recognisable as real people. 
 In a review of the book the reviewer stated that the author takes her time revealing the whole story, which is true; but if you can make past a certain point, the story that keeps looming cannot be ignored, impelling you to keep going until the end. I also think that there are so many genres this book covers that almost everyone will find something to enjoy. All in all it is a well-written story told in an interesting way with a different perspective on a very well-covered time and is definitely worth the effort.

Undermajordomo Minor is a sly, twisted fairy tale. Lucy Minor leaves his small village where he is deeply unpopular to take a job in a dark, Gothic castle as the assistant to the majordomo of the resident duke. Lucy is not your ordinary fairy tale hero as he is a compulsive liar, fairly amoral, and has a tendency to feel sorry for himself. And the duke? He might be the tragic figure of melodrama, but every time you think you have a bead on where this story is heading, it changes gears. DeWitt has mixed a potent brew of folk tales, coming of age stories, and gothic page-turners and come up with something completely unique.

While reading "Ashfall," I was transported back to my teenaged enthusiasm for Larry Niven's Lucifer's Hammer. What's not to love about a hero who defies the END of the WORLD? There are so many things to like about "Ashfall" that it is hard to know where to start. The premise is simple and believable: a super volcano eruption suddenly and completely transforms the Iowa life Alex has known into an ashen wasteland. The natural upheaval is devastating, but it is the way people change suddenly and completely that is most disturbing. It isn't quite The Road. Yet. As the events of Hurricanes Katrina and Sandy show (and tsunamis and earthquakes and on and on), mother nature is unforgiving, but it is people who make tragedy into obscenity. "Ashfall" raises the stakes beyond simple disaster survival stories, such that the devastation is believable and the lack of coordinated response is equally understandable. Mullin has done a fine job of weaving speculation in with elements of historical fact, of how food shortages and refugee camps work, of how people are both good and evil. 
 Alex is completely engaging as our sixteen year old protagonist and narrator. He is confused, determined, naive, altruistic, and adaptable. Alex eventually stumbles upon a companion, Darla, who is perhaps more engaging, a no-nonsense raised-on-a-farm practical gal. It is hard for me to think of a romantic relationship between teen characters that displays such respect for the real strengths and weaknesses people bring to relationships. 
 The realistic depiction of violence, sexual and otherwise, might give pause for some younger readers. Fans of "Survivorman" will feel right at home. And I hear that darker things are to come in the sequel. I'm glad I have Ashen Winter sitting on my shelf, as it would be a rough wait to see how this turns out.

As socialite Paxton Osgood is trying to restore the Blue Ridge Madam, she discovers the bones of an old mystery. She'll need the friendship of the unlikely Willa to get through the past and hopefully discover true treasures in life. 
 Yeah. This is not one of Sarah Addison Allen's strongest books, unfortunately. She has a lot of great books in the same vein (magical realism) that I would highly recommend, but not this one. She tries to take on a little too much in this book and fails at delivering any of it in full. She wants to take on a mystery, the budding friendship between two very different girls, two different romances, a character who comes to terms with his sexuality, a character who tries to understand what home means, reconciling two different generations, getting away from overbearing parents, etc. 
 TOO MUCH! Not enough pages. In the end, I feel very unemotional about all of it because there wasn't enough build up for these types of settings and emotions. 
 The mystery was just plain horrible. Hardly any mystery and more of an excuse to get the characters to bump into each other. 
 I just have very mixed feelings about the character relationships. On one hand, I like how Allen writes her romances and her friendships. On the other, they were so unbelievable in this book. 
 For instance, while I really love the idea of a socialite and a travel-gear shop owner becomes besties, I was completely unimpressed by Paxton and Willa's friendship. They opened up too quickly for me to believe that it would actually happen. I think I needed another 50 pages and three more scenes before I would believe they could become that chummy. 
 Same with the romances. The romances were fun to read because Allen does that type of slow exploration of emotions very well. But balancing these two romances felt incredibly rushed. From never-seen-you-in-years-or-even-talked to let's-get-married. 
 I did adore the Claire cameo. 
 Two stars. It was okay. Would not recommend to friends. But I would recommend her other books over this one.

 This is the 16th book in the series. The books have changed a lot over the years. They started off as your run-of-the-mill vampire hunter novel, tough heroine, nasty bad guys, lots of sleuthing, crime busting, general fighting and monster slaying. Eventually the books lost more and more of those standard items, the characters went through lots of changes in the process, it got more gory and more sexual as time wore on. Lots of fans didn't like that and stopped reading at some point. Others came to it later and some die-hard fans like me just stuck with it, despite lots of bitching about the amount of sex and the lack of plot in some of them. I have been with this series for so long, I just don't want to miss what happens to Anita. 
 Blood Noir does have a plot and the usual heavy smothering of sexual encounters. The gimmick of the doppelgaenger in this one was a bit lame in my opinion. It worked for the plot, but can we expect people to really be so stupid that they repeatedly don't get it? I am not convinced. I missed Jean-Claude in this one. He is my favourite character besides Anita. And I could have done without Richard. I really, really do not like him. And I wish Hamilton would kill him off already. But I guess that's really a no-go with him being part of the triumvirate with Anita and Jean-Claude. He is just such an idiot, I just groan as soon as he appears on the page. I like Nathaniel and Jason is growing on me.

Not quite as compulsively readable as The Hunger Games, this is at least as original a world as that of Scott Westerfield's Uglies trilogy. The world is more alien than that of Margaret Peterson Haddix's Shadow Children series, and even more sinister than that of The Giver. The first two chapters took some getting used to, but if a YA reader can muscle through them, the book is highly engaging. Todd is compelling every-teen, aware of the adult world and not quite able to make sense of it. Although the plot moves along, really the thematic issues are equally compelling: coming of age, the dishonesty of adults, the struggle to be a man and on whose terms. 
 Some high lights include a solid friendship between Todd and his dog, as well as between Todd and another teen. I suspect that mid-to-strong readers will enjoy this, especially as the layers of the story unfold. I look forward to the sequel.

DEEPER is everything a New Adult read should be! Gritty, real and makes the reader so emotionally invested that it feel like you are reading a diary. 
 I am so glad that all my high school/college blundering happened before camera phones and social media! My screw ups are a distant memory but kids these days have a permanent record that even their grandkids will be able to peruse. That is what happen to our protagonist Caroline. 
 Caroline had plans. She had her life planned out that included a public persona but that was destroyed the moment she trusted her first love, her first everything, to take pictures of her during an intimate moment. Pictures that he used against her when they broke up. Pictures that would never go away, that made people judge her, that made her a target for the sexually depraved. 
 Reading it felt like internet rape. I felt how exposed she felt. Her humiliation and her fear. The internet is for forever and it was never going away. 
 I really related to Caroline and she felt so real to me, maybe because we have all trusted the wrong person but not many of us get burned this badly. 
 West is is our hero but he's not the typical bad boy with a chip on his shoulder. West does bad things but out of necessity and love for his sister. He sacrifices himself as the price he feels he has to pay so he can build a better life. 
 He has a powerful organic attraction to Caroline but she isn't part of his plan. He wants to take care of her, like he does with his mother and sister and he does to a point but with working three jobs, going to school full time and a few shady dealings just to maintain his ambition of making a better life he is stretched too thin. 
 This is beautifully written, so compelling and so gut-wrenchingly real. I'm not going to lie, I cried and then I was pissed because I have to wait till summer to read what happens next. 
 Bravo Ms. Robin York! 
 If you like the New Adult genre then this is a MUST READ and put the next one on your TBR!!!

As her point in writing seems to be to instruct the reader, this may not strike some as valid criticism. Still, I object to reading a novel with all the linguistic vitality and joy of a furniture assembly diagram. It makes reading drudgery. Still, at 256 pages, it is at least digestible. When folks rhapsodize over Atlas Shrugged, hundreds of pages longer and just as plodding, I just don't get it.

See my review at: http://stephaniesbookreviews.wordpres... 
 PLOT 
 The First Phone Call from Heaven chronicles the lives of several members of a small town where a miracle has seemingly occurred - residents are receiving phone calls from deceased loved ones. When the town and the phone calls become worldwide news, there are staunch believers, insistent protestors, a skeptic pastor, and a man that will do anything to prove that it's all a hoax. 
 I felt like for most of the book we are supposed to believe that the phone calls are real. While I believe in Heaven, if this was to happen in real life, I would definitely be one of the skeptics. Because of that, I just kept waiting for when we would find out what really was happening and it was a good ways into the story before I figured it out - and even longer until it's actually revealed. Though I did figure it out, there was another twist that I didn't see coming. 
 Interwoven with the story is the history of Alexander Graham Bell and the telephone. While some of the information was interesting, I really don't see how it added anything to the story. It was one of those times where I felt like the author was just saying, "hey, look at all the research I did!" 
 CHARACTERS 
 There were a lot of characters, but most of them were not very developed. We skip from one to another so quickly that it was hard to really care that much about what was happening with any of them. The most developed character was Sully, a man recently released from prison for an incident that wasn't his fault and has also been recently widowed. When his young son keeps asking when he'll get a phone call from his mother, Sully starts his own investigation into the phone calls. I did mostly like him, as well as two of the phone call recipients, Tess and police chief Jack, who started a relationship after being brought together by the calls. 
 Though we didn't get enough investment into most of the characters, Albom did do a good job with varying each of their reactions to receiving the phone calls - some wanted to tell everyone, some wanted to keep it a secret, some were scared, some doubted. I just would've liked a couple more characters to get the same amount of attention as Sully did. 
 READABILITY 
 This is the first Mitch Albom book I've read and he is an excellent writer. However, the plot just jumped around a little too much for me. Instead of really investing in the characters of any given scene, it gave us just enough to know what was going on with one person before it jumped to what was going on with the next. 
 ENJOYABILITY 
 I'm just not sure how I feel about this book. It was different and it did keep me turning the pages, but at times I was just trying to get through it. I didn't know what to expect going in, but giving the author's popularity, I thought I would've enjoyed it a little more than I did.

Impressive conclusion to the epic Sci-fi saga that began with Pandora's Star. Not quite as unqualified a success as that previous volume, since I found the writing a bit uneven this time around and everything did fall into place rather neatly at the end. It was almost as if Hamilton was experiencing writer's fatigue at times. Understandable given that the two books are in fact one continuous 2,000+ page novel. 
 Those minor quibbles aside, Hamilton succeed admirably here. The scale and complexity is unlike anything I've read. But since Hamilton has complete command of the story and offers good character development and mostly smooth writing, I did not find it hard to keep track of the myriad plot threads and characters. The denouement, juggling 3 or 4 different climaxes at once, was exciting. These 2 books would make one helluva Sci-Fi TV series a la Battlestar Galactica. 
 There is plenty of political intrigue, mysteries, danger, explosive action, and exotic technology. There is gritty realism. Aliens are attacking. Yet, Hamilton also has a great sense of humor. I found myself laughing out loud several times. Like when one character visits the NYC of 300 years in the future: "As always, the antics of the city's yellow cabs drew a frown on her forehead; whoever programmed their drive arrays did an appalling job. Her own car had to break sharply several times as they cut in front". 
 Or this, when one of the characters encounters an alien: "Who are you?" Ozzie asked. 
 The Silfen's circular mouth opened wide, allowing the long slender tongue to vibrate between his rows of teeth. "I am the one who dances in the endless wind streams which flow along the tumbling white clouds as they circle in eternal orbit within the star of life." He gave a sharp whistle. "But you may call me Clouddancer. I know how you humans have to be so quick and shallow." 
 I found those two examples, and others, hilarious. You don't often find laugh out loud humor in Sci-Fi, at least not the books I've read. I've become quite a fan of Hamilton and his prodigious talent. Looking forward to Great North Road, Fallen Dragon, and the Void trilogy.

I read this book because I wanted to know what all the hubbub was about. It was released back in 1997 and sixteen years later, people still mention it. After the television series "The Middle" had an episode where they referred to this book, I decided it was time for me to pick it up. It's a quick read, so it would be easy to dismiss it as being too simplistic, but it really contains some food for thought even if it is a little too sentimental. This book was okay but it is more about the message than the skill of the writing. 
 When someone you admire and love develops a dreaded disease what do you do? Perhaps, like Mitch, you have good intentions but don't get around to doing much because you are so busy. Eventually though, like Mitch, you take time to visit that friend and realize that you just must spend what time you can with this beloved individual before you have no more time left. So it goes with Mitch whose mentor and friend, Morrie, battles ALS. Morrie is just glad to see his former student who promised to keep in touch when he graduated. The book contains a great story of friendship and learning not to take even life's smallest things for granted. Morrie Schwartz inspired something in Albom that enabled him to create a treasure that truly commemorates a great man. 
 This read has many messages not the least of which is it's never too late to find an old friend. From Morrie's viewpoint, one must live one's life to the best of one's ability whatever happens. Morrie's messages got to me as expected. It's never too late to apologize. It's never too late to renew an old friendship and spend some time with someone. It's never too late to let someone know that you love him or her. Be compassionate! 
 The audiobook was read by a paid actor but at the end, it contains Morrie's voice during some of the actual interviews recorded by Albom. That was a nice bonus even if it was repetitive since much of it has already been incorporated into the book.

Since becoming a blogger I've become a different reader. Before I wrote book reviews, I wouldn't bother finishing a book that wasn't working for me. Now, I make my best effort to read books in their entirety, because I can write more informed reviews that way. Still, I was only able to get through about two thirds of Magonia before skipping ahead to the ending and calling it a day. 
 Magonia is a Narnia-esque fantasy -- a girl living in the normal world discovers a magical one, just "through the wardrobe," as it were. Aza, the girl in question, has always been sickly, unable to breathe air effectively, for some mysterious reason. Her doctors say she's quickly running out of time. But, just at a fatal moment, Aza is whisked away to Magonia, a land of bird-like creatures and airships in the sky. Able to breathe the thin air, Aza comes into her own strengths for the first time, but must question the intentions of her new Magonian family. What do they want with her and are they being entirely forthright? Meanwhile, back on the ground, Aza's best friend, Jason, is determined to find her... 
 I have a lot of problems with Magonia. One of my main issues is that the book is stretched too thin. Headley wrote a stand-alone contemporary/fantasy -- with only 320 pages!! On top of that, the novel spends a good amount of time in exposition mode at its beginning. I think it was the author's intention to build up her characters and raise the emotional stakes of her story by fleshing out Aza's existing relationships before she's taken away to Magonia. It was a good idea, but I think the book would have been better served by jumping into action a little quicker. Because the beginning lagged, Headley had to start her fantasy world-building late in the game, which hurt the pace of the story. 
 On top of that, we were pulled away from Magonia over and over again by the chapters focusing on Jason's -- largely internal -- activities. He was a thin character, slavishly devoted to Aza. It bothers me when characters can't stand on their own, and Jason entire purpose throughout the novel was to worship Aza... who was over-worshiped. Her funeral scene left me alternatively sniggering and gaping. A moment that was supposed to move me, instead gave me the biggest laugh in the book! When Jason, who is wearing an alligator suit, with the words "Aza Ray was here" painted on the head, drives to the burial honking morse code messages to Aza... only not real morse code because he doesn't want anyone to know what he's saying.  Truly, the histrionics in this book turned me off. The emotion was always ramped up to ten, but because I was not invested, everything came across as clownish. 
 In case it hasn't come across clearly yet, I do not recommend this book. A good alternative would be The Blue Sword by Robin McKinley.

I haven't really read anything like Death of Bees. Which is quite impressive, because I have read a lot books over the past 25 years, excluding TRNs (trashy romance novels), urban fiction, and anything by James Patterson (how does he write all those books?) All in all this book had a lot of positives when it comes down to MY type of story: a well designed book cover, a kick ass summary, a creative writing style, and lots of suspense. 
 It saddens me to think that this would have been a five star if it wasn't for that damn conclusion. To me, a conclusion will make or break a good story. It is the last thing your reader remembers before you send them back to their reality. Just think about George Orwell's 1984. NOW THAT is a pretty awesome conclusion and still lingers with me years later. 
 But honestly, when a story starts out with two dead parents buried in the backyard, there are very few outcomes. 
 Death of Bees is about three people, told in first person perspective from each character. Marnie is a 15 year old girl who is intellectually gifted, but experiments with drugs, sex with older men... same as your typical juvenile delinquent. Nelly is a 12 year old girl who may be described as having some form of autism. She is very prim, proper and intellectual, while being emotionally stunted. Lennie is the girls' elderly neighbor who several years ago had been convicted of trying to solicit sex from a minor (albeit he unknowingly tried to solicit sex from a minor.) Though none of the three characters can be described as likable, O'Donnell somehow keeps me invested in the girls' fate. 
 Like most good suspense novels, the story keeps chugging along, and events build slowly. Are the girls going to be found out? Will they be put into foster care and separated? Why is seemingly nothing happening in the resolving of these mysteries? 
 And then BAM! Everything happens at once like lightening. The same as waiting in line for a roller coaster, when you finally reach in the end of the line after standing for 2 hours in 100 degree weather with no shade, a 2 min ride seems hardly worth the sun baked shoulders and the achy feet. 
 Just like waiting for the Top Thrill Dragster at Cedar Point, the conclusion of this novel did not give me the sweet satisfaction that it made me crave. 
 So if you are looking for something a little different and don't care for interesting conclusions, this may be your book. As for me, I think I might just have to reread 1984.

In a not-so-distant future, humanity faces the constant threat of extinction as a result of diseases unwittingly unleashed when scientists meddle with gene splicing. Entire nations have succumbed to these diseases, and the only people with the resources to stay ahead of the genetic plague are the very companies responsible for the outbreak in the first place. For the sake of survival, many nations have capitulated and ceded their autonomy for access to the latest disease-resistant crops. 
 Thailand is the only country to retain independence from these corporate powers, and only because their ruler had the foresight to create a stockpile of untainted seeds protected by a ministry dedicated to containing any outbreak of disease. Yet, the corruption inherent at all levels of society has created gaping holes for immoral power players to exploit. 
 The book revolves around at least five main characters, but their stories are so tightly intertwined that the narrative thread is never lost or confused. The plot twists are expected enough to be believeable, but still audacious enough to be rewarding. The world is also believable enough to make one worry about the possible effects of genetic modification accidentally slipping into an uncontrollable ecosystem. 
 This book would probably come off as dark, depressing and cynical to many, but I found it to be intellectually stimulating with plenty of themes upon which to ruminate well after the reading is done. Highly recommended.

 Wow! I purchased Carnage after hearing so many people and reading so many reviews about how amazing it was. Against my normal behavior, I didn't read any spoilers. I normally read spoilers because I like to prepare myself for heartbreak or mayhem...Good Lawdy. I ended up staying up until 5am because after plowing through the book until 2am, I couldn't sleep. This is the best type of book, isn't it? A book that doesn't leave you even after you've read the very last page- the events of everything your eyes have just consumed lingers and can't seem to dim even in the wee hours of the night. 
 Carnage was unexpected. I wasn't sure what to expect as I read the first few chapters but swipe after swipe, I couldn't put the kindle down. Georgia Rae, I wanted to hate her but I couldn't. I wanted to judge her but I didn't. There was something so innocent yet raw and gritty about her that I just couldn't write her off as just another timid and painfully naive heroine. She loved so freely and felt so deeply and I felt her pain when her world came crashing down around her. 
 The love story between Sean and Georgia was sweet and endearing. There's something about a pure love which starts at such a young and vulnerable age that plays at my emotions. I was rooting for them to conquer all and survive the dreadful battles they faced against such miserable and despicable human beings. But, feeling as I did for our heroine, I started hoping for a different outcome. 
 Enter Cameron King. The man was a walking fantasy. He was strong and powerful and he helped Georgia through dark times. I found myself in the unusual predicament of being torn between two amazing heroes. 
 Events in this book were so tragic and earth shattering that I find it difficult even writing this review. But I couldn't in good conscience not do so. I've now taken the time to read some reviews and I find it disheartening how so many people loved the book until they read an ending they didn't want. I myself have always preferred the HEA but applaud an author brave enough to buck the norm and write what they truly believe is the story that needed to be told. 
 Lesley Jones has delivered a story that packs a powerful punch to the gut. There's love and loss. There's tears and laughter. There's a family so entwined and connected that the destructive forces of life could never keep them apart. Do I love the ending? God no!!! But I can't stop thinking about this beautiful love story; I can't bring myself to not care about the characters Lesley Jones so beautifully introduced into my literary world. Now I just need a valium and some wine and I'll be good to go for Carnage 2. Hope that happens soon because I am eagerly waiting with my one clicking finger.

Forgive me if this review is a little fuzzy. I'm fighting a nasty virus which has left me able to do very little besides lie on the couch all day and watch the position of the sun change. During that time, I did manage to finish this book, so thoughts: 
 This book answered the pressing question of how to make Valerie interested in political drama: Set your drama in Disneyworld. Doctorow found the perfect microcosm universe in which to meditate on his philosophies. The book is a love letter to Disneyworld, and the theme I found most compelling was the idea of preserving the old attractions hundreds of years into the future when they are still just as beloved. It's nice to see speculative fiction that shows people don't really want everything to change. Doctorow's world has ended scarcity, plugged people into the net 24/7, and even learned to cheat death, but people still enjoy a trip down the Caribbean (with or without Jack Sparrow). Upgraded and tweaked sure, but Doctorow's future Magic Kingdom is still perfectly recognizable. I had a lot of fun just imagining the very serious conversations happening in full Haunted Mansion costumes. 
 This book deals with a ton of speculative themes which my stuffy brain is not really up to exploring, but I'll try anyway. First, the idea of Whuffie and meritocracy which I find both intriguing and terrifying. I'm glad that Doctorow doesn't give us too many details on Dan and Julius' arguments on the subjects because that would have been too forced philosophic, but I still have a lot of questions on how a Whuffie-based economy works. On how the whole Bitchun society works, really. We all like to think that based purely on our own karma, we'd do okay in the world, but if I really stopped to analyze mine, I'm not sure I'd come out on top. I'm also still curious about the different kinds of Whuffie. Again, I'm thankful Doctorow never departs from the story to expound, but I'd have loved to see more of these pieces of the world in action. 
 Dead-heading is another curiously blase topic. I love the logic that no one complains about it because everyone who had a philosophical bone to pick is already dead. Everyone left was raised to pretty much accept it. You were murdered? Oh big deal, ya baby. Get over it. I love that Julius feels bad about feeling bad about his own murder. 
 The theme that really hit home with me though was when Julius goes offline. As one of the few people left who haven't gone smartphone, I often feel like a backwater hick, but too much connection leaves me drained and ... well, disconnected. It's when Julius is offline that he has his idea of bringing in the human elements of the Mansion, crowd-sourcing its cast, and making it a social experience over an individual one. That's the part where we cheer for him, however melodramatic he may be at other points in the book. The idea that he will permanently lose life events because he is offline and doesn't want to visit a doctor, is terrifying and creates tension where a death-free society should have none. This part is just masterful.  
 I can't say I really like Julius (or Dan or Lil for that matter). I think I was so focused on the themes and the settings, I never really bonded with any of the people. The themes and setting were interesting enough to keep me plowing through the pages, though.  The Julius/Dan/Lil triangle was a bit predictable and seemed an easy way of building strife. I could have done without that, and Julius and Lil had enough problems as a couple that I didn't think Dan was necessary to make things worse. Dan changing his opinion from death to dead-heading was also kind of an anti-climax. It's one of those where I'm happy he's not dying, but I have no idea why he suddenly went back on all his principles. 
 Dan and Julius' relationship is so complex, and they so often just ignore the awful things that go down between them. I guessed Dan was part of the murder conspiracy in the beginning, but it's interesting that this doesn't really damage their friendship, less even than Dan's affair with Lil. Murdering someone is like stealing 20 bucks from their wallet. It's an awful thing to do, but really no harm done, right pal? A dynamic I do not understand, but did enjoy reading . 
 I'm definitely curious to read more of Doctorow's recent works now and see how he's matured after this first novel. He has such a crisp, easy to read style and never gets bogged down by science. It's the brand of social-science fiction that I enjoy the most. A great weekend read for anyone who loves Disney and Science Fiction.

I read the prequel, Elemental, and wasn't all that impressed with it, but I decided to read Storm anyways. I'm glad that I gave it a chance because I really enjoyed it. 
 The story is told in 3rd person POV between Becca and Chris. I felt that both of these characters were well-developed and I really liked them. Though I always feel that 1rst person gives a better emotional connection to characters, I think that 3rd person worked well here and still gave me the connection that I look for. 
 I loved the Merrick brothers. Michael, the oldest (and the focus of the prequel) is the guardian for his brothers and puts up with a lot of crap. He's also trying to find the balance between parent and brother and is resented for it. I felt bad for him for most of the book, but got some hope at the end that they'll all get along better with him. And even though I didn't care for the prequel, without reading it I probably wouldn't have liked Michael much in this book. 
 I liked one twin and was annoyed by the other. Nick is the peacemaker in the family. He's sweet and strong and I would've liked to have seen more from him. Gabriel is surly and impulsive. He also has that sarcastic bad boy thing going for him that's usually reserved for the male leads in YA. I'm usually into that, but here he mostly annoyed me. He's the one that really butted heads with Michael all the time and it got old after awhile. But as the book goes on we see that he's not such a douche. And I believe that the next book is focused on him, so I'm hoping he stays a little nicer. 
 Chris is probably my favorite of the Merricks, but that might just be because he was the most developed. He's struggling with learning to control his element, water, and also with fitting in with his brothers. He grows up a lot throughout the story. He became more confident, but also remained sweet and protective. I really liked him and Becca together. 
 One thing I really could've used more of was explanation of the Elements. We know that they each have some power to manipulate an element, but not really the how. Chris talks about feeling the power of water and that it can lead him to danger, but I would've liked more explanation on how exactly it worked. Or a better description of it when they were using their power. I also don't completely understand the Spirit element, but hopefully that will be explained more later. 
 Overall, I enjoyed Storm. I loved the relationship between the Merrick the brothers and look forward to reading more of them. I would recommend this book to fans of YA with sci-fi elements (ha, see what I did there).

Asking For It is such an important book. 
 Eighteen year old Emma O'Donovan lives in a small town in Ireland and like a lot of teenage girls she likes to go out with her friends and party. One night she goes to a party, gets drunk, takes some drugs and flirts with a few guys. The next morning, she wakes up on her front porch with absolutely no memory of what happened the night before. But not to worry: there are hundreds of photos posted to Facebook which show exactly what happened to her. 
 Emma O'Donovan is beautiful and she knows it. She's confident, she's selfish and not a very good friend. Emma is not a likeable character and the decision to make her so makes this story all the harder to read. Generally it is difficult to sympathise with unlikeable characters and that is the point here: we don't have to like Emma. Being unlikeable doesn't mean that you weren't raped. You can be the bitch of the century and no still means no. Emma being so unlikable opens the reader's eyes to the way we (society as a whole) tend to think about rape victims: their personal life is always dragged up. How promiscuous are they, how often do they get drunk, how often do they have sex, what kind of clothes do they wear, are they a nice person? Emma deals with all of this in the aftermath of her rape. The people of her town completely turn against her in favour of her rapists and the media are constantly discussing her. Is it any wonder that so few rape victims report their assault? 
 The reactions and behaviour of her friends and family (particularly her parents) were one of the hardest aspects to read for me. I really just could not believe the attitude of her parents and their utter unwillingness to just believe their daughter. They were more interested in their image and losing their "friends" and that was just utterly heartbreaking. Emma's brother is probably the only decent character in the entire book. 
 As for the ending: I think it ended in the right way. I was majorly pissed off at her parents for being relieved and happy at her decision but it is realistic. I'm glad that O'Neill didn't give us a happy ending or wrap things up nicely because it is never going to be over for Emma. She has been completely ostracised from the community she lives in, she's given up her dreams and she is forever going to be haunted by what happened to her. It reflects the society we live in where many victims don't get the justice they deserve.  
 I can't stress enough how important I think this book is, especially in today's society. There are countless cases in the media concerning rape, and what is defined as consent, as well as rapists who get off incredibly lightly whilst victims are left to suffer. Asking For It deals with the issue of not explicitly saying no but not saying yes either, a lack of memory of the rape, slut-shaming, victim-blaming and the increasing use of social media. This is a must-read for everyone.

 This is a very unique, interesting book. When it first came out, I wasn't sure if I wanted to read it. I wasn't into horror stories and read very few paranormal books. However, my tastes have changed and I decided to go ahead and pick this book up at the library. 
 The plot drew me in from the very beginning. I loved seeing the old vintage carny photographs and looked forward to seeing a new photograph as the story progressed. I think this added an eerie, intriguing touch to the book and made it unique. This book is definitely not scary. Creepy maybe. But not scary. I expected a true horror story (mostly because I never bother to read summaries before reading a book. I much rather read it and figure it out on my own as I go.) and was surprised to find that other than the vintage photographs, there isn't much of a horror element to it. It's more of a mystery novel with a bit of action thrown in it at the end than anything else. I enjoyed reading about all of the characters and their individual peculiar abilities. It did become a bit difficult for me to keep everyone's names and their abilities straight throughout the book so I wish that Riggs would have repeated their abilities again when mentioning a name so I wouldn't have had to flip back to the beginning to remember who was who. I also think that Riggs did a decent job explaining and setting up the world that the peculiar children live in. After reading some disappointing dystopian novels when it came to world building, it was refreshing to read this and find a writer who was able to sufficiently write a world. 
 I think this book is another John Green element to me. I like the idea of the book, but I don't think it was written to its full potential. There are very few true horror books in the young adult genre and I really wish that this book had been more of a horror story. I feel like I kind of got jipped after finishing it. The book seemingly promises you horror and creepiness with all of the cool vintage photographs laced through it and you come out with a mystery novel with a touch of creepiness. The writing was also pretty lackluster in my opinion. If the book didn't have the photos in it, it wouldn't have been as enjoyable and I don't think the writing is strong enough to have been able to carry the plot on its own. The plot started out strongly and engrossed me, but then it lost its captivity element for me when Jacob meets the peculiar children. The writing quality deteriorates from there in my opinion. Regardless, I did enjoy reading this book. 
 Likes: Vintage carny photographs. Emma. Unique characters with interesting abilities. 
 Dislikes: Doesn't deliver what it promises (no horror element to it). Writing is lackluster and loses its captivating-ness after Jacob arrives on the island. 
 Overall: 
 Recommend? Yes.

Actually 3.5 Stars 
 Don't ask why I feel a little underwhelmed by this book. 
 It wasn't a horrible read, in fact, I zoomed through it in a day. Seriously. 
 The WRITING was great (if you've seen the movies Ghost in the Shell and Valerian that's what some of the VR descriptions brought to mind). I think descriptions were actually my favorite part of the book. The augmented/virtual realities have always fascinated me and Marie Lu did a superb job of showing how they would integrate into the real world, especially the shopping aspect of it. I virtually applauded her every time I read a particularly fascinating description of Tokyo. The customizable walls, artificially intelligent cars, the virtual mannequins in front of stores and buy buttons above the items, the dark underworld. It all just made sense (although I did question the way VR actually worked... if it felt as real as a dream would, wouldn't the brain have to temporarily paralyze the body? That's what it does when you sleep *shrugs* Just sayin' but I'm by no means an expert.) 
 Then there were the CHARACTERS. They were good (not super realistic but that's fine). Emika was good. Hideo was interesting (though I've seen his kind in Japanese dramas and animes before). Asher, Roshan and Hammie (I use the same nickname for my cat btw, whose real name is Ame: "rain" in Japanese) were pretty cool. The rest of the peeps were decent too. But I didn't fall in love with any of them. Not a single one, except maybe the little robot who served drinks. Wikki! 
 The PLOT was interesting (I loved, loved the beginning but as the story went on, some moments felt rushed. And I could guess the plot twist ). Since this book was heavily driven by plot , the fact that I could guess the plot twist  made it less wowing. Sorry!! 
 But still it should have been at least a 4 star read by all accounts (I even gave it 4 stars because I felt bad giving it 3).
