I'm having a really hard time even approaching this review. 
 The subject matter was very personal to me, and I'm having a hard time verbalizing my reaction to this book. I have a history - not as an addict but as someone who has dealt firsthand with the devastating consequences of addiction on a family. As a result of that, I have a hard time relating to James, the fictionalized representation of the author of the book. He was repulsive, selfish and stubborn. He is hateful, self-loathing, and destructive. His rejection of the treatment at the facility, his insistence on the belittling of the Twelve Step program, his condescending, all-knowing persona is repellant. He is whiny, negative and hopeless for the majority of the novel. I found myself sympathizing and relating to his family more than the narrator. I couldn't stand James. While he progresses as a character throughout the book, I still find him equally repugnant. As I was reading it, I kept saying to myself, "If I knew him in real life, I would HATE him. HATE him." 
 That said, I read this novel after the controversy. For more information regarding the Frey scandal that went down after the supposed memoir was exposed to be (at least partly) a fictitious account, check out A Million Little Lies at The Smoking Gun. I really don't care about the scandal. Yes, I can understand the readers' frustrations and betrayal at Frey's exaggerations. Because I knew of it prior to reading, it didn't affect my reaction - I read it as fiction. As someone who loves me some J.T. LeRoy, I'm not terribly upset by authorial misrepresentation in memoirs. I think that Frey's insistence on representing the experience as truth was offensive to some people because of the delicate and personal nature of the subject matter at hand - addiction. Which leads me to believe that my hatred of James is not all fair. It is certainly colored by my own experience. But to represent fiction as fact can be damaging in this case. Frey represents himself as a hero, overcoming the sludge of a criminal past and life-threatening addiction; however, The Smoking Gun and Oprah (by the way - do NOT piss off Oprah) view Frey as a fraud - and I tend to agree. 
 It's a shame that the subject matter and narrator was so off-putting because Frey does know how to write - sometimes quite wonderfully and movingly. I would have to read something else by the author - this time something admittedly fictional and not related to addiction (aka not My Friend Leonard) - before entirely writing him off.

[page 3(PDF file) "Come on, Charley, what's the story? This is a difficult review to write for me. I was about two thirds of the way through when my Nan passed away unexpectedly. Yeah ok so she didn't die of cancer, but reading a book about life and death when you experience it's reality can be quite traumatic. At least that's what I expected! 
 My husband suggested I leave it where I was. Why put myself through the grief? I thought maybe the experience would be cathartic. But you know what? I am so pleased I read on and finished this book! 
 Is this book about cancer and pain and death? Yes! But it is also so much more! It is about life, love, beauty and humour! 
 What did I get out of this book? Life is a side effect of dying. But it is beautiful. It is a piece of forever. An infinity that maybe smaller than other infinities but an infinity nonetheless! 
 Having studied philosophy extensively I was no stranger to Zeno's paradox of Achilles and the Tortoise but I always looked at it from a metaphysical perspective never a personal one. This is the thing that really stuck with me in this book. "You gave me a forever within the numbered days, and I'm grateful". 
 There were lots of things that I loved about this book. I loved the raw honesty of it. I loved the humour. I loved the emotions. I loved the metaphors. I loved that we don't find out what happens to Hazel, just like how she felt about the book and how it always is with death . 
 I laughed and I cried but not soul destroying heart breaking tears. I cried life affirming isn't the world beautiful tears. Because there is pain and suffering and loss and death in the world, but each of us get our "little infinity" and I for one intend to appreciate every moment of it with the people I love. 
 Thanks John Green! It's on the favourites shelf and I will be reading again when I need reminding of how precious life and love is. It holds the same place in my heart as Through a Glass, Darkly which I have read several times.

I really felt for Sprout as she fought hard for what she wanted and what she believed in and was constantly put down by the other animals.

Quick thoughts: Fanboy fiction strong on flash and flair, weak on world-building and character development 
 2ND REVISION: I recently participated in a Q&A with Mark Lawrence in a Goodreads book club, which actually resulted in me bumping up my rating just a bit. First of all, any author humble enough to do that nowadays gets a standing ovation (not to mention that his personal bio is a truly inspirational story that totally outstrips his books). What got my attention in that discussion, though, was that there was no plan or outline to the book. The writing was spontaneous and pretty much stream of consciousness. I still have a lot of issues with the book, and with that style of writing in particular, but the problems I encountered seem a lot less egregious when the author readily admits how little thought went into planning or details. 
 Prince of Thorns really hit my radar earlier this year, when some of my go-to bloggers put in absolutely glowing reviews. When I saw ringing endorsements from authors like Robin Hobb, Conn Iggulden and Peter V. Brett, the excitement factor went up even more. Everywhere I looked, people seemed to be gushing over the book (with the exception of those offended by the gratuitous violence and such). So when I finally settled in to enjoy the ride, you'll understand my disappointment if the advertised Mustang started to feel more like a Pinto. 
 What started the bumpy ride was the brief postscript at the end of most chapters, which highlights some facet of a secondary character and appears completely unrelated to the story at hand. I started calling these segments "Pokemon cards" because they sounded just like trading card descriptions of the characters. I still have no idea what to do with these snippets. 
 A second speedbump was being immersed in a medieval world that had no relation to historical Earth, and suddenly finding that people are reading things like Plato and Plutarch in the original Greek and Latin. They have priests from the Church of Roma, a black man from Nuba, Spanard horses and the rivers Sane, Lure and Rhyme (Seine, Loire and Rhine). A lot of people obviously bought into the explanation for all that, but it didn't sit right with me before or after that point. 
 Nietzsche being referenced by name was really the breaking point for me. It took a good ten seconds to recover from my slack-jawed shock when his name was dropped. Monks are apparently illuminating leather-bound folios in dead languages, Christianity is the accepted state religion, yet we have "God is dead" manuscripts that haven't been burned and are obviously being copied by hand? 
 And here's a final rant that requires a spoiler tag: Even when we are told the setting is 1,000 years in the future, the twist still feels like willful misdirection. And who can really believe that ancient philosophers would survive the holocaust, but not small arms blueprints or scientific know-how? Or that people would be able to read Greek and Latin, but struggle with English? Or that a superstitious barbarian would be able to detonate a nuclear device but not be able to think of a better weapon than a sword?  
 The common issue here is that it seemed the book couldn't decide what it wanted to be. It's fantasy, but set in our own world. It's got zippy little YA features, but the main character is a 14-year-old psychopathic killer and occasional rapist. It often felt like I was being led down the garden path for big chunks of the novel. Just when enough clues were dropped to get me thinking one way, some new information would be dropped into my lap--but it was always something completely at odds with what I had been led to assume. Some people really thrive on that sort of misdirection or spontaneous development of plot. I don't, and it completely spoiled what would otherwise have been a terribly enjoyable read.

The Revisionists is that rarest of rare birds...a literary Sci-Fi novel. And it's a really good one too, deserving a place on the shelf along side the likes of A Handmaid's Tale, Cloud Atlas, The Sparrow, Oryx & Crake, The Book of Strange New Things. 
 Zed is an agent sent back in time to preserve events as they had already happened, while there is a subversive group going back in time to try to alter the future. A "Cataclysm" is mentioned and even though a shit ton of people died, this must be preserved in order not to compromise the perfect world humanity has constructed out of its ashes. Thus begins a kind of conspiracy thriller sort of plot involving several present day people ("contemps") and others sent back from the future. For some reason I had expected a more freewheeling adventure type story, but it has more of an elegiac tone, though certainly not stiffly written and overwrought like books with similar themes (looking straight at you, The Age of Miracles). 
 The writing is in fact quite exquisite, smart, erudite, poignant, yet concise, with precise language, but there is also a looseness to the writing that is natural and not the slightest bit belabored or pretentious (looking in your direction once more, Age of Miracles by Karen Thompson Walker). The viewpoint shift between four diverse, incredibly well drawn characters. it was a real treat to get into the minds of four fictional characters in one book that are not only vivid, but have their own distinct ways of thinking and interpreting the world around them. Bravo, Thomas Mullen, for some great, perceptive character development. 
 Very very minor weaknesses: The future world seems like standard Orwellian Big Brother stuff. Almost a cliche of Utopian societies where everyone lives in perfect harmony and it seems great except for the fact that no one gets to actually, you know, be human. And any deviation from the norm can get you Taken Away. Also, I liked, but didn't quite love, the way it all wrapped up. 
 That said, I really enjoyed this novel and would strongly recommend it it, particularly to anyone who is a fan of the books mentioned in the first paragraph. This is my first book by Thomas Mullen. Mullen seems to genre hop to some extent with his books, which I totally respect, and I plan to search out all of them, as he is a really gifted writer.

3.5 bumped down to 3. 
 What worked? 
 I thought the writing was competent and the mystery was well done. And though I found the protagonist to be annoying at times, overall she came to life and felt fully flushed out. I also felt that the author tried to explore some deeper issues like gender inequality that gave this substance. 
 What didn't work? 
 Much of the sex talk between the women just didn't ring true. Not saying that women are prissy, just saying that "we" (the women I know at least) have different ways of talking about sex. For instance, I don't think I've ever asked a friend if she got "fucked" last night. Too often it sounded like a man trying to sound like a woman but failing. 
 Several of the supporting characters were more caricatures who were either too over-the-top to be relatable or too cliche to be interesting. 
 At times, the inner dialogue felt preachy, as if the author was trying to enlighten me. Sometimes I don't mind a little philosophical aside, especially if I feel what the author is saying is worthwhile, but this was too much. As a result, this book was easily 100 pages longer than it needed to be. 
 The twist at the end was just too much (and actually ruined what I thought was going to be a fairly satisfying wrap-up) and the last two chapters almost felt unnecessary. 
 This is actually the fourth book in a series. The previous books were alluded to, but I felt this held up as a stand alone. 
 Final conclusion: Not bad. Some decent writing and a solid story (sans the twist). I would definitely read another series by this author, but I won't go out of my way to read the previous books in this series. The characters just didn't impress me.

Could she not know the man she loved and still loves? And if Daedalus gets their hands on the both of them together, what they want them to do - to produce - is much scarier than anything they could have ever imagined. In order to escape the government, Daemon must be willing to start an outright war on the U.S. government. But when the Arum and Luxen join the impromptu fight, will Daemon fight on Katy's side, or that of the other Luxen? Does he even have a choice?

After finishing this novel, I felt as if I had been caught in the crossfire of a huge argument. While standing on its own, aside from "To Kill a Mockingbird", it is a decent story, but not the revelation of its predecessor. The syntax and grammar are odd and difficult to follow at times. The story is written in the third person, but many times it shifts to Jean Louise's thoughts and switches to first person. This is acceptable, but it would have been better if it had been better had those instances been italicized. But that's just my opinion. Also, some sentences just didn't make sense and I had to often re-read paragraphs to fully understand what was being said. However, in the scenes where Jean Louise recalls memories from her past, those parts really resonated. They briefly touched on the magic of her first novel. I was initially apprehensive to read this book because I didn't want it to taint the amazing memories I have for "To Kill a Mockingbird." Thankfully, that didn't happen. But I am saddened that this book was published when Harper Lee has stated that she didn't think anything could ever compare to her original work. In my opinion, the publication of "Go Set a Watchman" was the publisher's way to make a quick buck. After all, anyone who read Harper Lee's first book would be intrigued to read the second. Yet despite this, I still have the utmost respect for Harper Lee, the memorable characters she created, and her iconic body of work.

I saw this hyped a lot on my social media sites and when it came through on sale (or maybe even free...I can't remember) I thought I'd give it a try. 
 Okay, I'm not one to be automatically turned off by infidelity. It's a sad reality for many marriages and, if handled well, there's a great deal to explore in those dynamics. Not every marriage ends in happily ever after, and not every "other woman" is a home-wrecking whore. So I'm not judging this book based on my own personal biases. 
 My gripes: this is riddled with obvious editing errors. Misspelled and misused words were everywhere. I get that it's harder to catch every tiny error when you're self-published, but this level of shoddy proof-reading is unacceptable. I also found the prose to be clumsy and unpolished. There were too many incomprehensible sentences that should have been cleaned up by a good editing. 
 As far as the story went, Vera wasn't my favorite character, but she was fine. Her abrasive attitude and snap judgments of others in the opening chapters set me on edge, but that improved as the book went on. 
 Mateo was appealing enough initially. At least, I could see what drew her to him. When he was in seductive, flirty mode, he was pretty swoony. It was when he was in relationship mode that I really began to dislike him. He couldn't figure out what to do with his life for nine years and chose to blame that all on his wife instead of manning up and taking control of his circumstances. Sure, there might have been more to that story, but the reader wasn't shown any so I can only judge him from what we were given. And then he made some pretty egregious missteps once Vera moved to Spain. Each one taken on its own wasn't unforgivable, but they were never addressed and/ or he didn't apologize for it, except for some cop-out blanket "I'm sorry I messed up" statement at the very end.  Frankly, by the end, all he had going for him was that he was hot and rich. The person inside all of that had proven to be pretty whiny and immature. 
 And I was really annoyed with how badly they handled their new relationship. Yes, they were in a difficult situation with his marriage ending and the custody fight and her being so much younger than him. So maybe proceed with caution? But no, she throws everything away to move to Spain right this second because he demanded that of her and then sure enough, it blew up in their faces.  If they'd have used their brains and not just their libidos, they could have held it together long enough for his situation to resolve itself and a lot of the drama would have been avoided. 
 Back to the writing... once things began to fall apart, the angsty overwrought DRAMA of it all was too much. two or three pages devoted to her wailing and her heart breaking and she's bleeding emotion out until she's dead and it was all just way too over the top. 
 So yeah... I don't mind cheating in a story in general, but I do mind when it's handled badly.

I think the author found a bunch of random photographs and said, "I bet I could write a story connecting these." Which is a fun gimmick, but I don't think it made for a particularly cohesive story. The way the plot would bend over backwards to justify the characters looking at a photograph was sometimes laughable. Couldn't the photos just be flavor that punctuates the story instead of a moment in which we stop reading to look at the photo that the characters in the novel themselves have stopped to look at? Gimmicks get old fast, man. Faster than a bunch of kids stuck in a time loop apparently. 
 Jacob is a mystery to me, and not in a good way. He's terribly unpopular, but I don't see why. He's rich, he's not a total jerk, and he has no obvious deformity of body or mind. But I guess because he's the protag of a YA book, he has to be alone. His one friend is basically bribed to be his friend, and he's so unimportant to the story I don't know why he exists at all. After page 30 he stops existing. Jacob's family is small, thinly drawn, and neglectful, but not even horrible to him in a memorable way. They're just there because otherwise he'd be an orphan and that would be too complicated and interesting. 
 When Jacob finds the Peculiars (which takes far too long), they immediately adore him. You might think that's because he's peculiar too, but he doesn't know that and neither do they. There's nothing weird about him that made him an outcast at home but accepted by these strangers. Harry Potter at least had magic manifesting accidentally, so when he found Hogwarts, it was a relief to know he wasn't alone. Jacob's just a loser, and I guess this is one of those fantasies losers have where they move to a new town and can start over and convince everyone they're cool? That never worked for me. 
 I like some of the peculiar kids and their powers, but I couldn't shake how unbelievable their situation was. These kids have been stuck in the same day for 80+ years. But they're still kids? Even though they remember each day? The young kids even still take lessons with the old bird? What do they learn after 80 years? I know they aren't aging, but they're experiencing each day and the older kids, at least, should grow up. They should be jaded, or wise, or something. But then Jacob wouldn't have like minded teenagers to suddenly accept him, so no, they're babies who sneak away to snog under elm tree. Is this junior high? Have the same six people been dating one another for 80+ years? Shudder.  
 So the protag is utterly boring, the plot is both predicable and slow, the stakes around the bad guys' plan are large, but the bad guys themselves are generic villains, and the photo gimmick didn't work for me. The novel ended and I realized this whole thing was really just a set up for the REAL story, which (hopefully) will develop in book 2. 
 And if I'm ever stuck in an endless time loop, maybe I'll get around to reading that.

Fallen had been sitting on my shelf for a year now. After watching an interview with author Lauren Kate at a book fair early November, I finally cracked its spine. My expectations weren't that high, nor were they exceptionally low. The considerable hype surrounding this series definitely had something to do with both the high and the low part. All the same, I ended up disappointed. 
 I just couldn't get into it. Part of that is the fact that it's written from a third person perspective, which nearly always makes me feel distanced from the characters and the events. I strongly prefer books with a first person narrator, books that make you - when you look in a mirror after you've read them - surprised not to see the main character's face looking back at you. 
 A second reason is the setting. It was bland and gray and boring and the fact that it was a disciplinary boarding school added little or nothing to the story - when it could've had. In my opinion, it would have been so much more interesting (and realistic. And creepy!) if Luce were sent to an asylum of some sort. 
 I also found myself being slung back and forth between my impression of the surroundings (being: rainy, dark, coldn gloomy - as Luce's mood) and the actual surroundings (being: sunny, warm, beautiful trees etc). Somehow it didn't seem to fit, leaving me confused whenever Luce commented on it being hot outside. "Wait a second, wasn't the sky weeping in despair just a second ago? No? Sunny skies all around? Well alrighty then ..." 
 Third reason: it took forever until something supernatural started occurring. 3/4th of this book is basically about a girl getting sent to boarding school, doing research, falling in love with 2 guys at once and being chased by rather harmless shadowy thingies. Yawn. Only at the very end things started getting interesting, but then there was too much happening all at once. I honestly couldn't be bothered anymore at that point. I wanted to get it over with. 
 Fourth reason: although the idea of Luce's incarnations always finding Daniel is, of course, extremely romantic, I didn't feel anything at their developing love. No nostalgic sighing, no latent butterflies. Nope. Nothing. Sorry. 
 Fifth and maybe most important reason: I - once again! - made the mistake of reading a translation from English to Dutch. As a general rule, they suck. And I suck for trying to keep reading them. From now on: only English books and Dutch books that were actually written in Dutch.

I loved this book! But the loose ends weren't tied up! 
 First, let me explain the plot (the official description doesn't do a good job and I was confused the first 100 pages). The story is told from four different POV's, all students going to New York City High School of Creative and Performing Arts (CPA for short). There are four main characters, but a lot of minor characters. 
 Emme. Don't even get me started on her. From the second I started the book, I loved Emme. She was so realistic, so alive. She's a member of the Teenage Kicks, along with Ethan, Jack, and Ben--imagine this band, but classier: 
 Emme is a songwriter whose whole life has always been about helping her best friend, Sophie and hiding Sophie's ten-note range which brings us to our next main character. 
 Sophie, the characteristic manipulator. From the very beginning, she has manipulated her best friend Emme to have songs that make her the star. She was the one who convinced Emme to attend CPA, but now she feels like Emme isn't thanking her enough. Sophie is also hanging out with a junior named Amanda, who you find out more about later on  and her role in convincing Sophie to use Emme . Sophie is dating our next character, Carter. 
 Carter is a former child star who just can't get out of the limelight. His first audition was at 6 months, and every since, his mom has been pushing him to become a bigger and better star. He finally got her to agree to let him attend CPA, but he does a soap opera anyway. Carter's whole life has been one big part, but now he's finally stepping out of the role to find out who the real Carter is. 
 Our last character is Ethan, the 'loner' in a way. Ethan has troubled history (minor spoiler, nothing major and is revealed early on, but important to the overall plot).  He once dated a girl named Kelsey, but he would constantly cheat on her, then get back together with her after writing an apology song about it. Finally, Emme confronted him about his behavior, and he's stopped.  Ethan has had a major crush on Emme since day one, so he's constantly trying to get himself to tell her how he feels. 
 I have very mixed feelings about this book. On one hand, the overall message of the book was amazing with the background singer finally coming out of her shell. On the other hand, Sophie and especially Carter seemed weak and unimportant. Carter's POV was practically pointless, with the author treating it only as a good way to communicate information about the band. Sophie was great until the end, when she vanished out of the picture entirely along with Carter. Both of them were practically ignored any time Ethan and Emme were 'on a roll', so to speak. 
 Overall, this book was good. I would have given it 6 stars out of five, but there was no real ending with Sophie and Carter was 'brushed' over in order to give an ending to the Teenage Kicks. This book had a great heart, but it was too focused on the main plotline and didn't wrap things up very well for any characters other than the Teenage Kicks. I still love it, but the author could have done a better job with the POV's.

I just wish I had known which side of the love triangle to pick in book 1, as the romance was really wonderful here -- I kept waiting for him to storm out, but he was just unendingly patient and good and supportive and appropriately worried about her, which was refreshing.

Carefully preserved family history will do the trick.

 I often find other user's review far more articulate than my own, and I find that when different reviews come together, it nicely makes up for my own multi-faceted opinions about a book which I never fully cover in my own reviews. Having said that, Carol's and Maxwell's review perfectly sums up my very-hard-to-gauge feelings for this book. 
 The Long Way to a Small, Angry Planet is reminiscent of Star Trek, minus the action. It is a feel-good, sci-fi space opera that -- more than anything -- feels like a cup of soothing hot chocolate tossed with mini-marshmallows on a cold, hazy winter night. It is first and foremost a character-driven story, so I wouldn't (and shouldn't have) go[ne] in expecting an action-packed plot because there is little of it. 
 Very little happens in terms of plot in the former half of the book, and it was almost tedious, but what had bothered me most was the lack of maturity-- I'm accustomed to dark themes and characters, and stories that bring out the worst in humanity. Stories that reflect the disturbing but very real corners of reality. This was too happy, too naive for my liking. What I mean is that the story does traverse through the themes of sex and sexuality, love, loss, acceptance, despair and xenophobia, but it doesn't handle them maturely, or I guess, pragmatically. They just happen to be; never quite developed. At times, it also leaves little for the readers to decipher on their own as it glosses over profound themes by being explicit, which would have otherwise served as a spectacular backbone as an underlying message for a drama- or action-packed plot, or perhaps for a more subtle set-up. Regardless, I still appreciated this charming little remedy, and the quirky, cheeky band of crew members onboard the Wayfarer eventually grew on me. 
 The pacing dramatically picks up in the latter half, just enough to sustain, if not pique my interest.  Especially after Rosemary approaches Sissix with her feelings. A newfound appreciation for the story blossomed-- I was internally gushing; it was such a lovely, humane moment.  
 Alright, so the book felt too good, and too cheesy most of the time, a sci-fi fluff without the gritty, action-packed sequences you would expect from a solid space opera. It also lacked a certain degree of maturity which I sought, but I appreciated how its monumental purpose is to serve as an exclusively character-driven story, one that is emotionally-packed, self-conscious, and is urging the world to retain all the goodness that is left. It was delightful.

This is the thing: i hardly ever cry in real life, but when it comes to fiction and imagination i can cry like there is no tomorrow. 
 1) Award winner for crying-my-eyes-out in the category Movies: Breaking the Waves by Lars Von Trier. A 3 hour gorgeous, but emotionally horrific movie with the fabulous Emily Watson. I started crying after 20 minutes and i didn't stop until the very end. I remember my mother forcing me to drink 2 glasses of water before we headed back home. She was scared i was dehydrated. And she was probably right. 
 Runner-ups: Schindler's List, The Deer Hunter, Todo Sobre Mi Madre (All About My Mother), La Meglio Gioventu (The Best of Youth) and Bambi (obviously!) 
 2) Award winner for crying-my-eyes-out in the category Music: Puccini's Nessum Dorma. Put it real loud, especially if it's raining and storming outside. Or in a church: Goosebumps and tears guaranteed. 
 Runner-ups: The cello concerto of Edward Elgar (the version with Jacqueline De Pre on cello and Daniel Barenboim conducting); Max Bruch's violin concerto; Handel's Lascia Ch'io Pianga; Jeff Buckley's Hallelujah; Elvis Presley's Always On My Mind and Radiohead's Exit music for a film. 
 3) The award for crying-my-eyes-out in the category Books might just have been grabbed by this one. A story about a very complicated family carrying loss and grief, and not always carrying that burden in an elegant way. The story is being told following two main characters: aunt Georgie, fabulous lady of 42, pregnant by her ex-boyfriend of 7 years ago; and Thomas Mackee, a twenty-something who, strucken by grief, blew up all his bridges. 
 I was impressed with Melina Marchetta's writing in Saving Francesca, but that's nothing compared to this one. This is not like Breaking the Waves, which is so sad and heartbreaking from 20min until the end (way after the credits). This comes like military salvos, with some light-hearted banter in between and then WHAM before you know it, Melina Marchetta hits you where it hurts most, again. And as of then you're in an emotional warzone and the salvos just keep coming. Because it's sad or even because it's beautiful. It doesn't even matter anymore. 
 I cried when Tara finally calls for the first time, even if the message was somewhat surprising. I cried when Tom joins his dad to AA meeting, to find out that at his worst he couldn't recall his son's name. And as of the road trip to Brisbane, I cried every 10 pages or so.  
 And as in any award-speech, I need to thank a few people: 
 Thank you Wendy for recommending this book to me after i liked Saving Francesca. 
 Thank you Karen, Wendy, Ceridwen for making it so clear in your reviews that i needed a stack of Kleenex nearby. So i read this book in the safety of my own flat, and not somewhere on public transportation. Pfew. 
 And thank you Melina Marchetta, for writing this fabulous book that i won't shelf as YA. To me, this is a 25-30-something novel (how do we call those? Sophomore adults?) because it will only really get to you once you've known loss and grief for a couple of times, you've screwed up a few friendships/relationships for no good reason and you've lost yourself a little. 
 And now, I've cried enough. 
 I need some good old fantasy that won't make me cry. Legend or The Well of Ascension, aka Mistborn 2 ?

I loved the characters in this book. At least most of them. I don't usually read books that have soldiers in them (that aren't historical fiction). It just doesn't usually interest me because authors tend to use those characters to make a political statement about war, etc. This book didn't feel like that to me at all. Most of the story was told from the POV of Skylar, a recent high school grad trying to enjoy her last summer before escaping the tiny town she grew up in. When her former co-worker, Josh comes home from Afghanistan after two years away, he is minus one leg and not at all the same man-whore party animal he was in high school. He is a bit damaged to say the least. The two start up a light friendship that gradually grows into something more. Both are afraid to take it to the next level though. Sky doesn't want to have any reason to stay in Creek View and Josh is afraid she won't really want him with all his baggage from the war. I enjoyed the occasional snippet from Josh, mostly in a monologue to his best friend, who was not so lucky in Afghanistan. You can see him really struggling with his growing feelings for Sky, his attempts to adjust to his new life and his return to Creek View, not to mention deal with the emotional and psychological damage he sustained in combat. Most of Josh's struggles are seen through Sky's eyes, which is perhaps why I didn't feel like it was a commentary on war. I am well aware of all the soldiers that return home changed and damaged, I just don't like it shoved down my throat. The author did do a little shout out to the wounded warrior program in the author's notes section, which is great in my opinion. To me this story was simply a love story between two individuals who both had real problems and real challenges to deal with. I liked that Skylar also had major roadblocks and challenges and that it wasn't just Josh. She had a mother that was falling apart, the responsibility of being the adult and taking care of things she should never have to be burdened with at her age. She was exactly what Josh needed because she allowed him to take care of her and she didn't avoid the obvious with him. She didn't ignore his lost leg or treat him with pity, which is the way most people dealt with him. She was real and that is why she was the only one to be able to help him on his path back to himself. I really did like this story.

Vampires in a hard science fiction novel. Ok, not really "vampires", but a genetically-engineered re-creation of the predatory sub-species of homo sapiens with intellectual super powers and strange weaknesses that spawned the vampire legends. If the idea fills you with the same intense sense of malaise as it does me, then you should probably pass on this review and this book. 
 Blindsight was nominated for the Hugo, Locus, and Campbell awards, and I can see why: the ideas are flowing fast and furious throughout. The plot and other story components that are inessential to the cascade of ideas are all pretty sketchy, so the concepts take the weight of being front-and-center, supporting the whole book. 
 Unfortunately, to me, there are some flaws in the idea-stream. For example, some of them are neat-but-miss-the-point; I'll put the vampires in that bin. (I don't really consider them a spoiler, since Peter has a very good presentation about them online.) 
  
 Other ideas, however, seem to me to fall into the not-quite-thought-out category. The narrator and protagonist has no sense of empathy, following a hemispherectomy, and yet acts as a translator, in a sense, from the shorthand used by the other super-intelligent characters to normal human language used by the decision-makers back home on Earth. Yet, it doesn't seem quite real; there are only a few scenes where his viewpoint is suitably strange. Most of the time he simply seems to be an asshat, and as a narrator, an untrustworthy one. On other hands, apparently all super-intelligent physical scientists have the same set of enhancements, including the ability to use the spaceship's sensors as senses (two such scientists are seen); apparently linguists all have multiple personality enhancements (implied, IIRC). 
 The book suffers from what I like to call Sherlock Holmes' syndrome (although Conan Doyle doesn't suffer from the problem, which may be why I like the term) in that it is very difficult to make a convincing story with characters that are significantly smarter than the author. Watts, unfortunately, doesn't handle it as well as Doyle. 
 Searle's Chinese Room gag features as an important point, but Watts seems to make a bit of a hash of that, as well: the real mind-blowing aspect of the argument is the idea that an entity could pass the Turing test without being "conscious" or possessing "understanding", not that such a test would turn up an entity that could almost pull it off but fail because it doesn't "understand". 
  
 So, I am going to have to give Blindsight only two stars, mostly out of disappointment. But I feel bad about it.

 I loved this book! It was such a well done psychological suspense and I did not want to put it down. 
 Lies She Told is about Liza, a once best selling author who has struggled with her last few books. Her editor doesn't seem to be very impressed with her newest idea, but she gets him to agree to give her 30 days to submit a first draft. As she writes, she is distracted by her relationship with her increasingly distant husband, David, who's best friend and business partner, Nick, has gone missing. She is also on an experimental fertility hormone that has some difficult side effects. She starts to write her new book about Beth, a new mother who suspects her husband is cheating on her and goes to drastic measure to keep him. 
 "To be a writer is to be a life thief. Every day, I rob myself blind." 
 The story is told in alternating chapters of Liza's life and her book. I really loved this! There are definitely parallels between Liza's book and her life. However, I also thought that Beth's story, while inspired by Liza, still felt like it's own plot. It was almost like reading two different books that gave clues to each other. Including a story within a story is not a new narrative device, but I thought it was done really excellently here. 
 While I don't think the conclusion to the mystery of what happened to Nick is really that surprising, there were still enough little twists to keep me guessing. We don't know if Liza's hormones are making her forgetful or if there are other things going on. On the other hand, we see exactly how crazy and manipulative Beth can be. While neither of these two characters were particularly likable, I thought both of them to be sympathetic and compelling. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Lies She Told. I loved the writing style and the alternating chapters made me never want to stop reading. I definitely recommend this one to fans of psychological suspense. This is my first book by Cate Holahan and I am now anxious to try out what else she's done.

 This isn't the kind of book I normally read. I tend to steer clear of contemporary novels, and novels with a male protagonist - not intentionally though. However when this book was released I saw so much about it, so many people raving about how good it was, and some people saying how much they hated it, that I had to put it on my tbr list. When I found it for PS3.99 in Sainsburys I bought it straight away and started reading it the next day. 
 I think it's the kind of book which you either love or hate. It takes you on a journey, a realistic and graphic journey, that is haunting and beautiful. Its hard-hitting, it deals with a scope of topics that are sensitive, but they are well handled in the novel. I was also impressed by how many bases it touched; whereas in a novel normally only one of these sensitive topics are touched on in great detail, which perhaps a couple others in the background, this book deals with them all right in the spotlight. There's self-harm, suicide, child abuse, drugs, disability, issues with sexuality and race.  It's not for the faint hearted. 
 One thing that really struck me is how accurately diverse the characters are. They're not 4 white men, or 3 white men with one novelty black man in to make it racially diverse. Nor is there a novelty gay man in there. There's a huge range of non-white, non-straight people in this book, which is fantastic. It's amazingly diverse. And it's accurate too. Straight white men are not the majority in this world, and I am so glad that Hanya was accurate and inclusive in her book. I also loved how the novel started when the men were in their late 20s, I'm not sure why...I feel like it could've been easily started when they were in college, and though we get flashbacks to college, it was just so refreshing to have the novel start when they were older. 
 Another thing was how beautifully descriptive it is. One of my favourite parts of the novel is the description of JB's studio. It was stunning, not only could you picture it in your mind, but you could feel you were there, as Hanya describes the ambience of the place, not just the aesthetic. All of the houses are so lovingly described, as are the characters. This was another thing that really impressed me; in the first chapter you are basically given a description and backstory to each of the 4 main characters, but rather than being dull and dry and just pages of long paragraphs, it was gripping. I've never been so engrossed in a description of 4 characters. It was just handled brilliantly, and you get to know them so well throughout the book. 
 I'm not normally a crier at books; with films and tv programmes I am, but books never seem to make me cry. Before I was halfway through this book I had cried 4 times. I was a mess. I just wanted to wrap Jude in a blanket and tell him that none of it was his fault. Of course he wouldn't have believed me and would have ran away, but still. Willem's death was so unexpected. Those couple of pages became quite sinister in a way, like you could tell something was about to happen, and I was reading warily not wanting anything bad to happen.  
 The relationship of the 4 boys is amazing. It's a great friendship, granted it has it's ups and downs, but you could tell their bond was strong. I also found Willem's and Jude's relationship really touching. I was thinking throughout the book that something might happen, it's kind of hinted at in the sensitivity and love of their friendship, it's just a touch above everyone else's. I think that the transition from platonic to romantic was inevitable and really well done. I just wish they had had longer together.

 I was recommended this book by another author, and I have to say, this cover wouldn't have usually pulled me in. The cover just isn't very beautiful or creative, it honestly feels like something someone with a very minimal design budget and experience would have made by themselves. I was genuinely surprised when I found out it was a book represented by a major publishing house. That being said, the description and the recommendation made up for the issues with the cover, and I picked it up. I'm glad I did. The plot is a refreshing perspective on the Robin Hood tale, painting him in an interesting light and bringing Marian into the story in such an interesting way. I did have a few issues with the way it was written, first of all, it is my opinion that to balance show and tell, you shouldn't be telling us the way a person speaks but showing us. This is huge for me. I cannot stand funky written out dialect, which is what we received from the main character, not only in her dialogue but also in her manner of thinking. I would much rather of had the first time she spoke have it described and then perhaps have it described as a thickening accent when she was upset or something, well, anything other than the jolting writing of her poor English. This one factor alone pulled one star away from the story. Lastly, the level of description was just a bit obtuse for my taste. In the bits where there was action, I found I had to skim to find the action instead of the inaction. This docked another half star rating for me.  One of the things that makes this book so brilliant: Abercrombie gives you a few jaw-dropping electroshocks along the way: Jezal king? Quai actually being Tolomei? The bloody nine killing Tul?  which distracts from the real nuclear bomb that has been dropped at the start and is slowly building to general destruction of everything you thought you knew. Of everything that was so carefully constructed in Book 1 when Abercrombie really took his time to build solid foundations for all his characters. 
  
 Tolkien learnt us to trust the grumpy old wise wizard that lives in seclusion most of the time, but comes out of hiding and heads to court when things get tough. Bayaz seemed to fit that profile, he even got himself a fellowship of his own, but it becomes clear that he is in fact a huge manipulator, power-hungry and he does not care about the consequences of his actions.

 "All this has happened before, and all this will happen again"

4.5 stars. Mike Godwin is right on target when he describes this book as the "manic apotheosis of cyberpunk science fiction," at least the manic part. What I both loved and disliked about this book was its deep interconnectedness of technology and reality, man and machine, and all the ridiculous Sumerian mythology. The idea that these "me"s of what are basically ideas spread subconsciously throughout people just like a virus, and that this nam-shub anti-virus thing can disrupt this, and how that connected with the story at hand, and what that means for ideas, computers, and virtual reality -- I mean, awesome. But I wished that stuff would have taken less of a "side explaining story" that is expounded upon at length in certain parts but is then forgotten. 
 That seems to be a pretty recurring theme in this book: that it goes pretty deeply on something, and then there's a big question mark on the follow through. Many holes of "why didn't x?" or "but what happened to y?" persist past the end of the story, which is frustrating. Similarly frustrating are the all-too-convenient aspects of the plot that crop up near the end. 
 But, the mostly fast-paced plot, crazy but, yes, recognizable dystopian setting, and the ideas of the meta-virus as a sort of agent of change a la Darwinian evolution or the root of consciousness or something like that, all that make this an insanely complex and engrossing story. The ideas of "me"s and nam-shubs as neurolinguistic tools of programming the mind are pretty wild, and the use of the Metaverse alongside reality was a fantastic blend that may tell us what we might expect from the combination of virtual reality and actual reality when it comes. 
 Flawed but compelling all the same.

While Hyperion was brilliant in its variety, the way it mimicked the Canterbury Tales in tonal shifts, Fall of Hyperion is brilliant in the way it brings those tales together. Time travel makes me a bit dizzy, and there are still some points I don't understand  Where did Brawne's superpowers come from? , but the way it connected memorable characters with themes very close to my heart (society's dependence on technology, what would happen to a world without the Web?) make this one of the top sci-fi series I have read. I'll definitely read Endymion, though I'll take a break first. One can only stare into Hyperion's lapis sky for so long. Lapis, lapis, lapis...

 I think it was just okay to good. There were perhaps just a few too many characters to truly love them and flesh them out. 
 A few quick things I liked: 
 - Ululenia and her penchant for virgin boys - this is particularly hilarious because it is basically the reverse of unicorn == chastity. 
 - that our main character was a black female that was desirable 
 - Dairy's name 
 - the opening scene to show off the main character 
 Aaand, those were the main pluses. The writing is decent, with a few too many shoving down the reader's throat reactions (like the political puppet shows with the audience's reactions - it was never funny, but the audience laughed to show that it was humorous). But very solid writing otherwise. 
 Things I didn't really like. Why did everyone have to end up in couples? That really made me angry. Especially since two of the women had a main conflict of fighting over a boy (seriously, let me roll my eyes here) and they all seem to be allocated to physical descriptions. I could tell you how every single woman in this book looks - but I couldn't do that for the men. Good grief. It's a little annoying. 
 The plot was just a sigh at the end. Like we all knew it was heading towards an old fashioned good vs evil battle - is there any surprises there? Mmm not really. I guess that's why I'm so ambivalent about this book. It just feels like a typical fantasy novel with nothing new. It's a good romp with tried and true tropes, but what else does it bring? I was hoping for something new, and got mostly expected scenes that you can probably guess way upstream in the book. 
 Ugh, in the end, I thought it was just okay because the book just never grabbed my attention. I didn't love the characters, I thought the con was a bit half-hearted and not particularly clever, the end plot was a bit forced, and *shrug. There wasn't much else besides that.

I struggled with this book all week. I wanted to like it and then happily work my way through the whole series. But I give up. 
 The highlights of why I don't like it: 
 There is a prequel in Skin Trade. I actually read it at some point, but can't remember it. I guess reading and liking that prequel was the reason for me to get the book. Anyway, I don't remember anything about that short story and as this is supposedly the first book of the series, it should not matter. But the short story is referenced several times and it bugs me that I don't remember it and it interrupted the flow of the story several times for me. 
 I should like Jane. Tough biker chick, shapeshifter or rather skinwalker. Can fight, knows weapons. Takes no bullshit. Instead she just comes across as rude, not very smart, stubborn and juvenile. She does not seem to like anybody she meets out of principle. And that leads to a sleigh of characters that are not explored or described properly. She apparently is surrounded by idiots. 
 And despite being this tough chick, she gets bent out of shape about her hair getting wet in the rain, waxes on about the shape of all those awesome teapots in her pantry, shops for frilly dresses and has to go shopping for lipstick after shifting. Because as a woman you can obviously not get anywhere without lipstick. 
 There is a lot of descriptions about every little thing. On and on and on. The story drags. A lot! 
 And then all of a sudden there is action and you have no idea why there is a fight or how Jane got to that point or found the perp. She shifts and is on the track of the bad guy immediately. What? How? Jane could not reason her way out of a paper bag. 
 I dislike the voice of Beast. To make it distinct from Jane's voice, Beast thinks like a caveman. It makes for very bumpy reading. Plus she does not stick to the same tense or the same perspective during those scenes. 
 I also struggle a bit with intentionally bad grammar, that only pops up every now and then to give the impression that the character is a hardass. Does not work for me, especially when that character uses words like "whence" and is then incapable of telling the difference between adverb and adjective in the same paragraph. 
 And there are no decent dialogues. It is just dry, with long descriptions, action that makes no sense, no sleuthing, no character development. Around page 100 it actually got a bit more interesting,but by that point I disliked the whole story and Jane Yellowrock so much, that I decided to give up on this book and this series.

I read this book on the recommendation of a friend, who, I am not afraid to admit, has led me astray more than once. We really disagree on what books we enjoy reading, but that hasn't stopped us from recommending to others. I picked up this book with apprehension. But, I was pleasantly surprised. 
 The Girl of Fire and Thorns stars 16 year-old Elisa. She is a princess. She is bring forced to marry to the King of a neighboring country for political reasons. She eats her feelings. And she was bestowed a Godstone upon her naming by none-other-than God himself. Thus, chaos begins. 
 This book is a well-balanced YA novel with a strong female heroine. 
 Yes, Elisa struggles with her weight and how she eats all her feelings. But this isn't done in a body-shaming way. Elisa struggles with this as any 16 year-old does. She compares herself to how others look and the societal pressures of what is beautiful. When she's emotional, she eats. And she LOVES food. She doesn't just eat because of her emotions, she spends time in the kitchens (even once she becomes Queen!)  chatting with the cooks about their favorite foods and best prepared meals. This is a woman who struggles with body image, other people's expectations of what she should be, and a passion for delicious things. I am actually really impressed with how real this depiction is. I'm sure I'm not the only woman who can relate to this. 
 Also, this book involved a high percentage of religion. What with God bestowing the Godstone upon Elisa. It's literally a stone embedded above her naval which shows she has been "chosen for greatness". However, the religion is well embedded into the story in a what which feels natural. The prophesy (which, come on, it's fantasy, there has to be one) is tied closely into religion, which actually made me accept it more.  The Godstone is just a device for establishing magic in a world without it, which I actually enjoy.  I look forward to seeing how far religion goes in the remaining books. 
 All in all, an enjoyable book. I recommend this book to anyone who likes strong heroines and light fantasy. This is an easy book to get swept up in.

I ended up liking this book a lot more than I thought I would. The beginning was really annoying and weird, but after the first 150 pages or so, the story started picking up, and it started getting interesting. 
 My favorite thing I think is Celaena. She's amazing. At first, I thought I didn't like her, but as we got to know her throughout the book, I realized how well-crafted her character is. She's an assassin, so she's tough and strong, but she also likes pretty dresses and puppies and blushes a lot around the attractive men in her life. She's realistic, and she's also likable. 
 I also really liked the writing style. Sarah J. Maas really does a great job in capturing the essence of her kingdom and her characters with her words. The tone fits the story perfectly. It feels like a fairytale but more intense. And I LOVED THAT! 
 The only thing I really didn't like was the love triangle. It just felt really unnecessary. And boring. So, so boring. And it felt really out of place because everything else in the story felt so natural, but this love triangle felt so contrived. 
 Overall, I really liked this book, and I would definitely recommend it.

I didn't know much about the plot to start, and I think the book was better for it, so I won't divulge much. Suffice it to say the book is set in Stalinist Russia, and follows the rise and fall of a MGB State Security Officer, chronicling his pursuit of truth in a country that refuses to acknowledge weakness of any kind. At the same time, he changes his entire perspective on his life, his relationships, and how communism affects his country. It's beautifully written, and for a debut novel is that much more impressive. I kind of want to stab the author for being so brilliant on a first try. YOU MUST READ THIS BOOK!

This was a cute, quick read. I'll be honest, I didn't expect to like it, partly because of the title. I'm not a believer of love at first sight and this comes off as one of those books that tries to prove that it can happen. Maybe people can fall in love a first sight. But that's not what this book is about at all. 
 This book is about all kinds of love. It's about the love that you feel for family members, ones that you know you can count on and ones that disappoint you. It's about the love that you feel toward an ex, someone who broke your heart or someone whose heart you broke. It's about the possibility of love, of meeting someone that you connect with almost instantly, or meeting someone that you are sure you're going to hate only to find out that there's something good inside them that you could grow to like. 
 It's only 236 pages and the whole book spans only 24 hours, but so much happens and it's more than a boy and girl meeting in an airport. It digs deep into what it means to love someone and the things you do or don't do to show that love or to lose it. 
 I enjoyed reading it and was surprised at how much I ended up liking it. If you are looking for something quick and light to read, I would recommend this one.

I walked into this with no idea what to expect. I only knew it was a small book and compared to the last book I read (which was unnecessarily long at 500 pages) I wanted something quick and easy. 
 It was quick, yes, but I wouldn't say easy. The book barely makes it to 100 pages but it's packed full of situations that make you think long and hard. Here I am a day later and I'm still trying to figure out how I want to address the book. I tried reading other reviews for it but found that most of the top ones try far too hard to show off their academia. I'm not in school anymore so I don't need to worry about my word count or using the big words I know. 
 Essentially, The Invention of Morel is a study in isolation and companionship all at once. Our narrator is alone on an island, until he isn't anymore. Only the other people really aren't people, despite our narrator's perceived love and adoration for one of them. He vies for a relationship he can never fully have in its entirety, but then it seems like precisely how he wants it to be in that way. 
 I'm not sure I'm making any sense, but it's a damn good book. Makes me think far too much.

CAPTURED by Erica Stevens (Paranormal Romance, New Adult) I first just want to say that this is categorized in Amazon under "Teen" but this is a New Adult (18-25 age range) read. Even the author discloses "New Adult. This book contains some language, violence, and sexual situations. Recommended for ages sixteen and up." 
 I have been reading about vampires since I was old enough to walk to the library by myself and sneak home Anne Rice books at the tender age of thirteen. My mother call them "the devil" but I call them happiness. 
 This paranormal romance had interesting well developed characters, great pacing and intriguing world, although there are a lot of unanswered questions. In "Captured" the vampires are the ruling class and humans are slaves or in hiding in the wilderness planning a rebellion. Arianna (the leading lass), is captured and chosen by a vampire (Braith) of the royal family, to be his blood slave. What should have been a master/blood slave relationship grows into something neither of them understand. While Aria settles on her fate, she can not kill the hope that she might one day be back in hiding with her family. Braith (vampire prince love interest), confused with feelings he's never had before, appreciates the short time with Aria in secret, hoping to protect her from the ultimate demise of a blood slave. 
 What I didn't like: It was short and ends abruptly. At only 188 pages which to me, is more like a novella. I understand a lot of Indie authors are using a formula of: First ones Free + cliff hanger = paid 2nd book. As a reader I like this because I get a free taste of the story to see if I like it and then, once I'm hooked I will gladly pay the $0.99+ for the next book.  Upon re-reading Magician's End, I was struck at how well Mr. Feist was able to link so much together, especially some of the finer, less memorable things. Few authors are good at that.  One aspect of this book that really hit me this time which I don't remember affecting me as much in my first reading was the use of bringing back dead characters to help instruct the major characters.  Not since Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows have I found reading a novel so difficult. Please excuse me if I digress a bit. In the mid 1980's I first picked up Magician: Apprentice, and was totally enthralled. The world was so vivid, the characters so real, the emotions and insecurities so sincere. This first book by Raymond Feist gripped me like no other. For the next 30 years I devoured every new novel, purchased two computer video games based on his fantasy world and characters, and just could not get enough of his work. 
 Of the 28 novels set in his fantasy world of Midkemia (hey, it's easier to spell than William Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha County (yes, I have read and retained 'real' literature too)), I would say only three were bad, and they were written as a basis for the video games and shouldn't count. 
 Magician's End wraps up the story in a similar fashion, bringing back the memories of old and beloved characters, making you feel the pain of losing long time favorites, and neatly enfolding all the previous story-lines into one unified climactic battle. 
 Everyone has their favorite author, book or series that they cannot get enough of. Knowing that this is the last of a 30 year series is like saying goodbye to a close friend. 
 I would highly recommend this book with the caveat that you have some familiarity with most of his books, as there are references that the reader will only understand if they know the backgrounds.

A slow start, but wow, what a finish. 
 This is a book that I bookmarked based on a good reads recommendation. I knew that it dealt with injustices within the legal justice system and thought it would compliment other reading that I have done...which it did. It was also a library borrow that I hadn't intended to read just yet, but found myself reaching for when I forgot to bring my current reading material with me on an outing. 
 So it is mere coincidence that I happened to be reading this book, which among other things discusses racism in the South, during the same period in which SC state officials finally removed the offensive Confederate Flag from the State House building. 
 Basically, Bryan Stevenson, the executive director of the Equal Justice initiative in Alabama and a professor of law at New York University Law School, outlines his fight to stop racial bias in the criminal justice system and to end unfair sentences in criminal cases, particularly as they relate to minors, minorities, and the mentally ill. 
 He cites many examples and case histories that include his successful effort to free Walter McMillian, a black man who was wrongly convicted of murder and sentenced to death. But the book really covers quite a bit of ground that goes far beyond any one example of injustice. 
 Bottom line, there is less justice for the poor and even less for poor minorities, and virtually none for poor, minority youths. 
 Reading this book, I was saddened, disgusted, outraged, and generally frustrated. The idea behind our legal justice system is a good one, but the execution is sorely lacking--no pun intended. The idea that we try youths as adults is preposterous. The idea that we then send them to adult prisons where they are routinely abused is madness. The state-sanctioned killing that we know kills innocents and is disproportionately applied to the least advantaged is absurd. And the racial bias and ignorance that all too often confirms our biases and fuels our prejudices are all too real and relevant to be denied. 
 There is one story Stevenson shares in which he is subjected to a demeaning strip search by an enthusiastic and overtly racist guard. Later, this guard accompanies him and a prisoner he represents, a man who was severely abused by the foster care system among a life of hardships which are offered as extenuating circumstances in his case. Afterwards, the guard approaches Stevenson with a much different attitude and shares his own horrible experiences in foster care. I felt this was such a wonderful addition to this particular book. In a sense, Stevenson has gone out of his way to not only empathize with the people he helps, but also to empathize with the kind of racism that makes his efforts necessary. I think this is an important point in the context of this discussion. Just as many of the men and women that Stevenson advocated for were victims in their own right and deserve to be judged within the context of their life experiences, so are many of the racists and pig-headed absolutists. In that sense, as he so eloquently points out...we are all broken, perhaps to different degrees and in different ways, but we are all affected by things outside our control. Thus, taking the time to understand why somebody is racist is just as important as speaking out against racism. Even the bigoted racist has his own story. This actually reminded me of some of Erskine Caldwell's works of satire in which he often shows the oppressed quick to oppress those beneath him, which I always felt was a powerful observation and true in many cases.  
 I'm going to end with a long quote which beautifully and completely expresses the essence of this book, making it worth all the extra typing. 
 We are all broken by something. We have all hurt someone and have been hurt. We all share the condition of brokenness even if our brokenness is not equivalent. I desperately wanted mercy for Jimmy Dill and would have done anything to create justice for him, but I couldn't pretend that his struggle was disconnected from my own. The way in which I have been hurt--and have hurt others--are different from the way Jimmy Dill suffered and caused suffering. But our shared brokenness connected us. 
 Paul Farmer, the renowned physician who has spent his life trying to cure the world's sickest and poorest people, once quoted me something that the writer Thomas Merton said: We are bodies of broken bones. I guess I'd always know but never fully considered that being broken is what makes us human. We all have our reasons. Sometimes we're fractured by the choices we make; sometimes we're shattered by things we would never have chosen. But our brokenness is also the source of our common humanity, the basis for out shared search for comfort, meaning, and healing. Our shared vulnerability and imperfection nurtures and sustains our capacity for compassion. 
 We have a choice. We can embrace our humanness, which means embracing our broken natures and the compassion that remains our best hope for healing. Or we can deny our brokenness, forswear compassion, and, as a result, deny our own humanity. 
 I thought of the guards strapping Jimmy Dill to the gurney that very hour. I thought of the people who would cheer his death and see it as some kind of victory. I realized they were broken people, too, even if they would never admit it. So many of us have become afraid and angry. We've become so fearful and vengeful that we've thrown away children, discarded the disabled, and sanctioned the imprisonment of the sick and the weak--not because they are a threat to public safety or beyond rehabilitation but because we think it makes us seem tough, less broken. I thought of the victims of violent crime and the survivors of murdered loved ones, and how we've pressured them to recycle their pain and anguish and give it back to the offenders we prosecute. I thought of the many ways we've legalized vengeful and cruel punishments, how we've allowed our victimization to justify the victimization of others. We've submitted to the harsh instinct to crush those among us whose brokenness is most visible. 
 But simply punishing the broken--walking away from them or hiding them from sight--only ensures that they remain broken and we do, too. There is no wholeness outside of our reciprocal humanity.

I actually liked this book. However, I feel like I need to deduct a star because of the truly unhealthy nature of Jude and Lucy's relationship. I know that's part of the issue Lucy's struggling with in the book, but I just can't condone it. Especially with the way it ended. 
 If it was just about the struggle, and Jude's anguish about it, I would have been ok. But what really gets me is that, at the end, Lucy's mother encourages her daughter to stay because "they're both passionate people". Ok, no. Passion and fighting is one thing, but throwing your drawers out the window? Not eating for 4 days? Driving 5 hours back and forth?  Yeah, it sounds romantic, but it's exactly this kind of stuff that encourages teenage girls to get into unhealthy relationships. 
 When I was younger, I read all these trashy historical romances where it was passion, fighting, drama. And throughout college and my 20s, I mistook fighting for true love. It wasn't until I realized that something hard and emotionally exhausting wasn't love, but chemistry created by drama. Yes, you need to work at relationships, but that's not the same thing as constant emotional roller coasters. 
 I feel like its sending a wrong message to teenage girls that could impact their lives. 
 There are other things that really, really bugged me about the book - SPOILERS AHEAD 
 1. Jude freaking out at Lucy's parents during Thanksgiving. Yeah, his dad going to prison caused him abuse. And I could understand his sentiments in the first book. But seriously - his dad murdered their son. He may have had a crappy life, but John is dead. Where is the remorse or guilt of the impact that his dad had on their family?? 
 Worse, why are Lucy's parents understanding of it??? It's all zen to believe that one shouldn't judge the son for the fathers sin, but for the to (a) take it, (b) apologize for it, (c) welcome him, and then (d) encourage their daughter to be with him? Come on. It would have been much more realistic if they struggled with Lucy and Jude being together because they loved her, but had a hard time being around him bc he reminded them of their loss. 
 2. These public declarations of love? Bugged me in the first book, seriously bugged me in the 2nd. At least in book 1, Jude was this bad ass who frequently caused disruption at school. But Lucy declaring her love at a football stadium??? And him proposing? *Roll eyes* 
 3. How did Jude suddenly go from bad boy juvenile delinquent to football star? Sure, he's an awesome player, but ppl don't make a 360 turnaround like that. He's got anger management issues, but now he's suddenly on the straight and narrow because of love? And what about studying? Football players still need to keep a certain grade point to play. He seems to spend all his time driving back and forth. No studying involved. 
 Plus, why doesn't anyone have him seem counseling for his anger and rage? It's not good for him or the people around him.  
 As I said, it was an enjoyable read - emotional, intense, dramatic. I guess once boy and girl are together, the author needs to create some drama to justify a 2nd book. 
 But there were just too many times I spent shaking my head that I can't justify 3 stars. There were so many other ways that this book could have continued their story - struggling with John's death despite their love, his anger issues, etc. Instead, Nicole Williams took the I'm-jealous-and-insecure path that made it like every other new adult/teen romance sequel. And she killed the strong, spunky, of grief driven girl Lucy was in "Crash" and made her a blubbering, insecure mess. 
 There were good topics that she dealt with in book 1 that would have made book 2 stand out. Unfortunately, she shot her own story in the foot by making it an unhealthy, unrealistic wannabe, and it looks like book 3 is headed in that direction as well.

Don't let the fact that it took me over a year to finish this book make it seem like I didn't thoroughly enjoy it! Blame two semesters with intense reading schedules (also, the fact that I could never read this while eating lunch, which is when I do the bulk of my reading). Luckily, this is easily put down and restarted due to the almost self-contained chapters. Mary Roach is an insanely talented writer, and I covet her ability to bring clarity and humor to potentially difficult topics. I loved her drive to follow through with questions that other people would drop because the answers were so uncomfortable, and I loved that she treated everything with a good sense of humor while still respecting the subject. Her choice to occasionally insert her own opinion on how people treat death and the body was a good move, and I thought the last chapter on her own choices for her body in the future brilliantly put in context everything she'd discussed. I think I'm going to give this four stars because I can't imagine feeling a need to read this again, and there were points when I started to feel like some of the chapters went on too long, while other topics were given too light of treatment (the chapter on the dead body used for religious purposes could have been greatly expanded) , but it's very close to five. (UPDATE: I'm changing my rating - I think about this book all the time!)

For the past few years, I can't imagine myself reading a chicklit-romantish novel. But now I'm in love with Rainbow Rowell. I loved Attachments. I loved Eleanor and Park. Attachments was written so whimsically that you can imagine yourself in the lives of different characters. Like you were there, inside the book (dating Lincoln/ Chris OR being Beth or Chris...or Lincoln. hihihi). I was overwhelmed with the idea that I can picture myself with the amount of stalking-investigating powers in Beth. I cried for laughing too much actually. I loved this so much. 
 Attachments is about a wholesome-multiple-degree-holder guy (Lincoln) and two brilliant ladies (Beth and Jennifer) dreaming about a perfect life. A perfect love life but then who knows what a perfect life is? There are different levels and views about a perfect life and a love life. Anyway, the three characters work on a same newspaper company, The Courier. The guy, Lincoln works as an internet security officer. A job where he is allowed to sneak and peek on other people's email so that they will not slack off during work. Honestly, I never thought that there is really a job like that before (welcome to the 90s! Haha). Well, this is how Lincoln indirectly met Beth and Jennifer, both writers and editors, he was amused with their wits and humor from their explicit emails. In the end, he finds himself falling for Beth. 
 Unfortunately, Beth, has been dating a handsome and hunk musician for nine years. She's dying to get married and have kids. But then she got dumped. Now Lincoln shows up being awkward, how can he tell her that he has been in-love with her? How can he approach her without being awkward? How can he approach her when he already knows so much about her (thru her email)? Is it already too late? Well, that's for you to find out. Read this funny and heartwarming novel! 
 Here's an excerpt from the book, I found it realistic (and I can relate to it. -- I don't know what to do in my life so I just study. Study. Study. Study again. Sigh.) and funny at the same time. 
 "I don't know how I feel about that, Lincoln. I'm starting to think you might have a problem. With school." (Lincoln's mother) 
 "I've never had a problem with school," he said, knowing how lame that sounded, knowing that refusing to take part in the conversation wasn't the same as avoiding it. 
 "You know what I mean," she said. She wagged a dirty spoon at him. 
 "A problem. Like those women who get addicted to plastic surgery. They keep going back and going back, trying to look better until there is no more better. Like they can't look better because they don't even look like themselves anymore. And then it's just about looking different, I think. I saw this woman in a magazine who looked just like a cat. Like a cat of prey, a big cat. Have you ever seen her? She has a lot of money. I think she might be from Austria." 
 Excerpt From: Rowell, Rainbow. "Attachments."
