Kresley Cole's female characters are the best! They are badass, wicked and flawed which is so much more exciting the typical virgin do-gooders who only want to do the right thing and make the world a better place. Kresley Cole's females will kick a jerk while their down and maybe even break their arm just for kicks. I know that awful but in the world of the Lore, it is the only way to survive. 
 Calliope was exiled from Silvan, the Fey realm, when she was just thirteen years old by her fiance, King Saetthe, because her parents had plotted against him. At least she wasn't beheaded like they were. She has lived in the human real ever since. She has been hiding from her mortal enemy Rune and his alliance, the Morior, all of her life. Sylvan has wards against the Morior so she was safe there but in the human realm, she was vulnerable. She adapted well and hid in plain sight, working at Disney World as one of the princesses. 
 She hadn't heard from Saetthe in over a decade when he showed up with Nix, the Valkyrie sootheayer, to tell her to go to hell...literally. They wanted her to go to Pandemonia, a hell realm, to spy on a demon named Abyssian, one of the Morior. Rumor had it that the Morior were going to invade this universe and take over. Saetthe told her that she could come back to Sylvan if she made this sacrifice. Nix told her it would be easy because Calliope or Lila as her friends called her was Abyssian's mate and she would need to seduce him. When she asked Saetthe if that would bother him, he told her he was above those sort of feelings. 
 Lila agreed so Nix told her she would set the plan in motion. She would have her captured and taken to Abyssian. Later that night, two Sorceresses captured her and opened a portal into Pandemonia and handed her over to a monster. 
 Abyssian used to be physically flawless. The ladies fought each other to get to him but when his twin brother was killed, Abyssian aka Sian had to take over Pandemonia as the king and had to take the curse that went along with it, turning slowly into a monster. He already had red skin, wings and huge horns but knows that it will only get worse. 
 Thousands of years ago Sian had found his mate. She was a Fey princess from Sylvan but she broke his heart and betrayed him then married another Fey. She had died shortly afterwards but he had always wanted to get his revenge on her. So, when the sorceresses opened a portal into his dimension and handed Lila over, he was elated to finally get his revenge on her. 
 Lila was surprised when Sian put her in a tower with no physical comforts. She realized that Nix and Saetthe had duped her by not telling her the whole story. Sian played games with her like making her spin spider webs into thread before the sun came up lest the gigantic spiders come for her. He believed they were impossible tasks but Lila was smart and crafty and outwitted him in a lot of his cruel games. Some of the things she did were hilarious. She hated him yet was somehow drawn to him at the same time. 
 Sian could not seem to separate Lila from Kari and made her suffer for crimes she didn't commit. He had lots of cruel plans for his mate but he couldn't help feeling for Lila. He was hot and cold but Lila was up for the challenge. 
 This book was fantastic! I loved all their antics. There was a lot of humor yet some heart-wrenching moments too. I had just re-read this whole series so I was ready for this book and had everything from the previous books fresh in my memory. I am not sure exactly what Nix, the mastermind of everything happening in the Lore, is planning but I can't wait to find out.

A brief review (more for me to remember): 
 I was thoroughly impressed by this book. If I read this before the Goodreads Best Fantasy 2014 poll closed, I would have actually changed my vote to this book. 
 The concept is absolutely fascinating. This book really teaches an old dog new tricks. There's the old tropes: fantasy gods, a murder mystery, a spattering of magic. Y'know, the usual. But dang, this was quite a ride. 
 My only complaint was that it is a little strangely written in the present tense. However, I only noticed (and was jerked out of the story) when going between the flashbacks (past tense) and the actual story (present tense). It's a little odd, but not overly so. 
 Characters are done extremely well. The flashback to the childhood and interactions between Shara and Vohannes was perfect for setting up their personalities. I love love love Sigrud (that scene of getting ready for war was hilarious and as strong as a Haka dance in my mind). No Mary Sue here, no flat 2D characters here. Motives are subtle and every action is colored by character, rather than forced for the plot. 
 The setting is lovely and has that ethnic, familiar, yet not-familiar feel. The characters's names themselves add color to this world. 
 The plot moved. It carried you into discovering the world and the characters. Fast-paced, always interesting. Never stagnated. A murder. The discovery of gods. The Warehouses. A fight to the death against a god's beastie. Political maneuverings. An assassination attempt. Family troubles. And of course, killing gods. 
 Ending... eh. I don't hate it. But I don't think I love it either. It is a little too clean.  Killing both gods in one go? Blah, it was too easy. I think I am also sad that Vohannes died - but I do understand it . 
 Solid 4 stars. The main reason I didn't rate even higher is that it has no re-read appeal for me. 
 -edit- 
 Reread because I wanted to read City of Blades and I had forgotten some details. I take it back. This holds up really well to a reread. I am still impressed at the world, characters, plot, and everything. Even more so the second time around. I think 4.5 stars rounded up now. If I end up rereading it again, I might have to bump it up to 5 stars entirely.

This book is satisfying as a companion to the Mistborn trilogy. Though it stands on its own with a host of new characters that all feel quite fresh and new, the world is very familiar. It's far more technologically advanced, sure, but there are plenty of references (some obvious and some wonderfully subtle) back to the trilogy. The magic system has evolved along with the technology of the world, and it's all quite logically thought out. 
 I had a minor gripe with the main villain, who served his part quite well but was fairly predictable. There was a lot of guessing in the beginning as to who was behind all the terrible crimes, and as soon as the notion popped into the main character's mind it became rather obvious to the reader. He didn't want it to be true, as the villain was someone he used to work with.. but the emotional impact of the "betrayal" was fairly mild, as all that was before the beginning of the novel. Despite that I enjoyed his scenes, and liked the semi-subtle comparisons to Kelsier. The idea of how such a wonderful, charismatic leader was so close to sprinting down the road paved with good intentions always intrigued me, and seeing a villain that was only a few steps further down the path was fascinating. 
 I also loved the development of the religions, a few of which began during the trilogy. Seeing how they changed over time was highly intriguing, as were the creative swears that went along with them. Well worked religions are a staple of Sanderson, though, so that's to be expected. (: 
 Oh, and the "lofty tongue" of the "High Imperial" had me in splits. That might have been my favorite part. 
 Overall, this was a fun little novel that wrapped up rather neatly despite the interesting hook at the end. It wasn't quite as memorable as any of the trilogy books, but it was great for a quick run back to the Mistborn universe.

I'm so irritated right now that I don't even know where to begin. But, everything will be a spoiler because I can't help it with this one. 
 First off, Tate. WHAT THE HECK, GIRL? When this book started off, I thought I was going to like her. She had spunk. I foolishly got my hopes up that she wasn't going to be the girl that always annoys me in romances. But, she was. As soon as she met Miles, ALL OF HER SPUNK DISAPPEARED. Suddenly, she was this lovesick puppy who couldn't stop thinking about Miles. All of her thoughts were about Miles. It was Miles this and Miles that. I wanted to rip my hair out! She is going to school and working as a nurse, but she can only think of Miles? Come on! Not to mention, she let Miles walk all over her. He was polite enough to ask if she was okay with it (and though he could have stopped it I'm not currently ranting about him) and even though she wasn't, she never said no. At the end, Miles says Rachel's name during sex and instead of Tate stopping him she tells him to finish. WHAT THE HELL? I don't know how I didn't through the book across the room. She thought that it was okay for him to use her to feel better. Then, he comes back and she accepts him with open arms because he finally admitted that he missed her. I'm sorry???? GROW A SPINE. 
 I briefly touched on it while I talked about Tate, but this relationship was unhealthy. It was emotional torture and painful to read. I had wondered about it when I heard it was compared to 50 Shades of Grey, but then I heard people disagree and say it was nothing like that. Now, in my mind, it wasn't that bad, but an unhealthy relationship is still an unhealthy relationship and there are no excuses for it. NONE. 
 Miles has a few things I like about him. For just wanting sex, he was polite about it. He was always honest with her and asked for consent. But, he could have put a stop to all of it! There was no way he didn't know what he was doing to Tate. He should have stopped it. What he went through was tragic, yes, but that doesn't mean he gets to be an ass. 
 I really wanted to like this book, especially when I first started, but I couldn't do it.

 Well, I was wrong, and I am glad that i was wrong. This is a fucked up story, it really is, and somehow i am left wondering just how the hell did I come to name a 'snatch and rape' story in one of the top "Feel-good" books of 2013????!!!

Kind of... weird? It's written as well as you would expect from Sayers and I enjoy her characters but 1) the introduced "romance", such as it is, is kind of weird and creepy 2) the mystery isn't very exciting. 
 This is related to 1) and it's "spoiled" on the back cover but just in case The very first time Wimsey sees Vane, while she's imprisoned on a murder charge, he says "I want to marry you". Uhhhhhhhhhh. I think the only reason I was OK with it is because Vane is similar to Sayers - mystery writer etc - so it was like "oh if she's ok with the creepiness then fair enough". But it's a really bizarre plot, with no reason for his attraction to her or why this is a reasonable way of doing things. Given that it was the major character plot, so to speak, it bothered me  
 With 2, massive massive ending spoilers There are only 3 possibilities ever brought up, with no other suspects or even red herrings: Vane killed him, he committed suicide, Urquhart killed him. We know from the start the first isn't possible because it opens with the crown trying to prove it was true and Wimsey knows they're wrong (just because HE KNOWS no other reason), the second is constantly undermined with 0 evidence for it and eventually firmly disproved about halfway through, leaving the third as the only possibility. So the suspense is entirely in why and how he did it. "He did it for the inheritance" is the oldest motive in the book and becomes pretty obvious from early on but you only find out for sure late on. I didn't guess the how but I feel you could pretty definitely work it out and realise it if you have more experience with mystery/crime stuff if only as an "elimination of the impossible and whatever remains" thing. There are also a few things not explained in the end, like whether Urquhart intended to frame Vane - it feels it must have been deliberate but it's not mentioned. He'd been planning it for *years* though so it seems strange he'd have worked out who to frame for it - but the coincidental timings of attacks seem impossible otherwise. And it's not as if the earlier poisonings were at all necessary and in fact just created more suspicion. So it's weird. Not that elegant.  
 Other people have complained about Wimsey not always being the focus, but I like Climpson a lot - Sayers has a pretty funny and recognisable speech pattern down with the italics being surprisingly effective. Her attempts at spiritualism are funny and some of the most enjoyable parts of the book

This was another disappointing read for me. Yet again, as it seems to be a running trend, I have turned into the equivalent of a 'Literary Grinch'. I really had high hopes for Eleanor & Park. Truly, I did! But there was so much crammed into this novel that did not work for me. 
 The characters, first-and-foremost, bothered me. I mean, we have a slightly chubby, redheaded be-freckled (is that a word? Fuck it, I'm using it!) girl named Eleanor, who, truth be told, comes from a fudged up family. She spends the whole book being snarky and hot/cold...also, crying, whining, abashed, nervous, self-concious, etc. A-typical teen behavior, for sure, and she has a rough life to boot, but she annoyed the living hell out of me-- Especially when it came to the half white/half Asian boy, Park. From a somewhat normal family, for sure (at least, in comparison to Eleanor's); Park does taekwondo, is pretty "cool" (and just "pretty", apparently), but how many goddamn times do we need to be reminded of his half-Asian heritage? Almost every single time he and Eleanor speak. I preferred, in terms of racial diversity, Eleanor's two friends, DeNice and Beebi. I really wish Rowell had them play a bigger role in this story, but alas, we're stuck with the teens who go from pretty much hating each other upon first glance, to being near-goddamn soulmates not 10 pages later. 
 That's another thing that I had a gripe with. The romance. It was so cloying at times I wanted to scream. Other times, way too melodramatic for sixteen year olds. Seriously, Eleanor and Park constantly talk about how they are the only ones for each other; They are all the other needs. It's incessant! At one point, Eleanor asks Park why he doesn't hang out with his other friends anymore. His response? "...I don't really miss them, I've never really missed anybody but you." It made me want to throw up. I get that they're young and "in love" (yeahfuckinright), and we're made to believe that theirs is not just some half-baked high school romance that will fizzle and fade (they even say pretty much the same), but it's just way too cutesy. Maybe it's just me. Although, I had a long conversation with my sisters today about what Park said in regards to his friends, and they thought he was being, well, a pussy. All this mumbo jumbo about Eleanor being the only person her ever needed is just nonsense. Love shouldn't shackle you, children. 
 Seriously, am I supposed to be heartbroken over an unrealistic, implausible, whirlwind romance possibly not lasting? 
 No. 
 Is this book a heartbreaking look at "brave and desperate" young "love"? 
 No. (Maybe?) 
 You want to know what is heartbreaking? -The amount of 1-star books I've been reading lately. Maybe 'Cynical Kyle' has been clawing his way to the surface more recently than not, but I'm not deliberately trying to hate these books. They're just not very good, 
 and Eleanor & Park just happens to be one of them.

The horrors of war in Germany. 
 What is death? Death is life's ending. Everyone will experience death. Death and dying are an inevitable part of human life. 
 Why did I define death? Well, this book is so deep and poetic that even Death itself narrated the novel. And because of that, the book created a depressing point of view. Death the narrator is the most human of all, he feels weakness, feels sadness, feels sympathy, feels love, feels fear unlike Nazis & ignorant people. 
 This book made my nose filled with mucus. 
 But do not feel disappointed, this book also speaks more about human survival. 
 "I guess humans like to watch a little destruction. Sand castles, houses of cards, that's where they begin. Their great skills is their capacity to escalate." 
 And now, I will end this review with the conscience-stricken last paragraph of the book: 
 "I wanted to explain that I am constantly overestimating and underestimating the human race - that rarely do I even simply estimate it. I wanted to ask her how the same thing could be so ugly and so glorious, and its words and stories so damning and brilliant... 
 I AM HAUNTED BY HUMANS." 
 I AM HAUNTED BY HUMANS.

I was SO HAPPY that Clark survived the plague. The book wasn't clear on if he had or not until nearly the end of the book, and I was so glad he did. He was one of my favorites.  I would have liked to hear more about Jeevan overall, and felt his story wasn't as fleshed out as I'd have liked it to. 
 I appreciated the familiarity but excitement of diving into this book. The premise reminds me of The Stand, but at the same time it's nothing like The Stand. I highly recommend reading it.

Book Review: The Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins 
 Okay, I may be a tad dilatory in getting to this, but I did it. Why did I read the first book of this top-shelf young adult action trilogy? Because A, I wanted to see what all the tweenie-boppin' masses were whining about, and B, because I was curious. 
 I'll admit, there's some speed to this story. It's a fast read and, in all fairness had me wondering how it was going to end. 
 Now, after admitting that, I refer back to page 100 where she decided to put this sentence in there. 
 "Don't. Don't let's pretend when there's no one around." 
 WTF does that mean!? I'm asking you out there because I don't know at all, and there's no valid excuse you can give me that would validate it. It doesn't make sense. Period. 
 However, book one of the Hunger Games was, I thought, well-crafted. Collins has a great idea and presents it well for a young-adult audience. I am not going to read books 2 and 3. I think it should have stopped with one book, but that's me. Who knows the reasons for why she kept going. 
 All-in-all, if you're up for something light and deals with mass killing and suited for young adults, by all means.

This is a really sweet, heart warming story. Shelter Mountain really pulls at your heartstrings. I think Shelter Mountain is one of my favourite type of books. Where you get to see the heroine grow as the story progresses and how she over comes the bad things in her past and becomes the best woman she can be. 
 Paige is on the run with her three year old son Chris from an abusive husband who has just beaten her for the last time. She's trying to get to a friend to hide and restart her life but ends up in Virgin River instead. When she wanders into Jack's bar on a cold and stormy night, with a face covered in bruises John "Preacher" Middleton who's Jack's cook is left to close the bar and feels instantly protective of Paige and her son and offers them a room for the night and a safe place to stay. 
 John who comes across in Virgin River as a bit distant is anything but in Shelter Mountain. John is such a sweetheart, right from the start of the book all he wants to do is protect Paige and her son and make sure they're safe and taken care of. The way John and Paige's son Chris bond really well from the start and its so sweet to see. 
 Paige is a wonderful character, she starts off as an abused and scared woman and as she slowly starts to trust John and the residents of Virgin River she really blooms and becomes of of the town. 
 I enjoyed the extras in Shelter Mountain, you get to see more of Jack and Mel and how they're doing as a married couple. There's a new development for Mike, who's one of Jack and John's marine buddies and a few others things. 
 This is a wonderful story and it's beautifully written. I would highly recommend this series!

A tomboy who doesn't know how to get close to people and makes assumptions rather than effectively communicate and has no clue what to do when she likes a boy? Well hello my childhood (and maybe my adulthood but I digress...). Only this book has a bad ass girl who may be all of the above but knows what she wants, fights for it, falls, gets back up, trains her ass off, learns humility and still gets to take out her frustrations in battle. I am blown away with this book, the characters and the storyline. The last few chapters I think I almost passed out from holding my breath. I won a copy of this title from the publisher via a giveaway on Good Reads. This does not impact my review. 
 This is a book I have been looking forward to reading for awhile and I was very excited to win a copy. It seemed to take forever to finally receive it, but once it did I read it in a weekend. 
 The Woman in Cabin 10 started out a little slow. The main character, Lo, was pretty unlikable. She seems to be kind of an alcoholic and mixes alcohol with anxiety medication and isn't really the most reliable witness. She's kind of belligerent with people, as well. Throw in some PTSD from a recent break-in at her apartment and very few people believe her when she insists the woman in the cabin next to hers on a cruise ship has been thrown overboard. Of course, there's also no record of a woman staying in that cabin to begin with. 
 Once we reach the part in the book where Lo tries to investigate what really happens is where the story really picks up and I had a hard time putting it down. The setting was kind of creepy and Lo's paranoia was really well written. I suspected many different people, including Lo and her questionable mental state. While this part of the book seemed to fly by for me, we reach a part where it's basically just a lot of Lo conjecturing with very little plot advancement and the book slowed way down again. The final chapters leading up to the end picks up a little again, but overall the pacing of the novel was just a little too uneven. 
 Overall, I did enjoy The Woman in Cabin 10. Though the pacing was a little off for me, there were definitely big parts of the story where I couldn't put it down. Though Lo was a pretty unlikable character for the most part, I did feel a connection to her by the end. I felt the conclusion was a little bit rushed and I think maybe an epilogue from a different POV could have really added something to the story. Overall, though, I think this is a book that I will read again and recommend to mystery/thriller fans who don't mind unlikable MCs.

She was the most interesting character in the book, and I wish she had been the protagonist instead. Her relationship with the guard(I don't remember his name) would have probably been more interesting to read about than what we were given.  I was really disappointed with this book. I loved the first two(especially One Good Knight), and had figured this one would be even better, or at least just as good as the other two. I'm really hoping The Snow Queen is better than this was. It has taken me a very long time to get through this book. Twice (and strangely at the same point each time) I've completely given up on it. Third time, well we're finally done but it took effort to actually finish it off. I'm glad that I did because I feel I got more out of it, but I couldn't say that I really enjoyed it. 
 I flip-flopped between 'this book is so pretentious' to 'Quentin is so pretentious' several times when reading this but as I approached the end I concluded that it was the author's intent to make the character this way, and perhaps that's an indication that character was actually quite well-written to be the odious cretin he actually is. This was particularly noticeable towards very end of the book when Quentin, now actually learning magic thoroughly when in Fillory alone, notes how he was learning things he 'didn't have time for' previously, when the reader knows full well this isn't case, particularly as after graduating all he did mess about.  
 Quentin is easily one of the most frustrating POV characters I have ever had the misfortune of reading. He is a monumental douche for most of the book and just completely rage-inducing with some of his actions, or lack of. Although the premise of such a flawed character was interesting, it was very overbearing at times and detracted from the enjoyment of reading the book. As many other reviewers point out, Alice's little speech about how 'this is reality and as good as it will get' massively highlighted Quentin's main problem. Another is that he very rarely takes responsibility for his actions and his own miserable state (arguably he does at the end after the climax, but as he uses it to excuse his current shoddy behavior it just seems like an excuse than regret). When he does blame himself, he's quickly distracted by the wrongs other people have done, which was definitely what I hated the most about him. I was practically foaming at the mouth every time Quentin was bitching about Penny and conveniently forgetting it was his indiscretions which motivated Alice to sleep with him in the first place. I wasn't impressed with how the author handled it either, with Alice actually apologising and Quentin not doing so and continuing to be a complete dick towards her - perhaps it's supposed to say something about the respective characters but if so it wasn't obvious enough.  
 The pacing was something that irked me, with years flying by in a few pages, journeys finished in paragraphs, and aftermaths of massively consequential events frequently only glanced over. In some places I was aware that the author seemed to be 'telling not showing' and this broke the suspension of belief. It also meant I really didn't care the supporting characters - though they were interesting on paper, I didn't see enough of them or the trials they went through with Quentin to actually like them or pay much attention to what happened to them. 
 That being said, I actually would recommend people read it if they were so inclined to do so, because it is a very different take on the fantasy genre (and as many have pointed out probably a satire of it, rather being in it). It was interesting in places and I actually quite liked Grossman's style though it did have it's moments when the cracks began to show. For some people, Quentin's realism (because I'm sure everyone has come across someone like Quentin to some degree) may be a positive attribute to readers. Unfortunately, for myself, it was an irritant. I liked the idea of the book, but I wasn't too impressed with the execution and probably will not be pursuing the second in the series.

The historical anecdotes underlying The Orenda's plot structure are ones with which I am fairly familiar, since they have appeared in numerous school assignements throughout my years of education. What Boyden brings to the [re]telling, however, is a First Nations perspective that doesn't feel forced or accusatory. The result is a dual-perspective narration that gives equal moral weight to the impressions and cultural assumptions of both the Jesuits and the Wendat people. 
 There are perhaps times when the magical folklore of the First Nations people is pushed into the realm of fantasy, but that potential overreach feels somewhat justified when you consider how many stories in the Christian tradition make saints sound more like magicians. There was also a bit of historical revisionism, such as when one of the Jesuits comments how the Haudenosaunee practice of torture was not much different from the Spanish Inquisition. But again, while this seems jarring when considered in historical context, it serves well here to raise a point of consideration. 
 The plot itself is well-paced, with the book being broken into three very distinct sections, each represented by some tangible turning point in relations between Jesuits and First Nations. And while the pace becomes a little more slow and introspective at about the two-thirds mark, the climax built into a gripping finale that had me staying up late to finish. Bravo, Mr. Boyden. A fantastic job of breathing new life into old stories.

But the man who snatches Delaney from her home isn't the murderer. He's Tighe, a dangerous Feral Warrior who needs her and her visions to stop the rampages of a creature as inhuman as he is evil. Tighe has little use for humans, but as he and Delaney join forces to track the dark fiend, he falls for the intense beauty and becomes wild with an obsession as untamed as his heart.

Intro: If you love blood and guts this is for you. If you like real world historical could have beens here you go. This is a a crazy good story. The only reason I don't give this a 5 star review is that there were a few sections that seemed to linger on quite a bit. 
 Summary: Covers the time periods between 876 - 878: Uhtred, tires of the peace between Alfred and the Danish king Guthrum, goes off raiding into Cornwall. He comes across a settlement ruled by the British king Peredur, who hires Uhtred and his men to fight an invading Danish force led by Svein of the White Horse. Uhtred and Svein however ally to kill Peredur and pillage his settlement, and Uhtred carries off Peredur's wife, the shadow queen Iseult. A monk named Asser who was at Peredur's court witnesses the betrayal and escapes to Dyfed in Wales. Uhtred and Svein then sail up the coast to Land's End where they part ways. Svein goes to Cynuit, where Ubba was killed previously, and Uhtred to the coast of Wales where he raids a ship laden with treasure. He returns to his estate and pious wife Mildrith, using his hoard of treasure to build a great hall and relieve his debt to the church. 
 The Witan summons Uhtred to an audience with King Alfred in Cippanhamm, where he is accused of using the king's ship to raid the Britons with whom Wessex is at peace based on the testimony of Asser, who has made his way to Alfred's court, and wrongfully accused of attacking the Cynuit abbey on the false testimony of the warrior Steapa Snotor, who is loyal to Uhtred's enemy Odda the Younger. To settle the dispute, a fight to the death is ordered between Uhtred and Steapa. During the duel, Uhtred carries only his sword, Serpent-Breath, whereas Steapa is fully armoured. The duel is cut short when Guthrum's Danes attack and the crowd is scattered. Uhtred, Leofric, and Iseult hide in the fields until nightfall when they enter Cippanhamm and free their friend Eanflaed at the Tornake Tavern. The four of them wander for a few weeks until they reach the swamps of Athelney. As they enter the marsh, Guthrum himself attacks Uhtred. Uhtred makes a fighting escape onto a boat that carries him, Leofric, and another passenger to an island within the swamp. The passenger insists that Uhtred should have left a Danish warrior alive, and turns out to be King Alfred himself. Uthred becomes Alfred's bodyguard and for a few months they hide in the swamp until enough men have joined Alfred's army. They then fight at the Battle of Ethandun and Alfred takes back Wessex, with Uhtred being instrumental in the death of Svein of the White Horse. However, during the battle, Leofric and Iseult are both killed.

We Need to Talk About Kevin is a pretty damn innovative book. It deals with a topic that's already heavy, and puts a spin on it that makes it vastly different than the other books that address this issue. The basic story: Kevin calmly and methodically attacked 9 students and 1 teacher from his school, fully aware of his actions. He planned the action and left a devastating blow to his mother in his wake. 
 But what makes it so different than, say, Forgive Me, Leonard Peacock, is that it's told through his mother Eva's point of view in very long letters to her husband, Franklin. In these letters, we learn that Eva's emotions in regards to her son ran the entire spectrum. Already ill at ease with motherhood (in the book she admits that all she wanted was a man to love her; the rest was secondary) she felt an immediate animosity emanating from her child as soon as he was born. Real or imagined, it didn't matter. Kevin would prove to be her greatest adversary. 
 The thing that I think infuriated me with Eva (and especially Franklin) was how little they took everything seriously. Franklin was blinded by the front that Kevin put up for him. Kevin knew his father wanted the attaboy, the kid who played catch with his dad and went to war museums, so that's what he gave him. His father never saw anything different. With Eva, whether because of her uneasiness or despite it, he was much more like himself--disdainful of everything and everyone, unwilling to show vulnerability through favorites, and with a cruel glint in his eye he didn't bother to mask. His actions steadily become more extreme, and yet nothing is done to stymie what he does. 
 Oh, his actions start innocently enough: ruining his mother's favorite dress, slinging food whenever possible, ruining a room in the house. Then it starts to progress: convincing a girl to scratch off a layer of skin thanks to her eczema, refusing to use the bathroom until he was six, openly masturbating in front of his mother. And still further: accusing a teacher of sexual abuse, physically (permanently) harming his younger sister, convincing an anorexic girl she's fat, not to mention the final act itself. The boy steadily gets worse. And while Franklin turns a blind eye to everything (how infuriating that was!) Eva knows what's happening and does very little to stop it. Maybe there's not really anything she could do. I don't know. But I know my gut instinct says that's bullshit and she should have warned someone, or videotaped him, or something. 
 What really caught my attention was this little passage: 
 "If it's a girl it's a Plaskett, then! But on one condition: None of thise Gara-souvlaki stuff for a boy's first name. Something American. Deal?" 
 It was a deal. And in hindsight we made the right decision. In 1996, fourteen-year-old Barry Loukaitis killed a teacher and two students while taking a whole class hostage in Moses Lake, Washington. A year later, thirteen-year-old Tronneal Mangum shot dead a boy at his middle school who owed him $40. The next month, sixteen-year-old Evan Ramsey killed a student and his principal and wounded two others in Bethel, Alaska. That fall, sixteen-year-old Luke Woodham murdered his mother and two students, wounding seven, in Pearl, Mississippi. Two months later, fourteen-year-old Michael Carneal shot dead three students and wounded five in Paducah, Kentucky. The next spring in 1998, thirteen-year-old Mitchell Jognson and eleven-year-old Andrew Golden opened fire on their high school, killing one teacher and four students, wounding ten, in Jonesboro, Arkansas. A month after that, fourteen-year-old Andrew Wurst killed a teacher and wounded three students in Edinboro, Pennsylvania. The following month in Springfield, Oregon, fifteen-year-old Kip Kinkel massacred both his parents, proceeding to kill two more students and wounding twenty-five. In 1999, and a mere ten days after a certain Thursday, eighteen-year-old Eric Harris and seventeen-year-old Dylan Klebold planted bombs in their Littleton, Colorado, high school and went on a shooting rampage that killed one teacher and twelve students, while wounding twenty-three, after which they shot themselves. So young Kevin--your choice--has turned out as American as a Smith and Wesson. 
 During these years I was in elementary school. I remember almost nothing of the wide world beyond my cartoons and movies and books. So I was astounded when I looked this stuff up to find that yes, this was true. There really was a fad. There was a huge burst of students resorting to extreme violence, whether for no good reason or no reason at all it didn't matter. 
 But I do blame Eva, at least in part. Her character was absolutely something that was reflected in Kevin. I don't know if it was learned or inherited--I suppose this book would be great in a nature vs. nurture debate--but there was absolutely some of Eva in Kevin. Her disdain for everyone is the most obvious. Eva believed herself to be above everyone else; her opinions were right and she had a biting comment for any situation. Kevin felt this same superiority, he just didn't speak of it. His contempt was only visible to Eva, and I suspect this was intentional. He recognized a somewhat kindred spirit, whether Eva wanted to admit it or not. And I think that ultimately he was proud of his mother, at least a little bit, for being better than the masses, because she understood his actions. She didn't need to question him the way the outside world did, because part of it was apparent in herself. And he knew it. 
 Frankly, the kid was a genius. In a really sick way, but aren't all the greatest villains? He never wanted to show vulnerability. So he would eat when no one was looking. He refused to give Eva any satisfaction as a parent; he learned how to count and how to read behind closed doors. He learned everything behind closed doors, truth be told. He refused to have any favorite shows or bands or even clothes or colors, because it showed a weakness. He learned this the hard way when his attachment to a water gun at a young age got it confiscated. He never made that mistake again. 
 The actual act itself in some respects wasn't as difficult to read as I thought it would be, and actually proved harder in others.  I felt little when the students and the school employees were killed. What got to me (I think for most people this would be the case) was when we finally learn that Franklin and Kevin's little sister, Celia, were killed as well. Celia was pinned to the wall with five arrows through her seven-year-old chest; Franklin had about the same, the ones I remember being the one in the throat, the one in the pectoral muscles, and the one in the groin. It was harsh and planned. Kevin set his sister up (a sister who never ratted him out and followed him around like a puppy) and shot an arrow straight into her chest. That...that got to me. I know it's the same for countless others: that pain purposefully inflicted on a child seems so much worse than when inflicted on an adult. Probably the most grotesque part of the whole affair was that Kevin took his sister's glass eye from her body and kept is as a memento. How fucked up is that?! And it really, truly disturbed me. Of course, Eva as the narrator leaves this until the end. We don't know her husband and daughter are dead. It's implied earlier in the book that they are divorced and that Franklin as custody of Celia. I'm sure this was intentional, to draw it out until the end. I had my suspicions, which were confirmed.  
 The only thing that I didn't really like about the book was how wordy it was. It took far too long for Eva to get her point across sometimes, and she would talk about things that really didn't have anything to do with the plot, only to draw it in somehow with one sentence. It was like reading about, I don't know, pick something. Drag racing. 2 or 3 pages on drag racing, about how the drivers must feel exhilarated by the start line. And then she'd be like "That's the same adrenaline I got when (blank) happened with Kevin." It was kind of annoying, and detracted from the plot for me. Parts of it were absolutely warranted, but other parts just didn't need to be there. I gather it was to show just how important Eva felt her thoughts were, that everything she thought needed to be put on paper. 
 But really, it's a great (if morbid) read. It deals with one of the tougher issues, one that can be categorized with abuse and suicide. I was captivated by it.

Since the first minute I saw Real on goodreads I felt in love. I love books with athletes, especially if they are fighters, men and this one stole my heart letting me without a chance. 
 Brooke Dumas is a 24-years-old woman, recently graduated in sports rehab - a career she chose after getting hurt and losing the chance to win a gold medal in the Olympics. One night her best friend, Melaine, takes her out to watch an underground fight and there she meets Remington 'Riptide' Tate for the very first time, and as soon as their eyes met they are attracted to each other. 
 Remy is a sexy, gorgeous and intense fighter who has some problems with self-control and for that he's already had been jailed once and in a lot of trouble, but he also is a quiet and introspective man due some bad things that happened, and still happen, to him. 
 The first time they talk, at the underground fight, they let the place in fire. 
 "Your name," he growls, panting, his eyes wild on mine. 
 "Uh, Brooke." 
 "Brooke what?" he snaps out, his nostrils flaring.With trembling efforts, I pry my hand free and glance frightfully at Mel, who comes behind him, wide-eyed. "It's Brooke Dumas," she says and then happily shoots out my cell phone number to my chagrin. His lips curl, and he meets my gaze once more."Brooke Dumas." He just fucked my name right in front of me, and right in front of Mel. He steps forward, and his damp hand slides into the nape of my neck. "Brooke," he growls softly, meaningfully, against my lips, as he draws back with a smile. "I'm Remington." 
 After that night Brooke is called to an offer of job. Guess from who? Exactly, Remington offers her a job as his physical therapist. She takes the job and goes to him and his team for a national tour of fights. 
 At first they try to be just friend, but as they will knowing each other the feeling is getting stronger and that they can't avoid anymore. 
 The author Katy Evans delighted me with this book, all characters are well built (I loved how the author created a logical explanation for Remy's excessive jealousy and protection) and the story is so cute (I want a love story like that) and the way she made them communicate through the music (~sigh~). 
 The narrative, in first-person point of view, is quite detailed, so that the reading flow quickly. I would rather if the point of view would be intercalate in the two of them, but that's not a negative point. 
 If you like books with strong, determinate and dominant then you'll love read Real by Katy Evans, give an opportunity to this wonderful book, you won't regret it.

Set in the year 1929, in Jazz-age Paris, this story takes us through the glittering literary and artistic set, into the depths of those who take things to extremes, indeed to the brink of insanity and then over the edge into a dark, hellish experience. 
 Harris Stuyvesant is an American investigator sent to find a young woman who has gone missing in Paris. The irony is that he had a brief affair with the girl and so his interest in finding her is tinged with personal regret and a sense of a failure to protect her. 
 The writing in this novel is vivid and evocative and though it is filled with historical nuggets and real world characters, such as Hemingway and Man Ray, it is in no way dry. 
 I found that I was drawn strongly into the story and that the fictional characters were written in a way that allowed me to identify with them and feel that all-important connection that makes me want to read on. 
 This is a story that I can highly recommend.

Even though we didn't get lot of it, the on-page lovin' was great and I feel like this was a very convincing and well-done double-gfy.

THUG was one of the most hyped ya books I've seen this year. Before it was published there were different publishing houses vying for the rights to publish it. Along with a movie deal in the works right now. I can only imagine how amazing that must have felt for the debut author, Angie Thomas, to have so much acclaim around her first novel. Knowing all that about the book I wanted to read it to see if it was as incredible as the ya community was claiming. After many months of being on hold for it from the library, I finally received the audio. It was well worth the wait. The story was one that brought tears to my eyes, made me laugh, and most of all made me reevaluate my words and actions towards others. 
 The Hate U Give is an interesting title and once you know where it comes from it makes more sense. It's part of a longer title based off of Tupac's tattoo: THUG LIFE. THUG LIFE is an acronym for The Hate U Give Little Infants Fucks Everybody. "Meaning what society gives us as youth, it bites them in the ass when we wild out." 
 The story was inspired by the Black Lives Matter movement and Tupac's THUG LIFE tattoo. The story explores what happens when an unarmed black male teenager is killed by a police officer when pulled over. Starr, our heroine, is the only witness and this is her journey to rise above her situation and be a voice for her friend who was murder. 
 I really loved Starr's family and her interactions with them felt authentic. Each character was flawed and how they handled the cards they were dealt was inspiring. No one had it easy but in each situation, they strived to be better and do better. 
 Bravo to Angie Thomas on her debut novel and I can't wait to see what she creates next.

Good from start to finish. Well, almost. The dangling, morally ambiguous end felt a bit preachy, but otherwise "Leftovers" is a good example of what writing for teens can be: propulsive, addictive, thrilling, and disturbing. 
 After completing the book in one four-hour sitting, I'm struck by a few things. First, as a reader I enjoyed Blair and Ardith's believably complicated characters. Secondly, as a male reader, I appreciated how Wiess did an outstanding job of bringing me into the minds of teen girls. Last, as a teacher of writing, I admire Wiess for telling a story that doesn't slack or go soft, but that keeps building tension; the back-and-forth between each girl's voice works well. 5 Perfect Stars 
 This was an Amazing story and I quickly fell in love with Ryan and Josiah and have a new appreciation for Naked Twister! 
 Annabeth Albert has proven to me that she can write stories that are deeply emotional, perfectly romantic, and hot as hell - yes, she clicks all my boxes on what makes a perfect story! 
 So, if you have not read the first two stories in this series - while I really think you should because they are amazing, you can totally understand this book with out them. It stands alone from the others yet connected by friendships and work relationships. 
 This story deals with some hard topics, disability and learning to live again, life changing medical conditions, being injured in the line-of-duty, mourning for a previous you when your whole world is turned up-side-down, and learning to adult, struggling with ADHD, being held accountable, and falling in love. So many of these issues many of us can either empathize with or know someone who has been affected which is why I think it makes this book that much more emotional. Annabeth does an excellent job portraying Ryan's insecurities as a recent amputee and his inability to ask for help, his annoyance at others wanting to help, and his struggles with adjusting his world from Lieutenant Ryan Orson to Civilian Ryan Orsan, and his resentment at others who are still living his dream, along with his feelings of failure at being disabled. These are such valid feelings for a person who has had a life changing event such as portrayed by Ryan's case that it was impossible not to fall in love with the guarded, sometimes burley man. 
 Then you have Josiah - we met him previously in other #Gaymers books and he wasn't always portrayed in the best of light, now we are getting his story. Josiah has struggled with severe ADHD and has to stay on a planned cycle of meds and lifestyle in order to function best. He is often accused of being flakey, not thought of as a "go-to" person, not self-assured despite his brilliance and talent with gaming development. When he meets Lieutenant Ryan Orson on a cross-country flight he tongue hangs out and his libido wakes up. He is in lust. Not even noticing that the man he is listing after is a double amputee - and puts his foot totally down his throat when he finally does notice. These two don't get off to a stellar start and I wondered exactly how Annabeth was going to weave them into a relationship, I should have never second guessed her brilliance! 
 I did a dual review of this story and both listened to the audiobook, narrated by Sean Crisden, and read the story. I will tell you I was driving too and from work and either laughing, crying, or needing a cold drink based on what these two guys were up to - so perfect narration again by Sean! 
 And dont forget Gracie, she has a huge roll in this book and I love that Annabeth included pets as therapy and service dogs - these animals do amazing things every day! 
 Worthy of 5 stars and I highly recommend this series and book!

In general I am not the biggest fan of contemporary fiction, but this book surprised me. I've never read a Sarah Dessen novel before, but now I'm sure I will pick up another. This book wasn't perfect, but it was very well written and I enjoyed the story. Let's get to some thoughts. 
 One thing that I appreciate about this novel is that it throws you right into the heart of the story. There is no time spent on setting the story up. We just fall right into it. All of the setting up details are revealed slowly, through portions where Ruby is thinking back. This is another thing that I love. I've read several books that use a similar technique recently and I love it. 
 The main thing that I appreciated most about this novel was that it wasn't just romance novel, in fact, the little romance that does happen is never the focus. There are so many relationships here. And so many weighty topics discussed in a great way. There was more focus on Ruby finding herself and building a relationship with her sister and brother-in-law, and learning to be a friend. I loved that. 
 More thoughts will come soon on my blog.

 I was mainly interested in this book because I was curious about the spiritualism era and the time period, but I ended up enjoying this book much more than I expected. 
 This book takes place in 1918 and which the war and Spanish Influenza, death is very common and many people are turning to spirit photographers, desperate for comfort. Mary Shelley Black moves to San Diego with her aunt after her dad gets arrested for treason (letting boys escape the draft). At the same time, Stephen, Mary Shelley's first love and childhood friend was drafted into war. When Stephen dies and Mary has a new death experience, she becomes haunted by him. She then begins to question what really happened to Stephen and why is he haunting her. 
 What I like the best about this book is how real the setting is. I knew about the Spanish Influenza and World War I, but knowing about it is completely different than actually seeing it, which is how I felt while reading this book. The time period is so accurately presented. Now, I'm not a history major, but I absolutely feel like this is how 1918 might have been like in San Diego. It was a horrible period and filled with death, despair, and fear. The author portrayed all this so brilliantly that I can actually feel all of this while reading this book. I applaud the author for being able to write such a vivid setting! 
 I felt like this book was a mix of a bunch of different genres, if that makes any sense. This book felt so incredible realistic, due to both the settings and the characters, even with the paranormal elements. This book was also a mystery. A majority of the book is Mary trying to figure out why Stephen keeps talking about the blackbirds, and why he is haunting her. I, honestly, had a very hard time putting this book down. 
 While this book is so brilliant, it is also incredibly sad. That's obvious based on the setting, but the events in Mary's life, in the one's surrounding her are so horrible. Gosh, I can't really describe this without spoilers Poor Stephen! I feel like crying whenever I think about it! How could someone do such a thing?????  The romantic in me wants this book to be so much happier and I almost have this book a 4/5 instead of 5/5, but this book would not be so vivid and brilliant without it. I also accept the fact that not everything is butterflies and rainbows. 
 IN CONCLUSION 
 Overall, I really loved this book. This book was incredibly dark and sad, but this book was also very brilliant and new. I thought that the setting was done very well and while the plot has been done before, believe me when I say that this book is not like any other. After reading this book, I am definitely going to pick up more from Cat Winters. In fact, I've already added The Cure for Dreaming to my to-read list. This is not a book (or author) to pass up!

I went to the library and looked for it on the shelf and it wasn't there! I was so disappointed. Imagine my surprise when I found it on my bedroom floor! Apparently my sister got to the book before I did and checked it out for me! 
 I loved and hated this book. Marak was his usual smug I'm-always-right self, if only for a few pages, and the girl. I love how Catpaw didn't like that he had to marry the elf and still wanted to marry Miranda. 
 What I hated was the elves. Well, it's not so much hate as a very strong dislike--I would hate to live in their world, never really doing anything useful. I like to keep busy--even with fun things (like reading). There never seemed to be much for Miranda--or Fox--to do. While she was annoyed with that at first, I think it's weird how she got so used to it. She's almost more elf like than Kate! Something else that annoyed me about the Elf King (although we didn't know he was such at the beginning) was that he always thought he was right and trusted his magic--without a tangible reason or result for him to do so! At first I thought it was because that's how all the elves were (since in my mind, he was a normal elf) but after we found out who he really was, I think now that those sort of actions are ones of a King--because those are the same things that infuriated me when Marak did them! I still consider myself more partial to goblins, however. Elves kind of creep me out (in her books at least). 
 I'm also glad the author didn't write a whole book about what happened to Till--What I think it was is that the author hated Till so much she couldn't bring herself to write a whole book about her. I think the way she did it was brilliant--told what happened to her (and tells how she retains her awfulness!) perfectly. (I still don't like that Till turned out that way because Kate didn't want to deal with her behavior.)

 This is one of the few books who will soon be considered as an academic material for philosophy class. It is still not credited in some schools because this philosophical text is pretending to be a novel (and I was a victim of it as well but it's a good thing). The book comprises of almost 10 philosophical topics but I summarized it and only wrote some of the major parts of the story, particularly: 
 The Garden of Eden- believed to be the first "garden of God" 
 The Top Hat- A creative chapter where it describes how we are similar to a magician pulling a rabbit from a hat. Hence, life itself is like a magic trick, and philosophers must always observe it with wonder. 
 The Myths- This part of the 'letter' explains the situation leading up to the beginning of Western philosophy and Norwegian philosophy (THOR, my love ;p), before the Greek philosophers and so, it explained how people live a life through myths--stories about the gods. 
 It all started with these three major concerns and the philosopher's first few questions to Sophie: who she is and where the world came from. Those (of course) made her think. These questions are undemanding and easy to ask but almost unattainable, but what is most astounding of all is that people already stopped asking those questions. That is where Sophie realizes that she has never really thought about these things before, and when she does she understands that nothing could be more important. It seems that knowing who we really are is necessary for our lives to have meaning and significance. Beyond that, we live in the world, and are in invariable interaction with nature, yet most people take that interaction for granted and do not stop to consider how the world itself came about. As little children we are tremendously inquisitive, and we wonder about everything, but as life goes on we begin to take certain things for granted even though we do not understand them. [I remember my old little self hanging on the cliche: "THAT'S NOT FAIR!". Even of the smallest child, I remember making such statement and I never thought that certain instance made me prove that I AM DEDICATED TO GO TO LAW. Justice is what I already know surprisingly since I was a child.] 
 The Natural Philosophers, Democritus, and Fate- Ancient Greece up to the present moment. In this chapter, Sophie finds that everything she learns seems to make sense to her and she finds it extremely applicable to life. Philosophy is not an activity that takes place outside of everyday life. In fact, philosophy has become a regular part of Sophie's life,like science. 
 The Major's Cabin and Aristotle- In a way, after reading about Plato, Sophie's life has become majorly intact with philosophy. Her sensory experiences--the postcards sent to Hilde, the mirror that blinked at her--are in direct conflict with what her reason tells her could be possible. The same conflict between what perception and reason that the ancient Greek philosophers struggled with has become valid within Sophie's life. Everyone faces this sort of conflict, but this time for Sophie, it has become critically real. 
 The Renaissance and The Baroque- Birth of modern diplomacy (I learned this from my history class and International Relations ;p). Aside from that, this is the part where Sophie learns about philosophy being a continual and integral part and task for humanity. Why? Well, in a way people ask questions that may not be answerable in an attempt to better understand life and existence. 
 Darwin and Freud- Darwinism. The ideas that have now pass through our time period, in spite that we probably cannot specifically identify them while we are in that certain period, it may lead to a large amount of problems that we soon are going to try to solve and set the limits for the solutions. 
 Our Own Time and The Garden Party-The author seems to wholeheartedly embrace existentialism (e.g works of ALBERT CAMUS). Although all of the other philosophy that has been studied has much to offer, it seems clear that one must find meaning within life. 
 Counterpoint and The Big Bang- Not much to say but we must ought to know that in an attempt to understand the universe is the same as an attempt to understand ourselves. 
 In short, the course chronologically covers thirty major periods, schools of thought, and philosophers from the pre-Socrates to Aristotle, Aquinas, and Hegel to the Big Bang. Each is presented in an accessible chapter of a dozen pages, with the philosophy teacher simplifying and clarifying points for Sophie. 
 "The notion of a separate organism is clearly an abstraction, as is also its boundary. Underlying all this is unbroken wholeness, even though our civilisation has developed in such a way as to strongly emphasise the separation into parts." 
 The Undivided Universe, 
 by D. Bohm and B.J. Hiley

This book has been on my 'to-read' shelf for a very long time. Truth be told the only reason I hadn't read it earlier is because I try very hard (and fail) to not spend too much money on books and there always seemed to be such good bargains out there. So I checked with my local, rural library regularly for this book coming in. I even had a lengthy discussion with the librarian one day on what New Adult was. He couldn't understand why they didn't have New York Times bestsellers on their shelves, and frankly neither could I. Anyway, I digress, it came in, I got it, first person so it felt like I'd gone out and bought it, it was so crisp and new. I was reading 3/4 other books at the time but as I walked home I let my son stop by the playground and play and I opened the cover of Slammed... 
 That was 12 hours ago, since then I made lunch and read, watched Mary Poppins, and read, made things out of lego, and read, made dinner, and read, played wii u, and read, read a bedtime story, poured a glass of wine and read, and read and read. Now I have to digest. 
 I think you can guess. I. Loved. This. Book! Yes I even just did that full stoppy sentence thing just to make sure the point really sinks in! 
 It's funny really because there are books that have affected me more, with characters I love more, with a romance that has me all fluttery or trauma that has me gasping with tears. But there's something about Colleen Hoover's writing in this book. It's just so brilliantly executed. It gave me goofy grins and slow tears. I loved the quotes at the start of each chapter, and the slam poetry and Kel and Caulder, oh and Eddie. Mostly though I think I liked how it didn't try to over explain itself. The book is so confident. I got it, I felt it, it wasn't necessary to have endless streams of consciousness, the tension was palpable, the love and tenderness were beautiful. 
 I mean really, what can I say. I guess I could say that it felt a little unbelievable and Layken sometimes a little immature, but who am I kidding, I loved the romance and well 18 is immature really. This wasn't 'I want your babies' good, or 'I can never stop thinking about it good', or 'I'm hurting I've cried so much' good. It was just nice, and satisfying, and I'm just going to sit here and smile for a little while good. 
 Now, how long will it take the library to get Point of Retreat in I wonder?

** spoiler alert ** 
 The first two-thirds of The Secret History are suspenseful, mysterious, and intriguing, then it drops off. The final third drags and follows a pattern of 1) a conversation that reveals some lurid secret, 2) binge-drinking/drug use, 3) repeat to end. This could be interesting if the characters really went off the rails, but it didn't read as though they were really unraveling or grappling with what they'd done. They were drinking too much and doing drugs from the start and none of them seem particularly remorseful - just scared of getting caught. 
 The pressure of getting found out is what they were cracking under, not that...idk, murdering your friend is probably a very difficult thing to cope with (but then again, maybe not, if that friend is Bunny). And I didn't really care either way if they got caught. I didn't care about them, I didn't care about Bunny (or the farmer), and Tartt never really prompts the reader to think about the morality of it all or what's at stake. The character's are never REALLY at risk of losing everything, or at least I never got that sense. So what's Tartt's point? I'm not sure. 
 I also couldn't peg the time period. The dialogue is the main reason this was so difficult. They all called each other "sport" and "old boy" and "son". I get that they're out of touch with the world around them because they're so involved with the classics and are so very rich. But it was so very distracting and prevented me from really visualizing the scene at Hampden. I kept thinking: When are we? Do rich people really talk like this? They're supposed to be in college? Stop talking like Jay Gatsby. Judy was the only believable college student in the whole book, and even she was a caricature, and a peripheral character to boot. 
 The characters never quite "got there". I'm not sure if we were supposed to hate them, admire them, fear them, envy them. Everyone likes a good villain, but they didn't feel particularly villainous. They never felt truly evil (except maybe Henry) or frightening , just entitled and beyond reproach. And aggravating. Maybe that's the point, but again, Tartt doesn't really bring us to a discussion on morality, good, evil, and the mundane. 
 One last thing - the bacchanal. I kept waiting for more on that other than the really vague and reluctant descriptions she gave us. I'm not sure why she left such a pivotal and wild event so obscured. Why even include a bacchanal if you're not going to get into it? Not necessarily the details of how they reached that level of ecstasy or transcendence (or whatever you want to call it), but what it was like, how belief fits in (other than that you need to truly believe...whatever that means), and how that belief system allows them to justify the chain of events that the bacchanal kicks off. 
 All that said, I actually did like it. It had shortcomings, sure, but in all I had fun reading it and will likely read other work by Tartt in the future. I'm sure there are structural techniques I'm overlooking and nods to Greek literature that went completely over my head. I'm pretty confident that someone who has a greater knowledge of the classics would get more out of this than I did. Still, I enjoyed it.

This book has been on my TBR shelf FOR-EV-ER. Based on the description above, I can't really remember why I wanted to read it. But I'm glad I did. It really is soooo much better than it sounds. 
 Jennifer wakes up to a life she doesn't remember. She knows she's been in an accident, but no one will give her the details. Her doctors tell her the amnesia will fade and she'll "be back to her old self" in no time. While Jennifer returns to her life, the memories do not come quickly and more than that - she can not understand why she chose this life for herself - a bored trophy wife in an unhappy marriage. She also feels a deep sense of loss for something she can't describe. When she finds a letter tucked (hidden) into the pages of a novel, she begins to put the pieces together. What she's missing is love - and the man who loves her back. She spends her days searching the house for more mystery letters and trying to figure out who wrote them. 
 Now for my major problem with this story. Obviously this great love affair is, in fact, an affair. Jennifer is married and Anthony, while divorced, has a married women habit. Not to be all judgey, but I think once you say your vows, you're in it. If you decide it's not going to work or that you want someone else, get divorced. I do recognize that times were different back then and a divorce was much harder to come by. Plus, Jennifer and Laurence's marriage was basically in name only. However, right or wrong, I became deeply invested in Jennifer and Anthony's relationship. 
 The story is effortlessly woven between multiple timelines and points of views to give. And, oh, the emotions! I loved Anthony. I liked Jennifer. And I desperately wanted them to find a way to be together. 
 Part three of the book brings us about 40 years into the future. We pick up with a new character, Ellie, working at the newspaper Anthony worked at all that time ago and is having an affair of her own. Unlike Anthony and Jennifer, Ellie and her married man is a more typical day affair. Secret e-mails and texts and clandestine meetings. When Ellie finds one of Anthony's letters to Jennifer she clings to it as a story idea to save her job, but also begins to believe in the possibility of being really loved - nothing like her relationship with John. 
 With the help of newspaper librarian Rory, Ellie tracks down the details of the relationship behind the letters to it's startling conclusion. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed this book. The pace was a little slow, but once I got into the story I didn't care and I really loved the multiple timeline style. The character development is ah-mazing. The story involved journalists and newspapers (that almost always gets me - I used to want to be a journalist and I still fantasize about it). The writing is terrifically emotive and I was dangerously close to tears when I finished the book during my lunch break today. I'm definitely going to read more from Jojo Moyes!

First, this is hard stuff to write about and Lawson has done something wonderful by putting herself out there. Her story speaks to tons of people and has undoubtedly made their own struggles easier to talk about and (hopefully) easier to bear. There were some things in here that made me laugh out loud; the belly button fart thing, for instance, really caught me off guard. There were also some strong passages where I thought she articulated her struggle with mental illness really well. These passages were far and away the best parts of this book - they were stripped down, honest, focused, and vulnerable. 
 I just wish the rest of the book was more like them. But - don't call me a jerk here this is personal preference and opinion - these little gems were couched in lots and lots of fluff, rambling, and a general aren't-I-so-quirky tone that is always a death knell for my attention span. I'm not familiar with Lawson's blog, but most of this book read like an amalgamation of blog posts. Some readers will find this super accessible and I'm sure fans of her blog will love it; again, it's just not for me. I don't have much else to say on this one. I could sit with it a while longer and come up with more, but reading this actually made me feel more anxious so I'm ready to move on. 
 (DISCLAIMER: not that it's really anyone's business, but on pretty much every less-than-glowing review I've seen of this, people jump right to "Oh you obviously don't know what it's like." I do. Personally and with loved ones. So take that invalid critique of my critique elsewhere, plz. It's just not the book for me.)

 , Feyre is on an undercover mission beginning here. This part should have been exciting and suspenseful. Sort of a, will she get caught, will she be successful? Instead, it was a lot of Feyre thinking she was being so cunning and cackling to herself on how evil she was being to her enemy. This was just so poorly written and executed that I still don't really understand how her plan worked she brought down Tamlin's court internally? I guess so, but it didn't seem like a brilliant, well thought out plan either . 
 After that first part, things don't really pick up. Instead, they slow down even more! There's a lot of strategizing and meeting even more characters, especially those of other unexplored courts. Honestly, with the announcement of more books, Mrs. Maas didn't need to include so much more information on the rest of the Faerie courts. She has more room now to explore them later and didn't need to squeeze so much of that in here. Instead there should have been a lot more action. There's a part in the middle of the book that I particularly had to laugh at because nothing was being done and even Mrs. Maas picked up on it: There are 70 pages of all the high lords meeting at the Court of Dawn to discuss what is to be done in the war against Hybern. This is the war that has been the focal point of the entire plot so far but no battles have actually taken place, and we are more than half way through the book at this point. At page 70, all of a sudden it has been learned that the King of Hybern tore down the wall between Faerie and Human lands, and is now advancing his army. This was probably supposed to shock me as a reader, but all I did was laugh. It felt like the author knew nothing was being done by all the lords talking, so she just forced the enemy to take action instead.  
 Things pick up towards the end of the book, but I lost a lot of interest in the characters and plot by this point, and I couldn't find myself caring all that much. 
 There are more companion books to be released in this series. I assume a lot of them will focus on the unfinished romances. I am slightly interested in finding out about them, but I don't know if I can commit myself to reading long books about them... for me Maas's romances lose a lot of their luster as they unfold, as was the case in this series. It's a toss up for now but right now I'd say I'm not going to bother...

 I'm heavily battling with myself on this one, so I'm going to go with a nice middle-of-the-road rating to assuage myself. 
 This has an incredible amount of potential, and for those potentials I may still continue the series. I was saddened by the typical YA tropes that seem to be prevalent in every single YA book these days, but it wasn't quite so eye-rolly as it normally is for me. 
 The story is extremely convoluted. It really seems like two separate stories mashed together--one about a girl rising above her bullies, and another about a supernatural wager. They're each really strong, but get too tangled up in each other and make it harder to follow along with what's happening. So I'll talk about each plot respectively, beginning with the non-supernatural. 
 Edie is a highly intelligent, socially crippled, fat, awkward, middle-class girl at an elite private school where money and beauty are everything. Rich kids are perhaps the most vicious because they have the time, money, and inclination to do truly horrible things; Edie's story is a good example of that. They do something truly horrible to her, then plaster it all over the internet for her to relive her shame over and over again. Their constant bullying is ruthless, and it drives her to suicide. 
 What stops her goes more along with the supernatural element, so I'll pass over that for now. Edie then goes through an utter transformation--from the shy fat girl to a beautiful and confident queen bee type, and works her way (quite easily) into the group of popular teenagers who made her life a living hell before. 
 Right here is where it starts to lose me. It would have made more sense to me if Edie slowly built her confidence up naturally, maybe with the catalyst of Vi's friendship. If she managed to find a niche for herself and to learn that things do indeed get better, it would have been a bit more heartwarming. 
 Instead, we're sold on this idea that it would be a gnarly revenge story, which was simply untrue. Sure, Edie wishes revenge in the abstract, but never actually does anything to make it happen. Instead, she makes passive wishes, and the supernatural comes into play with some kind of dark guardian angel. Whoever Edie wishes bad things about, bad things happen to in really unusual forms. And since Edie actually likes some of the people now that she's seen they're not one-dimensional demons, this becomes a problem in and of itself. 
 With that, we'll transition over to the supernatural story now. Remember when I said Edie was saved from suicide? It was by a drop-dead gorgeous boy who offers her 3 wishes--whatever she desires--in exchange for 3 wishes from her later. She agrees because on the precipice of death, what is there to fear? 
 I can understand that thinking process if you're quite literally on the edge. What I also expected, and was not disappointed with, was the urge for life she had once things started to go well. Thanks to one of these magic wishes, she's now the most gorgeous version of herself, she's made friends with the clique who violently ridiculed her, and she has a steamy boyfriend to look forward to as well. 
 Okay. Not my most favorite plot line, but okay. When it starts to get good again is when all these deaths suddenly come up. One girl basically gets crater holes in her face and dies. One boy hangs himself. One boy just kind of disappears and turns into the wind or something. 
 What won me over despite being totally confusing: the monsters. Give me some mythological creatures (besides werewolves and vampires) and I am in godly heaven. So when suspicious ones start cropping up, I did a little boogie. Father Frost, the sun god in several forms, Bloody Mary, hellhounds, the Oracle of Delphi, a creepy Krampus-like boogieman who takes heads away in sacks... it was deliciously creepy and I was so stoked about it. I was home alone when I started reading the bit about Bloody Mary, and it did a great job of giving me the chills and making me pull my blanket tighter around me. 
 The reason for the monsters sort of makes sense, I guess. It's a giant chess game where the two sides don't care if the pawns die. There's spectators, who also seem to get involved? And it's apparently any creature or god who people have believed in enough to force them into being....and for whatever reason, even though they're immortal they need future technology. Hence the reason they want Edie. She's a brilliant person with brilliant parents who are on the verge of time travel. 
 So you see. It has its good, and its bad. The good would include the sneaky inclusion of monsters, and the desire to include a girl overcoming her bullies. The bad is the really convoluted plot with fantasy/mythology, science fiction, and young adult bullying; the instalove with a stalker boyfriend; and the undercurrent of belief that once Edie is beautiful, she's more important and more popular. The author does make an effort to address this and have Edie scorn it, but it doesn't seem to work as well when Edie goes from a shy, stuttering, fat girl to a curvy-in-all-the-right-places beauty.

Wilhelmina Pursling (Minnie) tries to keep a low profile. She's in her late twenties and almost on-the-shelf for marriage, not that she has really thought about it. She then hears his whole discussion about marrying her and what he'll be able to get away with. Unfortunately there is another witness to this conversation, Robert Blaisdell, the Duke of Clermont. He was hiding behind the curtains to smoke a cheroot. When the ugly fiance is gone, he works out who she is and then he asks her why she would want to marry such a man, and she tells him. 
 The more time he spends in this city, the more the duke becomes fascinated by her. He sees through her carefully crafted meekness and plain looks.

 ***

 Minnie assumes that the duke has had a life filled with everything he has ever wanted only to find that he is just as scarred as her but less visibly.

I don't think she would have misjudged him that badly; she got everything else dead right. Oh... except for thinking that marriage was a way out and not just a smaller, tighter cage. That also seemed vague of her.
