5 Stars to The Tin Box 
 Oh. My. God. 
 Kim Fielding is ripping my heart out with The Tin Box 
 William Lyon's story begins with him taking a job at a former mental institution in the destitute and remote area known as Jelley's Valley. When William takes this job he plans to enjoy the remoteness and write his dissertation, nothing else. Little does he know that fate has other plans as he meets, Colby Anderson. Colby is Jelley's Valley resident gay man. William is at first undecided about Colby - he can't decided what makes him tick - all he knows is the man is totally gay and totally different than him. William decides quickly that he has nothing in common with Colby and attempts to only interact with him as he has too, when shopping or getting his mail. Colby on the other hand has other ideas and finds creative ways to insert himself into Williams life. As the two get to know each other Colby helps William come out of his shell and loosen up while learning to explore his sexuality. You see William is a repressed gay man who has not only been taught it was wrong to be gay but has his own horrific past that taught him being gay was wrong. Colby decides he is going to help William explore his sexuality, thereby increasing Jelley's Valley gay population to two! 
 One night while William is at the Jelley's Valley institution he starts to explore and finds an old tin lunch box, it is what is inside this lunch box that forever changes William. Because inside this century old tin box are letters from Bill to Johnny. Bill was a resident at Jelley's Valley institution and his illness was homosexuality. Let me just warn you these letters are not pretty and they speak to the horrific past that people who were different faced at a time when psychiatric care was not as strictly governed as it is now. As William reads these letters he starts to accept that his situation, being gay and not accepted by his family, is not even half as dire as Bill's was almost a hundred years ago. It is through these letters and with Colby's creative help that William learns to accept himself, love himself, and transition from an uptight-in-the-closet-man to a fun-loving-out-and-proud-gay-man named, Will. 
 As William transitions from William Lyon to Will Lyon he also transitions from in-the-closet to out-gay-man, one thing he doesn't anticipate is falling in love with the man who at one point puzzled him - Colby. He also doesn't anticipate the trouble that he will have convincing Colby that he is exactly what he wants. 
 This is a highly emotional story. The letters in the tin box ripped my heart apart. Watching Will and Colby fall in love put it back together again. The narrator K.C. Kelly does an excellent job in this story bringing emotion and depth to the underlying horror story that these men faced while trying to be accepted in a society that wasn't ready to accept their type of love. This book isn't for the faint of heart let me warn you now. It is however a wonderful love story.

After so many busy days, I was able to sit down and finish The Titan's Curse By Rick Riordan. This is the third installment to the Percy Jackson and the Olympians series. I will try my best to keep this review spoiler-free. 
 This installment follows Percy Jackson as he sets off on another quest to save a friend and of course, the world, but this time he is accompanied by a new companion- Thalia- and a new group of mythological beings. 
 I must say that this book is definitely my favorite of the series, so far. The plot was so full of adventure and excitement from the beginning til the end. Rick Riordan had definitely taken this series at a whole other level with the ah-mazing twists and turns of modernized Greek mythology. In addition, he's such a talented writer! He had this ah-mazing ability to pull his readers into the world of Percy Jackson and give them a ride of their lives. I am really enjoying the overall story development. The story gets only gets more interesting as the story develops and it always gets me excited to pick up the next book :D 
 In each book, especially in this one, the main character(s) faces several challenges that are unique in every way and each challenge are usually more difficult than the previous ones. What I'm loving the most is that these challenges show the audience the true nature of Riordan's characters in the Percy Jackson world, without having the author describe it word for word. I think the characters are developing really well so far. It's always so exciting reading about new characters and in this case- the Di Angelo siblings. They were quite the adorable pair and the bits about them towards the middle to the end of the book has me itching to start on the fourth installment!!!

First impressions: I completely fell in love with Jackson. His voice is strong, sweet, and funny. You can't help but root for him as he jumps to save his girlfriend and reconnect with his dead sister. 
 Lasting impressions: This is a book about second chances, and Jackson's journey is a heart-wrenching one full of mystery, loss, and love. It definitely brought a few tears to my eye. 
 Conflicting impressions: I wasn't totally feeling the connection with Holly. Because we see her in two different times, and most of that time is in the past, I wasn't able to piece together exactly who she was or why she was so perfect for Jackson. Since their love story is what drives the plot, at times I felt a bit distant while reading. 
 Overall impressions: I do love a good time travel story, and this one has the interesting perspective of being about small jumps. No centuries here - we're talking minutes, hours, and in a sudden twist, a few years. Jackson has never been able to travel far, so when he witnesses Holly's shooting and winds up stuck two years in the past, he's stumped. 
 The book follows Jackson as he tries to explain his presence in New York when his two-years-ago self is supposed to be studying abroad in Spain. He sets out to find 2007 Holly ("007 Holly" as he calls her) and through her meet Adam, who becomes their mutual friend in the future and has been helping Jackson study his time traveling. He needs Adam's help if he's going to jump back to 2009 and save Holly, and he uses the new time with 007 Holly to get to know more about her. In the midst of his travels, he also gets the chance to see his twin sister, who died from leukemia, as her younger self. Those scenes are beautiful and touching, sorrowful and sweet, and were some of my favorite moments in the book. 
 The story gets a little convoluted with the dual Adams, Hollys, and bad guys. Jackson's dad, Kevin, has a role to play in this mystery, and he comes with a cadre of other gun-wielding people that Jackson isn't so quick to trust. Around this point is where I started to see this book sort of similar to The Adjustment Bureau, with lots of guys in fancy hats running around and trying to stop Jackson and Holly from being together. 
 The book is very cinematic, so it's no surprise to learn that it's been snapped up by Summit Entertainment. As the trilogy continues, I hope we find out a lot more about Kevin's involvement in his son's time travel, and what consequences result from him traveling into the past. This is an exciting and fresh new story in young adult fiction and I highly recommend it.

4.5 
 Reader thoughts: I craved this book when I wasn't listening and kept looking for ways to listen longer (I should take another walk!). That's why it got rounded up to a 5, even though the story and writing itself didn't strike me as phenomenal. 
 Rhenn is honorable, hard-working, and has quite a bit of skill in both portraiting and imaging. (It doesn't hurt that he's young and healthy.) I adored him. 
 The plot was milder than I wanted. I don't need adventure at every corner (and I was glad he had some normal days), but the climax was short (about half an hour), and  Rhenn wasn't in that much danger. He kills one imager who tried to kill him, and then he explodes three people who were trying to kill him. He's a bit caught in the explosion. After reading the blurb for book 2 about his wounds, I expected more danger. Plus, the cover of book 1 looks like he's witness murders and chasing assassins like some sort of fantasy Jason Bourne. He wasn't.  
 I really wanted more desperation, more struggle. No one hates him (openly; there are the assassins), and he succeeds at everything he tries at the first or second time he tries it. He and his girl and her family and his family also get along splendidly. There was no tension! Everything was happy! More on this below. 
 Even the assassination attempts felt mild. Oh, someone shot at him. Oh, someone shot at him again. Someone shot at him again. It was always in public and always when his shields were up. The shots knock Rhenn over, and the bad guys run away. He picks himself up, dusts himself off, and continues. Is there no panic? Does no one ever try to shoot him when he's inside a building (and turned his shields off)? Does no one try to walk up next to him and knife him (which would get through a shield that only caught fast-moving objects like bullets)? So, the assassins seemed a bit dumb. 
 Another reviewer mentioned that there's more detail than necessary. Like, food is described more than it needs to be. Well, I mostly disagree. 
 **1st, one of the most detailed meals is described right after Rhenn learns how to detect poison. I was nervous through the whole meal, thinking he would find poison in the wine or the braised lamb or the vegetables. That was the perfect place to describe the meal. The readers are interested! 
 **2nd, food brings the story to life. It shows off culture! 
 **3rd, I mostly skim descriptions of food and get the basic idea rather than every single detail. What? I'm not lazy; I'm practical and efficient. 
 Despite all of Rhenn's one-on-one meetings with his master (and why did he qualify for such exclusive classes? What about working in a group? Is it because his coursework was accelerated??) about politics, I don't understand his world that well. Some countries like imagers, and some don't. Rhenn's country has a council with high holders and guild leaders. There is one country that Rhenn's country doesn't trade with right now because of some reason. I'll probably learn more in the next book. 
 The romance was sweet and clean. A bit too easy, but it wasn't too fast. They never disagreed on anything. Maybe they will in book 2. 
 I would totally buy book 2 in audio format right now, but I convinced the library to buy it instead. I hope the wait is worth saving the money! (It takes at least a month for my library to buy books and make them available. Sigh.) 
 Writer thoughts: Most authors take the approach of, "If anything can go wrong, it will." That's basically Murphy's law, and it works wonderfully in making a plot full of lots of danger and tension. Cressida Cowell is particularly good at this. 
 In this book, it was the opposite half the time. 
 It seemed like, if something could go right, it did. When Rhenn accidentally kills someone with imaging (twice), he's not charged for it, no one blames him, and he gets off with barely a warning. When he's told that imaging is dangerous if you're not careful, I expected him to accidentally hurt himself or try something risky at least once, but he never does (never! Why did the masters keep calling him reckless?). When students tell him things, he trusts them, and I kept expecting someone to play a prank or tell him the wrong thing (like, "Imagers have to do such-and-such each morning" or "You have to pay a fee in order to eat lunch") like people do for a laugh. Nope, all his classmates were nice (except for that one scene). He thinks that certain actions will make people mad or get him into trouble, and they don't. I really hope this changes with the next book.

Gwynneth Ever After is a lovely contemporary romance novel that is set in Canada. 
 An ordinary single mother, Gwynneth has built her life around her three young children, working as an architect from her home, so that she can meet their needs. While attending a play that was written by a friend, she accidentally meets Gareth Connor, a famous actor who is visiting the area and finds herself drawn to him, despite herself. 
 This story is notable for the quiet normal life of its heroine. She works, takes care of her children and home and juggles financial and maintenance issues, just like any single mother would. Many of the scenes are centered, not around glamor, but in quiet moments with which we can identify, because we live in moments like that daily. 
 The author, Linda writes with a descriptive flair that makes even the normal and small moments special. We have all had those times when we're just doing what we usually do and then a tiny thing happens and we suddenly realize how important that moment is? She manages to convey that in well-chosen words, drawing a vivid picture that keeps us involved in her story. 
 One line in particular stood out for me: "A sudden, icy blast of wind sliced through thoughts he knew he had no business having," 
 This is a well-written book and a calming, enjoyable read.

Anna Dressed in Blood borrows a lot of its tropes from Buffy the Vampire Slayer. But instead of killing vampires, its main character, Cas, slays ghosts. That's not the only comparable thing, though. Cas surrounds himself with a group of friends ("scoobies" in BTVS parlance) that include what is essentially a witch (though a male one), and there's even a Giles mentor-like character off in jolly ol' England. Also, Cas, the ghost slayer, ultimately falls in love with a ghost, just like Buffy fell in love with Angel and then later Spike . Having said that, Kendare Blake is completely aware of the similarities and even goes so far as to mention it in the book. I guess you'd call that being meta. But it does make me wonder why she chose to write the book in the first place. I mean, why write something that's essentially already been done? 
 I guess it's not necessarily a bad thing. I love Buffy the Vampire Slayer and maybe that helped me to enjoy Anna Dressed in Blood to a point. I will say this. It was sufficiently creepy, and I made short work of it, which usually means I liked it (though it does have a rather low page-count). I did think that Blake made some odd choices, though. At first, it seems like Cas is rather full of himself, but as the book goes on, it becomes apparent that he's aware of his shortcomings. Ultimately, he's a dynamic character and goes through some changes, which is a good thing. Another odd choice is that one of his good friends is the school prom queen. That's actually a lot different than you would expect. Typically the female sidekick would be the kind of nerdy but cool type. But Carmel (not crazy about the name) is the most popular girl in school. It is different, but I don't know if I buy that it would go down like that IRL. Also, the setting. Ontario? Really? What's scary about Canada? The villain of this story is a Cajun ghost , and I kind of feel like she should have carried that decision through to its logical conclusion and set it in the dirty South. Maybe she thought that would be too much like Sookie Stackhouse, but she's already basically copied the premise for Buffy so who cares? 
 All in all, Anna Dressed in Blood was exactly the kind of book I was looking to read this week, so for that I'm giving it a solid three-star rating.

I finished the book I brought from home while at Comic Con this year, so I needed something new to read when I got back from all that walking. As this was one I got the first day I was there and it was a slim enough volume, I figured it was a good choice (I didn't want to lug a giant book around when I was just collecting more books). 
 It helped even more when I realized that it was a dark retelling of Peter Pan. I loved The Child Thief and how it portrayed Peter as a selfish being only focused on his own fun. Lost Boy was just that, but it gave us an amazing backstory for our favorite villain, Captain Hook. 
 Only Captain Hook isn't a villain here. Before he was Captain James Hook, he was Jamie: Peter's first friend. He was the counterpoint in every way--where Peter was sporadic, Jamie was measured. Where Peter was flighty, Jamie was thoughtful. While Peter was conceivably the cool uncle for the lost boys to look up to, Jamie was the mother hen who made sure they all ate and bathed and kept themselves alive. 
 It was also Jamie who buried them when Peter's adventures got them killed. 
 I loved every minute of it. It draws Hook in such a new light that I did more than just root for him--I pined for him and his success in a way I haven't for a character in a very long time. And that ending.... well, it basically just ripped my heart out. Jamie will permanently be Peter's playmate forever.

In a sentence: This is a page-turner, but I wanted more character development. 
 I feel like this is what it so often comes down to in my critiques of books, these days: the characters don't feel real yet! I don't know them as people. They're too generic. 
 So, as with many novels, without some really, really fantastic character development none of it really resonates, no matter how fantastic the premise is. 
 In this case, you'll know from reading the Goodreads summary that the premise is really, really fantastic. I will confirm that it remains fantastic throughout the book. Lots of cool plot ideas. Still. 
 Mild spoiler ahead about exactly why that cool plot is not enough. Yeah, the multiverse is a gripping idea and a seemingly overwhelming obstacle to returning home again, but... for me to really care whether the protagonist overcomes that obstacle, or even decides to try to overcome it, I need to care more about the protagonist and his family. Otherwise it's only mildly interesting. This is a book where the protagonist is supposedly making a choice between two things he wants most in the world, his family and a stellar career, but... as soon as he realizes he's gotten the stellar career, he immediately rejects it, no struggle to decide, and meanwhile we don't know enough about what kind of people his wife and son are to understand fully what it's like for the protagonist to weigh his love for them against his desire to be a successful scientist. Talk about a letdown.  
 I was entertained throughout by the action and ideas of the novel, but that was about it. Daniela is so essential to the emotional resonance of the novel, but I feel like I don't know her yet. I haven't spent enough time with her. Their son, Charlie, is even worse. 5 minutes after finishing the book, and all I remember about him is that he liked anime, I guess, and had some skateboarding decorations in his room. Why should I believe the protagonist's burning desire to get home to Generic Teenage Boy? 
 Without the emotional resonance, I'm left with a book I feel like I'll soon mostly forget. I bet I'll have forgotten Charlie and Daniela's names by the end of the week.

This review is for The Moon Dwellers, which I purchased on my own. I was provided a copy of the boxed set in exchange for writing an honest review for a book in the set, so I chose the one I'd already purchased. 
 True rating: 3.5 Stars 
 Note: Spoilers may be present in this review, though I tried to mark them as best I could. 
 The Moon Dwellers is set over five centuries into the future, after a meteor has wiped out the surface of the Unite States. A select group of people has moved underground and developed a tri-level society (The poorest Star Realm, the almost as bad Moon Realm, and the rich Sun Realm). Adele, the female protagonist, hails from The Moon Realm. She's a strong young woman who must use her fighting skills to break out of jail, evade (and battle) the evil Enforcers, and rescue her family. The male protagonist, Tristan, comes from the Sun Realm. He's a swoon-worthy "black sheep of the family because he's a good guy" prince who spends much of his time chasing after Adele with his friend/servant, Roc, and trying to figure out his place in society. 
 Mr. Estes' writing is truly gorgeous and it's clear he has an incredible gift. What he chooses to describe and how he does so (excluding one of my bullets below) is unique and refreshing. He paints beautiful pictures that convey strong emotion and a realistic world. His premise is relatively unique for the genre and I enjoyed the characters, particularly the relationship between Tristan and Roc. Based on these things, this novel would have earned 5 stars from me; however, I had difficulties getting into it until I was nearly half-way through, mostly because I kept getting jarred out of my read by the following things: 
 1. Plausability - Fantasy is a genre where a reader is expected to suspend some aspects of reality to believe in the new world that's created. I actually love that, but for me to truly suspend reality, the fictional world has to be wholly believable. The majority of the time, The Moon Dwellers does a good job meeting this requirement; however, I had a hard time with the way the book sometimes handled dialogue and descriptions. Cliches and common, modern expressions were used throughout the book (some examples: "No problemo!", "Bring it!" "Bingo! Give the guy a prize" and "make mincemeat out of your face"). Although I'm not a fan of any author adopting the regular use of cliches, when a book is told from a YA perspective, this can be forgivable, and even expected within dialogue. In the case of The Moon Dwellers, though, the story is told from a YA perspective 500+ years into the future. Our language changes every year and often evolves drastically within a few decades (old phrases are replaced with new ones; cliches are forgotten and recreated), so using modern speak doesn't work for me. No matter how hard I tried to ignore this aspect of the book, I couldn't and wound up disbelieving the progress of the society for this reason. The real shame for me in this is that I loved (and I do mean truly LOVED) Mr. Estes writing style. When he chose not to use those tools, the end result was so much better than when he did use them (for example, "The pain on his face is utterly complete, cracking his cheeks with jagged lines"), so I think this situation could have been avoided. There were also a few other logic issues throughout the novel (such as a scene where it's pitch black, yet Tristan somehow knew they were in a hub) that bothered me, but not as much as the one I've detailed above. 
 2. Love at first sight premise - While I'm typically okay with love at first sight novels, I had trouble believing that  Tristan and Adele would think about their first meeting twice, let alone consider it as a sign of anything important. When they first saw each other over a large distance, they each felt pain (although neither of them knew the other felt it). This seems like a coincidental thing, so I'm not sure I understand why Tristan would change the course of his future, risk his life, and chase after Adele for it.  
 3. Editing - Every author has editing points that are missed; it's the nature of writing, but when those issues are prevalent, I start highlighting them. In this case, there were a few things that got to me. Incorrect semi-colon/colon use and missed commas were standard grammar issues, and some sentences could have benefited from tightening (for example, "...I think about when my next scheduled visit to the Moon Realm is."). 
 4. Character Development - While I did genuinely like most of the characters (particularly Cole and Roc), I didn't feel they grew much throughout the novel. The main focus of the plot is non-stop action, which will appeal to many people, but for me it came at the expense of getting to know the characters and their internal struggles. 
 5. POV - The Moon Dwellers is told from first person point-of-view, alternating between Tristan and Adele. While this is handled well throughout much of the novel, some scenes were repeated from the other person's perspective without adding value to the plot. This slowed down the pace at times. In one big fight scene, when the POV is switched in short succession repetitively, it also dampened the emotion for a pivotal moment. 
 Despite these personal quibbles, I enjoyed The Moon Dwellers overall and think David Estes is worth reading and following. I suspect we'll be seeing great things from him in the near future.

Forbidden is a very tragic and disturbing read, the book's main focus is on incest but it does not necessarily promote it, it rather gives you a very in depth close up perspective and experience about two siblings who are in love . 
 Before reading this book I battled with myself if I was personally ready to handle a book of this magnitude, just because it delves into a world that I personally don't believe I am comfortable exploring. After reading this novel I can honestly say I wish I never picked it up, it has left me shaken and the ending cut me to pieces, it was unexpected, sad, and I found this novel extremely, extremely dark for a Young Adult book. 
 The writing was decent, the story-line (specifically the family dynamic) was very well done, the romance left me uncomfortable, and the characters were all very interesting. 
 Lochan and Maya are the two main characters in this novel, they are also siblings, and are only a year apart. You have the middle brother Kit, Tiffin the little brother, and Willa as the youngest. Lochan and Maya have been forced to keep the family together at the age of twelve, after their father walked out on them, and their mother became an alcoholic. As a result Lochan and Maya are more parents than teenagers and find solace in each other. This aspect of the story was wonderful, I loved the whole family dynamic and would have read that story even without the romance between Lochan and Maya. It was all very endearing the way all the siblings loved each other and were such a strong unit, the siblings relationship was one of my favourite parts of the story. 
 Lochan and Maya's romance wow, I did not expect the author to delve at all into the physical aspect of their relationship, I was not at all prepared for it. To be honest I was not rooting for them, I knew that they could never be together, and to be honest I was a bit turned off by their desperate love for each other. I am a very open-minded person, but incest is just not something I can understand. The author did a very good job in showing the readers the mental struggle Lochan and Maya faced for their attraction for each other, however I just did not feel comfortable reading about the little romantic world they created for themselves. 
 Incest had always been a very tricky topic, a lot of authors sometimes border-line the concept of this, or brother figure/ friend to lover. For example in Cassandra Clare's Shadowhunter series the main character's Jace and Claire, realize that they are siblings, however before that knowledge is gained they first realize that they both are deeply attracted to each other. In the end we find out that they actually are not sibling's, but Jace was raised by Claire's biological father, and considers him to be his father. How is that not a bit disgusting? 
 As well as Nora Robert's Honest Illusion, where the main character Luke is adopted into a family of magicians as a child. He grows up and ends up falls in love with their daughter, a woman he grew up with, who loves him in turn. They fight off these feelings but realize because they are not biological siblings that it is not at all incestuous. 
 In Forbidden, Luchas and Maya have never felt like brother and sister, it has always been something more even as kids. So because of their biological connection they are not allowed to be together the way Luke and Roxy (the main characters from Honest Illusions), are allowed to be despite having the exact same upbringing. I'm not saying I agree with incest, or even rooted for Luchas and Maya, I'm just simply putting things into perspective. 
 All in all what I got from this novel is the fact that decisions, life, society it is all very difficult, how can people tell what is right and what is wrong, is it a feeling in the gut, or what society says is the norm, the characters in Forbidden ask "how could something that feels so right be so wrong?" And honestly we all want to be the one's who are accepting but at the end of the day whose to play judge and jury and what gives them the right, the power over our lives?

Before Tumblr was all over the idea of non-binary and transgender identities, neither of which are out of the realm of possibility if you want to read it that way, I gave this book a 5-star rating for how thoroughly it blurred the line between "feminine/gay?" and "angel?" and really made me think about intolerance. To my pleasant surprise, it still takes my breath away 10 years later. This is partly because it's two completely different stories depending on whether you think Lani is simply a human who refuses to be labeled, or something otherworldly. The latter is a brain-tingling possibility that makes you want to open up to your spiritual side, while the former makes it one of the most devastating stories imaginable. 
 Lani Garver is one of my favorite fictional characters of all time. Claire frequently says he's wise beyond his years, which is demonstrated by such things as his interest in casually discussing philosophy and noting when she displays signs of an eating disorder/finds a way to get her help. He's also very sweet and fairly tactile with his affection. At one point, he kisses her on the side of the head, and she complains he's like a dad, while I'm over here doing kicky feet and twirling my fist in a circle to cheer this care-taking on. 
 His friendship with Claire is particularly beautiful, because even though it seems to be all him helping her, she's also the only ally in the town, where even his own mother seems tired of dealing with the controversy that surrounds him (that first magazine scene, for example, punched me in the heart good after his resigned response). And while he is mostly very calm and collected, a paragon of "rising above," he can also be Sass Level Midnight when there's an opportunity dig someone good, which got more than a few giggles out of me. 
 Actually, all of the characters in this book are memorable, whether good or bad. I feel for both Claire and Lani's mothers, despite their poor coping mechanisms with their respective children's struggles and a tendency to distance themselves as a result. There's Claire's dad and stepmom, wanting to be supportive but less accessible due to living in the city. Lani's friends from the performing arts high school, whom I didn't give enough credit the first time, now make me wish I could read a whole separate book about his year going to school with them because they're such unique individuals, and so open and accepting of everything. And one of my other favorites, the optimistic city medic, Marcus,who introduces her to the concept of floating angels in the first place, having seen it all in his tenure. 
 The Hackett characters are less developed, which fits with their herd mentality and the promotion of blending in and going along with the crowd. It's particularly creepy when juxtaposed with the concept of "convenient recollections." On ringleader Macy's say-so, anything she thinks or decides to believe suddenly becomes infallible truth among her followers, and there is a parallel solidarity of the "fishermen frat." It chills my blood to think there could be a place in this country so doggedly homophobic that it escalates to physical violence, and not only can no one prevent it, there seems to be minimal hope of prosecuting it after the fact. 
 Now, back to Lani. 
 I want to say that I believe, as I did the first time I read it, that he was an angel. [because spoilers]  Fear doesn't sufficiently explain his total collapse at the end, which doesn't match up with how sensibly he's handled every situation up until now. Especially not after he was so deliberate in asking what Tony would most likely do, and then did exactly what would escalate the situation. That said, I feel guilty every time I choose this answer, because it's the convenient explanation. Maybe I shouldn't. But maybe I have to, because otherwise I cannot wash away images of some helpless kid curled up in a ball, sobbing and pleading in genuine fear for his life, ultimately in vain. And isn't it far more harrowing if that's the truth?  
 The ending is the most satisfying inconclusive ending I've ever read. The author allows Claire to explore plausible explanations for both scenarios, providing equal and ample evidence for both, and everything sounds so reasonable that it's impossible to decide which one is best. I don't always love open endings, but nothing could have been better here. 
 When I closed the book today, I just sat there in stunned, contemplative silence and stared into space for about ten minutes thinking about it. Not even thinking, really -- I just replayed my feelings and tried to process my emotions and how I could describe this book in order to recommend it. I don't know that I came up with a sufficient answer, I just know that this is a really, really powerful story and that Lani is a life-changing individual, not just for Claire, but for me.

 Strap in, this review is almost as long as the book because I don't want to let this world go. 
 It's probably because I have been desensitized to its biggest flaws longer than I have known what the plots of books 2 and 3 were, but since it is too late to be fazed by "body-destroying half-vampire baby" or inappropriate imprinting, with those shock factors negated I was able to concentrate on the story for what it is: half a book about newlyweds and half a book about a brewing confrontation with the Super Vamps and a bonus concentration on family togetherness. 
 Part I: As the fluffiest-hearted person of all time, I was head over heels for the extended wedding & honeymoon, particularly the latter. Although that first cut-to-black was too abrupt even for me -- I am all for G-rated bedroom scenes, but she literally went from standing in the water next to him to waking up in bed the next morning -- I really loved everything else. I like to think I am above wanting my life to be like Twilight, but all bets are off when it comes to how much I want an Isle Esme honeymoon. And as someone who got very frustrated on Bella's behalf when Edward made his ~nevermore shall I touch you whilst you are human~ speech, the payoff on that was spectacular. 
 Part II: I thought I would hate having to enter Jacob's head, but once we got past the first couple of chapters of his awkwardly juvenile first-person voice, I saw the wisdom of switching viewpoints. It was just a giant festival of "let's talk about how anguished and guilty Edward looks all of the time," with bonus descriptions of how loving and motherly Rosalie is (let me pretend they have bonded as sisters instead of Rose just trying to womb-snatch). 
 It was especially lovely to view that without Bella's interjections about her own unwarranted guilt or his obnoxious cold skin. This is hurt/comfort in its finest element and, in all deference to the story, hard to give a real-life counterpart. The closest example would be if you were pregnant while sick with cancer, but even then the baby isn't starving you to death/breaking your bones on the regular. Edward really is at his manic wit's end, and it's both sweet and heartbreaking. 
 Plus I nearly perished of adorable during the shift when he can suddenly hear the baby's thoughts and basically melts into a puddle of goo. 
 On a non-Cullen note, Jacob's breakaway from the pack and the addition of the Clearwaters following his lead helped his part a lot. Seth is such a cutie-patootie, and Leah is pretty much everything I've ever wanted her to be. I also loved Esme's unstoppable mothering instincts, leaving food and clothing for the werewolves and practically clucking over their well-being. 
 Part III: Excuse me while I go die of laughter at how apparently being a vampire = having all the crazy whoopee during the time most people are asleep. And then laugh some more at the thought of Virgin Edward dealing with a house full of it for decades. 
 Beyond that, my eyes started to glaze over when they wouldn't stop introducing "witness" vampires from around the world. It felt like the author kept thinking up more and more vampire stories she wanted to tell but knew she couldn't get book deals for them all, so they had to be crammed into this one. I was almost relieved when Aro and the Thug Brothers + the children's parade (Jane et. al.) showed up, because I can't stand them but at least I know them. At some point I also started laughing about how Bella is magically the most special and talented vampire that has ever existed, straight from birth, because heaven forbid anything should be a challenge for her. Super ridiculous, but I wasn't even mad. 
 I was disappointed that Bella never really connected with "Nessie," and so neither did I. She seemed bonded with everyone else, but Bella was just kind of...there, nearby. Like a visiting aunt. Or like Renesmee was a family pet, beloved by all but not really belonging to her. As important as Baby Cullen was to the plot, she made little impression on me. 
 Plot-wise, the closer we got to the end, the more of a nervous, shaking wreck I became. I hunched over the book for hours, terrified that a Cullen I loved was doomed to die (Emmett being the only one my heart can spare, and I'm pretty sure no one cares enough about him to make him a target), sure that Alice & Jasper would come back but not sure they'd stay alive. 
 And then...nothing happened. Like literally nothing. Irina paid for starting this whole mess in the first place and then everyone popped their collars and walked away. 
 And it was AWESOME. 
 Just pure, adrenaline-flooded relief and collapse.

I am sure that a lot of people hated this choice, probably because many people just want shiny action plots and then move on to the next book or show, but I am in the business of permanent world building.  This is one of the few series that lets me go home happy, and for that I am profoundly grateful.

I believe a reader's enjoyment of this short story will come down to one question: Do you believe a ghost can grow up? If your answer is no, you may be put off by the happenings of DARK CURTAINS. 
 That's what happened to me. I couldn't buy into the whole ghost becoming an adult after dying at the age of ten. So the first time James is seduced by the curtains, I was picturing a ten-year-old girl doing the caressing. Can you see why I was put off? It isn't until later that the author tells us that the ghost is actually a matured version of the ten-year-old dead girl, but by then it was too late. 
 Also, I feel there are some inconsistencies with the kids in the flashback/dream James has. At ten, he has a feeling of wanting and desire for the little girl who lives across the street, his best friend, yet when she kisses him, he wipes the kiss off. She kisses him again, and he kisses her back. This took me out of the moment. It's been 24 years since I was ten, but I don't remember kissing being a sensual thing. It was awkward. Something you did because you saw grown folks doing it. This is subjective, I suppose. Others might have had passionate kisses at the age of ten, but I wasn't one of them. This flashback also led me to believe that the ghost in the curtains was a sexualized ten year old because the author already described the desire of the kids, which put me off even further. 
 In summation: The story does manage to be thoroughly creepy, as long as you can get past the whole ghost-growing-up thing. Not my favorite Evans Light tale, but well-written. Oh, and I liked the alternate ending better.

I had only two complaints which happen to be spoilerish  Within the first sentence they introduce Eo, the main character's wife, it's obvious she's going to die. The whole reason she exists is to die, to give the main male character some angst to motivate him to overthrow the system. It's a tired trope and you can tell when it's going to happen because the wife/girlfriend/family is always presented in this idyllic, flawless sort of way. The other complaint, which literally made me stop reading and rub my eyes a little bit: Darrow teams up with Mustang after she saves him. She presents the brilliant idea--which ultimately allows them to win-- of not enslaving other people, but getting them to truly fight for them. then she defers leadership to him . because why? why shouldn't the smartest person with the best idea lead? because she's not the main character, of course! With only four girls left, Maxon is closer than ever to selecting a bride. Danger has escalated throughout the land as the southern rebels increase their attacks. Half the guards sent to protect the Elite's families have disappeared. Tension in the palace has grown as the girls zero in on the prize and the king increases the pressure on Maxon to end the Selection. Of course America continues to antagonize the king, but the people seem to love her more for it. He can't just get rid of her, but he tries to manipulate her into further his agenda. The leaders of the northern rebels approach Maxon with a deal, and America makes an alliance that will change the fate of the royal family. I thought this was a good conclusion to the trilogy. It had some twists and turns I didn't expect, as the two books before it also did. I should have known not to make up my mind about any character, because once again I was surprised. I think the author did a magnificent job of developing all these characters. The girls continued to grow and change as the story progressed and Maxon continued to surprise me as well. The king probably didn't like the changes in Maxon, but that made them all the better in my eyes. I even liked Aspen more in this book. I forgot to read his novella before I read this, and now I am definitely going to. I thought everything was wrapped up well, leaving just enough to imagine the future. I'm going to miss this series. Hopefully the author will start a new one just as good.

I watched the movie first and then decided to start the book series. While the book did contain some variants to the movie, they were very similar. I like it but don't have a driving need to read each one right away. 
 This is a futuristic world, sort-of mysterious dystopian, where fifty boys are stuck in a glade trying to figure out how to escape through a maze. Each boy has arrived monthly with no memory of their previous life. They each try all of the work positions until they figure out what they are good at doing. 
 When we begin observing the group, they have been there for two years and the latest "greenie" to join the group is Thomas. He is confused but eager to help and feels strongly that he should be one of the "runners" who enter the maze each day to map and track the changes. Two days after his arrival, another child is sent to the glade with a note that she (the first girl ever) is the last child who will be sent. She is the beginning of the end. 
 The children then ramp up their efforts to figure out the mystery and escape the glade. Some are killed during their attempts but eventually about half of them make it out. We are left with some answers but more questions about what is to come leading to the interest in the next books in the series.

When I started this book, I was pretty skeptical over whether I would actually enjoy it or not. I have read Ms. Bardugo's other trilogy, The Grisha Trilogy, and while I really liked the first book the series fell off quickly for me (the 2nd book bored me to death). That trilogy did have an all right ending though, and again, I did really like the first book. This series is getting a lot of love, and most people say that if you like good characters you will like this book. That fits me to a tee-- I read for characters. The plot, of course, must be decent, a good twist here or there is always good, but I don't care about what happens to characters I don't care about. I definitely care about what happens to all of these characters. There are six main characters and five of them are given POV chapters. (This is a series, and I do hope we get the 6th's POV in the next book). Each character is given a well developed backstory, so you really get to understand their motifs for participating in the heist. Their backstories are inter-woven into the plot, giving the backstory when the reader will understand it most given the current situation. It was so nice to get all of this information. Plus, for a rag-tag group of thieves/rouges, the characters are all very diverse. Again, this is in part to their glorious backstories, but we don't have a bunch of thieves just in it for the money. 
 The actual plot is also great. The pacing is wonderful and I could not expect it to be any quicker or slower. I stayed up late to keep reading to the end once the heist begins. 
 If I had any complaints, it would be that I was a little confused over what was happening at times. I think the world was just so rich that I had a hard time picturing some things happening. For example,  when they break out of the prison and are on their way to the White Island and they end up having to spilt ways due to the prison break not going smoothly, I was just like.... where are the actually standing in this court? There is a picture of the court provided in the book, and it looks like after the prison is immediately the ice moat. I understand that they were on rooftops for a period of time, but they are also spotting people entering the White Island by crossing the Glass Bridge. Where are all these incoming people standing? I don't know. I could re-read it to try and get some better clarity, but honestly it was me being really detailed orientated and I just wanted to know everything I could. Another example of confusing: Jesper and Wylan showing up to save Inej when she was caught pretending to be the Lynx of the Menagerie was a little unbelievable. I don't even understand how they got there, or exactly where this is occurring in the Ice Court either. I know Jesper and Wylan were bringing down a gate, but just how did they get to Inej then? How were they pretending to be a guard??  This is in part due to the reader being much more left in the dark of the heist plan-- the reader is more involved in its planning in the beginning and that changes later on. Like the heist not going as planned so Kaz has to tell each member what they need to do  This is to create much more suspense, and I was fooled at least once. 
 I am excited to continue on with this series. When Jesper and Wylan saved Inej, I was kind of disappointed because I wanted Kaz to develop a plan to save her. Now he has to do that anyway!!

 This is definitely a 3.5 book, but I'm not feeling like rounding up, even though I think there's a lot of good going on here and I'd definitely read another novel from Imbolo Mbue. First, I found the general story extremely compelling, and I loved that she illustrated the contrast of what the American Dream means to different demographics and how those dreams are wrapped up in each other, even for people that live on opposite sides of the economic spectrum. The irony that that the vast differences between the Jongas and the Edwards' are best shown when they are sharing the same small physical space inside the car was not lost on me, and I loved that she portrayed the Edwards as both kind of silly (complaining about possibly having to fly coach after the 2008 crisis) and completely justified in their fears of losing an entire lifetime's worth of work. In the meantime, Jende is worried about being deported and barely makes enough to scrape by, but calls it prosperity. She also perfectly captured the wonder and symbolism that New York City holds for outsiders, especially a new immigrant hoping to build a better life for his family. 
 On the other hand, I found the writing incredibly stiff in some places, while it flowed beautifully in others. I don't need paragraphs about economics: make it clear through dialogue and the plot. Most of the characters didn't stand out as individuals, and even the main characters were sometimes weirdly hard to discern from each other based on their speech. I liked the ending, but the story kind of petered out in the last 100 pages, even though there was potentially major stuff happening. Nothing had any oomph or lasting effect, and each plot point toward the end moved on to another one that felt nearly identical, like the author had written ideas for scenes on index cards and then put them all together and called it good enough. That definitely doesn't mean that every event had to be loud and dramatic, and  I liked that final scene between Jende and Clark was very quiet, but it didn't have the weight that would have made it memorable. It could have been dripping with tension, or with unspoken feelings on the past, but it felt so...blah. Too straightforward.  
 Anyway, this is a great premise, and there were a lot of good ideas, but there are definitely some things to iron out before the next novel.

 But the characters? Blah. No one I really cared about, and no one who felt truly original and human. The villains are cartoonish, and the protagonist? Ha. Jack Reacher is so stoic-badass-manly-man it's almost funny, plus he's totally inconsistent in his detective skills--making amazing deductions one second and missing ginormous clues the next. 
 The women characters are even worse, bland and mostly stereotypical, with no cool roles in the novel. For example, Jack's love interest, Roscoe the police officer, could've been really awesome, but as it stands, most of what I know of her is what she looks like and how sexy Reacher finds her. She quickly turns into the worst stereotype of a woman: breaks down sobbing at crime scenes because it's just too much to handle (meanwhile, Reacher sheds not one tear, instead remaining cool and ultra-manly), gets kidnapped by the bad guys, and can't even run out of a burning building but instead needs Jack to carry her out like a damsel in distress. Seriously, she's not tied up or anything but he still "drags" her out of danger. What makes that last one even more unbelievable is that she's perfectly fine aside from being exhausted, whereas he's exhausted AND has just had the crap kicked out of him. She should totally be pulling him up off the floor and out of harm's way, not the other way around. 
 Can't say I'd recommend this, but it was entertaining enough.

I received The Bedlam Stacks from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. 
 This is the first book by Natasha Pulley that I have had the pleasure of reading. I knew nothing of her previous work, but the synopsis of Merrick (employed by the East India Company) traipsing through Peru to get quinine coupled with an air of supernatural weaved through it, and having read nothing dealing with the East India Company and only knowing a little about their past, further intrigued me. This book, screamed. "Yes, read me." 
 However, within the first couple chapters I found myself bogged down in exposition. But, I kept going, and I am so glad that I did. Once I got a handle on Natasha Pulley's writing style, I couldn't put the book down. I found myself Googling the trees and Inca culture that Merrick found himself surrounded by. Pulley really did her research with this book and it spurred me on to find out more. Hence, the Googling. 
 Every character took a life of their own. I half imagined them walking off the page. My favorites by far are Randolph the mysterious priest, Minna (Clem's clever wife), and Keita the intuitive boy that Merrick took under his wing. They where the ones that helped slide Merrick into the places he needed to go. And I would die to have a side story about where Keita was in all those years in between leaving and meeting Merrick again. What did Minna do in all of that time that Clem and Merrick were off in Bedlam? Randolph alone is a man with many secrets who deserves an entire book to unlock them. 
 "Could I borrow him?" I asked. 
 "If I can borrow that dog." 
 "Yes. Trade." I gave her the dog. Sing followed me out. 
 "Was I just bought for a St. Bernard?" 
 Scenes like this make The Bedlam Stacks engaging and endearing. These simple quick witted exchanges are something I crave in books. It connects me to the characters. It makes me laugh. It sticks with me for weeks to come. Now to find a copy of the The Watchmaker of Filigree Street.

Whether or not Juliette ends up with Warner is still up for debate, but she won't end up happily ever after with Adam.

The survivors are holing up at Adam's old apartment - including the rescued Winston and Brendan! - when they (mistakenly) find out that Juliette has been killed.

I have very many mixed feelings about this book. The last book I tried to read, CRAVE by Melissa Darnell, reminded me so much of TWILIGHT that I had to put it down after 50 pages. 
 This book reminded me of TWILIGHT even more than CRAVE did, but for some reason, I still enjoyed it. For the most part. 
 One of the biggest reasons I kept reading the book was because the main character, Katy, was really interesting. When all of these weird things were happening around her, she didn't think "Oh, it's just my imagination and I'm just being silly so I'll just forget anything even happened" and then "take it really well" when the big secret is revealed, like she knew it all along. No, she actively thought about what was going on around her, tried to piece it all together, and then freaked out when it was explained to her. Like a normal human being. Which is what she's supposed to be. 
 Granted, there were the "You're taking this surprisingly well" moments throughout the book, but I felt like she'd also been given ample time to be a little crazy about it. 
 Also, about halfway through the book, there was a scene in which I knew my view of her would be sealed forever: was she going to run, or was she going to fight? I'm happy to say that she stayed and fought. And it was actually kind of an anti-climatic scene where she really did nothing more than run up to some guy and stab him in the back, but the fact of the matter is that she ran up to some guy and stabbed him in the back. 
 And she still didn't disappoint at the end, when all seems lost and the most powerful person Katy's ever known is incapacitated and there's really nothing more that can be done. Except, wait, there is! Katy somehow miraculously saves the day, in a way that I can't explain.  
 So, yeah. Not the most original, thought-provoking book, or the best writing, or really that great of a story in the first place. But I enjoyed reading it and I find myself interested in the next book. 
 P.S. For a novel about aliens, it didn't really feel much like a sci-fi to me. It should definitely go in the romance section. 
 EDIT: I forgot to mention so much more about this book because it was late last night and I just wanted to get some thoughts down before I forgot them all. 
 One thing that I didn't like about the book was the constant mention of Daemon's hotness. It gets redundant and a little bit distracting after the 50th time. I know he's hot. Every guy in every book like this is hot. It's just a given. So stop mentioning it every freaking time he opens his "poetic" mouth. 
 Now, despite the fact that Katy over-sold Daemon's hotness, the romance wasn't rushed. She admitted that she was attracted to Daemon, she sometimes thought about kissing him, but she never over analyzed it and she never acted like a love-sick fool. And when there was an opportunity for her to finally have a romantic relationship with him, she tells him no! Which I loved! Mostly because of her reason, which was that she wanted him to want her the way her father wanted her mother. 
 And that is how romance is supposed to be. None of this "We looked into each other's eyes and I was a gonner" garbage. None of that stupid "I'll do anything for him, just as long as he kisses me one more time" bullcrap. 
 No, she didn't let him get away with being a jerk and she told him how it was. And that was the end.  
 I like reading about girls like Katy. And I think ultimately that's why I liked this book enough to want to read the next one. 
 EDIT (agian): I've thought a lot about this book and I've finally come to this conclusion: it has a lot of good things that TWILIGHT didn't, plus it takes some of the things I liked about TWILIGHT and does them better.

The Strange Library has all of (or almost all of) the elements of a Murakami story that I love, distilled into one quick read. The illustrations and the recurrence of familiar Murakami themes and characters/character-types serve to elevate the story's dreamlike atmosphere. It was made both familiar and strange, as the best/worst dreams often feel. That said, those unfamiliar with his work will probably finish this with a sense of "what the f did I just read". It would be unfair to compare this to his novels. It's an experiment and a way for Murakami to play with new formats and new methods of expression. I for one really enjoyed it and hope he takes the experiment further next time. 
 I haven't quite worked out exactly what he's saying, I only just finished it 20 minutes ago. But I suspect that as with any other parable, or any other Murakami story for that matter, its meaning will become clear (and change and evolve) the longer I sit with it. What I do know is that I had an immediate emotional response and that's usually the first phase in understanding Murakami for me. I think those writing The Strange Library off as a failed attempt at scaring children into behaving are missing the point - taking it too seriously and too literally. I think it was originally published for adolescents, but being familiar with Murakami's decidedly NOT kid-friendly work makes this of interest to adults too.

What a wonderful end to this wonderful series! Winter was just about everything I was hoping it would be and I really couldn't be happier about it. 
 As with almost every series finale I try to review, I find it overwhelming to organize my thoughts into a cohesive review. So I will go with my trusty list of random observations and thoughts. 
 -What started as an ok book for me in Cinder just continued to get better and better in each installment and it became one of my all time favorite YA series. Meyer has developed a rich cast of characters that I love and ship and root for. While I'm sad to see them go, I'm so happy to see them reach their Happily Ever Afters. 
 -This book is long. In many books I feel the action and the conclusion often feel rushed towards the end, but that is not the case in Winter. Meyer definitely takes her time to set everything up. A revolution is not a quick or easy thing to start and we see every step, every hiccup along the way. There were a few times when I thought, "can we just get on with it, already?", but really I can't complain about spending more time with these characters. 
 -The Friendships. I love the friendships in this book so much. Cinder and Iko as BFFs just makes me smile. The sarcastic banter between Cinder and Thorne has made me laugh since the very beginning and I'm so happy that their relationship has remained just a solid friendship instead of turning into a possible romantic triangle - which is what I originally feared when Thorne's character was first introduced. Scarlet and Winter also became a fun friendship to watch evolve in this book. 
 -The Romances. Of course I have to mention all the romantic pairings in this series. Cinder and Kai's relationship has been developing since the first book and I loved every single thing about it in this book. From their first scene together to their last, I love them! Scarlet and Wolf have faced many, many obstacles in their short relationship, but they are solid and wonderful and adorable and I love them. Cress and Thorne! We did not get nearly enough Cress and Thorne chapters for my liking, but when we got them, we really got them. I'm incredibly happy with their big romantic moments in this book. And, last but not least, Winter and Jacin. I didn't really expect to love them as much as I do, but I should have known better. Their relationship also had their obstacles, but they never gave up and I ship it. And I also fee like I must mention that I have come to love Jacin just as much as the other guys in this series. He's sarcastic and smart and protective and I just really fell for him. 
 -The Perspectives. There are a lot of perspective for Meyer to juggle here and like each book before it, she handles it so well. Though I often got upset when a shift in perspective changed, it did not take me long at all to get into the new perspective. It really kept the story going and with our favorite characters often separated in different groups throughout the book it was necessary to keep up with everybody and see all the parts of the revolution coming together. My only complaint is that I don't think we got a single chapter from Thorne's perspective. He was around, of course, and had some big moments, but I wish we would've gotten some of his perspective since we got everyone else's. 
 -The Revolution. We've been gearing towards this moment since the first book and it was so satisfying to watch it play out. It was not without fatalities and sacrifices and heartbreak. Not every single thing went according to plan. But I loved seeing all the characters - old and new - come together. I loved reading the strategy and the twists and surprises. And, of course, I loved seeing it reach it's conclusion.

 I'm so torn right now. Because I did enjoy this, but I also... didn't. It's really hard to explain, but I'll try to do so as best as I can. After all, such is a reviewer's burden. But yes, I enjoyed this. But there were things that stopped me from loving it completely. 
 I feel like it's best to start with what didn't work for me. Get it out of the way, so to speak. So here we go. My main problem with this book is in the way it's told. Don't get me wrong, I like the letter stuff. And it's worked fantastically for me before. But in this one it just... made me feel disconnected from the characters for the most part. Because it's told in a letter format, I felt like I missed a lot of what happened. And some of the more feelsy stuff just didn't really get me the way it should because I felt like the story skipped over those important moments. I feel like I would have gotten more out of this story if it had only been partly letters. This could just be entirely my problem though. And though I loved the story for the most part, because of the aforementioned disconnect, the first half kind of dragged a bit for me. And with that, I also didn't really feel any connection whatsoever to ANY of the side characters. Because I never got to know them at all outside of what Cath and Scott mentioned in their letters. 
 But I really did like the story itself and the setting. It's set in the 80's and it has SO many great music references. Seriously. So much love for the amazing taste in music this book has. I also liked the friendship between Scott and Cath, our main characters. And I loved them too. Their voices were distinct and I rooted for them for the most part. I didn't really get into the romance because it felt a bit rushed at the end. Also, despite my disconnect with the characters, the second half really did hit me in the feels a few times. 
 I feel like I should say more positive things about this to convince you to read this. But I don't really have much else to say because the book itself wasn't all that long. I wanted to love it a lot, but I ended just liking it okay. But despite that, if you love YA Contemporary, give this a try. You might end up loving it more than I did. Especially if you're fond of books in this kind of letter exchange style.

So everyone in the blogosphere seems to be in love with Colleen Hoover, and especially with Maybe Someday. I was expecting to feel all the feels I've never felt before. I was expecting extraordinary romance and an un-put-downable book. However, after all the hype, I find I'm left disappointed. It's not that the book was bad. But it wasn't great. It was kind of just so-so for me. 
 Oh the drama! Girl gets cheated on. Girl is heartbroken - kind of, for a bit. Girl falls for new guy - someone way better. Girl becomes the other woman. Irony ensues. But, not as much irony as there should have been. It's supposed to be different because Sydney's ex-boyfriend and ex-best friend were just having a physical thing that meant nothing, while Sydney and Ridge are actually falling in love. Despite that he's still in love with his girlfriend. And has no intention of leaving her. But, cheating is cheating, folks. 
 I was pretty annoyed with Ridge for most of the book. I don't believe the whole "being in love with two people at the same time" thing. While you can love more than one person at a time, it's in different ways. And it takes almost the whole book for Ridge to realize that the love he feels for these two women are different and finally makes a choice a about it. 
 Song writing was a big part of this book. While it was an interesting addition to the story, it just wasn't done as well as I wish it was. I didn't think the song lyrics were anything amazing. I didn't find Sydney's writing ability to be as amazing as we're supposed to believe. However, I do like that all the songs have actually been recorded and you can listen to them here. 
 Where this book really worked for me was with Ridge being deaf. It's always interesting to me to see the disabled community represented and how it's handled. I liked how Sydney never once thought of Ridge as disabled and never lamented the fact that he was deaf. If anything, it intensified their intimacy. 
 Overall, Maybe Someday was an ok read for me. While it was probably one of the better New Adult books I've read, I can't help but be disappointed since it didn't quite live up to all the hype for me. I wonder if I would've liked it more if I had gone into with no expectations. While she's not a new auto-read author, I think I'll be checking out more books by Hoover in the future.

Read one-third if you're curious about Stephen King's becoming, two-thirds for the most practical (fiction-) writing advice, and finish the whole book for more tips on being a full-time writer. He also shares his views on reading, relationships, personal habits, and a list of recommended books. Fun and informative read. 
 Here are my brief notes of memorable parts from the book. The examples King has chosen from his own and other writers' work to illustrate are worth the time for a re-read. 
 1. "Write with the door closed, then rewrite with the door open." Because there's no need to pressure yourself until you've got your story ready for a second opinion. 
 2. "Life isn't a support-system for art. It's the other way around." Just as you need privacy to write, you have to live a life away from your desk and outside of your bubble to find stimulation. 
 3. "Books are a uniquely portable magic." I'm surprised that he often listens to audiobooks and have decided to follow suit. 
 4. "The basic rule for vocabulary is use the first word that comes to your mind, if it's appropriate and colorful." Over-editing could stray from what you really mean, and we all know it's ridiculous to dress up the vocabulary with long words. To cite King, "take a shit" does sound more appropriate and colorful than "perform an act of excretion". 
 5. "The object of fiction isn't grammatical corrections but to make the reader welcome and then tell a story... to make him/her forgot, whenever possible, that he/she is reading a story at all." 
 6. "[When revising] if you spot a few of these [logical] big holes, you are forbidden to feel depressed about them or to beat up on yourself." The stories he shares about changes he has made to his works will help you see how important this is. Also, why not accept a shitty first draft and the possibility of a better next draft if this can happen to experienced writers? 
 7. "Writing is magic, as much the water of life as any other creative art. The water is free. So drink. Drink and be filled up." If you're ever interested in writing your own stuff, this is him kicking you on to start now. 
 I've never read any of his fictions. This book makes me want to read lots of them, especially the ones he has discussed. He talks about how these stories progress and end, but I feel the urge to read them because I believe the way he tells the stories will make the plot only a part of the whole thrilling package.

 Getting Him Back is a new adult, male/male romance that tells the story of Ethan and his school and love life troubles as he makes the transition from high school graduate to college student. Ethan's longtime boyfriend Blake has been at college for a year and Ethan has decided he will follow Blake to Coborn College so they can be together as they begin their lives together. Since they have been apart for "three weeks, two days, five Hours and twenty-nine minutes" Ethan is very eager to get to school and spend some quality time catching up both in and out of bed. 
 Imagine Ethan's surprise when he finally gets to Coborn and is told by Blake: 
 "I still love you, but I don't love you that way anymore" 
 Ethan just cannot understand why his boyfriend broke up with him, he becomes depressed and regrets following him to Coborn College. He makes it his mission to not let his parents know that this has happened (as they warned him not to follow a boy to college) and to figure out the "why" of Blake's ending their relationship. 
 In his pursuit of Blake, Ethan meets his dorm roommate - Wyatt. At first Ethan tries to get information about Blake from Wyatt by acting like he wants Wyatt who is an engineering student to tutor him in calculus. Wyatt refuses to tutor him and calls Ethan on only attempting to use him for information. After much ado and persistence Ethan and Wyatt settle into a little bit of a rocky friendship, which then progresses as Wyatt confides in Ethan that he is not sure if he is gay. Their rocky friendship transitions to a friends-with-benefits relationship as Wyatt finds out he is most definitely gay and has been harboring a huge crush on Ethan even before he met him, as he used to stare at Blake's pictures of them and know he was in love. 
 Overall, this is a fun story and it would have been worthy of 5 solid stars from me. However, it is not a complete story leaving the readers to wait for the continuation of Wyatt and Ethan's story in the next few months. I am not sure if this is the start of a serial style story-line or if it will be just a set of novella's but as it is - cliffhanger or HFN story with slightly unresolved ending. I also felt that Blake was a bit of a flat character, you never really get to see why he made the choices he did and what made him not want to be with Ethan anymore. It is just them breaking up.. and then him changing his mind all throughout the story. I would have liked to see the "why" behind his actions as the two had been together for 2 years and he just casually breaks up with Ethan. 
 Wyatt and Ethan have a good start to a solid relationship and the passion between them is pretty hot. One of my favorite scenes between them is as follows: 
 "I backed him into the wall and started kissing him again. Hard, the way he liked it. The way I liked it. When your lips feel bruised against teeth and you can't catch your breath because there's a tongue deep in your mouth and there's nothing to think about but him." 
 I can't wait for the continuation of the story.

Diana Wynne Jones has been one of my favourite authors ever since I was a little girl. There's something almost indefinable about her books, something so magical that makes reading them a truly special experience. 
 And yet for some reason I have never read the Chrestomanci series. Don't ask me why - they're some of her most famous books. Perhaps they simply never had them at my library as I was growing up, and so I wasn't aware of them. Still, thankfully I'm now putting this right, beginning with book one: Charmed Life. 
 This was a lovely book. Its main characters are quite young children, and I would put its reading age a little lower than the Ingary (Howl) or Dalemark (Spellcoats, Drowned Ammet, etc) series, though there are some bits that could be frightening for very young readers. Of course, all of Diana Wynne Jones' books are hugely appealing to adults as well. As usual, it's about magic, but also about family, identity, growing up and gaining confidence in oneself, and it has themes relating to power and its misuse. As with Diana's other books, there is also a lovely sense of Britishness and a great charm to the story. Diana Wynne Jones's books tend to make me feel cosy, and this one was no exception. 
 The characters in the book are written very well, which is something this author has a particular knack for. The main character, Cat (Eric), is timid and passive, allowing his older sister Gwendoline to walk all over him. As the story progresses he gains confidence and is finally able to stand up for what he wants. Gwendoline is rash and selfish, and Diana Wynne Jones has done a fantastic job of making such an unlikeable character so interesting - the reader can see why she makes others laugh or admire her, even when they despair of her. Cat's relationship with his sister is also realistically portrayed. He resents her, but he also looks up to her, and even though she scares him he can't help leaning on her for support and missing her when she is gone. She's family and he loves her, and he's spent a long time looking to her as the leader. This is almost his undoing, as Gwendoline seems to be taking sibling rivalry a little more seriously (murderously) than Cat! 
 Chrestomanci might be the good wizard of the story, but this does not prevent him having character flaws, moments of bad judgement, and quite a bad attitude to the children. Both Gwendoline and Janet are very practical and brave, as is Chrestomanci's wife, a powerful magic-user in her own right, and the female characters in general are more decisive and less dithering than the men (even when they're being bad). Chrestomanci's children are sometimes antagonistic, sometimes helpful, and there are no clear-cut enemies until the very end of the book. Every character is more complex than a simple hero or villain (yes, even Gwendoline!). 
 The story is good, but quite simple and a very quick, easy read. I didn't think the levels to the story went as deep as in many of Diana's other books. Howl's Moving Castle has many themes and a number of subplots that begin to thread together at the end, but it is also quite a surprising love story between two unusual characters, and an extremely romantic book. The Dalemark series has incredible world-building and myth-making, and the story and themes do get quite intense, while books like Fire and Hemlock need at least two readings to understand their complexity. There's nothing wrong with Charmed Life being simpler, but it didn't take my breath away as some of her other books have done. 
 However, this is really the only criticism I have of the story - that out of a range of truly amazing books, this one is perhaps a little weaker than the others. Besides which, it's the first in a series - maybe the later books grow deeper as the characters grow older, and as the point of view shifts. I'll definitely be reading more, so I guess I will find out!

The reason I gave it such a low rating is because the ending did not feel authentic to me. There are so many things wrong with this book but the ending was just the worst!

It just felt like creating a twist was more important than giving us a realistic ending to the whole story. Every other amplifier died and did not come back so therefore Mal (the last amplifier) should not have come back either. Not to mention making him the amplifier did not make sense either. The last amplifier was suppose to be Baghra's sister. Mal just happens to be a decedent. But according to the rest of the story the other amplifiers lived very long lives and did not die or pass on the amplifier ability to their decedents. I am usually fine with the whole "everyone lives at the end of the story" happy ending thing as long as it makes sense within the story and this ending did not. Even making Alina the last amplifier would have made more sense than this. 
 Now onto the relationship between Alina and Mal. I have read several reviews about how Mal is just not good for Alina and I would have to agree. He never fully accepts her with her powers. She should have outgrown him in the third book. Even having her end up alone would have been better. Plus I thought she hated Duke Keramsov's estate orphanage so why did she end up living there with Mal after everything was finished? 
 I hate that Nikolai was treated the way he was in this book. He didn't even get a decent ending. Nikolai was one of the more interesting characters in this series but he was just kicked off to the side and felt like an afterthought in this book. Nikolai was my favorite character in this series. I really wish he had been treated as more than just a side character that did not deserve a decent ending or even a decent story line in this book. I really think that Alina should have ended up with Nikolai because he just seemed to treat her better than Mal ever did.  
 I am all for authors writing the endings they can live with, but they also need to make sure they are authentic to the story. There are plenty of books that I read that I did not agree with the ending but still felt like it worked for the story. This ending was so bad to me that I had to lower my ratings for the rest of the series by 1 star. I loved the setting and I loved most of the characters. Hopefully the Six of Crows series will be better.

 Sarah, her adopted cuckoo cousin is change averse but has to ship out of her current hotel room when one of the covenant agents picks the lock and just lets herself in the room. Worse, it's Margaret Healy, a distant relative from the family branch that stayed on the covenant tree. And she hates the Prices. 
 Uncle Mike comes in from Chicago to help but he's all the family is sending. 
 Dominic knows where Verity lives, so they are all shipping out to the dragon's old den in the meat packing district. 
 *** 
 This is, I suppose, a book of choices. Verity has to choose dancing or cryptozoology, Dominic has to choose a side, Sarah has to choose a behaviour, and the locals have to choose to back Verity or not. 
 They can't just kill the covenant agents, that would bring the whole shebang down onto them.

They sent the mice out to spy and then... they didn't. Why are the dragon ladies still pissed with Verity when she found the last remaining male and they have eggs and hope again? Jesus. Get over it. Cuckoos are all sociopaths except for the two in the Price family. *eyes narrow* 
 I do not feel the love between Dominic and Verity. I honestly think the Price women must have some kind of pheromone attraction to and for Covenant men. It just happens too frequently.
