Not that I want them to, but you know what I mean? They caught Verity, too easily, silly girl. There is literally a stripper bar that advertises how weird its staff are! And the covenant MISSED it?! 
 That makes me discount them as 'the big bad'. 
  
 Still firmly in the like box.

 This book was well on it's way to get about 4 stars, possibly 5. It's a first, "true romance" novel for me, I haven't read anything that specifically falls under romance genre fiction before. I thoroughly enjoyed it, at least until 60% of the way through. There is a really good amount of romantic teasing in the book and I loved that. It has a pretty good actual plot, too, even if it's fairly basic (couple gets together to investigate a murder). And I have no problem with the author's writing-- it's great for the genre. However, the overall mood was killed for me at slightly past halfway. I can't go into too much without spoilers, but basically that. Here's my explanation with spoilers: Temperance and Lord Caire finally "do the deed" right after Temperance's sister gets raped. Like, really? Literally what happens is that Temperance finds out from her family after a ball night out with Lord Caire that her sister, Silence, was missing. They go to look for her and find out she has spent the night with a pirate. Silence did so in exchange for the pirate returning the cargo he stole from her merchant husband whose career would be ruined by the robbery. Literally she finds her sister and then runs to Lord Caire's to have sex with him THEN. Never before this point, which as I said, there was good teasing before, but AT this point. It was such a mood killer. The last thing on my mind when someone from my family is harmed is to go sleep with that hot guy I've been dreaming about. I would rather comfort my family, you know? (side note: I know Silence says that she did not sleep with the pirate, only spent the night in his room, but no one in her family believes her anyway. They, including Temperance, all believe her to have been raped or at the very least whored herself to save her husband) 
 To top it off, Temperance runs to have sex again with Lord Caire right after finding out that her orphanage is out of money again and a baby is dying. What is this? Bad news=run to have sex? Oh my goodness, again, mood killer.  
 As I said it's my first book into romance genre fiction, I would also like to say that I definitely liked the pacing of the book for the first half much better then the last half. Essentially once Temperance and Lord Caire get together, all they have is sex from that point on. Most of the plot is not important at this point. I was also enjoying the plot, but once they slept together they couldn't keep off of each other. I think most of the investigations was all the author actually had for a plot as well, so after they sleep together they don't really need to investigate further, Lord Caire just needs to magically track down the murderer, which is what happened in the end.  There are also some side plots and characters mentioned that I know are only there to be expanded upon in future books in the series, but I did not mind them that much. I may continue on with the series to give the author another try-- maybe her next story won't have the same issue these characters did.

This book started out awesome. I loved reading about how Janelle's world had been torn apart by natural disasters and how they were trying their best to fix it.  Then Janelle went to go stop this organization, starting out by going to Prima and looking for Ben. And I got bored. I'm not sure why, but I actually decided to take a nap instead of read. Which is totally not something I would normally do. 
 When I went back to reading, I skimmed a couple of pages, and then picked up on the excitement pretty quickly again, especially during the prison break scene . 
 As I read the book, I marveled at the world - worlds - that Elizabeth Norris had created. I couldn't tear myself away from it, and I found myself imagining so many things that could be written within it. My favorite thing was learning about how each Earth was different than the last, and imagining how it became that way. I loved it. It felt real. 
 Oh, how I want to rate this book 5 stars.

 Another thing that kept pulling me away from the story: Norris kept repeating things. Especially when it came to Janelle's musings about Ben.  N. K. Jemisin attended a NASA-funded workshop titled Launch Pad which was meant to help "media influencers" understand science. This then helps media influencers such as a Sci-Fi/Fantasy author to write about accurate science since much of the public's misconceptions about science is from the media. This was in the acknowledgements section of the book and I'm glad I have that piece of information to go off of while writing this review, though my lack of actual Earth Science is going to be apparent. What I would just like to say is that I think N. K. Jemisin wrote a well-researched piece of fiction that involves people with the ability to manipulate the Earth. I don't have the time to fully research all of the Earth Science used in the book, but from what I remember from my primary schooling, I believe the terminology used works well with the concepts. Now, it IS a piece of fantasy fiction, so I'm sure it is still left to the author's own whimsy, but if I wanted to learn more about Earth Science I think I would find some similarities. If I ever gauge enough interest/time to investigate it further, perhaps I will update this review. 
 With that bit, I did spoil that there are people who can manipulate the Earth in the book, but that is where I will stop. I believe you should just go into this book blind. Mrs. Jemisin throws you into her world and you are left trying to figure it out. It takes a little time to grasp things, so you may be confused or find it slow at first. I definitely don't think I am "fluent" after reading just the first book, but part of reading a fantasy is the worldbuilding. It's good for a trilogy for more to be explored. Her world has many features including discrimination, repression, diversity, and more. I will leave it up to you to discover it all.

Here is the spoiler bracket: The fact that Essun, Damaya, and Syenite all end up being the same person. We start out following 3 points of view characters and each grow on me so much. I thoroughly enjoyed each person's point of view, and by the end when I find out they are all the same person, instead of liking that one character even more, I am saddened to find out that throughout the whole book there was only one character. Not to say none of the side characters are great, I love Alabaster and Tonkee and Hoa are interesting, but now I only know I get to follow this 1 super great main character in the next book instead of following 3 super great main characters. And isn't the more the merrier? And while Essun's point of view is 2nd person so it kinda gives hints to the timeline of the story, the fact that a lot of this could've been figured out by featuring a timeline at the beginning at each chapter is frustrating. It's literally the author leaving off that one piece of information that prevents giving it all away. It just feels like a cop-out or lack of creativity at the author's part. Also, Mrs. Jemisin uses the name changes THREE times to help with her trickery. Damaya changes her name to Seynite as she becomes a ringed orogene for the Fulcrum. Seynite changes her name to Essun as she tries to run from her past. Then we have Tonkee who ends up being Binof Leadership Yumenes from Damaya's past encounter while breaking into the chamber in the Fulcrum. It's the same trick on THREE separate occasions and who knows if she is done. Is it partially me being frustrated that I never saw it coming? Slightly, but at some point I did start thinking Syenite was also Essun because I didn't see how there could be ANOTHER free orogene that has been so clearly trained in her abilities. I just hope this trend of re-naming for the sake of a "twist" ends here. I do truly appreciate the opportunity to learn Essun's past this way; I'm just frustrated that leaving out just the time made me unable to piece it all together fully. 
 With that said, names are pretty important in this world, with all of the above and the fact that people's use-castes (kind of like a born job or role into society that is recognized by officials) are a 2nd name. I will definitely be paying more attention to names as I continue the trilogy.

So... I was very uncertain about this book. I wasn't even sure if I should request it but a lot of people were liking it, so I thought to give it a shot. The problem is, the impression I got was of a sad story about a girl struggling with cancer, doing a list of things before she inevitably dies, but then bam, she's alive and faces the consequences of her actions, but you as a reader deal with it alongside her and you all get closure or growth or whatnot. All right, essentially this is what the book is about more or less BUT I didn't get closure. Or sense much growth. I'm giving you guys a rant warning here, there may be spoilers. 
 Alice was diagnosed with cancer, and the first thing that came to mind to her when she thought she was going to die soon was to make a list of things she wanted to do before she died. She couldn't do it alone so she recruited her once upon a time close friend who she's pretty sure loves her to help her scheme and accomplish things. All goes well for Alice until she goes into remission... then? Not so much. She has to face the consequences of her scheming, which is not something she had counted on. 
 The idea of the story was intriguing at most. The going back and forth in point of views between Harvey and Alice both now and in the past, wasn't the best part of the story since there was no chronological order to the now and then, it could take place any time in the past and any time in the assumed present. I was prepared to deal with the entire book and hoping to be pleasantly surprised by the turn of things, and hopefully enjoy the book. I was pleasantly surprised, but sadly, not for long. What I didn't anticipate was hating the protagonist so very much. 
 I think Alice is one of the worst people ever. She's the most ridiculously self-centered, selfish, arrogant, egocentric, and vindictive people I've read about in quite some time. I guess one of the great things of having a religion or faith or even Karma, is that when life hands you bad news, like really really bad news, as in your much closer than anticipated imminent death, you kind of start thinking of your purpose in life, what you're leaving behind, what your legacy would be, how people will remember you. You start thinking about praying, or making it up for people, or helping others deal with your death when your gone. But oh no, definitely not Alice. 
 "I laughed. We were so different. Harvey wanted good. He wanted to leave the ones he loved in a good place. I'd just wanted the last word. But I wouldn't be sorry for that now. It's too late for sorry." 
 Instead of trying to forgive the transgressions that were committed against her, instead of thinking above it all, since she's dying and should probably be at peace rather than anything else, she plots her revenge. She wants to cause havoc, wreck things and people, so she can remain the centre of attention. All she cared about was making the year she was going to be alive for the most heavenly experience for herself, and if it included Harvey - because hello he makes her happy - then so be it. Who cares if this experience was tearing him apart? Who cares if he would never recover from the experience when she was gone? Who cares if she was potentially scarring him for life? What mattered was that she got what she wanted, how she wanted, when she wanted, and that's that. Why think of what she wouldn't be there to witness anyway? 
 "I think I'm going to die." There was an eerie calm to her voice that terrified me more intensely than any cancer. 
 "Don't say that, Alice." 
 "We all die. We are dying. I'm just in the fast lane, I guess, dying faster than the rest of you slugs." 
 The most thing I personally loathed her for, was her treatment of Harvey. She'd ignored him for years, but once she was about to die, she decided she might as well let him in her life again, because now that she has an expiration date, she can let him love her the way he'd always wanted to and just give him hope for the year she was staying alive. She dragged him through hell, put his heart on a freaking grinder and just tore him to pieces. Over and over and over again. She kept leading him on, giving the poor guy the impression his feelings were reciprocated and that even though she was dying, they were something. Until of course she was in remission and the poor lad excited over the potential of a future between them realizes that the Alice that survived was back to the one before she was diagnosed with cancer. Except much worse. I was upset for the poor guy. The thing is, she didn't want to be with him anymore, she treated him like freaking crap, but she had the gall to not want him with anyone else either. 
 "I'd always heard that when you truly love someone, you're happy for them as long as they're happy. But that's a lie. That's higher-road bull shit. If you love someone so much, why the hell would you be happy to see them with anyone else? I didn't want the easy kind of love. I wanted the crazy love, the kind of love that created and destroyed all at the same time." 
 And boy did she destroy. The problem is, I never got why Harvey loved her in the first place, not one freaking redeeming quality in this atrocious human being. Okay fine, I'll give her one act of kindness. But that's not enough to love someone so heinous, full of hatred and ugliness inside, so not worth it. Whenever Harvey talked about why he loved her, there was nothing solid, nothing from her core, just that she was a beautiful dancer, he loved her looks... I don't know, nothing about why he loved her made her sound like a person that one could love. More like an addictive drug that's so horrible for you but might seem just good at the time, except later on you realize the amount of damage it's inflicted, the harm it can do and you still come back for more. Harvey was one of the most singularly amazing people out there. I think I would have had a very big book crush on him if it wasn't for the fact that he was a doormat to Alice, a slave of her every whim, no backbone to actually save and protect himself from her. The poor guy was a hopeless goner. His life turned upside down when hearing she might be taken away from him for good. 
 "I have leukemia, Harvey." 
 Your life changes sometimes and it only takes a few words to bridge the gap between now and then. 
 In conclusion, the story had an interesting plot. However, hating Alice and her character as much as I did, made it very difficult to appreciate it. Alice did 'attempt' to redeem herself, but not in anyway that matters. I didn't get the right confrontations, I didn't get to see her understand how screwed up she made everyone, she never got to understand how wrong she was to treat Harvey the way she did, not in a way that counts. I didn't get closure, I was more angry by the ending than anything. 
 Rating: 2/5.

I read this book in spurts so I'll have to go over this book again before I write a full review. Nonetheless, one of the most important books I've read. Throughout the book, Sandel examines different systems of justice and talks about scenarios and the difficulties of each thing. Starting with utilitarianism, he then goes through libertarianism, Kant's categorical imperative, Rawls' theory of justice, and virtue ethics to talk about what the right thing to do is - how to maximize justice. 
 Perhaps in proof of how difficult this question is, where he ends up, a system of justice that incorporates a moral conception of virtue that is not fully based in choice but communal commitments, is not quite fully convincing. He argues what is, not what should be with his communitarian view. Further, he neglects to give enough examples of how this would play out in real life. Most crucially, however, he neglects to talk about the fact that people have different moral views on the virtue of something and there is usually no agreement on what the right virtue is. What this means is that such a virtue-based system can devolve into what is essentially majoritarianism. His level of rigor in attempting to disprove the theory he believes in is nowhere near the level of rigor he used to disprove competing ones. 
 While weak and unconvincing in its ending, perhaps due to some element of confirmation bias that I have as a left-leaning, reason-reliant person, the ideas he presents about the progression and the pitfalls of utilitarianism and libertarianism are very clear and I see the beginning of a strong argument about the incorporation of morals in deliberations about justice. Notwithstanding all that, it's still an excellent read that will not only teach folks about these different systems of justice but also how to approach them - how to poke holes in them, find alternative explanations, and understand the complexity of justice.

 Not only was there not enough time with their early relationship for me to believe that's the level they were at, but a soulmate arc - regardless of the implication that you'll find each other no matter what - loses a lot of its power when you are split up and go off to be with other people. I listened to this in audiobook form during my life on the road (driving an hour each way to and from work on southeast Iowa highways), and it was very fitting for those trips. 
 Steinem begins her book with stories of her own childhood trips, when her father would pack up the family and set off for Florida or California, buying and selling antiques along the way to pay the way. While my own family road trips were never so haphazard, the description brought back memories of the excitement that can only come with being about to set off traveling by car thousands of miles across America and not knowing what great things you'll see. 
 The book moves on to discuss Steinem's travels to India and "talking circles," which become a recurring theme. Her work with the women's movement and the amazing women she's worked with kept me enthralled, as I'm sadly ill-informed about a lot of our feminist history. 
 A section discussing the 2008 race for the Democratic presidential nomination particularly stood out for me, in part because I listened to it while driving from a Democratic caucus back to my newsroom. There are plenty of parallels between the party infighting in 2008 and what's happening now. 
 Steinem managed to elicit a desire in me both to travel more and to do more for justice. It's rare that I've ended a book feeling so inspired.

At long last the end of The Wheel of Time is here. I started reading the series shortly before Winter's Heart came out in 2000. Much has changed for me over the past thirteen years - especially my taste in books and life interests - but through all of that The Wheel of Time has been a constant for me. It's been with me through most of my teenage and all of my adult years. And now, at last, it's done. 
 I, and most other fans, would be lying if I claimed to have loved every moment of the series. At times it's been a frustrating and infuriating process. When Robert Jordan died in 2007, many of us assumed the worst that because he'd spent too much time writing on minor details we'd never see the end of the series. Thankfully, he spent his last days leaving careful notes ensuring that we would eventually see the end. 
 There's been plenty said - good and bad - about Brandon Sanderson's completion of the series. While many of those points on both sides are valid, I personally don't see much point in doing anything but thanking him for the work he's done. He took on an impossible task and gave us an ending worthy of the series. Was his work perfect? Nope. How could it have been? But it was respectful and more than worthy of Robert Jordan's legacy. 
 This last book is a whirlwind of action and resolution. The pace is absolutely relentless. Despite the 900 page length, the book absolutely flies by. Normally when reading a book like this, I'd find myself wishing for less action and more quiet, character driven moments. Reading A Memory of Light, I realized that that sort of complaint was really irrelevant. The series has transcended any individual scenes, dialogues or characters. It's a work of staggering complexity - more immersive experience than novel. It's triumph isn't in the style, characters, action or dialogue; it's in bringing the enormous complexity to a satisfying resolution. Neither Jordan nor Sanderson were particularly great novelists, but both were phenomenal world builders whose joint talents gave this series the ending it needed and the one fans deserve. 
 It's difficult to say what the series' legacy will be. On the one hand, there are few fantasy novels that have influenced the genre so much as The Wheel of Time. On the other, the genre has seemingly already passed Jordan by moving on from stories of good vs evil to the morally ambiguous worlds of Martin and others. Regardless of how the series is looked back upon in the years to come, it has undoubtedly left is mark on all of us who made it this far. Thank you, Robert Jordan, for sharing your world with us. It's been an incredible ride.

 Iris and Will have been married for 7 years and decide to start a family right before he leaves to go to a conference. Seeing him off, Iris is happy - her life couldn't be more perfect. A flight crashes and the presumption is that everyone on the ledger is dead. The relief that Iris feels when she finds out that this flight was going to Seattle and not to Orlando (where the conference is) is overwhelming. But then she gets the call. Will is on the list of passenger names. How could this possibly be right? Iris is now on a mission as she's convinced that Will cannot be dead. Her investigation into finding him leads to answers she never would have imagined. 
 The first 80% had me completely engaged. I loved the fast pace and the mystery about what the answers would be that Iris would find. It was a bit predictable, but that usually doesn't take away from the story too much for me if it's done well. And this is where I feel stuck. The writing is good. I'm engaged. But I started to lose interest around this point. I wish I could pinpoint exactly why... I did finish this in one day so clearly I needed to finish it to find out how the author was going to bring this to a close. With some things being predictable and some things being implausible, I still did enjoy this ride. A well done domestic suspense, but just lacking that joie de vivre for me.

I have to admit, I had no interest in this book going in because I loathe dystopian stories. The authors never do a good enough job of explaining why society changed so much, or why I should believe it did (this book is no exception). But everyone was so blown away by it, I thought I should read it just to make sure I wasn't missing anything. Yeah...I wasn't. 
 My first thought as soon as I finished was, "Why is this book popular? It is so ordinary. It is so not special or particularly captivating in any way." It was actually less explicitly violent than I thought -- the worst thing for me was the mention of a previous year in which spiked maces were used; that was some unsettling imagery -- but the sheer boredom almost made it worse. 
 The whole reading experience was just a long slog of, "Is it over yet? Is it over now? Will it be over soon? Oh my God, this is some pointless storytelling right here." What probably didn't help was me hating Katniss/Peeta. Going in, I was pretty neutral but assumed I would like that pairing best, since I thought they were canon.  The long wait is over, Divergent 3 or Allegiant is now on the rampage. Divergent fans are waiting for this moment to come. The cliff hanger moment Veronica Roth left us from the second (2nd) book, Insurgent made as crave for more of Tris's senseless yet selfless ways in saving the world. But let me get this straight. Initially, I don't know how to say this in a less overt manner but I'll say it anyway, I dislike this Allegiant (Divergent 3). I hated almost everything. There are too many conflicts, too many characters dead, too many romance scene, and not to mention, the almost-unpredictable and unlikeable ending. &^@Q$*(%(*&%#q*&%^*!~ 
 To the reader's convenience, I tried to widen the thoughts I have during and after reading the Allegiant. 
 (WARNING: TOO MANY SPOILERS AND HARSH COMMENTS AHEAD) 
 First off, Allegiant has too many conflicts, seemingly interesting conflicts, and WTF extra scenes 
 From the beginning of the story (almost 100 pages long), the book focuses on the battle between the factions and the factionless. And then another faction showed up and introduced themselves as the Allegiants. The narration of the story began focusing on the newly introduced characters (not necessarily new people in the story but new title or category of certain group of people) totally forgetting about the conflict about the factions and the factionless. I almost assumed that the story's pace to another conflict would resolve the first one out but then it seems like it was completely forgotten. 
 The seemingly super awesome, frightening and mind-boggling plot turned into romance and chaos (and by chaos I mean instances where foolishness and the like survive). The book started with Tris Prior still stuck in the shattered faction-based society that she once believed in. It was fissured by violence and power struggles by power hungry people which were blinded by a scarred past or by loss and betrayal. Tris and the other dauntless people were offered a chance to explore the world past the limits known to them. And when they ready, they got beyond the fence. *YES, BEYOND THE FENCE* *thrilling, frightening, yeah....NOOOOOOT!!!!!* Beyond the fence, Tris and Tobias have thought of finding a simple new life together, free from complicated lies, tangled loyalties, and painful memories. And as they think of themselves and their hopes to live happily ever after, a few supporting characters die (and other supporting characters from the first book shows up *crazy, I know*), but the readers wouldn't care anyway, because that is what the author intends to do; kill, kill and go for another KIIILLL!!! It's like; the author didn't bother spending time developing old and new characters so she let them die. And you were there, reading like you don't really care. 
 As the story progresses, we find out that Tris's new reality is even more alarming than the one she left behind (surprising? I guess not). The old discoveries are quickly rendered meaningless and were altered by the explosive new truths. And once again, our distressed protagonist, Tris must battle to comprehend the complexities of human nature and of her selflessness and selfishness while facing the apparently terrible choices about bravery, loyalty, sacrifice, and love. 
 Another thing I want to point out is the constant switch between Tobias and Tris's point-of-view (POV), although I appreciate reading Tobias's perspective but it was a little TOO annoying. Instead of having certain problems and conflicts resolved between characters and the openness of their feelings toward each other and most importantly made the readers understand the things happening in the novel's world, IT MADE IT MORE CONFUSING!!! 
 Lastly, the ENDING, tragic, sad, gloomy and UGLY. Don't get me wrong, I have to problems with happy endings, sad endings and cliif-hanger endings AS LONG as the ENDING makes sense with the story, with the WHOLE EFFING STORY!!!!!!! 
 I think the ultimate thing I hate about this book is how it made me dislike the author in so many ways. It was so frustrating and annoying. My review of this is actually quite irksome for me because I don't like criticizing books of famous and good authors so I sucked up a little bit and gave this book 2 (two) stars!

I still really enjoy this series. This book in particular was very, very heavy on the romance. I like the romance, don't get me wrong, but it doesn't progress the overall plot very much. The plot can be summarized in as "all the characters of the series get together with Aelin (except Chaol) to strengthen forces to defeat the evil demons and evil queens, and the cliffhanger ending gets Aelin kidnapped, so now her posse must go rescue her in the next book." "Oh, and sexy times" I do really love Manon's plot of finally leaving the Clan behind and betraying her grandmother. That was great. That was a lot of character development, and I think it's close to being the only character development throughout the whole book. Most other parts of the book is relationship development.  
 I really love all the side characters at this point, but barely tolerate Aelin and Rowan. Manon has been my favorite since she has been introduced, and she still is bad a** in this one. Elide surprisingly is a close 2nd favorite, but I think this is because she is the one character I can actually relate to. Most of all the main crew have super abilities or powers, and Elide is a cripple just trying to find her way to the one friend she had. She knows when to run and hide and when she can do something to help fight. and she has my 2nd favorite romance going on-- Manon and Dorian are first, but I can't help and ship the Fae who doesn't like humans, Lorcan, with her. She keeps proving him wrong and its great.  Aelin has just been way too over-reactive to everything, as she has been from the beginning. If she wants to lead her people, she must grow to make rational, well-thought out decisions. She can't be an effective queen otherwise, and it's just really annoying that she still acts this way after 5 books. I still am not a huge fan of her and Rowan as a couple, but at this point I am more than happy to throw them together because I don't care about either of them anyway. Rowan is a generic, strong and good-looking warrior. Well, all the characters are incredibly good looking at this point Mrs. Maas even acknowledges this with a character commentating on it during the narrative. , but really, that's all Rowan has going for him. He is a typical romance lead where he is 110% committed to helping his beloved. I still love Dorian, and Aedion and Lysandra (especially those 2 as a couple), so I am happy they show up and I get to read about them. Chaol doesn't show up though, which I understand would have made the book so much longer, but this is a whole book without one of the original three main characters showing up. It feels like sloppy storytelling only used to make money on novellas that will come shortly on what the heck Chaol was doing at this time.

Aelin (as Celaena) was secretly the heir to the conquered kingdom of Terrasen. She also hid the fact that she is part Fae and has a Fae form to perform magic. Dorian secretly held magic powers within him (was it due to his father being possessed by a demon? I don't remember). Manon is secretly half Crochan-witch and thus a Witch Queen.  When Kate's father is killed by a group of men she decides to go and avenge his death, and learn why they killed him, and why it looks like they didn't take anything before they destroyed the house. 
 Before she can go ride after the killers, though she has to keep a promise she's made to her father since she was little, that if anything ever happened to him she would go and find Abe. 
 But when she gets to Abe's house she learns that he is no longer there, instead his children are including two sons. Who decide to tag along with her until she reaches a certain destination where they say they'll separate. 
 Except that doesn't happen, instead the boys help Kate along the way including almost getting themselves killed multiple times. Kate also eventually gets a guide after she helps a Indian girl working in the saloon escape. But this ends up getting rather complicated thanks to the boys, being rude and prejudice of her. 
 I really liked this book. It does contain curse words though so if you don't like that then I don't think you'll like this book. I loved the interaction between Kate and the other people in her group. While she was stand-offish it was for good reasons, and when she did start opening up and talking you could tell that that meant she really trusted them and liked them as well. I was not expecting that about her parents. At times I did wonder what exactly happened to her mom, but after a while I just thought it was me being suspicious for no reason. 
 This was exactly what I was looking for in a YA western though and I really hope more like it come out. 
 While I am glad Kate and Jesse ended up together, I would have also been completely okay if that hadn't. Yes they had been through a lot together, but I also felt like maybe they weren't the best for each other at times. Did anyone else feel that way or is it just me?

What I Liked 
 -I enjoy re-tellings and while this was a little more of a spin-off than a re-telling, it still worked for me. I've always been a Phantom of the Opera fan (well, except maybe when I was pretty young and my family used to listen to the soundtrack on road trips and it kind of scared the crap out of me at the time...but I definitely grew into it) and it's definitely a unique topic in the YA market. 
 -The duel narration completely saved this book for me. We get Rune's 1st Person POV and Thorn's 3rd Person POV (I'm not really sure why they didn't both get 1st Person, but that's ok). While with Rune we were often stumbling around in the dark trying to figure out what was going on, with Thorn we get background and answers and insight. With him we get to see the actual Phantom of the Opera that I had been hoping for when I picked up this book. As a character I found him so much more interesting than Rune and I was always counting the pages until we got to see him again. 
 -The romance. Though it appears to be "insta-love", it does have a good excuse for it. I liked Rune and Thorn together and shipped them. 
 -That cover. It's beautiful. 
 -The Author Note at the end of the book where Howard details a lot of information from her research was almost more interesting than the book. A lot of the historical information in the book was accurate and it made me want to read more about the original book and it's inspiration. 
 What Didn't Quite Work For Me 
 -**MILD SPOILER** Two words: Psychic Vampires 
 -Ok, a few more words: This was a lot more supernatural than I was expecting it to be. While it, of course, needed a certain amount of fantasy elements there were a lot more than I expected or wanted. If you go into this knowing that, though, then I think you would probably like it. 
 -I spent a good portion of this novel confused. I think it took far too long to get to the point. Howard is an extremely detailed writer and I know a lot of readers love that, but for me a ton of description is hard for me to get through. Add that to the long chapter length and I found this book took me a lot longer to get through than a book normally does. 
 -Rune's new "friend" Sunny. I HATED her. She did occasionally have redeeming moments, but she spent the whole book sneaking around and spying and crossing all sorts of friendship lines that I found myself kind of hoping she'd be killed off. The fact that Rune viewed her as this great friend kind of enraged me. 
 Overall 
 RoseBlood was a very interesting idea that didn't quite live up to it's potential for me. Two likable main characters (especially Thorn) and lots of references to the original Phantom of the Opera story were really well done. However, the major fantasy/supernatural elements were unexpected and hampered my enjoyment a bit. I also thought it was a little too long and too descriptive. I do think that fans of Howard's Splintered series and those who are looking for a different type of re-telling will enjoy it. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 3 Stars

I honestly do not know how to express my feels for this book... 
 I was crying a river by the time I had finished the last page. Despite being an emotional wreck, I am comfortable to say that I was very impressed with this novel- and this is the first Patrick Ness novel I've ever read so I didn't know what to expect. I read the synopsis of this book a while back so I had a general idea of what was going to happen, but I didn't expect it to have so much... depth. 
 A Monster Calls follows a 13 year old boy named Conor O' Malley. He isn't like your average 13 year old boy who casually lives out his days with an easy going family, goes to school, returns home to do homework then immerses himself in video games/ computer games before going to bed. No. Conor's mom is a cancer patient, his dad lives in America with another wife and family, he's bullied by classmates and pitied by his teachers because of his family situation, and on most nights, Conor is visited by a monster once the clock strikes 12:07. 
 The plot to this story was certainly nothing I've ever read and was quite an unpredictable one. I'm not saying that this book was difficult to follow, no, it's just the way we (readers) are brought into Conor's world kind of kept me off balance in a sense where Conor's reality and the reality he jumps in when he's with the monster nearly co-exists on the same plane, but is separated by a very thin line. So yeah, it really gets you thinking about what each element to the story really means. In addition, the way this book was written really brings you into this world, where you just have to keep reading in order to find out what happens next. Oh and the feels... It will definitely trigger tons of feels, especially those really...sad ones, so I recommend keeping a box of tissues nearby :D 
 I really like Conor. I found him to be really well written and well rounded as a character. Patrick Ness was so descriptive with everything about Conor and I honestly didn't feel overwhelmed about it at all. Plus, I felt that connection with Conor- like I felt every emotion that he felt as the story progressed and he was just so relate-able and so... real. 
 Overall, I really fell in love with this book. It's definitely going onto my favorites list for 2014- oh I really can't wait to see this on the big screen. Yea, it's going to be a movie and I don't think that I'm even disappointed about that. I really recommend for readers to pick up this book. It's not like any YA fiction that you've read before. It'll get you thinking and it will get you emotional so don't say that I didn't warn you. It's a great story about love and loss... and simply trying to find one's way in the world and discovering yourself while on that journey.

 I'm not sure what I was expecting when I started reading this book, but I don't think I was expecting to love it as much as I did. But, I loved it! It was so cute and fun and was a well done Fake-Relationship story (which we all know are my favorite kind). 
 I thought both Vaughn and Oakley were likable characters. Oakley definitely had his egotistical jerk moments, but we see way more of him being sweet and funny and sometimes vulnerable. I liked Vaughn, but had to remind myself a few times when she did something or reacted to something in a way that annoyed me that she's only 17. But, seriously, as far as YA heroines go, she was a pretty level headed one. I also really liked Vaughn's family and Oak's bodyguard. 
 This book had all the things I love in a good Fake-Relationship story. I loved the awkwardness of hammering out the terms of the contract and the initial antagonism between Vaugh and Oakley. I loved their fake date outings and how they slowly started to become friends and then more. I thought they were so sweet together (even though things did almost get a little too sappy at times) and I shipped them hard. After reading 
 The Royals 
 series, which I thought was far too explicit for YA, I was a little concerned about how graphic the sexual content would be in this one. And though there was still a little more than I prefer for YA, it wasn't very graphic and I liked that the their feelings for each other were highlighted over the physicality. There was also some underage drinking and casual drug use, but it was also much less than The Royals series and more YA appropriate (if those things are ever appropriate for YA). 
 Overall, I really enjoyed When It's Real. The writing was addictive and I never wanted to put it down. It was funny and sweet and I just had so much fun reading about Vaughn and Oakley. There was one thing, though, that kind of brought my reading experience down and it's not the book's fault. The e-ARC I received had some major issues on my Nook with missing text - often paragraphs at a time. I hate to even mention that because it obviously won't be an issue with the finished copy (and I did find a solution by downloading a copy for the Kindle app for my phone so I could find the text missing from my Nook), but it kind of cast a shadow over the whole thing for me. However, as you can tell, I still loved the story. I definitely recommend it to YA Contemporary fans.

It is because of Goodreads that I got my hands on this book. Must have read someone's review somewhere and then shelved it 'toread'. 
 To me, it's nostalgia: a mix tape for every occasion. A road trip, a birthday party in eighth grade, I like you, my heart broke, etc. And Rob Sheffield must have made more tapes than anyone else. 
 On first sight, it's just that: a series of recollections from his past, fueled by the music he listened to. Every chapter starts with a cassette inlay containing all the songs and artists that were on it. And when you love music, there's more than enough to explore from that alone. I even found myself creating a Spotify playlist (and tweeting Rob about that) so as to place myself in his past. 
 But fortunately, it's much more than that. It's well written, a fast read but with enough food for thought. Humoristic. Chapter after chapter, hardly anything really happens, but you barely notice, since his writing is so entertaining. It's also an intimate lovestory, on a level that I can relate to. 
 Then his girlfriend dies and the book changes overnight. Which ofcourse is completely in place. There's a detailed and gripping description of her death and the funeral. And in the rest of the book I realized that I never really think about a sudden death of someone so close and that I can not even imagine the intensity of the impact.  
 I was surprised that I liked this book this much. On more than one level. It made me laugh, it made me think, it made me listen to songs and artists I had never heard of. And it made me realize that I'm lucky to be with the girl I am with, which I know sounds really corny, but is a very comforting thought.

"Undone" is book #4 in the Fiery Tales series, 
 but can be read as a stand-alone novel. 
 How are the sex scenes? 
 DiPasqua adds more depth to their relationship by showing the intimate moments and mentioning others that happened behind closed doors. 
 And the steamy scenes we do see definitely push the story. 
 How are the story lines? 
 Really loved those. The hero has a plan, the heroine has a plan, the hero interferes with said plans and all romance breaks loose. 
 Review 
 "Undone" by Lila DiPasqua is a full length historical romance novel set in France and the Republic of Genoa in 1660. 
 "It is a convent, sir." 
 Never would hero Simon Boulenger guess those words would inspire lust, yet after heroine Angelica straddled him while dressed in a habit he reconsidered. 
 Wait, what? The promiscuous hero is seduced in an instant by a nun? 
 LOVE it! 
 Detailing the plot, for this novel, is a spoiler. From the beginning DiPasqua layers meanings and readies readers for one of many reveals. 
 Angelica is wonderful. She doesn't take the 'easy' way out nor does she ask for help, because she can trust no one. Her secret is that dire. 
 Simon is the classic playboy pirate who wants the new shiny toy and refuses to stop pestering until he gets it. He's not always this childish with women, don't worry. His upbringing is tragic and the man he is today reflects a person wanting to save the world. 
 Simon often has an inner dialogue about how "he'd never done a rash thing in his entire life." Odd for him to think this, because when readers meet Simon he's in a precarious position and I can't imagine he planned that. 
 Angelica and Simon's physical attraction is intense. Simon sports a hard-on 90% of the book because Angelica is near. 
 "Undone" is a bit choppy in the beginning, with shorter sentences that are to the point - like what you'd expect at the end of a story or during an action scene. But man can she write descriptions: 
 "Raw lust licked up his spine." 
 "She placed her hand over her agitated heart, willing it to calm." 
 "Every inch of her quaked." 
 The start of the black moment is GENIUS. For the third time in "Undone," DiPasqua creates a conflict that no one can remedy. (And DiPasqua doesn't stop at three.) 
 What an adult approach to romance. Real people reap the consequences of situations and in "Undone" Simon and Angelica do too. 
 The only slight criticism I can give is that the black-moment-start is resolved too easily. A slight plot tweak would have hurt a few feelings, broken a heavy heart and added a bittersweet resolution instead of a neat and tidy one - making the 'start' all but forgotten. 
 Well done, Lila. Your books deserve much love.

FOUR POINT FIVE STARS 
 "I veer off to the left, taking the shortcut that Matthew didn't want me to take." 
 It was a dark and stormy night when Cass was leaving a party and phoned her husband to say she's on her way home. Her husband, Matthew, tells her to NOT take the shortcut home through the woods. He won't be up when she gets home because he has a migraine and he's going to sleep in the guest room. 
 Right away, I can relate to Cass because I'd probably take the shortcut and figure my husband would never know. I mean what can go wrong ... it's only late at night on a deserted road. Seems perfectly safe, right? 
 Just like Cass, it would be my luck to come upon a car pulled off the side of the road with their lights on. Cass can see there's a woman in the car but because of the downpour, she can't make out any details. Now she has a dilemma on what is she supposed to do: 
 A) Does she get out of her car to see if they're okay? 
 B) Drive on because hey she shouldn't have been in the woods at night by herself in the first place. The boogeyman lives there. 
 C) Drive to where she has cell signal and phone the police? 
 Cass picks option B and the next morning she learns that the woman in the car has been murdered. Now her guilt sets in because she questions why she hadn't stopped to help or at least called the police?!! Had she done that then maybe that woman would have been alive now! Or maybe Cass would have been murdered too! Gah! Her indecisions on what she had done continued to plague her throughout the story. 
 "Fear and guilt have become such constant companions that I can't remember what it was like to live without them." 
 Cass begins to spiral downwards with guilt. I began to feel like the story was gaslighting me because Cass couldn't remember anything. It makes the reader question their own sanity as they read about Cass doubt her own mental health. Cass lived in a state of constant paranoia to the point that she couldn't even hear the phone ringing without being sure someone was calling her torment her. 
 The last 25% is golden - it's where the rubber meets the road and we start to see pieces of the puzzle fit together. I called the book early on and to see it come fruition was fun. Especially, when Cass started to put it all together and gain her life back.

INBREEDING. 
 That is the one word that I can say the author didn't consider when she wrote this story, and scarily the only word I could focus on while I was reading this. And no, it's not because I am a squeamish person, or this was my very first brush with this kind of subject. It was the terrible way this book was written. 
 There are authors out there who have an extremely rare talent to balance a taboo subject in a way that a reader could relate to. The end result would be this - even though the readers would stay with their original conclusion and feelings regarding the subject, they would approach it from a different angle. They would strive to understand the driving force behind the actions of a character. That, my friends, is something that a good storyteller is capable of producing. 
 I am certain that the author chose incest purely for the reason of it being 'fresh' and 'edgy' subject, and in hopes that the controversy alone would be enough of an inspiration for people to spend money on her book. I read this on a dare, and I have read a few novels on the subject in the past. They all have the same commonality, something of a rather vital element that Diane Rinella simply doesn't understand, or seem to get. There is a damned good reason incest is wrong and it's most certainly not just simply society's fault. Rinella created her leading lady Lilly and almost from page one, you are being told that she doesn't care if she's gross, or what society thinks. 
 There is an documentary available on he internet somewhere, and if you look hard enough for it, I'm sure you'll find it, I can't be bothered at the minute looking for the link. It's about natural born instincts. The subjects being observed were babies up to a year and a half old, and they were seated in a room with their mothers, the room has one glass wall covered with a curtain. The curtain parts first time and there is a snake on the floor behind the glass. The baby stares at it, not looking away until the curtain closes. When the curtain parts the second time, there is a fluffy bunny on the other side. The baby looks at it for about five seconds before it starts to play and look elsewhere. The point is simple - even though the child is that young it may not understand the concept of a snake, it's instinct tells the baby it's dangerous. 
 Apply the simple human instincts to mate and reproduce and you will see natural selection at it's best. In history humans suffered the worst known deformations as a result of inbreeding, and even though it's painfully obvious that some people are just plain dumber then others, we can still rely on the fine tuned human organism to sear us in the right direction. We are simply not attracted to blood relatives because the gene pool is extremely undesirable. The mere thought of it is revolting. It's instinct, just like you wouldn't eat rotten meat. IT FUCKING STINKS. 
 Every other book I have read on incestuous relationships, the characters seem to be aware of these facts and understand that it isn't something as trivial as society's whim behind the general disgust once you mention it. Yet Rinella inflicts upon her reader the mind of her MC Lilly, and wow, what a disturbing mind it is. There isn't a sense of wrongness anywhere, no true realization that she is pursuing her brother as a sexual partner. Her mind is full of flirtation and jealousy, like she's dealing with the kid from next door. Second extremely disturbing thing is Lilly's behavior. 
 If one would go trough her actions through the eyes of a male character, you will get an very persistent sexual harasser. This is as well one of the subjects that is increasingly common in contemporary romances of late, where the female characters get away with so much more then we would dare to forgive the males. Like having a vagina has somehow became a get-out-of-jail-free card that allows females to do the exact same thing we do not stand for....but that's a bone to pick for another time. Lilly pursues her brother, insisting on closeness, on sexual contact that he is uncomfortable with, and even goes out of his way to let her know, but to no avail. She plots, pushes, touches, whines and throws tantrums when she doesn't get her way. The whole thing made me sick, it was like watching a rapist in training. 
 Not just that Rinella lost the plot, she lost her dictionary as well. I've read some books with a shitloads of spelling mistakes, but this is the first one where the author just invents a word. She wrote eunuch - unic. Friggin unic! 
 The story was disgusting, the writing was horrendous.

I remember the first time I read this book. I was in the 4th grade and my mom was worried about me because I hated reading, like seriously hated it. It's not that I was bad at it, or had a hard time reading, I even had an amazing imagination; I just didn't get the point of sitting down and reading a book. The reading teacher I had was *the* reading teacher to have if you wanted to get you child to love to read. She had these 2 floor to ceiling bookshelves that were packed with books. My mom talked with the teacher about how worried she was about my lack of love for reading. She told my mom not to worry, she would work on me. She lent me a copy of this book and told me to read just the first 2 chapters of the book, if I didn't like it after that, I didn't have to read anymore and that would be that. In one week, I had finished the book. I was brokenhearted because she had lent out the second book to another student, so my mom called my dad and asked him to get the book for me. The wonderful dad that he is bought all 4 books that were out at the time. It was all history from there. 
 So maybe I have a special connection with this series, but it is truly the best series in the world. It teaches you about life, friendship, hardships, diversity. And this is just the beginning of it.

I really enjoy Krakauer's writing, so much so that this is the fourth book written by him that I've read in the past year. I also purchased two other books (on this topic) and a documentary after reading his version of the Pat Tillman story. Thus it goes without saying that I gave this five stars. 
 What is the book about? 
 The obvious answer is Pat Tillman, the famous football player who gave up a multi-million dollar contract to enlist in the army after the September 11th attacks. Pat's story alone is a remarkable one.  
 A super athlete, who apparently was also a gifted baseball player, Tillman tackled his way into the NFL and eventually a starting position - something only a few talented men ever do - despite his relatively small size. 
 Receiving a full scholarship to ASU, he graduated with a 3.8 grade point average. He then pursued a master's degree while playing professional ball. 
 He married his high school sweetheart, whom he had known most of his life, and adored her until the day he died. 
 He was an atheist who believed in living this life to its fullest and whom people claimed never went any where without a book. 
 He turned down a lucrative contract from the Saints - stunning many - in order to continue to play for the Cardinals, the organization that had picked him in the last round and given him the chance to prove himself. 
 His decision to join the army - along with his younger brother - stemmed from a desire to do the right thing, even though it meant leaving his career at its pinnacle and his new wife - arguably a "perfect" life.  
 But it's not just a story about Pat, as interesting as his life was. It is also a recounting of America's complicated relationship with the Middle East, including early U.S. support of groups - which coincidentally evolved into al-qaeda and the Taliban - that could help nullify the Soviet threat. 
 It discusses how America helped to train, finance, and ultimately lay the groundwork for the terrorist forces that would become enemy number one. 
 In fact, some could say the U.S. played into Osama bin Laden's hands. He wanted desperately to drag the Americans into what he deemed an un-winnable, not to mention expensive and crippling, military conflict (mission accomplished). It turns out, our invasion of Iraq and removal and later execution of Saddam Hussein, a man Osama detested, was simply icing on the cake.  
 Except, that's not all. It's also a story about propaganda, lies, political whitewashing, and doublespeak.  
 When Pat Tillman is killed by friendly fire, the powers-that-be do everything possible to mislead the public. Not only do they withhold the fact that Pat is killed by his fellow Rangers (from his family and the public), but they instead suggest he is the victim of an ambush and then quickly prop him up as a hero,using his story to garner support for the war at a time when support was waning. Considering Pat's views on the matter, this was extremely disrespectful to the man who had made the ultimate sacrifice for his country.  
 And somehow, Krakauer weaves it all together into one cohesive and riveting read. 
 Would recommend to Krakauer fans - he does not disappoint - and/or anyone with an interest in Pat Tillman and his story. Complementary themes that might interest are the cover-up angle as well as the extraordinary sacrifices that military families make(that most of us are spared)during times of war.

Jay Asher's controversial novel "Thirteen Reasons Why" raises issues surrounding suicide. Clay's anxiety is resounding through the novel and it very easy for the reader to connect to him. I became attached to Clay. By seeing his emotions, I became as anxious as he to find out where he fits in this puzzle of, more or less, thirteen stories. 
 The reason I gave it four stars out of five was simply because of the credibility of this story. As many reviewers have pointed out, Hannah's reasons for suicide seems a bit superficial- but then again, who are we to judge? 
 Then, we find out that Clay does not fit in with the other people who hurt Hannah... Then why did she put him through the anguish of waiting for his turn? If she loved him, then why didn't she simply give him a disclaimer of some sort at the beginning? That part felt wrong to me, hence the removal of one star.  
 The book was, however, highly enjoyable. I did stay up past an appropriate time to get to the ending. I would take this book out of the library to read it again.

There are also some areas which I find unfathomable and illogical, for example  how the bird (or airship) could just "sink" into the sky through the swamp, or how the king and his men would not have noticed a presumambly huge "bird" or airship when Internment is such a small place and the whole city is on the highest level of alert possible, after the murder of the prince. For the record... I watched the movie before I read the book. It was one of those years were I haven't found my love for reading yet so I didn't care about this book at all - or any book, for that matter. 
 "...the first time you fall in love, it changes your life forever, and no matter how hard you try, the feelin' never goes away." 
 I was confused, dumfounded, even, by how the story started. The second chapter (entitled "Ghost") felt like it fast forwarded to when Noah was building his dream house and Allie was away at school and is engaged with Lon. I felt like I was being tricked, like someone tore the chapters from the book to screw with me. I searched the book if it did have missing pages but it didn't. So I just read on... 
 But I was completely saddened by this because I wanted to hear their love story first. It was like Nicholas Sparks just jumped into the conflict of the story without giving any knowledge to the profound love the two main characters had (unlike the movie). I wanted to feel, to hear, to understand their love first like I have through the movie and was expecting more from the book because that's where it was based off from. And besides that, I've read three Nicholas Sparks books already and knowing his writing style, I KNEW it would be especially heartfelt, well-told and awesome. So while reading the book I struggled with understanding the problems and pains the two protagonists were going through. I tried to not associate the movie with the book at all, for I know it would be different as to most books turned to movies. So I was left with no basis as to what they were going through because I didn't know how they fell in love and all their memories that came with that. 
 Honestly, the whole time I was reading I kept questioning myself, "Am I supposed to connect it with the movie?", "Did they purposely made the movie as a companion to this book?", "Were you supposed to link the two together to understand the story more?" I didn't know. I still don't know. :( 
 Anyway, as always, Mr. Sparks writing is breathtakingly beautiful. The way he explains things, events are so deep but have a simple meaning and I don't know how he does this. Sometimes I feel like flying in a fluffy cloud when reading his novels because the words he uses, the way he describes things are so celestial and pleasing that you kind of forget that your in the real world. Like your just floating through the story, watching the characters through a fluffy cloud. 
 The characters were good. They felt real but as I said above the book lacked memories they had before the conflict started. They also stuck through to their given personalities and I really applaud the actors and actresses who played these characters in the movie. Their acting is EXACTLY the same as how the characters are in the book. The only problem I have is that I loved the movie and only liked this book. It's like the movie gave more meaning to the book. Like the book was based on the movie rather than the other way around. I feel bad for saying this because Mr. Sparks is one of the best authors I know and to have me say this is heartbreaking. 
 *Note: Please, please, please inform me if I have picked up a false or damaged book because I really don't want to think and remember that this book wasn't magical. Thank you in advance!

The book summary describes the setting as "being inspired by Ancient Rome". While I am not an expert in Ancient Rome, I would say that yes, the setting is inspired by Ancient Rome, but definitely not quite like it. There are some fantasy elements that I don't believe existed in Roman mythology. The fantasy elements might not be part of the setting, I guess you can argue, but I think the fantasy elements are slightly of Indian mythology, though not quite sure. In any case, it has a pretty unique setting just from the fact that is has an empire with a strong focus on the military (Ancient Rome) and also fantastical creatures like Jinn, Wraiths, and Ghuls. Just wanted to get this little tidbit off my chest, I do LOVE the setting, by the way. As I said, it is unique to other current/popular YA Fantasy that is currently out there. 
 I also love both of the characters whose point of view the story is told: Elias, a senior student at the rigorous and unrelenting military academy close to graduation of becoming a full soldier of the Empire (known as a Mask), and Laia, a Scholar (a people conquered by the Empire who focused in knowledge), who lives with her grandparents and older brother in the free Scholar quarter of the capital (most Scholars are slaves). Going off that and back to the setting, the Empire is ruled by the Martials, a people who focused in military, and there are other groups of people in which the Empire conquered, like the Scholars, Tribesmen, and Mariners to name a few. I guess it gives a little of a Sorting Hat/District/Faction element, but is not completely integral to the story (at least not yet) and again contributes to a unique world-building. 
 The overall plot is amazing and I had a hard time putting the book down. I won't go into too much detail since part of the excitement is due to the fact that the book summary doesn't give more than like 20 pages of plot away, which is great. I think book summaries tend to give away about 100 pages sometimes, so it was just really nice to be surprised from the beginning. 
 A small complaint (small enough to give 5 stars still) is the complex love story built within. Each main character kinda has a love interest separate of each other, but of course when they meet there is a spark (this is kinda a pun given the title of the book ;) ). I guess not many books that I have read involve this kind of love sub-plot, but it just made me as a reader a little confused as who to root for at times. I am sure in more books it will be clearer and just better overall. 
 Re-read September 2016: I still really liked this book but not as much as the first time through. Again, the surprise of the plot was one part I really loved but knowing/remembering those points going it made it a little less exciting. The characters are still great though, and looking forward to starting the next book in the series soon! 
 Summary of this book with spoilers for my future reference.Laia is a free Scholar when her brother is captured by the Masks, a group of Martial solders, for working with the Resistance (a group of Scholars trying to take down the Empire of the Martials since most Scholars are slaves and mistreated). In order to save her brother, she finds the Resistance in town and strikes a bargain with them. In exchange for saving her brother, she will work as a spy on the Commandant of the Blackcliff Academy-- the training school for the Masks. She will be sold to the Commandant as her personal slave. The Commandant is a cruel, cold woman known for killing off her slaves. At the Blackcliff Academy, there is a senior student, Elias, who decides that he wants to desert the Masks after he graduates. However, the Agurs (sort of like Monks, holy people of the society) visit the school and proclaim that the Trials have begun. Elias is one of the 4 selected to partake in them. The Trials are to determine who will become the new Martial Emperor, as the current one will die soon (prophecy) and his line has come to an end. The other 3 are Elias best friend, Helene, and his rival, Marcus, along with Marcus's twin (but kinder) brother, ----. Laia ends up meeting Elias and there is a bit of an attraction between the two. Elias ends up bringing Laia some healing salve when he sees marks that the Commandant left on her. Laia befriends a kitchen-girl slave, Izzi, and also works with a slave known as Cook. Cook is distant and stutters when she talks about her past. She was part of the Resistance back in the day and knew Laia's parents who were core leaders of the Resistance before their death. They were caught and killed by the Commandant. 
 As for the Trials, the winner will be the first to win 2 trials. The 2nd place person will be declared the Blood Strike, the person who declares full service to the Emperor and commands his army. The other 2 will die. The first trial puts everyone in a deserted area that also scares them. Helene is placed in cliffs in a giant bird's nest since she fears heights. Elias is left stranded in the desert, but he sees mirages of the people he has killed over time. They have to make it back to Blackcliff within a timeframe.

I was worried going into this that I wouldn't like it as much as I'd enjoyed the previous books but I hoped I'd be wrong. I wasn't. There have been other books in the series that I haven't enjoyed as much - Mine to Possess comes to mind - but at least there was some warmth to that, at least there were plenty of background characters who made things better, and at least things improved as the book went on. 
 I struggled with this one. I was slightly interested in learning more about Ekaterina/Katya before starting to read, the little glimpses we got of her when she was working in the lab with Ashaya made me think that she could potentially be an interesting character but I felt that she was lacking something. I think some of the Katya criticism that I've read is a little unfair, especially when the same people are praising Dev (who I personally thought was a bit of an arsehole), but she didn't live up to her potential. She survived Ming's mental torture, she didn't break, but despite that which should have made her a strong person, she was kind of weak and came across quite childlike at times. 
 Dev... I really didn't warm to him at all. On the one hand, I understand him being wary of Katya. She's a Psy who has had Ming rooting round in her brain and he's the director of the Shine Foundation so there's going to be some distrust there but I didn't agree with the way he treated her. He thought it was awful the way she'd been treated before being dumped on his doorstep but there were times where he treated her exactly the same. 
 I also didn't feel anything for the romance. It left me empty. Not even cold. Just empty. There was no natural build up and although that could sometimes be said for the changeling romances, there was no reason why it should be the same here. There's the mating bond to explain things with the changelings, there's something bigger at work, something that pulls them in. There's nothing to explain how quickly it happens here. You've got a Psy (although one that can feel emotion) and a human with Psy ancestors. It doesn't make sense. It happens almost straight away. One second he's saying he might have to kill her, and the next he's kissing her, and I honestly felt that some of his advances were a bit pushy and a bit gross. 
 I did have a hope towards the end that things were going to go a different way and I was actually quite excited for it but of course Katya couldn't actually die. It just shows how bad the romance was, that I wasn't even upset when it seemed like she was going to die and I was excited for it. I did like that it was Noor and Keenan that saved her but at the same time it was a massive letdown because once again things worked out perfectly. If she had to have been saved, I would have liked her to have been left with some of the effects she'd had before she decided to die. Left with the weakness on one side, or left paralysed or something. It would have also been a bit more interesting to see this if she pops up in later books.  
 There were a few things I enjoyed. I loved seeing Judd help one of the Forgotten children. I loved seeing the Changelings pop up occasionally although I did really miss them. I think the series suffers when they are not main characters. I did enjoy seeing more of how the Shine Foundation works. Overall though, I was disappointed. I might take a break before continuing.

Single Malt is a thrilling, fast paced mystery that will keep you engrossed and flipping the pages as fast as you can! I loved the MC's, Agents Whiskey and Irish, and their personalities, how they interacted with each other, and that they were both already firmly aware and accepted their sexuality. 
 REVIEW: 
 Single Malt is book one in the new series, Agents Irish and Whiskey by author Layla Reyne. This is a book that you are going to want to run out and get, it is the type of story that keeps you on the edge of your seat - flipping the pages as fast as you can, as your pulse is pounding away and you are both trying to figure out the mystery of the story and loving the romance between the two MC. The combo is addicting. Although author Layla Reyne was new to me, prior to this book, she will be an author I keep my eye on and watch for new books to come in the future! 
 The MC in this story are: Jameson "Whiskey" Walker, who is a former basketball champion and is now with the FBI in the Cyber Crimes division & Aidan "Irish" Talley who is an Irish ex-pat and is just returning to the FBI after the car crash that shredded his heart and life into little pieces. This car crash occurs prior to the start of this book and takes the life of Aidan's husband, Gabe Cruz, and his FBI partner Tom. It has been only a little over 8 months since Aidan's life was changed forever by a wreck that was ruled a random hit-and-run; however, now before he is set to return to duty information has surfaced that supports his belief that the wreck that rocked his world, was not random - it was a hit. Aidan's sister-in-law/supervisory agent at work agrees to allow Aidan to investigate the wreck that took her brother but it has to be on the down low - nobody can know, nobody except his new partner that is - Whiskey. 
 When Whiskey sees his new partner strolling into work after being on an extended leave for more than 8 months - he is just as attracted to the sexy man in the three piece suit with the shamrock cufflinks as he was when he first met him. The only thing that has changed is now, Aidan is a widower and now, Jamie is paired up with Aidan - who he quickly nicknames, Irish. The sexual tension between the two is strong and working long hours together, depending on each other in life threatening situations, and being alone with each other for hours on end does nothing to quell the lust. Even if it is against regulation to fraternize with a fellow agent - there is only so much temptation these two men can take. "Walker knew exactly what he wanted, and fuck, the anticipation, the wanting, the end of the emptiness right there where he needed it most was killing him." The only problem is, Aidan is afraid of getting his heart shredded again - so he reverts back to a manwhore. While Jamie can't help himself and falls quickly for his partner. "I can't promise you anything. I can't get attached." Whiskey tries to abide by the rules that Irish sets up; but the heart wants - what the heart wants and he finds himself getting deeper and deeper, even considering if he is falling in Love. - Their bodies settled into the intimate embrace, fitting seamlessly together again. Fates and Furies has all the fixings of a classic Greek tragedy...or is it comedy? As Groff reminds us throughout, it's all a matter of perspective. This is a story of passion, betrayal, rage, loss, lust, revenge, hubris, plotting, epic love, and epic deception. All this peppered with the occasional omniscient aside, a la classic Greek chorus. At the center of this storm we find Lotto and Mathilde, an ambitious and enthralling couple whose marriage - the bedrock for both - is built on half-truths and misconceptions. 
 This framework allows Groff to be both playful and self-indulgent in her narrative. She introduces us to a group of preposterous characters who find themselves leading equally preposterous lives. She isn't exactly subtle, either, in hammering home her very meta intentions. Early on, Lotto's drama teacher instructs us on how to read this work. We read plays embedded within the larger narrative, go to operas, and attend art shows. Many of the characters' names are a nod to other characters from great works of art and myth - Lancelot being the most obvious. Her narrators regularly quote major players in the literary/art world. Art criticism and the creative process play a major role in their motives and moods. [The Greek chorus asides, though delightful, are yet another example.] And don't think those mentions of gesamtkunstwerk and ekphrasis went unnoticed. 
 In short, Groff makes sure we know that this is not just the story of a marriage. Instead, she uses it as a sounding board for her commentary on the creative process and the power of great art to tap into something visceral within us. Perhaps Lotto and Mathilde's marriage - charged, electric, painful, devout, ecstatic, consuming, devastating - mirrors the marriage between artist and expression, truth and beauty? It speaks to the struggle of remaining faithful to our truths while trying to contribute something meaningful to the world. Though at times overwrought, this story is, in the end, deeply moving and intimate, the pretense giving way to emotional veracity.
