When did we all start talking about Elena Ferrante, guys? I can't remember- was it last year? Maybe 2013? I know she's been writing for far longer than that, but it was definitely only recently that she became A Thing. Whenever it was, we should have been talking about her sooner. 
 And with different words. Better words. Words whose value hasn't been sucked out by the marketing blurbs they've been a part of, with the same accompanying modifiers (if I never hear "compulsively readable" again that would be okay with me, marketing departments). Too many eyes will glaze over when I use these words that would once have excited the grab-the-keys-and-run-to-the-bookstore response this book deserves. And that might make you, like me, not pick this up for absolutely years after you read this. 
 So I need better words. Words that will make you pick it up tomorrow. Because I still can't believe I somehow developed the impression that this was a book that I could miss. How did I somehow think this wasn't a series of books that I should have had on pre-order every time like it was Game of Thrones? (... or, you know, something better than that given the quality of the last installment.) 
 But in the absence of an unused vocabulary floating around somewhere I'll try to convince you with the words I have, because- and please read this in the tone of your dad giving advice at a crucial life moment-I don't want you to make the mistakes that I did, sonny boy. 
 How do I love this novel? Let me count the ways... 
 * * * 
 My Brilliant Friend is the first installment of Ferrante's Neapolitan trilogy. It is an old woman's memories of her friendship with a girl named Lila in the slums of 1950s Naples. They are both clever girls growing up in the midst of a grinding cycle of poverty and isolation generated by the problems of the post-war, post-Fascist Italian state (and the pre-war, mostly-in-name-only Italian "unification"). Both of them, along with the other children of the neighborhood, have a possibility of escaping the cycle and breaking out into the new Marshall Plan supported dolce vita- and some of the story is about that. But not mostly. Mostly it's about what it's like to be blessed/cursed enough to have a childhood friend who is the center of your universe, and how that friendship can literally change all the things in your life, and make you the person that you are in the process of becoming. 
 Straightforward enough, yes? You've read that before. Sure...but then why is it so poignant? Why did I spend hours upon hours with this book yesterday, unable to put it down? How did such an ordinary story work such undeniable magic? 
 There are many answers to that, but let's start with this: The story. The plot was the most natural, organic thing I've ever read. She started telling it and kept on doing it without pauses for literary reflections or metaphors, or for pretty much anything that might send the "oh right, this is fiction," signal to your brain. She let the damn thing be and run its course without interfering. She didn't shy away from having her character be involved in all the quotidian things of childhood or adolescence- zits, dresses, best friends, boyfriends, finding out what bad words mean, and endless status competitions. But never once did she make it feel tired or like something I've read a zillion times. Nobody came equipped with signifier clue words or pre-packaged, recognizable YA storylines, with immature emotional truths being repeated in italics, in between descriptions of clothing and hair. And you know what was fascinating? There totally was a popular girl everyone wanted here, there were mean bullies, nerdy intellectuals, hot jocks, slutty cheerleaders, apparently motivationlessly awful villains, and our heroine was even intellectual and had glasses. But that never occurred to me until I started to write this review. 
 This is mostly because Ferrante allows her characters a kind of full, honest emotional range of expression that I've rarely seen in books about children and teenagers. She conveys the pettiness and center-of-the-universe feeling that characterizes childhood without ever quite making you detach from or become disgusted with the characters involved. When someone's doll is thrown away, and another character retaliates, instead of rolling her eyes and refereeing whose fault it is, Ferrante just keeps staring at both characters and watching them go through that moment and what happens afterwards. There's no adult intervention, whether that's with an adult character or with an adult narrator. 
 As is typical with Ferrante, this is deliberate a choice that serves several purposes at once. One of which is to highlight the lack of fully developed adults anywhere in these children's lives. This is one of the many effective ways Ferrante finds to seep you in the atmosphere of the Naples neighborhood where this all takes place, right from the beginning, but beautifully, dropping it in between the cracks of action and thought: 
 "I waited to see if Lila would have second thoughts and turn back. I knew what she wanted to do, I had hoped that she would forget about it, but in vain. The street lamps were not yet lit, nor were the lights on the stairs. From the apartments came irritable voices. To follow Lila, I had to leave the bluish light of the courtyard and enter the black of the doorway. When I finally made up my mind, I saw nothing at first, there was only an odor of old junk and DDT. Then I got used to the darkness... We kept to the side where the wall was, she two steps ahead, I two steps behind, torn between shortening the distance or letting it increase. I can still feel my shoulder inching along the flaking wall and the idea that the steps were very high, higher than my own apartment across the way... There was an odor of sauteing garlic. Maria, Don Achille's wife, would put me in the pan of boiling oil, the children would eat me, he would suck my head the way my father did with mullets..." 
 Never once does she need to set aside pages and pages of description as some authors do, because it's given to us in pieces like that, while we're following the action, until we have a full picture of a crumbling courtyard of a creaky old apartment building on a beaten down street in a bad part of town without ever really knowing how we got there. 
 She also does a lot, effectively, with repetition. Repetition shows us a lot about why the characters are the way that they are. The violence of the neighborhood, in particular, is depicted with a frighteningly normalizing banality. We see violence happen over and over again- not as an isolated, cinematic horror, the fright of one's life- as something mentioned as an afterthought, "they argued, and then sometimes, after dinner, he beat her." The deliberate use of "sometimes" was chilling, like we're not even hearing about all the other times when it happens. It's not even worthy of comment. What's even more terrifying is the dispassionate, impartial gaze turned on it by a narrator who has never known anything different. It only occurs to the sixty year old character who is the actual narrator of the story about two-thirds of the way through to get outside of herself and mention that she realizes now that her neighborhood was not the norm- it's like in telling the story she put herself back under the spell and forgot that herself. It takes something 2015 Hollywood-level cinematically, publicly violent for anyone to feel the slightest bit bad about something that happens- like throwing your eleven year old daughter out a window into the street.  The pernicious, weed-like growth of a particularly violent form of aggressive masculinity is at the root of most of the problem, but its societal reinforcement and indeed, the respect shown for those who display it, is shown, through this enforced repetition, to be the true cancer that not even young boys with the best of intentions and a deliberate intent to break the cycle seem to be able to escape. (Not to mention the girls who never had a chance to begin with.) 
 Something that further increased the powerfully true impression I got from her writing was her gentle use of not-quite chronological time. Time in the novel wavers into being, then very slowly circles back to its origin point until you've almost forgotten where you started. But even this tried and true literary device never felt like a literary device. Again, it was so well and seamlessly executed it felt like a natural, organic process that was necessary to telling the story. It was like what happens when someone is telling you a story and realizes you don't have the context to understand it, so they back it up and up until they feel they've given you the whole story, and then only just remember why they were telling you the story in the first place. 
 But beyond that, the prose itself: Ferrante has that magical Tolstoy thing. The power of it isn't in the individual sentence, which I guarantee you will be perfectly ordinary, but a string of sentences put together in just the right order. It is almost never going to be a striking word choice that nabs you, but rather a continuous flow that lulls you into its depths so that you're surprised awake occasionally, just realizing that it's happened to you. I honestly can't think of anybody else except Tolstoy when he's not ranting or religious, or Austen when she wasn't being mischievous or clever, who can give the impression of being so utterly absent, as if someone simply left a kind of recorder on that would let you see what was going on inside and outside of the characters' heads. 
 But while the plot is compelling enough, the hot, poisonous atmosphere and her rare gift for naturalistic, barely-there powerful writing are more than enough reason to show up, that's what you notice later, after you're done and you can breathe normally again. 
 At the time all you really notice are these girls. It's Lila. Lila, Lila, Lila. If you've ever been friends with someone who was demonstrably smarter than you (or you were so convinced they were as to make no difference), then you know Lila. You know what it's like to know that no matter what you do you'll always feel inferior- whether they praise you or encourage you or not. It makes so much sense to me that Lila was the transformative experience for Elena. She's a heady thing for a child to experience. She is a person who is seemingly born free of gaze. She'll process what you say for the words you actually use- not the social status you have while you say it, not the yearning she has to be like you or not like you at all, nor does she care about the image she is projecting to you. One of the things the narrator worries about in Lila in 1950s Italy is that she doesn't have the instinctive, eyes down response that the other girls do when they are getting harassed on the street. Lila threatens people with a knife, or simply asks them curious questions about what on earth they're talking about when they do that to her. She literally stares down or completely ignores a gaze that is the all-encompassing foundation, path and walls of all the women (and, to be frank, most of the men) around her. That's an intoxicating cocktail of a thing to be around. A possibly dangerous, even ruinous thing to be around, if you're a smart, insecure teenager with an imagination and a constant societal message that you are not good enough. 
 Like Elena, the narrator. Her character development was very cleverly done. She had us, and Elena, so focused on her friend that her own story seems to happen under the radar, in asides, as if just necessary for context and to get us to the next Lila story. Which is a brilliant way to depict someone with the kind of self-esteem issues and brewing existential problems that are the major driver of most of Elena's choices. She becomes a person somewhere along the way, without even realizing it- she builds an entire personality around Lila, the only thing she can see as worth motivating herself for in her horrible little dirty world. But it makes her beautiful moment of self-awareness at the end of the novel all the more poignant. She is shocked to discover that a disappointment she has in her own life, unrelated to Lila in any way, is important to her. This realization of her own, independent being as a person means she is able to have her first out of body experience, and look beyond the isolation and suffocation of her neighborhood to see herself with a gaze that might actually benefit her, in the end: 
 "I discovered that I had considered the publication of those few lines, my name in print, as a sign that I really had a destiny, that the hard work of school would surely lead upward, somewhere, that Maestra Oliviero had been right to push me forward and to abandon Lila. "Do you know what plebs are?" "Yes, Maestra." And at that moment I knew what plebs were, much more clearly than when, years earlier, she had asked me. The plebs were us. The plebs were that fight for food and wine, that quarrel over who should be served first and better, that dirty floor on which the waiters clattered back and forth, those increasingly vulgar toasts. The plebs were my mother, who had drunk wine and was now leaning against my father's shoulder, while he, serious, laughed, his mouth gaping, at the sexual allusions of the metal dealer. They were all laughing, even Lila, with the expression of one who has a role and will play it to the utmost." 
 But most of all there is the friendship between these two girls. The content of it is some of the most honest that I've seen. It's neither a sentimental Victorian ode to sisterly support nor is it as cynical as some more modern reinterpretations of female friendship would suggest. It trusts you to understand that these are real people and to acknowledge that because you are willing to acknowledge it within yourself without ever telling you to acknowledge it. We know that the narrator doesn't mean it maliciously, necessarily, when she needs a boyfriend because she thinks her friend has one, that she throws her friend's doll down a hole because her friend did, that she feels better if she looks a little better than her sometimes. We also see that whenever something truly bad happens to her friend she notices it and she helps- she gets her through some tough situations when she has no obligation to. We also see how fixated she is on her friend, and how nothing is really worth it to her if she doesn't share in it with her: she shows us what it means when your life is really, as literally as possible, almost entirely about your perception of another person. We see this so often in the context of romantic literature, but almost never in the context of friendship. I think the latter is far more common 
 I do not claim the novel is faultless. There were two moments where her assured voice broke and she fell down into the exaggerated metaphorical exercises I was so happy to see absent from most of the book. (Though one of those times is forgivable, because it came from a dramatic adolescent who dramatically drew out the metaphor herself in the weird, obsessive way that teenagers do. I also did wish that we might have spent slightly more time with the narrator herself, in her own home and her own life so that we might have gotten to know her better. But that was a reader's wish for a sympathetic character to know herself better, mostly- that's not what this story was about. It would have been the poorer for following what I wanted it to do. The faults were mostly the faults of the character, put there deliberately to emphasize a character trait. 
 So perhaps it is nearly faultless after all. What did I miss? Maybe someone else can tell me where she went wrong, because I can't find it. Or I probably could, actually, but I think I'll be much too busy reading the next installment: The Story of a New Name. Which, I predict, is exactly what you'll be doing as soon as you finish this book.

Based on extensive research of historical texts, "The Red Tent" tells the story of Dinah, of the Book of Genesis of the Bible, as from Dinah's own perspective. Anita Diamant has a wonderful way of conjuring up the past, and it was easy to get lost in Dinah's world, from her sheltered upbringing to the famous biblical story of her encounter with Shalem, a Canaanite prince. 
 Like one of my all-time favourite books, "The Mists of Avalon" (Marion Zimmer Bradley) I savoured this novel and the opportunity to travel in space and time into a world we only know from legends. Diamant's characters are so alive that they literally leapt off the pages of the book. I loved the descriptions of the lives of Jacob's four wives, the mystery of the red tent and Dinah's childhood growing up with 12 brothers. But most of all, Dinah's early years are a celebration of womanhood, also reflected in her later role as midwife and healer, which made for fascinating reading. I only wish that I had had such support on coming of age and a similar initiation into womanhood, and that that there was more opportunity to celebrate the wisdom of generations of women who have come before me. I found Diamant's description of the birth stories especially haunting, reminding us that childbirth used to pose a real risk of death to women throughout history - and was feared and celebrated accordingly. 
 Unlike some reviews I have read, I did not find the story to be anti-male - rather, it seemed to me a pretty accurate description of the roles of males and females in early history. Diamant also provides acute insights into married life, love, passion and the different attitudes of different women to relationships and sex. And whilst Dinah may seem unforgiving to her brother Joseph later in the book, this is understandable given the circumstances ... but I won't give too much away here. 
 All in all, I recommend this book to any woman interested in historical fiction - or simply wanting to celebrate womanhood and the many generations of women who have come before us. Do not be turned off by the religious theme - this is not a religious book, merely an account of life in Biblical times. The Red Tent made for fascinating reading and will undoubtedly provide many discussion points for our next bookclub meeting.

historical m/m romance at it's best 
 I don't typically read historical romance - in fact I can count the number of them I have read on one hand, with probably three fingers, so yeah - not much. However, I had to see what all the hype was about this series as all of my book friends were ranting and raving about it's brilliance! So I succumbed to peer pressure and tried it! I have to admit, I liked this book. Now, remember I am not a historical romance fan, probably as historical as I get is back to the 1950's ... So when I say I "liked" this book that's a big thing! 
 This book made me think about how it must have been to live back in those times as a gay man when sodomy was illegal and a punishable crime, while I know it's probably a law still on the books in some places it isn't one you hear of people being thrown in prison for anymore. Not to mention the stigma of loving someone of the same sex.. It shows how far civilization has come and even though we are not as accepting of allowing everyone to love how they want...we have come a long way. 
 Beyond making me think, this was an enjoyable book to see that families behaved just as atrociously back then as they do now and to see how creative a group of gentleman were to come up with their little "don't ask don't tell" group where they were free to express themselves behind closed doors. 
 So yeah, I enjoyed this book and I think I might try book two! I am not however a convert to historical romance.

This book was selected by my book club. We thought it was a neat concept with the weird vintage photos and it was on bestseller lists so we figured we couldn't go wrong. 
 I had the physical copy from the library and also downloaded it as an audiobook so that I could multitask while listening if need be. 
 Initially, I flipped through the book and looked at all of the pictures. I wasn't sure how much of a part they would play into the story. Turns out, the author seemed to use those pictures as his inspiration and developed a story around each one describing them in the text and weaving his tale around each one. Some were more believable than others and some were a stretch. It reminded me of the psychiatrist test, similar to Rorschach ink blot test, where line-art pictures are shown and the subject is instructed to tell a story about what is happening in the picture. 
 Unfortunately, in some ways using the pictures actually hurt the story because it felt very fragmented. It was as if he "had" to include every creepy picture even when their result added little to the story. 
 Nevertheless, it was an enjoyable first book in a new fantasy adventure series. Not usually my choice (fantasy/sci-fi for children) but it is so unique with the vintage photos that I will read the next in the series once it arrives at the library.
I'm very 'happy'' to announce that this was a total waste of my free time.

Let it be known from the beginning that I am Team Jace. Yes, after reading Something Like Summer I was left very upset because of what i felt was an unfair ending to his story. So I was looking forward to reading his story even though the ending was somewhat spoiled. I wanted to know what made Jace the man that he became. 
 In short Jace's life story is one full of the search of love and commitment. His story starts with Jace deciding to take his life because he is afraid of ending up alone and unloved; this was his greatest fear.Luckily his suicide attempt ends up being just that and he is able to move on. Soon after, Jace meets Victor who becomes his first love. But Victor's vision of love and relationships is nothing like Jace's. Jace is bent on love and commitment but Victor is a carefree character that is cause for a lot of joy and pain for Jace. However, Victor teaches him two important lessons that later define Jace: Love is unconditional and it doesn't stop unless you let it stop. He also learns that commitment is nothing without a promise that is honored throughout time. 
 When Jace is with Ben these two lessons help him deal with Ben's relationship with Tim. Jace understands what Ben is going through because he himself still loves Victor. So he is willing to forgive what happens between Ben and Tim because he can finally see that despite it all their love is for each other is still intact. Then after they get married Ben once again honors his promise to love Jace above all and pushed Tim away one last time. 
 Even though half way through the book I was still feeling Jace got less than what he deserved in life, as the inevitable nears I can help but finally understand that Jace actually got everything he wished for in life and I was able to shed tears of happiness for him because what was happening was happening on the terms he always wished for. 
 Anyway, by far this is my favorite book of these series. And although I own Something Like Winter I have not been able to read it yet, as I am not sure I want to get to know Tim better. But reading Jace's story's has actually given me closure and I look forward to the final chapter Something Like Spring.

I liked this book but I didn't fall in love with it. I enjoyed the descriptions of Italy and the U.S. during the time period and I liked learning about the opera and sharing Enza's love for it. I had a hard time feeling emotions for the main characters and got annoyed with the many near misses that Ciro Lazzari and Enza Ravanelli had. The plot is somewhat predictable especially when we knew that Ciro would end up with Enza as indicated by the tile of the book. It felt contrived when they both made it to the US and found one another over and over again. Nevertheless, this book was inspired by the author's real grandparents so I had to let that go. 
 My heart did break for the Lazzari brothers when their mother left them to be raised by the nuns. I wanted her to get better and come back for them and had a hard time forgiving her when the boys found her as adults after Ciro was diagnosed and she still felt like she had done what was best for them. I really felt for the boys as they walked the line and tried to do everything right so that they wouldn't be kicked out of the convent. When the corrupt priest's orders to get the boys out of the convent were obeyed with a twist, I was at least happy that the monsignor didn't completely get his way. I found it funny that the nuns were willing to fib to get the money and send Ciro to the US. In a patriarchal society, the nuns were expected to be humble and obey the orders of the men. The priest had so much power that it was easier to pay lip service to obeying his orders and then skirt around them than it was to try to stand up to him. 
 I wasn't sure what made Enza sick on the crossing over to America unless it was seasickness and was glad when later in her life her son suggested that there was medicine that she could take now to keep her from getting sick. I hated that she sent money to support her family and help them build a house but would never be able to see the yellow house on a hill. 
 Enza was a strong girl and a stronger woman and she really did well to think of others first. I was proud when Ciro asked for her hand and told her father that he wanted her for those traits - because he needed to know that she could step up and care for his family if something ever happened to him. I was also proud when Enza stood up to Ciro and told him that if she was important to him as he professed that he wouldn't have let anything, even an ocean get in the way. 
 When Ciro and Enza's son was off at war, it was as if life was on hold and Angela, the girl who had come to stay with Enza, did not want to commit to chasing her own dreams and living her own life until Antonio came back from the war. I don't think Enza would have wanted that for her if she had known. Enza was wanting to go to New York to stay with Laura and downsize her Minnesota life anyway. This is an example of people making sacrifices without ever consulting the person they are sacrificing for. 
 Questions and Answers for Book Group: 
 1. The novel is split into three parts: Italian Alps, Manhattan and Minnesota. How would you characterize Ciro and Enza in each of these sections? How do they adapt to their new homes? In what ways did they change over the course of the novel? In what ways did they remain the same? 
 They each had their levels of growth and maturing in their respective destinations. Manhattan was important for both of them because this is where they found their individuality, had time to pursue their dreams, and matured. Ciro also had the war to help him put life into perspective. 
 2. How would the course of both Ciro's and Enza's lives have been different if they hadn't gone to America? Do you think they would have ended up together if they had stayed on the mountain? 
 If they hadn't gone to America, I think they still would have ended up together and probably sooner rather than later. However, I don't know if they would have had the sort of growth that enabled them to stick with each other over the years if they had stayed in their smaller worlds. 
 3. Enza and Ciro shared their first kiss beside Stella's grave. In what ways did digging the grave open up Ciro's heart? 
 Ciro saw vulnerability in Enza at the grave. This experience of loss would change her. For the first time he wanted to take care of someone else when they needed him. Not just because he didn't want to lose his spot in the convent, but because he felt a connection to her through their different but shared experiences in losing a loved one. 
 4. When Ciro opened up his duffle bag on the ship to America, "the fragrance of the convent laundry - lavender and starch - enveloped him, fresh as the mountain air of Vilminore" (p. 120). What other aspects of convent life stayed with Ciro and Eduardo after they left? What did they learn from the sisters? 
 Eduardo definitely embraced the compassion, faith and spirituality of the atmosphere of the convent. He took this with him throughout his life. Ciro learned a sweetness and calm (signified by the lavender) at the convent. He also experienced a rigidity and structure (signified by the starch) from his time at the convent and his banishment from it. 
 5. Enza "found a best friend in Laura, but so much more" (p. 195). What do you think made Laura and Enza's bond so deep from the beginning? In what ways did they support one another? 
 The friendship that developed between Enza and Laura when the two meet as factory workers was a wonderful example of making a family when the nuclear one is absent. Laura helped to teach Enza English and gave her the courage to go out on her own and reach for the job at the opera. Enza was a calming influence to Laura and helped to give he that added income and security that she wouldn't have had on her own. Also, Enza's love of the opera was what garnered her attention when she applied and her wanting share the job with Laura made a difference in the decision to hire them both. 
 6. Did anything surprise you about the characterization of Enrico Caruso? How would you describe his relationship with those around him? How did the time he spent with Enza and Laura affect them, even decades later? 
 No, I got the sense that he was just an Italian missing home. He found kindred spirits and a taste of home with the girls. 
 7. How does The Shoemaker's Wife portray the immigrant experience? Do any of your own families have a similar immigrant history? Did they have a different experience? 
 Hard but worthwhile for those who embrace it. No, those stories have not been passed on to me. 
 8. Enza and Ciro have different views of religion. In what ways do their beliefs shape their actions and relationship? 
 Ciro could always accept Enza's spirituality just as he did his brother's. He respected it in each of them and wished that he could feel the same about it. 
 9. How do you think Enza's life would have turned out if she had married Vito? If Ciro had married Felicita? What did Vito and Felicita offer them and what did they lack? 
 Enza would have had a comfortable life but none of the passion and deep connection with Vito. Ciro knew all of her including her past and the love for the mountain and Vito only knew the ex-pat version of Enza. If Felicita and Ciro had married, it would have been a lukewarm existence. With Felicita, it was more of a physical relationship. Enza and Vito would have lived a comfortable cultured life but there wouldn't have been the highs and lows to add the spice. 
 10. Carlo Lazzari warned Eduardo to "beware the things of this world that can mean everything or nothing". In what ways did this advice ring true throughout the novel? 
 We place our own meaning on experiences and objects. The kiss at the grave could have been dismissed as meaning nothing but instead it ignited the spark for the teens. There are many more examples of perception coloring experiences throughout the novel. 
 11. What effect did fighting in the Great War have on Ciro? Do you believe he returned to Manhattan a changed man, or did the war just force him to acknowledge what he had known all along? 
 I think it matured him and brought his life and what he should value into perspective. I think he was changed along with clarification of what is important. 
 12. When Ciro saw Enza on the steps of Our Lady of Pompeii church, moments away from marrying Vito, "it seemed like fate was on his side." Do you believe that fate brought Ciro and Enza together on that day? Overall, do you believe that Ciro and Enza were destined to be together? 
 It was fate sprinkled with determination. 
 13. Enza once said to Ciro: "I remind you, I imagine, of things you'd rather not think about." What do you believe Enza meant by this? What challenges did Ciro and Enza face in their relationship? How did they differ in their ways of communicating? 
 She reminded him of his immigrant past and all that he had lost. She also reminded him of his failures to join up with her at each of their missed opportunities. 
 14. How did Ciro, Enza and Antonio each react to Ciro's diagnosis? What were Ciro's fears and hopes for his family? In what ways will Enza and Antonio fulfill his dreams? 
 Ciro was shell-shocked and then resolved to put his affairs in order. Enza was heartbroken and placed her trust in her faith. Antonio did not fully understand the loss that would come. As an only child, he would share and experience it with his mother and she would lean on him. 
 15. At the end of the novel, Enza agrees to return to Italy with Antonio and Angela. How do you imagine the reunion between Enza and her family? How will Schilpario be different for Enza when seen through Angela and Antonio's eyes? 
 I think it will be much the same as how they greeted Ciro. Enza's memories of the mountain will probably be sweeter than the actual return. I don't think Angela and Antonio will feel the mountain in their bones the way that Enza will and she may be disappointed in that.

I was expecting an action-packed spy thriller. 
 I was expecting life and death situations. 
 I was expecting sappy romance. 
 I was NOT expecting the author taking all of these things, putting them into a blender, mashing them to bits, and constructing them as a masterfully humorous tale that feels like it's poking fun at the YA genre while simultaneously paying homage. In a good way. 
 So we have the bad boy and the good boy characters pursuing the intelligent, attractive female. But the bad boy and the good boy are really just abandoned kids trained in the arts of seduction and espionage. They are only vying for this girl because a spy is needed to be by her side day and night. To complicate things, our bad boy and good boy also develop feelings for someone other than the mark. 
 The book rapidly switches from jaunty romance to action craziness. Since I'm way more into action, this made the book even better for me. But I will say, I did enjoy the romance also. The characters were likable and sometimes felt a little underdeveloped. I am hoping this means there will be future books in a series featuring these characters and fleshing them out. There's plenty left to explore in the world Dietrich has built in The Love Interest. 
 I think it would be a good fit for fans of Kristin Orlando's "You Don't Know My Name" and ready for a David Levithan-esque twist.

A mix of historical fiction and magical realism, following three different women in three different time periods: Mer, a healer and plantation slave in cusp-of-the-revolution Haiti; the real-life historical figure Jeanne Duval in 1840's Paris, Haitian mistress to poet Charles Baudelaire; and Thais, an Ethiopian prostitute in fourth century AD Egypt. 
 Hopkinson links our main characters via a framing device: African goddess Lasiren/Mami Wata, fragmented by the slave trade's dispersion of her peoples, is adrift in time and space, and, while trying to reconstitute herself and help her enslaved people, jumps from human consciousness to human consciousness in various eras - sometimes influencing the actions of the person she is 'visiting', but often just passively observing. Each individual character thread advances chronologically when we (via the goddess) return to it, so we still experience narrative momentum despite the fragmented set-up. 
 The writing is strong, characters well-developed, and different historical settings well-evoked (Hopkinson neatly integrates a lot of historical detail into her scenes and dialogue while avoiding the weighed-down-by superfluous-'look at all my research'-details trap that some historical fiction falls into). There's also a good amount of explicit sexual content, of both heterosexual and homosexual stripes, that's impressively handled, because it's so easy for frank sex scenes to dip into the unintentionally ridiculous, and Hopkinson deftly avoids that. 
 The only issues for me was that I vacillated on which character thread I was most interested in, most often wanting to get back to Mer's story, and I wish Thais's thread (which starts about half-way through the novel) had been introduced or at least hinted at earlier, though I absolutely loved her resolution. One other spoilerly nit-pick: I also wanted some more mixed feelings from Mer towards Makandal after he/Ogu ripped out her tongue. I mean, she had mixed feelings and mistrust towards him and his revolutionary plans throughout the book and then he/Ogu RIPS OUT HER FRIGGIN TONGUE at the climax, and she seems way too accepting of this act of violence afterwards (not even really commenting on it?) - I could understand her not wanting him killed, but expected *some* kind of bitterness, or a 'He may have taken away my voice, but...' thoughts, given her attitude throughout the rest of the book. . But regardless, a unique and recommended read I likely wouldn't have found on my own, so thanks to the Sword & Laser group for making it a pick, and I'll check out more Nalo Hopkinson in the future.

I finished reading this book a while ago. It has a lot of things that I liked. To start with, it explores ideas about what it is like after we die. Lela's super popular bestie, Nadia, commits suicide. I cannot remember how, but Lela finds out that Nadia did not go to a good place and when she dies by accident, she leaves behind the good death place to go find and save her friend. 
 The city is not a safe place. And I loved it. Fine left plenty of places open where dark and fantastic things are. It was very clear we were only seeing a small part of the city. Sadly, though, Fine also decided to construct yet another land of the dead where suicides are punished even more because they have to get over themselves and become real people again. Meanwhile, the city gives them whatever they want. Only badly. For example, you can watch your favorite tv shows but your favorite episodes will never air and there will be lots of static. No one is really making an effort to help them. They can barely help themselves let alone each other. And it's pretty clear most them are never getting out of anything. 
 But they brought it on themselves, right? Because they killed themselves. I really hate this sort of victim blaming. But I knew it would be like this (cause when is it not?). I am reading this to explore this land of the dead and it is a cool land. There are different realms. There are agendas from on high going on and we can see that the characters are starting as very minor characters in a very deep game. I really liked all of that. 
 But the main character is yet another tough loved goody-two-shoes. And after I finished the first book and started the second where they leave the land of the dead, well...without the land of the dead in the background, I lost interest fast. Then it became yet another teenagery blah story with hot love interest in the background and...meh. Save the world on your own time, kids. I'm out.

*Shrug* I don't know. Maybe I need to cool it on the PNR for a bit because despite Kenyon's really interesting world of the Hunterverse, this felt a little formulaic to me. It was also incredibly depressing reading about all of the tortures Zarek suffered as a slave. How much of that did we really need? I expected there to be a bigger dust up over Astrid's secret, and the love story felt too easy. It was fine, just not my favorite so far. This is the last of the series that I own already, and now I'm not in any rush to buy the next ones. This may have to be a library series for me.

 The long wait is over, Divergent 3 or Allegiant is now on the rampage. Divergent fans are waiting for this moment to come. The cliff hanger moment Veronica Roth left us from the second (2nd) book, Insurgent made as crave for more of Tris's senseless yet selfless ways in saving the world. But let me get this straight. Initially, I don't know how to say this in a less overt manner but I'll say it anyway, I dislike this Allegiant (Divergent 3). I hated almost everything. There are too many conflicts, too many characters dead, too many romance scene, and not to mention, the almost-unpredictable and unlikeable ending. &^@Q$*(%(*&%#q*&%^*!~ 
 To the reader's convenience, I tried to widen the thoughts I have during and after reading the Allegiant. 
 (WARNING: TOO MANY SPOILERS AND HARSH COMMENTS AHEAD) 
 First off, Allegiant has too many conflicts, seemingly interesting conflicts, and WTF extra scenes 
 From the beginning of the story (almost 100 pages long), the book focuses on the battle between the factions and the factionless. And then another faction showed up and introduced themselves as the Allegiants. The narration of the story began focusing on the newly introduced characters (not necessarily new people in the story but new title or category of certain group of people) totally forgetting about the conflict about the factions and the factionless. I almost assumed that the story's pace to another conflict would resolve the first one out but then it seems like it was completely forgotten. 
 The seemingly super awesome, frightening and mind-boggling plot turned into romance and chaos (and by chaos I mean instances where foolishness and the like survive). The book started with Tris Prior still stuck in the shattered faction-based society that she once believed in. It was fissured by violence and power struggles by power hungry people which were blinded by a scarred past or by loss and betrayal. Tris and the other dauntless people were offered a chance to explore the world past the limits known to them. This is a difficult book to rate because at times it's a 1 and then a 3 and I can even see how readers could give it a 5 star rating. It's an inspirational romance that at times is quite heavy on the religious aspect in my opinion. If the idea of a kind of self-sacrifice to the extreme that doesn't seem to benefit anyone apart from God (but even then that's debatable) appeals to you, then you'll probably like this book. I didn't particularly enjoy it, but I could appreciate it. 
 It's not the greatest writing in the world. It's very simple in style and reminded me of something like the Good News Bible where Biblical verse is written in a more modern, accessible way with a simplistic approach to what is otherwise complicated religious dogma when you really look at it. The relationship between the two frontier families is a bit too utopian but fits in with this striving-to-be- like-God ideal and there's nothing wrong with that, but I think you have to like reading about that sort of "wholesomeness". There's a note from the publisher that says it's a PG 13 novel and maybe for people who read inspirational romances it is but I didn't think so. There was one very brief disgusting scene but given the situation and the period I thought that was misleading to brand it PG 13. There is virtually no physical intimacy in this book, apart from the odd kiss, and any sex is glossed over leaving you wondering if they had sex or not. The violence in the novel is treated the same way and I think it's a disservice not to "show" the reader what the author is seeing. You get these one liners about horrific beatings, great sex on a very spiritual level but no detail. The author shows a lot about God but not enough about the h/h together as a married couple. Emotional, spiritual and physical intimacy make for better rounded characters I think and I felt short changed not to get all that. The book could probably be a good 4 1/2 stars if this aspect of the writing had been developed. 
 The hero and the heroine are very well-drawn. Michael is a true saint and if you took away his devout belief in God he'd make one of the best romance heroes around. He gets kicked in the teeth so many times but he still keeps coming back for more. He reminded me of poor Job at times. His self-sacrifice skirts the incredulous and I still can't see what he got out of it during those years of waiting. His character's endless patience reminds me of Sarah McCarty's Asa in Promises Linger. As for Angel/Sarah, she is such an irritating/stupid woman. She has heaven in hand and she keeps throwing it away. Her life is a nightmare and it's a wonder she never killed herself to get out of it, but I had a hard time understanding that after so much unconditional love from Michael that she felt too she ended up leaving him. 
 It was difficult to believe all this love at first sight and God speaking to these people in mysterious ways. It's the Old Testament mysterious mean God in this story at times who takes everything away and you get to live in emotional hell. Why I don't know and that's what I really didn't like about this book from a romance perspective. Michael's a good guy why keep testing him? Angel has been through hell and back why have her leave her haven incessantly? I guess you could say that they both had things to do first before they could be together but I think they really wasted some very valuable time that they could've been better spent together. 
 The epilogue is quite moving and God finally decides to give something back apart from just his love which is supposed to be the true reason for living, but I didn't really see what kind of happiness it brought these people because without each other they were horribly sad and lost. 
 If you take the novel as a retelling of the Book Hosea(what little I know about it) it's pretty good, but if you read it as a romance you may be disappointed. So two stars for romance, four for the retelling of the Book of Hosea for me. 
 FYI: If devout believers who see God in everything as well as true faith being the only way to find happiness in life bother you, you may want to pass on this book.

I was approved an ARC of this book by the publishers via NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. This review in its entirety was originally posted at eclectictales.com: http://www.eclectictales.com/blog/201... 
 The atmosphere of the novel definitely reminds me of Hannah Kent's Burial Rites: that sense of isolation and stillness, the haunting mysteriousness of the cold landscape. Maija and her daughters endured much over the course of that winter, on top of the mystery concerning the mysterious and eerie death of Eriksson. It's the perfect setting for a mystery and a character drama. 
 The story itself had a bit of a slow start despite of its powerful opening of finding Eriksson's lifeless body as the relationships of the characters and their respective situations were established. It was interesting in order to understand where these characters are coming from-especially as the story progresses-but I felt it meandered a little too long before turning back to the main story. It's a tale of twists and turns, with political maneuverings and hints of the supernatural playing a role in Maija and Frederika's respective investigations into Eriksson's mysterious death and its effect on the community. Interwoven throughout is the changes happening within Maija's family as Paavo goes off to work at the coast for the winter and Frederika is transitioning to adolescence and Maija finds herself unable to keep up with the changes. 
 These are all excellent story threads and kept me turning the page-the reveal about the priest, Olaus, was unexpected-and provided complexity to the mystery of Eriksson's death. However, I felt the novel ended rather abruptly. There was the reveal behind Eriksson's death and the reason behind it, as well as hints on the general directions of where the characters go after the last page, but I felt it could've used a few more scenes at the end to wrap things up. I felt especially dissatisfied with the resolution to Maija and Frederika's mother-daughter relationship; does it improve afterwards or does it remain at stalemate forever? 
 Overall though I enjoyed reading Wolf Winter. The desolation of the story and the landscape really came to life and it had its lyrical moments to compliment the sparceness of the atmosphere. The climax and wrap-up of the story left me wanting, but for the most part kept me glued to the story once the narrative took off. I would recommend this book for readers who enjoy mystery in their historical fiction and who enjoy books set in the Scandinavian countries.

This book was on everyone's lips for a time so I had to see what the fuss was all about. While I read a lot of books known to stand the literary test of time, this was a new one when I picked it up so I was hesitant about its ability to live up to the hype. It was a fun read with varying vantages which brought a personal feeling to the situation. The old saying about walking in someone else's shoes comes to mind. It is so true to life that everyone seems to think that what they are doing is the right thing and we often don't realize how our words and actions affect others. 
 I'll be the first to admit that when an author writes in multiple voices it takes me a couple of chapters to keep everyone straight, with that being said, The Help is an exception. Kathryn Stockett clearly voices each character and smoothly transitions between them all in a way that has them portrayed more along the lines of actual people in the world rather than just single dimensional characters in a book. 
 1962 Mississippi is no place to be, white, privileged Eugenia, more commonly known as Skeeter because of her likeness to a mosquito has recently returned home from college and much to her mother's disappointment there is no ring on her finger. Aibileen has just returned to working for a white family since the death of her own child and Minnie, the best cook in the county is hard pressed to find a family to work for since she has quite of habit of speaking her mind, something that a white family just won't put up with. 
 As each woman's story is told a truer picture of the segregated south emerges. When they decide to work in unison to write a book from the black domestics perspective looking at the white families they have loved and served a whole new picture emerges. The fear of being discovered, of actual prison time becomes all to real, but it's a story that has to be told. A story that in a way will free them all. 
 At times you will be shocked, mortified, and laughing out loud, these women will have you hearing what they have to say for a very long time. Whether my heart was aching for the characters, feeling anxious right along with them or laughing at their antics they all came to life in a way that left me thinking about them long after I had finished the book. The Help spins a tale about common household "Help" & the families who employee them. Loved it!

 This is not your typical college love story. It is a nice reversal of the good girl and bad boy coming together. Here we have the more experienced, liberal Monica (scarred by a physical and emotional trauma) starting a relationship with the picture-perfect conservative governor's son, Trey. 
 The story started somewhat slow for me. There was too much politics involved at the beginning and the characters were presented solely through their political views. Gradually, though, they became much more real and likeable. I really liked the middle section of the novel with their romantic courtship, and there was real romance there (roses, dinners, morning coffees, etc.). The witty banter between Miss Remy and Mr. Chapman was particularly enjoyable and put a happy smile on my face. 
 The novel got somewhat heavier towards the end. The serious issues (rape, contraception  were dealt with in a realistic and convincing manner. They were presented in a graphic manner, yet their impact on everybody involved was presented quite successfully. 
 The ending showed the growth of the characters and the blend of the personal and the political without losing your personal values and beliefs. 
 There were also some things in the novel that I did not like very much, hence the 3-star rating. The political messages were too strong and they seemed to overtake the story at times. There were also too many repetitions (politician-in-making, political smile in reference to Trey, my only exception, etc. . I understand they serve to make a point but I find they were overused and became boring. At times the characters acted too good to be true and they did not sound very convincing. 
 Yet, overall I liked the book. It is a sweet story of true love, overcoming trauma and learning that there are always exceptions to the rules :)

Much of the story is focused on Dr Frankenstein's formative years, a quick undetailed creation story and then his pursuit of the monster he created. I'm still not quite sure what to make of this book. In many respects, I suppose that's indicative of some inherent level of quality. The writing tends toward exceptional, and there are so many rich themes lurking just under the water--visible, yet teasingly beyond simple definition--that quality was never in doubt. My wavering opinion rests more on the fact that I'm not sure whether I truly enjoyed the experience. 
 The conceptual layout of the book is picture perfect postmodernism. The Part A/Part B division was intended to reflect a concept album from the golden years of rock. Each chapter tells a new piece of the overall story through a new narrator, using their unique point of view in overlapping and concentric tales. The story bounces between past, present and future with the reader expected to sort out the details. Heck, one of the chapters is even a self-contained slide show! While all these elements combined to tease and tantalize, there wasn't enough narrative thread to pull things together tight enough for my tastes. 
 There were times when I felt I was reading a whole bunch of previously published short stories, all dealing with the same narrative core, that some enterprising author had decided to publish as a novel with some gimmicky features to razzle-dazzle readers into seeing more than what was really there. Then I reflected on how well everything fit together, and I must admit that there is some real genius behind what the cynic in me sees as gimmicky. And the more I reflect on the stories, the more I'm able to see thematic allusions that thread through several different chapters. This is a book that could easily work its hooks into me and have me raving about it in a few months or years, but my current response is rather mixed.

 Karou as a character was interesting. People that know me and have read this book have said to me that I remind them a lot of Karou. I too had blue hair, sported tattoos, was an art student (still am), and had a streak of an adventurous soul in high school. But all in all although I found Karou an interesting character I felt that all the potential to explore her character any further in this book ended once Akiva shows up, and ultimately led me to see Karou as a character I couldn't really relate too. 
 But in general.... 
 Things I liked about this book: 
 - The writing was strong and lyrical. It felt like I was reading a song. 
 - Highly effective imaginative world building 
 - Great cast of supporting characters. 
 - I was interested in the Chimaera world, and thought the different species of Chimaera were really interesting to explore. 
 - Interesting plot. I enjoyed the whole concept of the book. 
 Things I didn't like so much: 
 - GOD was this overwritten. I found at points that I had read pages without retaining any information from it, I would go back to see what I had missed, and it would turn out I hadn't missed anything because of how overwritten it was.

So... to be honest, I was not expecting to like this book very much. I recent read Delirium and heard this book was very similar, but that it wasn't as good as Delirium. So, my expectations were very low. I don't know if that's why I enjoyed the book so much, or not. 
 To be fair, there are a LOT of similarities between the Delirium series and this one... Main Character is a female, young and naive. Thinks that her perfect society is perfect and spotless only to slowly uncover the truths behind the twisted government. Love interest that then tears down the walls of the world the main character has believed in her whole life. 
 But really that's it. I really liked the way the author put together this world. It seemed real to me. There are a lot of dystopian novels out there, and so often the world is unclear or not explained well enough, but that isn't the case here. I don't know how the world got to the point it is in the story, but I still believed it when I was reading it. 
 I have also heard that this story mirrors another called The Giver, but I never read that one, so I don't know. Either way, I will stop comparing this book to other books and just review This one. 
 I loved the writing. It was fluid and even almost poetic at times. I loved that the author actually found some perfect poems to fit into the story, whether she worked the story around those poems or found the poems later, I don't know... and either way, it doesn't matter. It just worked. And I loved it. 
 I loved the world she created- and the way she showed that every person truly believed in this society that controlled everything in their lives, from what they ate (they couldn't even buy their own food and were never allowed to grow their own food) to what they wore, who they were Matched with, how many kids they could have and even when they would die. It seemed more like an ACTUAL dystopian novel, than most out there right now. 
 The characters were great. Though I never felt like I could feel Cassia's emotions. I felt like she was so subdued, and I should have been able to feel more. Though, I loved Xander and felt so bad for him. I loved Ky and felt we truly got to understand him, and his broken past. 
 I really don't like love triangles, and Im really tired of them. This is my biggest issue with this story. Xander is the logical choice. She has known and cared for him ( and he for her) for their whole lives... and just all of a sudden she loves Ky?? 
 I like Ky... but I don't get the decision, and as I already mentioned, I never really felt any of Cassia's emotions, so Its not like I felt her love for Ky... 
 Overall, I really liked the book. WAY more than I expected to. I liked Delirium better... but... I don't know. Im about to start Crossed, book 2, so maybe ill end up liking this series better.

This book is a space opera, but it's a space opera between the start of space exploration and settling on far-off galaxies. This world has people who inhabit Earth, Mars, and the Asteroid Belt (known as the "Belt"). There are some people who live off of some of the gas giants' moons (I can't remember which is the farthest out, possibly it was Neptune, but it isn't important in the story other than giving you a general sense of how far people have gone), but for the most part it focuses on those three. It's showing that humanity has expanded their space exploration and habitation, but it's not at the point of finding far-off alien worlds; we are still in our solar system. We deal with some prejudices and politics that arise when people live on other worlds, even if they aren't that far away. 
 Our chapters alternate between two different perspectives. Our first is James Holden, a 2nd-in -command of a space ship that hauls ice from the rings of Saturn to the Belt. Holden is an Earth-native and used to serve in it's Navy, but was discharged and now enjoys ice hauling. The Belt doesn't really generate any resources on their own, so they rely on services like ice hauling to get water and other life necessities. While out on a run, the ship receives an emergency signal from another ship, and it's law to go help out people stranded in the middle of space, so Holden and a set of selected crew take a shuttle out to investigate. 
 Our other point of view is of a Belter, ie someone born and raised on the Belt, Miller. He's a detective and his new assignment is to find a missing rich person's daughter, Julie Andromeda Mao. Julie is originally from Earth, so it's a bit of an interesting case as Miller learns more about her character. He gradually becomes obsessed with her and honestly it was creepy. 
 I'll stop the summary there, but obviously it's a bit of mystery plus action-adventure. I liked Holden a lot better than Miller. As I said, Miller was creepy. Miller isn't supposed to be a likable character, either, he's supposed to be giving a contrasting perspective. 
 I saw the 1st season of the TV show before reading this, and I can say that I like the chemistry of Holden and his crew a lot better in the book. It helps to get all the internal thoughts that you really only get from reading, but the TV show puts a lot of emphasis on drama between the characters when they don't really exist in the book. Well, except for Naomi and Holden, but that wasn't in the first season really. It's a romance,  and it's to be expected. 
 4 stars for the whole book, but I didn't like how everything resolved, so I want to lower it to 3 just for the ending. It was a dumb, as in stupid, as in not really making sense at all, ending. But I plan on continuing the series as well as going to watch the 2nd season of the TV show, so I'll stick with 4 stars which was what I thought I was giving it until the ending. REALLY? Miller ends up planning to kill himself on the infested asteroid, Eros, and then finds out Eros is really being controlled by Julie. We think Julie was killed off by the protogen, but it turns out this magical alien-virus took over control of Julie instead??????????????? What????? Then Miller, since he basically loves the girl he never met, convinces her to drive the asteroid into Venus instead of Earth, thus saving Earth from the disease (or whatever it actually is). It's not even a good twist, it just makes me uncomfortable. I also just HATED Miller's obsession with Julie, and the fact that it gets "redeemed" (for lack of a better word) just makes me angry.

I'm pleased to report that my second Rainbow Rowell went down nice and easy. Last week was Eleanor & Park, this week it was Fangirl. Also, I took a trip to the library today and procured Rowell's other two books. Attachments and Landline are waiting in the wings. So, why have I decided to binge on one author's written works? First of all, Rowell's prose is so very readable. She has a talent for conjuring compelling scenes out of character-driven plots and fashioning dialogue so real that you can hear the conversations play out in your head. I found this to be true in Eleanor & Park and the trend continued in Fangirl. Second, it's fun, every now and then, to consume one author's works in their entirety. You become so aware of an author's personal style and technique. There's also the added rush of achieving expert status on a certain writer. Think about it. For how many authors can you say that you've read everything they've written? Including short stories? For me, not very many. But anyways, onto the synopsis... 
 Fangirl follows freshman Cath Avery during her first year of college. Unlike her twin sister, Wren, Cath is not excited to be entering the halls of higher education. Cath is anxious and reclusive, a bit prickly, and prefers to spend her time engaged with her hobby -- writing Simon Snow fanfiction. (Simon Snow is a stand-in for Harry Potter.) During the school year, Cath's established lifestyle is rocked by... 
 Moving away from home, Omaha, Nebraska, to Lincoln, Nebraska 
 Leaving her bipolar father behind 
 Dealing with the growing distance between her sister and herself 
 Having a strong personality for a roommate 
 Having said roommate's boyfriend be around all the time 
 and Taking a fiction writing class with an esteemed professor who doesn't recognize fanfiction as a legitimate or acceptable form of fiction writing 
 Like I typically do with books when my ADD is bad, I started out Fangirl by listening to the audiobook, and switched over to page format once I got hooked on the storyline. (Once I get hooked, there's no prying me away.) This happened fairly soon with Fangirl; I'd say I was reading the e-book by chapter two. 
 I can't say that Fangirl was a life-altering book, but it was solidly written, had a good flow, distinct characters, great dialogue, and a sweet romance. I'd even say I enjoyed it slightly more than Eleanor & Park. In Fangirl, the characters are slightly older, which made them a bit more relatable to me. However, for both books, I was completely sucked in, emotionally -- both laughing and tearing up. 
 What got to me especially in Fangirl was the character of Arthur, Cath's father. He struggles with bipolar disorder and his storyline shot me right in the heart. I think he may go down as one of my favorite fictional dads. 
 Other highlights: realistic portrayal of twins, fantastic interactions between Cath and her roommate, hilarious bits of dialogue, honest depiction of romance, and emotionally moving moments. 
 Lowlights: I sped-read through a lot of the fanfiction excerpts, although I realize that their presence was necessary. The plot meanders, especially around the middle. 
 So, that's that. I give Fangirl four north stars out of five. 
 Be sure to stay tuned for my next Rowell review, of Attachments. Thanks, always, for reading!

Suspension of disbelief makes this a wonderful story. I am fully aware of that. Because if I truly sat and thought about how this sort of thing would work, it doesn't really make sense to me. How can someone exist without having a physical form? Is he just...a ghost, or something? And why are there rules about age and distance? 
 And I think A can be a little selfish. I think he should have stuck by his rules, and not screwed some people's lives up so much. The one that got me was when his host was supposed to leave for Hawaii with his family, and he forced him to miss the flight. What if that was the one time the family was able to afford a family trip like that, and he was forced to miss the trip? If they had to reschedule, flights aren't cheap. If he missed the trip, then it's a whole other headache of trying to get refunds. It didn't really seem fair. 
 What really got me was Rhiannon. I haven't read the first book, the original one from A's point of view. So going in, this was a brand new story for me. Rhiannon's story is one that I think is a little too familiar. She has accepted her lot in life, because she believes she can do no better. Her boyfriend, Justin, is not a kind person. He's stressed all the time, and extremely angsty. He's far too focused on things that don't matter--drinking and videogames are not in and of themselves bad things, but when those are the only things he cares about, it's a problem. He takes out all of that unhappiness, anger, and dissatisfaction and channels it all into Rhiannon--making her question everything. It was not a healthy relationship, and I was so frustrated that she allowed herself to be treated this way. It reminded me intensely of the phrase from The Perks of Being a Wallflower: we accept the love we think we deserve. It was pretty illuminating, and I can't help but feel that the first novel (from A's point of view) would not have been nearly as effective for me because of this lack. 
 Rhiannon is the girl who doesn't realize she has anything to offer. She's the girl who got a boyfriend and faded away--she no longer had her own individual identity, she took on the traits Justin had as an extension of him, like an extra arm. And although this is certainly bad enough, it is only made worse by how Justin constantly kept her in a state of uncertainty. It was a power play to show her just how worthless she was, and how important he should be. I hated it. 
 Which is why I loved A so much. I didn't necessarily need all the extra stuff about him hopping from body to body, though it was mildly interesting. What drew me in was Rhiannon's road to self-discovery. She learns to finally listen to her friends, the people who genuinely care about her happiness. She learns to look at her relationship objectively, and more importantly she learns to find something that makes her happy, not uncertain. A's ability to appreciate Rhiannon in a manner befitting her made her realize just how important she truly was. 
 So truly, my rating for the body snatcher thing is fairly low. It doesn't make much sense, and sort of seems to just make up arbitrary rules just because (though I loved that A did not relate to either male or female, since he (she) has always been both. Loved that.) The reason for my rating is because Rhiannon's self-discovery was the best part, and I liked seeing her strength slowly and discreetly grow.

Consequences ended in a way so that book two could be awesome... but all of the comments about how you will feel differently about The Abusive Asshole after reading the second book... I just don't know if I can stand seeing him portrayed in a sympathetic way. I don't care how unhappy his childhood was or whatever other bullshit excuses that will come up in the second book, that does not make the things he did in Consequences okay! 
 This book was very emotional. I chose this book partly because people described it as being a "mindfuck." I can't describe it with that term, but it is an emotional rollercoaster. With the main emotions from me being ones of anger, outrage, and sadness. I will say, I never once felt any sympathy for The Abusive Asshole, even when he was doing really nice and sweet things. In real life, abusive partners can be sweet and loving and caring, but it isn't real... It is a way for the abuser to keep their victim off balance. And it is portrayed quite well in Consequences how off balance Anthony makes Claire. 
 There is one scene in particular I need to point out to backup my argument that Anthony Rawlings is nothing more than an abusive and controlling man... This is the sort of thing I imagine a being said between a battered wife and her abusive husband: 
 Tony: "I can't promise I will never get upset. I can probably promise I will. However, I promise I will do my best to never hurt you like that again. But I need something from you. ... I want you to make me a promise. A promise, that you will do your best to follow my rules. That you will do your best - to never give me cause to hurt you again." 
 What kind of bullshit promise is that?!?!? I won't hurt you again as long as you don't make me hurt you. It is your fault that I hit you. If you would just do what I tell you to do, I won't hurt you. Why is that so hard? I don't want to hurt you, but you make me do it. Just imagine that being said by a middle class man to his wife who is curled up in the floor in the corner of the kitchen after he hit her because supper wasn't on the table when he walked in the door. 
 How is that different from multi-millionaire Anthony Rawlings beating Claire because she wasn't in his office at the exact minute he dictated she be there? It isn't, and it is not okay! 
 I don't know if I am going to read Truth or not. I want to, I want to see Claire get the revenge she began plotting at the end of Consequences  but I'm just not sure that is really going to happen and I just don't know if my heart and my nerves can stand to see Claire fall for Anthony after everything he did to her. Every nice thing he does and excuse he gives in Truth, I will flash back to the quote above... I won't hurt you if you don't make me hurt you.....

Colleen Hoover is a great writer and I don't doubt her abilities to create beautiful novels but This Girl just didn't hook something new for me. This Girl is not for me. After I have read 2 of the Slammed series (Slammed and Point of Retreat), I was in deep awe. As much as I don't want to get disappointed....I can't because I really feel discouraged to read more of this. 
 The Point of Retreat's mop-up led to Lake and Will's final statement of locking their selves into the real and legal adult life. Thus, came This Girl. This Girl more likely contains mixed up questions and answers from the star-crossed lover's life back in the Slammed and Point of Retreat. To sum it up, it is Lake's Post-Wedding Interrogation of Will". And the gist of all this is that, it is told through Will Cooper's point of view (while having their honeymoon). Did I just make that sound bad? If I did, it's absolutely not my fault. :p 
 I didn't hate This Girl but I didn't like it very much either. It wasn't bad at all, but there's lot of parts where I actually said, 'I read that already' and 'Yep, I can still recall it immediately from Slammed'. Hence, there was too much I already knew. I am not saying that the writing was awful. It is still congruent and nice but it was just too much of Slammed. There were glimpse of Honeymoon scenes after the flashbacks but it was too repetitive for me. 
 And don't get me started with Will Cooper. Will's perspective was just okay but I think he was too feminine. I might even get goosebumps and butterflies if he had sounded a little bit manlier. 
 I think the ultimate thing I hate about this book is how it made me dislike both characters in different ways. There were times I thought that Lake is being too paranoid and was being too much of a spoiled brat. And it was so frustrating and annoying. I cannot live with that! -__-

Warning - there were be spoilers from the first book and one spoiler from this book. 
 Plot 
 Now that the lines are drawn, Kami and the gang are focused on getting more sorcerers to join their side and trying to figure out how exactly to beat Rob. And now that the link has been broken, Jared has reverted back to his reckless, bad boy default and Kami can no longer read him, this boy she's always known as well as herself. While there are some developments and sweet moments, just not a lot happened. I felt like this book kind of fell into the sophomore slump, where it's mostly holding pace until the third book. 
 *SPOILER ALERT*Also, did I miss something somewhere? Jared and Kami cannot be linked again? I thought they could. Or is that only if he makes it through the suicidal ceremony in the Crying Pools? If that's the case, then Kami linking with Ash makes more sense because at the time I was a little bewildered why she just let Jared go out and fight and then linked with Ash. And Ash didn't really do much with the power surge. *END OF SPOILER* 
 Even though the ending made me a little angry, I wasn't entirely expecting it, so that makes up for it a little bit. I hate to be able to call everything that happens. And it guarantees that I'll be reading the next book (out sometime this year, but no release date that I've seen yet). 
 Characters 
 Pretty much every character is more developed in this book and I love it. In addition to Kami's POV, we also get Holly and Ash. While I can't say that getting their view has endeared either of them to me any more than before, I do feel like I understand them better. Ash reminds me a lot of Tobias in Allegiant - Spends most of the book feeling sorry for himself and desperately wanting the love of his parents, even though they're horrible people. I also enjoyed the more we got to see of Kami's dad, Lillian, and Rusty. I would've liked a little more Rob, though, just to see what the other side is up to. 
 Readability 
 Brennan's style is still clever and witty, but I didn't find it quite as good as the first book. I spent a long time being annoyed that we weren't getting Jared's POV, but after thinking about it, I think it was the smart move. Kami had always known how Jared was feeling, but now with the link gone she finds that she can't read him. By not getting Jared's POV, we are also like Kami, not always understanding his motivation or what he means. Though I will say, as I mentioned in my review of the first book, when it comes to Jared's feelings for Kami I think it's pretty obvious that he's saying one thing and meaning another. And I was pleased that we do get some of Jared's POV towards the end of the book. 
 Enjoyability 
 While I didn't love this book as much as the first, I still really enjoyed it. The writing style is still unique and while I felt the plot dragged a little, the character development really helped make up for it. This is a series I would still recommend and will be anxiously waiting for the next installment. 
 Rating (out of 5): 
 Plot: 3 
 Characters: 4 
 Readability: 4 
 Enjoyability: 4 
 Overall Average: 3.75 stars

What sets Graceling apart from other books in its genre is the writing. I often found the prose to be quite lovely. Normally, I'm content with adequate. After all, this is young adult, fantasy, quasi romance and not a literary work. I'd like to not be so surprised by a published author's authority over language, but here I am. Some wonderful descriptions, clever turns of phrase and snappy dialogue. That's what made this a page turner. The notion of the gracelings has the right touch of magical mystery: no one understands how they work, and some of the graces are a bit crazy, but everyone in the world is fully aware they are out there and accepts (well, not always accepts, but acknowledges) them as part of their world. 
 What fell short was the pacing, the plotting, and the aspects of the main character I didn't get. I liked Katsa, I really did. I'd even like to read more about her. In fact, I would have liked to read more about her in this first book so maybe I'd understand what drives her to make the decisions she does. I'll explain in spoiler la la land. 
 I get that Katsa is reluctant to be tied down by a man after being used by one most of her life. But really? It never occurred to her that she could have a lover without marrying him? Never occurred? Then Po demonstrates that he's not the controlling sort, that he won't ever tie her down blah blah blah and she clearly loves him. So why can't she marry him? Why is she so sure she'll never have kids? Are kids nothing but prison wardens? This smacks of that Edward/Bella "we can't be together because then there wouldn't be enough conflict to sustain a book" stuff. Also, there's a strangely preachy feel in Katsa's exposition.  
 It's not that I don't like Katsa's decisions, but she is so absolutely convinced that this is the only way she can be and I don't understand why. If she didn't understand, I could sympathize. If I understood, I could accept it, whether I like it or not. 
 There are two big confrontations in the book. They both build up nicely and their is tremendous tension and everything is reader goodness - then, in both cases, the conflict wraps up in less than a page and everyone walks away with no further trouble. So, pacing is bit funny. I enjoyed the writing a good deal, liked the characters and the world in general, so even when we seemed to be just kind of hanging out, I liked the experience, but then when the action burst into the room only to run straight out the other side without so much as a "how do you do" - well, I found that disappointing. 
 There are some cool characters in here, especially the main two of course. There are some other stand outs though. I do wish they all had better names. I don't think you can get much nit-pickier than this, but really? Bitterblue? Po? Randa and Raffin, father and son, introduced about the same time so I am constantly confusing their names? 
 Eh-hem. A worthy, quick, enjoyable read.
