I am so so torn on this book. I've been really enjoying this series, especially the Victorian England setting and the romantic tension. However, there are quite a few things that started to get to me by the time I read this final installment in Clare's trilogy. 
 1. The book is set in Victorian England, but the characters don't really speak as if they're from that time period. Fine, I can suspend my disbelief for that part. But then why do they write letters in the parlance of Victorian England? Let's be consistent! Either they do or they do not speak and write in the language of their time. You can't have it both ways. 
 2. And there are so many letters in this book. It feels like an unnecessary and at times clumsy plot device. 
 3. Jem. I cannot stand that Clare has Jem become a Silent Brother. It seems like such a cop out. Plus, we just learned 200 pages earlier why Jem was passionately against becoming a Silent Brother. I find his decision to do so unrealistic given what we know about him. 
 4. The epilogue.  And then to top it all off, Clare undoes Jem's Silent Brother conversion, conveniently after Will has died. So now Tessa gets to live a lifetime with both of her loves. Again, another cop out. And I'm pretty sure they mentioned that the Silent Brother thing was permanent, yes? How can you un-sew someones eyelids and mouth, anyway? I was fine with the whole Tessa loves both parabatai thing because of the special relationship between Jem and Will. But really. Pick one or the other. I feel like it just cheapened everything to end on that note. Though I'm sure those on team-Jem will disagree.  
 5. Finally, the cover! Ugh. Tessa would never make that ridiculous face. 
 So, yes, I was conflicted, and for that reason this one only gets 3 stars.

A Shade of Vampire 
 By Bella Forrest 
 A Shade of Vampire #1 
 Here is another one of those books that I downloaded a long time ago but didn't read because when I read the first few pages and discovered it was about a 17-year-old girl, I stopped reading it. I have a hard time reading romance books about protaganists who are in their teens because I can't take them seriously. Most of them have never lived life beyond high school, never had a job, never had an apartment or had to pay bills and never had the worries that go along with being an adult. They have never had a relationship while trying to earn a living. I try to avoid teenage romance books when I can but I came across this one again so I decided to give it another chance. I was pleasantly surprised. This book was a pretty good read. 
 Once I got past the weird alternating POV thing, I really got into this book. The chapters alternate first person POVs. One chapter, it will be Sofia's POV and the next Derek's and sometimes other characters. 
 Sofia Claremont was upset with her best friend Ben, with whom she has deeper feelings for than just a friend, because he forgot her birthday. She goes for a walk on the beach and gets abducted and taken to a hidden island where it is always dark thanks to a magical spell. The island is full of vampires who have human as slaves. She and four other girls are given to the Derek, the prince, who has just woken from a 400-year nap and is starving for blood. 
 Sofia and the girls are all frightened but she takes the hand of the blonde girl next to her to comfort her. Derek noticed this and for some reason it endeared her to him but Sofia has a cut on her lip, thanks to an earlier encounter with Derek's psychotic brother, so Derek's hunger took over. He pinned Sofia against a column of the temple they were in and almost sank his teeth into her neck when she talked him out of it. Since then Sofia has been his favorite harem girl. 
 She soon learns that humans are not treated well on the island named The Shade. Vampires think of humans as playthings and as slaves and think nothing of killing them. Once a vampire bites a human, he or she becomes addicted to that human's blood. The vampires show very little control and usually kill the human by draining them within days. The human is lucky if they last a week. The most attractive humans are made playthings of the vampires while all the others are put to work keeping the island running. 
 Derek Novak helped save the vampires in his coven hundreds of years ago when humans called the hunters were after them. He, along with the help of a witch named Cora, built The Shade into a sanctuary. He sent out vampires to abduct humans for slaves and for blood while Cora used her magic to hide the island and make it eternally dark. 
 There is a prophesy about Derek saving his kind. After all the horrible things Derek did to make The Shade possible, he believed his part in the prophesy was completed and had Cora put a spell on him to sleep forever. However, Cora knew there was more to the prophesy than what Derek knew. She made sure to build into the spell that Derek was to awake when a girl came along that would help him save his kind or something like that. 
 This book was not your typical vampire book. Usually, there are good vampires and bad vampires but every one of these vampires seem not to care one iota about human life except for Derek who is conflicted. Before he met Sofia, he had no qualms about using and killing humans. Derek's thoughts were sometimes disturbing. He'd think about why he shouldn't just take what he wanted from Sofia or someone else and bend her to his will because he was the prince and what he wants he gets. The author wasn't always clear if he meant just taking blood from a person or raping them. I don't think I could ever like a character, no matter what he did to redeem himself afterwards, if he raped someone. It's strange how I can accept a killer but not a rapist. Derek has something dark within himself but being around Sofia helps him have a conscience. Derek goes to drink the blood of a captured hunter and had every intention of killing her but stopped himself just before her heart stopped. He was able to control himself. 
 There was a lot more going on in this book that I could tell would be part of the future plot which intrigued me. There is the threat of hunters finding them or other vampire covens around the world coming up against them. There's a threat from within because now that Derek is awake, he is changing things and people are unhappy. 
 Of course, I have already downloaded the next book in the series and started reading it.

Ann Smith has always been in love with her boss Jasha Wilder so when she needs his signature on an important document she plans to go to his home and seduce him only to find out he can actually turn into a wolf.

 This is the first Christina Dodd book I've ever read and although I didn't give this book a great rating I'm really looking forward to reading the rest of this series and seeing how everything unravels and the ending. I'm really looking forward to the third book Into The Shadow with the missing third brother who's gone dark and twisted!

Jasha was a really great alpha male who was trying not to turn to the dark-side by changing into his wolf and letting his anger over take him! Ann made a pretty good heroine all in all considering I didn't really like the start of this book, she was struggling with her own secret and thought it would ruin any chances she had of a relationship with Jasha.

From the pact with the devil, the family that we're introduced to and the main couple in this book. I think this is a great book to start a series with and I'm really looking forward to the reading the rest of them!

Fifteen year-old Jason is dealing with the loss of his mother, and taking care of his father, who is mentally unfit to take care of him. In dealing with loss and mental illness, Jason must find a way to deal with his father, school, and nosey friends, without getting separated from his father. 
 Crazy is not the book that I was expecting to read. I love the idea of a story about the challenges faced by families and friends of those with mental illness; however, this story was not able to captivate me the way it should have. 
  Jason's character is unreliable and unreasonable. He knows deep down that his father needs help, and does not try and find it for him. Instead he decides to hide the fact that his father needs help and ignores any help his friends try to give him. Jason is a child, taking care of another child, or so it seems.  
 This story had so many opportunities to show exactly what families go through in these situations. I have dealt with a similar experience, and this book did not provide the emotions that emanate from those situations. 
 There was a moment in the book that I felt was a good representation.  Specifically, the moment when Jason finally finds his dad at home after he has disappeared. This was the only moment in the book that I felt was sincere, and did not feel forced. It is difficult to deal with a family member that disappears, but that sense of relief that washes over you once they are found, it leaves you breathless.

He laughed. "What's to say? Great paintings--people flock to see them, they draw crowds, they're reproduced endlessly on coffee mugs and mouse pads and anything-you-like. And, I count myself in the following, you can have a lifetime of perfectly sincere museum-going where you traipse around enjoying everything and then go out and have some lunch. But--" crossing back to the table to sit again "--if a painting really works down in your heart and changes the way you see, and think, and feel, you don't think, 'oh, I love this picture because it's universal.' 'I love this painting because it speaks to all mankind.' That's not the reason anyone loves a piece of art. It's a secret whisper from an alleyway. Psst, you. Hey kid. Yes you." 
 From an obverse perspective, that quote from The Goldfinch almost exactly captures my overall ambivalence toward the novel. It's the book that everyone seems to be reading. The marketing campaign has ensured that I see the cover everywhere I look. It could very well become the book which defines this decade of literature. But did it change the way I see, think or feel? Was there some irresitable sibilance luring me from the alleyway? Not really. 
 That's not to say I don't see the merit. There is plenty to praise, and much that I appreciated. It just didn't speak to me. My reading experience was largely devoid of emotion. In addition to not truly caring about any of these characters, I have a tendency to cavil when plot twists are too coincidental (of which there were an abundance here), when some odd element becomes ubiquitous (it came to appear as though everyone had lost at least one parent in some dramatic fashion), or when there is an overuse of dramatic foreshadowing in flashbacks ("If I had only known how things would turn out..."). These may seem like petty objections, but I'm sure we all have those irrational triggers which sap the enjoyment from writing which we would likely otherwise admire. 
 There is also a part of me that wonders whether a shorter version might have been more enjoyable, but I don't think it would have changed much. Judging by the high praise and the sheer volume of 5-star ratings on Goodreads, the editing process turned out a novel with plenty of appeal. The prose is honestly sharp enough that the pages flew by despite my indisposition toward the story, which speaks volumes to me about the quality of the writing. My issue was just that I never found anything here to love.

 "Joana still had her mother. Reuniting with her mother was her motivation. She would slay dragons to get to her. Mother was anchor. Mother was comfort. Mother was home. " 
 If you've been following me for a while then you'll know that I have loved Sepetys other books, and she is an auto-read author for me at this point. Every one of her stories is accurate to the time period and the way she writes the characters makes you feel like your right there with them. 
 We follow four teenagers 
 Florian - A "german" who is caring a secret, a secret that could not only get him killed but those he is now traveling with as well. 
 Emilia - A young girl who is lost, parentless, pregnant, and terrified of most men in general now. 
 Joana - A nurse who is taking care of Ingrid, the shoe poet, Eva, and the wandering child (Klaus). Not only does she feel responsible for these four people, but she also wants to help as many others as possible and get back to her mother to try and right the wrong she feels she has done that caused her extended family to be sent away by Stalin's soldiers. 
 Alfred - A German Sailor who lives more in his head than in real life. 
 Each chapter is only a few pages long, and as we get towards the end of the book it gets to just a few sentences as we switch back and forth between the characters. I got so attached to most of these characters ( I found Alfred's part a little annoying with his mental letters he was constantly writing). By the time they got on the boat and you could tell that the end was near I didn't want the story to end, I didn't want the boat to leave port, and when the torpedo's hit my heart broke for all of the people on-board. 
 "The Wilhelm Gustloff was pregnant with lost souls conceived of war. They would crowd into her belly and she would give birth to their freedom." 
 The water was freezing, and there weren't enough life boats (only 12) once again, and the ones that were on board weren't filled to capacity due to panic. When the few survivors were picked up surprisingly considering they were surrounded by Russian Submarines, they were taken to safety, and towards the start of their new lives. 
 I also really loved the connection this book had with Between Shades of Gray with Joana being Lina's cousin. If anyone knows of any other books about this tragedy or Lithuanian's during the WWII please let me know. 
 I'll leave you with, the authors note from the acknowledgement 
 Every nation has hidden history, countless stories preserved only by those who experienced them. Stories of war are often read and discussed worldwide by readers whose nations stood on opposite sides during battle. History divided us, but through reading we can be united in story, study, and remembrance. Books join us together as a global reading community, but more important, a global human community striving to learn from the past. 
 What determines how we remember history and which elements are preserved and penetrate the collective consciousness? If historical novels stir your interest, pursue the facts, the history, memoirs, and personal testimonies available. These are the shoulders that historical fiction sits upon. When the survivors are gone we must not let the truth disappear with them. 
 Please, give them a voice. 
 This is why I love Historical Fiction and Ruta Sepetys books, she always reminds you that these books are based on real stories and that this is what some people's lives were really like during this time period.

Just read the first story (The Bloody Chamber) itself but wow it's really powerful and scary and sinister with an incredible atmosphere of oppression and withheld violence and a lot of suspense even though it's likely you know what's going to happen from the start. What stood out to me was a bit in the middle which breaks open the suppressed violence when she opens the book of art showing sadistic, violent, murderous paintings - the description is suddenly very explicit.  I feel deeply creeped out after reading it, it's really good 
 None of the others blew me away quite like the first one did (although to be fair it's the longest story in the collection) but I definitely enjoyed them a lot. They're either retellings of or strongly influenced by fairy tales - for most of them it's obvious what it's based on very quickly but it's either told very well bringing out undercurrents and ideas in the original stories you wouldn't have thought about before or with a different take on it. The only odd one is "The Courtship of Mr Lyon" which seems like a really straight version of Beauty and the Beast  but I'm probably missing some stuff with that. The themes of misogyny, objectification of women, virginity, etc crop up a lot. The stories generally have a sinister/gothic/surreal vibe except for Puss in Boots which is humorous and bawdy. Her descriptions are really good at evoking an atmosphere although she uses a lot of really obscure words and I was glad to be reading on an ereader so I could look stuff up easily heh. Sorry for kind of shallow review but I liked it

Oh, god, feelings. This book was like a punch to the gut in the best way. I didn't think I'd enjoy it as much as I wanted to but by the end, I was almost moved to tears. (I say "almost" because I was in public, whereas if I had been on my own I definitely would have been weeping.) 
 Silvera tackles so much--depression, sexuality, teenage boyhood--with grace. It's beautifully written and really compelling, although I'll admit that the first chapter didn't grab me the way I wanted it to. Aaron is such a sympathetic character and I felt for him so much throughout the book that I wanted him to end up happy in a way I haven't experienced in a while for any protagonist. 
 One thing I LOVED about this book was the depiction of Genevieve. As Aaron's girlfriend who is also aware that he's gay, she was wonderfully sensitively written. I really appreciated how she wasn't the straw, villainous straight girlfriend, but nuanced and complex. Her love for Aaron shines through, and I loved the scene towards the end where they reaffirm their love for one another in a platonic manner. God. Feelings everywhere.  I mean, really, most of the characters (with the exception of some of the minor/"crew" characters--I couldn't really differentiate Brendan's personality from Baby Freddie's, if I'm honest) were so real, while living in a slightly different society. 
 The premise felt a little Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, but it averted a few tropes. There are twists and turns galore! I did not see it coming that Aaron had already had the procedure--I was about to put the book down to go do my yoga until that bit, then I read for another twenty minutes.  It was well-imagined and compelling. 
 If you're looking for a light read, this is not it. But if you're looking for something complex with layers of ambiguity--especially with that ending--this is the book for you.

Many people recommended Divergent to me as a book that I would enjoy. 
 It is exceedingly interesting (and telling) that after all those people had read Allegiant (but before I had) they came back and, in the most delicate, gentle way possible, rescinded their original recommendation. One told me she wished she'd never finished the books. One emailed: "Have you ever been on a cross country trip and had an unexpected delay at, say, an airport of the large Midwestern hub variety? You were just waiting and waiting and nothing seemed to be happening? And when things did finally happen you were so rushed and felt so unpleasant that you longed for a return to the lengthy delay? That is literally how you might feel." I did not realize at the time that he meant that "literally" literally.  
 I feel for Roth. I feel like she thought she had this great idea for a novel and then realized that writing science fiction--especially the world-building bit--is way harder than she expected. 
 In a science fiction book, the science either has to make some sort of sense or at least have a compelling reason for us to suspend our disbelief. Roth never pulled that off. She told us a lot about genetics and divergence, but none of it actually made sense or showed up in the actions in a rational way. 
 Almost nothing in Allegiant makes sense. Much of what we learn contradicts everything we thought we learned in the first few books. (This has the potential, used once, to be original and enlightening, but loses effectiveness logarithmically the more it happens.) Roth didn't execute the dual narration well. 
 The events of the ending didn't upset me quite as much as it could have because I was so proud of Roth for making a brave plot decision. (As she points out repeatedly, though, there is a very fine line between brave and stupid, and just because it's brave doesn't mean it's not also stupid.) 
 I'm glad we didn't get the trite, facile ending I thought we were. 
 It would have been nice if there had been any sort of resolution, any sort of message or lesson. But there wasn't other than, "Wow, humans are screwed up." I didn't learn anything. I didn't think any new thoughts (unless vivid and upsetting nightmares count). I didn't enjoy spending time with any of the characters. I didn't like spending time in their world, which was not only grim but nonsensical. 
 I can't recommend this book and I shudder to think about the movie.

Short version review: This started out really freaking weird, then downsized the weird to a more tolerable level, then had a pretty awesome ending. 
 Longer version: Shadow, for all intents and purposes a blank slate of a person, is recruited to help the enigmatic Mr. Wednesday gain popularity so people will join his side of an oncoming battle. Most of what's going on is hidden from Shadow, and therefore hidden from us as the reader. I found things out very slowly, and spent quite a bit of time trying to decipher which god was which. 
 I enjoyed that the most. Trying to guess which god was present based on the characteristics provided was fun in the nerdy sort of way. I know Greek mythology the best and only a basic understanding of several others. So I knew who Kali was, and Odin. I could guess the characteristics of the native American ones. I knew who the Morrigan were. And it was that sort of boundary crossing that drew me in--that, and the vagina sucking up a man. That's a good way of making me curious every time. 
 And the scheme!  Turns out Mr. Wednesday (Odin) doesn't actually care about winning the battle. He just wants to dedicate the battle to himself so any blood that is shed (god blood, no less) will strengthen him. He enlists the help of Loki (god of chaos) to make that happen....and Loki poses as Mr. World, the guy opposing Mr. Wednesday. Genius! Stupid Shadow and his dead wife for ruining it.  
 Yup. Also, Shadow brings his wife back from the dead, but her body is still rotting. At one point she feels maggots in her lungs. Gross.

I really enjoyed this book. Really, really enjoyed it. It was by no means a perfect book--Celaena was a borderline Mary Sue character at times--but there were far more good things about this book than bad. The world-building was superb. It was actually what motivated me to finally pick this book up after having it on my TBR for three years. I saw a lots of posts on Tumblr about the world and the characters, most of whom we didn't get to meet in this book, so I have confidence that this series will take off and deliver greatness to the fantasy genre. 
 Now as for the characters themselves. As I mentioned before, Celaena had a lot of Mary Sue qualities. She's the best assassin in the whole country despite being only an eighteen year old girl, and she was beatiful. Really, really, really beautiful. That is made perfectly clear. It made me roll my eyes occasionally that we were constantly reminded of her good looks and perfect badassery. However, being both good-looking and a badass isn't a crime if it's balanced well. And since it is also made clear that Celaena had to train for years to become the best helped create a balance, one which I hope will be made stronger as the series continues. I hope we get to see more of Celaena's flaws in later books, and that she becomes more well-rounded. One thing about her, though, that I really liked was that being a highly skilled assassin didn't stop her from being feminine. And in fact, once she got the opportunity, she went full-on girly-girl mode, with fancy gowns and jewelry and the whole shebang. Too often in fiction, you have female characters that are either feminine OR badass. You rarely see female characters who are both. This lack of traditionally feminine fighter characters sends the subtle message that femininity is weak, all while loudly claiming to have "strong female characters." I really appreciated that Celaena was able to switch gears from practical-minded assassin to feminine lady of court at the drop of a hat. I hope we meet a lot more characters like her, on a spectrum from traditionally feminine to not, because there are many kinds of strength. 
 Prince Dorian fell a bit flat in my opinion. It seemed like most of his characterization was based on his growing attraction to Celaena, at least throughout the first half of the book. He did become more developed and relatable as the narrative continued, which I appreciated. But I think he could have been presented this way earlier on, which would have made him much more interesting to read. I did appreciate his role in the love triangle, though (words I don't often say), mainly because although he was initially attracted to Celaena based on her looks, that reason ends up fading in favor of her actual personality. And though he doesn't forget that he finds her physically attractive (which would have been unrealistic), it's good to see a love triangle character forming a deeper bond with the main character. You don't see that very often, especially in YA. YA fiction has this bad habit of creating love triangles for the sake of dramatic tension and then not developing anybody beyond the main character, which makes them hard to believe. But the love triangle here was actually really believable, because it progressed slowly, and not always smoothly, and everybody involved was aware that there were way more important things to worry about (like who's killing all the champions and why?) than which man Celaena was going to fall in love with, if at all. 
 Continuing on the train of love-triangle characters, let's talk about Chaol. I think he was my favorite character in this book. Or at least favorite male character (because Nehemia was great, too). He's stoic, takes his job very seriously, and seems like the only sane man of the cast for a lot of the group. While Dorian is busy being Distracted by the Sexy, Chaol is constantly reminding him that Celaena was locked up in a death camp for a reason and he needs to not trust her so easily. And as time goes on, he gets to know Celaena better and grudgingly admits that she can be trusted, and despite being an assassin is still a regular person with a sense of morality, as opposed to a cold-hearted monster. His character development and growing friendship with Celaena felt the most realistic to me, out of everybody. 
 And finally, let's talk Nehemia. I LOVED her. She was sassy and fun and I really liked her friendship with Celaena. They both really needed it and it helped them both to grow so much over the course of the book. I want to talk more about her, but since so much of her character is a spoiler for major plot points, I won't. 
 I've already picked up Crown of Midnight. I have high hopes for this series. Keeping my fingers crossed that they're met.

This got rave reviews from most of my contacts/friends on GR. That said, while I can appreciate McCarthy's writing here, this book just didn't wow me the way I had anticipated based on my expectations. 
 The overall premise is an interesting one. A bleak post-apocalyptic world is a provocative story-line, always. And any story that focuses on a parent/child survival scenario is bound to hit us where it hurts the most (and hard). As a mother of four, I fully appreciate the parent/child relationship and the sacrifices one is willing to make as a result of that intense bond/love. 
 Stylistically though, this book just crossed the line too many times. I'm all for the artistic experience of literature, the lack of punctuation, the sentence fragments, the bleak imagery, the unusual paragraph formatting, the choice not to name any of the characters, and the simplistic Hemingway style dialogue. Okay. Okay. You sure. I'm sure. I get it. But one of my pet peeves is the artistic liberties established artists are allowed that would otherwise be a source of intense criticism, and for a valid reason. After a while, those liberties draw unnecessary attention to themselves and become distancing if not downright annoying. 
 Reading this, I was reminded of a short story by another critically acclaimed author, Fox 8 by George Saunders, where the author indulges in phonetic spelling as a literary device gone wrong. "Pure genius," some say. "Pooh-pooh," is my response. 
 I found this great review here on goodreads. In addition to being quite humorous, I think it summarizes my complaints so masterfully that I'm providing the link. 
 However, the stylistic indulgences weren't my only complaint here. The characters were undeveloped and felt anonymous, in addition to the fact that aside from things being bleak and desperate there is very little detail offered about their circumstances (arguably intentional but not for me nonetheless). And I kept getting the feeling that while already short, I might have enjoyed this more had it been 100 pages shorter. Didn't feel as if there was anything new here to warrant 250 pages. 
 Bottom line: powerful imagery (even if overdone) and a provocative premise, but just way too distancing to really be enjoyable or even thought provoking. Some might claim that the distancing was intentional, and maybe it was, but that doesn't mean it works for everyone. I didn't hate it, but I didn't love it either and I'm so glad I found this on consignment for 50 cents. 
 Also, if you haven't garnered this already, this is a dark book. I generally love "dark" but not so much this book. So be forewarned.

I'd give this book a pretty solid 3.75 stars. 
 The story is set in our world, however things have happened that have put strains on the environment. The air quality is frequently dangerous and citizens are required to wear O2 shields which regulate their air. They also have 7 day work weeks, with no breaks or vacations, and a pretty constant onslaught of acid rain. Things are pretty bleak. Enter Elusion. The perfect escape to get away from all of these problems. 
 The main character Regan is the daughter of the man who invented Elusion, but after her father's untimely death, accusations start to arise that there are problems with Elusion that could lead to deadly consequences for users. Regan is determined to prove these accusations wrong, but every time she goes into the virtual world of Elusion, she starts to wonder if the accusations might hold a little bit of truth. 
 The writing was really great and the descriptions of the Escapes and the world of Elusion were beautiful. The plot was really cool as well and I'm very interested to see where this goes next, however, I feel as though there was a bit lacking in the world building. There wasn't really much of a description or any background info given on how the world got to the point that the air quality is so poor, and that the clouds always pour down acid rain. 
 I did enjoy the characters and the romantic aspects even though I felt like there was a bit of insta-love going on between Regan and the male protagonist. (I say male protagonist instead of his name because there are kind of 2 male protagonists and I won't give away which one she ends up with, even though it's not really a love triangle either.) 
 Overall, I enjoyed this book a lot, and I will definitely be reading the next one, especially since this one ended in a cliffhanger!

 I bought myself and my godmother Tiger's Curse for Christmas two years ago. I figured it would be a fun way for us to do something together even though we now lived a couple thousand miles away from each other. I'll be honest, at first the story was slow, and my Goodreads updates were more complaints than anything else. I was getting bored and confused under so many details and different cultures AND FAR TOO MANY ITALICIZED WORDS. Luckily, all of these things quickly stopped bothering me and I was able to really lose myself in the story. 
 Most of the complaints I've seen about this book have about about the main character, Kelsey's, juvenile actions and thoughts. I agree 100% with these complaints. I think Colleen was going for a sense of naivety with Kelsey, but instead it came off as though she was just a little bit dumb. She didn't speak the way she should have, and her thought process usually resulted in me shaking my head. I mean, several times she discussed about her love for Ren has being a "love-plant".  That's just cringe-worthy. 
 With all of that said, Tiger's Curse is gripping - and I don't ever call anything gripping. I went from going, "Ehh, I can put this off right?" to being unable to put it down. It's obvious how much thought and research Colleen Houck put into writing this story. LOVED The Interestings so I wanted to try another Meg Wolizer book. Similar to The Interestings, this book is filled with relateable, realistic characters whose stories I thoroughly enjoyed reading. However, the stories were too single-faceted to really get a broad character picture the way that I have gotten in her other books. 
 The basic premise of this book is that when the new drama teacher at a local high school puts on a production of Lysistrata, Aristophanes's Greek comedy about women who intend to stop the Peloponnesian war by refusing to sleep with the men, all of the women in the town suddenly lose interest in sex. 
 There are essentially two parts to this book. The first is a brief look into the lives of many of the women in the town, all at different stages in their lives (from high school students, to new mothers, to older women) and the look at what sex means in the current stages of their lives. This part I found to be a very interesting study on female sexuality throughout a lifetime. 
 The second part of the book describes the mysticality of the "spell" that overcomes these women. It's constantly described as a "chill" that comes over the women. These intense descriptions do NOTHING for me and almost ruin the book. Not to mention the ending, where we find out that the drama teacher has been casting the spell on purpose all over New Jersey to "revitalize" peoples' sex lives??? I'm all for mystic powers, but for one person to reveal them in the last 10 pages of the book just seems terrible. This caused me to drop a whole star from my review. 
 There are some other interesting parts, and some storylines that are not totally wrapped up (is Eli going to come back from MI to be with Willa??). But for the most part, the various women's stories are not interesting enough to need clean, tidy endings.  
 Furthermore this book features the use of teenagers talking online using speak like "ru there" which is my biggest pet peeve in books because teenagers have not done that in real life since 2004.

Trudy, the daughter of a German immigrant mother, has lived under the shadow of her mother Anna's traumatic wartime experiences all her life, a past which is never discussed. Suspecting that she is the result of her mother's affair with an SS officer in Weimar during WW2, Trudy has always felt a sense of shame and guilt about her parentage. The only evidence Trudy has about her mother's time in Weimar is a small photograph she found hidden amongst her mother's clothes, a family portrait of the infant Trudy and a young Anna with a high-ranking Nazi officer. Now a professor of German history in Minnesota, Trudy embarks on a series of interviews with German women to explore their wartime experiences and attitudes, and how they're dealing with what they did during the war. During these interviews she meets another German from Weimar, who may have the answers to some of Trudy's questions regarding her heritage. 
 Jumping back and forth between Minnesota in the 1990's and wartime Weimar, the reader slowly learns about Anna's past. As an 18-year-old girl living with her tyrannical father in Weimar at the beginning of WW2, Anna violates the Reich's strictest rule when she falls in love with Max, a young doctor of Jewish descent. As anti-semitic actions intensify, Anna hides Max in the family home, but he is discovered by her father and sent to the concentration camp Buchenwald. Anna, who is carrying Max's child, flees from her home to live with the local baker's widow, a member of the resistance, helping her smuggle bread to the prisoners in an effort to be near Max. After the baker's discovery and execution by SS officers, Anna knows that it is only a matter of time until the SS will also come for her. But being a beautiful young woman, she catches the eye of the Obersturmfuhrer, a high-ranking Nazi officer at Buchenwald, who has been sent to interrogate her. Trying to ensure her and her infant daughter's survival, Anna must make a decision which may save her life but will ultimately cost her much more .... and which she will pay for the rest of her life. 
 How far would you go to keep your child alive? This question lies at the heart of Blum's novel, which also reminds the reader of the complexities of human nature and the danger of judgment without knowing all the facts. Blum is not trying to make excuses for Anna, but draws the reader into a place where her choice is only life or death. Would you sacrifice your ethics and morals to ensure your own and your child's survival? Or would you rather die for your principles? Anna makes a decision no mother should ever have to make, and loses a great part of herself in the process. Spending the rest of her life trying to forget the past, she becomes cold and remote, unwittingly bestowing the burden of her past on her child. 
 For me, the story was at times unbearably sad, especially witnessing Anna lose more and more of herself as she is caught in an impossible, hopeless situation. By saving her own life, she must also betray her love in the worst imaginable way, by having an affair with one of the people ultimately responsible for her child's father's death. Anna's disassociation becomes evident as the story progresses, and she is emotionally detaching herself from her actions, which is heartbreaking to witness. "The past is dead...and better it remain so", Anna says. But the past has a way of staining the future, and sometimes facing up to it is the only way to heal. Blum masterfully captures the dilemma of many Germans during the war, without making any excuses for their actions. Yet it reminds the reader not to be too quick to judge anyone's actions, without having been in a similar situation. 
 I could not put the book down, although it left me with a lingering feeling of hopelessness and despair that was hard to shake. As the story progresses and Anna becomes more emotionally withdrawn, it becomes harder to engage with her, which left a lot of my questions unanswered and took some of the enjoyment out of reading Anna's chapters. All in all, Blum does a fantastic job in exploring the far-reaching effect of our decisions on generations to come, and that healing may only be possible through understanding and acknowledging the past.

This is a great book. It's incredibly imperfect, but somehow it's better for it. Notably, it reads less like a novel and more like a series of short stories or fragments that cover a broad narrative arc - almost episodic, like a TV show. Comparisons to Firefly are not perfect, but are also entirely justified. 
 This does mean that sometimes plot points come as a surprise, one of the couples for instance, I did not see coming AT ALL, which is maybe because I am ignorant but whatever. Sometimes, things that seemingly need more airtime get less and vice versa, but somehow, this is still an utterly magical book. It's rich and character-focused, and the world the author has created is breathtaking for it's realism and understanding of humanity. It's also incredibly inclusive - the female characters are strong and rich, there's a lot of sexual and racial inclusivity, which to me is becoming a crucial element in the books I read - honestly, I just couldn't care less about a bunch of white guys doing a stuff anymore. 
 Borderline five stars for me, definitely recommend.

This is a book that you want to go into without knowing much about because much of the story is just that-- a narrative written by an "English Flight Officer" as her captors call her. So I will try to be vague. She is supposed to be writing about the British War Effort, but while doing so tells a story of a female pilot, Maddie, and their runnings into each other. There is not much action in the book, and the suspense is limited because what we are reading is her report of what has happened to her, so we know she didn't die from what happens to her  except for the way the end of Part 1 cuts off and we don't know what happens until the end of Part 2 . 
 Still, this book took me a while to get through. It is only halfway through Queenie's narrative that the book started to become interesting to me, and that was because she was finally telling the story of how she landed in France, and was subsequently caught. It is worth reading though however. I believed I was going to give this book two stars, and it jumped up to four. The writing style and interesting premise gave it the two stars, but  the revelation of Queenie's true character and my admiration of her  added two more stars. This book is filled with many technical parts regarding aircraft, which is why I found it hard to get through. She also recounts many small moments in her or Maddie's day to day life that I did not find interesting, though it adds to the character development of both girls. I almost feel bad that I did not find many of those descriptions interesting, because looking back on them now that I'm finished has me enjoying them more, and wanting to reread the book to see what I glanced or skipped over. 
 I did enjoy Queenie's descriptions of herself and her friend. Queenie is a very strong character and so is Maddie. I enjoyed how different they were though. Maddie was afraid of gunfire, but that didn't make her less of a strong character. Maddie was just afraid of different things than Queenie, the latter of whom had the additional luck to be able to hide her fears. The only problem I found with Queenie was in the beginning, when I thought she had given up code rather easily and that she was exaggerated some of the torture she feared (because she never recounted any truly horrible things happen to her). Later though we learn of some of the horrifying circumstances that she endured  to give them FALSE CODE. Maddie telling how she was still in control, even when she was being tortured was inspiring. I completely believed that she had given up her code and that she was Special Operations.

 I really don't know what to say, to assure you that this book is very very very good.

It's been a few weeks since I closed the cover on Illuminae and I'm rethinking my initial rating of four stars. I might be a hardass and lower it. As I've written this review, I've gotten crankier and crankier about certain aspects, although I do have to be fair -- this book grabbed my attention from the get-go, and it wasn't until late in the book that I started critiquing its faults. Let's get down to it. 
 The novel is narrated through documents and messages, a type of updated epistolary style. At first I thought that this would cramp the pacing, and it did to an extent, but not nearly as much as I anticipated. For having all of its action be related as past events, Kristoff and Kaufman did an amazing job at making the the narrative seem like the present. 
 Our novel starts off with a cover letter for a compilation of documents. The letter tells its recipient that the documents will relate the story of a catastrophic event on an illegal mining colony (in outer space). We start off with two teenage survivors of the catastrophe being interviewed (our protagonists). 
 Before the catastrophe, Kady was a spunky, punky young lady with aspirations of college and traveling the universe. Ezra was a talented G-ball jock with a close bond with his miner dad. The two kids used to date. Except, they messily broke up hours before the catastrophe occurred. They both made it off the colony, thanks to Kady's badassery, but are on separate rescue vessels. Most of the novel follows their independent activities on different ships. Ezra is drafted into the military as a pilot. Kady is taken under the wing of an accomplished computer hacker. 
 I don't want to get into the plot further, because of spoilers, but there is a lot going on in Illuminae. There's a pursuit across space, a deadly contagion, malfunctioning artificial intelligence, an evil corporation, and more! To be honest, it was too much at times. One or two plot points could have been excluded and the story would have been much more streamlined. 
 Another thing that could have been improved was the style of narration that took up most of the climax.  That of AIDEN, the artificial intelligence.  In my opinion, it was the least dynamic narrative style, and made the finale of the book annoying to read. It was like reading high school poetry. Blah. I can't emphasize enough how much I disliked  AIDEN  Speaking of high school, I hated the texting abbreviations and :P faces that littered the book. Just personal preference. 
 One MORE thing. I couldn't help but notice the extreme similarities between Illuminae and Kaufman's Starbound collaboration with Megan Spooner. In fact, they are ridiculously alike. Now, writing similar works isn't exactly a sin, but Kaufman is risking becoming a one-note author, which isn't exactly good. It definitely made me wonder, though, what traces of Jay Kristoff were in Illuminae? Did he serve to make the male lead more authentic? Is he responsible for AIDEN? I'm curious, because it's hard to tell. 
 Now that I've sufficiently ragged on Illuminae, let me spend some time praising it. The book was good. Period. There's a lot of bad YA out there and Illuminae floats to the top without breaking a sweat. I was sucked in the the story immediately and read the book in one sitting. I enjoyed myself. That is not to say, however, that there's no room for improvement. I think the novel could have benefited from adding dimension to EVIL Corps, or whatever it's name is, having the characters be fleshed out further, shaving off plot bulk, and more. 
 All in all, I can see Illuminae being a popular book, but I doubt it'll be a breakthrough hit.

A collection of stories, some better than the others. Although all concern the para/super/unnatural, not all of them relate to romantic love, or even love in general. 
 Michelle Zink, "The Assassin's Apprentice." Clunkily written, with poorly developed characters, a mere sketch of a romance, and sprinkled with malapropisms(ex: "They moved silently through the shadows of our world, doing their duty without worldly aplomb or association.") 
 Diana Peterfreund, "Errant." Marvelous. In medieval France, a unicorn hunter negotiates with a family to stage a traditional unicorn hunt. Fantastic characterization done entirely through the details and choices of their lives, complex relationships and moral decisions. Not sure why this is in a paranormal love collection, though, because by the end of the story Gitta and Elise are friends and haven't even had a thought about romance. 
 Karen Mahoney, "The Spirit Jar." A fairly new vampire helps a half-djinn free the soul of his dead ex-girlfriend. I liked all of the characters, and the action was well written. This seems to be part of a larger series--I'll try to track it down. 
 Justine Musk, "Lost." Hades tries to train a young woman to help the souls of the dead.  Once I figured out what was going on, I wanted this to have been spookier and tinged with more sadness. I wish the main character had had a few more qualms. 
 Sarah Rees Brennan, "The Spy Who Never Grew Up." Peter Pan becomes a secret agent, and eventually gets Wendy's descendent to help him on his spy missions. Fabulous, a bit dizzying, very funny--all the things I've learned to expect from Brennan. 
 Becca Fitzpatrick, "Dungeons of Langeais." An angel tortured a young duc into swearing fealty, and ever since has possessed him once a year for the last two centuries. The duc has discovered that the angel loves a woman, and uses her to bargain for his freedom. I have no idea who I was supposed to find sympathetic in this story, nor do I really know what happened. It's clearly part of a larger tale, and without knowing it this short story is basically unintelligible. 
 Caitlin Kittredge, "Behind the Red Door." A punk teen in a small town finds love in a haunted house. Creepy, spooky, twisty. Great imagery, very believable characters. Totally pulled me in! 
 Carrie Ryan, "Hare Moon." In the world of the Forest of Hands and Teeth, a young woman has to choose between duty to her village and her love for an outsider. This is the origin story of Sister Tabitha.  I liked this much better than Ryan's books, actually. 
 Michelle Rowen, "Familiar." A witch-in-training picks a kitten to be her familiar, only to find out the kitten is really a hottie shapeshifter on the run. So boring I couldn't finish it. 
 Rachel Vincent, "Fearless." A foster girl is annoyed to be sent to a group home, but horrified when she realizes that none of the other girls are afraid of anything. Sabine is a mara that feeds on nightmares, and without them she'll starve. I really liked the talk about consent with a mind-controlling boyfriend that she had, and the twist on negative emotions this story gave. The home's cook is sucking all the negative emotions around her and replacing them with positive ones, expecting the girls to become useful and good members of society. Sabine points out that this is unfair--these girls have earned their fear and anger, and it's part of them. Yet still, Sabine is a monster who multiplies the fear of those around her...I liked how complex the morality in this story was, and that no one person or viewpoint seemed to be totally correct.  
 Daniel Marks, "Vermillion." Am I supposed to like Velvet and Nick? They seem awful. As soon as they meet Amie they're calling her schizophrenic and making fun of her large ears. When Amie compliments Velvet's hairstyle, Velvet internally guffaws and makes yet more jokes about Amies gigantic ears. Then they start talking about their favorite foods: "The barbecue pork with hot mustard was my favorite." Nick's eyes rolled into the back of his head as he searched for the pleasurable memory. 
 "Fried chicken feet at Uncle's Dim Sum." Amie added, trying to join in. 
 Velvet startled, her mouth agape. "Chicken's feet?" 
 "Oh yeah, they're so delicious...and so crunchy. You could just suck the skin right off the bone..." 
 The girl continued to wax nostalgic about her disturbing meal, while Velvet glanced at Nick, happy to see that his face was as sour as hers. Uncle's Dim Sum must have been a mental institution. Maybe Amie just thought it was a Chinese restaurant...She glanced back at Amie and noticed that, at some point during the exchange, she'd stopped talking about gross things that weren't actually food and was staring directly at the two of them. Sooo that was horrible. It's rapidly followed by lots of talk about how slutty Amie is (I started counting the number of times she's called a slut and literally lost count) and fat jokes. And then it turns out Amie was evil all along, and everyone is like "way to go, Nick and Velvet, you two are the best!" Very weird.  
 Maggie Stiefvater, "The Hounds of Ulster." Overly stylized and the narrator's descriptions of their music are too precious. That said, I liked the last minute reveal that the narrator is a girl, and how that alters my perception of her decision to shave her head. And I liked that she doesn't convince her friend to stay away from the fairies with a guitar riff or a confession of love, either of which I'd have expected--instead, they have a conversation and she doesn't save him at all.  
 Daniel Waters, "Many Happy Returns." Not a good writer, ex: "He yelled orders, people moved. Cal Wilson was running. Mike moved. Other than she-of-the-fluttering-eyelids, none of the other bodies on the ground had moved. 
 Cal Wilson ran over too." Uh, yeah, I got that he ran over, thanks. Although the writing and tense choices are clunky, I actually quite liked this story, about a grieving father and his daughter's zombie boyfriend coming together.

 I fell in love with a person, not a prince; the rest is just circumstance. 
 The Royal We, as many others have discussed and as is perhaps apparent from even just the cover art, is clearly a William and Kate fanfiction. While they, and some of the broad details of their relationship, may have been the inspiration for this story, it is still very clearly fiction. For starters, Rebecca "Bex" Porter ("Kate") is an American who meets Nicholas "Nick" ("William") when she does a year abroad at Oxford. Her twin sister, Lacey, is an exaggerated Pippa while Nick's brother, Freddie, is an exaggerated Harry. Richard ("Charles") is Nick and Freddie's callous, emotionally detached father and heir to the throne, while Emma, their mother, is supposed to depict (to a certain degree) Diana. While in reality Diana is no longer alive, Emma is; but not mentally present. The pressures and anxiety that come with constantly being scrutinized and in the public eye have driven her nearly catatonic and withdrawn; she lives like a recluse and does not go out in public nor does she really engage or interact with other people. A tragedy perhaps not nearly as tragic as the physical loss of Diana, but still meant to somewhat evoke that sentiment: how sad to know that your mother has been mentally ill and unreachable for 20+ years when she's still living not a few miles away from you? So close yet so far, especially when your father is clearly incapable of warmth and devotion. As Freddie nicely states in his bonus chapter, "A Person can die without being dead." 
 Throughout the story of Bex and Nick's romance, as told through Bex's perspective, we are also introduced to their close-knit friend group. Only a couple of their close friends are actually considered royalty, Bea "Lady Bollocks" for one, while the rest have royalish connections: a parent who is the queen's gynecologist, press connections, etc. This seems mostly reasonable, as I imagine it would be difficult to trust people who are genuinely interested in you as a person rather than being tied to "the royals." Thankfully, they (mostly) have Nick's (and Bex's and Freddie's) back(s) and look out for bottom-feeding opportunists who are only looking out for themselves. Unfortunately, one of Nick's friends becomes one of these bottom-feeders and in the worst way. In other words, Clive's a twat and never trust the media, especially when your "friend" is so keen on making a name for himself as a "journalist" but is only ever really interested in gossip . 
 "Words only have the power we give them, Beatrix," Pudge said. "Open your spirit." 
 Gaz and Cilla, on the other hand, begin with a heated, contentious relationship that tropes itself into their eventual "happily ever after." Lacey is out of control. Bex is far too kind and forgiving of her twin; Lacey is a selfish monster. Freddie is wild, yes, but he is adorable. I loved the bonus chapter from his perspective and would gladly read more, please! And then there's Bea, who is so sour grapes at the start and in general but, come to find, is more complex and actually kinder than she may at first appear. Like a very fickle, hard to unravel onion. 
 I might be Cinderella today, but I dread who they'll think I am tomorrow. 
 All in all, this was a light, mostly fun, guilty pleasure read. It started out fairly decent, but then started to get heavily eye roll worthy. As others have noted, and I agree, this felt like it was genuinely at least 100 pages longer than it needed to be. Not terrible, but also kind of just meh.
The morale of this story is that, if you love someone, you should probably tell them. Or face dire consequenses.

I generally and genuinely enjoy (most of) Meg Cabot's writing. I don't mean to knock the Chick Lit genre, but these books are typically light, quick, and easy reads for me. They are usually fun and entertaining, especially as a sort of palate cleanse between books or as a means of decompressing after some really intense reading. Now, that's not to say that there can't be intensity in Chick Lit, but in those cases it generally doesn't stress me out like some other reads. At any rate, in these areas, The Boy Next Door pretty much delivered. Well, for the most part. 
 The Boy Next Door was certainly a light, quick, and easy read for me. I enjoyed the modern epistolary storytelling structure as viewed solely through email format, but a major missing detail really began to grate on my nerves: where were the timestamps? I would occasionally catch phrases or subtle references that would indicate how much time had passed, but it was still incredibly frustrating. Please, for the love of OCD, include timestamps! I know that this is Cabot's first work of adult fiction, so I will cut her some slack, but going forward I hope that she will include them. Now, I know that the rest of the books in this "series" have already been published, but still. Please. I shouldn't have to work that hard or do that much math to attempt to figure out the passage of time in a novel. 
 Overall, the characters were moderately enjoyable; eh, more or less tolerable, I suppose. The story was more or less predictable, especially regarding the fate of Mrs. Friedlander (and whodunnit). Though I realize that it is a work of fiction, and I knew that it was going to happen, I still couldn't help rolling my eyes at just how quickly (though not necessarily easily) Mel took John back. Three months (I think that's how long it was?) is a very short amount of time to make such an important decision regarding marriage, but whatever.  I'll try to refrain from analyzing my fun, light reads as much going forward. Now, for Boy Meets Girl...

This was a fun read, although I'd hesitate to call it quick. This is one of the more ~sprawling~ YA books I've read in a long time, and there were some points where I thought much could've been cut down--several points of Andie's internal monologue got redundant, or she kept thinking about things that had already been shown. In lesser hands, this would've really irritated me more (see also Da Vinci's Tiger) but it didn't so much here, probably because Matson did a great job of building this entire world. 
 The pros: 
 - For the most part, I loved the character-building. Andie's story is, for the most part, predictable--type-A overachiever learns to let go a little bit, grows closer to family, finds love, etc--but she still felt like a breath of fresh air. She was well-realized, as were her friends (for the most part--a little more on that later). 
 - I mentioned a moment ago that the story was pretty predictable, but at the same time it was something I enjoyed watching unfold. You know from the outset the internship will fall through, that she'll fall for Clark, she'll manage to break some of the tension with her dad. There were various things I kept predicting throughout the narrative, but it didn't actually bother me when they surfaced (most notably with Bri and Wyatt ). 
 - The excerpts scattered throughout from Clark's books  were well-written and better than something like, say, Fangirl to some degree--which was nice. I would've liked to read the full texts. 
 - The depiction of friendship--specifically the volatility of female friendship--was excellent. I was, for the most part, pleased with the depiction of Bri/Toby's friendship, which was all-consuming and unsustainable. It was a huge relief to see that they didn't make up to their former levels at the end of the story, nor was it dependent on Toby finding love. I did, for a while, think that Toby was in love with Bri, and I was kind of rooting for some weird queer girl drama, because that's exactly how the Toby/Wyatt/Bri thing read to me--Toby wasn't upset that Bri had Wyatt in my mind, but that Wyatt had Bri, with Bri being the lynchpin. Was Toby perfect? Absolutely not, she was profoundly irritating with her dogged pursuit of love, but I appreciated that nobody came out of that situation quite so clean. That's how it is in real life.  
 The cons: 
 - Everything felt a bit too neat. C. B. McAllister being Clark, the resolution of Andie/Clark's relationship at the book-signing, the signs from Andie's mum, etc.--it was all a bit much. I know the Toby/Bri relationship imploded, but everything else was a little unexpectedly tidy. Especially for a book called "The Unexpected Everything."  
 - I never actually got a great sense of Bri as a character, which was a shame, because she's pretty integral to a couple plot points. This was mostly when, during the Toby/Bri meltdown, Bri kept saying she'd never been able to put herself first and that it was always Toby who was more important--which I never doubted, per se, because everyone always wanted to protect Toby, but I also couldn't follow how Bri felt like she could never put herself first. She had sisters, sure, and I had a feeling that her family had immigrated to the US or was maybe second-gen, still setting down roots, but there was no other indication of socioeconomic status that I might've expected. I really wanted *more* of that, but sadly, no dice.  
 - I know I mentioned previously that I loved the snippets from Clark's books, but the last one was a little godawful, actually. Like... just change the names. Please, oh god, just change the names.  
 There was a lot in here to like, and I really did fly through this book. There was a depth explored that something like Since You've Been Gone didn't quite lack, but also didn't go all the way with. I'll definitely continue to read Morgan Matson's stuff, but I might need a little break after this one!

I was expecting to like this book less than I did. I will say that I absolutely LOVED that the main character is not white. Very rarely has there been a kids book (or movie or show) with a genius, quirky kid that wasn't white (at least from the books I've read), as well as her friends. 
 Outside of that however... 
 I felt the writing was pretty mediocre and honestly took away a lot from the story for me. The changing perspectives felt lazy (first person for Willow, third person for any other character). There wasn't really any urgency in the plot or situation the characters were in. Willow was in process for finding a new permanent family, but none of that was really brought up at all until the very last few chapters. When the court date was set and everyone was reacting emotionally to the possibility of her leaving, I couldn't really feel the emotion with them. The pacing was too slowly paced, but not in a way that felt right (to me, anyway). 
 Willow was kind of a hard character to relate to. I think the Manic Pixie Dream Girl trope, while it exists, is similar to 'Mary Sues' in that it's just another way to invalidate a female character. I totally think that there are a lot of characters who fit this trope, but I wouldn't call Willow one of them. My understanding of the trope is that MPDG is a quirky, cute, usually white female who exists for the benefit of a sad, jaded, also white male, and that doesn't happen at all in here. Willow was definitely odd and I found her hard to relate to and not very believable, but I wouldn't say she was a MPDG at all. I honestly feel the writing just wasn't up to snuff for this character, so she comes across as unbelievable. 
 That said, I loved the Nguyens. Mai was great, as was Pattie and I really would have liked to hear much more of their voices. I loved how strong-willed they were. However, I don't feel like the relationships between them (anyone) were properly illustrated. Pattie took Willow in, but there were never really any moments to show how the relationships had developed. There were a few here and there, but nothing very substantial. Also another review had mentioned Pattie's somewhat questionable parenting decisionsPattie is quite rich and makes her family live in a garage? How awful is that? . 
 Dell was a character I didn't quite like. He was questionable at best. His desire to change himself was admirable, but he was terrible at his job and his lifestyle was gross (as in he never, ever cleaned ever). He never really seemed to take responsibility for anything. 
 Overall, this was a decent and quick enough read, despite the writing not being the greatest.

I have been waiting for this book and I was not disappointed! This book was amazing! A total 5 star read and a great addition to The Cold Fury Series! I would recommend you start with Alex, then Garrett, then read Zack otherwise you really will miss the subtle connections and character traits that Sawyer Bennett brings from one book to the next. 
 Zack, he is a player of the Carolina Cold Fury Hockey Team and we met him in previous books of the series. Zack has been through a major tragedy and he feels like he had nothing to give. He just wants to play hockey, raise his son Ben and try to live his life as best ad he can. He had emotionally shut down. 
 "My insides feel dead, my capacity to care for much of anything seems lost, but there are two things that still keep me functioning. It's the prospect of playing hockey again, and, more important, my son, Ben."~Zack 
 Once Zack is cleared to return to playing by his Dr, he realizes he is going to need help with Ben. But never fear, his sister Delaney has already interviewed and hired a live-in Nanny, Roberta. 
 When Zack answers the door to meet his nanny the first time, he is shocked not only by her young appearance but that she looks like she is wearing clothes 3 sizes too big for her. Once he attempts to introduce himself, he is promptly told "Roberta is my first name, Kathryn is my middle and I go by Kate." This is the beginning of a very fun relationship! 
 Kate, she is quirky - often referring to herself as adorkable, and she frequently makes up nicknames for Zack and Ben such as "Glitter Skates" for Zack of which she won't stop calling him until he acknowledges her. Kate is a romantic at heart, she won't deny she is waiting for her Prince Charming. She is not all fun and games though. Kate has had a long hard life and she has struggled the entire way to achieve her dreams of being a child psychologist. Recently just graduating with her Bachelor's degree in psychology she divulges she had to take this job for Zack so she can save money for graduate school. Kate will quickly capture your heart and she is a great leading lady. 
 Zack & Kate together, well let's say it is combustible and Zack finds himself letting walls down he never thought he would. Is it enough, is Kate willing to take what Zack thinks he can give because he won't face his demons? Will there be a Happy Ever After? 
 Thank you Sawyer for bringing us another Brooding Alpha male who just needed the right woman to make him see, isn't loving and losing...better than never loving at all?

 "You make my world bright again. You make it brighter than it ever has been before. You were what was missing from my life and I'm not going to let that get away."- Zack 
 "And here is the truth of what I know. I found what was missing in my life. She's in my arms right at this moment. I love her with all my being and she will be my wife one day. We will have children of our own, and Ben will be the best big brother in the world. My life will be happy and whole, and it is all because of this amazing woman."~Zack

I just finished this book and am still trying to collect my thoughts on it... 
 I started this book not really knowing what to expect. I added it to my Want To Read shelf not too long ago but by the time I borrowed it from the library I'd forgotten the plot premise from the book cover. I'm glad I did because I got to experience the book without any preconceptions whatsoever. 
 First of all, I loved the main character, Ananna. She was tough, knowledgeable, and I enjoyed her narrative voice. At first I was unsure about the way the author wrote her narrative, using incorrect grammar and words like "ain't" to go along with Ananna's way of speaking, but I quickly grew used to it and actually ended up liking it because it gave me an even stronger sense of Ananna's character. I loved that she was not a Mary Sue, far from perfect and never described as beautiful. The author may have pushed it a bit by describing her as plain so many times, although I guess insecurity could just be a part of her personality (it somewhat clashes with her born-and-raised-pirate attitude though). I was a little worried that her antagonism with Leila was going to devolve into one of those cliche mean girl-Mary Sue pointless hostility over a guy things but fortunately Leila was a more complex character than that and the author stayed away from that. 
 The world-building in this book was great, although I wish we could have learned even more about the pirate Confederation and the Mists, though I'm guessing these will be explored further in the next book. I can't wait to learn more about the Order and its secrets as well. I loved how vividly everything was described. I could imagine clearly in my mind the desert, the night market, the river, etc. And the element of magic in this story certainly held its appeal. It's interesting to me that magic seems so widespread in this world, with many different elemental types and abilities. 
 As for the male lead, Naji, I enjoyed learning more and more about his character and watching his relationship with Ananna develop. Even by the book's end he still remained pretty mysterious and I liked how things never even came close to insta-love or dramatics (I talk about this in pretty much every book review I write but really I'm a simultaneous romantic and skeptic... I love the romance but only if I find it believable). He's not exactly the most likable character, but I loved him nonetheless. His powers, secrets, and emotionless facade fascinate me greatly and I'm excited to read more about him in the sequel. I love how we only got little hints at Ananna's feelings for him leading up to her realization at loving him... Even though I knew it was going to happen, the progression felt natural and believable to me, especially seeing as no feelings have been divulged or resolved yet. I won't lie, I love tension!  
 This book had a strong plot, though I felt little developments actually happened within this one book. I was actually surprised at where the book ended, though it was far from a cliffhanger and made sense. The pacing didn't actually bother me that much while reading, I only realized how little happened as an afterthought. So not a big deal. The big action/tension moments didn't feel insanely suspenseful or drawn out, but I didn't mind terribly. I can only hope for a bit more excitement and action in the next book, where no doubt bigger things will be happening.

 Mastering the Marquess is a story about a woman who does her best to honor her husbands memory as she searches for a new one, and a man who is, essentially, prepared to live two different lives in an effort to sate his desires. 
 I have to say right off the bat that this author has an amazing gift for detailing a scene and setting it up to make it feel like the reader is in the room watching as everything unfolds. She was so masterful there were times I felt like a voyeur. 
 I liked the main characters in this book. They were on an even playing field in that they were both so preoccupied with how things should be that they didn't realize how things could be. Louisa was a very likable heroine. She genuinely loved her first husband and took drastic measures to ensure his reputation remain intact even after death. While trying to be timid and bashful at times (as society demanded), who she was always shone through and she was a determined and, at times, feisty heroine. I enjoyed Geoffrey's character, as well. He knew marriage and an heir were his duty to his family, but he was torn between propriety and desire, certain that his two worlds could not collide. And though his marriage was his duty, he didn't treat his wife as though she was a burden. 
 I really enjoyed the pacing of this story and the way things unfolded. Watching Geoffrey's world get turned upside down and being introduced to a way of life he'd never considered was fun to see, and I loved witnessing Louisa's journey of self-discovery. These characters really complemented each other, and they both brought out facets of the others personality that had never been brought to light before. 
 The chemistry between Louisa and Geoffrey was established from the moment they 'met,' and it only escalated from there. The love scenes in this book were incredibly intense and sexy. 
 The reader does have to suspend disbelief a bit, as it's hard to imagine Geoffrey didn't recognize Louisa from their original encounter. But it makes for a fun story, and it wasn't something that bothered me. 
 Props to the author... 
 ...for putting Louisa in extreme danger and actually having horrible things happen to her. So often the heroine is rescued by the hero before any physical or emotional harm is brought to her, but that wasn't the case here. I think it made it much more realistic, and it also was a prime opportunity to strengthen Louisa and Geoffrey's bond.  
 Overall, this was a steamy, interesting read with great characters. I highly recommend this book if you like erotica or historical romance with a suspenseful twist.

  Me Before You first grabbed my attention when it's movie trailer was first released. I was so overwhelmed with emotion, I just knew that the book would make me feel that way and possibly more. So off I went asking for a copy for my birthday, after receiving a copy I wasted no time at all in starting it. 
 I always hate when people say "Don't judge a book by it's movie.", it's usually always correct, especially in this case. By just watching the trailer, I had assumed a bunch of things when going into the book. Most of which turned out wrong. 
 Me Before You is not primarily a romance, sure it's sort of there, but it's definitely not focused around it. Me Before You is a book of trying to convince Will to live, to show that life can still be like the way it was before the accident. With this being my first read with a quadriplegic, or really my first experience in general with one, I did not know what to expect, but it wasn't what I got. 
 From where Will started off, to where he ended up, I understood why he didn't have the motivation anymore. To live a life of travel, adventure, and excitement then suddenly not being able to do those or really anything anymore, it was be devastating. If I were put in a similar situation, I would hope that my parents would respect my wishes. 
 To be completely honest, I did not find anything romantic in the novel at all, it was all so bland for me. We were given a bland relationship between Louisa and her first boyfriend, then we were given the relationship that was Will and Louisa. But really, in same ways that could be only considered one sided because of the way Will treated it. Then there was the way Louisa viewed it, just because you made someone fall in life with you, that doesn't mean you're going to change their perspective of their life. 
 Where the novel was bland, the movie trailer depicts that the film will probably be taking a different route when it comes to the story, which will probably be for the best. I'll definitely be seeing it in the near future, reading the novel's sequel on the other hand, that won't be happening.
