 Better review to come.

How I feel about this book depends on how I look at it. As historical fiction, it does a great job of capturing the ache of the Dust Bowl and the life of a poor farming family. As a verse novel, it is so-so, although an early title in what has become a common format, so Hesse gets credit for being on the leading edge. As a Newberry, it holds up well but isn't at the top (The Giver and Holes are both more delightful and moving). My biggest complaint is that the second half moves a bit slowly for my taste. But worth reading.

SO GOOD. I loved this! It was a little long and difficult to get into also a bit confusing, but I still enjoyed. So much information and mystery in this book like I have no idea what's going to happen next. I wish there was more Gansey&Blue but I have a new love for Ronan so it was fine. Adam annoyed me and I wanted more of Noah too! AND the whole 'kissing' scene between Noah and Blue made me piss myself, IT WAS SO FUNNY AND SWEET. I loved the whole dream plot, I find it pretty cool and different. The Grey Men was so interesting, I liked him and Maura together! This series is so interesting, I'm very excited to see where it goes next! Also loved the cliffhanger!!

This was a really hard book. 
 It deals with some really tough subjects and a few times I wasn't sure if I was going to end up liking the book because I was questioning the MC's decisions. Not related to the abuse, I do still think she jumped into the marriage waaay too quickly. Also Ryle was a total prat for not telling Lily about his issues before they got married.  But by the time you get to the end, you realize that's the whole point. 
 The stuff in this book is hard to deal with. It's hard to make "the right choice" or even know what the right choice is. It's easy to make excuses. 
 Don't forget to read the author's note at the end, because that just reinforces EVERYTHING in the book. It cannot be skipped! 
 The abuse was handled very well. It had me so conflicted throughout the whole story, but by the end I realized that was the whole point. It was subtle enough each time that I could completely understand Lily's hesitation. She kept explaining it away, and I totally get why she did. The situation never really felt clear cut, and I thought it was a brilliant example of how real women in these situations must feel.  
 I knocked off a star because of Ryle. Aside from his rage issues  I felt like his development was a bit too perfect. 
 "I don't want kids. I hate the idea of marriage. I'm only into one night stands." 
 "Please please PLEASE let me have sex with you! Just once! That's all I need! To get it out of my system." 
 *sex happens* 
 "Woah. You were right. Once isn't enough. I'm going to need more." 
 *few weeks later* 
 "Marriage sounds good after all. So do kids." 
 I feel like he changed his entire outlook waaaay too easily. This was never even really a struggle for him. His complete 180 was just a little too perfect. 
 My only other issue was with Lily's business. This is sooo silly of me, but I kind of hated how easy she had it. Maybe because I'm a small business owner and it just irked me to see her start a business and have everything go PERFECTLY. 
 - Rich girl walks in on day #1 wanting to work for free and is super passionate about helping her get the business off the ground. 
 - She immediately has really busy days (and slow ones, to be fair, but we always get the impression that she's doing really well). 
 - She can suddenly afford to hire other employees pretty quickly. 
 - She gets noticed by the community quickly and nominated for awards. 
 I feel so stupid complaining about this but I really feel like the stars just magically aligned to give her a great, booming business, and I hate her a little for it.

I liked The Fault in Our Stars. It was the first time that I actually felt that I read a book that reflected how I would imagine it would feel to be dying. I agreed with most of Hazel's musings about funerals: funerals are actually for the living, people will suddenly speak of the virtues once the person is gone, it doesn't feel as if the person is really there. 
 Honestly though, it was a bit of a disappointment for me. Maybe because I had built up these ridiculous expectations for it. I don't know. But I wasn't as impressed with it as others seem to be. It is a cancer story with teenagers. It's been done before, only in this case the teenagers are witty and oh so clever and proud of themselves like in Juno. Which is fine, but I can't really extol the virtues of it as highly as others. It is a great book, and I enjoyed it, but it's not a favorite by any means.

I decided to read this as I have been watching the TV series Once Upon a Time, and was curious to see how the original resembles the TV show. This is a childrens' book so I will treat it as such and not point out weak writing where I feel that choice was in the best interest of the child. 
 While the themes were kept simple, as was the writing I found it fascinating to imagine children 100 years ago having the patience to sit and listen to te old style writing of this book. I cannot imagine being able to do that with children today. 
 Overall I found it a strange, but compelling tale with a sweet ending. I'm glad I persevered through some patches that seemed condescending and read it.
not one of the best, but interesting setting of Africa, spy thriller ish, a cute ending.

"Fallen Too Far" by Abbi Glines 
 I own this book and this review is my honest opinion. 
 This book kicked butt. It falls into the 'more than 5 stars' category. Abbi Glines is an incredible writer and she captivated me from the beginning. 
 I loved how sweet and bad@$$ Blaire was. It was awesome. I instantly fell in love with Blaire at the very beginning. The moment we met Rush, I fell in love with him too. I loved their story from beginning to end. They were made for each other despite all outside forces trying to prevent them from being together. 
 The drama and secrets were fantastic and heartbreaking. The romance and sex was beyond steamy. I wanted to jump in the pages and take Blaire's place with Rush...oh, did I just admit to that? Oh well, he's hot, and when you read this book you'll most likely feel the same way. An amazing blogger coined the term, 'Rush Crush.' I can honestly say I have a Rush Crush and I am proud of it! =) 
 The cover to "Fallen Too Far" is beautiful. I think that the models work perfectly with the descriptions of Blaire and Rush within the book. The girl definitely has Blaire's signature white blonde hair! 
 When this book was over, I was so satisfied yet craving more. I couldn't wait to dive into book two. I would absolutely recommend this book to New Adult Contemporary Romance readers. You will not be disappointed with "Fallen Too Far" by Abbi Glines. This 5 star book is one that I want to add to my print book shelf. I will be an Abbi Glines fan for life and plan to read EVERY other book she wrote, and all her future books as well! 
 Happy Reading!

This audiobook was provided by the author, narrator, or publisher at no cost in exchange for an unbiased review courtesy of AudiobookBlast dot com. 
 I felt at the beginning of the book that the world and characters were not well developed. Eventually the characters gained a bit more backstory and became very likable with the exception of Dash and Ryan. This first book only gives us a glimpse of Dash and it's not enough to find him likeable. It's only through his mother that we learn that he might not be a total scumbag. The story of Kane and Lena was very sweet and I found myself rooting for him and liking the other two couples in the story as well. The pack mentality in this book was a bit annoying with the continual reminders that females are supposed to be submissive and can't be alpha. 
 The love story makes this book worth reading and the likeable characters and investment in Lena/Kane story will bring me back for book #2. 
  
 This is not exactly a spoiler, but my speculation. I spent the entire book certain that Dash and not Kane would mark Lena. At the end we still haven't seen that happen, but I'm still certain that's what will happen and knowing that's coming created some frustration with the book. The fact that Kane and Lena continued to put off the marking was annoying. 
 Knowing this is going to turn into a triangle with a guy that so far is one dimensional leaves this book lacking something.

A much more interesting re-imagining of vampires than Twilight. Similarly centered around a romance where the vampire-man is creepily possessive of the protagonist-lady, but the romance is much more bearable because the lady seems to actually have a personality. And their world seems more realistic and interesting. Granted, this opinion is based on having read like two chapters of Twilight and not much of the preceding books in this series...

Picks up right were the first book left off. Brishen and Ildiko are an established pairing, so there is a little less romance, but due to the darker plot a whole lotta ANGST at first. 
 The story is told in alternating chapters. In the beginning one side is Ildiko and Brishen, the other side a group of travellers heading their way. Eventually that changes, as the plot develops. 
 I like the idea of the Wraith King and what they do, although the idea is not exactly new. Tolkien comes to mind. 
 The plot wasn't exactly mind boggling. The first half held more tension for me, with the fate of Ildiko in the balance. The second half, where the fight against the galla actually happens, was pretty straight forward and with little suspense and few surprises. Not as strong as the first half of the book, too predictable. I put the book down for a day, to read something else in between, and wasn't to fussed about picking it up again. 
 Bottom line, it was ok. I am somewhere around 3.5 stars for this installment. The next book will center around Serovek and Anhuset. I liked them as side characters. Not sure yet, if I will get the book when it comes out in 2017. Rigth now I am not too bothered. 
 There are quite a few editing mistakes in the ebook edition. The odd work or letter missing or a word too many. They were numerous enough to bother me and I hope future editions of the book will be better edited.
Gayle Forman is a great author. Very satisfying.

I love fairy tale retellings, and I really enjoyed this one. Too many retellings cling slavishly to the original story, but this one feels more like a story that would very normally happen in this fantasy universe and just happens to have some resemblances to "The Twelve Dancing Princesses." I especially liked the very realistic family relationships and the varying (and mutually incomprehensible) grief reactions to the queen's death. The characters were interesting, the magic was intriguing and (mostly) believable, and most of the action of the plot made sense. I was able to picture everything vividly, and I couldn't help thinking that this book would make a great movie. 
 And yet...it always frustrates me when a really good book is marred by little but annoying things. In this case, much of it involves the tendency of this otherwise very original story to slip into little cliches. For example, the unnamed (and theoretically unnameable) third kind of magic (in addition to blood magic and silver magic) turns out to be love, although never named as such , and some the things it manages to accomplish have a really sickly-sweet Disney feel about them. Likewise, the king's change of attitude over the course of the book is just a little too good to be true. While the action at the climax of the plot was exciting, it also slipped into cliches, such as the onlookers' dilemma that always results from the bad guy being able to look like a good guy  , that niggled at my enjoyment. But the biggest question looming over the plot for me was this: why on earth would people keep dancing a dance invented by an evil king to symbolize his evil powers? That was horribly artificial and undercut everything that was connected with it. 
 In spite of these little annoying things, I would still recommend this book to anyone who likes fairy retellings. It's certainly one of the better versions I've seen of this story, and with a more original flavor than most.

Alright, I finally had the opportunity to reread this. Cue in the "Yay!"s. 
 Kidding aside, this is more of a 3.5 for me. 
 Cameron Morgan or The Chameleon may be fluent in fourteen languages and capable of killing a man in seven different ways (three of which involve a piece of uncooked spaghetti), but the Gallagher Academy hasn't prepared her for what to do when she meets an ordinary boy who thinks she's an ordinary girl. Sure, she can tap his phone, hack into his computer, and track him through a mall without him ever being the wiser, but can she have a regular relationship with a regular boy who can never know the truth about her? Cammie may be an elite spy in training, but in her sophomore year, she's doing something riskier than ever - she's falling in love. 
 With that said, although the aforementioned blurb above appears to be a massive cheese fest, I adored Cammie. She is far from an annoying protagonist; instead, she has proven herself to be a witty, independent, hilarious heroine. Her naivety when it comes to boys is just amusing and not at all vexing... which is a tremendous feat, in my opinion. Reading this story in her point of view is just a pleasure. 
 The plot kept me interested the entire time and the dialogue between all the characters was always - and I mean always - entertaining. 
 On the other hand, the writing style could have been infinitely better. It wasn't bad per se; however, improvements won't kill anyone. Furthermore, I wasn't exactly a fan of the love interest in this book. 
 Nevertheless, the first book of Gallagher Girls is definitely perfect for a lighthearted read.

As per usual Moriarty-style, she wrote about such realistic and heartwarming relationships between sisters. Although I liked all three triplets from the start, Gemma slowly became my favorite  and I'm just so happy and relieved she found happiness with Charlie!!  I really loved the interspersed anecdotes by random passersby who had observed the seemingly happy-go-lucky family. It really brought home the theme of being stuck on representing yourself the way everyone else perceived you, even if that's not always the way you think you are or feel that you are.
I don't know when I've read a book that was this much *fun* to read!
Absolutely heartbreaking. And wonderful. But UGH.

If you are lazy like my two younger siblings who don't like (yet) to read books, watch the movie - it's completely the same. 
 Yup, even the dialogues. Yeah, even the transitions. Uh huh, EVERYTHING. 
 Yes, I watched the movie first but I really wanted to read the book because I thought it would be like other books-made-into-movies where they'd change or revise some part/s of the story. And I like knowing how or what these changes are. 
 So while reading this I was shocked by how it was EXACTLY the same as the movie. I love it when people from Hollywood or whatever follows the events, dialogues, message, setting, etc. of the book - especially when I LOVE that certain book. Although, I do appreciate movies in which events or the story line where changes but are better than the original story/book or are equally awesome. 
 Anyway back to the book review, this story shows a realistic point of view of love. And it's teen-fiction so it's easy to understand. I love how the story starts off at the very beginning and ends with an open-ending. It just makes everything more realistic. It's like everything in this book is real and that maybe Julie Baker and Bryce Loski are an old couple now still in love. 
 I love how I saw myself in Julie and Bryce - that I remember what it was like to be in love or to have a crush at that age. It made me go back to when I had my first crush and how I still have a crush on him now. This book was like a diary to my elementary love life and I LOVE THAT FEELING SO MUCH. 
 It rarely happens to me that I feel like I'm reading my life in someone else's story or that someone else is telling my life to me through their experiences. And this is why I recommend that you read and watch the movie. I don't care if you watch it first or vise versa, just promise me you'll do both. You won't be sorry... in fact, I think you'll thank me. 
 Happy reading and watching! :)

On one hand, The Broken Eye kind of reads like it was originally supposed to be the ending of The Blinding Knife that just kept expanding and expanding until it had to be its own book. On the other hand...that's actually a major strength of the story. 
 In contrast to the first two books in the series, The Broken Eye introduces few new characters, plot complications (well, MAJOR, previously unhinted at plot complications, anyway), or settings. It spends most of its time developing and explaining the set-ups, situations, and characters that The Blinding Knife introduced--when it's not hurtling headlong into a thundering climax that interlaces intrigue with massive action sequences. Not only is this is this the most successful Lightbringer book in avoiding huge wells of exposition, we actually start to get answers to questions or puzzles that have been hanging overhead throughout the series. (Of course, we don't get ALL the answers. There's still one more book to come.) 
 The Broken Eye reads as if Brent Weeks deliberately tried to avoid or fix the problems of The Blinding Knife. There are mercifully few Liv Danaveris chapters. Some of the morally questionable choices main characters have made receive consequences. There is less use of sexual violence against women as a shock tactic, and more emphasis on the brains, emotions, and personalities of the female characters, and less on their bodies. And, as mentioned before, there are many explanations given for events in previous books. Some readers may find all of the explanations satisfying, allowing them to silence niggling inner criticisms about how possible or plausible some things could be. Personally, I found some of the answers reminding me of how many questions WITHOUT answers we've already been given, and some of the explanations felt "patched on," not organic to the story. 
 The female characters take a step up in The Broken Eye. The White has always been amazing, but we see even more of her in this book. Karris benefits from a lot of character focus in this book. Teia reads almost like the heroine of most of the book (if this was the first one I'd read, I might be unsure if she or Kip was supposed to be the main character), becoming more likable and awesome along the way. (However, neither Weeks' attempt to redeem the whole olive oil thing into an actual character point or  the love triangle with her, Kip, and Tisis  worked for me). Liv...manages to not ruin the book? 
 By contrast, Gavin spends almost the entire story isolated away from the main characters, and while the development he undergoes might well be necessary for his morality, his character is less entertaining than usual. Kip... Kip has developed a lot, which makes him a more competent character, but self-controlled, self-confident, slimmed-down, and settling rather nicely into adulthood Kip just doesn't make the inside of your chest ache for him. He hasn't lost all of his Kip-ishness, but every step he takes seems to make him more of your generic fantasy action hero, and less of that awkward, hopeless loser that was so easy to identify with. I love his Blackguard squad, though, and Cruxer shines all the more because his amazingness isn't always been shouted from the rooftops. 
 The theology of Brent Weeks' books has always been a point of interest for me. After The Blinding Knife was comparatively light--we heard a little about the "mechanics" of religion in this world, but pretty little else from either a character or author standpoint--, The Broken Eye comes in hard. Too hard. And this is coming from a Christian who loves the Christian worldview in these books. Some parts worked, but there was just too much, and too much that was straight on the nose, barely altered from the Bible. 
 Oh, and that wholly unnecessary love triangle? Rage, rage, rage. 
 Still, warts aside, the last fifty pages alone are enough to send me running back to next Brent Weeks book, just as soon as it comes out.

I don't think I actually read the last book in Alexandra Ivy's Guardians of Eternity for some reason or other because when I read Hunt the Darkness I couldn't remember Roke and Sally meeting at all. Which is sad because other than that last book I've read them all to date and have the first half {which was the better half, in my opinion} on my bookshelves. But I still managed to read Hunt the Darkness without having read the book before it and following along perfectly well and enjoying it as well. Sally and Roke are great characters, that I found humours and charming, which reminded me a lot of the characters in the first books especially Dante and Viper. I enjoyed the accidental mating between Roke and Sally and what Roke would do for Sally. How it all turned out in the end was the best because it was humours and heart warming. Which is what Ms Ivy usually gives her readers and I was not let down at all with Hunt the Darkness. It was nice to see Levet {as always!} would it be a Guardians of Eternity without him making a few small appearances. I certainly think not! And a few other characters from the previous books. All in all a great eleventh book in a overall great series!

So it took me over a month, but I finally finished this afternoon. In fact, I read the last 300 pages in the last two days. Yes, it was overlong and could have been shortened by at least 100 pages, but it's still one of the most extraordinary novels I've ever read. It's a little funny to me that The Secret History has gotten so much praise over the past decade because as much as I really like that, it's nowhere near as great as this. As cold and hermetic as TSH could be, The Goldfinch is so suffused with warmth and beauty that it feels like it was written by a different person. This should win every literary prize out there.
Magical realism + hard boiled pulp = a fun, suspenseful, well-written tale that may go on for a bit too long, but is highly entertaining at the end of the day.

I normally don't write reviews about books here. And I definitely don't usually read books where women are older than the guys. I prefer the ones with older lads. However, I had to make an exception for this book. Because, oh my goodness! I really loved it! 
 Mia is Adam's mother who is Gray's best friends who's son of the new wife of Mia's ex-husband. Did you get it? 
 After being kicked out of his own home by his mother and stepfather, Gray is invited to live with Mia and Adam. And that's when everything start. 
 A massage. 
 A kiss. 
 To everything. 
 To nothing. 
 At first Mia tries to ignore it, being more than ten years older than him and his best friend's mother she gets a little hold back in giving it a try, but at some point she just can't deny it. Gray is very childish in the start, but he grows up through the book with has made me didn't care about his previous attitudes. 
 Mia and Gray are a such explosive/sexy couple. Mia and Adam are great people. Mia, Adam and Gray are such a lovely family. And Stella is amazing! 
 Although I think we could have had a bigger end (because I loved the book that much!), I really enjoyed this book and would highly recommend it.
Such a great narrator! Her voice jumps off the page, and she propels the story forward, not the characters around her.
Cool book. I think it is a 100 times better than the first part marked.

Still just as good the second time around! Doing a reread of the series before I read Opposition. 
 It's been over a year since the last time I read it and this time around I found that I was less patient with douchebag characters that get away with acting like a dick because "ohmygod he is just so hot like I can't control myself", but I somehow am still in love with this series <3

Fantastic! I was so excited to read this book that I started as soon as I could, and I was blown away. The main reason I'm giving this a lower rating is because it dragged a little, mostly, I think, because Raffe was MIA for most of this book. 
 But that ending was worth every moment that felt long and lonely. Every struggle. Every terror. Every fight that there was no chance of winning. 
 In this book, Penryn misses her enemy gone friend, Raffe. She wonders if he's safe, if he thinks about her, if he managed to get his wings back. While she wonders all this, she struggles to keep her mother and sister together once more. But this new world of apocalyptic proportions is against her. 
 I don't want to give too much away since this is the second book in a series, so I'll just say the following: 
 Read this series. I honestly can't believe I didn't read them sooner. THAT ENDING!!!! *scurries off to read the final book in the series*

When I checked how many pages were in this book, I was shocked. It felt at least twice that long. I really wanted to like this book, but there were too many plots and sub-plots and back stories getting juggled and I had a hard time following it all. Jane's shifts into Beast were distracting and I had a hard time reading those sections. I appreciated the diverse elements of the book, but not a favorite of mine.

Istyria book blog ~ B's world of enchanted books 
 I can always count on Kelly Oram to get me out of a slump. If I want a light, fun and sweet romance, I just have to read one of her books and I feel better instantly! V is for Virgin is one of the books of hers I hadn't read yet and now I have to wonder why that is because it's just as good as the other ones are! 
 V is for Virgin is about Valerie. After being dumped by her boyfriend because she wants to wait until marriage with sex, she starts the V is for Virgin campaign. It doesn't take long to excalade into something bigger than she could've imagined. The downside is Kyle. Lead singer of Tralse, the band that helped her campaign more than they realise. He's made it his personal mission to her change her mind. 
 Going into this I was afraid that I wouldn't be able to relate to the main character because we are so different. But of course I didn't need to be scared. I loved Valerie and I did understand how she felt. I didn't find this unrealistic either. In these times, I think it's very possible for something like this to happen. People have become famous for a lot less in the past few years. 
 I did hate Zach at first because of how he treated Valerie but he redeemed himself. I did love Kyle but I wanted to know more about him! I didn't buy the "romance" with Isaac. Didn't feel it and it felt a bit forced. I loved Cara at first, but I hated how she started treating Valerie after she got Shane as a boyfriend. He's Kyle's bandmate and best friend and while I didn't see enough of him to hate him, I didn't like how it changed Cara. I loved the rest of the side characters though. 
 Ugh this review is all over the place. That's how it feels anyway. I'm not feeling 100% so sorry for babbling away! I love this author and I needs to read more from her.

I was really liking this book up until Aspen showed back up. >_> 
 I thought this would be more of a "getting over a broken heart and moving on" type of story rather than a love triangle. I would have probably continued reading this series had America been a little bit more decisive about her feelings.

Midnight at the Electric evoked a lot of very strong emotions for me. It's a story about relationships, loss, and pining. It reflects on what makes relationships lasting and what draws people together. It's ridiculous really--it's such a small book about so many people, how does it make me feel things!? 
 Relationships are all entangled. Adri meets her long lost elderly cousin Lily and bonding with her first important person. Catherine realizing she must choose between the boy she loves and what she knows or leave it all behind for her sister. Lenore getting the closure she needs on her brother's death and finding solace in a new friend. There's so much want and need within each story and I seriously just wanted to give every single one of these women a big hug--even crochety young Adri. They all had lonely roads that they made worthwhile, and it was beautiful. 
 Stupid skinny book.

*GASP* I hated it. The hyperbole, the "romance", every single one of the characters. Hated it. It's a mildly interesting concept, but all the negatives kept it from being anything other than a mediocre YA dystopian. In fact, I'm taking it of my dystopia and sci-fi shelves because it hardly qualifies for them - it's 95% YA romance. The most interesting parts of this story (the superpowers, the pending conflict, the demise of our current society) were glossed over entirely. Maybe it gets better as the series goes on and these things are explored more fully, but this was such a snooze I can't even think about picking up the next one. Just the thought of trudging through another 300 pages of cringe-worthy makeouts, heart-fluttering, baffling figurative language, and wishy-washy characters is giving me anxiety.

Minor spoilers 
 I thoroughly enjoyed the story. I feel that many trilogies that I read the second books lacking. This is not the case for this book. The characters have grown and so has the world. While we don't get any resolution in this book, it's understandable because it's the middle of the story. The ending really perks a lot of questions that makes me want "The Doors of Stone" to be released asap. 
 I have to disagree with some of the other reviews who say that his time in Ademre and the Fae were wasted. I think that these were important events that will tie in strongly to the story-line...eventually. 
 All and all I am glad to have read this and would recommend it to people who don't mind waiting for a conclusion. If you want your stories wrapped up in a nice little package with a happy ending you may want to steer clear of this one.

3.75 stars 
 Caller of Light is a fantasy romance and the settings are fictional. 
 There are mythical creatures called Critons. Without going into a lot of detail, Critons are similar to dragons. There are Criton riders and the riders can be bonded to their Critons for life. This bond is a sacred thing and can only be done by the Caller of Light. That's a good fantasy element I enjoyed throughout. 
 This novel has a few action/battle scenes and, again, I liked them. Heroine gets to show her skills, Hero gets to show his love, and the reader gets to have their jaw hit the floor thinking, "That won't really happen, right?" I'm not telling. :) 
 Caller of Light is written with three Points of View. That was a bit strange, but mostly we only see the Hero and Heroine's thoughts. I could've done without the antagonist's. He or she was a bit juvenile (sorry, can't say who) and I feel that person's motivations lessened the story. (It took this novel from a 4 star to a 3.75 star.) 
 EVERY good fantasy/other world novel has customs the characters adhere to (Harry Potter, Hunger Games, etc.) and this novel does. LOVE that. Great element and these customs were used to show the progression of Hero and Heroine's relationship. 
 I wished the Caller of Light element was used more. I somehow got the impression the plot would keep growing and show the Caller of Light in action. That didn't happen so there seemed a bit missing. (I didn't read blurbs or reviews of this novel beforehand. My impression came from the text.) 
 But if a book two or series is published I will read it if the action and plot revolve around the fantasy element with the romance. 
 It's a good book; I enjoyed it.

An interesting dystopian novels with elements of historical events as well. 
  Ruby is sent to a 'reconditioning' camp because of something that happened on her 10th birthday - she erased her parent's memories of her. And she now has uncontrollable strange abilities - but I suppose that's better than death, the other result of a strange disease that is sweeping the children of the nature. Ruby is rescued from the camp and then runs from her new captors and joins up with the ragtag group of Liam, Chubs and Zu - three other camp escapees with abilities. Together they try to find 'East River' to hopefully find their parents once again and help them feel normal once again. 
 After running into problem after problem, they do find East River and the leader, the illusive Clancy. Clancy is only after power and control, but he convinces the people in the camp that what he's doing is for their benefit. While in the camp, he does teach Ruby a bit about her ability and how to control it, but in the end, he is stronger because he's had far more practice than she has. 
 The camps that the children are sent to for 're-conditioning' remind me of concentration camps, where the prisoners were divided into categories, kept separate, had jobs to do and eventually certain groups went away under the guise of 'being transferred'. 
 I cannot believe how the group was separated at the end - I felt so bad for all of them, especially Ruby because she knows about Liam, but now Liam doesn't know her.

The story is about a group of aliens that came from the planet Lorien. Their planet was destroyed by the Mogadorians and is now here on Earth hiding and waiting for their time to fight and avenge their planet. The book basically focuses on Four and his struggles as he tries to have a life and stay under the radar of the vicious mogadorians. 
 I read this book after seeing the movie so I was kind of hoping for some badassery and all that jazz. But as I was reading through the book I can't find the will to become emotionally immersed with the story. I mean it is written in the first person point of view but they seem to lack the emotion. There were some times that the characters seem to struggle to deliver a very good message, the one Henri keeps on persisting the one about hope. But I can't seem to find myself to connect with the message. Also I really felt that Sarah and John Smith's love were kinda superficial I don't know. I just can't feel a thing about this book. The only time I felt something was with what happened with Bernie (John's dog). Though, I still can't qualify that since I am really soft when it comes to animals and the fact that it just made me sad and did not tear my heart out just like what it usually does. 
 The action part was also a wreck. I can't clearly visualize what's happening. And John. GOD. He's such a loser I mean, he can't even fight and save his own ass in a cool way and he still had the guts to put his foot down and insist on staying in Ohio. I literally wanted to smack him whenever he puts his foot down. I mean if I was him I would listen to whatever Henri is saying because the guy obviously knows more than I do. Well, I think that's the logical thing to do. Though I can't really blame John since he's undergoing adolescence and this is a YA book, shit just happens. -__-" oh well. I really didn't expect that I wouldn't enjoy the book because I really did enjoy the movie. Oh and one question I don't know what Four looks like. @_@ I can't imagine him as Alex Pettyfer. I swear. I can't imagine Four. I don't know why. The thing I liked about this book is that I was curious as to what powers would Four develop in the long run. I was curious as to how strong he'll get (he's apparently a loser for now but who knows?) So yea, I don't know. The book was, just Okay. I don't hate and I don't love it. It was just okay. Though I think I prefer the movie over the book. Wow now that's a first. 
 Giving this a 2.5 :/

Poor Harry. It my personal opinion that this is the most difficult Harry Potter book. It's the most political, the most emotional, and we get, of course, the first truly heartbreaking death in the series (not that I didn't like Cedric or anything). That moment at the end where Harry tries to call to Sirius through the mirror gets me every time.

I borrowed The Selection from the local library. Now I own it. It's better than I gave it credit for and I'm glad to have it my library. 
 Quick summary: It's kind of like a Hunger Games meets The Bachelor. I know some of you must be thinking "What kind of story is this?" and I completely understand, but read on if you want to know why I love that it's in my library. 
 I really enjoy this story line. 
 The center focus is on love. The obvious love is Aspen and America, which develops into a love triangle with Prince Maxon-America-Aspen. However, there are other loves that come into play as well--love for your family, love between friends, love for the country. 
 I was so interested in knowing what happened next (I mean you have two rebel groups attacking the castle, are they working together? Who are they?) I bought The Selection and The Elite, pre-ordered The One, and then bought the two novellas, The Prince and The Guard because I just couldn't stand it. Dramatic? Probably, but it's okay, I approve it! 
 Feel free to check out my blog for a more detailed review, www.411junkie.com.

I LOVED THIS BOOK. I just really love these characters and this story. So action packed and full of mystery. It was a bit predictable at times but I still enjoyed it. It was a bit too short of a book, the next one better be super long. I'M SUPER EXCITED AND NERVOUS FOR THE NEXT BOOK LIKE WHAT IF JENNIFER KILLS OFF ONE OF THE BOYS OR EVEN ANNA LIKE I'M SO SCARED BUT STILL SUPER EXCITED OMG. 
 OH if you didn't know I love this series sigh

Sometimes, we just want lightly, fluffy, and romantic. And this book delivers. 
 There were perhaps a few too many convenient misunderstandings (and then resolutions) for my taste. Another reviewer compared it to the Hangover, and I'm glad I read that, because the storyline had puzzled me until I read that. I kept questioning why the characters were traipsing around this town, bumbling into everything without being able to piece together the night. And if you're looking for intense historical accuracy, or even more emotional depth to your characters - maybe not this story. 
 But you absolutely cannot fault the story-telling abilities of Jennifer McQuiston. Her novel is a light, bright, and well-woven tale. The author gives us exactly what she has promised to the reader: a lovely, fun romance set in Scotland. Sexy James MacKenzie is our ideal hero, and is a great foil to Georgette. Their story manages to maintain a high level of heat and tension all the way through. 
 This was a fun read that I would recommend to any romance readers.

It has been often said that the way a child has been treated by their parent can effect, and ultimately change the very essence of who they are capable of being. Beginnings regardless of environment will either make or break a child. But how can anyone know which way they will go? This story portrays a mothers struggle, both mentally and emotionally when faced with financial hardship, racial discrimination and how that can impact her own 11 children. 
 That saying from Forest Gump "Life is like a box of chocolates, you never know what you may get", rings true for all characters in this book, but one things for certain, life is hard. I now sit in wonder, had Hattie stayed with her decision of changing her future, was that her golden door of opportunity? I understood Hattie with her inability of showing love to her children. She had nothing left and was trying to hang on with every strength of the little energy she had. Without comfort for the spirit, what light will you ever see? A great first book for "Oprah's book club 2.0 choice. I loved it.

Ironic how it takes losing my hardcopy to realize I haven't reviewed this book, but really I'm praying that I just misplaced it somewhere, and that one day I'll find it buried in a corner underneath the mess that is my bedroom. 
 Whoever knows me know that I love Lauren and that Liesl & Po is one of my favourite children books. A tale of locked attics, alchemists, evil step-mothers, ghosts, creatures that are not-quite-a-cat-nor-a-dog and spaces between worlds, I mean, how could I NOT, and with Lauren's lyrical writing? And the illustrations... I need to get me another hardcopy.

Trite and predictable. Even though it was written for a younger audience, I wouldn't want them to read it because it continually insults the reader's intelligence. I will NOT be reading any more books in this series.

I really like Shelly Laurenston as an author. I throughly enjoyed her Pride series and I'm seriously hooked on the Call of Crows series, the first book, The Unleashing {review} was a strange but fun read and The Undoing is just as good, no wait, it's actually better! 
 The idea behind the Call of Crows is based on Viking mythology and several of the gods and goddess have clans who represent and do work from them. Most of the members of the clans have belonged to their clan for generations. With the exception of the Crows. The women who become members of the Crow clan basically die in awful and horrific ways and are then approached by the goddess who hears their cries and wishes and brings them back to life to exact their revenge and to join the Crow clan. 
 While each book in the Call of Crows series is technically individual, they are not standalone. You can't pick this one up first and think you can pick up the storyline! I actually went back and skimmed through the first book before reading The Undoing because it's been a whole year and I had forgotten some things. Which I definitely needed. 
 You first meet Jace and her quirkiness in The Unleashing so her attitude and behaviour follow on and while Jace is the very definition of an introvert she is still crazy enough to be one of the crows, even though she sometimes feels like she doesn't fit with them. 
 First paragraph: 
 "He packed more dirt on her body. She felt it now. Felt the dirt falling against her face, her arms and legs. He was trying to wipe away all evidence of her. Pretend she didn't exist. Pretend she'd never existed." 
 Ski is a Protector and is a really great match for Jace, other than of course his tiny problem with making small talk! Honestly, I really loved most of the Protectors. They're all into information gathering and books and protecting information. They seemed like a great bunch of characters. I really hope we get more from them. 
 Of course you see more characters from clan Crow and the ongoing storyline does carry on from the previous book. You also get to meet characters from the other clans as well as continuing seeing characters from clan Raven who were in the previous book along with the previous couple. 
 There's no clue, to me, who's book is next but I seriously enjoyed The Undoing, it's about 400 pages long and is a really great read. It starts well and ends just as well. I was a little sad when it ended! I can't wait for the next book! 
 Series order: 
 The Unleashing #1 
 This review is based on the ARC of The Undoing provided by Kensington Books

Holy cow. What a book. Compassionate, funny, weird, astounding, neuro-geeky, short, simple, to the point. If you've read anything in the New Yorker about agnosias and amnesias and the like, seen any movie Christian Bale or DiCaprio have ever appeared in, wondered about the mind/brain problem . . . you will like this book, trust me.

I freaked out when I saw this book was dropped! I've definitely been waiting. 
 And this book does pick up where Red Skies left off, leaving Locke a sliver away from death and Jean panicking out of his mind to fix him. Of course, only Bondsmagi have the solution and it's just another game they're thrown into. Heyo, they've survived anything, they should be fine, win, and prosper. Right? A certain Lady Bastard might disagree when they find out she's their opponent. 
 Sabetha. Ah, we finally meet her. The only person who turns silver-tongue Locke into a stuttering idiot. I am impressed that I don't hate her. I say that with all seriousness. Usually authors who only hint at potential women can't write them to meet up to the expectations that we've set. Sabetha comes very close to what I would have imagined. And Locke's stupid silly obsessive nature and love makes up for the rest. I love that she was written in such a way where she has reasons to dislike him, reasons to say no, where she's not perfect by any means, etc. She actually has personality, even though most of it is not entirely friendly. I can see why a lot of people won't like her, especially since most will root for Locke (and she turns him into a 7 year boy, ha). But I'd rather have the character with character flaws than the one who is perfect and boring. I can't say Sabetha is one of my favorite characters because she's still barely penciled in and shaded as a character. I haven't seen enough of her to say much besides she is a strong, female character that very closely lives up to expectations (which were high to begin with, so there is that). 
 I must say though... Locke did get a little annoying after a while when he doesn't have any confidence. Poor guy. 
 The other characters aren't really worth talking about because Locke and Jean don't really changes. And the rest aren't here to stay and play - they're just accessories for this one book. Oh, except for the flashbacks. 
 I loved reading about their younger days! And I was glad to have the Sanzas back. I really liked the two of them as a comedic relief pair. And seeing their dynamics when they were younger, thinking about Chains's difficulties with pubescent and hormonal Bastards, haha. It's great. But as much as I adored reading about the whole gang when they were younger, the acting stint arc was just so-so. He put too many pages of actual play dialogue for me to be happy. I rolled my eyes at the stupid lines and skipped on to the real plot. 
 I didn't like this book as much as the previous two. I think it's because the plot had less thought. Lies of Locke Lamora was meticulously planned out and it was fantastic. Plot after scheme after counterplot and betrayal and lies. It really was crazy. And then Red Skies got a little less intricate. And then Republic of Thieves definitely had the least amount of intricate plot. This was an "introduce Sabetha" book. The amount of plot was mostly paragraphs hinting at Locke's plans. But nothing truly deceptive or deep. Which made me feel a little lacking because I wanted to be blown out of the water with his ingenuity. I'm not entirely sure if that's fair of me because I know coming up with schemes means the author has to seriously plot something out and sometimes you run out of crazy ideas... but as a reader, I was still a little disappointed. 
 I also didn't like how Locke's true background was revealed. I thoroughly enjoyed book one because of how anonymous he was, even after the entire book ended. But here, the mysteries are starting to be peeled back, and it's not as wonderful and mysterious as it seemed from the far away distance of book one. ... I think I'm just afraid of how the next few books are going to turn out with the reveal of his background. I don't want it to follow too many tropisms. But already, it seems like it's heading in that direction. Ahhh!! I just hope Lynch knows what he's doing. 
 And (spoilers) pooh on the last chapter. I don't entirely approve of ending books with the rise of the villain for the next book. 
 Like Red Skies, book #3 only gets 2.5 stars, rounded up to 3. It was good and I liked it, but in the end, it's the plot that has to sell me and I really only bought two and half stars of it. 
 Definitely read if you've already become acquainted with Locke Lamora. And I definitely recommend the first book to anyone who's wondering what this series is all about.

Picked this up based on the cover art, the James Patterson blurb, and a hope that I can discover something for teen guys to read once they've exhausted Darren Shan and Anthony Horowitz. On the plus side, the cover is appealing for this serviceable prison-break story. Alex is an acceptable hero, who is both a petty criminal and noble when it counts. There are a few Frankenstein-esque monsters, some classic gross-out scenes, and once the action gets going - about 150 pages in - the plot is propulsive. 
 The writing was easy to follow, but took a long time to gear up after the strong opening. Of course, I felt the same way about Lord Loss, and readers gobble that up, so perhaps Smith is onto something and I'm just not in sync with the audience. I certainly didn't get much sense of character development, and Smith's last-minute interjection of 'what-does-freedom-really-mean' sounded flimsy. 
 Although there's violence and horror on a par with the books I've already cited, the absence of sex, drug use, and profanity makes this a good choice for a wide range of ages. While I didn't love it, I'll probably pick up the sequels, just to see how they turn out.

It seemed to take forever to read this because I was so busy, but I absolutely loved this trilogy! It was fantastic!! Lauren Oliver is now one of my favorite authors. I'm actually kind of sad the story is over.

This didn't start off too well, quickly becoming my least favourite of the series so far, but thankfully it picked up and while it isn't a favourite, I still ended up enjoying it. 
 Things were so up and down for the first 25% or so. Talin can't decide whether she wants to talk to Clay or not, or whether she wants him or not, or whether she's too scared of him or not. And I get that she has mixed feelings - she had such a fucked up childhood - and I understand her being afraid of him - the last time she saw him, she was eight years old and had just witnessed him tearing apart her abusive foster father - but it was incredibly frustrating to read. It didn't help that Clay was all over the place, being quite pushy with her, and then acknowledging why she might be reluctant due to her horrific past, but then going back to being pushy, and then getting pissed off with her because she'd been with other men. Um, hello? You've acknowledged that she had a fucked up childhood which would explain her views and hesitations and then a couple of pages later you're ignoring that and acting confused and pissed about it? Throughout the book there were times where I think that Clay pushed things a bit too far for my liking considering the issues that Talin had. 
 Also it kind of creeped me out a bit that his first thoughts were about how attractive he found her and how they'd been so close when they were kids. It wasn't so much they were friends as kids, that normally doesn't bother me at all, it was the fact that she was eight and he was fourteen when they last saw each other and for a while it made me feel uncomfortable. The friendship part was cute, him looking out for her, but the jump from that to instant attraction was a bit gross to me. 
 This is the first book in the series that isn't between a Psy and a changeling so I did enjoy the change there. This time it's between a human and a changeling. Different challenges. And there was a lot of backstory there to build a foundation between the characters, even if it did gross me out at times. We still got to see some more developments from the Psy side of things and wow, it's getting even more messed up and frightening and I can see it getting a lot worse. I find the whole PsyNet, NetMind, DarkMind stuff fascinating and now learning about the Forgotten. There's so much there! Really well thought out.

I had a lot of mixed feelings about this story. Tate was such a sweet girl and to read about how she was bullied continuously throughout the story was hard. Especially coming from a boy who was once her best friend. 
 Jared had a hard time after coming back from his visit with his dad when he was a kid. Once he came back he was a very different person and started to lash out at Tatum. 
 Finally a poem gets to him that she reads In school. And I start to see why he became that way even if I don't agree with it. 
 K.C I really liked to and hope she can have her own story. 3.5 star! !

Although I enjoyed this one better than most of the other House of Night novels (probably 99% due to the fact that IT'S OVER!), there were still several moments that made me roll my eyes so hard I gave myself a headache. 
 I don't hate this series. Sure the characters are annoying and I grew really tired of so much filler, but I don't hate it. It's simply a case of "I'm too old for this s---." I started reading these books when I had just finished Twilight and wanted more vampire books. I didn't yet know about the wide world of YA books, and vampires were new and exciting to me at the time. So I spent some birthday money on a House of Night box set. It started out too immature for me but the series actually did get better once I got past book 2, plus I wanted to read all the ones I'd already paid for. Logical, right? It was fun for a while, and I even bought a couple more of the books as they came out, but then I realized this series was stretching out way too much with way too little plot. For the past 5 books at least, it's been very much about continuing what I started, and since I still like some of the characters and wanted to see how everyone ended up, I stuck it out. 
 Overall I would give the entire series a 2-3 star rating. I don't regret reading them because it's such a long and known series that I feel I would have been missing out to know nothing about them. But it was just too much teen angst and same old recycle plots for me. 
 There were a few moments in this final book that I found exciting, but overall I didn't think it accomplished much.  
 -Neferet is once again banished, not actually killed. If Kalona, another immortal was able to be killed, why couldn't the same measures (taking pieces of her immortality) be done to Neferet? I think it would have served the overall plot better to have started on this a few books back and have the nemesis from 12 books actually be defeated in the end! I feel like I wasted my time! 
 -I REALLY felt like Erik and Shaunee was a huge cop out. I hate the way multiple characters have been treated like puppets over the course of this series. Erik has probably been the worst, how he flipped a switch to become such a such a jerk early on and now he's flipped another switch and suddenly everything is OK and he wants to be with Shaunee. And where are Shaunee's motivations for wanting to be with him? Nonexistent. 
 -Lynette served zero purpose. She gets her own POV sections, she gets rescued, then goes back and ends up dying. I don't see why Neferet's POV couldn't have covered what Lynette's did. And seeing as how NONE of our main characters ever even KNEW Lynette went back to Neferet, just why did you waste my time with her? It would have been awesome if the Nerd Herd had used Lynette to go back in and help defeat Neferet.

This was my introduction to Eggers' writing, and I now have absolutely no interest in reading anything else by him. Perhaps this was a bad place to start. I've heard plenty of good reviews about his other books. His efforts to raise awareness of human rights issues are commendable. Judging by this novel, however, he seems to assume that his audience will be aware enough of his real world efforts that he can now speak in shorthand. How else to excuse his bragging about not undertaking any research before writing The Circle? I can tell you that the lack of effort certainly shows. Take the huge revelation that (...gasp!) data in the cloud actually requires a physical server, or that pulling all online services under one umbrella would somehow make that service safer rather than giving hackers one big bullseye. The whole premise comes across as implausible, which handicaps the story from the get-go. 
 Even beyond that, the characters are so flat that they give 2D a bad name. The exposition is painfully self-aware, conversations are generally wooden, and we are never really given to understand why a character's motivation can so suddenly shift. So long as it slavishly serves to move the plot along, little consideration is given to believability. There are a few moments where I could feel something more real, but these all quickly devolved back to the status quo of overblown inanity. Definitely not my cup of tea.

More of a family drama or women's fiction than suspense, Girls in the Garden made me fearful for my little ones - a reminder that they're going to be teenagers one day, with teenager secrets and teenager justifications for all sorts of craziness. And scary not just because of what happens to Grace, but because it seems that no sort of parenting can prevent what happened from happening. 
 I kept thinking as I was reading this "only in England could this magical garden exist"; Americans would be too worried about child snatchers in the park to let their kids roam as freely as the kids here do. Especially if there had already been an earlier unfortunate occurrence. 
 So the suspense was less of a "who dunnit" kind of suspense - more of a growing and well-formulated sense of panic about a mom who doesn't know what's currently happening with her kids, both from a psychological perspective (when she doesn't even realize Grace has a boyfriend) and a physical perspective (where is my kid?). 
 We gradually see how clueless Clare is (though not in any sort of negative way - she's got a lot going on, what with her actually crazy ex-husband and all  ) about what's going between Grace and her boyfriend or her daughters and the other girls. Which again played on my own personal fear of "holy crap, my kids are going to be teenagers one day, and they're going to pull the same shit I did..." and probably a fear Lisa Jewell was very much aiming to elucidate. 
 And Adele, with whom I totally empathized and sympathized, was also, in the end equally clueless, despite her home-schooling, generally awesome parenting, and healthy habits.  Lisa Jewell seemed to be sort of winking at all of us hippy moms out there who, despite our best intentions, can't stop our kids from eating Twinkies and also, occasionally, from beating the shit out of another girl when she doesn't fit in.  
 There's almost a sort of wink here for Gordon's type of parenting, perhaps?

This was another of the books I'm reading for the Richard and Judy Book Club Challenge, hosted by Vicky at Books, Biscuits and Tea. I enjoyed the first book I read as part of the challenge, so I had high hopes for this one too, and I did really like it. 
 The book starts with the end of the story, when Alex suffers an epileptic attack while stopped at customs, with marijuana in the glovebox and an urn full of ashes on the front seat. Alex is in big trouble, with the whole country in uproar about something he has done, but we don't know what yet. The story is then propelled into the past as Alex decides to explain exactly what happened to him that led him to this moment. 
 I'm not often a fan of the 'start at the end' kind of story. Sometimes it works very well, but if it's not used for a story that really needs to be told that way, or if the events leading up to that moment are actually more boring than the event itself, then it can just be frustrating. Here, it largely works well. Alex begins by telling us about an unlikely but true event in which he was struck by a meteorite. This has a large impact on his life, and leads him down certain paths, which eventually causes him to meet an old American man, Mr. Peterson, who lives in his village. They strike up an odd but funny and heart-warming friendship. I loved the character of Mr. Peterson and really enjoyed the parts of the book where he and Alex interacted and discussed life and literature. 
 I did feel, however, that the 'middle section' of the novel dragged a bit. For me, this book was too long, and I would have preferred things to move more quickly towards the events that we saw at the beginning, and to the resolution. Alex sometimes takes too long to explain things to the reader that, while it makes sense that Alex finds them interesting, to the reader might be less so, and might not seem so relevant to his overall story. I think the book would have been more enjoyable, and the messages and emotional impact much stronger, if it had moved just a little quicker, focussing more on Alex and Mr. Peterson and less on some of the other things that happened. Having said that, it does have a very strong end, and I was quite surprised when I finally realised what Alex's mysterious, controversial actions (which were hinted at the beginning of the book) were going to be. 
 Alex is written convincingly and has a compelling voice, and though I sometimes found him a little hard to relate to, I did really like him as a narrator and main character. This is a very thoughtful book with a lot to say about the world and the assumptions and rules people make for themselves, and Alex's very simple, matter-of-fact way of telling the story really worked well for this. The book left me with lots to think about, and there were some very moving moments. 
 This review also appears on my blog.

[2nd time: After a re-read I find myself still in agreement with my earlier review below. This time I will actually read more of the series, however.] 
 In the forward, King says his inspiration to start this series was to somehow combine the widescreen spaghetti western feel of The Good, The Bad and The Ugly with an epic fantasy world of Lord of the Rings scope. At least in this first installment, the combo comes across more as spaghetti western + David Lynchian surrealness + random elements from forgotten horror comic books BUT somehow it works. 
 This was interesting as my first King read since junior high (read Pet Cemetery and The Shining then) because I'd been reading online criticisms of King's writing, and this seems to escape some of the most-often lobbed objections. For instance, he was charged with always having a simplistic good vs evil view, protagonist always clearly-identified good guy/gal fighting clearly-identified evil. Well, sure, the book's protagonist Roland is chasing a guy called only "the man in black" whom we see do a least hideous act ...but Roland himself is a deeply compromised character, not only does he gun down an entire town, men, women and children (admittedly, in self-defense)  but he sacrifices his dependent-upon-him companion, the young boy Jake, to get closer to man in black . 
 I also liked the flashback to Roland's younger days especially the whole tale of his enraged rush to take the rite-to-manhood duel early, fueled by his desire to challenge his mother's illegitimate lover - the brashness of the youthful action (spurred by the lover insulting him), his trainer's reluctance to duel him early, the way he won the duel -- all of that worked excellently as a mini-story . 
 The only thing that was disappointing was the very end - after such buildup, the man in black was pretty disappointing in that he ended up being just a (partial) exposition machine. Plus the fact that his exposition had a little too much of a weed-drenched "wow, man, what if our world is just a pebble in another world, and that world is just a pebble in another world, and..." feel to its idea -- although admittedly, Rudy Rucker could make the same idea work as complicated-physics-sci-fi..it's just that King can't. But even if the *idea* was working better, I don't know if this book's climax's way of handling it would. Well, there's much more of the series to develop the idea in better ways... . 
 A very odd mix, but I'm intrigued enough to try more of this series, and even try some of the other supposedly linked-to-this-series King books.

I think I've decided I don't like the star rating system. I like analyzing things too much, and my feelings on this book run the whole gambit. 
 I'll start by saying that as far as writer's craft, Paolo Bacigalupi is a five star writer. The way he plays with the language, his powers of description, his attention to minutiae are all skills I to which I aspire. This book surrounds you with post-crisis Thailand from the sweltering heat to the stink of plague. The world envisioned is also terrifyingly probable. I remember doing research back in college on genetically modified foods and the disease mutations produced by them, but I don't think my brain ever made the next logical leap to fear and horror until reading this book. 
 The complexity of Bacigalupi's plot is intense. There are so many crises facing each and every character, and just when one of them distracts you to the point you forget the others, boom! Also he has the plague! Or white shirts attack. Or a plan goes awry. It's a lot to keep track, and Bacigalupi does it masterfully, instilling suspense and surprise at every chapter. Add to that the normalcy of a world without cats or elephants or pineapples, of government balancing on knife edges, of humanity delving just a little too deep. It's a world just slightly twisted from the one we know, and one where we could end up with just a few mis-steps. 
 His characters too are complex, believable, and sympathetic. Kanya's life as a double agent, coming to sympathize with the people she still despises, is fascinating to watch, and I love how she ends the story. Jaidee is likable, direct, and therefore doomed, but I loved his muay thai approach to the world, and I don't think I'd like the book at all if his phii didn't come around to snark behind Kanya's back. Hock Seng's unstoppable need to prepare and survive at whatever cost is balanced out by his sympathy for little Mai. He's like a Thenardier with a heart. Emiko, naturally, is the character that held my attention the strongest. I love the way her alien nature comes through the prose, the steady fighting of her nature and training against the reality of a world she for which she was never intended. When Emiko murders the Somdet Chaopraya and his men, I just about cheered. For a title character, though, she gets remarkably little screen time.  
 I think that Emiko's lack of screen time is really what keeps me from loving this book for all of its craft. The title is "The Windup Girl," and I went in expecting a story about human hybrids surviving in a post-crisis world. I expected her to go North to the windup encampment. Instead, I got a story about Thai politics and genetically modified fruit. It's an interesting story, but it's not the kind of book that would normally peak my interest. For every heart-breaking or hear-stopping emotional chapter, there's five about political nuances and lychee. It was all necessary, but I found those chapters hard to sit through, especially in the beginning. If you have trouble with slow-starting novels, this one is really not for you. 
 I'd add to that statement that you should not try this novel if you are not okay with a lot of disturbing, often sexual, violence. I'm not accusing Bacigalupi of being gratuitous because that violence really cements the world and is vital to Emiko's character change, to the very idea that the mistreatment of just one person can topple the world (a theme I very much enjoyed), but it is graphic and again, hard to read. 
 It's hard for me to sum up my feelings on this book because they are so polarized. On the one hand, I have to respect the craft and skill that went into its creation as well as the entirely topical themes it introduces. On the other... it wasn't the book I was looking for. I didn't get enough time with the characters I wanted to follow, and I had to spend a lot of pages mired in stories I wasn't interested in. 3 stars might be harsh, but using the rating as my strictly personal opinion, that's about where it falls.

 Of course like so many supernatural romances since Twilight, everything hints at Twilight, we meet the hottie, in this case an actual badboy (not a badboy trying to be good), in biology. Where Nora is forced to sit next to Patch..., note to author I prefer for my characters to have an actual name, and she gets all the stay away vibes but who can resist a guy who loves wearing black...all the time and drives a motorcycle. But all of her hatred seemed to stem from not having anything, which just didn't seem to fit. If Mare acknowledged some of that privilege and how other families had suffered greater loss, it wouldn't have seemed so odd. I also think Shade being alive was a huge cop-out of the author. I don't mean to imply that her family didn't suffer, especially her dad, but it just seems way too unrealistic that none of her brothers died in war and being taken care of by the monarchy. It just felt irritatingly convenient.  
 This would have been a more enjoyable escape if I had had the time to just sit down and sink into it. If the author had spent more time developing the world and characters, this could have been really great. As it is, it's like all the worst parts of The Selection meets The Hunger Games with better writing but not world-building.

This book was really good and a perfect example of building anticipation with foreshadowing. For most of the book, we know something happened on Parents' Trivia Night at the school; possibly a murder. 
 The book centers around the parents of kindergarteners and the drama that ensues when one child accuses another of bullying on the first day. Of course there are parent cliques and lofty opinions about child-rearing leading to quite a bit of friction. Some of the parents even start a petition to try to have the purported bully expelled. 
 The plot intertwines among the lives of three women and their children, each at a crossroads: 
 Madeline is a force to be reckoned with. She's funny and biting, passionate, she remembers everything and forgives no one. Her ex-husband and his zen new wife have moved into her beloved beachside community, and their daughter is in the same kindergarten class as Madeline's youngest (how is this possible?). And to top it all off, Madeline's teenage daughter seems to be choosing Madeline's ex-husband and his second wife over her. 
 Celeste is the kind of beautiful woman who makes the world stop and stare. While she may seem a bit flustered at times, who wouldn't be, with those rambunctious twin boys? Now that the boys are starting school, Celeste and her husband look set to become the king and queen of the school parent body. But royalty often comes at a price, and Celeste is grappling with how much more she is willing to pay. 
 New to town, single mom Jane is so young that another mother mistakes her for a nanny. Jane is sad beyond her years and harbors secret doubts about her son who is the purported bully. But why? While Madeline and Celeste soon take Jane under their wing, none of them realizes how the arrival of Jane and her inscrutable little boy will affect them all. 
 Big Little Lies is a brilliant take on ex-husbands and second wives, mothers and daughters, schoolyard scandal, and the dangerous little lies we tell ourselves just to survive.

Disclaimer 
 : This book magically appeared in my PO Box. I have no idea where it came from. I didn't buy it and the author didn't send it to me. It seems I was meant to read this book and I'm so glad I did. 
 Review 
 : If you're anything like me you read the description of this book and rolled your eyes. It starts out strong and then you have a Were-Cheetah, guys named Zulu and the use of the word "raunchy". I knew this book was a risk when I started it. It was either going to be the best book ever written in the Supernatural Genre or it was going to be a complete tomato. 
 By the time I was two pages in I knew which it was - this was going to be an awesome book. I'll list out below the major things that pull Fire Baptized out from the crowd of crappy Supernatural Romance books out there right now, but the main thing that set it apart is that Wright buys into her own story so completely, it comes alive on the page. There is never a moment when it feels like the author is pushing too hard or where the prose comes across more tongue in cheek then actual. This book is written as fictional realism, contemporary mystery or literary romance, there just happen to be flying monsters and were-folk. It's presented as so common place that you can't help but believe the world created. Parallel to our own, it's a completely plausible alternate reality. 
 In addition there are a few points that separate 
 Fire Baptized 
 from the pack: 
 The Love Triangle: 
 Instead of some convoluted, unexplainable attraction, the romance in FB is believable and engaging. MeShack (the were-cheetah) is Lanore's ex-boyfriend, who is promiscuous and still madly in love with her. It's hard not to want these two to end up together, except for the fact that MeShack is led by his were-instincts more than his head and can't resist the seduction and conquest of a new lover. It seems like Lanore should just tell him to bugger off, but their love is the kind of soul-mate bond that isn't so easily broken. They were raised together and MeShack is conditioned, dedicated and biologically pre-destined to be Lanore's protector. Their childhood traumas and mutual devotion form a strong bond. 
 The other man in Lanore's life is Zulu (yeah, I laughed at the name at first, but it fits him once you get into his story). He's mysterious, political, influential and driven. As the leader of the MFE (Mixies For Equality) he represents a Black Panther or ACT UP! kind of movement. Lanore is drawn to him for his politics, his beliefs, his devotion to her as well as a sick body. 
 While there's definitely a choice for Lanore to make, there is no flip flopping or whiny "Oh it's so hard to be me" Twilight bullshit. Instead we have a sexual woman, with a past and a future which includes two wonderful men. Both have flaws but both are fully developed three dimensional characters. 
 The Diversity: 
 Thank Baby Buddah! For ONCE there is a book set in the supernatural world which includes people of multiple races. I've read a few who have tried to do this but it's usually a "hey, look! I have a book about black people!" Instead 
 Fire Baptized 
 is just a book, set in a world where diversity is the norm. Race is discussed, joked about and sometimes even an issue, but it's as much a part of their lives as it is for most of us who live in a multi-ethnic community. Lanore isn't just a black girl. She isn't defined or announced by her race, instead MeShack helps her wax her dreads after a shower. It's a normal and real part of her existence. This is the kind of writing which brings diversity into a story without making you feel like you're getting some kind of lecture. 
 Fire Baptized 
 could easily be seen as a exploration of race relations in America, with segregation and internment camps from our past coming to a speculative reality. If you dig deep, you can see issues of desegregation, inter-racial relationships and children as well as an us vs. them theme. These themes are there, but they aren't teaching us or lecturing us, instead Wright has built on the reality of racism/sexism/homophobia and used them to create a world which presents as true. 
 The Series: 
 Fire Baptized 
 is a stand alone book. The story is completed and the reader is satisfied with what they have read. However it is the first book in the Habitat Series. Book Two 
 Burning Bush 
 will be coming out in August and I have to say I am chomping at the bit for a copy. FB did what the best First Book of a Series will do, it made me want to read more, but left me feeling satisfied with the adventure I had been on. Wright also has a free ebook called 
 Caged View 
 which appears to be little character explorations for The Habitat MCs. I'll check it out at some point but I hate ebooks. However, I love this series so much I'm going to try and pick it up. In addition The Habitat World is used as the back drop for another series Wright is working on called Cage Punks. Book One 
 Chameleon 
 is coming sometime later this year. I'm a little giddy... 
 The Audience: 
 Another HUGE plus for 
 Fire Baptized 
 is the fact that it is NOT YA. When's the last time you read a good Supernatural Dystopian book that wasn't written for teens? Oh you can think of one? Bet'cha a nickel it was full on romance or erotica. Not so with 
 Fire Baptized 
 . Here we have characters who are strong and vulnerable, smart and emotional. We have a woman who isn't ashamed of her body but who also isn't a slut. Sexy men who serve as more than just masturbation material (although there's some of that too.) This is not PG or PG-13. This is a book meant from grown-ups, real people swear, real people fuck, real people cry. Lanore and her co-horts are more like us than one would expect from a book about Fairies and Were-Cheetahs. 
 In the end, 
 Fire Baptized 
 is what every Indie book should strive to be. I found ZERO typos or other editing issues. I'm sure there are a few (there are in every book) but I've gotten to be a pretty critical reader and they either aren't there or I was too wrapped up in the story to notice. The book is beautifully written, expertly constructed and fully realized. 
 If Sookie Stackhouse is a penny that Lanore Vesta is a million dollars. This is the next big thing, buy it now.

I looked and searched for reasons to keep going. Patty whining and self-pity was very annoying to me. Walter's wimpyness didn't exactly win a medal in my heart either, though at least he tried to be as genuine as possible and more so than other characters. These two "are incredibly wrong for each other and stuck in a monotonous and needy relationship." Richard and Joey were far from being angels. The one character that Franzen didn't really get into was Jessica, and I'm not sure why he didn't. 
 Despite all the things I didn't like about this book, I'd grown to care for the characters. Even though Patty was annoying, she tried to redeem herself and do right again. And when all the characters came back together in the end, I had a sense that everyone matured. All was forgiven and that we can mend broken relationship despite all the pains it had caused. 
 One of many parts that stuck out in my mind was by Walter when he, Lalitha, Richard, and Jessica were in brainstorming session about Free Space: 
 People came to this country for either money or freedom. If you don't have money, you cling on to your freedoms all the more angrily. Even if smoking kills you, even if you can't afford to feed your kids, even if your kids are getting shot down by maniacs with assault rifles. You may be poor, but the one thing nobody can take a way from you is the freedom to fuck up your life whatever way you want to. 
 Not that it was an eye-opener for me, but I liked how Franzen had summarized it. "...freedom to fuck up your life whatever way you want to." Patty knew that she was stuck in perpetual self-destruction, but she didn't want to get out. Similar to Walter. And similar to Richard. The only one that came out of it, to me, was Joey. 
 I wanted to hate this book, but in the end it left me too much to ponder. The book, however, could be a lot shorter. Editing, editing, editing next time, Mr. Franzen.
