I find myself somewhat conflicted by this novel. There were things that I really enjoyed and others that I just did not. The final few chapters of the novel were better than the rest, I thought. The story was a mix of fantasy and mystery set in a world where a once enslaved country has taken over the country that once suppressed them. That land was once governed by the divine-godlike beings who blessed (and cursed) their subjects. 
 The mystery was fairly interesting though I did find certain aspects a bit obvious. The writing style grew on me, though I wasn't very intrigued in the beginning. The characters, for the most part, were well developed and interesting. Sigrud was my favorite and I enjoyed getting to see more of him as the novel progressed. 
 Overall this was enjoyable though I didn't find it brilliant. I was rather invested in the story and wanted to find out what was happening (and see if my conjectures were correct), however. Which kept me reading even when I wasn't feeling particularly attached to the characters. I think a lot of fantasy and mystery fans would enjoy this, particularly those who enjoy gods and myths.

The characters and events of this novel appear and recede much like figures in a mist. 
 If you must have a clear and definite sense of conflict or plot, steer clear. 
 This is a story for those who have had their fill of the didactic tendency in literature. This is a story for those who take delight in an author's delight in illuminating the crevices of non-thought through sound. 
 So, try: this is a story for those who are content with beginning their readings from the final chapter and going on backwards, sussing out the mystery underlying each scene with a sense of calm detachment, eager only for the next break for tea. 
 This is a story for those who have no need of stories that lack the sometimes harsh poignancy of things as they are.

Carl Sagan, a brilliant and humble man. 
 This is a compilation of the Gifford Lectures on Natural Theology which he presented in 1985 at the University of Glascow. 
 If there were ever a champion for science, it was Sagan. And thank "God" for him. The beauty and eloquence of his words are only superceded by the beauty and eloquence of his ideas. 
 Some passages that stood out for me  
 These (referring to technological advances and advances in human right's issues etc) are all things that have happened very recently, and you can think of many, many other, all of which involve not just a change in the technical details of our lives but changes in how we think about ourselves in the world. Very major changes, and therefore not a circumstance where the wisdom of, say, the sixth century B.C. is necessarily relevant. it might be, but it might not be. And therefore, for this reason as well--for this reason especially--wisdom may lie not in simply the blind adherence to ancient tenets but in the vigorous and skeptical and creative investigation of a wide variety of alternatives. 
 This struck me as particularly poignant given the recent Supreme Court ruling in the US regarding gay marriage. 
 We kill each other, or threaten to kill each other, in part, I think, because we are afraid we might not ourselves know the truth, that someone else with a different doctrine might have a closer approximation to the truth. Our history is in part a battle to the death of inadequate myths. If I can't convince you, I must kill you. That will change your mind. You are a threat to my version of the truth, especially the truth about who I am and what my nature is. The thought that I may have dedicated my life to a lie, that I might have accepted conventional wisdom that no longer, if it ever did, corresponds to the external reality, that is a very painful realization. I will tend to resist it to the last. I will go to almost any lengths to prevent myself from seeing that the worldview that I have dedicated my life to is inadequate. 
 Oh my. BAM! I think he nailed this one dead center on its head. 
 One thing that seems especially striking in contemporary culture is how few benign vision of the immediate future are offered up. The mass media show all sort of apocalyptic scenarios, ghastly futures. And there tends to be a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy to these prognostications. How rarely is it that we see a projection twenty or fifty or a hundred years into the future into a world in which we have come to our senses, in which we have figured things out? We can do that. There's nothing that say that we will inevitable fail to meet these challenges. We have solved more difficult problems, and may times. 
 So true. Tune into any major news media outlet and there seems to be this discussion of how bad things are...this desire to "make America great again," "get this country back on track," a pining for the good old days when things were so much better, simpler. Jesus expected the end of times to occur in his lifetime...and still people are waiting for the world to end. 
 But really, the reality is that the quality of life for most of us has steadily increased. We have made tremendous gains in technology, human rights issues, medicine, morality. Sure, we have a long way to go, but as a history buff, it seems to me as if the gains we've made are substantial and speak to our ability to do the right thing. 
 I tend very much to agree with you, but I would say that purpose is not imposed from the outside; it is generated from the inside. We make our own purpose. And there is a kind of dereliction of duty of us humans when we say that the purpose is to be imposed on the outside or found in some book written thousands of years ago. We live in a very different world than we lived in thousands of years ago. There is not question that we may have many obligations to guarantee our purposes, one of which is to survive. And that we have to work out for ourselves. 
  
 There is also a wonderful question and answer section provided. Of particular interest are those questions designed to get Sagan to concede to the possibility if not likelihood of a God. I think one of the most important points he makes both in the lecture itself and during these questions is that a lot depends on how you define "God." Most atheists I know are not opposed to the idea of a powerful force that is beyond our immediate understanding. They are willing to go wherever the evidence takes them and many are agnostic. However, that broad, hazy interpretation of God is much different than the very specific and rigid Gods of various traditional religions, many of whom supposedly dictated religious texts filled with absolute truths about the world. 
 There are also some wonderful, thought-provoking, and humbling photos of the universe. Great read which I highly recommend.

The Maze Runner was pretty exciting as there's quite a lot of action going on throughout this book. I've got to be honest, though - I picked it up because I heard there's going to be a movie of it (with a cast that looks like a lot of fun!). Not the best of reasons for reading a book. And I've got to say, I'm also not the best adult to read YA books and to comment on them. 
 I liked the set up - mysterious, challenging. Pretty much the whole book takes place in a very limited world, which in many ways was still unknown even to the 'Gladers' who had been there for a long time (not so smart bunch, it seems like). Only as  they escape from the maze and we get some snippets re: what happened before and the craycray 'Creators' , we get a sense of just how limited. The second book must carry heaps of explanations of how their world works. 
 As for Thomas himself - not too bad. He seemed like an okay guy. Of course he's skilled and smart, but what YA book character isn't? What I really didn't like (and this has more to do with the writing than the character himself) was how he always felt tons of emotions at once ("Different emotions battled for dominance in his mind and heart. Confusion. Curiosity. panic. Fear. But laced through it all was the dark feeling of utter hopelessness,--"). He also had these sudden bursts of courage or anger, which seemed pretty odd, as he deflated soon after. Maybe just the ambivalence of a teenager, who knows. 
 The beginning of the story was confusing. On purpose. Oh, very much on purpose. So much on purpose that it got annoying that no one was willing to explain anything to Thomas. It's not a strange thing that the author wanted his readers to be just as confused as the main character, but the brusque brush-offs of the supporting characters and such just made it seem fishy. While there was no fishy-ness going on (not really among them, anyway). It made the first part a bit off-putting, actually. 
 The author very cleverly created a whole load of vocabulary to replace the usual crude words. It needs some time to get used to (as even these are not explained right away). Clever, because these teenagers get to cuss the hell out of everything while staying PG. 
 The ending was very obviously set up for a sequel, but I think in a good way. There's a major cliffhanger but also a sense of resolution, the closing of a chapter (or in this case, a book). It does grow a sense of wanting to know what happens next, I guess. I felt satisfied with how he ended this part, though, and am not planning to read the next installment. 
 Verdict: not bad for YA, not the greatest of characters, but quite full of action and a quick paced storyline.

 It all begins when new neighbors move in next door. Let me be more specific: It all begins when Olly moves in next door. Before Olly, Madeline is more or less content in the life she leads confined to her own sterile bubble of a home. She reads profusely, studies, and has her vitals checked every couple of hours. Due to her SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency), Madeline has never left her house. She only interacts with three people: Her doctor mother, her nurse, Carla, and her tutor. This is all perfectly fine until she starts spying on, then communicating with, Olly. 
 For the first time in a long time, I want more than I have. 
 Their communication is friendly and only mildly flirtatious at first. As things start to intensify, however, Madeline attempts to draw back; she knows that they cannot meet in person due to her illness. She decides that they should only be friends, which is all well and good...until Carla allows Olly to come over. 
 Madeline and Olly's first meeting is brief yet monumental. They are instructed to absolutely NOT touch and to stay on opposite sides of the room. After fifteen minutes, Olly is instructed to leave. They wait about a week before another meeting, to make sure that Madeline's immune system hasn't been compromised (it hasn't), and each subsequent meeting contributes more meaning and depth to their budding relationship. They touch. They kiss. They essentially say to hell with being friends, because let's be real here; it's definitely more than that. And when Madeline risks her life when she runs out of her bubble to check on Olly when his father hits him, things get even more complicated. 
 Madeline is cut off from Olly. Carla is fired. Madeline's new nurse, Nurse Janet, is obnoxious and restrictive and Madeline is going crazy locked up in her tower of isolation. Until she finally cracks and plots her escape, with Olly, to Hawaii.  
 Olly's math says that you can't predict the future. It turns out that you can't predict the past either. Time moves in both directions--forward and backward--and what happens here and now changes them both. 
 Hawaii is an adventure and experiment for Madeline in more ways than one. She discovers that her health holds up fairly well in the few days that she is outside of her house (until one day when it doesn't) and her relationship with Olly takes several important and intimate steps forward. Her hospitalization is another important milestone: She cuts things off with Olly, breaking both of their hearts, but with the hope that he will be able to move on and be happy. In her newly reinstated isolation, Madeline comes to learn some new things about herself and her mother: She does not actually have SCID. When her father and brother died, Madeline's mother apparently had a breakdown and, in an effort not to lose another piece of her heart, she isolated her daughter from the physical dangers of the world. Love can be funny and cruel that way.  
 I will be honest: I could kind of sense that the thing was coming before it actually did. When Madeline was fine after touching and even kissing Olly , I began to grow suspicious. I became more suspicious still after she ran outside and was fine. Even the few days of traveling and doing things in the world made me think, huh; maybe this girl isn't really sick after all . And then, BAM! Revelations. My heart broke with Madeline, both at the loss of Olly and with the distrust and resentment of her mother.  The resolution and ending is beautifully paced and well executed.

On a military base somewhere in England, a teacher instructs a strange class of children who must be kept in restraints and held at gunpoint. A certain Sgt. Parks keeps the base running while a team of government scientists perform their tests on these special children. If you have read enough zombie novels, you might be able to guess why even brilliant little Melanie can't be trusted when she smells the sweet, sweet flesh of her beloved teacher. In the zombie apocalypse, though, is even the strongest bastion of military power safe? Nope! And once their walls are breached, Melanie is on the road with her beloved Ms. Justineau, as well as her nemesis Dr. Caldwell (she of the scalpels and formaldehyde), and the ever-cautious Sgt. Parks. The characters narrate the story by turns, but Melanie's voice is the most interesting. She's always trying to puzzle out what the adults aren't telling her about their situation, and for a genius, it's not that difficult. Harder to figure out is the scary truth of what she is, and it's poignant watching her put it together that *she* and the creatures like her are the monsters they are fleeing. As always in an post-apocalyptic tale, individual deaths are highlighted against a deeper sorrow for an entire civilization that has been wiped away, in this case by a fungus (!). Carey ends on a hopeful note, with strains of Richard Matheson's "I Am Legend." Perhaps we can't bring the people back, but there might be hope for the civilization.

This book, despite all the glowing reviews totally missed the mark for me and for one reason (that I'll get into in a minute) it didn't get downgraded to a 2 star review. 
 This is a book about a tough, smarty-pants, badass little girl who has a terrible life. She is lucky when she is left to her own devices to catch fish and crabs, go hunting in the woods, and spend time by herself outside, and unlucky when she is being brutally abused by her father. This is giving nothing away. 
 I was so frustrated by the well-meaning people recognizing Turtle's abuse, but not doing everything they can to stop it, or at least confirm that it is happening. I wanted more of her relationship with her grandfather. 
 She seemed only truly free when she was in the woods, and eventually hanging out with Brett and Jacob. Then they all felt like real kids. But in her home life, she came across as less real. 
 The part that I found especially interesting was how Turtle was deeply embedded in her dual life with her dad. He was the only adult in her life, whom to an extent she loved and needed, but she was repulsed by his abuse of her. Despite her repulsion, she endured her horrible predicament until it further endangered someone younger and more vulnerable than she. I think this showed her character well.  
 I have dealt with a lot of brutality in fiction, and can often see past it to its beauty, but this one rubbed me the wrong way and I am uncomfortable with a man writing the role of a horribly abused young girl, even if he intends to show her strength.

Another great book by Kingfisher. One of the things that does bother me about fairy tales that you don't generally get answers for is why the hell the characters are bothering to do things and where are they really going to end up afterward? Kingfisher answers both of these things. The character herself ends up asking these questions and the answers take her in her own direction making this a wonderfully fresh take on the Snow Queen. 
 Sprinkled through are both light moments and dark. And even, if memory serves, a moment when the teenager realizes just how much the people at home might be missing her. Again, something that is often left out of fairy tale re-writes. Too many orphans in story land. 
 Finally, if you don't shed a few tears for the reindeer, you have no heart.

 Chase is still a bit mysterious but I like how he can be protective of Hartley and nope his sexy frame has nothing to do with my likeness in him.  Still, I wished Hartley had waited for him to drop his pants before halting him with the scream.

 As such, I recommend this book if you are traveling or on the beach, not enough to keep your head spinning at quad core speed, but enough to keep you from yawning.

Basically, the review I wrote with over 100 pages left to read still stands. Partially because those last hundred or so pages were completely superfluous to the mystery/character development/interesting bits. And partially because I don't even want to go into that ucky last page. 
 I don't like the mystery genre. I guess this book is also a family drama and a history and a critique of Swedish economy/politics. But I don't really like those things either. It's also a book with much casual sex. And abuse. 
 At the beginning, I was incredibly irritated with the writing style. 
 Too thorough in the details. I mean, who cares the precise amount of money that a certain character paid in taxes the previous year? Even if that character is important, THAT IS NOT AN INTERESTING OR REVEALING DETAIL. I guess some of the thoroughness in the introductory part's rambles about the characters was meant to establish how very good Lisbeth Salander is at investigating. But that doesn't excuse it, especially since this sort of uninteresting thoroughness repeats itself in the narration (Blomkvist woke up at 9AM! Then he had breakfast! Then he chilled in a coffee shop! It was cold! Here's the temperature! Here's the time again!) I guess it's a case of form echoing content, since the protagonist-people are a reporter-man and an investigator-lady. And they, like the writing which conveys them to the mind of the reader, are flat. 
 Speaking of flat characters, I am struggling against righteous indignation about the female characters. All of them. Okay, maybe Larsson just didn't know how to create perfectly realistic, flawed and interesting and non-caricatured characters. It kind of shows in Blomkvist, too. But the flatness comes across more as a lack of authorial understanding in the portrayal of female characters. (They tend to be abused, which seems like disgusting pandery shock-value but the little Swedish trivia factoids that precede the sections indicate that this is part of The Point....which I have trouble believing this artless book has but that's a matter of opinion I guess.) Every female character who gets enough narration to be considered "developed" or central to the plot is a sexual object. It doesn't take long for the reader to be presented with images of Lisbeth's/Ricky's/Cecelia's naked breasts. The positive (at least for the man involved...) sexual relationships of Ricky and Cecelia get glossed over while the disgusting (spoiler alert?) sexual encounters of Lisbeth get described in all-too-explicit detail. And, while I have a pretty clear idea of what all the female bodies look like, the male characters are ambiguous floating-personalities. Charming and older, mostly. While the women are mysterious and attractive and "fiercely independent" (but just happen to rely on men for pretty much any stability in their lives). 
 Maybe I'm not being fair to this book. It's definitely not a genre I seek out, and I went into reading it with a prejudice against the popular-crime-drama which I knew it to be. And with all my prejudices against its style and content and reservations about its overarching message, I'm still reading it. Not throwing a book against the wall in disgust has to indicate something about the book's merit, right? I don't like not finishing books, but still. This one is interesting enough to counteract most of the obligatory-feelings of sticking with it. 
 I'll probably end up giving this book a few stars, and feeling ambivalent about each one of those stars.

 I'm quite a fan of David Baldacci and I like all his action thriller books, and I had rally great expectations about his first adventure in the young-adult dystopian genre. I had, because in the meanwhile I recommended it to a friend and he found it disappointing (but I had to try for myself!)... and so my disappointment was not really unexpected. 
 But I certainly was disappointed! 
 In this book there is nothing of Baldacci writing skills: written from the point of view of (and with the language, the wugghis!?!, of) a fourteen year old girl, with the addiction of unnecessary awful words) 
 There is nothing of his characters building: even Vega Jane is not very likable!

Jane, Unlimited is certainly a fitting name. This book absolutely would not be corralled into any one genre--once I thought I had it figured out, Jane's decision would change and the whole plot would flip upside down. 
 It's not even an exaggeration! It's a spy movie and a science fiction movie and a whimsical fantasy movie and a coming-of-age movie all rolled into one. It's a choose-your-own-adventure book with all the wildness you'd expect from a book like that. It flits from horror to action to personal crises as if they're all nothing. 
 It's completely ridiculous and I loved it. There isn't any rhyme or reason to half the events, and truly half of the plots could be cut without ruining the overall story. But that's just it--the random plots that lead to radically out there moments were just too delicious. I'd like to see someone try and classify a genre for this. 
 P.S. I love all the nods to Rebecca!

As John Green says (and I'm paraphrasing), "It's about what happens when we choose distraction over engagement." I think that's an important message. I prefer engagement, but I often choose distraction, and it's not fulfilling and it's often not worthwhile. Engagement is better--it requires a longer attention span and it happens because I'm doing something I find really interesting. Distraction is just crude, unimportant, a time-filler and a means of unproductive procrastination (as opposed to productive procrastination, which often involves engagement). So, Fahrenheit 451 makes a good case for engagement over distraction. However, I don't think this is the best book for this message. I prefer Huxley's Brave New World. I could now go into a fascinating discussion of why Brave New World and even Fahrenheit 451 are more realistic depictions of potential future cultures than Orwell's 1984, but that would be getting off-topic, so I won't. I shouldn't even be reviewing this book; I should be writing an essay. So I'm going to stop procrastinating productively now. 
 P.S. Another reviewer commented, "It is currently axiomatic of literature that what matters is technique. Maybe characters. That's it. Ray Bradbury writes about ideas." That may be true, but I like technique and characters. Fahrenheit 451 seems weak on both. The best books--my favorites--are the ones that best meld together good characters, technique, and ideas. Definitely, though, ideas are important. I like a book that provokes deep thought in me, not merely entertains.

This book was AMAZING. I am actually regretting having given A Court of Thorns and Roses a 5-star rating because if that was 5 stars then this must be 7 stars. It's definitely going on my list of all-time favorite books. 
 The main reason I love this book? Rhysand. I think he may just be my favorite male lead in any book ever. Well, except for Mr. Darcy but he was my first literary love. As far as NA/YA fiction goes, he is #1 without question (I think this book is more NA, it seems a little mature for YA readers). He's the love interest I always hope for in a NA/YA story but never actually get. It's been over a year since I read the first installment in this series so I didn't go into this feeling particularly attached to any one character, though upon reading my own thoughts about A Court of Thorns and Roses from back when I read it, it would seem I loved Tamlin back then and hoped things with Rhys wouldn't evolve into a full-blown love triangle. Well, it didn't but pretty much from the first chapter he appeared in in this book I had forgotten Tamlin entirely and was falling headfirst into Team Rhysand. I suppose that makes sense since Feyre was essentially headed down that same path and I WAS following along with her POV. Despite me foolishly loving Tamlin in the first book, I definitely had been intrigued by Rhysand (so I guess I was at least somewhat sensible). I just loved every scene Rhys appeared in in this book. He is dark, flirtatious, powerful, intense... Gah. Plus, he smells of ocean air and citrus, who doesn't love that? I absolutely LOVED him and Feyre together. Waiting for them to finally get together already was near tortuous, but in a good way. The whole thing had a very Hades and Persephone vibe, which only made me love it more because that's my favorite Greek myth. I always root for the bad boy/underdog to get the girl yet it frustratingly never happens so this was a refreshing and wonderful surprise for me. Still, I had a lurking suspicion midway through that he would end up being Feyre's mate and boy was I glad to be right. The whole scene where he explains everything to her killed me. Finding out that he had known she was his mate and been in love with her all that time, even knowing she was with Tamlin was just overwhelming. My love for this couple led to me being panicked when I thought that Rhys and Feyre's mating bond was actually broken. I was freaking out for about an hour afterward, even after we found out that it was just their bargain that was broken. Even as I read through the bond-breaking scene, I tried to pull back from the story and remind myself it was just that, a story, but the book had me in its claws so that didn't really work.  
 Admittedly, I am a little irked at Tamlin's rapid shift in portrayal in this book, but at least it didn't just come out of nowhere. Unlike with Elliot from Dance of the Red Death, who was also rejected in favor of another and rapidly changed into a despicable character, the clues were there once I actually thought about it. Like Feyre, I was too distracted by the fairytale romance plot to notice the flaws, such as Tamlin not really doing anything to help Feyre when they were Under the Mountain, whereas Rhys stuck out his neck to do so. Though he may have loved her, Tamlin really was kind of just using her. I got irritated with him for being so controlling at the start of this book, even if it made sense after his experience with Amarantha. I do think he was a little overly vilified, betraying/murdering Rhys's entire family and joining forces with the sadistic King of Hybern.  At times, Tamlin's changes felt a little like the author was trying to convince me that since Tamlin was no good, I should switch over to Rhys, which didn't make sense because I already wholeheartedly loved Rhys on my own, no such contrivance needed. 
 I feel one of the elements that really made this book special was the setting. Up until this point, we had no information really about the Night Court, other than that Amarantha based her court Under the Mountain off of it, so that didn't sound too great. However, the actual Night Court, or at least the Court of Dreams, is amazing. I loved all the descriptions of it, from the jasmine-scented air to the magical city of Velaris. If I had to pick one fantasy locale to live in, I would pick that (of course, the Velaris before it got attacked and wrecked by the King of Hybern's forces) . Although I wouldn't really want to visit, I also loved the descriptions of the Court of Nightmares. They were both chilling and compelling. I loved the scene that took place there where Feyre pretends to be Rhys's pet. Not to mention, with Rhys's softer side being developed in this book, it was good to see the mask of the cruel, heartless High Lord of the Night Court again. As much as I love seeing the "good" side of Rhys, part of his appeal is that element of darkness from when we first met him in ACOTAR so I'm glad that he wasn't transformed into an entirely nicey-nice (read: boring) guy.  
 As for the new characters in this book, I loved them. It was a little odd to see so few of the characters from the first book, like Lucien, but I didn't notice as much with this new crew around. They all really brought out a different side of Rhys for us to see. The first character from said crew we meet is Morrigan, or Mor, Rhys's cousin. I loved her and her fierce personality. It was also interesting to learn about the Illyrians, a subculture within the Night Court, and meet its two strongest members (aside from Rhys), Cassian and Azriel, both of whom I loved. I loved their interactions with Feyre and I'm really rooting for Azriel and Mor to be together. It will also be interesting to see going forward if anything happens between Cassian and Nesta, I really liked their dynamic. However, my favorite of the new characters is definitely Amren. I had a feeling I was going to like her when she was first introduced, a petite yet insanely powerful force of nature. I'm curious to learn more about what she is and where she came from in the next book. 
 Speaking of the next book, the ending to this book was a whirlwind of action and emotions. As I said, the whole thing about the mating bond had me in a state of panic. I was unable to tear my eyes away from the page as the action unfolded, needing to know what happened next. I gasped when it was revealed Tamlin and Lucien corroborated with the King. I didn't know if the author would actually go through with making Feyre's sisters into faeries, but then it happened, and even more surprising, the twist of Elain being Lucien's mate. Definitely looking forward to further development on that. Also, I loved the twist that Feyre was secretly sworn in as Rhys's High Lady of the Night Court and will now be working as a covert operative within the Spring Court.  It's amazing to see just how far Feyre has come since her days as a desperate human huntress in book one. I cannot WAIT to get my hands on A Court of Wings and Ruin. I need more Rhysand ASAP and May can't come soon enough. Depending on how that unfolds, this may just end up being one of my favorite series. As it is on its own, though, ACOMAF has already earned its well-deserved spot on my favorites shelf.

I found this soppy, sappy, and embarrassingly, nails on a chalkboard earnest. Also, I have not seen so many vowels in females' names since my own ninth grade attempts at writing Regency romance. The magic created here is lazy (your standard 'let's-just-make-it-technology' fare, because writers think we can't relate to people without some modern accoutrements, such as, in this case- alarm clocks). The plot is all over the place, with far too much going on and not enough time to really get to know the more interesting characters created (Lars!). I know it is a multiple book series, but that's no excuse for poor organization. I expected all of the "twists" early on, so there wasn't much suspense. Furthermore, Hartmann writes possibly the most cliched "oh, he's too good for me!" sort of teenage love triangle tripe as its centerpiece. Finally, the whole thing with the dragons  cutting emotion out of their brains while the main characters make a cloying plea for Love and Caring  guaranteed that any layers we might have been interested in exploring in terms of the manifestation of emotions or how that works in our brains or what it is were jolly well stomped out in favor of simplistic conceptualization of emotions as a thing separate from thinking and logical thought, which I don't believe is always the case. It ended an interesting conversation and that annoyed me. 
 There were two redeeming factors for me that I must list as caveats that got this two stars instead of one. The first is the concept of "mental structure," Hartmann created around the dragons, along with the accompanying mental work that Seraphina has to do to maintain it. I was very interested in that as a possible side effect of her  inter-species-ness. It seemed like a very plausible thing to occur, much better than whatever magic powers she could get. This whole thing where all the half-dragons have some sort of unique magic power is pretty odd, especially given that some of them are not reflected in dragons themselves, but the mental structure made sense from everything we've heard about the dragons. . 
 The other redeeming factor, as I alluded to above, were some of the secondary characters, many of whom were the  half dragons  that Seraphina meets. There were some beginnings of exploration of "affliction" and "victimhood," as conceptualized by the people themselves experiencing it here. I do think it can sometimes be fascinating to see inside that and see how people conceptualize their disadvantages- how crazily we all put ourselves down and convince ourselves that everyone else's situation is better than ours. YA novels specialize in this- it speaks to the Special Snowflake ideas about our own suffering that we can develop at that age. So it was annoying in that sense, but there were some small moments that spoke true, like the one where  Dame Okra sees Seraphina's scales and is like, "That's it?" "That's all?", comparing them to the amount of scales on her body like a one-for-one comparison of the amount of suffering could be made by its physical manifestation, and the ultimate realization that of course that is not the case.  
 Also, Lars is pretty great. Just straight up. I would read a book about him.... though maybe not because then someone would turn him into a romantic hero and no thank you, he's excellent just as he is. 
 Yeah, though... I'd give this a pass. Not enough to see here to make it worth it.

Beautifully written. We have maybe 5 POVs now, in contrast to only 1 in the first book, and it's amazing how each character's line of thought is perfectly built. Their fears and even their stupidity are really realistic. I love the shape the story has taken. I have no idea where it's going to now, because there was a kind of closure at the end, but of course I'll keep reading. I think Voyager makes us crave with anticipation and have stronger feelings, but somehow I liked Drums better. I'm not sure I like Roger though. 
 Outlander has made me think about many things so far, but for some reason 3 are clearer in Drums for me: 
 The first is feminism. I'm not into feminism activities, but the men in this book make clear what feminism fights against nowadays. Jaime and Roger, not to mention other men, are so sexist that even I, who am not an activist, felt bad. And the worse part is that it doesn't mean they are bad of character (on the contrary, they really love their wives) because woman inferiority is the concept they were raised to believe in. Women were simply inferior in the time this story happens, so that must be present in the book. Fact. And horrible. 
 Motherhood. I'm not a mother, I don't even like children and I never thought I'd like my child if one day I have one. But the descriptions of motherhood here were so good and interesting that they touched me and made me think that it wouldn't be so bad after all. 
 It also made me think about true love. About what it is and what it would really feel like to have it, not the passion we usually mix it up with. And about why exactly I haven't found that yet, what needs to change inside me to be in the same vibration as that kind of feeling. 
 I wasn't surprised that Ian became an Indian. It's nice for him, although it's sad he won't be able to come bad. 
 Jaime being over jealous over Brianna was also very predictable, but I don't mean it in a bad way. It's just so like his character. I wish he would be more amiable to Roger though. 
 I love seeing how his relationship with Claire has developed, comparing with the first 2 books. 
 But I'm sorry for John. I really like him and it's heart-breaking that he can't be happy. I wish he could be closer to the Frasers without suffering by Jaime's presence or by Claire's dislike.

I haven't read the first two books in this series, but my tween mentioned that a main character becomes dependent on drugs in this book and I thought, "Here's an opening to talk about a tough issue, better check into this one." Glad I did. Other reviewers have said this third entry in the Ranger's Apprentice saga is off-the-mark, but I didn't notice shortcomings. The story moves quickly, alternating between Will's imprisonment at the hands of Erak and the Scandians, and Halt's quest to rescue him. There's plenty of tension and buddy humor, ending on a hopeful note. The reviews may be negative because Will essentially vanishes as a character for about the last third of the book, and the end doesn't conclude so much as point the way to the next volume. 
 I wouldn't hesitate to hand this book to a middle grade reader, but there would be appeal for older teens as well. The above mentioned drug use is handled appropriately, as are issues of chivalry, honor, vengeance, and violence. Flanagan isn't afraid to use words like "poltroon" and "quay", but generally the sentence structure and word choice is quite readable. In this book, there's only one female character. 
 Fans of fantasy will like this, even though there's almost nothing that couldn't actually happen and it could just as easily be historical fiction. I'll be checking into other books by Flanagan.

The Evolution of Mara Dyer (Mara Dyer #2) by Michelle Hodkin - 4 stars 
 This series... Wow. I love the twisted and creepy, and this series doesn't disappoint! I was on the edge of my seat with the need for answers. And - golly gee willikers - do we get some answers. My nerves were on edge for most of this book. 
 These people made me want to scream, rattle, and punch them. I hate that Mara is putting up with such awful characters! Not that they are awful. Just that they don't believer her. And it can't get much more frustrating than that! When people don't listen to you, don't believe what you know is true and real, especially those you love, it can drive anyone mad. Not clinically crazy though. 
 Thrilling. Riveting. Unnerving. 
 Mara is fighting her families belief that she is suffering from a mental illness. She knows what to do in order for people to see that she isn't losing her mind. But when things keep coming at her, when bad incidents occur over and over, she isn't sure she's not losing her mind. It's an inner struggle, an outer battle, and if it weren't for Noah Shaw, she would feel completely and utterly alone. 
 I'll walk forever with stories inside me that the people I love the most can never hear. 
 But honestly, for the first half of this book, I was frustrated with Noah. His silence and odd behavior was killing me. I was scared for Mara. What if he leaves? She'll have no one who believes her? But the more I thought about it and the deeper into the story we went, the more I realized we don't know much about Noah. About what he's been though. About what secrets he might be keeping. 
 Mara was beginning to fill with doubt about their relationship as well. 
 I want people to understand the reason I'm giving this book 4 stars. These stories haven't scared me. I am addicted to fear. I read Stephen King, Paul Tremblay, and more. I watch scary movies and television shows regularly. If there is a high to get from fear, I'm chasing it. Now these books, though they don't scare me to the point that they might with others doesn't mean that they aren't good. For a YA series, these books are spot on. So if you're too afraid to jump into the exceptionally dark SK books, then this series seems like an excellent choice! 
 And one final thought... The ending of this book? Ugh! I thought the first book ended with a bang. This one ends with a bite. Raw and savage. And I can't wait to open the third book! Which I think I will go do now!

 I think for me the concept and the main plot was a really difficult thing for me to grasp, furthering as to why I could not fully commit in loving it. 
 Basically the two main characters would possibly never had met if dire circumstances were not what they were, but because they were fate had placed them together... as prisoners of one another. 
 Please do take the title literally, they both are prisoner's to their desire. Both characters did horrific things to one another for different and understandable circumstances. However that being said I still could not see how their love for one another could grow from such a dark place, but alas it did. You must give absolute praise to Johanna Lindsey for making this love story believable and not a disastrous mess. 
 Amazing, amazing character development on the main heroine Rowena, and Warrick was undeniably a villain stuck solely on revenge. It is fascinating how the author transformed him from a character who you despised into something else entirely. However I do wish she played more with him. I really wanted to get deeper into him, his past, and his character and I was waiting for that one on one moment between the two characters, where they both reached a point of understanding and compassion. 
 That being said I will give Ms. Johanna Lindsey another attempt, for I do believable she does have the skills to capture me with another great story.

"EXCITING, UNIMAGINABLE, AND UTTERLY ASTONISHING. RAPTURE IS A PERFECT ENDING FROM MY FIRST LOVE" 
 Originally posted @: Jules Bookshelf 
 MY OPINION: 
 It has been days, weeks, heck months since I finished reading this, after I finished it I vowed to myself that I made a review and that day has finally come. 
 I'm gonna skip the detailed description of what happened since the beginning of the series. Basically "Rapture" is the last installment of the Fallen series. Ever since, Luce has always been drawn to Daniel Grigori, and she found out that she ALWAYS falls in love with him. But its different now, because not only is she being hunted down by everyone. She's slowly finding out the reason behind her tragic love story. 
 I've been reading the Fallen series since the beginning of time (when I first started obsessing over books), it has been the first book I wanted to buy. I first saw it in the library, and after reading the first five chapters. I decided that I had to buy it. It was my first love. It made reading much more than leisure time. I had to admit that I was a bit bummed out when reading the first two books(but I still love them), they kinda fell short from my expectations. "Passion" however was awesome, I learned a lot about Luce and Daniel's story. It showed more about how their relationship isn't just a soulmate-thing relationship. So yeah, you could guess how thrilled I am when I got Rapture. 
 I decided to-slow-read it, 'cuz I want to savor reading it. But I couldn't find myself to stop even for a second. It completely took over my body. I always held the book everywhere. Always reading it. Not wasting time because all of the SECRETS and REVELATIONS are being exposed now. Lauren Kate did a good job of building excitement and surprises in my opinion. Rapture is the best out of all the books in the series. 
 The plot was much more in detail and organized, which consisted mostly of Luce being in different places in just a span of 7 days. Which made me wonder if Lauren Kate ever visited the places that she talked about. The pacing was good, but the action scenes aren't that stellar. 
 The characters were still the same, but there are extra characters who popped up. Even Bill came up. Shocker is, some of the characters died. *gasp* I kinda felt bad when they died. Not that bad, but its sad to see friends dying. 
 Daniel was a little low key here. I wasn't amazed by him at all. I don't think he did much until near the ending. He mostly just held Luce, protected Luce, and had bonding with Luce. -.- 
 Cam was still the same, but by now I'm pretty sure of his feelings for Luce. I kinda like Cam here more than Daniel. Maybe because I can see Cam's intentions more clearer than Daniel's. Either way. I still felt like Cam is in action on this one. 
 Luce is a whole other story. She's constantly the solution for the problem. Kinda showing off but at least she isn't too dependent on Daniel now. I was a bit worried how she will react with people trying to get her. But at least she didn't act like a pathetic damsel in distress. She even seemed more cooler now than before. 
 But what really made me love this book was the twists and the surprises that happened. I will not be detailed 'cuz I'll just end up like a spoiler. But goodness, I loved the twist! It made me shriek(in midmorning) just because I kinda felt like HE was THE one. And I was right! ^^ 
 Moreover the BIG SECRET was revealed, and I also found that equally surprising and satisfying. Because it made it much more real and controversial. It kinda prove me wrong about INSTA-LOVE, and because of that, it became more awesomer(<- this is not really a word) 
 WHY WOULD I RECOMMEND IT?: 
 It was exciting, unimaginable and astonishing. I love love love it because it showed "true love" not just insta-love. It made me squeal with happiness, and giddy feelings. It surprised me. A lot. For all of those who swore that Fallen isn't a good series. I think that Rapture might prove you wrong. For those who haven't read the Fallen series. Don't let other bad reviews stop you from reading it.

3.5 Stars 
 Jackaby is a book that has been on my to read list for a while now, constantly popping up and demanding that I read it. And so I finally did. 
 The cover is one of the first things that drew me to this book. I love the various layers to the art and how there is just a splash of red in the dark blue and black. It just screamed mysterious to me. And I'm usually not the biggest fan of faces on covers, but this profile of a man, with the rest of the details visible through him really works. Every cover in the series is rather stunning. 
 Now that I've finished gushing about the cover, let's move on to the story. 
 While I found the overall mystery in this novel very predictable, the story as a whole just worked. The characters were all so vibrant and real, particularly the two leads Jackaby and Abigail. Jackaby has a gift for the supernatural and uses that to solve crimes, often landing himself in trouble along the way. And Abigail is a young woman searching for adventure, for someone who won't just dismiss her because she's a girl. So the two fit quite well together. And the side characters were rather brilliant as well. Jenny and Douglas were two of my favorites, but I also enjoyed Charlie and Marlowe. 
 This story is full of witty banter and laugh out loud moments. I was constantly entertained. And while the mystery was quite obvious, I still found myself invested in the story. I wanted to know what the characters were thinking, how they were drawing conclusions, what they would do to resolve things. 
 The setting was also excellent. I loved the New England town of New Fiddleham and the time period in the late 1800's. It just felt so right. 
 By the end of this I was smiling and laughing and wishing that I already had book two ready to read. This is definitely a series that I will be continuing. I might try the audio because I think it would be a lot of fun to listen to. 
 Parts of the supernatural aspect of this remind me of Delia's Shadow by Jaime Lee Moyer. The mystery also bears some resemblance to that series, in a good way. 
 If you like Sherlock Holmes type stories and want that mixed with a supernatural element, this would be a good book for you to try. It's fast paced, fun, and well written.

Try by Ella Frank is book one in her highly acclaimed Temptation series and if you haven't heard of it or the two MC's Logan Mitchell and Tate Morrison, you MUST be living under a rock. Seriously, this book is one of the first gay romance books I read, back when it was a new release - and I was hooked! I owe it all to Logan and Tate, they ignited the spark in me! So, why am I reviewing a book almost 4 years late? Well, back when I originally read this amazing story it seems I failed to review it! *hangs head in shame* So, to right that wrong...here we are! 
 A 
 So, let's talk about Try - there probably isn't a lot I can say that hasn't been said over and over in numerous reviews, but I must Try. (Hahaha...sorry, I am just a little dorky) - Ok, our MCs as mentioned earlier - Logan Mitchell, he is sex personified.  Tense and very enjoyable! It reads pretty literary fiction-y, but the plot then takes a quick turn towards genre. I like both literary fiction and genre, but they don't always make an easy marriage (not even talking about Nick and Amy!). My rule of thumb is that is that literary fiction could be about any of us -- the art is in the telling. Genre is usually about a situation so outside most of our experiences, that it becomes pure escapism (there can be a lot of art in that too, though!). 
 In this case, if an unreliable narrator is a turn in a screw, Flynn gives it another turn by having two very unreliable narrators. It's also a little bit "Real World: The Marriage Edition" as in, "we find out what happens when people stop being polite and start getting real." If you're a sociopath, the "getting real" gets scary fast. What I also liked was the non-sociopath is just as sick in his own way, and just as unreliable a narrator. Flynn shows how no narrator (except maybe teenage ones) wants to tell the reader all the gory details about themselves. I didn't always find everything in Gone Girl believable, but it's a very fun, almost breathless read nevertheless.

I love reality tv. I can't help it. So I knew I would be picking this book up at sometime or another. I tend to go for the competition shows (Survivor, Amazing Race) or home improvement shows (Property Brothers, Love it or List It), or my greatest guilty pleasure, Mystery Diner, more than the family-type shows (Sister-Wives, Keeping up with the Kardashians, 19 Kids and Counting), though. Something Real is definitely more of a play on the family-type shows, particularly the one with John and Kate Gosselin. 
 Once upon a time the young Baker couple wanted to have a baby, but were having trouble, so they pitched a show to a big network that they wanted "A Baker's Dozen". So fast forward several years and they now have thirteen children and their whole lives have been chronicled on a tv show. However, having a baker's dozen worth of kids and cameras in your face all the time is not as charming as it seems. Much like the reality show this is obviously inspired by, the patriarch of the family cheats on his wife with a much younger woman and then leaves the family and is an absentee parent. The show ends when Bonnie has an extreme reaction to the pressure. The mother moves the family and remarries and Bonnie is now going by Chloe and lies to all her friends about her reality tv past and things are going well, until Chloe suddenly finds out that the show is going back on the air. 
 I enjoyed large portions of this book. I liked all the behind the scenes drama of having one's life constantly filmed. I loved to hate the manipulative producer who stirred the pot and capitalized on every traumatic moment. I loved, loved Chloe's love interest, Patrick Sheldon. He was basically the perfect guy, with just a touch of Edward Cullen-eque obsessiveness at times. I loved the relationship between Chloe and her brother Benton. 
 There were, unfortunately, several things that didn't work for me, though. Chloe was way over-dramatic most of the time. She did have very valid points about not wanting to be on the show and having privacy and shouldn't have been threatened by the producer as much as she was, but she still took things way too dramatically. The mother was ridiculous. I think it would've been a little more realistic to give her at least a couple of humanized moments where she wasn't completely awful. I also felt like the ending left things way too open. There was a lot of time spent building up to certain things and the book ends before we find out the outcomes. 
 Overall, I enjoyed Something Real. Most of the books I've read so far this year have been kind of heavy, so it was definitely time for some light YA fun. While the book ran maybe a touch too long and was often a little over-dramatic, the romance was sweet, the characters were well developed and the premise was interesting.

 Dear Mr. Knightley is told in an epistolary format, which is quite fitting as not only does the reader learn more about Samantha this way through her perspective but it touches also on a dying art that reflects Samantha's interests and the sort of books she reads. The plot is pretty straight forward, following Samantha as she relays to they mysterious Mr. Knightley about her life and her experiences in the programme and the people in her life. 
 I thought Samantha was a very interesting character who clearly had a lot of issues to resolve at the start of the novel. I found myself very sympathetic to her plight, especially as some of the problems she had were issues that I can relate to on some level: failure, the desire to do her best, wanting to connect with other people but at the same time watching out for herself. It was interesting to see how Sam slowly overcomes her problems and her own personal feelings of failure and despair and become stronger, more courageous in facing the outside world and reaching out to those around her. I also appreciate how gradual these changes are and how everything contributes to her change. 
 While I appreciate Sam's character development over the course of the novel, I did find myself wondering a little bit about other aspects of her character (for lack of a better explanation). Save for a few kind people, she had a horrible childhood-to the point of spending a few months out on the streets-and I'm surprised that, for the most part, she's still relatively good-natured: she's not rude or nasty towards other people, she's not rough at the edges. She can be socially awkward and very distant but she's strangely self-contained, which sometimes felt a little inconsistent. 
 The secondary characters and the development of Alex and Sam's relationship was also wonderful to read. Overall, I enjoyed reading Dear Mr. Knightley, I couldn't quite put the novel down once I really got into the story because I wanted to know what was going to happen to Samantha and Alex next. While I more or less figured out the big reveal at the end, I thought the character journey was really interesting and how Samantha and Alex's story progressed.

 I was definitely hooked throughout the entire book. But it wasn't "amazing" or anything. It was a good, solid time travel book that explored typical things that time travelers do. It's just that it was well written. 
 The ending. It ended the only way it could have ended. And I sorta love it for that. I was actually really uncertain if he would have been able to  save JFK the first time or not . But I shouldn't have been, really. 
 I am just really impressed with his writing. This is window pane writing - where all of the words seem to disappear and all that is left is the story. It is not beautiful prose. It is not gorgeous and lovely, it is not purple. I feel the emotions from every word, yet I do not see the words. It is hard to imagine that a transcription of a play, even if it is Of Mice and Men, could well up such emotion. It is hard to imagine that we could feel as deeply as these characters do. I love them, when I read this story. 
 It was a really good book. 3.5 stars rounded down. There is a reason that so many people like Stephen King.

Benson Fisher gets a scholarship that takes him away from a cycle of unpleasant foster homes, promising an excellent education in a secluded boarding school. This was a solid escape/suspense novel that reminded me of many other YA titles. Upon arrival at Maxfield Academy, Benson must choose which 'gang' to join - Society, Havoc, Variant - so perhaps that's why it reminded be a little of Divergent. It is clear early on that the school isn't what it appears to be, and Benson tries to figure it out, which reminded me of The Maze Runner. There are some unexpected twists and a cliff-hanger ending. 
 There are several good things about this book, chief of which is that although several teens are killed during the story, all the serious violence happens off-screen; what appears on the page is several steps milder than The Hunger Games. The complete lack of sex, drugs, and strong language makes this a good choice for readers looking for peril without an R rating. 
 Wells could have done a better job developing characters. The plot rolled along - although slowly at times - but the characters always remained a little flat. And since Benson's primary motivation is to escape, the other issues raised by the story don't seem especially important. All-in-all, "Variant" was a good book, but not especially memorable. I'll recommend this to my students, but I won't be rushing out for the sequel.

Short Review 
 A better installment than the previous one, and an instance where Butcher largely abandons his normal two plots intertwined structure in favor of there really only being one plot - the search for The Word of Kemmler. An entertaining read, though there isn't a lot of mystery in this one like previous books. They have to find the book, but there's no real who-dunit kind of angle so it feels more like an adventure book than a detective book. Harry's still infuriatingly sexist, and there were some general inconsistencies and odd dialogue choices. It's entertainment, but don't expect depth. 
 Long Review 
 This book breaks with the normal Dresden structure that has been mostly followed up to this point in the series - namely there being two investigations which are apparently separate at the outset which then turn out to converge to bring about the resolution of both mysteries. 
 Instead of that, this book focuses entirely on the recovery of another book The Word of Kemmler. You could try and argue that Mavra's involvement was technically a side plot to the business with the pack of necromancers, but I don't think that holds up. Mavra's involvement was almost entirely unnecessary, other than maybe giving Harry the title of the book he just happened to need to find to stop the necromancers and giving Butcher an excuse to throw in a convenient, "I can't involve you! Murphy might get fired!" now and then to keep the plot from losing tension. 
 Butcher's prose seems to be improving. With the exception of some of the dialogue, which we'll talk about in a bit, his writing seemed a lot more polished than it used to be. The pacing was good, as I've come to expect, and the fight scenes in this one were also improved from previous books. 
 I also really like how you get the strong impression that the series is shifting into a larger, multiple book plot. Really, I think it's been moving that way since the Denarians were introduced, but I noticed it most strongly in this book. You also start to see some degradation in Harry and more anger, presumably as the result of the influence of his own denarius and Lasciel. It's not exactly subtly done, but it's interesting to watch happen. 
 The final big set piece was fun too. On one hand, riding into battle on a re-animated zombie tyrannosaur fueled by a one-man marching polka band is probably getting dangerously close to a textbook case of Jumping the Shark. On the other hand, it was fun. As long as you're approaching it as being intentionally over the top, I found it entertaining. 
 One of my biggest complaints about this book, and the series as a whole, remains the sheer un-likeability of Harry himself. The sexism is still there, of course. It's basically a defining character trait at this point. For example, take this bit from chapter 28: 
 "But dammit, I didn't want to see anyone else get hurt because of Kemmler's disciples. Particularly not anyone with such lovely breasts." 
 The book is full of things like that. It makes it hard to see Harry as a good guy. Even more so when, every time he makes note of his own sexism chivalry, he jumps through hoops to excuse it all with bullshit handwaving of how he can't help it. 
 Harry seems to be designed to hit all the stereotypical men's rights activist checkboxes. He's something of a loner who lives in a basement. He's nerdy enough with the tabletop roleplaying games and the geeky pop culture references to be relatable to that demographic. The black leather duster and the hat seem both relatable and idyllic to the fedora crowd. He has incredible power inside of him, but doesn't really get day to day respect for it because all the 'normals' just can't see how special he really is. He is surrounded by and gets enough attraction from beautiful women to be a fantasy, but still has enough women trouble to feel like one of those people, and he talks about his chivalry like he's on Reddit explaining why it's so tough to be a straight white male. 
 There were other little hiccoughs in the book itself. Billy and Harry take an elevator after we've heard tons of times how the power is out. Then Harry goes to another building and complains about having to use the stairs because the power is out. 
 Mavra's involvement felt really tacked on. Maybe it plays into events in a later book, but it seemed like she was just there to drop the name of the MacGuffin and then be inconsequential. It felt odd to me to involve such a big player in the overall narrative universe just to drop a hint to get to the real antagonists / plot lines. 
 The dialogue in parts was stilted, or just strange. American spelling is used for most things except the word 'grey', which shows up repeatedly. Another example is where Harry says to Mab, "Greetings, Queen Mab. I do beg your pardon. It was not my intention to disturb thee." He never really uses Elizabethan English with anyone else, it would make more sense if Queen Mab used it, but even then why that era? Why not Old English, or Chaucer style Middle English? She's much older than Shakespeare. Is that considered polite for some reason, and if so, why only use it in one word rather than something like, "I do beg thine pardon. T'was not mine intention to disturb thee." 
 Am I nitpicking? Yeah, mostly. It pulls me out of the story a bit. I still enjoyed it enough though for three stars, which is "I liked it" on the Goodreads scale. 
 If you love the Dresden series you'll love it, if you don't it's still entertaining at least.

I started this book because I get it in my head every so often that I'd like to do something adventurous and lately the Appalachian Trail has seemed appealing and what better to learn a little about the AT than through an author I've been meaning to read anyway? 
 Bryson was as funny as all the hype, though as another, much less enthusiastic, reviewer on goodreads wrote he is a bit smug towards people. However, he doesn't make himself out to be a great hiker, out to conquer the great AT - in fact it's not long before he realizes he is not made of the stuff thru-hikers are. Bryson really undergoes absolutely nothing unique or particularly dramatic, though to be honest he is rather dramatic sometimes - he claims after four days of walking in the woods that crossing roads is a forgotten and dangerous experience as if he was once again a child, a sentiment I have difficulty believing. Even though his experiences are on the trail are perhaps not equal to that of Bear Grylls he makes them much more humorous and how interest anyway. All the while to provides a nice history to the actual trail, geography, communities around the trail, and perhaps his favorite topic, the incompetence of the Park Services. 
 While he rues the destruction of the natural flora and fauna as well as commercialization and gaudy tourist attractions that besmirch the towns and landmarks. However, at the same time he bemoans how there is no longer farmland and certain man-made features, like bridges, pretty shelters could be used to enhance the natural beauty of the trail. He also seems to want a little town or lodge every night so he can have at least the simplest modern conveniences, good food and a shower most notably. I can't really argue with wanting to shower and eat well, and hear I should note that I'm not much of a hiker surely by anyone's reckoning, think that he is rather missing the point of backpacking through the wilderness. He most definitely is a wonderful day hiker where he can go home every night and enjoy his bed and wife's cooking. But I often thought that going to the backwoods to backpack was to rather escape the modern world, as one can, and enjoy what nature has to offer. Otherwise why would you walk for day's in the woods? I suppose there is the sense of accomplishing something hiking the trail, but I hardly think it ought to bend it's purpose to those people. Maybe I missed his point.

When I first started reading this book, I wasn't sure how I was going to feel about it by the end. The story was told in a bit of a roundabout way--lots of backstory was given upfront, in a sort of village-rumor storytelling style. It was cool, but I wasn't sure if it was going to benefit the book. But it did. It took a while for this style of writing to really benefit the book, but it definitely added to the story. I would have liked for more plot upfront, though, with the backstory woven between a bit more seemlessly. I think the style would have presented better that way, right from the beginning, rather than take half the book to be effective. 
 The second half of the book is really where the plot took off. The action began moving quickly, the mystery and magic finally bloomed, and the characters came fully alive. I really liked the depth this book took on the story of Dorothy and Oz. I was quite amazed how Ms. Paige had managed to put her own twist at the end of the original story. And her twist to it is a very dark one. Everything's all tipsy turvy. The good is bad and the wicked is good. But are they really? 
 It seemed to me that in the new Oz there is no good not evil just bad happenings. And the only people who are suffering are those who are not in power - the people of Oz; the munchkins, winged and wingless monkeys, other animals, trees, etc. 
 I really liked how Ms. Paige captured every part of Oz and explained it in not-so-full but imaginable details so that the readers get to visualize what the new Oz looks like in her world. I really liked the pace of the story too. It was a bit fast at the start - so that you get to know Amy's background and such. And after like 2-3 chapters, you just straight away get into Oz and the main story. I did wish that there was more background to Amy's "regular" life in Kansas because throughout her adventures and misadventures in Oz, the only things we know about her "regular" life is repeated. What I mean by this is she doesn't give out other memories and learnings in her life back home except for the stuff we read about. Like I wish there was something new that she felt or saw to relate or compare to that we didn't know before so we got to know her more. 
 Another flaw of this novel is that some of the characters in Oz didn't fit the mood or the essence of who they are in context to how they talk. This story originated as a CHILDRENS BOOK so all the cursing and such was a bit too much. I mean, I get it... A lot has changed and people turned evil or whatever but from how I know and have loved the original story, readers like me would need some sort of transition into how these characters have changed so drastically (imo). Or maybe I should've read the prequel first? 
 I also didn't enjoy how vague EVERYONE in Oz is or at least those that Amy has talked to. Oh and the Amy and Nox love thing? NO. NOPITY NOPITY NOPE. But I secretly want Amy and Pete to end up together, all right? 
 Nevertheless, this was a long but good read. I enjoyed it. I had some specks of annoyance and anger but it wasn't so bad. If it makes you feel better or whatever... 
 I want to read the next one straight away! 
 Happy reading! :)

It touches on all the right tropes: the line between sanity and madness, the role of literature in living a fully awake life, growth and survival through adversity, the need of friendsip. 
 I suspect that this will have strong appeal among kids who share qualities with Jam. She's quiet, sees herself as flawed and weak, and feels her pain acutely. There's a hint of romance, a splash of magic, and a dash of Sylvia Plath. Wolitzer has mixed them well here. 
 This could begin many discussions of the line between reality and fantasy, truth and Truth. I found it not quite as powerful as it could be, but I am closer to Ms. Quinell than the intended, teen audience.

Mitchell is one of my top five favorite living authors and I haven't disliked any of his books until this one. Of course, I wouldn't really even call this one a proper novel; it's more like his publisher called him up and said, "Hey Dave, remember that story you wrote for Twitter? Why don't you expand on that and make us a bit more cash?". 
 I couldn't figure out for the life of me why nearly every damn section of this ended in the same way either. It just felt lazy. The last 90 pages finally kick things into gear somewhat, but it's just too little, too late. The talented writer that Mitchell is still shines through, but if this is the first Mitchell you've read, please don't let it be your last because this is a very poor place to start the oeuvre. Don't make a snap judgment of him just because of this. In fact, if you haven't read the Bone Clocks yet, don't even worry about reading this one until you do.

This is my third Giffin book. Each one was rated pretty highly but I couldn't really see why once I read them. They are definitely Chick Lit of the beach read level and not of the book clubber's variety. Knowing that, I went into this book expecting an easy way to pass some time while I walked my dogs for the week. I was pleasantly surprised that I liked this book as much as I did. I liked the adoption theme (the young adult child finding her biological roots) and how it affects her adopted and birth families. 
 The adopted child is Kirby Rose, an eighteen-year-old uninterested in college and trying to figure out where she came from and what makes her tick in order to figure out where to go in life. Her adopted parents pay lip-service to their support of Kirby finding her biological roots but wish they could forget Kirby's origin and shield her from what she might encounter. 
 The woman who gave the child up for adoption is Marian Caldwell. She is thirty-six years old and finally feeling success as a television producer living in New York City. She has a boyfriend on the cusp of asking for her hand in marriage when she has to confess to him that there is at least one secret from her past that she hasn't shared with him. Will Kirby's appearance threaten Marian's relationship and success? 
 The biological father is no longer in Marian's life but when Kirby asks about meeting him, Marian is forced to face a past she thought she had put behind her. The title is apropos since each person is questioning where they belong now that they are confronted with where they came from.

Thanks to the publisher for an advance reader's copy.

It's rare to find novels for young women that don't involve a physically beautiful, thin girl as the protagonist (even if she's also strong and resourceful), and I know that even as a supposedly confident adult woman, I struggle daily with feeling like my lack of stunning looks makes me less-than. How much harder must it be for a regular teenage girl, especially one who is overweight? We need more voices who preach the value of all women, regardless of what they look like, and that they too are worthy of love.

Wow was that amazing. From page one I got completely wrapped up in this book. In fact, about halfway through my hold on the next installment of a series I've been reading that I've been waiting for for weeks became available, yet I chose to plow through this book first because it was just that good. 
 I first picked up this book because I was looking for more YA fiction based on non-Western mythology. I was thoroughly convinced upon learning that this book was loosely based off of One Thousand and One Nights (aka Arabian Nights), as I took part in a production based on these tales as a child and the Disney film Aladdin, based off of "Aladdin's Lamp" from the story collection, ranks among my all-time favorite films. Thankfully I was not disappointed. Rather, I was gifted with a very entrancing, entertaining read. 
 In the story, Sharzhad/Shazi (based off of Scheherazade from the original tale) volunteers to marry Khalid, the Caliph of Korasan, to avenge her best friend Shiva, who died as one of the many brides executed daily by Khalid. To keep him from executing her, she begins to tell him a story but refuses to finish it and manages to persuade him to spare her one day after another, outliving the daily threat of an execution at dawn. Meanwhile, her childhood sweetheart, Tariq, and her father plan to get her back from Khalid, by various means, both together and apart. All the while, Sharzhad begins to have feelings for Khalid, the very man who executed her best friend and whom she has sworn to kill. 
 I absolutely loved Sharzhad. She was funny and sharp, and mostly fearless. Her chemistry with Khalid was off the charts. I loved how their relationship developed at a slow pace, a refreshing change from the rampant insta-love I've been stuck reading lately. I mean, once things started happening they happened at breakneck speed (hatred mingled with curiosity grew to attraction then zoomed straight on to love)  but I hardly cared. I just loved the romance and the two of them together. This doesn't usually happen, but I was a total sucker for the affectionate names thing in this book (Sharzhad calling him Khalid-jan just about killed me).  I did feel bad for Tariq, but I'm glad the author seems to be staying away from a cliche love triangle, as it seems Sharzhad knows she loves Khalid now and not Tariq.  
 I liked the side characters too. The fact that Despina and Jalal were together  seemed a bit convenient. I did like them as individual characters though.

At last, after series of failure in search of a hard copy of this book at the bookstore I settled to read it in 'PDF'. I've been nagging friends to lend me a hard copy of this because I felt like it was one of those books you have to get...well, it is, I conclude. 
 If you try to look deeper in the simple content of this book, you will find different parts and philosophies (existentialism -- for the most part) of life. Although this wasn't so much engaging but it was intellectually stimulating.

In most of my time as a student, I have enjoyed the pursuit of learning. Though I majored in art and design, I attended a liberal arts school and studied a variety of subjects, and honestly, enjoyed most of them. But like most of my fellow art students, we considered math to be our nemesis (the irony here is that an art student does use quite a bit of math. In fact, students with an emphasis in ceramics or sculpture were required to take MATH TESTS in each of these classes. Needless to say, I chose an emphasis in painting.) And if you add economics or statistics to the mix, these two things combined cause me to have what I would call, "deer in headlights syndrome." It is like listening to an unfamiliar foreign language, where someone is really trying to tell you something important, so she starts shaking her fists and performing crazy hand gestures, which is like the witnessing worst game of charades ever performed. In the end, there is some semblance of understanding between the two of you, but you are still unsure of what exactly transpired. This is what math + economics/statistics does to my brain. So my understanding of this book is rudimentary at best. I will try my hardest to review "The Signal and the Noise," but I make no promises in my comprehension of this subject matter. 
 I first heard about Nate Silver when I happened to be watching The Daily Show. John Stewart was interviewing Silver about his correct prediction that this past election was not going to be a close battle between Romney and Obama. Silver stated that Obama would win by a larger margin than what FOX NEWS was predicting. Now this intrigued me, because if someone can make FOX NEWS look even more foolish, the guy is a winner. So I decided to read his new book "The Signal and the Noise," since Silver proved that he was pretty good at making predictions. 
 The first part of this book was dedicated to the types of predictors: the foxes and the hedgehogs. Foxes gather from many sources and is good at many things, while a hedgehog only digs blindly forward. Silver suggests that he is a fox; he analyzes past data and looks at current statistics in order to make a prediction. This concept to me is almost common sense; a flashy prediction (like I don't know, let's say predicting that the world is going end) is like shoot an arrow in the dark, sometimes you may get lucky and hit your target, but most of the time you... don't (not even close really.) 
 The rest of the book was dedicated to this past decade prediction failures, from the housing crisis to weather patterns. These chapters were not as hard to read since they were things that affect me directly (even though sometimes it looked like gibberish and my brain started to hurt.) The main problem I had was the chapters filled with topics that I had no interest in (like baseball stats, chess and poker games.... Yawn.) And the book was like an information overload; it is definitely something I could only read for an hour before my mind began to wander to a grassy meadow with pretty yellow flowers and blue butterflies, a world that operates on no MATH. 
 Though these problems may just be me... 
 In fact, I am pretty sure it is mostly my problem. 
 Oh well. #YOLO right?

 She takes a chance on a big city. A big dream. And an even bigger Russian.
