This is a book with both strengths and weaknesses. On the plus side, Mary is a compelling and complex girl. Locked up at nine for killing baby Alyssa, struggling with guilt, PTSD from that night and her subsequent incarceration. Her mother is a wackadoodle, her group home mates only slightly less so. There's a sympathetic and believable boyfriend in Ted, an unstoppable legal counsel in Cora, and a no-nonsense SAT-prep teacher in Ms. Claire. And there are sinister twists within twists: what happened to Mary's baby brother when she was fife? Who is Mary, REALLY? What kind of crazy is her mom? There are several moments with mirrors that are quite revealing. For teen fans of Gillian Flynn, this might present an easier entry into layered thrillers. 
 On the negative side, I struggled to keep track of the many girls in the house, as they blended together. Some of the feints - Mr. Middlebury, Ray - aren't given their due, which left me wondering. At almost 400 pages, it takes a while to get going, and then ends abruptly (with a twist to be sure, but many unresolved loose ends). And I didn't feel like the either mother character - Mary's or Alyssa's mom, Ms. Richardson - came together as forcefully and fully as necessary. 
 The book has violence and hinges on issues of justice and truth. The multiethnic cast of NYC characters is both refreshing and entirely organic. There's decorous sex and modest swearing of the sort necessary to make incarcerated girls seem plausible, but the book's real evil is the twisted things people can do to each other and the lies they tell, even to themselves. While this isn't a prefect thriller, I'm hopeful that Jackson will write more.

This story continues the line that began with Ender's Shadow. Its plot and development are highly dependent upon the previous Shadow novels; don't waste your time tackling this until you've read all the previous Shadow books. You'll be missing so much context it's just not worth the confusion, and the book will be mostly wasted on you. I'm going to be very deliberately circumspect in this review to avoid revealing much in the way of details that people who haven't read those stories wouldn't know, just to be safe. 
 Pros: We see the natural evolution of Bean's story and of a few of his kids. The developments that happen make sense. The presentation of his kids, as highly intelligent kids, yet kids nonetheless, is careful and subtle -- much in the same way, I think, that Watership Down anthropomorphizes rabbits while making their thoughts distinctly rabbit-ish. 
 Cons: It's small; Ender's Shadow was 469 pages of dense text; this book was 237 pages of 1.5-space larger text that I finished in a few hours. The story arguably didn't need to be told; previous books stopped things at a reasonable juncture (although one clearly designed for something like this book to fill in -- and sucker for the story that I am, I'm only happy to read whatever Card pumps out here). The amount of cleverness of thought can feel a little overwhelming at times; yeah, I know the characters are unnaturally smart, but sometimes the pace and certainty of thought feel too much to be realistic. 
 Thus far in the handful of Goodreads reviews I've written, I have a consistent and disturbing habit of rating almost everything a 4 or 5. I can't rate this a 5; it's too thin to be satisfying in the ways the previous Ender's Shadow storyline novels were. Yet I can't rate it a 3, either, because as a way to wrap up various bits of the Shadow storyline, it leaves me more satisfied than that. So 4 it is, probably closer to 3.5 if I could grant it. 
 How exactly does it leave me satisfied? I was reminded of bits of three other books that I think capture my feelings pretty well. I'll note them behind some spoiler tags since they relate to the final plot development of the book. 
 First, I was reminded of the story of the third brother in The Tale of the Three Brothers as told by Hermione in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: 
 It was only when he had attained a great age that the youngest brother finally took off the Cloak of Invisibility and gave it to his son. And then he greeted Death as an old friend, and went with him gladly, and, equals, they departed this life. 
 I was also simultaneously reminded of Dumbledore talking to Harry near the end of the same book: 
 [T]he true master does not seek to run away from Death. He accepts that he must die, and understands that there are far, far worse things in the living world than dying. 
 Second, I was reminded of the last several paragraphs of the epilogue of Watership Down. If you haven't read Watership Down, don't read this quote; read that book instead as soon as you can. If you have and are simply forgetting it, this page includes the relevant quote (search for "One chilly, blustery morning"). (But really, you should reread the book.) 
 Third, I was reminded of the way in which the mortality of humans is portrayed in The Silmarillion. I don't have exact quotes here; it's more the way in which the mortality of humans was portrayed as a blessing, as contrasted with the immortality of the elves.  
 Anyway. If you read the other Shadow books, I think this one does a good job of continuing the story, and it's worth a quick read for that purpose. If you haven't read them, I'd only recommend this if you read those and remain interested.

There were several very cute moments between her and Talon, but I thought Talon was a little too much of a jerk to really ever love him. A fun novella about the harrowing trip to the Winter Court. Ash has come to collect Meghan, fulfilling their contract by taking her to Mab. What should be a simple trek into Winter is anything but. An ancient Hunter is on their tail and will stop at nothing to get Meghan.

Not entirely dramatic and quite moving. All bits of the story draw you in, make you think you know what's coming up, and then surprise you and says you need a new guess. 
 The twist made me frown and gasp almost until the very end... call me evil, but I don't think a slightly open-ended happy ending works well for this novel.

Imagine Germinal crossed with Frozen. I haven't stayed up late into the night to finish a book for six months. Wonderful, beautiful characterization by an absolutely lovely, hilarious person. 10/10 WOULD READ AGAIN

Well this was quite a surprise! I don't understand why it is called a "companion" novel, because it takes place right after the first story and even gives more background and history into Seraphina's world. I was on the edge of my seat, lots of suspense but..I think the relationships between Phina, Kiggs and The Queen are...vaugely described... So much has lingered with me like subjects of religion, conciousness, spirituality and the mind. This story is so emotional, I'm still angry at some characters and parts of the ending. So much time was spent building up the tension toward the reader..like can Phina save "blank" or "blank" in time or will she fall apart? The ending was reduced to 2 chapters that left a lot for the reader to fill in..or wait for answers in another story? Other wise I loved the plot and mystery, and the deep meaning woven throughout this story.

I picked this book up at my local library (Thank god) because I heard so many people loved it and it had such a high rating on goodreads that I figured it must be good! 
 I was wrong of course... 
 To begin with this book is like every other YA paranormal romance out in the market. You have the "average" girl protag who isn't like other girls because she listen to cool indie music and doesn't dress like a "slut" or anything. Also she happens to have some interesting magical or paranormal power, and if she doesn't people are just attracted to her because she's so "different". Then you got the boy who's usually rich and attractive and falls in love with the girl protag because she isn't falling at his feet to worship him, even though she secretly is but doesn't show it. Then you got them falling in love somehow, and also a basic ass plot or no plot at all, and there you have it that's the book. 
 The reason why I picked up this book, besides the high rating, was the interesting premise, but of course it was wasted by the terrible writing and dull characters. I felt like the book had many opportunities to explore and go deeper into the paranormal aspect of the story but Hodkin instead chose to explore the cliche romance. I felt that the paranormal aspect was overshadowed by the romance in a really dumb way. Like you have all this crazy paranormal shit going on around you but you're worried about a boy??? Like come on??? 
 The romance was also terrible, unhealthy, and controlling. Almost like what I've read in "50 Shades of Grey." Noah is a controlling bastard at best, and for some reason Mara swoons over that??? Why I will never know I guess. I honestly don't know what else to say about the romance other than it is basically a combo between "Twilight" and "50 Shades" so there you go that's all you need to know. 
 Mara's view on mental illness was very disgusting honestly. She referred to herself as "crazy" , "psycho", and "broken" a lot of the times, and as a mentally ill person myself I felt offended and that she wasn't really educated well on the topic of mental illness at all. Also she believed that Noah could somehow save her from her mental illness which is a really negative and terrible thing to think, and I'm honestly shocked this is somehow still a popular trope for YA literature. 
 The writing wasn't good. I have no idea why people are calling it beautiful and lyrical. The writing was juvenile at best, and at times I felt that the author was trying way to hard to make things seem deep and meaningful. Also there was no plot? Like at all? Till maybe the end where they were setting up for the second book. Nothing was explained, nothing was resolved, and everything was terrible. 
 I have nothing else to say about this other than I just didn't like it. It was a bad book with no real redeemable qualities. The only reason why i'm interested in the second book is because maybe things will be explained finally, and maybe a plot will exist. For now though I think i'll take a break from this series.

Easily one of my favorite books this year! 
 The writing was very excellent. Riley was so completely believable and someone would have to have a heart made of stone to not empathize with them. It helps that Riley and all of their peers felt really authentic and never like a middle-aged person trying to sound 'like the kids'. It never feels like Garvin is trying to hard to sound hip or relevant to his target audience. 
 The strongest part of this novel was of course Riley, but Solo and Bec were great characters also. Both were great friends and strong allies. I'm really glad that they each had their own richly developed backgrounds. Bec and Solo enhanced the story in a lot of ways and it definitely would not have been as good without them. I also just really loved Solo, he is literally the best. 
 From a lot of the reviews I've read, there's a complaint of information overload, especially for those already familiar with the concept of gender fluidity. I felt like the information was presented in a way that felt natural to the story. Riley was on Bloglr, an obvious subsitute for Tumblr, where posts with information on such topics abound. Other than slowing the pace, I don't think this really detracted from the book at all. I honestly couldn't put it down once I had a chance to finally sit down and devour it! 
 This is another young adult book that I really think should be required reading for everyone, particularly with such awful discriminatory laws being written. Just reading this book made me so grateful with the awesome amount of diversity that is becoming more commonplace in young adult literature. I really, really hope it can help give a voice to kids struggling with the same thing. Or maybe even retire outdated notions about gender identity.
Cute and fun but nothing amazing.

To me, Anna Dressed in Blood read like a tv episode. An average one. There were parts that's nice, and parts that I can't wait for them to be over soon. Prose and pace were good (especially in the beginning), it's one of those books whereby I just read one word after another. Though it wasn't as consistent towards the end. And erm, let me get something over with, it's not scary - slightly creepy, maybe. There's nothing graphic that you wouldn't have already dreamt or came across before the book came along. The only thing that kinda spooked me is the cover. All in all, there were more of mystery elements than horror, really. 
 Anna Dressed in Blood follows our character Cas. He's basically a nomad, moving to one place to another alongside were his mother (a witch) and their pet cat. Such inconvenience comes with a unusual circumstance and that is, he is a ghost hunter. His routine includes moving into a town and hunting down their local ghosts that committed murders after their death. 
 The story begun when Cas travelled into a town in Canada. Their famous (but hushed) local ghost is Anna. Known to be murdered as she was walking to an event in white dress (only to be drenched in her own red blood later). After the event of her death, violent murders (from different time) started to happen at her home, unexplained and obviously linked(by how they died, not relations between those that died). Police closed those cases without much investigations and people just brush them off as they usually do, but they were aware of something that was out of their understanding was happening, so they stayed away. He was planning to go up to her and kill her, nothing he hasn't done before. (Well, except Anna was by far the strongest ghost he has come across) 
 Another thing that's different for Cas was he only did solo on his huntings, but this time round, he came across people that he only ever had intention to get them talking and gather as much information as he could on Anna, but soon those people turned to be his acquaintance, then friends and sidekicks. The two crazies that wanted a part were Thomas and Carmel. 
 I loved Thomas and Carmel. I wanted more about them, as in an individual and their backstory in details. That part left much to be desired for me. 
 There were certain parts of the story that just felt like a little more detail definitely won't hurt. Like Uncle Gideon? I felt like he's definitely not as unconnected with the whole incicent as it seemed. He appeared on and off in the beginning and totally disappeared in the end. 
 And,  the titanic-ish ending. That's a little silly and totally knocked off a star for me  
 Lastly, this book is popular and many said it's gripping. So read this book (for its quite okay content), don't read it - as in no rush if you've other books you can't wait to get cracking.

I just downloaded this book this morning and in less than 5 hours I finished reading it. Finally! A book that's not too mainstream or a cliche but was plotted in an interesting manner. Although the way that some part's written confused me a bit - one character's dialogue to another. I loved it. I loved the ending and the substories. I LOVE THE STORY AND I'M GIVING IT A 5/5 STARS!!!!!

Actual raiting: 
 4.5 
 This book had a rather sad feel to it and I didn't like it, it depressed me. But however it's still a good book and oh god love triangles, I just can't deal with them. I'm pretty sure I know who's endgame, because someone spoiled it for me, but I'll just have to wait and see I guess. Anyhow it's still a great book and I'm glad we finally learn more of Clara's mother's secrets. I can't wait to see what happens next!
Why do these covers keep getting worse? And, more importantly, why do the plots of the books deteriorate as well?

This is an entertaining entry in the McEwan canon and is more on the "amusing" side than the "profound". It's well-written, incredibly atmospheric, and very engaging. The last chapter will strike you as either convoluted and forced or very smart and clever. I was somewhere between those two spectrums.

Cop Town by Karin Slaughter is a book about cops set in Atlanta in 1974. It tells the story of Maggie Lawson and Kate Murphy, two of the few female cops in the force at the time. 
 The premise is a good one. A serial killer is on the loose. Cops are his/her target. Maggie and Kate take matters into their hands and prove the rest of the men in the police squad wrong, by being good cops. 
 The plot is OK. It kept me interested BUT it was a hard book to read. I had a tough time getting into the story because of the language. To say that the characters had a "potty mouth" is an understatement. They were so filthy and vulgar. Not only in their expressions but their behavior was disgusting. And I'm not talking about the men only. 
 The men were sexist pigs who couldn't imagine a woman could have any capabilities other than having breasts and a vagina. Needless to say that the two main characters in the story face sexual discrimination of the worst kind. Also, these men didn't know what a respectable law enforcing cop was. 
 The women weren't exemplar either. Even though they were given a hard time, they let the environment and the people around them get the best of them. They had to defend themselves by forgetting their morals and femininity, acting like tough, masculine at times and very vulgar women. Kate seemed like a respectable young widow in the beginning. I was rooting for Kate, until she knocked three times (I won't spoil it for you, when you read it, you'll understand what I mean). 
 All of this made it difficult for me to read Cop Town. 
 Read this book knowing that it juggles strong topics: murder, sexism, discrimination, race issues, sexual harassment, homophobia, antisemitism, betrayal, violence, corruption, and crime, to name a few. The language is crude, vulgar and profane. 
 The positive side of this book, is that I gained even more respect for women in police squads, army, secret service etc. It also made me reflect on women's roles in society today. My other train of thoughts was about corruption, antisemitism and racism. We're still living times in which many people still face these issues be it first world countries or those from the third world. And it's a little disheartening to see that times have changed, but we humans can't seem to completely change and live in true world peace. More about this on my blog 
 This was my first Karin Slaughter book. I'm not sure I would read more books if this one turns into a series. Cop Town is an OK book to read, that's it. 
 Check out the complete review and my other musings on my blog.

Male MC is sex on a stick, best buddy is gay. Female MC is very hot. Check, check and check. Fairly stereotypical paranormal romance? Surprisingly, not so much. 
 Fate marks people for death and our female main character, Cacia, and her family, the Ferrys, then help the souls of the dead to heaven or hell. 
 Title song for this book: "Don't Pay the Ferryman" by Chris de Burgh. 
 The setting is a dystopian, flodded Boston, surrounded by a country ravaged by climate change and disaster. Our heroes are members of emergency medical services, struggling to save lives. 
 I really like the world Sarah Fine came up with, although the world building ultimately left me unsatisfied. There are quite a few holes , that only get filled very slowly or late into the book. Some part did not really work for me and I kept wondering how they could exist at the same time in the same setting. What is there, is good though. New ideas, not the same old, same old. Well described, easy to visualize. 
 About 10% into the book my thoughts were: "I could like this book just as a climate fiction with a dash of mystery and romance, no need for the paranormal elements." 
 I liked the alternating POV, switching from Cacy to Eli and back. It kept the narrative lively. 
 The side characters were vivid and believable and some of them were even more interesting than Cacia's family members. I actually struggled a bit to tell her two brothers apart at times. And two of the Kere that kept popping up I couldn't keep straight till the end. 
 The romance built up slowly, in a fairly mature way. A third into the book I hadn't winced once--paranormal romance is not really my genre. Nice amount of subtle humour. 
 She folded her arms over her chest. "I have trouble thinking when I'm not wearing pants." 
 Eli laughed, a deep, husky sound, and took a few steps back. "I guess we have that in common. I also have trouble thinking when you're not wearing pants." 
 Eventually it got a bit more saccharine sweet, but the main characters did not loose their minds completely. They actually behaved like adults, which was refreshing. Halfway into the book they were in lust with each other, but in typical romance novel manner not communicating well. A little mystery, murder and suspense thrown in and I was entertained, despite all my misgivings about some of the world building. 
 Even the eventual sex was mature, no swords, rods or sheaths in sight. 
 And then the last part of the book happened. Flipping heck. The story really took off. Fantastic plot twist that I did not see coming. Followed by more awesome plot developments. All of a sudden the paranormal element was great and the action just went wham, bang, thank you, mam! I was glued to the page and couldn't read fast enough. I wish the whole book had been like that. Awesome stuff. I am really looking forward to the next book in the series! 
 Even the bad guy grew on my. I hope there will be a lot more of him. This story has a lot of potential. Almost five stars, small deductions for world building. 
 Thank you NetGalley for this great, free and wholeheartedly appreciated read!

Fantastic book. It really cements Vader's rise as a Sith as it shows the last remnants of Anakin fading away. With Kenobi and Yoda given up on fighting directly it's good to see some Jedi keep up the fight.

A solid book that introduces who introverts are, the extrovert ideal that's prevalent in all corners of society, the nurture vs. nature argument with relation to temperament, and how to nurture kids that are introverts. 
 Throughout the book, she talks about the advantages of disadvantages of both introverts and extroverts, and--if you're an introvert--how to make the most of your strengths, some of which are deep concentration, inner exploration, and having in-depth conversations with people, one-on-one. She also talks about how much we can break out of the negatives of introversion, such as fear of public speaking, large groups, and being sociable. 
 In general, this was a strong book talking about many aspects of introversion, its place in society, and how to make the most of it. I found myself being quite glad to be an introvert (though it does seem like she sings the praises of introverts a lot.) 
 The historical content and practical ideas in this book, coupled with the recent scientific research into temperament and how much we can stretch it, make it a very good book. I didn't find it incredible, but I related with the book to a strong degree. Worthwhile read.

Honesty I hated the beginning of this book. About halfway in I was feeling a little better about the book, but the series is getting a little too predictable. At this point I'm pretty much only picking up the books to finish the series. Since they are such quick reads, I figure, why not.

There is/was a lot of hype around this book, and I may have gone in with a little too high of expectations, but I still really enjoyed it. I only knew it was about two sisters' living during WWII. It paints a good story of peoples' (especially women's) lives during the War in France while they were home and the men were at the warfront. You see how rough it was for some of these people to live with the affects of war such as rations and dealing with the Nazis occupying France. 
 The story is told from the older sister, Vianne's, and then the younger sister, Isabelle's point of view. Vianne is married and her husband is away so she is the sole caretaker of her younger daughter, Sophie. Isabelle is 19 years old and quite rebellious; she wants to play a bigger part in the war. The sisters are not quite close due to their father sending them away when they were young after the death of their mother, and a young teen Vianne found closeness with new friends, ignoring toddler Isabelle. I think the way the sisters' relationship with each other is handled very well and I found it really believable. The whole story overall is quite believable, actually, which is a good thing for a historical fiction novel. 
 The reason I am not giving it a 5 full stars is that I was not incredibly emotionally involved. Honestly, I don't know why. There are parts where I was shocked or saddened, but nothing made me cry and nothing made me shout. I don't think I had a strong emotional connection to the characters maybe? Not sure. But I have been much more invested in other books. I enjoy a good romance, but I did not feel anything for Isabelle and Gaetan's story. It just felt very sudden and I don't think I understood either's feelings for each other and where it comes from. On the other hand, I really felt bad for Beck and Vianne. They had a very forbidden love. The fact that Beck died too while Vianne protected Isabelle really showed that the sisters cared for each other despite not being close, and family ties are very important.

The usual -- scary bad guys, boy raised in secret and protected by mighty wizard. Innocent, but eventually realises that something is up. Sets out into the world with a band of companions and saves the world. Does not necessarily mean that the book is not good, but this was boring. Sorry!

I can't even begin to describe how great Neil Gaiman is as an author. I lack the necessary poetic mind. Stardust is in turns clever, sad, and funny. I easily empathized with the star's longing for her home, particularly at the ending. I approve of Tristran's choices, despite him starting out as foolhardy. 
 I took the time to type out some of the more beautiful and whimsical descriptions from the book that I really enjoyed: 
 "There was once a young man who wished to gain his Heart's Desire. And while that is, as beginnings go, not entirely novel (for every tale about every young man there ever was or will be could start in a similar manner) there was much about this young man and what happened to him that was unusual, although even he never knew the whole of it." 
 Storm-filled eggshells!! 
 "Every lover is in his heart a madman, and in his head a minstrel." 
 "Lights flickered in the hawthorn bush behind him. He thought they were glow-worms or fireflies, but, on closer inspection, he perceived they were tiny people, flickering and flitting from branch to branch." 
 "It was sometimes said that the grey-and-black mountain range which ran like a spine north to south down that part of Faerie had once been a giant, who grew so huge and so heavy that, one day, worn out from the sheer effort of moving and living, he had stretched out on the plain and fallen into a sleep so profound that centuries passed between heartbeats."

I very recently discovered Elizabeth Eulberg and have been working my way through her books. While I've enjoyed all of the ones I have read so far (especially Better off Friends), Take a Bow has become not just my favorite Eulberg book, but one of my favorite books of the year. 
 I loved the characters. The story is told from the 1st person POV of four students at a prestigious arts school: Emme, Ethan, Sophie, and Carter. I really enjoyed each of their perspectives. I loved Emme and how kind she was. I loved her relationship with her band members, Ben, Jack, and Ethan. Ethan came the closest to the "tortured artist" persona I was expecting for the setting, but it was never over the top. While he messed up plenty, he did really try and I loved him. Carter was the former child star who just wanted to have a normal life. He was so nice and I loved the friendship he developed with Emme. His part of the story is really focused on finding himself and while I appreciated it and did like him, he came across a little pretentious at times. I pretty much straight up hated Sophie at first, but as the book went on I started to kind of love to hate her. She could not be more different than sweet Emme and I couldn't wait to see this mean girls get what was coming to her. 
 As I've mentioned, I've been binging on Eulberg books lately and I think the thing that keeps making me come back is the character development. All of her characters are really well developed and I become deeply invested in them. I almost start to feel like they're real people and I wish I was part of their friendships. This year I have been really into mysteries/suspense and have not had a lot of patience for anything else. These books have made me really start to appreciate a good character-driven story again. 
 The only thing I didn't really like about the book was how Carter's chapters were formatted. Every time there was dialogue it had the character name and then a colon and then what was said. It took me a little while to figure out that's it's supposed to mimic a script. It didn't work for me, though, because the rest of the text wasn't like that. If the whole POV could have been written out like a script I think it could've been a really interesting narrative choice, but as it was it was just kind of distracting. 
 Overall, I really loved Take a Bow. I read it in a day. I loved the characters and the friendship and even the catty egomaniac. I know this review does not do justice to how much I enjoyed this book. I can't believe how long it has taken me to discover Elizabeth Eulberg. If you are a fan of YA Contemporaries, you definitely need to check her out. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 4.5 Stars

I hate when I just can't get into and love a story as much as everyone else. This one for me was not one of my favorite K.A. books.

So much drama, I loved it! 
 I can't wait to read the next books!

I struggled! I think that this book needs more explaining of Mr. Grays past, instead of I love you, I love you too, oh I can't stay mad at your overbearing neediness...blah blah... The mystery was dragged out for too long and unexplained. First book was good but these last two.. Boring...

"Only way to reach the green grass of Oregon or the sweet gold of California is through hell itself." 
 MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS 
 It has been a long time since I've read a book that is a western so I wasn't even sure if I would like this type of book anymore, but I am so glad I did. I loved this book and how brave Leah is. 
 When Leah's parents are killed she is forced into making a very tough decision leave the farm she has worked so hard to keep up in order to go California or to stay and become trapped with someone who may want to harm her. With this choice she also had to figure out how to keep her "witchy powers" secret. 
 Once she has made her decision she realizes that she will have to hide her identity in order to make it their safely. While along the way she meets a wide range of people, some good, some bad, and some a little bit of both. She also makes a lot of new friends that are willing to help her along the way and keep her safe after they reach their destination. 
 I really did love this book. I loved how things that had never been talked about before were talked about. (How she dealt with hiding her time of the month and what confirmed bachelor meant) These were things that I had never seen be talked about before and while they were just briefly mentioned I found it refreshing and informative. 
 Every time Leah was almost found out it was stressful and made you feel like you were in her shoes as well and when she was finally found out it wasn't the end of the world like I thought it would be. Carson did an amazing job of keeping the "witchy powers" and the real history of wagon trains true to what we've mostly been taught about them and made them work together perfectly. 
 I can't wait to read the second book in this trilogy and see what happens to Leah and her friends next.

Lots of thoughts. 
 As I drove into work today (one of the primary reasons I started with audiobooks--I don't mind delays anymore in an urban setting), whereever I was in the book made me think that reading ("manually") is such an intrinsic part of my life, and has been since I was a young child, that I have forgotten the real visceral joy of it. I am grateful that this book has reminded me/given that back to me. 
 The parody (unfortunately NOT so much a parody) of education these days was hysterically (in all its senses) funny (to one who is and has been immersed in education--vocationally as well as avocationally--all my life). 
 The environmental message is pretty much "beat you over the head, repeatedly and hard" for adults. But as a tree hugger myself :-) I am delighted with the message to kids...those in awareness as well as years. 
 This is a really wonderful book (although I admit the first half was making me regret I thought I could give three stars at best; keep reading). 
 2016 reread: Still my favorite of this series.

I was looking for something similar to Cheryl Brooks Cat Star Chronicles and think Claimed was something similar to the Grabbed series by Lolita Lopez. 
 Olivia wasn't a great character for me personally but I really enjoyed Baird. I thought that Olivia should have been the one to persuade Baird that she was worth all the fuss he was going through and thankfully by the end she did!

Katie has just moved to NYC from Texas. She has a terrible boss and isn't paid much. She notices how truly strange NYC is. And then she starts getting these strange emails about a job. She gives it a try and is introduced to a whole new fantasy world--full of magic, fairies, etc. 
 Katie comes across as a very normal girl and is therefore easy to relate to. A quick, fun read, especially if you're into magical-type chick-lit.

This was a good book. It was very detailed and well thought out, almost to detailed. I loved Rex, yes he is the perfect man. Daniel - torn on him but grew to love him. I am rating it down a star from 5 to 4 stars because of how it ended. There was so much going on and then boom..done. I felt like I was cheated on the story. I know many may not agree, but It's how I feel at this moment - another part I didn't like was the book was so long, yet I was still left hanging. I want to read Colin's story and also get to the ending of Rex & Daniels story.

3.5 stars... or maybe 4. It started out a lot slower than the first one, only ramping up in the last third or quarter. That, and me not 100% loving the ending. But for most of the book, I was likely to only give three stars. Still totally an enjoyable read (especially the last 30%), but I wish it would have gotten into it faster. Also, shouldn't Brody have been at the party?

By all rights I should've hated this. On the surface, it's everything I dislike in YA fantasy novels: a helpless girl stuck in a gilded prison, bemoaning her situation while others have it worse. She questions her stance and wonders whether she made the right choice. 
 But it doesn't lack in huge plot developments, and that continuously managed to amaze me and keep me satisfied. Because fuck. Each one packs a mean punch. 
 This is one of those times where I actually care enough to not spoil it for the others who haven't read it yet. Rest assured, there's at least two or three things you probably won't see coming. And it's rough when you realize what's happening, because this author doesn't sacrifice story in the name of sentimentality. Our favorite characters are brutalized and tortured, shot and maimed. 
 So far the only thing I haven't been satisfied with is the lack of use that the Sultan had for his secret weapons.  Capturing and confining the Djinni.... that's an epic arsenal at his fingertips. I'm a little surprised they didn't play a larger role in this installment, but I expect that means they'll make a huge splash in the next book.  He's a ruthless ruler, and you can see why he's stayed on top for so long. I liked that he wasn't some idiot who was caught up in Amani's impulsiveness. He recognized the challenge in her and didn't underestimate her. He knows the true worth of his son. He knows just how much public opinion sways choices. 
 Honestly, I just really enjoyed this. It was worth the wait of starting the series and I am definitely looking forward to the rest of it.

I finally got a chance to read this book. I had to form a de facto book group at work to make it happen but it worked! I finally found the time to add it into my unending to-read list. So, I've got to post a bit of a review. I've already watched the movie series and there wasn't a lot of difference between the movie and the book in this case. Unfortunately, I've lived with Harry Potter so long that I didn't experience the wonder and enchantment that I think I might have if I had been one of the lucky people to read it prior to it becoming a phenomenon. Also, it is a juvenile level book and so was a bit simplistic for me in some ways. 
 What I loved about the book was the relationship (and family) that Harry got by meeting the Weesleys. I also loved that the author could create an entire world and her very own game. The action was visually descriptive making it easy to imagine it as I read it.

After an initially interesting premise, this book takes a turn for the overwritten and plodding. I raced through it to give it back to the person who lent it to me, otherwise, it probably would have languished in my "paused" bookshelf forever. At least I've got closure.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Wool Omnibus is a collection of five "books", each one can actually stand-alone (originally the first was planned to be one). The first two parts introduced the settings of the story -- the underground settlement called Silo and the punishment for breaking out the defined rules of the Silo by sending outside called Cleaning. These two are the core concepts of the whole 'Wool' plot. On the other hand, the last three parts focuses on the main character while she uncovers the secrets and how she got caught on the intricate web of her dystopian community. I treated this book as a whole continuous narrative and worked for me because the five divisions gave a resolution and something to look develop on each every part. 
 I liked the first two parts for its story-telling - serving as the introduction as said. Holston and Jahns lead the two parts, respectively, and their characters were driven by conflicts and own motives. Honestly, I would love their roles to be stretched throughout the end, but their untimely deaths provided a good ground for the successful and intriguing flow of the story. Note-worthy heartbreaking moment here is Jahns' death and Marnes reaction on it. 
 Part 3 to 5 focuses on the main heroine, Juliette, recruited by Jahns and Marnes to serve as the new sheriff. To start off, she was not a perfect character -- her actions greatly changed the whole Silo and its people. Though, she was strong-willed person that made her a likable character. There were highlights on supporting roles which gave more flavor and width to Juliette's world. I'm shipping Juliette and Lukas' budding relationship in here. Solo, on the other hand, was a great companion for the heroine as she traversed to the unthinkable frontier outside her Silo. There were a lot of depressing instances here (if you guessed death, then you are right) that it was hard to invest emotions anymore (I became quite numbed with it already). However, there were flashes of optimism and hope throughout that you cannot miss. One particular scene that I love is when the guys (Walker, Shirly and Courtnee) heard and was talking to Juliette for the first time after thinking that she didn't survived outside. The words of the author for the characters were swelling up with inexplicable emotions, which I found really endearing. 
 Overall, 'Wool' works on a wonderful and unpredictable premise. And 
 delivers well 
 . However, I did found some parts a bit dragging and slow (i.e. parts when Juliette was trying to find her way outside after her survival from the cleaning) and the last dozen chapters a bit cramped with integral events (that could be more spread out, ideally). The last point actually made me doubtful about how Howey will end this book as there were a lot of possibilities in a short amount of pages. Gladly, the ending was satisfying. It was not I expected and it was short of anything close of what I initially expected it to be in terms of narrative and plot, but it was a nice and smooth conclusion. The author didn't touch the post-apocalyptic world in a general sence but rather somewhat concluded the stories in the Silos involved only. 
 Satisfying 
 indeed. Excited to know that there is a possibility for a film adaptation soon of this material -- so please pick it up soon Ridley Scott! Also, can't wait for Howey to finish up the story of Jules with his new work coming out on October 2013 titled 
 Dust 
 ! For now, I'll read the prequel 
 Shift 
 within the year.

 Have to dock one star (but it'd be only a half if available) I simply can't believe/accept the speed and depth of Beauvoir's mental tailspin (both emotional and reason-ably/logically).

Another victim of oversold expectations. The reason I picked up this doorstopper in the first place is because of the hype over a PEN/Faulkner winner jumping into genre with both feet. I was looking for brilliant character development, and maybe even a unique structure or style of storytelling. What I got instead was little more than Stephen King's The Stand with less emphasis on the supernatural. That's not a bad thing. What ticked me off, though, was being promised one thing and receiving something completely different.

This was my first King book in some time. I don't even remember the last book I read by him. I had only read his earlier horror books before and wanted to see his take on fantasy. I wouldn't say it was something unbelievably good, but it was good. I'll just leave it at that right now. I am interested in the continuing the series because he has some good hooks in here. They're not strong, but they're good. I am by no means saying the book was bad; it just takes a bit to get into.  By having Roland be a guy who is into girls when they're there, has a heart for saving kids when they merit it, and still going after the tower, adds to the allure of the story.  
 It was a fairly strong initial setting. Again, we have to remember he was 19 when he wrote this, and that is the unbelievable bit. Who else can say something like that?
It does have humor...fairly subtle but that's the best kind. I enjoyed it a lot. New author for me; I'll read more.

For some reason, I was expecting this to be a vampire book, but it wasn't. Dante is basically a prince in his country and when American, Reece, bumps into him at the airport, a connection is formed. She is on her way to visit her dad for the summer in London, but a volcano eruption stops that from happening. So...she ends up in Caberra, at Dante's home. 
 Likes: I liked watching them fall in love--so complicated and gradual. I also liked knowing that Reece was so normal--thinking things and then saying them, without realizing it; feeling jealous and insecure; trying to find a friend in a strange place. But she wasn't over the top. Dante is such a gentleman--so different from American boys and I can totally see why he had Reece swooning--he had it all--looks, money, manners. 
 Dislikes: I'm not a fan of teen sex or teen drinking and I teach my kids not to go down those roads. There were a few scenes where you knew that was happening, but there weren't details, but that still bugged me. For those reasons, I wouldn't recommend it as a YA read, even though that's how it's listed. There was also a bit more language than I personally like--not just swear words, but crude Jr High words. 
 But...I loved the storyline and it was good, fluffy fun.

From the first page this is a compelling, character driven story. Cassie has been living in the wild of the Obed wilderness, taking care of her young, mute sister Jenssa while surviving the predations of a meth-using mom, limited resources, and haunting memories. When the girls are brought back to civilization by their almost-too-good-to-be-believed father, Carrie's adjustment and struggle make for heart-felt reading. Murdoch has crafted a strong, distinctive narrator, whose voice is a mixture of backwoods-bumpkin and autodidact-elevation. It was a pleasure to read. 
 The first section of the story is perhaps the strongest, as Carrie shares nuggets of her life in the woods, of how she managed to eek out a spartan existence that had its pleasures and beauty. The middle section of rejoining suburban teen life is slightly less compelling - there's a boy, mean girls, a dog - but I appreciated the way Murdoch wove in believable details of Cassie's mental state without becoming fixated on the horror show of her past. 
 The last section brings everything to a close in an honest way. Hand this to fans of Carol Lynch Williams's Glimpse or perhaps Beauty Queen and Crank. This is more character driven and lyrical, but still easy for even modestly engaged readers. I'm looking forward to more books from this author.

This books was atrocious. It is ridiculously over-the-top in a fashion that renders it nothing so much as an absurdity. It makes no cogent sense whatsoever. It is deeply flawed and thoroughly unbelievable. 
 I wanted to champion this book. The diversity of its characters, while painfully "let's checkmark the boxes," was a welcome change from other book's casts. But if you're going to tell a story from multiple POVs, they have to have distinguishable voices. The characters here do not. It is the same voice with different names attached. If the only way to know who's speaking is by reading the heading or because some "I got this off Google Translate" Spanish is thrown in, that's not a success. 
 And the dialogue. Oh, the dialogue--or what passes for it--is painful. Teenagers do not talk like this. Adults do not talk like this. People in the middle of a deadly emergency, watching a slaughter and wondering if they're next, do not read prepared speeches off a teleprompter. They do not think grand, sweeping thoughts usually reserved for everyone's "I am so deep, let me journal my very deep thoughts" phase. 
 Nothing about the law enforcement response rings the least bit true. Even pre-Columbine, the police would not have acted in as grossly negligent a fashion as they do here. In a post-Columbine world? Forget it. 
  
 The author seemed confused throughout as to what type of setting she wanted. It's a rural farming area, but the school has tons of kids, except then it doesn't, or maybe it does? There are really no places to hide? Really? Every classroom conveniently locked except the one a character firecrackers and no one has fixed--and this student has not been expelled? Nope. Not how it works anymore. 
 Everything is so over the top. The Very Villainous Bad Guy Shooter, who is incredibly well-armed and able to enter and lock down a school with NO ONE noticing, takes time out of his very busy murderous day to not shoot the school's resource officer, but instead run him over? He doesn't shoot or even stab the school's one janitor, but instead has time to bind and garotte him with zip ties? Where are the lunch ladies? The office staff? The teachers who are always left to patrol a hallway during an assembly? They do not exist. Because with a story this poorly plotted, they cannot. 
 The attempts to bookend sections with social media looking posts was also an utter failure. It muddled the "narrative" while adding nothing. By the end I still had no idea what or who I was meant to derive from half these messages. And I simply didn't care about the other half of them. 
  
 This book is an insult to readers, to history, to anyone with a modicum of knowledge about the psychology or criminology of school shooters. I can only imagine the deep disgrace it presents to survivors and victims of such horror.

I received a copy of this title from NetGalley. It does not impact my review. 
 The Mime Order will be available January 27, 2015. 
 According to NetGalley the version of the ARC I read is NOT the final, Americanized version that will be published. (Whatever that means.) 
 It's been awhile since I read The Bone Season, so it took me several chapters to get reacquainted with the world of Voyants and Rephaim and Scion and the Syndicate and Mime-Lords. Once I did, though, I really enjoyed it. I think I actually enjoyed this one a lot more than I did the first book. 
 When I first read The Bone Season and heard the series would be seven books, I predicted that each book would be from a different member of Paige's gang, The Seven Seals. Thankfully, I was wrong about that. The Mime Order is still told through Paige's 1st person POV, but we do get to know some of the other Seals better through her. 
 After breaking out of Sheol I, Paige is on a mission to warn the rest of the Syndicate about the Rephaim and their control over Scion and London. However, Warden is missing and no one is interested in hearing about it. Especially Jaxon, Paige's Mime-Lord. He rescued Paige, his Pale Dreamer, and now just wants her to get back to work and focus on their Sector. I love to hate Jaxon! He's such a great blend of confident and cocky; smart and devious. I spent the whole book questioning his motives and what he really cares about. 
 While Paige's main focus is getting the word out about the Rephaim, there are a lot of other obstacles thrown her way. Scion has named her enemy number one in London for being a dangerous clairvoyant, but it's not just Scion that's after her. While I enjoyed the book, it did run a little long and the number of times Paige gets jumped in an alley got a bit too repetitive for me. However, as the book goes on, the action definitely picks up and I had a very hard time putting it down. 
 I'm not sure how much more to say about the plot of the story, since the book doesn't come out until January and I don't want to be spoilery. I will say that there are some big shake-ups within the Syndicate and while the book doesn't exactly end in a cliffhanger, it definitely left me wanting more and I can't wait to see what happens next! 
 The character development was well-done in this book. We get to see Paige grow, as well as get to know Jaxon, Nick (love him!!), and Eliza better. There's also a continuation of the romance that started in the first book, but it doesn't overtake the story at all, which I appreciate. The writing I also felt was much improved from the first book. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed The Mime Order. It was a great follow-up to the start of a series, one that I think actually surpassed the first. I would definitely recommend it to those that have read The Bone Season and recommend the series to those that enjoy fantasy.

Fuck. 
 That was definitely one of those books that was far too stressful and enticing. The whole time I was absolutely captivated--much the same kind of emotions I felt while reading anything by Gillian Flynn. The book from the get-go is dark, and steeped in pop culture media. Everything relevant to this age is mentioned: Reddit, Facebook, Kickstarter, Nyan cat, you name it. I can imagine this would be kind of baffling for people who don't have much of an online presence, because the fundamental focus of this entire narrative is social media. And boy, does social media rear its ugly head here. 
 There's several main characters: 
 TK: the homeless guy who just tries to do what he can to help others. 
 Gabi: a single mom detective who is lead on the murders 
 Layla: Gabi's 16 year old daughter, who decides to make stupid decisions 
 Jonno: the lame wannabe journalist who forgoes basic logic to be famous 
 Clay: a guy who has been fighting off the bad things for far too long, and finally succumbs 
 There's some minor characters as well, characters that really are just as great as the main ones--Cas and Sparkles, namely. 
 Basically, all of their different paths lead to one explosion of activity. Cas and Layla learn that what gets on the internet stays forever. Jonno learns that his fame rides entirely on his ability to work the internet. And Clay's dream learns that all it needs is eyeballs. 
 Ugh. I'm getting annoyed because there's so much I want to say about this book but can't seem to articulate it. I loved the horror aspect that didn't come out until the end. I loved the steady build up of events, events that kept getting more and more rash. I loved that each character had their own issues to work through, all culminating (again) into one fabulous climax. 
  The dream is some kind of thing that leaks into Clay and takes him over. The dream only wants to return to its own world, or bring its world out. So it starts drawing chalk doors everywhere, and creating "art" in the form of hand-sewn satyrs in the hopes of bringing that world out. When it doesn't work, it becomes increasingly determined, going bigger and bigger with its ideas. The thing is, its tendrils have started infecting others, too. Because TK is starting to see things, and Layla, and Jonno. And the more that the dream is exposed, the stronger it becomes. And stupid Jonno decides his career is more important than, you know, the world. But rest assured, Reddit users think he's nutso and with poor Sparkles serving as the door for the dream to return to its own world, there is nothing left for him to do but bemoan his lost credibility.

While I started out being very skeptical of this, I ultimately really enjoyed it. The first several chapters are so filled with slang for the dystopian scifi novel that I spent more time than I cared to figuring out what the heck was being talked about. I was spending more time figuring out the diction than I was on the story, and I didn't like that. 
 Eo's part is silly to me, too. It's all very convenient, and sets up the rest of the story so perfectly. It couldn't have happened any other way, of course. It felt way too contrived, but it moved the story along so I suppose I can forgive it, if the story is good enough. 
 And it is, even if I think it's kind of a rip off. Maybe the second book (because no dystopian book is ever a stand-alone anymore) will branch off more, but Red Rising absolutely strikes me as a kind of rewrite of The Hunger Games, except with a boy lead and people are color coded instead of put in districts. 
 The good thing for me is that I loved The Hunger Games, so I didn't mind reading a rehash so much. In fact, I quite enjoyed it. 
 First off, I want to leave a key, because I think it's interesting and informational. Here we go: 
 Red: the miners, the lowest of the low. 
 Yellow: medicine and science 
 Green: develop technology 
 Blue: navigators, pilots 
 White: arbitrators of justice 
 Pink: pleasure slaves. You get the idea. 
 Gray: regular soldiers 
 Copper: run beaucracy 
 Obsidian: elite soldiers 
 Silver: currency and logistics 
 Gold: the very best, the smartest and most revered, etc. etc. 
 So what you see here is color coding. In every facet. Humanity has gotten so advanced that they can apparently engineer people to be monochromatic. Golds are born with gold hair, gold skin, etc. Reds are born red. No impersonations can happen, because your status in the caste system is worn plainly on your skin. 
 Or is it!? (dun dun dunnnnnn) 
 Our protagonist, Darrow, is a miner. a Helldiver, if you want to be specific. He lives on Mars and drills for chemicals that make Mars inhabitable for people. He's already married at the tender age of 16. After his "lost love" is lost, she becomes a martyr and Darrow somehow gets thrust into a rebellion. He undergoes some serious changes in order to appear (and be) gold. And then the Hunger Games happens. Teenagers forced to fight and play capture the flag all while being watched from the sky by Proctors, judging and manipulating. It made for an awesome situation, once we finally got there. It takes a bit of time to get to the meat of the story (the beginning is quite dull) but once it picks up, it's pretty damn near relentless. And I loved it. I thoroughly enjoyed the characters and their actions. The lieutenants were by far my favorite part, Sevro being my favorite. The Goblin is scrappy and I loved it. Darrow's choices grated on me sometimes, but as a general rule he was not one of those annoying main characters that makes all the mistakes just to make the book more dramatic. He does make mistakes, yes, but he learns from them and adapts accordingly. Imagine that! A protag who learns! And while he does rely on his lieutenants for some things, he does things himself too, and I respected his character for that as well. It made him much more admirable and I had no problem rooting for him. 
 I really enjoyed his ascension (literally and figuratively). It felt deserved, as the affections he earned from others felt deserved. Which was immensely refreshing. I'm thoroughly invested in seeing what happens to mister Darrow, which is kind of disappointing because this book doesn't even come out til February which means the next book will be at least a year--if not more--away.

 Sadly, the Confederation and Mists weren't explored as I hoped they'd be after reading book one. Still loved the world building though!  As for the villain, he did not show up nearly as often as I thought he would, and he was quite easily defeated. And the final cure was done very conveniently and easily. This plus the way the book ended made the plot resolution feel a bit rushed compared to the slow pacing of the rest of the series. I kept waiting for some last minute obstacle to appear to make things more difficult but things wrapped up very neatly and instantly. Ah well. And there weren't any crazy plot twists, at least in my opinion. As in, nothing really shocked me. For example, the moment Queen Saida said the starstones had been stolen by Confederation pirates I immediately thought to myself "I bet the pirates were Ananna's parents" and they were.  But that could just be my own personal problem from reading so many books in a row. 
 All in all, enjoyed this short series immensely and am happy about the relationship endgame for Ananna and Naji.

Daniel was the boy next-door for Jessica. But they both moved away from Willow Park. He became a pastor, married and then his wife was killed in a road accident. They renew their friendship and when Daniel wants to apply for the pastor's job back in their old home town, he is told he needs to be married. 
 Jessica makes him an offer. 
 *** 
 I was on board with this until after the marriage. 
 It seemed very obvious to me that Jessica has lied to herself. She wanted to marry Daniel because she loved him. She told him their marriage would just be in name only, and then once it happened, she changed. She got whiny, she nagged, she did not give him any space. She resented anything he did for the church and that the church did for him. She can't cook but she gets annoyed when people give them casseroles. Jeez, you just moved house. Think of it as a nice welcoming act, not a criticism of you. 
 She knows he adored his wife but she won't let him mourn her. 'It's been years'. So what? 
 Jessica has a raft of issues with what she thinks she ought to be able to do but she can't do them and when she fails she gets whiny about it. 
 But it's her lack of communication that makes me nuts. She prevaricates, she keeps telling herself 'it's not a normal marriage' and that somehow eradicates the friendship they had before they got married. He keeps asking her what she's thinking, what she wants and so on... and she won't tell him. 
 "We'll just go down to the cafeteria. We'll ask Randa to call if there's any news. But the surgery takes a long time, and you'll feel better if you don't sit and brood." 
 "I wasn't brooding." Her objection was mostly out of principle since she had been brooding and there was no reason not to go down to the cafeteria. (Willow Park Book 1) (p. 169). 
 An exchange like that just happens over and over. Even when he tells her she's beautiful, she argues with him. 
 I really dislike her. 
 I guess also it's the format. Often in romances, you get the guys pov as well and here, we don't. It's all Jessica all the time and I need a break from her. 
 So when Daniel asks if she's happy without love she has yet another fit about it. 
 They've been married a month! 
 Then she threatens to leave him at Christmas. He runs home to beg her not to go and it's all fixed and he loves her. I don't feel it. I just don't know when that happened.  
 2 stars

'For all the girls next door - and the boys who love them.' 
 I was all in when I read that dedication. The idea of the boy next door falling in love with the neighbor girl is iconic and one that has women saying, "Awe!" 
 "A simple story about a handsome prince, a good-hearted princess, and their sweet love." 
 Awe, doesn't that sound lovely and all it needs is the magical - "They lived happily ever after." As with any story nothing comes easy and especially second chances. Brent is the guy during his high school days that all the other males wanted to be and all the females fawned over. Now, that he's in his early thirties and has become less of the 'young and dumb' stage and more of mature adult, he's become a guy to be admired. 
 Kennedy, the girl next door, was more of the nerdy social circle during her high school years. Fourteen years has passed since she's seen Brent and she's back in town for work. Her first line of business is a criminal case against Brent's young client. 
 The case these two are trying against each other hits close to home for me. It's about a young teenage boy who feels unseen and does something drastic to get the attention of those around him. His actions were of the criminal nature but his intent wasn't. It was like Ms. Chase knew my son's friend who did something similar to the teenager in the story. This is the second book by Ms. Chase where a young male character has found himself brushing up against the law. Well, this made me bawl my eyes out. So I have to give it five stars. 
 Topher, Steve and Brand are sixth graders. They're the target of bullies, but they're also resilient and fun dudes. Topher is an artist with a wild imagination. Steve is a little like Spock, super logical and intelligent. Brand thinks there's nothing special about him, but the fact that his dad is disabled means Brand has taken on a lot of adult responsibilities, making him especially determined and capable. 
 These three friends each tell part of the story in turn. They go on a kind of quest to see their teacher Ms. Bixby in the hospital. It is, of course, part adventure and part comedy of errors. They have to skip school, take a bus into the city, and procure certain items, at least one of which is illegal for minors to purchase. 
 The heart of this story is each boy's connection to Ms. Bixby. She is a Cool Teacher (http://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php...) but it doesn't play like a stereotype. She gives each of these three boys what they need and they want to give her something back in her time of need. 
 Like The Great American Whatever, this manages to be both funny and heartbreaking, which is a winning combination like salty and sweet or comfortable and stylish. A perfect book for a 6th grader, just edgy enough not to be babyish (there's a little bit of swearing and just a touch of risque) but not beyond what an average preteen can handle. 
 There are allusions to great poetry, music and literature (you'll probably want to read or re-read The Hobbit after this and go look up Walt Whitman), which is a hallmark of the Cool Teacher. She turns you on to cool stuff. 
 Is it a drawback that Steve's character calls on a certain Asian-American stereotype? He has tiger parents and a perfect sister who's a pianist. In popular culture Asian people tend to be portrayed as logical, good at math, and socially reserved like Steve. But Steve is a well-developed character with a rich inner life. He is not just a series of stereotypical traits. Maybe his parents are, though. I'm not sure where I ultimately come down on this but I mention it because I'm sure there are readers who are tired of seeing this stereotypical set of attributes. But I did love Steve. To get into spoiler territory:  I thought there was a subtle implication that Steve is gay and feels more than just friendship for Topher. That definitely shades his character, right? To be 12 and dealing with an attraction to your straight BFF? That would explain being reserved in how you express your emotions.  And I liked what the author did with Steve's relationship with his sister. 
 So there you have it. Read with tissues at the ready.

This is a novel written from the perspective of a man with autism in a world that, for the most part, sees him more as a disability to be cured than as a human being. I loved pretty much every moment of it. But it's like a cross between Flowers for Algernon and The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time, so how could I not?? 
 Seeing the world through such a different perspective than my own and getting to know Lou kept me captivated. Lou's mind is a surprisingly beautiful place to inhabit. And he's just such an awesome guy, definitely one of my favorite characters in fiction. I just wanted to hug him whenever anything bad happened to him. 
 A great book for fans of Flowers for Algernon, The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time, or Submarine. 
 I'm usually all for happy endings, but this one gave me really mixed feelings--which I guess is actually a good thing because I keep thinking about it. Lou was happy and prospering, so yay for that, but my reaction was really bittersweet. It felt like Lou had died, replaced by someone else with Lou's memories but not his personality or perspective. It felt a lot like Flowers for Algernon.

Alright, alright, I finally decided to read this. 
 I read it in less than 24 hours. It's a fun page-turner that is hard-science-fiction-y. I read somewhere that this book is a love-letter to human ingenuity, and that's true. The situations that the protagonist gets himself into are a bit silly and the writing style could use some work (also silly at times), but it's still fun to see how he solves problems and gets around roadblocks, and it inspires me to get to that level of creativity to be able to solve problems like that. Although sometimes technical, it's accessible enough to follow the story and also teaches a bit about how all that space stuff works - which is really great. 
 I think the points that I didn't like about the book were basically uncanny valley points. It's so close to reality that the points that fail to match reality are glaring, like some at the end of the review. Either way, I really enjoyed it and could not put it down. The closest analogue I can find to this book is Ready Player One by Ernest Clide - both by first-time writers, both technical and pop-cultury, and both at a similar depth of story. Great read! 
 Some uncanny valley reservations: Would NASA really overlook the nose cone problem? They ran that many calculations but not that one? That Mark was able to get things fixed and batteries connected and all that stuff without an immense amount of work, that he just knew that stuff himself - plausible? etc.

Good dystopias construct a future that is at once distant and dangerously close, balancing the far-fetched with all-to-real. The best - this list includes The Hunger Games,1984, Feed - also establish characters who matter. They may not be lovable, but you want them to succeed. "Empty" falters on both counts. 
 Weyn's vision of a world without petroleum isn't adequately developed; it is told through the particular experience of some teens in Spring Valley and via news items from around the world. For such a profound crisis, the particulars feel false and under developed. And there's a global-warming caused storm. And there's some problem with genetically modified food. And even with all of this, things never seem to be more than inconvenient. I guess I was expecting something post-apocalyptic. 
 But the bigger problem, as other reviewers have noted, is that the characters are completely blah. They spout convenient bits of information about bio-diesel and growing your own food, but no one seems to be a real person. Their love lives and friendships just don't hold up. 
 This is an interesting premise in wait of a better telling.

Half-human and half-wyr, Pia Giovanni spent her life keeping a low profile among the wyrkind and avoiding the continuing conflict between them and their dark Fae enemies. But after being blackmailed into stealing a coin from the hoard of a dragon, Pia finds herself targeted by one of the most powerful - and passionate - of the Elder races. 
 As the most feared and respected of the Wyrkind, Dragos Cuelebre cannot believe someone had the audacity to steal from him, much less succeed. And when he catches the thief, Dragos spares her life, claiming her as his own to further explore the desire they've ignited in each other. 
 Pia knows she must repay Dragos for her trespass, but refuses to become his slave - although she cannot deny wanting him, body and soul. 
 I think every reader (and they're mum) has heard about Dragon Bound by now even if they haven't read it yet. After reading Smexy books review of Dragon Bound I was unsure if I wanted to read Dragon Bound but then I saw Katie from Babbling About Books and More tweeting about it and she seemed to like it and thought ah, why not give it ago. And I'm so glad I did! 
 I loved, loved, loved Dragon Bound. Gushing aside I haven't read anything like this before and I'm really looking forward to the rest of the series and hope it's just as good. I understand why some people have been saying that Dragos is similar or reminds them of Raphael from Nalini Singh's Archangels series and in some ways I can see it but in other ways Dragos is a million times more interesting character with a more interesting history, in my opinion. Dragos is as old as time if not possibly older, in today's world he is extremely powerful, wealthy and everyone is scared of him. He's ruthless, aggressive but also charming and extremely possessive of what he thinks of as his. In other words totally yum! I liked Dragos from the get-go and really enjoyed the way he was portrayed throughout the book. I immensely enjoyed his interaction with the secondary characters, who were his first and second in command, Rune and Graydon. Other characters such as Tricks and Tiago also helped add to the series and make it even more enjoyable. I can't wait to read more about them in the future. 
 Pia, where do I start with Pia?! I seriously loved her right from the first opening sentence, which doesn't happen often, normally it takes me a while before I like the heroine in most books, but not with Pia, right from the get-go like with Dragos I adored Pia. She was brilliant, funny, smart and resourceful. I really liked her take no crap attitude, even from herself and how she handled Dragos from the start of their relationship, even before they met face to face Pia made a lasting impression on him and even me. 
 Dragon Bound was an interesting paranormal adventure romance that really gripped me throughout the story. I was intrigued with the villain but not overly concerned because the story between Pia and Dragos had me thoroughly transfixed. I really liked how you don't find out what Pia's wyr half is until near the end and how special and unique it makes her. I liked how Dragos knows what she is but can't remember what it was from the smell of her. 
 Favourite Quotes: 
 "Pia was blackmailed into committing a crime more suicidal than she could possibly have imagined, and she had no one to blame but herself." 
 "It sucked so bad she might as well put a gun to her head and pull the trigger. Except she didn't own a gun because she didn't like them." 
 "If she were in a race for her life, that roar was the starter pistol. If God were the referee, He had just shouted Go." 
 "...smelled like wild sunshine and it was familiar in a way that pulled at all of Dragos's deepest instincts." 
 "He strained harder for that elusive time with a younger sun, a deep green forest and a celestial scent that drove him crashing through the underbrush-" 
 "I'm sorry I had to take your penny. Here's another to replace it." 
 "How could she be so damn charmed by such a primitive thug?" 
 "You might have noticed I'm a primitive kind of guy." He showed his teeth and got into her face. "All those centuries of civilization? Just a veneer." 
 Overall, Dragon Bound is a totally brilliant and wonderful story that had me totally enthralled from start to finish. It's a must read for any paranormal romance fan and I really can't wait to read the next book in the series Storm's Heart out 2nd August 2011.

Tiger's Voyage has a slightly different build-up when you compare it to the previous two books in the Saga. We get a good idea of the direction the story (or more accurately: the boat) is heading in very early on, but once again don't jump head-first into the action, which is something I like about these books. The research and preparations foregoing their quests, make their adventures feel a lot more realistic - well, as realistic as a tale about a girl with two tiger princes on a sea voyage can be, that is. 
 As Kelsey and her friends board the Deschen, they prepare for their next quests first and foremost by learning how to dive. A new character is introduced, thankfully diverting some of the love triangle-tension between Kelsey and the brothers. 
 I enjoyed this part of the book because of its 'holiday feel'. However, I did not enjoy Ren's company - nor Kishan's for that matter - in Tiger's Voyage. I felt both of our tigers kind of lost hold of their personalities, floating adrift into either Boring Boyfriendville of Arrogant Assholetown. 
 Ren has become this supremely arrogant and jealous manipulator, while Kishan has only about 2% of his 'bad boy with a big heart'-appeal left. This was somewhat of a dud. That being said, Tiger's Voyage is still a highly entertaining story with more action than the first two books in the series and plenty of conflicting emotions. Kelsey has grown up so much since Tiger's Curse and I feel more and more connected to her character. Consider me Team Kelsey now instead of Team Ren or Team Kishan! 
 Though some parts of the quest were a bit too lengthy for my taste (mostly the Green dragon's part), Tiger's Voyage is once again a fun, magical read where varying mythologies come to life and love has just the right amount of complications. Something that always manages to surprise me is how Colleen Houck answers even the tiniest questions or remarks I have throughout the book. 
 Tiger's Voyage ends on a cliffhanger but I think I'll leave it there for a while and wait to read book 4 until the release of book 5 is a bit closer.

 Brilliant! I was hooked from the first page until the last page. 
 I first met Van in "Deliver" and he seemed so detached and menacing that I held him at distance. I was unsure if I could soften to him or not. When Ms. Godwin announced that there would be a Van book I knew I had to read it. I needed to know what made Van so disconnected and yet so frightening. 
 Van happened upon Amber on one of his nightly stalking adventures of Liv (from Deliver). Amber has issues. She suffers from OCD and agoraphobia. In little ways I could relate to Amber: her use of sarcasm, doing things in symmetrical groups of four (I don't do that BUT four is my favorite number), and her OCD (I tend to be OCD when it comes to organizing my books, etc. I like to think of it as JUST being organized). One last way I could relate to Amber is with her former profession. My niece is also involved in that profession and I can see how it would make you very self aware of every thing about your body. To not ruin what her former job was I will refrain from saying anything else except to say- this is the first time I've read of this occupation in a book. :) 
 Amber's quirkiness brought out Van's need to train people. His desire to break her free from her prison was a real growth moment for him. His willingness to help her was oddly fascinating. Her idiosyncrasy had him feeling things he had not felt for another human. Van has a heart? 
 The enigma of the man beneath the hood was mesmerizing and Van won me over with his alluring ways. I enjoyed watching him coerce our needy heroine into the woman he realized he may actually love. Even though, he is possessive and controlling...he is also captivating with his fierce, protective attention he doted on Amber. 
 I kept an open mind about my feelings for Van when I went into Vanquish and I wasn't disappointed. I really liked Van in this book. Some things that freaked me out in the first book, his dolls and hair fetish, broke my heart when we learned the truth about the true purpose behind them. 
 The story was superb. Fascinatingly dark with a splash of sass and sarcasm. Although this is a dark book there are a few times that it made me laugh (for those of you who have read it, the needing to use the bathroom scene had me dying of laughter). Ms. Godwin's adds just enough humor in it to melt our hearts for Van. I've read 3 dark books written by Ms. Godwin and they've all been 5 star books. If you like dark books Ms. Godwin's books are an excellent choice to read.
