I also hated that he forgot everything that had happened to him, especially the fact that he forgot Tinker Bell, who saved his life several times.  
 I was expecting more, as it is considered one of the most beloved children's stories.

By the title itself I already knew what this book is going to be about and that's the main reason why I read it. I actually got my hands on Time After Time (the sequel) first so I kind of got a peek into what this book was. JSYK, I never read The Time Traveler's Wife so I don't really have any background of time traveling stories except in A Wrinkle in Time and Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban and some research from the internet. 
 This book had a lot of potential and I really thought that it would go beyond the usual scene of a distance or time difference in a relationship. It was like the author was trying to outdo or to make her own version of The Time Traveler's Wife (again, I have not read this so I may be wrong). 
 Anna is very blah to me, I couldn't find a connection with her especially since I have experienced difficulties in distance with someone I care about. I also don't understand how she willingly just goes for Bennett when she KNOWS the consequences and hardships she must face. It's like she's hurting her heart, herself on purpose. Like she wants to feel all this pain because this special powered boy came to her life and this instantly makes her special too. WTF? 
 Oh and let's take a moment for Bennett Cooper... 
 Yes ladies and gentlemen! BENNETT. EFFING. COOPER. 
 WHO IN THEIR RIGHT MIND CREATED A NAME OR EVEN POSSIBLY CONSIDERED A NAME AS 
 BENNETT COOPER?!?!? 
 I'm sorry Ms. Stone, I just don't understand how you can give this character such a douchebag name. With as his character seems like a nerd, a cool-guy type nerd. He's not the super smart kind of nerd but the safe average guy type of nerd. The mysterious nerd that is actually pretty cool... Oh and he has time traveling powers too! 
 Okay, okay... So Bennett Cooper... I also did not find a connection to him. I find him nice and very caring to Anna but then again here comes in the WHOOPING WTF DUDE?!!?!?! Why would you even bother to care for someone who is possibly freakin' 17 years older than you are in a normal sense. Like seriously? I mean sure give her a chance but to prolong something you know that is going to hurt her and STILL GO FOR IT. WHATTTT? 
 The only character I really liked was Justin. I was actually rooting for him to be with Anna in the end but I knew that was never happening in this book. I just hope in the sequel Bennett will sacrifice his love for Anna and give her to be happy with someone else, someone who might equally love her, someone like Justin. And then they'd have kids and maybe their daughter could bump into Bennett at 2012 and maybe they'd have a shot together. You know... SOMETHING UNEXPECTED. SOMETHING REAL. 
 Oh all the feelssss... WASTED on this book. I actually want to read the sequel just cause it's on Bennett's (ugh that name) POV. So I'll just see you then. 
 Happy reading! :)

Sanderson has done a good job of setting up a world of super heroes and then playing out his own version of comic-book fantasy. David is a wide-eyed protagonist who begins by simply wanting revenge. The story has plenty of action and a satisfyingly twisty conclusion. This reads a lot like Super Human; fans of one series should investigate the other. This is plot-driven fantasy from an author who writes a remarkable quantity of text. The quality of language suffers, but super hero action stories rely on motion, not poetry. This is all action. 
 As other reviewers have pointed out, Sanderson has constructed a fantasy that many 13-year-old boys will enjoy. However, the complete lack of female characters who exist as more than wish fulfillment is a glaring omission in an otherwise reasonable book. There is some comic violence and such, but there's nothing else prurient to trouble pre-teen readers. Hopefully the next book is as strong.

I picked up Ultraviolet after reading about the twist at the end, so my review may be a little different from those who read it without any spoilers. 
 First of all, let me say that Ultraviolet is a wonderful page-turner. I finished it in one day (after staying up late to see what happened), and I enjoyed seeing the plot unfold. The first part of the story unravels both Alison's past and reveals what's going on in the present, giving the reader just enough to want to read further. In regards to the twist about two-thirds of the way in, I actually noticed quite a few hints that pointed in that direction. 
 I loved the descriptions, especially in regards to the Alison's (the main character) synesthesia. The prose was fluid and fascinating to read, and I felt like I had a decent idea of Alison's surroundings without ever running into any infodumps that slowed me down. The characters also held my interest, and though I had a hard time keeping up with everyone at first, they quickly proved to each have something that made them easy to remember. There were times that I wondered how accurately the institution was being portrayed, but I don't know enough about Canadian psychiatric practices to say one way or the other. 
 I liked that the people who were antagonists were not all "bad," and that some of the protagonists who we thought were "good" actually had a bit of a dark side to them (except for one, who surprised me). 
 The main downside I saw to this story was the slight romantic sub-plot. It didn't work for me, and while I understand why Alison was interested in him, I kept wondering why she wasn't focusing on some of the more important matters at hand. He also felt a little... too perfect. 
 I found the end a bit hard to believe, mainly because everything escalated so fast that the end felt rushed. I think that if it had been built up as much as the first two-thirds of the book, the twist likely wouldn't have been such a problematic point. I did enjoy what was revealed that Tori is a very fun character to have around, and that Alison misjudged a number of things about her , but the mechanics toward the end felt too rushed. Alison is able to save the day thanks to her enhanced abilities. Personally, I would have preferred to see her use her synesthesia at her previous sensitivity to solve the problem. In a sense, the problem felt too big for her. On the other hand, the explanation Tori offers on the last couple pages of the book suggests that's the point.  
 Overall, Ultraviolet is an exciting read that kept me turning the pages to find out how the twist would play out. It's not for everyone, but if you like a bit of conspiracy in your reading, you might give this book a shot.

*This book was provided to me in exchange for an honest and unbiased review* 
 I feel quite mixed about this book. I thought it was a great idea but to be honest not expertly executed. 2.5 stars. 
 What I liked... 
 The plot really interested me. I knew what was going to happen for the first half (well it was in the blurb!) and so I read with real anticipation of the moment, wondering quite how it would play out. Then in the second half of the book it was great to see growth and new characters and I had no clue how it was going to end. Right up to the last chapter I couldn't have told you what HEA to expect! I liked some of the snappy wit Scarlet had too and the sense of place created. I like to be able to picture where people are and for there to be regular locations like the office and the shake place. I could picture these places really well. 
 What I didn't like... 
 Unfortunately, I didn't much like the characters. Sean was a selfish idiot and Scarlett was just plain irritating and not too bright, despite her supposed education. They both grated on me. I also found the dialogue stilted, and contrived and often vulgar. 
 I couldn't buy the history of the characters. I didn't feel like the characters were built gradually with their stories being pieced together throughout the book. It was just stated, in chunks that bore no relation to anything else. Like, all of a sudden the brother is her best friend forever and there's this family dysfunction that is never mentioned before. I don't get where Scarlet and Sean got their friendship from either. It would have made more sense if they'd been friends since little kids or something but you don't just get a friendship like that without something to explain it. 
 I don't want to come across as mean though because I did really think the idea of this book was great. It just read like it was made up as it was written and could really benefit from a rewrite, integrating the histories and character traits more fully from the start and softening the language.
I am going to say only one thing about this book: A girl needs warning! This story broke my heart.

*3.5 stars* 
 First of all, this book is super pretty. The cover is pretty. The pages are deckle-edged (which is my favorite!). The headers and page numbers are on the side of the page instead of the top and bottom which is something I've never seen before. I love the way this book was designed! A+ 
 I don't have too much to say about this book honestly. I enjoyed reading it. I thought it had an interesting twist with the blend of genres that Rutkoski used. I liked it enough to want to read the second one. But something was just missing for me. 
 This book is a blend of fantasy and historical fiction. It had fantasy elements of it taking place in a different world than us, and there were different races and names than we would use today. But it has an interesting twist because it's not dystopian but instead takes place in the past. I would guestimate that the time period this book takes place is closest to the mid-to-late-1800s based off of the societal rules that Kestrel, the main character, had to follow and the way that they dressed. Kestrel's world also includes slaves which is similar to our Civil War period (in the U.S.) during the mid-1800s. Since I have an interest in both fantasy and historical fiction, I enjoyed the book just based off of that and that I haven't seen another book with this blend of genres. 
 I think the main thing that kept me from enjoying this book more is that it is written in third person. I much prefer first person and connect much more with characters that way. The way the book is written I think it would have been a little difficult for Rutkoski to write it in first person without having to use alternating points of view, but I also think it would have made this book more relatable if she had written in first person instead of third person. But the book was also just lacking something for me. It never engrossed me. It never gripped me. I enjoyed it but I didn't feel much after finishing it and didn't feel any kind of connection with the characters. 
 The main characters were unique and developed. I loved the way that Kestrel is much different from other YA characters. Instead of being loud and tough and rebellious in her fight to make her way in the world, she quietly plots and manipulates people to her advantage. But Kestrel is also kind which was very much needed in a book such as this that includes slavery. It was refreshing to have such a smart lead YA character. Arin was also a likeable character to me regardless of how secretly devious he was . I liked that he was slowly revealed to us and the way that he developed along the storyline. His past was an interesting twist. I definitely wouldn't put him in my favorite male characters list, but I think he was pretty realistically characterized and I can definitely appreciate that. I do think there were some characters severely underdeveloped and some that were notably place-markers. Jess was very much underdeveloped and Kestrel seemed to have a stronger connection with Ronan than with the girl who is supposed to be her best friend. Enai was notably a place-marker and clearly was just a character that was meant to make Kestrel seem more compassionate. When Enai died,  there wasn't much emotion, in my opinion. Kestrel is upset, of course, but there was no desperation of someone dearly loved lost. I'm not even sure why Rutkoski decided to remove that character from the storyline as it wouldn't have made any difference if she hadn't with the way the plotline ran. 
 The plot ran very slowly for me up until the ending. In some ways, I understand that the characters all needed time to develop their relationships so that it wouldn't seem insta-lovey; but at the same time it made for a boring book until the end. The romance was pretty well-written and more "grown-up" (meaning the characters acted more mature, not that it was explicit in any way) for a YA novel which was nice. The action elements were interesting and engrossed me as the plot unfolded. I think the war setting brought some interesting parts to the book, especially where Kestrel and her father's relationship was concerned. The ending was good and I think it set up for a strong beginning to the next book. 
 Overall, I think it was mostly the third person point of view that threw me and kept me from connecting to the characters. I did like different parts of the book, but I think there was just something missing from this that ultimately left me feeling unsatisfied by the end. 
 Likes: Unique blend of genres. Kestrel. Her father. Arin. The war setting. The action elements in the end. 
 Dislikes: Plot ran very slowly for me. Third person POV. Some characters were severely underdeveloped. Never connected with the characters. 
 Overall: 
 Recommend? Only if you can handle third person POV well. Otherwise I would say skip this one because there are probably similar books out there better written. 
 Reading the Next One? Yes.
this was definitely my favorite book in the series! They've grown so much, I'm proud of them both!

This book is a book club selection which I found surprisingly enjoyable. We are provided a glimpse into the past and a look at Wichita, Kansas and New York City before the depression and during prohibition through two completely different eyes. 
 In reality an unnamed chaperone accompanies a rising star at the beginning of her climb but we can postulate who she was. Thirty-four year old Cora informs her husband that she will be gone all summer chaperoning a 15 year old dancer, Louise Brooks, to a famous dance school. For Cora this trip to New York City is more than the task at hand, it will provide the opportunity to unlock her past which she has been trying to figure out. Louise is a young ingenue who wants to become a celebrity in theatre and film, her big break takes her from Wichita, Kansas to New York City. She is a handful who both shocks, liberates and befriends the chaperone. 
 This book spans fifty years. I absolutely adored being able to see the change in times in both of these women's dress, words and actions. Although the book is told through Cora's eyes, the reader is given enough information to understand Louise's perception of the world evolving around her. 
 I loved the strong female characters who were trying to figure out how they would fit within the changing times. I love the subplots with Cora's mysterious orphanhood, relationship with her husband, and the way in which her family grows after her awakening in New York. 
 A historical fiction that didn't feel dated, which is my kind of read! I would recommend this book to the reader who is a little weary about historical fiction; an entertaining story that could take place at anytime. When you finish, Google Louise Brooks so you can read even more about her, see pictures and even watch her movie performances in videos.

If you have a lump of ice instead of a heart, beware! This book will melt it and you'll only have a sad, lukewarm puddle instead. I read this book in a day, and I had to take a break for about ten minutes in the middle because I was afraid something bad was going to happen to the characters. That's the kind of book this is.

This book was a lot better than the previous one, but I have to say that the love triangle trope is getting on my nerves. Lindsey comes off as a bit of a bitch, leaving both men hanging (although she shows clear favoritism to Sully while Robbie is out of town). And she does finally seem to pick Sully, although now Robbie has turned up divorced it could throw a wrench in the works. Who wants to bet she pity dates him in the next book, messing things up with Sully again?  
 But I did read this book in pretty much one go, so it kept me interested and entertained, even if I did gnash my teeth every time the Sully/Robbie bit was mentioned, haha. 
 The new librarian from the short story seems interesting, so I will look for her in the next book. But please, Ms. McKinley, end the love triangle, it stinks. (And yes, I am still taking off a full star for any book with that trope. It has become sooo common in cozy mysteries and annoys the snot out of me!)

I just couldn't do it. The writing was strong (if a bit too flowery and pretentious for my taste) and there was a decent plot that should have kept me engaged, but it wasn't up to par with all the buzz I saw surrounding this book. Now granted all that buzz was generated by the publisher, but still. I expected something that was riveting enough to capture and keep my interest the whole way through. The language was especially annoying at first, but ultimately I was forced to get used to it from exposure. Great for me I suppose. 
 The plot... really good. Could have been great if it wasn't for the damn language. The inclusion of mythical creatures was something I wholeheartedly agreed with, but their roles were sidelined so much that it just made it rather dull. The best part of the entire novel was the very end, when Zacharias brings Prunella in front of all the pompous buttheads that make up the aristocratic magical men. That meeting, coupled with Prunella's display of ruthlessness and leadership abilities later on made it a much better ending the rest. The portion spent in Fairyland was cool too, I won't deny that. I attribute that to the mythical creatures employed more so than the plot progressing. 
 Really, the short version of my review is this: it would have been better if the author hadn't tried so hard to show me her expansive vocabulary.

Not my favorite by him, although I liked the ending quite a bit. This one just seemed so full of lines that were obviously...lines. Intended to be quotable. Blegh. But those Hempstocks were pretty great. Gaiman is such a fun story teller that I'll always read him because even if there are parts of his writing that irk me sometimes the story is fun and heartfelt and entertaining.

Very fun. 
 My only misgivings would be the small amounts of innuendo and some suggestive behavior and brief nudity  and where the man attempting to rape Amaranthe groped her breasts before he was killed . 
 Otherwise, well plotted with good try-fail cycles and believable reactions. Bright characters who all felt unique. And Amaranthe was super clever and wily.
This book was pretty cute. Definitely one of the better New Adult books I've read. Though Kat annoyed me at times, I liked her growth throughout the story and I adore Alec.

YASSSS TO MORE SIMON! Although the scene with Isabelle ripped my heart out, but that's classic Cassandra Clare. 
 Onto the next one!

This didn't have quite the charm of the first book nor the pacing of the third. On the other hand, the climactic scene is great. I introduced myself to this series during the excitement generated at the publication of the third book, so I came to them as an adult, which may explain my unusually cool reception: clearly, Rowling's fans are legion.

Mostly, this was a great start to a new series in the Star Wars universe. My biggest issue was keeping all the characters straight. There were far too many introduced for me to remember them all, and mostly their varying roles didn't do much to initiate more of the plot. The Interludes were interesting but mostly a distraction--I always had a moment after I finished one where I tried to figure out whether it was relevant to what I was currently reading. 
 The other thing I was disappointed with was the lack of Jedis. 
 I know, I know--that's the whole point. There's only one Jedi left and his name is Luke Skywalker and right now with this book we don't know if there will even be more of them. So it makes sense that we don't see any Jedis. But still! They're the best part!!! 
 All that being said, I still liked it enough to rate it highly. I liked the variety of characters and how the interacted, and it felt like a great introduction to a new set of characters. I don't know if we will continue with the same ones over the series, but if we do then I'm satisfied. I particularly liked our ex-Imperial loyalty officer and the dialogue he brought to the table.

In order to get ratings the father (supposed holy man) wants them to play a vicious sports game..where anyone can get killed at anytime..more than usual in the Bitch Planet daily life. So he makes the women build the complex..men vs women..let the game begin?

Do you remember the Choose Your Own Adventure Series from the 80's? I loved those. This is not one of those, but it manages to capture that spirit somehow. Maybe it's all the references to the nerdom of the 80's and 90's, maybe it's just the same kind of free-wheeling quest. The story is clearly rooted in the tech world of today (it does take place in SF, after all), but looks back with affection to the world of books ("Old Knowledge" as one of the characters calls it). Sloan recognizes the allure of technology's promise - that we can build a simulacra that will be just as good. better!, than the messy, dying world we inhabit now. But I think with this book, he's clearly cast his vote for the other side: the world is too dense with conflict, beauty, joy, everything to be contained. There's not an operating system or a server big enough. The world, and the people who make it up, will have to be enough. I might be making the book sound more profound than it actually is. It's a fun, light-hearted, and pretty fast read, with characters who can be a bit too charming. I loved Mr. Penumbra, but if he called Kat "dear girl" one more time, I was hoping she'd slap him. But I won't hold that against a book as big-hearted as this.
Liked the book... Was great considering an Indian author... Definitly worth... And don't worry, its small so won't take much time...
Found it to be a very satisfactory re-entry into the world Steig Larsson created.

Slow in places, but worth the draggy parts. While it's a contemporary story, there's something nostalgic about the world Meloy's created. I guess talking animals have a long history in jf-ya history, and I'm glad to see a contemporary author giving that a try. I really enjoyed the illustrations, as well.

Belonging picked right up where Temptation left off, which was great for me, since I just re-read it. 
 Rose is trying to adjust to life as an Amish woman, in hopes of being accepted into the church so she can marry her soul mate. She falls into a good friendship with three girls, who may end up being her downfall. I can't imagine how it would be for her to give up all the "worldly" things she loves to be with Noah. I kept wondering if she'd end up regretting it down the road. 
 Noah was tough. Before, he could hardly keep his hands off her and now he won't even hardly spare a glance her way--most of the time. He's so dedicated to his way of life. 
 The twist in the middle took me by surprise and the twist at the end did the same. I like surprises. 
 I was a little disappointed in the content in the story, although some of it was necessary to the storyline. 
 Content: language, including one use of a very offensive word; innuendos and talk of intimate behaviors; consummation of relationships, although details were mostly behind closed doors; teen drinking; an instance of violence. This is another one that is technically clean in the romance department, but left me feeling a little uncomfortable. I would NOT recommend it for younger teens.

Fat Charlie Nancy is as average as average gets and he is perfectly content with his average life. When he returns home for his father's funeral, however, he sets in motion a chain of events that throws his life into chaos. He discovers that his father was the trickster god Anansi and that he has a highly unreliable, unstable, and potentially dangerous brother - Spider - who inherited all of the good stuff. In short order, Fat Charlie's life is in shambles and he finds himself on a dangerous mission to save Spider and protect the Anansi bloodline. 
 Neil Gaiman has a knack for writing books that are hard to pin down. True to form, Anansi Boys is an enjoyable read that does not commit itself firmly to one genre. He combines elements of myth, fantasy, urban fantasy, folklore, and adventure. He taps a broad range of human emotion, sometimes within a single scene, and does so with apparent ease. He sometimes loses his thread and transitions clunkily between Charlie's story and Anansi folktales, but all in all this is an engrossing story.

Here we meet Casey Simopolous, young girl who recently lost her grandmother to cancer. She is maintaining x2 jobs to make ends meets as far as finances go. 
 She works during the day at her own book store and by night works as a waitress at the local strip club "XScream" 
 It is during a night shift at the strip club that we are first introduced the heavenly god of a man "Theron" 
 We learn from an early start that Theron is an Argonaut, a descendant from the Hercules bloodline. So by now I'm guessing I've lost you about the whole Argonaut business, well let me give a little insight as to what an Argonaut is: 
 The Argonauts (Ancient Greek: Argonautai, Argonautai) were a band of heroes in Greek mythology, who in the years before the Trojan War, accompanied Jason to Colchis in his quest to find the Golden Fleece. 
 Their name comes from their ship, the Argo, named after its builder, Argus. "Argonauts" literally means "Argo sailors". 
 This particular hero "Theron" is the leader of the Argonauts / Guardians for his king Leo. 
 Casey knew from the first moment she laid eyes on Theron that he was different. She feels an instant connection to Theron, and she thought he the same. 
 We start to see both Casey & Theron getting close, which makes things harder when Theron learns that Casey is the one he is after. 
 Theron has to make a choice between serving his King and keeping his loyal duty, or sticking by Casey, his love, his soul mate (Sorry for the slight spoiler :( ) 
 As a reader you are thrust into some awesome Greek dimension, way of life and Greek mythology. This book is full of laughter, love and betrayal. 
 Casey finally learns of her heritage, learns of her illness, learns of her destiny and learns of betrayal of the worst kind! 
 I certainly can't wait to start to second book and continue this Greek mythological adventure

This is by far the cutest contemporary that I have read so far! This is such a great novel to read especially after my sci-fi/ dystopian binge that I've been going through lately. I have been wanting to pick this up for awhile now and I'm embarrassed to say that I've only gotten to it now :( But! Better late than never! I have heard nothing but awesome things about this book. It seems to be on everyone's contemporary list and now, I could definitely see why. Anna and the French Kiss was such a cute, light and fluffy read. And it certainly was a fast one! 
 !8 year old Anna Oliphant is sent to France to attend the School of America in Paris by her novelist of a father. There she meets a group of friends, Etienne St. Clair, was one of them. Now the two hit it off quite well, and Anna was instantly attracted to him (of course, who wouldn't?! Especially with that British accent!). But here's the kicker- St. Clair has a girlfriend and Anna supposedly has this thing with a guy back home (Atlanta, GA). Anna and St. Clair eventually become best friends and the attraction, that they "try" to hide from each other, becomes undeniable. Although the plot may seem a bit common, the chemistry between Anna and Etienne was pretty enjoyable. I fun reading about these two and their little escapades throughout one of the biggest cities of love. Although, I can't say that they're my favorite YA couple. And St. Clair...OMG, St. Clair!!! If only he were gal, he's surely be one heck of an eye candy ;) Anna, on the other hand, was an 'ok' character, now that I put some thought into what I had just read. 
 Now there were a two things that did bother about this book. The first one that I picked out were the stereotypical briticisms. These made me LOL from time to time because they were just so... stereotypical!!! I hope no one was offended by that- especially the British. The second thing that bothered me while I was reading this book was that I couldn't shake the idea of Anna interfering with St. Clair's relationship with Ellie especially towards the middle and end of the book when she started to ask "why are you still with her?!". She was basically the reason why he had broken up with Ellie. It's not that I don't like Anna, its just the way I see it and strongly feel. And I know that it's probably not her fault that Etienne was instantly attracted to her on the first day of school, when his feelings started to change. But the fact that she interfered by allowing to Etienne to become really close to her (ie., always out watching movies together, alone sometimes, sitting really close to each other in class, at breakfast/lunch/dinner, & allowing him to SLEEP with her on her bed in her dorm room) rather than allowing his relationship with Ellie run it's course without interference, was not something I liked. I mean c'mon! If Anna really respected his relationship with Ellie, Anna wouldn't have allowed him to sleep with her on her bed in her dorm room! She could've told him no, or let him sleep on the floor... But nooo- she allowed him to sleep beside her. I think I would've enjoyed the story (and the character) even more if she did not interfere so much. It is what it is. 
 Overall, Anna and the French Kiss was a cute, light, fluffy and fast read. I enjoyed reading the general idea of the story and would definitely recommend this to all seeking for a good, fun read (just try not to read into it so much) :D
Cool retelling of Snow White. I loved the fantasy elements, especially the Draconi king forced to be the huntsman. Very curious to see where the series will go!

I have to say that this isn't a book I'd normally read if I knew what it was about and how it ended. However, Colleen Hoover is so amazing as always that she has the power to make us envision ourselves as the character and it twist totally our feelings and expectation. The only thing I say about it is, give it a try!

I love the way the author wrote the book but It's not as brilliant as the other books I've read. It's very descriptive and specific. You won't have to ask about the details because it's there. 
 Let the ranting commence. 
 There were more thoughts and action than conversation. It should be balanced though. I was really waiting for them to have a normal conversation. Just like a normal couple, although they are far from normal. 
 Now on to the characters. Ava and Jesse. When I first read it I thought, "Wow this is gonna be a wild ride." There were sparks everywhere and although some have said otherwise, there is chemistry. But then again it makes me ask, does it really happen in real life? How can someone turn your world upside down the moment you meet him? I've never experienced that before. Please enlighten me if that ever happens. I can't put myself in the shoes of Ava in that part. It's too fairy tale-ish.  
 Then comes the running away part. Why can't Ava just freaking stay in one place and listen to explanations? Sure she's scared but she doesn't stop for a while and think. She doesn't use her head, it's just ridiculous . It's not like she's a virgin or something. This is not her first encounter with a man. 
 I hate Jesse for being so overbearing. It's not normal. The fact that Ava knows he's neurotic should make her run for the hills. It's not Fifty Shades of Grey kind of controlling and that's a bad thing. Ava is being shackled and I'm confused whether or not she wants to break free. I don't even understand Jesse's fear of Ava being taken away from him.  I only like him during the times that he's reasonable and loving. I'll understand if there was a reason behind his controlling aspect but there was none. None that I know of. There was no character building. Very little background for Ava and none at all for Jesse. Why is it so important to keep his real age a secret? It really bugged me not to know. It's basic information dude and you're f*****g the girl so she deserves to f*****g know. Speaking of f*****g, the swearing! For goodness sake Jesse's a big hypocrite for forbidding Ava to cuss. He has his fair share of cusses too so why can't Ava? I would never let anyone forbid me to swear. Believe me when I tell you that I adore alpha males and would even declare that I have a submissive personality, but this man is not the kind of alpha male you'd want. It's just too much.

Wow. This was an exhausting read. Between the epilogue, the afterword 1986, the last chapter 1989, the update: twenty years later 2000, and a postscript penned by Rule's daughter, I thought I might never finish this. 
 That said, it is considered by many to be the definitive work not only on Bundy the serial killer, but also on Bundy the charismatic, attractive, and promising law student. 
 And really. What are the chances? You're a struggling single mom of four, eking out a living writing true crime articles for detective magazines and suddenly not only have you received a contract to write a book detailing a string of grizzly murders, but once the murderer is caught you find out he is a friend and previous coworker. 
 Seriously. You can't make this stuff up. 
 At times, I found Rule's narrative to be repetitive and overly introspective, but I guess given the circumstances, it was hard to avoid. And what the hell. She deserves to get it off her chest. Plus, eventually, she makes some valid observations, particularly with respect to Bundy's final interview in which he tries to "blame" his actions on violent pornography and detective magazines (ie true crime stories). I had actually watched the interview earlier on in the reading process and admit that he almost had me biting--hook, line, and sinker. However, after reading Rule's analysis, I think she was spot on. Which, I think is the point. A sociopath, Bundy was a master manipulator, incapable of empathy and lacking a conscience. He certainly wasn't able to fully appreciate his culpability. Pointing the finger at society seems consistent with his character. 
 I personally found some of the add-ons to be of little value, with the exception of the afterword and the last chapter, which both document the remainder of Bundy's ordeal. 
 All in all, a fascinating story told with competence, at least for the most part. If you happen to pick up a later printing like I did, consider skipping the epilogue, the update 2000 and the postscript. 
 As an aside, though unintentional or not on the part of Rule, I think there is an interesting discussion of the death penalty. It took millions of dollars to put Bundy to death, far more than it would have cost to keep him alive. Furthermore, seeing that he represents a "diseased" brain, I wonder if "we" (society) missed an opportunity to better understand exactly what contributes to the making of a Bundy. 
 I also wonder if as a society we need to redefine what constitutes sanity and insanity and the legal implications. I'm not sure men like Bundy have the power to stop themselves, just like I don't think most of us with normal functioning brains can understand how a Bundy couldn't stop himself. Anyone who does what he did has to be playing by a different set of rules, and it seems to me they are suffering from something that may be no more their fault than a man who is stricken with cancer. What does that mean legally? I'm not sure. But while putting men like Bundy to death "feels" right on some visceral level, it doesn't even begin to address the underlying problem. 
 Of course, on the other hand, this is a man who escaped twice, murdering and/or brutally attacking a half-dozen victims before being recaptured. Had he the opportunity, he would have killed again. 
 Anyway, lots of food for thought.

However, the somewhat recent cover trend with the black and white picture and the soft color in the text is one that I really like. I also somehow missed the part in the synopsis that the loss of virginity was a plot point, which is also something I usually avoid. Despite those things, ever since I read Deanna's (from A Novel Glimpse) review of this book I was intrigued. I'm so glad I decided to give Trust a try because I ended up really liking it. 
 The story starts out pretty intense with Edie becoming a hostage in a convenience store robbery. Scott did a really good job of creating the threatening atmosphere and I could feel Edie's fear. John tries to keep the drugged up robber calm and it looks like things might be ok for awhile, before ending badly. During the fall out Edie loses her best friend and ends up changing schools, where she meets John once again. 
 The story is told in Edie's 1st person POV and I felt a pretty strong connection to her. I identified a lot with her insecurities. Her new attitude from walking away from the convenience store was basically that nothing that wasn't life and death mattered and that was kind of concerning. However, as the story goes on she does start to take the consequences of her actions (to both her and those around her) more seriously, while still being able to rise above the Mean Girl drama/insults that used to affect her. While I think she still has a way to go, I did appreciate her growth. And a lot of that had to do with John. I LOVED John. Before the convenience store he was a drug dealer and lived with his brother, who was also a dealer. Afterwards, though, he gave it up, moved in with his uncle, and started to take school more seriously. While he still indulged in some behavior I didn't really approve of, I really respected how he got his life together and how much he changed. I loved how he looked out for Edie and was so sweet with her and I really enjoyed their friendship and shipped them to becoming more. 
 There were a few bits I didn't like. Since John only dealt weed and not harder drugs and it was the only drug he sometimes did it was portrayed as no big deal. If I may get on my soap box for a moment, I think casual drug use is a really damaging thing to include in YA. While there was definitely an anti-"hard"-drug message, it felt counterproductive to include the casual marijuana use. The other thing I didn't love was the sexual content. While I did think the subject was dealt with responsibly, there were a few scenes that I thought were far, far too explicit for YA. 
 Overall, I really did enjoy Trust. I liked the characters, especially John, and the relationship between him and Edie. Though I had my issues with it, it was a fast, easy read that I did not want to put down. I've read a few books recently where I felt like I had to really push myself to finish, but this one I could not get enough of and is the reason I'm bumping up my final rating a bit. This is my first book by Kylie Scott and I'd like to read more from her.

I was a bit disappointed that, after all the controversy surrounding this book, it ended up being little more than Flash Gordon meets Johnny Comes Marching Home. Perhaps that's because I'm so far removed from Heinlein's real life controversies at the time, but I couldn't help wondering what all the fuss was about. 
 Starship Troopers tells the story of Johnnie Rico, a young man living on Earth who joins the army on what seems like little more than a whim. The plot is little more than following Johnnie through boot camp and a fairly abbreviated military career. While the tone is at times overbearingly didactic, that approach is difficult to avoid when the story is as much about his mental training as combat training. I'm pretty sure that the endless lectures on political structure was what gave the book a bad rap, especially when the tone feels like Ayn Rand in reverse (down with unbridled capitalism, and up with taking care of your fellow humans!). 
 The philosophical arguments on government (the cause of controversy surrounding the book) seem idealistic to the point of naivete. Perhaps we've just become so jaded by wrongdoing that we could never understand how the military could seize power without crossing the line into autocratic territory. Or how major corporations could willingly accept production limitations or instructions imposed by military fiat, without doing their best to undermine the system through bribery and corruption. The "ideal" government discussed by Heinlein can't support it's own weight, and would readily fall victim to the same issues of corruption and self-preservation as all the other systems of government sneered upon in the book.  I rationalize this unfounded optimism to myself by remembering that this was written when Scout leaders and priests were still considered the safest people to leave young boys with. A crude and unfeeling analogy, perhaps, but it certainly helped me put the author's idealism into perspective. 
 The descriptions of warfare tactics and military organization, however, were absolutely flawless, and hardly feel dated. That's a major accomplishment so many years after publication. Many times, it felt like I was reading a modern novel -- right up to the point where the narration goes all "gosh golly gee" about the better sex. The plot itself and the action scenes are fairly thin, but the book holds a quality of realism that I haven't seen in many books. 
 I have heard that this book is the main influence for a great many military sci-fi novels, and I wouldn't hesitate to believe it. Perhaps the reason it feels so modern is because so many current writers have started with this novel as the assumption of their own future reality. Either way, this novel gets a strong recommendation for any sci-fi readers -- not so much for the weak plot and almost non-existent action, as for laying the ground rules of future mechanized warfare that seem to have become the accepted norm among many sci-fi writers.

LGBTQ merit badge? Check. There is some interesting world building, as McCarry weaves contemporary realism and ancient mythology together in a way reminiscent of Neil Gaiman's American Gods. 
 The book appeals to and demands a level of intellectualism, as Tally moves from her work in a bookstore and obsessions with astronomy and physics to her mythic quest in the wilds outside of Seattle. Books, book stores, and reading figure prominently throughout. The frankness of several sex scenes makes this an older YA, although there's really nothing here that any youth hasn't already seen with a few mouse clicks. There are also narrative leaps that a familiarity with Greek mythology will make clearer. By the time our hero gets home, she has moved through the heroic journey to come back changed, without the thing she initially sought, but still wiser.

This was the first Agatha Christie novel that I've ever read and I was definitely impressed. This book started out so well. It was engaging and though the main character wasn't likable per se, he was interesting. I wanted to watch him find redemption and finally grow past his old sins. I also liked how the book seemed to effortlessly display the political situation - Hosseini easily drew me into the world of the Kite Runner. 
 Sadly, the book fell apart. The villain was utterly one dimensional, as was his likable childhood servant friend. I found it entirely unbelievable that the main character, after moving to the US, had no friends of any note until he met the love interest. I ultimately decided it was laziness on the part of the author - an excuse to gloss over what should have been important time periods. Oh look, a decade or so has passed. I'll just say he went to school and kind of flopped around for a few years without talking to anyone besides his father. Sure, sounds reasonable, Hosseini. 
 Finally the path to redemption appears, but it's a jarring change from the meandering of the earlier parts of the novel. Suddenly the book is put on a racetrack to the end.. but a very slow track, where things only get worse and worse for the new focus character. The ending is bittersweet in a style I like, but felt too crafted - like the author was trying to show something to the reader, rather than having his characters naturally arrive at the end. 
 It's all very heart breaking and empty, and quite a disappointment from the strong opening.

Neverwhere is one of my favourite books and the Marquis is one of my favourite characters, so when I saw this short story at the bookstore I just had to pick it up and read it instantly. And I loved it! I felt a sort of comforting nostalgia in being back in the world of London below - I first read this book in my teens, and it was my introduction to urban fantasy. I also instantly recognized the way the Marquis spoke, and just fell into that familiar rhythm. I was more into this than I was in the Sandman Overture, another of Gaiman's returns to his old stories, which was sort of a surprise. 
 I wasn't quite sure how to feel about one thing in this book. Spoiler-y thoughts follow: 
 It was the introduction of the Marquis' older brother. On one hand I liked the idea of two lovable rogues being in a sort of competition about which one is the most daring and awesome, and it also brings a nice addition of a bit of self-doubt to the Marquis, but on the one hand I couldn't help but feel that the introduction of the brother took something away from the Marquis' character. The idea that he has modeled himself after his brother sort of diminishes the Marquis de Carabas, in my opinion, makes him feel less unique and takes a bit of the fascination out of the character. I especially didn't care for the end where he disappears into the shadows, just like his brother did a couple of pages earlier. It makes him feel not like a daring, scheming puss-in-boots, but just like a copycat. I still love my Marquis, but was torn on this matter.

Lacked conviction. A disappointment. I would have given it 2 stars, but felt it deserved 3 purely for effort.

Never Let Me Go is my 1st book by Japanese-born British author Kazuo Ishiguro and it won't definitely be my last. I was taken aback by his style of writing and the way he created and twisted the idea of a Dystopian place. I believe I entered the realm of Gothic darkness while I was reading this novel. It's way more than Fantastic. 
 The story tells the readers one of the scariest ways of the government in dealing their people (I am not going to say how and what scariest ways are those, because I want to create curiosity in your minds. The probability now is that, you will have the motivation to read this novel). It was narrated by a girl named Kathy H. As children, Kathy and her friends, Ruth and Tommy, spend their childhood at a seemingly peaceful boarding school. As years pass by, they grow into young adults (of course), they find that they have to come to terms with the strength of the love they feel for each other, while they didn't notice that the seemingly peaceful school is preparing them for a dreadful reality. 
 *Spoiler Alert* 
 Sorry, but I have to share this heart-breaking scene in the book: 
 In that certain part of the book, A teacher (Madame) explains to the students that the boarding school they went to was paid for donations and fund raising by the government so that they could be brought up like normal people. Before that, they will be modeled on as clones. And the clones will be brought up in concentration camps and treated inhumanly. The whole point of that scene was that Madame and a few others were willing to make great sacrifices because they assumed the clones had the same rights and privileges as all other humans, while the rest of the world thought of them only as livestock that were being raised for consumption. 
 Never Let Me Go will stay with me forever. The ending left me with a lot of inquiries. What if this is really the reality that awaits us (people on the average social class)? Are we going to be used as lab rats and after we are "completed" we get nothing in return? However, we all in a sense, share a similar fate. Life is short, live and love while you can.

*2.5 stars* 
 I think this book was creative and interesting but overall the writing was substandard in my opinion. I think this is the very first sci-fi book I've ever read so I have nothing to compare it to and therefore don't have much to comment about in that aspect of the book. I was satisfied with the explanations given about how Adam was created and the gene program, etc. but someone who is an avid sci-fi fan might not be. The idea of creating a perfect person and discovering how different gene patterns create different people is a very intriguing idea to me and kept me interested. 
 This book definitely didn't go the way I thought it would. I thought it would mostly focus on Eve creating a new human being--Adam. But that's actually a very small part of the book which really disappointed me. We don't even get to see Adam come to fruition first-hand, just bits and pieces of him being formed.  I think the subplots brought some interesting parts to the storyline but I do wish that there had been more of an emphasis on what I thought was the actual point of the book. After Adam is created, we barely get to see him before the book is over. I think the story would've been much more interesting if we had been able to get to know Adam and been able to see how Eve's choices affected who he was and how a lab-created person would interact with various situations/people, etc. We get some instances where these things happen near the ending of the book but if the plot had focused more on the actual creation of Adam, we would've been able to see more of it. I also found it difficult to understand what exactly had happened to Eve in the beginning of the book. It took quite a bit of piecing together to figure out (as I understand it) that she was walking on the street when a car ran over her. There's lots of implications but it's never said what actually happened. 
 Although I did like the characters and found them to be entertaining, they pretty much all had the same voice. The book flip-flops between different POVs, yet all of the characters have the same sense of humor and way of talking. Even Adam sounds the same apart from a few dry comments that you would expect from a lab-created person. I found Adam to be very entertaining in his naive, child-like view of the world in some ways. I wish that there had been more character development of him and also of all the rest of the characters. We know that Solo is angry with Terra but we never know really what happened to make him hate her so much. Eve hates her mother but we don't really know why either besides her seeming to be neglected a bit. There were a lot of unanswered questions in this book. It seems like it should have a second book to it but I don't believe there is one nor do the authors plan to write one. 
 I was surprised when I got to the end of the book and saw that both of the authors were writers of the children's series of Animorphs. I read a few of them when I was in elementary school (mostly just the horse ones, I was obsessed with horses) and I remember liking them. Maybe the authors just got stuck in writing in the style of children's book and weren't able to amp up the writing for a young adult book. I'm not sure. But the book definitely could've been better written just purely grammatically let alone all of the loose ends left with the characters' backgrounds. 
 Likes: Easy, quick read. The idea was very interesting. The characters were all enjoyable. 
 Dislikes: All of the characters were basically the same. No character development. Actual pretense of the book (the creation of Adam) plays a very small part in the story. I also found the fact that every single person felt the need to gawk at Adam unrealistic. Everybody has different tastes and a seemingly "perfect" person will never seem attractive to everybody like how Adam is portrayed. Sure, lots of people might find him attractive but everybody he sees? Not so much methinks. The romance was too quick without enough interaction between the characters to support such a deep attachment in my opinion. 
 Overall: 
 Recommend? Yes. Because it was still enjoyable regardless of its lacking.

This was my second attempt at reading this and I'm not really sure what happened the first time around. The plot is engaging, the writing is brilliantly executed (if a bit flowery at times), and the overall effect is very, very pleasing. I do think it's a bit overrated though. The main feeling that I received from it was that the characters and their lives felt somewhat hermetic to me. As much as they are passionate individuals who live their lives fiercely, I couldn't entirely tap into them, empathetically speaking. I almost felt like I was observing the plot and the characters as if they were in a snow globe with an obstruction between us. 
 I also found it frustrating that there are not only so many characters with the same name, but it also bothered me that there were SO MANY CHARACTERS! I can understand that the Buendia family itself or even the town of Macondo is supposed to be the central "character", but without one individual to put the emphasis on, I felt like my focus ended up being a bit scattered and I couldn't quite find one person to laser in on in terms of storytelling. With no central focus, you definitely have to pay attention or even take some notes, or otherwise, you can easily get lost here.

I received a copy of this title from NetGalley. It does not impact my review. 
 This is only my second book by Lisa Jewell and I am once again wondering why I haven't read more from her? Her writing is so addictive and the way she creates so much tension without a very fast pace or big twists just seems effortless. 
 I wasn't really sure what I would think of having so many characters set in different locations, as well as a timeline from the past. While I am a fan of alternate timelines, I usually like them involving all the same characters and I wasn't sure how it would play into the central story. Of course Jewell was able to weave together the characters, locations, and timelines masterfully. It does not take long at all to know how the past timeline and characters fit into the present, but there is still a bit of mystery into the players. I thought Jewell did a good job of keeping me guessing and second guessing every time I thought I had it all figured out. 
 I thought the characters were very well done and well-developed. I liked Alice and her kids and even her dogs, "Frank", and Gray and Kirsty and their family. I did think that Gray seemed a little bit more of a jealous boyfriend than protective brother at times, though, and it made me a little uncomfortable. However, there was nothing to worry about on that front. I really didn't care for Lily, the young wife who's husband goes missing. Her behavior just really rubbed me the wrong way and I had a hard time feeling sorry for her position when she married a much older man after so little time. I found Mark, Kirsty's admirer who Gray doesn't trust, to be kind of intriguing and then kind of terrifying. Yet another book where Jewell's portrayal of teenage behavior scares the crap out of me. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed I Found You. It's emotional and intriguing and I could hardly put it down. I thought Jewell did an excellent job of juggling the characters and timelines. I definitely recommend this book and really look forward to reading more from this author. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 4 Stars

Arrrghhh. DNF at 50%. 
 The Star-Touched Queen is like Beauty and the Beast**, Alice in Wonderland, and The Matrix. 
 **or, more appropriately, (spoiler at 50%): Persephone and Hades  
 To some people that might be an awesome combination. For me, it's not. Probably largely because I'm not really an Alice in Wonderland kind of girl. 
 The world is... weird... Alice in Wonderland style. 
 The magic in the world is like The Matrix. Imagine it and it happens. There's even a scene where the MC stops an arrow heading her way and redirects it. Very Matrix. 
 The circumstances are Beauty and the Beast-esque. 
 It was the weirdness that got me though. It's certainly creative, I suppose, just not my cup of tea. 
 Then there's the romance, which I also wasn't a fan of. It was cheesy and came on too strong. Imagine some random dude coming up to you and being like, "You are my everything. Join me in my kingdom, where I shall make you the queen of the universe." Like, woah, dude, take me out to dinner first. But that's how the romance was. 
 "I know your soul. Everything else is an ornament." 
 "Come with me and you shall be an empress with the moon for your throne and constellations to wear in your hair." 
 "You are my hope and more." 
 As evidence that this is just not my style, I was constantly thinking, "Who really talks like that?" But some people are into this stuff, so... That's cool if you're one of them. 
 I really tried to give the book a solid chance, but somewhere around the 35-40% mark I just got bored. Really bored. And frustrated with the sappy romance and the guy who'd known the girl for all of two seconds before he was talking about how she's perfect and his soul mate. (I'm pretty sure there was something else going on that would be revealed to explain his obsession, but I didn't get there.) Also it was actually pretty confusing. My boredom wanted me to fall asleep, but I'd get massively confused if I didn't stay alert and reread passages to try to decipher what the fuck was actually happening. 
 So at this point I looked up some negative and DNF reviews of the book and saw that my thoughts aligned with theirs EXACTLY. And after seeing a few snippets they revealed, I was pretty confident that the book wouldn't turn around for me. So, alas, DNF. 
 I wouldn't necessarily say this was a terrible book, it was just so not my style.

I received a digital copy of this book from Netgalley in exchange for an honest review. All thoughts are my own and I am in no way compensated for my opinions. 
 I have so many good things to say about this book that I don't even know where to begin. 
 As a character, Isabel was well defined and rounded. I connected with her on an emotional level. Her struggle to fit in, to be "normal" even though she was extraordinary was something anyone could relate to. Every relationship she had was carefully thought out and showed her growth, or regression, as a person. This made every heartbreak, every insecurity, and every joy feel as if I'd experienced it myself. She was a brittle kind of strong, where she always seemed ready to break. I enjoyed her struggle to identify herself as Izzy Jenkins, teenager, instead of just Isabel Jenkins, MD. 
 Marshall was the perfect male lead, as well as the perfect balance to Isabel's character. He was sweet, with a strong love for his overbearing family and deep loyalty to his friends. He always put himself last, and in the way of heroes, this isn't such a terrible flaw to have. His personality was a great complement to Isabel's struggle. I loved watching them figure it out together. His eventual  sickness  was so tangible, so real, that I couldn't put this book down. 
 The pacing of Third Degree was spot on. I was never bored, nor did I figure things out before the characters. I opened the book and fell into perfection. Julie Cross...you genius, you. 
 If you've followed my reviews, you know that I haven't read a lot of NA because it tries too hard. I think authors are excited because they can finally write YA with all the sex. I prefer my romances heavy on the story with a side dish of sex as opposed to heavy on the sex with a side dish of story. I've been disappointed before, but basically, if Julie Cross could write EVERY NA book from here on out, I would be one happy reader. I need authors to focus on the story before they get to the sex. I need to care about the characters before you start throwing in words like "nipples". Cross, however, made me love the characters long before I got to the "good stuff". So when the sex happened, it was PERFECTION, not raunchy, nothing like the other NA books I've read. 
 NA writers, please, PLEASE reference Julie Cross. She knows what she's doing!! 
 I can't say a single bad thing about this book. Being in the medical field, I really enjoyed all the references to medicine, though I don't think it was overdone, just enough to immerse the reader in Isabel's world. It made Marshall's  condition  real. It made me ache for him. 
 Third Degree was perfect. (I know, I've said that three times, at least.) With a suspenseful, romantic plot and crush worthy characters, Julie Cross has nailed NA romance. This book will satisfy readers who want their romances with an original plot. Julie Cross is fantastic. 
 Read Third Degree. Seriously.

 I chose this book after reading Flynn's very popular Gone Girl. I liked Gone Girl but found it fell short of the praise and attention it has received. Still, I enjoyed the overall writing, and I wanted to sample another book by the same author, one that hadn't potentially been spoiled by high expectations. 
 Interestingly, the things I liked about Gone Girl are the same things I liked about this book. Flynn is one hell of a writer who explores the darker side of human nature in all its ugliness. Her characters not only pick their boogers...they eat them, with no apologies (okay...maybe that's a disgusting analogy, but I'm too tired and pressed for time to come up with another one and honestly, it somehow seems to fit with Flynn's writing). She obviously loves this stuff, and I get the sense she has read extensively in the horror, crime, and true crime genres. 
 Still, there was that moment when I'm chugging along quite enjoying myself and suddenly something happens that makes me go...really??? No, I don't think so...I'm not buying it. I mean, this is fiction and all but that is just too much. For Gone Girl that was the moment that we find out that the protagonist Amy is really dead and for this book it's when Crystal, Libby's long-lost niece cracks her over the head.  One thing I did feel that warrants mentioning is although the characters are deeply flawed, I found I was still able to root for them...which was measurably harder in Gone Girl. 
 In conclusion 
 Similar to Gone Girl I enjoyed reading this on a very superficial level. It is well-written, macabre, with lots of twists and turns, even if some of them leave you saying "un-uh, nope you can't do that." This is the kind of book that entertains but doesn't really bring anything new to the table, which is fine, because there's nothing wrong with books whose primary function is entertainment. Actually, on that front, Dark Places excels, and I debated giving it four stars, although I can't quite pinpoint why I settled for three instead. I think it's because like the Hunger Games and Twilight series, it's as if once you strip away their entertainment value, you're left with very little. But like both the above series, I could see myself growing to like her more with each book. 
 That said, I will be reading her other book Sharp Objects and I could definitely see myself reading her future books when I need a little escape. Interestingly, like Gone Girl I also think this would translate very well into a movie.

I cried from cover and cover and was full-blown sobbing at the very end. This is the most moving, tumultuous, emotional and emotionally devastating journey I have been taken on by a book in a long time. 
 The opening pages are dripping with beautiful imagery, majestic and carefully constructed sentences, sentimental but shadowed with a lingering sense of foreboding that lets you know this will not be a happy book. Somewhere along the line - namely, when the audiobook chapters begin - it starts to become a very dark book, so gradually that you almost don't notice until, like Hanna listening to it, you're in too deep to stop. [It reminds me of comparing the first Harry Potter book - or maybe the third, since this novel doesn't start so lightly - to the final one.] 
 I'm not sure why it got marketed as YA, because the teenager's POV only tells half the story, the rest given over to reflection from an old woman, and it has incredibly mature, complex themes that I honestly don't think I would have found that engaging before the age of 20-22. And even the teenager herself strikes me as more of the teen you find in adult books - she's annoying, difficult to relate to, and kind of a stupid cliche until she begins her community service; several times I found myself thinking that it would be a better book if her chapters were edited out. 
 That's part of why I'm struggling with the 4/5 star line (it's a PERFECT 4.5). The other parts are the overly numerous sex scenes - not terribly graphic, but there's still just a little too much detail for me to be comfortable, in both Hanna's life and in the audiobook chapters - and a certain line in the ending: 
 (serious spoilers follow) 
  
 "Only one person was brave enough to say that if, like Oregon, the state allowed for physician-assisted suicides, then instead of being forced to resort to extreme measures for lack of options, Gran would have been able to pass away with dignity, to go gently and peacefully surrounded by loved ones, not miserable, desperate and smashed to pieces." 
 That morally superior tone really left a sour taste in my mouth. I understand what they were trying to show, but I just can't see that as a good demonstration of true/passionate/eternal love. What is romantic in theory is unfathomable in practice if this is what it requires. Call it a spiritual block, but I'm uncomfortable with the message that death is best when voluntarily decided.  
 ---- 
 But as I said, this was an incredible book. The descriptive writing, the slow and overwhelmingly sad decline of Helen's health, the flashbacks and occasional present-day scenes spent building up the bond with Hanna. I connected with Helen from the first sentence or two, understanding her every motivation, and identified incredibly strongly with her the whole time. 
 When I finally stopped crying at the end, I walked around feeling inexplicably shaky and upset for hours afterward, having trouble processing and coping with the extreme flood of emotions I'd been through, and how horribly real it all felt. Part of me wants everyone to know how I feel, part of me wants to warn everyone away from experiencing the same devastation. 
 That is powerful writing talent, and this is the kind of book that should be widely known and/or spoken of in distinguished literary circles. Alas, I'm pretty sure the "MTV Books" publishing label slapped on it will ensure that never happens. A genuine shame.

When I started this series I hadn't quite realized that Bishop had made more of her own world than normal. Still loosely based on our own but where the paranormal peoples--who call themselves terra indigene--are the landholders of the continent we're on (humans hold another continent, but have spread out off of it). They call humans "monkeys" or "meat", equate fucking a human with bestiality and think it's just fine to eat the human afterwards. They do tend to have mercy for younger humans and will simply scare them back out of their territory but an adult human--especially one carrying weapons--will get deaded and then there will be "special meat" for sale at the butchers. 
 Humans on the other hand have limited resources because they're only being tolerated on the continent for the clever things they make. Even water resources can be cut off by the terra indigene if they are pissed. Yet humans have been there for generations and so still think of their homes as their homes (which offends the terra indigene). You still have very rich humans and then everyone else. These rich humans are the major problem of course because they consider the terra indigene a obstacle to making more profit and don't want to have to listen to them. I've had to gather this from the background noise because Bishop is focused on the main character and her cute murderer friends who come to love her and a few other harmless females so so much as the super special exceptions. 
 Yeah. You might be wondering why this book has such a high rating when I'm clearly bitching so much about the world building. Bishop writes a fast paced interesting story. Meg is a "nice" character and in the scope of their little friends group they are nice to each other. However, I've read all the way through the second book in the series and started on the third and realized I needed to stop. My heart can't take it. 
 Meg ran away from a very bad situation caused by rich humans and the terra indigene have given her shelter as their liaison. But she's still human. I'll give her time to adjust to her position and such but after the space of book one, I condemn her utterly for doing nothing to stop what I can see is coming. Not to mention that she lifted zero fingers to go back and help the other girls in her situation until she had a prophecy. Victim blaming of me to expect her to go back and rescue them, I know. At the same time this is a book and she's supposed to be the 'heroine' and since something does eventually happen in that arena for different reasons, I still choose to condemn her . Meg never looks at the bigger picture beyond cutting herself when a prophecy prickles. The minute that's over, it's back to dog biscuits for wolves and playing in the snow. 
 Meg is also sloooowly being paired with over-protective Simon the werewolf. I find little to like in their relationship past first glance. He's controlling and you'll see her over and over again hiding from him when she needs to cut for another prophecy. Bishop disguises this with hefty scatterings of cute moments (that were repeated so much that they became cloying and fake) and tries to play off his overbearing ways as acceptable caring ways. Nope. Meg has already left one situation where she was being controlled. She needs someone who will encourage her strength and cheer for her, not someone she has to hide her actions from and constantly worry about upsetting when she does assert her independence. Stop threatening to bite her, Simon. 
 I should have known better than to get into this series since I also had to reject Bishop's The Black Jewels series for being over the top stupid with emotion-jerking candy, poorly written, and with zero likable characters because they were too unrealistic on inspection. But Bishop's writing has definitely improved. I could probably read one-off books from her with great enjoyment. She writes exciting and interesting books. But a longer series just gives me time to question why it's so exciting and then I realize my emotions are being jerked around by stupid situations. Emotional ride too long. I want off. 
 And I'm sorry, but the terra indigene are monsters. Literally. She's showing their side, but they are an elitist pack of murders who consider other thinking people to be food that they can kill whenever. There is no acknowledgement from any characters that this is wrong-headed and no attempt to change it. The "good" humans are on Simon and his courtyard's side and want to make wolf cookies. The "bad" humans are everyone else. I'm pretty sure that "everyone else" mostly consists of innocent bystanders trying to raise their families and live their lives. Meanwhile her female characters are milk toast, short-sighted, thoughtless people who only seem to live to be earnestly nice in the moment. To the terra indigene. I don't want to spend time with women like that. So, yeah. I quit this series.
