I found absolutely nothing in this book to be even remotely worthwhile. It's one horrifying mess from start to finish in just about every way possible. If I could give this book negative stars, I'd do that. 
 But I digress. 
 Let me start by saying I'm biased. I'm a character person. I'd go for a strong character with a weak plot over the alternative and the character thing is a large part of my, erm, hate. I love McGuire's books. She's on my short list to buy when they come out. I think I may be stopping that. Well then... 
 Let's start with Alex... I can't stand this character. I finished this book with the hope that Alex would die at the end. I truly did and that didn't happen... Well, a girl can dream. He's the most boostful character I've ever read. If he's not whining about his 'duties' and how he never asked for any of this, he's tell us how strong he is and smart he is and how much he's sacrificed and bleh bleh bleh. 
 When Alex goes into one of this internal dialogues, this song starts playing a loop in my head: https://youtu.be/bolBQL_ztZo I'm seriously not kidding. 
 If that's not enough, Alex leaps head first into a great many 'I told you so's. He's not obnoxious enough, right? 
 I've come to the conclusion that McGuire just can't write decent male POVs. They're all so cliche it hurts. Which is baffling because McGuire is such a good writer and male POV is universal. I mean, we're basically raised on male POV books from our first books and McGuire is just so utterly terrible at them. The men in her books that don't have a POV are great, which is another layer of bafflement. 
 The story is, to put it mildly, horrible and stupid. The plot basically hinges on everyone being complete and utter morons. Every plot turn is because someone did something stupid. The characters reactions to everything is stupid too. It's stupid on the level of 'how are they still alive.' 
 Here are some examples: 
 The leaders of this group have an arsenal of weapons and all that. Do they treat this with the seriousness it warrants? Of course not! How then would the plot continue? So what did they do with this arsenal? They gave every member of the organization free access to everything. Seriously. There's not even a 'fill out yourself' log. 
 WTF is that? I've worked many jobs and even my first job in a movie theater had more responsibility in the way we dealt with the discarded 5 cent cups that this group does. Of course, this becomes a plot point. OMG! Someone switched their ammo out with fakes. COULDN'T SEE THAT ONE COMING A MILE AWAY. 
 This brilliant group is brilliant. For a morgue, they have a metal shed with a lock. This shed isn't guarded and it's in the summer. This made it conveniently easy for the villain to escape. When Alex asked about this, he was told that this is where they 'put the bodies' until they can feed them to the alligators. Let's just forget the part where he's possibly infected and animals can catch it by eating the infected. 
 It would be a fun parody except McGuire was being serious. I can't tell if this book was just a contract book and she didn't give a fuck or if ... Well, no. She's a great author. This was definitely a contract book that she shit out and tossed to the publishers. 
 Besides the stupid that's EVERYWHERE, we also get major doses of deus ex machina and a morality tale. Seriously. Ridiculous amounts of deus ex machina. The mice are deus ex machina. At the end there, he's basically saved by a doorbell. Seriously. They start up all this 'we're GOING TO KEEL YOU DEAD! And then seriously stop to answer the fucking door . At this point, you don't even care. It's so deus ex machina that you just it to end. 
 Then the morality bits are wonderful. If Alex wasn't obnoxious enough, we get his many, many, maaaaaaaaaaaaaany inner lectures about how terrible this group is for seeing the monsters as 'monsters'. Of course we get to the part where a 'monster' asks why Alex didn't kill them and Alex said, all innocent morality with shining eyes, 'but doesn't everyone deserve to live?' and we get another lecture from this 'monster' telling us how it's okay to kill these. 
 It brought back terrible memories of that horrible morality tale Card shoved in his book (where the lone character who wanted to save the planet turned around and said KILL THEM ALL and the people who had wanted to KILL THEM ALL get to shake their heads and share with this character that KILLING THEM ALL is a terrible thing.) 
 Now add all the above with a knowledge that the first 15% ~ 20% is spent largely on recapping what happened before and you start to suddenly wish you'd not learned how to read. I just can't anymore...

I received a free review copy of this book through NetGalley. 
 1.5 stars 
 Well, that was certainly...interesting. 
 I first want to begin by contributing to the sentiment of other reviewers that the synopsis for this novel feels misleading. It paints a picture of possibly dark secrets merely related to rich prep/boarding school kids, somewhat reminiscent of Kate Brian's Private series, but the story itself starts off creating a completely different image. The setting of an isolated island off the coast of Maine calls to mind a potential for some Stephen King level horror/suspense/supernatural thriller, yet this never fully comes to fruition either. Instead, the reader is thrown into a convoluted mess of nonsense that is so confused with which direction it (the story) wants to take, so it takes all of them; simultaneously. I attribute this primarily to the writing style, which isn't as strong as it could be, but is still more or less done well enough to keep the intrigue and mystery alive. What will happen next? Needing to know the answer to this question, among the several others that will undoubtedly come up while reading, will (probably) keep the reader hanging on through the awkwardness. 
 Starting at the beginning of the story, the dialogue is slightly awkward but not completely cringe-worthy...until around Chapter 4, where it starts to feel stilted, unnatural, and just continuously awkward throughout the rest of the novel. The beginning of the story itself starts out fairly strong in the Prologue. The scene setting is interesting and enticing, hooking the reader into wanting to learn what happened to Sarah: Why were her parents murdered? What is with the obsessive repetition of her (supposed) last name? Is there something else (supernatural?) at play here? 
 After the first couple of chapters, however, the plot seems to escalate too quickly and seemingly out of nowhere. What's with the secret society stuff? It's a bit unusual (to me) that Sarah, a foster child who has previously noted how she tries not to sleep the first few nights when she's in a new place due to (understandably) major trust issues, is so quick to trust and accept this "Wolfpack." Perhaps this is Stockholm Syndrome? Very strange. The Wolfpack in general is such an awkward social experiment: Is this supposed to be a teen sex cult? Because that's how it certainly comes off in many of the major Wolfpack scenes. I get being at a boarding school and being a teenager and BAM! Hormones. But still. The way that Sarah just so quickly, and even enthusiastically, accepts this Blutgrog is just...ugh.  
 I also have some (nitpicking) questions regarding the use of technology on the supposedly closed off island. At the beginning, Nate and Maya tell Sarah that they're on a closed server, which keeps them from interacting with the outside world with the exception of some research tools. How, then, is Sarah able to google Ethan and his family? How is this considered "research"? Nitpicking further, the constant mentioning of Sarah's "incredible memory" is a bit tired. When discussed with Dr. Diaz, as a scientific study, though, that's okayish. It's just kind of weird how clinical and awkward the descriptions are with her peers or even as repetitive narration. 
 Regarding the writing style, there are definitely times when it absolutely feels as though there are multiple authors, which is to say that the writing was either repetitive and/or there are clearly distinctly different authorial voices between some chapters. Additionally, the writing occasionally leans toward the side of talking down to the reader rather than merely painting a picture with the descriptions. 
 Overall, I really wanted to like Sanctuary Bay, and I still feel as though it has potential, but where it stands right now is all over the place and unnecessarily awkward and uncomfortable to read.

I'm having a hard time sorting out my feelings for this book. The rating is actually a weighted average because parts of it deserve five stars, but the flaws run so deeply, I almost gave it one star instead. Foer is clearly an excellent writer capable of writing deeply affecting prose. I don't mind that he tells some of the story in pictures either; as a visual person, I think it can sometimes be the best way to tell a story. But on the whole, the book is so clever and gimmicky, it makes the pathos of it feel cheap. Writing it from a grief-stricken nine year-old's point of view is too cloying and manipulative to boot. 
 For those who liked this book, I would recommend reading W. G. Sebald's _Austerlitz_. I think he's the best author I know for examining tragedy and for trying to salvage something it. Foer feels more like he's mining it for material.

Books about American girls/women in Europe are completely engrossing to me, even if I generally don't identify them as favorites. Thus I give it three stars. I wish I'd been able to enjoy this as a light "girl finds herself" novel, but instead of maturing and finding inner strength, the main character is infuriatingly co-dependent for much of the novel. I would have been cool with her starting out that way and growing into herself, but just when the author is taking the character into a healthy frame of mind, she reverts back to her obsession at the last minute in a way that really frustrated me. One of the most anticipated books has finally been released. Most of you have been waiting for almost a year, for me it was only some weeks but my excited was over the clouds nonetheless. 
 "She was the heir of fire. 
 She was fire, and light, and ash, and embers. She was Aelin Fireheart, and she bowed for no one and nothing, save the crown that was hers by blood ans survival and triumph." 
 Celaena is back. Back in Adarlan, back in Rifthold. She came back to take what belongs to her and the execute these, who took everything from her. The people she loved and her own identity. 
 I love how this book starts off. There are immediately old characters from former books. Some we know well, some we just might have heard of. We are back in places we been before but still it's not the same. The girl has grown into a young woman and she's not Celaena anymore. She's 
 Aelin Ashryver Galathynius 
 , rightful queen of Terrasen. 
 "I believe the title out esteemed friends in the empire now like to use is 'fire-breathing-bitch-queen.'" 
 And we all know that bitch-queen is quite a suitable title for her. She's bitchy, snappy and says what she thinks. She's as bad-ass as always. 
 Aelin is such a strong woman, who won't let herself bring down by anyone. 
 "She was a whirling cloud of death, a queen of shadows, and these men were already carrion." 
 We meet Arobynn and Chaol. 
 We all remember too well what Arobynn did to her. And we know Aelin/Celaena. She will not rest until she got her revenge. 
 The relationship between Chaol and Celaena is...weird and...stiff. There is a lot of bitching and accusations and he seems to blame her for everything. But to me he seems hurt. Hurt that she left him, hurt by what happened to her and hurt that she supposedly has moved on. 
 I'm sorry for all the CelaenaChaol-Shippers but they are officially over and out.  
 But I have to say that I actually liked all the bitchiness between them. It was sometimes really entertaining. 
 Of course the book couldn't go without Rowan. He seemed like a total jerk in the last book for most of the time but he quickly won my heart. And I'm squealing each time he comes up. OMG, I love him so much! 
 And I think it's great that she - for now - decided to be with him. They make a great couple because they are both Fae and he's an amazing addition to the throne. 
 "You make me want to live, Rowan. Not survive; not excist. Live." 
  
 We also get to meet Lysandra again. At first I was "Ugh...really?", but at the end I was very happy. It's funny how things can change. She definitely has won my heart. 
 "You and I are nothing but wild beasts, wearing human skins. Don't even try to deny it." 
 Kaltain, the King, Manoa Blackbeak and Dorian are back again. Oh, Dorian - what have they done to you? It breaks my heart, but I love how Chaol stands by his side nonetheless, but sometimes even the hardest decisions need to me made. And of course, there's Aedion. I'm still not sure whether I like him or not. To me, he still seems a little "off". 
 I still enjoyed the Witch Chapters. Maybe they are not that evil after all? And I'm sure we will meet her again in the next book. 
 And we also meet a new character: Nesryn. She's part of the rebellious group Chaol is a part of as well and we get to know interesting details. I can't really say I like her, but she seem like she can be trusted and I'm sure she will appear in the next book quite a bit. 
 As for the story; I love how things develop, all the happens, the actions, the twists, the expected and unexpected. At some points, it was a little slow but that doesn't do much damage. This book holds so many surprises and things I never thought about. It's so nice to see all the characters grow and develop. 
 The writing is so fantastic and it has grown so much since the first book. I said it before and say it again: Sarah is such a talented writer. Her stories really do come to life and soak you in. 
 "And at long last, Aeiln Ashryver Galathynius was home." 
 Damn, it was really good and pure enjoyment. I probably read the entire series again over Christmas or so. Haha! 
 PS: When does the next book come out?
I've only read the first issue so far, but I'm really looking forward to reading the others.

I read this book last week, and it's taken me some time to digest it. I have a few different reactions, and they don't seem to talk to each other, so I'm left a bit confused. First off, emotionally speaking, this book is a three-hanky affair. The subject matter is difficult to say the least. To her credit, Donogue made an risky choice for narrator that could have become very tiresome, and she handled it beautifully. She's really an excellent writer, and she's written a deeply moving book. 
 The problem came after I finished the book, when I felt a little manipulated. And then I started to wonder, don't we read books, watch films and TV, and go see art in order to be manipulated? We go to art to make us feel, or think in ways we normally wouldn't. Why should I have a problem with that? I came to the conclusion that the plot set-up made me feel manipulated in the bad way. Donoghue put her characters into the most horrible situation imaginable (although not unrealistic since it was inspired by horrible real life events) and the horrible situation did a lot of the emotional heavy lifting. In the end, I want to be manipulated by her art, not by the horrible situation. And even though I *was* moved, the set-up made me feel a little cheated in the end. It's a shame because she seems more than capable of delivering all that emotional impact with her writing alone.

There are lots of reasons why this book is very popular; one of the reasons is that - John Green is a gifted writer and this can be witnessed in this novel, The Fault in Our Stars. The novel revolves around the protagonist, Hazel. She is a girl of great sensitivity and humor knowing that her time on Earth is nearing its end. She's not struggling to make peace with it because she accepts it, that death had already found her. Unexpectedly, she met her whimsical soulmate, Augustus, a fellow cancer sufferer. 
 I love how the novel made me cry. I actually cried not because that death has found them but on how the novel tells us that life isn't always fair. The Fault In Our Stars is not a depressing read, then again, it isn't an entirely beautiful novel either. It is simply a truthful depiction of love, loss, and life. 
 The Fault In Our Stars is an insightful and moving novel that will not just leave you with a inspiring story to remember, but also with a more optimistic understanding of life. 
 P.S: I also love ANTM! :p

You know who's a good character? Simone Kegan. With the looks and one-liners of a Betty Draper with a career. Her impeccably closet of high heels and lacquered door are, by my lights, a feminist statement of that generation: I built this business, I did it without a husband, and I looked damn good doing it. 
 And she's not even a bad mother or a convincing narcissistic foil. She (correctly) points out her daughter is bedding a loser with commitment issues, and she's an attentive and loving grandparent. 
 Sure, she's bitchy about weight but it's Hollywood, baby. 
 Spoiler: She even leaves her awful Gen X spawn her house and all her money. Again, who's the villain?!  
 This novel took me to weird places, because my own Gen X mother never told me my birth father's identity although I'm relieved to report she never hooked up with him as a boring midlife crisis . It's a topic I've rarely seen handled well: either with too much sentiment or not enough. 
 I find myself thinking about Elijah's rant to Hannah, how she'll be a terrible mother, and she is. 
 Lady is a terrible mother, and a terrible person. If the novel leaned in to that (no corporate pun consciously intended), I think the ending would have felt more authentic to me. 
 In the end, I am left with that same letdown I had at the end of Girls. Really, is this all there is? A freaking baby? 
 At least the Millennials use protection and have their dumb guerrilla art.

I was expecting Look Behind You to be a fast-paced psychological thriller. While it had those elements, it was more of an in-depth look at the psychological and emotional effects of abuse, within a mystery. 
 Chloe wakes up in total darkness, bound and without knowing how she got there. Hodge does a good job of describing the terror and the physical exhaustion Chloe feels as she tries to escape. When she eventually does, she winds up at the hospital where she learns that she had recently been admitted into the psychiatric ward for hallucinations that sound startlingly close to what she has just experienced. When no one believes that she was really abducted, she sets out to prove that it really happened. 
 While Chloe starts to put together the pieces of the seven weeks she doesn't remember, she begins to suspect her husband, Liam. Liam is a verbally and emotionally abusive husband. He's manipulative and controlling and Chloe begins to wonder if he is dangerous, as well. A good deal of the book dealt with Chloe's feelings of loneliness and lack of self-worth that led her to initially fall for Liam. It gave a realistic view of living with abuse until something happens to eventually make her believe she's deserves more and wants to do something about it. 
 While the story was a little slower paced than I would've liked, there were some good twists that I enjoyed and didn't always see coming. I suspected several different characters throughout the story and was ultimately satisfied with how it ended. Overall, I enjoyed Look Behind You. I would recommend it to those interested in psychological exploration and mystery.

Ugh, I have such mixed feelings about this book. 
 The Lake was definitely written well. I enjoyed the slow pace and the casual yet often profound language. I thought Banana Yoshimoto's characters were well fleshed out and fairly original. The book didn't take me long to read, even with all the stuff I have to do for college. For a good part of the book, I thought it was going to be a favorite. Chihiro's memories of her childhood were particularly powerful. But The Lake never went anywhere. There was a lot of build-up to the big reveal of what happened to Nakajima, but after Chihiro recognized his mother's portrait and he finally told her what had happened to him  in the last few pages, I just sat there thinking, "That's it? That's the end? I read 200 pages for that?" I kept waiting for something to happen, but the reveal was decidedly anticlimactic (and never fully explained why Nakajima sleeps with that wire rack ). I feel like this book wasn't so much about Chihiro unearthing the details of Nakajima's past as it was about both of them just learning to love each other and adjust to the way their lives changed after the death of their mothers. Yoshimoto made Nakajima's past a small part of that story, when I thought it was going to be relationship-altering. When he finally narrated his past, most of it was really vague, and that was also a disappointment because it could have been an interesting tale if Yoshimoto had wanted to elaborate. 
 Because of the minimal plot and the weird dip into psychics/the supernatural , I probably wouldn't read this twice, but I did enjoy reading it once. 
 Favorite quotes: 
 ". . . You weren't even a wildflower blooming in a field, as they say, you were such an extraordinarily delicate, transparent person that, if anything, you were like a blossom softly unfurling its petals on a cliff somewhere, so high that no one ever came your way, no one but birds and deer . . ." (17). 
 "Because when you were relaxing with him, you always looked like a little girl. You were like children, both of you. Only society, the world at large, wouldn't let you be." (17)

 "Here, time didn't exist. We were cut off from the rest of the world. Just being with Nakajima made me feel as if we were detached from history, and had no particular age.

 "The sky was incredibly far away, and beautiful enough to make a person wonder why our hearts are never so free." (80)

 Or maybe that's necessary when two people are serious about each other? 
 We try our hardest not to feel that, to sweep it under the carpet, but I bet it's there.

I thoroughly enjoy Mrs. Meyer's writing and her story ideas, and with this novel being her first set outside of The Lunar Chronicles, it's nice to have another book to prove that she is probably my favorite author. Granted, I don't expect her to always write fairy tale twists and re-tellings, but I truly enjoy novels that involve them. Mrs. Meyer also has this wonderfully girly writing style that I just love, and it is very easy for me to get absorbed into her books. I think it's a really nice prequel to Alice in Wonderland about the Queen of Hearts. It's actually hard to see where the story goes in order for Catherine to eventually become said Queen given the way it begins, but I think it has a very smooth transition throughout the book. I felt very satisfied at the endingand sad... poor Jest and poor Cath was such a nice person until she gave up her broken heart to extract revenge.  
 I didn't quite enjoy this as much as The Lunar Chronicles (LC) series, but this is a standalone, and I think my favorite books of hers are the 3rd and 4th book of LC, which has all the build-up to it from the 1st and 2nd. I am a character-driven reader, so when you get 2-3 books leading up to a better book, it just naturally has more character growth and development. Not to say these characters did not grow on me, they certainly did. (And the Joker, Jest, was pretty much wonderful from his first scene.... he is definitely my favorite character). I think if you like Mrs. Meyer's writing style and storytelling you'll probably enjoy this book. :)

With the election of Donald Trump, J.D. Vance enjoyed a bump towards celebrity as a voice of the low-income, white, Midwestern voters who vaulted the man to office. I came to his book hoping for some insight, but am left wondering. Perhaps my expectations were too high? 
 Certainly, poor whites have had their chroniclers: Mary Karr, Dorothy Allison, even Gary Paulsen. Vance had been billed as and important new voice. 
 Memoir may succeed in many ways: the prose can be and end unto itself, either gorgeous, or funny, or sharp, or poignant (think Frank McCourt). The book can be original, exploring a new direction, perspective, or vista (see Ishmael Beah) . Or the plot can be a ripsnorter. Or it can be a rogues' gallery of character. Or the writer can be a captivating storyteller. Or genuinely captivating. And on all of these fronts, Vance didn't convince me. There were a few good anecdotes, but they were too few and too far between, sandwiched among scads of lesser-relatives, neighbors, and friends. His Mamaw is on every page, but hardly well understood. There are a few illustrative anecdotes (a Christmas memory of his uncle's is especially strong) but nothing essential. 
 By the time Vance offers up a thoughts on the problems facing hillbilly Americans - see Adverse Childhood Experiences - I didn't have much love left for his people's predicament.
The last few chapters really made this worth it! So cute.

I'm not a fan of short stories because I always feel like more should've been said/done. They feel short. I wanted to try this one because it's three authors writing one story but taking up different parts of it and for the most part they did a good job of giving it a good flow. All three stories showcase a particular character at a party hosted by the Earl of Briarly's sister who's determined to find him a wife. The novel blends well in terms of story telling, but the three authors are distinctly different. In between each story there are a few co-authored pages that allow one story to finish and another to start. 
 The first two stories are fade to black so there's virtually no steam. The characters there are underdeveloped so their story seems to end too quickly and gives you a "where did that come from" feel when they're suddenly "maddly in love". Julia Quinn's story (the first one) is a gazillion times better than Connie Brockway's (the second story). Quinn's is typically light with lots of fun dialog and an interesting heroine, while Brockway's is nothing but dense narration with a painfully boring and blah hero. The h/h of that story had a lot of potential but they were just mired in description and nothing really happens. I almost tossed the book at this point --thankfully I slogged on to the last one by Eloisa James. 
 James' story is well-written, the characters are well-developed (especially the sizzling hero), the story is spicy with very good tension building for a short story and there's none of that PG fade to black crap ;) 
 The Quinn story is a 3, the Brockway is a 2 and the James is a good 4.

Well after reading Liane Moriarty's Big Little Lies I thought I was ready to go into this and spend the next few hours/days going in circles wondering what the hell happened that day/night???? 
 Because that's what Moriarty makes you do. 
 I wasn't ready for it, I power read through this because like the Big Little Lies, I had to know what happened!!!! 
 Overall it was a great story, I enjoyed the complexities of each character; their flaws and their special quirks. 
 But I had issues with some of the plot so 3 stars outta 5. 
 Spoiler complaints & raves: 
  
 Biggest complaint: Harry. 
 Harry was very unnecessary as a character in this story. 
 He could have been deleted and then you would have still known all the same things you knew about his neighbors. 
 Erika could have just looked across and seen the coat in the fountain without Harry pointing it out to her. 
 His slightly tragic death running down the stairs to 'try' and save Ruby was sad, but didn't motivate any of the characters to do change or think differently. His death was meaningless. 
 Also: 
 Erika not having a 'brown out' of that day wouldn't have changed much. She could have just been cryptic in her thoughts LIKE EVERYONE ELSE was and we would have still found out what happened in that slow, cruel, taunting way Moriarty loves. 
 Last complaint: 
 The length. 
 Seriously, after the big what happened reveal, the story dragged. I don't care about your mom Erika. 
 Raves: 
 I loved Tiffany & Vid. Seriously, over the top and a bit too much to handle couple. 
 But still they're that couple you want to goof off with for a bit, a release from a boring normal vanilla life. They're fun and pretty harmless. 
 I liked how Tiffany really understood herself and her body but still didn't come off like a big hoe. 
 Tiffany watched Sam and Clementine look at each other, their faces flushed, their pupils dilated. It would be a kindness. A public service. She could see exactly where their sex life was at. They were tired parents of young kids. They thought it was all over, and it wasn't, they didn't need an affair or a midlife crisis, it was all still in them, they were still attracted to each other, they just needed a little electric shock to the system, a little stimulus, maybe some sex toys, some good-quality soft porn. She could be their good-quality soft porn. 
 Erika & Oliver at first are just weird, then after you learn about their tragically sad childhoods it makes sense. They make sense together. 
 To me they grew the most as a couple in this story finding out more depths into each other and realizing that they work as a team. Oliver telling Erika that he's really her best friend and not Clementine was one of the most bittersweet moments in the novel. Their decision to travel for a bit and then become foster parents was amazing. 
 Clementine & Sam. 
 Clementine is just a weird horrible name, but it does of course fit the character. 
 At first they are that cute, balance each other out quirky couple that seem to fun and light. 
 Then damn barbecue takes care of that for you. 
 They both seem to be thinking about their sex life but not talking about it to each other. 
 Sam's PTSD wasn't something I noticed till it was mentioned, then it made total sense and again it came back to needing to communicate to make the relationship work. 
 Clementine's weird 'friendship' with Erika was really sad from both points of view. 
 Erika growing up with a mom who 'picked trash, items everything else to love instead of her only daughter' was crushing. Clementine mom taking her in and being there for her as a child and an adult was so cool, but of course tormented Clementine. 
 Clementine feels like the lesser 'real' daughter and Erika feels like the 'unwanted' sister. 
 Where they had some nice moments together, over all, their friendship didn't seem important enough to work on or save. 
 Dakota & the other kids. 
 I mean I figured out something maybe happened to one of the children eventually, it was some what less big than what I thought. Don't get me wrong, drowning kid is super serious. But I felt let down. 
 Dakota torturing herself over blame that wasn't hers to have was so sad & holly blaming herself was actually accurate, don't push your little sister into bodies of water. 
  
 Overall worth reading but not as good as Big Little Lies.

He chases the boy and then decides to take him home and tell his parents what has happened - something that happened to him a lot when he was a wayward child. The boy, Rory, lives in a huge mansion - but instead of parents Jake meets the boy's aunt Chelsea. Rory's parents died recently in a car accident and his aunt is bringing up him and his five brothers and sisters single-handedly. I received a copy of The Regulars via NetGalley. It does not impact my review. 
 Addicting writing and short chapters helped make this a quick read, even though it was a little longer than it needed to be. I liked the style and I think the writing is what mostly compelled me to keep reading about these awful girls. 
 I appreciate a good character-driven story, but to really love one I either need to Love the characters or Love to Hate them. Unfortunately I felt slightly annoyed, but mostly ambivalent towards the characters in this book. While diverse (not all just straight, white girls), they were pretty cliched - Evie: The Angry, Feminist, Bi-Sexual; Krista: The Good Time Girl that flakes out on all responsibility; Willow: The Artist with a Tortured Soul. I also felt the character growth was pretty much contained to the final chapters and was kind of too little too, late for me. 
 I was surprised at how Pretty ended up working. I thought it would just enhance their features to a traditionally beautiful level, but it straight up changes their appearance into a new person. Because of this they come up with fake names and ignore their normal lives. It bothered me that there was virtually no consequences whatsoever to this. I also wished that we would have learned a little more about the origin of Pretty and how it works, but it pretty much remains a huge mystery that none of the characters are all that concerned about. 
 While I like the overall theme of feminism and self-acceptance, it just wasn't quite executed as well as I wanted it to be. The main characters were pretty selfish and kind of awful people and they didn't really face any lasting consequences to any of the bad things they did while on Pretty. The ending felt way too easy and they're only marginally better people than they were before. 
 Overall, The Regulars was a quick read with some addictive writing, but it's unlikable characters made the book kind of hard to enjoy at times. I wish that the character growth would have been more pronounced and that they would have had to face some consequences of their poor decisions. This book wasn't my cup of tea, but I think there are a lot of people who would really enjoy it. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 2.5 Stars

As a teenager, I always thought that the ultimate thing in life would be to have a celebrity fall in love with me. I don't know how many hours I've spent daydreaming about randomly bumping into my favourite celebrity and it being love at first sight. He would sweep me away from my boring life and we'd live happily ever after in his exciting world. At 22, I realize how completely unrealistic this is, but even so, I find myself thinking, what if? 
 What first grasped me about this book is how easily I could relate to Sophie. I too have experienced turning from an outgoing child filled with joy to being introverted and afraid of connecting with others. I didn't experience the kind of devastation Sophie did, but even so, I felt like I could understand her. My favourite thing about this book is probably Sophie's journey of self-discovery, her development and growth. 
 Billy and Me is about Sophie and how her life changes completely when she meets the famous actor Billy. Their relationship develops quickly and Sophie is thrown into a world so completely different from everything she's ever known. Overnight she goes from being an anonymous girl working in a local teashop to having her face on the front page. What could possibly go wrong, right? 
 Giovanna Fletcher obviously has quite a lot of experience with dating a celebrity and therefore has a good insight on what it's really like. Is it at all the dream-like state so many teenage girls imagine? It definitely has it's perks, but fame also has it's backsides and Billy and Me reflects on this in a very impressive manner. 
 To me, this book is as much about self-discovery as it is about love. It's about figuring out what's really important in life and about finding your place in the world. I think it's written in a quite realistic manner, I really believe in the story and I have to say it is quite a page-turner. It was hard to put the book down! I think parts of it was a bit predictable, but I don't think that really matters all that much. All in all, Billy and Me is an amazing debut novel and I really hope to read more from Giovanna in the future!

He's got a simple set up, a classic can't/must (can't find father, must find father!) with high stakes, and do you really need anything more? Turns out, Woodrell also has an ear for the music of the language, and an original way of describing nature especially. A short novel, but manages to pack a wallop.

I read a fair amount of steampunk because I want to wear steampunk. And also own a dirigible. Pretty hard to get road rage in something like that. Though I'm sure I'd manage somehow. 
 Anyway. The premise of this book is that the British Empire has taken over much of the world. It holds huge chunks of the American continent and is very powerful. The people in this book are revolutionaries who want to bring down the empire only they are more like the revolutionaries kids who have been sent away to "grow up in safety" until they're old enough to join their parents. The main character is a sixteen-year old girl and her love interest is an eighteen-ish boy who is engaged to another woman  and his older brother. I think it's pretty obvious the older boy is going to win because she sees right through how the younger is always trying to set himself up so he has a fallback. That's really unsexy when it comes to finding a life-partner, folks. My new favorite phrase is "sack up". Because balls are vulnerable and don't want to be hurt--just like people's feelings--but sometimes you gotta risk it. 
 So I did like how the girl stood up for herself against the younger brother and was like: "I deserve more than this. So, despite my pants-feelings for you, no." This whole book, though, made me wish to read something where the main character has fucked a few people and fallen in and out of love and left and has been left and has a normal, non-overly dramatic amount of baggage. The phrase I don't or can't be loved cannot even be touched on by the merest comma throughout the entire book. This book's teenage love shit was understandable, but not terribly interesting. 
 I could have gotten past the lack-luster love story if only the background made more sense. It felt like there was zero adult supervision at the catacombs where the kids were growing up. Why would you send your kids off to a place like that to raise themselves? And I couldn't figure out what the characters actually thought they were going to accomplish. Like, ever. Great. She went to the capital as a lady to be presented to society while the boys use her movements to disguise their poking around. What were they poking around for? They didn't seem to be poking around for anything but mysterious meeeetings. And she only goes to a minor ball and then leaves. wtf? I realize the formula for this sort of thing means that we have to find some reason for a person inexperienced with looking nice to suddenly have finery and look fantastic, but there needs to be some substance behind that. And this book/series/whatever does not have it. 
 Maybe next series, Cremer. Because even with these glaring faults, I still finished the book without falling into a rage over how awful it was. Because it wasn't awful. It just wasn't good in the ways I look for.

I was asked to read this book for my literary masterpieces class and I was sort of disappointed while reading it. 
 I was constantly having to stop reading to go do research because the author doesn't give explanations as to what he meant when he gave us African terms. I felt like I had to analyze everything that he wrote before I could fully understand what he wanted to say. 
 When he talked about the naming ceremony, he didn't say what it was or why it was done on the eight day after the birth of the child. 
 When he talked about " throwing away twins" , he never said why. And wasn't it mentioned enough for him to have to say why or explain their beliefs in that!? 
 When Ezinma was sick,and they talked about the medicine man, the author didn't explain much about the stone they were looking for. 
 Those are just some of the things that I wish the author would have explained while the book was developing and not at the end of the whole thing where they give the vocabulary. 
 The book itself wasn't bad, the story was understandable, and other than the explanation issues I appreciated the story and the play of events. Even though I KNOW the authors don't always give you information and you are expected to read between the lines, I shouldn't be required to stop every other page to look up a term or something he didn't develop on. 
 I was also sort of annoyed by Okonkwo's self esteem and his thoughts about him not wanting to be as weak as his father was. He used his 'daddy issues' as excuses for many things. We know he liked Ikemefuna and even though he was warned not to play a part in the killing he does it anyway because he doesn't want to seem weak to the rest of the clan. Could he have stopped the killing if he spoke up? Probably not. Could he have stayed home and not have been blamed ? Most likely. He definitely wasn't asked by the Oracles to do it himself. 
 Again, I'm not saying that this made the story horrible, but it was definitely annoying. 
 Um, if I wasn't asked to read this book for class , would I have picked it up? No. 
 Am I glad I read it ? Yes. 
 I did enjoy the book, it's not the worst book I have read but I definitely learned a lot. So if you want to have to look up terms to fully understand this book I encourage you to read it. 
 Happy reading. =D

First impressions: This book had me hooked straight through to Chapter Four. We are introduced to Briar Wilkes and her son, Zeke, both of whom are captivating. They live a hard life in 1880s Seattle, and there is some controversy around Briar's father and her ex-husband. Cherie Priest drew me into this world right away and I was totally absorbed... 
 Lasting impressions: ...and then it screeched to a halt. It took me 10 days to get through this book, because there was no urgency to the plot whatsoever. The characters have no internal conflict or growth. Every element of the story seemed held at a distance, so I could never invest in any of it. I don't remember the last time reading a book was so painful. 
 Conflicting impressions: Beyond the aforementioned pacing problems, this book had too many characters that served no function. Once Briar and Zeke enter the walled-off portion of the city, where zombies (here called "rotters") roam hungrily about, you expect some action. Instead, we get lots of scenes where they stumble across interesting and colorful characters, who help them get from one place to the next, and then disappear--only to then jump out at you in surprise later on, when you have already forgotten about them because you've met 14,527 new people since then. It was maddening. 
 Overall impressions: The only reason I finished this book was so I could give it a proper review. Though the process was like pulling teeth, there were portions of this book that were quite entertaining. The world was interesting, and I loved the idea of the rotters developing after a mysterious gas leak. The hidden society that Briar and Zeke stumble upon behind the wall is mildly interesting, but the ongoing is-he-or-isn't-he surrounding Dr. Minnericht as possibly being Briar's dead husband was more annoying than intriguing. 
 There is a big reveal at the end, but by the time the plot meandered its way to that point, I was so beyond caring that it hit me about as forcefully as a shrug. You ever see a movie where each scene is kind of exciting, and just enough happens that you don't turn it off because you're curious what will happen next, but when it's over you realize that every scene had exactly the same intensity? That's how this book was for me. Flat as a pancake, straight through. No real rise or fall to the action. Zero heartbeat. Flatlined. 
 The book is saved from one-star doom because there were flashes of light hidden away from time to time. I just wish overall there had been more of them, and they had been a thousand watts brighter.

Vampires and werewolves have been blood enemies for centuries, but now a new threat is rising...demons are escaping from hell and those demons are intent on wiping out both the vamps and the werewolves. In order to stop the demons, pureblood vampire princess Morgan LaBeaux agrees to the treaty offered by werewolf alpha Jace Vaughn. She'll mate with him, share her blood with him...and in return, the wolves will aid the vampires in this battle. But Morgan doesn't realize just how dangerous the wolves can truly be. Jace has been waiting years to claim her. He's set a trap for his princess, and now that he has her, Jace doesn't plan to let her go. He'll send the demons back to hell, and he'll keep his vampiress--forever. 
 I read a review of Bound by Blood by The Book Pushers and really liked their review and liked the sound of the short paranormal romance. 
 Bound by Blood was an amazing short story that just blew me away and made me want more! I really didn't want to finish Bound by Blood because it was soooo good! I really enjoyed it. After reading Cynthia Eden's romantic suspense Deadly Fear a few months ago I wasn't quite sure what to expect but there was no reason to worry because Bound by Blood was just brilliant, especially as it only cost me 70p! Via Amazon kindle. 
 I loved Jace and Morgan, Jace is a deadly lethal alpha werewolf (le sigh!) who's been watching Morgan for years, now he finally has a way to get his hands on her. Morgan doesn't know much about Jace other than he's a deadly werewolf and the vampires need her to align with him and share her blood with him so he can dispose of the demons coming through to their world. Although Morgan is meant to mate with Jace she isn't meant to sleep with him but there's something more between Jace and Morgan than just a business deal. Although Bound by Blood is a werewolf/vampire/demon book it's mainly a vampire/demon book as there's more information about the vamps and the demons than the werewolves which is a shame because Ms Eden writes some really interesting werewolves but I'm happy enough to wait for her next book which may be more werewolf orientated, Never Cry Wolf out June 2011. 
 Favourite Quote's: 
 "Jace Vaugh tensed when he saw her. He wasn't as drunk as the other wolves, not yet anyway, so he recognised the deceptively delicate woman instantly." 
 "When you were stuck between death and hell, sometimes, you had to turn to big, bad wolf for help." 
 Overall, Bound by Blood is a brilliant short story that is a must read for paranormal fans and a great way for romance readers to try a new genre at a cheap price, which I highly recommend!

The Sea of Tranquility by Katja Millay - 5+++ stars 
 I have given 5 star reviews on many books as the highest rating. I wish I could give this one 10 stars. It's that brilliant. After just finishing the book a while ago, I'm a hot mess. Every emotion. All over the board. 
 Love. Hate. Despair. Anger. Sadness. Longing. 
 It's all here buried in the pages of a book that I cannot believe I haven't read until now. This is probably one of the most amazing stories currently on my shelves. One of the most tragically beautiful, heartbreakingly wholesome, painfully real tales. This book didn't leave my hands all day Saturday and all Sunday morning. I honestly don't know if I was blinking besides for the moments I had tears in my eyes. 
 When I look at her now, I think for just one second, 
 that God doesn't hate me so much after all. 
 At first I was confused and conflicted. I didn't know what was wrong with this girl. Why she kept her mouth shut to everyone. Why she put on a show for the world, yet still never showing her true colors... And even with all this confusion, I couldn't put it down. 
 She runs straight to a boy who she doesn't know, but has seen at school. He, too, has been struggling in life with the loss of his family. She finds comfort in his presence. She has her secrets. He has his. But they both sit in the quiet, and grow closer in the silence. 
 "When you look at her what do you feel?... Joy, fear, frustration, longing, friendship, anger, need, despair, love, lust?" 
 "Yes." 
 "Yes, what?" 
 "All of it." 
 This is a powerful story that sweeps you away with the most realistic characters I've read. It has taken me three days to write this review. I had a serious case of book hangover. I didn't want to move on. Not because the story is beautiful, but because it is so real. 
 I honestly don't know what else to say other than READ THIS BOOK. I recommend it to anyone. Young or old, man or woman, this book deserves a place in everyone's heart.

This is Book 3 of The Giver Quartet. In this book, Lowry brings characters from book 2 Gathering Blue to the town where Jonah (now called Leader) found refuge at the end of book 1 The Giver. For the past six years, Matty (Kira's little friend from Gathering Blue) has lived in Village and flourished under the guidance of Seer, a blind man, known for his special sight. The blind man is Kira's father revealed as alive but blind at the end of the second book. For less sophisticated reader's their initial identity may not be so glaringly obvious but it was for me and I don't think it takes much away for me to reveal it in my review. 
 Village was a place that welcomed imperfect newcomers like Leader, Mentor, Seer and others but something sinister has seeped into Village and the people have voted to close it to outsiders. Over the years, Matty has been invaluable as a messenger ably traversing forest to other communities when so few can. Recently, a Villager is found tangled in vines, his life taken by Forest for not heeding its warnings. Now Matty must make one last journey through the treacherous forest to post notices of the closure of Village and bring Kira back with him to finally be with her father. 
 Matty's always been comfortable in Forest and one of the few it allows to traverse it. But Forest has begun warning even him that he is no longer welcome and unwelcome people in Forest are killed by it. Matty's only weapon, a power he unexpectedly discovers within himself will likely be expended if he uses it unwisely. As he and Kira limp along suffering more and more wounds inflicted by Forest, we wonder if they will get out alive. Lowry really begins to bring the special gifts of the characters into focus, and they become a central element in the progression of the story. 
 This book was interesting (and again, a bit creepy) because Lowry is starting to personify evil, to give it ground as it starts to manifest itself in various ways. The once-peaceful town is changing, the people are starting to turn on each other, and nature itself is starting to turn on them. It was a quick and interesting read and surely necessary in relation to the first two books. Nevertheless, it was more of a story and less of a statement as book one The Giver was.

Plot: A Professor of history relocates his family from Oxford to a small town in Germany in pursuit of some mythical ancient stained glass panels. When they arrive however the enigmatic townsfolk are unwilling to talk about the the stained glass panels that is believed to have a satanic curse on it. The Professor believes these panes of glass still exist and is on a quest to find them. 
 Narrator: This story is told entirely through the eyes of one of the Professor's teenage daughter, Lin. This means that a lot of the story deals with the family relocating to an unfamiliar country as well as more typical themes in teenage/YA literature. For example changing schools, difficult family relationships and some boy troubles. 
 I think some of my misgivings about this book comes from the fact that I was unaware that this book was YA when I picked it up. I was expecting story that was grounded much more in the supernatural and the mystery, than the real world problems. I've never read a YA supernatural mystery before so I don't think I'm really the right audience for this novel. 
 What I liked: In the parts that focused on the mystery it started to feel very much like one of Susan Hills ghost stories, (which I love). In these parts the pace was really great and made me want to finish the story very quickly. This was helped by the first person narration in the past tense which really did make me want to find out the mystery of the glass, this made it a really quick fun read. 
 What I didn't: As I've talked about previously some of the YA elements took away from the real mystery for me. I also only really connected to the narrator, the other characters were pretty distant and I felt we were supposed to really dislike the adult characters, which was a bit of a barrier to understanding them. 
 Under the spoiler section is discussion of a spoiler but it is also a type of trigger warning so if you feel triggered by certain things you may want to read it. (It isn't a piece of the main plot). 
  One of the subplots of the novel is of Lin's sister's eating disorder. This felt to me like it needed more time devoted to it. I picked up the ARC at BEA 2013, and there is no summary on the back of the book, so I literally had no idea what I was getting into when I read it. That said, THIS BOOK IS FANTASTIC AND EVERYONE NEEDS TO READ IT. 
 I'm one of those people who doesn't like it when people refer to something as "the next so and so", so I won't say that this book is the next The Hunger Games. Red Rising is what The Hunger Games SHOULD have been, and this is coming from someone who read THG series in about two days and saw the movie four times in theaters, including IMAX. This is what a dystopian world should be. 
 Darrow is a Red. Not just a Red, a lowRed -- the lowest of the low in a post-Earth society. The problem is, he doesn't know that. He, and the rest of his people, believe they are the pioneers of Mars, mining the all-important helium3 that will help terraform the planet and make it fit for human colonization. They live in tunnels beneath the surface because they've been told the surface is not safe. However, after his wife is killed and he is left for dead, he learns the startling truth -- Mars has been colonized for years, an empire built on the back of Red slaves who don't realize that they're slaves. 
 Darrow is hand-picked to lead the Red revolution by an as yet unknown entity named Ares. Ares' followers rescue Darrow from the brink of death and take him to the surface. They put him through numerous surgeries and training to turn him into a Gold, the apex of civilization, the color that all other colors aspire to be. Darrow endures the pain and humiliation so that he can take his place in Gold society and bring it down from the inside -- his wife's dream. 
 In order to join the society, he must first go through the Institute, where he is placed in a house (House Mars) and made to go through a series of tests in order to prove his worth. But even in this, the system is rigged, and Darrow must make allies out of enemies and fight those he once called friends as he tries to figure out just exactly what kind of game the Golds are playing. 
 RR is THG on steroids. This book is not going to be for everyone. It's violent and brutal and there were some parts I had to skim because reading them made me nauseated, but it so well-written and enthralling that I couldn't put it down. The characters are all complex, with hidden depths and motivations you would not expect. Darrow is a complicated individual, driven initially (and always) by vengeance, yet starting to befriend the very people he intends to bring down. 
 The idea of someone rising above his or her station is hardly revolutionary (except when it causes a revolution), but I've rarely seen it so well done. In RR, Pierce Brown has created a fascinating world unlike any I've seen yet, and it's as compelling as it is frustrating. 
 I devoured every page of this book (except the ones I couldn't bring myself to read), desperate to find out what would happen to Darrow, what he would do next, if he would be discovered. And now that I've finished the book, I am eagerly anticipating the sequel, which will be a too-long wait, considering that this book isn't even published until next year. 
 TOO LONG TO WAIT.
This whole book is like a punch of adrenaline, and I loved every minute of it.

 First of all, I have to gush about the writing. It's so beautiful and this is a debut novel, which makes it even more special. I was hooked to these words from the start and it never really faltered. The two voices of Denna and Mare were distinct and unique and it was easy for me to tell them apart.  The characters are all unique and though I didn't like some of them, I think that was the point. I liked the side characters Nils and Casmiel. I didn't care for Mare's father or brother at all. Both Casmiel's and Nils's death shocked me, though Nils's death hit me a bit harder because I spent more time with him than with Cas. But it made me sad either way.  BUT, they could've been developed better. 
 I feel like I have to mention the main characters seperately from the others, because, well, they're the main characters. Denna was smart and does what is expected of her and I connected with her instantly. She likes to learn new things, but always tries to remain neutral. Until she meets Mare that is. I really felt for her, but she didn't really grow all that much. Of course I liked her magic powers because I have a weakness for fire powers so why wouldn't I love them in this book. I also loved Mare a whole lot, though it took me a bit to warm up to her. BUT also, could've been developed even more. They both were the same throughout the story. 
 I like how these girls were almost each other's opposites. But not quite. Their romance, in my opinion, was done very, very well. It wasn't too fast or too slow and interweaved with the story quite perfectly. Though I do have to say that once the romance really kicked into gear, it didn't hold back. There was one scene in this book that I never expected to see in a YA Fantasy book with a f/f romance, but it was handled very well and I actually applaud it. So huzzah for that! 
 Now though I did like the story more as it went on, for the longest time it felt a bit boring outside of the development of the romance. It felt very politics-centered, which isn't really my thing. There was also some things about the religion and said politics that I didn't get, but it could be just me. At the end, I didn't really feel like anything happened. At all. Also, the names are quite stupid if you ask me. Amaranthine, Thandilimon, Dennaleia,... Really? xD Also, and this REALLY bothered me the most, but when one of the side-characters dies, there isn't much time spent grieving. Or any time, really. They're all just focused on who did it and they're not actually sad about the fact that that person just died. I get that everyone grieves differently, but that just didn't feel realistic to me. Especially Mare, who supposedly had a real connection with both people that died. 
 The ending was very satisfying for me personally. It closed the story, but it left things open just enough for a possible sequel. While I do think the story can stand on its own, I can't help but want more of Denna and Mare together. 
 Despite the things that irked me, I still loved this story and the romance. I welcome this kind of diversity in YA Fantasy books and wish for there to be more of it in the future. A lot more. I encourage you to check this one out if you're a fan of YA Fantasy.

What a wild story. Christopher Knight was a man was living in the woods for about as long as I've been alive. They talked about how there are so many big granite rocks dotting the forest to hide from but when I looked around on Google Maps I couldn't find any. When I looked up Knight online I didn't expect him to look like he did at all. But he does exude a reverent spirit about him. 
 The tricky part with this guy (among everyone else on earth) is placing him in a box. Labeling him. Right when I think I got him with the perfect label his behavior or actions contradict it and I get all stumped. For example, Knight would still listen to a radio and television. (He liked Seinfeld, yeah!) I found that strange because his behavior implied that he didn't want to be around people so why would he care about what people were doing? Does putting labels on people give us emotional insurance? I did like how he didn't think much of Thoreau and said he had no deep insight into nature. I agree. I think Thoreau is a phony and overrated. I like Emerson better. 
 I wonder if he heard news about him on the radio while he was in the woods. Did he know he was causing such a ruckus? 
 He loved his treats and candy so much. But that was because he was deprived of it as a kid. Let that be a lesson to all you parents out there: Give your kids candy all the time then they won't be hermits. I was surprised to learn that his teeth were rotting even though he was careful about brushing everyday. Yet I never understood that the teeth for those famous Cleveland kidnappings girls didn't rot away and they never brushed. Same with Elizabeth Smart. What accounts for that? They did eat some unhealthy foods but probablay not as much candy and treats as this hermit did. I guess that shows how powerful sugars are. New lesson to parents: don't give your kids as much treats and candy but still give them some. 
 He never got sick once while being out there. Neat huh? Where are you doctors at on that one? 
 You Are Not Special and Other Encouragements talked about Herman Melville not writing anything else after he wrote Moby Beep. We learn here that was because he was a hermit. 
 Heat sinks are neat. I had never heard of them before now. 
 I chuckled how he would try to talk to these hardened inmates about the Summer Solstice. I wanted to see the blank looks on their faces. I hated that there was no Spirit of the Law for his punishment. It was really harsh and unnecessary. People need to lighten up. Hopefully we'll get an update on his life in a few years on how he's adjusting to society. 
 This book was great for helping me to see a glimpse of humanity. What would a person be like if they weren't influenced by anything? You could say the joker was like that but even he was motivated by madness or people's reactions. This books makes me believe that there is no right or wrong. Except maybe love and hate but everything else doesn't matter. It also made me question what is Truth and understanding the solitude one would want in life. Especially the physiological differences that go with it. I thought that humans were created to have affection and being around loved ones. I suppose humans are also created gay too. So it's all OK I guess. Being in the presence of people made him physically hurt. This is why we need more biographies of neat people like this. Enough of memoirs from movie stars and famous people. They're all the same. Nevertheless I still wonder what was the tipping point that made him go out there. Even he didn't know (or didn't care to go deep into his mind enough to know). What was his shameful act? Yeah I know I'm putting him in a box but still. He holds grudges after all. There has to be something we imperfect people can relate to. 
 Noise and distractions are toxic. I just learned that from Deep Work: Rules for Focused Success in a Distracted World. Two hours of complete silence prompts all development in the hippo-campus or memory parts of the region. No wonder his memory was so good. Time amid the silence of nature makes you smarter. If you compared his brain to a regular person would they look any different? Would his have more or less grey matter? 
 Knight said people accused him of not living. Yet when you think about it who lived more him in the woods or someone stuck in a job for 30 years exchanging time for money? Reminds me of what Jack Reacher said in his 2013 film. 
 I bet Knight would love being in Microsoft's sound proof room. 
 An idea grew into a realization then solidified into a resolve. That reminds me of how I did my biking trip across the United States. 
 After all was said and done, the thing he learned after 27 years of being in the woods: Get enough sleep. That's peculiar. 
 The author started to get annoying at the end when he was badgering poor Knight. I can see where he was coming from though. He really was invested in his life and cared for him. 
 Silence intimidates. 
 The end.

First impressions: This series was definitely designed to be read together. The action picks up shortly after the conclusion of the first book, 
 Leviathan 
 , and as with that book, we are quickly launched into exciting events. Westerfeld is a master at drawing you in. 
 Lasting impressions: I actually read the last 60 or so pages slower than any other section of the book, because I did not want it to end yet. I have so much fun in the world of this series that I get grumpy when I'm forced to stop reading. 
 Conflicting impressions: Sometimes Alek wavers in TSTL (Too Stupid To Live) territory. The fact that he can't figure out Deryn is a girl is mind-boggling, especially as her feelings grow toward him. I was just glad that at least one character figured it out, but I think the total is still a bizarrely low 3 people that know or suspect her secret. Really? It's that easy to impersonate a boy? It's so easy for Deryn, in fact, that I no longer find that subplot filled with much tension. 
 Overall impressions: I thought I loved this Clanker/Darwinist world in Leviathan, but this book took it to a completely new stratospheric level. My god is Scott Westerfeld a genius! Everything about the voice, tone, action, setting, and characters pulls together into one cohesive whole that is so vibrant it is nearly cinematic. I can practically breathe in the Turkish air when the lady boffin leads a team to meet the sultan. I can hear the steam pistons firing in the giant walkers. I can smell the stale atmosphere deep in the Leviathan whale-ship's core. I didn't just read this book. I The-Neverending-Story-style lived it. 
 Deryn is still my favorite of the two protagonists, but Alek improved greatly in my esteem this time around. He was more confident and less arrogant, more careful and less reckless. He started to use his brain and consider the wants and needs of not only himself, but his people and the civilized world as well. Deryn, meanwhile, is still tough, humble, and a bit naive. They are great when they work separately, but brilliant when they work together. If only they weren't on opposite sides of this growing war. 
 The politics got a bit more jumbled as the hard lines are blurred and more countries start pulling into the conflict. It's no longer just Europe, but expanding into Asia as well. I found the Turkey setting in this one to be colorful, different, and exciting. Instead of clomping through the Alps or soaring through the skies, we see new communities and cultures and how they are affected by both the Darwinists and the Clankers. Westerfeld handles it all impeccably, and I found myself wanting to plan a trip to Turkey. 
 Alek and Deryn both are thrust into new levels of responsibility in this book, and we get introduced to a new beastie that should prove to be quite instrumental in the future (though I admit it was a bit of a letdown after all the book one buildup with the eggs). I loved seeing these two kids step up and experience the world in new ways. They really rose to the challenges presented to them and I look forward to seeing how they deal with what's coming in the final chapter, Goliath, due out September 20th. 
 This one was full of nearly nonstop action and scheming, with a tiny hint of romance thrown in. I hope we get more than just a taste in the next one, but only because I adore these two so much and am really rooting for them. This is certainly a book that can stand on its own without the romance element, but gets an added touch of that something special when the romance comes into play. 
 Westerfeld is a beautifully subtle writer, never hitting us over the head with extraneous details or descriptions. Instead, his stories unfold with ever escalating urgency, perfectly timed to the events and consequences the characters face, and propelling the plot forward with just the right balance of character and plot development. Throw in the fantastical steampunk elements (which never outshine or divert from the story), and now I'm glued to the page. 
 I cannot recommend this series highly enough. As much as I loved the first book, Behemoth has catapulted this series to the top of my favorites list, and I promise you I will be re-reading these books for years to come.

My feelings about this book are complicated, perhaps because the book itself is complicated. It is multi-layered, with essentially four stories: (1) a coming-of-age story of a 13-year-old boy, (2) a crime mystery, (3) an exploration of the psychological effects of violence, and (4) a depiction of modern life in a Native American reservation community. 
 I was captivated by this book, and especially enjoyed the shenanigans of the young boy and his friends. Many of their escapades were hilarious, and I was tickled by their devotion to Star Trek Next Generation as I'm also a huge fan. (For those of you who aren't familiar with STNG, you might be interested to know that the chapter titles coincided with some episode titles from STNG.) 
 But somehow, I didn't feel the other layers of the story were woven together quite successfully. Perhaps this is because the story is told in 1st person by the boy himself. (For instance, as he is only observing his mother's behavior after the attack, we cannot really know what's going on inside. Also, I didn't feel that his verbatim re-telling of the grandfather's myth stories was very effective.) 
 The somewhat disturbing ending leads the reader to ponder how the boy came to live with the action that he took, but that's a story that is left untold. 
 In some ways, this book reminded me of Alfredo Vea's "La Maravilla," which also weaves together a rollicking, multi-layered story of the people in a unique multi-ethnic Arizona community, while including somewhat mystical or spiritual elements. (The Round House includes aspects of Native American myth and spirituality.) However, I think Vea was more successful in weaving all those elements together in a beautiful, coherent narrative. 
 Still, overall, I think The Round House is a very good book -- I really enjoyed it, I'm glad I read it, and I recommend it.

I sat here racking my brain for a while trying to decide if I wanted to rate this 3 stars or 4. It was a pretty tough decision for me, but in the end I'm giving it 4. 
 I had such a hard time for a few reasons, and I'll start by naming all of the things that made me want to rate it at 4... 
 -I loved that the setting was in Austria. I have a very good friend from there (who I one day hope to visit), so it was really fun for me to read about her home town as well as nearby areas. I wish a little more description had been there about it, since Austria is absolutely freakin' gorgeous. 
 -I loved the idea of a soul collector. I wasn't sure what to expect since the very beginning had a pretty intense event (with her family dying in the car crash). I wasn't sure if the story would follow in the same vein and that taking the souls would therefore be harsh as well. I was pleasantly surprised that it was handled very well. The Soul Conversation in particular is what made it so calming and soothing. I loved that souls were different colors, and that they flickered when ready to die. I had an image of a dainty lightbulb in my head that couldn't decide if it wanted to power off or not, and I attribute that to this story (even if it's a bit odd to relate it to). 
 -I liked the characters. While Ana would get on my nerves a little bit at times, she is vastly improved over the countless YA heroines that are whiny and immature and selfish. While she could be all these at times, it was in small doses and didn't control her character. And as usual for me, I loved the side characters. Reiner and Rolf in particular were extremely captivating to follow. I wish Lucy made more of an appearance just because she was so cute. 
 -The overall plot is awesome. I want to know the name of the race that Ana is saving, and I want to meet all the other Elite. I want to know more of the tools of the trade for being a soul collector. I want to meet more creatures. I'm curious to see how Ana will put her musician skills to use, and how that will ultimately be something helpful and not just interesting. I mean I think we got a bit of that with the violin, but I want to see it in action. 
 Now for the things I almost knocked it down to a 3 for... 
 -Zig's whole "lovely Ana" thing got to be too much after a while. Literally every time the two interact he says it. It was too repetitive, and it shouldn't have been done so often. 
 -The secrets! I got so tired of the secrets!! I absolutely hate when characters won't just talk to each other!! If Ana's friends are so great they could handle the news.  we proved that with Reiner. After the initial shock he was fine!  The whole "Ana can only take information in small doses" was annoying behind belief and I was so tempted to skip ahead just to find out what the heck everyone was being so secretive about. Plus, the information was too few and far between. We'd get hardly any information and then we would have to make due for another inordinate amount of time until someone else deigned to offer some more information. It was infuriating. I suppose this is a compliment because I was invested in the story enough to care what the secrets were in the first place, which isn't the case when I don't care. 
 -Not enough happened. Here's the book: Ana's family dies, she trades their souls for hers. She learns soul collecting while everyone talks about her and won't tell her why. She acts weird, everyone acts weird. 
 I wanted more of the plot. I wanted to see more development of how she was going to be a heroine, and the people that were involved in helping her do that, and there just wasn't enough of it for my taste. 
 It's a solid book, and I do recommend it. If the second book in the series is more fast-paced I'd definitely be on board to read it.

Rosie and her classmates all take a pill to make them sleep utterly and completely for twelve hours. She and the others all wake up completely refreshed and completely happy, but she can't shake the feeling that she feels off somehow. So Rosie skips her pill one night, then the next, then the next. What she finds is that maybe there really is something to cause that weird feeling she gets. 
 What makes this so strong is that the farther we go, the less we know. The author does a solid job of making it difficult to believe Rosie--is she truly just falling apart from not taking her pills as prescribed, or are there insidious things going on at the school at night? She has no proof, and no one to back up her story. All she has are these faint inklings that something isn't right. 
 For most of the book, I was indifferent. I didn't hate it, but neither was I driven to finish it as fast as humanly possible. I didn't sneak read at red lights like I am wont to do, or stay up late to finish it. That all changed as soon as we got to the last third of the book--then it was just BAM BAM BAM BAM with all the craziness! 
 I loved how crazy and surreal the reveal was at the end. When we get that last glimpse into Rosie's mind, I was practically bouncing with anticipation. 
 And then...confusion. I don't really know what happened in that last scene. I reread it a couple of times, and I have an inkling of what I think it might be, but I am not totally sure whether I am right or wrong. I don't think that was the author's intention either. What I do think her intention was, and what worked quite well, was that last bit of terror before the book ends. Because that was one hell of a zinger, and THAT is on par with what I would like to see from this author. 
 So by and large this was a rollercoaster. Cruising along, nothing happens, then woah! big climax! then a dip down, where we build up momentum for the dramatic showdown! and then you're done and questioning what the hell just happened to you, but it was a pretty fun ride, even if it had its boring bits. 
 (In case you couldn't tell by my lack of mention of it, I didn't care either way for the reality show thing. I can take it or leave it.)

I'd wanted to read it for a long time; at least post-Jim Carrey/pre-Neil Patrick Harris as Count Olaf. So, I've finally taken the plunge and my overwhelming thoughts? Meh. Yes, I know; generally a wildly unpopular opinion regarding this series, especially in my field. Sorry not sorry? 
 I first attempted to read The Bad Beginning when I happened upon an actually available copy at my library. This was no easy feat considering the resurgence in popularity thanks to the Netflix series and summer break. I stalled after about 18 page before deciding to go the route of listening to the audiobook, because a) Tim Curry is the narrator and b) why the hell not? I thought that, if nothing else, this would make it a little easier to trudge through the awfulness of life with the Baudelaire orphans. What I found instead was an unusual radio show type production (not entirely unpleasant, though pretty awkward) with various different sound effects and nonsense that I found to be too distracting to fully enjoy the book. Awkward audio production aside, I found the constant definitions of terms and phrases to be obnoxious and belittling rather than helpful. Yes, I realize that I'm an adult, but I can almost guarantee that I would have felt the same way had I read these books as a child. 
 I will say that in general I do appreciate and even enjoy the darker nature of these books. I think it's important for kids to read a wide variety of books, especially ones that don't necessarily have a "happily ever after" type ending, because, let's be real: life isn't always so happy/awesome all of the time. That being said, these just aren't for me.

The narrator of this section is an omniscient Voice, a kind of cosmic, tough-love therapist that exists outside time and space and maintains a "long-standing policy of supportive neutrality." It speaks directly to Junior as though conducting an experiment: "Throughout your life, no matter how long or brief, the choice is, in the end yours.
