I'm really at war with myself here. My first instinct, my gut reaction, is to rate this low. There's a lot that I didn't like, that didn't work for me in whatever capacity it was supposed to. But then, I swing the other way and sort of want to give it 4 stars. 
 Kestrel and her friend go to the market, and Kestrel impulsively buys a slave because reasons. The reasons don't really make sense, because the logical reason for her to buy that slave isn't the reason she bought the slave. It was just some "feeling" that she had while looking at him, because he was defiant I suppose. Cue the first two thirds of the book, where we have yet another heroine who is in a gilded cage and whining about how she suffers from lack of freedom. Arin, the slave she purchased, is anything but a slave. He's rude, insolent, recalcitrant. He's every other word you can think of that is basically the exact opposite of a slave. And Kestrel, despite being the general's daughter, lets him walk all over her. He talks back to her, he insults her daily, he touches her and comes near her all the while. 
 I think we're meant to see a friendship and then love evolve slowly, but the origins of it were just so shaky that it never felt real to me. He makes a few half-assed remarks that sort of sound like he's surprised she's not a vile bitch like he thought, but never to the same capacity as friendship or love. The same could be said for her--she treats him like she would treat a talking parrot--interesting, and brings him along everywhere so she can observe him and see what else he'll do. It didn't feel real, so when the author tried to make it into more it just fell flat for me. 
 The other issue I have is the whole slave/owner thing. Never once did I feel like I was actually seeing that kind of dynamic. Arin was never forced to do anything humiliating. He had the run of the house, was able to smuggle who-knows-how-many weapons out of the GENERAL'S estate, and then wander where he pleased. Kestrel does nothing to prevent any of this, of course. In fact, she makes his job particularly easy by giving him free reign to go into the city whenever he feels like it (which conveniently gives him a way to tell secrets to the rebellion!) He reads military strategy books from her own library. She flat out tells him when the entire army is leaving, thus allowing the rebellion to attack the unprotected city. It was so ridiculous that I couldn't fathom how I was supposed to believe this girl was a brilliant strategist. 
 I just don't get it. 
 But then, I kind of do. 
 Because the final third of this book is where it really shined for me. I never once thought that Arin's people were in the wrong for trying to take back their freedom. Not once. But I could still understand the betrayal Kestrel felt when she realized that Arin was one of the leaders of the rebellion--the rebellion that killed almost everyone she knew. So Kestrel's hatred for Arin is what fueled my reading desire. I finally felt like I was seeing a real emotion, not the staged love. She was angry, and it showed in her unwillingness to let Arin touch her and in her cruel and biting remarks meant to hurt him. 
 In one page, that was squashed. Suddenly she's back to loving him again, and then my enthusiasm waned with it. I liked the struggle she had with herself to come to terms with the fact that the man she loved was able to upend her life so completely. He had every right to do so, but I wanted to feel that betrayal from her, that hurt. The author did a fantastic job of it when it was there. It just got taken away so quickly. 
 The whole thing was very PG-13, too. Kestrel is incensed that when she is captured, she is forced to wash the man's feet. Never mind that Arin's people had been enslaved like that for ten years, forced into subservience and being treated like dogs. This one injustice gave her all the self-important martyrdom she could need. Oh, and never mind the one slave that Kestrel supposedly loved, Enai. When Enai died Kestrel didn't have a lick of regret for never even bothering to learn the names of Enai's family. All that mattered was that Enai belonged to her, so she was the only one who had the right to mourn at her death. It was beyond selfish and very representative of just how special is, and not the Herran people. 
 The heinous parts of slavery are never really discussed either. It is pleasantly glossed over in most of the book, like when there is an inference of rape or when a slave getting whipped is only briefly mentioned. Like I said, the whole thing was very PG-13 and didn't truly do the conundrums of a slave/owner relationship justice. 
 With all that being said, I was interested enough in this to read it all in one day. It sparked my interest and then didn't let up until I was done. I just sort of drooped more and more as I kept on reading, because it ultimately didn't blow me away like it should have.

Theodore Finch is an unpredictable, death-obsessed teenager with ever-changing style. Violet Markey is popular, pretty, and reeling from her sister's recent death. Finch and Violet meet in their high school's bell tower, and the two recognize the sadness in each other that they see in themselves. When a school project takes the two on a tour around state landmarks, they fall in love and find comfort in the other's company. But as Finch's actions become more and more erratic, Violet must try to help him before it is too late. 
 I put off writing this review for a long time because I wanted to mull over my feelings until I was sure that I wasn't missing something. The internet is littered with 4 and 5 star reviews praising this book and setting it alongside Fault in Our Stars and Eleanor and Park as one of the best realistic fiction titles of the decade. Movie rights were purchased and a big name star was attached (Elle Fanning) before the book had even been published. There is no doubt in my mind that Jennifer Niven could be the next juggernaut in YA fiction. But this just didn't work for me on a number of levels. 
 I will start off by admitting that any comparison to John Green or Rainbow Rowell has me instantly skeptical, not only because I love both of these authors, but mainly because nearly every new realistic fiction title with a less-than-happy ending seems to court these comparisons. But when I read "reminicient of Green and Rowell," I don't think "this is a book where teens fall in love and overcome tragedy." I think of a book with a simple plot, filled in by incredibly skillful, character-driven writing. I think of characters that feel achingly authentic, that are distinct and unlike any others. And I think of a writing style that is a little cerebral and truly unique, a book that doesn't feel like anything I've ever read. That's the trickiest thing when this comparison is made - if it's accurate, the book doesn't read anything like Rowell or Green. It's its own smart, heart-breaking animal. 
 And it's in these ways that All the Bright Places fell short for me. The writing was good but not special, the characters were interesting but not fully fleshed out. And while I loved that Niven tackled a very serious subject to which many teens would be able to relate, the depictions of depression and suicide didn't feel quite authentic to me. Depression runs in my family, and I know that suicidal thoughts aren't always, or even often, triggered by something serious. Spilling coffee or missing the bus can suddenly make life seem unbearable. But there's always a degree of worthlessness and catastrophic thinking that I didn't get from Finch's narration at all - his discussion of suicide seemed romantic rather than depressive. There had to be a deeper, inner dialogue that the reader wasn't hearing, and keeping that hidden felt more like a plot device than selective narration. Violet's narration, too, felt superficial given the complicated thoughts she must have regarding her sister's death  but not to such a dangerous fault, given that Finch follows through on his thoughts and kills himself at the end of the book. Amanda's explanation of depression toward the end of the book offers far more insight into what it feels like to have suicidal thoughts than anything Finch says within his own narration.  My advance copy did not include the help line resource guide included in the regular print copy, but I'm thankful that the publisher included this guide for readers seeking help or more information. 
 I would personally give this book two stars, but the teens I work with wouldn't likely take issue with the faults I found and would enjoy the romance, so I'm bumping it up to a three. While I would recommend this to teens looking for a tragic love story, for more realistic depictions of depression and bipolar disorder I would steer teens toward Matthew Quick's books.

Final Girls - named by the horror industry as the only girl left alive after a massacre. In Quincy's world, there are three of them - the first being Lisa, the second being Sam and then Quincy. Quincy survived a night with her friends at Pine Cottage that was supposed to be a fun weekend. Stabbed and somehow left alive, Quincy's tried hard to make her life as normal as possible. With a successful blog on baking and an understanding boyfriend, she's moving forward as much as she can. For ten years she's managed with the blessing (?) that she remembers almost nothing about that night. But she does hold secrets on how she handles some of her post traumatic stress and she keeps that secret close to her chest. 
 Then one day, she gets a call that Lisa has been found dead in her bathtub and shortly after, Sam shows up on her doorstep. Bound by their survival stories, Lisa brings Sam into her home. Sam tests her and pushes her to remember and deal with her residual feelings of anger. But can Sam be trusted? Can she trust her own memories? 
 This book has been EVERYWHERE and it holds up to its hype. Written almost like a slasher film, it's taut, tense, action packed and keeps you on your toes. Trust me when I say that what you think it is, probably isn't... and it isn't THAT either. Flashing back to the night in question, we get a deep look into Quincy ten years ago and to her today - building up into a final reveal you really won't see coming. Riley Sager has a way of seamlessly building Quincy's world and everyone in it. I read this in one sitting and couldn't put it down. After turning the last page, I immediately went into conversations with others who have read it and we all readily agree - it's a shocker... and a good one! Already being touted as the thriller of the year, this book will be talked about for quite some time - get yourself a copy and join the conversation!

 I just finished the Sword of Truth series by Goodkind which left me asking if its author ever dated, but this book's honest and tender romance was exactly what I was hoping to see in such a work. 
 The protagonist, Soren, is a wonderfully darkly complicated moody teen angst but one with an utterly viable reason that makes you empathize while you cringe at his bouts within the coming of age journey. 
 Astrid - is my my hold out - I'll await the rest but I've had the initial impression of the cliche manifestation of various tropes archetypes. 
  
 Fenris is, in contrast, a character with which I'm looking forward to getting more acquainted. In a wonderfully unique reinterpretation of its mythos, she is a creature of appetites and truly comes across as Loki's kin. 
 (I still think she may be Loki). 
 I'm also curious on the shift between traditionally Dwarven roles being recast by Goblins. 
  
 I did not give this 5 stars, though it is an excellent book. 
 I love the concept, its execution, and the likely story arc; however, I feel Gratton hasn't stretched her literary legs fully. 
 I was told a quote from Gratton that shattered a paradigm of mine with effortless grace - and I'd like to see more of her insights in her work.

When I noticed that Jon Krakauer had a new book, I immediately logged into my local library's website and put it on hold. 
 I'm a fan of his writing style and the topic seemed interesting enough. 
 I often learn things from reading books, but it takes an exceptional book (or writer) to teach me something about myself. I'll be honest. I was surprised by my visceral reaction to many of the non-stranger rapes described in this book. There seemed to be a constant battle between my logical brain (who openly cheered for the victims) and my emotional gut (that occasionally and silently rooted for the accused). 
 Had this book been written by a less skillful author, I think I may not come to the same conclusion, that I do have some biases regarding this topic that are both unfair and the result of buying into various myths even if unconsciously. 
 I am also more convinced now than ever that how we view a situation is largely impacted by our perspective and thus we need to constantly question our beliefs about the world, which were often put there without our consent or even knowing it. 
 Krakauer does of good job of baiting those who might disagree with the book's final conclusions, that we need to reevaluate our attitudes about rape to acknowledge the prevalence and destructiveness of non-stranger rape that doesn't necessarily fit our preconceptions about what rape is. In essence, he gives an inch only to take back a yard. By acknowledging your reservations about buying into his assertions, it makes questioning your reactions more a process of self-discovery and thus a lot easier to do. 
 That said, there does seem to be a gray area here that Krakauer acknowledges but only in passing. In some cases, it really comes down to "he said, she said." I can't even count how many times my husband and I will recall the same situation (ranging from casual conversations to serious matters) differently. 
 As always, Krakauer manages to cover several different though related topics (entitled status of athletes, our treatment of victims, and our ideas and misconceptions about what constitutes rape)that converge almost seamlessly. 
 Ironically, I had already picked up a book that chronicles the Duke Lacrosse players (who according to Krakauer represent the minority as they were wrongly accused of rape) prior to getting this book, so it will be interesting to read that now that I have read this.

I received a copy of this title from NetGalley. It does not impact my review. 
 Eeny Meeny is an intense thriller that kept me glued to the pages for days. 
 Helen Grace is a detective investigating a disturbing murder. In a Saw-like scenario, two people are trapped with no escape and are left with a gun with one bullet. Once one of them is dead, the other will be freed. After the first "winner" of the game escapes, it is not long before another couple go missing. The cases get even more disturbing for Helen when she suspects the victims are somehow connected to her. 
 I really liked the writing style of this book. It's told in 3rd person POV and we get the perspective of Helen and her fellow officers Charlie and Mark, each of the victims, the killer, and a BDSM dominant who may have feelings for his mysterious client (don't worry, it's not as Fifty Shades as it sounds). The shift in perspectives, as well as the short chapter lengths, really made the story clip along at a quick pace and kept me engaged. 
 Helen was not an easy character to like, but I was definitely rooting for her throughout the book. She's a good cop, but struggles with all personal relationships. I liked Mark and was really hoping for his happy ending. I felt like the character development was done very well, especially when juggling so many characters and some of them are only seen for a few chapters. 
 One word of caution is that the book can get quite graphic at times. No detail is spared when describing the precarious conditions the victims are facing, especially after they've been trapped for a couple days. 
 Overall I enjoyed Eeny Meeny. It was an intense thriller with well-developed characters, smart writing, and a plot that will make you question your own humanity. I recommend it to fans of crime/mystery/thrillers, who don't mind a little bit of the graphic and resolutions that aren't necessarily Happily Ever After.

I really enjoyed this book, because I love these characters and this world so much. But it doesn't quite capture the magic of the original trilogy...the first half is slow-paced, with alternating chapters causing a bit of narrative whiplash. Lirael's section recaps much of "Creature in the Case", which is wasted words considering the second half of the book feels a bit rushed. 
 After the ending of Abhorsen, the climax of Goldenhand lacks drama. Even having read Clariel, I'm not sure that her brief reappearance  adds enough to overcome the fact that you can't top binding the world-Destroyer as an ending. 
 I also feel like Sabriel should have been more involved in that -- she had history with Chlorr, after all. Or Mogget! And it would have been nice to see Lirael and Sabriel working together - would have been a good chance to expand the mechanics of the magic a bit (what can two Abhorsens in tandem accomplish that one can't?). I understand why Nick was there (though he was essentially just a passive plot device) and that Nix wanted to have them together. But I think there were ways to make the final confrontation stronger. 
 And then there was the expansion of the world -- that map! -- which we see for perhaps all of a chapter! There was so much potential in the Rift, in the steppes, that hardly got realized. 
 I think I just wanted more than could be accomplished in one book. Sabriel was a fairly self-contained arc, though it led into the events of Lirael/Abhorsen. But after such a well-rounded arc, and a whole book of setup in Clariel...Goldenhand should have been the start of a new arc rather than try to rush through it all in one go. Another sort of Lirael/Abhorsen duology, to give all the relationships (Sabriel/Lirael, Lirael/Nick, Sam/[REDACTED]) room to breathe, and to play with the new areas of the world, the new aspects of Free Magic revealed in Clariel, expanding the magic system, maybe even exploring the Charter Magic/Free Magic relationship more. It's briefly touched on in the Nick subplot, but not enough. There was real potential there. 
 I don't know. I'm glad this book exists, and I'm glad I read it, but I'm disappointed because it felt like there was so much more there and Nix was just skimming the surface. I think if/when I revisit the series in the future it will be only the first three books.

 I received a digital ARC of this book (via NetGalley) in exchange for an honest review. Thank you, Megan Gaudino, Evernight Teen and Xpresso Book Tours! 
 Always Kiss Me Goodnight left me undecided with a lot of mixed feelings. On one hand, I can't possibly deny that I enjoyed reading the story Gaudino has weaved. Despite the book's title, Always Kiss Me Goodnight offers more than an unlikely love story; its pages hold a fascinating, fantastical, supernatural realm that readers will definitely eat up. On the other hand, however, the book did not quite keep me as engaged as I hoped it would. 
 Sophia Destino was all right, I guess; but for the most part, she lacked appeal as a female lead character. While I did sympathize with her every now and then, I felt that she needed more personality to further strengthen her character. Still, I haven't given up on her and I can only hope that she will be given the opportunity to really grow as a strong, dimensional heroine in the next book. As for her love interest, Leo Knight, I had a lot of mixed feelings about him as well. I mean, technically, Leo was a stalker. He literally followed Sophia around, without her knowledge, to keep tabs on her. I get that it was all part of his duty and all, but it's kind of hard to imagine myself falling for someone who knows too many intimate moments in my life without needing me to open up about them. Aside from that, Leo was very likable and I would really love to read more about him. 
 The relationship between Sophia and Leo was great, in my opinion. I really think that the two balance each other out. And I definitely prefer Leo over Aiden any day, any time of the week. However, the element of forbidden romance was not played out well. I would have appreciated a lot more struggle. It seemed to me that Sophia and Leo almost easily overcame all the obstacles that threatened their relationship. Aside from that, I was also slightly disheartened by the presence of overused YA literary tropes such as the lack of familial presence, guy saving the girl's life, and other whatnot. Seriously, guys, what is up with these trends? Enough is enough. 
 On a more positive note, I really loved how Gaudino expertly put a twist in the idea of Fate. In her book, Fate appears to be an actual entity, and there actually exists a divine order that carries out Fate's will. I found this concept to be incredibly imaginative and refreshing. I don't think I've encountered anything quite like it in any of the books I've ever read. Plus, Gaudino's execution was totally on point! 
 Overall, despite the book's shortcomings and flaws, I had a good time reading the story. I am very much interested in reading the next book. 
 What makes this different: 
 In Always Kiss Me Goodnight, Gaudino plays around the traditional ideas of angels and grim reapers, consequently introducing a supernatural twist that is unparalleled to anything I've ever read: Guardians of Fate whose primary role is to protect the ways of Fate and to ensure the execution of Fate's plan. I found this highly intriguing as it challenges our current perception of the ethereal and the divine. This is definitely something worth looking into!

This book had me terrified to make a call using my cell phone. Everything in a moment changed. Clay, the main character, watched in horror as everyone around him turned into something more primal. They lost all human thought and reasoning, and he was trapped in the mayhem miles away from his family - his son. 
 In Cell, Stephen King takes you on the arduous journey of making his way through the "phoners" to get back to his son. While his son may have been lost to the same incident, he wasn't about to leave his son on his own if he managed to stay normal. The journey is long, and with the help of a few other normals he finds on the way, they try to rid the world of these atrocities of beings while fighting to stay alive and keep their sanity. 
 The way Stephen King weaved CELL and that humans were suddenly corrupted by a program, much like computers can be, kept you at the edge of your seat, wondering if really, we, too, are nothing more than programmable beings. 
 While on his journey, Clay and his two followers ran into an older man and a young boy. An old professor and a student who were able to teach Clay all that they had discovered about these strange beings since the Pulse happened and cell phones cleared most of the populations minds. The professor said one thing that stuck with me through the entire book... 
 "Our core is madness. The prime directive is murder. What Darwin was too polite to say, my friends, is that we came to rule the earth not because we were the smartest, or even the meanest, but because we have always been the craziest, most murderous motherfuckers in the jungle. And that is what the Pulse exposed five days ago." 
 While not one of Stephen King's more frightening reads, I still found the story to be amazingly written and well-spun. I connected to each of the characters: Clay, Tom, Alice, Jordan, the Professor, Denise, Ray, and Dan. I could feel their hopelessness and fear, and their will to save what was left of the human race. I thoroughly enjoyed reading this book, and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys a taste of what the end of the world might become.

Louie is a cat. Nothing else makes sense--there's no other way to describe how he managed to survive everything his life threw at him. His childhood stunts alone were epic--he's the kind of kid that turned into a legend once he left his hometown. No way you can live in the same place and not hear about the kid who stole everything from everyone and had stories always end with, "and then we ran like mad." 
 Then his amazing track career in high school and college. Then the Olympics. Nothing seemed to stop him. That became all the more apparent when he went into the military and got stranded in the middle of the ocean for more than a month, barely surviving and punching sharks. I mean, come on. 
 The bulk of the book is spent on his time as a POW in a Japanese camp. That was ruthless. Most of the time, books focus on the western stage--Poland and Germany. For me, this was the first time I'd read anything that focused exclusively on the east, and specifically Japan's involvement. 
 Holy crap, Louie--all those guys, really, not just him--survived SO MUCH. The brutality is a harsh reality that history tends to forget about, and hearing (almost) first hand about how these guys had to deal with it was a hard thing to choke down. It's a gorgeously uplifting story though, in the end. I'm glad we got our happy ending.

In a future where humanity has spread to other stars and has contact with various intelligent alien races, Binti, a mathematically-gifted young woman from a remote African desert community is the first of people to leave Earth to attend the galaxy-renowned Oomza University, and her journey will see her face not only discrimination for her origins, but also a deadly alien threat. 
 I really liked the main character, and the set-up is captivating, but two major plot problems kept me from fully getting into it: 
 1. The edan was just way overpowered - not only activating exactly when she needed, but having exactly what she needed: not only a weapon but a perfect universal translator of the Meduse language and her own. I could have bought it more if it were powered by her mathematical thought-fugues or if the Meduse language was somehow mathematical - *something* to give it more of a connection to Binti. I know this is #1 of a series so maybe further books will explore it more, but this story is pretty self-contained, and as is, the edan's just a Totally Unexplained Superpowered Thing Just Because the Protagonist Needs It.  
 2. Her becoming pals with Okwu at the end just felt very rushed in order to enhance a happy-ending feel. It's one thing to understand why the Meduse attacked/their grievances, and to broker a deal between them and the University to prevent more bloodshed, as she bravely did. It's another thing to *also* feel trusting and friendly towards a Medusa who was part of the group who she saw slaughter her defenseless friends *right in front of her just days before*. That has to either be some heavy Stockholm syndrome stuff going on that would need to be explored with more nuance, or a much longer process of seeing her not just understanding Okwu but growing to be comfortable around him, to be believable. Yes, I guess her getting the "sting" that transforms her hair into the Meduse strands means she's part Meduse now and *that* could explain her comfort level. But I could've easily seen her feeling horrified that she's been transformed without her consent instead, and, since that doesn't seem to be the case, I'd like to see her contemplating how strange it is that she doesn't hate him for murdering her friends or *something*...

Police officer Seth Colter got shot during duty and is on leave, during his leave he helps out at a soup kitchen. While Seth is serving he see's Lily and he's horrified over the idea of her being on the streets cold and alone. More baffling is the dark, possessive instinct that tells him she belongs to him. For Lily, home means a secluded nook in an alley until Seth offers her a place to stay. Seth is convinced Lily is the one. The problem is, when his brothers lay eyes on her, the same primitive instinct comes roaring to the surface. The Colters never imagined they'd follow the unconventional path of their fathers, but they can't ignore their mutual need to offer Lily their protection and their love. But before Lily and the brothers can forge a future together, they must heal the deep wounds of her past. 
 This is the second book in the Colters' Legacy, I would suggest you read the first book Colters' Woman as it would help you understand the background of the Colter family. 
 Colters' Lady takes place roughly after 30 years of marriage between the first Colter brothers, Adam, Ethan and Ryan to Holly. They had three sons, police officer Seth, veterinarian Michael and pub owner/entrepreneur Dillon, and a daughter Callie who's running from someone or something that will be revealed in 2011 in Colters' Daughter. 
 I'd like to point out that I didn't see Lily as much of a Lady and more of the role of a lost and alone bird that needed looking after and healing but the brothers weren't planning on letting her go once she was healed. My main problem with the storyline was the Colter brothers seemed so easy to trust Lily and not nag her or hassle her about the reason she was homeless and living on the streets. 
 When I found out why Lily was on the streets I did feel sorry for her and her former situation and in a way was glad she'd found the Colter brother's as they had healed her and made her stronger to come with her ghosts from the past. 
 This is the sort of book where you have to suspend your normal ideas and views on relationships and typical romance novels and just remember it is a good romance read with a bit extra because they are several times when you go 'but that's not...' and 'why didn't he...' and 'how did...' so it does really help to read Colters' Woman which I think is a better read than Colters' Lady. 
 I do however, always enjoy reading a Maya Banks book.

Over the years Robin Hobb has become an absolute powerhouse in the world of fantasy. After devouring all her Elderling books, it was time for the odd trilogy in the bunch: the soldier son. A lot is different in this trilogy, and yet a lot remains the same: there are mysterious plotlines brewing (excellent for speculation!), but at the end of the day, it's all about the characters. 
 I'm more than ok with that - I'm a very character-driven reader. Yet what this book didn't have versus all the other trilogies is an instant connection with the main characters. Perhaps that will still follow, but I didn't get there yet. 
 Like Farseer, the Soldier Son is written in one fixed first person narrator. That narrator is a New Noble son called Nevare, but I've come to know him as Little Stick In The Mud. He's one of those fairly inactive protagonists: things happen to him, but he doesn't do much. And that makes me impatient. 
 Nonetheless, the book sets up some interesting storylines. The boarding school feel (buddy reader David Sven compared it to Hogwarts which was an excellent call) is really well done, comraderies are formed, not so much by choice as by coincidence, but it works and it will be important in the following books I'm sure. 
 There is a lot of 'unfairness' in the story, which worked for me, but me rooting for all the little Davids in the story would have worked better if I would actually have loved the little Davids. (At least I already loathed the cross-generational Goliath Stiets, so no issues on that account.) 
 In short, this book isn't a homerun for me, but it's promising and I'm looking forward to see what she does with it. And even more so, I'm curious to find out whether I will ever come to like our little Stick-In-The-Mud.

 I also really dislike this cover. I love that they use orange, but this cover just bothers me so much! Where are the glasses? Where is the crazy hair? Why is the title so small? I personally think it would've been better to have a flat design over someone that doesn't even resemble Dimple.

All of the characters were well developed, even if I think Dimple's character was a little over-developed. 
 I love that this took on a lot of topics as afterthoughts. It wasn't like this book was set out to crush the patriarchy, or diminish arranged marriages, but it wanted you to see those things and give insight about them. Talk about the real struggles that girls, immigrants and first generation individuals, and many other people go through on a daily basis. It shed light on how male-centric the world can be, and it shows it to you from an own voice, person of color author's perspective. 
 This book is amazing, and I hope you all have a chance to read it.

Reading back through these books is always rather nostalgic for me, as I grew up with these stories. However, the older I get, the less I like them. I still enjoy the plot lines and the characters, but there are many small things that make me dislike the stories a bit. 
 Each of the characters tended to annoy me more than they have in the past. The reactions the characters have can be fairly extreme, and I feel as though that wouldn't quite be realistic. However, I do believe that it shows the truth that ignorance and fear can blind us to the truly amazing people and wonders around us. The prime example of this would be  when Uncle Andrew's fear and ignorance when it comes to Aslan and the animals he creates and the refusal (and disability) to hear them when they speak to him.  
 When rereading this one, I still loved reading the Narnia creation scene. It's a wonderful blend of bizarre and inspiring. 
 C. S. Lewis still did a phenomenal job creating a new children's tale, and I know reading these books, especially The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe has given many children inspiration and belief that they are capable of anything (with or without the aid of others) and that they can truly change the world. I know all these books certainly inspired me and helped me believe that I was capable of great things, growing up, and that certainly includes this one. 
 The Magician's Nephew also taught me to take responsibility for my actions and helped me to see that every action has consequences, whether good or bad. 
 I recommend this book to those who want to reengage in the magic that surrounds them or want to teach their children to see the world as full of wonder and possibilities.

 I went into this world blind. I haven't read Leigh Bardugo's Shadow and Bone trilogy and didn't know anything about the Grishaverse. I have to say that I had to try this book twice in order to get into it. The first time around, the prologue killed me. The second time around, I sped through it and actually got to the good part (so if you're like me and didn't like the prologue then know that there's light at the end of the tunnel). 
 The first chapter was a piece of awesomeness wrapped in a shiny, black package with golden stars. It was magic. The plot was tightly woven and fast-paced. The characters were a lovely surprise (seeing as I usually dislike books with multiple POVs). And the writing was very atmospheric. 
 The only thing I wasn't a fan of was the very long backstory dumps. Don't get me wrong, I loved learning more about the characters, but it's just that's when I found it easiest to put the book down and go do other stuff (like sleep). 
 Anyhow, I suggest that you pick up this book and experience the magic for yourself.

I love the first line of the blurb--Pippa has always wanted to go to Italy...but not by herself. Well, by herself is exactly what she got. I was amazed that Pippa's parents would sent her there by herself--she is only seventeen, after all. I barely send my sixteen year old to the store by himself, let alone halfway across the world. Anyway...Pippa isn't too excited about going, since she almost feels forced into it. Her best friend is determined to help her make the best of it by giving her a journal with some goals to fulfill. 
 I was impressed with Pippa's maturity in letting someone know exactly where she was and what was going on, since she decided to ditch the art program and go after the summer of her dreams. This experience is a growing experience for her--she learns a lot about herself, about the world around her, and about how what you really want might not really be what you want when it comes down to it. 
 I loved Pippa. She is brave, determined, and is easy to get along with. She feels deeply and throws herself wholeheartedly into life. Bruno is very charismatic with a bad boy vibe. It's hard not to like him even when he's unlikeable. Darren, the American, is real and down to earth. He seems to be a little hesitant, yet very spontaneous. 
 I really enjoyed all of the characters, misunderstandings, adventure, setting, and relationships. Fun, cute story! 
 Content: Clean romance (kissing, mild innuendo); very mild language; mild violence (non-descriptive fight).

I have not read something quite like this before. Sadly, I wasn't so much as scared as creeped out. Maybe it's because I'm such a fanatic of scary things that it's difficult to scare me now. So don't let it deter you just because I wasn't feeling the fright! 
 Let me start out by saying, there are some slower parts of this book, but they are there for a reason. 
 For a moment, it felt as though Ania Ahlborn crept into one of my personal nightmares and brought it to life. Again, I wasn't scared, but it creeped me out. I was shocked, to say the least. 
 This book doesn't just give you all the creepy-crawly chills, it gives you all sorts of emotions for the main characters. Pity, love, sorrow. All I wanted to do was hug the ever living hell out of Stevie. For such a little boy, he's gone through so much, and it just keeps coming at him. 
 And so many people give him the look. You know, the one that says, stop being such a loser and a freak... 
 The ending though. WOW. I'm blown away. That was the best part of the book by a long shot. 
 Throughout the entirety of this book, all I could hear was Jud Crandall from Pet Cemetery by Stephen King: 
 Overall, this book was a breath of fresh air. I've been reading romance for a while and needed something that would crawl under my skin, work its way into my head, and hold on for some sleepless nights. This book did almost all of those things. It was still a good read! 
 Rating: 3.5 stars!

This book was a mess y'all I'm sorry...

 Things I liked about this book:

 - I enjoyed Dorian's character and arc a lot in this one. In fact, he was probably my favorite character in this book, although he was one of my least favorites from the last book. It happens you know. 
 - Nehemia continued to be the BEST DAMN CHARACTER IN THIS ENTIRE SERIES. I swear this book should have been about her. 
 - The action/magic was good and had me interested.

 Things I didn't like about this book: 
 - Calaena is still my least favorite character, and I still find her immensely annoying sorry not sorry honestly. 
 - Chaol was actually terrible in this book, but it saddens me because I loved him so much in the first book. I find he was only terrible during the first part of the novel, and in the second he got my heart again though so... 
 - I hated Chaol and Calaena's romance. It was cheesy and just terrible? I honestly hoped Chaol and Calaena would be platonic life partners. You know "Best Friends Forever" and that kind of stuff. I never saw that it would be fitting for them to be romantic partners, but you know it's YA what do you expect. 
 - Characters felt like they were entirely different people. Not even like character growth wise or anything, just that they were literally entirely new people. It was strange. 
 - I felt like the entirety of this book were parts that were really interesting and action packed, and then really slow. I felt like I was on a bad rollercoaster the whole time. 
 -  [Nehemia's death enraged me so much. Not only did Maas kill off the best character in the book, but she also killed off the only POC in the book so far. Like thank you for adding to the token brown friend dying Maas. We all really needed that one.]  
 - Predictable. Incredibly predictable in fact. I literally knew the big "Twist" once it was even barely mentioned. I figured everything else out in the book almost immediately, which lead to a fairly dull read. 
 In general, yeah it was better than "Throne of Glass" but not by much. I was still kind of disappointed, and i'm still waiting for this series to wow me. Will I continue on with this series? Maybe? I don't really know yet? I'm definitely taking a LOOOONG break that's for sure.

I'm a big Susan Mallery fan, but I didn't enjoy this book as much as I was expecting too. I thought it sounded like a great contemporary romance and a great new series. But I feel that I may have out grown Susan Mallery's stories but as I'd already bought the first two books and the novella I had better read them all. 
 Charity's nomadic childhood has left her itching to settle down, and she immediately falls in love with all the storybook town has to offer everything, that is, except cyclist Josh Golden. With her long list of romantic disasters, she's not about to take a chance on another bad boy, even if everyone else thinks he's perfect just the way he is. But maybe that's just what he needs someone who knows the value of his flaws. Someone who knows that he's just chasing perfect. 
 Chasing Perfect just doesn't hit the mark for me. I felt that it was too simple and too everyday. I liked Charity, I thought she was a great character but Josh just didn't appeal to me at all and he really put my off the book! The strangest part of Chasing Perfect was that Charity's job was to build something to bring men to Fool's Gold, because the problem with Fool's Gold is that men just don't seem to stick around, there's plenty to see and do and people to meet but they're mainly women.

After the cliffhanger ending of the first book, I was surprised when I struggled to invest myself in the second. The book starts out exactly as it has to, with Elisa assuming the throne. However, I just didn't care. I wasn't particularly interested in the pageantry and the intrigue. Luckily, I feel like Rae Carson wasn't enthralled with it either-- so when I hit 14% completion, I started running through the book. 
 Later, I realized why I wasn't as interested. Elisa is an incredible leader. She led the Malficio ruthlessly and understood the sacrifices she must make for the greater good. However, she is a terrible royal. She was not bred for that life, and she is not good at hiding her emotions or being involved in the political intrigue. I was actually was incredibly surprised we didn't hear more about the court politics in Brisadulce. There was still some intrigue and there were lots of court politics at play. However, Elisa tended to avoid them as they exhausted her.  Hindsight is 20/20, and not until she is betrayed in the end does she realize what a terrible royal she has been.  Once we moved past the politics/intrigue, I was engaged. But that was where Elisa was in her element. 
 We have lots of great new characters in this book. I particularly warmed towards Tristian, and I was sad we didn't see more of him. He brings a lot to the table. Plus, he's a dashing rouge. ;) 
 Religion was downplayed in this book. It was not as overtly discussed, but it was still a key focal point. I think the real transition in this tone is due to the addition of Storm to our cast. His people, the Invierno, don't view religion the same as the Joyan people. This helped temper all the religious gusto. While it's still there, the balance was obvious. 
 I found towards the end of the book I was addicted. The ending of this book was only a minor cliffhanger. My heart needed that after reading the end of The Girl of Fire and Thorns. I received a lot of contentment from the ending, but I still immediately opened the next book. 
 I strongly recommend this series to anyone who believes in themselves, and anyone who believes ignorance is not a form of protection-- but of repression.

 THE RUN-DOWN 
 Cassie has the gift of reading people. She can look at a person and be able to tell who they are, the kind of life the live, and what they may possibly do next. When she catches the attention of an FBI group, she's asked to join. The group of Naturals, filled with other teenagers with natural gifts similar to Cassie's (one just like hers, another good with emotions, and the last good with statistics and numbers), are meant to solve cold cases. But when a current case, homicides targeting women with red hair and/or "psychic" abilities, may be related to her mother's murder, which was never solved, the situation gets even more serious. 
 MY THOUGHTS 
 I really enjoyed reading this book, which surprised me since I wasn't actually planning on reading this book in the first place. I was actually invested in the story and breezed quickly through the book. But, I've read books like this before. There are a lot of mystery books that have either the same or very similar story line as The Naturals (the first one that comes to mind is The Body Finder series). And while I did enjoy reading this book, I can't give it a higher rating due to how the plot of the book is so common and the fact that there was a few things that were very predictable.  In every single mystery book I've read, involving killers, the killer ALWAYS comes after the main character! Always! Always! Always! So, I predicted that at some point, the killer would go after Cassie in some way, which did happen. This disappointed me since I hate it when books are predictable, but there was some redemption (which I'll talk about later)  
 I also have to say a few things on the romance. 
 You tried, romance, but you failed. 
 The romance of this book basically an attempt at romance, and you could tell that there was supposed to be romance, but we didn't get any romance. Sure, there was some strange kissing scenes, but there was no hint of any feelings from Cassie for either of the boys (yes, there's two, but I would not consider it a love triangle. Mostly since I don't even consider it as romance.). I also had no idea what the two guys were feeling, so the entire romance was basically a few awkward-ish kisses. That's all. 
 I'm glad that this book did not go the route of plot taking the back seat, while romance takes the front, but I also don't particularly like it when romance is thrown into a book for seemingly no reason. Maybe there's more to it in the next book? I don't know, but it's possible. 
 I know it seems that I was not a fan of this book, based on the fact that all I'm doing is complaining, but I actually did enjoy reading this book. While the romance was kind of stupid, it was only a very small part of the book. And the fact that the plot of this book is a common one did not mean that I didn't like it. There is a reason as to why I have read enough of these books that I recognize how common the plot is. 
 I mentioned earlier that the book was a bit predictable, and yes, that's true, but only in some ways. As with most mystery books, there is something that is, well, a mystery. In this book the mystery surround the serial killer. I had no idea who the killer was. None. When the killer was revealed I was taken completely by surprise! And I loved this! This was not a case of "oh, the killer is actually this person", but there are absolutely no clues or hints that would lead up to that person. No, there were many hints throughout the book, very subtle ones that are not obvious until you know who the killer is. Looking back, I could the genius in this and, of course, I loved the fact that the book took me by surprise. 
 IN CONCLUSION 
 This is a very quick read, barely 300 pages, and the story is when that you can quickly breeze through. It's a bit of a common serial killer mystery, which I have seen many times before, but while predictable at times, the book will take you by surprise. The "romance" is kind of unnecessary. In fact, I hesitate to call it a romance. 
 But, all in all. I did like this book. It was very entertaining and I definitely plan on reading the next book in the series!

This lady is totally kooky and nuts, but I like some of her ideas a lot. This book probably won't help a really bad packrat, but for the rest of us, it might be enough. If you feel like it's too much time and effort to go through your stuff, you can space it out over six months or so. Just think about all the time and effort you spent acquiring it, storing it, digging through it to look for that one thing you really wanted to find, and it won't seem like so much.

Some books just don't age well, and this is one of 'em. Being a high school teacher, I tried to keep an open mind. After all, it is a classic, right? When our 16 year old protagonist describes the morning as 'effulgent', I gave up. This pleonasm is just one example - there are many others - I ran into, where Knowles' prodigious vocabulary works against the coherence of his characterization. What kid in the history of ever speaks that way? As I read, I noted that Gene is one of the most annoying narrators of all time. He's insecure, pretentious, melodramatic and yet alien to almost every version of teenager I've encountered in the last 15 years, in that he has almost no appealing facets. 
 Knowles is trying to say something about the nature of friendship or regret or grief or the pall of war or whatever, but rarely are such meaningful topics hitched to such tedious characters and such stuffy prose. So while this might have been edgy stuff in 1965, contemporary readers will find little to admire here beyond stodgy formality. 
 Perhaps I'm just over the sufferings of white guys at prep school? Well, that can be interesting: exhibit A, Looking for Alaska, exhibit B, Winger, exhibit C, Spud. Why teachers usher the generations though "ASP" instead of those others is really inexcusable.

 This book has been recommended to me many, many, many times. After much ado, I finally took the initiative to read Perks. (Actually, that's a lie. It was more of an accident. But I digress.) I could see why people felt drawn to this novel. See: 
 "So, this is my life. And I want you to know that I am both happy and sad and I'm still trying to figure out how that could be." 
 With an introduction like that, it's pretty hard not to get hooked. Quite frankly, The Perks of Being a Wallflower is the most quotable book I've read so far (which isn't really saying a lot, but eh). Moreover, it was ridiculously easy to relate to and it touched all four chambers of my heart. The writing style was impressive and neat as well. 
 What I love about Charlie is his wit, innocence and perceptiveness. Although at times, he appeared to be naive, his insight remained uncanny and entertaining throughout the story. He was a strong narrator and an intelligent kid through and through. It was amazing to read about someone so selfless and conflicted. In fact, it was just beautiful. (This is what realistic fiction is about, yo.) 
 Consequently, I have grown fond of all the characters especially when it came to Sam, Patrick and, of course, Charlie. They were really an almost inseparable trio and I liked how they interacted with each other. 
 I'll admit, I wasn't blown away by this particular quote: "And in that moment, I swear we were infinite." I don't know. It felt pretty darn cheesy, overused and overdone for me. Perhaps I've seen it too much on the internet. Nevertheless, my eleven favorite quotes in this entire book are most likely the following: 
  
 Eleven. "I have decided that maybe I want to write when I grow up. I just don't know what I would write." 
 Ten. "I don't even remember the season. I just remember walking between them and feeling for the first time that I belonged somewhere." 
 Nine. "I am very interested and fascinated how everyone loves each other, but no one really likes each other." 
 Eight. "Craig said the problem with things is that everyone is always comparing everyone with everyone." 
 Seven. "I don't know what's wrong with me. It's like all I can do is keep writing this gibberish to keep from breaking apart." 
 Six. "I would die for you. But I won't live for you." 
 Five. "And I guess I realized at that moment that I really did love her. Because there was nothing to gain, and that didn't matter." 
 Four. "And even if somebody else has it much worse, that doesn't really change the fact that you have what you have. Good and bad." 
 Three. "I think the idea is that every person has to live for his or her own life and than make the choice to share it with other people." 
 Two. "Things change. And friends leave. Life doesn't stop for anybody." 
 One. "So, I guess we are who we are for alot of reasons. And maybe we'll never know most of them. But even if we don't have the power to choose where we come from, we can still choose where we go from there. We can still do things. And we can try to feel okay about them." 
  
 With that said, I guess the only thing keeping me from giving this book a total of five stars - aside from the fact that the word "incidentally" kept being use here and there - is my slight disappointment with the ending. It was such a massive and unexpected curve ball for me, and I honestly think that Chbosky could've wrapped Charlie's letters with a more poignant and heartwarming angle. One that would really knit the story into one thought that would be engraved in every reader's memory bank. One that would make people whisper excitedly to themselves, "Hey. I'm a wallflower." Quite honestly, my initial reaction to the last paragraph was, "... ... ... ... ... ... Buffering... ... ... ... ... ... Hold on, that's it?" I guess it didn't really strike me with much impact. It really could have been better. Nonetheless, Perks of Being a Wallflower has definitely left a good impression on me. 
 4 stars.

Not only is NPH's autobiography enlightening. It also has a certain characteristic flair, not to mention some legitimately poignant moments along with some great name-dropping. 
 It came as a surprise to me that I yet again found an amazing autobiographical narrative. I started with Amy Poehler's Yes Please earlier this month, read a couple books in between, then started this one. And at the time of finishing Poehler's book, it was my favorite autobiography. 
 No more. 
 To start with, the "choose your own adventure" format was fan-freakin'-tastic. I hate missing out on anything, so while I did flip through the pages when told to I always kept one finger back to mark my page, so I could read linearly. Cheating, maybe, but with good reason. There's some pages that don't have anything leading to it!  And even reading linearly, for the most part it stays in chronological order so it's not a terrible way to do it. Plus referring to himself as "you" is odd but fun but totally in line with the theme. 
 Next, Neil's witticism is absolutely hilarious without being over the top. I just recently read Stephen Colbert's I Am America and it was just too much after a while. Poehler's was by and large more serious, with little funny bits thrown in with funny pictures. Still hilarious, but not quite as catching. 
 There was just pure gold in this, and I actually lol'ed. Here's some of my favorites: 
 on page 79, when referring to his first gay hookup: On the plus side, you did have an orgasm, which, like Andy himself, is nice to come by. (See what he did there?) 
 on page 142, when discussing his costars on How I Met Your Mother: I think [Alyson Hannigan] was the heart of the show whereas Josh was the brains, Jason the spirit, Cobie the soul, and I was the cock. 
 on page 194, which had you dying of laughter (regarding NPH's journey to his new adorable twins): but alas, try and try as you might, you and David simply cannot get pregnant. You attempt everything. You stand on your heads, follow lunar cycles, try special diets, and have sexual relations in every conceivable position. Nothing. Is God punishing you for your lifestyle? Are you just naturally infertile? Impossible to know for sure. All that is certain is that neither of you is with child. 
 There's so many delicious moments too, where NPH reveals his nerd side. My favorite is him "squeeing" when he gets a compliment and then an offer to hangout from Sir Elton John. There's also the adorable bit about how when he first met David, he secretly kind of hoped he and his then-boyfriend would break up, so NPH could sneak in. Plus, the whole chapters about his kids were amazing. If anyone has ever doubted the ability for a gay couple to love and take care of their kids, all they need to do is read this book. The love and devotion for David and their twins (Gideon and Harper) just oozes off the page. It's a wonderful book full of funny and love and random bits about celebrities and random bits from celebrities. 
 This is the sort of book that, if you loved NPH already, you'll end up loving him even more, and if you disliked him/ignorant of him, will make you like him anyway.

This is the 2nd book in the Penton Legacy series and I'm getting pretty involved in the plot and the characters.

The book version of the town has it being a virtual ghost town, a textile mill town that has died out thanks to the textile industry moving overseas. A master vampire named Aidan Murphy has made it his new home and has brought the town back to life. 
 A pandemic flu has hit the world and a wreaked havoc on the elderly, sick and very young but scientist were quick to invent a vaccine for it and almost everyone in the world has been vaccinated against it. The Pandemic Vaccination has made the blood of anyone vaccinated with it poisonous to vampires which, of course, humans are unaware of. There are very few humans left who are unvaccinated so vampires are starving and fighting over the ones they can find...mostly drug addicts and the homeless who were too high or down and out to bother going and getting the vaccine. 
 A master vampire named Aidan Murphy has come up with a solution. He has built up a scathe, vampires bonded and loyal to each other, and has recruited humans to live in the town. He believes that humans should be treated as equals and with respect instead of as food as most vampires treat humans. He has taken unvaccinated humans from the streets and homeless shelters and helped them withdraw from drugs or helped them with whatever problem they had and then made them an offer to live in the tiny town of Penton for the exchange of blood with the vampires who live there. If they refuse, he simply erases their mind of their encounter with him and lets them live their lives but if they agree, they can have a great life in Penton. All humans are bonded to a scathe member which makes it impossible for other vampires outside the scathe to feed off of them. If they ever want to leave, he will erase their minds of their time in Penton and take them to wherever they want to live. It is a great setup and the town is doing well.

His son ran away from Matthias and avoided him for decades but Matthias learned that William was hiding out in Penton and he wants him back. It was just too soon to tell. 
 In this book, one of the humans whose husband was killed during one of Owen's attacks wanted to leave Penton so Mirren, the only other master vampire in the Penton scathe, took her to her desired location and erased her mind. He left her with plenty of money to start over again and then headed back towards Penton. He stopped at one of their safe houses along the way to get his day sleep but Matthias had people watching the house and six of them kidnapped him. 
 Mirren has a dark past. In his human life he was a warrior who fought most of his life. As a vampire, he worked for the Vampire Tribunal as their assassin until they asked him to kill a child. He was known as the Slayer because he always got his target, he tortured for information and he could kill twenty men with his sword or battle axe easily. He realized the Tribunal was more evil than the people he was hunting and faked his death and hid from them for a very long time until he hooked up with Aidan and his scathe and Matthias' intel exposed him.

 Matthias is keeping Mirren downstairs with his hands tied in silver which weakens a vampire and his cell has silver bars so there is no escape. Mirren is being starved.  William Ludlum, Matthias' son, is basically a genius. He can hack almost any computer system and is good with puzzles and architecture. I end up telling on myself or putting my foot in my mouth or offending someone. Glory is one of those. Mirren won't admit it but he likes her. He decides to sponsor her while she is in Penton which he has never done for any other human. He keeps to himself and not even Aidan knows much about him except he is a man of few words and he used to be the Slayer. Melissa drops Glory off at Mirren's house while he is in his day sleep and tells her that she will be staying with him until they find her a permanent house or she decides to leave. 
 Glory loves to cook and has a dream to be a chef or open her own restaurant one day. She borrows money from Melissa and insists on paying it back even though Melissa tries to explain to her that Mirren is rich and is sponsoring her. Glory will not allow anyone to pay her way. This is the staple of modern science fiction. I'm not sure how I feel about it being made into a movie. I just hope they do it some degree of justice.

A modern update to von Arnim's Enchanted April holds such possibility. This story tries to bring the characters and their personal trials into the 21st century, but the revisions aren't entirely successful. Strangely, in some ways it is too close to the original, and in others it has played too loosely. Perhaps it is the choice of which elements to keep pure and which to contemporize that do it a disservice. 
 My primary complaint is that the tone was erratic. One of the gifts of the original story is the languid, reflective air, even when contrasted by moments of drama. This is crafted by beautiful depictions of setting and contemplation, all with evocative language. Bowen's foursome is much less isolated, interacting with people all over the island, and that doesn't allow for the self-discovery or refreshment each sought in choosing this getaway. The rough edges of personality seem heightened here, and the backstories are awkwardly inserted. 
 One other significant change I found disheartening, though revealed early in the story, might be seen as a mild spoiler: the introduction of a male character to the group changes the dynamic. Too much of these women's lives -- even in the modernization -- is defined by their relation to men. Beverly is older and gay, but his presence seemed an almost formulaic way to update.  
 I realize this seems a game of comparison between this book and its inspiration, but that isn't the sole source of my dissatisfaction. On the contrary, were I evaluating this story on its own, I'd probably have even less patience with the characterizations and outcomes. 
 This has some lovely moments, and the book as a whole might be the diversion some readers need. Others, like this reader, might better find classic respite in a Italian villa.

I really enjoyed this book. The pace is fast and there's a lot of action. I don't usually like a lot of action, but Lee really made it work in Runner. Too often I feel like the author details it to death, to the point where it's almost impossible to follow what's actually happening. Here it was detailed without going overboard and it was all plausible. I also felt the pace was pretty perfect. It wasn't just Go, Go, Go, but more like Go, Go, Go, Pause, Go, Go, Go, Pause, etc. The story moved along quickly, with lots of action, but it took time with quieter moments where there was character development and plot reveals. 
 The main character, Sam Dryden, is very likable. He's a smart, caring, stand-up guy that always does the right thing. His experience in Special Forces makes him uniquely qualified to help Rachel escape her attackers and try to figure out the secrets that live in her head. Rachel was an intriguing character with lots of sides to her. My only complaint with her is that she almost always seemed much older than her eleven years. Martin Gaul, the man leading the hunt for Rachel and Dryden, is another interesting character - mostly despicable, but still a little sympathetic. 
 There were a lot of twists and turns in this book, perhaps the most surprising to me was that there is a large sci-fi element to the story. It's not a bad surprise, I just didn't expect it. Despite that, the story still seemed realistic in all its other aspects and contained enough surprises to keep me guessing the whole way. 
 While most chapters focused on Dryden, Rachel, or Gaul, there were other chapters that focused on Gaul's competitor, Hager, and those he was training. While those chapters were interesting and informative, they also contained perhaps the only thing I didn't care for in the book - the slightly graphic use of sex as motivation. Maybe it's just a guy thing, but I didn't quite see the need and it made me a little uncomfortable. However, since there were only a few examples of that, it didn't really hinder my enjoyment of the rest of the story. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Runner. It was suspenseful, fast paced, and action packed, but also smart and sweet. This looks to be the first book in a series based on Sam Dryden and I look forward to the next. I would recommend Runner to those who enjoy mystery, suspense, action, and a little dose of sci-fi.
