Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants. Certainly good advice, but unfortunately, Michael Pollan should have stopped there. 
 Ugh...what a huge disappointment. This is a perfect example of why journalists should not give nutritional advice or write these kinds of books. 
 Pollan starts out by stating the obvious, but then quickly learns what many nutritional professionals and public health advocates do, the obvious isn't sexy and it certainly doesn't make a bestseller. As a result the chapters that follow his iconic slogan are little more than poppy-cock for the masses. 
 I'm going to break this review down by sections, because in fairness, some were better than others. 
 Section I: The Age of Nutritionism - 1 star 
 I guess the first step in any straw man argument is to give it a name, in this case nutritionism. 
 The problem is like others before him, he argues against an opponent that never existed. 
 According to Pollan a bunch of questionable studies led some incompetent (if well-meaning) scientists to determine that saturated fat was bad. As a result the government developed anti-fat nutritional guidelines that the public embraced wholeheartedly, but that ultimately made them unhealthier. 
 He repeatedly points to these "nutritionists" (which he somehow lumps in with greedy capitalists and which almost feels like a derogatory label the way he uses it) that misled the public with their "junk science" and continue to do us all an injustice in their efforts to further our understanding of the nutritional sciences. 
 Interestingly, I happened to be a college student in the eighties studying, of all things, Nutritional Sciences (and while I usually avoid reading these types of books). As such I can tell you that his characterizations are incorrect and best and dishonest at worst. In the late seventies and early eighties there was a push toward limiting fats to 30 percent of total calories. It was further recommended that less than 10 percent of total calories should come from saturated fats based on the belief that it was related to CHD. 
 The merits of this recommendation have since come under fire and has spurred more research...because after all that is what science demands (that it constantly improves upon itself). But the important part of the discussion that is left out is that this was only one small part of the guidelines. The USDA also recommended that of the carbs ingested at least half those should be from complex carbs and not from processed sources. And they didn't stop there. They recommended eating one serving of fish at least two times a week. They recommended eating 2-3 servings each of fruits and veggies daily. They recommended limiting salt intake to under 2300 milligrams. They recommended eating a diversity of food. They recommended eating foods high in fiber. They recommended limiting sweets. Okay...so you get where I'm going with this. 
 However, as is so often the case, capitalists saw an opportunity and the food companies began a massive anti-fat campaign that would help to distort certain aspects of the USDA recommendations to the point that low-fat became the most important aspect of a healthy diet. Of course, even Pollan admits that people didn't cut out fat, they simply ate more low fat foods in addition to the fat they were already consuming. Mostly ultra-processed foods whose fat had been replaced with sugar and salt. 
 Bottom line, people didn't get fat because they followed the USDA dietary guidelines of the eighties which by the way with the exception of a few tweaks based on additional research and changing needs of society (and saturated fat has still not been completely vindicated), the recommendations have changed significantly. People got fat because they became ultra-consumers of the cheap and easy...just like they have become ultra-consumers of cheap and easy everything from clothes, to shoes, to electronics, to home decor. The West is a culture of excess everything. 
 Pollan further contends that "nutritionists," which by the way is a poorly defined and meaningless term then and now so I'm not exactly sure who he is referring to, were obsessed with isolating nutrients...again, totally not true. In fact, the food pyramid, despite its flaws, was designed to encourage consumption of a wide range of foods to ensure that Americans ingested a diversity of nutrients. Vitamin supplements were also discouraged and seen as inferior to eating real food as nutritional scientists and dieticians have always acknowledged and appreciated the symbiotic relationship of various nutrients within food as well as those that exist between various foods in the diet. 
 Pollan then blasts the science itself, pointing out all the shortcomings innate in nutritional research, shortcomings that those who actually study nutrition appreciated long before Pollan pointed it out. But just because something is difficult to study doesn't mean we shouldn't try. It also doesn't necessarily invalidate the research. Ironically, Pollan himself has no problem citing these flawed studies later on in support of points he is trying to make. And again, Pollan's misrepresentation is huge. Anyone who attempts to study nutrition understands the difficultly in isolating the effect of any one nutrient. And yet we somehow know more now than we did say 50 years ago. The fact that we aren't any healthier as a nation isn't necessarily a reflection of what we know or don't know. Using Pollan's own argument about the futileness of trying to tease out all the cofounding factors. He seems to suggest that our anti-fat campaign, which led to an increase in the amount of highly processed carbs being eaten is responsible for the rise in obesity and diseases like diabetes...and he may be right...or partially right...or completely wrong. It is widely accepted that the obesity epidemic is probably the result of several cofounding factors. 
 Anyway, I cringed reading this first section. I expected so much more from Pollan. Ironically, despite disagreeing with his characterizations and the logic employed, I agree with a number of his conclusions. In short, I agree that we need to look at foods as greater than the sum of their parts. I also agree that science can have limitations and can be flawed. In that sense, a recommendation is just that a best guess based on what we think we know at any given point and people need to understand this.  
 Section II: The Western Diet and the Disease of - 3 stars 
 I felt this was the strongest of the three sections. Whatever the culprit, it does appear that the Western Diet contributes to poor health outcomes. 
 Pollan makes some good points about the food chain and our interconnectedness with our environment. Ironically, the most recent panel of experts that propose changes to the USDA guidelines for the first time ever suggested that the new revised guidelines should take into consideration not only the internal impact of our eating habits but also the external factors. To Pollan's credit, I think his efforts have played a crucial role in this type of thinking. 
 His argument for whole foods is sound. If the nutritional research to date seems to agree on anything it is that whole unprocessed foods are generally superior. 
 His argument from quality to quantity also has some merit, though I think there is still some debate about the significance. For example, there are several studies (probably flawed if you bought into section one of Pollan's book) that suggest industrially produced produce is lower in nutrition than its locally grown, organic counterpart. However, the relevance of this in a society where our food options are endless, is debatable as it may be a non-factor. The reality is in the US we have access to superior nutrition. We might not always make the right choices, but given a little vigilance 99.5% of us should be able to meet our nutritional needs even if the products we are eating are nutritionally inferior, not organic, and purchased from the grocery store. 
 The whole omega-3 section is a little weak. He spends the entire first third of the book telling us why these nutritional studies are flawed and can't be trusted and why we should not be isolating nutrients and then seems to put the omega-3s on some sort of nutritional pedestal, repeatedly referencing the science to make his case.  
 Section III: Getting Over Nutritionism - 2 stars 
 While I applaud and agree with many of Pollan's recommendations, I have a feeling they were recommendations that could only be made by a man in his unique position. 
 Unfortunately, I think many of Pollan's ideas are shortsighted and impractical for the average family. They look good on paper but are too idealistic as to really make a difference. 
 Pollan's plan to buy local in season produce, to cook more and eat together paints a nostalgic picture that panders to our natural bias. But really... 
 Listen, I'm a part-time working mother of four. And unlike the families Pollan references who supposedly spend less than 10% of their income on food, we spend almost 2-3 times as much on food as we do on our mortgage. In fact, food is by far our biggest expense. I also only work part-time which gives me significantly more flexibility than those moms out there working full-time. I have a degree in nutritional sciences. I teach a personal training certification course. I'm currently pursing an advanced certificate in Sport's Nutrition. I actually like to cook. I totally embrace and accept the importance of eating and living well. Heck, in my free time I run a facebook page dedicated to healthy living. I read Medscape articles for fun. But he is really setting the bar high. 
 Seriously. I see how the average American eats and it isn't pretty. And I know from talking to them that most of them want to do better. But they are struggling to meet the demands of their job and family. They need real world solutions for their world and while some of Pollan's suggestions may be helpful most don't even come close to reaching the people who need his help the most. 
 At one point Pollan claims that you wouldn't be reading this book if you already got it...but I would argue he's wrong. This book most certainly speaks to the people who already get "it," but offers little for the people who really, really need it. In fact, I would be willing to bet that the majority of people who bought this book are college educated, or at least educated, do not have diabetes, don't regularly eat at McDonalds, and aren't obese. And if you are, I'm not sure this book offers substantially more than the government's nutritional guidelines he was so quick to criticize.  
 So by all means...Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants. 
 As far as the book...if you already get it and are interested in reinforcing your commitment to eating healthy, then maybe this is worth your time. If you're currently struggling and looking for real life strategies to overcome obstacles, go somewhere else. 
 I should add, despite not "loving" this book, I am a fan of Pollan and what he is trying to do. His common sense approach to diet is admirable and I think he has done a lot of good and reached a lot of people.

This review is written after a re-read, but my initial review gave this book 4 stars. Rereading it I did not enjoy it as much. I read it when it first came out because the concept sounded really awesome-- using creepy, real photographs to convey a story. And while the idea is still cool, as a slightly older reader I see that the story is actually kind of choppy. It throws things in there to include the photograph as part of the story. I am also still disappointed that the story itself isn't creepy or horror. It's basically just paranormal YA. Sure, there are some "scary" points, but unless you are a super wimp you won't find it remotely terrifying. I want a home of peculiar children and old creepy photographs to be scary, you know? Also, the children themselves really only have a small superpower which labels them as peculiar. They don't have any other traits to make them peculiar and definitely act like normal children/teens. Overall the book is marketed strongly on creepy photographs and peculiar children, and it doesn't deliver much more than the surface of that. 
 The plot is simple-- I don't think it leaves any surprises. Socially outcast boy investigates grandfather's mysterious past. Turns out those old goofy photographs of floating girls and the like were real, and he is able to go through a time loop to where the children reside. He makes friends with these people, finds out he too is peculiar as he can see the monsters that are after the children. One of those monsters steals Miss Peregrine, the children's headmistress, and they have to go and save her. They do, but in the process Miss Peregrine is stuck as a bird, so the next book's plot will involve fixing that. The romance is awkward. Really, Emma was Jacob's grandfather's sweetheart, and he has the hots for her? His feelings also spawn from nowhere, though I guess he is a teenage boy who was a social outcast in his real life, so any girl who gives him the time of day is beautiful. I bought the sequel to this book some time ago and waited until the release of the movie to give this book a reread. I think I will try to read the 2nd, but I'm not super excited to go into it, only mildly curious.

Leave it to the wayward and whimsical Roald Dahl to write his memoirs in a very unorthodox way: a collection of memories that prove he didn't only have a vivid imagination, but always had a way of looking at the world that would become golden in writing children's books. 
 My favourite scene without a doubt is about the candy store where they sell liquorice bootlaces which they are meant to believe are made from rat's blood. 
 "Every ratcatcher in the country', the father had said, 'takes his rats to the Liquorice Bootlace Factory, and the manager pays tuppence for each rat. Many a ratcatcher has become a millionaire by selling his dead rats to the Factory." 
 And from his description of the lady who runs this sweet-shop, it isn't hard to imagine some of the gruesome characters he would write about later. 
 Her name was Mrs Pratchett. She was a small skinny old hag with a moustache on her upper lip and a mouth as sour as a green gooseberry. She never smiled. She never welcomed us when we went in, and the only times she spoke were when she said things like, 'I'm watchin' you so keep yer thievin' fingers off them chocolates!' Or 'I don't want you in 'ere just to look around! Either you forks out or you gets out!' 
 But by far the most loathsome thing about Mrs Pratchett was the filth that clung around her. Her apron was grey and greasy. Her blouse had bits of breakfast all over it, toast-crumbs and tea stains and splotches of dried egg-yolk. It was her hands, however, that disturbed us most. They were disgusting. They were black with dirt and grime. They looked as though they had been putting lumps of coal on the fire all day long. And do not forget please that it was these very hands and fingers that she plunged into the sweet-jars when we asked for a pennyworth of Treacle Toffee or Wine Gums or Nut Clusters or whatever. 
 Is this an extraordinary autobiography? No, but's entertaining and fun to read if you like Dahl's writing. 3,5 stars, upped to 4 because this is the whimsical Roals Dahl we're talking about.

Rating Clarification: This book deserves a 5 star rating for the graceful writing and realistic depictions of real human beings with real life concerns (see also: poverty, marriage problems, children problems, and, above all, environmental problems). I've lowered the rating to account for the pacing of the first 200 or so pages. The beginning of the book (minus Dellarobia's discovery of the "miracle" on the mountain) was dreadfully slow, and it left me questioning my willingness to continue on. I'm glad I soldiered on because the second half was much better - though the ending seemed abrupt - it came on too fast with a flurry of revelations which brought about too much change for my idea of a happy ending. Perhaps, that's the point: there is no happy ending. With the threat of global warming - so much is changing unseen and the change will threaten everything and everyone. 
 But I digress. 
 Flight Behavior was my first introduction to Barbara Kingsolver; however, her best-sellers have been on my vast and never-ending "to-read" list for quite some time. I'm glad that I was introduced to the author in this way because I'll be sure to continue on to her other titles in a much more timely manner now :) Kingsolver is an expert, weaving flight metaphors throughout the entire novel. It particularly pertains to the main character, Dellarobia Turnbow, who finds herself in the midst of a controversy surrounding millions of monarch butterflies that have migrated from Mexico to roost in her husband's family's woods. However beautiful the spectacle is, it is unnatural and a subject of concern for entomology expert Ovid Byron who believes that the butterflies are a sign that climate change could be destroying the environment as we know it. In the midst of evaluating her life's choices, her marriage, and her faith, Dellarobia becomes the spokesperson for the butterflies and a research assistant for Byron. The end of the novel is bursting with change - not all for the best. 
 As a woman, I'm kind of repulsed that I am saying this - but - for all Cub's shortcomings, I thought that he was somewhat endearing. Yes, he's a horrible mama's boy, but I thought that he had evolved as a character throughout the book - becoming bolder and more mature. I was disappointed in part by the ending in this regard. I won't go into absurd detail for fear of spoiling a good read, but I was left unsatisfied - you know, apart from all the horrible predictions of climate change that will ravage Earth and all of the species that live dependent on its resources. That wasn't exactly a feel good take away, but, like the book points emphasizes, you can't see or recognize what you don't know. Knowledge is power. Go hug and tree and watch a butterfly while they are still here because this book has made it abundantly clear that they might not be here forever - or even tomorrow. 
 I wish I could be more eloquent in my review, but rest assured, there are plenty of reviews that summarize the book beautifully. It was, indeed, a good read, and I want to thank Barbara Kingsolver and Harper Collins for this advanced read opportunity. I'll recommend it to other with the caveat that readers should be ready to trudge through some slow spots for a book that rushes to take form like a violent, unexpected summer storm. Those interested in environmental concerns, farming, quirky women characters, and Appalachia would do well for themselves to make notice of Flight Behavior's release date: November 6, 2012.

It took me an exceptionally long time to read this book. I picked it up while pregnant and working with a midwife (CNA) who is also a really good friend. I set this book aside a couple of times. I think my life got in the way more than this book was boring but I admit that I did have a hard time getting into it. Once I dedicated time to finishing it, it was a page turner for me. 
 On an icy winter night in an isolated house in rural Vermont, a seasoned midwife named Sibyl Danforth takes desperate measures to save a baby's life. She performs an emergency cesarean section on a mother she believes has died of a stroke. But what if Sibyl's patient wasn't dead and Sibyl inadvertently killed her? As Sibyl faces the antagonism of the law, the hostility of traditional doctors, and the accusations of her own conscience, Midwives engages, moves and transfixes us as only the very best novels ever do. 
 Narrated by Connie, a present day doctor and the now-adult daughter of Sybil (she was a 14-year-old during the events), Midwives moves back and forth in time, fitting vital pieces of information about what happened that terrible night like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle into its complicated plot. As Connie looks back on the events that changed her mother's entire world and which shaped her own life in significant ways, she is still trying to understand what happened and why.
Lovely contemporary romance with some great characters!

I picked this book up from the library knowing nothing about it. I liked the idea that sign language might be used. I did not know this was one of Oprah's book club picks until I was writing the review and I did not know that it was re-imagining of Hamlet (which I have not read.) 
 The main character is a boy with no vocal ability to speak. He has enriching relationships with his family and has exceptional bonds with the family dogs. Although I did enjoy the portion of the story where Edgar runs away, by and large this book was tediously long. Had I not been listening to it as an audiobook, I doubt I would have finished it. 
 Throughout the book, the author provided pages of information about dog breeding, and the importance of certain features in the Sawtelle dogs, which created the expectation that this information would become key to the narrative - in other words, I expected that the Sawtelle's dogs' breeding would enable them to make an independent choice at a crucial plot moment, but it never happened. It was very repetitive in regards to the dog training too(yes, I get it, the dogs were well trained!) most dog people know that but what difference did it make to go into such detail? I expected Fourte, the boy's dog, to play a key role in the ending, but it never happened. 
 The book felt like several books in one. The first fourth of the book felt like a Steinbeck novel, then it abruptly changes - part Call of the Wild, part Fugitive, part ghost story, all wrapped up in a coming-of-age story of loss and redemption. It is definitely not an uplifting book. 
 If you are looking for a way to kill a lot of time and are in the mood to look deeply under the surface of a book, then this book is for you. If you want to sit and relax while you enjoy a good narrative story, I don't recommend this book. It takes work to appreciate it.

 Fury was SUCH a wonderful book! 
 I was actually a bit nervous since all the reviewers on GR rated it 2-4 stars. 
 It's still a mystery to me as to why, because i LOVED it! 
 Fury has never known compassion or love. He's spent his life in a cell, chained and abused by humans. The one woman he allowed himself to trust betrayed him. Now he's free and set on vengeance. He vows to end her life but when she's finally in his grasp, harming her is the last thing he wants to do to the sexy little human. 
 Ellie is horrified to discover the pharmaceutical company she works for is doing illegal experiments. Company scientists have spliced human and animal DNA, creating exotic new species. One such "experiment" captures her heart and she'll do anything to save him--even if he hates her for it. 
 But loving Fury is one thing...taming him is another. 
 I have been wanting to start this series for SUCH A LONG TIME. I think it's been 2 years now. Finally got some sense into myself and brought it. 
 Let me tell ya something - after the 1st chapter i called myself a genius for picking it up. 
 A lot of readers have been saying this is extremely similar to Laura Leigh's Breeds series. I don't know as i haven't read them. But i think it's mean saying Fury is a poor copy version of it. 
 I haven't read anything quite like Fury. So i found the plot very refreshing and new. 
 It was awesome and one of the reasons i loved it so much. 
 It's good to read something unique once in a while. 
 What i thought of Fury?: 
 Fury has that name for a reason! He is filled with rage on everyone who inflicted pain upon him and his kind and who betrayed him. Who gained his trust and then crushed it right in front of his face. 
 I felt emotional reading about his past and the pain he injured when he was locked up and experimented on. 
 Let's not forget he is NOT human! Only partly. He is also canine (or something like that - can't remember the name but it's some sort of animal). And OMG do i wish i could have my own Fury to do the things he does in bed! YUM! 
 What i thought of Ellie?: 
 I thought she was a fantastic heroine! She was very brave, caring and tenderhearted. Fully human of course. 
 I don't remember ever being annoyed with her. 
 She had suffered a bit from bullying and people who couldn't accept her for who she was. 
 However, Fury changed that and showed her just how beautiful he thought she was, and that her looks didn't even matter to him. 
 This book had some flaws, don't get me wrong. I felt like the characters were sometimes repeating the same things all over again and that bored me a little. I admit a skipped a tiny bit of those parts. 
 But Fury was action packed and i didn't want to stop reading. In fact i stayed way past bed time cause i couldn't force myself to put it down - yes it was that good. 
 I even didn't go to university for the day because the urge to finish it and find out what will happen next was very strong. Too strong to resist. I got in shitload of trouble for that. 
 Overall... 
 Fury was an AMAZING book that i could not put down and i thought about constantly. The characters and plot are realistic and epic. Sex scenes were freaking HOT! The ending was very cute and a great HEA! 
 CAN.NOT.WAIT.FOR.BOOK.2! 
 Definitely pick it up, ladies!

"Happiness comes from moving toward something. When you run away, ofttimes you bring your misery with you." 
 I had a feeling going into this one that it would break my heart and I was right. Something had to go wrong eventually. Well, I mean, stuff had already gone wrong, but something else was going to go wrong. And it did. There was plenty to break my heart here. There was also plenty to love. 
 It's no secret that Royce is my favorite character and this installment did nothing to lessen him for me. His character has been building through the series, his layers being revealed one by one, and we get yet another layer (or more) here. His story is extremely sad, but so real. And that's what I love about him. Honestly, I have a hard time putting into words just how much I like Royce. 
 Hadrian and Royce are separated for most of this installment, each dealing with different aspects of the same problem. Hadrian's portions were quite entertaining, for the most part. There were darker, harsher moments, because what he was trying to do was tearing him apart, but so many little things happened that made his story quite humorous. Which is excellent. A story can't always be dark; that's just not how life works. 
 I don't know how Sullivan manages to build every single character so well, but he does. All of the side characters are brilliant and either have me loving or hating them. Sometimes both. Nimbus really shone here and he was hilarious. Seriously. Which makes me curious about his past. Hopefully we get more about that in the next installment. 
 Another new favorite is Sir Breckton. The guy is pretty much perfect, but not in a bad way. He was just great. I really want to see more of him in the last book. 
 And of course there is Arista. She isn't as involved in this one, which makes sense if you've read The Emerald Storm. But she manages to have some good scenes and make a difference. She has probably grown on me the most through the course of the books. 
 Modina and Amilia each have important roles to play here. And I really like both of these women. Modina more than Amilia, probably, but both of them have their moments. And some of those things are brilliantly executed. 
 The plot really gets amped up here, taking us to a new level. Most of the questions that have been building through the series are yet to be answered, but the setup for the conclusion is excellent. The stakes are high, higher than ever, and I'm ready to see what happens. The subtlety with which Sullivan is able to weave his story honestly amazes me. The smallest things done or said books ago come back time and again with huge impact. Piecing all of that together is so much fun. 
 The ending of this shattered me. It tore my heart out and broke it into a million pieces. What will happen next? I really have no idea. 
 I was going to pause for a day between books, but I don't think I can keep myself from starting that final journey. I need to know what happens.

And I Darken started out so strong and then dwindled into typical YA. Lada was a badass, a girl who had no qualms about hurting whoever stood in her way. She did not turn away from torture displays and was not particularly bothered by gore. She was a girl that I was 100% amped to root for. She maintained this personality for perhaps 50% of the book. 
 Then she abruptly changed. No more ruthlessness or vengeance-seeking or scheming. Suddenly she's in love with the boy-king and loses all of her awesomeness that makes her awesome. Then it becomes a typical YA love story where nothing happens for 2/3 of the plot and then suddenly DRAMA! DRAMA WE DON'T NEED! But drama we welcome because the drama that should actually be happening isn't happening at all. So you just kind of shrug your shoulders and accept what you can get. 
 I guess I just don't really understand why we needed to add anything about Vlad the Impaler at all. Literally nothing in this book ties back to that, so it seemed unnecessary to tack that name on. I kept holding out hope that Lada would show herself to be as ruthless as her father, but no such luck there. Murad was the only one crazy enough to do stuff like that and it's only briefly glossed over in the beginning of the book to let us know she's basing it on the real guy. 
 It just isn't enough to keep you interested the whole way through. It's a fairly hefty book but truly you could skip most of the middle section without missing anything, simply because nothing happens. Lots of talking. Radu is jealous of Lada, and Lada is jealous of Radu. Miscommunication. Random bits about how apparently amazing Mehmed is, but I don't really see why. It just became very meh. The only reason I'm rating it three stars instead of two is because I loved Lada in the beginning of the story.

Based on the title and cover, Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children did not seem like my cup of tea at all. It came across as more of a horror story, so I hadn't been meaning to read it at all. After seeing some videos of Ransom and Tahereh though (they really are adorable together) and reading some positive reviews by fellow bookbloggers, I guess it kind of lingered in the back of my mind and I even ended up having a dream about it. 
 Well, I had a dream about some children in an old house. Seen as how my subconscious appeared to be drawn to this idea, I decided to follow suit and give Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children a chance. 
 At first I was quite curious to discover these peculiar children. I wasn't entirely grasped by those first few pages but held onto that curiosity for as long as I could. Unfortunately, it quickly dissipated seen as how 1/3rd of this novel consist of seemingly endless build-up. Once the story finally started going somewhere, I couldn't really be bothered anymore and just wanted the book to be over. 
 The addition of old (and at times slightly unnerving) pictures between the written pages was something unique, but in the end I don't feel it was necessary. I could imagine what the pictures looked like perfectly fine from Jacob's descriptions. 
 Only when I discovered that they were all authentic images and not modern fakes made to look old, did they regain some of their worth. (The clown twins with the coil was most disturbing to me - how is that a real picture? Creepy.) 
 The second half is considerably better than the first. Thanks to an at least sort of unexpected plot revelation, the end managed to somewhat salvage my impression of the novel. But in its entirety Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children lived up to my initial impression of it: not my cup of tea. 
 The main reason why I couldn't get into this story is the unlikeability of the protagonist, Jacob. He appears to be a mere tool to tell this story instead of an actual character. On the rare occasions where he does display an ounce of personality, he comes off as a spoiled brat, a whiner and just an all-round dull individual. This is kind of the point I guess, but for me it missed its mark. 
 Riggs seems to have thought that the way you write a realistic character is to give them as many flaws as a non-fictional person. But to me - in this case - it rendered the protagonist very very unlikeable. 
 The romance between him and Emma was completely unnecessary and actually quite inappropriate. This is one of the reasons I feel the story would better have been told by a younger protagonist (let's say 12 or so) and written towards children instead of young adults, giving Emma and Jacob a profound connection without having them randomly sucking face here and there. To me, (someone who loves romantic stories!), this was quite off-putting. 
 I had expected a timeless setting, loads of mystery, a dash of horror and most of all: a boundless originality. What I got was an at time foulmouthed tale framed in boringly normal modern times with a romance that should have never been. 
 I can't say it's bad, per se (I can certainly understand why some people love it), but I personally did not enjoy reading it at all - thus: 2 stars.

"A girl who sees murders in her dreams, murders that happen in real life" 
 See reviews first on my blog! 
 This is a story told in duel perspectives by two characters Nina and Warren. 
 Nina was adopted by her mom at ten months old and soon thereafter they moved to Vermont where they have lived a normal life. Except for the part where Nina has seen somebody else in her dreams since she was little. Things were pretty normal in her dreams, but one night things turned sinister and she has never been the same since. This is when she started calling the person in her dreams the Thief because of what he did to others that was so calculated and covered that he would never get caught. 
 Then we have Warren who was Nina's childhood best friend, but they grew apart when Nina started acting different. 
 "I'll do my best to protect Nina from her obsession, her nightmares, but I won't be pulled in." 
 With Warren's help Nina is able to start feeling better about what she's seen and thinks that maybe she isn't so crazy after all. Not only do these two find out where the thief lives. Things really start to take a turn though when they go on a road trip and Nina starts forming a plan on how she plans to deal with this thief and to stop her dreams forever. It sounded so simple to do, until she learns how she knows the thief and how he just might not be as sinister as her dreams make him seem. 
 "The key is to pretend to see him the way he sees himself. Not a monster, but a boyfriend, a son, a brother who just happens to kill strangers now and then." 
 This story had me on the edge of my seat throughout the whole thing, not only did it keep me up at night because of how creepy it was, but I even had to take a bit of a break from it for a few days and then come back from it because of how creeped out I got. The best way I can think of describing this book is do you remember the show Medium where Patricia Arquette was the main star who would see things happen to people in her dreams? This was like that except think more of when the daughter started having the same types of dreams, and how scary it was for her to see those things. It was like that, except instead of it being multiple people it's just one person who Nina has always seen for as long as she can remember. 
 "The boy's inner voice isn't snarky or snide. It's flat, assessing the terrain like he's a soldier on a mission." 
 This person she has seen change for a little boy, to a man, she seen him fight in a war and make it home safely and then one day he kills someone and covers it up. Then it happens again and again, each one cautious so he's never caught. But then you also seem him with his family and it's hard to believe that he could ever do those things. 
 As for the friendship between Warren and Nina, I loved it. Warren thought Nina needed help, but the closer they got to each other again he realized that she wasn't crazy or making things up. That this was something that was real and if they could find a way to stop the thief, Nina would get a good sleep and no one else would die at the hands of the thief. 
 If you want a YA thriller that will keep you wanting to know what happened, while scaring you then this is the book for you.

If you have been an avid reader of the Harry Potter series you will notice the shifting of tones from bright to dark, darker and the darkest respectively from each series. Apparently, just within two (2) chapters of this Harry Potter series I became aware of the gloomy atmosphere it created. And that certain experience was and still is indescribable.  Oh by the way, prior to the movie adaption of this film, I would like to give a small statement. I remember watching the film but as a huge fan of the book, I must be very unrealistic. I knew there have been a lot of information left out in the film adaption. There were few parts of the book that I wish have been included in the film because it could have made the story richer, but I won't go into detail so I don't give away any of the film's changes and this is a book review, as I remember. :p 
 All the same, let us start with the awesome heart-thrilling story of the fifth book shall we? 
 If you can recall in its predecessor book: The Goblet of Fire. Harry Potter was in the state where people thought he was just another boy who cried wolf. (And I shall boast, that is the best among the rest example of Harry's condition.:p). Anyhow, Harry thought his life cannot be at any worst circumstances but it did. While he was strolling around near his house in the Muggle world two (2) dementors attacked Harry and his fat cousin, Dudley. And of course, he defended himself (using magic, obviously) but he was underage, as a result he received a letter from the Ministry of Magic (the Government of the Wizard World) saying that he has done something against the law. Consequently, Harry with all the help of his friends, Sirius and the secret organization: The Anti-Voldemort or Order of the Phoenix (ruled by Professor Albus Dumbledore) members, he had successfully convinced the government that he was innocent because he just did magic just to defend himself from grave danger. Unfortunately, some of the authorities believe that Harry was just dealing with the same feelings of teen angst, emerging love that any ordinary teen finds stressful and consuming and that he was just a bigheaded-know-it-all-freak. The government is covertly not convinced with how Harry Potter was taught in Hogwarts as well, heck, they believe that Hogwarts is not ruled properly by Albus Dumbledore so they decided to ruin everything (that's the way I see it) and created a High Inquisitor (A job taken also by a ministry of magic, Dolores Umbridged) at Hogwarts. 
 Order of the Phoenix is the best Harry Potter series for me (so far) for various reasons. First, there are numerous amazing characters and some old characters have unlocked their personalities throughout the story. You will love them all and you will also learn to develop hatred to some characters as well which is truly remarkable. Second, this book has a lot of breathtaking battle scenes! And lastly, this is also the Harry Potter series that actually caused me to get so teary because of the heartfelt portrayals of friendship and family and Harry Potter's relationship with his friends and Sirius Black. I don't want to spoil the story for you guys, but I am going to miss Sirius Black. :( 
 I love Siruis Black. 
 Note: It's funny how I learn to love different characters per series. haha! As I bear in mind that I was inlove with Harry Potter (of course) in the first series, (*No one for the second series), Professor R.J Lupin for the third, Neville Longbottom (4th) and Sirius Black for the last. hoho.

You know that a character has a certain shaped chin and a voice like a saw, or whatever the case might be.

As I was reading I was really struck by how fun and genius the concept was. It's simple, yet makes a lot of sense. How hasn't this been done yet, I wondered? And yet, this is a fun, fresh story.

 "When someone needs to be protected, does it matter who they are?" 
 "What will it take for you to understand that freedom is fragile, and we must never forget what man, or woman, is capable of."

Holden is a bit of a cowboy, a little immature, but a capable captain who tries to always make the best of any situation. Miller is an alcoholic, depressed homicide investigator who has very little faith in humanity left. They come together in the midst of an investigation into a mystery that spans the entire book, and manage to teach each other some important lessons along the way. What is the price of justice? When is it okay to bypass protocol and act on self-preservation instincts? This book had fascinating insights into how Earth may begin populating the rest of the solar system and the ways in which our choices on where and how to live in that greater system would divide humanity's priorities. I'm really looking forward to reading the rest of the series, and to see it brought to life on screen.

You know what? I know the globe worships Brandon Sanderson, and I must admit he is a good writer, but boy does he take his sweet time getting to the point. 
 I just can't. It's a massive book turnoff for me when I start to space out while waiting for things to develop in the plot. Chalk it down to writing style preference, and although I like Brandon Sanderson's world-building, I don't like his writing style. There just isn't enough to keep me on my toes for a book a book sporting this kind of page count. And it is impressive... 
 The concept was beautiful I must admit. A band of thieves, some of them who shouldn't even exist join forces to try and overthrow a tyrant who rules over a world filled with ash, misery and hate with an iron fist of cruelty. Working the ash fields as the beating heart of the entire Empire are the poor skaa, the slaves. The setting was taken from the old American south, with the barracks, field work, beatings, and 'masters'. The masters ware few, the slaves were many but fear and pain breed ignorance and superstition needed to keep people in line. 
 Masters are gifted with Lord Ruler's powers, as a thank you for their services all those years ago and the masters guard those jealously. If a master would take a skaa woman, after he was done with her he would have her killed, to ensure that there would be no child, no bastard, no halfbreed. Even a concept of a halfbreed is dangerous. The poor and the enslaved do not need someone like them developing any hope. But like everywhere, there are the few that manage to survive. 
 That leads us to the band of misfits and thieves that are the best in their field because of that power. Their leader Kelsier and Vin the sweet girl just beginning to understand who and what she truly is. 
 See what I mean? It sounds so good, and honestly it is very good, just boring at times. I felt like every powerful moment was diluted with inconsequential conversation and the sheer amount of time that passed between two important events. 
 What didn't help the story any was the fact that it was PG13. I am not complaining about the absences of scenes of a sexual nature, rather than that connection with adulthood. It was all so smooth and cushioned at moments and that is simply not the way life works. Especially in a world so dark and twisted as this. 
 Would I recommend this to other people? Yes I would. Just not my cuppa; and although it was good I won't finish the series any time soon.

I really enjoyed this read a lot - it's been on my to-read shelf for far too long and I'm glad that I finally got around to it :). As it's often the case with books that have had many readers in the past, there is a lot of pressure associated with reviewing this one - I want to do it well (also for the purpose of discussion with my friends who've already read it). So here I go... 
 This is quiet an original BDSM story - I am new to Cherise Sinclair, so I am definitively excited to see what else she has penned, but I'm getting ahead of myself - back to my point regarding originality. We're in the country side, Jessica is on her way home from an unsatisfying date, her car breaks down and she ends up in Master Z's quarter, in more ways than one. She's new to BDSM and also new to some feelings that reside deep inside her. Here is where the novel develops a little differently from what I've read before - these are adult characters who are real and at times a little nutty. The novel is very sexual, very focussed on BDSM play and not the fluff that more often than not comes with it. Don't get me wrong, sometimes I enjoy great revelations, deep thought-provoking novels and yes, sometimes when it's a really rainy day I may even enjoy reading about a damsel in distress. But here's the thing - if you want good BDSM fiction, a quick and naughty read, if you are entertained by aspects that BDSM erotica is mainly supposed to be about (at least in my opinion), this read is for you. 
 Sinclair's writing is solid, her characters are easy to remember (hey, I even remembered their names *without* checking and that doesn't happen often at all) because they have a personality - you don't need to like them, I don't think Sinclair is trying hard for readers to do so, you just have to go with the flow and take the story as it comes and enjoy it as a whole - again just not a lot of fluff here. Again, what I want to highlight here is Sinclair isn't trying so hard that things become stiff and fake - it's easy, natural, again what makes a good read for me. 
 But I had one problem with the book which is why it's four stars not five and it's gonna be difficult to explain as it's been discussed by many but I want to present it at a different angle - the story, though not particularly fast paced, is about 50 pages too short in my opinion. I'm not exactly saying that about the beginning, initially it felt very fast but I just went with it and afterall Jessica is an adult making her own choices and Zachary wants her and acts upon it - I think that's all there is to it. However, I am more addressing the scenes where Jessica shows her concern for other subs and the fact that there are some pretty shitty Doms running around Club Shadowlands (just a couple I know but still) - I felt that this could have been explored in a little more detail, the scenes felt rushed to me and also it felt a little forced when everything else was quite natural. 
 That's it, oh wait, one last thing... 
 ;)

This book wasn't nearly as bad as the reviews suggest. The story was fairly enjoyable, and Wendig's style is a bit haphazard. But that's okay. 
 I think a lot of the criticism of this book had to do with the fact it's not really about any of the main characters people were expecting to read about. And I can understand that. People want to know what Han, Luke, and Leia got up to after the destruction of the Death Star II. Not Snap Wexley. But really I was fine with getting a story about peripheral characters. It's a big galaxy, after all. 
 The other reason for a lot of criticism was because of the inclusion of a gay character. Really it wasn't a big deal and didn't make any difference to the story at all. In fact, one might wonder why it needed to be brought up at all. The revelation definitely felt shoehorned. It comes when Jas randomly (and in the middle of a rather tense situation) decides to tell Sinjir it's cool if they get together at some point, to which Sinjir replies that he's into men. This was so random to me because at no time do we ever have any indication that Jas would be interested in Sinjir. And she brings it up at such a weird time, interrupting him when she thinks he's about to bring it up himself. But why would he? They're in the middle of busting a big mission. It just felt awkward. An earlier implication that Sinjir is gay comes when he's telling Norra about an Imperial he interrogated. Sinjir says he was "beautiful." I think we got the picture at that point what Sinjir thinks about dudes, but Wendig unnecessarily wants to make it all too clear by bringing the subject up at the weirdest time.  
 So does the author have an ax to grind (which is frankly something I really dislike in my book/movies/whatever)? Well, I might've said no if it was just Sinjir  we're talking about. But Wendig also includes a lesbian couple and mentions in another part randomly that a character has two fathers.  So, yeah, given those three separate references, it really did kind of feel like he wanted to drill it in that, "hey, the SW universe has gay characters in it, so get used to it." Okay, cool, but you don't have to be so heavy-handed about it. Okay, maybe it wasn't really "heavy-handed," but it seemed so obviously ax-grindy. Personally I don't care about any romantic elements in my Star Wars, not even Han and Leia really. I mean, I understand we have to create a new generation of Skywalkers/Jedi/What-have-you, but it's not why I'm tuning in is all I'm saying. Just keep it PG-13, and we'll be cool. 
 All in all, I enjoyed the story and will definitely read Life Debt. In fact, I've heard it's really good, and I'm looking forward to it because I hear there's a really cool twist.

I've read several novels in my life, and through those indulging occasions, I've been exposed to several writing techniques, some of them are effective and shamefully, some of them are not. This novel, 'It's Kind of a Funny Story' was written effectively though the first-hand familiarity of the author, Ned Vizzini (or Edison Price Vizzini). More accurately, Vizzini suffered from depression, spending time in a psychiatric ward in his early 20s and authoring several works about the illness (and under those days of confinement, he allegedly wrote It's Kind of a Funny Story). And clearly, nobody nobody will understand depression unless they went through it. Truly unfortunate, the great Vizzini was found dead in his native Brooklyn, New York after an apparent suicide from a fall, aged 32. [Yardley, William (December 20, 2013). "Ned Vizzini, 32, Dies; Wrote Teenage Novels". New York Times. 12/21/13] *goosebumps*. And so, many writers like Vizzini felt the urge to write about what he actually saw, what he knew, what he have essentially experienced, capturing the readers hearts (like mine). If it wasn't for writers like him, we would all have been short of understanding specific social, human, psychological and cultural issues or even pastimes. In fact, perhaps we could've gone into a complete oblivion. 
 It's Kind of a Funny Story is about the life of clinically depressed 17 year old named Craig. He felt so much pressure about things he does not know he wants or wanted, and is grabbing for connection and help that does not seem out of his reach. He feels misunderstood by his parents; his father who appears to be there but obsessed with his son's goals of academic prominence, and an achingly overreaching mother who just wants what is best for him. Craig gets a new jump of his life after he checks himself into an adult psychiatric ward two blocks away from his home. He's been treated for a moment of five days. During those five days, he seems to become a normal teenager again, and his hopes have been opened for a new beginning. I have been contemplating about life after reading this. I think we are all "used-up" individuals that could use a five day break from our lives so we can just enjoy the moment and relax without following a strict schedule that forces us to rush around. 
 Just a random (connected) thought: In our adventurous life, there are always unbearable and mind-boggling questions which we sometimes ask ourselves. For instance, we ask: why does this keep happening to me? or What did I do to deserve this? these questions are only struggling feelings inside and/or just plain emptiness we feel deep inside ourselves. Almost every day, these gloomy feelings are there and waiting to swallow you anytime around. And you realize something so simple that you oftentimes forgot: it's just life. It's not what you called suffering. It is what makes life worth fighting for; worth living. In other words, life in all its forms and dealings, it's still worth a try, worth whacking, wacking, waaaaaacckiiing for, because you only have one life to live. Don't waste it on suffering. 
 Final Thought, It's Kind of a Funny Story is really a kind of a funny story and it's kind of an awesome novel too. :)

As the final part of the Brilliance trilogy - something i discovered only courtesy of NetGalley, which provided me with all three books that I devoured in a row - Written in Fire is an extremely satisfying conclusion to the series. They are based on "our" world - with the exception that in the 1980's, about 1% of children born going forward were considered 'abnorms' - that is, genetically brilliant in ways that gave them huge advantageous. This inevitably leads to a confrontation between these 'abnorms' or 'twists' and "normal people." 
 I really liked how Sakey veered away from both tried and true tropes with subjects like this, as well as avoided being too preachy about the obvious allegories between the way any privileged majority looks at new, 'strange' new minority groups. (The point comes across without feeling as if it is being shouted down from Mount Pious.) 
 It's a very satisfying and engaging conclusion .. with the only complaint I have is that at the very end, it resulted in a few pages of "and here's how all the other loose ends were tied up and resolved" that was likely necessary for space (and also because it wouldn't have been as interesting to play out after the events that preceded it)....but it felt a bit lazy and rushed. 
 Marcus Sakey has written a LOT of terrifically engaging books and this is no exception. I really recommend the series - even if, like me, you're not particularly drawn to sci-fi or fantasy. It's well worth your time.

MY OPINION: 
 Gone, Gone, Gone is a very different kind of book because it dwells more in realistic problems, in a more deeper sense. I've read books that deals with realistic situations, and I all found them very interesting and inspirational, this is not an exeption. The book talks about Craig and Lio. Two boys that are friends, but polar opposites. The only thing common in them are that they are gay, and that they experience they're own share of trauma. Whereis, Craig clings to his animals, and talks without filter. Lio is quiet, and keeps to himself. 
 This is a really different read for me because I never read a book that talks about two boys like Craig and Lio. When I started this, I was surprised that it would talk about heavy problems like 9/11, leukemia, heartbreak, divorce, and other things. Plus it has touchy subject. Though I was a bit uncomfortable with it, I still decided to read it, because I felt like there's something to like in it. 
 As I progressed through the story, I slowly got to know what kind of persons Craig and Lio were. Craig, other than his animals and his word diarrhea. Really irritated me at first. I just didn't get why he was so clingy on someone like Cody(FYI: The EX-Boyfriend), to the point that he looked very desperate and clingy. 
 I want to email him, but if I do I'll stay up until he answers, I'll stay up,worrying, I'll stay up freaking out that he's hurt and wonder why he isn't screaming at me with capital letters from my inbox. 
 The heck? Why would you still want to be with someone who sends things like that?! I just don't like it. At all. I don't think Craig deserved to receive such hateful words from someone who he claims that he loves. Its just unfair and sad. But yet, he kept thinking about this Cody guy, he kept crying at night because of him. It was so frustrating sometime I want to enter the book and shake some sense into him. Then there's Lio. The situation with Lio was quite different and also a bit sad. He's more closed off than most people and he has the most colorful hair (I mean that in the most literal sense). 
 Reading this was a blur actually, its like I'm reading it in slow motion. Every detail was given, and I just take and take in everything that was happening. I had to admit that I was overwhelmed with how deep the story was. That was probably what sets this apart from other inspirational stories. It deals with two boys, (I say boys because they're only 15 and 16) that are very much affected by the 9/11, shootings and safety. They were broad minded, unlike most boys that just dwell on normal topics in life, they think about such mature things. Though I didn't understand why it was like this at first, after finishing the book. I've finally had a little grasp what the real message Gone, Gone, Gone says. 
 Gone, Gone, Gone is a becoming of age kind of book (if the meaning is what I think it is), I saw how much topics like shootings, terrorism, and the 9/11 could affect even the youth. I saw how it could change them, with how they are, how they live, and how they think and act their lives. I saw how Craig change from someone who's paranoid and confused. To someone who's firm. Someone who know what he wants, someone braver and stronger. Though I do admit that Craig irritated me most of the time, it was good to see him change for the better. Lio, who at first was closed off, almost fearless, and independent, learned how to depend of someone, he tried to talk, and actually connected with Craig. His change was the most memorable for me, because he holds this tortured feelings inside, that when he decided to let it all out. It became much more significant. 
 The relationship between Lio and Craig is something new to me. I had to admit that I am a bit uncomfortable reading about them being intimate, not because I think its disgusting or gross. But because it was something new to me that will take some time for me to absorb.(P.S: I mean no offense to anyone) But technicalities and my feelings aside. I admire how they really became a couple. Lio is very patient with Craig, who was still in love with his ex, Cody. I love that they became each others pillar of support, they were there for each other, and their relationship was based more than just attraction, it grew out of friendship, acceptance and trust. 
 WHY DO I RECOMMEND IT? 
 Its something that can make you see in a different perspective. It was refreshing, new, and something that could make you think and see a different opinion

This is a difficult book for me to rate. I love the Old Kingdom series, and Clariel sounded like it had a lot of potential. In part, it delivered -- it was interesting to see a decadent Old Kingdom, in the beginnings of its decline and fall but prior to the breaking of the Great Charter Stones. Clariel herself was interesting to read about. She resists the plot the whole way, but that's true to her character; the events of particularly the second half of the book do a good job of suggesting how and why she might be tempted by Free Magic sorcery. 
 I was also so happy to see a canonically aroace character in a YA novel! So Clariel is dear to me for that reason. 
 Unfortunately the book left me unsatisfied in a number of other ways. The most unique feature of the series is its take on necromancy and death magic, but these make no real appearance in the book. The second half does become much more interesting, developing the berserk nature and the nature of Free Magic sorcery, but I was still disappointed to see no death magic. Interestingly, and a little confusingly, Mogget even makes a point of noting that Clariel is a naturally inclined necromancer. And yet, aside from some early mentions of Clariel having the Abhorsen's death-sense, there's very little support for that in the text. 
 Then, too, the choice of end point: Nix is just showing us the beginning of Clariel's descent. Her first temptation, if you will. The rest is left up to our imaginations...which is possibly better, to be honest, but then I sort of question why this book exists at all. It's a historically significant interlude, yes, and an interesting peek into the world's past, but it doesn't stand well on its own. I wonder if it would have worked better at novella length -- if Clariel's story could have been streamlined to cut out some of the politicking of the beginning of the novel, which was of medium interest at best, to focus more on Clariel's succumbing to the lure of Free Magic. The real meat of the story is located in chapters 16/17, and 23 on, and I think much of the rest could have been trimmed or removed entirely, leaving behind a much more concentrated story. 
 Having it be a novella would also fit better with its overall standing in the series -- an excerpt from backstory, a snapshot of history, but not so much a full story on its own. 
 Ultimately I would say if, like me, you are a die-hard fan of the series, it's worth reading this entry. (I have also heard that having read it adds something to the experience of reading Goldenhand; I'll soon see if that is indeed the case). But it's certainly not the strongest entry.

I was not expecting this book to be so good. I had set my expectations low because I had just re-read my favorite series and thought that any new book I read afterwards could not compare but I was wrong. I've read so many vampire books and series now that it is rare to find an original concept but this author found a way to make it more interesting. 
 About five years ago, after a worldwide pandemic where many humans died, scientist came up with a vaccine for it. Unfortunately for vampires, the vaccine made human blood poison to them. Now, vampires are starving and desperate to find humans who have not been vaccinated to feed them and still keep humans unaware of them. 
 Aidan Murphy is a four hundred year old vampire who has taken an old ghost town and made it thrive. He and some other vampires loyal to him have found unvaccinated humans and bonded them to themselves. Most of the humans were from troubled backgrounds and had nowhere else to turn. Aidan and his scathe, a group of vampires who are bound to each other, have taken these humans and given them a better life in exchange for blood. Aidan believes in treating humans as equals and not just food and the town is working well. 
 Matthias Ludlum is a rich vampire living in New York. He is on the Vampire Tribunal which makes and enforces vampire law. He is also the head of the Tribunal Justice Council. Matthias wants Aidan Murphy's town of Penton, Alabama shut down...not only because he thinks having such a large scathe of vampires could dangerous to the power of the Tribunal but because his son William has joined Aidan's scathe and is loyal to him and not his father. Matthias wants his son back and will do anything to get him back. 
 Matthias uses his power as the head of the Justice Tribunal to release Aidan's brother from prison where he is to be executed for killing humans and carelessly leaving them on the streets of Dublin where the authorities could find them. Dublin's newspapers were calling the deaths the Vampire Murders so the Justice Tribunal caught Owen Murphy and scheduled him to be put to death. Owen is a psycho who has made Aidan's life miserable whenever he could. Matthias makes a deal with Owen. If he kills Aidan and breaks up his scathe, he'll let him live. 
 Aidan knows his brother is out and after him when the town's doctor turns up dead with the word "food" carved into his chest in Gaelic. He also believes Matthias is behind his brother's sudden release from prison because his son refuses to have anything to do with him and is loyal to Aidan instead. Aidan has to figure out how many people Owen has and where they are hiding and if any other Tribunal members are behind it. He has to be careful how he handles the situation and he also needs a new doctor. 
 Krystal Harris has worked hard to become a doctor. She left home when she was seventeen and never looked back except to go to her mother's funeral. Her father was a controlling and abusive man and her mother allowed the abuse because she was too frightened of him to do anything about it. Krys is now fresh out of medical school and has a boatload of debt to pay back. She has been offered a ton of money to head a rural clinic in Penton, Alabama and is on her way to an evening interview. She is just entering the town when someone steps out in front of her car and flags her down. She steps on her brakes and stops right before she hits the man. 
 The man turns out to be the man she was going to interview with, Aidan Murphy. He asks her to help a friend who has been stabbed and has something carved into his chest. She gets the feeling Aidan knows what the letters mean but he says he does not. She tells him to call an ambulance but he tells her there is no time. Another huge man pulls up in an SUV and they throw the victim in the back. She rides with them to the clinic to save the man who Aidan says is his business manager. 
 After helping the man, she has her interview and is offered the job but she is getting a weird feeling about these people so she tells them she will think about it. The next thing she knows she comes out of a fog and Aidan is drawing blood from her arm. He looks surprised that she is cognizant and his eyes change to an eerie light blue almost silver and he says something to her. She wakes up in a nice room with a fuzzy memory but knows she has been kidnapped. 
 Aidan feels really bad for kidnapping Krystal but he explains to her that his town really needs her and gets her to agree to stay for one month and then she can leave if she is not happy after that. She still doesn't know that Aidan is a vampire but she is starting to figure it out. 
 Krystal gets a crash course in Vampire 101 when Owen attacks Aidan and his right hand man Mirren Kincaid. Owen's lackey shot Mirren in the back with buckshot covered in vaccinated pandemic blood and Krystal has to remove the buckshot as fast as she can before it gets into Mirren's system. Aidan tells Krystal what they are and why his wounds are closing up and healing so fast. She is freaked out but keeps calm to save Mirren. She learns about the town and its secrets. She keeps thinking that she really needs to get out of there. 
 Aidan and Krystal have an intense attraction towards each other which scares them both. Krystal thinks she has Stockholm's Syndrome and Aidan just doesn't want to have a relationship because of what happened to his wife four hundred years ago....something bad which involved Owen. 
 Aidan and his town have a lot to overcome. There is the immediate threat of Owen and then there is Matthias who is super powerful and resourceful. There is also the Tribunal to worry about. If they feel that Aidan and his scathe are a threat to their power, they could find a reason to shut them down. Aidan does have a few friends on the Tribunal but none that would openly back him. No other vampires can feed from the humans in his town because they are each bonded to a member of his scathe so they are safe there but not from outright being killed. 
 I immediately liked this book. The characters are solid and the author has made them complex enough to peek my interest and want to know more about them. The one thing I don't like is that her characters are straight up evil or straight up good...too black and white...and I like characters who have some grey in their personalities. There is one character who may struggle with his morality and that is Mirren. I believe he is the subject of the next book which I am getting ready to read now.

Every Other Day: Paranormal Creatures With a Pinch of Darwin 
 3.5 stars. I love it when authors know what they're talking about. 
 It just feels me with such joy to know that I'm reading something by someone who's actually put in the effort to do the research. It shows that the author cares about this story, and that's the first step in convincing me that I should care too. In books like Every Other Day, you get this sense that the author loved the story and worked incredibly hard on it, because suddenly, the impossible has become possible and the absurd has become probable. And so the story is just that much more enjoyable and believable. That's good fiction. 
 Every Other Day. This book was rooted in science . Jennifer Lynn Barnes anchored the whole fantastical aspect of this book in the kinds of things they taught us in those high school science classes we never paid attention in. Darwinian evolution, genetic alleles, physics and dimensions and more, all served a role in explaining the existence of these "preternatural beings." It sounded so legitimate that I never questioned a single ounce of it. I was convinced that these weren't some whimsical, wishy-washy creatures that conveniently frolicked out of their designated pages in the Brothers Grimm, no, these were real, scientific creatures that were discovered by Darwin, have evolved since then, and merited an entire field of scientific study. They were real. Terrifyingly so. The living dead? Yep, zombies. Classification: homo mortis. Quite common. And like any second now, one can barge into my house and kill me with in one bite because its saliva contains a species of mortis bacteria that's lethal to humans. 
 And then there are the characters. Man oh man, what a hardy lot they were. With the exception of Skylar, none of them had really stunning, likable personalities that made you want to befriend them. Kali routinely displayed symptoms of social phobia, Elliot was forever suspicious and skeptical to the point of being a hindrance to the story, Reid wasn't exactly cuddly, and Bethany could be a real witch at times. But despite that all, they were still a very varied and interesting cast to read about, and though Kali won't be winning any Miss Congenialities anytime soon, her snark and her wit still made her narration a very fun one to read. 
 But the plot didn't seem to really start moving until the halfway point. This really is just a personal complaint, but I really don't enjoy knowing that the narrator is holding out on the other characters. It's maddeningly frustrating for me to read. So for the first third of the book, I was impatiently waiting for her big revelation. Granted, I can understand her reluctance, given the scope of her secret, but still. I was so peeved at her. 
 But even then, the story was hard to latch onto at first. There would be pages upon pages of set-up and exposition, and then an action sequence that felt so rushed and flew by so quickly that you'd be left hanging without the full effect of what had just happened. It took a while to adjust, but just about around midway, the story accelerates and rockets to a strong, powerful finish. 
  Speaking of which, the ending. The emotions. Skylar. SKYLAR. It was such a Prim Everdeen moment. My gosh. It was so sudden and swift; one second, she's smiling at the will-o-wisps, and the next second, she's gone. Caught in a mine explosion. My gosh. It's not exactly a completely unnecessary, unreasonable death, but really just tragic. Gosh.  
 Jennifer Lynn Barnes is so very underrated. Underrated might not even be the proper term for her, since it seems like virtually no one has heard of her. But what baffles me even more is how she has stayed under-the-radar for so long when her books are so enthralling. Granted, they're not perfect. But I've thoroughly enjoyed every single book I've read by her so far. Her writing is spunky and entertaining. Her stories are unique. And her worlds are golden. 
 4 out of 5 stars for Every Other Day. What a thrill ride of novel. 
 P.S. And who doesn't love a good fantasy stand-alone ?

When Grace lowered to her knees to listen to Shane play for the first time in the studio I gave a mental sigh of relief because for some reason I felt like I needed to sit down as well. I was going to put a quote from that part here, but it's one of those things you just need to be there to experience. 
 It wasn't like a litany of stuff being thrown at you, either. Each piece you can tell was hand-picked to move the story forward and give it a feeling. You really feel, too, the scenes where Shane and Grace sing together. Despite the fact that they are constantly sparring, those few moments we get to see what they are like together when they let all their pretenses down are really sweet and touching. I'm kicking myself for not remembering where I read it now, but I recently came across a quote that was something to the effect of: the entirety of history is present in any given moment. This book was not what I had expected it to be at all. Ignore the rating for now-- I never once thought ratings could justifiably define a book anyways. 
 I am really at a loss for words. After a few chapters in, the word which struck me right away was wierd, because that was what this book was-- completely nuts (or I had thought so at least). I'm even well aware that there is already a surfeit of the word wierd being used as a conspicuous adjective for this book in several other reviews, and you're probably thinking that the redundancy isn't necessary. But now, having gone through this insanely crafted tale from cover to cover, the word weird seems hardly appropriate. 
 In its own right, it's one of the most unique, bizarre, and refreshing stories that I've read. Its creative and unconventional originality reminded me of books like Grasshopper Jungle-- which was hella weird too (it's about a very hormonal teenage boy who unleashes a virus that turns people into horny grasshoppers, which ultimately leads humanity to its doom. Like I said, weird stuff-- but hilarious and surprisingly good!) On the other hand, its unique sci-fi aspects reminded me of hidden gems like Ultraviolet. 
 The writing seemed to be ameturish at first, which frankly, put me off, but as the characters transitioned from adolescents into more sophisticated adults, the writing evolved into a more mature narrative style-- one that kept me from losing interest entirely. I felt like there was a lack of visceral connection between the reader and the characters, and by the time they've developed into tangible, somewhat likable individuals, it was far too late; the story never quite appealed to me as much as I had hoped it would, hence the three stars. I'm all about emotional attachments with fictional characters, so it's probably a personal thing. 
 I have come to strongly appreciate this book rather than adore it because I have a feeling that its presence will make a difference. I'm glad Jane Anders decided to write this book. In its own way, the story is an eye-opener, questioning the fate of our future and the consequences of tampering or dealing with forces that we don't quite fully understand. It explores interesting and salient themes on the surface about human interaction, ethics and morals, and just the world in general-- the sort of science vs. magic notion, and all the horrible things humans are doing that will one day unleash catastrophe on the world (hint: global warming-- or perhaps even by loony witches or evil mad scientists, who knows). 
 All the Birds in the Sky is one of those bold, ambitious, genre-defying novels that audaciously misses hitting the right note of perfect by a long shot, but proves itself to be extraordinarily delightful nonetheless. It's a wonderful fusion of magic and sci-fi elements, with a sprinkle of magical realism.

Is it just me or was this ever a reoccurring dream throughout many females adolescence? You are becoming aware of your sexuality and your body's potential for creating life and it all just seems so alien and miraculous. So often, from the age of 12 to...even now sometimes, I dreamed that I just up and woke up pregnant. Never really questioned how it was possible, but with the shifty logic of dreams just started thinking about how to deal with the situation, how embarrassed I'd be at school foremost in my mind. In waking life I'd often entertain this as a thought experiment. I had a plan in mind for this eventuality, similar to my plans for other impossible situations like finding a genie. ( I'd do it if there was some kind of reassuring 'annunciation', but if it happened without warning I'd immediately terminate and have myself sterilized, because there's no way it's not a Village of the Damned alien takeover. If I found a genie I'd wish that I could wish for more wishes, duh). 
 We've seen similar premises before, whether it's ancient mythology or Xena, Warrior Princess, or(..ugh) midichlorians. This trope, mystical parthenogenesis, is older than dirt and is not going away any time soon. While it can be...problematic, what with the use of a young woman as a "vessel" for a supernatural entity, this version at least has some nice, realistic character interactions, and really focuses on how it affects her family and female friend relationships. There is also a modern cyberbullying twist that gets unrealistically out of hand, in my opinion.  Does some high school facebook drama really merit local news, let alone national, and eventually INTERNATIONAL? The most that would happen to Mina in real life is that people would make fun of her, maybe the media would make a story about the state of sexual education in the United States, forget about it after a week, and Lifetime would make a fictionalized tv movie about it. There would not be a religious uproar, an angry televised protest in a firehouse and a parade on a residential street without a permit  But what do I know, maybe it could happen. 
 Some other things that annoyed me: The Mina's assumption that in her small town, teenage pregnancy only occurs to the "girls you'd expect it from"( i. e., sluts) is never addressed or challenged. She never interacts with any other pregnant teens in her high school. I thought there was an opportunity missed there. 
 At one point a room in a firehouse is filled to overflowing capacity. In a firehouse. Think about that for a minute. And nobody said anything. 
 The mysterious messenger from the beginning, Iris, is incompetent and bumbling. Perhaps she isn't a supernatural being after all, but an insane person who has been drugging Mina and artificially inseminating her in her sleep with random semen. 
 Just nitpicks, though. Some people may like this book.
