I enjoyed this book. The characters were pretty messed up, but I loved the various relationships. Not all of them, but Jill and her dad, Jill and Claire. Jill's head has been spinning since she walked in on an unpleasant scene, only to have her mother be gone the next morning with nothing but a post-it note as a good-bye. In one night her family fell apart and she had her heartbroken by longtime bestfriend and love, Sean. If only he saw her the same way she saw him. Claire is determined to bring Sean and Jill back together, torturing the two with cross-country training and time together doing silly things. If she makes them spend time together, perhaps Claire can get Jill to quit hating Sean and start talking to him again. Their friendship is one of the things that Jill is in need of fixing. Her relationship with her father is awesome. The two are super tight, spending the majority of their time at her father's garage, fixing cars and working together. Jill loves to fix cars, and has an inner drive to fix everything she possibly can. When Daniel moves in next door he is yet another thing she longs to fix. His first night in the new home, Jill overhears his mother yelling and throwing things at Daniel. Trying to stop the fight, she throws a can at the house and breaks a window. It brings Daniel outside and a friendship blossoms between the two. He has a horrible life story and you can't help but feel sorry for him. All he wants to do is save his mom from his abusive father, the problem is she doesn't want to be saved and hates Daniel for getting between them. Jill and Daniel are drawn together immediately, with romance blooming, only to come to a screeching halt when he discovers that she is only 16. At the age of 21, he knows a relationship with her is wrong. If only that had stopped him. He is hesitant and holds back, but in the end he gives in to his feelings. I'm glad that Jill is able to be there for him, but the two in a relationship bothered me. That is just too big of an age difference, at that stage in life. I'm glad the author didn't push for that happily ever after. Overall, Jill has to decide if fixing Daniel will be detrimental to her own desperate need to be fixed. She has to face her mom and the some pretty awful truths. She has to face Sean and the truth she has been running from. She has to face all the broken bits of her and decide what is important to her and what is worth fighting for. All the characters in this book experience a little bit of fixing. Overall I enjoyed the book and the relationships made and broken in this story.

I know that when I feel bad about slut-shaming my friends who are having affairs with married men, I immediately learn my lesson by sleeping with the first hot guy who offers because it turns out that hormones ARE totally uncontrollable. Who knew!! Especially for virgins in 1907).  
 Really, though. I have a very hard time finding general/adult fiction that holds my interest, so when I find a treasure trove like this I want to clutch it to my chest and then maybe hoard the library's copy for the maximum-allowable nine straight weeks because I want to keep it nearby for easy access. I was worried that Amanda's "affair" would be a dealbreaker, but we didn't really spend a lot of time with him, and it was a little easier to swallow after hearing they were high school sweethearts. She made plenty of pathetic choices, but I liked her anyway. Or maybe I just liked pretending I was in her shoes, breathlessly reading through a discovered diary. 
 I liked Olive even more, as she had a great sense of self without ever coming across as abrasive. I particularly loved the detail of her day-to-day work in the fashionable department store. It really was fascinating to read about life as a single and career-minded woman (with extremely minimal work experience) trying to make it on her own. In this era of Self-Rigehtous Outraged Tumblr Feminism, it was almost overwhelming to remember why feminism was born. The theme was definitely heavy-handed, but in no way caustic.

 Long Review 
 I will preface this by saying that I was born in '87 so I mostly missed out on growing up during the period this book fetishizes. That being said, I grew up with an Atari from an early age thanks to older siblings and a nerdy engineer Dad, and watched a lot of older movies. So while I didn't have as much of a nostalgia factor, there weren't any references I didn't get. 
 Outside of the decade of birth thing, I'm probably this book's target demographic - an unabashed nerd. Unfortunately, I found it to be just kind of mediocre. 
 The plot is fairly plain and straightforward. That isn't always a bad thing, but in this case it's also paired with characters who experience no real growth or arcs. In my opinion a main character should either change or remain steadfast in the face of change in relation to the problem presented by the story. Neither can really be said to happen here. 
 Technically Wade decides he'd rather split the money and feed the poor, starving people of Earth rather than escape into space but it's not exactly a big change for him. None of the other characters really get any time to develop either and you're left feeling a lot like a person in a simulation surrounded by people who you really know nothing about and have no close connection to. 
 The plot is clearly just a structure upon which to hang pop culture references. The actually references are unimportant, you could replace all the '80s trivia with anything else at all and it would be the same exact book. Even so, long passages are devoted to rattling off details about things like his DeLorean or his Firefly class ship when they make no difference to anything other than to let he reader go, "Oh! I remember those things from those [shows/movies/games]!" 
 It marks an overall larger problem of falling hard into a habit of telling, rather than showing. Portions of the book are so deep in infodump territory they read like the transcript of a PBS documentary. If I had the time, I would interested to know how many words are devoted to showing us things Wade is actually doing in the story, and how many words are devoted to explaining the world and things that happened in the past in the style of a voice over narrator. 
 There are also semi-frustrating examples of poor story construction that damaged my experience of the book. For example, at the finale of the book Wade intends to use his portion of the $200+ billion prize, presumably along with Art3mis's, to help save all the starving impoverished people around the world. They all still idolize Halliday while glossing over the fact that if all that money could've helped feed, clothe, and shelter millions to billions of people then Halliday is at best a huge dick and at worst a total monster for making it a prize in his contest. 
 Additionally the repeated use of Deus Ex Machina got somewhat tiresome - the biggest example being the 'Oh, I forgot to mention I bought these super-admin codes' bit of Wade's IOI indenturement gambit. 
 For all its faults it was at least an entertaining read. Like many of the '80s movies it fetishizes it's enjoyable so long as you don't expect anything of substance out of it.

Seems her predations have left Archie with a case of whatever we call PTSD's bigger, badder brother. 
 Susan - a newspaper reporter - is also quite interesting as a foil to Archie and a woman with her own demons. And there are a bevy of partners, sidekicks, colleagues, and long-forgotten friends to populate Portland. 
 That's the source of some of the tarnish on the title. Cain's third-person narration drags a bit in the first act, with many named bit players and red herrings galore. The characters were never developed and the diary entries were sometimes only a sentence or two, so it functions as a daily account of the happenings in Mazie's life, but they never have the depth needed to get a sense of her as a character. 
 I know that book is meant to be a post-mortem account of her life, and that we are left to the fake historical record told by those who knew here, but it never really came together for me. 
 For a very well done fictional account of a headstrong woman artist, read Siri Hustvedt's The Blazing World. For a more documentary fictional book, try the Life and Death of Sophie Stark. While the main characters of those books both never get to speak for themselves, they are much more realistic. 
 I wanted to know whether Mazie wanted Tee to be her lover, and whether she ever struggled with that. I wanted to know her relationships to the people she helped. I wanted to understand her relationship to her sisters better. Everything was told and not shown. Disappointing, but still an interesting concept.

 Rites of Passage 
 has me a bit torn. There were definitely pros and cons with this book. 
 Things I Liked 
 For the most part, I LOVED Sam as a character. That girl is tough as nails! She gets an insane amount of shit thrown at her at the Denmark Military Academy, but she never backs down. There were tons of times when I wish she'd stand up for herself more, but that's just not military style, so I understand why she didn't. If I were her, I probably would have punched everyone in the face 5 times instead of standing there and taking their shit. 
 The whole military aspect of this book was REALLY interesting. I'm so not a military person and I know very little about it. But reading about a hardcore military academy was pretty cool. This may seem weird, but Rites of Passage gave me the strongest urge to go to the gym. I read all about Sam running 5Ks, doing 5 million push ups, running through obstacle courses, etc. I wanted to jump up and get in on that! ...I'm sure I'll feel differently by tomorrow. 
 However, the shit the recruits got was insane. It was crazy to see how anti-women some of those guys were. What fucking century are we in? Sam beats half the guys in the training exercises, but the guys don't get shit for it--Sam does.. just because she's a girl. So even though she rocks, she's "not cut out for this". Whaaaa?? 
 What I Didn't Like 
 This book was long--416 pages. But the thing is, I don't feel like it needed to be that long. There were a few times where the book felt slow. There was a ton of build up, but then nothing was happening, or there would be long periods where the plot felt like it was stalling. I think it could have been cut down. 
 I didn't hate the romance, but I feel like it wasn't developed well. At the beginning of the book, Sam actually has a half romance with a different guy.. this "half romance" went on for so long that I actually had to go and reread the synopsis, because I remembered it saying she falls for her 
 drill sergeant 
 , but this "half romance" was with someone else... It just had me confused. Then when the romance with the drill sergeant finally came into play in the second half, I LIKED it, but I feel like it never came off the ground. It wasn't the focus of the story so I guess it wasn't intended to be super heavy/detailed, but it still felt really awkwardly half developed (especially by the end). 
 And finally: the ending. Rites of Passage had A TON of build up. The hazing gets more and more violent and brutal.. then I feel like the end was really abrupt and not super satisfying. Without spoiling it, the ending was sort of like: the war isn't over, but we've won the battle.. but actually, even that's generous. It's more like: the war isn't over, but the bad guys don't feel like taking bad PR so they're letting us win this one battle. I was hoping for a lot more. Mostly, I wanted Karma to kick Matthews's ass but it didn't. The guy can still stay at the school! Also I wasn't pleased with Sam's brother's role. He was a total asshat to her the whole time, then at the end he was just like, "I couldn't let them know I was onto them. That's why I was an ass. I didn't mean it." Seriously? That's it?  
 Overall 
 I enjoyed a lot of Rites of Passage. It was interesting and felt different from other YA books just because of how military-heavy it was. Even other military books I've read have nothing on this one. Rites of Passage is more like: a day in the life of recruit. It's very cool! If only the romance and ending were a bit better, then thiss could have easily been a 4.5 star book!

Across the Universe is Beth Revis's first book, and in some ways it shows. However, despite some hiccups, the book was overall a good read. 
 I've read interviews with the author that have indicated that her initial idea was for a closed-room mystery in space. 
 Honestly, the mystery part was not that interesting. 
 First of all, there were only a certain number of people on the ship who would have been capable of murdering the frozens, so it was less of a whodunnit and more of a whydunnit. If the ultimate motivation had been particularly interesting, I would have been fine, but honestly it didn't make a lot of sense. I suppose a case could be made that Orion went a little crazy after he was drugged  but that seems like a cop-out. 
 Plus, the big reveal that Orion was the missing, presumed dead, Elder  was...not a surprise at all. I saw it coming immediately. The 'clues' were a bit heavy handed. 
 Having said all that, I did enjoy the book. I liked seeing how the generation ship worked, and finding out the reason behind all the weirdness was enough to keep me reading. I also liked the romance between Elder and Amy - namely, that it was slow to develop and isn't resolved yet. 
 Amy was a good character. Her reaction to being awoken seemed realistic - she didn't sit around and whine but she also was appropriately upset about her situation, as any person her age would be. 
 I also enjoyed Elder's struggles to determine what makes a good leader, and the conclusions he comes to. He wasn't perfect, but he grew as the book went on. 
 All in all, it was a pretty good book and I've got the sequel on my to-read list. I'd like to see what Revis does with the next couple books, and any future books she may write.

 So we all know by now that I love the Lux series. It often makes it onto my Top Ten Lists and favorite character lists. I've been looking forward to Opposition for what feels like forever. While I think it was a good ending for Katy and Daemon, I was not overwhelmed by it. 
 10 things i hate about you gifs 
 The story focuses on Daemon and Katy as they face the alien apocalypse, but I didn't really feel satisfied with any of the details. It almost felt like JLA had this great idea of an alien invasion and then didn't really want to take the time to develop it. And the government's only lines of defense is to kill millions of innocent people or to let Daemon, Katy, and their friends make negotiations with the only possible ally? 
 In between the occasional ambush or fight sequence, Daemon and Katy are busy being young and in love. While I love seeing them as a happy and together couple, it was almost redundant at times. Yes, they are adults now. Yes, they are in love. Yes, they like to physically express that love at any and all opportunity. It just got boring, honestly. 
 In Origin, JLA killed off a lot of characters and I was a little nervous that there would be no one left standing at the end of this book. While she doesn't hold back on a lot of the violence, there is only one major death in this book and it definitely packed a real emotional wallop. 
 One thing that really bugged me was that we didn't get an answer to this: 
 Onyx note: I get a lot of requests from readers wanting to know what was in the note that Daemon passed to Kat in Onyx during class. Currently, I do not have permission from the publisher to share that note or what it contains. Sorry! As soon as I do, you guys will be the first to see it. 
 That quote is taken directly from JLA's website. In the final pages of Opposition, that note is referenced, but other than it "scalding her cheeks" in embarrassment, we don't get any more information. However, I guess if all it is, is sexual innuendo, we don't really need to know. I just thought that since it was such a secret it would be something bigger. 
 Overall, Opposition was a decent end to the series. I feel like the arc of Daemon and Katy throughout the entire series was very well done. Where the series went a little off the rails for me was when it started to center more on the government project and alien politics than on Daemon and Katy and their friends (what happened to Lesa!?! Did she die? Did she escape? Did she go to college? Couldn't there be just one sentence on her?). And I enjoyed seeing how things ended up with Daemon and Katy, Dawson and Beth, Dee and Archer, and Luc - though I do feel like it left things open enough that there could be an Origin spinoff in the works! Despite my mostly negative review of this book, I still really enjoy the series on a whole and still recommend it.

I know that Snape had a reason for everything he did, and we find this out in the 7th book, but his betrayal hits me hard every time. However, it makes me very happy that he does not allow Draco to kill Dumbledore.  
 This entire book is dark. I feel like it is the darkest of all the books. I remember reading it for the first time and not grasping all of it because of that. However, as I got older and read it again (and also once the movie came out and helped), I understood some of the subject matter better and I enjoyed the story better.

I did like that the author tried to show that young women can have sex, enjoy it and not necessarily want to have a boyfriend and all the attachments. I liked that she tried to present this character with no judgements. Did she succeed? Not entirely, but that's okay. The reason I am not giving this higher is because the reason that Mercedes does what she does is so flimsy and badly developed, that instead of sympathizing and feeling sorry for the main character, you end up disliking her even more. It was obvious the author WANTED you to like and sympathize with the main character, but she doesn't give you enough reason to. It was obvious that Mercedes had a very skewed and bad relationship with sex, who can blame her considering what happened to her? And it made sense that she wanted to control her experiences afterwards, and the her spiralling out of control all made sense. Just the way or what she did to justify her methods is where it fell apart for me. I am glad that in the novel she had really great support system and friends to have her back when things inevitably went wrong and she faced consequences for her actions. It is obvious though that a Canadian wrote this novel which makes me wonder why she chose California for her setting if she was going to use Canadian slang and lingo. A mickey means something completely different in Canada than it does in the States so that scene where she drinks a mickey can be confusing. A mickey in Canada means a small bottle of hard liquor whereas in the States, I believe it actually means a date rape drug.

 Q: Have there been fans rooting for Julian and Lena? 
 I have, there's a Team Julian. I think in young adult books, it's always the first love that's hard to beat but you know the truth is, in real life people almost always never end up with their first loves, and it's not usually the right thing either. 
 Q: Is that a spoiler? (laughs) No, it isn't!

 I thought something would happen when they were alone in the room. It was too tempting to have two people on opposite sides, who hate each other, locked in a room together, to not have something major to occur. Is she falling in love with Julian? Yes. Is she in love with Julian by the end of Pandemonium? It's not clear, you know. It's not exactly like she just tumbled head over heels. 
 Q: Did you anticipate uneasiness from readers with the introduction of Julian and the love triangle element?

Think I might have enjoyed this more if there hadn't been so much hype. Interestingly, for each point I liked, I could find a counterpoint. 
 For example: 
 The fact that Flynn does not back away from the nasty side of human nature is a huge plus for me. However, her characters are so unlikable and so despicable it's hard to invest yourself in them. So, while I don't need to like a character, I do need to empathize with them. Even a psychopath can have a redeeming quality. Sure, maybe they lack a conscience, and maybe they themselves lack the ability to empathize, but in all the true crime/abnormal psychology/profiling books I've read and in all the sociopaths I've encountered, none of them were so "evil," so "cold and calculating" (like Flynn's characters) that I couldn't find a redeeming quality. 
 I appreciated the plot twists...I mean, who doesn't? It's what keeps the reader on his/her toes. However, after a while the "bait and switch" gets annoying. I think her choice to write this as a "he said/she said" is an interesting one...but to also write two first person accounts...maybe too ambitious. There's a fine line between creating suspense and purposely misleading the reader so that you can then "wow" them. 
 I like that Flynn is a talented writer who can pen a witty phrase with the best of them...except even cleverness can be overdone. Sometimes, it felt as if her need to dazzle us with her prose surpassed her desire to tell us a story. I suppose this is a stylistic thing, but for me it detracted from the overall story. 
 I like that Flynn obviously reads true crime books; however, the similarities between characters and other true-life characters became distracting. A good portion of the book felt like a marriage between the Scott Peterson case and the Jeffrey MacDonald case prior to the big reveal that Amy isn't really dead...of course . For example, the staged crime scene is incredibly similar to the supposedly staged scene as presented in Fatal Vision, while Amy's parents are loose interpretations of the Kassabs (MacDonald's inlaws). Interestingly, Colette MacDonald was also the only daughter of Mildred Kassab, who (like Amy's mother) miscarried repeatedly. Nick's mistress, Andie, also seems like a loose interpretation of Amber Fry. Reading the interview Andie gives the press, I couldn't help but picture Amber. Both Laci and Colette were pregnant at the time of their murders  though we quickly find out Amy wasn't actually pregnant . Obviously, real life influences fiction, but for someone (like me) who is very familiar with the other cases, it made the story feel more contrived than it should have. There were several scenes in the book that were almost identical to details and events in both cases. Perhaps coincidence...but I doubt it. Either way, it begged comparison to the other cases and blurred the characters in my mind's eye.

Much better than The Lost Symbol, not as good as The Da Vinci Code, Dan Brown's Inferno is pretty much everything you would come to expect, to the point where the unexpected is completely expected. His books have a rather rote form at this point, plotting by numbers, such that many of the plot twists are entirely predictable: you might not know precisely which way it will turn, but you know the turn is there and the broad outline it will contain. 
 A very nonspecific spoiler-like example: 
  
 If you've read any of his books, you know that at least one character who he trusts will turn out to be a "bad guy" and at least one "bad guy" will turn out to be a "good guy". This pretty much means you're looking for the clues and misdirections to figure out which is which well before the reveal is supposed to occur. 
  
 In fact, certain elements of the plot twists are so telegraphed that I almost wondered if it was a double blind. It's like a giant red fish was jumping up and down yelling "Hey, look at me, I'm a red herring." At some point I felt like I was watching a magician, but rather than watching the trick I was entirely focused on the misdirection, looking for the deliberate missteps. A generic example would be Character A makes a phone call to end a chapter. The next chapter starts with character B hanging up the phone. You are clearly meant to believe that A called B, but the very nature of the book and the manner in which the exchange was portrayed (nor not portrayed as the case may be) made me suspect that it was deliberately set up to create an incorrect conclusion. And more often than not, I was entirely correct in this assessment with most of my predictions and guesses as to where certain elements were going to end up. 
 I also feel that Brown's over-appreciation for art masks a lack of appreciation for the rather blase nature of modern people. At some point early in the book there is a flash back to a talk about Dante's Inferno and the Botticelli map of hell, and the audience gasps in horror when it's shown. Uh...no. Wouldn't happen. We're exposed to way too many images of grotesque horror in art and culture to get more than a reaction of mild curiosity from most people. 
 Despite this I generally enjoyed the book. It's not high literature, despite its pretension to be about high art, but it serves its purpose as brain candy with a twist.

Okay so... what to say about this book...

Margo Roth Spiegelman. That's the name on everyone's lips. And when she appears at his window and drags him along on a midnight escapade, she irreversibly turns Quentin's life upside down as graduation nears. Especially when she disappears the next day. 
 This is my first foray into John Green's books. After seeing so many people reading all of his works, I had to pick one up just to see what all the fuss was all about. 
 And... I couldn't like this book. It was all teen-angst and teen emotions and teen notions. The book was all about teens trying to figure out whether the "paper town" world is worth it or not, to walk inside the drawn lines, to be spontaneous and wild and crazy or a good kid. If I were perhaps a high school senior all over again reading this book, maybe it would have resonated with me and I would have given it 5 stars for writing down the emotions in my heart onto paper. 
 But. I'm not. And I'm not nostalgic about those emotions this book tries to evoke. 
 I didn't care for any of the characters, sorry. They just felt like random people. Margo was obviously a fantasy girl - the one that all teenagers imagine they would like to be deep down inside. And Quentin was the boy who was supposed to appeal to everybody who imagines that they are a little too normal and boring. 
 Yawn. 
 As for pacing, I wanted to just flip to the last chapter to see the inevitable meeting and see how it ended. Most of the middle of the book could have been cut out and I would have lost nothing. It's too much of a "slice of life" book for me. And those types of books need either humor or love for the character. And this book is certainly not comedic, and I didn't love the characters enough. 
 John Green does have a penchant for quotable sentences though. Which actually makes it more teen-angsty in a way. All teens (most teens?) go through that angsty phase where they question the meaning of life, where deep universal truths should be said aloud until it pierces someone's heart, where they want to make an impact on the world without appearing to try too hard, to read and maybe write poetry like a misunderstood artist, to be effortless, to be a rebel. This book appeals to that sort of teen. 
 It was just too young for me. 
 And I'm just not nostalgic enough to care to remember those times that fondly. 
 Two stars. It was okay. The writing and the plot was solid. The slice-of-life feel of the book and searching-for-meaning-despite-the-transition-of-life will appeal to many people. But I'm probably not going to pick up another John Green book though because it seems that he writes for a certain age group. 
 Recommended for teenagers and people who want to remember that period of their life.

Laurence didn't really need to hang out with Patricia at school, because he only needed her to vouch for his after-school time, and maybe weekends. But he felt awkward sitting by himself when she was also sitting by herself, usually frowning out the nearest window. And he found himself curious to ask her stuff and see how she responded--because he never, ever knew what Patricia would say about anything. He only knew it would be something weird. 
 Mentally filing this book under "Things that started out fantastic but ended in tears and disappointment." 
 For the first third or so of this book, when the protagonists (Patricia and Laurence) were children, I was SURE this was about to be my next favorite book. It had this quirky/absurd/satirical vibe to it that was like the best ever blend of Lemony Snicket, Harry Potter, Jonathan Safran Foer, etc. etc. Basically, you have these two weird and gifted children in terrible circumstances becoming unlikely friends... while being pursued by a ridiculous creepy/adorable assassin. 5-star material for ~100 pages. It was great. 
 Then the novel skips forward to Patricia and Laurence's young adulthood, and BLAH. It's cynical urban hipster-land, kind of like The Magicians except not as good. The writing goes downhill. Some of the charming "wtf"ness of the first part of the book just becomes plain old "wtf," such as this line: "Ernesto came and stood so close to Patricia, he was in danger of touching her and making her body a bacterial and fungal playground." Why did I just read this sentence with my own two eyes? 
 I could go on and on. The world-building gets slipshod, the plot starts hopping around erratically, cliches and sentimental dribble appear, the characterization flies out the window, and there's a hetero romance (no spoilers, but you can probably guess it anyway) that was so forced I literally cringed and got angry at this book for letting me down so hard. Dear Charlie Jane Anders, I DIDN'T SHIP THEM, AND EVEN IF I DID, I WOULD RATHER SEE THEIR FIRST KISS THAN DISCOVER THE EXACT STYLE IN WHICH LAURENCE SHAVES HIS PUBES. Or witness Patricia idly wondering in the middle of a love confession if she's just accidentally magic-viagra'ed her lover's penis. Page 223 for the curious among you.  Please delete all the random explicit sex details from this book, thanks. 
 Also, this reminds me: Is there such a thing as writing the straight male perspective a little TOO well? Post-puberty Laurence narrates like the worst cliche of "straight male writer" whenever he gets in range of a woman. For example, Laurence and Patricia are innocently sitting in the park, in the middle of a deep conversation about ethics, and he still finds time to mention that she's "raising her shoulders so her breasts lifted up inside her white T-shirt." Like, okay, Laurence, thank you for this irrelevant status update on Patricia's breasts. Reminds me of this hilarious tumblr post. 
 Anyway. The last few pages were okay, tying up loose ends in a fairly satisfying way, but it still couldn't make up for all the wasteland that came before. 
 I don't want to say, "Skip this one," because you really don't want to miss out on Patricia and Laurence's childhood, but... I would recommend reading this book to about the one-third mark (Books 1 & 2) and then forgetting about the remaining two-thirds. You'll save yourself some excruciating disappointment that way.

Immediately preceding this book, I read the original Island of Dr. Moreau. This one dovetails nicely with it. Juliet Moreau is fourteen and struggling to make a living as a maid. She is young, penniless and close to being homeless. It didn't used to be that way. Her father, Doctor Henry Moreau, was a very successful surgeon and they lived very well. Then the accusations came and Juliet's life as she knew it changed. Her father disappeared, rumored dead, and as years pass, her mother dies. So it's a fluke that Juliet runs into medical students performing an experiment with one of her father's papers. With some investigation, she finds Montgomery James. He was a servant in their household and disappeared when her father did. He explains that he left with her father and they now reside on an island. Juliet insists she go back with him. She wants to see her father alive for herself and ask him directly if the accusations were true. 
 On the long journey, a boy is found near death in a small boat. They bring him aboard and Montgomery brings him back to health. He says his name is Edward. It's here that the love triangle begins to make itself known. Juliet finds herself drawn to both young men, and they her. When they arrive on the island, Juliet is delighted to reacquaint herself with her father, and he insists on pairing her up with Edward and marrying her off. He wants to do his fatherly duty, then send her away so that he can get back to his important work. 
 Things aren't right on the island though. Those who are familiar with the Island of Dr. Moreau won't be surprised by what Juliet finds when she goes to her father's island. The good doctor experiments and creates islanders that are at times horrific and others docile and humane. The heartfelt event which led Dr. Moreau to first began his experiments was teased at enough that I could guess it early-on but some readers may find it to be a surprise. That Dr Moreau's experiments have moved well beyond their initial ethical reason does not trouble him. 
 When a monster makes itself known on the island, bodies piling up left and right, it has many in the compound questioning who it could be. Juliet not only questions that, her father's choices and her own matters of the heart, but she also questions her own morality. Although she believes what her father is doing is wrong, she is also intrigued by it all. 
 Juliet is a believable character who is not only strong, intelligent and curious, but also gullible, witty and sassy. She is easy to admire and engage with. There is a bit of medical talk in the book since Juliet has been learning from all of the medical books her father left behind and this also shows that she is a contemporary woman before her time. The other characters on the island are similarly interesting. You are constantly wondering why Montgomery continues to work for Dr. Moreau and what Edward's mysterious background is. There is just a lot of mystery hidden within all of these characters. 
 This book begins a series which I hope to find my way back to eventually.

 These are the quotes worth sharing from the novel: 
 "Yet all around you, timekeeping is ignored. Birds are not late. A dog does not check its watch. Deer do not fret over passing birthdays. 
 Man alone measures time.

I'm not someone who is usually attracted to memoirs/autobiographies. I'm not sure why since I've enjoyed the ones I've read...yet still I approach them with less enthusiasm than their fiction counterparts. 
 Maybe it's because I've often tried to forget my own childhood, exchanging it in my mind for something less dysfunctional, and thus I am leery of those who not only open their dark, messy closets but also invite all their neighbors over to take a tour. 
 I think Maya Angelou does just that, and probably better than most, and suddenly my closet doesn't look so messy, or at least not in need of hiding. 
 Written with the unique skill of a talented poet, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings is the story of a bright young black woman growing up in a still blatantly and shamelessly racist America just before and during World War II. Her story is touching, enlightening, and inspiring. 
 A sample of Angelou's powerful and skillfully constructed prose: 
 The men in the Store stood away from the walls and at attention. Women greedily clutched the babes on their laps while on the porch the shuffling and smiles, flirtings and pinching of a few minutes before were gone. This might be the end of the world. If Joe lost we were back in slavery and beyond help. It would all be true, the accusations that we were lower types of human beings. Only a little higher than the apes. True that we were stupid and ugly and lazy and dirty and unlucky and worst of all, that God Himself hated us and ordained us to be hewers of wood and drawers of water, forever and ever, world without end. 
 We didn't breathe. We didn't hope. We waited. 
 Would recommend this to anyone who appreciates honest (at times painfully/brutally honest) and important writing that sings.

I read The Kite Runner several years ago, and I loved it. I told myself I would soon get around to reading Khaled Hosseini's next novel soon. It took longer than expected, but I finally started A Thousand Splendid Suns and quickly finished it. It was certainly a page-turner and very hard to put down. Hosseini's writing style is excellent, simple yet powerful with a mix of Pashto words that soon seep into your vocabulary. Every character is vibrant and multidimensional. Even those you hate have their own moments that make them human. The only people portrayed as flat are those who instigate the wars that ravage Afghanistan. Even then, war itself seems to be a living entity, one with character and a sick sense of ironic, twisted humor. 
 Of all the characters, Laila and Mariam are of course the most memorable. Their separate backgrounds, each tragic in its own right, are brought together and eventually become inseparable. I loved the fact that their relationship was the focus of the book, even more than the one between Laila and Tariq.  
 The novel portrays the harsh conditions in Afghanistan following the Cold War as a fact of life, a state of existence which the people of that country must cope with. However despite all of the war, death, and horror, there is an underlying message of hope that perhaps some day Afghanistan can be restored to its former glory. It's a novel that underscores the human condition and a book well worth reading.

From the girls perspective, about this scenario, that is your worst nightmare to have a group of guys thinking you're in the bathroom doing number 2. From the guys perspective, they just screwed up big time because they just told a stranger through a closed door to "nip it off" thinking it was a guy and it turned out to be a gal.  Chess is a ferociously independent woman who is accomplished in her own right as a photographer and business owner. Her bluntness mixed with her sarcasm keeps Finn on his toes.

 At the core of their relationship is a friendship. A friendship that is coated with friendly flirtiness. They both are dancing around in their attractiveness to each other because it feels safer to pretend they're only friends than to explore their feelings. 
 I love that just like Gray's mom did in "The Friend Zone" Finn's mom offers her wisdom to her son: 
 "Just remember, Finnegan. Love with your heart, not your head. Think about things too much and it all turns to shit."

I've always wanted to read Beastly so when I finally had the chance of getting it and this book, I thought it would be a good idea to read this first. I've heard about this book through the movie but I haven't seen that in a long time so when I got the two books I thought it'll be great to revisit the story and actually read where the film came from since we all know books and movies differ the stories from time to time. 
 So why did I choose to read this story in the opposite's perspective from the original book and film? Well, it's because of that different perspective. When watching films or reading books, I always wonder about the other people's voice or perspective on the events that unfold in the story. Like in this particular story, I've always wondered what Lindy felt, what her thoughts were as the story goes on. Sometimes I even think about what Kendra must be feeling, what led her to what she did - I mean the author did mention in the books but I always had a feeling there was something more to that or I just basically wanted to know her history on how she became who she is or why she is that way. 
 The reason why I read this first was because I loved knowing how people in the same story take on the things happening in their life differently. It was something that I couldn't do in real life - and being someone who had a real tough time reading and understanding social cues and such, this opportunity to know someone other than the protagonist or main character's perspectives and feelings was a learning experience. I guess reading someone else's take on "their" story is my way of understanding what others may be going through in my own. 
 But what bothered me most about reading this story afterwards and immediately reading the original one was that I've always been biased of male povs. I mean, I'm currently reading the same story in Kyle's perspective but I'm more invested in it than when I was reading Linda's. There's just something about the male's perspective that captures my attention and interest more than a girl's. Maybe its because I don't understand guys and being a girl makes it easier for me to "get" that perspective. Or maybe its just because it's difficult because its so different. Or maybe its being different in general. I don't know but what I'm trying to say is that I really like Kyle's voice in this story more than Linda's. 
 Although, I did feel this connection between me and Linda, especially when she was confessing how common or mainstream it was to have a crush on a boy who isn't typically your type of guy but because of their extreme hotness level they are. I mean, let's be honest, I don't know anyone who hasn't had that affection for someone who is in their own definition "hot" or "handsome". And I also liked her values especially with being true to herself... but that also kinda died down on me on the last chapters of the book because that romance they had went a different way than I would have liked. 
 Nonetheless, it was a good read and I enjoyed it. 
 Happy reading! :)

This is a love story disguised as a mental illness story. 
 I had hoped that we would have a story that allowed a teenager to be every part of himself without the mental illness defining him, at least at the end. I wanted something where we saw him come to terms with it and grapple with how to handle himself. 
 Instead I got a supremely idiotic scheme--one that no sane person would ever agree to, even a hormonal teenage girl--that not only proves he's incapable of making rational decisions, but also that this whole book is a travesty on contemporary realism. 
 Seriously, it was so ridiculous. You find out your best friend is schizophrenic, and he wants to travel across a frozen lake; a process that would take at least a couple days. Is your response to: 
 1) immediately call a doctor and tell them your friend is having an episode? 
 2) talk your friend down from the precipice of stupidity 
 3) laugh in his face, because you're close enough that you can do that 
 4) decide that yes, hiking across a frozen lake with no real expertise is a great idea! 
 It was just silly. Which is a big bummer because I was looking forward to this book a lot. Mental illness is massively stigmatized and I thought this would help shrink that mentality.

3.5 rounded down to 3 
 So, yeah. 3 stars. 
 What I liked... 
 1. Despite its faults, this is a page turner. Setterfield takes her time getting where she's going, always giving the reader just enough at just the right point. 
 2. This is a book for book lovers that celebrates writing, storytelling, and reading with equal enthusiasm. 
 3. The writer has some interesting insights and managed a few quote worthy passages. 
 4. The commentary on the twin relationship was well done. 
 5. Finally, Setterfield works the otherworldly element, which is always a plus for me. 
 What I didn't like... 
 1. I'm a pretty adaptable reader who is generally willing to go with the flow. I rarely find myself thinking...that could never happen. Yet, much of this story lacks credibility and requires a huge stretch of the imagination. In such cases, it's up to the writer to sell it, and I'm not sure that Setterfield does to my satisfaction. 
 2. I can appreciate a good plot twist, but Setterfield's grand reveal was just too much. I was four stars up until she revealed that there were actually 3 girls instead of two.  I felt kind of cheated here, as if the author purposely misled me rather than letting me mislead myself. 
 3. The ending was a little too contrived. 
 4. For the most part the writing is strong, yet there were times where it was over the top. The fact that the story was not grounded in time also bothered me a little, though one could argue this is a positive. Me? I generally like to be well-grounded with respect to time and place (though there are always exceptions--this wasn't one). The author does a great job with place but not so much with time. 
 Overall, a solid read with some strengths and some weaknesses. Had it not been for the ending, I would have rounded this up to 4. Think this will appeal most to the fan of the suspense novel as suspense is what Ms. Setterfield seems to excel at.

This is a prime example of a book that I initially felt conflicted about reading, but went ahead and kinda did it anyway. A Man Called Ove is one of those books that's been on bestseller and book club lists for the past couple of years, so naturally it piqued my interest. For mostly the same reasons, however, it made me not want to read it (see: Sweetbitter). When I took over the Fiction Book Club at my library and saw that this book was already selected by the previous librarian for our August read, though, I had no choice. So, with only slight pause (read: groaning and eye-rolling), I trudged forth and conquered. Bless you, audiobooks. 
 Honestly, as I was listening to this audiobook, I started out thinking, uh, okay? What's the big deal with this book? I admittedly had to speed it up significantly to finish it in time and may have tuned in and out here and there, but I found that after I finished it and stepped back to evaluate (plus research questions and reviews for book club), I found myself reflecting positively on Ove. For starters, the book begins with the delightful curmudgeon attempting to buy a computer. He wants absolutely nothing to do with an iPad or any other such nonsense tablet. He wants a computer with a keyboard. No frills, please; just pure, unadulterated machinery that can't fit in a pocket or other convenient means of transport. I fell in love with his curmudgeonly disposition immediately. 
 Ove currently lives alone, his sourpuss facade masking a deeper, underlying sadness. He has had more than his fair share of bad luck, the most recent of which being the death of his wife. Ove's sadness compounds and manifests in his multiple (five?) attempts at suicide throughout the course of the novel. The chatty, boisterous neighbors who have moved in next door, however, keep interrupting him in a darkly humorous way. The family, complete with two small children and a third on the way, and a determined stray cat wriggle their way into Ove's life and eventually win him over. By the end, the neighbor kids are referring to him as grandpa and Ove is mourned and celebrated by several people at his wake . 
 I found it a bit hilarious that Ove was described as such an old man...then it was revealed that he was only 59-years-old. What?! I was certain, until his actual age was revealed, that he was in his eighties. This detail aside, however confused or bored I may have felt at times, this book was definitely overall intriguing. The dark humor, the bitter curmudgeon descriptions; it made me think of a relatable grumpy old man, which I found entertaining and enjoyable. 
 Throughout my read-through, the story kind of waned in and out with my interest level. I found some of the flashbacks a bit confusing to sort through and organize, though this may have been due to any combination of my time crunch, increased audio speed, and the very nature of the audiobook in general. In hindsight, and perhaps in the future, I should have/will read this with my eyeballs instead of my ears.

I mean, really, what can I say about this? 
 I have loved Harry Potter since I was 5 years old, and my parents took me to see the Philospher's Stone in the cinema, because people had told them it was a good film for kids. I'm pretty sure they regret that decision. From that moment on, I have been utterly obsessed with the world of Harry Potter. I read the books as soon as I could get my grubby hands on them, went to midnight releases, went to see each film the day it came out, bought all the merchandise I could (which has gotten worse now I'm an adult and earn my own income), read the series at least once a year, managed to get my 4 year old sister obsessed with it. Harry Potter has been of a massive importance to my me whole life, and I honestly cannot comprehend a world without it. 
 So, naturally, I pre-ordered this play the second that Waterstones e-mailed me telling me that I could. And during that wait, I was faced with masses of negativity on Tumblr. Some people had found some spoilers for the play, and as people on Tumblr are apt to do, they become outraged and ranted about the play. I avoided all spoilers, and didn't let this negativity affect me, because how can you judge something you haven't seen or read? And I'm glad I did avoid them, because this morning I went into the play with only my excitement, and no negativity to cloud my judgement. 
 I read it in just under two hours, and I have to admit that I cried a few times. Actually, I welled up on my walk home, just thinking about what I was about to experience. I locked myself into my room with a cup of tea and half a packet go Tyrells vegetable crisps, and read. I only had one loo break, during which I brought my book with my for good measure. I feel kind of at a loss as to what to do now I've finished it. 
 I don't even know what to say about the actual play. Reading about Albus and the next generation was fantastic. It's something we all want, to read about these children. For me, it didn't disappoint. I'm glad Albus was sorted into Slytherin. We all know Harry was going to be, it only makes sense that one of the Potter's were. I'm glad he and Scorpius are friends, I feel that it made up for what Harry and Draco failed in. It brought them together though, and I feel that post-Cursed Child the Malfoys and the Potters/Weasleys will be closer friends. Well, especially because of Rose and Scorpius. I know they're shipped quite a lot, and I'm so happy that they are (sort of) canon. I loved who the next generation are, all of their personalities. I love how Scorpius is like a mini Hermione. I loved seeing the trio as adults, and their relationships, and how even now they still argued with Draco. I loved the cameos of Dumbledore and Snape and Minerva and every who was even briefly mentioned in passing. 
 I loved the plot as well. I loved the use of time-turners and I loved the alternate universes when things went wrong. I loved that Harry is scared of pigeons and that Ron wants to renew his vows with Hermione. I loved that Albus got to see his grandparents and that Harry got to see them die, even though that broke my heart. I loved how Albus has inherited his fathers sassiness. I loved it. The only thing I didn't love with Voldemort's suddenly having a child, but to be honest that doesn't bother me that much. I hope that Jo does an interview or something just to clarify exactly when Bellatrix had her, and how.  
 I just really love Harry Potter.

This book tells the story of Gabe Williams, an eighteen year old who's in the process of transitioning from Liz Williams. At the beginning of the story, the only people who know that that Liz wants to be known as Gabe from now on are his parents, brother, and best friend, Paige. Gabe's super nervous about people finding out about his true identity, because he comes from a small town in Minnesota where people aren't very open-minded. He's also incredibly passionate about music and has his own radio show called Beautiful Music for Ugly Children. The story basically follows Gabe's coming out to the rest of his town, and it's also about his transition as he figures out what to do with his life after graduation from high school. 
 I think it's safe to say that the main goal of this book is to inform people about the transgender community and to make people more open-minded about people who are born in the wrong body. In my case, I would definitely say it was successful. It's for that reason that I gave this book such a high rating: it made me more informed about a topic that I had previously known nothing about, and it made me so much more open-minded toward that topic.

If I had to sum up this book in two words, they would be "Cute" and "Frustrating". 
 The Cute 
 I love Friends to More Than Friends stories. I love watching the relationship grow and change and all the sweet moments along the way. I liked how close Kennedy and Graham were and that they were not only roommates, but best friends. I have to say the roommate angle appealed to me so much because I had a male roommate for a couple of years - however, while we were friends, our relationship was nothing like the characters in this book. 
 The story didn't just focus on the romantic relationships, but on family too. Both characters have some family issues of varying degrees. I liked seeing some resolution come about by the end of the book. 
 Kennedy and Graham's banter was pretty entertaining. I love a good sarcastic couple. 
 The Frustrating 
 While I liked Kennedy's sarcasm and sense of humor, there were times it was just too much. She could hardly ever take anything seriously and she kept blaming Graham for "missing their chance", but I think he gave her plenty of chances that she blew by being so immature. She did finally have some good moments where things were resolved, though. 
 The love triangle could've been better. Blake kind of comes out of nowhere and goes after Kennedy right away, despite knowing how she and his brother feel about each other. While Blake and Kennedy did spend some time getting to know each other, I never really bought their possible romance. 
 It was obvious from the beginning that Graham has feelings for Kennedy, but she spends most of the book thinking the opposite. Graham also gets super jealous super easily and spends a lot of time refusing to believe that he and Kennedy will work out. It was annoying. 
 Overall, though, I enjoyed Roomies. The Cuteness definitely made up for The Frustrating. I enjoyed the banter and the burgeoning relationship. I would recommend this to fans of the Friends to Lovers trope and contemporary romance.

I was entertained, interested, and invested the whole time. The way that the various storylines have come together and the way that the plot and history were laid bare in Empire of Storms has made it my favorite installment in the series. 
 Things I enjoy in fantasy storytelling that this book did: 
 -Ensemble casts with multiple POVS that give a large scope to a large story and world. If this were first person POV from a single character, we would get such a tiny portion of the story. 
 -Information being withheld from the reader until it's needed. 
 -Having storylines intertwine and information be unveiled before the final conclusion. This gives us more time to process what's at stake. 
 -All of the major players are females. Friends, allies, enemies. The women are in power here. 
 Some thoughts on the sex scenes: 
 I could do without them to be honest, but despite how much they are being talked about, there are less than 20 pages of graphic sex scenes in this 689 page book. That's around 3%. If someone is telling you half the book is smut, that's just not true. Two erotic scenes does not equal an erotica novel. One of these scenes I found very unnecessary (the Dorian and Manon one. I guess I just needed more build up for that? ) and they are both quite graphic and kind of comical because of the magic elements used. 
 Some thoughts on Chaol: 
  
 I literally do not care that he was removed from this book. I have never been a fan of Chaol and honestly what the heck would he have been doing in this story other than griping at everyone for not doing things his way, or complaining that, despite being Captain of the Guard, he has to fight or kill. I do hope that he returns in the final book, but him being gone during this one was a GOOD thing. Did we really need his POV? No, let him do his thing and bring him back when the time is right, which was not in this installment. 
  
 My thoughts on the diversity (or lack of it): 
 With so many conversations about diversity in books going on around the time that I read this, and with Maas being under fire so frequently about her lack of diverse characters, I was paying more attention to it while reading this book. What I noticed was good (non-food) skin color descriptions, several side characters that were "bronze," "deep tan," or "brown," multiple same sex romances mentioned, a POV character who very clearly told us they were attracted to both men and women, and a main character with a disability who is so much more than just their disability. The POC and LGBTQIA+ mentions are mostly minor characters, so of course I am not arguing that this is great representation or that the book should be considered diverse, but I wanted to comment on this because I was personally glad to see that Maas had included acknowledgement of other races, sexualities, and disabilities. She's seeing the real world and reflecting it in her fictional world without trying to tell someone else's story. (This only speaks for this book though, as I do not remember descriptions from previous ones, aside from Elide.) 
 Anyway, I really enjoyed this. I've been a fan of the series since the start, it appeals to me personally (it's fine if it doesn't appeal to you though) and I'm excited and anxious for the conclusion.

2.5 stars. I don't think I've found characters quite as horrendous and despicable since Gone Girl. Some people should never be allowed to be parents. Poor Delphine. I felt sick to my stomach whenever she came into the plot. She was so pathetic and damaged by her horrible parents. If Rosie had never fled to Kate for a few minutes of safety and normality, Kate never would have gotten involved in trying to find her killer. Of course, then we wouldn't have had a story. Kate took it upon herself to befriend and take care of Jo, the grieving mother, constantly getting dragged in further. The narration would occasionally switch to Rosie, the dead girl. It was through her we saw flashbacks of her whole life, including her murder. At times it felt forced when Rosie was the way for information to be revealed. I guess I felt there was a better way to show us flashbacks of Jo's life. It didn't need to be seen through the eyes of her dead daughter. It felt like it was just a way to keep Rosie in the story, and it wasn't necessary. Overall, the story was a little too slow paced to be considered a psychological thriller. To me it was way more a story about people and the secrets they keep. It shows that you never really know people. That the person they let the world see may not be who they are at all. I don't know how I felt about the book as a whole. There were parts I liked and other parts I didn't. It just didn't pull me in that much.

As always, the main problem with this is that it was too long. It didn't actually take me four months to read; I had a massive break in the middle. It seemed to make almost no difference to my knowledge as to what is going on. Jordan re-explains everything each chapter switch, so it' s easy to jump back in. I'm pretty sure this is a bad thing: the book would probably be much shorter if he didn't. 
 On the whole it's okay. Yes, it's got a big scope and blah blah blah, whatever. So have lots of books. (Spoilers coming, if anybody actually reads this review). The thing is, I don't get the feeling that Jordan really knew where he was going. It seems like the wanted to do anything other than start coming to a conclusion, and bear in mind that at this point the WoT series was already more than four times longer than the LoTR series. Jordan introduces a whole batch of frankly unnecessary plot elements. A new Aes Sedai woman, the best ever (tm)! A new baddie type, even deadlier than a Mydraaaaaaaal!! A whole new group of women who can channel!!! I just don't think any of these things were necessary. They seem like pointless complications. 
 On top of that, there are so many annoying mannerisms. Nynaeve's constant braid tugging. Women with eyes like dark pools that a man can lose himself in. Women crossing their fucking arms under their breasts! Why is that last detail necessary!! I'm pretty sure women don't sniff to express disapproval either, but maybe I just haven't noticed. On top of that, there's a really questionably arc, where one of the main characters is effectively raped by a woman. I think we were meant to find this funny, but he is basically repeatedly coerced into sex, and I can't help but find the whole thing a bit unpleasant. 
 So there we are. Rant over. Two stars is possibly a bit stingy, but mostly deserved.

I took a few days to mull this book over before writing any sort of review. First, the non-spoilery stuff: 
 The first book of the Stormlight Archive, The Way of Kings, had a significant learning curve, and the end of the book paid off big time. This book is a bit different in structure. He builds this book off the last one, but it is its own monster. 
 From page one, you go into Words of Radiance as a fully established world, so in a lot of ways there is no learning curve at all. That's an accomplishment in and of itself, but Sanderson set up more than just the world in the first book, he also set up characters, and all that set up came together and built the foundation for this book, which starts out great and just keeps on going. 
 Sanderson also sets this book up so that you don't just have one big climax but at least five throughout the course of the book. Each part of the book feels like an episode in a longer epic, and yet it all ties in so well that it never feels disjointed. Even though I felt I could put the book down at the end of the day after finishing a part, I only wanted to get back to it that much more the next day. 
  
 Finally seeing all the characters from the first book come together and interact was amazing. It's so different than other fantasy that I've read where the group starts together and then splits up. It was refreshing. 
 Adolin's interactions with the other characters made him one of my favorite characters where he was a character I could have taken or left in the first book. Throughout this book, though I felt he really grew. When he stayed in prison with Kaladin, I was very impressed. The biggest surprise of the entire book was when Adolin killed Sadeas. I hated Sadeas so much and wanted someone to kill him. I wanted to cheer, but the scene was so dark, and so emotional, and character driven, that I just sat there in awe when it was over. 
 I absolutely loved Shallan in this book. She's come a long way, and so much stuff about her was revealed that made me retroactively like her more in the first book. Her killing her father was one of those things I didn't see coming, but when it was revealed I felt it couldn't have been any other way. Her and Kaladin worked so well together, too. I don't know why, but I was worried that they wouldn't, but they worked better than I thought. Not a fan of the love triangle aspect, but what can you do. At least it was handled with class. 
 Kaladin was great. It was strange seeing him through everyone else's eyes, and I think Sanderson did a really good job showing us his back story in the first book because it humanized him. He's the grim and determined soldier from every book who you can never really relate to, except that in this series, you can't stop relating. Good stuff! 
 Because it was Sanderson, I expected a twist ending, which I guess we got with the whole Jasnah thing, though I saw that coming a long time before (though I didn't know it'd be in this book). Her working with Wit was a cool twist. Throughout the book, the series seemed to be building toward a higher concept clash soon. Can't wait to see what Hoid has been up to this whole time. I'm hoping we get his entire story. 
 There's so much more to say about this book, but I'll save it for 17thshard.com!

I received a copy of this title from NetGalley. It does not impact my review. 
 I've read two Cassie Mae books before and thought one was pretty cute (Switched!) and one was pretty ridiculous (we don't need to get into that one). When I saw this book I wanted to give her another try since I enjoy the best-friend-becomes-more trope, if done properly. I'm pleased to say that I did really enjoy The Real Thing. 
 Before this book I read another one that also employed the best-friend-becomes-more trope and it didn't really at all work for me. I think one of the biggest differences between the previous book and this book (where it does works) is that in The Real Thing Eric and Mia are friends that have an attraction for the other, where the previous couple were friends that were already in love, but not admitting it to each other. And even though we know Eric and Mia will end up together, there's still a lot more build up and tension in their relationship throughout the story. 
 I also enjoyed the bit of role reversal that deviates from the usual NA. Mia is confident and knows what she wants. She's neither trampy nor innocent. That's not to say she isn't without her problems. She's addicted to the internet and her phone to an unhealthy degree. While I thought this was a bit over the top, I'm sure there are many people out there that could totally relate to that. 
 Then there's Eric. He's insecure about his weight, has anxiety attacks, and doesn't like to be touched. I can not even tell you how much I related to him! I thought Mae did a great job of realistically portraying what it's like to live with anxiety. I also think she handled the treatment of it much better than most books that have anxiety prone characters. Eric has coping techniques, family support, therapy, and medication. 
 My only real complaint with the book is all the sexual content, though it seems to be a requirement for the NA genre. Mia seemed way more interested in moving their relationship ahead physically than in really getting to know Eric. I get that they're best friends and know a lot about each other, but they've been apart for three years and there's obviously a lot more they need to find out about each other. It was, however, not as graphic as a lot of other books of this genre are. 
 Overall, I enjoyed The Real Thing. The characters were mostly very relatable and likable. I especially appreciated the way Eric's anxiety was portrayed and handled. I would recommend this book to fans of NA, especially to those who are looking for something a little different than the normal NA plotlines.

Upon reaching the halfway point or so in this novel, I became curious about what the Goodreads community had to say about Blood Meridian. I logged on and found Josh's review below, in which he mentions that many people stop reading the book when they reach the tree of dead babies. 
 Let me repeat that: Tree of Dead Babies. My brain underwent some kind of chiropractic shift when, upon reading his comment, I realized I had breezed past that horrific scene, and many more besides, with an "Eh", and a kind of mental Gallic shrug. That is what this book does to you. 
 A deadpan catalogue of the atrocities westbound American settlers visited on the natives and each other in the mid-1800s, Blood Meridian is a novel more to be admired than enjoyed. The action is copious and violent, the landscape vast and soul-numbing, the characters-- those that register at all--dwarfed by the enormity of their situation, both in geographical space and historical moment. 
 Even though I can bring to mind other books that contain extreme violence or horror, in those stories such incidents usually form the climax of the narrative, or at least significant turning points. In Blood Meridian, armed fights, casual murder and mass slaughter are part of the landscape, so that a description of the posse encountering their murdered scouts hung from a tree by their heels is no more (or less) appalling than that of the blasted heaths they cross later on. 
 It took me a while to really "get" this book--to see the larger structure that holds it together--but I'm glad I did: if I'd just read the story literally, I'd probably have ended up hating this book, for all the reasons some reviewers below hated it. Yes, much of this book is a repetitive travelogue; yes, McCarthy's prose tends toward the run-on sentence more than I'd like--and some sentences are almost unreadably long; yes, the characters, with the notable exception of the judge and Glanton, are little more than stock figures. I'm not here to excuse any of that. 
 Where the book did resonate with me was on the mythic level. Accept that the American West is a stand-in for Dante's Inferno, the posse doomed souls, and the judge the impartial figure of Fate floating above it all, untouched by time or circumstance--and everything falls into place. McCarthy employs a detached, omniscient narration that prevents the reader--purposefully, I think--from becoming attached to any character. The characters are perhaps mere sketches to underscore that they don't matter in the larger course of human history, which itself may be a pointless exercise in an uncaring, fundamentally random universe. 
 Perhaps fittingly for the material, I'm not sure if Blood Meridian adds up to anything beyond that, but I'm not sure it has to, either. For any readers tired of novels that end in an artificial redemptive arc (and there are many more of those), Blood Meridian is refreshingly nihilistic reading. Just bring an iron stomach and check your emotions at the door.

This book is a breathtaking work of art. It is not a novel, as the cover so boldly claims, but an in-depth photo essay, with only a few snatches of independent dialogue serving as text beyond what can be found in IMs and occasional notes, e-mails, and other paper memorabilia. In some respects it's like a scrapbook - there is nothing interactive, but there are all manner of things from drawings and personal photographs, to photographs of things you can imagine taking out and looking at, to mix CDs and YouTube clips and newspaper articles. The artistic photographs of the main characters, though, are the ones that stand out. It reminds me of a movie stilled to individual frames, that's how rich each spread is, with not one wasted page, or even part of a page. 
 It took me at least 30 minutes to "read" through the book the first time, drinking in every page and scanning all the items presented on each spread. I was skeptical, wondering how I would possibly understand what the story was without real text. The answer is: just open it and start trying. The story will develop before your eyes, like magic. Another part of the magic is that the images give you an outline, but only a few of the intimate details are given. Everyone will read a slightly different story out of it, and I think that's pretty cool. 
 What's it actually about? Generally speaking, an 18-year-old piano prodigy disappears from a rest home one night. We then flash back 18 months and, after a brief history lesson about her childhood, watch her fall in all-consuming love with the new boy next door, and their frustration at being separated when she and her father leave to pursue her gift on an international level. While they maintain an intense long-distance relationship, his grades spiral down as her mental well-being destabilizes under pressure, developing an obsession with playing Chopsticks. 
 I initially knocked a whole star off of this because the relationship wasn't appealing at all. It wasn't even the Romeo-and-Juliet levels of melodrama, because I would be happy to believe that this is a story of a star crumbling and that love may not be all you need, but sometimes it's exactly what holds you together. No, the problem was that boy-next-door Frank was the most unappealing loser I've ever seen, getting in fights and failing most of his classes besides art because apparently there's just no point in trying when you're an immigrant in ESL. Stupid America! Not relaxed and cool like Argentina at all! 
 I have since read a lot of other reviews, and apparently I fail at determining whether books are ever more than they present themselves on the surface. Minor spoilers for theories: In that case, the question of just how deep Glory's madness is and how early it presents is fascinating. I did notice the oddly identical letterhead on the school/rest home, but thought it was just meant to show that they were managed by the same property owners - not until later did I realize it was also the same signature, same address. If I can pretend Frank and/or their relationship is a figment of Glory's imagination, I am still disappoint in her lack of ability to imagine someone desirable, but I am also way more invested in the story of Glory alone.  
 This is a book to which you can absolutely go back again and again, whether for the purpose of seeking new "clues" or simply to relive the experience and enjoy the artwork. I don't have any way of utilizing the app, but it sounds like one of those rare times where technology actually does enhance a book, and I look forward to testing it out one day in the distant future.

Rylie has to go summer camp. Unhappy, she leaves the cabin at night and is attacked by something. Seth, the boy she met in the woods, tells her she's becoming a werewolf. 
 *** 
 Rylie is not a very sympathetic character. She's selfish, whiny, and just awful. She describes herself as the richest kid at her HS. 
 Rylie's friends back home were mostly guys, since all the girls she knew were catty and stupid. And these ones hated Rylie for no reason at all. 
 See? It's coz she's a super skinny, vegetarian with white blonde hair. *shudders* 
 She's very unlikable and dumb as a rock. [I started this is April] 
 Her father dies and she's allowed to go home for the funeral, but intends to come back the next week to see Seth. *frowns* 
 She says her father was like her friend and the only person she could talk to, but there was no evidence of that. And while she's at camp, she never messages him. (before she breaks her phone - no wait, she lost it but found it again and I don't know why she isn't using it to message all those guy friends she has.) 
 And the first night home she goes to a concert with her friend and is annoyed that he shows up with a girl. Grief is a funny thing but this the day after her father died and he's not even buried yet. More weight on the unlikable side of the scale. 
 Girlfriend: the dirtiest of dirty words. Girlfriends interfered with friend-time and turned her guy friends stupid. Rylie hated it every time one of the boys she hung out with got a new girl because it meant their fun was over until the relationship ended. No matter how much she liked the band, Rylie never would have come if she knew it meant tolerating a girlfriend. 
 Ugh. It's really piling on there now. 
 Conveniently she's now rich. (but forgets to buy a new phone.) Her father has left her everything which is odd, because the divorce was just finalised and he should have paid off his wife. They sent her to camp so they could do it. And her mother doesn't seem worried that her kid has the business she ran AND all the money. Nor does she seem to be worried about where her underage daughter will live. 
 It's all a bit too convenient. [she steals a car and can miraculously drive, and on wilderness roads] And it's so cliched. I'm going to guess Seth knows too much about werewolves, and is probably a hunter. 
 I keep getting Teen Wolf vibes. She has an inhaler, gets chained up, they use aconite, the info is all in one book. This was published in 2011. Which is when the show started. *shrugs* 
 So the wolf IS who I thought it was, the second wolf is not a surprise either, and Seth IS a hunter. The camp doesn't get shut down after one death and there's no one official investigating. When she wants to stay human she thinks of her mother's condo, rather than anything idk... humanising. I skimmed to the end.

I really wanted to like this. I absolutely love the cover with the hourglass filled with the two realms. When I read the blurb and saw it was about the afterlife, I was even more sold on it. When I finally got to read it.... 
 It makes no sense whatsoever. Seriously. I have no reasons to justify all the biggest portions of this book. First: why doesn't Ten want to decide between the two realms? She's literally withstanding months of degradation and torture, sexual condescension, etc. but for what? I mean, I know that her parents want her to go to Myriad. Ten knows that both places probably aren't the best. Yet instead of choosing the lesser of two evils like most others....she stays in a prison cell (sorry, asylum) stabbing herself in the finger over and over again. Ooookay. 
 Second: the two realms send their "best" people to try and lure Ten to their sides. I'll disregard the fact that in ETERNITY, their best people are random 17 year old guys. Figures. Anyway, why do they send their best people to get Ten? Because Ten is special. Why is Ten special? It takes more than half of the book for us to finally get an answer, and it's a half-assed one. They think another eternity soul fused with hers. Also, she can somehow bring light or dark or something? Which doesn't really make sense because there's been no proof of any magic powers up to this point, only a little bit of science fiction and fantasy with souls traversing different realms. So these guys are pulling out all the stops to drive her to their sides....first by impersonating a girl, then by seducing her, then lots and lots and lots of badgering her. 
 Third: everybody REALLY wants Ten because they're waging a war between the two realms. So...why are they fighting? What is the reason for them to dislike each other so strongly, for them to be at war for eternity. I just don't get it. I mean their fundamental ideas are very different, but that doesn't constitute war. 
 On top of all my constant questions, I get a love triangle and instalove. Dates and kisses and pining for one another. It was ridiculousness on top of confusion. So yeah, this whole time I was just thinking that it is a dramatic disappointment of a book. 
 Oh! I just remembered! There was a random part about how Ten's mother was a 16-year-old mother or something, and it was almost implied that it was normal for everyone to be pregnant around that age. I wish I could find that part to remind myself, but whatever.

 Unlike the best YA, "Darkest Minds" doesn't have characters that fix my imagination. As I read, I kept wondering about practical matters that seemed convenient but ultimately inexplicable. There are other plot holes that just don't make sense and aren't really explained, just moved on from. And if these are the sorts of threads I'm pulling as I read, I'm skimming the surface.
