You sigh, uncertain if you will ever again find that slim tome you began reading in that labyrinth off of the avenue so many moons ago. For the life of you you are not sure how it began, much less the title or author, or even where in the book you picked up the story's thread. You can hardly even recollect the end of the story for all its glory. Spying an old favorite, you pull if off the shelf, dislodging a torn fragment of something else entirely. Consumed with the writer's carefree charm, you begin to read. 
 And read. 
 And read. 
 Until you forget what you were looking for before, and after . . . 
 Italo Calvino's If On A Winter Night A Traveler is a novel nonpareil in terms of the richness of its language and the innovations taken in form. This little masterpiece is all the more curious in that you are the character: much of the novel is written in the second person and your very act of reading it drives the plot forward. And the plot is at heart a mystery, one that will appeal to any true bibliophile.

Though I am of the generation that grew up with Goosebumps, both the books and the television series, I admittedly never completely got into the series. I recall watching an episode here and there, but at the time, in the '90s, I was more of a Babysitters Club kind of girl. I have been wanting to get into the Goosebumps/Fear Street series for a while, though, so when I received an ARC for the upcoming third book in the Fear Street relaunch (The Lost Girl), I knew I needed to pick up from the (relaunched) beginning. Though theses books are generally standalones, I wanted to have some familiarity, be eased into the content at hand. Familiar tales and literary settings from my childhood began to emerge the further I delved into the subject...or at least the prepackaged description. 
 Rachel Martin is invited to a birthday party thrown by the popular and "weird" Brendan Fear at his family's mansion on their self-named Fear Island. Despite warnings from her best friend, Amy, and her newly ex-boyfriend, Mac, as well as the ominously placed dead rat (warning sign?) in her bed, Rachel goes with hopes and expectations of getting closer to her crush, the birthday boy (Brendan). Things start out fairly normal with the slight exception of a seriously injured house staff member, but suddenly turn strange and deadly once the teens embark on their scavenger hunt game. Following the creepy elevator, the hall of aggressive bats, and the floor with seemingly no escape is the first second serious event of the evening: A classmate is found dead, limbs twisted unnaturally and with an ominous, "gamey" note. Two more teens drop dead, thoroughly terrifying the survivors, before Brendan makes his grand reveal: This has all been a part of his latest game. Brendan explains everything, following with an invitation to party the rest of the night away, until two unknown masked men show up with rifles and threats to shoot anyone who doesn't follow their directions. Brendan at first assumes that they are just his hired actors, pawns in his game, but when they use force and make demands (think kidnap and ransom), Brendan's twisted game turns into a dangerous reality. 
 The pace of this work starts out somewhat dull with tons of characters who are introduced only to be lost later on in the thrill of the dangerous adventure. This was confusing and seemed unnecessary, especially since half or more of these characters weren't even part of the party (or they initially were, then completely disappeared). Further, certain slang and dialogue felt forced or unnatural to teens nowadays (I imagine YA readers rolling their eyes about as much as, if not more than, I did) as well as the point to make sure that everyone was of legal drinking age, while responsible, seemed a bit over the top. I honestly was a bit bored up until Randy hit his head, when things started getting Fear-weird and thus somewhat interesting. I was hesitant to get wrapped into the plot, though, until we were led to believe that Brendan might be hanging dead. When kids started dying, though I (accurately) had a feeling that this was only the true plot of Brendan's game, I started to really get drawn into the quicker pace and darker tone of the story. Even with the slightly underwhelming reveal, I wasn't let down for too long before the masked men came in to take us on a wild and dangerous ride all over again. 
 The supernatural elements of this title were unfortunately quickly dismissed or explained away, yet I still felt chills from the possibly haunted Fear mansion and the creepy ghost of Victoria Fear, whose intense interest in taxidermy led to the creepy rumor that she was her own last taxidermy project. Though not entirely as creepy as the tales I remember from my youth, Party Games is still a promising and mostly exciting adventure back into Fear Street.

The Nightingale is a historical fiction novel which tells the story of two French sisters, Vianne Mauriac and Isabelle Rossignol, during the German occupation of France in World War II. This is an amazing book inspired by a real-life nineteen-year-old Belgian woman who led downed airmen over the frozen peaks of the Pyrenees Mountains on an escape route out of Nazi-Occupied France. It is also inspired by all of the women left behind in a country full of women without enough food or rations who furthermore had to accept that the occupiers would take over or share their homes. Additionally, it is inspired by those who chose to find ways to help the Jewish avoid the concentration camps at all costs. It is about the courageous, ordinary French women who put their lives on the line to save others. I love that this book tells the story of ordinary women making extraordinary sacrifices and performing acts of heroism during such a horrific period. There is just something so dramatic and important about this story. Like many historical novels of this period, it tells a story of how horrific it was to live with the Nazis. It's a sad story that can bring tears to the eyes of the reader. Yes, it has sadness and cruelty but it also has suspense, redemption, love, and hope. 
 Fifty years after the end of the war, a recently widowed woman in a coastal town in Oregon is preparing to move to a nursing home because her cancer has returned. Her son, a surgeon, comes to help her and finds her in the attic going through a trunk of old things he has never seen. She insists that the trunk be taken to the nursing home with her in its entirety. She gets an invite to a reunion in France and decides to attend. We occasionally cut to her story as we learn about the past. We aren't told the identity of the woman until near the end. 
 The book is told from the perspective of two sisters prior to and during the German occupation of France in WWII. Two sisters, as different as they can be, were sent away as children by their alcoholic father, Julien Rossignol, whose WWI experience changed him so much that when his beloved wife died, he could no longer be father to them. He dumped them off on relatives or at boarding schools and pretty much left the girls to fend for themselves. The sisters didn't get along well and weren't close. Vienne, the older, marries as a teen and leaves her nuclear family behind. Isabelle, the younger, is sent away for refinement and education but her life is void of love. She determinedly runs away and tries to rejoin her father or her sister but is repeatedly turned away. The book details the lives of the sisters involving the father only when their lives somehow intersect. 
 In August of 1939, Britain and France, despite having declared war on Germany, have not engaged in any military battles with the German Reich. Tensions are high among the French citizenry as they await the start of the war. The sufferings of the Great War, and the millions of lives lost, are still fresh in their minds. As WWII rushes into their lives all three confront it differently. The father seems to go deeper into drink while he works in Paris at the administrative headquarters of the enemy. The older sister, Vienne, sees the love of her life march away leaving her ersatz widowed with her young daughter to survive as best she can in the small town in which she resides. The younger sister, sent to live with Vienne, rushes headlong into resistance groups doing whatever she can. Each plays a specific part in resisting German occupation until at long last France can be liberated.

"Never Too Far" by Abbi Glines 
 I own this book and this review is my honest opinion. 
 I jumped into this book immediately after finishing book one - "Fallen Too Far." I'm glad I started reading this series after all the books were already available, because it would have been torture having to wait to see what happened after the cliffhanger in book one. 
 Book two, "Never Too Far" started off with a bang. I already fell in love with the characters in the first book and was eager to see what they were up to now. I'll tell you that my mind was blown very early into this book. And when I say very early, I mean right away. It was great. 
 I love when I am so drawn to the characters in a book, and Abbi Glines sure knows how to create a character. I love all the drama in Blaire and Rush's life, but I love when things are happy too. All the drama makes the happy moments more special. And the sex is as steamy as ever. Of course I love it! 
 Rush's family is still very unwelcome with Blaire and that takes a major toll on her and Rush's relationship. Understandably so. Nan is a very hard person to deal with. As much drama as she causes for Rush and Blaire, I would like to see her happy and find her own love. It'd be better on everyone. 
 Once again, I love the secondary characters surrounding Blaire and Rush. Bethy, Grant, Woods, Jace...I love them all. I like being able to connect with people in a story even if they are not the main focus. It's another sign of good writing. 
 I would definitely recommend "Never Too Far" by Abbi Glines to readers who love the New Adult genre with Romance and drama. I'd also strongly encourage you reading book one first...otherwise, you'll be lost. You don't want to miss that great story anyway, though. I will definitely continue reading books from Abbi Glines and highly recommend her work. 
 Oh yeah, and I love the cover of course! Fits the story so well!

The best part of the Reckoners series, in my opinion, is the way in which Sanderson plays with that traditional black-and-white dichotomy between the hero and the villain. He first introduces these Epics, corrupted beings with superhuman abilities, and then throughout the course of the series, makes the reader question whether their potential for harm and destruction is an inevitability. This is especially apparent in Calamity, where Sanderson uses the climatic events in this finale to make a distinction between innate good/evil versus chosen good/evil. And in doing so, he provides a thought-provoking commentary on the nature of human goodness. 
 Mmm. Good stuff. 
 There's not much else I have to say about this. The action sequences were fast and snappy as always, the characters compelling. The worldbuilding was solid -- I mean Ilditha was a city made of salt that periodically crumbled away only to reform somewhere else and I was still sold -- and the witty humor was spot-on. Cody's Scottish-Southern sass was sort of the best thing ever, and David's metaphors, as per usual, gave me life. There were so many hilarious ones this time around, but I do think that "like bread at a rock party" and "like a barrel of green ducks at a Fourth of July parade" take the cake. (The second one being Megan's, but David took it seriously of course.) 
 But that doesn't mean I didn't have issues with Calamity. 
 The first gripe that I had with this conclusion is that Calamity didn't read like a conclusion. Seventy percent of this was David and crew plotting another one of their schemes, which was fun and all, but the problem lies in the fact that this isn't just another installment in the series. It's the end. But only in the last 40 pages or so did that become clear. And by then, everything just felt maddeningly rushed. 
 And it's disappointing, because Sanderson is usually so solid with his plots. I could have let the pacing problem slide, had the resolution not been so convenient. Everything was a bit too easy, almost as if Sanderson were trying to cater to a younger--and thereby "easier"--audience. This comes up time and time again, where fantastic authors, either because of their publishers or some other factor, are told to "dumb down" their writing and spend less time developing their plots because young people don't actually care about quality right? They're just in it for the action and some entertainment. The way in which this massive, Epic conflict was resolved felt weak and as much as it pains me to say it, cheap. 
 The reveal about Larcener being an extension of Calamity was strange, and then there was the fiasco with Prof that was riddled with deus ex machinas. Megan suddenly is in complete control of her dimensional powers and can pull a full-fledged rtich out of them, after having spent the rest of the series crippled by a single illusion. Everyone is conveniently wounded in action, leaving David as the only possible person to save the day. And Prof's weakness, to me, did not take me by surprise. The only thing I liked about the end was the way in which Sanderson used Calamity's fears to highlight the difference between internal and external goodness was fascinating. What made the Epics of David's world become corrupted, and what made the Epics of Firefight's world stay good? And what made this even more interesting was that in Firefight's world, there were still Epics who had chosen to become tyrants and terrorize civilians.  
 And finally, in honor of this being another conclusion to a Sanderson series, I thought I'd share my favorite quotes from Calamity: 
 (396) "The world?" "It's broken. Terrible. Horrid." "Yeah," I said softly. "Beautiful." 
 (388) "He was afraid of stepping up, of becoming everything he could be--not because the powers themselves frightened him. But because if he tried, then the failure was far, far worse. At least if he held something back and failed, he could tell himself it wasn't completely his fault. Or that it was part of the plan, that he'd always intended for it to go this way. Only if he gave his all, only if he was using every resource he had would the failure be complete. What a terrible burden the powers were I could see how they'd become a focus for him, how they represented the whole of his competence--and how they also represented his potential for true failure."  
 (403) "Divine powers don't make you a god." 
 (411) "Do you fear that? Does it terrify you to now that deep down, men are not monsters? That we are, instead, inherently good?" 
 (415) "They're people. Free to be people, as it should be. And that means some of them are still going to be selfish, or messed up, or whatever."
You can see how her writing has improved since her first book. However there is still something missing for me. not enough to write anything negative about this book, it is a good book.

However, once the initial introductions were over, the story really kicked off nicely. As it stands, Brady Hartsfield is one of King's more despicable villains that he's created in recent memory. There were no redeeming qualities with him, and I raced through the book wanting to see how (if?) he would get his just desserts. With regards to the fate of Bill Hodges and his cancer diagnosis, I was fearful that King would pull a body switch and then have Brady return to his own body with the cancer and everyone would live happily ever after. Such was (thankfully) not the case. Hodges does succumb to the terrible, silent, suicidal killer. It's not how I wanted his story to end, but it was the way it was meant to end. 4.5 stars rounded up 
 While reading this, I jokingly referred to it as "Howl's Moving Castle for Grownups" as it deals with a magician who loses his physical heart to a female magic-user, and the woman who braves all odds to save him. And I'm all about that life. 
 I enjoyed all of the characters immensely - but knocked off the .5 star because I felt Lira was rather one-dimensional - and I get it. We're seeing all of this through Ceony and Emery's viewpoint and their opinions are obviously skewed, but she came off as very manipulative and "muhahaha"-evil. So why and how would a person like Emery fall in love with her to the point of marriage? 
 As for the other characters: the way in which we learned about Emery Thane as a whole was so clever and inventive and really just made you come to care for the man as Ceony did. I love that we didn't just see how heroic and romantic and kind he is, but also saw how he could be cruel and selfish and petty. And Ceony Twill made my heart sing - a sassy, strong female character who didn't come off as insipid or arrogant or annoying. 
 The magic system is very cool! People with the capability for magic attend the Tagis Praff Magic Academy (or some such) to learn about the different forms of magic and upon graduation pledge their magic-performing life to one man-made material. They can then only perform magic through that material for the rest of their lives. The author shows us plenty of cool and clever uses for Folding (paper magic) throughout the book - animated paper animals, giant paper gliders that humans can pilot, paper chains of healing and defense, paper fans that create gusts of wind - but also drops mentions of cool things from other magics - enchanted bullets that always hit their target, magical cannons and so on. My imagination had fun mulling over the magics from this series, and I would read this book before bed to fill my dreams with man-made magic. 
 The plot itself moved along at a brisk pace and I was never bored or counting pages. I greatly enjoyed this imaginative little read and can not wait to get my hands on the rest of this trilogy!

The second book of the Sarantine Mosaic. We follow the potential war between cities, the chariot races underlying the tension between Blues and Greens, and of course the characters that are trying to stay afloat and survive in their daily lives. 
 I almost hate that it ended so well because it makes me really want to give 3 stars when I feel like it only deserved 1 or maybe 2 around the middle of the book. I seriously almost dnf around page 200 (about 50%) of the book because it got so boring and annoying. 
 Again, the only redeeming factors were the court scenes, the chariot races, and the ending. How many ways can I praise the way GGK writes the court scenes? Court was brilliant as usual, with people vying for power and showing how hidden knowledge is power. Tension in every word. 
 Like the first book, the chariot races were full of passion and energy and heart-stopping moments. Brilliant. And I ended up loving all of the chariot characters for their passion. 
 And the ending. THE ENDING. Just wow. What a strong finish. The imagery of  three women vying for the throne  is too great. 
 However, I was not convinced that  Alixana would actually end up with Crispin. Seem like too much of a neat and tidy way to wrap up characters's endings . 
 But let's talk about characters. What can I say? I just don't really like Cripin. He's such a dull (and fairly unlikable) main character. But whereas I hated/was ambivalent toward every single character in the first book, there are quite a number of characters I like here. Of course Scortius, First of the Blues. He's brilliantly written. Shirin of the Greens and how she wears her perfume. Strumosus the fussy chef and Kyros (that medic scene was heart wrenching). Alixana and Valerius are just too snarky and adorable together. But Crispin.... yeah. No. 
 Another little thing: there was no resolution with the birds. Kinda gimmicky because they were hardly used in this second book. The entire "magic" of these series was a underused. 
 But as much as I complain about the problems, I just have to return to praise GGK. The prose... How does GGK write so beautifully? It is not flowery, it is not whimsical, or wispy around the edges. It writhes with emotion. It paints pictures in the mind. 
 If I ever need to find beauty in words, I know which author to read. 
 Three stars.

We have two very serious things to discuss before we jump into this book. For one, you know a book is really good when I don't feel the need to make a ton of Goodreads updates. This book just sucked me right in, just like the show initially did. I had not one single complaint. So, the rest of this review is going to be a ton of gushing. Which brings me to the second serious thing to discuss. I was a huuuuuge Veronica Mars fan. I was completely devastated when the show was prematurely cancelled by The CW all those years ago, and I was one of thousands to donate to their KickStarter campaign to make a movie. I wanted Veronica back in my life so damn badly. So while I am a very proud Marshmallow, I want this review to be taken seriously. Because I am not just squealing with delight at how perfect the book ended up being just because I am a Veronica Mars fan. It is truly a wonderful book, and I honestly have no complaints. I never have zero complaints. Not even with a John Green book. So this is fantastic. 
 Just as some backup, Veronica's dad was a sheriff-turned-private-investigator while Veronica was a teenager, and as the cases started piling up she used to help out. Ten plus years late, she's back in her home town as a PI in her own right, and she's called in to help with a missing persons case. The girl is in Neptune on spring break when she goes missing, and Veronica has to find her and bring her home before Neptune loses all of their tourists. That's basically the initial premise, anyway. As the story unfolds more and more obstacles start popping up, and more and more bits from Veronica's past start bubbling to the surface. 
 This is a perfect mystery, as most Veronica Mars episodes were. Just when you think you know what's going to happen or who did it, another twist is brought in and the whole thing changes direction. For those of you that aren't familiar with Veronica Mars you can read it without needing to watch the show or the movie. There's enough there as a story to entertain you. But for us VM fans....... phew. This was flawless. This takes place just a few weeks after the ending of the movie. There's old characters, old references, everything you could possibly want. And yes, There is even some LoVe (heh, get it) between Veronica and Logan.  When I tell you I have no complaints, I truly have no complaints. The book was wonderfully written and it felt just like watching an episode back in the day. I heard the characters voices in my head. I pictured their movements. It felt wonderful to be reunited with my old friends. Amazing even. But you'll have to read the book yourself, and then come back to fangirl with me, because there is nothing else I can say without spoiling things. 
 Side-note: While there's no news about whether or not there will be another Veronica Mars movie (fingers crossed though, you literally can't ever count anything out with these guys) there will be another Veronica Mars book coming out on October 28th. It's called Mr. Kiss & Tell and I'm so damn excited. I've missed being a Marshmallow.

I've been having no luck with Anna Campbell's latest books and this one was no exception :( It's a story that tries way too hard making every emotion and action so extreme and over the top that nothing seems plausible and it gets irritating. The characters are pretty good at the beginning and show some originality, but then the heroine turns into every other heroine I've ever read and the hero is just plain unlikable reminding me more of Anne Stuart's mean/unfeeling/uncaring sob historical heroes which I don't like. The steam scenes are smoking hot for a historical and a little different which was good to see, but with the non-stop "emotional highs" it missed out on the feeling sometimes. The author did do a good job of tension building so that when the two finally came together you could certainly appreciate the sizzle, I just would've liked more variety in the emotions which tends to make the reader connect more with the characters. 
 Some of the writing skirts the edge of purple prose with the crazy adjectives one after another. The revenge story is well-done for the most part as the hero sets out to destroy the charge of the woman he really loves. He goes pretty far too but then the story veers into the stupid and stereotypical romance  where the hero fights in a duel for the heroine and is on his death bed because he gets himself shot like an idiot suddenly thinking of her beautiful eyes--what the???!! . The way he handles the duel doesn't coincide with his character so the story went downhill from there. 
 There are a few too many "coincidences" from the  long lost heroine's lover who accidentally stumbles across the hero and later her, to the heroine's brother suddenly finding out that she's not dead. . It was just too much. Campbell can create an amazing story (just read Claiming the Courtesan and Tempt the Devil) but here it's as if she ran out of ideas and fell back on the same ol' cookie cutter regarding writing and just tried desperately to make it all work. Thanks to The Hunger Games, dystopias are hot among the teens I teach. "The Line" offers a curious branch on that tree, not as action packed or dramatic, but driven by the relationships between three women. This is clearly the set up for future books, and "The Line" just stops, rather than ends, with a climax isn't all that tense. So for such a lengthy lead up, the payoff wasn't there for me. 
 What I did like is that "The Line" concerns a girl, her mother, and the woman for whom they both work. Cultivating orchids takes up a significant portion of the book. In a word, it is a bit 'girly.' Say what you want about other YA speculative fiction with strong female characters - Leviathan, Ship Breaker, Mortal Engines, Airborn - they aren't 'girly.' 
 The pace is leisurely. If you have a capable reader who wants something squeaky clean and isn't put off by character-driven writing or an all-female cast (yes, there are a few guys, but they aren't central to the plot), this might be a good read.

Just a couple nights ago I glanced at Stay, but I wasn't looking for a new book to read at the moment, I couldn't tell what it was about by the title/cover, and--this is my bad--I didn't even finish reading the whole blurb. I don't remember why (I think the shark metaphor made me worry that there would be a lot of flowery prose, and that's not my thing), but part of it is probably that I'm so used to being disappointed by many of the dark romances I pick up. But then Emily Goodwin popped up in my FB newsfeed doing an author takeover on a blog I follow, and she used the r-word that never fails to excite me--research. She said she wrote a dark romance that involved human trafficking, and then mentioned some of the research she did to prepare to write about this. 
 I was pretty much sold on that alone. Too many authors these days don't bother doing any research, and then I read their books, don't like them because they're insanely unrealistic, and I feel like a meanie. It's an unpleasant experience for everyone involved. When I saw how seriously this author (rightly) took her research, I got all giddy. I didn't reread the blurb that I never finished (I rarely go into books that blind, but I made an exception this time) and I didn't look at a single review. I saw that it was on sale and snapped this little book right up in my greedy, gluttonous Kindle. 
 Now, first I want to say this is not erotica. It was classified on Amazon as erotica so that's what I expected, but it really isn't. (That doesn't bother me, as I don't read a ton of erotica anyway, but I thought it was worth pointing out.) Also, the romance in this is not dark. The circumstances are dark, but the romance is not. There's also rape (obviously). 
 I won't totally reblurb here, but a very brief synopsis--this is a story about an ordinary girl just going about her life, she's in the wrong place at the wrong time, and she ends up getting abducted by a group of human traffickers. 
 This was a very readable book. I read the whole thing in one day. Lost many hours of sleep! It's also pretty unique. While it's not altogether uncommon these days for trafficking to be a plot-point in dark romances, this one certainly didn't go about it in the same way. In a sense, some parts reminded me of Trafficked (that one was much less graphic/not as dark and featured domestic servitude, not prostitution, but it also focused on the girl's life during the trafficking experience without the captor-romance that sometimes develops in the dark romances). There's another one it reminds me more of, but I can't remember what it was called at the moment. THIS one is really gritty, but it's based on real events. Trafficked: The Terrifying True Story of a British Girl Forced into the Sex Trade (In this one, that whole fear making you pass obvious escape thing...that actually applies in this one. The times she could escape and doesn't are enough to make you pull your hair out, but...it happens. The fear goes deep.) 
 My interest in this book was very uneven. It didn't immediately grab me, but I was pretty determined to love this book, and once I read a little more and got accustomed to the writing style, I got sucked in--obviously, since I read it all in one day! I was really excited, not only because of the research, but because there's an author's note at the front of the book that reads, "One thing I hope you understand is that fear controls the victims. There may be times that seem ideal for escaping or calling for help that are not taken because the fear of getting hurt or having loved ones hurt is so deep." 
 I basically vibrated with excitement when I read that, because that goes through my mind, almost word for word, every time I read a book with this storyline and the heroine acts like a headstrong hellion, but magically survives, even though in real life, someone who needlessly provokes dangerous criminals to that extent would be dead and buried in a shallow grave. That note made me think this one was going to be different. The heroine would be more of a survivor, smarter than that, more wily, able to bide her time and...I won't even bother finishing, because unfortunately that was not the case. 
 Unfortunately Addie was exactly the sort of heroine that I don't like in these kinds of books. She isn't a survivor, she's a headstrong pain in the ass who confuses bravery and strength with stubbornness and stupidity. I'm not a soulless criminal, and I can tell you beyond a shadow of a doubt, if I were Nate, Addie would have died about halfway through this book. Without question. 
 "You don't want to become more trouble than you're worth." 
 I was not even remotely intimidated by the bad guys. Rather, at the beginning I thought they had a lot of promise, but as the book went on, they lost all credibility for me and eventually became complete afterthoughts. There were occasions when I thought the so-called bad guys needed to either respond to Addie's constant, stubborn rebellion, or just turn in their bad guy cards altogether. Not that I want her to suffer, obviously, but I need to be shown these guys actually mean business, and they put up with way more crap from her than I would have in their positions. If I'm more merciless than your bad guy...that's a problem. In real life, the "strong," and "spirited" things she did would have gotten her killed. Her life means nothing to them. Less than nothing--she's an inconvenience! So the logic didn't hold up for me. I'm sure others will admire her fighting, "never give up" spirit, but for me, when it reaches the point that I cannot for the life of me understand how you are alive, but the soulless baddies just slap your wrist and ground you...this is a huge issue for me. I need my bad guys to convince me/behave like bad guys. Otherwise, what's the point? These guys tolerated way too much and threw around empty threats way too often. I learned in management that you never issue a threat you can't/won't follow through on if you want to be respected/feared, so how can that be left out of the successful bad guy manual? 
 The heroine was also...man, I don't even know. She may have been made of stern stuff, but to me she came off as an outsider looking in rather than someone living in those horrific conditions. I hate to say it, but I think some of it was because of all the research; Addie often sounded like someone who had learned a lot about trafficking victims trying to educate the audience...which is okay in a sense, educating people who don't know is admirable and all, but it stuck out like a sore thumb and was not how the character should have thought. The author was also apparently so concerned with circumventing victim-blaming that realistic portrayal was sacrificed--even in the moment, when anyone in the world would be horrified at what resulted from their actions/apologizing, etc, she made a point of having Addie say how she's not sorry for anything, nothing is her fault. Frankly, she just made Addie sound like a bitch. Even victims who don't blame themselves do not take it this far--she was defensive and there was no reason for it as far as the circumstances were concerned. It pulled me out of the story every time because it felt so out of place. She was also WRONG in every instance--the things that happened to the other people DID happen because of her actions. If she would have been shrewd/kept her mouth shut on both occasions, there would have been no consequence to the people around her. Simple as that. Cause and effect--it has nothing to do with what's right or wrong, what people should or shouldn't do, if you provoke someone you know to be violent intentionally and for no reason (it certainly can't benefit you to do so), you're just kind of an asshole when you don't feel bad that you running off at the mouth/doing something painfully stupid caused your friends to get hurt. 
 I also hated Addie's high and mighty attitude toward the other girls (not Phoebe, but Rochelle and Lily). Her attitude toward the girl who had Stockholm syndrome really rubbed me the wrong way. You don't choose to develop Stockholm syndrome--it just happens to some people under the right circumstances as a means of coping. You don't get to judge them for that--it's a real thing! It really happens. Often in books Stockholm syndrome is totally misrepresented (like, the heroine gets it ten minutes after meeting the anti-hero, etc) and that was definitely not the case here, but the heroine's clear disdain (and condescension) toward the girl who was experiencing it really made me stop liking her. Also her condescension toward a "brainwashed" tween-prostitute. Maybe it made the character feel better/superior to separate herself from the other girls at every turn, but it slowly drained away her likability for me. (I also felt sometimes the portrayal of how smitten Rochelle was came off a little heavy handed. Skipping up the stairs? Really? And I think that happened two or three times.) 
 This is probably less of an issue for most people though. I'm sure most readers will simply be impressed by her "strength" and fortitude. Personally, I consider a strong character a smart character, someone who can feasibly survive terrible circumstances because they are shrewd enough to make it, not someone full of attitude who only makes it because they're a main character and the author says so. And most people probably won't look at the story from the perspective of the bad guys, either, to make sure their actions/motives make sense. But I do, so these were problems for me. 
 There were little things that bothered me as well. Editing issues (which I wasn't even going to mention when I was loving it, but...); Zane beginning the story as a potentially interesting, really compelling character (and there was even some build-up of his character, describing how compelling/manipulative he could be!), but then eventually fading into nothing but a one-line bully who made an occasional appearance to cackle and say something thoroughly unclever; the stereotypical portrayal of all the johns in the beginning (all fat with BO and some obvious interest in fast food); lots of blurting and more dialogue tags than were necessary. I also didn't really warm up to the romance until the very end, it felt based out of their bond on the inside, but there was nothing about it that made me think they would be together if they ever escaped. Then I was pretty upset when after finally escaping, this poor barely-20-year-old girl gets saddled with a pregnancy! Yeah, babies are great, but come on. Give the poor girl a chance to get counseling and move on with her life. It would even be more understandable if she would've been pregnant by one of the johns, or there was some mystery as to whether or not the baby was Jackson's, but to just stop taking your birth control like that, and then sleep with your captive boyfriend with nary a thought to possible repercussions... It just felt so unnecessary. If she had to have a baby, couldn't she have just announced her pregnancy in the epilogue, once she was home and had actually been with Jackson in the real world and they were sure they wanted to be together?  
 "Addie, I'd rather live one day with you than a hundred without. You're the best thing that's ever happened to me." 
 Overall, I did like the book, but the issues I had with the heroine and the lack of conviction of the bad guys put a real damper on things for me. I would still recommend it, unless you share my feelings about how-in-the-hell-did-she-survive heroines...maybe even then, if you're feeling patient.

Hamish Wolfe - a convicted killer spending time in jail for the brutal murder of 3 young women who all just have one thing in common: being overweight. 
 Pete Weston - the detective who found the evidence to put Hamish behind bars. But did he catch the right guy? 
 Maggie Rose - the reclusive and somewhat eccentric young lawyer who has already freed several convicted murderers. Hamish still claims he is innocent - will she take on his case? 
 And who is the mysterious Daisy? 
 Playing out as a narrative from the perspectives of the three main characters and a series of letters and case files, Daisy in Chains takes the reader on a roller coaster ride of crime, lies and deception, where no one is to be trusted and dark secrets can raise their ugly heads at any minute. 
 It is impossible to say any more without giving away a piece of the puzzle, so there is only one thing left to say: this is a must read for all fans of Sharon Bolton and anyone who enjoys a solid, well-written and suspenseful crime novel. Executed with Bolton's usual flair for words and eye for detail, Daisy in Chains will shock and surprise at every turn of the page, as will the ending. It firmly proves why Bolton is a master of her game and firmly entrenched on top of my favourite authors list. It also shows that she can turn her hand to a slightly different writing style to her previous novels, and excel at it. Gone are the dark gothic undertones which once earned her the name "Queen of Rural Gothic", but the story's increasingly dark and sinister undertones are initially hidden in a more formal voice fitting for a crime novel which is partly set in the prison system. It is more towards the end that the setting becomes more creepy and sinister, as only Bolton can conjure up, fitting for the shocking finale. As in previous books, Bolton uses a strong professional female lead to drive the story, but this time with a twist you may see coming as the story progresses, but will never guess the full extent of. As the story gets darker and the reader is constantly forced to question every preconception they may have held, it is impossible to put this book down for even a minute. Best read under the doona with plenty of time to spare. 
 All I can say is: run to the bookstore and get a copy for yourself, then bolt all the doors, put the phone on silent and enjoy! It is so worth it. Firmly on my favourite list for this year.

A rather interesting almost "Fringe" (tv show) like book. 
 Two cities, but one city space. Two different cities exist, in what appears to be two separate realities the overlap in a specific areas "Crosshatch" zones. The citizens of the two cities are required and trained to ignore their counterpart reality. Recognizing, or *gasp* acknowledging the "Alter" city denizens is a thing called "breach" which is the penultimate crime in the two existences. 
 To manage this Breach (Capital B), an organization of both realities - oversees such crimes, was crafted to investigate and somehow be a shadow organization whose members can interact with both sides. 
 The book appears to be a political mystery with a distinct sci-fi - multi-reality flair. 
 I find the ubiquitous elements of the term Breach becoming a bit tiresome, its completely appropriate to the story and narrators point of view, but I am beginning to feel like I'm reading Wolfe, with his idiosyncratic of avoiding the obvious question of "why??"

Three Things: 
 (1) I really, really enjoyed reading this book! 
 (2) The format of this review is extremely unoriginal. 
 (3) I don't know why, but I really love the cover of this book and am really happy that it ties into the story. Though also oddly disappointed that it's not a bigger role. 
 Three More Things: 
 (1) I loved the banter in this book. It was so fun and witty and kept me smiling throughout so much of it. I loved the e-mail/texting/IM formatting and honestly wouldn't have minded if the whole thing was written like that. While I think that shifting to texting/IM-ing made sense, I did miss seeing the e-mail subject lines, as they were pretty funny, too. 
 (2) While there was a lot of fun banter, the other half of the book was pretty heavy. While the banter did a good job of helping balance out the heavy, I don't think it was done as effectively as it could have been. It would be all fun and texting one page and the next was a lot of introspective moments of grief. The transitions were a little jarring at times. 
 (3) The family aspect of this book was lacking for me. While things start to get better by the end, I really didn't care for any of the parental figures in this book. I thought the blended family aspect would play a bigger factor in the story, but it was mostly used to give Jessie one more thing to be upset over. 
 Another Three Things: 
 (1) Jessie is dealing with a lot, though - the loss of her mother, moving away, new step-mother and step-brother, new school, new friends, mean girls, bullying, absent father. I mean, the list goes on. Plus, she's only 16, so if she spends a good deal of the book feeling sad and lonely and a little self-indulgent, I can excuse it. There was actually a lot of Jessie that I could identify with and even though I didn't always love how she handled something, she was a likable character and she did really grow throughout the book. 
 (2) I love the Anonymous E-mailer, Somebody Nobody. This could have been creepy, but I'm just going to blow right by that and go for how cute it was. Because it was cute. Though, was I supposed to be surprised by SN's real identity? Because as soon as his character was introduced he was my guess on who it was and I just became more convinced as the story went on. Like, it couldn't have been anyone else. And while I wouldn't have minded if it was revealed to Jessie before the final chapter, I was ok with it. I shipped it. 
 (3) I don't really feel like I can mention any of the guys/potential love interests without giving away SN's identity. So I'll just say, I think you will be satisfied with the romantic portion of the story. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Tell Me Three Things. It was such a cute story with fun, witty banter that I couldn't get enough of. And while I didn't always think the heavier moments were well balanced, they did seem raw and relatable and in that regard, was well done. This is definitely a YA Contemporary I would recommend. I already want to read it again. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 4 Stars

 After reading Wait for Me and seeing some potential with the plot, I wanted to give this author another shot. Unfortunately, this book didn't work for me for a lot of reasons. 
 The characters...ugh. I just couldn't like either one of them. Tess was a dancer who was recovering from an injury that might mean she'd never dance again, but aside from a few moments thrown in haphazardly to remind you of that, you'd never know it. If you have an injury that upends your entire plan for the future, I would think it would be something that constantly weighs on your mind. It rarely crosses hers. Yes, she thinks about her injury and pain a lot, but she rarely thinks about dancing. She didn't seem to be into her health in general, and I can't help but think someone who was into such intense training wouldn't be downing cheeseburgers and cupcakes all the time. And Jase. Poor Jase. His character had a lot of potential at the beginning of the book, but his words became sweeter than the cupcakes he was presenting to Tess. It was hard for me to picture a guy saying the things he said, and in the end, he just wasn't a believable character for me. His indecisiveness was so unattractive, and the timing of when all his issues came to a head was too hard to buy into. The 'wham, bam, no thank you, ma'am' didn't work here. 
 There were times when this book just seemed to drag. Some of the scenes went on and on and on, and some of them just didn't fit the story. 
 I'll hide some of the other things that didn't work for me, as they might spoil parts of the story for you should you decide to read it: 
 The whole 'no kissing' thing. It was too Pretty Woman for me. Maybe I could believe that from an older man, but for a young robust guy who supposedly has as much prowess as Jase...he got those girls into his bed somehow, and I'm guessing a lot of them would have been lured with some hot and heavy kissing. 
 The situation between Jack and Jace. It was obvious from the second Jack appeared who he was. 
 Jase feeling Tess up when they're at lunch sitting across the table from Cam and Avery. So...you're telling me that Jase was nervous about dating Cam's little sister, but he's going to stick his hand in her pants while he's having lunch with him? No. Just no. And maybe it's just me, but if I'm sitting across the table from my brother and my boyfriend is feeling me up, the only thing I'm going to feel...is mortified. 
 Cam constantly swooping in to save the day and Tess letting him. She had backbone on occasion, but not nearly enough. He needed to be stood up to and put in his place. It seems like every time he was a jerk, something happened to her that she just 'needed' to be rescued from, and there he was! 
 The 'oh, I've never laid eyes on the person who lives in the suite just off mine' was so predictable. Aside from the fact that it was obviously going to be someone Jase had hooked up with, there wasn't even any drama when the identity of the roommate was finally revealed. I didn't understand the build-up that essentially led to nothing. 
 Tess being mad at Jase for hitting Erik after Erik had a hand in injuring her. It felt like a plot device used simply to create drama, and it fell short for me. It just made it seem like Tess was looking for reasons to be mad at Jase.  
 The whole book was predictable - it was one cliche after another, and they just didn't mesh in a way that was plausible. The drama was never ending right up until the last page, and the characters were too one dimensional. If you're a fan of this author's other works, you may like this. Her books just don't do it for me.

I am a bit wishy-washy about this. I'm glad I finally read it, what with all the hype going around about it. I would say there is very little in the way of comparison between this and Gone Girl, unlike some people. 
 Here's the thing. I've read a lot of books lately about fucked up females. I read Eeny Meeny, I read everything by Gillian Flynn, I read As Night Falls, and now I've read this. It's getting to the point now where I sort of feel like it is overused, and I am losing interest in these stories now because they're the same thing every time. We have a main character who is unreliable--in this case, it is Rachel, who is so blind drunk all the time she doesn't realize she was beaten by her husband . Then we get a mystery or a conflict that needs to be solved--in this case, a woman Rachel spies on has gone missing--and then unreliable, completely-twisted-up-female-narrator tries to solve it. 
 One thing I have noticed about books that change the point of view of narration: it is so obvious who the bad guy is when you don't get to see into his head. When everyone else gets a chapter, process of elimination tells you exactly who it is. I figured this out fairly early on, and I was disappointed that I was right. 
 Yet now that all of those opinions are on the table, I can honestly say that I enjoyed the book too. I was totally engrossed, and I was definitely one of those stereotypical people who bought this just so I had something to read on my flight. (If it gives me brownie points, I bought it on my Nook instead of at the airport!) It is a quick read, and an easy one to get through. Rachel is just absolutely pathetic, but you start to really care about her and wish that you could help her out through the pages. She was pitiful, and that made her a nice change from the typical "I can do no wrong" thing happening in all books lately. But again, these fucked-up-females are surfacing more and more... 
 I don't know. I guess for me it was a good fun read, but starting to feel like run-of-the-mill.

Going into reading this book, I had high expectations. I had heard great things about it, but my core group of "reader friends" hadn't hit it hard yet, so I'm not certain why I had my expectations set so high. But I was not disappointed. 
 I don't know how to express my feelings about this book without spoiler alerts everywhere. I will start with the writing style. This writing style really speaks to me. I was instantly pulled into the worlds of Eleanor and Park. I use the word "worlds" because with the perspective changes, you can tell they see the world in a very different way. I didn't even feel like I had to keep track of who knew what; it was simple enough to follow along without filing specific details away. I love that there are chapters, but within a chapter the PoV switches often. In particular, when Eleanor and Park are both simultaneously reflecting on a moment and the PoV switches back and forth after short sentences. 
 I also really enjoy how love is portrayed throughout this book. Annnd...  
 There are many different types of love and variations of love portrayed throughout the book. There is so much love. Eleanor and Park are obvious. But there is also: 
 * Eleanor and her siblings 
 * Eleanor and her mother 
 * Mother and Richie 
 * Richie and Eleanor (<>) 
 * Park and John 
 * Park and Steve 
 * Park and Tina 
 * Eleanor and Tina 
 * Park and his Mom 
 * Park and his Dad 
 * Park's Parents 
 * Park's Grandparents 
 And each of these relationships has it's own form of love-- both subtle and not. The most compelling relationships to me are Eleanor and Park, Eleanor and her mother, and Park's parents. 
 Eleanor and Park experience the extreme emotion of first love. They are lucky that their first love it together; often with high schoolers it's not. I can relate to the extreme emotional spectrum they are experiencing and how they flip between forever and not. 
 Eleanor and her mother are also fascinating. They are incredibly similar. Both of them live in fear for the rest of their family. Each of them are trying to keep the other happy and is willing to make sacrifices to help the other achieve that. But, they are terrible at communication, so they don't see themselves in the other. It's both inspiring and heartbreaking. 
 Park's parents are incredible. They really love each other. I love seeing their interactions. The constant making out and visible signs of affection are something I hope to keep in the future. I am also most impressed with how they talk to each other. They allow each other the space to be upset, but they also won't back down on what the right thing to do is. It's amazing.  
 All in all, this book is incredible. I would recommend this novel to anyone who has ever been in love, is looking for some light reading with a deep message, or who is into YA.

Proxy was an enjoyable read with an interesting take on the Dystopian genre. It worked well in some places and not as well in others. 
 The world building was just enough to get the gist of the new society, without delving too far into the how and why. There are Patrons, the rich society who live super hi-tech, lux lives. Then there are the poorer population in the Valve. They live in kind of the sewers of the Patrons. The whole society is based on debt. Just being "rescued" from the outside wilderness gives you ten years of debt. Every medical appointment or purchase can add on years to your debt. The Patrons buy your debt and in return you work it off as their proxies. Inspired from the idea of whipping boys, when a Patron misbehaves, his Proxy is punished. There is a resistance, The Rebooters, who want to forgive all debts and start over, there are the wealthy Patrons who are happy with the way things are, and there's Syd, a Proxy who just wants to pay off his debt and be left alone. 
 Of course, Syd is the reluctant hero of the story. When an especially severe punishment is handed down from Knox's behavior, Syd's debt, which is just a couple years of being repaid, is almost doubled and he goes on the run to escape it. With the help of his best friend, Egan, his Patron, Knox, and a Causegirl, Syd runs head first into his destiny. 
 There's some confusing back story and unlikely coincidences that leads to the final chapters. All Syd wants is a choice, but all choices seem to already be made for him. A twist at the end brings redemption to one character and hope to another. 
 I thought Syd and Knox were both relatively well developed. They both have demons they face and both have some growth throughout the novel, but ultimately I never found either of them particularly lovable. I found it refreshing that this is a YA novel that didn't revolve around romance. I also liked that Syd's sexual orientation is just another part of his character and was not used as some greater platform. 
 Overall, I enjoyed Proxy. While I thought the world building and the the back story could have been a ittle more developed and explained, the plot was interesting and pretty fast-paced. I look forward to reading the next book in the series.

While both books center around the immersive virtual realities of video games, Ready Player One this book is not. Sorry folks. I loved Ready Player One - LOVED it. And I struggled to love this one just as much. I mean, the author worked on EPIC MICKEY. What more needs to be said for his impressive credentials - not to mention his hardcore gamer street-cred. (Side note: If it seems I'm mocking Epic Mickey, I'm not. I own it for the Wii. Played it. Loved it. Never beat it. And...now I'm thinking of restarting that game...but NO...reviewing, reviewing, reviewing must be a priority here). While I'm still digressing, I should come out of the closet as a minor RPG fan and sometime video-gamer in my previous life, pre-baby. I really loved the Paper Mario RPGs, played Animal Farm and Harvest Moon, and my brother was (IS) a hardcore gamer - all platforms, most computer games (especially World of Warcraft in its heyday) , Mortal Combat tournaments - the works). So, that said - most of the terminology and video game references we not lost on me, but... that doesn't me that I necessarily LOVED the heavy-handed approach to recaps and in-depth game description. I didn't really LOVE the book, but I did appreciate parts of it. It really captured the wonder and awe that was associated with how video games (and computer technology) changed reality for a whole generation of youth. I was part of that generation. I know. But not to the extent that this author knows - because it's clear he has done his research (if not lived the part). 
 Our narrator Russell is an early middle-aged closet nerd who ran out of opportunities (or personal ambition) in the "real" world of adult jobs. In high school, he ran with a handful of misfit of technies who were grouped together to program a video game for a project and, later, at a computer summer camp. While Russell attempted to pursue a more traditional career (however unsuccessfully or misguided), the others formed a highly successful video game company. With little else available to misguided, middle-aged Russell, he throws himself on the mercy of his former friends and begins a career as a video game designer. This story is his account of settling into this new environment, all the while plagued by the unexplained death of one of his former friends, Simon, the genius behind the company's success. Russell throws himself into his work, attempting to fix a mysterious virus that has started to plague players in unpredictable ways. While the description of the game world became a bit of a drag, the book shone in the passages that dealt with the high school relationship dynamics of the gamers. I wish that there had been more reality - and less virtual reality. 
 All in all, it was so-so. Not good. Not bad. There wasn't enough substance and resolution to the plot.  About three-quarters of the way through this book, I had to stop reading for a day or two. I just couldn't bear to go on, I dreaded to think what would happen to the man and his son. The dangers are myriad in Cormac McCarthy's post-apocalyptic world, and lie in wait around every corner. It's a bleak book. McCarthy keeps the dialogue terse and the color limited to a palette of gray and ash. Only the boy is described with color. He's golden, carrying the last flame of compassion in his heart. 
 The book is driven by their journey south to the coast, where the man hopes for a warm winter. I had some questions about the ultimate purpose of the journey. But I think it suits McCarthy's purposes symbolically that they are itinerant, constantly vulnerable. We seem to have destroyed our home for good in the apocalypse, so the man and the boy are forever homeless, scrounging, hiding, living on borrowed time. 
 McCarthy's writing, which I found lean in _No Country for Old Men_, seems to have gone on a starvation diet. The language is spare, as if the same disaster that has pared the characters down to their essential motivations has worked on the book itself. The boy asks at one point about their "long-term goals" and the man questions him about where he heard the term. In this world there's no such thing. Survival, the shortest-term goal ever, is the only goal. This makes for a simple, powerful narrative, and compelling--who doesn't want to see good protect innocence and triumph over evil (marauders! cannibals!)? But was that really what was going on? Clearly there were bad guys, but the father's attempts to "protect" the son seem to ensure their isolation as much as their safety. I was left frustrated by the neat, vague ending. It's so easy all of a sudden! It's something to debate with friends, I suppose, whether we are to take this ending at face value or as a dream of death.

So I know there is a TV Series of this out there, like with so many other things. No I have not watched it. 
 My sister would tell me why read it when you can watch it... 
 My answer..."Cause maybe I'm a Freak that would like to have a better background than I know the series will give me." 
 So Alison is at the centre of a circle of five BFF's. They share everything, and Alison (Ali) is the glue that holds them all together, they only became friends because of her after all. They share everything from cloths to secrets and promise to protect one another at all costs. 
 Then one night when the girls have a sleepover to celebrate the start of summer vacation there's an argument. As usual Ali is trying to get them all to do what she wants, everyone reluctantly agrees until Spencer decides she's had enough of being bossed around and kicks Ali out, the minute Ali goes waltzing out the door Spencer regrets it but Ali is gone. 
 On the night she goes missing, no one can find her, has she been kidnapped or murdered. 
 Fast-ward three years later and it's been proven that Ali was the glue that held, Emily, Hanna, Spencer and Aria together as a group. All the girls are now living their own lives separate from any friendship they might once have shared, still at the same school but they pass one another on a daily basis without so much as an acknowledgement. 
 But something sinister begins to happen that might bring the girls back together whether they want to or not. Each begins getting cryptic messages hinting at secrets that only Ali would have known about each of them. Secrets none of the girls shared as a group or with anyone else in our outside of the group. 
 Not only does this person hint at knowing the secrets the girls believed long buried but they seem to know things that is happening to each of the girls now, secrets that no one could know. To make it even worse the messages have all been signed "A". 
 Is it someone messing with them or is Alison still alive? 
 This not a tediously taxing book to read, it's just plain guilty fun. It does keep you guessing, Shepard gives you new suspects all the time that has you wondering who it could be. So it's enjoyable and keeps you reading. 
 Especially because "A" keeps threatening that they knows the biggest secret that all the girls the girls share (or think they do) connecting them to Spencer and Ali's creepy neighbour across the street Toby, and his stepsister Jenna. 
 If anything I kept reading just to find out what the secret was. 
 All the girls lives seems to begin falling apart, was it something that was going to happen anyway or does "A" have a hand in it. 
 Just when the girls believe that A could be Ali come back from the dead, Ali's body is found when the new girl, Maya's family who's moved into Ali's hold house, dig up the old gazebo area to build a tennis court. 
 Is it really Ali's body? If it is and "A" isn't Alison, who is it that knows every secret past and present? 
 All these girls are from fairly well off families, the embodiment of "poor little rich girl" syndrome, everyone of them as a credit card, the designer cloths and of course everyone is buying from Tiffany's or stealing from them.... 
 One reason that I enjoyed the book, even though the girls tend to be a but melodramatic at times, is that it shows that teens lives are not just parties and who's dating who, exam dramatics. They actually do have some serious issues and for the most part these girls aren't who they are because this is the path they've chosen but because in some way they are pushed into it by their parents or because they feel it's what they have to do to be accepted or to be a cut above looser. 
 Hanna 
 Was the overweight one of the group, she began eating more than normal after her parents' divorce because she didn't know how to deal with anything. Now three years later she much thinner and has re-invented herself into Ms. Popular and Sleek making fun of everyone she considers a looser. She hasn't seen nor spoken to her father in the three year since her parents' divorce and what she views as her father's subsequent replacement of her with his girlfriends perfect daughter, she thinks her father left her for a better more beautiful family (daughter specifically). Now she finally has everything she ever wanted including the boy she's been in love with since before Ali went missing. Or does she? 
 Hanna doesn't seem to ever see her mother and when her mother is at home she's working and on her phone. But she has given Hanna everything and anything that money can buy. Hanna has a number of secrets, one of which is she's actually bulimic. That's how she lost weight, binging and throwing up, but of course she's convinced that she has control over this. Also although she can afford to buy anything she wants...she steals anyway. Why? Because it gives she a thrill. 
 Hanna is looking for someone to accept her and love her, she feels imperfect because of the way she used to look and is determined to do everything in her power to make sure she stays beautiful and popular. The one positive thing about Hanna is that when she didn't like the way she looked she took it into her own hands to change it, but in the process changes her personality as well. Becoming someone she doesn't like, a bully, yet she doesn't even seem to see it. All she sees is that she is now the perfect physical package, yet at the same time she is still so very insecure. She even has a new best friend who has also re-invented herself right along with Hanna, that's how they become friends in the first place, she seems to encourage Hanna to do everything she probably shouldn't be doing. But could Mona really be called a friend, as she doesn't seem all that supportive on other levels and only seems to want to be friends with Hanna because they have been able to snub others together, the same people that used to probably snub them. Also their friendship basically seems to hinge on Hanna maintaining the perfect image and going alone with what Mona wants. 
 Aria 
 Like all teens she is trying to fit in, but in a more conventional way. She tries different looks and different interests to find her place. Only when her family moves away, after Ali goes missing, for three years to live in Iceland does she finally find herself. In that time she is guarding a horrible secret her father has been keeping. A secret that can destroy her family, but up until they move back everything seems picture perfect. Aria seems the more balanced of the four. 
 Spencer 
 She is the super achiever of the group, she's a top grade student, plays sport and is the head of more school groups than I can count. Ali was the only one of her friends who she competed against but with Ali gone she is top of her friends not that she seems to have any. For all her brains and smarts and the fact that she is a joiner Spencer seems to be completely alone. 
 Even where her family is concerned. 
 She seems to be in constant competition against her sister Melissa who is older than what she is and it should no longer be the case, yet everything Spencer does she measures against her sister's achievements. Which classes her sister took, what grades she got on her papers, was her sister the head of this group, what did she accomplish while she was. Her main goal in life seems to be to outdo her sister. But this isn't just from Spencer's side. Her sister Melissa also seems bent on never allowing Spencer to shine. She constantly finds ways to remind Spencer how much better she was at school. At first I thought it was all only in Spencer's mind but through the first book, whenever Spenser mentions an achievement of the day Melissa has to point out something she did better than Spencer in the past and "Oh I also did this great thing today-kiss my feet mom and dad". 
 Talk about walking in your sisters shadow (as far as Spencer is concerned). 
 But Spencer's parents encourage their children to compete against one another, they even have a game they play call "Star". Where each person names an achievement of the day and the person who's done better than everyone else is the star of the day. I'm all for encouraging you kids to do the best they can but that is kind of ridiculous. The minute Spencer messes-up, she is shunned by her whole family. No one speaks to her or even acknowledges her existence. Yes I get that messing around with her sister's boyfriend (not the first time) was really messed up, but at least Spencer tried to keep it quiet not wanting to hurt Melissa (and it only happened once and also she did try a to avoid the guy). But for some reason her parents won't even give Spencer a chance to tell her side of the story. Even through she apologizes profusely, they don't seem to care nor see that there might be more going on, which pushes Spencer to keep seeing her sisters ex and even starts to fall in love with him. Melissa meanwhile, after making it clear she wants nothing to do with her ex, and also knowing that Spencer is falling in love with him sees him on a continuous basis and then after he breaks it off with Spencer Melissa brags to her that she's been seeing him all along but now she doesn't think it will work. In other words, now that Spencer is in love with him and Melissa has made sure to cheat with him with the express purpose of rubbing it in Spencer's face and then dumping him (now that is really sick). 
 It is also very clear that the only reason her parents want their daughters to do well is so that they can tell others about how great their children are. 
 Emily 
 What can I say about Emily, to me she is the saddest one out of the lot. Nothing she seems to do is in anyway for herself. She's an amazing swimmer, but only because every one of her siblings has been and because her parents want her to be. She is a parent's dream child. Doing everything that's asked of her even dating a boy that her parents approve of, because he's on the boys swimming team. 
 The minute she expresses a desire that swimming might not be what she wants, her mother acts as if she's just found out her daughter in using hard drugs. I mean really. 
 Even worse! She might be friends with a black girl and who wants that kind of association. 
 Alison 
 The person we never really meet, except through the eyes of her old friends, yet she is still at the center of everyone's world. 
 In a way it's sad when they remember her, how she brought them together and made each of them feel unique and special. She always seemed to be right there when they needed her and she was the center of all secrets not just the center of the circle. 
 But as the novel continues we begin to learn that maybe Ali wasn't as perfect and nice as the initial picture each of the girls gives. There seems to be something darker beneath the surface. 
 A 
 We never meet A either or hear anything from A's point of view, but A is just as much a developing character as the others, maybe even more so. as A is in some ways more ahead of the other characters. A has goals and drive and knows exactly what it is that he or she wants. Whereas the other girls are still growing and learning, the fact that A is also set on such a path of destruction is in itself disturbing. Cause let's remember these girls are still mostly only 16, they are still experimenting and trying to figure out who they are. And let's face it not one of them as a clue. All of them is living only to please their parents and to please their peers. But A...A is manipulative and somehow their actions seem, yes childish but also more mature at some points because it is very clear that A is carefully positioning them. But for what is the question. 
 At first A only hints at the past, which all though it's horrible there is no actual proof, since the one person who knew is still missing and probably dead. But when A begins to talk about secrets the girls have shared with no one, not even Hanna's so called best friend Mona knows everything that's going on in Hanna's life it even set me on edge because suddenly A seems to be everywhere all at once. 
 One thing that I found annoy, besides the fact that everyone one of these kids don't seems to lack not a single thing (no wonder they're so messed-up) is that all they seem to do is drink. Hell not only do they drink but they drink right alone with their parents at supper, come home totally sloshed and not one of these people seem to bat an eyelash. The reasonable parents seem to not existing in this world! 
 I mean does Hanna get in trouble when she's caught steeling....? Hell no! Mother dearest covers for her and even buys her other things to make up for the loss of returned the stolen items, then disappears off to work. WTF! Some perspective people!  
 A is not going away, A definitely loves playing with them. So who is A? My money is till on Alison. 
 Definitely a fun read!

I've had this on my to-read list for a long time and finally got around to reading it. I don't know what I was waiting for--I loved it!!! This story is based on the twelve dancing princesses, one of my favorite fairy tales, and I loved the twists and unique way that the story was told.

It's easy to be dismissive of rich white people problems. Having just finished Cristina Henriquez's excellent "The Book of Unknown Americans," featuring a protagonist who is vulnerable in every way that poverty, race, and disability can make her, it was hard to have sympathy for Lockhart's Cadence. By the end of the book, though, she seemed less untouchable. Her tragedy is not enacted systemically, or implicitly sanctioned by a state that views her as second-class. But it is a tragedy. And strangely enough, the book ended up in much the same place as "Unknown Americans," with characters struggling to forgive themselves. Harder to forgive is some of the writing quirks and adolescent drama (maybe that's unfair to complain about in a YA novel?), and--come on, amnesia? Still, I think high schoolers will enjoy the twisty plot and possibly even the "it's rough all over, Ponyboy" ethos. Echoes of fairy tales and King Lear resonated enjoyably.

Yeah. To start off, I don't know why Sally Green went in that direction with the ending. Was it for the shock factor? It was shocking. Was it for the sake of tragedy? It was tragic. I just don't understand the reasoning behind that decision. If I did, if it were clear to me in some way, then I might excuse it somehow and accept it. But I don't quite understand the reasoning behind killing Gabriel and writing the most miserable last couple of chapters for a trilogy, followed by the protagonist turning himself into a tree, because he's done living as a person, at the young age of 22.  Why end a book like that ever? 
 Also, I may be in the minority here, but I seriously don't get the hate for Annalise's character. I really don't. She's a pretty decent character that got a lot of hate solely - let's admit it - for the fact that she was cockblock. She stayed decent until the very end too. She did what she did to Marcus because her own family was being shot down in front of her. She didn't exactly have a great time risking her life for Nathan before or after what she did. She didn't have to do any of it because she had all the privilege that white witches get and yet, she chose to stand by Nathan. I admit she was a mildly annoying character on the whole, but I didn't understand the hate. Nathan is no walk in the park with all the brutal killing he's done, so he can cool it on the hate and judging. I'm glad she got her happy ending. 
 This is the part where I'm going to confess that the ending got spoiled for me (damn you Tumblr!). So I knew Gabriel bites it, and as I read on, it became sadder and sadder knowing what happens in the end when I would read the dialogue between the two characters and the life they had planned for after the war.  And here's the thing, I was accepting in some ways because I'd had the time to prep before I reached the end of the book (YEAH WE'RE TALKING ABOUT THE ENDING AGAIN!) but then it happens and the last chapters of the trilogy that followed were so damn depressing. Was this truly what was to become of Nathan in the end? Really? 
 And can we please talk about how Green glossed over the whole he-has-a-son bit and turned him into something, quite frankly, crueler than Marcus? Did he really not want to see his son ever? Even though there's no premonition that his son is going to kill him like the prior (perhaps almost legitimate) problem. (Also, the fact that the author plugged in a son at the end was eternally confusing. Why dump that in all of a sudden and do nothing about it?) That bothered me. 
 I might have enjoyed this book had the author not blundered the ending so badly. I would have accepted what she had done if she had tried to offer a little more solace or comfort to her readers at the end of a trilogy.

This book was very interesting. I accidentally spoiled myself for most of it, but that didn't stop me from reading, which is a good sign. 
 One of the things I didn't like about this book that kept me from rating it 5 stars was that it said the F word way too much. I get it. Teenagers swear. But that doesn't mean it's okay for it to be in books where it has no business being. I felt like half the time, the word was thrown in just because the author felt like having it in there. It was distracting and annoying. 
 Other than that, it was pretty good. Janelle was a good character and I found myself caring about her father and his partner Struz, her brother, and her best friend pretty early in the book, which I loved. 
 There were a couple characters that I feel like don't really need to be in the novel. If the author had decided to take one of the characters out, she probably would have cut only about 15 pages out of the 450, that's how often the character was mentioned. So even though there wasn't a lot of development or even relevance to the plot in that area, I wasn't too bothered by it because of the insignificance. 
 One thing that I want to mention about this book: it totally reminded me of the TV show Fringe, which is a good thing. I'm excited to read the next book.
