This was a pretty darn fun book about surviving an alien invasion/apocalypse. I loved the first half; Amy finding Baby and the two of them surviving together. I liked that we saw some growth from Amy; before, she was a snotty little know-it-all who cowered in her house until the food ran out. Then she had to grow up and survive, and I loved that she wasn't afraid to do the stuff that needed to be done. (If a guy tries to rape ME in a post apocalyptic world, best believe I will be feeding him to aliens!)I enjoyed her transformation, it was definitely something I really appreciated. 
 The second half still had me thoroughly entertained, although not with the same gusto. Perhaps I've read too many YA dystopian novels, but I'm kind of tired of the safety compound with ridiculously restrictive rules and ubersecrets thing. The twists  the one with Baby and the thing about what the aliens really are  were fairly easy to guess and didn't leave much of a surprise. This didn't bother me all that much though. I still was interested enough to keep reading this book and managed to finish it in a day. The romance was kind of lame, and you know what? I ABSOLUTELY LOVED IT. No love triangle? No stupid "does he like me? Does he hate me?" flower-petal-picking, not pining from afar. It was such a refreshing change from every other YA book out there I did a little happy dance! 
 And I really loved Baby. She started out as being too good to be true, and then became a little more like a regular seven-year-old, one who resented her friends being taken away and pouting and getting all hyper excited about little things. Again, a nice change from the abnormally calm and mature children you face in other YA novels. 
 Oh, except I didn't like the flashes between the Ward and the past. It was confusing at first and didn't need to be done; it could easily have been written normally without any issues and without the confusion. 
 Thoroughly enjoyable and a fun book, all action and nearly no time wasting.

This deserves a four star rating simply because it helps de-stigmatize anyone who suffers from a mental illness.

But no one should be dictated by their mental or physical illnesses--and suicide is one of those things that is still brushed under the rug. The start of Girl in Snow is one I've read before -- a beautiful young girl named Lucinda is dead, and a small town is reeling trying to figure out whodunit. But that's where the similarity to other novels I've read ends. Instead of being focused on the action of the murder mystery, this book is really a character study of three individuals who are all somehow involved: Cameron, the strange boy who loved Lucinda from afar; Jade, the angry girl who hated and envied Lucinda; and Russ, the police officer with a complicated history who's part of the investigation. The book weaves through each character's perspective, teaching us more about them than about the murder. I thought the character development was good, if a bit contrived at times (particularly in Jade's inner monologue), and I was definitely invested. 
 The ending --while an interesting twist that I didn't see coming -- felt like it wrapped up a bit too quickly/nicely, and I found myself wanting a bit more. But overall it was an enjoyable read. 
 Thank you to the publisher and NetGalley for the ARC.

So how did he do it? Hadley! She provided the encouragement and belief he needed to accomplish what he did. But knowing the arc of the story beforehand, I chafed every time she expressed her devotion to him. "Get out of there!" I wanted to yell at her. "Run for your life!!" But of course, she couldn't hear me. Sigh.

Walking. It's not so difficult. But for these 100 boys who have to keep at a pace of 4 miles an hour, endlessly, it becomes near torture. 
 This simple seeming premise was executed in such a chilling way because it just revolved around boys walking. No more, no less. But in the span of their time, we see a corrupt world, an eerie spectator game that involves death, casual shootings, and musings on what it means to dig deep. 
 There is not much plot, as mentioned, but still. This book was entirely captivating from beginning to end. 
 Each character is unique, but at the base of it all, there's only the last sounds of the gun. 
 I was biting my lips at the end of every chapter. 
 This is a horror story, but not in the typical monster-in-the-dark, scare-me type novel. It's a slow horror that creeps in after the hundredth mile. It builds up on you because you're starting to realize that you want all of these characters to survive, even the angry Barkovitch. The miles keep going, the descriptions of the pain and the fear and the numbness... you almost imagine you can feel it too. 
 The worst was watching McVries die. Especially because Garraty ignored their pact to try to get him to live. But the simple response, "No Ray, it's time to sit down." 
 That is just chilling. And heart-breaking. 
 I am not certain I appreciate the ending (especially as it seemed to end a little too abruptly), but this is definitely a book worth reading. 
 3.5 stars rounded up. Recommended for anyone who likes Stephen King. And for anyone who wants to read a bit of a dark book.

There's a teaser out there for this book that goes something like this: 
 We don't have one night stands, Georgia. We have forever-night stands. 
 Total cheese factor 500, and it was almost enough to make me walk away from this book. I decided to tough it out because I love Sarina Bowen, and I don't typically find her dialogue to be so cheesy. I will say the cheese in this one was minimal, but I didn't care for this book for other reasons. For one, this book felt as padded with information I didn't need and too much description; it really hindered the pacing for me. For another, Georgia was so immature at times I wasn't convinced she's ready for an adult relationship. There was a scene where Leo was spending the night at her apartment, and her father (who disapproved of Leo,) had stopped by unexpectedly. I think the whole scene was supposed to be funny while she tried to hide Leo's presence, but to me it just felt like, as with the entire book, Leo was getting the shaft. (And not in the good M/M way that Sarina writes the hell out of.) Georgia hit the jackpot as far as I'm concerned. She found a sexy man who loves her to bits and will forgive anything she does, no matter how stupid and shallow her reasons are. In line with the pacing, this book relied too much on the past to make the intensity of Georgia and Leo's love credible, but it didn't work. The timing was off so bad that at the end when Leo proposed, I was shocked as hell. Not because it was supposed to be a surprising scene, but because this was not something these characters were ready for. I have to wonder if Leo won't come to regret this decision further down the road. And that's not something I want to feel at the end of a romance novel. . Leo and Georgia, sadly, were the most boring characters in this book. I didn't really connect with any of the Brooklyn Bruisers, but I did love Nate (the team's owner) and Becca. Should they get a book, I will give it a try. 
 If you've never read Sarina Bowen before, please do not let this review deter you from giving her a go. Her NA is on a plane by itself as far as I'm concerned; no one writes it better. Especially the aforementioned M/M. Rookie Move just didn't do it for me.

This was a disappointing ending to a good series for me. Multiple things that may be little to some people just added up to me really disliking it. 
 First of all, Cole and the amnesia. Yeah, no thanks. Cole is pretty much my favorite part of the entire series. I immediately started to dislike this book when Cole turns up without any Cole personality. It killed it for me but I kept thinking it would get better and that there would be a twist and the Cole I loved would reappear. Needless to say, I was left disappointed. It was a bit fun to see some of Cole's past, but I was too overwhelmingly upset about Cole not being Cole that I really just didn't care about the glimpses we got. 
 Jack. was. so. annoying. I never liked Jack the entire series, but I think even if you were a fan of him in the first two books, you would have been left annoyed by the end of this one. He was just so overbearing and jealous and pigheaded that I wish I could've punched him through a wall like he was so fond of doing to other people. He was immature and his actions really conflicted with the way that Nikki's and Jack's love is portrayed. They're made out to be this sort of old-married-acting couple where they're super comfortable around each other and secure in their love yet every five minutes--almost literally--Jack is throwing a hissy fit over Cole--who isn't even really Cole because of the amnesia thing--making innocent comments about Nikki being pretty or with him having to feed her. It was so frustrating. If you're so secure in your feelings for her, why are you so upset about her being fed when the alternative is for her to die?! Nikki should've dumped his giant, overly-muscular, overbearing, pigheaded behind and forgot that she ever knew him. Any slight admiration I had for him with his actions when the first book ended went right out the window in this one. Plus, um, hello, Cole helped you return to your life, jerkface. Get over yourself for two seconds and maybe you'd realize how stupid you're acting. 
 It became too Percy Jackson for me with the plot. The first two books were pretty unique with their plot. They had a hint of mythology to them but overall they were just contemporary fantasy reads for me. This book just became Percy Jackson with quests. Don't get me wrong. I LOVE Percy Jackson. But it felt out of place with this. If the previous plots had been about quests and gathering special items, etc. like this one was so heavily characterized, I wouldn't have been so unhappy with it. But the series just felt like it did a 180 on me and went from unique underworld to Percy Jackson quests and it was just strange and lost its uniqueness. Plus, it was nowhere near as good as Percy Jackson quests. It was like a half-butt attempt with the whole sword (which mysteriously disappears and they need for a whole .2 seconds after making such a big deal out of getting it) and beetles thing and just, no. If you're going to try to emulate Rick Riordan, at least try to make it a little better than that. 
 Lastly, the ending. Ugh. The ending. I hated it. I absolutely hated it. I would've been okay with the overall, big idea of the ending, but the way the characters ended up, I hated it. So many of the characters that I had become attached to come to bad ends and I am so unhappy with it. Cole's bandmates dying in front of him was absolutely terrible.  Even though they weren't prominent characters, I hated seeing the way they ended up. But I may have been able to get past that and let it go if it weren't for the way the main characters ended up. COLE FREAKING DIES. HE FREAKING COMMITS SUICIDE. Like, I know that the whole idea was that Cole had come so far in this book with his character that he loves Nikki so much that he kills himself so that she gets what she wants but NOOO THAT IS NOT OKAY.  I'M SO UPSET. How could Ashton do that?!?! It was COMPLETELY out of character. I don't want to give away any spoilers but it was completely out of character in so many ways that it was ridiculous to have that character come to that end. 
 I could go on with more things that I disliked about this. Little things like Ashe and his actions, and the weird professor who makes way too many, spot-on educated guesses about the Everneath and the way it works with so little information and without thinking any of it was weird. But I hit my most important issues with this, and I think I'm just going to leave off with those. 
 Likes: The overall big idea of the plot ending. The Everneath being destroyed.  
 Dislikes: THE CHARACTER'S ENDS. Jack and his ridiculous baby-ness--like get out of here already. Although I never liked Nikki and Jack together, their relationship dynamic completely crumbles in this and I'm really left wondering why Nikki has any feelings for him whatsoever. It deteriorates into this ugly, unhealthy relationship that feels like Nikki is just with him because she used to want him and not because of who he is any longer. COLE'S AMNESIA. WHAT THE EVEN HECK? Percy Jackson plotline. 
 Overall: 
 Recommend? NO. Just stop at the second one and pretend that there is no third book. I wish I had.

It's taken me a while to write this final review for A Discovery of Witches since I absolutely ADORED it and wanted to do it justice. (Not that I ever could - my reviews are as scatterbrained as I am.) 
 Anyways, it was basically everything I could want from a novel: it had vampires, a strong yet relatable female lead, medieval castles, alchemy, centuries old profecies, secret societies, BOOKS ... and Matthew. (Imagine him as Richard Armitage whilst reading - you won't regret it!) 
 In a lot of ways, the experience of reading A Discovery of Witches was very reminiscent of my first reading of Twilight. Even though there are about a 100 differences for every single similarity, this imaginary connection of mine between the two of them made the book all the more precious to me. I kept thinking: "How lucky am I, I've found another one!" 
 As a Twilight-fan who's technically to old to be one, this "grown-up Twilight" came into my life at exactly the right time. (I could well imagine Edward becoming rather like Matthew after 1500 years without his Bella, by the way.) 
 Overall, the writing was bewitching (yet too advanced for a non-native speaker at times - I learned a lot of new words!), the plot keeps thickening and the characters are vivid - quirky even at times. There's an equal amount of humour, romance, action and academics in this book. This makes the endless amount of pages seem far less endless. 
 The only criticism I could possibly come up with, was that the last part (spoiler: the first being Cambridge, the second Sept-Tours and the third Madison) was a tad bit lengthy and that the end didn't provide any closure on, well, anything. It was more of a new beginning than an end. However, I'll gladly overlook this, as it is the first in a trilogy and the story needs a lot of world-building. 
 To wrap things up (don't want the review to be as long as the book itself): this is one of those books I love so much, that I'm actually afraid to read the next in the series. Not only do I wonder if it will live up to my extremely high expectations, but because it's a story I care a lot about and I don't want to see any characters (or relationships) get hurt. 
 Since somewhat of a war is brewing, I'm afraid I'll be in for a heartwrenching read when Shadow of Night arrives in my mailbox!

The Game Plan (Game On #3) by Kristen Callihan - 2.5 stars 
 This story follows Fionna, Ivy's younger sister (second book in the series), and Ethan Dexter (Dex). While I still enjoy this series as an easy and enjoyable read, I find that with each book, the story line isn't as strong. 
 While I did not hate the book, I just didn't like it the same way I thoroughly enjoyed the first two books in the series. I didn't believe in these characters the way I believed in the those in The Hook Up and The Friend Zone. 
 Fi and Dex fall together instantly. While some people might like that, I prefer more angst, more chase, more tension. There just wasn't much in this book. There may have been minor setbacks, mostly because of Fi not wanting to be with a Football player, but I feel like that was pushed aside quickly. I have standards in dating too, and if I were to make an exception to the rule, it wouldn't be after one night of sleeping alone and thinking of the guy. The story seemed to be built on instalove, and I just can't understand it. Don't get me wrong, the other stories were coming close to instalove for me, but they at least held off. The characters fought against it. There was a build up. 
 In The Game Plan, it just felt like, wam, bam, thank you man. It was too much, too fast, and I felt there was just so much that left me thinking why. 
 Dex could have been my next love - like Drew & Gray. But unfortunately, you don't learn much about him at all... Other than his virginity which was hinted at in the other books. I wanted to love Dex. He was the large and oddly attractive man sitting in the corner keeping mostly to himself. The quiet type. He seemed like such a big sweetie, but my heart wasn't in this story. And to be honest, it didn't feel like the author's heart was either. 
 The last half of the book was lagging. There wasn't much draw. I kept skimming over paragraphs, uninterested in the overall story or where things were going. There was potential in the end with the big media blowout. When I reached that point, I was thinking finally! But it, again, fell flat. I was disappointed to say the least. For the amount of potential it had, the author didn't live up to the fullest potential here. 
 So overall, I'm sorry to say, it just didn't cut it for me. While Kristen Callihan is a fantastic writer as you can read in the first two books of this series, this one didn't do it for me. I'm hoping the next book isn't as much of a letdown as this. 
 While many have enjoyed this book, it just wasn't my cup of tea.

For some reason, I don't read very many gothic novels, even though when I do read them I love them. Is it that there aren't many of them written? Are they just not flashy enough to compete with their dystopian brethren? Or do I just not keep them high enough on my radar? This gothic beauty has been languishing on my TBR for a long time, and I'm kicking myself for not getting to it sooner. 
 Immortal had everything going for it - sweeping romance, eerie moors, haunting ghosts. In the first 100 pages, I was enthralled. Evie arrives at Wyldcliffe, only to be nearly run over by a dark, mysterious, and handsome (naturally) boy on a horse. It was a scene ripped from Jane Eyre, that gothic novel to end all gothic novels. I was anticipating the love story to come and finding the secrets hidden in the passageways of the boarding school. 
 Around the midpoint of the book I realized that I needed to adjust my expectations. Evie isn't really haunted so much as she experiences visions. She has odd dreams and keeps seeing a girl who looks like her lurking around the school, but she's never really frightened by any of it. This means, of course, that I was never scared as a reader, either. It took a lot of the fun out of Evie's trips down musty passageways and out onto the moor to meet up with Sebastian. 
 Sebastian, the boy from the horse, runs into her again late one night after Evie has snuck out to get some air. They begin to meet up nightly, and Evie falls in love. I guess. Well, she says she falls in love, but I certainly didn't get swoony over it. This was one romance that just wasn't for me. 
 You see, the book intersperses Evie's story with excerpts from Lady Agnes Templeton's diary from 1882 to 1884. Agnes, the daughter of the owners of Wyldcliffe manor, writes about her friend "S." who introduces her to the Mysticke Way. "S" is kind of a jerk, and as they unlock their mystical powers (witchcraft, though no one in this book wants to call it that), he gets worse. 
 SPOILER ALERT! (I think, though it seemed pretty obvious to me.) I mean, clearly, "S" is Sebastian, right? So I'm reading all about this douche from the past who treated Lady Agnes like complete garbage...and then I'm supposed to be happy that Evie is falling for him? Nope. Not going to happen.  (Carry on.) 
 The witchcraft bit doesn't really come in to play for Evie's story until late in the book, at which point she has to rush to understand her role in the history of Wyldcliffe much too quickly for my taste. 
 Once Evie finally starts to put together the pieces of the large and obvious clues in front of her, there are only a few chapters left. She has so much to learn and do, which gets rushed into a couple of scenes, only to build to a climax that is resolved so quickly and lacks so much (or any) confrontation that it feels too easy. 
 Instead of wrapping things up with a genuine conflict between Evie and some badass witches in this story, it seems like the author left that for the next in the series. What a letdown! I would have liked to have seen more of Evie developing her own powers and working with her friends. I would have liked to have seen her then use those powers in a manner that actually accomplished something instead of seeming to delay the conflict for a bit. 
 Still, I'm only really complaining because overall I really enjoyed the book. I liked the mystery of Lady Agnes and "S" and how it all tied in with Evie. I loved the setting (boarding school!) and the isolation of this old manor on the moor. I tore through this book - devoured it - to find out what would happen next. It was thoroughly engaging, even if it didn't turn out to be quite the book I wanted it to be.

Very happy to have received my first ARC! Took me a while but I finally got around to writing my first review. And what better way than to start with Lauren Layne. She is one of my favorite contemporary romance authors, who can reel you in and keep you up all night until you finish. 
 As all her books, Lauren found ways to help readers relate to her characters. So, if you are one of those who plans their future 10 or even 20 years ahead of time, you would definitely enjoy Made for You. In order to be successful, Brynn Dalton needs to plan her life down to every detail. It all comes down to what clothes to wear, what job to have, what type of guy to marry and most importantly: by what age. 
 And guess who changed that plan: Will Thatcher. The guy who has always been a thorn in her side since the first time they met...15 years ago. Love the flash backs!  Now what changed? Why now? You'll just have to read to find out... 
 Lastly, life does throw curve balls so you might as well go for the ride.

I was assigned this book for a young adult literature class that I'm taking in the fall. I was definitely intrigued about it - I'm not a sci-fi fan, but I heard that it was comparable to the Hunger Games, and while that isn't my favorite series, it's definitely a good one. So I was really excited to start The 5th Wave. 
 At first, I wasn't really impressed. It's well-written, especially for YA - it's not overly simplistic but it's not overwhelmingly challenging either. However, at first I didn't like Cassie, the main character. She's very snarky and frankly she's really unnecessarily nasty sometimes (which, looking back, I guess she's entitled to - after all, pretty much everyone she knows is dead). Also, as stated before, I'm not a big fan of sci-fi, so I found it really hard to get into the whole alien apocalypse thing. And on top of all of this, the first section is really scattered; it's a mix of Cassie's memories and the present and it can be difficult to differentiate between the two and remember exactly what's happening when the story does finally come back to the present. So for the first quarter of the book, I wasn't feeling it at all and was only really reading it because it was required of me. 
 But then, out of nowhere, it started to get really, really good. Soon enough, I couldn't put it down. Everyone is interconnected somehow, and I love books like that. My favorite character by far was Evan. At times, he was a little TOO perfect, but I just really couldn't help loving him; he's just wonderful. If you think about it, the plot is a little predictable, but if you just allow yourself to get engulfed in the story, you might not be able to predict it. 
 I would recommend this book to anyone high school age or older. There is some pretty offensive language that I personally wouldn't allow middle school students to read. I would definitely recommend this to reluctant readers, especially boys. It's not a typical YA book at all and I think it could really appeal to reluctant readers in ways that other books might not. Definitely a good read!

Confession time! I started reading The Maze Runner because the movie adaptation has Dylan O'Brien in it and, well ... what a waste would it be to NOT get on board with that, right? Otherwise I probably wouldn't have picked it up, because I usually have a hard time getting into books that are narrated from a boy's perspective - especially if the story is not romance-centered. 
 Okay, you can start throwing rocks with the word 'shallow' written on them at me now. Or ... hold off a while longer and let me explain! 
 Because this book is the glorious exception to the rule (a rule I will have to see revised after reading The Maze Runner!). 
 I loved every page of it, despite the fact that 99% of the characters are in fact smudge-faced teenage boys and that the only girl present doesn't say a word until about halfway through the book. 
 As far as my juvenile need for romance in novels goes ... it still stands, because there IS some romance in The Maze Runner and it's adorbs. Let's just say I have a feeling it's going to be worth it at the end of the series. If it isn't, there's going to be A LOt of crying on my part. 
 Ugly crying, that is. 
 Dashner's writing style is of the highest level you will encounter in YA lit. Colourful characters come to life from the second they are introduced and will stay with you until long after you've read the last page. 
 The unfamiliar surroundings and feelings you experience through Thomas are described in such a colourful and detailed way that you really feel like you are in The Glade with them. 
 Dashner truly has an amazing eye (errr, pen?) for detail, all the while never slowing down from the 'running' (get it - running?) pace with which the story develops. 
 Okay, what more can I say about the characters? That I loved each and every one of them in their own way? Sure did. 
 That Thomas is an amazing protagonist and my new personal hero? Jup, sure is. 
 That the "secondary characters" (in this case, I hate referring to them as such because they are all so alive) were unforgettable? Sure are! 
 I especially adored Newt (great casting choice for him by the way) and Minho. Oh, Minho! Can we start a Team Minho, please? 
 As prejudiced as I am/was against so called 'boy books', I have always enjoyed books with bite-sized chapters and their own vocabulary (ACross the Universe by Beth Revis for instance). The Maze Runner has both! Guess that helped in alleviating my prejudice. 
 Almost every chapter ends in a cliffhanger (seriously wtf is going on in here?) and I'm sure to start calling people "slinthead chuck-faced shank" from now on. 
 If I have to give one single tiiiiiiny point of criticism ... [SPOILER] the letter at the end was a bit to Maximum Ride in my opinion. Though I like Maximum Ride, it didn't fit the general style of this book. I felt it to be rather unnecessary to be honest. [END OF SPOILER] 
 Conclusion: regardless your age or you preferred genre, The Maze Runner is a must read. Buy the book asap, turn of your computer to avoid spoilers (I had the unfortunate luck of coming across some grave ones on Tumblr) and READ THIS BOOK BEFORE THE MOVIE! And then go see the movie anyways because, you know ... Dylan O'Brien. 
 PS: Thank you to everyone on Tumblr who convinced me to read The Maze Runner despite my previously adressed and now non-existing prejudice! 
 Five well-earned stars to you, James Dashner!

Short Review 
 A dark military fantasy novel that lends a small amount of realism to an otherwise extremely magical universe. It's a refreshing change from most fantasy books in that you get the feeling the real protagonist isn't the main character, and that they may not even been on the side of the 'good guys'. Worth reading just for the refreshing difference. 
 Long Review 
 The Black Company really shines in the areas that make it most different from other fantasy novels. 
 For one, the story is told through the voice of Croaker, annalist and physician for the company. Though he definitely takes on a primary role in the story, you get the strong feeling that he's secretly the sidekick in a more traditional fantasy story about Raven. 
 This puts you in the action, but a little to the side of it, and it really makes Croaker feel like a guy who got caught up in something bigger than himself who was tasked with the job of writing it all down. 
 He's not the best fighter, not even the best physician really, and he only takes on a primary role in the events that unfold in the novel because he's likely to die a horrible death if he tries to refuse. 
 The nature of the Black Company's service to the Lady and Soulcatcher also defy general conventions in that you're pretty sure they're working for the 'bad guy'. Soulcatcher's death seemed almost realistically anticlimactic in that the general story trope would've had her defeating the Lady and being revealed as a surprise good guy (er... girl?). Instead, she gets her head knicked off and we're done with it. 
 You get a lot of archetypal characters (the gruff captain with a heart of gold, the brooding mysterious new guy with a dark past, the mute orphan girl who's clearly going to fulfill a prophecy) but you see them from a little off to the side, and that change in viewpoint makes it feel more fresh. 
 Through it all Croaker has a strong narrative voice, and he feels like a real person. The antics of the handful of wizards like Goblin and One-Eye are entertaining, and all of the people in the company you really get to know feel like they've got a little bit of background behind them and aren't just there to fill a narrative role, despite their general archetypal format. 
 The two areas the novel fell a little short for me were keeping up with the nicknames and the actual descriptions of the military engagements. 
 I understand the stylistic reasons for the naming conventions, I also get that more arbitrary fantasy names can be hard to keep up with, but at times I started losing the threads of different characters and until I'd gotten well into the book I frequently found myself a little lost with the names. 
 The battles as well felt very... Hollywood. 
 They were all more Conan the Barbarian or at best Lord of the Rings movie battles than something that would approach historical accuracy while adding in the presence of magic and sorcery. 
 For a book that was ostensibly written to focus on the gritty realities of this mercenary company, I was a little let down that the combat was so stylized and artificial feeling. 
 If you're getting sick of standard fantasy and would like something that exists in a fantasy universe but isn't presented from the same kind of viewpoint as all the others, this is a book you'll enjoy.

I received a copy of this title from NetGalley. It does not impact my review. 
 The Forgotten Girls 
 will be available February 3, 2015. 
 What I didn't realize when I requested this book from NetGalley was that there were previous books involving the same characters. According to GoodReads this is book #7 in the Louise Rick / Camilla Lind series. However, most of these books are in Danish and there are only four, including The Forgotten Girls, that have been translated into English. I was a little confused by this and was afraid I would be missing too much, but Blaedel kindly answered my question on Twitter and this is the first book in the Special Search Unit trilogy and can be read without reading any of her previous books. That said, there were still a few times that I worried I was missing something from previous books, but Blaedel did a great job of including enough background information and context that I never felt lost. 
 Louise Rick is starting a new job heading up a special search unit for missing persons. As most of us feel when starting new jobs, it starts out not being what she expected and is having second thoughts. This is especially true when she's assigned a detective that she didn't want, Eik Nordstrom, who she finds passed out in a bar on his first day. I enjoyed watching how their relationship changed and developed throughout the story. Louise starts out very closed off and almost cold and Eik seems like an extreme chain-smoking slacker, but the more they work together, the more their true characters are revealed and they end up working very well together. Their relationship outside of the office evolves, as well. They actually reminded me a lot of John Tomasetti and Kate Burkholder from the Kate Burkholder series which is probably one of the reasons I liked them so much. 
 Their first case is to identify a woman found dead in the woods near where Louise grew up. The woman has very distinct scarring and they figure it will be an easy case to solve. However, no one matching her description has been reported missing. After releasing the photo to the public, the woman is identified as Lise. She and her twin sister, Mette, so close they were often referred to as just Lisemette, were patients in a home for the mentally disabled. The twist is that Lisemette died thirty years ago. Once Lise is positively identified, Louise and Eik begin the search for her possibly still missing twin. 
 It took a few chapters for the story to really take off for me, but once it did I was hooked. There were lots of twists and turns throughout the book. Woven along with the mystery of Lisemette is a killer rapist on the loose. As Louise and Eik investigate Lisemette, they find themselves involved in the rapist investigation, which also has ties to Louise's past. There was also some definite darker themes. The twins, who were mentally disabled, were put into a home when they were three. It was heartbreaking to read the way the mentally disabled were treated back then. Parents just gave up raising their children and institutionalized them. They were then discouraged from visiting their children and they became known as "forgotten girls". 
 In addition to Louise, we spend some time with her best friend, Camilla, who is a major bridezilla. As the stress of the wedding begins to wear on her, she dusts off her old journalist instincts and delves into the case Louise has told her about. I have to say for most of the book I didn't really care for Camilla. However, once she stopped being so uptight about the wedding, she became a little more likable. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed The Forgotten Girls. Though there were a few times I felt some of the writing was a little lost in translation, the plot of the story really made up for it. I was surprised by the resolution of the central mystery and it left just enough of a cliffhanger about a mystery from Louise's past that I will be eagerly awaiting the next book in the series. I'll definitely be reading Blaedel's other books in the meantime. I would recommend this to fans of mystery/crime novels.

I think I'd give it a 2.5. At times I really liked this book, but other times I was just annoyed. Lexi's mother was horrible. I wanted to knock her upside the head a gazillion times, but I don't think it would have knocked any sense into her. I was mad at the dad for being unwilling to step in and take his children away from her. The whole anti-pageant world agenda was annoying. I am in no ways a supporter of that world, nor do I agree that it is at all healthy for young girls or their families, but it got a little annoying at times. I understand that is the world Lexi is stuck in, but sometimes I felt like the author was simply using Lexi as a tool to stage her personal protest. I always hate it when authors spend the majority of a book setting up the dream guy as this nice, friendly, wonderful human being, only to have them end up being a shallow tool at the end. I realize the point is the girl sees her crush as something other than what he actually is, but in this book she set up the audience to think that as well. I appreciate when the girl finally gets the dream guy, only to realize she has no actual chemistry or real interest in him. That is reality. I don't like when, as a reader, I'm not really given any clues ahead of time that he may not be the dreamboat the crush sees him as. I don't know why I'm ranting. Logan wasn't even why I didn't like this book that much. It was more the anti-pageant push and some of the situations Lexi created that I felt were perhaps a step too far.

Her Ladyship's Curse is a book set in an alternate history where the United States lost the Revolutionary war and thus we are still ruled by England. Women are still treated as chattel and have very few rights and privileges. Magic works in this universe and the technology is consistent with the steam punk genre. 
 A young woman who is a disbeliever in magic, Charmian "Kit" Kittrege has set herself up as an investigator of sorts, though most folks hire her to remove curses, she sees her job as finding out what the real problem is and fixing it for them. 
 Lady Diana Walsh visits her office and asks for her help. It seems that she is being attacked at night and insulting words are being carved into her person. She can't tell her husband or family, so asks Kit to investigate and end this curse for her. 
 Kit agrees to help the woman, but things get complicated, not the least because of the fact that she is a commoner interacting with the aristocracy. Since she has no male to protect her, she is vulnerable to accusations that she might not otherwise face. In addition, she has attracted the attention of two very different men, one, a death mage and the other a police inspector who each add their own level of complexity to her life. 
 No matter, whatever the others say, Kit can not see abandoning Lady Diana to the vicious attacks. 
 This was a wonderful tale with complex world building and characters that jumped right off the page for me. There were aspects to the steam punk technology that were unique to any that I have previously read and very interesting. I loved the web of friendship and loyalty that Kit had, despite her being largely alone in the world and the idea of her bartering in her business transactions, thus gaining favors from people that would be useful to her later. 
 I am very much looking forward to seeing more of these stories! An Excellent Read!

Its kinda funny seeing that soon enough, it looks like Jamie will end up right where he didn't want to be in Quinn's shoes. I have a feeling he'll get used to it and love it though.

Still awesome! Looooved it!

Will there be another book in this series?! Someone needs to tell me. I just don't know... But I hope. This is one of my favorite YA fantasy series ever! I don't want it to end. I don't want to say goodbye to all these wonderful characters. I don't want to leave this world. I don't want to say goodbye. 
 I would have come for you. And if I couldn't walk, I'd crawl to you, and no matter how broken we were, we'd fight our way out together-knives drawn, pistols blazing. Because that's what we do. We never stop fighting. 
 Kaz and the Crows are at it again. Scheming, thieving, and being the Barrel thugs that have earned them their ruthless reputation. This book was not a let down. I don't know how Leigh Bardugo does it, but with the character development and world building, this series will blow you out of the water! 
 This can't be how it ends. It can't, it can't, it can't! I am desperate to know where our characters go, what their lives become. 
 Sorry, Snape, but I don't think I can do that... These characters will get under your skin and make themselves a new home. There's no getting them out of your minds or hearts. I don't know what to say other than read these books. I haven't read something this fascinating in YA fantasy in so long, and I feel nothing will quite compare. 
 And that was what destroyed you in the end: the longing for something you could never have.
Somehow the things in this book didn't quite match up with the series and how the other girls remembered things but it was nice to see things from Ali's point of view.

 Oh gosh! Valentine Napier is one of those characters that you love to hate in a series. When you know he's going to get his own book you want that villainous character to remain villainous, because this is why you fell in love with that character but, you also want that villainous character to be redeemed because he's such a great character but you don't want him to turn into a goody, goody and lose all those villainous quantities that you fell in love with and well that's exactly what you get with Duke of Sin by Elizabeth Hoyt. 
 Elizabeth Hoyt has written a truly brilliant read with Duke of Sin! Prior to reading Duke of Sin I had only read Dearest Rogue and Sweetest Scoundrel so I knew enough about Val to know he was a great villainous character and to know there was more to him than met the eye because he does love his sister but he's still an unscrupulous rake who was up to no good. 
 To make Val a redeemable character though you had to give him a woman he would want to redeem himself for and Bridget Crumb was that and so much more. Bridget who you meet in the previous books is up to no good too or that's what you're lead to believe when in actual fact she is helping those Val has tried to ruin. 
 Bridget has such a strong backbone and I liked her just a much as I liked Val. She doesn't give in to Val and she has her own secrets that make her more unique. Bridget has a real depth to her, she's more than just a housekeeper but it's not until the story unfolds that you find out how much more. You can see how Bridget appeals to Val but it's more than he just enjoys her backbone and secrets. It's how he comes to care for her, her opinions, her vulnerability and her power over him. 
 There are a few worse places for a housekeeper of impeccable credentials to be caught than kneeling on her employer's bed. 
 While yes I loved to hate Val and wanted him to get his HEA, I didn't want it to be an easy ride for him because of all the bad things he had done previously. Sadly for Bridget and Val their HEA isn't easy to come by but god damn by the end of the book it was so very, very worth it. 
 "I don't wike you," said a familiar infant voice. 
 There was a lot of humorous banter in the Duke of Sin with all the different characters and I adored the way it was delivered to us and by whom and how. However, because this is Val's book and is the means to his HEA and to redeem him somewhat, he could no longer be the villainous villain that we knew before and therefore while he still got up to some dastardly deeds the true evil of the Duke of Sin was the Lords of Chaos that we were introduced to in Sweetest Scoundrel. I was slightly expecting the Lords of Chaos arc to be finished with in Duke of Sin but it wouldn't have meshed well with the rest of the storyline but I like the way Ms Hoyt brought it about. 
 While the Duke of Sin is the tenth book in the series it is no means the last and it was delightful to bring all the previous characters together and to see how everyone continues to mix. 
 Val smiled evilly at the child and reached into his pocket. "Do you," he asked, "like kittens?" And he held out a black, fluffy kitten with a white chest.  I love the way that Heidi McLaughlin writes. She is a great storyteller and her characters have so much emotion. They're like real people. "My Unexpected Forever" had some heavy topics, such as moving on after your spouse's death. There really is no right and wrong way to move on (or not) after someone you love dies.  So I liked the idea of The Kill Order. I feel like the Maze Runner series overall lacked some clarity in certain aspects. Thus, I wholeheartedly welcomed an entire prequel devoted to explaining the Flare and its origins.

 I was severely let down. 
 Never have I ever so vehemently disliked an installment from a series that I, on a whole, quite liked. I cared about the Gladers. I loathed WICKED. I invested time and effort and love into the Maze Runner series, and you may disagree, but it was well worth it in my opinion. 
 Likewise, I invested time and effort into The Kill Order, and I came up with...nothing. Nada. Zilch. 
 The characters felt flat, the action sequences far too long, and the whole plot seemed to revolve around evading hordes of savages, driven to barbarism and insanity by the Flare. I have nothing against crazy people. But when you have too many crazy people doing too many crazy stunts, well, that makes me a little crazy. 
 There was plenty of punching and kicking, but not much else. 
 Furthermore, the whole "justification" and "reasoning" behind the release of the Flare really irritated me. I didn't buy it. Not one bit. And one could argue that it shouldn't bother me the PFC's motives don't really matter when what's done is done and that those of us who have read the rest of the series already know the outcome of that incredibly poor decision, which is a valid argument. But still. Really?  They decided to mess around with biological weapons and wipe out a good portion of the population with a highly contagious virus all in the name of preventing human extinction? And they thought that they could control the epidemic?  I mean, really? The rationale behind that decision was dubious at best. 
 I never did truly latch onto the story and begin to care. My interest and attention kept rolling off the pages, like water droplets on wax paper. 
 But there were a few redeemable qualities in The Kill Order, the first being the technology in the story. Hijacking the Berg was the best decision the characters made in this book, and Transvices are things of nightmares. Then there was the epilogue.  THOMAS.  It was like getting a little wave from an old friend. And finally, Alec. "The bear." He saved Mark's hide countless time and each time he, my fondness for that soldier grew. He may be old, but he was leagues better than any of the other characters.  And thus, his ending (it's implied at least) made me very very disappointed.  
 I tried, guys. I truly did try. I tried to love this book, but I just couldn't. I don't despise it, but I don't necessarily like it either. 
 The Kill Order, loaded with lunatics, lacking in everything else.

 As for the actual story... Well, what do you want me to say? I love it. I went through all the feels about a hundred times and it was flinging me back and forth and I loved every second of it. Cather and Wren (Catherine), twins, started college together. Cath decided on an English Major, while Wren wanted to be a Marketing major, and work in advertising like their father. In High School the two sisters did everything together, even write fan fiction about the uber popular Simon Snow Book Series. Fanfixx was their domain; Magicath and Wrenegade were their aliases for writing fan fiction, Simon and Baz love stories. Magicath has 20,000+ fans! Cath went on alone to write her story "Carry On Simon" It's to be her version of the 8th and last novel of the series. She wants it done before the famous Gemma T Leslie (GTL), releases her last novel of Simon. Cath's version is basically a love story between Simon and Baz. 
 Cath and Wren's mother left when they were little and never came back. Their father, who is technically a "Mad Man" in more than one way. He has bi-polar and is very manic at times. He raised the twins on his own in Omaha, Nebraska. 
 Cath was dating Abel for 3 years in high school, but he went to college at MoTech. Wren always said "He's an end table", someone to dump on and be comfortable with. It wasn't really a relationship, so when he called to break up because he found Katie.. well it wasn't a real big deal and now Cath could celebrate being truly single! 
 It just so happens that Cath's roommate is Reagan, who has a tag-along ex (Levi) that always hangs out in their dorm (Pound Hall 913). Reagan and Levi (both from Arnold), try to get Cath out of the dorm and experience life. Cath was too afraid to ask anyone where the dining area was, she lived on protein bars for two weeks before Reagan asked if she had an eating disorder. Levi even stole some Blueberry Bliss to help out. This is when Cath became her special pity project. 
 Cath also liked to stay in the dorm because she was trying to finish 'Carry On Simon', but in class with Professor Piper she thinks to herself... 
 Why do I write? 
 "To be somewhere else" 
 "To get free of ourselves" 
 "To stop being anything or anywhere at all" 
 and "To disappear". Now we can see Cath really has some anxiety issues, and is troubled inside. She believes her twin has abandoned her on her quest to be independent and experiment with the drinking/party life with her roommate Courtney. 
 Cath slowly comes out of her shell and has adventures of her own, especially in the boy department. She met Levi in her dorm, an Agriculture Major, and she meets Nick in her Intro to Writing 3rd level course with Professor Piper. Professor Piper doesn't believe in Fan Fiction, she thinks it plagerism. She tells Cath to write her own story after Cath turned in a story about Simon and Baz. 
 Will Cath forever be in love with Simon and Baz? Or will she fall for Nick or Levi? Will she be able to write a story that is not Fan Fiction?? Will Cath and Wren start talking again? 
 I think that Simon Snow is a parallel of Harry Potter, and also the quotes interspersed throughout the book tie in to what Cath is going through emotionally and physically. 
 "Simon Snow is an 11 yr old orphan from Lancashire recruited to attend Watsford School of Magicks, to become a Magician. As he grows he joins the Mages fighting against the Insidious Humdrum, an evil being trying to rid the world of magic" Characters Include: 
 Penelope~red hair in pony tails with old fashioned glasses (the smart friend like Hermione) 
 Simon Snow~ Main Character Caramel Brown hair, roommates with Baz (Harry Potter) 
 Tyrannus Basilton Pitch aka Baz~ Slicked back Black hair, cool grey eyes 
 Apparently the Crucible cast Baz and Simon to be roommates and they are to watch out for each other like brothers. 
 Baz seems like a cross between Draco and Ron. 
 Agatha is the pretty girl so she must be Ginny who gets married to Harry. 
 The Insiduous Humdrum is Simon, so it is Harry and Voldemort tied together. 
 Quote from Chapter 23 Book 7 of the Simon Snow Series 
 "You're the most powerful magician in a 100 ages. The Humdrums face is Simons own boyhood face, looking dull and tired. Nothing glinted in his blue eyes... Do you think that much power comes without sacrifice? Did you think you could become you without leaving me behind? 
 This quote sounds like a girl version of Levi to Cath 
 "Every smile from Agatha was like waking up to a perfect sunny day. Agatha knew it and she smiled at everyone who crossed her path." 
 Another Quote on page 275, Chapter 34 about Agatha not being able to choose between Simon or Baz, is like when Cath doesn't know to choose Nick or Levi as they both make mistakes and both have good qualities... but I won't tell you which one wins...:) 
 I enjoyed this book, it was a fun read. It was just hard for me to put together all four of the stories going on in the book. I had to read just the Simon Snow book quotes from GTL and then just Carry On quotes, and other fan fics by Cath to really understand how it all folds into one another. The four stories are Simon Snow Series by GTL, Fan Fic by MagiCath, Cath's real story and the story by Rainbow Rowell.
It broken my heart. A little. And it put it back together (even if the end was a bit abrupt, READ IT.).

Entertaining. But in this format, without Rowlings writing style, it's basically fan fiction, and it reads like fan fiction. The characters were 1dimensional but the overall plot was intriguing. A good play, a pathetic book.

 I loved the buildup of their relationship. I felt their connection almost instantly. It helps that Stacey Kennedy wrote 2 very likable and interesting characters. 3.5 stars for story bumped down to 2.5 stars for "bad" writing/editing 
 I was conflicted about how to rate this book. 
 After the first hundred pages I was ready to give up. All the smiling was starting to make me frown. Seriously. Characters smile when they're happy, when they're sad, when they're angry, and even when they're tired. And sometimes...they smile twice in the same passage. See spoiler for examples  
 'I'm not sure I did tell you,' she said, smiling at the memory. 'We met in the park - I was out walking, and there was a sudden downpour.' She smiled. 
 I gathered up the next batch of completed letters and smiled as I pulled on my coat to go and post them. I would hunt again tomorrow, and the very thought lifted my spirits. I smiled. I couldn't help myself. 
  
 I'm sorry, but that's way too much smiling for me. Still, it wasn't just the out-of-control smiling that turned me off. The smiling might not have bothered me so much if not for all the pale faces and gloomy, foggy days (yeah, I know it's 19th London and two serial killers are on the loose and all, but still). 
 Add to that a plethora of typos (way too many for a professional publication) and the author's repeated and somewhat awkward use of the phrase "here and there*" and I thought I'd reached my breaking point, the point where I admit I've wasted my money and my time then lick my literary wounds and move on to something more readable. 
 *In the author's defense, maybe the phrase "here and there" was a commonly used phrase during the late 1800's. If so, I've never come across it. But every time I encountered it in this manuscript I immediately formed an image of Dr. Seuss' 'Sam I am' from Green Eggs and Ham. 
 Then right when I was about to give up, I got sucked into the story. After all, it's a paranormal take on the Thames Torso murders which overlapped the famous Jack-the-Ripper murders. This is the kind of book that seems written just for me. Plus the cover art is quite intriguing and the quality of the book and pages...all top rate. (I'm someone who still enjoys holding a book and this met all my tactile expectations.) 
 In the end, I'm not sure whether the writing improved or I was just more invested in the story, but I no longer found myself repeatedly stopping to brood over the "bad writing". With the exception of a few typos, I was enjoying myself. 
 Amid all the smiling, pale faces, and gloomy, foggy days/nights there's some good stuff here. For example, though it took a while, I eventually felt invested in the protagonist Dr. Bond and read the last 100 pages in two extended sessions. There was even a handful of Sherlock Holmes-esque moments and a satisfying ending. Still, when I read a book, I expect a minimal level of professional editing that seemed absent here. 
 Will I read another book by this author? Well, seeing as when I ordered this book, I also ordered another based on the description, yes, I will. 
 Bottom line - I didn't hate this book, but feel strongly that it could have been so much better. I liked the premise and some of the writing was quite good, still some of it wasn't, and why my rating dropped from 3.5 stars down to 2.5.

I remember hearing about this book when I was a child after my mother read it and brought up the concept of multiple personalities. As an adult, I got it in a box of books but never got around to reading it until it was requested by someone through my paperbackswap.com account. Needless to say, this book has been on my shelf for a long time. I read this book concurrently with another one (review also posted by me on Goodreads) written to disprove it. Knowing that there are so many arguments against this being a true story, I looked at it as a novel and a testament to the many facets that the modern woman has to maintain. As such, there were some gripping moments but one of the major weaknesses of the novel was its pace. 
 The beginning of the novel throws the reader right into the action and confusion as Sybil wakes up from one of her "blackouts" in the middle of a strange street during a snowstorm. The novel keeps this steady pace for the first part, but then, after the author introduces us to many of Sybil's child-like multiple personalities and describes Sybil's childhood, the pace slows to a crawl. During Sybil's formative years she was subjected to mental traumas and physical tortures that most people don't even want to imagine. It is explained that Sybil's psyche dealt with these traumas by creating walled off personalities who were forced to face them. The abuse is so malicious and despicable it is hard to even read about it. It makes us wonder what the hell was up with her parents. During the middle of the book, Schreiber describes Sybil's parents' backgrounds and religious beliefs. While this is necessary for the total picture, it is still very tedious and could cause the reader to become uninterested and stop reading the book. The pace accelerates once again during the third part of the book, but towards the end in the final chapters of the book the plot goes by faster and faster. Not as a page turner but more like a skeleton described in very clinical term which will never be fleshed out. On some occasions years will go by on a single page. It seems as though the author wants to end the book as quickly as possible so she stops explaining how Sybil's treatment is working and just tells the reader that it is working. 
 I followed up my reading of the two books by borrowing the four hour made-for-tv-movie starring Sally Field from the library. The biggest difference between the book and the movie was that a neighbor/love interest was created for Sybil.

 Reading The 5th Wave by Rick Yancey is like watching an action movie crossed with one of those sci-fi movies that follows the lives of several Americans meant to be absolutely typical and relatable, like the football jock and the teen girl with a crush on the most popular guy at her high school. 
 Once The 5th Wave really gets going, it's un-put-downable, but it doesn't have the quality of character development I look for in a favorite book. I had trouble relating to most of its characters, particularly Cassie (the typical blonde teen girl with the crush) and Zombie (the jock whose interests are "cars, football, and girls"). These characters have big, bold personalities it's easy to like; I just felt like I already knew most of them from other books and movies. That said, I did really enjoy reading the sections told from Sammy's perspective, as that felt the most authentic and relatable, and Evan's short section near the beginning was fairly good, too. Unfortunately, the reader sees through Cassie and Zombie's eyes for most of the book. 
 The so-so characterization is okay for this kind of book because it's mainly driven by plot and the post-apocalyptic situation, not by character development. Nevertheless, there were some scenes focusing purely on character that made me roll my eyes because the dialogue was cheesy or else zone out a bit because I just didn't care. As an example, here is a mild spoiler (that you should see coming a mile away) about a romantic moment in the book: When Cassie and Evan kiss for the first time, it's set off in its own paragraph, like it's some big surprise, but the lead-up to it is quite obvious. Then they continue to grow closer, yet almost all I know about Evan as Cassie falls head over heels for him is that (1) he looks like a "teenage version of the Brawny paper towel guy" (p. 159) and (2) he's weirdly obsessed with Cassie--lurking outside her door all the time and sneakily reading her diary--and tells her repeatedly that she's his only reason for living now. (It's like a more wholesome version of Edward Cullen.) I don't see what sets her apart in his eyes. She can be funny and spunky, and Evan says she's pretty, with blonde ringlets and a young-looking face, but my impression of her was still fairly ordinary. Their relationship felt mostly physical to me. Not a compelling reason to betray one's own species  and risk one's life. 
 The first hundred pages or so were a bit slow, despite some gun battles and explosions, because it took me so long to warm to the characters and because, I admit, I was nitpicking the writing a bit, like Cassie's statement on page 9, "If you can't trust anyone, then you can trust no one." Duh? 
 But once I started to care about them (which was around the time Yancey writes from Sammy's perspective for the first time, on the school bus), I grew more and more engrossed in the book, and I ended up staying awake until way past when I'd meant to go to bed, just to read to the end. I found myself feeling some affection for the characters for their appealing tenacity, ingenuity, and humor. I was left with a few questions, some of which will probably be answered in Book 2, but I don't think Yancey ever plans to address why Evan lived his life as a human farmboy yet has soft hands . Despite a few unanswered questions, I closed the book feeling fairly happy with the ending (with one glaring exception:  did Evan really die? really? He can't be dead. I won't believe it unless I see a body. ). 
 The 5th Wave might not be one of my favorite books, but it is entertaining, fast-paced, and touched by tender and thought-provoking moments. I also enjoyed its frequent, unexpected little jolts of humor. 
 I'll end as usual with a few favorite quotes to give you a feel for the writing style and humor.* 
 "He had given into hope, and that will kill you. It kills you before you die. Long before you die." (p. 13) 
 "Thousands of people took off for the mountains . . . or the desert . . . or the swamps. You know, somewhere else. The Majewskis' somewhere else was Disney World. ... 
 'You need to get out,' she said. 'They'll hit the cities first.' 
 'You're probably right,' I said. 'They'd never dream of taking out the Magic Kingdom.' 
 'How would you rather die?' she snapped. 'Hiding under your bed or riding Thunder Mountain?' " (pp. 18-19) 
 "Sometimes in my tent, late at night, I think I can hear the stars scraping against the sky. That's how quiet it is." (p. 29) (WHOA!! THIS LINE!!) 
 "Sammy was sitting on the floor in his room, playing with his X-wing starfighter, destroying the Death Star, 'Shroooooom, shroooooom. I'm going in, Red One!' And outside, my father knelt in the freshly turned earth. Brown dirt, red rose, gray sky, white sheet." (pp. 54-55, when  Cassie's mom dies and they bury her. ) 
 "I did my best to answer Brogden's questions without popping him with my free hand. What were our names? Where were we from? Was anyone in our party infected? Was there anything we could tell him about what was going on? What had we seen? What had we heard? Why were we here? 
 'You mean here at this camp, or are you being existential?' I asked." (p. 59) 
 "Oh look, my belt even has a holster for one of those ten-inch, wicked-looking knives! Hi there, ten-inch, wicked-looking knife." (p. 408) 
 " 'Yes sir, sir!' Sir, sir? Oh God, Cassie. 
 'Why aren't you with your unit?' ... 'Where's your name tag, soldier? And what are you doing with a suppressor on your weapon? And what is this?' He pulls on the bulging leather satchel holding Bear. 
 I pull back. The satchel pops open and I'm busted. 'It's a teddy bear, sir.' " (p. 411) 
 "... the pretty dark-haired girl called Ringer, who's about my age, who not only has very shiny and very straight black hair, but also the flawless complexion of an airbrushed model, the kind you see on the covers of fashion magazines smiling arrogantly at you in the checkout line. Except Ringer never smiles ... so I've decided to cling to the possibility that she's missing some teeth." (p. 455) 
 *from my copy of the book, which is an uncorrected galley. They might appear slightly differently in the final copy of the book.

Bravo, Dani Atkins. This was very much a run of the mill story for almost all of the book. It was well written, but bland. Your typical girl is blind to the boy next door until it's too late and then--BAM! It's not too late after all! Her continued obstinacy is rewarded! 
 Okay here's what I mean by that: throughout the whole book, in Rachel's alternate reality, she KNOWS Jimmy loves her. The signs are so friggin' obvious a thirteen-year-old could figure it out. But, Jimmy pulls back from her. Why!? Because she's, I don't know, engaged? Or just woke up from a coma? You know, that sort of thing would make ANY man hesitant to get involved. Yet Rachel decides to take this as a rejection because apparently she's a hormonal teenager instead of a twenty-three-year-old woman. And instead of handling it like an adult she decides to sulk and never actually broach the subject with Jimmy. 
 That got extremely irritating. And for much of the building romance, I was rolling my eyes. 
 Plus: why the heck was she so hellbent on proving that she was right!? Her life was horrible before, she was "deformed" (I don't really call that a deformity, but oh well), her best friend was dead, she had a nothing job, and her ex-boyfriend is now with the bitchy skank. So, why does she want to prove to everyone she's right? Because it helps the plot, that's why. There's no other real reason, because nothing makes sense. 
 But. 
 But. The ending justified it, at least enough that I added one more star to the review. I liked that it actually had a reason for everything, instead of just being a bad plot.  Rachel being in a coma and dreaming all of it isn't necessarily the most original idea, but it's the first time I have seen it in a YA novel. It was clever, and justified all the sappy moments and the seemingly perfect environment. And I liked that the final scene was her plugs being pulled in the hospital room while she's riding off into the sunset with Jimmy. Her dying and joining Jimmy in the afterlife was well demonstrated in the writing.  
 Kudos.

Oh dear, dear J. K. Rowling, 
 Even though I was disappointed by your last attempt at prose, I must say that your second attempt is better. Not by much, mind you, but better nonetheless. You are much more practiced in the way of the mystery, considering that most of the Harry Potter Series was exactly that. Your strong suit in writing is your ability to foreshadow events, provide us with clues so we as the reader cannot let go of your book; we clutch it till our hands bleed and our eyes blur. So thank you for an enjoyable story overall. 
 However, I do have some problems with your writing style. You tend to over describe the scene in which your characters inhabit, so much so that I find myself wondering why you tell us these things in the first place. I think you would really benefit from limiting the amount of pages, let us say no more than 350. This would cut down on the amount of pointless clutter that seems to fill most of the novel. Harry Potter also suffered from this problem but we didn't care; we wanted you to keep writing and we feared the end. But for mysteries such as this one, it becomes an exhausting marathon that we did not choose to run. 
 All in all I must say that I will not read your next attempt at adult literature. I suppose it is of little consequence to you, because millions will still read whatever you write anyway. If you do decide to return to children's lit I may join your fans again, because I do love your imaginative storytelling. 
 Sincerely, 
 Barbara

Months after the first murder, in the small town of Lake Eden, Minnesota, a bake off happens in town and everyone is getting ready for it. When a judge has to call in sick, they have a substitute who is none other than Coach Boyd Watson. After the first night of the bake off, Boyd is found in his garage dead. Hannah Swenson, the Cookie Lady, who owns her own bakery, knows something isn't right, especially with town reporter Lucy, is having new car and clothes even though she doesn't make much from her job. Hannah knows Lucy is getting money from somewhere and its not exactly the legal way. With the Dessert Bake-Off in full swing, and list of suspects, its going to take some time for Hannah to figure out who the killer is.  I didn't really like the motive for this. Mason killed Boyd because he was going to suspend his son off the team for using steroids which was given to him by his father. And he killed Lucy because she had a picture of him and was going to show it to people.  
 I had initially thought it was Danielle, Boyd's wife, for obvious reasons if you have read the first book. Because she was sick so she didn't make it to the Bake-Off, and she was the one that found him. I am still interested to see how she is taking this and what she is going to be doing in the third book. I didn't feel she had much closure and how she felt about the death of her husband.

This was what made the book worthwhile reading for me, and kept me interested to keep reading to the end. There is not a lot of action in the book, nor mystery or intrigue, but it offers an emotional journey into delayed grief, family dynamics, relationships and personal growth. Unfortunately the character of Melanie, who featured strongly in the beginning of the book, nearly dropped off the scene towards the end, though in my opinion she had a lot more to offer and would have given another perspective to the emotional load involved in her mother's death and the hidden family secret. All in all a fairly enjoyable read if you don't expect too much in terms of mystery or action.

4 Stars & lots of Feelz 
 Goodbye Paradise is a great story by Sarina Bowen. It is full of heartfelt emotion, lots of feelz, eye opening situations, some hot as hell moments, and great support characters who you fall in love with as well. Caleb and Josh are two MC who you just want to get their happily ever afters and as a reader become emotionally involved in their plight to freedom, love, and happiness. 
 So, why is this rated 4 stars instead of 5? Well, I had a bit of trouble grasping how a commune such as Paradise Ranch could exist without someone knowing what was going on there, one of the castoffs, or a nosey neighbor, or a freaking forest ranger. Someone would have wondered about this self-sustaining commune that basically allowed women to be treated as birthing/sex machines, isolated and kicked out the smart ones, and forced their rhetoric and divine beliefs on each member, as law. I just couldn't fully buy into that aspect. In Posey Roberts Naked Organics series that was also about a commune at least they had a "cover" of being an organic farm and interacted with the community by selling their products at a farmer's market. So, there was that aspect of the story that bugged me. Then, I hated that NONE of these people stood up for themselves and pressed charges, especially Miriam, and all the others before her who ran away or were kicked out, like Josh. They just left. They allowed the situation to continue and left others to the fate they escaped. So, yeah...those were my main issues with the plot that caused this to be a 4 star story versus a 5 star story, for me. 
 On the other hand, this is a beautiful bestfriend to lovers romance. Josh and Caleb will grab your attention and never let go. Watching them figure out it was okay to love one another was pretty emotional. Then as they worked to overcome fear of rejection and possible hate from others, those fears and feelings were well portrayed. 
 The audio book was well done and brought life to the story. I enjoyed it on my way back and forth to work, finding myself captivated by Caleb & Joshes story. 
 I would recommend this story to anyone who loves a friend's to lovers romance, with a side of forbidden, and a strong HFN ending.. 4 Goodbye Paradise Stars!!

I'm going to do a review of the full series in general on the first book in the series, its just easier that way because it didn't take me all that long to finish the series, about a week (-+) I think. 
 I love a fairy tale re-telling, the problem is there aren't that many good re-tellings out there, I've been disappointed time and again. Show White and Cinderella redo's are very popular and either there is to much sap or so much action it just isn't appealing to me. 
 Picking up this series I didn't have all that high hopes for anything really remarkable, I cringed thinking it was going to just okay since it was based in the real world happening in everyday life... 
 After the first chapter, though it was worse than what I initially thought: bleh kill me NOW, stab my eyes out with a red pen. 
 Why?! 
 The grammatical and language errors made my eyes burn, not to mention the words that just didn't fit with what she wanted to say or the idea that was trying to be conveyed, things just didn't...."gel". 
 And right through to the second book she seemed to forget key things that she's mentioned earlier and the way Mina, our clumsy, unsure annoying protagonist reached her conclusions just didn't make sense. There was nothing that lead up to how she managed to figure things out. For example : when she figures out Jared is Fae...how she reached that conclusion before he stated doing magic I have no idea. Because the words used clearly indicates that she had already reached that conclusion. 
 There is a great lack of world building, if that had been stronger toward the middle of the first book the novel would have been a lot stronger. And Mina was just completely annoying throughout both books, there isn't a single page where is isn't complaining about her lot in life, she was a total whiner baby! 
 Here's this girl who literally has all this power at her finger tips and she's in constant tears because the boy she likes doesn't really know what he wants... Blah blah blah. Started wondering if maybe Mina was suffering from depression and becoming a little crazy. 
 But the twist at the end of the second book was definitely a turning point for the series. 
 After that the last three books became really good, and the language problems weren't as bad. The concept was something very different, and each time Mina had to overcome something it wasn't a re-telling, it just had elements from the original tales. For me who always wondered if there had been some grain of truth to the Grimm stories; like a serial killer who ate children, it was just enjoyable. 
 Also the good guy wasn't always annoyingly good and the love triangle you initially think it's about is definitively not the triangle you should be looking at. My initial problems with the crazy Brody and Mina episodes of crazy possessive/infatuation started to make sense later in the series. The author actually cleared up a lot of things that didn't make sense at all by book four and five. The loss Mina experiences during the course of the other books is something you do feel with her and for her because time has been taken to build the relationships between the characters, which is one of the things that has been done quite well. 
 In the end I was glad that I'd pressed through with this series because by the end it really wasn't all the bad. So although the first two books only got about and iffy two stars the rest of the series I'd give a 3 1/2 stars, for surprising me. This is a fun series that just takes some getting into.
