The Plot Thickens in Torch 
 Torch by Jocelynn Drake and Rinda Elliot is book three in the Unbreakable Bonds series. These books, while they are technically "standalone" in that each story has an ending, they are NOT standalones meaning you can't pick up book three and start the series there...you will be so lost with the details. This book focuses on Rowe - his story is heartbreaking and his world was shattered in book 2 of the series when his wife was killed in a car wreck. Now, the authors are bringing Rowe back to life and putting him and his broken pieces back together with the help of Lucas, Snow, Ian, Andrei, Jude and his old friend Noah Keegan. 
 There is a lot that happens in this story. First, we watch Rowe as he struggles with grief and moving on with his life. Does he dare give his heart away again...what if something happens to the person, will he survive another loss? This is what Rowe struggles with throughout a large part of the story and it is brought on by the arrival of his old Army buddy Noah Keegan and the resurfacing of his attraction to the man. The authors did a great job of revealing Rowe's history and his sexuality - he is what I would describe as demisexual, he falls in love with the person - male or female. 
 "Rowe was into this and he wasn't an idiot. It had everything to do with the man. Not just any man would make him feel this way." 
 Noah Keegan is a man that we don't really get a huge backstory on as he is introduced to us. He is someone that Rowe has known since his Army days, his best-friend outside of his family of friends, and someone that has been in love with Rowe for years. He happily stepped aside and never told Rowe his feelings when Rowe met and married Mel...but now, he is back and he isn't denying his attraction and feelings any longer. 
 "Noah couldn't think, didn't want to think. He was so damn tired of fighting this when all he wanted was Rowe." 
 These two are hot. Hot. HOT! Rowe takes to being with a man like he has been doing it his whole life. No shyness or hesitant touches. 
 "I'm working on instinct here, but I'm all in." The wicked grin he got in return sent butterflies into his belly. 
 "Instinct is how we all do this at first." Noah ran his hands down Rowe's chest, scraping his short nails through the T-shirt. 
 "It takes practice to learn how to do it right. Practice with the same person." He kissed him. "Over." He kissed him again. "And over." 
 "Lots of practice," Rowe breathed before he spun Noah around, hooked his foot behind his knee, and sent him to his back on the bed. 
 Yeah, the sexual attraction between Rowe and Noah isn't the issue these two have to get past, it's the fear of the "what if..." and guilt that is eating Rowe alive that Noah is up against. 
 The "what if" game follows each of the guys in this story until finally...during Thanksgiving dinner, Ian sets them all straight! 
 "Enough! We're done playing the fucking blame game. Andrei, you feel guilty for getting kidnapped and pushing Lucas into being reckless. Lucas is drowning in guilt, because he thinks what he did led to all this recent hell, including Mel's death. Rowe has undoubtedly twisted the events in his head to feel guilty about Mel. Snow probably feels guilty for attacking Gratton all those year ago." 
 "Nope," Snow interjected and just flashed him a wicked grin. "Just guilty about not killing him the first time we met him." 
 "Whatever," Ian said with a roll of his eyes. "You want to get technical? This is my fault. If Snow, Lucas, and Rowe had never met me years ago, had never tried to help me, then Jagger would never have entered your world. But you know what? Fuck it! I love my life. And I love my family. And this entire shitstorm comes down to one man: Boris Jagger." 
 Ian suddenly swung around to face Snow, poking him in the chest. "You want to get Lucas back here? You call him and tell him I'm going after Jagger. We are done with this bullshit and we are bringing Jagger down for what he's done to this family and other families." 
 Beyond the romance the plot around who is trying to kill this group of men and why gets pretty thick in this book. We learn of some new connections, some covert-ops in progress, and there are of course several attempts to kill our guys throughout the story. Trust me you will be flippin' through the pages as fast as you can to see what happens next! 
 In addition to Rowe, we get glimpses into each of the characters lives. 
 Lucas & Andrei - it takes another catastrophe for Lucas to finally admit his feelings. While Andrei knew he loved him..Lucas has been a stubborn man in actually saying the words. 
 "I love you so fucking much. I should have told you that every day for the past year. God knows I've thought it a hundred times each and every one of those days, but I was too much of a coward to say it. Not anymore. You will never doubt how important you are to me." 
 Snow & Jude - they are settling into couplehood and all seems well on the surface. Who knows if our authors have something brewing for them... 
 Ian & Hollis - There is actually a little progression in this book and I am sure we will get much more back story in the upcoming story, Devour 
 Overall, 5 amazing stars - now to see what our guys go up against in Devour and of course hopefully watch them all settle into happily ever after!

Picked up an ARC from the Sourcebooks booth at BEA. Thanks! 
 I did not know this was part of a series. (That seems to be an ongoing trend with me.) I liked the description and the cover and had absolutely no idea that there are four books that come before it. That said, this isn't a series the way HP is a series, in that you need to read the other books to understand what the heck is going on, so don't let that knowledge deter you from picking up Breathe, Annie, Breathe. 
 Annie is still reeling from the death of her long-time boyfriend, Kyle. She has started training for a marathon to honor his memory, as he wanted to run one and never got the chance. But it's during her training that she meets Jeremiah, and for the first time since Kyle died, she actually feels. Unfortunately, one of the feelings she feels is guilt that she is moving on, and with Jeremiah's penchant for getting injured, she worries about the possibility of falling for someone else only to lose him as well. 
 Funnily enough, I finished this book on National Running Day. I thought it a fitting tribute. 
 I have never trained for a marathon. In fact, I don't run. But I felt for what Annie was going through, with her messed up stomach and her bum knee and her leg cramps, and it seems that the health issues associated with running long distances were the perfect not-really-a-metaphor for dealing with the death of a loved one. It sucks, and it hurts, but the only way to get past it is to push through the pain. 
 I liked Annie's story and was eager to read it. Knowing that she would eventually both a) finish the marathon and b) allow herself to move on did not diminish the giddiness when it actually happened. (I will confess that I spent a good portion of the book worried that something awful would happen to Jeremiah -- there was too much emphasis on how dangerous his activities were, and how much she hated that he participated in them -- so I was pleasantly surprised that nothing did.) 
 At times I found the dialogue a little too ridiculous, but I've learned that it's not always easy to write really good dialogue, and so I generally forgive it unless it's truly atrocious (which this was not). I liked Jeremiah as a character but I found him a bit too unbelievable -- he talks about how the rush he felt when he first met her was bigger than any of the ones he felt while doing his extreme sports, and I cannot stand when books use "love at first sight" as a way to jump start a relationship. But then maybe I've just never felt that rush and am being bitter and cynical about it. 
 I don't know anything about the other books in the series, so I can't speak to the cameos that apparently made other people giggle and squee. 
 Overall, I enjoyed the book and may consider going back to read the others in the series...once I fight my way through the massive stack of books I got from BEA.

This book and I had issues. I first of this book in my Reading Videogames class, where I with my casual gamer knowledge attempted to learn more about videogames and other games. I've been requesting this book since about the beginning of the semester (around Feb?) Apparently, it came in like 2 or 3 times and the e-mails telling me when it arrived never came, or I didn't check my eReader in time... 
 Such frustration. The semester ends in one week and I've finally FINALLY finished this book. 
 Phew~ Now that that is out of the way on to the review!! 
 Brief Summary: 
 Why live in reality when you can live in virtual reality? In the year 2044 reality sucks and most people spend as much time as they can as their avatars inside the VR game/program OASIS. There is pretty much nothing you can't do in OASIS. The creator of OASIS passes away and in his will he says that the person to find the hidden egg within OASIS will inherit his mass fortune and ownership of the company. This starts a mad hunt and a revival of 1980s culture since he was obsessed with his childhood. Wade Watts is determined to find the egg and rise up out of his poor life. Unfortunately, he has no money to travel within the game, therefore unable to actually search for the egg. 
 After years of no clues of progress by anyone, Wade (Perzival) stumbles upon a clue and starts the hunt up once again. It isn't just normal people he is competing against either, a vicious money and power hungry company (IOI) will do anything in order to have the egg. Anything. 
 -------------------------------------- 
 This book was a wild ride. There is just so. much. here! There is so much information needed to understand the riddles given to aid people in their quests to find the egg so, I felt like I just had to hang on and enjoy the ride. 
 I do not know 80s pop culture all that much. I recognize names and places, most of the games really, but not to the extent of the characters. --I sometimes found this to be a downside of the book because the author had to explain out the games, the movies, pretty much everything so that the readers could understand. It adds to the book but, I also thought it took me out of the book. 
 But the world of this book was really so cool. I mean... it sucks big time but, OASIS and the way the author set everything up was so awesome. OASIS is an utopia with no limits. Yet, this makes the story a dystopia because as the book mentions, the real world sucks and is more obvious because of OASIS. Sometimes while reading I would forget that Wade wasn't really in OASIS. 
 The characters were interesting. It is one of those cases where 'beauty is on the inside.' Personality is much more important than looks. And it really shines here. Also there is character growth. Wade goes from being a nobody -to- a celebrity. He has to deal with this change and he isn't perfect. He has to learn from his mistakes and mature. 
 Since the characters are geeks, some with anxiety issues and afraid of the outdoors there are lots of issues that are brought up and addressed. Trust is lost and earned and in OASIS one of the biggest pieces of showing trust is knowing the other person's face and name. 
 --One little thing I had a problem with was that Wade developed a fear of the outside (Doesn't affect story much so I don't think it is a spoiler). But, he gets over it really quickly with no mention ever again... I wanted a little more on this. 
 LOVED the diversity of the characters and mention of variety of shows and games -- not just American ones. So, seeing Gundam and Ultraman mentioned was super cool to me. 
 Really enjoyed this book and I'm glad I finally got to it. I might read the author's next book Armada but, it seemed most people in class didn't like it so, I might pass. 
 If you like 80s references, shows, classic arcade games as well as futuristic aspects --this is a book I think you should read. 
 If you like adventures and/or quirky characters -- probably a book you should try out.

 Not a long novel, but one which I expect to think about for a while. Yeong-hye has some bloody, disturbing dreams and decides she just can't eat meat anymore. It doesn't seem earth-shattering, but from there her situation spirals into complete catastrophe. Divorce, estrangement from her family, and institutionalization in a mental hospital all follow her seemingly innocuous decision. And each of these developments locates itself on Yeong-hye's body as she's assaulted, violated, seduced, restrained, and eventually force-fed. Is this a comment on Korean society's strictly homogenous and hierarchical organization? Is it a criticism of how we've divorced ourselves from the natural world to which Yeong-hye yearns to return? Is it a comment on how we treat the mentally ill and whether they have the right to seek a different state of being, even if it leads to their deaths? Or is it an existential horror novel with all of these rolled in, along with darker, abstract concerns about subversion, submission, and violence that implicates us all? I felt it was an update on Bartleby the Scrivener, who asks again in a different voice if she could be allowed to not work, to not eat, to not live.

 I read some mixed reviews about Criminal before starting this book, but I have to say that it's my favorite Karin Slaughter book yet! 
 The story is told in alternating views and timelines, but all revolves around the same case (or cases involving the same villain). One timeline focuses on Amanda Wagner, Will's boss at GBI, in the seventies when she was just starting out. When women were employed by the force, but not treated like cops. When Amanda and fellow female cop Evelyn (Faith's mother - before she was Faith's mother) realize a murdered woman was wrongly identified, they start their own investigation. 
 I really enjoyed the chapters from Amanda's past. She's been such a frustrating, inscrutable character thus far in the series and it was great to see her origins story. We get to see her influences, her emotions (yes, she actually has them), her growth, and most importantly, her connection to Will Trent. 
 In the current timeline, Will is finally happy, settling into his relationship with Sara (despite that pesky detail that he's technically still married to Angie). However, the happiness is short lived when news is announced that a young girl has been abducted and his father has been paroled from prison. 
 From both timelines we get a lot of background on Will - on his parents, on his childhood, on his career with the GBI. Everything that's been lacking for me in Will's backstory was satisfied in this book. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Criminal. There were times the story got a little bogged down with too much detail (especially in the forensic explanations) and I still find it off-putting that Sara and Will fully committed to their relationship before Will even tried to divorce Angie, but those were really the only parts of the book I didn't like. The story was fast-paced, the mystery was interesting - especially how it connected to the present - and the character backstory and growth was very satisfying.

The Martian Chronicles follows multiple people and their stories, beginning with the native Martians and ending with humans from Earth. It absolutely serves as a commentary about people and the way we interact with the environment. We must prove to ourselves that we are bigger and better always; and we do this by tearing down whatever was there before us and building on its shambles. 
 This is what we did on Mars. Little respect was given for the civilization that came before ours; instead, it was demolished with nary a second thought and turned into the very exact likeness of settlements on Earth (or mid-West America, I should say). 
 And the Martians, the poor Martians! They held no compulsive need to stop the onslaught of change, and instead tried to ingratiate themselves into the hearts and minds of the humans by impersonating long-dead loved ones. And it worked, too. For a little while. 
 The Usher house is by far my favorite. Deliberately disturbing and diabolical, and yet fascinating. What a novel! This faux memoir/alternative history envisions what might have happened if fascism had emerged to become public policy in the U.S. in the 1940's. Philip Roth grew up at this time so he names his protagonist after himself, which gives this a flavor of memoir as well. The fictional Roth narrates what 'happened' in the U.S. when FDR lost his bid for a third term and Charles Lindbergh was elected instead. The results are terrifying. Since Lindbergh was a very vocal anti-Semite in real life, he becomes a near monster in this alternate universe. The novel is a long one but it kept my attention rivetingly-well throughout. The only problem with it is that it gets to a be a tiny bit anti-climactic towards the end. Couldn't it have been a little bit more conclusive in its resolution? I'm not asking for a neat little bow with ribbons, but a little bit more of a structural coda would have done wonders. Lest I quibble too much though, this is still a pretty great novel. When I saw this book on a must read before the movie comes out list, I snatched it up and I am so glad that I did. I don't give a lot of five star reviews. I have described the opening scene of the novel to my husband and my book group (it wasn't our selection but I recommended the book to the members for their personal reading) hoping that it's intensity would emphasize what is so great about the two layers of the book - the horrors of starving in a war torn country and the quest to stop a serial murderer in a country that is supposed to be a crime-free utopia due to communism. 
 It really captures the bleakness of Russia (USSR) in the 30's and then in the 50s before Stalin dies. This book explores the psychological aspects of the politically minded very well. It's matter of fact tone sits well with the plot, and the (not often) action within is worthy of a Bourne-like movie. It's an excellent look into the communist's frame of mind, and the way people have to behave and act for their very survival. The plot is good, the pacing is good and if you have access to the audio version, give it a try! 
 The story follows one man's hunt to catch a serial killer of children. In typical thriller fashion, different chapters reveal what is happening with the protagonist, the killer, and occasionally victims or other side characters. Most chapters end with a cliffhanger before checking in with another character in the next. 
 Where Child 44 differs from the usual thrillers is in its setting - the story takes place in a Soviet Union ruled by Stalin. Clearly the author did quite a bit of research into that era, and he does a good job of showing the horrors and difficulties of life during that time. Much of the novel is spent developing the characters and setting - the murder investigations don't really rev up until the second half of the book. 
 "There is no crime." Stalin's Soviet Union strives to be a paradise for its workers, providing for all of their needs. One of its fundamental pillars is that its citizens live free from the fear of ordinary crime and criminals. But in this society, millions do live in fear . . . of the State. Death is a whisper away. The mere suspicion of ideological disloyalty - owning a book from the decadent West, the wrong word at the wrong time - sends millions of innocents into the Gulags or to their executions. Defending the system from its citizens is the MGB, the State Security Force. And no MGB officer is more courageous, conscientious, or idealistic than Leo Demidov. 
 A war hero with a beautiful wife, Leo lives in relative luxury in Moscow, even providing a decent apartment for his parents. His only ambition has been to serve his country. For this greater good, he has arrested and interrogated. 
 Then the impossible happens. A different kind of criminal-a murderer-is on the loose, killing at will. At first he tells the victim's family that no crime has happened but when the bodies start stacking up, Leo knows he must investigate even though the higher-ups would rather cover up. 
 Soon, Leo finds himself demoted and denounced by his enemies, his world turned upside down, and every belief he's ever held shattered. The only way to save his life and the lives of his family is to uncover this criminal. But in a society that is officially paradise, it's a crime against the State to suggest that a murderer - much less a serial killer - is in their midst. Exiled from his home, with only his wife, Raisa, remaining (sometimes reluctantly) at his side, Leo must confront the vast resources and reach of the MBG to find and stop a criminal that the State won't admit even exists. 
 Although the dialog is sometimes over-earnest and the who-dunnit aspect of the story is not edge-of-your-seat exciting, this book is still worth a read because of the dark but fascinating world and time it draws the reader into. This book should appeal to mystery/thriller fans, as well as those who enjoy historical fiction or even a dystopian story.

Oh god. I'm going to say a lot of things because I just finished this and I don't know if any of them will be coherent. I think, I think this is somewhere between 3.5 and 3.75 stars. But maybe I'll save it at three, because there is just... there is so much. And I don't know what or how to think. 
 My short review is: This is the best novel Handler has written (as Handler) since The Basic Eight. I love Adverbs, but I don't quite count that as a novel; if you know me, you'll know that I was NOT ENAMOURED with Why We Broke Up and I DNF the incest book that I pretend doesn't exist (because god, why, why, why was that written. why did that need to be written). The prose remains Handlerian--Handler is a stylist, I get it, he has a huge crush on Nabokov (and why shouldn't he)--but at the same time, it's toned down. One of the reasons I couldn't stand WWBU was because of how pretentious it felt, except for the giant paragraph at the end where Min says everything she isn't. I know him well enough to spot the hallmarks of his style ("I thought," he said, "that I said that"; not a direct quote but he does have a habit of putting his dialogue tags in strange places in the dialogue, so you've got to wait for it), but at the same time, they weren't overwhelming. They didn't distract from the story. 
 I've gotta say one thing on language, though. Let's talk about race, Daniel. Let's talk about some of the weird stuff you have in here that, frankly, I don't know how it made it in. Especially after the National Book Awards. You made a good apology, you put your money where your mouth was, and you didn't phrase it as "sorry if you were offended"--it was legitimately "sorry I said a racist thing." But? But? A woman "screamed the way the appearance of a black man makes everything suddenly scary." What the actual christ, Daniel. Yes, Manny is black, yes, he shows up, yes, the woman screams because of piracy, but just... dear lord. I hate that sentence. There are a few others, a strange comment about (black) police officers working "twice as hard, due to injustice,"one about a "knocking, clasping ritual believed at the time to be favoured by black people," and there's one other. The first sentence I've mentioned is absolutely not okay, and it bothered me throughout. The others were just... strange. They felt unnecessary. Unneeded. Why did you put those in there, Daniel? Why? 
 Okay. Now to the actual plot of the book: 
 The basic plot is there's a dad who's in radio and he's floundering in life. His infinitely more interesting daughter, Gwen, has been caught stealing. As punishment, she's has to go to an old folks home and talk to old people there. Suddenly, piracy happens. And we watch that unfold. 
 Interesting plot. I found this a really gripping story, and I had to keep reading to find out what would happen next. 
 Character-building was weird. I didn't like Phil a whole lot; he's kind of a sleazebucket and I never quite trusted him. Yet he shares equal screen-time with his daughter, Gwen. I found myself less interested in Phil's parts, partially because I had a hard time following what was happening, but also because he reads as a terrible person. I don't quite know if he's supposed to be sympathetic. Part of me doesn't think he is, mainly because of the way he treats Levine and ignores Marina, HIS WIFE, and is a bit of a snooper. See also: him reading Levine's personal file on her computer, where she's writing an erotic note, and he Gets Ideas . On the other hand, he's billed first on the book blurb, so he's clearly one of the protagonists. No doubt he's flawed, and I really don't mind flawed protagonists, but on the whole he turned out kind of bleh. 
 Gwen, though. Gwen's intriguing. Fourteen-year-old who's frustrated with everything, alter-ego who commits crimes, suddenly swept up in ideas of piracy? Yes, that's more like it. To be honest, I found myself wishing this were more overtly her story, rather than flipping back and forth between the two. I felt bad for Phil once or twice (when Gwen goes missing, but that was more regarding the horror of a missing child ) but Gwen I sympathized more with. This isn't because I read a lot of YA, although maybe it is--she was just more interesting overall. 
 As for other characters: they didn't feel as defined. In some, that's okay. In some, that's not. I wanted more Marina, Phil's wife, Gwen's mum--she intrigued me more than her husband did. The Glassermans were occasionally sketchy, although I was okay with that. Amber was fascinating, perhaps a little thin but nonetheless amusing. I also thought this was going to be a tale of reconciliation between Gwen and Naomi, and I never quite got why Gwen broke off her friendship with Naomi. Oh well. Can't win 'em all.  
 As for the actual piracy: Okay. I should've seen bloodshed coming, but I was absolutely shocked that Gwen was prepared to kill. That's such a drastic action, especially for a fourteen-year-old. Yes, I've read TBE, I know Handler writes this grand tradition of teenage murderesses, but also, that's... that's so big... and it didn't ring true, not quite, not for me. I also didn't get Gwen's sudden PIRACY!!! obsession. It happens as soon as she meets Errol, but I really would've loved to watch it expand. It felt, eh, not quite shoe-horned in, but dealt with too quickly. There was a lot that worked, a lot that didn't. Eh.  
 Oh, and there's a twist at the end that makes you want to re-read the book. I guess I should've seen it coming that Gwen and Errol were related, that Errol was grandfather, that he would die, but I didn't. Don't know how I felt about it, although I didn't feel like it was a cheapo plot device. So that's good.  
 Aaaaaand one last thing that I loved: I shipped Gwen/Amber all the way through and then they KISS on the BOAT and it's described as ROMANTIC and it was actually pretty glorious. SO THAT WAS REALLY NICE.  
 OVERALL: I don't regret reading this, I had a lot of fun with it, although it's less of a fun romp than I would've liked. Be prepared for strangeness and terror and feelings.

This story was great. It was heartbreaking and heartwarming all at once. The characters were wonderful. I just loved Finch. He burned so brightly, he was bound to burn out eventually. Labels were what he fought against from the beginning, constantly reinventing himself and trying to figure out/decide who he wanted to be or who he really was. Bipolar was the label he ran from the most. He didn't want that to define him, and because of that, he let it destroy him. Following him through the manic stage was very interesting. It was easy to see why Violet would latch on and let him pull her along. He was able to pull her out of her funk and help her to start living again. I loved watching her come back to herself and start to get over her sister's death. While Violet was surrounded by loving parents, Finch had nothing really. I didn't envy him his home life. It was such a fun way for Violet and Finch to get to know each other and make memories. Finch is one of those characters I will continue to think about even after the story ended. I do wonder what his life would have been like if more people had truly cared about him. Violet seems to be the only one to have done so. He tried his hardest to avoid the darkness for her. This really was a powerful and impactful story. It is one I will think about for awhile to come. That is not true of a lot of books. Even ones I love are often forgot a couple days later. This one will leave a lasting impression.

Short Review 
 A one off book dealing with characters that we're not likely to really see again. Not one of the best Discworld books, but the time spent in the Assassin's guild makes up for most of the shortcomings. Also does a decent job of making fun of religion. 
 Long Review 
 I have mixed feelings on this Discworld installment. On one hand, I found the protagonist Teppic to be kind of forgettable. Sandwiched in literary order between Granny Weatherwax and Commander Vimes he has tough competition when it comes to memorability and ultimately loses out. Many of the other characters are a bit tedious, like our main 'antagonist' Dios. All in all the last half of the book has a fair number of good jokes but was a little flat to me. 
 On the other hand, the time Pratchett spends at the start of the book fleshing out the Assassin's Guild was fantastic. Rather than just letting it be kind of a goofy self-parodying place he crafts a really believable (within the context of the Discworld universe anyway) institution that fits in a believable way into Ankh-Morpork. I think I would've enjoyed the book a lot more if we'd stayed in the realm of the Assassin's Guild the whole time. 
 I also enjoyed the parodies of ancient Egyptian and Greek culture, and the thorough manner in which he ridicules religion - a topic I think doesn't get made fun of enough considering how ludicrous it all is. 
 In the end then you're left with half of a great book, and then half of a so-so book with some good jokes peppered about in it. 
 If you like Discworld in general, or ancient Egypt and Greece as general topics, you'll enjoy it - you just probably won't rave about it like people do for Wyrd Sisters or Mort. If you're kind of on the fence with the series though, you might want to skip it and come back to it later once you're more hooked. You won't be missing out on anything huge.

This book made me mad. Not at Corey Whaley, who wrote a book I didn't particularly like. That's common enough, and I am well aware that I'm not the only reader out here. The best thing about "Noggin" is the concept: part cancer story, part Rip Van Winkle. And everything else was kinda ho-hum. The funny wasn't so funny, the poignant wasn't pointed, the protagonist wasn't particularly sympathetic. The central conflict revolves around Travis wanting to return to boyfriend-status with the girl he had been dating. That Kate is older, obviously changed, and engaged doesn't deter him. His mooning about her is several clicks past annoying. 
 There are many other unsatisfyimg bits that could have worked but just don't. Need examples? How about the title? The titular nick- name Travis gets upon his return to school appears to be some sort of embrace of his new identity, but it only gets mentioned again in passing, leaving narrative chips on the table. Or how about the importance of Kate's artistic pursuits? That she's dropped them is never explored. There seems to be some noise about making peace with the past and accepting the present, but it never came into focus. The positive LGBTQ thread is an idea I usually favor, but here it didn't connect to themes of relationship and affection that could have made it powerful. 
 I'll add this to the list of so-so books that maybe, some day, one reader may like. Note I don't say love.

I feel like most YA books that feature people of color are focused on navigating racial politics in a serious and sobering way. I think that it's incredibly important to tell those stories, but sometimes you just want an angsty teen novel about how horrible your parents are and how you don't know how to talk to the boy you like. The Education of Margot Sanchez delivers both. This isn't a frothy book (it covers weighty topics like gentrification, class division, prejudice, drugs, and more), but the serious stuff is wrapped in a package that feels light. It was refreshing to see a summery teen drama with a Latina heroine when so often those kinds of books are limited to white, female protagonists.

 I read the print book and immediately turned around and listened to the audiobook. I feel as though this re-read helped me absorb a few things better. 
 1.  I do think the book would have benefited greatly by telling the reader much closer to the beginning that it was a demon that Piper and Neeve had woken in the cave at the end of the previous book. We do not learn this until we get a Piper chapter halfway through this book, but by that point we'd already seen the corruption of the trees in Cabeswater, Adam's hands and eye going rogue, and the possession of Noah. The characters had casually mentioned maybe it was a demon before, but we were really in the dark about what was truly causing this until we get that first Piper scene. I understood those earlier scenes and how they tied into the overall story much better upon the reread. That Piper/demon chapter really should have been moved up in the book.  
 2.  The fact that Noah had passed on is marked only by the line "he quietly slipped from time." With all of the time loops in this story, I thought that meant he went back to the present, not that his ghost disappeared forever (reviving Gansey as his last act). I spent the rest of the book waiting to see Noah again and was QUITE enraged when there was no mention of him in the epilogue. I do think his passing should have been stated more concretely because I totally did not get that that's what happened until I re-read it knowing we'd never see him after that scene.  
 3. Glendower did not resurrect Gansey the first time with the bee incident because Glendower was already dead. It was Noah's voice that Gansey heard, but did Noah have the power to resurrect him? Cabeswater exists outside of ordinary time. When it healed him at the end, I believe it was simultaneously healing him at that other point in time through Noah, whose spirit had been blessed by the ley line since he died as a sacrifice. And that's why Gansey had the ability to command small things in Cabeswater with his words. Because he'd had a part of the ley line in him all along. Yes, yes! This is the kind of wibbly wobbly timey wimey stuff I wanted!  
 Overall, I felt there were too many new characters being introduced for a finale, and not enough closure for the ones we'd known all along (Maura, Grey Man, NOAH).  Although that felt like a lot of loose threads, I don't hate it because Maggie's characters are so unusual and so interesting. She really shows the bigger picture of this town and how things have a larger impact. I do appreciate that, I just wish more time had been spent with our main group. In particular, I felt the women of Fox Way were brushed aside too much in the end. 
 As a finale, I felt this was imperfect in how open to interpretation it was (not to be confused with an open ended plot). The meaning I got above in point 3 was mindblowing for me, but was I just making an assumption? Is this really what Maggie intended? It was never stated implicitly so even if this was 100% correct, what's the likelihood of everyone catching it? It took me reading it 3 times to really grasp on. I think a finale should be a bit more absolute. 
 However, it was a delight to spend time with these characters again. Even on my first read I thought there was a fairly obvious meaning to the plot that  chasing dreams and favors from others won't solve your problems, or give meaning to your life. In the end these characters were the kings of their own lives with the power to change their destinies.  And that's lovely.

Okay, so yeah, cancer sucks. Most of us, adults at least, learned this the hard way as we know and/or have loved someone who has died from cancer (young and old). We've watched as some parasitic form of the dreaded "oma" consumes them, sometimes to the point that we pray for their death just so that the suffering can end. We are all too familiar with the helplessness and fear and pain associated with the deadly C word. 
 So this is a poignant topic, one that touches many deeply because it is something we have experienced. And even for those who lack firsthand experience, cancer's prevalence is so great, it's still something the masses can relate to, something they can embrace. 
 That said, this story is a tearjerker. How could it not be? I think there are few things more tragic or more disheartening than a child diagnosed with a terminal illness except of course the death of that child/young adult. 
 Yet reading this story I was disappointed and not really sure why. Then I hit page 250 something and I began to have a change of heart. The point were Gus dies.  
 At first, I was like...this is it. This is why everyone loves this book. So what if I knew the twist from the beginning. Gus dies  So what if the characters seem less than genuine and scripted as opposed to organic. So what if the level of convenient coincidences defy mathematical probability. SO FREAKING WHAT...I get it. Finally, I get it. At least until Van Houtten shows up at the funeral no less ...all the way from Amsterdam...and then I understand why this will only be a 3 star book for me, regardless of the tears. 
 The way I see it, there is a fine line between a skillfully crafted story and a contrived story (even for a YA audience). And maybe that line is different for everyone. For me, this line was crossed too many times. Everything was just too scripted, too convenient, too expected, too predictable, too June Cleaver (the way we think life and death should be rather than the way it really is) from the dialogue to the characters to the book written by Van Houtten, who just happened to have his own tragedy to tell. Really? Just when I was willing to jump on board. Van Houtten lost his daughter to cancer. The same Van Houtten that wrote a book that both characters, who both have terminal cancer and who fall in love, quote throughout the dialogue. The same Van Houtten that returns their emails, even though he is a recluse/drunk who shuns his fame and hasn't opened fan mail in over a decade. . 
 I'm obviously in the minority here and not trying to take away from what this book does offer, an emotionally charged story capable of reminding us how precious life is, not to mention some interesting insights about life and death/living and dying, and probably one of the best titles I've come across in a long time. 
 Overall, an okay read with some shining moments, sure to make you cry a lot, yell at the kids less, and hug them more. Personally, I loved some of the philosophical musings about the universe, though at times their delivery felt contrived. I think this is also an interesting subject matter for a YA audience, who probably doesn't think much about illness/death/dying. 
 I will add that I think this would work better as a movie, which is probably already in the works.

Oh, and she messes around with any hot guy she can get her hands on, but she flips out when being called a slut. Or a bloodwhore - which she (by definition at least) kind of is as well. 
 Good thing Dimitri's there to teach the girl some manners. I have to admit I enjoyed there forbidden romance (gosh, I'm such a sucker for those ...) And Rose does grow less annoying towards the end of the book. The development of her character definitely went in the right direction, but she really had me rolling my eyes the first few chapters and I haven't quite forgiven her for that. 
 The overall story wasn't too bad though. Entertaining, at least. And the writing is fun, honest and easy to read. I bought the first three books in the series in a discount-pack so I'll read them anyways and hope that Rose gradually earns my respect and appreciation in Frostbite and Shadowkiss.

First 7/8 of the book? About 3 stars. Last few chapters? Negative stars. 
 Reader thoughts: We'll ignore the ending for a bit. 
 So, I liked seeing the friendship developing. Aaron, Callum, and Tamara have a lot of good times together. Havoc seems to be a fun pet, and he certainly affects the plot more than I'd expect. The three friends care for him a lot and actually take him on walks without treating him like a stuffed, growling animal or something (some fantasy characters treat horses like motorcycles). 
 The friends were extremely reckless, however. They steal, sneak into off-limits prisons, talk to dangerous elementals, practice illegal magic, consort with suspicious adults at midnight (twice), and ignore some semi-obvious warning signs. They hardly get in trouble, either. 
 "Now you three must apologize for breaking into that teacher's room and taking her stuff. Apology over? You're good to go." 
 The one fire test felt wrong. Why would Callum resort to using chaos magic? There were, like, a dozen other things he could try. Pull water from the earth, tunnel through the earth, use fire magic to shape the flames, use air magic to shout for help, etc. The whole situation felt like a cheap way to put him in some fake danger. (If those were impossible, he should have thought of them and discounted them.) 
 The Magisterium never seems to be doing much to help the children. Why do they have any guards stationed outside the school entrance? This is, like, the third or fourth time children got kidnapped off the front driveway! (Especially since the adults knew an assassin was targeting the children.) There didn't seem to be many protection spells, either. Why do books have to act like adults are so stupid? 
 So, the ending. Aaron dies. 
 It's almost as bad as Star by Star, which kills Anakin Solo, or as bad as Earthquake!, which kills Ryan, or as bad as Beyond the Summerland, which also kills its MC. 
 In this book, the MC's best friend dies instead. And he didn't have to. I suppose we're now going to see Callum turning to the dark side just like Constantine. We'll see him decide to try necromancy and bring Aaron back to life or something. We'll see Callum go as moody and twisted as Gen in The Queen of Attolia.  
 It won't matter about the other books. I won't be reading them. They're not fun anymore. 
 Writer thoughts: The events were layered well. This book felt like a lot happened in every scene, something to further the plot, further the danger. That was well done and is a credit to the experienced authors. Newer authors might have taken an extra 50 pages to tell the same story. 
 These books only cover about 2 or 3 weeks of the school year, and then the next one picks up a year later. Why is that? J.K. Rowling chose to skip most of the summer in each of her books, which made sense, but why would HB and CC skip much of the magical school year? I have two guesses. 
 1, it makes these books different so that they're not direct HP ripoffs. Fair enough. 
 2, it allows for a much faster pacing. If readers are waiting nine months for a bad guy to finally attack, it would be difficult to keep up the tension. If readers are waiting for only a week or two for an assassin to strike, the tension is maintained. 
 It does make me wonder what in the world happens in the other 8 months or so of school, though.

A fine tale about Janie, her community of Eatonville, FL., and living in the early part of the 1900's. Hurston is exquisite in her use of dialogue, revealing equal parts humanity, individuality, unique character. She then blends this with third person narration, weaving in and out of colloquial speech and elevated prose. 
 Some readers will complain that not much happens in this story, that Janie winds up where she started without taking much charge of her life. I would counter that this is a story that relies on character, rather than action (although there is action a plenty, especially in the final few chapters: hurricane, flood, fending off wild beasts, burying corpses, murder, insanity, grief). But Janie is the sort of character that is perhaps too familiar, a person who acts but also is acted upon even more. If you like your heroes to be of mortal scale, she's a good one.

Welcome to a world where "Lipstick, fishnets, and sequins [are] optional." As Lane Hayes takes you on an amazing journey and gives you a fantastic story! This is the first story in a new series by Ms. Hayes, the series is perfectly called "A Kind of" and this book focuses on several "Kind of Truth's". 
 Rand O'Malley is a character we met back in a previous series when he was a support character and Seth's best-friend. We didn't get to learn much about him back in Better Than Safe other than he had a band and appeared a bit high strung. Well now we get the full scoop and wow, what a story it is - Rand is a very complex guy with a dream of being a Rockstar and a plan in place to make his dreams come true. What he doesn't plan for his meeting William who literally rocks his world. 
 William "Will" Sanders / Billie Sanders is a self proclaimed band geek and if you didn't know better by the amount of names he has you might think he has multiple personalities. He doesn't. What he does have a several aspects of his life neatly compartmentalized -- so much that when the parts start to mesh, Will has trouble dealing with the consequences. William is a prodigy in music, he can make multiple instruments do his bidding and bend notes and harmonies to create unique musical masterpieces. When Rand is in need of emergency guitar lessons, Will is recommended - and as soon as Rand meets Will he is enamored and drawn to him, causing him to act like a bit of a spazz at times as he works his way into Wills heart. 
 When Rand is out at a local club one night after a show and sees a man in a blonde wig, fishnet stockings, makeup and a sexy dress - he can't believe his eyes when he realizes the sexy man dressed in drag is his guitar tutor. This also brings out a bit of a protective side to Rand as he asserts his claim on Will - ends up literally following Will home and then passing out in Wills cramped apartment. From that moment on, things are never the same. 
 I loved this story! It was the perfect mix of humor, angst, romance, passion, hot sex, innocence, rebellion, and drama while watching two characters find themselves and each other and fall in love. Perfection! An awesome start to a new series and I cannot wait for the next book! I highly recommend this book. As for the audio, wow! I loved the narrator. Seth Clayton did a fantastic job bringing life to this story, he gave personality and nuances to each character that added another layer of perfection to the story! I truly hope he will be narrating all the stories in this series! 
 I leave you with a conversation between Rand and Will that I loved: 
 "You're missing the point that the glitter and eyeliner is what got me here. It's why you're in my bed now, Rand. The part of me you like the most isn't the real me." 
 "I think you're like a caterpillar outgrowing his cocoon. You have these wings you know how to use, but you don't, because the bright colors make you nervous. You'll figure out on your own that you're the one who's kinda like magic."

Love, Love, Love it! 
 I rarely do more personal reviews but this book touched me on so many personal levels that I can't help it. If you care about a more objective review of the book, I will put something like it on my blog and leave the emotional stuff here. 
 So, here goes nothing. 
 It's Rafi's book through and through, not just because the story is told from his POV. Don't get me wrong I loved Denny quite a lot and he has a strong presence in the story but Rafi got me teary eyed a time or two in this book and I felt so, so close to him. 
 It is uncanny hom much I could relate to some of his college experience given how differen him and I are. I'm a 36 yo white het woman from a small country in Europe and he is a 20 yo gay African-Latino guy in what I understand to be one of the best white-boys(and girls) colleges in US. 
 Fresh out of high school at the age of 18 I got accepted in the best University in my country to study English philology (British and American studies). Now, it's my home city, so I lived with my parents at the time and didn't suffer from racial or sexual abuse like Rafi but the pressure to fit was real. 
 Some background info - this all takes place less than 10 after the fall of socialism/communism in Bulgaria and many things that are common and taken for granted in the Western culture were still new to us and it was yet another thing to navigate and get used to. All Western philology studies were sort of reserved for children of the political and party elite until recently and even in my day - many of my colleagues came from such families. And there was me - none of my parents had gone to University, none of them knows any foreign language. I had to figure most of the universtiy stuff on my own. And I have to tell you it was a struggle. Because I'm an overachiever, because I was studying something I loved but it was not easy. Some of my professors in the first year did their best to break the little confidence I had. I've always been good at school stuff, if nothing else and there was I, sudenly feeling like I didn't know how to write or read literature any more. The icing on the cake was 2 semesters of Latin which came of the blue and I didn't even know where to start with. The academic pressure felt brutal and i thought of giving it all up. The only reason I didn't search for professional help?support like Rafi did)  was because of my family - my father complete faith to the point of irrationality that I can do anyhting I set my mind to and my mom's constant encourgement and support. 
 I didn't have the complcations (and benefits) of a love relationship at the time but suddenly I had to navigate the dymanics of an all-women classes which was yet another complication for me. 
 In short, for long stretches of of the story I felt like Rafi's thoughts were mine. His struggle to make sense of this new, unfamiliar place, to be good enough/to deserve his place there (since he got there on a scholarship). His experience was powerfully presented and his anxiety felt real and true to life, especially to me as someone who is pretty anxious about a lot of things in life. 
 And I absolutely loved that the story made me look back on my own expereices in university with just a touch of melancholy and no real sense of regret. 
 I loved how the story included Rafi's life in its complexity - the romance, the college, the family stuff, the rowing. There is even a brief and rather sweet appreance of Steph and Cash (with Tom and Reese on the side). Rafi struggled with so many new things in his life and it all was interconnected and affected deeply his relationship with Denny. 
 The chemistry was really strong but they had to deal with a lot of issues on practicle level, basically they had to find a way to be together. I liked how Ms COusins didn't gloss over their difficulties and made their romance a perfect one. The love to each other and both felt they belong together but that didn't save them from making mistakes along the way. They are too different in terms of sociel, ethnic background, financial situation, family situation and their love didn't just magically erase those difference. They had to learn how to be togther while still being different. there was no sacrfice on oneself just to make the other happy. Rather what we got were two young people making compromises for each other. 
 There is an element of coming-of-age to this story. Both Rafi and Denny had to figure out what they wanted in life and how to go about getting it. The ending Rafi's marriage proposal  came as a bit of surprise but I think it fits the characters and I see it as promise, something that helps them to be happy together. 
 I want to end this rambling trip down memory lane with a quote about Denny which I think fits Rafi as well and pretty much sums up me in love - "Denny needed to take care of him because that was how Denny loved." 
 Thank you, Amy Jo, for writing this story!

I was hesitant to start this series cause I didn't want to have to wait long for the sequel, the torture! Hehe. But I also was just too tempted to stop myself, who isn't! Specially after such huge success on the Night Huntress Series! Which btw, I could not get enough of! It was just sad when that series ended. I still miss Bones and Cat. And will probably be re-reading the series again soon. Anyway, needless to say, I am diving in this one with I guess with some expectations. That part just cannot be helped. ;) 
 And surprise surprise, right away the action starts and it was non-stop! Wowser! I loved it! 
 Here we meet the heroine, Ivy, who is looking for her missing sister... And she realized what she thought were hallucinations of strange realms, were actually real! And that her sister is trapped in that parallel realm. 
 Enters our hero, the hot and mysterious, Adrian. He saved Ivy from the hands of a minion.. and then promised her he would help rescue her sister. But first, together, they'll have to search for this powerful relic that can save her sister. 
 One of the things I liked and is quite intrigued about is the concept of the story/series. It is centred on destiny and prophecy that has something to do with a popular biblical story/stories . As much as I want to say what that prophecy or destiny is about but then it would be a total spoiler. So instead, I will just say that that powerful relic that they are looking for is David's slingshot, from the story David and Goliath. I can't help but loved the genius of the story. 
 Ivy's, the heroine, character was off to a good start. She wasn't whining or acting out after the shock of discovering the otherworld and being hunted by minions... I thought her reactions were pretty cool. 
 But, sigh, her character did fail me near the end. Betrayal is such big word in this story. But is it just me or does it feel like the person who is so afraid to be betrayed was the one who did the deed?! I'm sorry but I find it very hypocritical of her to be screaming "betrayal", when all that other person did was help and protect her... and it's not as if he had a choice! As if she has a choice too if she wanted to rescue her sister! That part just irked me. 
 That said... I feel for Adrian. He is paying penance for a past he had no choice of. And now he has to prove himself worthy?! The poor guy! The constant emotional battle... his fear... He needs to overcome all this and just be the bad-ass hero that I want him to be! Lol. Give me something! Anything! Lol. ;) 
 Okay, before I lose it... let's just say, characters wise, I'd wished for more ... more maturity maybe? ;) 
 But moving on... 
 I enjoyed and loved the humour, specially when Zach glamoured Ivy to look like an old guy... or to look like a hellhound. Well can you imagine this hound in leather bikini? 
 Those scenes were just too funny (in my head anyway)! 
 On to the romance area, there is the attraction and sexual tension... then there is this supposedly "bond between them" that grows every moment they spent together. And while I did felt that attraction.... when it comes to love? Not so much. 
 I loved the non-stop action and suspense... And that much awaited turning point of the story was really fascinating. I keep picture it like a movie with special effects, hehe... :D 
 If I were to rate this accordingly, I'd say : 
 Writing : 5 stars 
 Worldbuilding : 5 Stars 
 Storyline : 5 Stars 
 Ivy & Adrian : 3.5 Stars 
 Action & Suspense : 5 Stars 
 Romance : 3.5 Stars 
 A great start of a series. I find it different. Definitely looking forward to the next one.

This is a tough one for me to rate. On the one hand, I absolutely adored Nevernight. I consider it, still, to be a personal favorite. And then, here with book 2, everything that I loved in this first installment went belly-up and let me down time and time again. 
 I found the whole 'school for assassins' plot to be such a fantastic idea in book 1, and found the writing style, the expansive world building, the burgeoning characters, and the twists and turns to be so totally nuanced and developed and exciting. It just worked. Having left that behind completely this go around was well and truly a disappointment. I know that in the first book, our young anti/hero, Mia, had completed her schooling, so there really wasn't much left to do there, but I didn't think that the plot would shift so dramatically... and to something not as interesting as assassins-for-hire. That was scrapped entirely. 
 Instead, we follow Mia, still on her quest for revenge, but training to become a gladiator of sorts throughout the course of the novel. Here's the rub: it's boring as fuck. I mean, what happened here? It's as if everything I loved about book 1 was snatched from the page, beaten into an ugly mess, pissed and spat on, and tossed back between the bindings a stinking ruin. 
 And those ooooooh, aaaaaah "shocking twists"... anyone could see those coming from a mile away. I knew from the get-go Tric was still alive (hint: it's the same with film & television- if you don't find/see a body, they're not fucking dead) . A major revelation that was obvious from book one was finally proven fact: Mia's brother is alive and well. The fact that Consul Scaeva has a son the same age as her own brother would've been should have been a BIG FUCKING GIVEAWAY. Seriously, how, after all this goddamn time, and after all the fucking clues about him still living, has Mia not wondered what became of her young brother? You'd think she would've questioned further the subtle hints to the contrary, but no. She continues to say he's dead for the sake of future "suspenseful" plot devices. And her being the Consul's daughter was just a non-shocker. It was expected. . It was simply too easy to predict almost every single "plot twist", as if Jay Kristoff just up and decided to stop trying to achieve anything. It's not fun when you know from the very beginning how a book will end, but still have to suffer through the 400+ pages of meandering redundancy. 
 It was boring. The story never truly gained momentum, because all the burning questions were set aside (it's even mentioned in the text- that there were bigger things at play, with nothing being done to further those plots), and yet we're stuck reading about these lame gladiatii games over and over and over. We also have beloved (and love-to-hate) characters from the first book show up, only to be quickly dispatched of early on, as if they hadn't been integral parts of the first installment. Literally all the new characters weren't interesting in the SLIGHTEST. You could also tell who out of the new batch of side characters was going to bite the dust before the nove's end. It was plain as day, and dampened the blows when their times finally came. It's really a shame when you know the outcome of an entire book, and realizing it for what it is-- an overlong sideplot that goes nowhere. 
 Something that rubbed me the wrong way was the treatment of Mia's new "relationship" with Ashlinn . The sex scene between the two went on for a number of pages in graphic detail. There's just something too exploitative about a male author writing about this; just a macho sexual fantasy he seemingly needed to fulfill. This completely takes away from the moment and the story. I am not saying a male author can't/shouldn't write this kind of smut, but I just read it as Mr. Kristoff getting his own rock's off, rather than make character development. Plus, the two just don't fit: Ashlinn killed Mia's lover. Mia killed Ashlinn's brother. How is it so easy to move past that??? . 
 Lastly, I'll have to point out again the countless instances in these novels of senseless violence against animals. Murdering camels, kittens, horses, dogs... it just has no rhyme or reason, and there is little empathy shown by the author. It's disgusting. I know there are innumerable human deaths to contend with, but those are expected in a mature fantasy fiction novel of this nature. I go in knowing that; not to read about a dog vomiting blood, camels being torn asunder, etc. etc. It upsets me to no bounds. 
 *** 
 I'll give this book a 2.5/5, if only because the last few chapters moved the plot further along than the rest of the goddamn 400 pages.

Caitrin is a scribe running away from her past when she stumbles into a strange, enchanted city. At the heart of this place filled with whispering townspeople and strangle ghosts in the woods is Whistling Tor - the home of Anluan, master and cripple. He hires her for a summer, but when war seems to be on the horizon, Caitrin must be able to overcome her fears in order to help save this place she starts to call home. 
 I love this book. Marillier is such a talented writer for these re-imagined fairy tales. This story pays a near-perfect homage to Beauty and the Beast. It is absolutely beautiful because it takes the story but makes it completely new. I don't say that lightly. We can see the shell of the original fairy tale, but these characters, the situation, the struggles are all new. Beautiful. 
 The characters are written so well. I love how Caitrin is a strong woman. Not through physical strength, but through her convictions. 
 Marillier does such a wonderful job writing a woman who can be strong without punching idiots left and right. Usually strong women in books end up as a stereotypical "kick-ass" heroine who asserts her strength by actual muscle and playing ball with the big boys. Here, Marillier accomplishes it by letting Caitrin face her fears and stick to her convictions. She doesn't run away when the chips fall, she doesn't shirk her duty even though she bone-scared. And she presses on forward. Strength in the subtlety. A rare find in books these days. 
 I love how Anluan is not the stereotypical beast, but rather a cripple. A homage to the true story of a man who is no longer a man, reduced to something else. I love the way the relationship develops. Not the ridiculous insta-attraction, but something slow and sweet from care to friendship to love. It is so real, so raw. 
 And though these two are the main characters, I loved every single character in this book. Fleshed out, important side characters. 
 I loved how the two main characters were given time to face their fears alone on their two feet before the war begins. Their strength isn't goopy, sappy, imagined strength from the ohmigahd power of love! (sarcastic). Rather, it's found within themselves first. They fix themselves first before falling into something so deep and committed as a relationship. It's a relationship done right.. 
 Perhaps the only weakness in the story is the amount of history that was thrown at us in the beginning - but that is also fairly necessary for reader understanding, so it's fine. But I had a little trouble sifting through what was important and what was extraneous. Ah well, that's history for you. 
 Four and a half stars because it was so, so lovely. I haven't read a beautiful fairy-tale adaptation like this is a while. I rounded down (and didn't give it that last 0.5 star) because even thought it was beautiful and I have pretty much nothing but compliments and declarations of love for this book.... it didn't give me the shivers, if that makes sense. It didn't make my heart ache as much as I hoped. Despite the brilliant story and wonderful characters, I wish there were more parts that made me gasp and hurt and love and hate. But that isn't something that one can just prescribe to an author. But it is a requirement for that last 0.5 star for me. 
 Very highly recommended for anyone who loves a slow, beautiful romance with a bit of a fairy tale twist.

I didn't understand how much I was looking forward to this book until my friend Natalie acquired an advance copy and I was buzzing with excitement for days. This really has been my favorite series of recent years. It's an excellent fantasy story in its own right, as well as a therapeutic examination of the flaws inherent to the YA fantasy genre -- it's Chicken Soup for the Post-Narnia Cynic's Soul. 
 This is an emotionally rough series overall, and the final installment doesn't pull any punches either. But the heroes are older and more mature now, and watching them finally take charge of their lives was not only satisfying as a story, but deeply cathartic for me. When I saw what direction the ending was heading in, my first instinct was to be disappointed that it seemed to embrace the hopeful "I'm a magician so I should be able to do whatever I want" mentality that was punished with cold hard realism in the previous books. (Did these books make me cynical or was I cynical already?) But really, the characters weren't unhappy in previous books because they were too hopeful or ambitious, or even because they rely on magic -- they were unhappy because they were always expecting someone else's world to be exactly the way they wanted it to be. I loved that in the end, this book was about building your own world, mentally and physically, and yet still pays homage to that initial inkling of inspiration and yearning that you get when you see how wonderful someone else's creation is. 
 I really loved this book, but there were just a few areas that didn't quite mesh. The arc involving Alice was introduced too late in the story and felt like it was rushing to reach catharsis in time for the finale. I'm disappointed that even after she delivers an amazingly scathing monologue pointing out everything that's wrong with Quentin, he doesn't seem to struggle at all with whether he did the right thing, or even whether he's a good person. Being Quentin Coldwater, like being a niffin, means that you burn with the total conviction that you're always right. A few more conversations between Quentin and Alice could have reached the same conclusion but with more of a sense that they both grew from the experience. 
 But my most nitpicky issue is that there are WAY too many references to internet memes and trendy internet slang, primarily from Janet, who should know better. First of all, I can't help but cringe whenever I see phrases like "for the lulz" in print. And secondly, is anyone even going to know what that means ten years from now? It really hurts the re-readability of an otherwise great book.  
 The amount of time I spent thinking about these nitpicks was nothing compared to the time I spent gleefully breezing through this book. I can see how this series might be irritating or unappealingly dark for some people. But for me it's been so relatable and satisfying -- I think I'm actually a better person for having read it. I can't wait to see what Lev Grossman will do next.

There is a border between the two cities--but is it purely out of superstition that the two groups of citizens keep it there? Is there truly a supernatural line, one that is manned by a supernatural agency? Is there truly a third city hiding between the two cities? 
 I am pretty sure I know the answer to these questions. I'm sure many will disagree with me, but I will say that I don't think this has anything to do with the author's ability to make things cool and weird and implausible but plausible. No, I just think that we were given vague enough information to flounder around in the mud while the author stands over us going, "You'll get it! Just keep thinking about it!" 
 And really, I just don't think I should have had to work that hard. No real concrete answers were given ever, only half answers and what one character says is real, and another one says isn't. I was too busy being confused the entire book. 
 So yeah, maybe I've been out of school too long and I don't know how to do critical thinking anymore. Sure. Or this author just wants to be too fanciful and it fell flat.

Rebecca is the pinnacle of gothic literature. While there's no true ghosts, the way that you'd think of. No spirits of white wisping in the corner. No creaks and groans that sound suspiciously like steps. Yet there is still an ominous presence--in the form of our narrator's constant reminder of who Rebecca was, and Mrs. Danvers the creepy old goon. 
 Our narrator is extremely unsure of herself. She's an introvert, painfully shy, and assumes that everyone believes the worst of her. This is in stark contrast to Rebecca, the always-warm and personable first Mrs. de Winter. And Maxim's stern refusal to talk about Rebecca compounded with everyone else's desire to talk of nothing else makes the new Mrs. de Winter feel like an unwelcome outsider to Mandereley. 
 There's many little things that build up--Maxim's obvious refusal to go near certain places because it reminds him of Rebecca. The servants who still pluck the flowers from the garden and arrange them the way Rebecca liked them, and who stand looking as if they don't hear when the narrator asks for something different. The constant reminders of those calling: "There were such splendid balls before!" Before: when Rebecca was alive. And of course as a result the narrator is entirely at a loss as to how she's supposed to act. 
 It's sometimes painful, the situations she makes for herself. The costume she chose to wear at the party. Her accidentally breaking the cupid and stashing the broken pieces instead of owning up to it. Hiding her feelings from Maxim, which would have saved herself a lot of heartache. 
 What I loved the most though was Rebecca. The imprint she left. I couldn't deny that I would have had the same obsession as our narrator had--the way everyone described Rebecca, she sounded unattainable. As though she were a legend, and not a person that had died a year previously. And when the narrator finally learns the secrets of Mandereley, I was duly impressed. I hadn't seen that ending coming. 
 Rebecca very much reminded me of Amy from Gone Girl--and I can't help but think that maybe Gillian Flynn may have gotten her inspiration for Amy from Rebecca. They're so similar with their ability to deceive and manipulate, it seems logical.

 Dear Reader, 
 I just got back from my book club meeting; the group is what finally forced me to get around to reading this book that I've been intrigued by for several years. But I wanted to wait to see what others had to say about it before I got my own thoughts down on paper. And whew, now I have so many thoughts! I don't know where to begin. 
 We started off the discussion commenting on how "flat" the narrative was - not in a bad way, just in the sense that everything that happened seemed so emotionless. One person mentioned that Jane Smiley hated the book for that reason. Another compared it to the writing style of Cormac McCarthy; having only read The Road from him so far, I can still see where she was coming from. We also discussed the "picaresque" genre, a term I'd never encountered before today. The feel of the book really appealed to me, although I think it is one of those types which a reader either loves or hates. I myself enjoyed the dry humor, the quirky banter, the odd wit, and the deadpan way everything was executed. 
 We also discussed how alchemy and chemicals played a very large part in this book - clearly most evident in "the formula", but also in the various other incarnations, including the use of some sort of novocaine, the drinking of copious amounts of alcohol, and the introduction of toothpaste. I commented on how it was a very interesting time when the nation was transitioning away from snake oil doctors and into embracing more scientific medical practices, so the book was fascinating from that aspect. I also loved how it was centered around the era of the Gold Rush, so it featured outlaws and hired guns and shootouts and general lawlessness - all of which culminated in their arrival in San Francisco, which was the epitome of the town with no rules and no discipline. 
 There was so much said in book club (I am still absorbing it!) and there is just so much to so about this book, but I think ultimately what I took away from the discussion was the way the brothers had grown. I got the impression that they kind of ended up exactly where they started, with nothing having changed. But everyone dissuaded me from this notion by pointing out that Charlie & Eli really do become different people throughout the course of their odyssey. It is subtle but you do get to see a big shift. So the dry, somewhat surreal novel really does have something to say. I had initially just enjoyed it for its adventure, but there is certainly more to the book than meets the eye. (Which also jibes with the amazing book cover design, too!) 
 Yours, 
 Arianna 
 P.S. When I finished the book, I noticed that John C. Reilly was thanked in the book's Acknowledgments section, and I was curious as to whether it was the actor. Turns out it was, and Reilly has optioned the movie into a film - I could so see him playing Eli Sisters! Apparently DeWitt and Reilly worked together on a different movie, which is how they met. It leads me to wonder whether DeWitt wrote the character of Eli with the actor in mind. In any case, no word on the production of that movie yet, but I am eager to see it happen!

I'm not a very sentimental person, so I probably should have known this wouldn't be the book for me. But a while ago I picked up a sample booklet that had an excerpt of the first chapter of this, its sequel, and...another book by Forman. I thought the writing in those excerpts was good. So when I was on a library-splurge the other day, pillaging the YA section, I decided to check out the full version of this book. 
 Having read the beginning of the sequel, of course I knew how this ended. Maybe that kind of contributed to my dissatisfaction with this book. But mostly I was irritated by the flatness of the characters. They were all such wholesome, good-to-one-another people. Mia was so loved. Her family was so "cool" (scare quotes because I found the evidence of punk-rock-hip parents and rockstar-boyfriend somewhat unconvincing). But more than that, their voices were all so similar. When Mia's grandfather is talking to her (in a flashback), his speech was so unconvincing as speech, I had to pause in my reading for a hearty eye-roll. He's not the only one who talks like an eloquent narrator rather than a human being, though. Everyone does it. Except the token non-white nurse, I guess... 
 Also: I was supremely annoyed by a particular flashback between Mia and her boyfriend. I don't think it's possible to spoil this book, because it's more about sentimentality than plot, but I think this scene was supposed to be important, so here's a spoiler tag. (I also want to hide this bit because it's embarrassing to even write about this sensual/awkward scene.)  The part where they take turns pretending the other person is an instrument. Not only did being played like a flamenco guitar sound supremely uncomfortable (is he, like, plucking at her belly fat? while she is awkwardly splayed over his lap? or is this supposed to be more sexual?), but I just couldn't visualize what either of them could actually have been doing. Was this a metaphor for the first time they have sex? It seemed like it was supposed to be literal, because they'd been awkward with one another before, and this was their way of getting over the discomfort of being physical with one another. But was she actually, literally, using her cello bow on him? Like, rubbing the rosin'd horse-hair of her bow on his crotch? Sounds like a great way to ruin your bow. And by "Great" I mean  Ridiculous.

I loved Max Barry's Machine Man, so when I saw he had a new book out, I bought it immediately. I have to say, it was a disappointment. The best qualities of Machine Man were its humor, premise, and pacing, while it flailed somewhat in developing relationships between characters, and Lexicon, while showcasing Max Barry's skill with pacing and creative plot yet again, was even worse with character development and had much less humor than Machine Man. I didn't hate Lexicon. Indeed, I rushed through it. Even though it was really confusing at first (and there are still parts that I feel weren't satisfactorily explained or explored), this book was easy to get lost in, and I wanted to know what would happen next. But I didn't care much about the characters because they were never developed enough. Sure, they were unique, but most of them lacked that something that would make me feel that they were real and allow me to care about their fate.

I did very much enjoy reading this trilogy. But... I cannot put my finger on what made them so readable! 
 My list of criticisms and frustrations is fairly extensive: 
 Firstly, there are way too many characters (many of which with similar sounding names). I spent a great deal of time working out who's who and what role they play in it all, only to find a little further on they are actually of no importance and have disappeared from the story...or they'll disappear long enough for me to disregard them only to reappear and have me searching back to refresh my memory. 
 Along with the abundance of pointless cast members, there is also way too many sub plots and silly little story segments which have absolutely no reason for being there- they neither draw the story on nor add depth to character. 
 Most of the sex (and sexual violence) bits are unnecessary and obviously there just for shock value. 
 As for the characters, they are all very much 2D. Character traits are undefined, flitting about all over the place depending on what best suits the plot at that given time. I didn't relate to, get any real sense of or very much care about any of them. 
 The plot is fantastical, unbelievable and overcomplicated made worse by Larsson's uncontrolled need to batter the reader over the head with all his knowledge. Yes, Stieg Larsson knows his stuff, but I really don't think we, the readers, need to know even a fraction of it in order to follow the goings on. 
 So, I did read all 3 books through fairly quickly and I did get drawn in, but they are mighty frustrating and not understanding quite why I did like them is driving me nuts. Hence, 3 stars.

Refreshing. Finally - a fantasy world that I would actually love to be in, because both males and females seems to be seen as individuals rather than their gender only. I would love to be a citizen of Skala. :-) Memorable, interesting characters. A very beautiful romance, I love the fact that it takes some time for the main characters to end up together. 
 I look forward to reading the rest.
