Ah, another book that I hoped I would like more. For some reasons I just couldn't connect with the characters. It wasn't because the story was depressing, but I thought it was a blah. I also couldn't get over how annoying Jack was. I didn't hate everything about the book. Some parts were very touching, but for the most part... not so much. Some parts just dragged. Good thing it was a fast read. Here's the review on the Tournament of Books that shared my sentiment: 
 Did I mention that Room is narrated by the five-year-old, Jack?... Yes, it is. The whole entire thing. And let me start by saying that this literary device excites very much the people who love this book--and those include most critics and most people who bother to express themselves online. Most people say that this was a bold and startling and heartbreaking choice for Donoghue to make. They mean that in a good way. 
 It drove me nuts, however. For a few short chapters the point of view was interesting; then for another chapter it was poignant; and then for a few more pages it was cute. But then I wanted out. The baby talk started to grate on me, even as the story continued to humble and intrigue. Every page started to feel, to me, like one of those TV commercials for a charity, where a kid is made to say lines composed by adults who are trying to make you cry. I felt manipulated and ... confined! (The irony!) 
 This review was by Matt Dellinger, who picked Freedom by Jonathan Frazen over this book. There was another review by Jennifer Weiner, who gave a more favorable perspective. My guess is that she's mother and can relate; Matt and I... not so much?

I am having a hard time choosing whether to review this with my head or my emotions. I think because I'm in a good mood I'll rate with emotion, because why not spread the love? 
 Windfall is entirely predictable. You can see most every plot development from a mile off, and the characters are very cookie cutter. Alice is the quiet, nice girl who is in love with her loud childhood friend. He's the guy that attracts girls and is charming in all the right ways. When she buys him a lottery ticket and he wins big, things snowball and he becomes larger than life. 
 Do you think they'll end up together? Do you think Teddy will learn how to be normal and not go overboard with his winnings? Will Alice learn to open her heart and stop acting like she's all alone in the world? 
 If you can't guess the answers to any of those questions, you haven't read enough books. 
 The thing is, the author had some beautiful narration. When Alice is realizing that she doesn't have to be the lonely island, for example. It's an honest take on how people can be their own worst enemies, and it was executed brilliantly. That you can damage your life just as easily as anyone else can is something our characters learn and must adapt to. 
 Hell, it even got me emotional in the end. When Teddy springs his big surprise on Alice, I got all wishy-washy in the eyeballs and had to stop reading for a second because it was just so darn cute. 
 There's definitely a market for this, and I'm hoping younger readers will read this and learn how to be good people.

Pike's writing is flawlessly fluid and utterly enticing. Her faeries are rather traditional (unlike those in Wicked Lovely and TMI: "Plot twits - the faeries are evil!") but I think this allowed for a more authentic form of orginality, which lies in the details. For instance, the faerie reproduction system and hierarchy. I really enjoyed learning more about those aspects of faerie life. 
 The love triangle is subtle and nuanced, which doesn't divide the readers into Team Tamani or Team David. The action parts are actually my least favorite, though equally well-writen: I would have loved to have spent the better part of the story in Avalon and the rest of it with David and Chelsea, in stead of being chased around by trolls. But hey, I guess Laurel feels the same! 
 Because Pike's description of Avalon is just SO lush, you feel like you're right there, with the loose soil under your feet and the summer breeze twining through your hair. I would love to see Spells become a movie, if only to see Avalon take shape in CGI. 
 As far as dream casts go: dye Molly C. Quinn's (Alexis from Castle) hair blonde and she IS Laurel. Dylan O'Brian (Stiles from Teen wolf) would be a perfectly loveable David and Kiowa Gordon (Embry Call in Twilight) is my stand-in for Tamani, at least for now.

Me Before You was a really thought-provoking novel about life and the choices we make about how to live our lives, and it was devastating and beautiful and I cried. I think that pretty much sums it up. 
 Update: I've been thinking about this book lately, in the context of the movie coming out and the backlash I've been seeing, and it has tempered how much I enjoyed the book. Although the book has a lot of stuff in it that is meant to encourage disabled people about how well they can live their lives, and places they can go, ultimately, Will sticks with what he had decided to do, which was kill himself. And I don't like that it sends a message in favor of killing yourself, especially when there is a lot already in our culture telling disabled people that they will never be happy, or never have a fulfilling career or life, or find love, etc.  So I've downgraded it from a 5 to a 4. I still think it was written well, but I don't think I can endorse it as wholeheartedly as before.

Where do I even start?! Rachel Van Dyken is one of favorite authors, who never disappoints with a new book release. 12 series and over 50 books...there is nothing she can't write about that leaves you laughing, swooning, breathless and excited. And luckily, The Matchmaker's Playbook contains all four! 
 Thoughts: 
 PLOT LINE - Have you ever had a crush and never had the guts to approach them? Well, with a little help from Wingman Inc., they can show you the ropes on how to hook your crush in seven days. SEVEN DAYS. If not, you don't have to pay for their services...they are THAT good at what they do. Just follow their creed and you'll never fail. From flirting to kissing, they make sure you are prepared to catch your crush. Blake Olsen has known her crush for ten years. Growing up and being like one of the guys doesn't quite catch his attention. With the help from Ian Hunter, Blake transforms from a sloppy tomboy to sexy woman. Along with one sassy personality, Blake may have Ian break his cardinal rule by the end of the week: never date your clients. Since Ian is almost as sassy as Blake, you will be laughing at every conversation throughout the process. 
 While I was reading this book, it reminded me of the movie The DUFF. Not the book...the movie (since the movie is so different from the book!). If you have watched the movie, you'll love the book. If you've never watched the movie, you should...after you finish this book of course. There a couple similarities along the lines of hot guy trying to help a hot mess of a girl get noticed by a guy she likes. 
 CHEMISTRY - Their meet-cute basically set off the chemistry in the book. When Blake is enlisted as a client, not only does Ian laugh the fact...he knows it will be a piece of cake. Once he shows off the fact that Blake is in fact a woman, things get a little heated. When small touches leads to smoldering kisses, there may be some confusion on where this is all headed. All their interactions will make you want the sexy times because their chemistry is off the charts. 
 LEX & GABI - Two of Ian's best friends, they can create their own set of drama in this book. They are a like a ticking time bomb waiting to explode. All that tension will eventually lead to on hot and sexy book. When you get to the ending...it might feel like a cliffhanger. I'm so excited for their story!

This book was pretty good. It isn't necessarily the most original-- 3 separate kingdoms with growing tensions and need for power that sparks a war between, but the characters involved are written very well. We get at least one character from each kingdom, and everyone of them has to deal with tensions between politics and morals. Magnus is the Prince of Limeros who has learned in his life to never disobey his bloodthirsty king father's wishes, but he has to constantly show no emotion or reaction to what his father does, and question what it takes to be a prince. He has fallen in love with the wrong person as well and has to struggle with his feelings. We also get to know Lucia, the Princess of this kingdom. No spoilers, but she has some interesting things happening to her. Princess Cleo of Auranos is involved in an event that ends up being the final spark for the war to start and feels bad that she did nothing to stop it. She also has an older sister who is sick with a disease who will kill her, so she works to find a cure for her. She is definitely a spoiled princess and usually that makes her hard to like, but she is strong in other areas and ends up being pretty likable. Jonas of Paelsia is a winemaker's son and was on the receiving end in the final spark event. He wasn't necessarily my favorite character in this book, but he is very intelligent and I think he will really grow on me over the course of the series, given the ending of this book. 
 The writing was pretty simple, but simple is nice. Again, the plot and worldbuilding isn't the most original, but really enjoyed how the cast of characters is portrayed. And I agree that it is like Game of Thrones in that Mrs. Rhodes is not afraid to kill somebody off-- no one is safe.
The story was very slow and seems quite confusing at times. I wasn't a huge fan of those love triangle that was alluded to but hopefully the third book is better.

A possible spoiler alert, in the form of a question, to share: Anyone else puzzling about the "Charlie Tango" helicopter crash?  Considering that Christian Grey tracked Ana Steele -- via her cell phone -- to that bar in a matter of minutes, my plausibility meter pinned when none of Grey's highly-paid security wizards could track the helicopter, "Charlie Tango?" Seriously, eyeroll? Even I, a non-gazillionaire, can track a plane via publicly-available websites, e.g., FlightAware, if one knows the vehicle's tail number?  
 This question falls under the category of what some clever movie reviewer once identified as a refrigerator thought. Why refrigerator thought? So, you've just returned home from the movies, you're standing at the fridge deciding what to eat since the movie popcorn didn't really constitute dinner: you stand there, with the fridge door open, puzzling through the movie's plot points. And somewhere, there is a disconnect, something that says to you, "Nah, no way Jason Bourne could NOT have figured that out.." That's a refrigerator thought. 
 No one in the world of Grey Holdings could track the downed helicopter, nor trace either Christian Grey's or Roz Bailey's phones pings? I mean, come on? Okay, okay.. I'm expecting comparable precision to a Jason Bourne movie. I know. Silly me. Haul out the floggers. That is all. LOL Fifty Shades Darker

I would like to be able to use half starts here. I'd give it 31/2. I enjoyed the book. The protagonist is interesting and I like Jeaniene Frost's version of Vlad. I usually prefer books where the romance is just a sub plot (though I love Cat and Bones) but there was enough action. Everyone once in a while, however, I found the protagonist to be stupid as opposed to spunky and assertive. I was glad that she grew out of avoiding her problems and hiding her powers, but she seemed to swing too far the other way into taking needless risks.  There is no reason in any reality that she would not tell Vlad about the bad guy's tunnel under the castle, or insist that she personally needs to rescue her people even if that makes it more likely they will all die. At the very least, she could have given Vlad a heads up right as she went in because it would be too late to stop her but not too late to coordinate the attack.  When the heroine wasn't being unnecessarily stupid and foolhardy, I liked the story well enough. I will read the next book when it comes out.

This a very emotional book. And that is an understatement. This is the pivotal moment. The very essence of Tristan and Danika's love story. Very heavy stuff that I was not prepared to handle. Much better than the first book. I really saw the love in this book.

This was so much better than the first book. It's still far from perfect, but I think Rick has gotten used to writing something that isn't Percy/Camp Halfblood centric. However, there's still something that's a bit off about this series. I can't figure out what exactly wrong, but something about it is a bit boring. I usually enjoy it, but occasionally it got really dull. 
 I really liked how Rick Riordan handled diversity. In The Sword of Summer, I found that the conversations about diversity were stilted and oddly placed. While topics such as gender identity and religion weren't seamlessly placed within this book, they were much more natural than in the first. 
 I'm really staring to like the characters! They seem a lot less bland than in the last book. Magnus and Sam are really starting to grow on me. Magnus's hall mates finally got some characterization. They're still pretty bland, but likable. Of course I still love Blitz and Hearth. Last book was really about Blitz and his history, but this book was really about Hearth's backstory. And Alex. She really grew on me. She got on my nerves at the beginning, but by the end of the book she was one of my favorite characters. She didn't have a ton of page-time, but she was very well developed. (She's gender fluid btw, but I'm using female pro-nouns because she said she usually feels female.) 
 Rick Riordan has written quite a few of my OTPs, so I don't understand why he can't write romance in this series. Halfborn and Mallory are supposedly dating and in love, but I don't see any chemistry between them. And while there isn't any explicit romance between Magnus and Alex, I feel like they'll get together in the next book. Magnus spends quite a bit of time staring at her. It was kind of annoying actually. 
 About the ending, I'm super excited! We're going to see Percy!?!?! Part of me knows that it's a cheap ploy to get me excited for the next book, but most of me is just fangirling <3  
 The Hammer of Thor was so much better than The Sword of Summer, and I can't wait for the next book. :)

I really didn't like Almost Perfect and don't see myself continuing with the Fool's Gold series. 
 In High School, Liz Sutton fell in love with Ethan Hendrix until she caught him bad mouthing her to his friends. Devastated and pregnant, Liz tried to talk to Ethan only to find him in someone elses bed. So Liz left Fool's Gold forever, she thought. But now she's back to take care of her brother's children and deal with the man who doesn't know she had his son.

 I know Liz was at fault for not trying hard enough to tell Ethan himself that he had a son but everytime she tried she was put in an awkward situation. 
 I felt that Almost Perfect went round in circles at times, with Liz being mad about what Ethan did to her in there youth and Ethan being mad at Liz for not telling him about his son. 
 Eventually (only a handful pages before the end of the book) Ethan realises the errors of his ways and tries to make amends for the wrongs he's done to Liz when she was younger and how he's behaved since her return and how the town has treated her since the news of their son got out.

 In addition to being hailed as a multiple SF award nominee, N.K. Jemisin is also being promoted with a host of descriptive nouns like feminist, political activist, African-American and practicing psychologist. Taken collectively, that makes for a pretty heady introduction, and one that certainly had me eager to see what intrigues this rising SF star had to offer. 
 The Killing Moon begins with Ehiru, a Gatherer priest of Hananja, the Goddess of Dreams, as he collects the "dreamblood" of a devout follower. This is done in a dream world where the Gatherer peacefully guides the dreaming soul into paradise, the essence of those dreams flowing into his body as the mortal connection of the dreamer is severed. His second Gathering of the night is a foreign unbeliever named as a tithe to the goddess on account of his corruption - an effort which goes horribly astray. This Gathering gone wrong eventually serves as the lynchpin for the revelation of internal corruption that threatens to destabilize the entire created world. 
 Although Ehiru is the character that serves as the connection to virtually every element of the story, the tale is mostly told through the eyes of Nijiri, Ehiru's apprentice Gatherer. As a counterpoint to the unshakeable faith in Hananja possessed by these two gatherers, the world-weary cynic and religious critic is played by Sunandi, an ambassador and spy from a neighbouring nation. Once she becomes a target in a hidden power struggle, fate manages to throw all three of them together in a quest to uncover a nefarious plot and save the world. 
 Well-researched, inventive and innovative, this is a book that won my admiration for all the things it is not: It is not European in flavour or tone; the underlying mythology is not Greco-Roman or Norse; it is not filled with Caucasian northerners fighting the evil southerners (rather the other way around, in fact); and the female characters are strong, perceptive and politically adept. Yet despite so much that I admired, it ended up leaving me cold. Even at the most climactic points in the story, I had to take breaks between chapters in an effort to redouble my wavering focus. 
 I have this same glassy-eyed reaction with other SF writers, like Guy Gavriel Kay or David Weber, whose books are intelligent, well-written, and possessing an almost scholastic attention to detail. What's missing in all these books is simply a hook for my individual sensibilities, something to drag me into the story. There was nothing here to grab my attention; nothing that prompted any emotional investment. 
 In many ways, The Killing Moon reminded me of a Hieronymus Bosch painting. Dreams and nightmares are portrayed through the pictorial lens of religion, with layers of allegory and allusion abounding. Another similarity is that I also fail to connect emotionally with any of Bosch's works, despite their obvious quality and merit. I'm disappointed that I wasn't able to enjoy my introduction to Jemisin, but at least now I can see why she's made so many waves in so little time.

I was a bit hesitant to pick up this book, because 1) its massive hype - and I tend to be disappointed those, 2) I am born in '94, don't play games (apart from zoo tycoon, but that doesn't help) and hardly watch (or enjoy) any movies, so I was scared of all the references this book is so well known for. 
 Now, I get the hype. It is most definitely an entertaining book and I had fun reading it. The idea of this story is great and very original. The idea that humanity can lose itself so much to a game is scary, but it is certainly something that could happen. It has its pros (like the amazing school Wade goes to, people can spend time with each other even though they live very far apart) and its cons (the fact that people only seem to live in this fake world and only go out of it to have a piss, while the real world is rotting away). 
 But... I did not like this book as much as I hoped I would. This is mainly because of two reasons. 
 One, most of the references went way over my head. Anything that wasn't Star wars, Star trek, Lord of the Rings, Hitchhikers guide or Pratchett, just ended up confusing me. I might recognize it by name but apart from that I had in most cases no clue. And that was so annoying at times. Something would look/sound like this thing/room/person/car/etc. from this movie/music video/game/etc... that doesn't help me at all. Just tell me what it looks/sounds like, cause I'm too lazy to look everything up (which would have been quite a lot in my case). 
 And then there were the characters... I'm sorry, but they annoyed me so much. The love interest, Art3mis, was described as this really funny blogger, but never said Anything funny and was basically just a bitch. All the characters kept cursing, not because they were pissed about something, but to look cool (it seemed), while it just made them seem like bigger losers to me. Not only the cursing did that for me, a lot of the conversations were just, I don't know, weird. Maybe this had something to do with the fact that I read it in Dutch and it was weirdly translated. When Wade tries to act all not-caring while he has his meeting with Sorrento, it feels so Awkward.  Wade, the main character, in general feels awkward and annoying at times. Dude, you are 17, what are you doing hanging out at brothels? If you are so worried about 'still' being a virgin, maybe not lock yourself in a room for a year and you know... see people. Then there is the fact that loads of people, among which his aunt and his only 'real-life' friend, which doesn't really seem to bother him That much throughout the book, until almost at the end, where he is willing to risk Everything to take revenge.  And then there is the way he looks down to everyone who isn't as clever as he is and may not know everything about IT, but are not scared to ask for help. Of course, his dedication and intelligence is very admirable. I have no idea how he managed to learn All the things he did in only 5 years. 
 I never had the feeling anything bad could happen. Maybe this is because it all takes place inside a game.  But to me there was never any doubt that the 'good guys' would win. And even if they didn't, it wouldn't be the end of the world. It is all just a game. (Of course, something bad does happen to one of the characters). It may have even been better if they didn't win, then people might finally wake up and start to clean up the mess they made in the real world.  
 I'm sorry, now it seems like I hated the book. I definitely didn't. It was a quite enjoyable read and I ended up giving it 3.5-4*. It does deserve the love and attention it is getting. The idea is great and original, it is entertaining, and if you get the references it is amazing and weirdly satisfactory.

I keep on being pleasantly surprised by this series. 
 I started Under the Never Sky a couple of weeks ago, not sure what to expect. I mean, Savages and Moles? Aether? Smarteyes? Auds, Scires, and Seers? Just what was I heading into? 
 Something awesome . 
 And now I've read Through the Ever Night, and I'm itching to get my hands on a copy of Into the Still Blue. I. Must. Have. It. 
 Now. 
 Onto the review. Through the Ever Night 
 I. The POVs are so well written. Veronica Rossi is so talented. I don't have a preference of one POV over another, nope, I enjoy the Perry chapters just as much as the Aria chapters. That, in itself, is pretty rare for us readers. But anyway, yeah, I'm digging the dual perspectives. 
 II. Outsiders vs. Dwellers I just love the stark contrast between the two, and seeing how different they are. The Dwellers are so scientifically advanced and "futuristic" I guess you could say, while the Outsiders are definitely more primitive, but they have what I call "magic". Aria can think it's a mutation or whatever, but supernatural hearing/sight/smell abilities? Magic. 
 I find the Marked abilities so fascinating. You can hear thoughts and scent emotions--how cool is that? We aren't really given much about Seers however, besides that Perry can see in the dark. 
 Holy cow guys, when the Outsiders and Dwellers clash in the next book...it's going to be interesting, to say the least. I'm super excited to see how they collide and eventually work together. 
 III. Kirra . The moment she appeared in the story, I nearly dropped the book in horror. I was thinking, "No, Veronica Rossi, you can't do this to us. You're above this. DON'T YOU DARE MAKE THIS A LOVE TRIANGLE." Fortunately, it didn't become one. Kind of. Perry remained loyal to Aria, in the end, thank the heavens. 
 IV. Although, I'm interested to learn more about Brooke. That girl was a witch in this book, but I bet there's something more...She's obviously jealous, but she's also lost her sister. I just want to see her character develop more. 
 V. Then there's Liv .  I did not see any of that coming. I was thinking along the same lines of Aria, in which Roar had made Liv sound amazing but the moment we meet her...she's a brat who doesn't want to leave. But then we get to know her better and she's slightly rough around edges, to say the least, but I bet you all let out sighs of relief when we learned that she still loves Roar. 
 But then came her death. Just why. I felt like we hadn't nearly known her long enough, and she could've developed so much more, but then she just dies. Why.  
 VI. I'm curious about all the other Pods in this world. It can't just be Reverie and Bliss right? Yet virtually no other Dweller dwellings are mentioned. Oh! Cinder revealed a bit of his history to us. He comes from a place where the other kids can manipulate Aether just like he can. I feel like this is going to play a major role in the next book. Also, I'd love to see Cinder developed more. He is one of the most unique characters in this world, and his ability to control Aether--huge. 
 VII. Aether . Cool, original concept. It's like lightning strikes on steroids, with electromagnetism and whatnot. 
 VIII. Finally, Perry and Aria . I love their relationship. They love each other, but they put others--Perry's tribe and Aria's people in Reverie--first. They aren't blindly obsessed about each other. But they know that they'll pull through in the end. It's so sweet. 
 So, that's that. This series. Read it, if you haven't. Then you can join us in our impatient wait for Into the Still Blue!

This is the first Dean Koontz novel I read so I decided to do a little research about him; and here's what I read: According to his official website and book blog sites, Dean Koontz is one of the good authors who brought several of his books to appear on the New York Times Bestseller List. He is famous for his novels which can be perfectly described and categorized as suspense thrillers with elements of classic horror, science fiction and satire. 
 Frankenstein (Book One: Prodigal Son) is one of Dean Koontz's best known novels. It is a combined science fiction-horror mystery, and satirist novel. It is actually a modern version of Mary Shelley's highly-acclaimed novel Frankenstein or The Modern Prometheus in 1818. Mary Shelley's version of Frankenstein is about an eccentric mad-scientist, Victor Frankenstein who creates a grotesque creature in an unorthodox scientific experiment (dead bodies, electricity, lightning and some other stuff). Although Dean Koontz didn't change the horror/goth-ish like theme of Shelley's version, he, however, contemporized Victor Frankenstein's image and "WORKS". Imagine the change from ugly stitches into unnoticeable beautiful sew patches and Dean Koontz named them as the "New Race". 
 Dean Koontz made me like Science-Fiction and Horror novels. His talent in writing didn't fail to meet my expectations. I'm going to read more and more of his works! :)

 Shazaam. I wasn't quite sure what to make of Shazaam. It was like a cartoon brought to life. Weird. But then when it was revealed that he was a cuddly toy my heart just broke for Dani/Jada. Just thinking that she'd spent those five years in the silvers with a cuddly toy she'd brought to life in her head... I may have shed a couple of tears. It was like a punch to the gut. But then it was revealed that he's real and still in the silvers and I'm back to thinking wtf. I don't think I like that he is real and the cuddly toy was just a surrogate in the real world.  
 I still can't completely connect Dani and Jada as two parts of the same person especially when it comes to Dancer and Ryodan. Hopefully that will resolve itself at some point. I'm hoping the two parts melt together to make a new version or whatever. 
 I did notice a lot of references in Feverborn. Chapter One immediately made me think of that Jack, Rose, floating door scene in Titanic and scattered throughout the text were Lord of the Rings, Harry Potter and Castaway references which made me smile at first but got a little bit old. 
 I've also realised through reading this and through my partial reread of the series in preparation, that the writing can have a touch of the over-dramatics about it. Luckily, at this point, I'm pretty much in love with the world and attached to the characters so it doesn't bother me much although I would completely understand if it bothered other people. 
 A really enjoyable read. I can't wait for the next book and I'm sad that I'll have to wait a while for it (hopefully only a year rather than years - I don't want another GOT situation over here!)

I received an ARC of this novel courtesy of the publishers in exchange for an honest review. This review in its entirety was originally posted at eclectictales.com: http://www.eclectictales.com/blog/201... 
 The Well was a curious novel, the unravelling of the story slow and setting up Ruth's story through memories and dealing with the present time (why was she under house arrest? Why did Mark lose his job? What happened to Lucien exactly?). It's hard to explain my feelings about this novel, but it does do a good job in setting up the eerie and strange atmosphere of the story; it wasn't what I expected. I was also expecting the fanaticism to balance out with the everyday/political/social concerns about The Well but I was surprised that the Sisters of the Rose really slipped in and became such a major part of Ruth's life. Their presence added to the very eerie and tense atmosphere of the novel, wedging into Ruth's life and unbalancing her already-fragile relationships further away, isolating Ruth even more. 
 Despite of the set-up of the story and the thematic elements of it, I found myself not really caring for the characters. I'm not sure if it's because of the set-up of the story or how the narrative indulges a bit too much into Ruth's memory, or the creepy nature of the Sisters and how they found their way into Ruth's life, but I just wanted to know what happened to Lucien. The apocalyptic element of the setting also was a bit of a letdown; you know that there's a major water shortage going on and there's all these government policies and announcements mentioned in passing, but the Well is just so isolating, I never really got that sense of place. 
 Overall, The Well was an interesting read, though it wasn't quite what I was expecting and in the end not quite the read I would've checked out. Nonetheless the structure of the storytelling was interesting and the question of what happened to Lucien and what led to Ruth's house arrest kept me around to the end.

I wanted something fun and light to read after I had read "Sharp Objects" by Gillian Flynn and it destroyed me emotionally. Since this book has been sitting on my shelves since the Twilight boom I figured "Why the heck not" you know? Basically it delivered what I hoped it would "light and kind of fun, but also a bit forgettable." 
 Aislinn is a girl who can see faeries, a rare ability. She is fearful of the faeries because she has seen them do terrible things to mortals and to other fae all her life. She ignores them mostly until a certain faery takes notice of her, after which her entire life changes. We learn that Aislinn is important and special to the faery world and they need her for their survival. 
 In general this book wasn't bad. It met the expectations I had for it, which was low honestly, but it still had me captivated as much as it could with a novel where nothing happens. 
 Characters: 
 Aislinn: Had no personality other than fear. Forgettable character, kind of cool sometimes though, but ultimately indifferent toward her. 
 Seth: Had a bit more of a personality than Aislinn, but still forgettable. Basically every 2006/07 girls dream indie/pop punk dude. 
 Keenan: The blandest character ever probably. 
 What I liked about this book 
 - The amount of research poured into this book is something to be noted and admired. Marr definitely did her fair amount of reading for this book which I appreciated. 
 - The amount of Fae variations in this book where also something I enjoyed a lot. The description of each fae was strong, and had me interested in learning more about them. 
 - The concept of the book was interesting and strong. Marr created a strong Faery Mythology that was effective and interesting. 
 - Also...possible consensual polyamory?????? Maybe?????Please??? 
 What I didn't like about this book 
 - Writing was overly simplistic, and the narration over all confused me. I often had to go back and reread certain pages over because I was so confused from the narration. 
 - Characters in general were bland. I felt that some of these characters could have been explored way more, but they fell short for me. 
 - Nothing seemed to happen in this book. Like nothing at all. Even the little conflict there was seemed to be settled pretty fast. 
 Ultimately if you enjoy books in the same vein as "Twilight" or "Hush Hush" then this book is for you. Fast read with little plot, and kind of forgettable. But hey! it was fun you know sometimes you need some dumb YA to cleanse your palette.

Reader thoughts: I loved this book! This was almost as good as book 1. It was deep and funny. It had conflict with human relations and Medean empires. It had baron traitors and guard pranks. It had true love. 
 Basically, Costis is a guard who despises his new king. He is assigned as the king's personal bodyguard. Soon after, he sees that the king is not as foppish and lazy and idiotic as he pretends to be. It takes awhile to convince the rest of the palace and kingdom that the king is worth following. 
 I could listen to this book again tomorrow, I think, and have just as much fun. Not very many books are good enough to read again right after you finish them. 
 My 2 favorite scenes are the dancing scene and the dueling scene. And maybe the assassination scene. :) 
 In the dancing scene, Eugenides and the queen dance. His left hand compensates for his missing right hand, and he pulls off all the dance moves as if he has both hands. Somehow, while he is doing this, he steals the queen's hairpins, and her hair falls loose. I loved it! 
 The dueling scene is where Costis forces the king into dueling him (with practice sword, which Gen uses so creatively!). This duel takes place in front of the other guards, and it's just epic. Through it, Gen complains about a headache, how tired he is, and he makes bets with other guards. It's like he wasn't even paying attention to the duel. 
 When Gen is nearly assassinated, three assassins jump at him before his guards can reach him. Two seconds later, all three assassins are dead. Costis walks Gen through the gardens back to the palace. Only when they reach stairs does Costis realize the king is injured. Gen starts complaining loudly about he almost died and that his guts are spilling out and how weak he is and that someone should carry him. People laugh, and he makes his slow way up stairs. When Gen reaches his bedroom with the physician, everyone realizes that Gen's injury is actually quite serious. 
 Costis sees that Gen was complaining in order to cover up the seriousness of the injury and to hide it from the queen so that she wouldn't worry. After the stitches are in, the queen faints, and Gen tries to force himself out of bed. It's a very good scene, and Costis comes to all sorts of revelations while he watches.  
 Writer thoughts: This is a perfect example of where the MC (Main Character, usually the pov character) is NOT the protagonist (the person who makes everything happen). The pov character for 90% of the book is a palace guard, Costis. The character who is doing all the scheming and action is definitely Eugenides, the king. 
 Why would MWT choose to write the book this way? What does she gain? 
 Well, some characters can be more interesting from the outside than they are from the inside. We already saw Gen from his own pov in book 1. We saw him from his close friends' povs in book 2. Now we see him from a stranger's pov in book 3. His quirks, lies, and attitude look very different from this perspective, and it is so fascinating.

 Originally I read this book, I was attracted by the cover and said "Why Not?" I found out that although I really tried to love the story it just felt like it was missing something.  Judging by all the amazing reviews, I expected 
 The Iron King 
 to wow me, but it sooo didn't. 
 The #1 problem for me was my lack of feeling towards this book. I didn't care about any of it, really. I never cared about Meghan or her fate. I felt like I barely even knew her. She, along with most of the other characters, were so two dimensional. I never got invested in any of them. I didn't care if they lived or died. 
 But to make matters worse, I often found Meghan to be annoyingly naive and sometimes just plain stupid. At the beginning, she accepted the existence of the Fae and the Nevernever far too easily. She was basically like, "Okay, there's this entire other world full of creates that I never knew existed. That's fine. Now what do we do?" There was no resistance or denial; she just accepted it. But then, she was told that she's actually the daughter of the faery king and there are multiple pieces of evidence to support that, but she refuses to believe it for, like, ever. And she's told that because she's his daughter she has some powers, but again she refuses to believe it's even POSSIBLE. 
 "I will never understand humans," he muttered. "With everything you have seen, magic, fey, monsters, and miracles, you still could not believe you could become invisible." 
 Or, another example, she's gone in and out of the Nevernever multiple times. She walks in through one part of the US, trots around the Nevernever, and comes out a few states away. Then, when they get ready to do the same thing later, she suddenly acts like these Nevernever "wormholes" just don't exist and she can't effortlessly travel around the country like the Fae can. It's like she's forgotten all the magical traveling they've already done before. 
 "You're talking about New Orleans. [..] That's hundreds of miles away!" I protested. "I have no car and no money for a plane ticket. How are we going to get there--or were we planning to hitchhike?" 
 You're traveling around with Fae in the Nevernever and you seriously think you're going to have to take a plane ride or hitchhike to get somewhere? 
 I was also annoyed with Meghan's refusal to kill anyone. People would be trying to kill her and her friends, then her friends retaliate in self-defense, and she scolds her friends for killing them. Fair enough if you don't want your friends killing people in cold blood, but these people are trying to kill you! The only way to come out unscathed is to attack them back, but she's standing there playing peacekeeper. 
 Then, Meghan just had a few stupid, WTF moments. Example: it starts raining, then this happens: 
 Water splashed over my jeans, and I yelped as something burned my skin. 
 We examined my leg. Tiny holes marred my jeans where the drops had hit, the material seared away, the skin underneath red and burned. It throbbed as if I'd jabbed needles into my flesh. 
 My first thought would be: acidic rain. As in, stay the fuck away. But Meghan's first impulse is to stick her hand outside to feel for more: 
 "What the heck?" I muttered, glaring into the storm. It looked like ordinary rain--gray, misty, somewhat depressing. Almost compulsively, I stuck my hand toward the opening, where the water dripped over the edge of the tube. 
 Awesome logic. 
 The final straw for me was the romance. There is no romance for 90% of the book. Literally, none. Not a single flirty conversation or romantic hint. Then all of a sudden, at 80% Meghan and Alex randomly make out. Randomly. I shit you not. One minute they're fighting an iron dragon, the next minute we get this quote: "I looked up at him, and then he was kissing me." Uhhh WHAT?? Where did that come from? And when they finally come up for air, they act like they're immediately dating and need to explain this to their parents. O_O I have no idea where that came from, but I'm not onboard with it.  
 Overall, I just didn't like this book. I didn't like the tone, which felt childish and very "Alice in Wonderland" (in terms of vibe and target audience). Meghan was annoying as hell. And the romance just popped up out of thin air. 
 A few people have told me that the series gets REALLY good after the second book, but I'm not sure if I'm going to make it that far.

Karina Tucker is a widow with one child, six year old Emily. Driving her minivan full of kids home from a school excursion - her friend panics about the school bus not having seat belts - she pulls in at a rest stop. The people there are odd; they call her a 'donor' and they attack her. She flees; protecting the kids, but is poisoned. A creature of darkness saves them and she agrees to be his. He needs something in her blood and she needs his venom to heal the poison. It's a monkey's paw deal; dead if she doesn't agree and permanent if she does. She hasn't got many options. What would happen to Emily? 
 But now the two are caught up in a battle between weird creatures and are transported to another world. Getting home won't be easy, if at all possible. 
 *** 
 This showed up in my Kindle and I had totally forgotten I pre-ordered it. I think there will be a few upset fans because this is not in their usual urban fantasy genre but is far more sci-fi and a lot darker than most of their other works. I inhaled it last night. 
 There was a great debate on Tumblr recently about how rest stops are the 'between places' of the modern world; places where you can pull off and end up in another plane. 
 The world-building is detailed and very intriguing. There are a few info dumps but that's the nature of it when characters are literally trying to explain to Karina (and the reader) where she is and what happened to her. Hint: she's not in Kansas anymore, Toto. 
 Lucas is the the creature of darkness, and when he appears human he is an enormous and still dangerous looking man. Most beings in this world are terrified of him but Karina does her best to try to pretend she isn't. He has to literally gnaw on her for the symbiotic relationship to work. 
 A man walked into the kitchen. Tall, corded with muscle that bulged his T-shirt, he dwarfed the doorway. He wasn't just large, he was massive and wrapped in menace, as if he were a whirlwind of violence, barely contained in the shell of his body. Black hair fell on his hard, aggressive face in long strands. He glanced at her, his eyes green and merciless. She met his gaze and gulped. It was like looking into the eyes of a tiger. His stare promised death. (Kindle Locations 234-237). 
 There is less humour than they normally have, too. 
 "Is a slave better than a payroll supervisor?" Emily asked. 
 "They're not that different," Karina lied. (Kindle Locations 515-516). 
 Snorts... 
 An interesting take on angels and demons. That's not much of a spoiler given that the short originally appeared in a short story anthology Angels and Demons, with Nalini Singh as the headliner. But a bonded pair of angel and demon? All kinds of possibilities. 
 There are a lot of loose ends: the lover turned traitor, how Arthur will take Karina's new form, and what Emily will become (she has to be a donor, too). Plus, there is mention of thirteen Houses, and we have only seen one; the house of Daryon. And Daniel didn't get his chocolate cake.  
 There are so many ways this could be extended and to an infinite number of worlds, but the author pair have already shelved The Edge series, and the second book in the Hidden Legacy series has been pushed back by the publishers, plus they are still working on the Innkeeper series. And they are messing with the Grey Wolf spinoff, too. I just can't see how they can continue this one as well. They are human when their characters are generally not. 
 The cover: sighs. Their covers are so often wrong. This screams urban fantasy with the cityscape in the background and it really isn't. Fans are misled as a result. I can already see some angry one stars over this. 
 The writers are brilliant at making enormous beasts more human and they certainly do that here. By the end I was rooting for them. 
 4 stars

 In Cavallaro's cleverly crafted world, Sherlock Holmes and John Watson were real. These are the stories of their descendants. 
 Under the guise of a rugby scholarship, James Watson transfers from his comfortable home in London to Sherringford, a Connecticut prep school near his estranged father. A descendant of John Watson (yes, the John Watson), James also aspires to be a writer, has quite the temper, and is fascinated by the Holmes family. It is thus just his luck that Sherringford also plays host to Sherlock Holmes' great-great-great-granddaughter, Charlotte. Holmes has quite the reputation at Sherringford both for her weekly poker games and her...odd disposition. Just as Sherlock was known to be both a genius and drug user, so is Charlotte (oxy is the new cocaine). She is a bit surly, but this doesn't dissuade James from wanting to get to know her. Plus, her British accent helps with his homesickness. 
 Watson is eager to introduce himself to Holmes, but she is immediately skeptical: "Who put you up to this? Was it Dobson?" Lee Dobson, we come to learn, is not only James' fellow rugger but also a complete creep. He technically sexually assaulted Holmes (she was under the influence of oxy and did not consent) and he somehow thinks it appropriate to say nasty, degrading things about her in the company of others (and in general); pig. Watson shows his temper by starting a physical altercation with Dobson, spurring ire from Charlotte who can defend herself and doesn't much care for such displays of "machismo." When Dobson turns up dead, all signs point to Watson and Holmes. The cause of death, the clues at the scene of the crime; straight out of John Watson's case files. Watson and Holmes thus begin their own investigation to clear their names...and find the true culprit. 
 In the span of the 300+ pages, Watson and Holmes narrowly avoid a bomb threat, uncover bugs and cameras in James' dorm room (thus revealing his roommate's involvement along with a teacher hoping to profit off of the unfolding story of this case), and discover a connection to the still presumably dead (or simply missing/hiding in action?) August Moriarty. In the end, James reconnects with his estranged father, enjoying time at his house with his stepmother and young half-brothers; quite (unrealistically?) mature for a teenager, but a decent reconciliation. Holmes and Watson make further plans to spend time with each other across the pond at her family's estate in Sussex.  
 In general, this was a mostly enjoyable read. There are some homages to the original series, most obviously the title (A Study in Charlotte/A Study in Scarlet), and both Watson and Holmes felt similar to their respective counterparts, if even only from the BBC Sherlock perspective (which I thoroughly and completely enjoy). That being said, there came a certain point when it felt as though the book was perhaps a touch too long; as though it were dragging. It makes it feel as though the last 50-75 pages potentially could have been condensed and still gotten the same, though a much more interesting, result. I am still curious to see what Watson and Holmes get up to in the next installments, though I move forward with slight pause and reserve.

Once upon a time...the Blood Sorcerer vanquished the kingdom of Elden. To save their children, the queen scattered them to safety and the king filled them with a need for vengeance. Only a magical timepiece connects the four royal heirs...and time is running out. Nicolai the Vampire is renowned for his virility, but in a cruel twist of fate "The Dark Seducer" has become a sex slave in the kingdom of Delfina--stripped of his precious timepiece and his memory. All that remains is a primal need for freedom, revenge--and the only woman who can help him. When the wanton vampire summons Jane Parker, she is helpless to obey. She's drawn to his dark sexuality and into his magical realm. But for this human, all is not a fairy tale. For saving Nicolai could mean losing the only man she's ever craved. 
 Lord of the Vampires is the first in the Royal House of Shadows series by four different authors, Gena Showalter, Jill Monroe, Jessica Anderson & Nalini Singh. They all have the same element to the series that "Once upon a time...the Blood Sorcerer vanquished the kingdom of Elden. To save their children, the queen scattered them to safety and the king filled them with vengeance. Only a magical timepiece connects the four royal heirs...and time is running out..." each author has one of the siblings and each story will unfold what has happened to Elden and how these events have changed the siblings and will eventually bring it all together to close the story. 
 I was quite surprised with Gena Showalter's story because it was something much different from what I'm used to, also it defiantly wasn't what I expected. I didn't love Lord of the Vampires because I found the heroine Jane rubbed me the wrong me from nearly the beginning and I think this is one of the hardest things I had to get through because normally I love and adore Gena Showalter's heroines but Jane just didn't work for me. I found her to be quite annoying however, at times I also felt Nicolai was a bit too overplayed with his extremely alpha attitude and memory loss and whacked out behaviour however, there were things I did like and enjoy about Lord of the Vampires, I enjoyed how Jane became a stronger person and more independent also how she never really gave up and was quite a determined person and I enjoyed parts of Jane and Nicolai relationship from the middle of the story to the end were what I enjoyed most. 
 Favourite Quotes: 
 "Nicolai was walking death. His expression, what few times she glimpsed it, considering how quickly he was moving, was cold." 
 "Nicolai fascinated her. He was bossy and arrogant, yet protective when it mattered. He was a killer with a lover's hands." 
 Overall, Lord of Vampires was an interesting and intriguing start to a new series that I'm interesting in reading more on.

I feel hoodwinked--so many great reviews, but this book was awful. The whole thing felt contrived, especially the world-building. In fact, I'm pretty sure Snyder just created arbitrary rules and customs to make the plot work. What kind of society makes a rule that the leader's poison taster must be someone slated for execution? This is a person charged with protecting the leader's life, and they're trusting criminals for the role?! 
 I just didn't believe in a single one of the characters or their motivations. Supposedly ruthless and powerful characters are tripping over their feet to protect Yelena the moment they meet her. They know nothing about her other than that she's a convicted murderer, yet they'll devote all of their time to helping her? They're going to teach her how to fight and pick locks too, because that makes sense. Frankly, all of the characters felt flat. I see a number of reviewers swooning over Valek, which leaves me utterly confused because he didn't have a personality. 
 And don't get me started on the Code of Behavior. 
 If someone committed murder, the punishment was execution. Self-preservation or an accidental death were not considered acceptable excuses. 
 So then if you attempt murder and don't succeed, are you off the hook? This must be a land peopled of complete idiots to blindly obey a system that doesn't distinguish between action and intent. And for living in a country with such an unforgiving attitude towards killing, the characters sure do attempt--and get away with--a lot of it. I guess the Code only applies when it's convenient to the plot. 
 Perhaps most frustrating is that Snyder doesn't trust her readers at all. She's convinced we won't connect the dots, even the ones she's already explained. If you want a book to treat you like an idiot, here it is. Snyder spells out everything, and I mean everything: 
 I hadn't realized he had drunk that much wine, which would explain why he had been so desperate to find me. Alcohol poisoned the mind, exaggerated the emotions. 
 No shit, Sherlock. Is that what alcohol does? 
 Finally, this book is just plain boring. (There's a brief section about 60% of the way through where things pick up, but don't worry, it gets boring again by the end.) It's like a diary of Yelena's every action and thought. We know every time she eats, every time she sleeps, every time she bathes, every time she trains, every time she gets new clothes. The amount of detail is excruciating. It is not world-building; it is drowning the reader in irrelevant details. I'm sorry, but we don't need to know the shape of every room Yelena enters. 
 Needless to say, I have a hard time imagining anything more painful than continuing with this series. Spare yourself the pain of starting it.

Firsts is really freaking accurate in all its sexified glory. Mercedes is the quintessential teenager, all angst and self-induced drama and willingness to go to extremes. It's a time I remember well since it wasn't all that long ago, and the author's ability to show the thought processes that Mercedes went through in each step was exceptionally well done. This is an author who knows not only how to write, but how to evoke strong emotions in the reader based on characters you may not necessarily like. 
 Here's what I mean by that. Mercedes and Angela both are probably not people I would have been close with in high school. I had a lot of friends, I talked to people from every stereotypical high school group that we had. I got along with most everyone, but even then I wasn't able to find common ground with some people. 
 The ones I had a hard time with were the ones who were completely closed off, like Mercedes. Mercedes, the girl who has only one friend and won't really talk to anyone else outside of that one friend. The girl who keeps to herself, rebuffs any attempts at conversation or friendship. This is works perfectly for her, because of her secret: 
 She has sex with virgins so that they can give their girlfriends the amazing "first time" they deserve, and what she never got. What's awful about this is her reasoning isn't too crazy to follow. Something bad and traumatizing happened to her. She compartmentalizes it, and instead of working through her anguish, she deflects it and decides another way to help herself is to help others. In this way, she justifies her choice to sleep with guys who have girlfriends. She's not doing it out of spite, or out of some need to show the girls that she can take what they have. It isn't that at all. She just wants to make sure the bad thing that happened to her doesn't happen to them too. 
 It's a lovely sentiment, if a little misguided. That's what makes this difficult for me to write about: I can't blame Mercedes for doing what she does because she believed she was doing a good thing. She didn't have a good influence she trusted to give insight and advice; someone to tell her it wasn't a good idea. On the other hand, I think it's pretty safe to say that having sex with someone that's already in a relationship is usually considered a no-no. 
 Mercedes' life goes up in smoke when someone reveals her double-life to the rest of the school. She made some idiotic decisions that didn't help her case (like keeping a log book of all the boys that came in her bedroom), and when shit hits the fan, it REALLY hits the fan. Suddenly, she has to deal with the fall out of her well-intentioned (but poorly planned) volunteer work. And that is where the story really shines. 
 When Mercedes has to essentially pay reparations for the damage she's caused, she knows she's in trouble. She's public enemy number one, the cause for relationships falling apart, and the cause of her own life's implosion. And suddenly, she learns what she should have known all along--there were people she could rely on, people who wouldn't judge her for what happened to her and what she did after. People who love her and don't want to see her fall. 
 It's a beautiful story, all the more so because it follows an imperfect protagonist who makes the wrong decisions. I am stunned that this (debut) author was able to create such a real, viable character dealing with self-inflicted but tough issues. I'm happy I chose to read this, and I wholeheartedly believe you should read it too.

Earlier today with only about 40 pages to go I called this a wonderful, beautiful train wreck. A goodreads 5-star rating type of wreck, the type that not only can you not be engrossed in but long to keep reading when you actually drag yourself to bed hours late and to work in the morning (only a little late). Then the end comes and you are left empty. 
 Not the good type of empty when the author feels like the story is complete and you understand that it is probably for the best even though you still crave more-that vignette was wonderful-but I want to know where the rest of their lives go. Not the empty where the bad guy wins and the world is a desolate, hopeless place - at least that is a fair if not depressing outcome. But no, this is an empty where you ignored your hate for the well crafted characters because you want some sweet sweet catharsis and are instead left with only apathy; the characters, their lives, everything. There's no they got what they deserved; they deserved each other; how depressing, but that's how it needed to end. Not the annoying left with doubt ending, is he or isn't he innocent. What you got was an abundance of patheticness. 
 With that said, the whole story was pretty over-the-top-crazy, but that was what made it so fun for the first 9/10 of the book. Flynn's characters are great. The book is so terrifying, at first, because Flynn makes Amy and Flynn seem so possible. You can see yourself in these two characters; your relationship in their relationship and as things careen out of control you picture your relationships doing the same thing. Everything always starts off so perfect, but eventually as you learn more about them and be yourself more you discover how unperfect people are and they discover the same of you - and it's scary. You wonder if you know the person closest to you and think could this really happen to us? 
 Then, Flynn goes over the ledge. And then you know. No, in fact none of this could ever happen to me. But by this time I was addicted, and I wanted more. It was fun now, I know she had manipulated my emotions (played me like a fiddle in fact) and though I begrudged her my snatching at the bait like an eager trout I was impressed and wanted more. So I willing nipped at the rest of the bait, enjoying my wriggling worm until she hooked me, dragged me onto the shore and left me dead with that crap ending.

So. The Fiery Heart. I just don't know. Sometimes I really enjoyed it. Sometimes I was just getting through it. I'm going to try to collect my thoughts.

However, I felt like Adrian's POV chapters could've been a little more Adrian. While I didn't have trouble forgetting who's POV we were in, they weren't really that different. I expected Adrian's head to be a little more funny and sarcastic than it was. His dialogue still had it, but I would've liked to have seen it in his thoughts. I also felt like this allowed more to be added to the story instead of just being stuck with Sydney the whole time. 
 -We get to see a little of Lissa, Rose, Dimitri, and Christian from The Vampire Academy series, which I liked. I would've liked a little more, though. We finally get a little more Lissa, but Christian is still getting the shaft. 
 -There wasn't a whole lot of development of secondary characters. I still despise Angeline. And I especially dislike that Trey is still into her. Trey was one of my favorite characters in the first couple of books, but he wasn't given a lot of time in this book.

 I liked the concept of the story. Any time a book or movie centers around a writer, I'm in. I am also a sucker for cold case mysteries. I had many theories about what really happened and kept changing my mind from chapter to chapter. Carpenter really did a good job of keeping me guessing and ultimately surprising me with an unexpected twist. I also really enjoyed the excerpts from the book that was inspired by the mystery Megan is looking into. It paralleled the story really well and I thought it was a really clever narrative device. 
 While it started off a little slow, it did eventually suck me in once we got further into the story. The island - and some of it's inhabitants - was pretty creepy and I really felt Megan's paranoia. I liked Megan, but she frustrated me often. For being as paranoid as she was, you would think she'd be a little smarter. I kept wondering why she wouldn't password protect her computer. Or how her inner monologue would go on and on about how certain people were liars and untrustworthy, but she just kept trusting them anyways. 
 Overall, I enjoyed The Weight of Lies, but it didn't quite live up to my expectations. The mystery played out to it's conclusion well, but I thought the actual ending of the book was pretty anti-climactic. I think I was expecting a more horror-inspired ending and was kind of disappointed it didn't go that route. Also, while there is some good psychological suspense, I was expecting more. It was still a well-done, enjoyable book, though, and I think fans of the genre will like it.

 Yeah yeah, Noah's way too perfect. But Mara isn't. And it's well and slowly built, as is her sense of terror and feeling insane. Who doesn't want a man like Noah? Makes me wish I was 16 again (and stunningly beautiful, of course.). Cliche it may be, but that scene with the notebook and Anna still makes me smile. I received a copy of this title from NetGalley. It does not impact my review. 
 I don't really know what I was expected from Making Faces, but the emotional tornado I lived through while reading it definitely wasn't it. This book is incredibly heartbreaking. But, it is also incredibly hopeful. Incredibly beautiful. 
 I found so much of this book really relatable. Like the characters, I was a senior in high school when the 9/11 terrorist attacks happened. I remember sitting in Physics class watching as one of the towers collapsed. I also really related to Fern's awkwardness and insecurity issues. And how, as a child of a pastor, you know that when the phone rings at an odd hour something bad has happened. 
 I think my very favorite thing about this book is that it positively portrayed Christian characters and the Christian faith. So often in mainstream fiction Christian characters are portrayed as wackos or extreme hypocrites. That is not the case here. Fern is kind and loving and not at all judgmental. Scripture is shared and not mocked. There is also a great message of having faith in God's timing and His plan, even when you can't possibly understand them. This all worked really organically within the story and never felt like you were being "preached" at, if that's something that bothers you. I can't even begin to explain how much I appreciate this aspect of the book. 
 I obviously shipped Ambrose and Fern. I really liked how their relationship developed and how they also grew as characters - and felt like there was so much more to them than just a romance. One major character that's really central to the story and isn't mentioned in the synopsis is Bailey. Bailey is Fern's cousin and best friend and the son of Ambrose's wrestling coach. He has muscular dystrophy and is confined to a wheelchair. People with muscular dystrophy do not have very long life expectancies, but Bailey has such an amazing attitude. He tries to live life to the fullest every day and do as much as he can. He has a great sense of humor. He loves his family and friends and Fern and wrestling. He was such an amazing character and one that turned me into a blubbering mess while reading. 
 There were only a couple of things I didn't like. There were several times the flashbacks seemed to come out of the blue. While in most cases there was a definite separation between present and past, there were a couple other times where it just randomly switched from one paragraph to the next and it was a little jarring. Perhaps this is just a formatting issue with the ARC, though? I also did not really like the character Rita. I felt like she was so selfish and that she wasn't so much developed as her own character, but as more of a catalyst for storylines involving Fern and Bailey. 
 The paperback copy includes bonus content, which is two interviews between Ambrose and ESPN - one during his senior year in high school and one that takes place sometime between the final chapter and the epilogue. I really liked both of them and the extra bit of insight it gives into Ambrose. 
 Overall, I just loved Making Faces. It's not a light book. It hurt to read at times. But it was beautifully written and included some amazing characters and really important messages. I really don't think I can recommend this book enough. I'm definitely going to be looking up other books by this author in the future.

Unlike the first four books in the series, I've only read Wolves of the Calla once when it was initially released. My thoughts on it - both good and bad - actually held up pretty well to what I remember from the first time around. 
 I'm going to divide my thoughts on the book into two parts: the main plot and then the twist at the end. The main plot about the Wolves is pretty fantastic and more than holds its own with the other volumes in the series. The Magnificent Seven gets most of the inspiration credit but I enjoyed that King worked in just as many references to Seven Samurai. I hadn't seen either movie back in 2003 when the book first came out, but I'm now a huge Kurosawa fan so I loved that part of the book. 
 The main story at first seems to be a bit more stand alone, but King ties it in big time to the Breakers and Maerlyn's Rainbow. The pop culture tie ins toward the end are a bit much for me but they're about on the same level as the Wizard of Oz stuff from book 4. 
 The only major complaint I have about the main story is that the actual battle is over way too quick. I'm not a fan of drawn out action scenes, but even by my standards that was abrupt. 
 So much for the main story. Now let's talk about the twist, which I'll enclose in spoiler tags. Read on only if you've read the book or don't care about being spoiled. 
 In the great movie Adaptation contains this wonderful exchange 
 Charlie: I've written myself into my screenplay. It's eating itself. I'm eating myself 
 Donald: Oh. That's kinda weird 
 Charlie: It's self-indulgent. It's narcissistic. It's solipsistic. It's pathetic. I'm pathetic. I'm fat and pathetic. 
 That scene is the only thing I could think of when I got to the point where Stephen King writes himself into the series. I hate this twist so much. I hated in 2003. I hate it more now. 
 In King's defense, he does lay the groundwork for it. Thematically, Wolves of the Call is about fiction, reality, and the very thin line between the two. It's a really well explored theme, and one that can fit comfortably in the Dark Tower series. But going so far as writing yourself into the novel is several steps too far. 
 Imagine if when Daenerys finally makes it to Westeros she walks into the Red Keep and finds George R.R. Martin sitting on the Iron Throne. Maybe he'd use that moment to explore some interesting themes. Maybe that would be really well written and set up in the previous volume. But it wouldn't matter, because A Song of Ice and Fire is a series with the fourth wall firmly in tact. You don't just get to change that halfway through and be able to pull it off. 
 But that's what Stephen King tried to do. It doesn't matter that he does a pretty good job of using that twist to explore meta-fictional themes. It's still doesn't work for this series. 
 There are certainly cases where that type of thing can work well. Adaptation is one great example. Dan Simmons has never written himself into a novel, but he's been exploring meta-fictional themes heavily since the early 2000s. I have no doubt that Stephen King could write an interesting novel that breaks the fourth wall, but that's not what THIS series is. The Dark Tower was 100% the wrong place to do it. 
 It would go too far to say that it makes the series jump the shark (though it feels close). King is still writing well and telling a compelling story. But while this twist doesn't destroy the final volumes it definitely taints them. It's part of why I'm so excited about the movies. I simply can't fathom them keeping this twist in the story. I really hope the movies succeed so that I can experience The Dark Tower without this blot and distraction.

"Who will save me?" 
 The real question is what could've saved this book? 
 Having a stronger heroine, or at least a stronger character arc. 
 Many reviewers have noted how Twylla is a weak character. It's true -- she is highly reactive. Throughout the entire book, Twylla instigates nothing of importance. All of her actions are in response to other characters and forces; she's pushed around. It makes for a boring protagonist and a boring read. Twylla's passivity would have been okay as a starting point for a larger character arc, but such development never materialized. Having such a lame lead character was a deathblow to the novel. 
 Developing the hook of the story further. 
 The hook for this story is that, as a goddess embodied, Twylla's touch causes death. That's pretty awesome. Many people were predicting The Sin Eater's Daughter would hold similarities to Graceling because of this. I wish! However, Twylla's is too frightened of her ability to do anything but execute selected people selected by higher-ups. She is so afraid of herself, she spends the rest of her time practically rocking in a corner. I longed for her to either embrace her gifts or to endeavor to find out more about them so she could understand them and, you know, weild them. This never happens. 
 Presenting a less cartoonish villain. 
 Our antagonist is an evil queen. Salisbury does a fantastic job at making her quite diabolical. However, she's never fleshed out and made three-dimensional. There was a gross and shocking reveal at the end of the book that fell flat for me because the queen's motivations were never revealed or even hinted at. Boo. 
 Getting rid of that ridiculous love triangle. 
 Maybe this is a matter of personal preference, but I, in almost all cases, believe love triangles weaken a story. I'm not opposed to forces getting in the way of a relationship, but love triangles come with a whole host of problems. They can make characters seem pathetic by appearing weak-willed and not self-aware or decisive. They can also hijack and plot and turn things into dumb soap operas. In The Sin Eater's Daughter, both the characters and plot are diminished because of the cheap drama. 
 Forming a more coherent plot. 
 Nothing streamlined occurs in The Sin Eater's Daughter. Horribly, Twylla is given nothing to do. I longed for there to be a mystery for her to solve or a journey to go on. Any kind of action. But nothing happens. 
 Bottom line is, the book wasn't a total disaster but it was still irredeemably flawed. Two stars.

Bloodlines was kind of confusing for me at first. I haven't read the Vampire Academy series and really have no desire to, so a lot of the background was lost on me. I wished numerous times for just a little plot summation so I could understand what was going on with everyone. 
 Yet it was still a fun read. I breezed through it in a day, and was suitably interested throughout. It was fun trying to figure out who the bad guys were in each little mystery, and I'm proud to say my guesses were correct--yay me. Lee being the bad guy was fairly obvious if only because the hints that the author dropped were fairly obvious. The fact that a school administrator recognized him but couldn't place his face was pretty damning, especially since we knew that a girl from the school was murdered years previously. Plus, the whole thing with Keith was pretty obvious once we knew it was an Alchemist who was helping the tattoo artists. Because really, it wouldn't be an Alchemist we never met in the story, because then it wouldn't be any fun for us as the readers. So it HAD to be someone we had already met, and since it wasn't Sydney there was only one other option. 
 Sydney got on my nerves quite a bit though. I had a serious problem with her passing judgment on everyone else for having opinions different than her own. She was condescending when it came to Angeline the Keeper, yet she herself sounds very much like a close-minded religious zealot, brainwashed by her religion and upbringing to believe everything is tainted and evil when all the evidence in front of her points to the contrary. 
 That being said though, she's a good narrator in that she's thorough enough without being dry. I'd love to see how this progresses.

Deliciously disturbing. A stomach-churning, page-turning romp through the woods and back into the cruelty and camaraderie of childhood. This will become an instant recommendation when talking to others interested in up-and-coming contemporary horror. 
 I received an ARC of this book through Netgalley but it has been on my "to-read" shelf ever since I read Karen's review a few months back. I was absolutely stoked when I got approved to read it, but I had some reservations because when I tend to want to read something for a while and then actually read it later on down the line, I am often disappointed - not because it was lacking but because my expectations that had been building over time were so unattainably high. This book exceeded those expectations as much as a book about tapeworms can exceed any expectations. 
 Even though this book is set near Canada's Prince Edwards Island, it ain't no Anne of Green Gables. It was scary - in every permutation of the word scary. Scary as in psychologically gripping, a frightening look into adolescent psychopathy. Scary as in vomit-inducing descriptions of gore that will have you skimming paragraphs just to get past the gross horror. Scary as in paranoia-provoking conspiracy theory that will make you trust the government just a little bit less than you already do. Scary as in science and nature gone terribly wrong. Scary as in boy scouts trapped in the woods on a quarantined island ravaged by something contagious. Scary as in CAPITAL LETTERS SCARY. 
 I loved it. Ate it up with a spoon. I've heard others compare it to The Ruins (which I hated - this book is much better) and The Lord of the Flies (which I remember loving - but only vaguely remember anything but the premise and poor, poor Piggy. (Side note: Piggy lovers, beware. This book will effectively give you a new chubby nerd to love, pity and cry over. A Piggy 2.0, if you will)). The boys were lovingly rendered, each given such character and history that the reader is almost enamored with each one despite their glaring, typical teenage flaws. Except for Shelly. He, I hated the whole way through. His scenes were the ones that made me grit my teeth and read just a little bit faster, glossing over the sentences to try to escape the awful detail and imagery. (Shelly, in general, and the lab experiments involving hamsters and gorillas were the most difficult parts to read). 
 I really, really loved the use of the mixed media to inform the reader of details the characters were unaware of on the island. The new releases, the court transcripts, the lab recordings, the magazine interviews all served to add another layer of disturbance to an already disturbing situation in the woods. It disoriented the reader, alerting them to the reality of the seemingly unrealistic situation unfolding on the island. It was masterful and haunting. Something like killer tapeworms could (and should) be the subject of a B-rated horror movie that is more humorous than frightening, but Cutter managers to "cut" away all the potential comedy of the situation - leaving room for fear alone. 
 Bravo. Five star excellence. A certain re-read.
