This is what I would called mostly a character driven story, because even though there is plenty of mystery and a lot of weird things happening, the characters make the story. Having such a different cast of characters, portrayed in such an incredible way, each with their fears and dreams. 
 I remember that after my first read I didn't like Adam that much. He was tiring to read, like I really understand his points, but the way he approached things, made the blame for some actions shift, when there shouldn't even be blame in the first place. When he finally decides to press charges against his father, he thinks that Gansey is happy about all this, because he has this stupid idea that Gansey thinks about him as his object. And I get why, maybe on some level, given his past, he would put such a blame on Gansey, but he is also his friend. That really pissed me off, the first and the second time.  I came out of this reread with the same feeling, like he did develop, but he has a long way ahead to see what he wants to be. 
 I like Ronan and Noah, and I am curious to see what becomes of their characters. I think the second book focuses more on Ronan, which is a very interesting character to watch, don't know how much fun he is to follow though, given his dark past. 
 I love Gansey, I don't know why or how, but he gets me everytime. People, and by people I mean the characters, have this weird perception of him, but reading his perspective was the most interesting one. I also love Blue, she is such a normal perspective, like you wouldn't see in YA. Normal in a good way. I am so curious to learn more about her past and ability. 
 And I'm digging the romance, the future one, because here there is hardly any. And I don't like this relationship anyway, meaning Adam and Blue. I've heard there is a love triangle, and by now I foresee a lot of drama, but I'm team Gansey from the damn prologue, so I really don't care.  
 Also amazing writing style. It's just so damn good. I've had no problem on the second read. To me it seems flawless. Highly recommend 
 In conclusion go read this book and if you feel like you don't get it in the first 20 pages, just give it more. It really is more than what you expect. Higly higly recommend. And I'm definitely bumping my rating. 
 Onto the next book, I am so damn excited.

 "You can either die tonight or offer your life to Prythian by living in it forever, forsaking the human realm."

 WALK THROUGH FIRE is a great second chance romance by Kristen Ashley. 
 "For three years we lived happily. But we didn't live happily ever after." 
 As young twenty year olds, Millie & Logan, were a happy couple. Their lives ran perpendicular to each other with him being part of an mc and her in college. But that didn't deter them because they were in love and had found their other half. 
 "I've been walking through fire for you for twenty years, Logan." 
 Whoa! WHAT?! Twenty years ago something happened that made Millie walk away. Logan is totally clueless, as are the readers, to what it was that made her fall off of his radar. When Logan and Millie encounter each other 20 years later he's angry that the love of his life up and disappeared on him. At first I wasn't sure I was going to like Logan because he was a grade-A Jerk with a capital j. I know he was hurt by Millie but he treated her so poorly I wasn't sure he was going to be able to redeem himself in my eyes. 
 BTW- I can't tell you what made her run from him because that's a huge part of the story. Just know that the secret isn't drug out for the whole story line. 
 "You hooked your star to an outlaw, baby." 
 When they reconnected they found a lot of had changed between the two of them over the last 20 years. They weren't those two young kids with stars in their eyes, they were older and little more jaded. Now, they're trying to fit their lives together and are running into some challenges along the way. Plus, Logan's outlaw life is skirting around the edges of messing with Millie's quiet life she has built for herself. 
 "Millie, I was given one good thing in my life, the family I was born into. I found one good thing, my Club .... But in all my life, I only earned one good thing. That's you." 
 I really enjoyed this second chance romance. I've been on a KA binge lately listening to her books and I can already tell this will make an awesome audiobook. Walk Through Fire has KA's signature flair that will have fans one-clicking her book.

Oh God, I just sobbed my heart out for a good 5 minutes after finishing this just now. Proper 'can't get my breath back' wracking sobs. I'm completely emotionally spent. So glad I know there's another book because no way could I recover from that book easily! I only wish it wasn't gone 2am so I could start book 2 straight away. 
 Okay, so I've slept now and can give a more coherent review... 
 This book started as a 3* for me. I didn't like that it jumped straight in without introducing the characters first, and I didn't buy the attraction between them at all. It wasn't until around 20% that I got into the book. 
 Then as the complex and screwed up life of Drew started making itself clear I began to like the book more. Fable's blunt but caring personality started to shine through and Drew started to have feelings. I liked the conflict and insecurities of the two of then as they struggled with the blurry lines between fake and real. The crazy awful family life for Drew was an interesting and unusual element of this book so often do we read about women being sexually abused as youngsters, or men having been beaten when younger, so this was unusual and refreshing . I think it was pretty obvious what the secrets were in essence but then I don't think it was supposed to be a surprise so that's fine. I liked the way it was dealt with particularly that the male main character had issues with having sex  
 As the story continued I liked the main characters more and more. I loved how much Fable cared about those she loved, her fierce possessiveness of Drew, her confidence with her body, her insightfulness, and the fact that she wanted more than her lot but wasn't going to feel ashamed of what she was doing for her brother and wasn't going to let anyone make her feel small for it. 
 As for Drew, yeah he was messed up, but the heart underneath his facade was so evident. He didn't lash out at his Dad, he still adored his sister, he sought to hurt no-one and took all the blame, guilt and shame upon his own shoulders. His struggle was heart-breaking. Ok so they were a little cliche, and that was even admitted in the story, but the struggle was so unique and intense it didn't matter one bit. 
 Together Drew and Fable were such a lovely couple, both so thoughtful of the other, so appreciative and respectful of each other. I have never read such tender and emotional love scenes in any book. I was actually welling up in some, really beautiful. 
 But I was still at just 4*'s by this point, having not quite gotten over the slow start for me. The jump to 5 came right at the end because any book that has me literally sobbing has clearly affected me so intensely that it deserves that. Distraught at that beautiful letter doesn't even begin to cover how I felt. I was heartbroken! I am so pleased that book 2 is already out, I don't think I could have rated 5*'s if I had to end like that and then wait for the next book. I'm too impatient so I would have been cross to have been left in such an unresolved state of utter grief  
 So, this was a brilliantly intense and yet tender story that I am desperate to have more of. On to book 2 right away...

In a war-torn world where Fallen have destroyed almost everything, the Great Houses are the source of power in Paris. Phillipe finds himself unwillingly bound to House of Silverspires, with only a strange connection to a young Fallen. But there is something dark and brewing underneath this Great House. 
 I was actually incredibly excited to read this book because I like a lot of the premise elements. Fallen angels, power, strange magic, an apocalyptic world. What's not to like? I immediately thought of Angelfell by Susan Ee (a YA book with a similar premise), but this book is does not feel as YA. I was prepared to give this four stars a quarter into the book, but it just couldn't keep up its momentum. 
 We come into the book at full steam ahead, and I love it. It's a rush of information about this world, what are the Fallen, and Phillipe seems to be an interesting main character. I love his anger and his backstory. It's all fascinating and a world that I could vividly imagine. But then somewhere in the middle, things go wrong. The characters don't change or adapt, the plot is very mild and almost boring, the politicking between the Houses not exactly rapier wit, etc. 
 I had a lot of problems with the characters in the latter half of the book. I liked them all when they were first introduced, but then they all sort of stayed stagnant. Even Isabelle! who supposedly seemed colder and harder than the beginning. But I would only really know that from the author explicitly telling us that, rather than her words and her actions. 
 The mystery was so underwhelming. The who-dun-it was not satisfying at all mostly because  you could not have guessed it on your own since the character was not introduced until the reveal. Ridiculous. That barely counts as a mystery then. . 
 I might have too high expectations for political talk because of Guy Gavriel Kay. But I really do expect rapier wit. Dark and cutting, words with hidden meanings, rudeness hidden under acceptable courtesy, etc. But this book had none of that. All of it was blatant threats, no sign of intrigue. Y'know? Sigh, it's just disappointing. 
 I am also incredibly unhappy with ending for a multitude of reasons. First, I really don't believe that  Isabelle should have died. I'm not saying that as a omg i love this character why'd she have to die!!!, but rather in the sense that it felt forced. It was just a way to force some sort of "tragedy" in the ending. And I didn't even feel that sad, to be honest. Probably because I never really connected with Isabelle. . Second, it was just too rushed. I am impressed that this is a shorter book - since many fantasy novels have now spanned into the 400-500 pages. But the ending was not a climax or an explosion for the reveal, but rather the book just slowly puttering out its last bit of steam. And it was so incomplete. The character storylines didn't feel resolved. I could swear there ought to be another 50 pages or so. I mean, obviously there will be a sequel - but a good book should still have some closure. Gah. It's annoying. 
 So... I focused on mostly the parts I didn't like. But I do swear it is a good read, or at the very least a decent read. The magic is interesting, in which you can ingest parts of Fallen for a magic boost. There is addiction in magic, there are different types of magic, etc. There are still many parts of the world that are yet to be explored, and I would love to find out. I want to see Heaven and the reason why these Fallen choose to fall. I want to see Annam and the Jade Emperor. There is still so much potential in this world. 
 Some other random notes: 
 - I liked that the backdrop was ruined Paris and the main character was of Vietnamese descent. And even better when I found out that the author is French-American of Vietnamese descent. 
 - I liked that there were a few same-sex relationships casually thrown in. There wasn't a big brouhaha about it; they were just laid out normally. 
 - I really hope the sequel will be more about the Annamites. 
 Three stars. I would recommend this book, but not heavily. It's a good book, but nothing that amazing. I will be waiting for the sequel though.

The visuals were nice, the setting for Caraval was interesting and engaging. Caraval is a magical carnival that has the players questioning what is real and what isn't real and has the reader second guessing their own perceptions and what they thought to be true as well. It wasn't by any means an amazing book, I did think it was missing something, maybe a bit more depth to the characters and their relationships, but overall it was a really captivating book. The ending leaves you wanting more but also answers a good number of questions and so it also leaves you satisfied. Some things I wish had been expanded on or explained include: why did Scarlett see colours? Does she have magic? I hope this is explained in the next book. Also why did everyone believe Legend seek revenge on the female line in Scarlett and Donatella's family when it wasn't true? Had he gotten revenge on any other females in the family before? Wouldn't that be a big giveaway that he was not seeking vengeance on the Dragna females?  There was one point that bothered me and that was the whole madonna versus whore analogy going on with the sisters. Also the random Australian/British lingo thrown here and there was a bit off and uncharacteristic for the language of the book. It really stood out. However, if you go into this book looking to be entertained and just sit back and enjoy the ride without questioning it too much, I think you would have a great time.

This is going to be one of those times when I read a book that everyone else seems to love and I just don't get it. Riddled with sadness and ambiguity, I didn't truly enjoy the story at all. The closest I could come to liking this book was appreciating that author Nikki Loftin created something unusual and touching. There's a lot of good stuff here, but it didn't come together in a meaningful way for this reader. The writing was only so-so and the symbolism heavy-handed. Still, here we go: 
 Little John is a boy in a lamentable situation. His little sister recently died in a tragic accident. He's estranged from his best friend because he's too proud to admit that his family is nearing poverty and falling apart. Little John's teachers make him feel stupid, his mother makes him feel invisible, and his father treats him like a hired hand. 
 Enter a mysterious new girl who's taken in as a foster child by the awful Cutlin family in the same small town where Little John lives. She calls herself Gayle, though the Cutlins insist her name is Suzie. She reminds Little John of his sister because she's small and feisty, but her most marked characteristic is her beyond-beautiful singing voice and belief in her own magical abilities. 
 Little John and Gayle become friends. He tries to protect her and at the same time can't resist extorting her for money that his family desperately needs. The villain here is Mr. King, the richest man in town. Known by town folk as "The Emperor," Mr. King is obsessed with recording Gayle's voice to add to his collection. His villainous qualities are ambiguous, though. Gayle fears him and is traumatized by his presence, but why? We don't exactly know. She says he's like a crow. Little John has a built-in reason to loathe King: his father is employed by Mr. King and resents him for being haughty and rich. 
 The plot is driven by something you know is going to happen, even though it seems so unlikely. Gayle makes Little John promise to protect her tree and her nest because she believes her parents will use these as beacons to find her--but it's somehow inevitable that Little John will break his promise. It also seemed inevitable to me that Little John would redeem himself. 
 Just a few other details to mention: 
 1. Little John lives five miles from Mr. King and the Cutlins. In the heat of summer, he runs those five miles (ten round trip) so many times! At first, it's portrayed as a difficult journey for Little John, but then it becomes something he just does without comment. I thought this was convenient for the plot and not very believable. 
 2. It also bothered me that Raelynn's death was set up as a something the family still needed to deal with, but in the end they went around the issue instead of through it. 
 3. I'm not a fan of stories that end with poor people conveniently coming into a lot of money and voila! Everything's better! (Also it would've made more sense for Mr. King to leave all his money to Gayle instead of Little John. It's like Gayle was a just a tool that Little John controlled. I would've liked to understand the relationship between Gayle and Mr. King better. ) 
 4. This story bears only a slight resemblance to Hans Christian Andersen's "The Nightingale". I wouldn't call it a re-telling or say it was based on it. I believe the book jacket says "inspired by" and that's fair. I encourage you to go read "The Nightingale" online. It's short and tells a very different kind of story--one about valuing an imitation above the real deal. Also, in Andersen's story the main relationship is between the nightingale and the Emperor.

I am in love with Simon vs. the Homo Sapiens Agenda. It is an incredibly sweet love story, all the more admirable because it is two boys in love. I remember sending and receiving texts like that with my boyfriend my senior year of high school. I remember that rush of happiness when he texted me first.  Simon was experiencing all of that, which to me is one of the most amazing things about being a teenager. You're learning yourself, your environment, and others; and that can be both horrible and beautiful. Thomas wakes up to find a world where he understands nothing, not even the language. He remembers nothing of his past life, and feels completely lost. He's in some sort of jungle. There are boys around him, boys who have formed something like a community between them. There is a boy named Alby who is sort of the leader of this ragtag band. Then he meets Gally, a boy who seems to really hate Thomas. Thomas can't help but feel like he's been in this world before. 
 He learns that the boys take shelter in a place called the Glade, which is the only place safe from the Grievers, gigantic robotic bugs that kill all in their way. They are safe in the Glade because at night, gigantic walls come out and protect their fort from these bugs. Outside the Glade is the just a gigantic jungle that is referred to as the "Maze" because it changes every day. 
 Thomas is put under the charge of Chuck, a boy who was sent to the Glade only a month before Thomas. They find out that Ben has been stung by one of the Grievers. if you are stung, then you are must have the Serum administered to you or you will die. 
 From this point on, I'm going to give the summary of the entire book. 
  
 Ben gets the serum, but it also has the added side effect of being very painful. 
 Thomas is attempted to have himself incorporated into the life at Glade. However, he wants to be a Runner, one of those people who map the changing Maze outside of the Glade every day. 
 Then a random girl is deposited into the Glade. The boys take this as a bad omen because a) it has always just been boys, b) she was sent a day after Thomas and boys only come once a month. She is in a coma however, and doesn't wake up. 
 Alby, the leader of the Glade goes out with Minho, the Keeper (aka leader) of the Runners to check out something in the Maze. Alby and Minho return but only at sunset and Alby has been stung. Thomas runs out past the gates to save the two and the gates slam shut behind him, leaving Alby, Minho, and Thomas all alone in the Maze at Night. They are attacked by the Grievers, but Thomas and Minho manage to outwit them by tossing the Grievers down the cliff. 
 They survive the night. Thomas is revered as a hero. Gally gets angry and tries to hurt Thomas. He runs off. Thomas is now a Runner, exalted for his actions. Alby goes crazy because another affect of the serum is that you regain part of your memories. Then the girl wakes up and Thomas finds out they can telepathically communicate with each other. Then the sun stops, and food stops coming into the Glade. The walls also stop moving, leaving the boys to be sitting ducks for the Grievers. Gally comes back and says that a boy will die every day until they all die. 
 Thomas and Minho figure out that the only way out of this crazy world is to go through the Grievers' nest hole. Thomas willingly gets stung by a Griever so he can regain his memories. 
 They're actually part of a gigantic government experiment, trying to figure out who were the best of the boys and now the experiment is over and they want to go home. 
 Alby who has regained some memories knows that the real world is worse than the fake world and chooses to sacrifice himself so the boys can escape. The boys escape and they end up in a laboratory. 
 THE END 
  
 Well at least the mystery was somewhat solved. The Maze Runner is a very suspenseful novel, and when you first start out, you feel like you don't know anything. On top of that, everyone refuses to tell Thomas any answers, and there are secrets upon secrets that aren't even really explained by the ending. 
 Gally was a terrible character. Usually, you want villains to have some sympathy, or likeable train. But he's just mean, and hates Thomas for no reason. He also bloody got in the way of everything, only to not actually have a point in the end. Why is he in this story? no one knows. 
 Thomas is a decent character, quick on his feet, creative, has super special bond with most beautiful girl ever aka Teresa, and becomes a Runner in around a week. 
 Plotwise, I had no idea what was going on half the time because the whole point of it was to keep you on your toes. We were just as lost as Thomas was, and you can really feel his frustration because dangnabit, I'm just as freaking frustrated. 
 Also the ending. I'm sorry, but just making Thomas remember everything is a bit of a deus ex machina. Suddenly everything is explained because Mr. Dashner couldn't figure out another way to resolve the story or provide explanations for everything. Even though everyone else who has gotten the serum has shaky memories at best, Thomas can recollect everything about this experiment! Gasf 
 Then why the HELL did Chuck die? there was NO point in that death. Really. 
 Finally, Teresa herself. Why do you have to keep telling us she's the most beautiful girl ever? why don't you just show us how she is beautiful, instead of just cramming that adjective down our throats? I don't see why having pale skin and black hair can make someone beautiful. Also, she lacks a bit of a personality there, pretty much being revived to be another source of "plot". She doesn't even seem to be of any interest to Thomas, just having "WICKED is good" on her arm. whoo for pen tattoos. 
 But despite its faults, The Maze Runner is still a beautiful book. I almost felt like I was in the maze and running for my life as I was being chased by the Grievers. Even if the plot was a bit confusing, I think it still provided a very exciting and enjoyable read, especially as a scific dystopian novel. I only wish the characters were more relateable, or more realistic. There were many times I didn't care if someone died simply because I had no emotional connection to them. 
 Also unresolved endings. I know it's meant to be a sequel. But -sigh- I wish that books would just end in one sitting because it feels like all ya are series nowadays. 
 Great Job Mr. Dashner. Loved how quickly I flipped through the pages. Loved how Minho was Asian. Loved the craziness of a boy community. Three stars!

This book had me on such a ridiculous roller coaster I can't even explain it. At first I hated it and was just going to stop, but then I continued, and things got a little bit interesting, then a bit annoying, then very very hooking, and then I hated it, but then I liked it... and it was like that the entire book. What did I finally think of the book? I liked it. 
 To those who were equally as confused as I was by the synopsis - because really, is cool as it sounded it was still all over the place and not giving you anything - here's a better way of explaining the storyline. Paisley has always had a hate-hate relationship with her older sister Caroline. While Paisley always felt her hatred for her sister was warranted, it still ate at her why her sister hated her back. Which is what drives a very drunk and depressed Paisley to make two announcements at her sister's wedding to try her hand at hurting her sister as much as she'd hurt her. But of the two announcements, only one is true. Now, seven years later, Paisley is back to try and fix past wrongs, but is it time to tell the truth and fix that lie? 
 I don't want to spoil anything else, so no more details on the story although I may share particular spoilers with apt warning below as a I ran about the parts that did bug me. 
 At first I found Paisley to be a new, unique and interesting character, but the more I read on, the more I kept hating her over and over. The best thing about this character in my opinion, is her Spanish Catholic background. I like the diversity, and how the author went into details with her entire family, it was definitely a new aspect I'd never seen before in contemporary stories. But Paisley herself was a complete and total provocative tease. I mean, who else hits on her sister's fiance so bad and tries to do everything in her power to compromise him just because he challenged her and she didn't like it? She's also an alcoholic teen who just got out of rehab for being a drug addict. Basically she's the kind of character that would completely disgust me that I'd just close the book and never read more of it again. Only... that's not all there is to her, and you slowly come to understand the very screwed up way her mind works and why she acts the way she does. Her family is so screwed up in so many ways I can't even begin to explain it. I mean, I think I'd be a wreck too if I lived in that environment. 
 Since the book is from Paisley's point of view, you don't get much into James' mind, which sucks because I think he would have been an equally as complex character with interesting views on things. There are so many parts of the story that are only told from her side and I never got closure on because she either never confessed them to James, or he didn't respond or give ample explanation to what he thought. But both characters were equally as messed up. 
 I'm not really sure if Paisley's roommate Marcia and her friend Tarzan get their own story, but I'd be intrigued if they did, though I'm not sure if I'd be waiting impatiently for it. It's more of a story I'd warily open to see where the author goes with it if she does. 
  
 Now one of the reasons this book seriously bugged me was the whole 'reading each other's eyes' thing. It gave the story a more fantasy vibe which I don't appreciate in a fully contemporary story. As if by looking into someone's eyes Paisley can completely get into their minds and know every good or bad thing they've done. It sounded like a pathetic superpower not a 'gift' or 'skill'. At some point she and James can actually READ each other's minds. Yeah, that part annoyed me to no end. There's seeing someone's expression and knowing them so well you'd understand their every emotion, and then there's just reading their every freaking thought. Yeah, no. I hated it. 
  
 But I highly appreciated how messed up Paisley's character was, she was so broken but in a very realistic way that you just admire her for all she's accomplished in her time away before she comes clean on things. She's turned from a druggie teen with no control over the crap she does or says to a mature adult out to show the world she's a better person. I admired that. The story was very condensed though and so much happened in it, but I think all in all it was a good read.

 Originally rated 4 stars. 
 I was shying away from this book because I'd heard so much hype for it but it didn't really sound like my thing. Finally, I picked it up for a debut novel challenge and I could tell I was going to love this book from literally page 1. 
 The best thing about this book was how easy and quick of a read it is. The author was very concise with telling the story she meant to tell, and there are many illustrations and charts that propel the story along without needing a lot of words. It was so easy to let my brain melt into this and go on auto pilot while reading and sometimes you just need that kind of book. I absolutely devoured it! 
 Everything about this book that would have annoyed me in other stories (coughINSTALOVEcough) was SO believable here. If you were in Maddy's shoes and had lived your entire life with no friends and never going outside, of course the first person your age that you meet would stir new emotions very quickly. On Olly's side, if you were new in town, had a horrible family life, and met a mysterious girl who never came outside, of course you'd be curious about her. It was such uncharted territory for both of them and newness= thrilling. Would they be together in 50 years? Who knows, but I completely bought that this teenage relationship would progress in this way, in these circumstances. 
 I know that people are split on the ending and I can see both sides. If you love contemporary romances, you will probably enjoy this one. But if you are really wanting a hard hitting book about a main character with a debilitating illness... this won't touch on that in the way you want. 
 The problematic elements are hard to talk about because the book sets them up to be spoilers... 
  I wish her mother's illness had been named. I'm pretty sure she had Munchausen Syndrome by Proxy, not just "she's too overprotective." Naming it would spread awareness and be informative. I've talked to friends who read this book and weren't familiar with MSbP. This was such a missed opportunity to bring attention to this disorder and child abuse. (Granted, I'm only assuming that the mother did indeed have MSbP here, I'm not sure what the author's full intentions were, but it's so similar that I wish it had at least been brought up.) 
 As far as being a plot twist, many real children in this type of situation also do not know. They depend on their parent and take their word for it that they are sick. The fact that her mom's illness was revealed to us along with Maddy felt very realistic of this situation. So, I can't say it's a mistreatment of child abuse or MSbP (it IS a mistreatment of Maddie's supposed disability though), it just makes it hard to discuss. People wanting the disability rep the book promises won't get what they expected, while people who need to see themselves in a story about a victim of child abuse won't know it's in the book. It's just not going to get into the hands of the people who really need it, and will get into the hands of people who will be hurt by it.  
 Overall, I really enjoyed the story and especially the storytelling format. Despite the problems mentioned above, it was one of my more enjoyable reads of this year. I would highly recommend it to anyone that loves contemporary romance, is looking for a quick read, or is looking for a book that features a POC main character.

She was leaving a happy teenage life until one day, she woke up in a hospital to discover that her world had been shattered. Literally. She's diagnosed with PTSD -- Posttraumatic stress disorder. It is a severe anxiety disorder that can develop after exposure to any event that results in psychological trauma. This event may involve the threat of death to oneself or to someone else, or to one's own or someone else's physical, sexual, or psychological integrity, overwhelming the individual's ability to cope. As an effect of psychological trauma, PTSD is less frequent and more enduring than the more commonly seen acute stress response. 
 Diagnostic symptoms for PTSD include re-experiencing the original trauma(s) through flashbacks or nightmares, avoidance of stimuli associated with the trauma, and increased arousal - such as difficulty falling or staying asleep, anger, and hypervigilance. Formal diagnostic criteria (both DSM-IV-TR and ICD-10) require that the symptoms last more than one month and cause significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. [PTSD's Wikipedia page] 
 What the doctors thought they conclude was that, she's been traumatized by the death of her best friend, boyfriend, and boyfriend's sister and the sudden guilt she has for being the only survivor, with barely a scratch on her--and she has no memory of that night. I thought this book was just going to be about a poor teen in an impoverished country who figured out how to build a windmill. Turns out it was that in the last half of the book and so much more than expected in the first half. It was a heartbreaking story of farming, famine and disease in Malawi and how this child, his family and friends got through those years. It is also an inspiring story about building something from nothing in order to ensure that his family will never have their lives threatened by drought again. The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind will inspire anyone who doubts the power of one individual's ability to change his community and better the lives of those on an entire continent. 
 William Kamkwamba was born in Malawi, a land withered by drought and hunger, a place where hope and opportunity were hard to find. His family struggled on their farm to make enough to support the family before the drought and famine so they had an even more difficult time when it ravaged their country through the seasons. William was forced to leave school because his family could not afford the tuition. His family had to choose food over his education so he went to the library (which contained only four shelves of books) and read the books which would further his knowledge as well as try to self-study to keep up with his peers. In one of the few library books available to him, William had read about windmills and dreamed of building one that would bring his family electricity and running water, luxuries that only two percent of Malawians could afford. He was dubbed the crazy villager who spent his days digging through junk yards to find the nuts, bolts, lightbulbs and other items needed to build a windmill to generate electricity and later water. He used scrap metal, tractor parts, and bicycle halves to forge a crude machine that eventually powered four vehicle bulbs, complete with homemade switches and a circuit breaker made from nails and wire. Due to the frequent power outages that plagued the country, people began to pay to have their cell phones charged at the windmill. A second windmill turned a water pump that could battle the drought and famine looming with every season. 
 The windmill was spotted by someone who decided to ensure that the boy's story got out. This led to news stories, a trip to America, sponsors who ensured his education was furthered and success. 
 This book was in the alternate book club kits, what the library dubs book-talk-kitkeeper-2-titles and sends out to other library systems but does not loan to our branches. I added all of those kits to my to read list because they had previously been read by my book clubs prior to my joining them.

Abandon all hope ye who enter here. This is a labyrinth in which you will get lost, and the temptation to immerse yourself in the minutiae and symbolism is stronger than a row of slot machines in Vegas. Point in case: there is an entire website (www.houseofleaves.com) dedicated solely to the discussion of this book. 
 The genius of the author is undeniable, and I never ceased to be impressed with the various approaches to the narrative. This is a story told in three layers. First is a pseudo-scholarly attempt by a blind man to relate the story of a...well, let's call it a haunted house for lack of a better description, with footnotes and academic trappings aplenty. The second layer is a young man named Johnny Truant, who gets his hands on the manuscript after the original author's death and marks it up with copious footnotes that tell a story about his own life and the onset of some sort of delusional mania. Then add the third layer of the publishing editors with their own notes and interjections on the annotated manuscript given to them by Johnny Truant. Layers upon layers upon layers... 
 The narrative structure is also toyed with, and all manner of subversive elements are introduced. One chapter is a labyrinth in and of itself, with text running up, down, sideways and backwards, and if properly followed the footnotes run endlessly like a Mobius strip. Sometimes the pages are packed so densely with words that it takes an eternity to read a page; at other times there may be one word per page. One page is written in braille, another in sheet music. Footnotes occasionally change from an ordered set of numbers to symbols which may or may not have meaning. 
 My only problem with overly clever books like this is that there really is no definitive answer. All interpretations are subjective and equally valid, which leads to the temptation of reading far too much into the book. The text refers to labyrinths and stairways and nautilus spirals--all of which are apt metaphors in more than one way, since trying to prise meaning from this tome is an endless and circular task. And there is so much material to work from that one could probably spend half a lifetime sifting through the intended and unintended clues that litter this tome. 
 This is a book which should only be attempted by the heartiest of readers. 700 pages of what could be described as avant-garde horror is not exactly a great option for the casual reader. But if you feel in the mood for a reading challenge that is out of the ordinary, this is a book you should strongly consider.

I have very recently written a post where I stated I was breaking up with the New Adult genre. And then I saw Definitely, Maybe in Love which is a re-telling of Pride and Prejudice! Obviously I couldn't pass that up. I told myself that I'd start it and if it started going down the semi-erotica trail that most New Adult does, and make Jane Austen roll in her grave, I would DNF it. I'm happy to report that this is a New Adult book that I can support! 
 This book was very cute. It had a few eye-rolling moments, but overall, just cute. As I said, this a re-telling of Pride and Prejudice and for the most part I think it was really well done. College junior, Spring, is our Elizabeth Bennett. She's very into the environment and is a little on the hippie/feminist side (I was totally picturing Cosima from Orphan Black). 
 When her thesis advisor tells her she needs more research from an opposing viewpoint, her new neighbor Henry Knightly (our Mr. Darcy), who is the son of a wealthy land developer, volunteers to help, despite their disastrous first impressions. I was a little afraid the book was going to veer into really political topics, but this aspect of the story was pretty downplayed, thankfully, other than helping provide a cause of conflict between Spring and Henry. 
 In addition to our Elizabeth and Darcy inspired characters, there's Henry's best friend and roommate Dart (Mr. Bingley), who has an awful sister (Caroline Bingley), Spring's roommate, Julia, who falls for Dart and then gets herself into some trouble (a combination of both Jane and Lydia Bennett), and Alex, Henry's old high school rival who tells some suspicious stories of the past (Wickham). 
 There were also some twists on some of the iconic Pride & Prejudice scenes. There's a party where Spring overhears Henry say unflattering things about her and Julia and Dart instantly hit it off. There's the letter Henry writes to explain to Spring the real story between him and Alex. There's Spring showing up at Henry's childhood home, unaware that he was there. And there was Henry rushing to Julia's rescue when she's in a compromising situation with Alex. I loved all of these, but it also made things pretty predictable. There were some parts that I think would have been predictable even if I wasn't familiar with the original source material. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed Definitely, Maybe in Love. It was very cute and was a well done re-telling of one of my favorite books. I also very much appreciated that it's an NA book that isn't borderline erotica. It still dealt with growing up, future careers, first loves (and all that goes with it), but without going into the crude or graphic. Some NA fans might think it reads more YA than NA, but I'm ok with that. I would definitely recommend it to fans of re-tellings, Jane Austen, and non-graphic NA. The next book in the series, 
 Someday Maybe 
 , is a take on Persuasion, and I'm really looking forward to it.

This book. It broke my heart so many times, yet still managed to leave me smiling (through the tears, but hey). 
 Morning Star does not have the frenetic pace that Golden Son had before it. Though there are plenty of battle scenes and action, this book is focused so much more on character development. While it didn't have quite as many shocks and surprises as the first two books, I can't be too upset about that because the character growth was just phenomenal (and let's be real, good character development is what I crave from all my books). 
 One of the things I have come to appreciate most from Brown's writing is his ability to surprise me over and over again. As I said above, this book doesn't have quite as many surprises for me, but it still had a few (or maybe I'm just getting better at guessing them earlier?). There was one big event that shocked me and then made me immediately think (hope), "Oh, that's a misdirect." But then the chapters went on...and let's just say the writing will always keep you on your toes. 
 Sevro, my little Goblin, has always been one of my favorite characters and in this book he's given much more page time. He's definitely been feeling the pressure of keeping things going after the heartbreaking events of Darrow's Triumph and let's just say he hasn't exactly handled it very well. I went from loving him, to being really annoyed with him, to wanting to just hug him, to loving him again. He remains the comic relief when things get heavy, but he also confronts his emotions in a way we haven't really seen from him before. My Howler heart will always be his. 
 In any book with war there are many deaths and Brown has never pulled any punches when it comes to killing off some of my favorite characters. Morning Star is no exception. I may have shed a few tears and yelled, "Screw you, Pierce Brown!" on more than one occasion. 
 It's been a long time since a series has had such an emotional impact on me. I don't even know why. It has beautiful writing, despite the blood and the death and the horror. It's just beautiful. And it's clever. And the characters! They were flawed and empathetic and I just loved so many of them. Darrow was an amazing protagonist that made me laugh, broke my heart, made me cheer, and made me hope. The deaths of some of his friends and allies (and even some enemies) made me tear up (and occasionally shed a few) and when I wasn't reading about these characters, I was thinking of them. And I think that's really the mark of a great book. When the characters and the stories live with you, outside of the pages. 
 Overall, Morning Star was a bloodydamn great ending to the series. While it didn't have quite the same "fun factor" as the first two books did for me, it made up for it in the characters, the emotion, and satisfying conclusion. This series will go down as one of my favorites of all time and will be one I read again and again. If you haven't read it yet, you really need to.

Reading a Murakami novel is a tricky preposition: yes, he is somewhat of a one trick pony, yes, he can be sexist (his female characters are either insane, sex objects, two dimensional, or a combination of all three), and yes, he can be annoyingly obfuscating. 
 So, why have I read half a dozen of his novels and keep coming back for more? I'm not really sure. He's obviously a talented writer, so maybe I'll just leave it at that. Colorless Tsukuru is possibly his most human, most empathetic novel that I've read. The plot is a more grounded one this time and contains very little of the supernatural. This one is more about human relationships and the turns that our lives take. 
 His moral seems to be that no matter how much we think we know about people and how much we're hurt by their actions, there's still more to situations than meets the eye, no matter how much we think it's just about us. I was intrigued by this novel. A family of female morticians? Um, awesome. A murder Lily is a suspect in? Oh my god yes. The cliche romance? Eh, not so much, but finding YA without romance is like finding authentic Chanel on ebay: frustrating. 
 The Secrets of Lily Graves has a great set up but the limpest plot - I was intensely reminded of the Dinner Theatre episode of Bob's Burger's where Linda plots that terrible play and at the end, says 'the murderer was me!' with literally no clues or evidence. And that's a really sad thing to say about a murder mystery. And holy info-dump, Batman. This book is suffering from a fatal case of telling, not showing. 
  - Matt bored me. He was bland and uninteresting, but still manager to come across as a bit of a creeper. If I have to look up the name of the love interest to write the review, that's a bad sign. I didn't find their friendship or romance interesting at all. 
 - Lily was intriguing. Her obsession with death! Her complete contentment to stay at home and follow in her family's footsteps! Oh man, I loved Lily, she was so original. Five seasons and a movie, seriously. And her family? Awesome. 
 - Erin. Erin and Erin's death was so cliche. How about the murder of a teenage girl that doesn't involve a secret, sordid life that involves drugs, rebellion and a SHOCKING pregnancy? Because none of those things are even vaguely shocking at this point. They are done. They are over done. They are charcoal and ash they have been over used so much. Nothing about Erin stood out or shocked me. 
 - Erin's friends were generic, boring and completely transparent as a way to trick us from the 'real' murdered. Ditto that Stone guy. Seriously, if I can mentally replace your characters with a brick and make no genuine change to the plot, then they aren't good characters. 
 - Sara. Oh man, Sara. I do not understand why Sara, Sara's arm and Sara's Russian adoption was at all relevant to the plot. Was it meant to reinforce how much she 'owed' her parents? How much she loved them? Ditto with all the college stuff. It was just an info dump. 
 - Okay, so the murderer is Dr Ken. And basically, other than the info dumps about Sara, her life, Erin, her life etc, there seems to be no actual clues that Dr Ken is the murderer. Zero. It just sort of happens for no reason. I think the singular clue was the cop's line about Matt and Lily being in the graveyard and 'no friend of yours'. That's the only clue that Sara's family is responsible for the crime. Plus, how deep was Sara involved - did she help her father hold Erin down? Drain the blood? AND WHERE WAS ALL THE BLOOD? And the random missionary trip? The drunken mother? Her silent brother? Blargh.  
 Ultimately, this book is kind of a mess. Just a way to end the story. It's a genuine shame, because I kind of liked Lily. She was a different kind of protagonist. 
 TLDR a singular intriguing character, but ultimately a nonsensical murder mystery that uses every trope and a parade of forgettable characters to stumble to the end.

Back in the fifth grade, at the humble age of ten, I discovered that apparently clothes were important, like life or death important. And so began my strange journey into the world of baby tees, hush puppies and glittery pants (Do you remember glittery pants? You would wash them once and they would just be pants again. This was such a waste of glitter really.) I would buy any fashion magazine I could find, just so I could be the first to wear a new 'fad' to school. My friends would always comment, "I love your sparkly bell bottom jeans with the glittery pink flowers on them. Where in the world did you get that?" I was a fashion maven. I reveled in knowing everything there is to know about clothes. 
 In the Tipping Point, Malcolm Gladwell writes about epidemics and the 'tipping point,' when a fad, disease, or trend, saturates the market and becomes mainstream. Basically this means that someone, somewhere down the line accidently spilled glitter all over their pants and just went with it. Gladwell talks about several ways that this can happen and refers to three different types of people, who are able to sell an idea and create a full blown epidemic. There are connectors, people who have several acquaintances, mavens, people who invest a lot of time into a certain idea and product so that they become an expert, and salespeople, who are able to sell a product to a mainstream audience. Little did I know that I was a maven and was selling pants for someone else just by being invested in their glittery product. 
 This book is an excellent read, and Malcolm Gladwell writes in a straight forward and clear manner. I recommend this book to anyone who is interested in the social sciences. I found that I wondered where I fit on the social spectrum when it comes to epidemics, especially when it came to my pre-adolescent choices in clothing. The only downside to the book is that is it dated (pre 9/11 so there is less cynicism and a more hopeful feel.) But if you can look past the fact that he talks a lot about outdated shoes and ad campaigns, you will get some insight on how you just happen to be wearing those ballet flats.

 I knew what I was signing up for when I read the book's synopsis. By that I mean: loads of sexual references, dark themes (i.e. rape, harassment, suicide), mature situations and other adult content. And I was right. The book did deal with them. However, I was hoping to see actual substance - which was located at no point within the story. 
 Honestly, I didn't have a problem with reading about those topics. There is nothing wrong with expressing one's sexuality, regardless of gender. I genuinely admire women who are brave enough to handle their sexuality in stride. My problem was with how the book dealt with sexuality, rape, violence and all these other sensitive topics. I am all about burning the misogyny to the ground. However, nothing of the sort happened. I wasn't expecting another Katniss Everdeen or June Iparis or any drastic, violent rebellion against the political leaders; but it would have been nice if Lila, the story's heroine, thought of things other than losing her virginity and indulging her voyeurism and other sexual fantasies. 
 I thought her desire to not get raped by the military personnel would catapult her into fighting for the humanity and equality her community was bereft of. That wasn't the case at all! Lila thought of no one other than herself. While she did earn a few sympathy points for being devoted to her family, it wasn't enough. The little vigilante group she's a member of was nothing but a half-assed detail thrown in the story to deceive readers into thinking that she actually served a purpose. Seriously, all she cared about was getting deflowered. At many points in the book, it didn't really matter to her whom she fucked first as long as it wasn't a soldier and as long as she consented. Rather than developing into a strong, independent woman, she instead falls putty into the muscled arms of the General. 
 Speaking of, General Faust was a sort of decent love interest, but I hated how overly dependent Lila was on him. It sickened me how often he had to intervene just to save Lila's idiotic self. Also, I didn't like the fact that he was genetically engineered to become impossibly strong and insanely gorgeous. So, like, what--Lila isn't okay with having sex with a soldier but it's okay for her to lust after the general because he's inconceivably hot? 
 The copy I received had errors and grammatical mistakes too numerous to ignore. Sometimes the passages were repeated twice. Also, the lack of character development and the senseless plot annoyed me. The book had a few moments to redeem itself, but mainly, reading this novel was torture. The only thing that made this book slightly bearable to read was Lila's sister, Azalea. 
 Azalea looks a lot like me and as her green eyes scan my face, I squirm. My sister has developed acute observation skills. She knows all about my plans, and blocks me as I approach our shared room, brandishing a carrot. "Why don't you put this inside you and get it over with?" 
 To put it crudely, what could have been an opportunity to incite women empowerment was instead an excuse to write crappy erotica between a sexually enthusiastic voyeur and a genetically engineered hulk of a man.

I Hunt Killers has been on my radar for a while now, but it's not an e-book at my library and I'm super stingy about buying books from authors I'm unfamiliar with so it's just been sitting there patiently on my TBR shelf. I recently won a giveaway for a Nook Book of my choice and it seemed like the perfect opportunity to finally check this out. 
 I'm a fan of serial killer plotlines. The psychological impact on the characters always makes for some compelling characters, which I love. I Hunt Killers is a new twist on the genre that I haven't read before. The main character is not the cop/law enforcement officer chasing him down or the serial killer, but his son. Billy Dent is the world's most notorious serial killer and has over 120 kills to his name. He's used several different personas, "The Artist", "Green Jack", "Hand-in-Glove", and has taught his son, Jasper ("Jazz") everything he knows in hope that he will carry on "the family business." Jasper has no intention of following in his father's footsteps, but the brainwashing he received from Billy all those years has seriously messed with his head and he is constantly on alert for the stray thoughts or incident that could easily push him over the edge to becoming his father. 
 The character development in this book was phenomenal. I really felt like I got into Jasper's head throughout the story and it was not always a pleasant place to be. I'm a fan of the tv show Dexter and this book has a bit of a Dexter vibe at times. Dexter's struggle with his "dark passenger" is similar to how Jasper struggles with Billy's voice constantly in his head - telling him how to kill and that he should. Jasper tries to combat the increasingly alluring inner voice by repeating a mantra of, "People matter" to remind him that they aren't the insignificant and disposable things to be used for his own purposes, as Billy taught him. He keeps pictures of all of Billy's victims on his bedroom wall to be reminded of what he doesn't want to be. When a new serial killer shows up in town he's desperate to help - not just to prove to the town that it isn't him, but to prove to himself that he's on the right side. 
 While he tries to ignore the most gruesome of Billy's teachings, he has become a master manipulator and often utilizes those skills to get him what he wants. He usually knows that it's wrong, but he also justifies it to himself and this peek into the possible sociopathic mindset is part of what makes his character so interesting. 
 I really enjoyed Jazz's best friend, Howie, as well. He was a great side-kick, comic relief, but also got in on some of the action. His hemophilia is also an interesting addition to his character. He's physically extremely vulnerable and thus an easy target, which makes for a surprising choice of BFF for a could-be serial killer. I also liked the sheriff, G. William, and Jazz's girlfriend, Connie. 
 Overall, I enjoyed I Hunt Killers and am glad I finally got to read it. I haven't encountered many YA books that pull off suspense and creepiness the way that this one does. It's dark and slightly gruesome, but it's balanced out with a bit of humor. While there were a few predictable moments, I was often in suspense. I loved the characterization of Jasper. I'm looking forward to see what happens in the rest of the series. 
 I struggled a bit with what to rate this, but I think because of the unique plot idea and the great characterization, I'm going to bump up my original 3.5 to 4. 
 Overall Rating (out of 5): 4 Stars

I've been sitting on this for a while, which is weird really given that I'd been so excited that I'd preordered it. I think what had me hesitating was that I couldn't see where the story could go that I would be happy with. I was sure that the story would be dragged out needlessly, or else something painful to read would have to happen to bring the tension that could then be sated with a HEA. I was right in a way. One book was really enough for me (for Ella and Micha in any case, I still want to read about Lila and Ethan!) 
 So, you may wonder why on earth I have rated this book 4 stars when I was so obviously disappointed? Well, it would be really difficult not to. Ella and Micha are such unique and beautiful characters with a connection and mutual devotion to be envied by all. Jessica Sorensen writes in a way that makes every detail seem important. She builds atmosphere between the characters, it is raw and passionate and tender and beautiful, but also kind of ugly. 
 What this book did for me was remind me of how much I loved the first book. It was like reminiscing about old friends, reliving their pain and their joy. (4.5 stars) So... oh. 
 Kinda, like, fuck this book? Because it's so depressing yet so uplifting? Hmm... Let's get out of the emotional range and go for the rational review: 
 Samantha McCoy, valedictorian of her senior class and debate champion, finds out that she is going to lose her memory. She's been diagnosed with Niemann-Pick Type C, a genetic disease. Her memory book, a Word doc on her mini laptop, chronicles her life between diagnosis and whatever comes next. As someone whose brain is her #1 most important feature (she doesn't care for her body, has awkward social skills, never had a boyfriend) she is terrified that her diagnosis will mean that she won't get to graduate from her small Vermont high school and move to New York to attend NYU. 
 I loved the language in the novel; Sammie's mental acuity ebbs and flows when she is having an episode or when she's feeling strong. It read a little bit like Flowers for Algernon. Sammie isn't the only one writing in the doc; her family and friends sometimes add a bit to it. 
 There are a lot of stories happening within the story: Sammie's family and how they are coping; her crush-turned-love-interest Stuart and the evolution of their relationship; her neighbor-turned-friend Cooper and the evolution of that relationship; her debate partner Maddie and her reaction to the news... 
 I liked that Sammie acted like a real teenager who couldn't get a lot of stuff right, even though she was trying her best. She was a brain but bad with social cues, so she ended up doing odd things like blurting out her feelings to her crush, asking blunt questions about the nature of their relationship, making decisions on whether or not to tell people she's close to about her diagnosis, and so on. She felt like a real person. 
 And even though the disease is terrible and steals Sammie's mind in pieces, this book didn't feel like an "issues" book. It was just Sammie's story. 
 My biggest nitpick about the book is that it's pretty abrupt. I understand that maybe Sammie had a sudden decline or that she was doing so poorly that she didn't write in the book near her end, but because the rest of the story is so rich, it felt too sudden.

This book was, too put it simply, amazing. I absolutely loved it. I think I like it too much to write an actual review, so I'm just going to write down some bullet points on what I loved. 
 - Hatta is one of my new favorite characters ever!!! I loved him to bits. The ending killed me. When he went crazy and admitted he was in love with Jest I just... 
  
 - The world building in Heartless was phenomenal. I read Alice in Wonderland in preparation of this, and I think that Marissa Meyer did a great job in portraying Wonderland in the same way that Lewis Carroll did. Everything was so weird and illogical, and yet it seemed so normal. There are talking animals and food that can make you shrink, but it seems commonplace and completely normal.

 Basically, I loved this book and thought it was near-perfect. I definitely recommend it!

First impressions: I was really happy to get back into the lives of Emma and Brendan and Angelique. Starting this book felt like slipping under a favorite blanket - warm and comforting. I appreciated the quick recap that Shultz was able to work in so I remembered where everything left off last time, and it didn't feel out of place or like an interruption of the narrative. 
 Lasting impressions: With a lightning-quick pace and lots of action, I tore through this one. I couldn't wait to find out what would happen next. A pure joy to read. 
 Conflicting impressions: There were two big things that kept me from loving this one as much as last year's 
 Spellbound 
 . The first was the too-obvious villain, and the second was the narrative jump at the climax. 
 Overall impressions: Cara Lynn Shultz has a definite knack for engaging the reader. She doesn't just make you want to read the book. She makes you want to devour it. The last few months have not been good reading months for me, and very few books made me excited to pick them up again - until this one. As soon as I started it, I settled easily into the story and the pages flew by. 
 Emma and Brendan are such a likable pair, it's hard to not enjoy reading about their lives. Private school wealth with down-to-earth personalities, these two are further kept in check by Angelique's snarky barbs and the good humor of bright and bubbly side characters. Everyone in this series feels like a real person, and someone I would want to spend time with. 
 The witchcraft gets an expanded role in this book, with Emma starting to explore her own powers with help from Angelique. She's under attack again, and the suspense of this plot keeps things chugging along. Lots of obstacles and fights, as well as the usual teen angst about relationships and intimacy. It reminded me a bit of one of my favorite guilty pleasure movies - The Craft. 
 Perhaps because of this familiarity with that movie's plot of witch-gets-power-and-turns-evil, I found the antagonist in this book very easy to spot. Since it takes Emma and crew a while to wise up to this, I got a bit impatient in the middle sections of the book. When it started to snowball toward the ultimate showdown at the climax, I was excited to see it all play out nevertheless. 
 But. 
 In a frustrating move, Shultz interrupts a pivotal decision-making moment for Emma during this climactic battle to transfer the narrative reins to Angelique. We wind up backtracking and following Angelique's experience of the events, leading up to her reuniting with Emma after the battle.  Only then do we find out what happened and what Emma decided - we get it told to us instead of experiencing it. 
 The narrative switch happens one other time at an earlier point in the novel, so it wasn't completely out of left field, but the placement of this one really bothered me. If the story needed the benefit of multiple viewpoints, perhaps a move to a close 3rd person narrative would have been better. I felt like the voices between Emma and Angelique weren't distinct enough, and would have enjoyed the story just as much if we'd been freed from Emma's limited perspective. Since Shultz chose to stick with 1st person, however, I really wanted to see the ending play out in full. I felt cheated by the decision to take us out of Emma's head at such a crucial point in her story. 
 If you liked Spellbound, this is a great follow-up story. I thoroughly enjoyed myself and hope this isn't the last I see of Emma and Brendan.

What I love about Alice Clayton books: 
 1. The main characters are grounded, independent and smart. Yes, they swoon, but don't lose who they are. They get into stupid, embarrassing, funny as hell situations. And they're real. 
 2. THERE IS NO CONFLICT OR DRAMA JUST FOR DRAMAS SAKE. I cannot emphasize this enough. It's refreshing to read about two people falling in love - genuine love, not I-love-you-I-hate-you-I'm-leaving-you-I-can't-be-away-from-you shit. Not instalove, crazy-sexual-attraction-I-must-fight love, or you're-making-me-miserable-therefore-you-must-be-my-soulmate love. In other words, a healthy and normal relationship where two people make each other happy - the kind of love we should all be so lucky to find. 
 3. They are funny as hell. Like crying from laughing funny. 
 4. The guy's not an asshole, a bad boy, or someone who's got tons of baggage. you can actually see why some girl would fall for them in real life. 
 I know that books need drama to be interesting, but it's so refreshing to read romance novels where romance equals two people getting to know each other, rather than be in perpetual love-hate.

Alina and Mal's lovestory felt kind of rushed, because it's a trilogy I didn't expect them to confess their love/get together until the last book, so I assume and hope that something happens in the 2nd and 3rd book to throw a spanner in the works there. Furthermore the chapters where they're walking and trying to escape The Darkling just seemed very coordinated...like they just confessed a lot to each other is such a short amount of time, it just felt very unreal and just like the writer wanted them to say that stuff but didn't know how else to do it. On the other hand I really liked Genya and David's romance, though it hasn't even really started.  
 I did predict most of the big plot twists and points in this book very early on. It can be really hard to delve away from YA Fantasy and to mark your mark as totally original, and I don't think Bardugo 100% did that, though the book was very good. It did remind me a bit of Deathless with the Russian influences. I'm excited to read the 2nd and 3rd book soon!

 My one complaint about the book is that there are so many characters - I count 19 and that's not including minor side characters of the "guy who found the body" sort - it can be very difficult to keep them all straight. That said, I stepped into the middle of a series with this book, so it's likely they would all have established space if I had read from the beginning. 
 One of the highlights for me is that this book treats mental illness, eating disorders and severe obesity with kindness and legitimate insight. That's incredibly rare and it makes me love this author. 
 This book reads just fine as a standalone even though it is #6 in a series. The very end scenes leave some of the main characters in doubt, but it works well as a teaser for following books without affecting the resolution of this one. Well crafted.

Here With Me could be the love child of the movie Castaway and the TV show The Client List. Even though those two shows don't have anything to do with the military they have elements that are in this book. The premises are similar but the settings are different. 
 "Time doesn't heal anything. It just prolongs the hurt and pain." 
 The plot line is one of intrigue and heartbreak. Evan was deployed on a secret mission for 6 years. SIX YEARS! He left behind a pregnant fiancee along with a twin brother, and his parents. When he returns his fiancee, Riley had moved on because she was informed by the military he was dead. SIX YEARS! I know, I already pointed out how long he was gone for but I want to emphasize that is a long time to think someone is dead. A lot of pain and confusion ensues when your dead lover shows up after six years. 
 "It's messy. Our family life is complicated. ... This family needs help!!!!" 
 Poor, Riley! Gah, I wouldn't want to be in her shoes. In that six years since she's buried Evan her life has moved on. Which is a normal part of life ... it's the fact it's with his twin brother, Nate, that makes me cringe. WHAT NOW?! Nate's deployed on a mission when Evan shows up thinking he's coming home to his waiting fiancee and son. He had no idea his family thought he was dead. Something was botched with Evan's secret military mission! Is the military covering up their mistake? Did Nate know Evan was alive all these year? I need answers!!! 
 "It would be so easy to fall back into a routine with Evan, and I wish that I could without consequences." 
 From their meet cute when they were teenagers until now Riley has always loved Evan. But now she's promised herself to his brother! How can this end good? Whose heart is going to be broken? Whose ring will she wear? 
 Eenie meenie miney mo! 
 I choose no one . . . actually I'm totally rooting for Evan BUT I haven't heard Nate's side of the story. I'm sure after I read the next book with Nate's pov I will be totally confused on who should get the girl.

Do you know the most satisfying thing about Want? 
 That the MC didn't end up with the brooding, abusive asshole. She ended up with the guy that genuinely loved her, was there for her and only wanted the best for her. 
 This book was unique in so many ways. Parental mental illness does appear in a lot of YA, but rarely manifests itself as a physically and mentally abusive mother. Julianne is a character that desperately needs someone to speak up and say that it is not okay. 
 Isaac was totally and utterly unlikable as a character, but I honestly didn't believe he was a predator until he took off at the ball. I figured, teens aged 15 and 17 are stupid, and playing with fire if one is still under the legal age of consent, but not sinister. But by the end of the book, I am convinced Isaac has some serious issues about his past, and he is a danger to teenage girls and himself. 
 Dave was a great character - one that burst off the page as someone real; flawed but genuinely kind and good. 
 Julianne was flawed. She was screwed up and irrational and mentally ill and she was a wonderfully complex character, this desperate girl was on a crash course of disaster. Everything That Can Go Wrong, Will Go Wrong, so I was utterly thrilled when she made it into NEC to be mentored by her idol. That Dave cared enough about her to stick around, even when she rejected him. I honestly believe that it was Juli's damage and her mother's influence, her father's distance and her brother's absence that caused her to seek out Isaac. 
 I felt that the build up between Juli and Isaac was paced appropriately, but I think the fall-out needed to be dealt with more - an epilogue of Juli arriving in Boston to meet Dave; Juli's mother arriving home permanently; years in the future, married Juli and Dave running into Isaac; Juli at her psychiatrists... the possibilities are endless; I really thing that would have been a more satisfying ending. 
 The book mentions the fallout at the ball from the discovery of Juli and Isaac, but that's really so close to the end that it feels like it takes too long to get to some so feted. This book is really about Juli's destruction and rebirth at the hands of Isaac, Dave and her mother.  
 It's a great, unique read and I'd absolutely recommend it.

1.5 stars. I started reading this book months ago, and I just today finished it. It was just so dull to me. At this point, I don't really care about the characters, and I was only reading it because I read the first two and wanted to finish the series. I guess I'm a glutton for punishment.

March has been a pretty slow reading month for me so far and My Soul to Take is the first book that's inspired me to write a review. The Soul Screamers series is one that's never been on my radar, but was part of the haul I won in a giveaway recently and I'm glad I gave it a go. 
 Kaylee is a banshee. A different term is used in the book, but it's two words and pronounced the same, so I'm going with "banshee". I haven't encountered books about banshees before, so it was an interesting new twist for YA paranormal for me. For those unfamiliar, banshees are not-quite-humans who scream (or "sing") for a soul that is about to be taken. Kaylee sees shadows and feels crushing grief whenever someone around her is about to die. While banshee myth is traditionally women, there are also male banshees and they can't tell when a person is about to die, but once it's happened, they can see the soul and can sometimes "redirect" it back into the body. However, doing so means someone else will have to die in the person's place. 
 Kaylee has had a few episodes when the need of uncontrollable screaming takes over and her aunt and uncle, who she lives with, explain it away as panic attacks, but Kaylee has always known it's a little more than that. When she has an "attack" at a club she's calmed down by hottie-hot-hot Nash. Cue Typical YA Trope where the "Special Girl" who is more beautiful than she realizes falls head-over-heels into insta-love with the Hottest Guy Ever Who Has Never Noticed Her Before. Despite the cliche, I was ok with Kaylee and Nash's relationship. While Nash has to explain a lot to her, they felt like pretty equal characters, needing to work together to save anyone. I'm still trying to decide if he's mysterious or shady. There's a lot that he holds back and by the end of the book I still feel like there's a lot more about him that we don't know.

 Model Spy just fell flat for me on so many levels. I did not enjoy reading it, and found the story quite cheesy and unbelievable. 
 Model Spy is about a teen genius (yeah, right) who hacks into a government database. The government finds out, and she gets recruited by an angency called the specialists. She soon has to go undercover in Ushbania as a model to try and locate her friend's father. 
 Bleh. 
 So, Kelly hacked through 9 out of the 18 levels in the government database, which is as far as anyone's ever gotten. She mentions that the passwords were very cleverly coded in the numbers of Pascal's triangle. 
 Firstly, the pattern of Pascal's triangle is incredibly simple. I could recite all the lines to you right now, even though I suck at maths and only passed my exam by 4 marks. I seriously doubt that the GOVERNMENT would encode their passwords with such simple pattern, and that she was the first one to figure it out. I bet heaps of people try to hack into the US government. I find it hard to believe that Kelly was the best at it. 
 Many points of the story were also incredibly lame. The specialists are quite lame and unbelievable. They were such a small group, and almost everyone there seemed untrained and unremarkable. I find it hard to believe that they're all very special as the book suggests. The characters were also given very lame codenames, like Beaker and Bruiser (for a chemist and a fighter). 
 One of the most annoying parts of the story was Kelly. 
 If I hear one more YA characters whine on about how klutzy they are, I will kill them. 
 She had an irritating crush on David for most of the book, often talking about how hot he was, but never acting on it. Considering that both Kelly and David were crappy, flat characters, I had no interest in the romance between them. There were often facefalm inducing parts such as this: 
 "The air conditioning kicked on, sendiing his cologne shooting up my nostrils. They flared in immediate response. My heart kicked into light speed, and my head whirred on a dizzying wave. 
 SERIOUSLY. It's just cologne! 
 My biggest problem with Kelly was that she was a teen genius, but she really didn't seem like it. A 191 IQ is incredibly high. Very rare, and anyone who would have such a high IQ would have to be very organised and have very complicated thought processes (like Sheldon Cooper, but less annoying). Kelly was stupid. She wasn't smart at all. She always mixed up her words, like this: 
 ""Sorry, I was proton spread analyzing the." I shook my head. "I mean, I was analyzing the spread of a proton."" 
 Yep. You're a genius. 
 It's hard to write such a smart character, because most of us are only of average intelligence, give or take. It is hard to adopt the thought processes of someone who is very smart. The author really needed to show us why Kelly was smart, instead of just telling us. Sure, she'd drop a fancy word or two sometimes, but I hear people in year 12 maths speaking like that two. Just cause you know what the nth term of a geometric sequence is doesn't mean you're a genius. 
 The rest of the characters were also crappy, empty shells. I would've thought that the head of a secret organisation would be incredibly smart and skilled at everything. The head of the Specialists, TL (I have no idea what it stands for) is very unremarkable. Just bleh. 
 So, they all go on a secret mission. You would think that the mission would be intense, exciting, and interesting, but it really wasn't. The mission bored me just as much as the rest of the book. I didn't really care about it, and it wasn't complicated enough. They go into the house, find the statue, and leave while being chased by random guards . Everything was resolved to quickly. 
 I also find it hard to believe that a top secret spy group and a bunch of guards have no guns. Kelly was hardly trained at all before going on the mission, and firearms weren't even mentioned in this. 
 It was a hard slog to the end, and I contemplated putting the book down many times. It was childish, cheesy, crappy, and boring. 
 I would not reccomend this book to anyone.
